archetypes.name: The Self
archetypes.oneLine: Totality of the psyche: the centre and circumference of conscious and unconscious.
body: The Self is where the map folds back on itself: the whole of the psyche, conscious and unconscious together, and the centre toward which a life is drawn. It is never met directly. It shows itself through images of wholeness, above all the circle and the quaternity.
On this globe the Self is the quiet field behind every other presence, reached through images as far apart as Upanishadic light and the alchemical stone.

definition.text: Psychologically the self is a union of conscious (masculine) and unconscious (feminine). It stands for the psychic totality. So formulated, it is a psychological concept. Empirically, however, the self appears spontaneously in the shape of specific symbols, and its totality is discernible above all in the mandala and its countless variants. Historically, these symbols are authenticated as God-images.

archetypes.name: Anima
archetypes.oneLine: The inner feminine in a man: life itself, personified as soul, muse and guide.
body: The Anima is the figure through which a man's unconscious turns toward him: siren and sophia, nymph and guide. She is watery, shifting and bipolar, and she draws the soul toward images rather than arguments.
She appears wherever a threshold is crossed by water, by song, by an unknown woman.

definition.text: Like the 'supraordinate personality,' the anima is bipolar and can therefore appear positive one moment and negative the next; now young, now old; now mother, now maiden; now a good fairy, now a witch; now a saint, now a whore.
definition.cite: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i) ¶352

archetypes.name: Animus
archetypes.oneLine: The inner masculine in a woman: spirit, word and conviction.
body: The Animus is the masculine counterpart within a woman's psyche. It speaks as opinion and as spirit; at its best it is a bridge to the creative mind rather than a chorus of verdicts.
Its images are quicker and cooler than the anima's: the wind, the horse, the hero-lover who arrives from elsewhere.

definition.text: I have called the projection-making factor in women the animus, which means mind or spirit. The animus corresponds to the paternal Logos just as the anima corresponds to the maternal Eros.

archetypes.name: Child
archetypes.oneLine: Beginning and futurity: the newborn possibility of wholeness.
body: The Child is the archetype of what has not yet happened: the threatened newborn, the abandoned and invincible one, the little figure who turns out to hold the whole.
It is dawn-coloured in this atlas: soft, rising, unfinished.

definition.text: The child motif represents the preconscious, childhood aspect of the collective psyche.
definition.cite: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i) ¶270

image.title: Statuette of Harpocrates

archetypes.name: Great Mother
archetypes.oneLine: Giver and devourer: earth, womb, cave and the realm of the Mothers.
body: The Great Mother holds both sides of origin: the nourishing earth and the swallowing dark. She is goddess, cave, well and tree before she is anyone's personal mother.
Her images sit at the instinct end of the spectrum: dense, warm and terrestrial.

definition.text: The “mother,” as the first incarnation of the anima archetype, personifies in fact the whole unconscious. Hence the regression leads back only apparently to the mother; in reality she is the gateway into the unconscious, into the “realm of the Mothers.”

image.title: Venus von Willendorf 01

archetypes.name: Hero
archetypes.oneLine: The struggle toward light: slayer of the dragon, bearer of renewed life.
body: The Hero is consciousness fighting its way out of the mother, the monster and the night. Solar and lucid, the hero's journey is descent and return; its dangers are inflation and identification with the light.
Its colour is the lucid white-gold of the risen sun.

definition.text: Taken purely as a psychologem the hero represents the positive, favourable action of the unconscious, while the dragon is its negative and unfavourable action—not birth, but a devouring; not a beneficial and constructive deed, but greedy retention and destruction.

image.title: Saint George and the Dragon

archetypes.name: Kore
archetypes.oneLine: The maiden: youth before transformation, soul in bloom and in descent.
body: Kore is the maiden figure who is carried off, hidden or crowned: Persephone in spring and in Hades. She stands between the anima and the Self, both a young girl and an intimation of wholeness.
Her images are green and early, always about to change.

definition.text: The 'Kore' has her psychological counterpart in those archetypes which I have called the self or supraordinate personality on the one hand, and the anima on the other.
definition.cite: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i) ¶306

archetypes.name: Mana-Personality
archetypes.oneLine: The charged, fascinating figure who holds numinous power over the ego.
body: The mana-personality is the figure who has absorbed more power than any person should carry: magician, prophet, hierophant. The ego is fascinated by such a figure and tempted to become it.
It sits between the wise old man and the hero, closer to the numinous than either.

definition.text: The hero is the protagonist of God's transformation in man; he corresponds to what I call the "mana personality." The latter has such an immense fascination for the conscious mind that the ego all too easily succumbs to the temptation to identify with the hero, thus bringing on a psychic inflation with all its consequences.

archetypes.name: Psychopomp
archetypes.oneLine: Guide of souls across thresholds: mediator between conscious and unconscious.
body: The Psychopomp leads across: Hermes with the dead, the bird that carries the soul out of the vessel, the unexpected companion on the road. It is a function more than a face, and it keeps the passage between worlds open.
Its colour is dusk, between the instinct and spirit ends.

archetypes.name: Shadow
archetypes.oneLine: The hidden, rejected side of the personality; everything we will not see in ourselves.
body: The Shadow gathers what a person or a culture pushes out of sight: the guilty, the primitive, the unlived. It is met first because it is nearest, and it tends to arrive as an enemy, a double, a dark beast or a stranger on the stair.
Its images are dense and low in the spectrum: dragons, apes, the blackened sun, the devil as the other half of the sacred.

definition.text: The first of these is the SHADOW, that hidden, repressed, for the most part inferior and guilt-laden personality whose ultimate ramifications reach back into the realm of our animal ancestors and so comprise the whole historical aspect of the unconscious.

archetypes.name: Syzygy
archetypes.oneLine: The divine pair: masculine and feminine joined as one image of wholeness.
body: The Syzygy is the paired opposite: king and queen, sun and moon, anima and animus held in one picture. In alchemy it is the conjunction at the centre of the work; in dreams it often arrives as a wedding.
Its images show up wherever a tradition has pictured the two as one.

definition.text: This youth is an animus-figure, the embodiment of the masculine element in a woman. Youth and young girl together form a syzygy or coniunctio which symbolizes the essence of wholeness (as also does the Platonic hermaphrodite, who later became the symbol of perfected wholeness in alchemical philosophy).
definition.cite: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i) ¶322

archetypes.name: Trickster
archetypes.oneLine: Shape-shifter and fool: archaic, unconscious cunning that unsettles the order.
body: The Trickster is the joker and boundary-crosser: half divine, half beast, careless of rules and strangely generative. Out of his blunders something new, and sometimes something healing, gets made.
Mercurius, the quicksilver spirit of alchemy, carries the trickster into the laboratory.

definition.text: The trickster is a primitive 'cosmic' being of divine-animal nature, on the one hand superior to man because of his superhuman qualities, and on the other hand inferior to him because of his unreason and unconsciousness.
definition.cite: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i) ¶473

archetypes.name: Wise Old Man
archetypes.oneLine: Spirit as meaning: the guide who appears when thought has run out.
body: The Wise Old Man is meaning given a face: a sage, a magician, a prophet, sometimes an animal or a gnome. He comes with knowledge the dreamer lacks, and with the reflection and resolve to use it.
He sits near the spirit end of the spectrum: fine, clear, cool.

definition.text: Mostly, therefore, it is the figure of a 'wise old man' who symbolizes the spiritual factor. Sometimes the part is played by a 'real' spirit, namely the ghost of one dead, or, more rarely, by grotesque gnome-like figures or talking animals.
definition.cite: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i) ¶397

occurrences.title: Maiaurli - the ancestral fire-sparks seeking wombs (Central Australia)
occurrences.label: Maiaurli - the ancestral fire-sparks seeking…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: These fiery sparks, which they call by the Swiss-sounding expression maiaurli, are supposed to be the souls of ancestors and to live in particular rocks or trees, and any woman who passes must use special charms in order to ward off the maiaurli that jump out to impregnate her
body: The aborigines - "like paleolithic men" - believe "that the falling stars were really souls descending from heaven to embody themselves in human bodies" and "that man was a fiery spark": "Those people believe that the soul of man consists of a little fiery spark, and when such a spark-they are very swift and cunning-is flying about and happens to enter the womb of a woman, she immediately becomes pregnant".

"These fiery sparks, which they call by the Swiss-sounding expression maiaurli, are supposed to be the souls of ancestors and to live in particular rocks or trees, and any woman who passes must use special charms in order to ward off the maiaurli that jump out to impregnate her-they are always looking for a womb to enter." Jung sets this beside the Gnostic idea of the soul as "a fiery spark which fell down into the sea, or the creative womb, and then became a human soul, building a body round itself" - and against the star piercing the vision-woman's heart.

occurrences.title: Abraham holds God to His word at the altar — Talmudic legend
occurrences.label: Abraham holds God to His word at the altar
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Talmudic legend (drawn up ~5th-6th c.; cited from 1920s compilation)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)
jung.locator: 'Transformation Symbolism in the Mass' n.25 (pdf p729)

occurrences.quote: \"'And I,' cried Abraham, 'swear that I will not go down from the altar until you have heard me. When you commanded me to sacrifice my son Isaac you offended against your word, \"in Isaac shall your descendants be named.\"'\
body: "How Jewish piety reacted to this sacrifice" — the aqedah rewritten as a lawsuit in which Abraham refuses to leave the altar until God answers for breaking His own promise:

God concedes the point, provides the ram, and institutes the shofar of New Year's Day as a remembrance-clause binding Him to temper justice with mercy. The human partner morally outmanoeuvres the deity — the exact structure Jung develops in Answer to Job.

occurrences.title: Abraham's pond at Harran: the carp of Astarte
occurrences.label: Abraham's pond at Harran: the carp of Astarte
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: it was full of carp which are the fishes of Astarte.
body: Jung's Near-Eastern parallel to Cupid asleep by the well: "the famous Abraham's pond in Harran; that was a pond for Astarte, and it was full of carp which are the fishes of Astarte. So this well can be called the Well of Astarte, the love goddess, and here is Cupid her son, the dying and resurrecting god". Footnote: Harran, home of Abraham's family after the migration from Ur; beside the pond a mosque and pavilion.

When Zarathustra says of Wisdom that "the oldest carps are still lured by her," Jung answers: "Those are the fishes in the pond of Astarte" — the sacred fish of the love-goddess surviving under the patriarch's name, the same well-water coupling as Cupid and the deep.

occurrences.title: Adam in the bath of the dragon, found by Venus — Basilius Valentinus
occurrences.label: Adam in the bath of the dragon, found by Venus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Adam sat in the bath which the old Dragon had prepared, and in which Venus found her companion.
body: "Adam sat in the bath which the old Dragon had prepared, and in which Venus found her companion." In the poem Venus is "the fountain that flows from the stone and submerges her father, absorbing his body and life into herself" — a parallel to Beya dissolving Gabricus into atoms.

Jung at cw14 ¶546-548: a bold Baroque stroke whose psychology is exact — the inner man (Adam Kadmon) swamped by the goddess of love, the Gnostic love-affair of Nous and Physis; the "old dragon" who prepared the bath is "a personification of the instinctual psyche, generally symbolized by reptiles": the unconscious itself initiates the process of renewal.

occurrences.title: Adam chooses intelligence out of three gifts — Islamic legend
occurrences.label: Adam chooses intelligence out of three gifts
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: But they refused, invoking God's own command never to part from intelligence.
body: When Adam left paradise, God sent Gabriel with an offer of three gifts — modesty, intelligence, and religion — of which he should choose one. Adam chose intelligence; Gabriel commanded modesty and religion to return to heaven, "But they refused, invoking God's own command never to part from intelligence, wherever it might be found. For the Prophet had said: 'Never submit to one who has no trace of intelligence.'"
Jung at cw14 ¶584: closing the account of the excellent equipment of the first man — "a legend which is not without a deeper meaning."

occurrences.title: Eve hidden unnamed in Adam — 'Rosinus ad Euthiciam'
occurrences.label: Eve hidden unnamed in Adam
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: here hast thou named Adam and hast been silent concerning the name of the woman or Eve
body: The Rosinus ad Euthiciam instructs: "Take Adam and that which is made like to Adam" — deliberately silent about the woman's name, "for thou knowest that that which is made like unto thee is Eve." The feminine is implicite in the prima materia Adam.

Jung's reading: opens the Adam-and-Eve chapter's documentation of the hidden Eve — the feminine contained in the masculine substance, elaborated by the Congeries Paracelsicae into "Adam the true hermaphrodite and microcosm" whose stone is "a living thing" bearing "his invisible Eve hidden in his body." Parallels: rebis, moon-luna-adoption-mutus-liber-1702, adam-four-colours-pirke-rabbi-eliezer-8c.

occurrences.title: Adam's dust from the four corners in four colours — Pirke de Rabbi Eliezer ch. 11
occurrences.label: Adam's dust from the four corners…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: He [God] began to collect the dust of the first man from the four corners of the world; red, black, white, and green.
body: Pirke de Rabbi Eliezer ch. 11: God collected the first man's dust from the four corners of the world — red (blood), black (entrails), white (bones and sinews), green (body); other sources assign green to skin and liver. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 38a, cited in the same note-cluster) maps Adam's body-parts onto the countries of the earth.

Jung's reading: the four-coloured quaternionic Adam as rabbinic parallel to the alchemical colour-series of the prima materia; he notes the instability of the series (three vs four colours, seven vs eight sleepers — n. 32). Parallels: adam-eve-rosinus-ad-euthiciam-13c, dream-portrait-four-colours-cw12-1933, lapis colour gradation.

occurrences.title: 'Ye are Adam': Adam as the general soul of Israel — Knorr von Rosenroth
occurrences.label: Ye are Adam' — Knorr von Rosenroth
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: And you were his sparks and his limbs.
body: On Ezekiel 34:31 ("Ye are Adam"): "out of your souls was composed the microcosm of Adam... And you were his sparks and his limbs." §20: "The son of David shall not come until all the souls that were in the body (of the first-created) have fully gone out."

Jung at cw14 ¶593-594: Adam appears as the body of the people and its "general soul" — a projection of the interior Adam; "the homo maximus appears as a totality, as the 'self' of the people." The going-out of souls is the projection of a psychic integration process: the Messiah cannot come "until all parts of the psyche have been made conscious."

occurrences.title: Adam's creation from four elements and burial at Golgotha — Cave of Treasures
occurrences.label: Adam's creation from four elements…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: And the earth opened in the form of a cross, and Shem and Melchizedek laid the body inside.
body: The Syriac Cave of Treasures: God takes "a grain of dust from the whole earth, and a drop of water from the whole sea, and a breath of wind... and a little warmth from the nature of fire" — the four weak elements in the hollow of his hand. Adam's dust is red, black, white and green from the four corners; he stood on the world's centre and is buried there, on Golgotha: when Shem lays the body down "the earth opened in the form of a cross"; over the grave grows the tree, there stands Melchizedek's altar; "Golgotha, because it is round."
Jung at cw14 ¶552-556 reads it as the quaternary Adam at the centre — cross, circle, and Above-Below reunion; God promises: "I shall make thee God, but not now."

occurrences.title: Adam as the iota, the small hook of the Yod — Naassene psalm (Hippolytus, Elenchos VIII, 12)
occurrences.label: Adam as the iota, the small hook of the Yod
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Naassene exegesis (a Gnostic paraphrase of John 1) on the smallest letter: Adam signifies not even a letter but "only the small hook at the top of the Yod" — Jewish tradition per Shaare Kedusha III,1; the iota of Matthew 5:18, "one tittle of the law," is its echo (cw14 ch. II nn.24-25). Jung's verdict: "All this is a Gnostic paraphrase of John 1 and at the same time a meaningful exposition of the psychological self."
The primordial Man contracted to the minutest point — the seed-point of consciousness/self within the pleroma of the text — feeds Jung's point/scintilla family and his reading of Adam Kadmon.

occurrences.title: Adam Kadmon, primordial man of the Sefiroth — Kabbala denudata
occurrences.label: Adam Kadmon, primordial man of the Sefiroth
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: in his soul, all souls, and in his body, all bodies.
body: Knorr von Rosenroth's 'De revolutionibus animarum' (Kabbala denudata II, 3) with the Scholem-annotated translations: Adam Kadmon is "the soul of the Messiah" (1 Cor 15:45–49); the survey literature calls him "a second God, so to speak, or the divine Logos," first emanation before or as the Sefiroth; for Luria the ten Sefiroth went forth from him in ten concentric circles, which are his nefesh-souls.

Jung's reading: Adam Kadmon as the homo maximus "who is himself the world" — man and heavenly prototype "twins" (Sanhedrin 46b); the "highest man" of the Merkabah, the Kether, the anima generalis; in him are represented "omnium rerum ordines." Parallels: purusha instances, tree-sefiroth-inverted-cabala-1677, ophite-diagram-origen-contra-celsum-6c.

occurrences.title: Adam Kadmon as One, Two, Three and Four — Rabbi Abraham Cohen Irira
occurrences.label: Adam Kadmon as One, Two, Three and Four
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: And to that extent he is Three and Four.
body: "Adam Kadmon proceeded from the Simple and the One, and to that extent he is Unity; but he also descended and fell into his own nature, and to that extent he is Two. And again he will return to the One, which he has in him, and to the Highest; and to that extent he is Three and Four."

Jung at cw14 ¶619: the Tetragrammaton (yod, he, vau, he) is a triad and at once a quaternity — "a perplexity which coincides most strangely with the Axiom of Maria." The doubled feminine he that is yet one unit corresponds "exactly to the anima, who... bears all the marks of non-differentiation."

occurrences.title: Adam created as a lifeless bodily statue — the Mandaeans
occurrences.label: Adam created as a lifeless bodily statue
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Thereupon Ptahil tried to 'throw the soul into the statue.
body: According to the Mandaeans Adam was created by the seven "in the form of a 'lifeless bodily statue' which could not stand erect." Ptahil, the world-creator, tried to "throw the soul into the statue," but Manda d'Hayye, the redeemer, "took the soul in his arms" and completed the work without him.
Jung at cw14 ¶566: the recurring "bodily statue" recalls the Chaldaean myth handed down by the Naassenes — man's body created by the demons and called a statue.

occurrences.title: Adam as a lifeless statue — Mandaeans and Naassenes
occurrences.label: Adam as a lifeless statue
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "According to the teaching of the Mandaeans and of the Naassenes, Adam was a 'corporeal' or 'lifeless' statue" — the anthropos first formed as dead matter awaiting the soul. Jung sets this at the origin of the alchemical "statua": the Komarios passage (Berthelot IV, xx, 14f.) where the soul, after the dark shadow is removed, awakens the shining body from Hades; Rosarium: "Venerate the souls in statues: for their dwelling is in them"; Lully's Codicillus: "Always extract oil [= soul] from the heart of the statues"; Senior: "We warm its water, which is extracted from the hearts of statues of stone"; Hegemonius: "when the statue shall come."
The statue is the dead body-vessel that must be ensouled — the matter-reduced human awaiting animation by the arcane substance.

occurrences.title: Adam as prima materia pierced by the arrow of Mercurius — Miscellanea d'alchimia (14th c.)
occurrences.label: Adam as prima materia pierced by the arrow…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Adam as prima materia, pierced by the arrow of Mercurius
body: Plate 131: "Adam as prima materia, pierced by the arrow of Mercurius. The arbor philosophica is growing out of him." It accompanies the anonymous text: "I pray you, look with the eyes of the mind at this little tree of the grain of wheat, regarding all its circumstances, that you may be able to plant the tree of the philosophers" (¶357) — which Jung reads as "active imagination as the thing that sets the process really going."

The plate fuses the anthropogony and the opus: the first man as raw matter, wounded by the Mercurial arrow, sprouting the tree of the philosophers. Its pendant (fig. 135) shows the skull of Eve with the tree growing from her head — "the mortificatio of Eve, the feminine aspect of the prima materia."

occurrences.title: Adam an androgyne with two faces, sawed in two — Midrash Genesis Rabbah VIII
occurrences.label: Adam an androgyne with two faces, sawed in two
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: God sawed the body in two and made each half a back.
body: In Midrash Rabbah VIII, 1 Adam is "an androgyne, or a man and woman grown into one body with two faces. God sawed the body in two and made each half a back." Adam is masculo-feminine also elsewhere in Jewish tradition; Rabbi Jeremiah ben Eleazar read Psalm 139:5 ("Thou hast beset me behind and before") as Adam's two faces.
Jung at cw14 ¶587-588: the Rabbinic ground of the alchemical hermaphroditic Adam; the Islamic parallel has the pre-created soul refusing the clay figure until God put it in by force.

occurrences.title: Adamanus created from 360 spirits — Arabic Hermes-text
occurrences.label: Adamanus created from 360 spirits
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Three hundred and sixty spirits in all, mixed them together and created out of them Adamanus, the first man.
body: When the virgin (Eve) came to power, the angel Harus (Horus) arose from the unanimous will of the planets; he took "sixty spirits from the planets, eighty-three from the zodiac, ninety from the highest heaven, one hundred and twenty-seven from the earth, three hundred and sixty spirits in all" and created Adamanus, the first man, "after the form of the highest heaven."
Jung at cw14 ¶587: "The number 360 and the 'form of heaven' both indicate his circular shape."

occurrences.title: Adamas the chief corner-stone in the foundations of Zion — the Naassenes
occurrences.label: Adamas the chief corner-stone…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This, they say, is Adamas, the chief corner-stone.
body: For the Naassenes Adam is a "rock": "This, they say, is Adamas, the chief corner-stone, who has become the head of the corner. For in the head is the characterized brain, the substance from which the whole family is named, the 'Adam whom I place in the foundations of Zion'" — the inner man fallen from Adam the archman on high.

Jung at cw14 ¶627: around it, the Korybas who comes "from the head on high and from the uncharacterized brain" and dwells in the "image of clay" — "This is the God who dwells in the flood" — read by Jung as the longing of the unconscious for consciousness.

occurrences.title: 'O Man of the Great Name' — the Naassene hymn to Adamas
occurrences.label: O Man of the Great Name
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: From thee the father, through thee the mother, the two immortal names, parents of the Aeons.
body: "These men worship as the beginning of all things... a Man and a Son of Man. But this Man is masculo-feminine and is called by them Adamas." The hymn: "From thee the father, through thee the mother, the two immortal names, parents of the Aeons, O citizen of heaven, O Man of the Great Name!"
Jung at cw14 ¶587: Adam's dual nature reflected in his hermaphroditism (with the Midrash's two-faced androgyne, Plato's sphere-shaped Original Being, and Gayomart).

occurrences.title: Paracelsus: Adech the self, Scaiolae the four (De vita longa)
occurrences.label: Paracelsus: Adech the self, Scaiolae the four
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: one can almost speak of Adech as hostile
body: "In De vita longa, Paracelsus describes the 'four' as Scaiolae, but the self as Adech (from Adam=the first man). Both, as Paracelsus emphasizes, cause so many difficulties in the 'work' that one can almost speak of Adech as hostile" (¶150).

Jung invokes the pair while reading dream 11 (the croquet ball, "a symbol of wholeness, that is, of the self, here shown to be hostile to the intellect"): the alchemists already knew the self and its fourfold periphery as personified agents that resist and complicate the opus. Adech's Adamic etymology ties the self to the original man.

occurrences.title: Nebo hands Asurbanipal to the divine Queen of Nineveh — adoption hymn
occurrences.label: Nebo hands Asurbanipal to the divine Queen…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Hymn of Nebo to Asurbanipal: 'Small wert thou, Asurbanipal, when I left thee with the divine Queen of Nineveh, Feeble wert thou... when thou didst sit in the lap of the divine Queen of Nineveh, Of the four udders that were placed in thy mouth thou didst suck from two, And in two thou didst bury thy face' (cw14 ¶384). Jung sets it in the adoption-complex of the Cantilena: the child hidden under the mother's skirt and drawn forth (an ancient rite, still practised by Bosnian Turks), Heracles 'adopted' by Hera, the 'tutelary Madonna' whose mantle adopts the believer (¶383-385). Ripley uses adoption to 'circumvent the scandal of the customary incest' (¶383): renewal through the mother without consummated incest.

occurrences.title: The Enigma of Bologna: epitaph of Aelia Laelia Crispis
occurrences.label: The Enigma of Bologna
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Bologna (villa near the Porta Mascarella, 'Junonia' in Roman times)
occurrences.yearDisplay: first reported 1548 (Venice); claimed antique; probably a 16th-c. joke
occurrences.quote: Aelia Laelia Crispis, nec mulier, nec androgyna,... sed omnia.
body: The "monument" that never quite existed: "Aelia Laelia Crispis, nec mulier, nec androgyna, nec puella, nec iuvenis, nec anus, nec casta, nec meretrix, nec pudica, sed omnia... Nec coelo, nec aquis, nec terris, sed ubique iacet... Hoc est sepulchrum, intus cadaver non habens. Hoc est cadaver, sepulchrum extra non habens. Sed cadaver idem est et sepulchrum sibi" (¶51).

Jung calls it "sheer nonsense, a joke, but one that for centuries brilliantly fulfilled its function as a flypaper for every conceivable projection" (¶52). The commentary chain is the real locus: Maier and Barnaud (1597) alchemize it — uroboros "devours itself," "slays itself with its own dart, like the scorpion" (¶58); Malvasius (1683) collects 45 interpretations; Aldrovandus makes Aelia a hamadryad in the Junonian oak; Richard White reads the androgynous soul, "a girl has a masculine and a man a feminine soul" (¶92); Turrius, prima materia "conceived solely by the imagination" (¶94); Gevartius/Veranius, Eros; Schwartz (1727), the Church. Jung: "the philosopher stared at the paradoxes of the Aelia inscription, just as he stared at the retort, until the archetypal structures of the collective unconscious began to illuminate the darkness" (¶88).

image.title: Pietra di Bologna

occurrences.title: The aerial trigon and intelligence — Flambart's hundred nativities (Paris, 1921)
occurrences.label: The aerial trigon and intelligence
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Jung reports the statistical test he wants astrology to repeat: the aerial trigon — Gemini, Libra, Aquarius, the air-signs ("air means mind or spirit"). "Flambart took one hundred nativities of men remarkable for their intelligence, and he found that, though the birth-dates were everywhere on the circle, there was an extraordinary accumulation on each point of the trigon, so one could say that the majority of such nativities were associated with the corners of the aerial trigon, with intelligence. This is of the nature of a scientific truth, but astrologers are proverbially reluctant to make such researches. They prefer to swim in intuition" (p419).

The sting: "Astrology is a dark science, a Hecate science." The editors link the passage to "Synchronicity: An Acausal Connecting Principle" (CW8 ¶869 n64) — this seminar anecdote stands in the pre-history of that essay, beside Swedenborg's correspondentia (p313).

occurrences.title: Agdistis — born of Zeus's seed in the earth, chained and castrated
occurrences.label: Agdistis — born of Zeus's seed…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "Agdistis was a hermaphrodite who owed his existence to the fact that once Zeus in his sleep lost his semen; it fell into the earth, and the earth brought forth Agdistis, but the gods did not like that fellow so they chained him and castrated him."

Jung: "It is again the union of a pair of opposites. Zeus is the god of the blue sky, and the sky and the earth, or spirit and matter, are united in the hermaphrodite, the son." The gold grows out of the earth in the same way — "out comes the hermaphrodite and the gold follows": the hermaphrodite precedes individuation, the creation of the precious centre.

occurrences.title: Ahasuerus — the eternally wandering Jew
occurrences.label: Ahasuerus — the eternally wandering Jew
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "Ahasuerus is the eternally wandering Jew. That is not a Jewish legend, it is a medieval Christian legend which dates back to about the fourteenth century. And this wandering Jew Ahasuerus, according to the legend, did not offer Christ help, he was one who refused Christ."

Jung's use in the blind old man's fourth self-naming: "it is the character of the unconscious not to be completely expressed in any symbol... The collective unconscious is never entirely expressed by any symbol, it is always wandering on, seeking new forms, and thereby it creates the world... he will never be satisfied with any formula that could be invented." Meyrink's The Green Face gives him the cross-mark under a bandage — the one sacrificed yet never sacrificed.

occurrences.title: Aion leontocephalus wrapped in the zodiacal snake at the Mithraic altars
occurrences.label: Aion leontocephalus wrapped in the zodiacal…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: "Time symbolism also played a great role in the Mithras cult. The figure of Aion usually stood at the main altar of the Mithras cult—he is a man with a lion's head, enveloped by the Zodiacal snake, Zrvan akarana, meaning 'boundless time'".

Distinguished from the Arles/British Museum leontocephalus (where lion and snake are identical in one body): there "lion and snake are identical. So this is man in the state of his spinal cord: it is unconscious man, strangely enough in no visible connection with the Mithras sacrifice. He assists, so to speak, in that act of salvation in which Mithras kills the bull. The bull is Mithras himself; he is sacrificing himself. It is a simple variant of the Christian idea, but Mithras is older" (p246).

occurrences.title: 'Horridas nostrae mentis purga tenebras, accende lumen sensibus!' — prayer of an alchemist-cleric from the nigredo
occurrences.label: Horridas nostrae mentis purga tenebras, accende…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "Thus an old alchemist—and he a cleric!—prays: 'Horridas nostrae mentis purga tenebras, accende lumen sensibus!' (Purge the horrible darknesses of our mind, light a light for our senses!)" (cw12 ¶41).

Jung's dating of it to the work's first stage is exact: "The author of this sentence must have been undergoing the experience of the nigredo, the first stage of the work, which was felt as 'melancholia' in alchemy and corresponds to the encounter with the shadow in psychology." The prayer stands in the row of those who "seek direct experience of the eternal roots" when the Christian dominant decays.

occurrences.title: Alchemist meditating in the initial nigredo — Jamsthaler, Viatorium spagyricum
occurrences.label: Alchemist meditating in the initial nigredo
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The word meditatio is used when a man has an inner dialogue with someone unseen.
body: Plate 137: the artifex seated in meditation while the work stands in its initial blackness. Jung prints it against Ruland's Lexicon definition of meditatio as "an inner dialogue with someone unseen … with God, or with himself, or with his good angel" (¶390).

His reading: the alchemists' meditation was not cogitation but "a living relationship to the answering voice of the 'other' in ourselves, i.e., of the unconscious" — the technique Jung formalized as active imagination. Khunrath's companion injunction: "Therefore study, meditate, sweat, work, cook … so will a healthful flood be opened to you."

occurrences.title: Aljira: the half-animal ancestors of the timeless land sink into the earth
occurrences.label: Aljira — the half-animal ancestors…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Australia (Aranda country; cf. Lincoln, The Dream in Primitive Cultures)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: The aljira ("land of no time") myth as Jung tells it: "In primordial times, when there was no time, there lived the half-animal ancestors, the great creators. Everything was wonderful, everything was done by enchantment. All things were created very wisely. Then these aljira gods or heroes sank into the earth and were no longer seen, but they did leave traces. These traces are now objects of ritual worship".

"When the primitives, for example, perform dances, they make strange patterns in the sand... This is something the ancestors did in ancient times. When it is repeated, the ancestors are still alive." Digging into the ground opens the aljira — dangerous, but also the source of life (p187). Jung equates it with the child's prenatal psyche, the Bardo world, and the Golden Age: "Consciousness, time consciousness, grows out of the aljira" (p255).

occurrences.title: The burial of Alleluia (Toul cathedral register, 1497)
occurrences.label: The burial of Alleluia
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1497 (MS of Nicolas, canon of Toul; custom much older)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: Alleluia is buried.
body: The 15th article of the Toul register, quoted by Jung: on the Saturday before Septuagesima the choirboys procession "with torches, holy water, and incense, carrying a clod of earth on a bier, through the cloister, wailing, to the place where Alleluia is to be buried" — Alleluia being believed a woman ("a" is a feminine ending), "a sort of queen of the past year."

Jung: "The clod of earth is the ball, and the ball is the sun, which is renewed at Eastertide... Alleluia was simply Mother Earth, a feminine potency made to suffer death, burial, and resurrection, and supposed to be responsible for the new sun." Grouped with the Pueblo sun-support ritual — the sun would not rise again if not ritually sustained.

occurrences.title: The fish brings the black stone that becomes beating amber — the Tao moment (Visions)
occurrences.label: The fish brings the black stone…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: vision read 24 Feb - 2 Mar 1932 (painted late 1929/early 1930 for Jung)
occurrences.quote: A fish cast itself out of the water at my feet. I picked it up, put my hand in its mouth and drew forth from its mouth a black rough stone. I rubbed the stone against my breast and it turned to amber. Within the amber I saw a face of suffering.
body: Among the villagers for whom the volcano "only smokes", the precious experience is lost in the ocean "like the ring of Polycrates". On the shore:

Rubbing fills it with her libido; amber is "a most preservative substance" holding the memory of suffering. Then "I felt the amber beating with a strong pulse… soon the ground and the trees about me beat also. I began to feel the pulsation everywhere" — "it is a sort of synchronistic phenomenon… a realization of Tao": "Tao is a sort of semiconsciousness-almost unconsciousness… the beginning and the end". The stone is "the middle condition": "on this side it is a piece of amber, and on that side it is the great mystery" — a talisman, the Lapis grown in the crater-retort. Only her blood spilled on it will break the amber.

occurrences.title: St. Ambrosius and the knight: 'Your face is black; wash it first'
occurrences.label: St. Ambrosius and the knight — wash it first
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: "You find this same connection between ablutio and self-reflection in the beautiful legend of St. Ambrosius. Ambrosius was addressed by a young knight, who asked for instruction. Thereupon Ambrosius told him: 'Your face is black; wash it first.' Then he ordered him to look at himself".

Jung's use: the bathroom-mirror dream of the four-year-old repeats the sequence wash → behold oneself; "the mirror is a frequent allegory of self-reflection," with Schopenhauer's mirror held up to the blind will as the philosophical pendant. Looking at oneself reestablishes identity after the archetype's dangerous intrusion.

occurrences.title: The alcheringa grandfather transformed into rice, bird, and hoe
occurrences.label: The alcheringa grandfather transformed…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: alcheringa tradition (rice-planting peoples; told in Zurich)
occurrences.yearDisplay: ethnographic present; Alcheringa = 'the time when there was no time'

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: So it is clear that the grandfather was transformed into rice. And from that he transformed into something else, perhaps a bird.
body: Jung's example of the half-man-half-beast alcheringa ancestor as "the first model of what a hero should be": the primordial being came to a spot, planted rice, and became the rice — the stalk's roots, stem, grain and spikes are read as feet, body and neck, head and hair — then became a bird, and even a hoe, "which clearly consists of a head and a neck and a body."

Creation as transformation, "not creation out of nothing"; the ancestors "have only gone underground," leaving stones, trees and hillocks as relics, so rites are bound to one spot — and a farmer ploughing that spot kills the primitive's world.

occurrences.title: Androgynous deity between the sun-serpent and moon-serpent — Late Babylonian gem
occurrences.label: Androgynous deity between the sun-serpent…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 183. Androgynous deity standing between male serpent with sun and female serpent with moon.—Late Babylonian gem
body: Late Babylonian gem: an androgynous god flanked by the male serpent bearing the sun and the female serpent bearing the moon.

Jung prints it at the pivot where the Gnostic myth — Nous and Physis — collapses into the single hermaphroditic natura abscondita of the prima materia: "the devourer is a sort of material earth-spirit, an hermaphrodite possessing a masculine-spiritual and feminine-corporeal aspect" (¶447). The gem shows the dual-serpent polarity carried by one androgyne — the pre-alchemical form of the rebis.

occurrences.title: 'Masculofoemina' — Priscillian's androgynous God
occurrences.label: Masculofoemina' — Priscillian's androgynous God
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: God's antithetical nature is also expressed in his androgyny. Priscillian therefore calls him \"masculofoemina,\" on the basis of Genesis 1:27
body: In the Trinity essay's argument that God's antithetical nature presses toward quaternity, Jung adduces the 4th-c. Spanish bishop Priscillian, who on the authority of Genesis 1:27 ("male and female created he them") names the Godhead "masculofoemina."

The androgyne surfaces here on the highest tier — the God-image itself carries the united opposites that the alchemists later project into the Rebis. Priscillian, twice cited by Jung in CW11 (unicorn, wheel of generation), is one of his key witnesses for suppressed heretical quaternity-thinking inside Western Christianity.

occurrences.title: Andromeda chained for Cetus - Perseus the hero liberates the anima (Greek myth, sky map of 8 June 1932)
occurrences.label: Andromeda chained for Cetus - Perseus the hero…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Andromeda is his anima, his soul, who was to be captured by the monster in the sea, just spirited away.
body: Reading the sky map: below the zodiac lies Cetus the whale - "the great monster of the unconscious, ever threatening to swallow the conscious world"; above, Perseus, "one of the old heroes of Greece, like Heracles and Theseus," son of Zeus and Danae (the golden shower through the iron room's roof), conqueror of the Graeae, with helmet of invisibility "like Siegfried," winged soles and a diamond sickle "like Hermes." Andromeda, the king's daughter, "was fastened naked to a rock and the monster was making for her," until Perseus petrified Cetus with the head of Medusa.

Jung's reading: "These were not fairy tales, they were really myths, they were sacred texts to be narrated for healing or magical purposes, and they were invented by medicine men, they are absolutely masculine. Andromeda is his anima, his soul, who was to be captured by the monster in the sea" - "the soul was always in the possession of the unconscious... only sacrifice could sever the connection." "The hero who overcomes the dragon liberates the soul from the curse of unconsciousness." Cf. the earlier constellation note perseus-gorgon-head-constellation-greece (sem-childrens-dreams).

occurrences.title: Angami tiger funeral — day of mourning for an elder brother
occurrences.label: Angami tiger funeral
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: the chief ordered a day of rest in mournful memory of the death of an elder brother.
body: From Lévy-Bruhl's The "Soul" of the Primitive: all the Naga — at least the western group — claim that humans and tigers have a common origin; all Nagas fear the tiger as a being particularly closely related to humankind. When the villagers of Angami killed a tiger, the chief ordered a day of rest "in mournful memory of the death of an elder brother." Cited with the Sakai (all tigers are humans in animal form) and the Mantra of Johore (a tiger is a man bewitched by evil spirits) as the mystical-identity background of the tiger dream.

occurrences.title: The angel who stirs the pool of Bethesda (Jerusalem, ~1st c. CE)
occurrences.label: The angel who stirs the pool of Bethesda
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Johannine legend: at certain moments an angel descends and stirs the waters of the Bethesda pool, and the first to step in is healed. Jung (laying out Ritschl's religious psychology) uses it as his concrete example of how a miracle-feeling is generated: a witness remembers the angel-event; the remembered feeling of value is later re-attached to the bubbling water; the "emotionbased hallucination of an angel stems from an unconscious confusion of a feeling felt in the past, which is now merely remembered, with a truly existent feeling produced by objective causes" (¶254).

It is student-Jung's first full psychological demystification of a biblical miracle — the method (memory-image + feeling of value) he then turns on Ritschl's unio-mystica denial (¶255ff). Note the ambiguity he leaves standing: "Let us suppose that at one time an angel really did stir the water" (¶254) — the reduction presumes but does not assert the absence of the angel.
Verbatim: "In the time of Christ there was a legend that at certain moments an angel would stir the waters of the pool at Bethesda."

occurrences.title: Angel as image of death — the suicide-drowning hysteric's amnesic chain (Burghölzli, 1905)
occurrences.label: Angel as image of death
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: With angel the image of death and the hereafter immediately appeared.
body: In "Experimental Observations on the Faculty of Memory", a 23-year-old hysterical woman with only 13% incorrect reproductions shows an "island-like amnesia": the chain water (no reaction) / to sting–bee / angel–"inn" (21.0 sec) / long–knife (9.0) / ship–"steam" (7.0) is amnestically blocked across four reactions. "The stimulus-word water had awakened the memory of a suicide-attempt, as was subsequently shown through psychoanalysis. With angel the image of death and the hereafter immediately appeared". Jung reuses the chain in the evidence essay: "In angel / inn the reaction-time is extremely long, because angel reminds her at once of the suicide attempt again, of dying and the next world... the emotional tone of the complex lasts over the next three reactions". The angel — Engel; Engelhof, the Swiss farm-name pun — is lived, not amplified: the death-messenger image carrying a real attempted drowning.

occurrences.title: The angel on the walls of Jerusalem — collective vision of the Crusaders (1099)
occurrences.label: The angel on the walls of Jerusalem
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung's example of collective vision alongside the glacier cabir: "The vision of the Crusaders when they first reached Jerusalem is an instance: they saw an angel on the walls of Jerusalem who signed to them that they would take the town, and they actually did take the town on the same day. That was also a collective vision".

His theory: "I assume that there is so much participation mystique through the shock that they get into the same mood" — several people hear or see the same thing at the same time under strain; "under the strain of such a situation extraordinary things do happen. I myself have observed them."

occurrences.title: Fall of the winged daemon in the vast edifice — Nerval's opening dream, Aurélia
occurrences.label: Fall of the winged daemon in the vast edifice
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1841 (dream at the onset of Nerval's psychosis; Aurélia publ. posthumously 1855)
occurrences.quote: The daemon represents the self, which no longer has any room to unfold its wings.
body: The opening dream of Gérard de Nerval's Aurélia (the novel Jung calls the history "of his anima and at the same time of his psychosis"): a vast edifice, and a winged daemon falls fatally. Jung's brief 1945 note is dense with diagnostics. "The dream has no lysis" — unlike a compensatory dream it resolves nothing, because it is the outbreak itself. The daemon "represents the self, which no longer has any room to unfold its wings": the totality figure crushed by the overpowering collective edifice.

Sequence Jung reconstructs: anima projected onto "une personne ordinaire de notre siècle" and lost — "he lost his 'pied à terre' and the collective unconscious could break in"; the real Aurélia dies during his psychosis, severing the last reality-tie; suicide, the MS found on his body.

occurrences.title: Jung's dream: the patient on the donjon balustrade (Zurich, 1935)
occurrences.label: Jung's dream — the patient…
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: My dream showed me that this was a mistake, and I knew that I had been a bad doctor.
body: Treating a girl born in Java whose instinctual life had been "tainted" by the natives' terror of the whites — nicknamed "the great whore of Babylon" for her gaudy acting-out — Jung found her forbidding and "looked down" on her. His unconscious answered with a dream: a highway at the foot of a high hill, a castle with a donjon, and on its balustrade sat an elegant woman — the patient. He had to look up so hard his neck ached afterwards.

Jung's reading: the dream compensated his devaluation, and telling her so plainly — "I have looked down on you" — "worked miracles," ending the transference trouble (¶336). A paradigm of the analyst's own dream as corrective instrument (cf. ¶333: the analyst's dreams correct his attitude to the patient).

occurrences.title: The stranger contracts the Chinese couple — war dream, Bombay, 20 Dec 1952
occurrences.label: The stranger contracts the Chinese couple
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: I demand a formal employment contract for the Chinese couple. To their delight he agrees.
body: Dreamt in Bombay during the India journey whose God-figures at Elephanta anchor the "dance of Siva" reflections. A war is won alongside a Chinese couple; when the fighting stops the "stranger" appears, and at the dreamer's demand he grants the couple a formal employment contract — "to their delight."

Pauli's reading: a further stage in confronting the unconscious — the Chinese couple (anima side) is no longer alien but hired, and a new light-dark masculine figure, the "stranger," emerges as superordinate authority. He would later rename this recurring figure the "master" — "in the meantime he has lost all his strangeness" — and liken him to Mercurius, who likewise "emerged from the river," the river being the mother. In 1946 the stranger appeared "as a Persian who was trying to get accepted at the Technical University".

occurrences.title: The Chinese woman opens the trapdoor to the auditorium — dream 28 Sep 1952
occurrences.label: The Chinese woman opens the trapdoor…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: Her movements are oddly dancelike; she does not speak but only expresses herself in mime, almost as in ballet.
body: The anima as the "Chinese woman (or the Exotic One) with the typical slanted eyes" leads the dreamer down a trapdoor, dancelike, mute, into an auditorium where "the strangers" wait for a lecture. The Chinese woman is the "holistic" anima — "herself that holistic union of psyche and physis" — bearer of psychophysical secrets "ranging from sexuality to subtle ESP phenomena"; the strangers are preconscious, inadequately understood ideas (cf. Jung's 1950 comment on earlier strangers).

The lecture the dream demands is the confession of a refused professorship — resistance of the rational ego. Jung: "the dark anima lives or is to be encountered in Esslingen"; here the same dark one appears Chinese, above the Catholic–Protestant opposites.

occurrences.title: Daemonic woman, companion of Zeus — Spitteler's Olympian Spring
occurrences.label: Daemonic woman, companion of Zeus
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In Spitteler's epic-ironic Olympian Spring, Zeus consorts with a "daemonic woman" — a figure Jung deploys in the Definitions chapter of Psychological Types as his literary example of the malevolent soul-image: the inner attitude that turns dark and hostile when the outer persona is all good-naturedness and compliance. "In men with a good-natured and unaggressive persona, the soul-image has a rather malevolent character. A good literary example of this is the daemonic woman who is the companion of Zeus in Spitteler's Olympian Spring" (cw6 ¶811).

The locus belongs to Jung's long Spitteler series: alongside the Imago of Prometheus and Epimetheus (see anima-figure-imago-spitteler-switzerland-1906, anima-figure-prometheus-soul-lady-spitteler-1881), it shows Jung reading contemporary Swiss literature as a projection-screen for the unconscious feminine.

occurrences.title: The dark girl at Esslingen — reaction dream to Answer to Job (winter 1952/53)
occurrences.label: The dark girl at Esslingen
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: The next station is Esslingen, and we are nearly there.
body: Reading Answer to Job, the dreamer rides out with Mr. Bohr (theoretical physics), changes trains, and finds "the dark girl" surrounded by strangers in a small local train bound for Esslingen — a provincial village "only loosely connected with the city of Zurich, which is where I pursue my main activity, theoretical physics." He wakes annoyed at the bore of the place.

Jung's reply: the dream intentionally lands the dreamer "in an insignificant (inappropriate) place... that is where you find what was missing in your reaction — namely, the dark anima and the strangers." "What good can come out of Nazareth (Esslingen)? Physics, on the other hand, resides up on the Zurichberg". The dark one is the counterpole to Protestantism, "the men's religion that has no metaphysical representation of woman"; the opposites pair appears in the table Fludd–Kepler / psychology–physics / intuitive feeling–scientific thinking / Holland–Italy.

occurrences.title: Anima figures 'Among Daughters of the Desert' — Zarathustra's only anima appearance
occurrences.label: Anima figures 'Among Daughters of the Desert'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: the desert (Also sprach Zarathustra IV, 'Unter Töchtern der Wüste')

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The erotic poem "Unter Töchtern der Wüste" ("Among Daughters of the Desert," Part IV) contains the only anima figures in the whole of Zarathustra: "Only very near the end anima figures appear in the erotic poem".

Their lateness is diagnostic. Zarathustra is "the most perverse phenomenon, the wise old man appearing as identical with Nietzsche himself without the anima" — so "it is quite unavoidable that Zarathustra sometimes shows symptoms of being the dancer, the anima. It takes the whole development of Zarathustra to call Nietzsche's attention to the fact that there is an anima". Jung adds the cultural geography: "the anima problem only reaches about as far as the Rhine. East of the Rhine the problem either of the wise old man or the Puer Aeternus comes up" — Nietzsche belongs to the masculine-psychology side, which is why the anima arrives only at the end, "when he was becoming crazy."

occurrences.title: Antinea, queen of the Sahara — Benoit's L'Atlantide
occurrences.label: Antinea, queen of the Sahara
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: Benoit's immortal Saharan queen, collector of a "salon" of embalmed lovers. Jung's verdict: "Antinea is not a real woman, but the anima of a Frenchman, and here we have a typical difference between the French and the Anglo-Saxons" (sem-1925). Compared with Ayesha she stands lower: "'She' is tortured for thousands of years till she admits [higher values]. Antinea is not even so far along that she admits or sees their existence" — but she has "all the charm of the native woman, all the erotic power and instinctiveness."

The ending is "a sort of apotheosis... the idea of La Gloire. There is a pantheon of fallen heroes, and there the whole thing ends in vain ambition" — against She's "mysterious side of promise." Aldrich's minority report split the hero: Saint-Avit (sensuality) vs Morhange (conventional spirituality) — the one-sided man "aroused a devil in Antinea."

occurrences.title: Ayesha, 'She-who-must-be-obeyed' — Rider Haggard's She
occurrences.label: Ayesha, 'She-who-must-be-obeyed'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Rider Haggard's She (1887), the tale of the immortal, beautiful and deadly Ayesha, enters the Aion Conclusion through the English editors' footnote to Jung's remark on novelists' anima-figures: "[In English literature, perhaps Rider Haggard's She.—EDITORS.]" (cw09ii ¶424 fn 1). The attribution is theirs, not Jung's sentence — a distinction this vault keeps (Jung elsewhere, e.g. CW9i, uses She at length). Ayesha instantiates the anima as numinous seductress and devouring great-mother in one: the "glamorous, possessive, moody, and sentimental seductress" of ¶422, "working now for good, now for evil" as a numen (¶425).

occurrences.title: The man and woman in black at the precipice — colonial officer's suicide dream (Europe, ~1907)
occurrences.label: The man and woman in black at the precipice
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Europe (dreamer on leave from the colonies)
occurrences.quote: he saw, on a rock, a man dressed in black covering his face with both hands. Suddenly he set out towards a precipice, when a woman, likewise clothed in black, appeared and tried to restrain him. He flung himself into the abyss, dragging her with him.
body: A colonial official, on leave in Europe, reports a dream from two years before: in a wild, desert place he sees on a rock "a man dressed in black covering his face with both hands," who hurls himself from a precipice dragging with him "a woman, likewise clothed in black" who tried to restrain him. Jung's single question — "Who was that man?" — moved the dreamer deeply: the man was himself. Two years earlier he had broken off an engagement rather than take his betrothed back to the murderous tropical climate where he was posted, had despaired, and had then led an expedition "relentlessly pursued by the savage inhabitants" in which members of the party died.
Jung reads the dream as the discovery of the essential complex — the relinquished beloved and the death-wish bound together — while declining to follow the wish-fulfilment further (¶78).

occurrences.title: Brolante the harlot, negative anima — 'The Tale of the Otter' (Schmitz)
occurrences.label: Brolante the harlot, negative anima
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1932 (posthumous publication of Schmitz's tale; author d. 1931)
occurrences.quote: the shadow is burdened with a still more inferior, feminine component, a negative anima figure (Brolante, the harlot).
body: Oskar A. H. Schmitz's fairytale "The Tale of the Otter," which Jung introduces in one of his last memorial duties to his dead friend, stages the inclusion of the shadow in the transformation of the personality. The second, harder half of the tale must integrate "the useless, adolescent traits" — and the shadow carries a still lower feminine component: Brolante, the harlot, Jung's named example of the negative anima.

Jung's reading (¶1721–22): the masculine components are reconciled with the vital instincts (the animals), "but there is a final separation between the spiritual and the physical nature of the anima. The masculine half is rescued from evil, but the feminine half becomes its victim." The tale as a whole is "an all-embracing and all-transforming initiation" which Schmitz fulfilled in death.

occurrences.title: Brünnhilde as spirit-mother of Siegfried — Wagner's Ring
occurrences.label: Brünnhilde as spirit-mother of Siegfried
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Who am I If I am not your will?
body: The Valkyrie who favoured the brother-sister incest and banished for it; she sends Sieglinde east with the child — the night sea journey of the spirit-mother (¶555). Her avowal "Thine own self am I / In the bliss of thy love!" (¶606) makes her "the mother-sister-wife" (¶607); her flood-longing (¶608–609) gives the anima's water aspect, and the regeneration she offers "is a deadly embrace" (¶609). She stands to Wotan as the Kore of the Acts of Thomas, the "Mother of Wisdom" (¶560–563).

image.title: Siegfried and the Twilight of the Gods p 110

occurrences.title: Courtauld on the Ice Cape: six weeks of darkness, the persona lost (North Greenland, winter 1930-31)
occurrences.label: Courtauld on the Ice Cape
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: He lost his persona absolutely. He looks effeminate and sentimental, exactly like his anima: a morbid woman.
body: The explorer Augustine Courtauld, stationed alone for meteorological observations, was buried by snowdrifts; the relief expedition could not find him until Watkins dug down to the air shaft. Six weeks without light and tobacco. Jung reads the published photographs as a natural experiment on the persona: cut off from every human expectation, the young airman "got absolutely ground to dust in the darkness" and looks "effeminate and sentimental, exactly like his anima: a morbid woman" — masculine force being chiefly a matter of persona. He died a few months later (editor's note). Mentioned in the seminar to explain why the patient's robe must burn in the fire of the cavern: the persona is treacherous, a compromise between ego and milieu.

occurrences.title: 'His name was Mary' — the house-painter's transforming voice-of-God experience
occurrences.label: His name was Mary
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: A lunatic house-painter's religious experience: "The voice of God told him that he no longer had a man's name; from now on his name was Mary — he was really the mother of God." Like a true prophet he objected — "how... is it possible that I should be Mary, since I am made like a man?" — and God answered, "Oh never mind, that can be mended": to look like a woman he attempted to amputate his external genitals and was brought to the asylum.

Jung's analysis: "when he heard the voice of God he would not have accepted it if he had not already been in a feminine condition" — a complete transformation by identification with the spirit, the extreme case of the femininity-role Nietzsche enters when overcome by the storm.
Verbatim: "The voice of God told him that he no longer had a man's name; from now on his name was Mary-he was really the mother of God".

occurrences.title: Imago — Carl Spitteler's anima novel
occurrences.label: Imago — Carl Spitteler's anima novel
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Carl Spitteler's novel Imago (1906) — whose title Jung borrowed for his own 1912 word-association study of the unconscious imagos — is named by Jung as the supreme literary case of the anima: fn 1 to the Aion Conclusion reads "The outstanding example in Swiss literature is Spitteler's Imago" (cw09ii ¶424). The context is his claim that "anyone who has a little knowledge of belles-lettres will have no difficulty in forming a picture of the anima; she is a favourite subject for novelists, particularly west of the Rhine." Spitteler's Sidelike woman belongs to the glamorous, possessive seductress phenomenology of ¶422.

occurrences.title: Lilith — George MacDonald's visionary novel
occurrences.label: Lilith — George MacDonald's visionary novel
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "There is a wonderful English book by MacDonald — I think it is called Lilith — which you ought to read as a most gorgeous example of a man whose anima is in the conscious." It opens with the anima problem — Lilith, the demon, Adam's first wife — "and it finally ends in an orgy of babies... he finds an anima that produces millions of babies, eats babies and drinks them. It is something awful!" but "marvelous as a pathological manifestation".

Diagnostic complement to the same page's animus dictum: the animus in a woman's consciousness means opinionating and dry convictions; the anima in a man's consciousness means mother-feelings — he "will schwarmen for babies and such things."
Verbatim: "it finally ends in an orgy of babies... he finds an anima that produces millions of babies, eats babies and drinks them".

occurrences.title: Minerva as Goethe-Prometheus' soul — Prometheus Fragment
occurrences.label: Minerva as Goethe-Prometheus' soul
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: His soul is Minerva, daughter of Zeus.
body: In Goethe's 1773 fragment Prometheus is "the defiant, self-sufficient, godlike, god-disdaining creator and artist. His soul is Minerva, daughter of Zeus" (¶289). Jung stresses the structural identity with Spitteler's soul-relation ("And when I deemed it was myself, / A goddess spoke") but marks the essential difference: Goethe's Prometheus is essentially and exclusively creative, self-activating, defying the gods out of his own creative power, while Spitteler's merely suffers the pangs of the creative soul within him (¶292). The relation is an introvert's, yet carried by an extraverted (creative) temperament — hence Jung's conjecture that Goethe belongs rather to the extraverted type (¶288).

occurrences.title: Molly Bloom's Penelope monologue — the anima's final 'Yes' (Ulysses)
occurrences.label: Molly Bloom's Penelope monologue
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Spirit in Man, Art and Literature (CW15)

occurrences.quote: O and the sea the sea crimson sometimes like fire and the glorious sunsets... and then I asked him with my eyes to ask again yes
body: The unpunctuated monologue that closes Ulysses: "the voice of easygoing Mrs. Bloom," sleepy at two in the morning, remembering Gibraltar — "yes and his heart was going like mad and yes I said yes I will Yes" (quoted cw15 ¶200).

Jung's reading. Mrs. Bloom "perhaps conceals an anima entangled in worldliness" (cw15 ¶185). She is the book's last word: "just as Faust was dissolved in the Eternal Feminine, so it is Molly Bloom (whom Stuart Gilbert compares to the blossoming earth) who has the last word in her unpunctuated monologue, putting a blessed close to the hellish, shrieking dissonances with a harmonious final chord" (cw15 ¶191). In the counterfactual ego-reading, the wanderer "would sink down at nightfall into the arms of the Great Mother, who signifies the beginning and end of life" (cw15 ¶193) — Penelope "need no longer weave her never-ending garment... for her husband is home again" (cw15 ¶202).

occurrences.title: Mona Lisa — the speaking silence of the anima-type (Leonardo, Louvre)
occurrences.label: Mona Lisa — the speaking silence…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: an indefiniteness that seems full of promises, like the speaking silence of a Mona Lisa.
body: Leonardo's portrait, taken by Jung as the visible formula of the "anima type": the sphinx-like, equivocal woman whose elusiveness is "not an indefinite blur that offers nothing, but an indefiniteness that seems full of promises, like the speaking silence of a Mona Lisa" (¶339, "Marriage as a Psychological Relationship"). The type is "both old and young, mother and daughter, of more than doubtful chastity, childlike, and yet endowed with a naïve cunning" — women "made by nature to attract anima projections" (¶339). Grounded in ¶338's definition of the anima as the inherited eternal image of woman, projected on the beloved.
Literary sisters in the same essay: anima-figure-ayesha-rider-haggard-she-london-1887 · anima-figure-antinea-benoit-latlantide-paris-1919 (both cited at ¶341 and fn. 3).

occurrences.title: Pandora as Epimetheus' soul-image — Goethe's Pandora
occurrences.label: Pandora as Epimetheus' soul-image
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Make her an offer and she'll raise your bid.
body: Epimetheus, "entirely given up to fantasies, dreams, and memories," hymns Pandora his wife in verses Jung reads as the textbook voice of the soul-image: "For Epimetheus, as these verses clearly show, Pandora has the value of a soul-image—she stands for his soul; hence her divine power, her unshakable supremacy" (¶304–305). The famous line gives the daemonic reinforcement mechanism of projected contents. Where Spitteler's Pandora belongs to the gods (the unconscious sphere), Goethe's is wholly the creature and daughter of the Titan — the difference between the two Prometheus conceptions.

occurrences.title: Prometheus' soul as 'Lady and Mistress' — Spitteler, Prometheus and Epimetheus
occurrences.label: Prometheus' soul as 'Lady and Mistress'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: But it does not lie with me to judge of the face of my soul, for lo, she is my Lady and Mistress, and she is my God in joy and sorrow.
body: Prometheus' answer to the angel who demands he free himself from his soul: "she is my Lady and Mistress, and she is my God in joy and sorrow." Jung reads this as the introvert's unconditional surrender to "the function of relation to the inner world," which gives the soul "a mysterious, metaphysical character" (¶278) — she gleams through with the collective unconscious and therefore appears daemonic, "embodying the totality, the utter polarity and ambivalence of the world of images" (¶281). Her first face-to-face apparition (tiger behind the eyelashes) is a separate locus.

occurrences.title: Psyche imprisoned in matter, awakened by the voice — Iranian redemption myth (Reitzenstein)
occurrences.label: Psyche imprisoned in matter, awakened…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: She wanders through the whole realm of matter and thus endows it with soul, but she can never find the way out-the border always stops her. Finally the god appears again, and leads her up to a heavenly marriage.
body: Reichstein's reconstruction from the syncretistic fragments: "The serpent-shaped son of the Prince of Darkness desires the daughter of the King of Light, and finally obtains her. (He represents matter and she, the Psyche, the soul.)" He promises a magic palace and holds her prisoner; her misery begins.

Then "there comes to her an invisible, divine messenger whom she only recognizes by his voice. He reminds her of her descent and of the home she has left." Psyche breaks the demon's power, "wanders through the whole realm of matter and thus endows it with soul," but cannot find the way out — until the god appears again "and leads her up to a heavenly marriage." Jung pairs the myth with the Mandaean/Manichaean soul asleep and narcotized in the World of Darkness — "comparable to the condition of Muladhara".

occurrences.title: Rhoda becomes the heavenly lady — Shepherd of Hermas, first vision
occurrences.label: Rhoda becomes the heavenly lady
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The repressed erotic impression has activated the latent primordial image of the goddess, i.e., the archetypal soul-image.
body: Hermas, sold as a slave to Rhoda in Rome, sees her bathing in the Tiber and thinks only: "How happy I would be if I had a wife of such beauty and distinction" (¶382). The repressed erotic libido "wrought a powerful transformation in his unconscious, for it imbued the soul-image with life" — on the road to Cumae, in a somnambulant ecstasy, "the heavens opened and I beheld that lady for whom I yearned, who greeted me from heaven and said: Hail to thee, Hermas!" (¶383). Jung's reading: "The repressed erotic impression has activated the latent primordial image of the goddess, i.e., the archetypal soul-image" (¶383). The transformation of Rhoda into a divine mistress breaks the object's spell and hands Hermas his collective task; she is then replaced by the old woman (Ecclesia), and finally by the tower.

occurrences.title: The double salamander vision — young Benvenuto Cellini
occurrences.label: The double salamander vision
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The double vision of a salamander, of which Benvenuto Cellini tells in his autobiography, would be an anima-projection caused by the music his father was playing.
body: In the Kore essay Jung footnotes Benvenuto Cellini's autobiography: as a child, sitting by the fire while his father played lute and sang, Cellini saw in the flames a salamander — doubled. Jung's reading: "The double vision of a salamander... would be an anima-projection caused by the music his father was playing" (¶310 n5). A fire-creature seen double at music's onset: the anima as shimmering apparition in the element of passion, exactly the fishtail/nixie register of the maiden's "superhuman nature".

occurrences.title: St. Anthony's phantom women in the desert
occurrences.label: St. Anthony's phantom women in the desert
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Mrs. Sigg, asked how the "Old and Young Women" chapter follows the creator's solitude: "When St. Anthony went into the desert he had visions of women who tempted him." Jung: "St. Anthony had quite a time with those phantom women in the desert."

The general law behind the locus: "to any solitary anchorite, women specters appear: women come up"; "a real fire can never burst forth without a personified opposite" — the dark side must take a body, or the conflict stays academic.

occurrences.title: Case Z — the 'unknown woman' dream series: eleven transformations of the anima
occurrences.label: Case Z — the 'unknown woman' dream series
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: A white bird perches on a table. Suddenly it changes into a fair-haired seven-year-old girl and just as suddenly back into a bird, which now speaks with a human voice.
body: Jung's densest single anima dossier: eleven dream-fragments in which "a mysterious feminine being with qualities like those of no woman known to the dreamer" (¶370) recurs — a white bird changing into a seven-year-old girl and back; the blind dancer-daughter of a magician-prophet in an underground house; a Gothic Madonna holding "a sort of flame or a snake or a dragon"; a black-clad countess with red hair and pearls surrounded by the spirits of the dead; a female snake speaking tenderly "only 'accidentally' shaped like a snake"; a helpful bird; the unknown woman on the tip of a church-spire; an old attendant in an underground public lavatory at forty below; an over-life-size goddess clad in blue "looking like Athena"; and finally the woman standing in the church in place of the altar, veiled. Jung: "Every conceivable shade of meaning glitters in her, from the highest to the lowest" (¶370); as snake she plays the negative role, as bird the positive (¶376).

occurrences.title: Verlaine's 'Mon Rêve familier' — the unknown woman who understands (1866)
occurrences.label: Verlaine's 'Mon Rêve familier'
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung closes the Miller drama with Verlaine's sonnet: "Je fais souvent ce rêve étrange et pénétrant / D'une femme inconnue, et que j'aime, et qui m'aime, / Et qui n'est, chaque fois, ni tout à fait la même / Ni tout à fait une autre, et m'aime et me comprend" — the recurring unknown woman, neither the same nor another, who alone cools the fevered brow "en pleurant."

He sets it as the poetic proof of his etymological thesis that to understand (verstehen, comprehendere, κατασυλλαμβάνειν) means "to stand round about something" — embracing — "and there is no doubt at all that nothing in the world ever embraces us so completely as the mother. When the neurotic complains that the world does not understand him, he is telling us in a word that he wants his mother" (¶682). The dream-woman who "me comprend" is therefore the anima-figure at her most maternal: the soul's understanding twin — precisely the figure Chiwantopel seeks as "she who will understand" (Ja-ni-wa-ma).
Verbatim: "et m'aime et me comprend" (¶682).

occurrences.title: The writer's irreducible woman — origin locus of the term 'anima' (Zurich, ~1920s)
occurrences.label: The writer's irreducible woman
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

body: A "very clever," thoroughly rational writer, analysed by many schools, whose dreams eventually produced a woman-figure he could not trace to any memory or personal experience — "she walks, she talks—she must be a ghost" (sem-kundalini pdf p148). Jung proposed that she had "not had its origin in your personal experience but is coming in all by itself"; the patient's resistance collapsed into the recognition of "the objective autonomous factor."

Jung then states the terminological origin directly: "I invented the term anima in order to designate such figures, which, according to our Western prejudice, should not be". The case is his clinical hinge to the Kundalini analogy: "this is the moment where the analogy with the Kundalini process begins, when something stirs up and develops all by itself".

occurrences.title: Kundry, messenger from the other side — Grail myth
occurrences.label: Kundry, messenger from the other side
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: It is as if the anima were standing on the other bank and I on this bank, and we were talking to each other, deliberating about how to produce a function in between.
body: Asked what the bridge symbol means psychologically in the "Redemption" chapter, Jung reaches for Kundry: "In the myth of the Grail, for instance, Kundry is the messenger from the other side, a sort of angel in the antique sense of the word, angelos, the messenger."

Jung's reading: the bridge between conscious and unconscious is the transcendent function, and "we must build a bridge from both sides, not from one side only. If there were no such figure at the other end, I never could build the bridge. It needs such a personification".
