Kundry is the anima standing on the far bank, the unconscious's own contribution to its connection with consciousness — "wherever we encounter the animus or anima it always denotes that the unconscious is inclined to form a connection with consciousness."

occurrences.title: Ramón Lull and the lady's cancer-eaten bosom (Spain, ~13th c. legend)
occurrences.label: Ramón Lull and the lady's cancer-eaten bosom
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Spain (Mallorca, inferred from the hidalgo tradition)
occurrences.quote: Silently she opened her garment and showed him her cancer-eaten bosom. The shock changed his life: he became a holy man.
body: Jung's exhibit of sudden transformation through affect: "the famous case of the Spanish hidalgo, Ramón Lull, who after a long chase finally succeeded in meeting his lady at a secret rendezvous. Silently she opened her garment and showed him her cancer-eaten bosom. The shock changed his life: he became a holy man."

The context is his claim that reflective consciousness itself may have begun in "violent emotional clashes and their often disastrous consequences" — the shock that makes people "wake up and pay attention to what they are doing" (¶542). Courtly pursuit turns to sainthood at one unveiling of the flesh's truth — the beloved as memento mori.

occurrences.title: The dreams of a lustful woman — Zarathustra, 'On Chastity'
occurrences.label: The dreams of a lustful woman
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: the city of the lustful (Zarathustra I)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "Is it not better to fall into the hands of a murderer, than into the dreams of a lustful woman?". Jung identifies her immediately: Nietzsche's anima, "who always tried to persuade him to come down from the balloon and look after the inferior man."

The reading frames the whole balloon-man psychology: the man in the clouds and the lower man "below, heavy like lead, absolutely identical with the lowest things," are bound by the anima — "the anima means a conflict." Because he lost his body, "he is a ghost and a ghost casts no shadow," so the woman below seems a stranger and is projected. Key theoretical statement attached to this locus: "very often she appears as split in two, an upper and a lower, a fair and a dark anima. And that is so real that men fall in love accordingly". When Nietzsche collapsed, his madness produced erotic writing "so crude that his highly respectable sister knew no better than to burn it up".

occurrences.title: Anima mundi, guide of mankind, herself guided by God — de Bry engraving for Fludd's Utriusque cosmi (1617)
occurrences.label: Anima mundi, guide of mankind, herself guided…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Engraving by J.-T. de Bry for Robert Fludd's Utriusque cosmi historia, captioned by Jung: "The anima mundi, guide of mankind, herself guided by God.". Set at the head of the dream series, it announces the guide-figure theme the dreams will develop.
Jung touches the anima mundi concept at cw12 ¶116: the alchemical vessel must be round "so that what comes out of the vessel shall be equally 'round,' i.e., simple and perfect like the anima mundi."

image.title: FLUDD: Utriusque cosmi

occurrences.title: Anima mundi = sensus naturae = Holy Ghost — Guillaume de Conches
occurrences.label: Anima mundi = sensus naturae = Holy Ghost
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

occurrences.quote: He identified the anima mundi, this same sensus naturae, with the Holy Ghost, just as Abelard did.
body: The Platonist scholastic Guillaume de Conches (1080-1154), teaching in Paris, "identified the anima mundi, this same sensus naturae, with the Holy Ghost, just as Abelard did. The world-soul is a natural force which is responsible for all the phenomena of life and the psyche." His source-chain runs forward to William of Auvergne (bishop of Paris, d. 1249), who insisted animals also possess the sensus naturae, and to Agrippa von Nettesheim's "luminositas sensus naturae" (De occulta philosophia, 1533).

Jung's reading: "this view of the anima mundi ran through the whole tradition of alchemy in so far as Mercurius was interpreted now as anima mundi and now as the Holy Ghost" (¶393) — the doctrinal bridge by which the world-soul became available to the alchemists' psychology of the arcane substance.

occurrences.title: The sun-woman crowned with twelve stars and her man-child (Revelation 12)
occurrences.label: The sun-woman crowned with twelve stars…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: "A vision of the sun-woman, 'with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars.' She was in the pangs of birth, and before her stood a great red dragon that wanted to devour her child" (¶710). Jung insists on the plain words: "Note the simple statement 'a woman' — an ordinary woman, not a goddess and not an eternal virgin" — an anima mundi and feminine Anthropos, peer of the primordial cosmic man. The vision opens with the Ark of the Covenant: a prelude to the heavenly hieros gamos whose fruit is a divine man-child (¶711).

She contains "in her darkness the sun of 'masculine' consciousness… She adds the dark to the light, symbolizes the hierogamy of opposites, and reconciles nature with spirit" (¶711); the birth borrows the pagan Leto-Apollo myth (¶713). The child is "caught up to God" and kept latent for the future; the mother hidden in the wilderness. Jung reads the episode as "the coming to consciousness of the self" (¶714) and as the prefiguration fulfilled by the dogma of the Assumption (¶743-744).

occurrences.title: Anima Mundi — Thurneisser zum Thurn, Quinta essentia (1574)
occurrences.label: Anima Mundi — Thurneisser zum Thurn, Quinta…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The idea of the anima mundi… coincides with that of the collective unconscious whose centre is the self
body: Plate 91: "Anima Mundi," from Thurneisser's Quinta essentia (1574). It illustrates the dream-40 commentary where the Pole is "the heart of Mercurius… Mercurius is the world-soul, and the Pole is its heart. The idea of the anima mundi (fig. 91; cf. fig. 8) coincides with that of the collective unconscious whose centre is the self" (¶265).

One of the load-bearing identifications of the whole volume: the Renaissance world-soul picture, the alchemical Mercurius, and Jung's collective unconscious with its self-centre are asserted as the same idea in three idioms.

occurrences.title: The old woman and the whip — Zarathustra, 'Old and Young Women'
occurrences.label: The old woman and the whip
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Zarathustra, alone at sundown, meets an old woman who asks him to speak of woman; he delivers the anima's whole repertoire ("Everything in woman is a riddle..."; "Man is for woman, a means: the purpose is always the child"; "The happiness of woman is, 'He will'"), and she answers with the little truth: "Thou goest to women? Do not forget thy whip!"

Jung: the chapter "had more to do with the anima" (Dr. Whitney) — a man too young in consciousness dreams an old anima; "she is his anima devil... The eternal Eve is playing her role in himself" — and the whip is symbolic: "Remember thy whip when you go to such women, or, when you go to your anima remember your whip... He first must learn to whip his anima."
Against two thousand years of "woman = serpent = devil" as "an organized truth".

occurrences.title: She — H. Rider Haggard's Ayesha, 'the classic anima figure' (1887)
occurrences.label: She — H. Rider Haggard's Ayesha, 'the classic…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: Haggard's She-Who-Must-Be-Obeyed, named in the 1925 seminar as "the classic anima figure": "As we have so often observed in connection with Rider Haggard's 'She,' the classic anima figure, we can never be too sure either of her goodness or of her evilness; now it is the one, now the other that grips us. Her potency lies in large measure in the duality of her nature". When a man sees in a woman "the magical quality that is the essence of She, he at once begins tremendous projections of the unconscious upon her." Jung places Ayesha in the old-man/maiden row and cites Haggard's Wisdom's Daughter beside the Elijah-Salome pair. The novel was one of three assigned to seminar committees for anima analysis (with Benoit's L'Atlantide and Hay's The Evil Vineyard) — the reports follow Lecture 16 of the seminar. Jung cites She repeatedly in later writings ("Mind and Earth," CW10 ¶75ff.).

occurrences.title: The insane boy who was his sister and a Buddhist — Zurich clinic, ~1930
occurrences.label: The insane boy who was his sister and a Buddhist
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Consultation case in the anima lecture: "Not very long ago I was called in as consulting physician to see an insane boy in a clinic in Zurich... he greeted me very politely and said, 'You will probably not believe it, but I am my sister and I am a Buddhist.'" The anima-sister, "more real than himself", carried an invented Indian name of three syllables, the middle one dava ("divine") — "the meaning was divine-mistress-sister" — half Italian, half Hindu/Sanskrit, a bit of Greek. Evidence for the anima as "a definite entity... She may become an hallucination", to the primitive mind a ghost.

occurrences.title: The stillest hour as angry mistress — Zarathustra
occurrences.label: The stillest hour as angry mistress
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: Yesterday towards evening there spake unto me my stillest hour: that is the name of my terrible mistress.
body: The chapter-personification: an unknown command calls Zarathustra from his pupils, and he names it "my terrible mistress", the "stillest hour" that speaks "without voice": "Thou knowest it, Zarathustra?... but thou dost not speak it!" He weeps and trembles "like a child"; she answers "What matter about thyself, Zarathustra! Speak thy word and succumb!" and "Humility hath the hardest skin"; finally the cryptic "The dew falleth on the grass when the night is most silent."

Jung's reading: "That is the anima, of course, and in a still hour one hears naturally what the anima says — one hears the voices of the other side". "The anima speaks absolutely to the point, as if she were a first-rate psychotherapist!". The dew-saying invokes Gideon's fleece — keep quiet and the revelation will come "as the dew came to Gideon": "an excellent example of what the anima can do in a critical moment of life". Nietzsche "passes by" such critical moments.

occurrences.title: The unknown woman — 51 anima dreams in three months (patient-anon)
occurrences.label: The unknown woman — 51 anima dreams…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Just as water denotes the unconscious in general, so the figure of the unknown woman is a personification of the unconscious, which I have called the 'anima.
body: A three-month male dream series in which the "unknown woman" motif appeared fifty-one times. Jung catalogs her metamorphoses: a throng of vague female forms; a woman on a step; veiled, then unveiled with a face shining like the sun; a naked figure standing on a globe seen from behind; dancing nymphs; syphilitic prostitutes; a doubled savage (Malay) woman; a mancatcher of a robber-band; a guide up a high mountain; a bird (marabou or pelican); a fair-haired guide with a dark Indian sister who owns part of the dreamer's sister's soul; a piece of broken pottery meaning a part-soul; a servant-girl to be watched; a dog that changes into a woman; once an ape; a spiritual guide who brings him bread and meets him in church — and when the dreamer draws her portrait, an abstract ideogram containing the trinity emerges instead.

Jung's reading (¶17): she is "a personification of the unconscious, which I have called the 'anima'" — of "exceedingly contradictory character," a fairy-being whose mythological row is "nymph, oread, sylph, undine, nixie, hamadryad, succubus, lamia, vampire, witch."

occurrences.title: The unknown woman above the diffraction screen — dream, 20 May 1955
occurrences.label: The unknown woman above the diffraction screen
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: The more unconscious the woman, the more... the power of the dark anima over the ego.
body: In a laboratory — no longer secret — Einstein conducts experiments intercepting rays on a screen; above the screen stands the "unknown woman" (resembling a certain Miss M.). An optical diffraction pattern appears: one central and two subsidiary maxima, "it looks something like a leaf"; marks appear on the leaves, the woman fades and disappears, and children appear on both sides.

Pauli links the children to the "cloverleaf" archetype (plants, lower Trinity) and to biology "the material substratum of life" — following his Dialectica speculation that biochemistry might one day formulate the laws of life in concepts nearer to "archetype" than today's physics. The woman's vanishing inverse to the dark anima's power "remains to be seen."

occurrences.title: 'That is art' — Jung's dialogue with the anima voice (November 1913)
occurrences.label: That is art' — Jung's dialogue…
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

occurrences.quote: Then a voice said to me, 'That is art.'... 'Perhaps my unconscious is forming a personality that is not me, but which is insisting on coming through to expression.
body: While writing down the fantasies after the Europe vision, Jung heard a voice pronounce his work "art." He knew "to a certainty that the voice... had come from a woman" — a patient with a strong transference to him (the editors note the speculation that this was Sabina Spielrein). He argued back; told her to use his own speech centres, "and she did, and came through with a long statement." In the 1925 seminar he names this the birth of his technique: "This is the origin of the technique I developed for dealing directly with the unconscious contents".

The identification followed: "it must be the soul in the primitive sense... the name 'anima' was given to the soul. Why was it thought of as feminine?". Personifying the interference — "I was in analysis with a ghost and a woman" — stripped it of power; taking the fantasies as art would have left only "a perceptional conviction" without moral obligation.

occurrences.title: Wagner among silk cushions and pink ribbons — the transvestit composing Siegfried
occurrences.label: Wagner among silk cushions and pink ribbons
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Wagner's study (Zurich period); bed canopy in Paris

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The anima-identification behind the Ring: "when Wagner was composing that aria where young Siegfried is forging his sword with a hammer and anvil, he was sitting in his study on silk cushions with millions of ribbons, in a silk dressing gown and a velvet cap. The air was filled with perfumes and he was adorned exactly like a woman, the most grotesque sight you could imagine. That was his reality, he was completely identical with the anima, he was a transvestit".

Prof. Fierz adds the Paris detail: over his bed "a silk canopy with roses and a mirror in which he could look at himself. And he never paid for it; Meyerbeer had to pay for it. Then five weeks later Wagner wrote Das Judentum in der Musik". Jung's "Isn't that marvelous?" leaves the sequence — mirrored self-adornment, debt, anti-Semitic pamphlet — as a single psychological figure, the counterpart to Nietzsche's grey top hat in Basel.

occurrences.title: Vision: the closed face opens — the eyes of the animal (8 Dec 1930)
occurrences.label: Vision — the closed face opens
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "I beheld a face with the eyes closed, I besought the face: open your eyes, look into my eyes that I may behold them." The face opens: "eyes full of beauty and woe and light and I could bear it no longer." Her painting shows "that of an animal, adarkhairyfacewith the melancholy eye of a beast" [OCR]. The Dionysian cortege has led her back past Greece into the animal age; she looks into the soul of the animal, "an equal sum of pain and pleasure, the capacity for joy and the capacity for suffering".

Jung: this is the essential experience of the Dionysian mysteries — "the purpose... was to bring people back to the animal — not to what we commonly understand by that word, but to the animal within" (p218). She touches bottom, "the regions of the blood", where mind is still at one with nature: "The break between man and nature has been abolished, there is a bridge once more" (p219). The eyes are "the eyes of the beginning, of the creator, who was unconscious because in the beginning all was unconsciousness". Hence the unavoidable conflict: she is animal as much as spiritual being (p225).

occurrences.title: Animal saviors folk belief — 'a Dr. Fox, a Dr. Snake, a Dr. Hare' (Black Forest)
occurrences.label: Animal saviors folk belief
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Don't you know that at the same time that Christ came for human beings, the savior of the chickens came into the world too? He preached the Evangel for the chickens.
body: Jung's mother's cook, a girl from the backward eastern Black Forest, beheads a troublesome rooster and reports: "'at least he repented before he died, so now he will go to heaven... when I chopped his head off he cried: "Verzeih mir, Forgive me! Forgive me!"' Pressed, she explains the local creed:

Local people confirmed the peasants' "conviction of an absolute parallelism between man and animal": when Christ appeared, a savior appeared to each species — "a Dr. Fox, a Dr. Snake, a Dr. Hare, and so on... in order that all creation should be redeemed together with man." Jung files it as "the idea of the apokatastasis in a very primitive form... I am quite certain that that is printed in no book, but it is printed in the hearts of the people."

occurrences.title: Animus as huge black bird over the primordial waters — two paintings in Jung's collection
occurrences.label: Animus as huge black bird over the primordial…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the animus is also in a way a spirit that hovers over the black waters and is often represented as such; I have two pictures in my collection where the animus is depicted as a huge black bird hovering over the primordial waters.
body: Two pictures from Jung's own collection depicting the animus in its bird-form:

Introduced while the Indian is pushed into the black pond: the animus "impersonates the unconscious, as the anima impersonates it in a man's case" — the anima is "the woman who emerges from the water, like Aphrodite arising from the foam of the sea in a shell", the animus the black bird above it. The pair illustrates the mediator-definition: figures on the surface of the sea between ego-consciousness and the depths.

occurrences.title: The animus in a sweat of blood — 'I must enter the mouth of that snake' (Visions, 13 Dec. 1933)
occurrences.label: The animus in a sweat of blood
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: After the vishudda-scale vision of the rearing serpent, only the animus is moved: "The man beside me shook and I saw drops of blood stand out all over his body like sweat. He said: 'I must enter the mouth of that snake, I cannot avoid it. If I remain here with you I will become black.' I said: 'I thought you could be my guide but I see that you are too weak.'".

Jung: an "electromagnetic storm which only affects the telegraph wires" — she is untouched by a vision of "extraordinary and far-reaching importance" and leaves the emotion to him, like Romans at the games while the Vandals besiege Rome (pp1305-1306). The Kundalini here is "not the luciferian snake that brings enlightenment, it is the devouring darkness, and into that darkness the animus has to disappear". The "black" animus thinks on the level of an unconscious woman — the nil-thinking suited to extending biological life (pdf p1307; period racial language quoted in the mentions record).

occurrences.title: Men in chariots rushing over the precipice into the void (Visions Seminar, 8 March / 3 May 1933)
occurrences.label: Men in chariots rushing over the precipice…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: After passing the archaic mother by another door, she descends the steep path and looks into the valley: "men in chariots rushing madly and frantically over another precipice, men and horses falling into a great void."

Jung: an animus battle raging beyond the archaic mother — a stampede, "her animus is stampeding... a typical animus panic", ending in the void. Passing by a fundamental fact (the shadow, the mother) drops one among the animi, into opinions instead of acceptance. Clinical form of animus panic: a misheard word, torrents of tears, then "the whole thing ended in smoke"; men fall into anima panics instead — a fortnight of gloom.

occurrences.title: The furry man dwarfed — 'I will tear at your garments' (Visions, 29 Nov. 1933)
occurrences.label: The furry man dwarfed
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: The incubus-animus (the furry man of the sylvanus/Pan species, pp1265-1266) catches the patient up on his horse. By a tour de force she wrenches the bridle: "The horse and rider fell to the ground. The man freed himself from the horse. As he approached me he turned into a little black dwarf". Jung: she de-possesses her horse — her own libido — and thereby reduces the demon to "an autonomous complex in one's unconscious, which can be held in check," whereas "a demon fills one with panic".

The resentful dwarf threatens her persona ("I will tear at your garments") — the imp of slips of the tongue, wrong medicines, the enfant terrible, the hunchback of the folk song (pp1275-1276). Commanded to "assume your proper shape," he becomes her own mind on equal terms, guide "down into your country": reality itself, not the unconscious (pp1276-1277).

occurrences.title: Latimer, the learned animus-husband — Marie Hay's The Evil Vineyard
occurrences.label: Latimer, the learned animus-husband
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: The 1925 seminar's animus case: Mary, having repressed her instincts, marries the learned Latimer. "Because he represents her projected unconscious, and is in short an animus figure to her, Mary is utterly powerless to free herself from him until she comes to love another man in a real way" (sem-1925).

Jung corrects the committee: the animus "is not necessarily a power figure" — Latimer first appears "as a learned man who appealed to her as a source of wisdom, a man representing wisdom," and became a power figure only through the tragic misunderstanding. On his side, the repressed anima is projected into the "uncannily unconscious" girl: "The vaguer she became, the more the anima had a chance to play her role" — "there we are launched upon the battle between the anima and the animus."

occurrences.title: The animus bound with thongs and arrows, freed from the amber (Visions)
occurrences.label: The animus bound with thongs…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: vision read 2 March 1932 (painted late 1929/early 1930 for Jung)
occurrences.quote: Then I knew that only my blood spilled on it would break the amber. So I cut my breast and blood fell upon the amber which vanished. In its place there stood a man bound with thongs and pierced with many arrows. I drew the arrows forth as gently as I could and freed him of his fetters.
body: The suffering face in the amber proves to be her imprisoned masculinity:

Jung: "in the making of the stone a man has been included in it… this is her masculine counterpart that has been locked in the stone" — "obviously the positive animus". The old opinionating animus was suppressed as the Yin material rose; imprisonment in the test tube is "the beginning of the alchemistic procedure… for the purpose of transformation". The arrows are "thoughts, shafts of light or of insight that pierce the veil of the animus"; drawing them restores wholeness after the "extreme violence" of suppression. Freed, he runs to a precipice — "Then he called like Icarus: 'I will fly.' I answered: 'And like Icarus you will be killed'" — and kneels beside her.

occurrences.title: Dream: seeking the doctor whose house is by the sea — the medicine-man animus
occurrences.label: Dream — the medicine-man animus
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I was going to see a doctor who lived in a house by the sea. I lost my way and desperately asked people to put me on the right path so that I could get to him.
body: Same night as the music dream: she must reach a doctor living by the sea, loses her way, asks desperately for the right path. Jung refuses the obvious reading that the doctor is himself ("If the unconscious wanted to convey the idea that it was Dr. Jung, it would say so", p78) — Freud's wish-fulfillment reading granted partial truth only (p80). Behind the daily facts looms an archetypal image that "puts one right back into prehistoric ages" (p78): the primitive woman haunted by a god seeks the medicine man who "has mana, prestige, healing power... and are therefore supposed to stand between the gods and the ordinary crowd" (p79) — always far away, in an inaccessible place (Rider Haggard's big-headed man; the Uganda head-sorcerer). The healer is again the animus: "This time he is no longer a musician, he appears in the guise of a doctor, and you will see later that he takes on many different forms" (p81).

occurrences.title: Hélène Smith, somnambulist of Geneva — 'a great animus love story' (Flournoy's From India to the Planet Mars)
occurrences.label: Hélène Smith, somnambulist of Geneva
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: Théodore Flournoy, the well-known psychologist and philosopher from Geneva, provided evidence of similar cases in his work, From India to the Planet Mars. The title may be fantastic, but it is a scientific book. Flournoy describes Hélène Smith, who had created a sensation in Geneva with her somnambulism.
body: Jung's second cryptomnesia exhibit, and his animus reading of the most famous medium of his youth:

The Hindu cycle, the Martian language, the Sanskrit fragments — all traceable to forgotten sources; yet Jung's aside frames the whole production as animus-driven. Distinct case from his cousin medium-trance-personalities-helene-preiswerk-basel-1896.

occurrences.title: The pyramid struck, the man freed from the earth (Visions patient)
occurrences.label: The pyramid struck, the man freed from the earth
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Then I struck the pyramid with the knife. It crumbled away and I saw, standing where it had been, a man.
body: Continuation of the pyramid episode. The patient seizes the sacrificial knife, cuts off a blood-dripping hand issued from the pyramid, then strikes the pyramid itself:

The knife is the discriminating intellect — "Logos is too beautiful, too ecclesiastical". The man who appears instead of the Self first embodies the animus, now projected onto a real man: "The Self is always on the other side to begin with; for a woman it is in a man". But "his feet and hands grew into the earth and were formless" — he begs: "You have liberated me from the pyramid. Can you now give me my limbs?" and cries, "If you cut me off I will bleed to death". Her most valuable possessions, projected, are in danger of being claimed by the earth — the danger of every attachment, and of none.

occurrences.title: The husband who ran after the servants — animus projection case (Zurich, 1935)
occurrences.label: The husband who ran after the servants
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: A respectable youngish woman consults Jung about her husband, who months after the long-wished birth of a child began compulsively running after the servant girls. Questioned, "somebody was walking over the stage behind her closed lids": a medical-student cousin had "made her a child" when doctors found nothing wrong with either spouse.

Jung: the husband, unconsciously working out whether he was the father, "had to try, to experiment with the nearest women, though they didn't interest him at all. That is the way she brought about his peculiar behavior."

Theory: "Perfectly harmless, nice people become fiends when they receive such a projection from the unconscious of the partner. Men sometimes have an absolutely fiendish anima that they cannot help projecting, so it concretizes in the wife."

occurrences.title: Dream: her music outplayed by the rich Jew — first animus figure (Visions Seminar patient)
occurrences.label: Dream — her music outplayed by the rich Jew
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I was trying to play some music and all the different members of my family were interfering. I was on a terrace looking out over the sea, when a rich Jew at the next table began to play also.
body: First dream after the personal layer of the analysis closed: the patient tries to play music on a terrace over the sea; her family interferes; then "a rich Jew at the next table began to play also" so beautifully that she stops. Jung reads the music as her feeling function (compensating the intellectual day-attitude, like Socrates' daemon commanding music, p74); the family as conventional resistance; the rich Jew as the animus — "the unconscious man in her," an animus "of great wealth, which means great power, great authority, and he is in possession of her feelings" (p76). The Protestant's unconscious is Jewish: "his religion is not the religion of the New Testament; he has never heard of St. Paul" (p75).

occurrences.title: Dream: the Swiss boy and the accordion — the animus as new Swiss thinking
occurrences.label: Dream — the Swiss boy and the accordion
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The boy says, \"No, you have kept me waiting so long that now you will learn what I have to teach.\
body: After the fire alarm, the dreamer keeps a Swiss boy (an accordion teacher) waiting while she dresses, then announces she will play the tune she has learned; he retorts that now she will learn what he has to teach. Jung: music = the art of feeling (Socrates' flute); a peasant instrument would already suffice for one so inarticulate. The boy is not Jung in disguise but "a new animus... a function," a subjective figure created in Switzerland — "a sort of mental visioning, a system of views, a kind of thinking, that originated in Switzerland and that advises music" (p97). The lesson of the exchange: the inferior function cannot be used at will — "when she touches feeling, she does what it wants" (p98); "The problem now begins to work by itself, spontaneously... For the fire is kindled and the process of disintegration is on the way" (p98).

occurrences.title: Antaeus and mother earth
occurrences.label: Antaeus and mother earth
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The giant Antaeus, invincible so long as he touched his mother earth, was strangled by Heracles holding him aloft.

Jung's reading: image of the temporary withdrawal into oneself — "in loving this inheritance they... turn back to the mother of humanity, to the psyche, which was before consciousness existed... It is the problem of Antaeus" (¶259).
Verbatim: It is the problem of Antaeus, who could only keep his giant strength through contact with mother earth. (cw05 ¶259).

image.title: Hercules and Antaeus

occurrences.title: The anteater portent and its bull-sacrifice expiation (south of Mount Elgon, 1925–26)
occurrences.label: The anteater portent and its bull-sacrifice…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: south of Mount Elgon, East Africa
occurrences.yearDisplay: Elgon custom, recorded during Jung's 1925–26 stay
occurrences.quote: The oldest maternal uncle of the man who saw the anteater must then sacrifice a bull. The man descends into the sacrificial pit and receives the first piece of the animal's flesh, whereupon the uncle and the other participants in the ceremony also eat.
body: The shy, nocturnal anteater is almost never seen by day; when one is, it is a transgression of the natural order — "a portent, an omen, comparable to a comet or an eclipse" — and it demands extraordinary placation: the neighbouring villages are aroused, the animal dug up and killed, "the oldest maternal uncle of the man who saw the anteater must then sacrifice a bull. The man descends into the sacrificial pit and receives the first piece of the animal's flesh," and the participants eat — "in this way the dangerous caprice of nature is expiated" (¶118).

Jung's reading: the ritual answers a real datum, the tendency of chance events to fall into series (¶121ff); portent and expiation restore the coherence of a world in which striking occurrences are all "brought into connection with the unusual event" (¶120).

occurrences.title: Anthropos as anima mundi with the four elements — Albertus Magnus, Philosophia naturalis (1650 ed.)
occurrences.label: Anthropos as anima mundi with the four elements
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Deus terrestris, Salvator, or filius macrocosmi… we can only compare with the Gnostic Anthropos
body: Plate 117: "Anthropos as anima mundi, containing the four elements and characterized by the number 10, which represents perfection (1 + 2 + 3 + 4)." Jung cites it in the vessel chapter as the goal-figure toward which the one vas tends — the stone as "an altogether mystical being… Deus terrestris, Salvator, or filius macrocosmi, a figure we can only compare with the Gnostic Anthropos, the divine original man" (¶335).
The decad (1+2+3+4) stamps the original man with the completed quaternity — the same 1-2-3-4 arithmetic as the Axiom of Maria in this very chunk (¶209).

image.title: Anima Mundi, Christ, Adam Kadmon with the four elements

occurrences.title: The Primordial Man as bait for the powers of darkness — Manichaean hook myth
occurrences.label: The Primordial Man as bait for the powers…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Manichaean myth behind Dorn's allegory: God threw out a hook — the Primordial Man himself as bait for catching the powers of darkness. "The Primordial Man was named 'Psyche,' and in Titus of Bostra he is the world soul (psyche apanton). This psyche corresponds to the collective unconscious, which, itself of unitary nature, is represented by the unitary Primordial Man" (cw13 ¶450; Bousset, Hauptprobleme der Gnosis p. 178).

In the Valentinian revision (cw13 ¶452) it is no longer the Primordial Man but the feminine Sophia-Acham oth who is cast in to the darkness — see sophia-achamoth-fall-plenum-2c. The hook with which God the Father catches the Leviathan is, in medieval allegory, the crucifix (cw13 ¶450).
Verbatim: he used the Primordial Man as a bait for catching the powers of darkness. (cw13 ¶450ocr)

occurrences.title: Basilides: three sonships and the Passion as discrimination of natures
occurrences.label: Basilides — three sonships and the Passion…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Alexandria? (Basilides; reported in Hippolytus, Elenchos VII, 26-30)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Hippolytus reports Basilides: "Now Jesus became the first sacrifice in the discrimination of the natures, and the Passion came to pass for no other reason than the discrimination of composite things" — the motto of Aion itself (Elenchos VII, 27, 8).

The non-existent God begot a threefold sonship (spirit/soul/body), mirrored by three Christ-figures of Ogdoad, Hebdomad, and Jesus son of Mary. The third sonship lies hidden in amorphia — "formlessness," which Jung reads as practically the equivalent of "unconsciousness" (par. 119). Jesus is the prototype "awakener" of the seed slumbering in unconscious humanity.

occurrences.title: Jakoby's 'The Fire Sower' — fiery Anthropos sowing flames over the city
occurrences.label: Jakoby's 'The Fire Sower'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: He sows flames, and instead of water fire falls from heaven.
body: A contemporary painting born of "the fundamental fear of our age": a round, fiery object rotating above a darkening city, personified as a head separated from a body of flame — "the gigantic figure of a spectral 'sower, who went forth to sow.'" He sows invisible fire, an inextinguishable "fire of the Philosophers," and the city takes no notice: "two worlds which interpenetrate yet do not touch."

Jung's reading: the figure "is in every respect archetypal... like an archaic king or a god"; the severed head recalls the omega-element that "originated with Zosimos of Panopolis" (¶728); it is a homo maximus, "an Anthropos and filius hominis of fiery nature" evoking Enoch, Christ, Elijah, Daniel and Ezekiel — and Boehme's wrath-fire, for "the name 'Lucifer' applies to both Christ and the devil" (¶733). "It is a 'uniting symbol'... a bringer of salvation and disaster at once" (¶734).

occurrences.title: First Man armed with the five elements, wrapped in the Mother of Life — Acta Archelai
occurrences.label: First Man armed with the five elements, wrapped…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Mesopotamia (Manichaean mission); Latin transmission via Hegemonius
body: The Manichaean descent myth in the version Jung quotes in the king chapter: the good father, perceiving that darkness had come over his land, 'produced from himself the virtue which is called the Mother of Life, with which he surrounded the First Man' — the five elements, wind, light, water, fire and matter, with which, clad as with war-gear, they descended to fight against the darkness. Jung adduces it beside the regenerated king to whom God gives the (four/five) elements as weapons — the elements conceived as circles, with the crowned Maid (Quinta Essentia) in the fifth, 'in whom we recognize the crowned Virgin... the anima media natura or anima mundi' (cw14 ¶450).

Verbatim: produxit ex se virtutem, quae dicitur mater vitae, qua circumdedit primum hominem, quae sunt quinque elementa, id est ventus, lux, aqua, ignis et materia, quibus indutus, tamquam ad adparatum belli, descendit deorsum pugnare adversum tenebras.

occurrences.title: Gayomart, spherical like the world-soul — Persian tradition
occurrences.label: Gayomart, spherical like the world-soul
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: 'Psychology of the Transference' §5 n.5 (pdf p422); §10 n.17 (pdf p434)

occurrences.quote: The Persian Gayomart is as broad as he is long, hence spherical in shape like the world-soul in Plato's Timaeus. He is supposed to dwell in each individual soul and in it to return to God.
body: The Persian First Man, Gayomart, cited twice by Jung in the transference essay: first for his radiance ("The radiant quality is characteristic of Mercurius and also of the first man, Gayomart or Adam," §5 n.5), then for his form:
The spherical Anthropos dwelling in every soul — the microcosmic self-structure in Persian dress, bridging Plato's world-soul and the alchemical rotundum.

occurrences.title: The man of light (phos) in Zosimos — Thoyth-Adam and the daemon Antimimos
occurrences.label: The man of light in Zosimos
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In Zosimos the "man of light"... is simply called φως. He is the spiritual man who has clothed himself in Adam's body.
body: The man of light (ἄνθρωπος φωτεινός) imprisoned in Adam, whom Jung places behind both the Cabalistic Adam Kadmon and the alchemical filius philosophorum: "Originally this figure may have been the ανθρωπος φωτεινος, the 'man of light' who was imprisoned in Adam, and whom we encounter in Zosimos of Panopolis (third century)" (¶166). In Zosimos he is simply called φώς (man = ἄνθρωπος, light = φως, a wordplay Jung notes); "He is the spiritual man who has clothed himself in Adam's body. Christ let Adam approach and accepted him into paradise" (¶166 n.52; cf. Psychology and Alchemy ¶456). The man of light is "an echo of the pre-Christian doctrine of the Primordial Man," popularized in the fifteenth century by Ficino and Pico della Mirandola and absorbed into alchemy.

Jung's literal translation of the Anthropos doctrine in the Zosimos texts (cw12): the Son of God becomes all things to draw souls out of the dominion of Heimarmene. The first man is Thoyth (Thoth) to the Egyptians, Adam to Chaldeans, Parthians, Medes, and Hebrews — "virgin earth, blood-red earth, fiery or carnal earth" — his name spelled by the four quarters (Anatole-Dysis-Arktos-Mesembria), the cross-structured Anthropos. The Man of Light (phos) in Paradise is persuaded to put on the earthly Adam; Hesiod knew him as Prometheus, bound, with Pandora — Eve — sent after. Jesus Christ "made himself one with Adam and bore him up." Against him stands Antimimos, the jealous imitator who falsely claims to be the Son of God and whose Persian forerunner's name has nine letters. Nikotheos alone knows the Man of Light's secret name.

Jung: this Son of God is "a Gnostic Christ who has more affinity with the Iranian conception of Gayomart than with the Jesus of the Gospels" (¶457); Antimimos is the dark twin whose chemical parallel is Mercurius duplex in the Uroboros (¶460).

occurrences.title: The man rising from the river — Splendor Solis, Plate VIII
occurrences.label: The man rising from the river
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: he is the "man rising from the river," probably a reference to the vision of Ezra.
body: In the very old "Dicta Belini" (Belinus = pseudo-Apollonius of Tyana), Mercurius is "the man rising from the river" — "probably a reference to the vision of Ezra" (IV Ezra 13: the man coming up from the midst of the sea). "In Trismosin's Splendor solis (sixteenth century) there is an illustration of this" (¶268 n.33: Aureum vellus 1598, Tract 3, Pl. VIII of the 1920 facsimile).

Jung: "The idea itself may go back to the Babylonian teacher of wisdom, Oannes" — the Anthropos rising from the waters, one of Mercurius's avatars; he is also "the 'high man'" and the "Philosophic ambisexual Man."

image.title: Splendor Solis 08 resurrection out of swamp

occurrences.title: 'Gloria mundi': man the little world (microcosm, Musaeum hermeticum)
occurrences.label: Gloria mundi: man the little world
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "Man is to be esteemed a little world, and in all respects he is to be compared to a world. The bones under his skin are likened to mountains, for by them is the body strengthened, even as the earth is by rocks, and the flesh is taken for earth, and the great blood vessels for great rivers, and the little ones for small streams that pour into the great rivers. The bladder is the sea, wherein the great as well as the small streams congregate. The hair is compared to sprouting herbs..." (cw13 ¶122).

Jung: the idea of man as microcosm "is a remnant of an original psychic identity which reflected a twilight state of consciousness"; personification and microcosm thinking underlie all alchemical projection (¶122, ¶123).

occurrences.title: Man as 'miniature heaven' bearing images of the constellations — Philo, De opificio mundi 82
occurrences.label: Man as 'miniature heaven' bearing images…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: Philo on the frame of creation: God made heaven the beginning and man the end, man "a miniature heaven" who "bears about within himself, like holy images, endowments of nature that correspond to the constellations."

Jung's reading: "Here the great principle or beginning, heaven, is infused into man the microcosm, who reflects the star-like natures and thus, as the smallest part and end of the work of Creation, contains the whole" (¶926). Philo is Jung's bridge-text from the Hippocratic sympatheia panton to the correspondence theory of the Middle Ages — and, implicitly, to the collective unconscious as the microcosm "containing the images of all creation" (¶931).

occurrences.title: Plato's round primordial man — Aristophanes' speech (Symposium 189d–193d)
occurrences.label: Plato's round primordial man
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939
Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "The idea of the Platonic primordial man, which is still going strong, is a symbol for the self, the all-round being." — Plato narrates as myth what the pre-Socratics still projected into nature.

On 22 January 1936 the figure returns as the hidden content of Zarathustra's golden ball: "the globe, the all-perfect roundness expressing the primordial man, the man that was before he had been dismembered, cut up or separated — before he became two. And it is the idea of the alchemistic hermaphrodite that unites the sexes." Editor: Aristophanes' spherical hermaphroditic beings, divided by the jealous gods — "a favorite of Jung" (CW11 ¶47n; CW9i ¶138n).

occurrences.title: The Poimandres vision — light, the coiling darkness, and primal man's descent and ascent (Corpus Hermeticum I)
occurrences.label: The Poimandres vision
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1st c. CE ('roughly the first century after Christ' — Reichstein)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: At first, all was light (the Spirit, or God the Father). Out of it came the darkness coiling down like a snake.
body: Reichstein's resume of the Poimandres ("shepherd of men") cosmogony-vision: "At first, all was light (the Spirit, or God the Father). Out of it came the darkness coiling down like a snake." A holy Logos leaps from the moisture as fire and air; the male-female primal god creates the demiurge, "he who holds the fire," who makes the seven planets, the visible world and fate — and is "supposed to be an evil demon."

Primal man breaks through the partition of the spheres, "breaking the power of the bad demon," shows lower nature god's beautiful form, and takes his home in the body out of longing: "man alone has a double nature, mortal through the body and immortal through his essence, primal man." Salvation is the stripping ascent: "Then thou traversest the seven spheres (Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn) returning to each its malevolent influence. Completely stripped, man enters the eighth sphere" — and ascends to God. The Poimandres community influenced early Christianity and Hermetic alchemy; "the Alchemist Zosimos was a member."

occurrences.title: The Anthropos beholding his reflection: shadow on earth, image in water
occurrences.label: The Anthropos beholding his reflection
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: His shadow falls upon the earth, but his image is reflected in the water.
body: The Poimandres-type myth Jung rehearses from the Neopythagoreans: Nous, the god Anthropos, appears alongside the demiurge as adversary of the planetary spheres; he rends the sphere-circle and leans down to earth and water. His shadow falls on the earth, his image is reflected in the water; the elements kindle with love, and he, charmed by his own reflected beauty, descends — whereupon Physis locks him in her embrace, and from the union are born the seven hermaphroditic beings: the seven planets, the seven metals, the hermaphrodite Mercurius.

Jung: "In such visionary images … there is expressed the whole phenomenon of the unconscious projection of autonomous contents. These myth-pictures are like dreams, telling us that a projection has taken place and also what has been projected."

occurrences.title: Prajapati alone, speaking with his own greatness — the Upanishadic cosmogony
occurrences.label: Prajapati alone, speaking with his own greatness
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Against the inflated ego of the marketplace discussion Jung sets "the original philosophic mind": "you find in the Upanishads the cosmogonic myth of Prajapati, the first being who, when he found that he was all alone, that there was nothing which was not himself, began to talk to his own greatness, or the greatness within himself spoke to him". Zimmer's note: feeling lonely, "he brought forth the universe to surround himself with company."

The distinction matters: the ego thinks "I am all alone… a pretty miserable condition. But there is also a greatness which is peculiarly myself, yet it is not myself; it speaks to me and even tells me that which I did not know." Consciousness's opinions are of little importance; "it is a greatness behind that consciousness which speaks the truth. But if one is unconscious of it, then naturally one has an inflation and behaves as if one were the greatness". The activated archetype "is like a rising sun" warming the ego from within.

occurrences.title: The Valley of Factories: the Purusha with the flaming bow, serpent below (16 November 1932)
occurrences.label: The Valley of Factories
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: That figure of the sun god above, and the black snake underneath is in a way a reconciling symbol, they are together though in a monstrous form.
body: First vision of the second book ("The Twelve Circles"), titled "The Valley of Factories" [plate 33]: an artificial volcano — manipura harnessed by man. In the sky a being surrounded by great light holds a flaming bow; stars fall from his head; his lower body is a snake reaching down into the seething earth.

Jung's reading: the Purusha / Theos Anthropos / Adam Cadmon — and, as sun-god above and black serpent below, the Gnostic Abraxas, the 365 time-god. Her breast-flame rushes to merge with the figure and would inflate her into the monster — a madness of opposites too close together; the vision extinguishes, and the flame falls and runs along the streets until ants ("water of fire," madji yamoto) stamp it out: regression from failed anahata into manipura.

occurrences.title: Purusha, the Person 'no bigger than a thumb' — Shvetashvatara Upanishad
occurrences.label: Purusha, the Person 'no bigger than a thumb'
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Upanishadic Person behind the sun: "There is one Rudra only, they do not allow a second, who rules all the worlds by his powers" (¶176); "I know this mighty Person (purusha), who is like to the sun, transcendent over darkness"; and the dwarf-formula: "That Person, no bigger than a thumb, the inner Self, seated forever in the heart of man" (¶178), matched by the Katha Upanishad: "burning like flame without smoke... that is Self" (¶179). The paradox completes: "Without feet, without hands, he moves, he grasps... Smaller than small, greater than great" (¶182).

Jung's reading: the All-Creator behind the winged sun (fig. 11, Bes with Horus-eyes); the thumb-sized creative Person belongs with "Tom Thumbs, dactyls, and Cabiri" — personifications of creative forces with phallic aspect (¶180). The same disparity of great and small reappears in Faust's key that "leads you to the Mothers."

occurrences.title: Puruṣa 'smaller than small, greater than great' — Katha Upanishad 2.20-21
occurrences.label: Puruṣa 'smaller than small, greater than great'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)
jung.locator: Lecture 2 (pdf p89, fn13); also cited CW6 §329

occurrences.quote: He discovers the puruüa in his heart, the thumbling, \"Smaller than small, and greater than great.\
body: In anāhata the yogi beholds the puruṣa, "a small figure that is the divine self" — the thumbling, "Smaller than small, and greater than great" (Katha Up. 2.20-21). Jung: in the center of anāhata Śiva stands again as liṅga, and "the small flame means the first germlike appearance of the self" — that which is not identical with blind causality, from which "one detaches... and when a man discovers this, he really becomes a man."

occurrences.title: Purusha Sukta — the cosmic Man sacrificed to create the worlds (Rig-Veda X,90)
occurrences.label: Purusha Sukta — the cosmic Man sacrificed…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Purusha Sukta: the primal Man who "encompassed the earth on all sides and ruled over the ten-finger place" is itself sacrificed — "the gods sacrificed with him, and the saints and the sages" — and from the offering arise the hymns, metres, animals, and the cosmos ("from his mind the moon; from his eye the sun; from his breath Vayu; from his navel the atmosphere; from his head the sky; from his feet the earth"). Adjacent, Vishvakarman makes the world from an unknown tree ("What was the wood, what was the tree, from which heaven and earth were hewn?" ¶646).

Jung reads it as a psychological cosmogony (¶652): Purusha is "a sort of Platonic world-soul" (¶649) with maternal character — "the encompasser and the encompassed, mother and unborn child, an undifferentiated, unconscious state of primal being" (¶650) that must be sacrificed so that "discriminated entities—i.e., conscious contents—may come into being." Anchors the cosmic-sacrifice argument of ch. VIII.
Verbatim: "The world comes into being when man discovers it. But he only discovers it when he sacrifices his containment in the primal mother" (¶652).

occurrences.title: The pre-existent Son of Man, chosen and hidden — Enoch's Elect One (1 Enoch 48, 62, 71)
occurrences.label: The pre-existent Son of Man, chosen and hidden
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: The Son of Man "chosen and hidden" before the creation of the world, with whom dwells "the spirit of wisdom and the spirit which gives insight"; under him earth and Sheol give back their dead (¶678-679). The Head of Days presents him: "This is the Son of Man who is born unto righteousness, and righteousness abides over him" (¶681) — announced by the angelic quaternity Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, Phanuel, in the heaven of heavens with the house of God "built of crystal".

Righteousness is his leitmotif — "only where injustice threatens… does such an emphasis on righteousness make any sense"; "It looks as though, with this, Enoch had unconsciously given an answer to Job" (¶682). Enoch himself, addressed as Son of Man, "experiences that godlike elevation which, in the case of Job, we merely assumed" (¶684), his wafting away prefiguring the resurrection of the dead (¶686).

occurrences.title: Solomon Trismosin's verses: 'Study what thou art… All that is without thee also is within' — Splendor Solis
occurrences.label: Solomon Trismosin's verses — Splendor Solis
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Augsburg → London, British Library Harley MS 3469
occurrences.yearDisplay: Splendor Solis (German ed. Augsburg 1532; Harley MS 1582)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: All that is without thee Also is within
body: The six verses Jung quotes from Trismosin: "Study what thou art, / Whereof thou art a part, / What thou knowest of this art, / This is really what thou art. / All that is without thee / Also is within."

They cap a series of admissions Jung assembles that the arcanum is man himself: the homo albus of the Visio Arislei, the Book of Krates' dialogue on knowing one's own soul, the Zosimas-attributed "Thus it comes from man, and you are its mineral… it remains inseparably in you," and Dorn's cry "Transform yourselves into living philosophical stones!" (¶153–154). Trismosin "expresses it most clearly of all." Jung's conclusion: the sought-for "hidden nature" is a consciousness-transcending content of the unconscious — the self, never identical with the ego.

occurrences.title: The three manifestations of the Anthropos: body, soul, spirit — Ripley Scrowle
occurrences.label: The three manifestations of the Anthropos
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 196. The three manifestations of the Anthropos during his transformation: body, soul, spirit. Below, dragon and toad as preliminary forms.
body: Plate from the English Ripley Scrowle rolls (1588): the Anthropos shown in his three transformations — body, soul, spirit — with dragon and toad beneath as the preliminary (animal) forms.

Picture verified against the plate render (cw12 pdf p360): the caption block identifies it as "Ripley Scrowle," MS. Add. 5025 (1588), British Museum, No. 2, detail — three labelled figures (spiritus/anima/corpus) on a columned, crenellated platform, a large winged dragon in the register below (the toad of the caption is not separately legible in the B/W render).

Distinct from uroboros-ripley-scroll-dark-sphere-frog-british-museum-16c: that note anchors the seminar's verbal walk through the whole scroll (chaos as dark sphere with vaporous exhalations, nyagrodha tree roots-in-heaven, ouroboros; pdf 1441), and its "dragon persecuting a small frog" motif (pdf 1452) is at most this panel's lower register — while the seminar's "female with a salamander's tail and the feet of a frog" belongs to the Melusina/Lilith register of the tree panel (cw12 fig. 257; melusina-anima-ripley-scrowle-bm-sloane-5025-1588), not to this panel. Kept as separate loci (batch-2 picture check).

Jung sets it against Zosimos' doctrine of the Man of Light who puts on the earthly Adam, and against the homo philosophicus "who is the One, i.e., the tincture or elixir of life, but … also the everlasting inner man, identical or at least connected with the Anthropos" (¶476). The same Scrowle carries the plumed king plucking his own feathers for food (fig. 228).

occurrences.title: Abarbanel: Messiah expected at the Jupiter-Saturn conjunction in Pisces
occurrences.label: Abarbanel — Messiah expected…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Ferrara (Ma'yene ha-Yeshu'ah on Daniel, 1551); Abarbanel b. Lisbon 1437, d. Venice 1508

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Abarbanel's commentary on Daniel expects the Messiah "when there is a conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn in Pisces": in anno mundi 2365 such a great conjunction stood three years before Moses' birth (legendary); the House of the Fishes is "the house of justice and of brilliant splendour". Saturn is the star of Israel, Jupiter the "king (of justice)."
At par. 168 Jung adds that in Abarbanel's Mashmi'a Yeshu'ah the Messiah ben Joseph "actually is the Antichrist." Cf. R. Abraham ben Hiyya (Messiah in 1464) and Solomon ben Gabirol.

occurrences.title: Nostradamus, letter to Henry II: the second Antichrist and the year 1792
occurrences.label: Nostradamus, letter to Henry II
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: France (letter of June 27, 1558, to Henry II)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Nostradamus' astrological letter: from 1792, "the infernal power shall rise against the Church of Jesus Christ. This shall be the second Antichrist" — a Northern king, an eleven-year persecution, the sanctuary destroyed by paganism (cw09ii pars. 151-152).

Jung (par. 150): the course of Christian religious history "could have been predicted more or less accurately... from the precession of the equinoxes through the constellation of Pisces." With Nostradamus' prediction "he placed himself firmly in the antichristian phase and served as its mouthpiece" (par. 159).

occurrences.title: Pierre d'Ailly, Concordantia: change of sects and the coming of Antichrist
occurrences.label: Pierre d'Ailly, Concordantia
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Basing himself on Albumasar, d'Ailly tied the eighth coniunctio maxima (calculated for 1693) and the completion of ten Saturn revolutions in 1789 to "many and great and marvellous changes... especially as concerns law-giving and religious sects": "after the sect of Mahomet none other will come save the law of the Antichrist".

Jung: "Fantasy could do the rest, for the archetype had long been ready and was only waiting for the time to be fulfilled" (par. 156). Saturn periods: 289 Manichaeism, 589 Islam, 1189 Innocent III, 1489 schism.

occurrences.title: Jackal-headed Anubis bending over a mummy — Thebes, XX Dynasty
occurrences.label: Jackal-headed Anubis bending over a mummy
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Pl. XXXIIa: Anubis the corpse-devourer and psychopomp ministering to the dead.

Jung's reading: "Here the dogs and jackals, devourers of corpses by night, assist in the reconstitution or reproduction of Osiris" (¶354) — the necrophagous helper whose deeper meaning Creuzer reads in the dog-star at solstice: "death being made equal to the sun at its highest point", i.e. entry into the mother's womb for rebirth (¶354).
Verbatim: Actually Isis collected the pieces together again with the help of the jackal-headed Anubis. (cw05 ¶354).

image.title: Theban region, Deir el-Medina, TT1, tomb of Sennedjem, 1905-1914
image.credit: Archivio fotografico Museo Egizio, Turin - online catalogue

occurrences.title: The sun-worshipping dog-headed baboon — Egyptian monuments
occurrences.label: The sun-worshipping dog-headed baboon
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

occurrences.quote: motivated by the same preconscious archetype which the ancient Egyptians, on their monuments, also ascribed to the sun-worshipping dog-headed baboon
body: The ancient Egyptians, on their monuments, ascribed to the dog-headed baboon (the cynocephalus) the same sun-worshipping gesture Jung observed among the Elgonyi: at sunrise the animal raises its hands to the sun. Jung's point is precise: the Egyptians did it "in full knowledge that this ritual gesture was in honour of God" — while the Elgonyi, and the Westerners with their Christmas tree, perform the identical gesture without any knowledge of its meaning.

Jung's reading: both are "motivated by the same preconscious archetype" — the archetype is "pure, unvitiated nature... which causes man to utter words and perform actions whose meaning is unconscious to him" (¶412). Preconscious archetypes never conscious, established only indirectly through their effects.

occurrences.title: Thoth's dog-headed ape on the balance — Book of the Dead judgment scene
occurrences.label: Thoth's dog-headed ape on the balance
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: This ape is a form of Thoth as the god of \"equilibrium.\" Perhaps it is a symbol of the equinoxes.
body: From Reichstein's report on the old wise man: in the judgment scene the dog-headed ape sits atop the support of the beam of the balance in which the heart of the deceased is weighed; "his duty is to watch the pointer and tell the Ibis-headed Thoth when the beam is exactly level."

Reichstein (approved by Jung's later discussion of Thoth as the anticipating Logos): "This ape is a form of Thoth as the god of 'equilibrium.' Perhaps it is a symbol of the equinoxes." The ape is a hybrid between man and animal, like the frog — an equilibrium-figure between the weighing of the dead man's heart and the god who records it.

occurrences.title: Aphroditos of Cyprus — the bearded Aphrodite and the hybristica at Argos
occurrences.label: Aphroditos of Cyprus
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The prehistory of Hermaphroditus: "The earliest traces were found in Cyprus where there is evidence of a cult of a masculine Aphrodite; there are images of a woman with a beard. This particular deity was called Aphroditos, and sacrifices were performed where the men had to appear in female garments and the women in male garments. A similar cult existed in Argos in Greece, and the ceremony there was called hybristica."

Jung: the name comes from the herm-stele, not from Hermes + Aphrodite (the late legend); introduced to Athens ~5th c. BCE, it sank to an occult domestic cult of plural Hermaphroditi, "just as there were always a certain number of cabiri." The double nature expressed "the unconscious intuition of a peculiar condition which was neither male nor female as an attribute of the divine" — not fertility, the hermaphrodite being sterile.

occurrences.title: Plurimi pertransibunt, et multiplex erit scientia — Daniel 12:4
occurrences.label: Plurimi pertransibunt, et multiplex erit…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Book of Daniel (set in Babylonian exile; composed Judea?)
body: The eschatological promise to Daniel: "many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased" — here quoted by Jung in the Latin variant "Plurimi pertransibunt, et multiplex erit scientia" as the closing line of his final Zofingia lecture (editors' translation: "Many shall perish, and manifold shall be knowledge!"). In Daniel it is the end-time sign given to the seer of the last things; Jung deploys it as the motto of the scientific age, immediately after his genealogy of the "dangerous interpretation" of Christianity running "from its birth in the theology of John until its decline in Schopenhauer" and his warning that "we have not yet seen the last lightning bolt flare up out of its dark reaches" (¶291).
The 23-year-old thus ends three years of lectures on an apocalypse of knowledge — multiplication of science as the eschaton's sign, perils included (the motto is double-edged: many shall perish).
Verbatim: "Plurimi pertransibunt, et multiplex erit scientia" (pdf p142, trailing footnote-marker OCR noise).

occurrences.title: The initiate elected Helios — Apuleius' Isis-mysteries apotheosis
occurrences.label: The initiate elected Helios
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Rome/Corinth (Isis mysteries as narrated in Metamorphoses XI)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: In the Metamorphosis of Apuleius, the initiate — "an ordinary human being" — is elected to be Helios: "he is crowned with a crown of palms and clad in the mystic mantle, whereupon the assembled crowd pays homage to him" (¶229). "The suggestion of the crowd brings about his identity with the god."

Jung's reading: prime example of identification with the cult-hero within the transformation experience; and in the 1936 essay, the ritual transformation into the Deity "is attested by Apuleius in the Isis mysteries, and moreover in the form of a Helios apotheosis" (¶107) — the frame for reading his 1906 solar-phallus patient, who felt himself the sun-god creating the wind.

occurrences.title: Apuleius' prayer to the Queen of Heaven (Isis as Venus and Proserpina)
occurrences.label: Apuleius' prayer to the Queen of Heaven
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: he associates "heavenly Venus" with "Proserpina, who strikest terror with midnight ululations
body: Apuleius' "magnificent prayer to the Queen of Heaven" in the Isis book of the Metamorphoses, which associates "heavenly Venus" with "Proserpina, who strikest terror with midnight ululations" ("Nocturnis ululatibus horrenda Proserpina").

Jung's reading: "it was the terrifying paradox of the primordial mother-image" — the loving and the terrible mother united in one figure; entering the realm of the syzygies leads "directly to the experience of individuation, the attainment of the self" (¶194).

occurrences.title: Arbor philosophica: tree from Adam's genitals, tree from Eve's head — Codex Ashburnham
occurrences.label: Arbor philosophica — Codex Ashburnham
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: One picture shows Adam struck by an arrow, and the tree growing out of his genitals; in the other picture the tree grows out of Eve's head.
body: Two pictures of the arbor philosophica in the fourteenth-century Codex Ashburnham: Adam struck by an arrow, the tree growing out of his genitals; Eve's tree growing out of her head, her right hand covering her genitals, her left pointing to a skull.

Jung's reading (¶519): "the man's opus is concerned with the erotic aspect of the anima, while the woman's is concerned with the animus, which is a 'function of the head.'" The prima materia — the unconscious — is represented in man by the "unconscious" anima, in woman by the "unconscious" animus; out of it grows the philosophical tree, the unfolding opus. In their symbolical sense the pictures accord with the findings of psychology: Adam as the woman's animus generating "philosophical" ideas, Eve as the man's anima who, as Sapientia or Sophia, produces the intellectual content of the work from her head.

occurrences.title: The archaic many-breasted mother inside the golden idol (Visions Seminar, 8 March 1933)
occurrences.label: The archaic many-breasted mother inside…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Seizing a glass-eyed worshipper by the neck, the patient forces the idol's secret: "We passed through the circle of worshippers and entered a little door at the base of the idol." Inside sits "the statue of a primitive woman sitting cross-legged... many breasts... loathsomely archaic." She wants it dragged into the light; her animus guide refuses: "It is covered by the great idol... It must not be shown."

Jung's reading: the idol is a hollow casket of personal complexes; within it, dimly perceived through the personal veil, stands the true archetype — the unconscious under its mother aspect, "like a mother with many breasts, nourishing innumerable children". Compare Artemis of Ephesus; negative aspect = Kali, enantiodromia of the Madonna; behind her waits the aimless animus battle.

occurrences.title: Ardhanari: Shiva and Parvati united — polychrome clay figure
occurrences.label: Ardhanari — Shiva and Parvati united
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Pl. XXIII: the half-male, half-female Ardhanari — Shiva has "given one half of his body to his wife Parvati as a dwelling-place".
Jung's reading: the god as both male and female, image of continuous cohabitation whose architectural form is the lingam-in-yoni (¶306).
Verbatim: The god Shiva, as Mahadeva and Parvati, is both male and female: he has even given one half of his body to his wife Parvati as a dwelling-place (pl. XXIII). (cw05 ¶306).

occurrences.title: Argei dolls thrown from the Pons Sublicius by the Vestales
occurrences.label: Argei dolls thrown from the Pons Sublicius…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: Chanting hymns and prayers, the Vestales threw these dolls into the Tiber.
body: Every May a procession visited the twenty-four chapels of the Argei, took from each a doll (Argeus) shaped like an old man, and — chanting hymns and prayers — the Vestal Virgins threw them into the Tiber from the Pons Sublicius, Rome's oldest bridge. Read (per the Encyclopaedia of Religion and Ethics, cited in the seminar) as a relic of an epoch when old men no longer fit for service were sacrificed as yearly tribute to the river god affronted by the building of the bridge.

The seminar frames it with the bridge-ghost idea: a water demon dwells under every bridge, first appeased with human beings, later with man-shaped dolls; chapels on former sacrificial sites remain the "last relics."

occurrences.title: Armillus, son of the stone — Midrash of the Ten Kings
occurrences.label: Armillus, son of the stone
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: And Satan will come down and have intercourse with the stone in Rome. The stone will conceive and bear Armillus.
body: The Midrash of the Ten Kings: "Satan will come down and have intercourse with the stone in Rome. The stone will conceive and bear Armillus" — the stone, shaped as a beautiful girl made in the six days of Creation, is the wife of Belial; her son has "squinting red eyes, two heads, green feet," hair "red like gold"; he will tell the Edomites "I am your saviour."

Jung's reading: the "lower stone's" evil counterpart-birth — a Typhon-like adversary of the second Adam, corresponding to the three-headed Azi-Dahaka of Persian legend who subdued Yima the Anthropos (Murmelstein; Hurwitz, Die Gestalt des sterbenden Messias). Parallels: antichrist-nostradamus-letter-henry-ii-1558, antichrist-abarbanel-pisces-messiah-ferrara-1551, ullikummi-stone-kumarbi-boghazkoy-1200bce.

occurrences.title: The square sheet of metal upheld by four gods (Visions Seminar, 7 December 1932 / 18 January 1933)
occurrences.label: The square sheet of metal upheld by four gods
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: So the armor, the four-cornered sheet of metal, symbolizes individuation.
body: At the great wheel the ground opens: "a square sheet of metal upheld by four gods, one at each corner, Osiris, a Greek goddess, a Mexican god and an Indian god. Red and green fire leapt from them." Wrapped in the metal she passes the wheel; where the ground closed "appeared a pool of blood."

Jung's reading: an international meeting — Egypt, Greece, Mexico, India, "the totality of ancient civilization" — one conscious female function counterbalanced by three male (animus) functions, an unconscious pagan Trinity. The armor symbolizes individuation, "the right protection against that wheel with the grasping hands"; the pool of blood is the sacrificial blood of the birth of the Self, paid for by the body. But the hollow sound of the hands striking the armor hints that perhaps nobody is inside. Read against Ezekiel 1 (four living creatures, wheels, fire) as an autochthonous re-invention of the same archetypal pattern, paralleled by Black Elk's boyhood vision.

occurrences.title: The arrow of love transfixing Mary's soul — Bernard of Clairvaux
occurrences.label: The arrow of love transfixing Mary's soul
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: God's word is an arrow; it is lively and effective and more penetrating than a double-edged sword.… And the love of Christ is a choice arrow too, which not only entered, but transfixed, the soul of Mary, so that it left no particle of her virgin heart free of love.
body: In the Return of the Soul section Jung sets Bernard's Mariological arrow beside the alchemists' telum passionis of Mercurius: "The alchemists regarded the arrow as the telum passionis of Mercurius" (§9 n.22).

Sermon XXIX, 8 supplies the wound: Mary "received a great and sweet wound of love in all her being" — quoted by Jung via Macaulay's motto of Book I. The arrow of the coniunctio pierces the soul-bride through and through.

occurrences.title: Philoctetes wounded at the shrine of Chryse — the wounded-king prototype
occurrences.label: Philoctetes wounded at the shrine of Chryse
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Chryse (island and nymph of the same name)
occurrences.quote: the prototype of the wounded and ailing king, a motif that is continued in the legend of the Grail and in alchemical symbolism
body: Sailing for Troy, the Greeks must sacrifice at the hidden shrine of the nymph Chryse; only Philoctetes knows the way. A scholiast records what the island cost him: Chryse offered the hero her love, and on being scorned cursed him — the snake-bit, unhealing foot-wound whose stench makes his companions maroon him.

Jung draws the line forward explicitly: "Philoctetes, like his forerunner Heracles, is the prototype of the wounded and ailing king, a motif that is continued in the legend of the Grail and in alchemical symbolism." The rejected goddess and the incurable wound are one complex — the wounded king as the land's sickness.

occurrences.title: The crystal bowl, seven golden arrows and the winged all-seeing eye — Jane Leade's vision
occurrences.label: The crystal bowl, seven golden arrows…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the last, the seventh arrow, is the symbol of an all-seeing eye with two wings, which enable the arrow to fly over the pool.
body: Dr. Reichstein's contribution, from Jane Leade (1623-1704), the English mystic and Pordage's soror mystica: a vision of a bowl of crystal and seven golden arrows shot at the goal "where the insurmountable power is located." A week later the same vision recurred — five arrows had reached the goal; two are hindered by a pool of slime; the seventh arrow bears the symbol of an all-seeing eye with two wings, which fly it over the obstacle into the secret chamber. Jung's reading: arrows = directed units of libido, golden = value; seven = mana quality, not arithmetic; the winged eye = winged thought that carries the libido across the last stretch — the Shiva-bindu goal, cousin to the patient's eye on the black wall.

occurrences.title: Heart pierced by triple beams ending in arrows — stigmatization of Anne Catharine Emmerich
occurrences.label: Heart pierced by triple beams ending in arrows
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The wounding and painful shafts do not come from outside, through gossip, which only pricks us on the surface, but from the ambush of our own unconscious.
body: The nun's heart-trouble "as if her heart were continually pierced by arrows" (¶435); Jung reads stigmatization as "an incubation with the Saviour, a slight modification of the ancient conception of the unio mystica as cohabitation with the god" (¶438) — the wounding shafts "do not come from outside … but from the ambush of our own unconscious. It is our own repressed desires that stick like arrows in our flesh."

occurrences.title: Dorn's 'Tour of the World' and 'Way of Truth' — Speculativae philosophiae
occurrences.label: Dorn's 'Tour of the World' and 'Way of Truth'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Hence it has come about that men have built for themselves a great Workshop on the left-hand side of the road... presided over by Industry.
body: In his Speculativae philosophiae (Theatrum chemicum I, 1602, pp. 286ff) the Frankfurt physician Gerard Dorn describes the "Mundi peregrinatio, quam erroris viam appellamus" — the tour of the world which we call the way of error: mankind builds a great Workshop on the left-hand side of the road, presided over by Industry, then crosses "the bridge of infirmity" to a great Hospital presided over by Medicine. The "way of truth", the right way, leads to "the camp of Wisdom" where the traveller is "refreshed with food far more powerful than before", beside "a stream of living water flowing with such wonderful artifice from the mountain peak. (From the Fountain of Wisdom the waters gush forth.)" Jung found in Dorn the exact map of his own mountain dream (¶335-337) — the archetype of the two ways verified in a text he had never read.

occurrences.title: Celestial seed fetched by the ascending elements — Dorn, Physica genesis
occurrences.label: Celestial seed fetched by the ascending elements
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)
jung.locator: tail of ch. XIV, before ¶421 (pdf p281)

body: Gerhard Dorn's Physica genesis (in Theatr. chem.
