I; Jung's fn 119 cites p. 391) describes the volatilized elements rising to fetch seed from the stars and carrying it back down into the elements: "But during their ascent the volatilized elements take 'from the higher stars male seeds, which they bring down into the four matrices, the elements, in order to fertilize them spagyrically'" (cw09iiend of "The Structure and Dynamics of the Self"). Jung frames this celestial insemination as the "circular distillation" that closes the opus into a cycle — the physical projection of a psychic to-and-fro between spirit and nature.

occurrences.title: Eckhart's deepest place, deeper than hell — the introvert's self-turning
occurrences.label: Eckhart's deepest place, deeper than hell
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Therefore do I turn back once more to myself, there do I find the deepest places, deeper than hell itself; for even from there does my wretchedness drive me. Nowhere can I escape myself! Here I will set me down and here I will remain.
body: Jung's footnote to the Spitteler chapter's Eckhart excursus (the soul as microcosm where introversion becomes mystical self-possession):

Jung reads this as the introvert's formula: turning back into oneself as into the deepest place — below hell, i.e. through the whole shadow-side — because the self cannot be escaped. The companion footnote in the same series: "According to Eckhart, the soul is as much the comprehender as the comprehended" (fn 162, Evans I, p. 389) — knower and known united in the ground of the soul.

occurrences.title: Elijah's ascent in illuminated MSS — modeled on Mithras' ascent
occurrences.label: Elijah's ascent in illuminated MSS
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Western Europe (medieval MSS); iconographic model from Roman Mithraic monuments
occurrences.quote: In illuminated MSS, the model is followed of the Mithraic representation of the ascent of Sol inviting Mithras to join him in the fiery chariot.
body: A case of iconographic assimilation across 1,000 years: medieval illuminated manuscripts depict Elijah's fiery-chariot ascent by following "the model... of the Mithraic representation of the ascent of Sol inviting Mithras to join him in the fiery chariot" (Bousset, "Die Himmelsreise der Seele"; Cumont, Textes et monuments, I, p. 178, fig. 11). Tertullian (De praescriptione hereticorum 40) says of Mithras: "imaginem resurrectionis induit" (¶1528).

Jung's reading: one more item in the unbroken chain of "phenomena of assimilation" proving Elijah "a living archetype" — the Christian prophet's ascent literally wears the Mithraic sun-ascent's garment, the same garment later passed to "Helyas Artista" in alchemy. Companion locus: ascent-descent-elijah-fiery-chariot-israel.

occurrences.title: Elijah carried in the fiery chariot
occurrences.label: Elijah carried in the fiery chariot
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "As Elijah was carried in the fiery chariot to heaven, or as Christ in his transfiguration ascended into heaven."

Jung cites both as the classical forms of levitation — "it is important that the perfect saint should be able to rise, to perform the miracle of levitation; many of the great saints have been seen rising into the air before the altar." Ascension is the fate of the subtle body, "that body of breath which would become heavy if filled with substantial food" — the ascetic's fasting as lightening for flight.
Verbatim: "as Elijah was carried in the fiery chariot to heaven, or as Christ in his transfiguration ascended into heaven."

occurrences.title: The false guide: 'Now we are on top of the mountain' (colleague's dream, told 3 June 1931)
occurrences.label: The false guide — Now we are on top…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Swiss village in the mountains (dream); Zurich practice (teller)
occurrences.yearDisplay: case from years before, told 3 June 1931
occurrences.quote: there the guide said: 'Now we are on top of the mountain.' The man thought it was impossible, but certainly the guide must know, he was such a reliable fellow.
body: Jung's colleague with a latent catatonia (dilated pupils, livid skin) dreamt twice, nearly identically: a winter mountain climb with a big, trustworthy-looking Swiss guide who stops halfway up a shoulder and declares "Now we are on top of the mountain" — and, in the twin dream, "Now we are down in the valley" when they have not left the village. The dreamer's trust in the guide's authority; the dreams' message, "your dreams say you have learned enough," ended the analysis and the psychosis: "He became human and normal again". Jung's exhibit of the double/psychopompos intervening at an impasse — the unconscious performing the tour de force the ego could not.

occurrences.title: Girl's dream 2 — pagan dances in heaven, angels doing good in hell
occurrences.label: Girl's dream 2 — pagan dances…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1938-39 (dreams dreamt at age eight; presented at ten; died of an infectious disease about a year later)
occurrences.quote: Ascent into heaven where pagan dances are being celebrated, and descent to hell where angels are doing good deeds.
body: Dream 2 of the twelve dreams an eight-year-old gave her psychiatrist father as a Christmas booklet: "Ascent into heaven where pagan dances are being celebrated, and descent to hell where angels are doing good deeds."

Jung's reading: "a motif appears that is definitely non-Christian and a reversal of values... This suggests, if anything, a relativization of moral values. Where did the child hit on such a revolutionary and modern idea, worthy of Nietzsche's genius? Such an idea is not strange to the philosophical mind of the East, but where could we find it in the child's milieu?" (¶534). He compares Lao-tze's "high stands on low" (¶536) — the milieu yields nothing, the archetype everything.

occurrences.title: Levitations of D. D. Home witnessed by Crookes (London, 1870–73)
occurrences.label: Levitations of D. D. Home witnessed by Crookes
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The great physical-mediumship locus: Crookes, "the famous English physicist", reports in the class "The Levitation of Human Beings": chairs rising with ladies seated, children raised "in full daylight", and above all Home — "On three separate occasions have I seen him raised completely from the floor of the room" (¶719). "There are at least a hundred recorded instances of Mr. Home's rising from the ground" (¶720).

Jung's reading: Crookes "was completely convinced of the reality of his observations", yet his honesty and intelligence make him "an unsolved psychological enigma" (¶722); observation depends on "the strength of his prejudice for or against" miracles (¶738). Jung brackets the physical question for the psychological one (¶723) — but in 1948 he numbers himself among scientists "completely convinced of their reality", though unable to choose an interpretation (¶750).

occurrences.title: Jung's mountain dream — the brook with metallic shimmer and two serpent paths
occurrences.label: Jung's mountain dream
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: I was climbing slowly and toilsomely up a mountain... Night was coming on, and I saw, on the dark slope opposite, a brook flowing down with a metallic shimmer, and two paths leading upwards, one to the left, the other to the right, winding like serpents.
body: Jung's own dream, told to prove the method: climbing a mountain, he finds himself only on the edge of a plateau; the real crest rises far off. Night falls. "On the dark slope opposite, a brook flowed down with a metallic shimmer, and two paths leading upwards, one to the left, the other to the right, winding like serpents"; to the right on the crest a hotel; below, the brook runs left under a bridge. "Not long afterwards" he found the same structure in Gerard Dorn's Speculativae philosophiae as the Mundi peregrinatio and the Via veritatis — Workshop and Hospital on the left, the camp of Wisdom and the Fountain of Wisdom on the right (¶335-336). For Jung the point is methodological: an apparently "individual" image is "an archetypal image such as can be reproduced over and over again in any age and any place" (¶337).

occurrences.title: The heavenly journey — Platonis liber quartorum (Harranite treatise)
occurrences.label: The heavenly journey — Platonis liber quartorum
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Harran? → Latin print (Theatrum chemicum V, Strasbourg)
occurrences.yearDisplay: printed 1659 (Theatrum chemicum V, p. 145); Harranite material older

jung.locator: fn 28 to ch. V, The Song of the Moth (pdf p691)

body: Jung fixes the earliest appearance of the alchemical journey motif: "The earliest appearance of this motif is probably the heavenly journey of Plato (?) in the Harranite treatise 'Platonis liber quartorum' (Theatrum chemicum, V, p. 145)." The heavenly wanderings of the soul — a "special instance of the journeys of the hero" — "was continued as the peregrinatio in alchemy" (cf. Psychology and Alchemy, par. 457). The treatise, spuriously fathered on Plato, carries the Sabian-Harranite astronomy of the soul into Latin alchemy.
Verbatim (fn 28): "The earliest appearance of this motif is probably the heavenly journey of Plato (?) in the Harranite treatise “Platonis liber quartorum” (Theatrum chemicum, V, p. 145)."

occurrences.title: Poliphilo's ascent to the Venus mystery and descent to daily life — Hypnerotomachia
occurrences.label: Poliphilo's ascent to the Venus mystery…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung reads the whole first part of the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili as 'the dreamer's ascent to a world of gods and heroes, of his initiation into a Venus mystery, followed by the illumination and semi-apotheosis of Poliphilo and his Polia'; the smaller second part is disenchantment and 'a descent to earth, to the reality of daily life' (cw14 ¶297). Whether Poliphilo 'preserve[d] in secret the nature of the heavenly centre which he acquired by the ascent' Jung doubts. Still: 'his exciting adventure has left us a psychological document which is a perfect example of the course and the symbolism of the individuation process' (¶297).

occurrences.title: Circular distillation repeated a thousand times — Rupescissa, quinte essence
occurrences.label: Circular distillation repeated a thousand times
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)
jung.locator: tail of ch. XIV, before ¶421 (pdf p281)

body: The Franciscan prophet-alchemist Johannes de Rupescissa (De consideratione quintae essentiae, ~1351) prescribed that the distillation of the fifth essence be endlessly iterated: "This is the 'circular distillation' [119] which Rupescissa says must be repeated a thousand times" (cw09ii; fn 120 cites the Lyons 1581 quinte essence, p. 56). Jung uses the thousand-fold repetition to mark the difference between a mere technical procedure and the circular opus: the iteration is the practical form of the ascent-descent cycle, the physical shadow of an individuation process that never completes in one pass.

occurrences.title: Stairs with mother and sister dream — young man (Zurich, ~1916)
occurrences.label: Stairs with mother and sister dream — young man
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I was going up a flight of stairs with my mother and sister. When we reached the top I was told that my sister was going to have a baby.
body: Jung's lesson in how NOT to interpret. A young man, months out of university, paralysed by the choice of a profession, dreams of climbing stairs with mother and sister; at the top, the sister is said to be expecting a baby. Jung first plays the Viennese: stairs = the sexual act by rhythmic climbing, the rest follows (¶540). Then the methodological turn: if stairs are symbolic, why not mother, sister, baby? (¶541). Analysed, the images turn prospective: mother = his long-neglected work; sister = "love for a woman"; stairs = "career — growing up, becoming great"; baby = "rebirth — becoming a new man" (¶542–546). Not infantile wish-fulfilment but "biological justice" (¶547); sexuality in dreams "a means of expression" (¶548).

occurrences.title: Ascent and descent in the Tabula Smaragdina (Emerald Tablet)
occurrences.label: Ascent and descent in the Tabula Smaragdina
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Arabic sources (Balinas tradition) -> Latin Europe (Ars chemica, Strasbourg 1566)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The Tabula Smaragdina — the shortest and most-cited text of the Hermetic corpus, known from Arabic sources (pseudo-Apollonius/Balinas) and transmitted to Latin Europe — carries in its "ascend... and again descend" formula the root scheme of the circular opus. Jung names it the locus classicus of the idea: "The basic idea of ascent and descent can be found in the Tabula Smaragdinaj [sic] and the stages of transformation have been depicted over and over again" (cw09ii ¶421). He treats the Tablet not as chemistry but as the textual seed of a picture-series tradition running to the Ripley Scrowle — "indirect attempts to apprehend the unconscious processes of individuation in the form of pictures."

occurrences.title: Watts, 'Love and Life' — the rocky path whose Love is always missing (London, 1884)
occurrences.label: Watts, 'Love and Life'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: It comes from a painting by Watts, 'Love and Life.' A female figure (Life) drags herself wearily along the rocky path, accompanied by the figure of Love.
body: G.F. Watts's allegorical painting: "A female figure (Life) drags herself wearily along the rocky path, accompanied by the figure of Love" (¶183). Prince's patient had studied it, and it becomes the recurring scaffold of her dreams 3, 5 and 6 — always the same dark rocky path, always "minus the figure of Love": in dream 5 the cats take Love's place, in dream 6 the warning figure ("Don't look, you will be blinded"). Jung exploits the structure diagnostically: what the waking picture carries as allegory, the dream empties of Love and refills with the affect actually due — a demonstration that the dream-image is a lived symbol, not a remembered picture.

occurrences.title: The ashvattha rooted in heaven — Bhagavadgita XV
occurrences.label: The ashvattha rooted in heaven — Bhagavadgita XV
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Krishna: "I am the Himalaya among mountains and the ashvattha among trees"; the Gita's fifteenth chapter sings the fig tree "Rooted in heaven, / Its branches earthward", its leaves songs of the Vedas, its buds the sense-objects, its roots "Reaching downward / Into this world, / The roots of man's action" (cw13 ¶412).

Jung: "The ashvattha (Ficus religiosa) pours down from above the drink of immortality, soma" (¶412); n.12 collects the nyagrodha of the Shatapatha-Brahm ana and Chhandogya Upanishad VIII, 5, 3, and Plato's "heavenly plant" (Timaeus 90A). The Gita's inverted tree is "a process of enlightenment... through knowledge" — the Veda as deliverance (cw13 ¶413).
Verbatim: There is a fig tree In ancient story, The giant Ashvattha, The everlasting, Rooted in heaven, Its branches earthward (cw13 ¶412)

occurrences.title: The feast of the ass — Dionysian orgy in Zarathustra
occurrences.label: The feast of the ass
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Jung refers forward to the later chapter in which the higher men worship the ass — "the feast of the ass is a Dionysian orgy."

His reading: it is the "hysterical" overcompensation of the ugliest man ("a sort of miserable Christian") — "In the cult of Dionysos it is even the main purpose to be drunk and unconscious, to end the psychological worry, to forget in the embrace of nature all the things that bother you as being too small." The god enters the mystes; individual worries vanish; "that is a way to deal with worries when they become too great" — the way of the alcoholic, the introvert's opposite.
Verbatim: "To get drunk with the figures of the unconscious is Dionysian; if you have read farther, you remember that the feast of the ass is a Dionysian orgy."

occurrences.title: Gnostic gem — she-ass suckling her foal, sign of Cancer, 'Dei filius'
occurrences.label: Gnostic gem — she-ass suckling her foal, sign…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: A Gnostic gem showing "a she-ass suckling her foal, surmounted by the sign of Cancer and the inscription 'D.N.-IHV.XPS.': Dominus noster Jesus Christus, to which is added, 'Dei filius'" (¶622). The Christ-child is figured as an ass's foal at the udder — Cancer, the zodiacal sign of birth/nursing, presiding.

Jung deploys it inside the Dionysus-Christ argument: Justin Martyr's indignant observation that the Christian legend's connections with Dionysus "are unmistakable (e.g., the miracle of the wine)"; the ass as steed of Silenus; the ass pertaining to the "second sun," Saturn, "the star of Israel and therefore to some extent identical with Yahweh" (¶622). The gem sits between the Palatine mock-crucifixion and the Dionysian vine of Hölderlin's "Man" — the god of the vine nursed by the beast of the second sun.
Verbatim: "There is a Gnostic gem showing a she-ass suckling her foal, surmounted by the sign of Cancer and the inscription 'D.N.-IHV.XPS.'" (¶622).

occurrences.title: The ass in the lion's skin — Aesop's fable, reproduced by a simulator (Zurich, 1903)
occurrences.label: The ass in the lion's skin
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Greece (Aesopic corpus); reproduced at the Zurich asylum
occurrences.quote: Then he took the skin and wrapped himself in it. He ran round roaring like a lion. Then the other animals tore him to pieces. The meaning is: Do not make yourself bigger than you are.
body: Aesop's fable: an ass finds a lion's skin, wraps himself in it, and roars until the other animals tear him to pieces. Jung uses its reproduction as an apperception test on I.G., the millhand simulating insanity — with a telling slip: the patient spontaneously adds that the ass found the skin "with a dead lion inside it," and draws the moral "Do not make yourself bigger than you are" (¶396). The resonance is exact and unremarked by Jung: the man dictating these lines is himself wearing a borrowed skin (catatonic madness), courting the fable's ending. The mask-that-devours is ours to infer, not his to claim here.

occurrences.title: Lucius the ass eats the roses of Isis (Apuleius, Metamorphoses)
occurrences.label: Lucius the ass eats the roses of Isis
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: He snatches at the roses and eats them, and from that moment he becomes spiritual, he becomes an initiate.
body: Jung closes the Yin-way session with the pagan novel: the youthful philosopher Lucius lives the natural sensual life of a Roman gentleman, is bewitched, and becomes an ass; used for abominable theatrical atrocities, he is miserable until the day the procession of the priests of Isis passes and the High Priest carries a wreath of roses: "He snatches at the roses and eats them, and from that moment he becomes spiritual, he becomes an initiate." Jung's point against moralizing: the book, "written by a pagan, not a Christian," shows the psychological necessity of the time — live the natural life entirely and you become an animal, and therefore need a spiritual initiation.

occurrences.title: The three-legged ass in the ocean, with the golden horn — Bundahish XIX
occurrences.label: The three-legged ass in the ocean…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The cosmological unicorn of Zoroastrianism: "it stands amid the wide-formed ocean, and its feet are three, eyes six, mouths nine, ears two, and horn one, body white, food spiritual, and it is righteous … The one horn is as it were of gold and hollow, and a thousand branch horns have grown upon it … With that horn it will vanquish and dissipate all the vile corruption due to the efforts of noxious creatures" (¶535). When it stales, "all the sea-water will become purified"; ambergris is its dung.

Jung: "as a cosmological being, it recalls the monstrous personifications of the prima materia (fig. 256) in Arabic alchemy" (¶536); the ass and the tree Gokard "both represent the power of life, procreation, and healing. This is a truly primitive equation: both are or have mana" (¶537); and "the ass is a daemon triunus, a chthonic trinity … identified with Mercurius, salt, and sulphur" (¶539). With Og, the re'em, Behemoth and Leviathan it personifies "the daemonic forces of nature" (¶547).

occurrences.title: The dogma of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin (1950)
occurrences.label: The dogma of the Assumption of the Blessed…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: The 1950 dogma that elevated "the Christian version of the mother archetype... to the rank of a dogmatic truth". Jung's ADDENDUM (asterisk-marked, ¶s unnumbered in this OCR): the Queen of Heaven has shed her Olympian qualities; "Isis and the Horus-child [are] iconological exemplars", and "the ascension of Semele, the originally mortal mother of Dionysus, likewise anticipates the Assumption" — her son being a dying and resurgent god, youngest of the Olympians; Semele herself an earth-goddess, as Mary is "the earth from which Christ was born".

Jung's reading: proclaimed in the hydrogen-bomb age, the Assumption is "a compensating symptom" — a heavenly figure split off from the chthonic realm taking counter-position to the titanic forces of the earth; understood symbolically it acknowledges matter ("utriusque capax") and anticipates the union of spirit and matter that alchemy had foreshadowed in the hieros gamos of opposites and science now approaches from the other side (synchronistic phenomena, Rhine).

occurrences.title: The Aten disk with ankh-bestowing hands at the ends of its rays (Amenhotep IV / Akhenaten)
occurrences.label: The Aten disk with ankh-bestowing hands…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: At the end of each ray emanating from the disk of the sun is a little hand bestowing the sign ankh upon the king and his family. Those would be the arms of the sun when it is spending, giving life.
body: Amenhotep IV introduced monotheism and took as his symbol the sun disk "rejoicing in its two horizons," the sun represented as the emanating deity bestowing life: at the end of each ray a little hand holds the crux ansata (ankh) out to the king and his family. Jung brings it in as the exact positive of the patient's black sun with its red outstretched arms: there the arms give life, here the darkened sun "does not emanate or create. On the contrary, darkness sucks in and swallows, so she is threatened by being drawn into those arms of death."

occurrences.title: Androgyne Atman creates the world and fire by rubbing — Brihadaranyaka Upanishad I.4
occurrences.label: Androgyne Atman creates the world and fire…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Atman, "as big as a man and woman joined together", divides in two; begets men, cattle, horses, goats, sheep, "everything down to the ants"; then rubs hands before mouth and brings forth fire from "the fire-hole (yoni)".
Jung's reading: "a monument of Indian literature which describes this conversion of libido into fire-making" (¶227) — the fire-hole (yoni) in the mouth, fire as child of the conjunctio.
Verbatim: Thereupon he rubbed thus [holding his hands before his mouth]. From his mouth, the fire-hole (yoni), and from his hands, he brought forth fire. (cw05 ¶227).

occurrences.title: 'This world in the beginning was brahman solely' — Vedanta (Bṛhadāraṇyaka I.4.10)
occurrences.label: This world in the beginning was brahman solely
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: This world in the beginning was brahman solely... I am brahman.
body: Jung quotes the Upanishadic opening — "This world in the beginning was brahman solely; since brahman was alone it was not unfolded. It knew itself only, and it realized: I am brahman. In this way it became the universe" — as the mark of a mentality that begins in sahasrāra, "speaks the language of the gods and thinks of man from above down." Were a Western lecture to open thus, "We would rightly be taken for mad, or at least it would be thought that we were holding a revival meeting."

occurrences.title: Kena Upanishad — 'know that as Brahman'
occurrences.label: Kena Upanishad — know that as Brahman
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'By whom willed and directed does the mind fly forth? By whom commanded does the first breath move?... The hearing of the ear, the thinking of the mind, the speaking of the speech... That which speech cannot express, by which speech is expressed... know that as Brahman' (¶348). Jung sets it beside Yajnavalkya's Brihadaranyaka definition of the inner controller (¶349) and Monoïmos' 'Seek him from out thyself' (¶347) — the purusha/atman teaching as the tradition through which alone the self becomes conscious (¶257). Parallels: atman-self-light-yajnavalkya-brihadaranyaka-700bc, monoimos-monad-iota-2c.

occurrences.title: 'Self is his light' — Yajnavalkya, Brihadaranyaka Upanishad
occurrences.label: Self is his light
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Self is his light. It is by the light of the self that a man rests, goes forth, does his work and returns.
body: The saying of the wise Yajnavalkya with which The Spirit Mercurius ends: "When all visible lights are extinguished one finds... the light of the self. 'What then is the light of man? Self is his light. It is by the light of the self that a man rests, goes forth, does his work and returns.'"

Jung sets it beside Augustine's cognitio matutina and the days of creation: "Thus, with Augustine, the first day of creation begins with self-knowledge, cognitio sui ipsius, by which is meant a knowledge not of the ego but of the self, that objective phenomenon of which the ego is the subject" (¶301). His footnote finds here the source of the lapis designation "filius unius diei" (cf. Mysterium Coniunctionis).

occurrences.title: Attis castrates himself beneath the pine — Phrygian cult
occurrences.label: Attis castrates himself beneath the pine
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Attis, son and lover of Cybele, wearing the pileus of Men, Mithras and the dadophors; driven mad by his mother he mutilates himself under a pine-tree and is hanged there in effigy (fig. 42). Fig. 20: Cybele and Attis, Roman coin.

Jung's reading: "incest leads logically to ritual castration in the Attis-Cybele cult" (¶299); "he did so because the tree has a maternal significance" (¶321); the self-castration as expiation of the incestuous longing.
Verbatim: Hence when Attis castrates himself under a pine-tree, he did so because the tree has a maternal significance. (cw05 ¶321).

occurrences.title: Attis initiates fed with milk for eight days (Rome)
occurrences.label: Attis initiates fed with milk for eight days
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Rome (Attis cult; Vatican area over the old taurobolium ground)

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: ...after the baptism people were fed with milk for eight days as if they were little babies, and they got a new name.
body: After the baptismal rite in the cult of Attis, initiates were "fed with milk for eight days as if they were little babies, and they got a new name" — rebirth as literal re-infancy. Jung strings the cult into his svādhiṣṭhāna argument: Attis' grottos like the Mithraic spelaeum; Christ's Bethlehem birthplace said to have been an Attis sanctuary; St Peter's built where the taurobolia (blood baptisms) took place; the Attis priests' title Papas inherited by the pope — "showing the continuity of true history."

occurrences.title: Heliopolitan cosmogony — Atum unites with his shadow (self-fertilization)
occurrences.label: Heliopolitan cosmogony
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'I, even I, had union with my clenched hand, I joined myself in an embrace with my shadow, I poured seed into my mouth, my own; I sent forth issue in the form of Shu, I sent forth moisture in the form of Tefnut' (¶322). Jung cites this beside Amen as Ka-mutef, 'husband of his mother', and the Indian Prajapati who has intercourse with his own split-off feminine half — the world-creator as self-fertilizing hermaphrodite. In the Interrogationes vision world-creation gives place to spiritual renewal: the seed is the logos spermatikos, 'a living water springing up into eternal life' (¶323).

occurrences.title: Augustine — the two fishes of the feeding of the five thousand
occurrences.label: Augustine — the two fishes of the feeding…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Augustine interprets the two miraculous fishes as 'the kingly and the priestly person or power, because, like fishes surviving the tempests of the sea, they outlast the turbulence of the multitude'; both are united in Christ, king and priest after the order of Melchisedek (¶228). Jung uses the exegesis to show that 'the fishes were regarded as ruling powers', though the Cathar two fishes cannot be read uniformly as Christ — they are Satanael and Christ, the yoked pair of the Pisces-aeon (¶229). Parallels: cathar-two-fishes-osob-revelation-1111, lambspringk-two-reversed-fishes-1678.

occurrences.title: Aurora consurgens: Sapientia and the alchemical reading of scripture
occurrences.label: Aurora consurgens — Sapientia…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Rheinau (Codex Rhenoviensis, Zurich) / Paris (Codex Parisinus Latinus 14006)
occurrences.quote: I am the only daughter of the wise, utterly unknown to the foolish.
body: The Aurora consurgens opens with the Wisdom of Solomon and Proverbs and identifies alchemy with the Sapientia Dei: Sapientia is the Queen of the South who came from the east "like the rising dawn." Its seven parables run scripture into the opus — the Song of Songs' bridegroom is the filius philosophorum (Christ); the "second Adam, who is called the philosophic man," enters eternity from pure elements; Senior's "One thing that never dieth" carries the lapis into the Creed's resurrection of the flesh.

Jung dates it to the first half of the fourteenth century (latest author quoted: Albertus Magnus), the author a cleric who knows the Vulgate by heart. The 1593 printer Waldkirch suppressed Part I for profaning the incarnation "by turning it into the mystery of the lapis."

occurrences.title: The Ave Praeclara and Albertus Magnus' dream of the Virgin
occurrences.label: The Ave Praeclara and Albertus Magnus' dream…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Osnabrück Register of Santa Maria (via Rémy de Gourmont)
occurrences.yearDisplay: Middle Ages (hymn ascribed to Albertus Magnus)
occurrences.quote: Fac … anguem aeneum in cruce speculari
body: The hymn Ave Praeclara — "Hail, clear-shining star of the sea, Mary, divinely born for the enlightenment of the nations" — weaving the sweet stream from the rock, the sea-bathed loins, the crucified brazen serpent to be gazed upon, and the Virgin made mother "by the sacred fire and the Father's word, which thou didst bear like the Burning Bush."

Rémy de Gourmont's legend from the Osnabrück Register: a virgin in royal raiment appeared to Albertus Magnus in a dream and reproached him for ingratitude to Mary — whereupon he composed the hymn. Jung: "An alchemist would find it full of alluring allusions"; Melchior Cibinensis made the Ave Praeclara the "testament of the art," in which "the whole chemical art is figuratively concealed."

occurrences.title: Axiom of Maria Prophetissa: 'One becomes two, two becomes three, and out of the third comes the one as the fourth'
occurrences.label: Axiom of Maria Prophetissa
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Maria Prophetissa's saying, "One becomes two, two becomes three, and out of the third comes the one as the fourth" — for Jung "one of the central axioms of alchemy… which runs like a leitmotiv throughout almost the whole of the lifetime of alchemy, extending over more than seventeen centuries" (cw12 ¶26).

In the even numbers "which signify the feminine principle, earth, the regions under the earth, and evil itself" are interpolated between the uneven numbers of Christian dogma. At ¶31 the axiom returns as τὸ ἕν τέταρτον: the inferior function, becoming conscious, "brings up among others the archetype of the self as well."

occurrences.title: Axiom of Democritus — 'Nature rejoices in nature'
occurrences.label: Axiom of Democritus — Nature rejoices in nature
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~2nd-1st c. BC (revealed to Democritus by Ostanes, per Synesius)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The axiom — 'Nature rejoices in nature; nature subdues nature; nature rules over nature' — was, according to the story, revealed to Democritus by his deceased teacher Ostanes (¶244 n.26). Dorn quotes it: 'nature seeks after a nature like to itself, and rejoices in its own nature; if it is joined to another, the work of nature is destroyed' (¶244). For Jung it grounds the magnes-magnesia pair and the whole like-cures-like logic of the opus — the self as the like that alone can unite the opposites. Parallels: axiom-maria-one-becomes-four, morienus-thing-extracted-from-thee-7c.

occurrences.title: Apparition of the Aztec — Miss Miller
occurrences.label: Apparition of the Aztec — Miss Miller
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: The continuing hypnagogic vision: "Suddenly, the apparition of an Aztec, complete in every detail: hand open, with large fingers, head in profile, armoured, with a head-dress resembling the plumed crests of the American Indians."

Jung's reading: confirmation "that a masculine figure was hidden in the Sphinx" (¶266-267); the personification of the masculine component of the woman's personality — later named the animus (¶267); "appears with all its 'heroic' qualities", the demon lover whose exalted spirituality forecloses any mortal marriage (¶273); eagle-feather crest = crown = sun-rays (¶268).

Verbatim: Suddenly, the apparition of an Aztec, complete in every detail: hand open, with large fingers, head in profile, armoured, with a head-dress resembling the plumed crests of the American Indians, etc. (cw05 ¶266).

occurrences.title: Aztec temple-pyramid sacrifice — the man who climbs as the rising sun
occurrences.label: Aztec temple-pyramid sacrifice
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
jung.locator: Jaffé's paper on the pyramid dream (pdf p306)

occurrences.quote: Once he reached the top, however, he was sacrificed: the sun begins to set.
body: A man slowly climbs the steps of a temple pyramid, symbolizing the slow rise of the sun; at the top he is sacrificed — "the sun begins to set." Jaffé sets this beside the suffering of the heroes in the triple glass house of the Visio Arislei: how much pain and sacrifice of light-day consciousness the transformation at the summit costs. The apex is both glorification (Ka, Atum) and death.

occurrences.title: Adam's helpmeet and Eve as 'salutary counter-institution' — Franz von Baader
occurrences.label: Adam's helpmeet and Eve as 'salutary…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: God, recognizing this possibility, thereupon created Eve as a 'salutary counter-institution.
body: Under Boehme's influence, Baader asserted that God gave Adam a helpmeet through whom Adam "was to have brought forth without an external woman," as Mary did without a man. Adam's fall into bestial copulation endangered his divine androgyny, so God created Eve as a "salutary counter-institution [rettende Gegenanstalt]" to prevent a deeper descent into animal nature. The androgyny departed from Adam but was preserved in Eve as the "woman's seed."
Jung at cw14 ¶581: "he who was born in the Virgin Mary is the same who had to depart from Adam on account of his fall."

occurrences.title: The mistletoe that killed Baldur
occurrences.label: The mistletoe that killed Baldur
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: All things pledge not to harm Baldur save the mistletoe, "too young" to be asked; Loki's dart of mistletoe kills him.

Jung's reading: the mistletoe as "child of the tree" — "That which grows on the tree is the child (pl. XXXIX), or oneself in renewed and rejuvenated form; and that is precisely what one cannot have, because the incest prohibition forbids it" (¶392); Baldur the puer aeternus, "only a dream of the mother", taken back into her.
Verbatim: The graceful Baldur is such a figure. This type is granted only a fleeting existence, because he is never anything but an anticipation of something desired and hoped for. (cw05 ¶392).

image.title: Baldr's Death by Frølich

occurrences.title: The bamboo-belt of Mount Elgon: abode of the spirits
occurrences.label: The bamboo-belt of Mount Elgon
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: was supposed to be the abode of the spirits.
body: Jung's ethnographic proof that the land of the dead is projected onto real places: "in the part of Africa that I saw, an especially dense growth of bamboos in the forest, the so-called bamboo-belt on Mount Elgon, was supposed to be the abode of the spirits." His own traversal gives the phenomenology: wind only over the treetops, moss and dead leaves deadening footsteps, no birds, "a sort of greenish darkness as if one were under water. The natives were scared to death of the ghosts and tried all sorts of tricks to escape being forced to go into that part of the wood."
Set beside Swiss glaciers haunted by the dead as the comparative row for Nietzsche's "silent isle": the unconscious, projected, is a landscape.

occurrences.title: Baptism of the Japanese ivory figure — the youth's second dream (Zurich, c.1920s)
occurrences.label: Baptism of the Japanese ivory figure
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: with the Jews circumcision is a sort of baptism.
body: Second dream, told before a consultation in which the first was never mentioned: in a great Gothic cathedral a priest stands at the altar; the dreamer and his friend (his lover, same fraternity) hold "a little Japanese ivory figure" that is to be baptized; an elderly woman — a friend of his mother's, "like a mother to me" — takes the fraternity ring from the friend's finger and puts it on her own; organ music peals.

Jung's reading: the figure is "a tiny, grotesque little manikin that reminded me of the male organ" (¶177) — circumcision as baptism (¶179), the homosexual tie cut and a heterosexual step beyond the mother substituted (¶180). The music confirms progression, not regression (¶181). Both dreams are "astonishing anticipations" that compensate the patient's conscious resistance (¶182).

occurrences.title: The baptism of the penguins (Anatole France, L'Ile des Pingouins)
occurrences.label: The baptism of the penguins
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: St. Mael said that if the sacraments were exact, if the rite had been performed in the proper way, it must give souls to the birds
body: St Mael baptizes the penguins; if the rite was exact, it must give the birds souls. When the baptized went on sinning, the flaw was sought in the form; some received baptism twice; the stubborn cases were finally declared "children of Satan, meant for eternal baking in hell, and that closed the thing."

Jung quotes the story to show "how strongly mankind believed in the efficiency of the invocation by the true name" — the sacraments are "magic devices... of forcing the grace of God" — and that such belief, however nonsensical, "represents a psychological fact". He had already used it on 23 Jan 1929 and 19 Feb 1930 (c01, c04).

occurrences.title: Easter Vigil: the hydor theion fertilized by the candle in the uterus of the Church
occurrences.label: Easter Vigil — the hydor theion fertilized…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Jung's Christian parallel to the hydor theion of the alchemists: the baptismal water "is made in a very similar way. In a complicated ritual, the baptismal water is composed of exorcized water, exorcized salt, oleum unctionis (the consecration oil), and Chrisam, the oil of anointment". "The hydor theion, which had been prepared in advance, is fertilized by the immersion of a candle, so that it may give birth again to man in the uterus of the Church. It is an extremely meaningful rite, a kind of hierosgamos" (p219).

"It is one of those secrets that constitute the power of the Catholic Church over the unconscious." The consecration is performed on the eve of Holy Saturday; instructions in the Missale Romanum. The rite parallels Zosimos' divine water, "the means to make incomplete bodies complete."

occurrences.title: Barabbas — the yearly released criminal of the old Babylonian custom
occurrences.label: Barabbas — the yearly released criminal…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: old Babylonian custom (Jung, 1934: 'to a great extent legend')
body: "You remember the prisoner Barabbas was released instead of Christ when he was taken to be crucified, which was according to an old custom in Babylon that each year one criminal was released and given the freedom of the city; he could steal what he pleased but he must clear out before sunset... if caught within the city walls he would be put to death".

Jung: "this was a remnant of the old myth of the god king from the time when they had a new king every year; if the year was good, he was confirmed as a god king, and if the year was bad he was put to death. He was supposed to emanate the mana quality of fertility." The king as superior man "was represented on the ancient monuments as several times bigger and taller than his subjects" — whence the pyramid, "a perfect mathematical form," for his burial mound.

occurrences.title: Barbelo — the upper mother whose name is read 'in the four there is God' (Irenaeus)
occurrences.label: Barbelo — the upper mother…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: Her name is interpreted as 'in the four there is God.
body: In the quaternity survey: "in Irenaeus we find the idea of the upper mother (Anometer), the Barbelo. She is the female appearance of the deity. Her name is interpreted as 'in the four there is God.'" Cited with the Gnostic Anthropos (primordial man as city with four gates, the Autogenes, surrounded by two parental couples) and the tetrapeza (Son of God on a platform of four pillars = the four Gospels) as Gnostic quattro-structures against which Jung sets his thesis: quaternity is pagan, older than Christianity, while the dogma is the Trinity.

occurrences.title: Lama's recitation of the Bardo Thödol over the corpse — Tibet
occurrences.label: Lama's recitation of the Bardo Thödol…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: terma tradition (~14th c. onward), still practised

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)
Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: The Bardo Thödol is not a burial ceremonial but a set of instructions for the dead: "The text of the Bardo Thödol is recited by the lama in the presence of the corpse" (cw11 ¶831). The recitation guides the dead man through the forty-nine-day bardo between death and rebirth.

Jung's reading: the instruction is "at bottom, nothing less than an initiation of the dead into the Bardo life, just as the initiation of the living was a preparation for the Beyond" (¶841) — the only living Western analogue being analysis of the unconscious (¶842). The cult of the dead rests psychologically on "the need of the living to do something for the departed" (¶855); these instructions are "the highest application of spiritual effort on behalf of the departed" (¶855).

occurrences.title: 'Allegoria sanctissimae trinitatis et lapidis philosophici' — Basilius Valentinus
occurrences.label: Allegoria sanctissimae trinitatis et lapidis…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: So, too, is the gold without flaw … yet, for the sake of its imperfect and sick brothers and sisters, it dies and rises again, glorious and redeemed.
body: From the 1700 complete edition of the pseudonymous Basilius Valentinus (Johann Thölde of Frankenhausen, c. 1600, is the likely author; Maier's Symbola aureae mensae of 1617 already cites the texts with the remark "Rather than become notorious he preferred to remain unknown to everyone"): the Father begets the Son, God and man, who needs no death yet dies freely for his brothers and sisters; so too the gold, "without flaw … for the sake of its imperfect and sick brothers and sisters, dies and rises again." The Spiritus Solis is Mercurius corporis; the two together are Mercurius duplicatus; God the Son is the homo glorificatus, "like our glorified and fixed gold, the lapis philosophorum; wherefore this lapis is also called trinus."
The author is strongly Paracelsian — Archaeus, astral and elemental spirits.

occurrences.title: Batak ancestral-souls wand (Miss de Witt's specimen)
occurrences.label: Batak ancestral-souls wand
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Miss de Witt's wand: "These wands usually consist of a series of figures standing on top of each other, the legend being that they are ancestral souls which derive from the primordial incest between brother and sister." Source: Warneck, Die Religion der Batak (1909), with the doctrine of ghosts, magic and tondi — "their word for mana."

The tribal teaching folded in: a father dying while the son is a boy leaves a "small" ancestral soul (black hen; a black pig if he was good — good people become dangerous dead); when the son has children he rises to grandfather, "a duke in ghostland" (a bull). Showing the wand "touches upon a living feeling... of the existence of that historical psychological tradition within... the collective unconscious must vibrate, the archetypes must be active" — the sorcerer's instrument for constellating the ancestors.

occurrences.title: Dea arcto — bear goddess of Gallic-Roman Berne (Historical Museum)
occurrences.label: Dea arcto — bear goddess of Gallic-Roman Berne
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Berne, Historical Museum (bear cult of Roman-period Berne; the Artio of Muri group)
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~2nd–3rd c. CE (Gallic-Roman; Jung: 'long before the Berne Zofingia')

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar
Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: In the Historical Museum you can see a dea arcto.... The believers of Artemis call themselves arktoi, the bears. The bear represents the female instinctual world.
body: Jung's exhibit of a totem surviving in civic heraldry: "the Swiss city Bern, where the cantonal coat-of-arms carries a bear and they still keep bears in a pit there — their totem animal; this used to be explained as a bad etymological joke, bear for Bern, but when they excavated the old Roman settlement nearby, they found a temple with a perfectly preserved figure of a Celtic goddess surrounded by bears" (p348). The point of the pair (with the Carthage crescent-star tombstones): modern emblems sit on buried cult-strata, and the dream-interpreter needs that archaeology — "it gives one a most precious impression of the universality of the human mind, our own little minds being reproductions of archetypal patterns" (p348).

Returning to the same artifact in the tiger-dream discussion, asked why the devouring, instinctual force should be feminine, Jung points to the animals in which "the female instinctual world" appears — felines, snakes, and bears: "In Switzerland, after all, we had a bear goddess. In the Historical Museum you can see a dea arcto. Long before the Berne Zofingia, there was a Gallic-Roman bear cult in Berne. The believers of Artemis call themselves arktoi, the bears." The bear-goddess artifact (conventionally the Artio of Muri, kept in Berne) is his evidence that the "devouring feminine" of the tiger dream has a local, pre-Christian cultic pedigree; Artemis's votaries at Brauron were the arktoi, the little bears.

occurrences.title: 'I belonged to the Bear Totem' — Jung's ascription at the Pueblo (New Mexico, 1925)
occurrences.label: I belonged to the Bear Totem
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: The Pueblo Indians declared in a matter-of-fact way that I belonged to the Bear Totem—in other words, that I was a bear—because I did not come down a ladder standing up like a man, but bunched up on all fours like a bear.
body: The Pueblo Indians told Jung, matter-of-factly, that he belonged to the Bear Totem — "in other words, that I was a bear — because I did not come down a ladder standing up like a man, but bunched up on all fours like a bear" (¶132).

His reading: the bush-soul logic concretizes what Europe keeps as metaphor. "If anyone in Europe said I had a bearish nature this would amount to the same thing, but with a rather different shade of meaning" — with the primitive "the poison of moral judgment is absent. He is too naturalistic for that" (¶132). The episode is his exhibit that primitive attribution is concrete identity, not rhetoric: to say leopard-woman, bear-man, is to state where a piece of the psyche lives.

occurrences.title: 'Unless ye slay me, your understanding will not be perfect' — Dicta Belini
occurrences.label: Unless ye slay me, your understanding will not…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~11th–12th c. (Dicta Belini; source likely Artefius' Harranite Clavis maioris sapientiae)
occurrences.quote: unless ye slay me, ye cannot be called sages
body: The Dicta Belini's dying speech: "I announce therefore to all you sages, that unless ye slay me, ye cannot be called sages. But if ye slay me, your understanding will be perfect, and it increases in my sister the moon according to the degree of our wisdom, and not with another of my servants, even if ye know my secret" (¶164). The Rosarium's variant ("Unless ye slay me, your understanding will not be perfect, and in my sister the moon the degree of your wisdom increases") is one of its "approximate quotations."

Jung untangles the speaker — "the father-son, whose mother is the son's sister-wife," Sol as reborn father — and reads "unless ye slay me" as "the slaying of the dragon, the mortificatio of the first, dangerous, poisonous stage of the anima (= Mercurius), freed from her imprisonment in the prima materia" (¶168). Sol's stages — dragon, lion, eagle, hermaphrodite — are "a new degree of insight, wisdom, and initiation, just as the Mithraic eagles, lions, and sun-messengers signify grades of initiation."

occurrences.title: The two kinds of dreams — Elgonyi dream-doctrine, Mount Elgon
occurrences.label: The two kinds of dreams
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: there are two kinds of dreams: the ordinary dream of the little man, and the ‘big vision’ that only the great man has
body: The Elgonyi of the Elgon forests taught Jung that there are two kinds of dreams: the ordinary dream of the little man, and the "big vision" that only the great man has — the medicine-man or chief. Little dreams are of no account; but a man who has a "big dream" summons the whole tribe to hear it, "on the psychologically correct assumption that it is of general significance" (¶277).

Jung's reading: the distinguishing criterion is an instinctive feeling of significance that impels communication — the same "collective dream" feeling found in Europe, where such a dream "springs from a conflict of relationship and must therefore be built into our conscious relations, because it compensates these" (¶277). The Elgonyi doctrine is his cleanest ethnographic witness that the unconscious produces contents "valid not only for the person concerned, but for others as well" (¶275).

occurrences.title: The boy who dreamt out his father's erotic-religious problem
occurrences.label: The boy who dreamt out his father's…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: early practice; retold in lecture publ. 1928
body: Among the "big dreams" of early childhood Jung long explained through parental psychology was the case of a boy who "dreamt out the whole erotic and religious problem of his father." The father remembered no dreams at all, so for a time Jung analysed the father through the eight-year-old son's dreams — until the father began to dream himself, "and the dreams of the child stopped."

Jung's later conclusion (the passage the CW editors flag as authorially revised): the peculiar dreams of small children are genuine, "since they contain archetypes which are the cause of their apparently adult character" (¶106). Participation-mystique channelled into dream content.
Quote. "There was the case of a boy who dreamt out the whole erotic and religious problem of his father."

occurrences.title: 'I am a crane' — B.St.'s Ibycus identification (Burghölzli, ~1905)
occurrences.label: I am a crane' — B.St.'s Ibycus identification
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: He who is free of guilt,' etc. is a well-known quotation from The Cranes of Ibycus. The patient therefore identifies herself outright with 'crane.
body: Neologism in the B.St. analysis: "I am a Switzerland... I am a crane — Switzerland cannot be shut up." Jung unpacks the condensation: the tertium comparationis is "free" — Switzerland cannot be imprisoned, and neither can she; and the supporting quotation, "He who is free of guilt and sin / Preserves the child's pure soul within," is from Schiller's Die Kraniche des Ibycus, itself built on the Greek tale of the cranes that betray a murderer. "The patient therefore identifies herself outright with 'crane'" (¶254) — the innocent soul under accusation takes wing as the bird that witnesses guilt.

occurrences.title: The Cranes of Ibycus — murderers betrayed by a crane-flight
occurrences.label: The Cranes of Ibycus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Greek tale of Ibycus (6th c. BCE); Schiller's poem 1798

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: The editors' footnote to Jung's bird-flock case: the Greek poet Ibycus, murdered by robbers, called on a passing flight of cranes as witnesses; later, seeing cranes over the marketplace, the murderers cried out and betrayed themselves. Schiller made the story a ballad in 1798. The footnote adds: "when a flock of chattering magpies settles on a house it is supposed to mean death... Cf. also the significance of auguries."

Jung's reading: the Ibycus story is the literary specimen of the mantic significance of bird-flocks that his clinical case instantiates — "The flock of birds has, as such, a traditional mantic significance" (¶850). The bird appears where the unconscious already "knows" of a death: an archetypal symbolism at work outside dream-space.

occurrences.title: Eagle over the concentration camp — dream of 'Y' (The Philosophical Tree, print 342–47)
occurrences.label: Eagle over the concentration camp — dream of 'Y'
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: The Philosophical Tree, final dream series — ¶ pin tbd (print 342–47)

body: The closing clinical example of "The Philosophical Tree": an eagle circles over Y's internment/concentration camp and the dreamer thinks of shooting it down from a rocket-propelled aircraft. Jung reads the eagle — the "king of the air", here a war-machine thought — as the spirit-bird (birds as "winged thoughts", print 266; eagle at 343n, 347; "eagle 'eye', 344") that must be caught rather than shot, the same captura spiritus the alchemists staged in their bird-flocks and flasks.
Verbatim: EXAMPLE: An eagle circles over Y's concentration camp; he thinks of shooting it from a rocket-propelled aircraft, 342-47.

occurrences.title: Flocks of birds at the deaths of grandmother, mother, and husband (Switzerland)
occurrences.label: Flocks of birds at the deaths…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Switzerland (the wife's family home; husband's death-route from the specialist)

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: The wife of a patient of about fifty told Jung that at the deaths of her mother and her grandmother birds had gathered outside the windows of the death-chamber. When the husband's neurosis cleared but apparent heart symptoms developed, Jung sent him to a specialist, who found nothing. On the way home, medical report in pocket, the patient collapsed dying in the street — while a whole flock of birds alighted on the couple's house, and the wife, remembering the earlier deaths, feared the worst (¶845).

Jung's reading: the third coincidence was verifiable only when the dying man was brought home (¶851). The interpretation as omen rests on the earlier events; the mantic tradition confirms it — "The flock of birds has, as such, a traditional mantic significance" (¶850), grounded in the Babylonian "feather dress" of the dead and the Egyptian ba-bird (¶845).

occurrences.title: Wingless bird of Hermes with bitterness in its throat — Rosinus ad Sarratantam
occurrences.label: Wingless bird of Hermes with bitterness…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The wingless bird of Hermes: 'Take the stone that is black, white, red, and yellow, and is a wonderful bird that flies without wings in the blackness of the night and the brightness of the day: in the bitterness that is in its throat the colouring will be found' (Rosinus ad Sarratantam, quoted cw14 ¶245). Jung uses it to bridge the salt/amaritudo chapter: the bird is a parallel of salt because salt is a spirit, a volatile substance 'which the alchemists were wont to conceive as a bird' (¶246); its throat-bitterness is the origin of the colours (¶333). The colour sequence black-red-gold-white anticipates the Hermas beast and the Ortus.

occurrences.title: Ibis 'dear to Hermes, the father of words' — Aelian, De natura animalium
occurrences.label: Ibis 'dear to Hermes, the father of words'
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Aelian (De natura animalium) reports the ibis 'dear to Hermes, the father of words, since in its form it resembles the nature of the Logos; for its blackness and swift flight could be compared to the silent and introverted Logos, but its whiteness to the Logos already uttered and heard, which is the servant and messenger of the inner word' (quoted cw14 ¶250). Jung cites it for the origin and meaning of the avis Hermetis: the black-to-white moulting of the bird enacts nigredo to albedo, the passage of the inner word into speech — the same sequence the salt-bird of Rosinus carries in its throat.

occurrences.title: Understanding the language of birds (patient: anonymous, Zürich)
occurrences.label: Understanding the language of birds
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: case-index [26], ref. book p402 ≈ pdf p369 (harvested from index, pdf p580)

body: A patient "understood the language of birds" (case [26], book p402n) — the archaic gift of decoding the spirit's language, filed by the index beside the schizophrenic's star-relation. Jung elsewhere ties understanding's etymology to inner events ("understand," etymology, 440); the birds speak what the dreamer cannot yet.
Verbatim (case-index): "Patient who understood the language of birds. — 402n"

occurrences.title: Dream: cutting the claws of the mole and the canary — wild vs domesticated function
occurrences.label: Dream — wild vs domesticated function
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Someone said the mole goes deep down into the earth. I took the canary out of its cage. It did not fly away. I had expected that it would.
body: She cuts the claws of a mole and a canary, fearing she has cut too short; someone says the mole goes deep into the earth; released from its cage, the canary does not fly away. Jung's pair-symbolics: the bird = thought/spirit ("Everything that pertains to thought or spirit is air. The word spiritus means breath. Animus, mind, means wind. Pneuma means wind and spirit", p118); the mole with snakes, mice and aquatic animals = "sexuality and all sorts of earthly desires or instincts" (p118). Her mistake: handling the wild function like the caged one. The canary is her domesticated thinking — "it remains within reach, it is sterilized by domestication. Such birds never soar away, they never function like Noah's dove or Wotan's raven" (p121). The dream's verdict: "she can expect nothing from her mind. But she can hope for something to come from her wild function" (p121) — the descent into the abdominal seat of the inferior function, located on the body-center ladder (abdomen-heart-head, pp119-120) that shadows the chakra system.

occurrences.title: 'The bird of Hermes which never rests' — Novum lumen chemicum
occurrences.label: The bird of Hermes which never rests
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: These are the epithets of the bird of Hermes, which never rests.
body: The anonymous author exclaims: "O our heaven! O our water and our Mercurius! O dead head or dregs of our sea!... And these are the epithets of the bird of Hermes, which never rests." And: "the head of the art is the raven, who flies without wings in the blackness of the night and the brightness of the day."

Jung at cw14 ¶727: the raven as name of the nigredo — a restless, unsleeping spirit, "our aerial and volatile stone," at once heaven and scum of the sea; in Christian tradition the raven is an allegory of the devil, yet the night raven (nycticorax) is an allegory of Christ: the ambivalence of the primitive archetypal form of spirit.

occurrences.title: Two birds, friends, in one tree — Rig Veda I.164
occurrences.label: Two birds, friends, in one tree — Rig Veda I.164
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: One of them eats the sweet berry, the other looks down only composedly.
body: "Two closely united friends both embrace one and the same tree. One of them eats the sweet berry, the other looks down only composedly" — quoted by Jung to illustrate the fruit of yoga-detachment reached through deepening analysis: consciousness "removed to a sphere of objectlessness," watching while its counterpart lives. The verse is the Vedic original of the two-birds image later carried by the muṇḍaka and śvetāśvatara Upanishads.

occurrences.title: The bird that built its nest beside him, sitting on golden eggs
occurrences.label: The bird that built its nest…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Zarathustra I.5 'On the Joys and Passions' (1883)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: But that bird built its nest beside me: therefore, I love and cherish it-now sitteth it beside me on its golden eggs.
body: Zarathustra's earthly virtue nests in him as a bird on golden eggs. With the seminar's help Jung reads it through the Holy Ghost's motherly quality (Mrs. Sigg), the hamsa (Mrs. Fierz), rebirth, and gold as 'the value beyond time' — 'this is a symbol of the self... still enveloped by the symbol of the wise old man, in this case by the wise old bird, the hamsa.' Parallels: hamsa-steady-flame-anahata-shat-cakra-nirupana-16c · markandeya-god-body-baby-hamsa-india.

occurrences.title: Dream of the spirit-birds drowned by the carnival rattle — woman patient
occurrences.label: Dream of the spirit-birds drowned…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: So we never hear what they say.
body: A patient who "tried in her way to hear the spirit" could never remember a dream that often repeated itself — until one night she did. She stands in a beautiful sunlit park, birds singing, and feels the moment approaching when she will understand what they sing. "Then suddenly she found herself holding one of those noisy instruments children have at carnival time, and she was making such an awful noise with it that she could not hear what the spirit birds were singing."

Jung's gloss doubles as a definition of the spirit's humility: "She preferred to make her own noise, for what the birds say is so humble that we have to assert ourselves. So we never hear what they say". The ego's rattle against the still, small voice — set beside Nietzsche, who speaks exaggeratedly "in order that the voices of the soul should not be heard".

occurrences.title: Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane — the impossible condition (Macbeth IV.i)
occurrences.label: Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: like the wood coming to Dunsinane in Macbeth; or the coming of a man not born of woman; or water running up hill
body: Schmitz names the motif — "one cannot have a thing without an impossible condition attached, as the wood coming in Macbeth" — and Jung generalizes: "Such an initial condition is often found in prophecies or fairy tales, like the wood coming to Dunsinane in Macbeth; or the coming of a man not born of woman; or water running up hill — perfectly impossible conditions like those in this dream."

The coffee-export-from-sterile-North-Africa of dream 27 belongs to the row: the Redeemer "comes from a place where one never would expect it", and the dream must shock the rationalist into expecting the exception.

occurrences.title: The black animus with the white back — the red bird and the severed head (Visions, 24 Jan. 1934)
occurrences.label: The black animus with the white back
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "The man caught up with me. He had become black." — "He walked ahead of me. I saw that his back was white and upon his back I saw the face of a man looking up into the sky at a white bird" (pp1319-1320). The white bird is "the dove, the Holy Ghost, the pure white thought"; the front is a "Janus-faced monster" — the repressed white man concealed behind the Negro animus.

On the white back a living picture: "A red and mangled bird tore at his chest but he did not see it" — the birds that infested her New York skyscrapers, "thoughts or desires, or just hopes that were injured by the clash with her New York world". Then "The red mangled bird gnawed at the throat of the man until his head fell off. A new head grew. This time the head looked down and saw the red bird. The man seized the bird and killed it" — the unconscious attempt to undo the shock. Her parenthetical repetitions ("This was the picture that I saw") betray the veil of the personal unconscious drawn across perception (pp1321-1322).

occurrences.title: The 'dirty black Brazilian' — Spinoza's hypnopompic vision (Netherlands, ~1660s)
occurrences.label: The 'dirty black Brazilian'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Spinoza had a hypnopompic vision of a 'nigrum et scabiosum Brasilianum' (a dirty black Brazilian)
body: Waking one morning, Spinoza saw before him a "nigrum et scabiosum Brasilianum" — a dirty, scurvy-marked black Brazilian — whom he knew to be a phantom because the man had been his frightening servant years before in Amsterdam. Jung cites it in a footnote cluster of hypnagogic/hypnopompic apparitions (with Cardan's bed-foot images and Goethe's Ottilie) during the dissertation's discussion of visionary states. The case is the earliest dated dark-humanoid apparition in the corpus: a threatening colonial Other surfacing at the limen of sleep, remembered from waking life. The tie to shadow (the repressed, "scabious" servant of the rationalist philosopher) is our inference.

occurrences.title: The black city, the white column and the man from the green silence of the deep sea (Visions, 16 Mar 1932)
occurrences.label: The black city, the white column…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: \"Who are you?\" I asked him. He answered: \"I am he who lives in the green silence of the deep sea.\
body: A road paved with black stones runs beside a stream of molten metal to the black city with many flags - "the shadow of the individual monad... the shadow of the white city" in infernal heat. A creature with a human body and two animal heads opens the door - "a sort of devil, the chthonic element," possibly one of the two-headed figures "chiefly on Gnostic amulets" (King, The Gnostics and Their Remains). In the hell-garden stands a tall white column where the pool was: "A phallic symbol instead of the pool, the mother symbol... the pool meant a descent... and the column would be an ascent"; the whole structure is the Tai-gi-tu reversed - "a white city with a black pool, and now a black city with a white column."

A small crowned man with trident and seaweed - "a minor sort of Neptune," the dwarfish water-demon animus - prophesies: "By that column you shall lose yourself." He comes from the water sphere now that she has accepted fire; the Yang she refused to receive as Yin now leads and torments her (cf. kun-refused-proposal-case-zurich-1932).

occurrences.title: The black figure in the wish-fulfilling prison delirium — Godwina F. (Zurich, 1902)
occurrences.label: The black figure in the wish-fulfilling prison…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich asylum (Burghölzli); delirium began in a prison cell
occurrences.quote: She dreamt that she received the expected 10,000 marks and put them on the table; a black figure suddenly comes in and gives her a violent fright; she leaps up; the hallucinations vanish, leaving behind them the delusions of being robbed, poisoned, etc.
body: Godwina F., a German woman arrested on a theft charge (later shown false), develops a delirious state in solitary confinement. The episode "began like a vivid dream with a wish-fulfilling illusion": she receives the expected 10,000 marks, lays them on the table — and a black figure suddenly enters and gives her a violent fright. She leaps up, the hallucinations vanish, leaving "delusions of being robbed, poisoned" (¶283); the scene then inflates into a grandiosity delusion (luxurious hotel, millions). Jung reads the whole as the standard prison-psychosis mixture of "hallucinatory wish-fulfilment and delusions of being wronged," triggered by unabreacted detention affects (¶283, ¶298–299). The dark intruder that wrecks the wish-fantasy is the same nocturnal-adversar figure the corpus elsewhere renders as the black man; the tie to shadow is ours, not Jung's here.

occurrences.title: The Black Madonna of Einsiedeln
occurrences.label: The Black Madonna of Einsiedeln
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Einsiedeln, Switzerland (Benedictine abbey, pilgrimage center southeast of Zurich)
occurrences.yearDisplay: abbey 10th c.; statue's dating contested ('black from the effect of a fire')
occurrences.quote: There is a black Virgin at Einsiedeln, though they say it is black from the effect of a fire, but they always say that!
body: The Swiss black Virgin, anchor of Jung's amplification of the patient's black-veil dream: "There is a black Virgin at Einsiedeln, though they say it is black from the effect of a fire, but they always say that! The fact is that there are a number of black Isis figures made of basalt that have served as Madonnas in Catholic churches" (p132). Black virgins as black-Isis relics — the black goddess of the black earth (Augustine's Mary, p132), the Demeter-layer under Mariology. The editor notes that Einsiedeln's black Madonna "became an example of a powerful feminine archetypal image for Jung and his followers." Its energy runs straight into the patient's series (the Ancient Mother with the grain of wheat; her own blackness read as "saintly in her blackness", introduction p55).

occurrences.title: The black man clutching her arm — hypnagogic vision of the heat-head hysteric (Burghölzli, autumn 1905)
occurrences.label: The black man clutching her arm
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: pdf p198 (¶793 area — print ¶ unmarked in chunk)

occurrences.quote: he looks like a ghost, 'like the black man whom I used to see when going off to sleep.
body: The 24-year-old hysteric of "Association, Dream, and Hysterical Symptom" (heat sensations in the head, hallucinations of figures at night, admitted autumn 1905) saw, going off to sleep, "a black man who stretches his black hand towards her and clutches her arm", with dim white female apparitions besides. Jung returns to the vision in dream IV (Dec 2, 1905), where the tall black man in Vehmic-court judge's dress leads an indistinct figure down the hospital corridor: "The black man is the disease-producing sexual complex that brought the patient to the mental hospital", and "Symbolically expressed: death is stretching his hand towards her" — the pursuer who takes her not to the grave but to the asylum.

occurrences.title: The wicked black man with a sword on the bed — dream of the 8-year-old boy (Case 4)
occurrences.label: The wicked black man with a sword on the bed
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: it seemed to him that a wicked black man with a sword or a pistol was lying on his bed, a tall thin man who wanted to kill him.
body: Falling asleep, the boy feels "a wicked black man with a sword or a pistol" lying on his bed, "a tall thin man who wanted to kill him"; he also dreams "that something terrible was going on in the next room, as if there were great black snakes or evil men who wanted to kill Mama" (¶733). The father was "a tall thin man" who washed standing naked each morning in full view of the boy (¶734) — the nocturnal noises the primal scene.

Jung's reading: the boy identifies with the mother through a homosexual component that feels feminine toward the father; the same black terror that threatens her threatens him (¶736). Black = the unconscious (¶737); the father rendered as dark nocturnal assailant = the 'father animal' motif. With the black snake this is the earliest documented black-man/black-snake pair in the corpus.

occurrences.title: The Black Mass for Mme. de Montespan — reversed rite and child sacrifice (affaire des poisons)
occurrences.label: The Black Mass for Mme. de Montespan
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The Mass was celebrated on the abdomen of a living woman, and the cross was reversed.
body: Jung's amplification of the peacock vision's dark side: when the good God fails, worship his opposite. The French peasants after the Black Plague "began to celebrate the Black Mass-they reversed the Christian rite for the worship of Satan" (p81), a devil-worship "which still flourished in the eighteenth century" (p82). Its most notorious form: "Three times the Black Mass was said for Mme. de Montespan in order to keep the love of the king, and each time they sacrificed a living child. The Mass was celebrated on the abdomen of a living woman, and the cross was reversed. Instead of wine, the blood of the slaughtered child was in the communion cup" (p82). "It was the Evil One, Sheitan, the creative principle, whom they worshipped, and it was under the symbol of the peacock" (p82) — the same spring-unfolding power the early church called resurrection.

Retold 18 Feb 1931 as his closest-to-hand historical evidence that children were really sacrificed as late as the seventeenth century: "There is historical evidence that Madame de Montespan sacrificed three children in order to retain the king's love." "And she succeeded in doing so-that is the amazing thing." There he suggests the Black Mass originated in the thirteenth century's war, famine and epidemics — when God's good will failed, people tried the devil — and ties the patient's sheep-tossing Indians to the whole rumor-complex from Carthage through the Gnostics to the jeu de paume. (The historical locus: the affaire des poisons, Paris, 1670s.)

occurrences.title: Algernon Blackwood, 'The Descent into Egypt' - the Egyptologist absorbed (1914)
occurrences.label: Algernon Blackwood, The Descent…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: He was sucked in and disappeared, he lost himself in the mystery of the still living archetypes of ancient Egypt.
body: The story of an Egyptologist "interested in the antiquities there, but instead of just excavating and explaining them, he suddenly discovered the extraordinary life they contained, their magic became revivified. Egypt got at him, as it does in a very subtle way. He was sucked in and disappeared, he lost himself in the mystery of the still living archetypes of ancient Egypt".

Jung: "That is not an invention, such things happen in reality. It is the spell of the primitive countries, the going black" - the same danger the vision's deserted temples would have posed "if they had been full of people she would have been submerged again, swept into the antique mentality". "A very poisonous writer," Jung adds, "but very good from a psychological point of view"; he discusses the book in Analytical Psychology (p139).

occurrences.title: The blessed waters awakening the dead — 'Instruction of Cleopatra'
occurrences.label: The blessed waters awakening the dead
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: how the elixir of life comes to them and awakens them, rousing them out of their sleep
body: One of the earliest Greek alchemical dialogues: Ostanes (the already-legendary Persian alchemist) and his companions ask Cleopatra how the highest descends to the lowest "and the midmost draws near to the lowest and the highest, so that they are made one with it; how the blessed waters come down from above to awaken the dead, who lie round about in the midst of Hades, chained in the darkness." Cleopatra answers: when the waters come in, the imprisoned bodies and spirits "bestir themselves, rise up, and clothe themselves in bright colours, glorious as the flowers in spring."

Jung connects the passage with the spring coniunctio of De vita longa: the Aniada as "powers that confer everlasting life," corresponding "to the blessed waters of Komarios and also, apparently, to the Communion substances" (¶193); the opus should begin in spring, in the month of Aries.

occurrences.title: The blond beast prowling in its underground prison — the 1918 forecast
occurrences.label: The blond beast prowling in its underground…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1918 ('The Role of the Unconscious,' written at the end of WWI)
occurrences.quote: As the Christian view of the world loses its authority, the more menacingly will the 'blond beast' be heard prowling about in its underground prison, ready at any moment to burst out with devastating consequences.
body: The seed of the whole turn-arc. In 1918 Jung publishes the mechanism that will become the 1936 Wotan essay: Christianity "split the Germanic barbarian into an upper and a lower half" and, by repressing the dark side, domesticated the bright one; "the lower, darker half still awaits redemption and a second spell of domestication." As the Christian view of the world loses authority, the collective unconscious it had dammed "is subject to a peculiar and ever-increasing activation," and the repressed god-form breaks out — individually as psychological revolution, socially as the eruption to come (cw10 ¶17).
