Retrospective confirmations in Jung's own hand: the German patients of 1918 whose dreams showed "primitivity, violence, and cruelty" in non-personal mythological motifs (¶447, written 1946 — self-report, no case records survive in the corpus); "I saw it coming, I said in 1918 that the 'blond beast' is stirring in its sleep and that something will happen in Germany. No psychologist then understood at all what I meant" (cw18 ¶371); the 1934 seminar re-reading of the 1918 text as "a rather good diagnosis of the present political conditions" (sem-visions pdf p1415, 14 Mar 1934).

Preserved-as-claims: ¶¶17-19 carry Jung's ethnic-psychology distinctions (the Germanic "chthonic quality," the Jew "badly at a loss for that quality in man which roots him to the earth," pdf p23-24) — documented, not softened; see the-turn Honest gaps.

occurrences.title: Blood baptism: robe turns scarlet, the blood-swirl carries her upward in spirals (patient vision, 25 Feb 1931)
occurrences.label: Blood baptism — robe turns scarlet,…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: And a great swirl of blood encompassed me, vibrating with a strange and terrible throbbing.
body: The head animus "initiates her to the blood": he spills blood upon her head and her white robe of perfect innocence becomes scarlet — "a blood bath, the reconciliation to the blood, exactly as it was done in the taurabolia." She hears "a strange rhythmic beating all about her" and lies back in a swirl of blood that carries her upward in spirals — blood flows up as well as down. Being in the blood means being in the instincts, in nature as it always was; the terror is the discovery that things are real (Jung's Tartarin de Tarascon aside).
The spiral — Bernoulli's eadem mutata resurgo — is "the very symbol of unfolding": surrender to the blood leads not down into hell but up, by the plant's law of growth, toward development.

occurrences.title: The woman in the blue robe — guide into the ghost world (Visions, 31 Jan. 1934)
occurrences.label: The woman in the blue robe
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Opening of "The Ghosts": "I entered a great cavern. Water dripped from the rocks. It was dark... Suddenly I beheld a woman in a robe of blue walking ahead of me". One story beneath the fire of manipura — svadhisthana's dripping dark. The blue celestial robe suggests Mary ("far from being dear old Mary") or the former earth-mothers; catching at it like a child repeats the Madonna's protective mantle (p1330-1331).

She assumes the psychopompos role: "She put her finger on her lips and said: 'Follow me. You enter upon a fearful place'". Later "old and withered": "I said: 'Why should I follow you? You may be a witch. Who are you?' She said: 'You have little faith'". Jung: a female psychopomp is unusual — this is "the Self that unites the pairs of opposites," impersonating the old woman who compensates the patient's childish consciousness and anticipates her post-midday attitude (pp1336, 1345).

occurrences.title: The girl who had never seen her body — balloon dream (reported 3 May 1933)
occurrences.label: The girl who had never seen her body
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A 28-year-old woman, "by no means insane," did not feel her steps on the pavement; on examination she said she had never seen her body — "No, I cover the bathtub in order not to see it." Told to go home and study her body, "she dreamed she was on top of a balloon and I was aiming at her and brought her down."

Jung: an exceedingly intuitive type, habitually outside the body — the seminar itself confesses the condition ("Are you in your body?" — "Not very well. The connections seem to be a bit loose"). Entering the earth/rock in the patient's visions means precisely this return into the body never before inhabited; hysteria's wandering anaesthesias and headless people show the pathology of the same relation.

occurrences.title: Christ 'a virgin in mind' and the woman's seed — Boehme
occurrences.label: Christ 'a virgin in mind' and the woman's seed
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: She is given to be a companion to thee in thy soul.
body: Boehme: Christ was "a virgin in mind," an "image of the holy number Three," eternally uncreated; where the Word is, there is the virgin. She is the "woman's seed" that bruises the serpent's head (Gen 3:15) — so Christ appears identical with the seed of the woman or with the virgin. "She is given to be a companion to thee in thy soul," yet as divine power and wisdom she is in heaven — corresponding, Jung notes, to the Indian Shakti; God took her to be his "spouse."
Jung at cw14 ¶580: in Boehme the virgin has "the character of an anima"; the androgynous unity of Shiva and Shakti is depicted in Tantric iconography as permanent cohabitation.

occurrences.title: The threefold illumination of the one day — Bonaventure's Itinerarium
occurrences.label: The threefold illumination of the one day
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This is the threefold illumination of the one day.
body: St. Bonaventure on the one day (Genesis 1:5): "We must enter into our mind [mentem], which is the eternal spiritual image of God within us... we must pass beyond ourselves to the eternal and preeminently spiritual, and to that which is above us... this is the threefold illumination of the one day."

Jung at cw14 ¶718: the triplex illustratio parallels Dorn's three stages of conjunction, "which obviously originated in the exercises for spiritual contemplation in the early Middle Ages" — turning from sense, turning to the inner mind and the celestial substance, contemplating the unus mundus.

occurrences.title: The Jung Codex — Coptic gnostic papyrus (Nag Hammadi)
occurrences.label: The Jung Codex — Coptic gnostic papyrus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Nag Hammadi, Upper Egypt → Zurich (C. G. Jung Institute) → Cairo (Coptic Museum)
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~4th c. codex (found 1945; acquired 1952; presented 15 Nov. 1953; to Cairo by agreement)

jung.locator: Address at the Presentation of the Jung Codex, 15 Nov. 1953 (pdf p1030; fuller addenda text pdf p1069)

body: A gnostic papyrus codex in Coptic, dug up in 1945 near Nag Hammadi, Upper Egypt, and bought in 1952 for the C. G. Jung Institute — hence "Jung Codex". Jung's address for the convocation at the Gesellschaftshaus zum Rüden, Zurich, 15 Nov. 1953 (draft pdf p1030; augmented final version published by Quispel 1975, per addenda pdf p1069) welcomed the codex as the gnostics' own voice returning: "The Jung Codex is a Gnostic papyrus in Coptic found in 1945 near the village of Nag Hamadi in Upper Egypt and acquired in 1952 for the C. G. Jung Institute." Provenance chain per the addenda: funds from George H. Page; purchase from the estate of the Belgian dealer Albert Eid; by the original agreement later given to the Coptic Museum, Cairo. Its first published text was the Valentinian Evangelium Veritatis (XREF christ-figure-light-bringer-evangelium-veritatis-2c).

occurrences.title: Forced to swallow the little book — Revelation 10
occurrences.label: Forced to swallow the little book
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "Take it, and eat it up; and it shall make thy belly bitter, but it shall be in thy mouth sweet as honey" — John forced to swallow the little book (footnote echoes Ezekiel 2:8–10; Jung adds from memory the live coal of Isaiah 6).

His point is the phenomenology of revelation: "one receives the shock from the fact that it is against one, the object thrown against one. (Objicere means to throw against one.) It comes with the authority of a reality". The list — swallowed book, Hosea's harlot, Paul blinded on the Damascus road, Jeanne d'Arc — shows revelation is not sudden conviction; resistance comes first.
Verbatim: "that peculiar symbolism in the Revelations of St.John where he is forced to swallow a book, causing an upset in the stomach".

occurrences.title: Borobudur — the Buddha vanishing up the terraces
occurrences.label: Borobudur — the Buddha vanishing up the terraces
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
jung.locator: pyramid amplification, paper by Aniela Jaffé (pdf p303)

occurrences.quote: finally completely eludes the human eye on the uppermost terrace.
body: Jaffé's second pyramid instance: in the pyramid of Borobudur the picture of Buddha is clearly visible on the lower terraces, surrounded by scenes from his life; on the middle terraces it stands alone, without narrative; higher up it is hardly visible; on the uppermost terrace "it completely eludes the human eye." The monument enacts dematerialization — the same movement as the Egyptian pyramid's surfaces narrowing to a single dimensionless point — and, as central edifice over a quadratic base, a body mandala.

occurrences.title: The snake-charmer's boy — Bedouin catcher of horned sand-vipers (Egypt)
occurrences.label: The snake-charmer's boy
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1920s (told to Jung; cf. his 1926 Nile journey)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: A Bedouin snake-charmer, called in "when snakes were really a pest" of the horned sand-viper among native labourers, "always went about holding a little boy on his arm while he was catching snakes... He said the child was absolutely necessary to give him protection". From bush to bush he pulled the vipers out "in a completely stiff and charmed condition."

Jung cites the story for the boy as indispensable magical companion and medium — boys "are very often used for crystal-gazing or for other magic performances" — in the run-up to the trance-boy of dream 30 who raises the great-grandmother. (Cf. H. G. Baynes's 1926 Nile film of a snake-charmer, footnote 7.)

occurrences.title: 'The sacrifice is Brahm' — Bhagavad Gita 4.24
occurrences.label: The sacrifice is Brahm' — Bhagavad Gita 4.24
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Krishna: "All's then God! The sacrifice is Brahm, the ghee and grain / Are Brahm, the fire is Brahm, the flesh it eats / Is Brahm..."

Jung's reading: "The affinity between this line of thought and the Christian symbol is obvious" (¶241) — the same self-sacrificing mediator structure as Agni (Max Müller's fire "both the subject and the object of a sacrifice", ¶240).
Verbatim: The sacrifice is Brahm, the ghee and grain / Are Brahm, the fire is Brahm, the flesh it eats / Is Brahm, and unto Brahm attaineth he (cw05 ¶241).

occurrences.title: Moses' serpent of brass: the one snake that overcomes the many (Numbers 21)
occurrences.label: Moses' serpent of brass
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Jung's key parallel for the many-snakes dream: "An example of this is the metal snake in Numbers 21:6-9. There you find the many snakes that bite the Israelites on their journey. Jehovah tells Moses to make a serpent of brass and to set it upon a pole, and whoever looks upon it will be protected against the snakes. For if you fall prey to the many, you will be dissolved. There is always the danger that an instinctual process will bring us down, and then we are dissolved in the multiplicity".

"Therefore, Christ is the One. — Yes, just as Moses exalted the snake on the pole, Christ was exalted on the cross. That's why the Ophites said: Christ is the snake of salvation, the sotēr snake. This idea persisted far into the Middle Ages" (pp237-238).

occurrences.title: Epiousion — the super-substantial bread of the Lord's Prayer
occurrences.label: Epiousion — the super-substantial bread…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Matthean text (Novum Testamentum Graece et Latine)
occurrences.yearDisplay: Gospel text (1st c. CE); Jung reads the then-new critical edition

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: In the newly revised Greek-Latin New Testament, the petition Jung had learned as "give us this day our DAILY bread" reads: Panem nostrum supersubstantialem da nobis hodie — the Greek ton art on tone pious ion, "the super-substantial one."

Jung's rendering is Eckhartian: "In German it would be, in the pure style of Master Eckhart: das uberwesentliche Brot." Ousia is "the being of the world"; epiousion "means that which is beyond the world... the concept of a metaphysical world." The coarse rendering to daily bread "was not exactly what Christ meant" — the petition is for the food of the subtle body.
Verbatim: "Ousia is the being, the being of the world that is, das Sein der Welt; and epiousion means that which is beyond the world."

occurrences.title: The Mithraic Host — cross-stamped bread, bells, and baptismal water (Roman Empire, ~2nd-3rd c.)
occurrences.label: The Mithraic Host — cross-stamped bread, bells…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In the cult of Mithras they used bread stamped with the cross, or divided into four; they used the little bells; and they used baptismal water
body: Tracing the Mass below Christianity, Jung asserts: "very important parts of the Mass — for instance, the Host — belonged to the cult of Mithras. In the cult of Mithras they used bread stamped with the cross, or divided into four; they used the little bells; and they used baptismal water — that is quite certainly pre-Christian. We even have texts that bear this out" (¶616).

The locus grounds his larger claim that "the ritual is the cult performance of these basic psychological facts" — hence ritual invariance: "if you change one little point in it, you make a mistake" (¶617). The mystery "reaches down into the history of the human mind; it goes back very far — far beyond the beginnings of Christianity" (¶616).

occurrences.title: The breaking of the vessels — Lurianic Kabbala
occurrences.label: The breaking of the vessels — Lurianic Kabbala
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: This elimination of the shards took place in what is described in the cabalistic writings—particularly of Luria and his school—as the \"breaking of the vessels.\" Through this the powers of evil assumed a separate and real existence.
body: The editors' note (at Jung's "allusion to an idea found in the later cabalistic philosophy") gives the full scheme: the kelipot ("shards" or "shells") form ten counterpoles to the ten sefiroth, originally mixed with their light; the Zohar describes evil as the by-product of the life-process of the sefiroth.
Evil as real by-product of the divine life-process, not privatio boni — the cosmological shadow, cast at the very act of emanation. Jung's Answer to Job is thinking alongside this structure.

occurrences.title: Brethren of the Free Spirit roving with 'transmittere in aeternitatem'
occurrences.label: Brethren of the Free Spirit roving…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: That was a colleective movement in the Germanic countries in the 13th century
body: Jung's example of the tarantula as old heretic-burning in new form: a "wide-spread movement of the spirit" with "absolutely communistic ideas and a wonderful way of dealing with capitalism." They held that everything should be spent, "offered or sacrificed," robbing travelers like bandits "always using the phrase transmittere in aeternitatem" — send worldly goods into eternity until money has no value "and we shall all be equal."

He folds the movement into the era's collective reaction: liberation of unruly spiritual powers answered by the great autos-da-fé; even the clergy infected — "Torquemada was the worst of the doubters," burning heretics whose convictions he feared to dream himself. Footnote cross-refers to CW 9i ¶139.

occurrences.title: 'Bridal bed in the field' — copulation rite for the field's fertility (rural Europe, Mannhardt's record)
occurrences.label: Bridal bed in the field
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: European agrarian folk custom cited in "On Psychic Energy" from Mannhardt's Wald- und Feldkulte as a canalization ceremony of the same type as the Wachandi piturja: "The 'bridal bed in the field' is a canalization ceremony of this kind: on a spring night the farmer takes his wife into the field and has intercourse with her there, in order to make the earth fruitful" (cw08 ¶85). Related usages: the "magic touch" of rolling (walzen, waleri) in the field; the farmer who feels work-fatigue as being "sucked dry" by the daemon of the field (¶86, fn).

Jung's reading: sexual analogy "acts like a channel that conducts water from a river to a power-station" — instinctual energy binds to the field, cultivation acquires the value of a sexual act, and a permanent flow of interest (libido) assures the work. Agriculture arose partly from such formations of sexual analogies (¶85).

occurrences.title: The bridge of Arta — the builder walls up his own wife
occurrences.label: The bridge of Arta
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Arta, Epirus, Greece (seminar text erroneously says 'Italy')

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: legend has it that human sacrifices were made in a bridge building, of the bridge in Arta in Italy, whose pillars collapsed until the bridge builder walled up his own wife in them.
body: Legend, cited in the bridge series: the bridge of Arta kept collapsing "until the bridge builder walled up his own wife in them [the pillars]." Quoted verbatim; the seminar text's "the bridge in Arta in Italy" is an error — the famous walled-wife bridge legend is Greek (the Ballad of the Bridge of Arta), kin to the Master-builder motif across the Balkans and Near East. Set beside London Bridge "made durable by being sprinkled with the blood of little children," it carries the same structure: a structure spanning the uncanny water demands a life; the bridge phobia of moderns is its ghost.

occurrences.title: The Chinvat bridge, where angels and demons fight over the crossing souls (Persia)
occurrences.label: The Chinvat bridge, where angels…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: A Muslim legend tells of a bridge between the Temple of Jerusalem in the East and the Mount of Olives in the West. Below is hell, into which those who are not righteous must fall. A Celtic legend tells of a bridge of horrors, not broader than a string.
body: Chief of the bridge parallels offered for the dream's breaking board-bridge:

The bridge's mythic weight rests on "the idea that a spirit or a god is at the bottom of the abyss," evaded by bridge-building and appeased by sacrifices (later puppets; chapels on bridges, Paris money-chapels, a clothes market in a Leeds bridge chapel). Psychologically the bridge "represents the weak spot of consciousness, the place where it might cave in" — for Jung the continuity of consciousness the child lacks.

occurrences.title: The Bridge of San Luis Rey — Wilder's five deaths
occurrences.label: The Bridge of San Luis Rey
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: when the bridge fell, the people on it were all at the end of their rope; that was very convincing from a psychological point of view.
body: Miss Kaufmann offers Wilder's novel as evidence for Jung's conjecture that 'people die at the right time.' Jung endorses it: the victims were all, psychologically, finished. The exchange belongs to his doctrine that the self may finish a man 'when he is no good any longer for the purpose of the self.' Parallels: luccheni-solitary-confinement-geneva-1898 · nietzsche-lucid-moment-weimar-1898.

occurrences.title: Bridge over hell, thin as a string and sharp as a sword — Qur'an
occurrences.label: Bridge over hell, thin as a string and sharp…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
jung.locator: bridge amplification from the 1936/37 seminar (pdf p286)

occurrences.quote: It is said that in a text of the Koran a bridge over hell is mentioned, thin as a string and sharp as a sword, which only the righteous can cross.
body: In the bridge amplification for a child's water-dream, Sachs (citing Jung's own 1936/37 seminar, seminar 2 §5) quotes the Qur'an's bridge over hell — thin as a string, sharp as a sword, crossed only by the righteous. Alongside it stand the Muslim legend of a bridge between the Temple of Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives with hell beneath, and the Zoroastrian Chinvat bridge: the bridge as place of judgment and passage to the beyond, "from the sorrowful to the sorrowless existence."
Jung's line: the bridge is man-made, a dangerous, precarious part of consciousness, the transition (puberty, death, "everything is transition") — carried historically by the Pontifex Maximus.

occurrences.title: Buddha threatened by Mara: the empty throne
occurrences.label: Buddha threatened by Mara: the empty throne
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: ...the throne of Buddha is empty—he is simply not sitting there any more.
body: "Mara and all his demons assail him, but the throne of Buddha is empty—he is simply not sitting there any more." Jung's chosen emblem for the analytical endpoint he has just described: consciousness severed from its objects, emigrated "to the other center, to the foreign yet originally own," the deliverance from tamas and rajas — what was panic-inducing seen without agitation, "not apathetic but freed from entanglement."

occurrences.title: The bugari (alcheringa) world of the Central Australian aborigines
occurrences.label: The bugari world of the Central Australian…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: a mythical period in the past of mankind, a sort of heroic age when men were demigods and animals; and it was like a dream. They call dreaming by the same name.
body: Levy-Bruhl's bugari world — the eternal dream-time one enters in dreams — is Jung's frame for the wise old man's 'absolute memory': 'the world outside time... which lasts during the transitory world in which we are actually living.' Passing through the animal stage is necessary to reach it. Parallels: aboriginal-maiaurli-fire-spark-australia · aljira-ancestors-sink-earth-aranda-australia.

occurrences.title: Apis high-priestesses buried in eternal embrace with the bull-god
occurrences.label: Apis high-priestesses buried…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: she was buried in an eternal embrace with the god.
body: The high priestesses of the Apis cults were buried in cohabitation with the bull-god: "the phallus of a bull was put into the genitals of the dead high priestess... meaning that she was buried in an eternal embrace with the god, a very beautiful idea but of course represented in a terribly naive way." Jung's exhibit, beside the ram-prostitution at Mendes, of primitive animal-assimilation rites — the bodily level of what the patient's swallowing of the black snake enacts in tamer, taste-conscious form ("a concession to good taste": the gods' scandalous love affairs are what broke their necks).

occurrences.title: Nine ears of wheat devoured by oxen — dream of Archelaos (Judea, A.D. 6)
occurrences.label: Nine ears of wheat devoured by oxen
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The ears of wheat signify the years of your reign, and the oxen the change of things. The nine years are fulfilled and there will be a great change in your fate. The hungry oxen mean your destruction.
body: The Tetrarch Archelaos, cruel Roman-appointed governor of Judea, dreams "nine big ripe ears of wheat eaten up by hungry oxen" in the tenth year of his rule, while a delegation against him travels to Augustus. His court interpreters refuse the dream; Simon the Essene (of the independent Essene/Therapeutai circles near the Dead Sea) dares the omen: the ears are the years of his reign, the oxen the change of things — "The nine years are fulfilled." Days later a Roman ambassador deposes him and exiles him to Gaul (¶241–242).

Jung's point is methodological: the 1st-century interpreter "understood the dream exactly as we would" — the dream image read on the collective layer, confirmed by the event. Paired in the same source with the Glaphyra ghost-dream as antiquity's dream evidence.

occurrences.title: The bull with tied feet under the net, fed milk and white flowers (patient vision, 11 October 1933)
occurrences.label: The bull with tied feet under the net, fed milk…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I saw brought into the market place a great bull. Its feet were tied and over it was a strong net.... They gave it milk to drink and threw white flowers at it.
body: When the war-between-the-sexes impasse needs a third factor, "a mythological factor" enters the market place: a great bull, feet tied, covered with a strong net, given milk to drink and white flowers. Jung's triple reading: (1) manipura instinctual force domesticated — "self-control"; (2) the antique animal-god, sun and fertility bull (Zagreus, Mithra the toreador, the Sufi world-bull whose left horn is the earth); (3) the reconciling symbol for the optimistic and shadow worlds, "the god caught in man, caught in his own creation" — the net the veil of Isis/Maya, the web of fate, the creator trapped in his own web; only man has the cunning to bind the bull's feet.

occurrences.title: The bull that broke its leg — dream of an elderly woman-patient (Zurich, WWI)
occurrences.label: The bull that broke its leg
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: While she was singing it, she saw a bull tearing around madly in front of the window. Suddenly it gave a jump and broke one of its legs.
body: An elderly woman-patient, whose faith had been shaken by the war, dreamed she was singing hymns of belief in Christ ("Christ's blood and righteousness...") when a bull tore madly in front of her window, jumped, and broke its leg; she thought someone ought to kill it, and woke.

Jung's reading (¶31–33): the hymn's emphasis on Christian belief constellated "that animal element in the unconscious which was personified by the bull — just the element that is represented by the Christian symbol as having been conquered and offered up in sacrifice." Christianity's sister-religion Mithraism sacrificed the bull outright; Christianity kept only the "little ram," the Lamb. When the absolute validity of the faith is shaken, the suppressed animal surges back — but "instinct cripples itself": the bull breaks its leg. The dream compensatorily offers, not sexual reduction, but reconciliation with the animal through compassion; "no religion is so defiled with the spilling of innocent blood as Christianity" (¶32).

occurrences.title: The calving cow — old chief's true dream, Mount Elgon
occurrences.label: The calving cow — old chief's true dream, Mount…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: But the cow and the calf were found just where he had dreamt they would be.
body: The only dream reported to Jung during his stay with the Elgonyi: an old chief dreamt that one of his cows had calved and was standing with the calf down by the river, in a particular clearing — "too old to keep track of his many cattle," he could not have known. The cow and calf "were found just where he had dreamt they would be" (cw18 ¶1291). Jung uses it to show why primitives hold certain dreams as "the voice of God": such dreams fulfil the thinking function the tribe does not yet consciously control, and leadership itself rested on "dreams that came true" (¶1291).

occurrences.title: The golden bull upon the pedestal descends to lie beside her (patient vision, plate 18, 25 November 1931)
occurrences.label: The golden bull upon the pedestal descends…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: So I drank from a goblet which had been left upon the pedestal as a libation. When I had done so the bull descended and lay down beside me.
body: Inside the white city she finds not bliss but a crowd worshipping a golden bull on a pedestal — the Mithraic bull god or the golden calf of Apis, "the worship of the sun bull, which is extremely archaic. It belongs to a period between two and four thousand B.C.". The bull asks where she lost herself; she drinks again from the libation goblet; the bull descends and lies down beside her, and upon the pedestal a green tree shoots up with many birds. Jung reads a compensation to her intuitive flight from life: by accepting the earth's blood-wine she domesticates the divine power of the instincts (she becomes the divine cow, Isis-Hathor with the crescent), and the animal principle is succeeded by the vegetative — the tree of yoga.

occurrences.title: Mithras carrying the bull — taurophory monuments
occurrences.label: Mithras carrying the bull — taurophory monuments
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: he had to shoulder his animal side.
body: Illustrating the ancient difficulty of the transitus — the dangerous passage to a new condition — Jung cites the monument type in which Mithras bears the bull on his shoulders (distinct from the tauroctony proper): "Mithras is represented on monuments as carrying the bull, meaning himself in the animal form; he had to shoulder his animal side."

Jung's reading: "in the ancient mysteries the transitus was always difficult; the hero had to undergo the transmutation by performing difficult tasks". The parallels are structural: "the transitus is shown in the passing of Christ on the cross — that is, going from life to death, carrying that symbol of the cross. In the cult of Mithras it was carrying the bull that is himself... And in the cult of Attis it was the carrying of the tree, which was Attis, into the cave of the Mother. Also the so-called athla, the heavy work... belong to the transitus". Zarathustra's mountain-crossing and sea-voyage are the same athla.

occurrences.title: Fiery bulls breaking through a barrier — patient picture shown by Prof. Heyer
occurrences.label: Fiery bulls breaking through a barrier
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: Yes, those fiery bulls breaking through a barrier. He was so frightened that he overlooked the fact that there were very positive signs in it which showed that the thing could be reconstructed.
body: Participant report (Mr. Baumann): "Professor Heyer showed a picture of such an explosion" — the eruption of a dangerously full unconscious. Jung: "Yes, those fiery bulls breaking through a barrier. He was so frightened that he overlooked the fact that there were very positive signs in it which showed that the thing could be reconstructed."

The image is Jung's illustration of the analyst's hazard discussed on the same page: touching an unconscious "full and ready to burst forth" may cause "a most terrible explosion-insanity really" (the lay-analyst suicide and the hidden asylum case follow).

occurrences.title: Vision: horse→ram→bull; the Indian on the pinnacle, the supplicating crowd (8 Dec 1930)
occurrences.label: Vision — horse→ram→bull
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The Indian and the bull crossed a high bridge over a swift mountain stream.
body: "I beheld a horse which changed into a ram and then into a bull." The Indian rides and then leads the bull up a high hill to a pinnacle of rock; below, many people surround the rock and raise their hands in supplication. Jung reads the transformation chain as the spring sequence of the zodiac (Aries the first shoot, Taurus "the fuller fertility, the greater generative force") — renewed animal libido — amplified by the Basel wild-man raft ceremony and Dionysian processions as "the new mana for the whole town for the whole year" (p207). The supplicating crowd is the collective unconscious itself, "a sort of audience within herself... composed of the parts and particles and atoms of the collective unconscious", waiting for rebirth.
"The Indian on his bull is the redeemer; the savior and his bull is the Mithra figure" (p210); the scene is St Paul's apokatastasis — all creation expecting revelation (p208).

occurrences.title: The prayer that became the bull before the world — Rig Veda 10.31.6
occurrences.label: The prayer that became the bull before the world
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: And this prayer of the singer, spreading afar, / Became the bull which existed before the world was.
body: Jung's key exhibit for the polarity built into the libido concept: Brahman as "a combination of prayer and primordial creative power, the latter resolving itself into the opposition of the sexes" (¶337). The singer's prayer "became the bull which existed before the world was," supporter of earth and heaven; the hymn then asks the cosmogonic riddle "What was the wood, what was the tree, / Out of which heaven and earth were fashioned?" and images the barren cow made to bring forth. Prajapati's later self-division into bull and cow, and into manas and vac, is the same scheme (¶338–343).

occurrences.title: Dream: the graveyard in the devastated area — the bull gnawing the saint's fingers
occurrences.label: Dream — the graveyard in the devastated area
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I saw that the bull was gnawing the fingers of the saint. I felt nauseated with horror and walked away, shaking my own hand as though to free it from the bull.
body: The dream that opens Lecture V: in a graveyard of red sandstone in the devastated area of France, over a mass soldiers' grave, a large tombstone carved with a saint and a bull — "in spite of the fact that both figures were carved in stone, they were alive-half dead and half alive. I saw that the bull was gnawing the fingers of the saint." She feels partial identity with the saint ("shaking my own hand as though to free it from the bull"), then a car races down a steep hill with doubtful brakes. Jung's frame: the opening locality carries the atmosphere (p136) — this graveyard is the Great War, "a psychological locality" (p137); the war shattered the vital formulas/mantras by which Western man lived, exposed the Church's powerlessness ("Even the Pope could only wail", p138), and produced the modern turn from parson to doctor (p140). The bull-gnawing-saint interpretation proper falls beyond this chunk's page range.

occurrences.title: "The Bull is the father of the Serpent, and the Serpent is the father of the Bull" — Firmicus Maternus
occurrences.label: The Bull is the father of the Serpent…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: A Greek saying quoted by the Latin astrologer (in CW5 ¶596 as "dragon" for serpent): each opposite generates the other — "That formulates it" (p287). Jung unpacks: the Bull is "the month of May, the marvellous fertility of the spring," Taurus, "the house of Venus... the uncontrollable power"; the Serpent is "the cold-blooded animal, the earth deity... darkness, night, humidity... death, fear."

Jung's use: the formula for the paradox of neurotic sexuality — "Neurotic sex trouble is Janus-faced": a disturbance of sexuality or a disturbance expressing itself through sexuality; "both are probably true" (p287). It says the same as the Chinese "At midnight midday is born and at midday midnight is born" (pp287-288) — "one of the intrinsic qualities of the unconscious mind."

occurrences.title: The Bull-Tamer — modern painting seen at Lugano (Jung's prime example of the archetype in modern art)
occurrences.label: The Bull-Tamer — modern painting seen at Lugano
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: C. R. Aldrich's exhibit A in the seminar's discussion of modern art: a painting of a man struggling with a bull against a flat blue ground set with six stars or planets — "so that the man and the bull seemed to suggest that they were the seventh." The bull "was not just a bull, he was The Bull"; the man "was more than any one man, he was Man." Crucially, Aldrich questioned the artist: he "had never even heard of Mithras and the bull: the picture was pure fantasy that had come up from the unconscious".

Jung's reading: the criterion of art is "that it grips you"; such a picture is a return of "Plato's conception of the eidolon" — "it is the bull he has painted, it is yours or mine—God's bull"; "The Bull-Tamer is a collective idea of tremendous power gathered into an image. It speaks of discipline—only a man of heroic attributes overcomes the bull". Modern art, like analysis, leads back "to the creative source within us."

occurrences.title: Dream of the transfiguration of a bull into a divine white sun-bull (reported 22 February 1933)
occurrences.label: Dream of the transfiguration of a bull…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Jung reports a recent dream "of a woman who saw the transfiguration of a bull into a divine white sun-bull, which was of course very beautiful." The dreamer was satisfied with the beautiful bull on its pedestal and never asked what it meant.

Jung's reading: "her god is an animal... she is under an inhuman, or subhuman principle" — whatever she does will be done "blind like a bull," with tremendous push and no regard for fences. "God is always the supreme force in our psychology... if the god is an animal, as he can be because he can be anything, then we are forced to act in an animal-like way—auto-erotic, blind, inconsiderate, shortsighted, instinctive".

occurrences.title: The world is a bull's horn — Somali legend told at Mount Elgon
occurrences.label: The world is a bull's horn
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: He told me that Allah had made the world in the form of a bull, which he then killed, transformed it into stone, and threw it into the sea.
body: One of the Somali boys on Jung's Elgon expedition answered his globe-argument (ships appearing over the horizon: first the smoke, then the funnels) with the old legend: Allah made the world in the form of a bull, killed it, transformed it into stone, and threw it into the sea; it sank so deep that only the left horn protrudes — and that horn is the earth we live on, so ships naturally come up over the curve. Jung identifies it as "a bit of old Persian mysticism, which was taken up by the Mohammedan mystics and, passed on by Sufism, went down the East Coast as far as Zanzibar." Told beside Mithras carrying the dead bull: the world-bull, the life of the earth.

occurrences.title: Cattle breaking into the cathedral during Mass — Jung's dream (1910)
occurrences.label: Cattle breaking into the cathedral during Mass
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: A pre-descent dream of 1910, offered as evidence that the Mithraic layer was stirring before the 1913 visions: "In 1910 I had a dream14 of a Gothic cathedral in which Mass was being celebrated. Suddenly the whole side wall of the cathedral caved in, and herds of cattle, with ringing bells, trooped into the church" (pdf p119; footnote number as printed). Jung connects the cattle and the ringing bells directly to the Mithraic cult — the editor notes his correspondence with Freud of February 1910 already awash in mythology ("My dreams revel in symbols that speak volumes"), and that Jung cited Cumont's Textes et monuments and Die Mysterien des Mithra constantly in Wandlungen. In the same breath he reports Cumont's remark that had Christianity been disrupted in the third century, "the world would be Mithraic today," and his view of the Mass-bells and Christmas (Sol invictus, Dec 25) as Mithraic survivals (pdf p119; cf. pdf p124).

occurrences.title: Fire in the basement of the clinic Hirslanden — dream of a boy
occurrences.label: Fire in the basement of the clinic Hirslanden
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: This night I dreamed that there suddenly was a fire at the clinic Hirslanden, in the basement, coming from the heating. We wanted to go down the stairs near the elevator for goods, but the staircase unexpectedly broke off.
body: Second dream of the boy series, presented by Jung himself. The child had been a patient at the clinic.

Jung: "The place where one is cared for often takes on a motherly meaning" — the clinic becomes an extension of the family web, a dream figure for the boy's psychology. The basement is the underworld, the abdomen; the heating the digestive fire; "Feuer im Dach" stands for an emotional outbreak threatening the whole system. The staircase breaking off: he cannot go down. The little children on the first floor — his own childlike quality — are in danger; one part wants the hospital (infantile dependency) to burn down, another hopes the children are saved.

occurrences.title: Cadmus and the dragon of Ares; the sown teeth — Thebes
occurrences.label: Cadmus and the dragon of Ares — the sown teeth
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Cadmus holds fast to Harmonia while the opposites in projected form slaughter one another.
body: Cadmus, kinsman of Hermes Ithyphallikos, forbidden to seek his sister Europa (taken by Zeus-bull), follows the moon-marked cow to the founding-site of Thebes, slays the dragon of Ares that guards the spring, and sows its teeth: "Immediately armed men sprang up, who fell to fighting among themselves until only five remained. Cadmus was then given Harmonia to wife" (¶85). Philaletha's addition — the serpent spitted to the hollow oak — "represents the banishment of the dangerous daemon into the oak" (¶85).

Jung's alchemical reading: Cadmus is "Mercurius in his masculine form (Sol)"; the sister-anima "acting as a psychopomp in the shape of a cow" leads him to his destiny as dragon-slayer; the dragon is "disharmony," and the self-slaughtering sown men exemplify "nature subdues nature" — "nothing less than the uroboros conceptually formulated" (¶86). The dragon's skin offered to the hollow oak = return to the mother; Cadmus and Harmonia end as stones, snakes, "and even into a basilisk" (Pernety) (¶87).

image.title: Danish: Kadmos kamp med en drage title QS:P1476,da:"Kadmos kamp med en drage" label QS:Lda,"Kadmos kamp med en drage"

occurrences.title: The caduceus: serpents heads-inward, two apples of Sun and Moon — Servius' commentary on Vergil
occurrences.label: The caduceus — Servius' commentary on Vergil
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Mercury causes these two fierce animals to agree, so surely we also ought to agree with one another.
body: Servius explains the caduceus: the serpents' heads look inward "to signify that ambassadors ought to discuss and agree among themselves"; ambassadors of peace are called Caduceatores; "to those Caducei are added two apples, one of the Sun and one of the Moon.... Mercury causes these two fierce animals to agree." Mercury as Medicurrius, "the mid-runner, because he is always passing between heaven and the lower regions." The medieval Pierius: he "will bind together the two serpents, that is, mutual hatreds, into one by the rod of his doctrine."

Jung's reading: the oldest full articulation of the caduceus as union-of-opposites symbol — Mercury the mediator between sun and moon, heaven and underworld. Parallels: monas-hieroglyphica-dee-antwerp-1564, mercurius family, ophite-diagram-origen-contra-celsum-6c.

occurrences.title: The camel pushing through the window, and the yellow glasses inside — dreams of a boy of five to six
occurrences.label: The camel pushing through the window…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: So I've got yellow glasses, and when I look through them things just are that big." — "Where have you got the yellow glasses?" — "I've got them in here!
body: Jung's parallel case to the lion-and-mirror dream: a boy of five to six with vivid fantasy life, endangered by the impression of death (a canary, a dog, a neighbor died; he was nearly run over by a truck). He tells his mother of an enormous horse or house "such as doesn't exist in reality," and explains:

He dreams of mounting a high tower on rotten wooden stairs; the stairs cave in, he falls, is dead; the mother picks him up and he comes alive again. Or of "big animals, a big camel. It comes from the street and then wants to push in the window of the bedroom to eat him. Father and mother stand before the inner side of the window, but the camel gets through nevertheless" — "This is the parallel to the lion!". Jung: such endangerings occur at certain moments of psychological development; "then one has to be careful".

occurrences.title: The Cantilena Riplaei: the sterile king's return to the mother's womb
occurrences.label: The Cantilena Riplaei
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: He then wished to return to his mother's womb and to dissolve himself in the prima materia.
body: The 'Cantilena Riplaei' legend: a noble king (the caput corporum), sterile though "nurtured under the wings of the sun," learns by the mouth of Christ that he shall be born anew; he resolves to return to his mother's womb and dissolve himself in the prima materia; she conceals him under her robe and incarnates him again; eating peacock's flesh and drinking the green lion's blood she bears the child who resembles the moon and then the splendour of the sun. The Crowned Maid (Virgo redimita) stands amid the four elements, the green lion bleeding in her lap; the king emerges "a supreme victor triumphant, a great healer of the sick and a redeemer of all sins."

Jung's reading: mother-son incest (Ripley) parallels brother-sister incest (Visio Arislei) — both "constitute the prototype of the royal marriage," an "endogamous mating [that] is simply a variant of the Uroboros." The king is "the domineering conscious mind" swallowed by the unconscious into the nigredo and reborn.

occurrences.title: Celebes rite: the captive stabbed, his blood licked from knife and spear
occurrences.label: Celebes rite — the captive stabbed, his blood…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: In the clay-eating discussion of "the other way of eating," Jung cites the explorers Fritz and Paul Sarasin: "A captive is tied to a column in the house of the spirits, then all the men of the tribe come, stab him in the skin, and lick the blood from the knife or the spear. This is a mysterious, ritual sharing of blood".

The frame: "Eating bread is human. The other way of eating is no longer human, it is a mystery. That is why these meals are taboo" — set beside the totem meals of the primitives, the taboo host of the Catholic Church, and the Spanish lapdog-host case. The boy's clay is this "more than bread" food: incorporating the other being, the world itself.

occurrences.title: The imaginary carcinoma — neurotic fear as a psychic growth (patient-anon)
occurrences.label: The imaginary carcinoma
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: case undated; lecture Vienna, Nov. 1932 / essay 1934
occurrences.quote: the idea of the carcinoma has imagined itself in him without his knowledge and without his consent.
body: A neurotic suffers from an imaginary carcinoma: he "knows, and has been told a hundred times before, that it is all imagination, and yet he asks me brokenly, 'But why do I imagine such a thing? I don't want to do it!'" (¶313). Jung's answer: "the idea of the carcinoma has imagined itself in him without his knowledge and without his consent" — a psychic "proliferation" growing in the unconscious (¶313). The fear is therefore "not imagination, but the consistent expression of a psychic fact that exists in a sphere outside consciousness" (¶315). The neurosis is a defence against the objective inner activity of the psyche, an attempt to escape the inner voice and the vocation: "Behind the neurotic perversion is concealed his vocation, his destiny: the growth of personality" (¶314).

occurrences.title: Images rising and falling at the bed's foot — Cardan's hypnagogic pageant (De subtilitate, 1550)
occurrences.label: Images rising and falling at the bed's foot
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: At the foot of the bed I saw images, consisting as it were of small circles and curves, and representing trees, animals, men, towns, troops drawn up in line, instruments of war and of music and other like things, rising and falling in turn, and coming one after another
body: Jerome Cardan (Girolamo Cardano) records a hypnagogic vision: at the foot of his bed he watches images "consisting as it were of small circles and curves" — trees, animals, men, towns, armies drawn up in line, instruments of war and of music — "rising and falling in turn, and coming one after another." Jung cites it (Latin given) alongside Spinoza's Brazilian and Ottilie's seeing in a footnote on hallucination-like states of the dissertation. It is the corpus's richest early description of autonomous image-streams between waking and sleep: a parade of micro-worlds that ascends and descends of itself, an ascent-descent mechanics of imagery two centuries before Romantic psychopathology codified it.

occurrences.title: The train that fell — dream of the child 'Anna'
occurrences.label: The train that fell — dream of the child Anna
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: After the gardener "buried" her in a hole and her father took her deep into the lake water ("Papa wanted to drown me, didn't he?" — ¶49–50), Anna woke screaming from a dream: a train went by overhead and fell down.

Jung's reading: "a parallel to the 'stagecoach' story of Little Hans" (¶52). The mistrust had turned on the father who must know the secret and keeps it; love blocked from transfer to the parents converts into fear, and the vehicle-crash image carries the repressed question about what fathers do.
Quote. "Anna had dreamed that 'a train went by overhead and fell down.'"

occurrences.title: Children's remains in pots at the temple of Astarte, Carthage (Tophet excavations)
occurrences.label: Children's remains in pots at the temple…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~8th-2nd c. BCE tofet deposits (Jung: 'perhaps in the seventh or eighth century B.C.')
occurrences.quote: In the excavations of old Carthage they found a series of pots in the temple of Astarte containing the remains of hundreds of slaughtered little children that had been sacrificed to the goddess. That was not mere cruelty, it was great devotion.
body: Jung's argument on the two levels of the sacred: "Like throwing the children to Moloch. That might be called ordinary murder and a terrible perversity... But before that it was a divine sacrifice and most efficacious because it was real." The rite lives only while the exaltation holds — "As long as it works it is real, but when it is understood it collapses and there is need of other forms." Paired with Abraham: the voice that stops the knife is "projected supreme consciousness... It is a voice, it is the god" — the transition to seeing child-sacrifice as murder, with the animal substituted. Tertullian's catechumens offering themselves to the wild beasts show self-sacrifice belongs to the same economy of human blood.

Retold 18 Feb 1931: the French excavations of the temple of Astarte uncovered hundreds of skulls of little children — "evidence that child sacrifices were often carried out there." He concedes the date is "too remote... perhaps in the seventh or eighth century B.C.; we need more recent evidence and we have only rumors" — the rumors being Roman charges against the Christians, Christian charges against the Gnostics (tossing a child in a circle till dead), and the medieval and pre-1914 Russian projection of ritual child-murder onto the Jews: the rumor-chain behind the tossed ball of the jeu de paume and the Black Mass of Madame de Montespan.

Retold again on the destructive-mother side: "Children were sacrificed to Baal and to Astarte, so they would be the destructive father and mother. When they excavated the foundations of the temple of Astarte at Carthage, they found in jars the bones of hundreds of children who had been burned. That would be more the activity of the mother naturally, the mother eating the first born; she herself does not eat it, she offers her child to the goddess instead." The destructive mother of the patient's vision has real cultic parallels; the destructive father has his ogres too — Cyclops, Kronos, Uranos "also eat their young."

occurrences.title: The carpenter who planed off her genitals — dream of the child 'Anna'
occurrences.label: The carpenter who planed off her genitals
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Watching a carpenter plane an ill-fitting cupboard door, Anna stood by; that night she dreamt the carpenter "planed off" her genitals.

Jung's reading: the dream asks "will it work with me? oughtn't one to do something like what the carpenter did, in order to make it work?" (¶66) — the problem of what makes generation "work" is active in the unconscious precisely where it is still unclear. The craft-tool image marks the doubt whether the genitals as given are sufficient to the function.
Quote. "That night she dreamt that the carpenter 'planed off' her genitals."

occurrences.title: The cat as Bastet of Bubastis, mirror of the sun (Egypt, 11 May 1932)
occurrences.label: The cat as Bastet of Bubastis, mirror of the sun
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The cat was an incarnation of Bastet, the goddess of Bubastis. It was also sometimes regarded as a personification of the sun, because, like the eagle, it showed its divine quality in the fact that it could look straight at the sun.
body: Amplification of the cat at the old man's feet in the hold: asked about cats, Jung turns to Egypt - the cat as an incarnation of Bastet, goddess of Bubastis, sometimes a personification of the sun "because, like the eagle, it showed its divine quality in the fact that it could look straight at the sun".

Jung's correction of Mrs. Crowley: the cat "should never be taken as a symbol of consciousness" - "It symbolized more a divine quality... For the sun was really the visible god; at the mental stage of sun worship there was nothing behind, the god was the actual sun." And: in old Egypt "there was only the consciousness of the pharaoh and of nobody else, because he was the only individual". The cat is "the most undomesticated of the domestic animals," at home in woods and household - "absolutely in accordance with a woman's nature" - and it sees in the dark.

occurrences.title: Egyptian cat sculpture that consumed its owner (patient's study, Zurich, ~1930s)
occurrences.label: Egyptian cat sculpture that consumed its owner
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: patient's drawing-room, Zurich (sculpture of Egyptian origin)
occurrences.quote: When he understood his general projection of the feminine image — for, of course, the cat symbolized the woman — then the whole charm and fascination of the sculpture was gone.
body: An unusually intelligent man bought an old Egyptian cat sculpture for 40,000 francs on sight, and it wrecked his peace: he kept leaping up from his office desk downstairs to visit it, moved it onto his desk, then had to lock it in the attic against his own temptation.

Jung's reading: the man had projected his unconscious image of woman into a real woman, and once that was clarified the cat's meaning surfaced — "for, of course, the cat symbolized the woman." Withdrawing the anima projection dissolved the artifact's numinosum entirely (¶325-326). Jung uses the case to show that activated archetypes project into things as readily as into persons ("There are even transferences to animals and to things," ¶324).

occurrences.title: Namazu the earthquake catfish — Japanese legend
occurrences.label: Namazu the earthquake catfish — Japanese legend
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Edo period; namazu-e prints flourish after the 1855 Ansei earthquake (legend older)

jung.locator: fn 17 to Discussion, Lecture I (pdf p924)

body: The namazu is a monstrous catfish of Japanese legend that carries most of Japan on its back and, when annoyed, moves head or tail and so provokes earthquakes. The motif crystallised in Edo-period iconography: after the great Ansei earthquake of 1855, namazu-e prints flooded the market, showing the catfish as world-shaker and, ambiguously, as agent of yo-naoshi — the shaking-loose and redistribution of a stagnant world.

Jung reached for this image in an aside on Japanese earthquake lore during the Discussion after Tavistock Lecture I (1935); the editors document the legend in fn 17. The general index anchors the allusion at CW18 print p33 ("Japanese: and earthquakes, 33&n"). The ¶ pin for the lecture-text aside is owed to the Tavistock Discussion (earlier chunk).
Verbatim: "According to a Japanese legend, the namazu, a kind of catfish of monstrous size, carries on its back most of Japan, and when annoyed it moves its head or tail, thus provoking earthquakes."

occurrences.title: Cathar 'Revelation of John' — two fishes yoked like oxen on the primeval waters
occurrences.label: Cathar 'Revelation of John'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: early 12th c. (Basilius' confession before Alexius Comnenus, 1111)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Christ's favourite John asks what Satan was before his fall. Descending through the elements he finds 'two fishes lying upon the waters, and they were like oxen yoked for ploughing the whole earth from sunset to sunrise' at the command of the invisible Father, and his 'Osob' — his own fire, which he could not pass (¶225). Cast down, Satan creates the world in a week on the model of Genesis 1 (¶226). Jung: the yoked fishes 'can refer only to the zodiacal fishes' — Christ and Satanael, the two principles of the Pisces aeon, whose ploughing begins in the west like the alchemical nigredo (¶229-231). The fishes were found 'in the beginning', when the spirit brooded on the dark face of the waters.

occurrences.title: 'Cathedrals should be built for isomorphy' — voice dreams, 2 & 6 Sep 1954
occurrences.label: Cathedrals should be built for isomorphy
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters
jung.locator: 'Statements by the Psyche' + Jung's Letter 71 (pdf pp201-204, 218)

occurrences.quote: Cathedrals should be built for isomorphy.
body: Two dreams Pauli calls "really fundamental," following the eating of the cherries. First a voice: "At the place where Wallenstein atoned for his sins with his death, a new religion shall arise" — taking him to the 17th century, Bohemia, Kepler, the Thirty Years War as "a general cultural split (dissociation)." Then, in a major war with censored dispatches, his Hamburg mathematics colleague A. appears with his wife and says:

Pauli's reading: isomorphy — "identity of form, reproduction of the same form," learnt from dream language and met again in Aion chap. XIV (CW 9ii par. 440) — is "the secret of the multiple forms of appearance of the archetypes, the multiplicatio with the coniunctio known to the alchemists". Cathedrals ritually capture the multiplicatio against "a pointless and aimless, psychotic or catastrophic repetition," and are themselves "a multiplicatio of the original and unique new house." Jung: "you do well to opt for 'chthonic wisdom' and for a union of oratorium and laboratorium".

occurrences.title: Schiller's 'Song of the Bell' recurrent association — fifteen-year-old girl
occurrences.label: Schiller's 'Song of the Bell' recurrent…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A fifteen-year-old girl under Jung's analysis kept returning, in free association, to the passage of Schiller's Song of the Bell in which "the dark prince of the shadows" snatches the wife and mother from her spouse's arms — though she had only once glanced at the poem and recalled nothing but "something about a cathedral tower" (¶7).

Jung's reading: the year before, the mother had left the girl alone with her father; now mother and daughter were to go away together, and it was the "little wife" being snatched from the spouse. The intrusive funeral-bell fragment marks the place where the girl's own situation and the poem's scene coincide — an association betraying the "kill/die = get rid of" logic of child language rather than any death-wish against the mother (¶8–9).
Quote. "I once had to treat a fifteen-year-old girl who, under analysis, had a recurrent association, and kept on thinking of Schiller's 'Song of the Bell.'"

occurrences.title: Gothic cathedral as tarantula's nest — temple ruins over the spider's den
occurrences.label: Gothic cathedral as tarantula's nest
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: instead of the tarantula's den it is a temple, and of course the temple he envisages is the Christian church, obviously a Gothic cathedral-and that is the nest of the tarantula.
body: Zarathustra's intuition: "Here where the tarantula's den is, riseth aloft an ancient temple's ruins." Jung amplifies through two lectures: life builds itself "with columns and stairs," then suddenly stands static — "that building is a static, petrified system of ideas. It is petrified spirit". The cathedral is congealed life: "It is wood that has become stone, or spirit that has become incorruptible matter"; vault and arch "strive against each other, the divinely striving ones," no longer striving.

Norman man-versus-monster carvings, Notre-Dame's flying buttresses "catching so much spirit in matter," Michelangelo's stone that "began to move with a surplus of life" — the whole read as the enantiodromia of the preachers of equality into the pillar-saint.

occurrences.title: Dagda's cauldron of plenty and Bran's cauldron of renewal — Celtic mythology
occurrences.label: Dagda's cauldron of plenty and Bran's cauldron…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Ireland / Celtic world (→ Britain, Grail romance)
occurrences.yearDisplay: pre-Christian Irish myth (dateless; material underlying medieval romance)
occurrences.quote: Further evidence of the pagan root of the vessel symbolism is the 'magic cauldron' of Celtic mythology.
body: Jung's documentary footnote on the pagan root of the vessel symbolism (ch.5, on the vas): "Further evidence of the pagan root of the vessel symbolism is the 'magic cauldron' of Celtic mythology. Dagda, one of the benevolent gods of ancient Ireland, possesses such a cauldron, which supplies everybody with food according to his needs or merits." The Celtic god Bran "likewise possesses a cauldron of renewal" — the same regenerating womb-vessel Jung elsewhere finds in the hero's immersion.

Jung reads the cauldron as ancestor of the Grail: "the name Brons, one of the figures in the Grail legend, is derived from Bran," and Alfred Nutt sees Bran, lord of the cauldron, and Brons as "steps in the transformation of the Celtic Peredur Saga into the quest of the Holy Grail." Acknowledged with thanks to Dr. Maurice Nicoll.

occurrences.title: Hadrian's temple of Attis beneath the Church of the Nativity
occurrences.label: Hadrian's temple of Attis beneath the Church…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Jung reports the archaeological scoop of his day: excavations beneath the Church of the Nativity (fourth century) revealed Roman masonry — "the remains of a temple of Attis built by the Emperor Hadrian in about 136; and this was erected in order to desecrate the place of the Christian cult."

The desecration proves the priority: "There must have been a very early local tradition that Christ was really born in this spelaeum, and that it was actually a spelaeum of Attis." Jung adds the Vatican: an Attis temple stood where St Peter's stands, its head priest the papas — "the priest who is still ruling there in the old place is the papa or pope."

Verbatim: "recent excavations in the Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem have shown that below the Christian church, which dates from early in the fourth century, is Roman masonry, the remains of a temple of Attis built by the Emperor Hacirian in about 136." (pdf p188, OCR as in text)

occurrences.title: The cave descent: ruby crystal, murdered hero, scarab, sun and serpents — Jung's first active imagination (Nov–Dec 1913)
occurrences.label: The cave descent — ruby crystal, murdered hero…
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: Jung's first deliberate descent, made with the "boring method" — fantasizing himself digging a hole "and by accepting this fantasy as perfectly real": a corridor of black slime, a cave of bat-like insects, a rock bearing "a light, a luminous crystal... like a ruby" covering a hole. Through it: rushing water, the floating body of a fair-haired man ("That is the hero!"), a big black scarab, then a dark-red luminous sun — upon which "hundreds of thousands of snakes threw themselves on the sun and obscured it." Withdrawing, he saw blood gush from the hole "as from a severed artery".

His 1925 interpretation: the crystal = the stone of wisdom; the beetle "an ancient sun symbol"; the fair-haired hero = the day sun / superior function; the black scarab = night; what appears after is not a new hero "but a midnight sun"; the murdered hero = the secret murder of one's own ideal of efficiency, confirmed weeks later by the Siegfried dream. The hole itself: "an archetype of considerable power... the mystery attaching to caves comes down from immemorial times; one thinks at once of the Mithraic cult, of the catacombs".

occurrences.title: Hal Saflieni hypogeum initiations — Malta
occurrences.label: Hal Saflieni hypogeum initiations — Malta
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The neophyte dies like the seed-corn, springs up again and gets into the winnowing-basket.
body: The neolithic underground sanctuary as the deep-time background of the spelaeum initiations Jung lists from the Attis spelaeum to San Stefano: the tomb-womb where the neophyte "dies like the seed-corn, springs up again" (¶536).

image.title: Malta Hypogeum Modell

occurrences.title: Diocletian's crypt of Hecate with 365 steps — Antioch (Malalas)
occurrences.label: Diocletian's crypt of Hecate with 365 steps
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: As the “spirit-mother” she sends madness, the moonsickness.
body: The solar count of the stairs leading down to the spook-goddess: "That this cavern is in fact related to the subterranean mother of death can be seen from a note in Malalas" (¶577). Hecate — night and phantoms, Empusa, lamia, the "Bride of Corinth," key, whip, dagger, torch, dogs — "a real spook-goddess"; as spirit-mother "she sends madness, the moonsickness" (¶577).

occurrences.title: The Holy Sepulchre spelaeum of San Stefano — Bologna
occurrences.label: The Holy Sepulchre spelaeum of San Stefano
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: It can scarcely be doubted that the underlying meaning of the Church is the mother’s womb.
body: "The Church is, in a sense, the hero's grave (cf. the catacombs). The believer descends into the grave in order to rise again from the dead with the hero. It can scarcely be doubted that the underlying meaning of the Church is the mother's womb" (¶536) — with the Tantric garbha griha ("seeding-place or uterus") as the architectural parallel.

occurrences.title: Flooded Mithraeum beneath the Church of San Clemente — Rome
occurrences.label: Flooded Mithraeum beneath the Church…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~2nd–3rd c. mithraeum (excavated in the modern era)
occurrences.quote: In Rome a Mithraeum has been discovered ten feet below the surface of the Church of San Clemente. It is still in good condition but filled with water, and when it is pumped out it fills again.
body: A Mithraeum discovered "ten feet below the surface of the Church of San Clemente," still in good condition but permanently flooded: pumped out, it fills again from an adjoining spring that has never been found (¶259). Jung pairs it with the spring by the Mithras grotto at Saalburg and a Provençal Mithraeum with piscina and Tauroktonos rock — the cult of Mithras is "always connected with a spring," which the early Christians hated as pagan nature-worship.

The ever-living spring under the church is the exact architectural image of Jung's claim that the crypt/mystery-place survives beneath the Christian layer (¶256) — and of the water-cistern under the cathedral of Toledo in the dream.

occurrences.title: Hippolytus: Christ's birth-grotto was a sanctuary of Attis
occurrences.label: Hippolytus — Christ's birth-grotto was…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Jung: "Hippolytus, an early father of the church, says that the grotto in which Christ is said to have been born was, according to tradition, the sanctuary of Attis."

For Jung this text, with the Bethlehem excavations (see parallel), proves the Attis-Christ continuity "perhaps even closer than Mithraism" — the same spelaeum serving son-god and Christ-child, the cave as "a burial place or a mystery place — they are indistinguishably the same."
Verbatim: "Hippolytus, an early father of the church, says that the grotto in which Christ is said to have been born was, according to tradition, the sanctuary of Attis."

occurrences.title: Plato's parable of the cave (Republic VII)
occurrences.label: Plato's parable of the cave (Republic VII)
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: He tries by that rather clumsy parable to explain the subjectivity of our judgment.
body: Cited twice as the classic symbol of the subjectivity of judgment: people with backs to the light watching shadows cast on the wall — "the same idea which was called later on in the history of philosophy the theory of cognition." Jung's gloss: "a rather clumsy parable" that needed "more than two thousand years until that problem was formulated in a philosophically abstract way in Kant's Critique of Pure Reason" — i.e., Plato could symbolize what only symbols can carry, exactly like the cakras.

occurrences.title: Plato's cave parable — true symbol of the theory of knowledge
occurrences.label: Plato's cave parable
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Spirit in Man, Art and Literature (CW15)

occurrences.quote: When Plato, for instance, puts the whole problem of the theory of knowledge in his parable of the cave, or when Christ expresses the idea of the Kingdom of Heaven in parables, these are genuine and true symbols
body: The parable of prisoners in the cave who take shadows for realities, by which Plato "puts the whole problem of the theory of knowledge" (Republic VII).

Jung's reading. In the 1922 lecture the cave is his exhibit A for the true symbol against the Freudian sign: "these are genuine and true symbols, that is, attempts to express something for which no verbal concept yet exists" (cw15 ¶105). The reductive counter-reading is rehearsed and rejected: "If we were to interpret Plato's metaphor in Freudian terms we would naturally arrive at the uterus, and would have proved that even a mind like Plato's was still struck on a primitive level of infantile sexuality. But we would have completely overlooked what Plato actually created" (cw15 ¶105).

occurrences.title: Pueblo emergence myth: mankind climbs through four caves
occurrences.label: Pueblo emergence myth
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Pueblo peoples, American Southwest (from Jung's Pueblo friend)

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: ...after untold time of a dormant and absolutely dark wormlike existence, two heavenly messengers came down and planted all the plants.
body: Humanity generated far down in a pitch-black cave, living a dormant, wormlike existence until two heavenly messengers plant all plants and find the jointed cane long enough to reach through the roof; ascent cave by cave to the fourth, with its "incomplete and ghostly light," and finally the surface, where a brilliant light is made and becomes sun and moon. Jung: "Those were cakras, new worlds of consciousness of natural growths, one above the other. And this is the symbolism of all initiation cults."

occurrences.title: Theseus and Peirithous grown fast to the rocks of the underworld — Athens
occurrences.label: Theseus and Peirithous grown fast…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The Theseus myth is therefore a representation of the individuation process.
body: Theseus and Peirithous descend through a chasm in the grove of Colonus to abduct Persephone from the underworld. Resting below, they find themselves grown fast to the rocks and cannot rise: "they remained stuck in the mother and were lost to the upper world." Theseus is finally freed by Heracles "in the role of the death-conquering hero"; Peirithous is left.

Jung states the reading in one line: "The Theseus myth is therefore a representation of the individuation process" — the descent that fails when the ego is stuck fast in the chthonic mother, and the rescue as liberation from below.

occurrences.title: The virginity test in the serpent's cave — Greek custom
occurrences.label: The virginity test in the serpent's cave
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: If they were bitten, it was a sign that they were no longer chaste.
body: The cave-serpent as jealous test-mother — the direct antecedent of the Roman dragon-legends in which girls descend to the cave-dragon and are slain for unchasteness (¶572–574), and the clinical inverse of the patient bitten in the genital region while freeing himself from the mother-complex (¶585).

occurrences.title: Zoroaster's cave with many springs dedicated to Mithras — Porphyry
occurrences.label: Zoroaster's cave with many springs dedicated…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~3rd c. CE text (Porphyry's De antro; Zoroaster mythic)
occurrences.quote: Porphyry relates that Zoroaster, the founder of the Persian religion, dedicated to Mithras a cave containing many springs.
body: "Porphyry relates that Zoroaster, the founder of the Persian religion, dedicated to Mithras a cave containing many springs" (¶259). Jung cites it inside the row proving that the cave-with-springs is the standard sanctuary of the mysteries — the natural temple that Christianity replaced with the crypt, and that the Toledo dream re-creates as the serpent's flooded cistern.
Text-locus rather than a single monument: its value in the vault is as the ancient literary witness joining cave, spring, and Mithras (cf. Orphic cults associating the underworld with water, same ¶).

occurrences.title: The New Jerusalem, foursquare, of Revelation 21 (Patmos, ~95 CE)
occurrences.label: The New Jerusalem, foursquare, of Revelation 21
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: And the city lieth foursquare, and the length is as large as the breadth... And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; every several gate was of one pearl.
body: The vision-seminar's central amplification of the white city, read aloud from the English Bible: the holy city coming down from God as a bride adorned for her husband — "The mandala is a yoni, female, so it is here a bride". Twelve gates (three on each side), twelve foundations, wall of jasper, street of pure gold like transparent glass, twelve gates of pearl, no temple, no need of sun or moon, no night. Jung: "You see that is a most beautiful mandala, the foursquare symbol... like the cloister in the center of the Buddhist mandala. The mandala is the symbol of individuation, so the white city is the city of individuation".

occurrences.title: The white city beyond the giant (patient vision, 11 November 1931)
occurrences.label: The white city beyond the giant
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Beyond him I saw a white city. I said to him again: 'I must pass you', but he only laughed.
body: Beyond the giant of public opinion she glimpses a white city — the city of promise, amplified by the New Jerusalem of Revelation 21 and the diamond city of Brahma on the Himalayas. Jung names it "the city of individuation," the symbol of the Self: "in the white city, one is surely in a state which is fortified against the surrounding destruction". But entry disappoints: "The light was blinding, the white stones hurt my feet" — she is not ready; the Self "can be, and very often is, the most difficult task; it is almost insupportable". Only after the faun's goblet, the white bird, the golden bull and the tree does the way stand open.

occurrences.title: The glorious celestial water is Wisdom — 'Consilium coniugii'
occurrences.label: The glorious celestial water is Wisdom
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)
jung.locator: 'Transformation Symbolism in the Mass' n.27 (pdf p724)

occurrences.quote: Sed aqua coelestis gloriosa scil. aes nostrum ac argentum nostrum, sericum nostrum, totaque oratio nostra, quod est unum et idem scil. sapientia, quam Deus obtulit, quibus voluit
body: In the Mass essay's water-spirit footnote chain, the Consilium coniugii collapses every alchemical substance-name into one identity — and names it Wisdom:
The celestial water = the sapientia of God — the Sophia-water equation that runs from the Odes of Solomon's living stream through aqua permanens to the Mass's water-and-wine.

occurrences.title: Chained cult images — Melkarth, Jupiter Ammon fettered to prevent escape
occurrences.label: Chained cult images
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: they used to chain the image of Melkarth or Jupiter Ammon with heavy chains in order to prevent him from escaping and depriving them of his assistance; they actually fettered the images of the gods in a panic of fear lest they might leave them.
body: In antiquity, Jung tells the seminar, cult images were literally chained:

From this he derives the ambivalence of the divine image: any object designating the god threatens him with destruction — an unskilled painter could make him ridiculous — so "a temple, particularly in a religion where there are images, icons, etc., is always a sort of burial place for the gods because the gods are then stone, which becomes an argument against them". Hence, by contrast, the Swahili insistence that Allah is shapeless "like the wind, a puff of cold air": shapelessness protects the god from the discriminating mind.

occurrences.title: Descent on the backs of chained old men (Visions Seminar, 24 May 1933)
occurrences.label: Descent on the backs of chained old men
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: The steps down between the black rocks "were made by the backs of old men chained to the rock... I spoke to an old man, asking him why he was chained. He answered: 'Your world has refused us. Therefore are we chained. But by our wisdom you shall descend.'"

Jung: a whole series of animi — ancestral beliefs and convictions, like caryatides holding the entablature of the Erechtheum.
