Every old opinion was once a way of consciousness; "each animus is really a different attempt at consciousness," and the traces survive in the brain cells. Science forgets its own old men (the corpuscular theory of light abandoned for oscillation, then readopted). Church dogma "contains the most finished theory of the unconscious" and will be understood when our own explanations fail.

occurrences.title: Cakra illustrations of The Serpent Power (Madras, 1919; enlarged copies used in Jung's seminar)
occurrences.label: Cakra illustrations of The Serpent Power
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Madras (Woodroffe's Serpent Power) → Zurich, Psychological Club

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: Mrs. Hauer had painted enlarged copies of the illustrations of the cakras from The Serpent Power, which were used for the lectures.
body: The traditional plates of the seven cakras (muladhara's elephant through sahasrāra's thousand petals) reproduced from the fifteenth edition of The Serpent Power. Mrs. Hauer painted enlarged copies for Hauer's lectures; Jung described them as "very wonderful"; C. A. Meier later donated them to the Jung Institute. These pictures are the visual anchor of every chakra reading Jung gives: elephant, makara, ram, gazelle, white elephant, winged seed.

occurrences.title: Shat-chakra-nirupana — Pūrṇānanda's description of the six centers (Bengal, 1577)
occurrences.label: Shat-chakra-nirupana
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Bengal (Śrī-tattva-cintāmaṇi, ch. 6; trans. Woodroffe as The Serpent Power, 1919)

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)
jung.locator: whole seminar, esp. App. 1 (pdf p126-127); App. 4 = translation

occurrences.quote: The ûa°-cakra-nirÖpaõa (Description of the six centers) was the sixth chapter of Purõanvnda-Svvmz's åri-tattva-cintvmaõz, composed in 1577.
body: The root text of Jung's Kundalini seminar: the sixth chapter of Pūrṇānanda-Svāmī's Śrī-tattva-cintāmaṇi (1577), which Hauer expounded and Jung interpreted psychologically in October 1932. Sir John Woodroffe's translation (The Serpent Power, London 1919) — heavily annotated in Jung's own copy — carried it to Zurich; Mrs. Hauer's enlarged paintings of its cakra plates hung in the lecture room. Jung mined it for per-cakra detail (sleeping Kundalini coiled round the liṅga, the makara, Laktini, the kalpataru, the itara-liṅga).

occurrences.title: Vishnu with four arms worshiped in the navel — Dhyanabindu Upanishad
occurrences.label: Vishnu with four arms worshiped in the navel
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: The great and powerful with the four arms, that is, Vishnu, should be worshiped in the navel.
body: "The great and powerful with the four arms, that is, Vishnu, should be worshiped in the navel" — Jung's evidence that before the tantric system, the Upanishads distributed the approach to brahman across four cardinal points appearing "in the head, neck, heart, and navel": an early stratigraphy of the later cakra ladder, with maṇipūra's navel already a seat of the god.

occurrences.title: Christ among the vines — the Chalice of Antioch
occurrences.label: Christ among the vines — the Chalice of Antioch
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~4th–6th c. (hidden during Julian the Apostate's persecution, 361–63)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Mrs. Baumann names it (7 Dec 1938): discovered with other antique silver vessels at the bottom of an ancient well — "part of the treasure of an early Christian church which had been thrown into the well at the time when Julian the Apostate was persecuting the Christians"; it has even been suggested the bowl is the vessel of the Last Supper. "The chalice is most remarkable for its symbolism: Christ is represented as sitting among the leaves and grapes in the branches of a huge vine which is like a tree" — the traditional antique form of the Caesars linked with Dionysos/Bacchus.

Jung: the image links Christ "up with the age-old traditions about the tree of life, and the crucifixion would mean... a retrogression or a recession of Christ into the tree from which he originally came." Companion locus: the Orpheus-Bacchus crucifixion seal in Berlin.

occurrences.title: The divining cup of Joseph and Anacreon — Hippolytus' Naassenes
occurrences.label: The divining cup of Joseph and Anacreon
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Hippolytus closes his Naassene report with the cup (κόνδυ) from which "the king, when he drinks, draws his omens" — the cup of Joseph and the tankard of Anacreon: "My tankard tells me / Speaking in mute silence / What I must become." "Anacreon's cup is dumb; yet Anacreon affirms that it tells him in mute language what he must become, that is, spiritual and not carnal" (¶550). The secret in the cup is the water Jesus changed into wine at Cana — "the kingdom of heaven that lies within us as a treasure."

Jung's structural reading: the "third and fourth" members of the quaternity are water and earth, "the lower half of the world in the alchemical retort," and "Hippolytus likens them to a cup (κόνδυ)"; water = content, earth = container; the Jordan as the water = the Logos, "bringing out the analogy with the Chalice" (¶551).

occurrences.title: Frogs leaping from the chalice in the Gothic cathedral (Visions)
occurrences.label: Frogs leaping from the chalice…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: vision read 27 January 1932 (painted late 1929/early 1930 for Jung)
occurrences.quote: The priest ascended the steps to the altar and lifted on high the sacred chalice. As he did so small animals and frogs leapt forth from the chalice.
body: Constellated by her extreme Yin-blackness, the Christian counter-image: Gothic cathedral, Te Deum procession, a gargoyle clutching the priest's gold robe — the chthonic factor not repressed — and then:

Jung: the frogs "do not mean a defilement of the sacred chalice, they mean the healing substance or the healing symbols that emanate from the womb of the chalice"; the chalice as antique medicine-bowl needing "a drop of poison" from the serpent (pdf p603, Quentin Matsys' St. John chalice, Gnostic Christ-serpent); virgin = vas insigne devotionis who brings forth frog as well as prince — "it is an animal symbol of the child"; the frog = "man under his chthonic aspect, his 'nothing but' aspect". The scene culminates in the hooded snake winding itself on the cross ("I am he who has taken the place of Christ") — see serpent-black-hood-cross-vision-zurich-1930 (plate 20).

occurrences.title: The cup full of fire-coloured water — IV Ezra 14:39–40
occurrences.label: The cup full of fire-coloured water
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In Ezra's revelatory dream: "Then I opened my mouth, and Io! there was reached unto me a full cup, which was full as it were with water, but the colour of it was like fire. And I took it and drank; and when I had drunk, My heart poured forth understanding, wisdom grew in my breast, and my spirit retained its memory" (¶551).

Jung cites it for the cup whose "content gives life and healing" — the same trinity the alicorn bestows (strength, health, life) and the alchemists attribute to the stone. Water with the colour of fire: the divine water (hydor theion) of Mercurius in a Jewish-apocalyptic vessel.

occurrences.title: Frederick the Great's pendulum clock stopped at his death (Sans Souci, 1786)
occurrences.label: Frederick the Great's pendulum clock stopped…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: There are numerous well-authenticated stories of a clock that stopped at the moment of its owner’s death, like Frederick the Great’s pendulum clock at Sans Souci.
body: Jung's example of symbolic patterns in which "not only the unconscious but even inanimate objects" seem to concur: "There are numerous well-authenticated stories of a clock that stopped at the moment of its owner's death, like Frederick the Great's pendulum clock at Sans Souci; of a mirror that broke, or a boiling coffee-pot that exploded, just before or during a crisis."

He hedges deliberately: even if the sceptic refuses the facts, such stories are "ever renewed and are told again and again, which is ample proof of their psychological importance" (¶480). The locus sits beside his acausal-connection material — a cultural chance-series rather than an observed one.

occurrences.title: Transoceanic ESP experiment — Durham, NC ↔ Zagreb (Rhine & Humphrey)
occurrences.label: Transoceanic ESP experiment
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Durham, North Carolina ↔ Zagreb, Yugoslavia (~4,000 miles)
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1938–41 experiments (reported J. of Parapsychology VI, 1942, pp. 52–74)

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

occurrences.quote: With the aid of synchronized watches experiments were also conducted between Durham, North Carolina, and Zagreb, Yugoslavia, about 4,000 miles, with equally positive results.
body: The long-distance wing of the Rhine series: after the first card-guessing experiments, the spatial separation between experimenter and subject was increased — in one case to 250 miles (average 10.1 hits per 25 cards; same room 11.4, next room 9.7, two rooms away 12.0) — and then, with synchronized watches, across the Atlantic between Durham and Zagreb, about 4,000 miles, "with equally positive results" (¶834; Usher and Burt had already scored positively at 960 miles).

Jung's reading: distance-independence rules out force or energy, "for otherwise... the score would fall proportionately to the square of the distance" — therefore "distance is psychically variable, and may in certain circumstances be reduced to vanishing point by a psychic condition" (¶835). With the time experiments (¶836) this grounds the "psychic relativity of space and time" first argued in "On the Nature of the Psyche" (¶440) — the experimental keel of the synchronicity concept.

occurrences.title: Marriage-horoscope moon-conjunction triad — Jung's astrological experiment
occurrences.label: Marriage-horoscope moon-conjunction triad
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Zurich (birth data from donors in Zurich, London, Rome, Vienna)
occurrences.quote: that it should single out precisely the three main positions of the horoscope from among 47 other possibilities is something supranormal and looks like the most gorgeous falsification in favour of astrology.
body: Nearly a thousand marriage horoscopes, evaluated in three batches by Frey-Rohn, tested whether classical marriage aspects (conjunction/opposition of sun–moon, Mars–Venus, ascendant–descendant) occur more often in married pairs. Statistically every maximum fell inside chance; qualitatively, all three batches peaked on a moon conjunction, and the three maxima together singled out sun, moon, and ascendant — "the three main pillars of the horoscope" — from 47 other possibilities, imitating the tradition Jung dates to Ptolemy. Jung's point is not astrology but the behaviour of chance itself: figures "meaningless in themselves" arranged a result that looks intentional — his demonstration piece for synchronicity (cw18 ¶1181).

occurrences.title: The split oak table and broken steel knife — Jung's youth
occurrences.label: The split oak table and broken steel knife
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1890s ('when a young man'); retold to J. B. Rhine, 27 Nov 1934

jung.workTitle: Synchronicity: An Acausal Connecting Principle (CW8 extract)
jung.locator: Fordham editorial preface (pdf p12) — unique to the Princeton standalone edition

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)
jung.locator: cited as the biographical germ of the synchronicity problem

occurrences.quote: When a young man, Jung saw a solid oak table suddenly split right across. Soon afterwards a strong steel knife broke in pieces for no apparent reason.
body: The founding anecdote of the synchronicity complex, as the 1973 editorial preface tells it: a solid oak table split right across before the young Jung, and soon afterwards a strong steel knife broke in pieces for no apparent reason — his superstitious mother "looked at him significantly," and he later learned that relatives attending seances with a medium had been wanting to ask him to join them.

Jung's reading (preface): the occurrences "apparently separate, became linked together in a meaningful way" — yet neither by conjuring ("it was unlikely that the split table and broken knife were caused by the thoughts of his relatives") nor by the medium "seeking to impress him magically." Synchronicity was introduced precisely "to strip off the fantasy, magic, and superstition" that gathers around such events. The episode propelled his dissertation research on occult phenomena (1902) and was still being documented for Rhine in 1934 — with a photograph of the knife (Letters i, pp. 180f.).

occurrences.title: The three tumbler rims that snapped in succession (Jung's acquaintance, ~1930)
occurrences.label: The three tumbler rims that snapped…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: About five minutes later she heard the same tinkling, and again the rim of the glass had broken off. This time she was greatly disquieted, and had a third glass brought.
body: A woman Jung knew was woken by a tinkling on her night-table: the rim of her tumbler had snapped off in a ring about a quarter-inch wide. A second glass was brought; five minutes later its rim broke off the same way. A third glass: "within twenty minutes the rim broke off again with the same tinkling noise." Three identical accidents in immediate succession — "She gave up her belief in natural causes on the spot and brought out in its place a primitive 'collective representation' — the conviction that an arbitrary power was at work" (¶123).

Jung's point is double: such series really do happen ("Misfortunes never come singly"), and the modern who meets one reverts to the primitive science of chance. The case is a first sketch of what he would later theorize as synchronicity (CW8).

occurrences.title: Vision: walking over the animus-bridge; the woman in the pileus, the golden boat and the rainbows (4 Feb 1931)
occurrences.label: Vision — walking over the animus-bridge
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: So the figure of the Self is the divine above and the animal below, like the vision of the satyr-god.
body: Patient and youth run hand in hand to a great chasm; the summoned animals are dismissed; "setting foot on either side of the chasm, the youth told me to walk over him to the other side. This I did." Then he falls into the water; alone in the dark woods, she lies by a stream and the animals come and lick her face; a woman rises from the water in a high peaked cap, laughing, as she steps into a golden boat pulled by a white sea horse; rainbows arch everywhere.

Reading: the animus at last "in his proper place... as a bridge" — mediator between conscious and collective unconscious (p263-265; compare the Viennese patient whose animus bridges the world-chasm). The licking animals show her together with her instincts — "people who are more or less on good terms with their own nature are friendly with animals" (p277). The cap is the pileus of Mithra; the golden boat and self-made rainbows complete the antique deification: "she herself is the sun now."
Jung's verdict: magnificent, but two thousand years behind — the next series must "reconstruct the Christian experience in an entirely new way" (p279-280).

occurrences.title: Egypt as the black of the eye, 'Chemia,' compared to a heart — Plutarch, Isis and Osiris 33
occurrences.label: Egypt as the black of the eye, 'Chemia,'…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "Egypt moreover, which has the blackest of soils, they call by the same name as the black portion of the eye, 'Chemia,' and compare it to a heart" (Plutarch, Isis and Osiris 33; cw14 ch. II n.91). Jung calls this an "important passage" for the relation between the eye and "Chemia" — the same discussion reports Typhon, the wicked brother-shadow of Osiris, tearing out the eye of Horus, interpreted as the new moon.

The locus welds three of Jung's chains at once: Egypt/keme as the black prima materia, the eye (of Horus) as the arcane pupil-point, and the heart as the bodily centre — Chemia as black, seeing, and living.

occurrences.title: The chen-yen, the true and complete man — Wei Po-yang's Ts'an T'ung Ch'i
occurrences.label: The chen-yen, the true and complete man
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Wei Po-yang, "the oldest Chinese alchemist known to us (2nd cent. a.d.)", describes the chen-yen, "the true or complete man, who is the beginning and end of the work: 'He is and he is not. He resembles avast pool of water, suddenly sinking and suddenly floating'"; in him are "mixed the squareness, the roundness, the diameter, and the dimensions... having been in existence before the beginning of the heavens and the earth: lordly, lordly, high and revered" (cw13 ¶432).

Jung's reading: the "closed region" of intercommunicating labyrinths protects the work; the black mass — "the massa Confusa, the chaos or nigredo of Western alchemy... black outside and white inside, like lead" — is the chen-yen hidden in darkness, "threatened by the rational and correct conduct of life" (cw13 ¶433). Giving way to the self's urgencies and perishing is "a true thysia of the self" (cw13 ¶433).
Verbatim: “He is and he is not. He resembles avast pool of water, suddenly sinking and suddenly floating.” (cw13 ¶432)

occurrences.title: Chidher, the eternally young one — Rückert's poem after al-Qazwini's legend
occurrences.label: Chidher, the eternally young one
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Germany (Deutscher Musenalmanach, 1830, pp. 39ff; legend translated in the 1820s)
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1830 poem; legend via 1820s translation of al-Qazwini

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: the poem by Rückert about Chidher, the eternally young one who returns every five hundred years. Rückert took this story from the translation of a legend that was published in the 1820s.
body: The route by which Khidr is known "in our regions": Rückert's poem about Chidher, "the eternally young one who returns every five hundred years," taken from a legend translated in the 1820s — by al-Qazwini, whom Jung describes as "a Persian poet who lived around the year 900" (in fact the great 13th-century cosmographer; Jung's dating preserved as a discrepancy). In the legend a young man loves his friend Khidr; the king, hearing of the wonderful storyteller, summons him and wants to be taught and follow him — and Khidr says he cannot do that. Jung adduces the poem as evidence of how little-known Khidr is (no "Chadir" entry under "Islam" in Hastings's Encyclopaedia), before turning to Sura 18 itself.

occurrences.title: The massacre of the innocents — Herod at Bethlehem (Matthew 2:16–18)
occurrences.label: The massacre of the innocents
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~6–4 BCE (Herod's last years); Gospel of Matthew
occurrences.quote: The hero's birth and the heroic life are always threatened.
body: Warned by the Magi of a newborn "king of the Jews," Herod orders all male infants of Bethlehem and its region killed. The tyrant's counter-move against the threatened divine child; liturgically commemorated as Holy Innocents.

Jung's use (¶321, "The Development of Personality"): the third member of his triad of threatened hero-births — "The serpents sent by Hera to destroy the infant Hercules, the python that tries to strangle Apollo at birth, the massacre of the innocents, all these tell the same story." The point is structural, not confessional: wherever the hero/inner voice announces a new way, the old order (Hera, Python, Herod) rises to strangle it at birth — "To develop the personality is a gamble" (¶321). Sits beside ¶318's solar birth of the hero.

occurrences.title: Bereshith Rabbati: the Messiah child plunged into the sea
occurrences.label: Bereshith Rabbati — the Messiah child plunged…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: France? (Moses ha-Darshan of Narbonne; midrash compilation)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Elias finds in Bethlehem "a young woman sitting before her door with a newborn child lying on the ground beside her, flecked with blood" — born at the evil hour when the temple was destroyed; "he neither walks, nor sees, nor speaks, nor hears, but lies there like a stone." Suddenly a wind from the four corners "bore the child away, and plunged him into the sea": 400 years in the great sea, 80 in the rising smoke of the children of Korah, 80 under the gates of Rome, wandering until the end of days (cw09ii par. 167rom Wunsche).
Jung: the sea = the Beyond = the unconscious; the endangered, latent Messiah explains the delay of his appearing — near enough the Talmud's critical 530 years to compare.

occurrences.title: Adepts as 'children of the golden head' — Greek alchemy
occurrences.label: Adepts as 'children of the golden head'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In Greek alchemy the adepts were called 'children of the golden head.
body: In Greek alchemy the adepts were called "children of the golden head"; the "simple" (arcane) substance was called the "Golden Head, after the god-sent Daniel, God's mouthpiece." Jung at cw14 ¶626 connects the motif with the Splendor solis' dismembered man "whose body was white like salt" and "His head was of fine gold," with the golden head as oracle-giver of Pope Sylvester II, and with the head as corpus rotundum — the arcane substance.

occurrences.title: 'Chiwantopel, a hypnagogic drama' — Miss Miller
occurrences.label: Chiwantopel, a hypnagogic drama' — Miss Miller
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Miller's third unconscious creation: after an evening of anxiety, lines, sparks and spirals of fire, an invocation, the sphinx and the Aztec, and finally a name forming "bit by bit" — "Chi-wan-to-pel", son of an Inca of Peru — awaited with "positively mystical expectation".

Jung's reading: the finest symbol of the libido is "the human figure, conceived as a demon or hero" (¶251); the birth of Chiwantopel from Popocatepetl means "I make, produce, invent him out of myself" — anal-birth of the hero-figure (¶279); the name-giving as baptism (¶274).
Verbatim: Lines, sparks, and spirals of fire passed before my eyes, symptoms of nervousness and ocular fatigue (cw05 ¶251).

occurrences.title: Christ's marriage consummated on the cross — Augustine
occurrences.label: Christ's marriage consummated on the cross
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: He came to the marriage bed of the cross, and there, in mounting it, he consummated his marriage.
body: "Like a bridegroom Christ went forth from his chamber, he went out with a presage of his nuptials into the field of the world. He ran like a giant exulting on his way, and came to the marriage bed of the cross, and there, in mounting it, he consummated his marriage... he yielded up also the carbuncle, as the jewel of his blood, and he joined the woman to himself for ever."
Jung at cw14 ¶568: Augustine (possibly behind Vigenerus) here supplied "the model for the language and ideas of the alchemists" — the sponsa as the Church presented as a chaste virgin (2 Cor 11:2).

occurrences.title: Jesus-Christ crucifie par les vertus — Besancon codex
occurrences.label: Jesus-Christ crucifie par les vertus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: He is being crucified by all the named virtues; one is hammering the nails into his feet and his hands, another one is stabbing his side, and so on.
body: A 13th-century French miniature Jung brought to the seminar: Christ crucified by the virtues of which he had been the model. 'It was his virtues, his greatness, that really led him to the cross... the named virtues killed him, tore him to bits' — and the cross is 'the well-known individuation symbol': individuation is the necessary outcome of moral development. Parallels: christ-figure-crucifix-pulling-nails-nuremberg-1050 · mantle-divided-dice-john-19-30ce.

occurrences.title: The twice-born Christ and the God who departs — Doketic Christianity
occurrences.label: The twice-born Christ and the God who departs
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Jung's excursus on "the individual himself is still the latest creation" reaches the Gnostic idea of Christ: "he was not born a Christ; he had to be twice-born, baptized in the Jordan, in order to be the real God Christ." The Holy Ghost generated the man miraculously, "but he was still only an ordinary man though his generation was a miracle. So the Holy Ghost has to descend a second time in order to make Christ into a God, and the God left him in the garden before his execution took place".

Therefore the cry from the cross — "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" — meant "only the man… found himself hanging on the cross… He had been entirely instrumental, and the tragedy was that the God had gone out of the man before he was dead. That is the belief of the Doketic form of Christianity which was a very serious competitor of the Christianity that survived".
The twice-born king continues the Pharaoh-Osiris line: coronation "is the equipment of a human being with the sun or the cosmic quality".

occurrences.title: The Alexamenos mock-crucifixion graffito — Palatine, Rome
occurrences.label: The Alexamenos mock-crucifixion graffito
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Palatine Hill, Rome (wall of the Imperial page school)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: as is shown by the mock crucifixion scratched on the wall of the Imperial Cadet School on the Palatine
body: Jung (¶463) invokes "the mock crucifixion scratched on the wall of the Imperial Cadet School on the Palatine" (reproduced in Symbols of Transformation, pl. XLIII) as proof of the old vulgar prejudice "that the god of the Jews... was an ass — a prejudice which extended to Christ himself". The graffito — an ass-headed figure on the cross, with the taunting inscription about Alexamenos worshipping his god — is the oldest known depiction of Christ's crucifixion, and for Jung a document of the theriomorphic danger that always shadowed the incarnate God: the trickster-beast at the boundary of the most sacred.

occurrences.title: Council of Chalcedon: the Dyophysite formula (451)
occurrences.label: Council of Chalcedon: the Dyophysite formula
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: once more asserted the standpoint of the abstract and inconceivable as against the sensuous and naturalistic formula of the Dyophysites
body: Jung's third christological type-conflict, after Ebionite–Docetist and Arian: "the revolt of the Monophysites (who upheld the absolute unity of Christ's nature) against the Dyophysite formula of the Council of Chalcedon (which upheld the inseparable duality of Christ, his human and divine nature coexisting in one body) once more asserted the standpoint of the abstract and inconceivable as against the sensuous and naturalistic formula of the Dyophysites" (¶31). The Monophysite position = accent on the abstract, inconceivable; the Dyophysite = sensuous, naturalistic. Jung further notes the psychological kinship of the Monophysite view with Nestorianism's opponents (Cyrillian physical oneness), and the persecuted Pelagians' advocacy by Nestorius (¶33–34).

occurrences.title: The pious patient who lets Christ decide (tax-cheating case)
occurrences.label: The pious patient who lets Christ decide
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "A very pious woman patient — she is not in the Oxford Movement, but in the Middle Ages": whenever anything goes wrong, or she wants something immoral like cheating, "she simply unloads it on Christ." Christ then "decides upon a very modern trick, how to cheat the state of taxes" — five francs may move from the poor-box envelope to the taxi driver; if conscience pricks, she asks Jung, who "as a rule" happens to agree with Christ.

Jung's reading: the principle of unloading must be broken through — one cannot live by principles without necessary exceptions; she cannot decide herself "on account of too narrow a consciousness." But the mechanism carries her: "he can carry her way beyond her moral scruples... And that is of course her emotion — Christ is her emotion". Mrs. Sigg hears animus contents projected into Christ; Jung half-concedes — with her it is "a real thing, not only a façon de parler. It is bordering on magic."

occurrences.title: Eleventh-century crucifix: Christ pulling the nails out of the cross (Germanic Museum, Nuremberg)
occurrences.label: Eleventh-century crucifix
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: a so-called crucifix of the eleventh century, which represents Christ pulling the nails out of the cross and coming away from it.
body: In the Germanic Museum, Nuremberg, Jung saw an eleventh-century crucifix "which represents Christ pulling the nails out of the cross and coming away from it, a most extraordinary thing" — the extreme case of the early type where Christ stands before the cross with outstretched arms, not nailed to it. It documents his iconographic argument: the equilateral sun-disk cross of early Christianity slowly elongated into the Gothic cross set upon the earth (Calvary's three lines), the detached deity descending until the symbol "lost its divinity" and took on human form.

occurrences.title: 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' — the cry from the Cross
occurrences.label: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: The one breach in Christ's lack of self-reflection: "the despairing cry from the Cross: 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' Here his human nature attains divinity; at that moment God experiences what it means to be a mortal man and drinks to the dregs what he made his faithful servant Job suffer. Here is given the answer to Job" (¶647).

The moment is "as divine as it is human, as 'eschatological' as it is 'psychological'" — the God-man experiences God's own dark side from below. This passage gives the book its title and its hinge: the wrong done to Job is answered from inside the Incarnation itself.

occurrences.title: Christ in the grapevine pergola — silver goblet found at Damascus
occurrences.label: Christ in the grapevine pergola
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: found in a well in Damascus; now in a safe in America
occurrences.quote: The goblet is of very thin hammered silver, argent repousse, and on it Christ is depicted sitting in a sort of pergola of grapevines and looking exactly like Dionysus.
body: A famous goblet of very thin hammered silver (argent repoussé), found down a well in Damascus — probably church treasure hidden in the sixth century during the persecution of Julian the Apostate, now "in a safe in America." On it Christ sits in a pergola of grapevines "and looking exactly like Dionysus." Jung's concrete proof that there were "plenty of opportunities for Christ to be mistaken for Dionysus besides his sacrificial death," and the perfect artifact for the diabolical-anticipation debate.

occurrences.title: 'The dog and monkey troupe wanting to play the Saviour' — the lucid interval of a delusional patient (Burghölzli)
occurrences.label: The dog and monkey troupe wanting…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A patient with whom no sane conversation was possible — "only a crazy mixture of delusional ideas and queer words" — fell seriously physically ill, and changed completely: friendly, obliging, patient, his eyes "shone quietly and with understanding." One morning he forestalled Jung's greeting with his fixed formula: "Here comes another of the dog and monkey troupe wanting to play the Saviour" (¶360). "Then I knew his physical trouble was over. From that moment the whole of his reason was as if blown away again."

Jung's reading: the returning refrain is the diagnostic sign — "reason still survives, but is pushed away into some remote corner by the mind's preoccupation with pathological ideas" (¶361). The delusional world's inversion of the Saviour — doctors as animal-troupe mocking divinity — shows the God-image still structuring the psychosis, only pathologically placed.

occurrences.title: The headless Christ with the sun-disk of Autun cathedral
occurrences.label: The headless Christ with the sun-disk…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Cathedral of Autun, Burgundy (photograph shown in seminar)
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~12th c. figure; Jung suspects an esoteric sect of the 13th-c. mysticism
occurrences.quote: The spiritual sun in Christianity is the specific truth of Christianity, it is the Logos, and it is symbolized as the circle with the cross.
body: "I have a photograph of the god without a head to show you. The sun, with the early Christian cross of equal branches, is in the place of the head". Jung later identifies the figure as from the cathedral at Autun and reads the headless god as esoteric Christianity: the disk is "a spiritual sun," the Logos, symbolized as the circle with the cross — "in the East is called a mandala... the symbol of individuation". The body is the past, the world of heretofore; the new light rises not identical with the body — exactly the structure of the patient's giant-egg-black-head sequence. The Latin inscription "Quisque resurget ita quem non trahit impia vita..." seals the meaning. Baumann's report of 12th-c. headless gods with a disk for a head feeds the same stream.

occurrences.title: Jung's anthology of the sayings of Jesus — Zofingia research notes (Basel, 1899)
occurrences.label: Jung's anthology of the sayings of Jesus
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.yearDisplay: January 1899 (research notes for the Ritschl lecture)
body: Forty-one numbered sayings of Jesus compiled by the 23-year-old Jung from Matthew, Mark and Luke — his own research dossier for the Ritschl lecture, preserved with the manuscript (ed. n.1: "These are Jung's research notes for the lecture on Ritschl"). He groups them under his own headings: "Knowledge" (mysteries of the kingdom, parables, Son of Man in glory, the Transfiguration), "Miracles" (faith as mustard seed), "Appearances after death" (Luke 24). His very first entry carries the editors' note that these "first words to the human race" were spoken by John the Baptist.

The dossier shows student-Jung reading the Gospels esoterically: the kingdom's mysteries given to disciples, spirits made subject to the apostles, the Son-of-Man parousia sayings, Satan falling as lightning — the occult thread of his earlier lectures touching the Gospel text itself.
Verbatim: "Christ's first words to the human race: Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. [3:2]"

occurrences.title: Christ the light-bringer of the Evangelium Veritatis — Jung Codex
occurrences.label: Christ the light-bringer of the Evangelium…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Hellenistic-Egyptian milieu; codex found in Upper Egypt (Nag Hammadi) → 'Jung Codex', Jung Institute Zurich
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~2nd c. (Valentinian text); ~4th c. papyrus; presented to the Jung Institute, Zurich, 1953
occurrences.quote: It belongs therefore to the series of numerous “phenomena of assimilation,” its purpose being to assimilate this strange and hardly understandable message to the Hellenistic-Egyptian world of thought.
body: Jung's address at the presentation of the Jung Codex (1953) — the papyrus purchased with Mr. Page's money and housed by Dr. Meier (¶1826) — singles out the Evangelium Veritatis, "an important Valentinian text that affords us some insight into the mentality of the second century A.D." Less a gospel than a commentary on the Christian message, it belongs to his "phenomena of assimilation": pagan-world psychic reactions that assimilate the strange message to Hellenistic-Egyptian thought.

His reading: for the Valentinian author "Christ was primarily a metaphysical figure, a light-bringer" whose work is "deliverance from agnosia" — leading the individual "back to his origins through selfknowledge" — a direct link to Hippolytus's accounts of the Naassenes and Peratics. The assimilation reaction shows "the unconscious of that age" interpreting the phenomenon of Christ with archetypal images (fish, snake, lion, peacock, ¶1827–28), a process continued in Kabbala and philosophical alchemy (¶1830) and prefiguring the modern Son-of-Man transformations (¶1832).

occurrences.title: Christ as 'the sun of the East' — Melito of Sardis, Peri Loutrou (~170 AD)
occurrences.label: Christ as 'the sun of the East'
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Melito's treatise Peri Loutrou calls Christ "The sun of the East... As the only sun he rose in the heavens" (¶158) — the sharpest single witness in Jung's dossier on Christ as Sol novus. The dossier runs: Philo Judaeus (sun as image of the divine Logos), Ambrose's "O sol salutis," Pseudo-Cyprian (Christ born "on the same day on which the sun was created, the 28th of March," Malachi's sun of righteousness, ¶159), the Pseudo-Chrysostom De solstitiis (Dec 25 as "the birthday of the Unconquerable One," ¶160), Eusebius of Alexandria (Christians praying to the rising sun into the fifth century, ¶161), Augustine's corrective ("he through whom the sun is made," ¶162), the nimbus and halo, apostles as zodiac signs, Tertullian's heathen, the Manichean sun-God, and the dedication Διὶ Ἡλίῳ θεῷ μεγάλῳ βασιλεῖ Ἰησοῦ (¶163).
Jung's thesis: the sun-coronations of the mystery religions are "the psychological roots" of this imagery — visionary light-processes congealing into liturgy (¶158).

occurrences.title: The 'Christ' who makes obscene jokes in church (Jung's old patient)
occurrences.label: The 'Christ' who makes obscene jokes in church
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: That old patient of mine tells me that Christ sometimes makes obscenejokes, particularly in church, which is shocking and makes it hard for her to maintain the theory that it is Christ.
body: An elderly woman patient reports that her inner "Christ" sometimes makes obscene jokes, especially in church — which "makes it hard for her to maintain the theory that it is Christ." Jung refuses to pathologize it: "I don't say this is wrong: it happens as a necessary compensation for a pious attitude which is not too real." The obscene fantasy shows "who you are," and illustrates the seminar's larger point that one is "never quite sure whose voice it is" when an inner command speaks — hence prufet die Geister (1 John 4:1).

The sacred figure contaminated by the obscene is the trickster-face of the numen — cf. the aischrologia of the mysteries. Parallels: holy-ghost-demon-god-sculptor-patient-1920s · trickster-delight-makers-pueblo.

occurrences.title: Orpheus-Bacchus crucified — the Gnostic gem of Berlin
occurrences.label: Orpheus-Bacchus crucified
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "The seal to which I referred is in Berlin, and it represents quite indubitably the crucifixion, with the inscription 'Orpheus-Bacchus,' so those two heathen gods were obviously competitors of Christ in those days". Christ was closely associated with Bacchus and Orpheus at the beginning of our era — old mystery gods of the period; Eisler's Orpheus-The Fisher gives the Bacchic fish symbolism (Pompeii).
An "Orpheus" who was crucified: the mystery god explained by the same symbolism as both Orpheus and Dionysos — evidence for the savior-mystery syncretism into which Jung reads Nietzsche's superman.

occurrences.title: Pistis Sophia: the spirit like unto Jesus bound to the bed
occurrences.label: Pistis Sophia — the spirit like unto Jesus…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Mary tells Jesus how, when he was a child in the vineyard with Joseph, "the spirit came down from the height, and came unto me in the house, like unto thee, and I knew him not, but thought that he was thou" — she seizes and binds him to the foot of the bed until Jesus finds him; the two gaze at each other, embrace, "and you became one".

Jung's reading: Jesus is "a double personality" — "truth sprouting from the earth" rising from chaos/hyle, and pneuma descending as "justice looking down from heaven" — the Gnostic Redeemer's discrimination of natures exemplified.

occurrences.title: The apocalyptic Christophany — Son of Man with the two-edged sword (Revelation 1)
occurrences.label: The apocalyptic Christophany
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: The initial vision: "Christ blended with the Ancient of Days, having the likeness of a man and the Son of Man. Out of his mouth goes a 'sharp two-edged sword,' which would seem more suitable for fighting and the shedding of blood than for demonstrating brotherly love" (¶699). John falls "as though dead" — overcome by fear, not love, despite the epistle "God is love".

The letters to the seven churches follow (¶700-705): threats, "synagogue of Satan", Jezebel struck dead, "Those whom I love, I reprove and chasten". Jung's verdict: "This apocalyptic 'Christ' behaves rather like a bad-tempered, power-conscious 'boss' who very much resembles the 'shadow' of a love-preaching bishop" (¶706).

occurrences.title: Toldoth Jeshu: Jesus the son of Pandira (medieval Jewish anti-legend)
occurrences.label: Toldoth Jeshu: Jesus the son of Pandira
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Jewish tradition (book burned repeatedly by the church in the Middle Ages)
occurrences.quote: the boy born out of that illegitimate union was called Jesus-Jesus, the son of Pandira.
body: In building the anima scale — Chawwa, Helen, Mary, Sophia — Jung produces the counter-legend: "In that book, it is said that Mary, though of royal blood, was very poor. She was a woman's hairdresser, and she had an affair with an Egyptian soldier named Pandira, and the boy born out of that illegitimate union was called Jesus — Jesus, the son of Pandira". "So the story of the Holy Ghost is reduced to a very personal, rather delicate affair. Yet that illegitimate relationship to the Holy Ghost is always on a higher level": the prostitute of the spirit, bridged by the hierodule (cf. Mary of Egypt). "If you look at it with unprejudiced eyes, Mary was an adulterous woman too."

occurrences.title: The two Jesuses of the ward — inflated patients compared
occurrences.label: The two Jesuses of the ward
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Jung's clinical exemplar of inflation: one patient declared himself Jesus; a second patient in the same ward made the same claim. Jung put them in one room to settle it. Half an hour later he found one behind the stove, the other tapping on the window. Asked who was the real Jesus, one pointed at the other: "Of course that is a mad ass."

The lesson: "He saw right away that he was a mad man but that he himself was mad he could not see." Inflation is functional — "still in a liquid condition" — unlike congealed psychosis; the cure depends on whether the patient takes "a sort of compensatory or contrasting attitude."

Verbatim: "But it happened once that I had another man in the same ward who said he was Jesus too; we had two.Jesuses, and how could I make out which was the one? I simply put them together in the same room to let them have it out." (pdf p163, OCR as in text)

occurrences.title: Valentinus: Christ 'cast off the shadow from himself'
occurrences.label: Valentinus — Christ cast off the shadow…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Rome? (Valentinus; reported by Irenaeus, Adv. haer. I, 11, 1; II, 5, 1)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Irenaeus records the Valentinian teaching that Christ, born of the mother outside the pleroma, came forth "not without a kind of shadow," but "being masculine, cast off the shadow from himself" and returned to the Pleroma; the mother, left in the shadow, bore the Demiurge.

For Jung this is the Gnostics tackling the problem of evil "on a broader basis than the Church Fathers": the cut-off counterpart is recognizable in the figure of Antichrist. At par. 171 he re-reads the shadow as the Yahwistic law under which Christ was born.

occurrences.title: 'Jesus, our grasshopper' — the mission boys' hymn (Africa)
occurrences.label: Jesus, our grasshopper' — the mission boys' hymn
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: when one asks about Jesus, they say he is a grasshopper and sing a hymn "Jesus, our grasshopper.
body: The "mission boy," severed from his ancestor-ground and schooled in a religion he cannot digest, answers the question about Jesus:

Jung's verdict is double-edged: "To preach a highly developed religion, which even we do not understand, to such people is utterly ridiculous. Our missionaries work pure magic out there" — prayers repeated "with their lips, but their hearts cannot follow." The locus shows a symbol cut loose from its living context degrading into a magic token (indexed as an anecdote of the volume, print p1530); it is the trans-cultural mirror of his European claim that Christianity persists as headless psychology.

occurrences.title: Christ hanging on the living tree (German Middle Ages)
occurrences.label: Christ hanging on the living tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "in the German Middle Ages, Christ was represented as hanging, not on the cross, but on the tree of life, and according to the old legend, it was the wood of that tree of life which was used for the cross. You probably have seen such pictures in galleries, where Christ is depicted as hanging on a tree with branches and leaves, a living tree."
Placed between Odin's windswept tree and the Bremen Odin-cross: the cross-tree identification that lets the reviving Germanic cult clothe itself in Christian form.

occurrences.title: Christ 'compared and united' with the stone — Aquarium sapientum
occurrences.label: Christ 'compared and united' with the stone
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Aquarium sapientum (1608): the raven's-head blackness of the decomposed stone is compared with Christ 'full of griefs and sicknesses... a worm and no man' (Isa 53, Ps 22): 'it is not unfitly compared with Christ when the putrefied body of the Sun lies dead, inactive, like ashes, in the bottom of the phial, until, as a result of greater heat, its soul by degrees and little by little descends to it again, and once more infuses, moistens, and saturates the decaying and all but dead body' (cw14 ¶485). Christ at the Mount of Olives and on the cross was 'roasted by the fire of the divine wrath'; his resurrection and 'roseate Tincture' heal 'us sinful men in body and soul'; the stone's 'material and preparation... an outstanding type and lifelike image of the incarnation of Christ' (¶485). Jung: the adept's Passion 'happens to the alchemist... in the form expressed by the alchemical myth' (¶492); cf. the 'furnace of the cross' passage (¶494).

occurrences.title: Christ the artist 'fashioning living men' — van Gogh's letter to Émile Bernard
occurrences.label: Christ the artist 'fashioning living men'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Miss Hannah quotes van Gogh: Christ "got beyond the period where he had to carve stone or paint, and worked on humanity direct". The letter itself (editor's footnote): "This unbelievable artist… made neither statues, nor pictures nor books; indeed, he said clearly enough what he was doing-fashioning living men, immortal beings."

Jung's response qualifies the artist's projection: "that is the point of view of an artist with reference to Christ. Obviously Christ never thought of painting." The comparison goes both ways — a doctor might equally say he "gave up general practice and became a psychotherapist." Yet Jung concedes the underlying thought through Mani, "who was the founder of a religion" and "also a fine painter… said to have decorated two temples with frescoes" — creative power can take many forms; the field open to Christ's time was simply narrow.
The locus belongs to the discussion of whether the creative impulse can be turned inward upon individuation: van Gogh's letter is the artist's version of that question.

occurrences.title: 'Christ is our locust' - the mistranslated hymn in East Africa
occurrences.label: Christ is our locust' - the mistranslated hymn…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The missionary, who did not understand the language very well, translated a hymn, \"Christ is our hope,\" but he put the accent upon the wrong syllable, so the word meant locust, and for years the Negroes sang: \"Christ is our locust.\
body: A missionary who "did not understand the language very well" translated the hymn "Christ is our hope" with the accent on the wrong syllable, "so the word meant locust, and for years the Negroes sang: 'Christ is our locust.' They were quite satisfied, it meant much more to them than the original version". Only the bishop who really knew the language "discovered to his horror what they were singing."

Jung: "You see, that fits in with the old belief that God also appears in the form of animals" - against the dissociation that begins "when animals are no longer included in the religious symbol or creed".

occurrences.title: 'If thou knowest what thou art doing thou art blest' — Gnostic morality logion
occurrences.label: If thou knowest what thou art doing thou art…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: If thou knowest what thou art doing thou art blessed, if thou knowest not then thou art cursed.
body: The sabbath logion Jung sets beside the "near the fire" fragment: "If thou knowest what thou art doing thou art blessed, if thou knowest not then thou art cursed." — "That is also a bit of the Gnostic morality which has, of course, been cleared out of the canonical text." Consciousness, not conformity, is the decisive thing: the same act blessed or cursed according to the doer's knowing.

Jung generalizes it into a formula for the educated: "it is surely a formula which would help philosophers and educated people to live; since they could not be as naive as the masses, they had to have such a formula, otherwise they would not have become Christian" — the same stratum Karpokrates served with his subjective reading of the Sermon on the Mount.

occurrences.title: Christ in the mandorla with the four evangelists — Saint-Jacques-des-Guérets
occurrences.label: Christ in the mandorla with the four evangelists
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The Son of Man is an anticipation of the idea of the self
body: Plate 101: "Christ in the mandorla, surrounded by the symbols of the four evangelists," mural at Saint-Jacques-des-Guérets. It stands in the world-clock commentary's time-symbolism cluster: "There is also a connection with the symbolism of Horus: on the one hand, Christ enthroned with the four emblems of the evangelists—three animals and an angel (fig. 101); on the other, Father Horus with his four sons, or Osiris with the four sons of Horus" (¶314). "The Son of Man is an anticipation of the idea of the self."
Christ-in-mandorla-with-four is the Christian member of the centre-and-quaternity family the world clock vision joins.

occurrences.title: Christ so poor the devil did not recognize him — Le Conte du Saint Gral
occurrences.label: Christ so poor the devil did not recognize him
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: Christ was so poor that the devil did not recognize him.
body: "Recently I read Le Conte du Saint Gral, a French account of the Grail legend. There it also says that Christ was so poor that the devil did not recognize him." Jung sets the line beside the Gnostic view of the mutabilis — the shape-changing Savior who "goes up, unrecognized, through the orbits of the planets, and is not recognized by the Archons." Khidr belongs to the same family: able to appear in every form, the sudden wanderer whose doings seem to go wrong but prove exactly right.

occurrences.title: Christ as rider on the white horse — North German sect
occurrences.label: Christ as rider on the white horse
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In North Germany there is a sect that worships Christ in the form of a rider on a white horse.
body: A sect in North Germany in the neo-pagan years worshipping "Christ in the form of a rider on a white horse" (cw18 ¶1329). Jung reports it alongside the Wotanistic symbolism of the three-million-strong neo-pagan movement as evidence of the "eruption of the collective unconscious" (¶1329): the ecstatic, Germanic Christ of Revelation 19 surfacing exactly when the national unconscious regressed. It "does not go as far as collective hallucinations," but waves of enthusiasm and ecstasy run high.

occurrences.title: 'By Christ's love I have been wounded unto death' — Mechtild of Magdeburg (~1250–80)
occurrences.label: By Christ's love I have been wounded unto death'
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung's example of "nice... ambivalence... in the language of mysticism": Mechtild of Magdeburg says, "By Christ's love I have been wounded unto death" (¶1079). Love and killing in one act — the erotic wound of the mystical marriage, death received as grace.

Jung sets it beside the erotic jokes of Apuleius' Golden Ass and the Mithraic formula "The bull is the father of the snake and the snake is the father of the bull" — creation through the killed god, as with Christ's death redeeming "for life eternal" (¶1079). The mystic's wound-of-love is the Christian register of the ambivalent libido whose oscillation Jung has just fixed "between the symbols of the lion and the snake" (¶1078).

occurrences.title: Christ as the great serpent carrying the twelve signs of the zodiac
occurrences.label: Christ as the great serpent carrying the twelve…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: From the fourth-dimension meditation on man-as-serpent: "Christ is represented as a great serpent who carries twelve signs on his back, meaning the twelve signs of the zodiac and also the twelve apostles. He says, 'I am the vine, ye are the branches.' He is the zodiacal serpent and they are the manifestation of the months." Resumed 29 Jan 1930: Christ's body was the Church year; the vine and branches, the twelve disciples, the twelve months and the zodiacal serpent are one organism of time.

occurrences.title: Christ as the snake carrying twelve stars on its back — early Christian drawings
occurrences.label: Christ as the snake carrying twelve stars…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: In the time-discussion of the fairy dream: "Religious heroes were often portrayed in connection with time. In the Upanishads, too, Prajapati is the year, is Chronos, the creator of the world. Christ is also the ecclesiastical year; in certain early Christian drawings he was depicted as a snake carrying the stars on its back—twelve stars representing the twelve disciples. It is the time, the year with its twelve months".

The locus gathers Jung's time-snake series: the Zodiacal snake, Prajapati as the world-year, and the Mithraic Aion at the main altar, "enveloped by the Zodiacal snake, Zrvan akarana, meaning 'boundless time.'" For the dream: "The three snakes in our dream are probably a reference to time."

occurrences.title: Morienus — the law of time and the fearful final transformation
occurrences.label: Morienus — the law of time…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Basel (print; Morienus legendary — the monk who instructed Prince Calid)

jung.locator: 'Faust and Alchemy', Psychological Club lecture, 8 Oct. 1949 (pdf p1040 n.5)
'The Psychology of the Transference' ¶407 n.18 (per cw18 pdf p1040 n.2)

body: In his 1949 Club lecture 'Faust and Alchemy' Jung adduced Morienus on time as the great transformer of the operator himself: "For the long lapse of time upsets man, who is under the law of time, and transforms him … after the final transformation, however, fearful death follows" (Artis auriferae, Basel 1610, II, p. 14). The opus outlasts the artifex: duration itself does the transmuting, and the opus's completion (final transformatio) borders on the mortal transitus — the same sub specie aeternitatis logic Jung heard in Faust II. Other Morienus material in the vault concerns the lapis as self ('thou art its ore'); this locus is Morienus on time.
Verbatim (as quoted in cw18 pdf p1040 n.5): “For the long lapse of time upsets man, who is under the law of time, and transforms him … after the final transformation, however, fearful death follows.”

occurrences.title: The mascot doll to be strengthened — South American case (Lecture 13)
occurrences.label: The mascot doll to be strengthened
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: Jung's exhibit of the Latin-American fusion with the primitive level: the son of Austrian parents (European household within, Indian world without), nearly driven crazy, is set by a beloved professor on a course of fetish-strengthening. The mascot is a doll: first carried about the streets in his arms despite great shame; then swung three times in the face of the president of the republic through the police cordon; finally — "the doll was not yet as strong as it ought to be!" — a little girl must be throttled over the doll "till she was nearly dead. Then the force of her agony as she approached death would go into the doll and it would be really strong." The boy broke down and stayed neurotic, fearing that speech would let the strength out of the doll. Jung reads the doll functionally as the churinga: an object into which power and sickness pass; the case shows what "keeping out of the split between the conscious and the unconscious" costs the Latins who mixed with the primitives — "they have lost their superiority".

occurrences.title: Rubbing the churinga to absorb sickness — Arunta healing rite, Central Australia
occurrences.label: Rubbing the churinga to absorb sickness
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: Jung's illustration that the primitive deals with the unconscious by work: the sick man "goes to a place where his churinga8 is hidden in the rocks. He rubs it. The churinga is full of healthy magic, and when he rubs it, this gets into his system and his sickness goes into the churinga which then is put back in its place in the rocks where it can digest the sickness and refill itself with healthy magic. That replaces prayer". We get strength from God through prayer; the primitive "gets strength from God by work" — all ceremonies are work, even the "most laborious dances for the spirits." The rite backs Jung's once-attacked claim in Psychology of the Unconscious that regular work is the greatest help against the dangers of rebirth. Source: Spencer and Gillen's Northern Tribes of Central Australia (1904), his constant ethnographic quarry.

occurrences.title: Rubbing the snake-ancestor churinga while singing its Alcheringa history — Arunta rite (Spencer & Gillen, 1899)
occurrences.label: Rubbing the snake-ancestor churinga…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: Jung's prime exhibit, in "On Psychic Energy," of the churinga as a transformer of libido, quoting Spencer and Gillen (p. 277): "A man who owns such a Churinga as this snake one will constantly rub it over with his hand, singing as he does so the Alcheringa history of the snake, and gradually comes to feel that there is some special association between him and the sacred object—that a virtue of some kind passes from it to him and also from him to it" (cw08 ¶119). Fetishes become recharged by standing for weeks near a stronger fetish (Pechuel-Loesche).

Jung's reading: the primitive "rubs his churinga rhythmically and takes the magic power of the fetish into himself, at the same time giving it a fresh 'charge'" (¶92) — the churinga is a libido analogue, an energic concept meaning (1) the ritual object, (2) the body of an individual ancestor from whom the life force comes, (3) the mystical property of any object (¶119).

occurrences.title: Soul-stones of the Birs cave and Burgaschi lake-dwellings (Switzerland, prehistoric)
occurrences.label: Soul-stones of the Birs cave…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Birs river cave near Basel; Burgaschi lake, Canton Solothurn
body: "A cache of 'soul stones,' similar to churingas, was found in a cave on the river Birs near Basel, and during recent excavations of the pole-dwellings on the little lake at Burgaeschi, in Canton Solothurn, a group of boulders was discovered wrapped in the bark of birch trees" (cw13 ¶129).

Jung's evidence that the magic-stone idea — otherwise Australian, Melanesian, Indian — is found "in Europe itself" (¶129): prehistoric Alpine soul-stone caches, material for the argument that the alchemists' stone-God-image rests on something far older than alchemy.

occurrences.title: Churinga — soul-stones of the Central Australian tribes
occurrences.label: Churinga — soul-stones…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Australian child-stone complex: "the view of the Australian aborigines that children's souls live in a special stone called the 'child-stone.' They can be made to migrate into a uterus by rubbing the 'child-stone' with a churinga. Churingas may be boulders, or oblong stones artificially shaped and decorated... The Australians and the Melanesians maintain that churingas come from the totem ancestor... and are full of arunquiltha or mana. They are taboo, are buried in caches or hidden in clefts... In order to 'charge' them, they are buried among the graves so that they can soak up the mana of the dead. They promote the growth of field-produce, increase the fertility of men and animals, heal wounds" (cw13 ¶128). Daubed with red ochre, anointed with fat, bedded in leaves, copiously spat on ("spittle = mana").
Jung's use: the stone-symbol's prehistory behind the alchemical God-stone (¶128) — matter carrying soul and mana.

occurrences.title: Churning of the Milky Ocean for amrita — Rajput miniature (plate XV)
occurrences.label: Churning of the Milky Ocean for amrita
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The gods churn the ocean of milk with the serpent Vasuki as rope to raise the amrita, the drink of immortality; the stir is "like the fire".

Jung's reading: soma and fire "are united in Agni" — "Soma is also the 'nourishing drink'. Its mythological characteristics coincide with those of fire" (¶246-247); the drink of immortality as libido-symbol parallel to the Eucharistic blood.
Verbatim: The drink of immortality, Amrita, was stirred by the Hindu gods like the fire. (cw05 ¶247).

image.title: The Churning of the Ocean of Milk title QS:P1476,en:"The Churning of the Ocean of Milk " label QS:Len,"The Churning of the Ocean of Milk "

occurrences.title: Circle to Adam, square to Eve — Glauber
occurrences.label: Circle to Adam, square to Eve — Glauber
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Glauber attributes the sign of the circle to Adam and the square to Eve.
body: Glauber attributes the sign of the circle to Adam and the square to Eve. The circle is usually the sign for gold and sun; Jung at cw14 ¶587 connects it with the Cave of Treasures' Adam whose countenance burns "in shining splendour like to the ball of the sun" and whose body is like crystal-light.

occurrences.title: 'The eye is the first circle' — Emerson's Circles
occurrences.label: The eye is the first circle' — Emerson's Circles
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The eye is the first circle; the horizon which it forms is the second; and throughout nature this primary figure is repeated without end.
body: "Here is your great American mind, Emerson": The eye is the first circle; the horizon it forms is the second; throughout nature the primary figure repeats without end — "the highest emblem in the cipher of the world," with St. Augustine's God as a circle whose center is everywhere and circumference nowhere. Life is an apprenticeship to the truth that around every circle another can be drawn. Jung uses it to crown the eye-vs-star debate: Emerson, "a grand introvert," links the pupil through which we perceive with the symbol of God — the eye as equivalent of God, the creative eye as Shiva-bindu.

occurrences.title: 'God is a circle whose center is everywhere, and whose periphery nowhere'
occurrences.label: God is a circle whose center is everywhere…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Hippo (ascribed; cf. Liber XXIV philosophorum tradition)
occurrences.yearDisplay: ascribed to Augustine (~5th c.; proverbial by medieval times)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: The Self revealing itself in time is represented by the instrument that determines time and fate, the watch. As a mandala, the circle also expresses the deity unfolding in space. Hence the circle metaphor of St.
body: The closure of the school-dream interpretation, where the swelling watch is read as the Self:

A compact late-1930s statement of the circle-mandala-Self equation (cf. CW12 §§44ff, cited by the editors at this passage): the mandala as concentration on a midpoint that is Self or deity at once — the human character itself "determined by the point of time of birth," like a vintage wine.

occurrences.title: God as circle whose centre is everywhere — Bonaventure, Itinerarium mentis in Deum V
occurrences.label: God as circle whose centre is everywhere
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: ch.11 fn 74 (pdf p612; main text ¶791, pdf p420)

occurrences.quote: Deus est circulus cuius centrum est ubique, circumferentia vero nusquam (God is a circle whose centre is everywhere and the circumference nowhere)
body: The editors' footnote to CW6 ¶791 (the self's numinous empirical symbols: mandala, "Deus est circulus…", tetraktys, quaternity) traces the dictum: "In this form the saying is a variant of one attributed to St. Bonaventure (Itinerarium mentis in Deum, 5): 'Deus est figura intellectualis cuius centrum …' (God is an intelligible sphere whose centre …)". The proverbial circle-form — "Deus est circulus cuius centrum est ubique, circumferentia vero nusquam" — is thus documented back to the Seraphic Doctor's intelligible-sphere of God; the editors add Mysterium Coniunctionis par. 41 n.42 and Borges' essay "Pascal's Sphere" for the wider genealogy.

Jung's use: the God-circle is one of the distinct numinous symbols of the self, alongside mandala and tetraktys (¶791) — the God-image drawn as a centre without periphery, i.e. the self's centrosymmetric field.

This note resolves the pin on mandala-deus-est-circulus-formula-latin-west-12c: the formula's full wording and its Bonaventure attribution come from this footnote, which the c03/c04 chunk text lacked.

occurrences.title: The sphairos — 'the most blissful god' of Empedocles
occurrences.label: The sphairos — 'the most blissful god'…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "the golden ball... is the globe, the all-perfect roundness expressing the primordial man, the man that was before he had been dismembered, cut up or separated — before he became two... it is of course the alchemistic gold and the all-roundness of the Platonic being and the sphairos, the most blissful god of Empedocles."

Jung: Nietzsche "never would think that this ball had anything to do with the all-round primordial man of Plato, or with the sphairos of Empedocles. Yet these ideas keep on coming back again and again... He is simply a repetition of one of the old alchemists."
Empedocles (editor): the four elements pulled apart and united by strife and love.

occurrences.title: The ring of eternal return — Zarathustra, 'The Virtuous'
occurrences.label: The ring of eternal return
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: this ring is the idea of totality and it is the idea of individuation naturally, an individuation symbol. It means the absolute completeness of the self
body: "Es ist euer Liebstes selbst, eure Tugend. Des Ringes Durst ist in euch" — the thirst of the ring, every ring striving "to reach itself again." Jung seizes it: "Yes, the ring of eternal return... this ring is the idea of totality and it is the idea of individuation naturally, an individuation symbol. It means the absolute completeness of the self." The circular movement round a center is "the famous circumambulatio, namely, the concentration upon the central point is the virtue"; the act of virtue is a star whose light travels on after it is spent.

Philological care marks the locus: the English "your dearest Self" is a misprint — the German selbst is lowercase here ("euer Liebstes selbst," your dearest) and only becomes Selbst paragraphs later ("Dass eure Tugend euer Selbst sei"); virtus read etymologically as dynamic power, "virtus dormitiva."

occurrences.title: The Egyptian hieroglyph for 'city' — a St Andrew's cross in a circle
occurrences.label: The Egyptian hieroglyph for 'city'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The Egyptian hieroglyph for 'city' is a St. Andrew's cross in a circle.
body: The Egyptian hieroglyph for "city" (nw.t): two crossed lines within a circle. Jung cites it (¶435) as the objective counterpart of a psychic schema: the quartering of the tribe and settlement through the crossing of a matrilineal by a patrilineal division — "The basic pattern is a square or circle divided by a cross; it forms the ground-plan of the primitive settlement and the archaic city, also of monasteries, convents, etc., as can be seen in Europe, Asia, and prehistoric America."

Context: the moiety system's marriage classes, whose practical purpose is the separation of cross-cousin marriage groups — for Jung "the original model for the peculiar psychologem which we find in alchemy": the marriage quaternio, re-emerging on the mystical level as the alchemical quaternio of adept, soror, king, queen.

occurrences.title: The city of Brahman on Mount Meru — four mountains, four gates
occurrences.label: The city of Brahman on Mount Meru
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the discussion of the Self as ordering pattern: "In psychological symbology, the Self is always expressed by a geometrical pattern, which means order. For instance, Brahman is expressed by the city of Brahman on the mountain of Meru, which is a mathematical pattern, four mountains, four gates and so on; it is like a sort of molecule, or an atom of carbon with the four elements".

Jung's immediate context is the Self as "a certain scheme or law of crystallization, a law of order... a Grenzbegriff, as Kant says... a sort of auxiliary structure," like atom, electron, or ether. The carbon-atom comparison ties the quaternity of the mandala to the four-valenced structure of living matter.

occurrences.title: Zschokke's mind's eye at the Brugg inn — the young desk-breaker unmasked
occurrences.label: Zschokke's mind's eye at the Brugg inn
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Suddenly Zschokke saw in his mind's eye this young man standing at a desk, breaking it open, and pocketing the money he found.
body: Heinrich Zschokke, lunching at an inn in Brugg, "saw in his mind's eye" the young man opposite standing at a desk, breaking it open and pocketing the money — "Zschokke even knew the exact amount and was so sure of it that he took the young man to task. The latter was so flabbergasted by Zschokke's knowledge that he made a confession on the spot."

Jung's use: exhibit for the "bad conscience... for no demonstrable reason" — in conversation, an archetype constellated in the other's unconscious can be parallel-constellated in one's own, or "The psychoid archetype has a tendency to behave as though it were not localized in one person but were active in the whole environment" (¶851), the fact being "transmitted... through a subliminal perception of the affect it produces." Bridge case between conscience, projection and synchronicity.

occurrences.title: Symplegades — the clashing rocks at the Black Sea entrance (Argonauts, Aeneas, Zeus's doves)
occurrences.label: Symplegades — the clashing rocks…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Black Sea entrance (Bosporus); also Scylla and Charybdis (Aeneas's passage)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
jung.locator: pdf p449–451 (Bash's paper on the grids dream)

occurrences.quote: the Argonauts between the Symplegades, the gigantic rock formations at the entrance to the Black Sea, which clashed without warning and crushed the poor seafarer.
body: The rotating grids of a six-year-old's womb-cave dream send Bash to the passing-through motifs of mythology: Aeneas between Scylla and Charybdis; the Argonauts between the Symplegades, "the gigantic rock formations at the entrance to the Black Sea, which clashed without warning and crushed the poor seafarer"; the doves bringing ambrosia to Zeus, the last of the consecrated birds regularly crushed. Phineus's advice — send a dove first — saved only the tail feathers of the dove and the ornamental tip of the Argo's rudder. Frobenius's catalogue (Das Zeitalter des Sonnengottes, 1904) extends the motif worldwide: Maui's rising and falling rocks (spell learned from the mother), Bogda Gesser Chan, the rock gate of North Korea and ancient Mexico, the North Indian clashing rocks behind the blessed dead, the Northwest American biting door, the collapsing tree trunk of Japan, Samoa's and the Navahos' split versions — the Navajo sun-wanderers pass rocks, cutting reed, cactus field, boiling sand, then gate wardens "two bears, two snakes, two winds, and two flashes of lightning." Dante's ascent under Satan's raised wings belongs here too. Meaning: passage at the sole right moment, with the indispensable tribute — "This is the age-old 'die and become'!"

occurrences.title: The Clear Light instruction to the dying — Chikhai Bardo, Bardo Thödol
occurrences.label: The Clear Light instruction to the dying
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: O nobly-born, thy present intellect, in real nature void, not formed into anything as regards characteristics or colour, naturally void, is the very Reality, the All-Good.
body: The opening instruction of the Bardo Thödol, spoken "not presumptuously, but in a courteous manner" to the dying man:

Jung's reading: this is "the Dharmakāya state of perfect enlightenment" — psychologically, "the creative ground of all metaphysical assertion is consciousness" (¶838). "Thine own consciousness, shining, void, and inseparable from the Great Body of Radiance... is the Immutable Light—Buddha Amitābha" (¶839). "The soul is assuredly not small, but the radiant Godhead itself" — the West finds this blasphemous, or suffers theosophical inflation from it (¶840).

occurrences.title: Clement of Alexandria — 'to know oneself is to know God' (Paedagogus III, 1)
occurrences.label: Clement of Alexandria
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'Therefore, as it seems, it is the greatest of all disciplines to know oneself; for when a man knows himself, he knows God' (¶347). Jung quotes it with Hippolytus' Gnostic saying 'knowledge of man is the beginning of wholeness (teleiosis), but knowledge of God is perfect wholeness' and Monoïmos' letter — evidence that 'many of the Gnostics were nothing other than psychologists' (¶347). The gnosis strand that runs into Dorn's self-knowledge and Jung's own method.

occurrences.title: Clementine Homilies — pneuma and soma; the devil as psyche of this world
occurrences.label: Clementine Homilies — pneuma and soma
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'In God, pneuma and soma are one. When they separate, pneuma appears as the Son and "archon of the future Aeon," but soma... divides into four, corresponding to the four elements'; 'from the mixing of the four parts there arose the devil, the "archon of this Aeon," and the psyche of this world' — 'God rules this world as much through the devil as through the Son, for both are in his hands' (¶400). God unfolds in syzygies (heaven/earth, day/night, male/female) down to Adam/Eve, then returns to the beginning (¶400). Jung lists the alchemical parallels: hostile brothers, tetrameria, Mercurius duplex, lapis uniting the opposites (¶401). Cf. god-image-clementine-homilies-two-hands-150 (the two hands).

occurrences.title: The cobra's head-diamond: the Indian tale of the scholar and the snake
occurrences.label: The cobra's head-diamond
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: "The Indians believe that the cobra carries a diamond in its head; and an Indian fairy tale recounts that a snake daily brings a scholar a gold piece for reading to it from spiritual works in a garden, until the old man's greedy son hits the snake on the head and breaks the jewel inside; the snake kills the son in revenge and disappears, lamenting: 'Woe, who has shattered my jewel?'".

"The particular reason why I presented this fairy tale is because such an association may resonate in the expression of our dream text: 'eyes sparkling like diamonds'" — von Franz's bridge to the ten-year-old's vision. The diamond in the serpent's head is the lapis it carries: instinctual nature in possession of the highest value.

occurrences.title: The Monad and the Monogenes dwelling in Setheus — Codex Brucianus passage quoted by Jung
occurrences.label: The Monad and the Monogenes dwelling in Setheus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Egypt (Coptic codex; Codex Brucianus / Codex Jung portion)
body: Gnostic description of the Monad as ship, field, and walled city with twelve gates — the Mother-City of the Only-begotten (Monogenes). Jung quotes: "From Him it is the Monad came, in the manner of a ship, laden with all good things… and in the manner of a city, filled with all races of mankind." (cw12 ¶138).

His reading (¶139): ship/field/city = the temenos idea; the crowned Monad recalls the dream-hat; as metropolis the Monad is feminine "like the padma or lotus, the basic form of the Lamaic mandala"; Setheus dwells in the Pleroma-city with four gates, equivalent to the City of Brahma on Mount Meru; the Monogenes stands on a tetrapeza, quaternion of the four evangelists.

occurrences.title: Dream of the shooting party and the tall man who says 'Don't worry' (reported 8 March 1933)
