occurrences.label: Dream of the shooting party and the tall man…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A man dreams he is in a room with his own party; hostile intruders, exactly like his own men, burst in. Firing at them, he notices they wink — it is only for show — and walks away; "a huge fellow, who reminded him slightly of his own father, took him by the shoulder saying, 'Don't worry,' and walked away with him."

Jung: very clearly a collective, not a personal problem — the dreamer had acquired new ideas and felt his community drifting from him. The tall man is "that greater man within himself, who is the totality of his being inclusive of his ancestral souls"; a new idea is taken in only at the top of consciousness while the totality remains untouched, "as if you had the whole unconscious against you" — wait until both sides are informed.

occurrences.title: The comet's tail sets the Earth on fire — cosmic childhood dream (girl 3–4)
occurrences.label: The comet's tail sets the Earth on fire
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: early childhood, recurring thrice in one year (reported 25 Oct 1938)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: A long tail of a comet swishes over the Earth; the Earth catches fire, and people perish in that fire. The child then hears the terrible cries of the people and awakens from them.
body: Jung's exhibit of what he calls "cosmic childhood dreams" (kosmische Kindheitsträume): a girl between three and four dreamed this three times within a year, and it "stayed burned into her memory ever since."

Jung: "From where does the child have the idea of the end of mankind in a firebrand? It is a completely archaic image: the terminal fire of the world that destroys the world." Such dreams are alien phenomena, strictly uninterpretable in personal terms; an ancient dream-reader would say the child has a special destiny. In antiquity such dreams were officially reported — to the Areopagus in Athens, to the Senate in Rome; primitives sat in council over them. "It is as if the dreamer should be prepared for a collective part... One is torn apart by the collective destiny".

occurrences.title: The Comma Johanneum — 'these three are one in heaven' (1 John 5:7)
occurrences.label: The Comma Johanneum
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: late interpolation (entered Vulgate tradition ~800; defended into the 16th c.)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: The so-called \"Comma Johanneum,\" which would seem to be an exception, is a demonstrably late interpolation of doubtful origin.
body: The one seemingly explicit Trinity text in the New Testament is, Jung notes with the editors' grammar-point, a forgery: the Greek text's three neuter nouns are followed by a masculine plural participle — the seam where the clause was stitched in.
Psychologically telling: the doctrine's strongest proof-text had to be manufactured — the trinity had to be read into scripture, as dogma crystallized what the text only half contained.

occurrences.title: Eating the dead by village exchange — Bugishu, Mt. Elgon
occurrences.label: Eating the dead by village exchange
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Bugishu, western slope of Mt. Elgon, Uganda

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: On the western slope of Mt. Elgon Jung found "relative anthropophagists" — they did not eat enemies taken in war, "quite nice, gentle people," but they had "the somewhat peculiar custom of eating the dead": a bereaved village sends word to the next, loads of food and beer are exchanged in the Bush, and the neighbours chop, boil, and eat the corpse; hyenas clear the bones.

Jung's gloss: mana is assimilated by eating — "because I am your cousin, I will eat your uncle" — the same instinct the Host satisfies: "the real communion with the qualities of human beings... only takes place when you can eat them." (A West African cemetery-cleared-in-one-night case is reported via Budge)
Verbatim: "they were quite nice, gentle people, but they had the somewhat peculiar custom of eating the dead."

occurrences.title: Peter's vision of the linen sheet with unclean animals — Acts 10
occurrences.label: Peter's vision of the linen sheet…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: At Joppa Peter sees a linen cloth let down from heaven containing the impure animals orthodox Jews were forbidden to eat, with the voice: "What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common."

Jung's exhibit for revelation versus intuition: "when the time had come for Christianity to be spread to the Gentiles, he had a vision... And the voice said that what God declared to be pure could not be impure. So he had to eat it, which means that he had to assimilate the Gentiles. But he surely did not like it; he had to have the shock of such a vision in order to be shaken into accepting it." Had it been an intuition it would have been "an ego business" with the secret power tendency creeping in; the true revelation is against the receiver.
Verbatim: "he had a vision that God let down a linen cloth in which were the impure animals which the orthodox Jews were forbidden to eat".

occurrences.title: Therese of Konnersreuth living on the Host alone
occurrences.label: Therese of Konnersreuth living on the Host alone
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "The little saint Therese of Konnersreuth is said to have lived upon the Host alone. People who were in a position to know reported that as a fact; they were absolutely convinced of it."

Jung neither asserts nor denies: "I cannot understand it, but I would not deny it; it is possible that such things might happen... We cannot say anything is impossible except a logical contradiction." In the argument, eating as symbolism: ascetics "refrain from eating in order to attain spirituality," food made "of a super-substantial nature, that the body may also lift itself." (Editors: Jung's "little saint" conflates Therese Neumann of Konnersreuth with Teresa of Lisieux, "the little one.")
Verbatim: "The little saint Therese of Konnersreuth is said to have lived upon the Host alone."

occurrences.title: The thiasotai — Roman burial-insurance societies and the origin of the mass
occurrences.label: The thiasotai — Roman burial-insurance…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: First-century Roman societies — thiasotai, originally companies of Bacchic revellers (editors) — functioning as burial insurance, some guaranteeing a daily meal: a room, a hired cook, the members eating while the cook read them the gospels "which were not then considered to be inspired truth, only very good books."

Jung draws from it a genealogy of the mass: "the altar is the cooking range, the hearth, where the magic or spiritual food is prepared, and the priest is the cook who gives it to the people." Decent burial was guaranteed "because otherwise the soul would begin to work havoc."

Verbatim: "There were Christian societies in Rome in the first century, sort of insurance companies, which guaranteed a decent burial; they were called thiasotai, and some of them were to guarantee to members one meal daily also."

occurrences.title: Communion table with 3 loaves and 1 fish — Roman catacombs
occurrences.label: Communion table with 3 loaves and 1 fish
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: It corresponds to the vas hermeticum (and the early Christian communion table of the catacombs with 3 loaves and 1 fish.
body: An early Christian communion table in the Roman catacombs "with 3 loaves and 1 fish" (¶1697), cited by Jung as the Christian structural twin of Faust's underworld tripod (Diana–Luna–Hecate and the Phorkyads) and of the alchemical vas hermeticum / Tripus Aureus ("the one that Hephaestus cast into the sea").

Jung's reading: the 3+1 arrangement — the axiom of Maria in liturgical miniature — shows the chthonic-feminine vessel (tripod, vas, table) bearing the quaternity-structure that pervades both pagan underworld imagery and the Eucharist; the fish is the ichthys-Christ (cf. Aion's fish study, named by Jung at ¶1520).

occurrences.title: Transubstantiation invented — Paschasius Radbertus at Corbie
occurrences.label: Transubstantiation invented
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The doctrine of real flesh and blood in the eucharist "only became dogma in about the ninth century when Paschasius Radbertus invented transubstantiation: that was a concession to the barbarous mind." Radbertus, abbot of a monastery in Corbie, Picardie, was himself one of the Frankish invaders' line. In the same house the monk Ratramnus still held the meal to be memorial; John Scotus Erigena (d. 889) fought for the memorial view.

Jung's frame: originally "there was no question about the communion... a sort of memorial rite"; the symbolic bread and wine hardened into flesh and blood as the message reached minds that demand the concrete — the same modification Zarathustra's message undergoes when Nietzsche teaches it to imaginary disciples.
Verbatim: "The idea of real flesh and blood only became dogma in about the ninth century when Paschasius Radbertus invented transubstantiation: that was a concession to the barbarous mind".

occurrences.title: Medieval paintings of the Conception: the tube from God's throne
occurrences.label: Medieval paintings of the Conception
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Medieval paintings depicting the fructification of Mary "with a tube or hose-pipe coming down from the throne of God and passing into her body, and we can see the dove or the Christchild flying down it" (¶108). The dove is the fructifying agent, the wind of the Holy Ghost.

Jung's reading: the third independent testimony (with the Mithraic Liturgy tube and the patient's vision) proving "the idea of a wind-tube connected with God or the sun exists independently... at other times and in other places"; the patient could never have seen such a rare picture — there was none in Zurich's public gallery, his native town (¶109). Association of sun and wind "frequently occurs in ancient symbolism".

occurrences.title: The hieros gamos of hierophant and priestess in the dark — Asterius on Eleusis
occurrences.label: The hieros gamos of hierophant and priestess…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The descent into the earth is a piece of womb symbolism and was widespread in the form of cave worship.
body: "This clearly points to a hieros gamos which was celebrated underground. The priestess of Demeter seems to have represented the earth-goddess, or possibly the ploughed furrow" (¶528). The descent into the earth as womb symbolism opens Jung's cave-cult catalogue: Magi sacrificing to Ahriman in a sunless place, Mithrobarzanes, "Sister Fire and Brother Spring," the Attis spelaeum.

occurrences.title: Christ the bridegroom consummating his marriage on the cross — Augustine
occurrences.label: Christ the bridegroom consummating his marriage…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The various forms of the crux ansata have the meaning of “life” and “fruitfulness,” and also of “union,” which can be interpreted as the hieros gamos of the god with his mother for the purpose of conquering death and renewing life.
body: Augustine's nuptial reading of the crucifixion: "Like a bridegroom Christ went forth from his chamber … he lovingly gave himself up to the torment in place of his bride, and he joined himself to the woman for ever." For Jung this shows the old mythologem — the hieros gamos of the god with his mother to conquer death and renew life — "has passed into Christianity" (¶411).

occurrences.title: Christ's marriage-bed of the cross — pseudo-Augustine, Sermo suppositus 120
occurrences.label: Christ's marriage-bed of the cross
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "Like a bridegroom Christ went forth from his chamber, he went out with a presage of his nuptials into the field of the world.… He came to the marriage-bed of the cross, and there, in mounting it, he consummated his marriage. And when he perceived the sighs of the creature, he lovingly gave himself up to the torment in place of his bride, and he joined himself to the woman [matrona] for ever" (¶671).

St. Augustine "actually interprets Christ's death as a hieros gamos with the mother, similar to the feast of Adonis, where Venus and Adonis were laid upon the bridal couch" (¶671). Jung: "Matrona in the language of St. Augustine means the Church, the bride of the Lamb. The feeling-tone of the classical hieros gamos has here changed into its opposite: torment instead of lust" (¶672) — the union of God with his congregation, the corpus mysticum, which psychologically "signifies the conjunction of conscious and unconscious, the transcendent function characteristic of the individuation process" (¶672).
Verbatim: "He came to the marriage-bed of the cross, and there, in mounting it, he consummated his marriage" (¶671).

occurrences.title: The royal pair crucified for union and rebirth — George Ripley
occurrences.label: The royal pair crucified for union and rebirth
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Ripley (Opera omnia p. 81) crucifies the royal pair, the supreme opposites, for the purpose of union and rebirth: "If I be lifted up, [as Christ says,] then I will draw all men unto me... From that time forward, when both parts, having been crucified and exanimated, are espoused, man and woman shall be buried together and are afterward quickened again by the spirit of life" (cw13 ¶446).

Jung's frame: the tree was brought in to connection with Christ's cross partly by the legend that the cross's wood came from the tree of paradise, partly by the quaternity — "the tree possesses a quaternary quality by reason of the fact that it represents the process by which the four elements are united" (cw13 ¶446). A sibling locus holds Ripley's Scrowle with its Melusina-top tree: tree-ripley-scrowle-bm-sloane-5025-london-1588.
Verbatim: when both parts, having been crucified and exanimated, are espoused, man and woman shall be buried together and are afterward quickened again by the spirit of life. (cw13 ¶446ocr)

occurrences.title: Faust with Helen: the coniunctio becomes subjective — Goethe's Faust II
occurrences.label: Faust with Helen — Goethe's Faust II
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "The essential Faustian drama is expressed most graphically in the scene between Paris and Helen. To the medieval alchemist this episode would have represented the mysterious coniunctio of Sol and Luna in the retort (fig. 268); but modern man, disguised in the figure of Faust, recognizes the projection and, putting himself in the place of Paris or Sol, takes possession of Helen or Luna, his own inner, feminine counterpart. The objective process of the union thus becomes the subjective experience of the artifex: instead of watching the drama, he has become one of the actors" (¶558).

The price: the goal of the opus is missed — "Euphorion, who is supposed to be the filius philosophorum, imperishable and 'incombustible,' goes up in flames" (¶558); "every archetype, at its first appearance and so long as it remains unconscious, takes possession of the whole man and impels him to play a corresponding role." Yet the identification "brings the coniunctio back from its projected state into … consciousness … the solution of the alchemical riddle" — with inflation as its danger (¶559). Faust's sin: "he identified with the thing to be transformed" (¶560); his perfected figure is named "Marianus" — Morienus.

occurrences.title: Flowing Light pursues Dark Water — Hippolytus' blue woman
occurrences.label: Flowing Light pursues Dark Water
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Behind these figures may be discerned a coniunctio Solis et Lunae, both the sun and the new moon appearing in their unfavourable aspect.
body: In Hippolytus' report, a woman of "celestial" blue hue ([kyanokrokon]) is pursued by "a grey-haired, winged, ithyphallic old man." "He is named [Rhou], Flowing Light, and she is [Kyanokome?], 'which means Dark Water.' Behind these figures may be discerned a coniunctio Solis et Lunae, both the sun and the new moon appearing in their unfavourable aspect. Here too there arises between them the 'harmony' of an intermediary spirit, roughly corresponding to the position of the filius philosophorum" (¶177).

A coniunctio of the darkened luminaries — the sexed pursuit at the bottom of the cosmos whose offspring is the harmonizing third. Greek proper names OCR-garbled in the chunk (flagged in the mention record).

occurrences.title: Gabricus and Beya — brother dissolved into sister, becoming the serpens mercurialis
occurrences.label: Gabricus and Beya — brother dissolved…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Latin alchemical corpus (legend of Hellenistic origin)
body: "Alchemy has the legend of Gabricus and Beya, the royal brother-sister pair. During the hieros gamos, Gabricus gets right inside the body of his sister and disappears completely; he is buried in her womb, where, dissolved into atoms, he changes into the soul-snake, the serpens mercurialis" (¶676, cf. fig. 6).

The coniunctio in its most radical alchemical form: the male partner's total bodily dissolution into the female, out of which the mercurial serpent-soul is born — brother-sister incest, burial, and transformation into the transformative agent itself. Jung cites it as the culmination of the snake-as-instrument-of-sacrifice survey ("the snake symbolizes the numen of the transformative act as well as the transformative substance itself"), and immediately adds the patient who crawled into her mother as a snake (see serpent-fantasy-enter-mother-anon-patient-cw05). The locus that later anchors his CW14 treatment of the coniunctio.
Verbatim: "dissolved into atoms, he changes into the soul-snake, the serpens mercurialis" (¶676).

occurrences.title: "I am God and the Devil. I am man and woman. I am love and hate." (Visions plate 27)
occurrences.label: I am God and the Devil. I am man…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich (patient's painting; plate following p. 272 of the edition)
occurrences.yearDisplay: painted late 1929/early 1930 for Jung; vision from the 1926-32 series

jung.locator: plate 27 caption (pdf p18); discussion in later sessions

occurrences.quote: I am God and the Devil. I am man and woman. I am love and hate.
body: Plate 27's declarative text: the visioner's assertion of the united opposites — God/Devil, man/woman, love/hate — the coincidentia oppositorum formula spoken in the first person. This is the patient's late-series arrival at the moral problem Douglas's introduction places at the seminar's heart: "the problem of what one could call the morality of evil, the question of the usefulness of evil" (Jung, quoted in the introductionrom p136 of the seminar) — the theme that leads toward Answer to Job and Mysterium Coniunctionis. The plate series around it (tentacles drawing the seeker down, the mandalas of plates 29-32) shows the same conjunctio being fought out imaginally.

occurrences.title: 'When there is wisdom the left and the right are in harmony' — Acta Joannis 98
occurrences.label: When there is wisdom the left…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Footnote to the Transference essay, quoting Acta Joannis 98 (via James, Apocryphal New Testament, p. 255): "… Harmony of wisdom, but when there is wisdom the left and the right are in harmony: powers, principalities, archons, daemons, forces…". The gnosticizing Acts give the cosmic left-right polarity gathered into one wisdom — an early parallel to the alchemical coniunctio of opposites Jung is building there. The Greek original is lost in this chunk's OCR (flagged in the mention record).

occurrences.title: Isis as heavenly cow receiving the seed that begets Horus — Heliopolitan autumn rite
occurrences.label: Isis as heavenly cow receiving the seed…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the heavenly cow with the moon-eye, Isis, receives the seed that begets Horus
body: The feast-day of Jusasit, "the arrival of the sister who makes ready to unite herself with her father" — daughter becomes wife, the rejuvenated mother given to the sun-god, "the 'father of his mother,'" for self-reproduction (¶408, ¶496). The moon as guardian of the seed is the key phrase Jung repeats for Nokomis (¶487).

occurrences.title: Father and mother sleeping together in the lake-dwellers' valley — Swiss soldier's speech (WWI)
occurrences.label: Father and mother sleeping together…
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: One man said: “Now, damn it all, we have dug into the depths of this blooming old valley where the old lake-dwellers lived and where father and mother are still sleeping together.
body: Digging an emplacement for a heavy gun in refractory soil, a soldier cursed the blocks and said: "Now, damn it all, we have dug into the depths of this blooming old valley where the old lake-dwellers lived and where father and mother are still sleeping together." Jung, hidden behind a rock with his pipe, heard it as "the same idea [as the Tao], very naïvely expressed" — the primordial union of the opposites in the ancestral ground (¶262).
A living vernacular witness to the archetypal image of male-female primordial unity, flanking the Negro calabash myth cited in the same paragraph.

occurrences.title: Picasso painting with the conjunction of the light and dark anima
occurrences.label: Picasso painting with the conjunction…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Spirit in Man, Art and Literature (CW15)

occurrences.quote: One painting (although traversed by numerous lines of fracture) even contains the conjunction of the light and dark anima.
body: The endpoint Jung descries in Picasso's latest work: "In Picasso's latest paintings, the motif of the union of opposites is seen very clearly in their direct juxtaposition" (cw15 ¶213).

Jung's reading. The alchemical key is explicit: the Nekyia's katabasis eis antron is followed, in his patients' material, "by a recognition of the bipolarity of human nature and of the necessity of conflicting pairs of opposites. After the symbols of madness experienced during the period of disintegration there follow images which represent the coming together of the opposites: light/dark, above/below, white/black, male/female, etc." One painting — "although traversed by numerous lines of fracture" — "even contains the conjunction of the light and dark anima." The violence of the palette is diagnostic: "The strident, uncompromising, even brutal colours of the latest period reflect the tendency of the unconscious to master the conflict by violence (colour = feeling)" (cw15 ¶213). The state is "neither the end nor the goal," and the conjoined opposites may still "burst asunder" (¶214).

occurrences.title: Ptolemy's three degrees of marriage harmony — sun and moon in the partners' horoscopes
occurrences.label: Ptolemy's three degrees of marriage harmony
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Alexandria → Cardan's Commentaria in Ptolemaeum (Opera omnia, V)

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: The astrological marriage tradition Jung chose as the fixed fact for his statistical experiment: "Since antiquity, the main traditional astrological and alchemical correspondence to marriage has been the coniunctio Solis et Lunae, the coniunctio Lunae et Lunae and the conjunction of the moon with the ascendent" (¶869). Ptolemy's three degrees of harmony: sun in the man's horoscope and sun/moon in the woman's (or moon in both) in trine or sextile; moon in his and sun in hers; mutual reception. Cardan adds: harmony of the luminaries makes life together "long and constant."

Jung's reading: the classical moon-sun conjunction topped his first batch (2.14: 1) — "the confirmation of the traditional astrological and alchemical correspondence between marriage and the moon-sun aspects" (¶886); fn. 66 instances Goethe and Christiane Vulpius.

occurrences.title: Triple coniunctio maxima in Pisces at the nativity (7 B.C.)
occurrences.label: Triple coniunctio maxima in Pisces…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Christ's birth "is characterized by all the usual phenomena attendant upon the birth of a hero… the coincidence of the birth with the thrice-repeated coniunctio maxima in the sign of Pisces, which at that precise moment inaugurated the new era" (¶644; the Greek astrological term is dropped by OCR). The catalogue continues: annunciation, virgin birth, recognition of the king, persecution of the newborn, flight, lowly birth, the twelve-year-old in the temple, breaking away from the mother.

The aeon-dating matters for the book's frame: the thousand-year binding of Satan "correspond astrologically to the first half of the Pisces aeon" (¶725), whose enantiodromia Jung sees breaking in the present ("Luciferi vires accendit Aquarius acres", ¶733).

occurrences.title: Bridal mysticism — Mechthild of Magdeburg, The Flowing Light of the Godhead
occurrences.label: Bridal mysticism — Mechthild…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: While, in Church mysticism, the primordial image of the hieros gamos was sublimated on a lofty plane and only occasionally-as for instance with Mechthild of Magdeburg-approached the physical sphere in emotional intensity
body: In Church mysticism the primordial image of the hieros gamos was "sublimated on a lofty plane and only occasionally — as for instance with Mechthild of Magdeburg — approached the physical sphere in emotional intensity" (¶295, fn39: The Flowing Light of the Godhead). Mechthild is Jung's limit-case of the sublimated coniunctio: the sponsus-sponsa union carried so hot it nears the body. The rest of the world kept the image "very much alive" below the official sublimation — a tension the alchemists would inherit as the coniugium solis et lunae.

occurrences.title: Miss X, Picture 14 — coniunctio of the royal pair over Fifth Avenue (Sept 1929)
occurrences.label: Miss X, Picture 14
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: On the blue flower in the centre the coniunctio of the "royal" pair is represented by the sacrificial fire burning between them.
body: The mandala floats over the lit-up ravine of Fifth Avenue, New York. On the blue flower at its centre the coniunctio of the "royal" pair is represented by sacrificial fire between them; King and Queen assisted by two kneeling figures, a man and a woman — "a typical marriage quaternio," for which Jung refers to his "Psychology of the Transference" (¶613). The inner bond is a compensatory consolidation against disintegrating influences from without, after the shock of New York. Picture 15 answers it: blue snakes penetrate the red flesh — the enantiodromia sets in (¶614).

occurrences.title: Shakti in everlasting embrace with Shiva — the Maya mirror (Tantra)
occurrences.label: Shakti in everlasting embrace with Shiva
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "It is the female that forms a ring round the male in the Tantric Yoga also; the Shakti in everlasting embrace with the god Shiva is an eternal symbol, and it is one of the most complete symbols of the self."

Jung's metaphysics of it: the self as superpersonal Atman (Paramatman, Prajapati, Purusha) is alone, "therefore, he emanates a world which is his mirror... The mirror is the shakti that creates the real illusion, the veil of Maya, round the god; the god sees all his millions of faces mirrored in the magic mirror of Maya."

Applied to Zarathustra's circle of disciples: "They form a circle round him like the earth snake that bites its own tail... the self only exists inasmuch as you appear. Not that you are, but that you do is the self."

occurrences.title: Coniunctio solis et lunae — Splendor solis (Harley 3469, 1582)
occurrences.label: Coniunctio solis et lunae — Splendor solis
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Splendor Solis plate of the sun-moon coniunctio, cited where Jung discusses the anima standing on the globe worshipping the sun.

Context ¶112: "the sun is a symbol of the source of life and the ultimate wholeness of man… the anima still seems to be a sun-worshipper, that is to say, she belongs to the ancient world." The coniunctio plate stands behind the whole sol/luna row of the volume.

image.title: Splendor Solis 04 solar king and lunar queen meet

occurrences.title: The coniunctio of soul and body as ecclesiastical marriage bath — Grandes heures du duc de Berry
occurrences.label: The coniunctio of soul and body…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Da nobis per huius aquae et vini mysterium, eius divinitatis esse consortes, qui humanitatis nostrae fieri dignatus est particeps.
body: Illumination from the Grandes heures (1413) showing the mingling of water and wine at the Offertory as a bath of the two figures — which Jung captions "an ecclesiastical version of the alchemical marriage bath."

His reading: in the Greek rite after the transubstantiation "a piece of the host is mingled with the wine, thus producing the coniunctio of the soul with the body and establishing the living body of Christ." The transformed bread is Ambrose's medicina, the pharmakon athanasias — the drug of immortality uniting body and soul, exactly what the alchemists sought in their bath and their stone.

occurrences.title: The stone's masculine and feminine killed and raised — Mylius, Philosophia reformata (1622)
occurrences.label: The stone's masculine and feminine killed…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: "Mylius (Phil, ref., p. 106) says that the masculine and feminine components of the stone must first be killed 'that they may be brought to life again in a new and incorruptible resurrection, so that thereafter they may be immortal'" (cw11 ¶? pdf p698). The stone is "also compared to the future resurrected body as a 'corpus glorificatum.'"

Death of the two, resurrection as one incorruptible: the alchemical opus mapped onto the paschal mystery — Jung's documentation that this is no private fancy of the alchemists but a citations-chain (de Hoghelande, Consilium coniugii, Djabir's Livre de la Miséricorde, Livre d'Ostanès, Comarius, Zosimos, Turba, Maier, Rosarium illustration).

occurrences.title: De Tinctura alba — the queen's conception speech
occurrences.label: De Tinctura alba — the queen's conception speech
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: …concipiam et ero praegnans et tempore meo pariam filium potentissimum, dominantem et regnantem prae cunctis regibus et principibus terrae, coronatum aurea corona victoriae.
body: The white tincture speaks as the beloved in the first person, describing the double conception: her parents, drunk with her milk, wed in her bed and beget "a son of the Moon"; then her beloved drinks from the red tomb of the stone and the fountain of his mother, copulates with her, and:
Cf. "Cons, coniug." (Ars chem., p. 129) and "Rosinus ad Sarratantam," pp. 291ff. The full hierosgamos cycle — milk-wedding, fountain, copulation, crowned filius — in one speech.

occurrences.title: Woman and dragon embracing in the grave at new moon — Maier, Scrutinium
occurrences.label: Woman and dragon embracing in the grave…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung recalls 'the gruesome conjunction at the new moon in Maier's Scrutinium chymicum, where the woman and the dragon embrace in the grave' (cw14 ¶293), illustrating the waning of the soul-Luna into the embrace of terrestrial sulphur — 'which here signifies death and corruption' (¶293). It is the nigredo-face of the coniunctio: union consummated not on the wedding-bed but in the tomb, under the sign of the new moon with its 'uncanniness and snakiness' (¶437).

image.title: Michaelis Majeri Secretioris naturae secretorum scrutinium chymicum - per oculis et intellectui accuratè accommodata, figuris cupro appositissimè incisa, ingeni

occurrences.title: Consilium coniugii: the philosophical man of the four natures, the red gum
occurrences.label: Consilium coniugii
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the union of the two is a kind of self-fertilization
body: "The old treatise 'Consilium coniugii' explains that the 'philosophical man' consists of the 'four natures of the stone.' Of these three are earthy or in the earth, but 'the fourth nature is the water of the stone, namely the viscous gold which is called red gum and with which the three earthy natures are tinted.' We learn here that gum is the critical fourth nature: it is duplex, i.e., masculine and feminine, and at the same time the one and only aqua mercurialis. So the union of the two is a kind of self-fertilization, a characteristic always ascribed to the mercurial dragon" (¶209).
The fourth nature "leads straight to the Anthropos idea that stands for man's wholeness… a unitary being who existed before man and at the same time represents man's goal" (¶210).

occurrences.title: 'Of all grain, wheat; of all metals, gold; of all birth, man' — Meister Eckhart
occurrences.label: Of all grain, wheat — of all metals, gold
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The innermost nature of all grain meaneth wheat, and of all metals, gold, and of all birth, man.
body: Miss Hannah's contribution at the wheat-field illumination: Eckhart's dictum that "The innermost nature of all grain meaneth wheat, and of all metals, gold, and of all birth, man" — the essence-series grain/metal/birth = wheat/gold/man. Jung builds on it: wheat is bread, the fruit of the earth, almost "the essence of vegetative or plant life"; since plant life symbolizes the spiritual qualities of man, the wheat-field vision carries Iacchus in the winnowing fan, Osiris' wheat-grown sarcophagus, and Christ as Host born of Mary the virgin earth.

occurrences.title: Corn as 'the old woman' sprung from a slain grandmother — Cherokee myth
occurrences.label: Corn as 'the old woman' sprung…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This view is corroborated by a legend of the Cherokee Indians
body: The corn as the killed mother: the grain sprouting from her blood — the sacrificial underside of Mondamin's burial in the earth his mother (¶523).

occurrences.title: The mown ear of corn held up at the epopteia — Eleusis
occurrences.label: The mown ear of corn held up at the epopteia
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Brimo has borne Brimos!
body: The final vision of the Eleusinian mysteries: the cut grain as the son of the mother, the Brimo-borne Brimos in vegetable form — the dying-and-rising corn-god contemplated in silence (cf. pl. IVb).

occurrences.title: Dream: sitting in the harvesting machine cutting wheat — the eternal answer
occurrences.label: Dream — the eternal answer
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I am sitting in a harvesting machine and cutting wheat.
body: A same-night fragment answering the doubt about playing Mother of God: "I am sitting in a harvesting machine and cutting wheat." Jung: "since time immemorial the miraculous child has been symbolized by the wheat. That is the reason why the Host must consist of flour of wheat, why Osiris is symbolized by wheat" (p127) — and the Eleusinian epopteia: the priest lifts the ear of wheat crying "Brimo has given birth to Brimos" (p127-128). Meaning: "if we do not submit to the pains of the task, we shall not reap our reward... It is the eternal answer by which the unconscious has always replied to the doubts of man" (p128). Toni Wolff adds: harvest fixed in the month of the Virgin's birth, under the sign of Virgo, related to the Demeter-Kore myth — the dreamer as harvest goddess and modern woman by way of the machine (p131-132). Jung confirms: "the Virgin in herself is already the harvest. That is again an archetype" (p132).

occurrences.title: Hiawatha wrestles and buries Mondamin the maize god — Song of Hiawatha
occurrences.label: Hiawatha wrestles and buries Mondamin the maize…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: His hunger … his longing for the nourishing mother, calls forth from the unconscious another hero, an edible god, the maize, son of the Earth Mother.
body: After three days' fasting and wrestling in the purple twilight, Hiawatha conquers Mondamin, buries him in the earth his mother, "and soon afterwards, young and fresh, the corn sprouts from his grave for the nourishment of mankind" (¶523). The mystery: "It is not man who is transformed into a god, but the god who undergoes transformation in and through man" (¶524). The Christian parallel is the eucharist; Sahagún's Huitzilopochtli is the ethnographic anchor.

occurrences.title: The 'Papas' of the Attis temple on the Vatican hill
occurrences.label: The 'Papas' of the Attis temple…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Vatican hill, Rome (site of St. Peter's)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: There was already a 'Papas' several hundred years before there was a Pope in the Vatican.
body: Decoding the dream-saint's name Papatheanon, Jung moves from papa through the Pope to a pagan predecessor: "The cult of Attis had a temple on the site of St. Peter's in Rome, and the high priest was called 'Papas' so there was already a 'Papas' several hundred years before there was a Pope in the Vatican."

The point is genealogical: the father-guide (the guru, the spiritual adviser the patient's unconscious invokes) has an institutional lineage running from the archigallus of the Phrygianum through the papacy — the patient, speaking Greek and Romanian, "adds a particular, symbolic form" to plain Papa. The saint in the dream "means the guru, the leader, guide, and spiritual adviser."

occurrences.title: Tages, the fresh-ploughed boy springing from the furrow — Etruscan legend
occurrences.label: Tages, the fresh-ploughed boy springing…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the son being the edible fruit of the field
body: "The plough has a well-known phallic meaning (cf. fig. 15), and the furrow, as in India, stands for woman. Psychologically this image is a symbolical equivalent of copulation, the son being the edible fruit of the field" (¶527). The lexicographers' "Demeter's daimon," identified with Dionysus-Zagreus.

occurrences.title: Corn-god vessel — Chimbote culture, Peru
occurrences.label: Corn-god vessel — Chimbote culture, Peru
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: A corn-god Clay vessel, Chimbote culture, Peru
body: Plate caption, the American parallel to Mondamin: the corn-god as vessel-god, the edible divinity of the grain — Jung cites pl. LII for the Mondamin motif (¶522, ¶523).

occurrences.title: Coronatio Mariae — the crowning of the Virgin — Rosarium picture
occurrences.label: Coronatio Mariae — the crowning of the Virgin
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The coronation picture that illustrates this text proves that the resuscitation of the purified corpse is at the same time a glorification, since the process is likened to the crowning of the Virgin.
body: A picture in the 1550 Rosarium (beside the main series) of the Coronation of the Virgin. Jung cites it at Figure 9: the resuscitation of the purified corpse is at the same time a glorification, "since the process is likened to the crowning of the Virgin" — the glorification of the white, moonlike (purified) body.

The surrounding texts invert the royal symbolism into its opposite: Morienus' ash as "the diadem of thy heart"; Senior's beloved who brings forth "the son of the moon"; the diadem appearing "in menstruo meretricis" and the "foul deposit" preserved "for it is the crown of the heart." In the Aurora consurgens the crown is given to the regina austri, Sapientia ("I am the crown wherewith my beloved is crowned") — the crown as bond between mother and son-lover. Jung: the alchemist, like the unconscious, gives every idea both a positive and a negative expression, mirroring "the indefiniteness of the archetype with its multitude of meanings."

occurrences.title: Coronis the crow-maiden, mother of Asklepios — birth-myth read as an opus
occurrences.label: Coronis the crow-maiden, mother of Asklepios
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The birth-myth of the physician: Apollo surprises Coronis — the "crow maiden," black, of new-moon nature, kin of therapist Ixion and the "incendiary" Phlegyas — bathing in Lake Boibeis; pregnant with Asklepios she consorts with the chthonic Ischys and is slain by Artemis; the child is cut from her body on the funeral pyre. Jung, following Kerényi's MS ("Asklepios: Archetypal Image of the Physician's Existence": the primordial physician as "wounded wounder" — Chiron, Machaon), notes the Mysterium's own Prince, the vir fortis who surprises Diana bathing, repeats the type.

Pernety already read "Coronis as putrefactio, nigredo, caput corvi, and the myth as an opus" — "surprisingly apt, since alchemy, although the alchemists did not know it, was a child of this mythology, or of the matrix from which the classical myth sprang as an elder brother."

occurrences.title: 'Like to a body which is glorified in the day of judgment' — Aurora Consurgens
occurrences.label: Like to a body which is glorified in the day…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Artis auriferae I, p. 201 (printings 1572/1593; material early 15th c.)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: "The 'Aurea hora,' or 'Aurora consurgens' (Art. aurif., I, p. 201) says it is 'like to a body which is glorified in the day of judgment'" (cw11 ¶? pdf p698) — the lapis described in the language of the resurrected body, the corpus glorificatum of scholastic eschatology.

Jung marshals this as the Latin-alchemical member of a series running from Greek alchemy (Comarius, Zosimos) through the Turba to Maier's Symbola (1617, p. 599) and the Rosarium's fol. 2a illustration: the stone as the future glorified body — matter's own assumption.

occurrences.title: Sea of blood and fire — the archaeologist's psychosis-dream (Burghölzli, ~1900s)
occurrences.label: Sea of blood and fire
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A foreign archaeologist of great learning — hermit scholar, weakly, stammering, secretly devoted to a student love he never declared — fell into his first catatonic attack and "left the orderly world": a chaos of an overmastering dream, a sea of blood and fire, conflagrations, earthquakes, nations hurled on nation, in which he saw himself at the head of great armies and, as the victor's prize, gained his loved one — whereupon "the illness ceased, and he awoke from a long dream" (¶352). The second attack, years later in the same town, was a milder replay: gymnastics, love-songs, "the border between two different worlds" (¶353).

Jung's reading: the psychosis as compensatory wish-fulfilment for the arid, repressed life — "Demon or destiny?" (¶353); the so-called cure only closes "the door of the underworld" on an unsolved problem (¶353). The same essay's image of chronic patients: "the hands of the world's clock remain stationary" (¶356).

occurrences.title: Earthquake dreams at the Tantric lectures — the lady warned off the unconscious (Zurich, ~1932)
occurrences.label: Earthquake dreams at the Tantric lectures
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1932 (Jung's lectures on a Tantric text; retold 1956); schizophrenic attack 25 years earlier
body: A highly educated lady, unknown to Jung, was attending his lectures on a Tantric text "that went very thoroughly into the contents of the unconscious." She grew fascinated and excited, unable to formulate the questions arising in her, and had "compensating dreams of an incomprehensible nature, which rapidly led to destructive images" — the isolation symptoms. "Her dreams of earthquakes, collapsing houses, and floods showed me that, on the contrary, the patient had to be rescued from the already menacing invasion of the unconscious by effecting a drastic change in her present situation" (¶561). Jung forbade the lectures and prescribed Schopenhauer's World as Will and Idea — chosen because its Buddhist-inflected author "lays express emphasis on the redeeming effect of consciousness." "The symptomatic dreams immediately stopped." She proved to have had a short schizophrenic attack twenty-five years earlier.

The case instantiates Jung's warning rule (¶560): isolation dreams in latent psychoses are "threatening signs" requiring immediate precautions — even "strict avoidance of any concern with... dream-analysis."

occurrences.title: Earthquake phobia of the child 'Anna' after the Messina earthquake
occurrences.label: Earthquake phobia of the child 'Anna'…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: family home (case of 'Anna'); triggered by the Messina earthquake
body: The 1908 Messina earthquake, "much discussed at table," ignited a nocturnal phobia in four-year-old Anna: the house would fall and kill her; every stone in the road was from the earthquake; a house under construction was a house destroyed (¶19). The fear sublimated into an "unnatural craving for knowledge" — geological atlases, volcano pictures — which Jung reads as converted, neurotically introverted libido (¶20).

The phobia vanished overnight when the children's "big brother" fantasy placed an all-powerful brother in dangerous Italy, in a house of cloth and glass that does not fall down (¶28–29): the archetype-made-wish dissolved the catastrophe-image.
Quote. "Will the house be standing when we get home? Will Papa still be alive? Are you sure there's no earthquake at home?"

occurrences.title: The approaching globe and the bifurcating path — girl of ten or eleven
occurrences.label: The approaching globe and the bifurcating path
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1937 (girl of ten or eleven; dream often repeated)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: I call them cosmic dreams of childhood.
body: Jung's second "cosmic dream of childhood": "She is in empty cosmic space, walking on something like a path, and far in the distance ahead of her, she sees a round light, which as she approaches becomes bigger and finally is an enormous globe that comes nearer and nearer, and of course she grows afraid. Then when the globe is close to her, the path bifurcates and she doesn't know whether she should go to the right or to the left, and in that moment she wakes up. It is a nightmare".

Named an archetype of the prenatal: "strong memories of what the Tibetans would call the Bardo life, a prenatal condition of the mind" — the psyche shown "under its absolute aspect, an empty, dead world to which life is absolutely strange." Hence too the claim that "the psyche is at variance with the conditions of our space."

occurrences.title: Hildegard of Bingen — earth quartered, ringed by ocean, air and heaven (Lucca codex)
occurrences.label: Hildegard of Bingen
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: the earth surrounded by the ocean, realm of air, and starry heaven. The actual globe of the earth in the centre is divided into four.
body: Manuscript picture from Hildegard of Bingen (Fig. 48 of Concerning Mandala Symbolism): the earth surrounded by the ocean, the realm of air, and the starry heaven — and the globe of the earth in the centre is divided into four. Jung sets it in his row of collective mandalas between the Egyptian Sky Mother (Fig. 47) and Boehme's XL Questions mandala (¶704), as the Western visionary form of the quartered world-circle.
Distinct from the Liber divinorum operum cosmic-man illumination (CW12 ¶456): same visionary, different picture, here a cosmological quaternio.

image.title: Hildegardis-Codex, sogenannter Scivias-Codex, Szene: Das Weltall

occurrences.title: The crab at the ford — woman patient's crossing dream (Zurich, c.1920s)
occurrences.label: The crab at the ford
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: a large crab that lay hidden in the water seizes her by the foot and will not let her go.
body: Jung's paradigm dream for the synthetic method: a woman at the border between personal and collective analysis is about to cross a wide river at a ford when a large crab, hidden in the water, seizes her by the foot. Associations: river = obstacle; ford = the treatment; crab = Krebs = carcinoma (Mrs. X died of it), an animal that walks backwards.

Jung's reading: on the objective level, repressed homosexual desire for the friend/mother; on the subjective level, "something 'animal'... which moves backwards and downwards, threatening to drag with it the whole personality" (¶132). The crab is "the symbol for the unconscious contents" (¶138), the untamed instinctual element that is also "the germ of a future sound personality" (¶79 end). Jung reads the whole against the hero-at-the-ford / night-sea-journey parallel (¶160) — the archetypal "danger at the ford" (¶162).

occurrences.title: The crayfish-dinosaur and the divining-rod — dream of the man with mountain sickness
occurrences.label: The crayfish-dinosaur and the divining-rod
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: The dreamer is in a plain house with a peasant woman. He tells this woman of a long trip to Leipzig. On the horizon there appears a monstrous crayfish, at the same time a dinosaur, that catches him by taking him into its claws.
body: Jung's worked example of interpreting a dream wholly without personal associations, "an exclusively objective method." The dreamer was a man of too-great plans whom the unconscious drove into a neurosis at the climax of life — he got "the mountain sickness, vertigo."

Jung: the peasant woman is the primitive mother; the monster is "also the mother, but the other mother, the one who brings death... The mother is also a sarcophagus ('carnivore')" — life and death as Hine-nui-te-po, as Matuta's womb. Amplified through Barlach's Der tote Tag: "Such a man has to bury his mother first." The divining-rod is a charm that does not really rescue. Dream structure: locale — exposition (plans) — peripateia (the claws) — lysis (the collapse).

occurrences.title: Hindu legend: the bored creator contracts and bursts into reality
occurrences.label: Hindu legend — the bored creator contracts…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Finally he got a tremendous headache and something really had to happen. So he did the only thing he knew how to do, which was to contract, and this he did to such an extent that he burst, and then there was reality.
body: An "old Hindu legend" on the solitude of consciousness before creation: "in the beginning the creator was all alone by himself, there was nothing but himself, and that bored him most terribly."

Told beside the parallel Jewish legend of the contracting God to frame the modern condition: "That all modern people naturally assume that nothing exists in the psychical world which they have not made up is the best possible demonstration of their God-Almightiness" — the psyche that takes itself for the sole creator is exactly this bored, headachy god, until something objective (an un-invented image, a touch of moisture) happens to it.

occurrences.title: Crescent-and-star tombstones from Punic graves — Carthage, 7th-8th c. BCE
occurrences.label: Crescent-and-star tombstones from Punic graves
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Setting the seminar its cross-and-crescent research task, Jung notes that "the old Turkish flag showed a crescent and a star. And in digging up some Punic graves, below the Roman remains, tombstones of the seventh and eighth centuries before Christ were found with the same symbols" (p348). Islam's emblem thus rests on a Mediterranean symbol-stratum a millennium and a half older.

Jung's genealogy: "the crescent and the star have also to do with Ishtar, Astarte, the Magna Mater, the mother goddess of Asia Minor, and the Egyptian Isis, as well as with Islam. Then it has to do with a pre-Islamic Sabaean astrological cult, which leads to Babylonian history" (p348). The immediately preceding example is Bern's bears and the excavated Celtic bear-goddess: "That kind of knowledge is needed to have any safety in the technique of dream interpretation."

occurrences.title: The dead woman whose bush-soul was the shot crocodile (Mount Elgon, 1925–26)
occurrences.label: The dead woman whose bush-soul was the shot…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: They explain that the crocodile was a certain old woman in their village who had died at the moment when the shot was fired. The crocodile was obviously her bush-soul.
body: A white man shot a crocodile; a crowd ran from the nearest village demanding compensation, because "the crocodile was a certain old woman in their village who had died at the moment when the shot was fired. The crocodile was obviously her bush-soul" (¶129). Jung pairs it with the leopard-woman episode: a man shot a leopard lying in wait for his cattle, and "just then a woman died in a neighbouring village. She and the leopard were identical."

His reading (¶130, ¶133): these are the facts of participation mystique — "a state of identity in mutual unconsciousness" (¶70) — in which a split-off portion of the psyche is concretely located in a wild animal. "The world is still full of bîtes noires and scapegoats, just as it formerly teemed with witches and werewolves" (¶130): the structure survives in our moral projection.

occurrences.title: The doctor-crocodile of Lake Victoria (Jinja, Uganda)
occurrences.label: The doctor-crocodile of Lake Victoria
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Jinja, north shore of Lake Victoria, Uganda

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: It was the friend of man, a doctor animal.
body: From Jung's own journey: "There was one on the west bank of Lake Victoria which the Negroes fed because they said that crocodile protected the whole coast, it chased away all the others. It was tremendously big and fat — they fed it with fish, and it never ate human beings. It was the friend of man, a doctor animal."

Set against the rule that "the crocodile symbolizes the voracious quality of the unconscious, the danger from below which suddenly comes up and pulls people down", this tamed crocodile shows the positive face of the saurian: the instinctual, cold-blooded fundament as healer and protector when related to rightly.

occurrences.title: The crosses of Yucatan — the devil's foresight and the bishops' synod
occurrences.label: The crosses of Yucatan
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: When the Spanish Conquistadores reached Yucatan they found, among the remains of Aztec civilization, many stone crosses and signs of bloody sacrifice — the Christian symbol in a country that knew nothing of Christ. The case went to the bishops, who held a synod and concluded, after long researches, that the devil had foreseen the Spanish discovery of America and pre-planted the crosses centuries earlier, so the natives could say "we know all about your god."

Jung tells it as the historical twin of Justin Martyr's diabolical anticipation of Dionysos: "That is the way people think when a thing is new. First they call it nonsense, and then when several hundred people believe it, they say it is true and they knew it long ago."
Verbatim: "they put the case to their bishops, who held a synod and came to the conclusion after long researches, that it was a very similar case to that mentioned by Justin."

occurrences.title: Thoth's annunciation and the crux ansata of Kneph and Hathor — Luxor birth reliefs
occurrences.label: Thoth's annunciation and the crux ansata…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~14th c. BCE (divine-birth cycle of queen Mautmes)
occurrences.quote: the bird-headed Thoth, the Logos and messenger of the gods, is shown announcing to the young queen Mautmes that she will give birth to a son.
body: In an Egyptian picture of the birth of a king at Luxor, the bird-headed Thoth — "the Logos and messenger of the gods" — announces to the young queen Mautmes that she will bear a son; in the next scene Kneph and Hathor hold the crux ansata to her mouth, "thus fertilizing her in a spiritual or symbolic manner" (fig. 27).
An annunciation-type iconography fourteen centuries before the Christian one, with the cross itself as the instrument of divine impregnation — the word announced, the life-sign applied.

occurrences.title: Cross amid the doves — apse mosaic of San Clemente, Rome
occurrences.label: Cross amid the doves
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: Cf. also the mosaic of St. Felix at Nola, showing a cross surrounded by doves. There is another in San Clemente, Rome
body: In the Answer to Job footnote on the quaternity's manifestation ("The quaternity, earlier hinted at in the vision of Ezekiel, is patently manifest in the pre-Christian Book of Enoch"), Jung points to two Roman-rite mosaics in which the cross stands in a roundel of doves:
The garland of doves (the Spirit) around the cross of the One continues the ancient mandala row: four living creatures, four angels, doves in the round.

occurrences.title: Cross surrounded by doves — apse mosaic of St. Felix, Nola
occurrences.label: Cross surrounded by doves
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: the mosaic of St. Felix at Nola, showing a cross surrounded by doves
body: The earlier of the two dove-cross mosaics Jung cites for the quaternity-surround: the cross "surrounded by doves" in the apse of St. Felix at Nola, the cult-church of Paulinus of Nola.

occurrences.title: Dürer's Trinity — God the Father carrying the dead Christ
occurrences.label: Dürer's Trinity — God the Father carrying…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Mrs. Sigg's contribution to the corpse-carrying motif: "our greatest painter, Dürer" used it "in his picture of the Trinity, where the King, the God-Father, carries the dead Christ in his arms" — the same motif she finds in Paul Gerhard's hymn (set by Bach in the Passion music), the Germanic-Dürer face of the king-and-corpse law: "it seems to be a law for a creative person that the king in him must carry the corpse."

Jung's gloss: "the corpse represents the corpus, the body"; the burden is protection "against inflation, against possession through an archetype". (Date/place of the panel inferred — Jung gives neither.)

occurrences.title: 'Cross, thou art the evil stepmother of my son' — Mary and the cross (old English legend)
occurrences.label: Cross, thou art the evil stepmother of my son
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "I quoted in The Psychology of the Unconscious an old English legend, a dialogue between the mother, the cross, and Mary. Mary accused the cross: 'Cross, thou art the evil stepmother of my son.' It is the same as the mother, the mother cross — exactly the idea which underlies the cult of Attis".

The cross as the tree that gives birth to Christ and takes his life again — the feminine face of the crucifixion, doubled in the medieval "Crucifixus dolorosi" motif and in the recession of Christ into the tree. Carrying the cross = carrying the mother.

occurrences.title: The cross made of four kinds of wood — Vitis mystica (ascr. St. Bernard)
occurrences.label: The cross made of four kinds of wood
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Witness no. 5 in Jung's quaternity-in-Christian-iconography series: "'It is said … that the cross was made of four kinds of wood,' St. Bernard, Vitis mystica, cap. XLVI, in Migne, P.L., vol. 184, col. 752; cf. W. Meyer, Die Geschichte des Kreuzholzes vor Christus, p. 7" (cw11 ¶? pdf p689).

The four-wood legend makes the instrument of redemption itself a quaternity — the cross as assembled totality, "a boundary-stone between heaven and hell", set in the centre of the cosmos and extending to all sides.

occurrences.title: The cross of light vision — Acts of John
occurrences.label: The cross of light vision — Acts of John
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: For there are [places] of the right and of the left, Powers, Authorities, Archons, Daemons... and the Nether Root whence proceeded the nature of whatever comes to be.
body: On the "mountain" (a Platonic supra-celestial place), John sees a cross of light with a formless multitude about it, and above it the Lord himself — with no outward shape, only a voice. The cross is named "now Logos, now Nous, now Jesus, now Christ, now Door, now Way, now Bread, now Seed, now Resurrection, now Son, now Father, now Pneuma, now Life, now Truth, now Faith, now Grace," and defined as "the Boundary of all things."

Jung's reading: Docetism here is "almost epistemological" — the historical crucifixion below in Jerusalem is real but the symbol expresses "a parallel psychic event in the beholder" (¶430). "Since it is a quaternity, a whole divided into four parts, it is the classic symbol of the self" (¶430); for the Gnostics the cross had exactly the function the atman or Self has for the East (¶433). The diorismos (boundary) at the centre, not the periphery, is the point of transcendence (¶434).

occurrences.title: Mock crucifixion with ass's head — Palatine graffito
occurrences.label: Mock crucifixion with ass's head
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The mock crucifixion on the Palatine shows the Crucified with an ass's head
body: The famous graffito (pl. XLIII, plate at pdf p289), used by Jung in the horse-and-ass excursus of ¶421: the ass-headed Crucified belongs to the theriomorphic underside of the god-image — the ass as priapic animal and mount of the god (Balaam, Christ on the ass, the ass-headed Jerusalem idol).

image.title: Graffito G-68 (PSF)

occurrences.title: Cross of ropes stretched over water — Muyscas sacrifice
occurrences.label: Cross of ropes stretched over water
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Here the divinity is evidently the water, not the cross, which only signifies the place of sacrifice.
body: The divinity is the water (the womb), not the cross; the intersection is the "point of union where the 'crossing' takes place" — sacrifice offered where the roads of the rite cross, on the analogy that fertility magic increases the things marked for sacrifice (¶407).

occurrences.title: The Nestorian stele of Sianfu (781 CE)
occurrences.label: The Nestorian stele of Sianfu (781 CE)
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The Christians, also, went into China; the famous Nestorian monument in Sianfu was erected in 781.
body: "the famous Nestorian monument in Sianfu was erected in 781, with the inscription in both Chinese and Syrian". Jung cites it as material evidence of the caravan roads by which Western religions penetrated to China — Nestorian Christianity and Manichaeism together, the latter's documents found in East Turkestan translated into Chinese and Uiguric. Richard Wilhelm speaks of it in The Secret of the Golden Flower, and Jung allows that "it seems not unlikely that even the text of the Golden Flower was affected by Christian ideas". Shown with the Gandhara and Turfan pictures on 25 November.

occurrences.title: Palenque Cross with child offering — Yucatán
occurrences.label: Palenque Cross with child offering — Yucatán
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: one of them holding out a child for either sacrifice or baptism
body: Mayan relief (pl. XLIa, plate at pdf p286), cited by Jung alongside the Fejérváry codex as proof that hanging victims on crosses was a religious custom in Middle America (¶400). The cross here is "tree of our life or flesh" — a sacrificial and baptismal tree with a bird at its crown.

occurrences.title: The world-soul split in a chi (X) — Plato's Timaeus
occurrences.label: The world-soul split in a chi — Plato's Timaeus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The idea of union expressed in the cross symbol is found in Plato’s Timaeus, where the demiurge joins the parts of the world-soul together by means of two sutures, which form a X (chi).
body: The demiurge joins the parts of the world-soul by two sutures forming a chi; the world-soul "contains the world in itself like a body", an image which "cannot fail to remind us of the mother" (¶404). Jung reads the self-contained bliss of the world-god as the vessel motif — the Indian god in the lotus or the embrace of his Shakti, Diogenes in his tub (¶405) — and notes that the image of the soul "somehow coincides with the mother-imago" (¶406).

occurrences.title: The cross as Mary's stepmother — 'Dispute between Mary and the Cross'
occurrences.label: The cross as Mary's stepmother
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In the Middle Ages the cross was therefore logically understood as the mother.
body: Middle English debate poem in which the cross, the instrument of her son's death, is a "false tree" that "destroyed Mary's fruit with a deadly drink." Mary laments: "My sonys stepmodir I thee calle." Sancta Crux answers: "Lady, to thee I owe honour... Thi fruyt me florysschith in blood colour" (¶26).

Jung uses it to show that "the moment of the eclipse and mystic marriage is death on the cross. In the Middle Ages the cross was therefore logically understood as the mother" — the wounding of the sponsus (Honorius' "Thou hast wounded my heart," ¶¶24-25) read by the vernacular imagination as a family drama between the mother and the fatal tree.

occurrences.title: The crucifixion between the two thieves — paradise and hell (Luke 23)
occurrences.label: The crucifixion between the two thieves
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: The great symbol completed by its margins: "This picture is completed by the two thieves, one of whom goes down to hell, the other into paradise. One could hardly imagine a better representation of the 'oppositeness' of the central Christian symbol" (¶659). The dividing sword is Christ himself; the Christian is marked out by being wounded through.

Returned to at the book's climax as the form of mediation: "the mediator hangs between two thieves, one of whom goes to paradise, the other down to hell" — the symbolism of Christ's fate already indicated the mediation between opposites which John's sun-woman vision anticipates (¶739).

occurrences.title: The clergyman's childhood dream — carrying the water-closet house
occurrences.label: The clergyman's childhood dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich (dreamer's childhood, reported in the seminar)
occurrences.yearDisplay: dream at ~5 years old (late 19th c.); reported 9 Nov 1938

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: A dream a clergyman "had as a child: when he was about five years old he had the clergyman's dream. He dreamt that he was in a water-closet which was outside the house, and suddenly somebody forced him to take that whole little house upon his back". The dreamer later drew it for Jung — "in reality such a house would never have such a form": the ground plan of the house was a cross.

Jung: "and that is where we are all closeted — in this corruptible body of dirt — and we have to carry it. A child five years old had that intimation from the unconscious." The transitus-burden row: the king and the corpse, Mithras' bull, the fir tree of Attis, Christ's cross as "a symbol for the mother."

occurrences.title: The world-soul cut crosswise — Plato's chi (Timaeus 36)
occurrences.label: The world-soul cut crosswise — Plato's chi
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Timaeus 36: the Demiurgos, having made the world-soul, "separated it crosswise" — Plato's image of staffs bent into two wheels pushed obliquely into each other so that, seen along their plane, they cross like an X: the Platonic chi, the fourfold division of the world, legible in the sky as zodiacal light against the Milky Way.

Jung's reading: "This peculiar symbolism is the mythological remnant of that primordial experience of becoming conscious; in the moment when consciousness appeared, there was division." — the dawn of consciousness as a split running through the whole world, still preserved in Plato's myth.
Placed beside Tauton/Thateron (same lecture): consciousness IS discrimination, and the cross-shaped soul-diagram is its cosmological projection.

occurrences.title: The jagged cross-shaped wound on the animus — opening of 'The Rising of the Serpent' (Visions, 29 Nov. 1933)
occurrences.label: The jagged cross-shaped wound on the animus
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: First image of the series "The Rising of the Serpent": the dwarfed creature "became a man. He no longer had the black hair of an animal. After I had spoken I saw appear upon his breast and arms a jagged bloody wound in the shape of a cross. Tears streamed down his cheeks. He bowed his head and walked ahead of me to lead me down the black and rocky path".

Jung: "the mind and the animus together carry the symbol. The symbol here is the cross, and it is marked on his breast: her mind is marked by the symbol... carrying the symbol is a sort of transitus" — Christ carrying the cross, Attis the pine, Mithra the bull (pp1277-1278). Since whatever the patient omits is done by the animus, "when the animus receives the wound, it is the wound which she is avoiding". The cross gathers St Paul's cosmic meaning, the East, and mandala symbolism.

occurrences.title: The diadem — Malchuth ascending to Kether, bride and Shekinah (Kabbala denudata)
occurrences.label: The diadem — Malchuth ascending…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: [Corona] sic vocatur Malchuth, quando ascendit usque ad Kether; ibi enim exist ens est Corona super caput mariti sui.
body: Jung's kabbalistic reading of the crowning in the Return of the Soul: "It is just possible that the idea of the diadema is connected with the cabalistic Kether (corona). The Diadema purpureum is Malchuth, 'the female,' 'the bride.'" Purple is the vestmentum of the Shekinah, "the Garment and the Palace of the Modus Tiphereth."
N.16: the paradoxical relation of Malchuth (lowest) to Kether (highest) is the parallel to the crowning of the lapis from below. Goodenough, "The Crown of Victory in Judaism," cited.

occurrences.title: The staff withdrawn, the wound healed - 'Too long have I fructified the earth' (Visions, 22 June 1932)
occurrences.label: The staff withdrawn, the wound healed - Too…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The wound instantly healed and the woman arose. I said: \"Why has this happened to you?\" The woman answered: \"Too long have I fructified the earth.\
body: Continuation of pegasus-crucified-woman-star-vision-zurich-1932: "I drew the staff forth from the breast of the woman... The wound instantly healed and the woman arose. I said: 'Why has this happened to you?' The woman answered: 'Too long have I fructified the earth.'"

Jung: "an abbreviated resurrection, the three days in the grave in a moment". Fructifying the earth = "to give libido to the earth... the biological libido of the morning of life"; the crucified woman "has lived only the first part of life, and the other aspect of herself is to live the second part... the impersonal form of life". The crucifixion read as vernal sacrifice - arnion, the little ram of Aries, sacrificed when the spring point left Aries, "Therefore Christ was called Ichthys, the fish"; the ver sacrum; Goethe's "Die Natur verlangt einen Tod". "The sacrifice... is meant only as a transformation" - yet historically the body is left behind: "the two separate apparently, and the one with the white horse takes the star, the symbol of individuation... and we are left in doubt as to what has happened to her shadow, to her poor body". The wound "is really like the wound of Amfortas".

occurrences.title: The crucifixus and the voice on redeeming — vision of a Jewish-born patient
occurrences.label: The crucifixus and the voice on redeeming
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: But Christ is not able to redeem you. If you could redeem yourself, he would be bleeding less. When men in general are able to redeem themselves, he will cease to bleed. It will then be like a song that has lost its significance.
body: Jung's opening exhibit for the suffering-God discussion: "a vision given me by a patient… a youngish, educated man, who was originally a jew," religiously indifferent, who "suddenly had this vision of the crucifixus," fell into ekstasis, and heard a voice.

Jung reads it against Nietzsche's anti-Christian destructiveness: this vision "is very much more human because it shows pity" — carry your own burden and Christ bleeds less; redemption is a function of mankind's self-redemption. "There is nothing schizophrenic in the case… they are truly psychic phenomena-what one calls mystical experiences"; later trancelike syncopes brought the same voice. There are almost no relevant dreams before or after — the vision arrived unprompted.

occurrences.title: Cupid asleep beside the well among the dancing maidens
occurrences.label: Cupid asleep beside the well among the dancing…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Zarathustra II (1883); imagery of Nietzsche's parents' era

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: beside the welllieth he quietly, with closed eyes.
body: In the Dance-Song Zarathustra finds "a green meadow peacefully surrounded with trees and bushes, where maidens were dancing together," and in the dark wood "banks full of roses under my cypresses" — "and even the little God may he find... beside the well lieth he quietly, with closed eyes." Jung dates the feeling-fantasy precisely: rococo faded into Biedermeier, the phil-hellenistic decor of Nietzsche's parents' drawing-room — proof that "a man who is entirely unconscious of his anima will first... fall into his mother's feelings."

The sleeping Cupid chasing butterflies (psyche, the soul) is Eros wholly in the unconscious, never reaching a woman. Well and Cupid are not opposites but a couple — "a sort of mandala... it is one and the same mood" — Astarte and her son; the whole arrangement "a sort of Venusberg, or a temple of Astarte where he should touch the earth," used illegitimately as a satire of the spirit of gravity.

occurrences.title: Nicholas of Cusa's sermon: Jacob's well, the well of reason, the well of wisdom
occurrences.label: Nicholas of Cusa's sermon
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Here, then, we have Jacob's well of the senses, the well of reason and the well of wisdom.
body: A sermon of Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa, a contemporary of the alchemists, on the parable of the Samaritan woman: Jacob's well of the senses (drunk from by father, children, and cattle), the deeper well of reason (drunk from by the philosophers), and the deepest well of wisdom in Christ's humanity, "which brings bliss and immortality."

Jung cites it (¶485) to show that the Rosarium's falling dew is the aqua sapientiae — "the dew falling from heaven the divine gift of illumination and wisdom." Cusanus' further images: "Whosoever drinks the spirit, drinks of a bubbling spring"; reason as an intellectual seed generating in itself "the water of understanding," from which the streams of science flow — for Jung, a demonstration of how easily the water of wisdom could be mistaken for philosophical knowledge alone (the books that must later be destroyed).

occurrences.title: Cinedian fish and the dragon's stone — Cyranides
occurrences.label: Cinedian fish and the dragon's stone — Cyranides
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The Cyranides describes a round transparent fish, six fingers long, living on the Syrian-Palestine-Libya coasts, carrying two stones in its head and one in the third tail vertebra (spondilo) — the cinedian stone, potent as a love-potion ('ligature of Aphrodite') and pertains to Saturn (¶214). The stone is 'twin or twofold': one opaque black, one black but shining 'like a mirror' — the dragon's stone (dracontius lapis), known to Pliny and the medieval alchemists as draconites (¶214-215). Jung reads its double nature as the polarity of opposites that gives the lapis its uniting significance, extended even to Christ (¶215-216).

occurrences.title: Cautes and Cautopates — the Mithraic dadophors
occurrences.label: Cautes and Cautopates — the Mithraic dadophors
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The bull-sacrifice flanked by two torch-bearers, one with raised, one with lowered torch; sometimes holding bull's head and scorpion (Taurus/Scorpio, equinoctial signs); Cumont connects them with sepulchral Erotes and makes them offshoots of Mithras' triadic nature ("the threefold Mithras").

Jung's reading: "One would stand for death, the other for life" (¶294) — the Dioscuri pattern of the mortal and immortal sun, flanked also in Christ between the two thieves and Baal between Aziz and Monimos.
Verbatim: They form a pair of brothers whose characters are revealed by the symbolic position of the torches. (cw05 ¶294).

occurrences.title: Inspiration as mediumship — Ecce Homo on the poet's daimon (Turin, 1888)
occurrences.label: Inspiration as mediumship
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: One hears–one does not seek; one takes–one does not ask who gives; a thought suddenly flashes up like lightning, it comes with necessity, without faltering–I have never had any choice in the matter.
body: Nietzsche's late self-description of inspiration in Ecce Homo (written 1888, published 1908) is the corpus's locus classicus for creation as automatic, necessitated influx. Two passages are quoted in cw01's cryptomnesia apparatus. First: one must "hardly be able completely to set aside the idea that one is the mere incarnation, mouthpiece, or medium of an almighty power" — "One hears–one does not seek; one takes–one does not ask who gives; a thought suddenly flashes up like lightning, it comes with necessity, without faltering–I have never had any choice in the matter" (fn 120). Second, the physiology of ecstasy: "a feeling of being completely beside yourself, with the most distinct consciousness of innumerable delicate thrills tingling through you to your very toes", where pain is not the antithesis of happiness "but as its condition … necessary shades of colour in such an excess of light" (fn 123).
