Jung reads these as Nietzsche's own testimony that consciousness "only plays the role of slave to the daemon of the unconscious" (cw01 ¶177, ¶184) — inspiration as possession by the autonomous complex, with "beside yourself" as the doubling datum. Written weeks before the Turin collapse, the text is also evidence in Jung's later Nietzsche case.

occurrences.title: Leopold the control manipulates Hélène Smith's body (Geneva, ~1895–1900)
occurrences.label: Leopold the control manipulates Hélène Smith's…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: as though her vocal organs were being manipulated or removed, she began to talk in a natural voice
body: Hélène Smith (Catherine-Elise Muller), Flournoy's celebrated Geneva medium, is governed in trance by a "control" personality, Leopold, distinct from the somnambulistic roles (Marie Antoinette, the Martian dynasty). Jung flags two of Flournoy's observations in the monograph's apparatus. First, voice-transfer with bodily invasion: after "a séance in which she suffered acutely in her mouth and in her neck, as though her vocal organs were being manipulated or removed, she began to talk in a natural voice" (Flournoy p. 103, fn 106) — the medium experiences the other personality literally working her larynx, possession imagery in physiological dress. Second, a simultaneous split of the body between two automatized selves: "while H. S. speaks somnambulistically as Marie Antoinette, her arms do not belong to the somnambulistic personality but to the automatist Leopold, who converses by gestures with the observer" (Flournoy pp. 130f., fn 108). Jung cites both as evidence that somnambulistic personalities are automatized complexes operating the body against, and alongside, the ostensible role — the splinter-psyche datum behind his daemon-of-the-unconscious language (cw01 ¶177, ¶184).

occurrences.title: The God figures of Elephanta and Siva's dance — Pauli before the caves (late 1952)
occurrences.label: The God figures of Elephanta and Siva's dance
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~6th c. CE (rock-cut caves); visited by Pauli late 1952

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: To the Westerner, however, after he has gone through the scientific age, it seems naive and erroneous to project the experience in concretist terms into rhythmic processes in the physis.
body: On the basis of "experience extending over a lengthy period of time" of rhythmic sensations in dreams — "an inner perception of 'archetypal sequences'" — the dreamer reports that seeing the God figures on the island of Elephanta near Bombay convinced him "that the rhythmic movements of the transmigration of souls and the world ages [Weltzeitalter] in India, especially Siva's dance, are based on similar experiences."

The remark sits inside the anima-dance dream of 28 Sep 1952 (anima-chinese-woman-trapdoor-auditorium-dream-1952) and Pauli's India journey, whose cost — his wife's illnesses since the trip — he reads as "a relationship problem".

occurrences.title: The two elves and the Lord's Prayer — 'Our Father, who art not in heaven' (Danish folklore)
occurrences.label: The two elves and the Lord's Prayer
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: A tale Jung retells in "A Review of the Complex Theory" to characterize the autonomy of complexes: "the elfin beings so aptly characterized in Danish folklore by the story of the clergyman who tried to teach the Lord's prayer to two elves. They took the greatest pains to repeat the words after him correctly, but at the very first sentence they could not avoid saying: 'Our Father, who art not in heaven.' As one might expect on theoretical grounds, these impish complexes are unteachable" (cw08 ¶202). Jung cites no source; the anecdote circulated in 19th-c. folklore collections.

Its place in Jung's argument: complexes "behave like Descartes' devils," slip in the wrong word, trip the latecomer over the chair — they are the elfin beings and "little people" (with the lares and penates of ¶209 and the hobgoblins of ¶203) that folklore everywhere projects as nightly house-spirits: personifications of the splinter psyches seen when no inhibiting consciousness suppresses them.

occurrences.title: The Danish pastor and the soulless elves on the moor
occurrences.label: The Danish pastor and the soulless elves…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: Our Father which art not in heaven...
body: Jung's story for the anima-type of the dream girl: a Danish pastor, returning at midnight from a dying man across the moor where only one path is safe, meets two little figures walking where no human could — elves. Asked what a pastor is, and told his work is praying so that souls are saved, they moan that they have no souls; taught the Lord's Prayer, they can only repeat "Our Father which art not in heaven..." — so he must dismiss them, "and that is why they never received immortal souls."
The dream-girl is such an elfish being: the soulless one who fascinates — "these elfish beings are a preliminary stage of a magical female being that we call anima."

occurrences.title: Dante's heavenly rose (Paradiso XXXI)
occurrences.label: Dante's heavenly rose (Paradiso XXXI)
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: a flower that spreads over the whole starry heaven
body: At the beginning of dream 26 a shooting star falls "in a curious leftward curve," and the dreamer notices the curve "corresponded exactly to the line he drew when sketching the picture of the eightfold flower": "Thus the shooting star traces the outline, so to speak, of a flower that spreads over the whole starry heaven. What is now beginning is the circulation of the light. This cosmic flower corresponds roughly to the rose in Dante's Paradiso (fig. 83)" (¶229).

The rose of the celestial assembly — the mandala of the blessed arranged in petals round the divine centre — is Jung's closest medieval parallel for the cosmic mandala-flower of the dream-series; it also links to the "rose garden of the philosophers" of alchemy (¶155, ¶235) and the rosa mystica of the Litany (¶257).

occurrences.title: Dante's flame of purification at the summit of Purgatory — Virgil must stay behind
occurrences.label: Dante's flame of purification at the summit…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: he himself steps back-because he is a heathen, he cannot pass through that flame-but Dante, baptized a Christian, can enter the fire of pure love where everything earthly is burned out of him, and then ascend to heaven.
body: In the last circle of purgatory, approaching the celestial sphere, Virgil leads Dante to the wall of flame and steps back — "because he is a heathen, he cannot pass through that flame" — while Dante, baptized, passes through "the fire of pure love where everything earthly is burned out of him" and ascends. Jung uses it twice: as the archetype of the purifying emotion that precipitates the imperishable substance ("the zone of fire in which every desire is burned out... the pure gold that stands the fire forever," pdf p1123), and in the chakra mapping of the Commedia — hell as muladhara, purgatory's fire as manipura at the diaphragm, Virgil the pagan prophet of the Child (per the medieval reading of his Eclogues) who cannot enter the flame.

occurrences.title: 'Dust of the earth is their food, and clay their meal' — the dead of the Gilgamesh epic
occurrences.label: Dust of the earth is their food…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Dr. Wespi's amplification for the robbers'-den dream: "What is of special importance to us is the tradition that clay was the food of the inhabitants of the Babylonian-Sumerian underworld. In the Epic of Gilgamesh, too, it is said of the dead: 'Dust of the earth is their food, and clay their meal'".

Jung continues (p166): "In Babylonian texts we find the idea that the dead eat their own excrement; the dead have to eat the heavy, indigestible clay.... just as the earth eats up the dead, the dead now have to eat earth, too. The dead eat earth like a sarcophagus." Chain: Genesis 3:19 ("dust thou art"), the serpent condemned to eat dust (Gen 3:14), and Mephistopheles' "He'll eat the dust" in the Prologue in Heaven. The boy forced to eat clay swallows the mortal world.

occurrences.title: Five-year-old girl: pyramids of ash, parents' death masks; crater landscape, father calling
occurrences.label: Five-year-old girl
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: age five, remembered; consultation ~1930s; presented 17 Jan 1939

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Two first-remembered dreams of a woman who consulted Jung at about thirty, shortly before an outbreak of schizophrenia. (1) The father calls at night; in the parents' bedroom stand "a pyramid made of ash above each bed, and above each of those the death masks of father and mother." (2) A desolate place full of craters; far away, the father stands in a crater calling for help. Presented by Dr. Nothmann; amplified with Egyptian pyramid religion (Ba, Ka, embalming, Osiris), Chinese geomantic graves, cremation prayers, the phoenix, and the I Ching's Splitting Apart.

Jung: both dreams end without lysis — an unfavourable prognosis. The ash-pyramids are a correctly executed archetypal cremation burial; the masks, like the Egyptian Ka, preserve the parents' identity "as a provision for a possible rebirth" (p186). The craters are open graves, the mouth of the great ancestress; the world is "naked cosmos." The dead father-spirit alone survives — animus possession, later fulfilled in the woman's life.

occurrences.title: The deification: serpent's coils, crucifixion attitude, Salome's sight and the lion face — Jung's vision (December 1913)
occurrences.label: The deification — Jung's vision
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: The culmination of the descent series. After the serpent-duel, Jung and Elijah climb to a cyclopean ring-wall — "a Druidic sacred place" — whose walls grow immense while the altar, the house, Salome and the snake shrink tiny: he is at the bottom of the world, in the crater-house of Salome and Elijah. "Elijah smiled and said, 'Why, it is just the same, above or below.'" Then Salome worships him — "You are Christ" — he resists ("This is madness"), and the snake encircles him, coils to his heart: "I realized as I struggled, that I had assumed the attitude of the Crucifixion." He sweats until water streams on all sides; Salome rises and can see; and his face becomes "the face of an animal of prey, a lion or a tiger".

Jung identifies the sequence as the ancient mystery of deification: the lion face is "the famous [Deus] Leontocephalus of the Mithraic mysteries,10 the figure which is represented with a snake coiled around the man... the face of the man that of a lion" — Aion, from the Persian Zrwanakarana, "the infinitely long duration" (pdf p118; footnote number as printed). "All this is Mithraic symbolism from beginning to end"; the Gnostic reversed cones and Dante's Inferno give the above/below geometry; "in this deification mystery you make yourself into the vessel, and are a vessel of creation in which the opposites reconcile".

occurrences.title: 'Thou shalt have become God' — Hippolytus on Christian self-knowledge
occurrences.label: Thou shalt have become God
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Hippolytus's account of Christian doctrine in the Elenchos (X, 34, 4): "But thou shalt speak with God and be joint heir with Christ... For thou wilt have become God. For whatever sufferings thou didst undergo as a man, thou hast shown that thou art a man; but whatever is appurtenant to a God, that God has promised to bestow... That is the 'Know thyself,' the knowing of the God who made thee. For to him who knoweth himself it is given to be known of Him by whom he is called" (cw13 ¶372).

Jung cites it directly after the Theosebeia exhortation as the Christian counterpart of the alchemical self-knowledge: "The moral equivalent of the physical transmutation in to gold is self-knowledge" (¶372).
Verbatim: For thou wilt have become God (cw13 ¶372)

occurrences.title: Gnostic myth: the Demiurge beholds a light he did not create
occurrences.label: Gnostic myth — the Demiurge beholds a light he…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: when he suddenly beheld a little light far above his head and knew that that he had not created. Instantly he traveled up and up until he reached that light...
body: The Demiurge creates the world, withdraws to admire it — "'That is damned good,' he said and was quite vain about it" — then looks up to receive praise and instead:

"That is a Gnostic myth, and that is a psychological experience": the precise record of an initiation — the discovery of something in the psyche one has not made, identical in structure to the Catholic patient's un-invented "touch of moisture in the air". Vanity of creation (the maker-god's, and the ego's) is broken by the superior light it cannot claim.

occurrences.title: Ptah — the creative word (Memphite theology)
occurrences.label: Ptah — the creative word (Memphite theology)
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939
Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "It is like the old Egyptian ideas about Ptah, the creative word; what he speaks, is. Of course our rational standpoint would say it always had been. Yes, but it did not exist for us because we did not exist." — Jung's counter to Mrs. Baynes's "is the opposites-in-the-cosmos a projection?": "they are, but they are not operative inasmuch as you don't know it."

The second engagement shifts to Ptah as self-begetter: "Like the old Egyptian texts, he is the builder of his own nest, the maker of his own egg: he forms himself upon his own potter's mold" — the god creating himself, the Phoenix myth, Eckhart's godhead born in the soul. Editor: CW5 plate XLIV shows Ptah shaping the world egg.

occurrences.title: Ulysses as demiurge — Joyce's creator-god of detached consciousness
occurrences.label: Ulysses as demiurge
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Spirit in Man, Art and Literature (CW15)

occurrences.quote: Ulysses is the creator-god in Joyce, a true demiurge who has freed himself from entanglement in the physical and mental world
body: Jung's culminating figure for the book: "Ulysses is the creator-god in Joyce, a true demiurge who has freed himself from entanglement in the physical and mental world and contemplates them with detached consciousness" (cw15 ¶192). The demiurge myth is retold at ¶199: "The demiurge first created a world that in his vainglory seemed to him perfect; but looking upward he beheld a light which he had not created" — whereupon "his masculine creative power turned into feminine acquiescence" (Goethe's "The Eternal Feminine / Still draws us on").

Jung's reading. "He is for Joyce what Faust was for Goethe, or Zarathustra for Nietzsche. He is the higher self who returns to his divine home after blind entanglement in samsara"; "the book itself is Ulysses, a microcosm of James Joyce, the world of the self and the self of the world in one" (cw15 ¶192). The negativity of the world-picture is dated: "After the optimism of the seventh day of creation the demiurge must have found it pretty difficult in 1914 to identify himself with his handiwork"; the book was banned "to avoid the scandal of its contradicting the creation story in Genesis" (cw15 ¶192).

occurrences.title: Demon eating the sun — stone, eastern Java
occurrences.label: Demon eating the sun — stone, eastern Java
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Stone relief of Rahu-type eclipse demon swallowing the solar disc.

Jung's reading: the sun-devouring demon — cf. Hanuman bursting "another sea monster, who was the mother of Rahu, the sun-devouring demon" (¶311); the whale-dragon as Terrible Mother whose conquest wins eternal youth (¶374).
Verbatim: Demon eating the sun Stone, eastern Java, 15th century.

occurrences.title: Deucalion and Pyrrha cast the bones of the Great Mother
occurrences.label: Deucalion and Pyrrha cast the bones…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: After the flood, the oracle bids the sole survivors throw "the bones of the Great Mother" behind them; the stones they throw become human beings. The nymph Anchiale similarly casts dust from which the Dactyls spring.

Jung's reading: the motif of throwing behind one as anal-birth imagery — "The idea of anal birth recalls the motif of throwing something behind one" (¶279); creation of mankind by the infantile route.
Verbatim: They thereupon threw stones behind them, from which mankind sprang. (cw05 ¶279).

occurrences.title: The stillness criterion: devil noisy, Holy Ghost still — Athanasius, Vita Antonii
occurrences.label: The stillness criterion
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: It cannot be the Holy Ghost, for that is a stillness
body: Athanasius' report on the desert anchorites: the devil "even occasionally reads the Bible to them or sings hymns," but comes "with a great noise"; the Holy Ghost is the opposite — "when everything is quite still then they can be sure it is the Holy Ghost." Jung uses it twice as the type-criterion for a problem he declares "very fundamental": influxus diabolicus vs the working of the Holy Ghost, mirrored in analytical psychology as archetypal invasion vs the releasing symbol of the transcendent function.

His commentary: the criterion worked for hermits "in the year 100 or 150" whose air was "full of ten thousand devils" — the turba — so that "the great stillness that came after, and the purity of the air, would give them the feeling of being redeemed". "We are living under entirely different circumstances and must have... an entirely different criterion".

occurrences.title: The bearded man who demanded he 'take a sin' — visions of the epileptic boy
occurrences.label: The bearded man who demanded he 'take a sin'
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: From about age seven an epileptic boy was seized with terror of an unseen presence, then saw "a short man with a beard," never met before, describable in fine detail, who pursued him demanding he accept something unspeakable — "It was murder." Jung needed hours to win the confession. The boy had already thrown scissors at his little sister, the point piercing her skull (¶137). From nine to twelve the figure changed into a nun whose unveiled face was pale and deathlike; the rage-fits ceased and manifest epileptic attacks began.
Jung's reading: "the vision of the nun signified the changing of the incompatible criminal tendency symbolized by the bearded man into obvious disease" (¶137).
Quote. "This man tried to make me take a sin." "But what sort of a sin?" I asked. [...] "It was murder."

occurrences.title: The binarius, Eve and the devil — Dorn, De tenebris contra naturam (1602)
occurrences.label: The binarius, Eve and the devil
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Dorn's numerological theodicy: God created the binarius on the second day — separating the waters — "and that this was the reason why he omitted to say … that 'it was good.'" From the binarius issued "its quaternary offspring" (sua proles quaternaria). Since 2 is feminine it signified Eve; 3 was Adam; the devil, "armed with a certain likeness of binary to binary, made his attack on the woman. For all even numbers are feminine, of which two, Eve's proper and original number, is the first" (cw11 ¶? pdf p693).

"The reader will have noticed how Dorn, with great cunning, discovers in the binarius a secret affinity between the devil and woman." Jung credits him as "the first to point out the discord between threeness and fourness … thus—albeit unconsciously—cutting the thread of alchemical projection"; Dorn suspected "something ungodly in the quaternity, which was intimately associated with the nature of woman."

occurrences.title: Black daemonic figure vs. white figure at the bedside — sister's vision (Zurich, 1899–1900)
occurrences.label: Black daemonic figure vs. white figure…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: the black figure seized her by the throat and started to choke her; then she awoke.
body: Three of S.W.'s sisters began to hallucinate as the circle's atmosphere charged; the married sister's repeated night-vision is the sharpest: a black daemonic figure arguing with a beautiful white figure at her bedside, the black seizing her throat, and on waking a "black shadow with human outlines" beside a "cloudy white figure", gone only when the candle was lit. Jung reports it as evidence of the hallucination-contagion within the circle and of the systematic, dramatic quality of the medium's world radiating outward.

The dark/light pair reappears systematized as Connesor/Magnesor (¶70) — the occult field polarizing into devil-figure and luminous helper. Parallels: devil-black-man-cold-hands-cell-zurich-1902 · magic-mirror-child-mirror-devils-face-zarathustra-1883 · serpents-toads-red-mantle-swedenborg-london-1744.

occurrences.title: Black man with cold hands — Godwina F.'s cell vision (Zurich, 1902)
occurrences.label: Black man with cold hands
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: it seemed as if the door suddenly opened and a black man came in, with bent head, who seized her by the shoulders with cold hands and pushed her into the pillows.
body: Recovered from total amnesia: on the second or third night in the cell, Godwina F. — awaiting 10,000 marks she was sure had been placed on the table — saw the door open and a black man enter, head bent, who gripped her shoulders with cold hands and pushed her into the pillows; the thought "Christ, he's after my money!" broke the trance, and the money was gone. The terror organizes the hysterical stupor that follows ("It was just like being dead"), with the jailer's wife as the bearded man who "hits her" in every later retelling. A hallucinated intruder at the exact pressure-point of loss and guilt.

occurrences.title: The black mass in plague-time France (12th-13th c.)
occurrences.label: The black mass in plague-time France
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: They reverted to the devil because they said God didn't hear them any longer.
body: Asked how to avoid devil worship once the devil is admitted into the quaternity, Jung distinguishes the psychological act from the historical cults — and gives this one: "in the 12th and 13th centuries in France, in those times of terrible plagues and wars and famines, they worshipped the devil by means of the black mass. They reverted to the devil because they said God didn't hear them any longer. He had become quite inclement and didn't accept their offerings, so they had to apply to some other factor."

Jung's reading: such worship is not the model. "But of course it has nothing to do with all that; when you come to psychology you cannot keep on thinking in the same terms as before" — the psychological equivalent of devil worship is rather "to consciously take into account the existence of an evil factor", the constructed devil-vessel between neighbours. A created devil "will be a poor vessel because you will be eaten away by doubt all the time you are constructing it", hence cannot be worshipped.

occurrences.title: Blumhardt's exorcism of the two possessed sisters — Möttlingen
occurrences.label: Blumhardt's exorcism of the two possessed…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: He once healed a case of spirit possession, a very interesting case. And the son continued the ways of the father and was the spiritual medicine-man for all the theologians of my set and my time.
body: "The elder Pastor Blumhardt — his son was also a pastor — became famous for his exorcism of the devil, who was in possession of two sisters" (Jung's footnote, citing Zündel's 1880 biography; the case is the historical Möttlingen exorcism). In the seminar text: "You know Blumhardt was a famous man in his day. He once healed a case of spirit possession, a very interesting case."

The son "continued the ways of the father and was the spiritual medicine-man for all the theologians of my set and my time" — including the cousin whose confession drew the famous reply: "Do you really think God takes notice of your dirt?" Jung uses the pair to show a conception of God that is not 'thou-shalt'.

occurrences.title: Devils hidden in the marble of the painted chapel — Case D at Burghölzli (1886)
occurrences.label: Devils hidden in the marble of the painted…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: between the veins of the marble he had drawn little figures of devils and also a not unskilful caricature of the asylum’s priest.
body: Set to painting in the asylum, Case D (the manic vagabond painter) depicted the asylum chapel; only afterwards was it discovered that "between the veins of the marble he had drawn little figures of devils and also a not unskilful caricature of the asylum's priest." The official image carries its negation concealed inside its ornamental field — trickster-work in the sacred frame, aimed (with the caricature) at the asylum's own clergy.

An early Jung-reported psychogenic artwork — proto art-therapy datum and a dated devil-locus. Parallels: devil-black-daemonic-figure-sister-vision-zurich-1899 · devil-black-man-cold-hands-cell-zurich-1902 · devil-gravediggers-joke-zarathustra-1883.

occurrences.title: Diabolical mimicry — Justin's explanation of the Dionysus-Christ resemblance
occurrences.label: Diabolical mimicry
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the devil went to Greece and told them all about it; he arranged that the myth of Dionysus should be made known
body: The church father's answer to why the pagan myth so startlingly prefigures the Christian one — retold by Jung over the Mayan crosses: "the devil knew-his intuition, I suppose-that God was going to send his only son to rescue man, and that it must be checked somehow. So the devil went to Greece and told them all about it; he arranged that the myth of Dionysus should be made known, in order that, when Christ came, they could say: Oh, we have heard all that before!-which would of course deflate Christianity" (pp100-101). The Spanish conquerors applied the same "diabolical mimicry" to Yucatan's crosses; Jung reverses the verdict: "their crosses were really the expression of an eternal truth, the four arms of the cross and the idea of the sacrifice in the center" (p101). The doctrine is the negative mirror-image of Jung's own archetypal-repetition thesis.

occurrences.title: The fall of the angels — Samiazaz, Azazel and the giants (1 Enoch 6-8)
occurrences.label: The fall of the angels
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: The "fall of the angels": "two hundred angels under the leadership of Samiazaz descended to earth, took the daughters of men to wife, and begat with them giants three thousand ells long. The angels, among whom Azazel particularly excelled, taught mankind the arts and sciences" (¶669). Jung reads them as "extraordinarily progressive elements who broadened and developed man's consciousness… an inflation of the cultural consciousness" — answered by the counterstroke of the Deluge.

The archangels' peroration before the throne ("All things are naked and open in Thy sight… Thou seest what Azazel hath done") shows Yahweh once more not consulting his omniscience (¶670-671). The sciences of the fallen angels return at ¶742 and ¶746: modern man's dangerous knowledge was "originally taught by the fallen angels".

occurrences.title: 'I saw Satan fall like lightning' — Christ's vision (Luke 10:18)
occurrences.label: I saw Satan fall like lightning
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: "a curious metaphysical phenomenon which Christ witnessed: he saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. In this vision a metaphysical event has become temporal; it indicates the historic and—so far as we know—final separation of Yahweh from his dark son" (¶650). Satan is banished from heaven but not into hell — "upon earth"; he keeps "his dominion over the sublunary world" until the end of time.

The fall explains Satan's comparatively inferior role in the Incarnation history, and answers the missing punishment of the Job story "in a strangely limited form" (¶650). Cf. the duplication in Revelation 12, where the dragon's fall is staged again (¶713).

occurrences.title: Devil in the garden shaft — dream of a girl of five (12 November 1940)
occurrences.label: Devil in the garden shaft
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
jung.locator: pdf p438–444 (presented by Dr. Emma Steiner; paper text lost)

occurrences.quote: I am seeing my father at a shaft in the garden. The earth moves, and I think: there's the devil down there. And I call my father for help. But my father laughs and pushes me down. I land in a tool shed with a cold frame full of seedlings.
body: A five-year-old girl dreams her father stands at a shaft in the garden; the earth moves, she thinks "there's the devil down there," calls the father for help — and the father laughs and pushes her down. She lands not in hell but in a tool shed with a cold frame full of seedlings. Jung's reading against the tiger dream of the same age: this consciousness is already "much better prepared," conflict-laden; the father aborts an incipient father complex at the outset (otherwise "a father complex as high as a house, a fille à papa"). The devil is so out of place — no hell, only shovels and seedlings — that he is "a modified devil," a vegetation demon: the child is planted like a seedling into fertile earth, an Osiris-like life demon of budding future life; Seth-Typhon is simply "the shadow of Osiris."

occurrences.title: The grave-diggers' joke — stealing the bite from the devil
occurrences.label: The grave-diggers' joke
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Grave-diggers mock Zarathustra carrying the corpse: "Will Zarathustra steal the bite from the devil?... If only the devil is not a better thief than Zarathustra! — he will steal them both, he will eat them both!"

Jung reads the joke as "characteristic of the style of Zarathustra in general" — brilliant yet painful, a pathological joke with a "stabbing pain" in it. Beneath it: anthropophagy. The devil means utter destruction, so the carrion is "only good for utter destruction"; Zarathustra who steals it becomes a carrion-eater — "he becomes the sarcophagus of Mr. Nietzsche... the tendency of the wise old man to be a vulture."
Verbatim: "as the devil is the principle of utter destruction, this morsel is only good for utter destruction."

occurrences.title: Jan Hus at the stake — 'O holy simplicity!' (Constance, 1415)
occurrences.label: Jan Hus at the stake — 'O holy simplicity!'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The Bohemian reformer Jan Hus (Jung, following Mrs. Jung's prompt: "Johann Jakob Hus"), burned at Constance at the instigation of the church. At the stake he saw a little old woman bringing wood for the fire and said: "Oh holy simplicity!" — she thought she was doing a good work.

Jung's frame is Zarathustra's warning "be on thy guard against holy simplicity... fain, likewise, would it play with the fire of the fagot and stake": the holy simpletons "are the great power behind the good and the righteous... they only become efficient and dangerous when millions of simpletons are marching behind them." The masses "really bring the fuel for the stake — it doesn't need to be a real stake of course: there are moral stakes too."
Filed under the better-man-is-the-worse logic: Christ chosen instead of Barabbas; Hus as the creative man the righteous burn.

occurrences.title: Luther throws the inkstand at the devil (Wartburg, 1521–22)
occurrences.label: Luther throws the inkstand at the devil
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The legend: while Luther was planning his reformation at the Wartburg, the devil appeared to him and he threw his inkstand at him.

Jung adduces it, with Nietzsche's seven devils, as the confrontation with one's own opposite: "that was his devil. And the same psychological critique could be applied to Christ; when the devil tempted him it was his devil, the power devil... he is only man when he meets his own devil. Then he is human."
The apologetic point matters to him: "I hope that Christ was a human being, otherwise he is of no use to us... For a god, it would be nothing. But he was always checked by himself, by his own devil."

occurrences.title: The Lutheran pastor and the devil in the straight line — clinical case
occurrences.label: The Lutheran pastor and the devil…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: treatment before the war (inferred); Jung met him again after 1918

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: In the case of that Lutheran pastor the real reason for his neurosis was a great inner rebellion against that principle of the straight line, and the devil got loose in him and literally raised hell with him.
body: "Once before the war I treated a Lutheran pastor, a pretty hard analysis." The case fills out the dragon-'thou-shalt' discussion: the pastor's neurosis was "a great inner rebellion against that principle of the straight line, and the devil got loose in him and literally raised hell with him. He fought me like the devil himself, but finally he came round."

After a year of digesting the analysis he reached the conclusion Jung wants: "neither the decalogue nor any other code of morality could be identified with God." His parting word is quoted too: "the church is the work of the devil, but if you want to live you must even make use of the devil" — a parson who "very much believed in the living god that is not a 'thou-shalt'… he is not codified."

occurrences.title: The devil as patron saint of the hunted animals — patient dream
occurrences.label: The devil as patron saint of the hunted animals
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Dream reported in the footnote apparatus to the sulphur chapter: "Animals were being hunted. The devil, their patron saint, appeared. Suddenly all the colours appeared in his dark-brown face, and then a vermilion spot in his cheek".

The devil appears as protector of the hunted (animal) unconscious contents; the sudden irruption of colour into the dark face, crowned by the vermilion spot, is the red of sulphur showing in the dark chthonic figure — the devil face of Mercurius-sulphur before its colour transformation.

occurrences.title: Satan falling as lightning — Luke 10:18
occurrences.label: Satan falling as lightning — Luke 10:18
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Christ's word to the seventy returning from their mission: "I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven" — the pre-cosmic fall of the light-bearer seen in vision, Luke's one independent fall-logion, standing right beside the disciples' exorcistic power ("the spirits are subject unto you", No. 47 in Jung's anthology). Jung compiled it without comment in his 1899 dossier for the Ritschl lecture — the devil who fascinated him in the Faust lecture of the same cycle (index: "Faustian beings, 70") here in his Gospel source-text.

Inferred reading: the fall-as-lightning is the devil family's cosmogonic scene — the autonomized light-figure cast down, which Jung later reads as the shadow that was once highest light (expresses_inferred, not stated in this chunk).
Verbatim: "I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven. [10:18]"

occurrences.title: Satanael, God's first son — Bogomil legend
occurrences.label: Satanael, God's first son — Bogomil legend
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: the devil, as Satanaël, is God's first son, Christ being the second.
body: In certain Gnostic views (which Jung's footnote traces into the Bogomil tradition), the devil appears as Satanael, God's first son, Christ being the second. Jung introduces it at the hinge of the Trinity essay: if the devil, as the adversary of Christ, "would have to take up an equivalent counterposition and be, like him, a 'son of God,'" then "a further logical inference would be the abolition of the Trinity formula and its replacement by a quaternity" (¶249).

The same Judaeo-Christian schema resurfaces in the Werblowsky foreword: Clement of Rome's Christ as the right hand and the devil as the left hand of God (¶470). The monotheistic difficulty — everything that goes against God must be traced back to God — is what keeps the "highly influential personage" unaccommodated in the trinitarian cosmos.

occurrences.title: The devil in the street, hanging in mid-air — 16-year-old's compulsion-neurosis dream (Zurich, ~1910s)
occurrences.label: The devil in the street, hanging in mid-air
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: In deathly terror he leaps into the air and hangs there suspended. This dream was repeated twice, a sign of its special urgency.
body: The initial symptom of a severe compulsion neurosis in a sixteen-year-old patient: "He is walking along an unfamiliar street. It is dark, and he hears steps coming behind him... Finally he turns round, and there he sees the devil. In deathly terror he leaps into the air and hangs there suspended. This dream was repeated twice, a sign of its special urgency" (¶285).

Jung's reading: the universal problem of evil and sin "produces collective compensations" (¶285). The dream anticipated the whole neurosis — the patient's ceremonial keeping of a "provisional" or "uncontaminated" state of purity against the transitoriness of human existence — by showing "that if he wanted to come down to earth again there would have to be a pact with evil" (¶286). The suspension in mid-air is the literal refusal of the earthly.

occurrences.title: The temptation on the pinnacle of the temple (Matthew 4:5–7)
occurrences.label: The temptation on the pinnacle of the temple
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939
Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Satan sets Jesus on the pinnacle of the temple and bids him cast himself down. Jung's radical inversion: "I and the Father are one" is the identification with the Father, and casting himself down — taught as the devil's temptation, "the greatest evil" — "could also be understood as casting himself out of the archetype... the serpent or the devil was that darkness behind man which invites him to jump down from superhuman heights, to come down to the level of the ordinary being living in the here and now, disidentified from eternal images."

On 22 January 1936 (Mr. Allemann's question) he separates the figures: the historical Jesus was right to refuse — "the devil makes promises only in order to destroy one"; but the symbolical Jesus, the clavis hermetica, cannot exclude the world — "as soon as Christ becomes a real symbol you are a philosopher, for Christianity has then come to an end". "About 90 percent of all the idealistic people in the world believe that to be identified with the archetype is right."

occurrences.title: The devil offers Jesus all the kingdoms of the earth — wilderness temptation (Matthew 4:8–10)
occurrences.label: The devil offers Jesus all the kingdoms…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This devil was the objective psyche that held all the peoples of the Roman Empire under its sway, and that is why it promised Jesus all the kingdoms of the earth, as if it were trying to make a Caesar of him.
body: The third temptation: an exalted devil shows Jesus all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time and offers them, if he will fall down and worship. Distinct scene from devil-temptation-pinnacle-temple-gospels-30ce (the pinnacle of the temple, Matthew 4:5–7); Jung here works the kingdoms offer.

Jung's reading (¶309, "The Development of Personality"): the tempter is "the power-intoxicated devil of the prevailing Caesarean psychology" — the objective psyche that "held all the peoples of the Roman Empire under its sway"; the promise of all kingdoms is made "as if it were trying to make a Caesar of him." Jesus, obeying the inner call of his vocation, voluntarily exposes himself to the assault, lets it act on him consciously and assimilates it — "Thus was world-conquering Caesarism transformed into spiritual kingship" (¶309). "The religion of love was the exact psychological counterpart to the Roman devil-worship of power."

occurrences.title: The three-headed Satan — Dante's Inferno and the umbra trinitatis
occurrences.label: The three-headed Satan
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: This would point to an infernal Antitrinity, a true "umbra trinitatis" analogous to the Antichrist.
body: Dante's Lucifer at the bottom of hell chews on three traitors in his three faces. Jung: "Medieval representations of the triune God as having three heads are based on the three-headedness of Satan, as we find it, for instance, in Dante. This would point to an infernal Antitrinity, a true 'umbra trinitatis' analogous to the Antichrist."

Context: the devil remained outside the Trinity as the "ape of God" because the Christian definition of God as summum bonum excludes the Evil One — though in the Old Testament he was still one of the "sons of God." The devil is "the 'odd man out' in the Christian cosmos," whom people minimize by euphemistic ridicule, or by laying the blame at man's door.

occurrences.title: St Anthony's devil-visions — Egyptian desert (~3rd–4th c.)
occurrences.label: St Anthony's devil-visions — Egyptian desert
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The devil is, of course, the voice of the anchorite's own unconscious, in revolt against the forcible suppression of his nature.
body: Athanasius' biography of St Anthony supplies Jung with the locus classicus of the Church's suppression of the individual unconscious (¶82). The devils sing like a loud song, mimic scriptural voices, rouse the monk to night prayer, accuse him of secret sins, appear as a brother monk carrying bread; a "haughty and insolent" devil declares "I, even I, am the power of God"; and Satan himself knocks at the door one night — a tall strong man who complains that the monks curse him, and vanishes "like dust" at the name of Christ. Jung's reading: these apparitions are what befalls those who "pray and fast in solitude" — the devils are the voice of the suppressed nature.
The quotations "show how, with the help of the general belief, the unconscious of the individual was rejected despite the fact that it transparently spoke the truth" (¶83).

occurrences.title: The wager in heaven — Satan and Yahweh over Job (Job 1-2)
occurrences.label: The wager in heaven — Satan and Yahweh over Job
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: The prologue in heaven: one of the sons of God, "the unscrupulous slanderer" (¶579), raises a doubting thought; Yahweh bets Job's person and family without a stake. "And the Lord said to Satan, Have you considered my servant Job… He still holds fast his integrity, although you moved me against him, to destroy him without cause" (¶615/¶616).

Jung's reading: Yahweh's readiness to deliver Job into Satan's hands proves "he doubts Job precisely because he projects his own tendency to unfaithfulness upon a scapegoat" (¶616); the dark deeds that follow — "robbery, murder, bodily injury with premeditation, and denial of a fair trial" — violate three commandments of Sinai (¶581). Satan is God's dark son, concealed "in his own bosom" (¶594).

occurrences.title: The Prolific and the Devouring — Blake, The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
occurrences.label: The Prolific and the Devouring
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: These two classes of men are always upon earth … the Prolific and the Devouring. … Religion is an endeavour to reconcile the two.
body: Jung closes the Spitteler chapter with Blake, "the English mystic": "These two classes of men are always upon earth... the Prolific and the Devouring... Religion is an endeavour to reconcile the two" (¶460). The epigram compresses the whole argument — Epimetheus' kingdom of correct values versus Behemoth's animal dynamis, Prometheus and Epimetheus reunited in the child Messias — into a formula Jung treats as the spontaneous formulation of the same collective process in England a century earlier.

occurrences.title: The heavenly dew (Ros Gedeonis) on the black corpse — Rosarium, Figure 8
occurrences.label: The heavenly dew on the black corpse
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Here falls the heavenly dew, to lave / The soiled black body in the grave.
body: The eighth Rosarium woodcut: the heavenly dew falls from above to lave the soiled black body in the grave — the mundificatio or purification.

Jung (¶483-493): the dew is the Ros Gedeonis (Gideon's dew), synonym for the aqua permanens and hence for Mercurius; Senior quoting Maria: the water is "a king descending from heaven" (Rex de coelo descendens). The whitening (albedo/dealbatio) is the sunrise after darkness — "Azoth and fire cleanse the lato and remove the blackness." The Rosarium follows with its long disquisition on Wisdom (Septimum Sapientiae Salomonis) — water as the aqua sapientiae, traced by Jung to the Samaritan woman at the well and Nicholas of Cusa's three wells. Psychologically: the enantiodromia of nigredo into albedo, and the demand that realization engage all four functions — "the books must be destroyed, lest thinking impair feeling and thus hinder the return of the soul" (¶488).

occurrences.title: Gideon's dew on the fleece — sign of Jahveh (Judges 6)
occurrences.label: Gideon's dew on the fleece — sign of Jahveh
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: Jahveh let the dewfall to show that he was on Gideon's side. It was a miracle, a revelation.
body: Gideon lays out the fleece and asks for a sign: dew soaks the fleece while the ground stays dry, then the reverse. Jung adduces it when asked about the anima's riddling word to Zarathustra, "The dew falleth on the grass when the night is most silent" ('The Stillest Hour'). Miss Hannah calls dew an alchemical symbol; Mr. Baumann names Gideon.

Jung's reading: "Yes, that was the sign from heaven... It was a miracle, a revelation". The anima "would be saying, 'Now keep quiet, don't talk, particularly don't try to teach people, because in the stillest hour the revelation will come to you, as the dew came to Gideon.' That is an excellent example of what the anima can do in a critical moment of life." Dew = silent-night revelation against Zarathustra's babbling; the alchemical ros is its later descendant.

occurrences.title: Diana of Ephesus with the mural crown — Roman statuette
occurrences.label: Diana of Ephesus with the mural crown
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Pl. XXIVb: the many-breasted Ephesian Diana wearing the mural crown.

Jung's reading: the city is "a maternal symbol, a woman who harbours the inhabitants in herself like children", hence Rhea, Cybele and Diana "all wear the mural crown" (¶303); Old Testament cities addressed as women (Isaiah 47; Jeremiah 50:12).
Verbatim: It is therefore understandable that the three mother-goddesses, Rhea, Cybele, and Diana, all wear the mural crown (pl. XXIVb). (cw05 ¶303).

occurrences.title: Diogenes with his lantern, seeking a man in Athens
occurrences.label: Diogenes with his lantern, seeking a man…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 4th c. BCE act; ~3rd c. CE source

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: He lit a lamp in broad daylight and said as he went about, 'I am looking for a man.
body: Jung follows Diogenes Laertius against the 'honest man' legend: Diogenes lit his lantern at noonday because there were no men in Athens. The image illustrates his thesis that consciousness is nature's answer to darkness — 'only if it were dark would one produce an illumination.' Consciousness is 'the only seeing eye of the deity.' Parallels: god-eye-triangle-radiating-churches-europe · light.

occurrences.title: Dionysian reconciliation — the veil of Maya torn away (Nietzsche, Birth of Tragedy)
occurrences.label: Dionysian reconciliation
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Nietzsche's great Dionysian set-piece, quoted by Jung as the closing amplification of his 1913 typology paper. The car of Dionysos "heaped with flowers and garlands," panthers and tigers striding beneath his yoke; the slave free, "all the rigid, hostile barriers" between men broken down; and then: "each feels himself not only united, reconciled, merged with his neighbour, but one with him, as though the veil of Maya had been torn away, and nothing remained of it but a few shreds floating before the mystery of the Primal Unity" (cw6 ¶878).

Jung's comment is a single line — "Any commentary on this passage would be superfluous" — letting the passage stand as his full description of the extraverted, Dionysian state: "the unleashing of a torrent of libido into things" (¶877). It is the counter-image to ship-schopenhauer-mariner-principium-individuationis-1818: dissolution of the principium individuationis instead of its serene defence. The Upanishadic borrowings (Maya, the Primal Unity) mark Nietzsche's Greek god as already a hybrid of East and West.

occurrences.title: Vision: Dionysian youth with cymbals checked by the blind old man; the ancient mother's lap (21 Jan – 4 Feb 1931)
occurrences.label: Vision — the ancient mother's lap
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "A beautiful youth with golden cymbals, leaping high in the air with joy and abandon", black-haired, in a leopard skin, followed by leaping dogs — comes upon an old man in a turban, arms outstretched. The cymbals drop; the old man gazes at the earth and flowers spring up at his feet; the youth falls and buries his face in the flowers. "His face was dark but his eyes were white. He was blind."

Reading: the Apollonian principle called up by the Dionysian attempt — Delphi's temple "originally been the property of Dionysus... later on divided really with Apollo" (p250). The old man's way is the East: wu wei, "the Eastern principle... sit still and give things a chance to grow" (legendary invisible emperor, p253-254). Blindness is the technique: the seeing intellectual eye "kills the growth... like the face of the Medusa" — contemplate without understanding (p254-255). The vision continues (4 Feb): the youth drops onto the lap of the ancient mother (her painting: a colossus), dives into the pond below "like a dolphin", and emerges with golden hair — "a sort of reborn sun": the rite de sortie from deification (p255-260).

occurrences.title: Dionysos made shareholder in Delphi — the Greek settlement with the Dionysian
occurrences.label: Dionysos made shareholder in Delphi
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The Delphic settlement: "there was some trouble over the Delphic oracle and they finally settled that claim in such a way that Dionysos became a shareholder in Delphi having equal rights with Apollo. They were fifty-fifty and so it worked; in that way they could arrange themselves with that Dionysian spirit without upsetting Olympus, and Zeus remained on top."

The foil is Wotan: "he is not alone but all the others are of a somewhat different character — Loki, for instance... Yet Wotan is the supreme god. There is no Zeus above him and therefore he is an uncontrolled factor... So Dionysos could be assimilated while Wotan is an unassimilated element. He is the spirit of the lion, and out of that spirit the child is born".
Verbatim: "Dionysos became a shareholder in Delphi having equal rights with Apollo. They were fifty-fifty and so it worked".

occurrences.title: The devil told the Greeks the myth of Dionysus — Justin Martyr, 190 CE
occurrences.label: The devil told the Greeks the myth of Dionysus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the devil told the Greeks the myth of Dionysus, foreseeing that God would later on send his son to redeem the world.
body: Justin Martyr's diabolical-anticipation doctrine: about eight hundred years before Christ the devil told the Greeks the myth of Dionysus, foreseeing the redemption, so that when God's messengers came the Greeks could spoil the effect: "Oh, that is an old story." Jung relishes the apologetic mechanics — Christ performed the same miracles as the temples of Dionysus (water into wine), and iconography confused the two (the Damascus goblet). The same argument returns 11 & 18 Mar 1931 as the frame for the patient's regression: she does not go back to Dionysus for fun, but because "he is the great competitor of Christ."

occurrences.title: Nietzsche's Dionysian explosion — the retort, the shaft, 'The Drunken Song'
occurrences.label: Nietzsche's Dionysian explosion
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1885 (Zarathustra Part IV, chs. 74, 76, 79 per editorial footnote)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: Then suddenly he discovered that he was filled with a new orgiastic enthusiasm which he called his experience of Dionysus, the god of wine. You see, that is the spirit. Dionysus is the god of prophecy, of prophetic dreams, and he is the god of the body.
body: Jung's account of how Nietzsche, having "crept into his own retort," suddenly "discovered that he was filled with a new orgiastic enthusiasm which he called his experience of Dionysus, the god of wine." Jung glosses Dionysus as "the god of prophecy, of prophetic dreams, and he is the god of the body" — the original effervescent spirit, not the intellect.

He points to the late poems in which Nietzsche "describes how he was digging down into himself, working into his own shaft," till the digging produced "the explosion of the most original form of spirit, the Dionysian." This is the body-as-alembic teaching turned biography. Distinct locus from Nietzsche's Turin psychosis (see nietzsche-psychosis-crucified-dismembered-dionysus-turin-1889).

occurrences.title: Dionysus dismembered by the Titans, reborn of Semele (Greece)
occurrences.label: Dionysus dismembered by the Titans, reborn…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: after he was dismembered by the Titans, Hera gave his heart to his father, Zeus, who swallowed it.
body: The Titans tear Dionysus apart; Hera gives his heart to Zeus, who swallows it; Semele then bears the new Dionysus — or Zeus encloses him in his own thigh till maturity. Either way it is "rebirth or resurrection symbolism, so it approaches the Christian idea." The early church answered by declaring Dionysus an anticipation insinuated by the cunning of the devil (Justin Martyr), while claiming the Osiris-Isis myth as a positive, Pope-sanctioned anticipation of Christ — Jung's twin exhibits of how antiquity's dying god was metabolized by Christianity.
The patient's own series will live the sequence: back through the Dionysian phase toward "the great competitor of Christ."

occurrences.title: Dionysus dismembered by the Titans — diffusion into all things (Orphic)
occurrences.label: Dionysus dismembered by the Titans
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: By being torn to pieces by the Titans, Dionysus diffused into all things, so that all things contain Dionysus.
body: In the Khidr exposition Jung judges the Islamic Green One "probably most closely related to the widespread views on Dionysus in antiquity": the vegetation god, life god, life spirit "who is nothing but spirit, a whole, who appears in everything." The mythological warrant is the dismemberment: "By being torn to pieces by the Titans, Dionysus diffused into all things, so that all things contain Dionysus." Mystically Khidr likewise can appear in every form — which "brings him closer to other views of a Gnostic nature," the mutabilis Savior unrecognized by the Archons. The same "undivided and divided spirit" formula is applied to Khidr directly at pdf p466.

occurrences.title: Eckermann's dream — Faust and Mephistopheles falling as a double meteor (Weimar, ~1830)
occurrences.label: Eckermann's dream — Faust and Mephistopheles…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1823-32 (dream; reported in Conversations with Goethe, publ. 1836)

jung.workTitle: The Spirit in Man, Art and Literature (CW15)
jung.locator: fn 19 to Psychology and Literature (pdf p168)

occurrences.quote: Eckermann's dream, in which he saw Faust and Mephistopheles falling to earth in the form of a double meteor, recalls the motif of the Dioscuri
body: Goethe's secretary Johann Peter Eckermann dreamed that Faust and Mephistopheles fell to earth together in the form of a double meteor — the paired flame of the Dioscuri. Jung reads the dream as diagnostic of Goethe's own psyche: it "recalls the motif of the Dioscuri (cf. the motif of the two friends in my essay 'Concerning Rebirth')" and thus "sheds light on an essential characteristic of Goethe's psyche" — the two-souled constitution Jung elsewhere treats under the Faust double.

The subtle point, Jung says, is Eckermann's remark that the swift and horned figure of Mephisto reminded him of Mercurius — "in full accord with the alchemical nature of Goethe's masterpiece." The twin-meteor image therefore binds the Faust pair to both the divine-twin motif and the trickster-mercurius current in one image.

occurrences.title: Diotima — the anima of Socrates (Plato's Symposium)
occurrences.label: Diotima — the anima of Socrates
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: the anima of Socrates who made such apt remarks.
body: Jung's yardstick for the wisdom-aspect of Nietzsche's Life-figure: her teaching is "not the highest wisdom, but is only a very clever remark, one which would be worthy of Diotima for instance, the anima of Socrates who made such apt remarks. What she had to say in that famous dialogue about the Eros sounds exactly like this passage".

The distinction matters: the wisdom in "my wild Wisdom" is borrowed — "the aspect of wisdom is due to the identity with Zarathustra" — whereas Diotima stands for the anima whose speech genuinely carries Eros-teaching (footnote: Socrates says he learned about Eros from the priestess Diotima). Sophia, by contrast, "would be the highest form of anima," and Nietzsche's figure is not yet that.

occurrences.title: Dionysos dismembered by the Titans — the heart rescued (Orphic myth)
occurrences.label: Dionysos dismembered by the Titans
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "He is caught by the Titans, the chaotic powers of nature, and they dismember and devour him; so a part of Dionysos is everywhere in nature, and only his heart, in the nick of time, was rescued from the cooking pot of the Titans. That was swallowed by Zeus who thus gave rebirth to Dionysos."

Jung's law of the creator: "If you assume the divine prerogative of creation, you will suffer the punishment which is meted out to the creative god: you will be dismembered... The fate of the creator is dismemberment in matter." The mystery was "taken over into Christianity as the creative principle": the body distributed to mankind, the mantle divided under the cross — "the wine we drink as the blood of Christ is Dionysos."

occurrences.title: Zosimos' vision: the sacrificer and Ion, priest of the inner sanctuaries (Egypt, ~3rd c.)
occurrences.label: Zosimos' vision — the sacrificer…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Panopolis / Alexandria, Egypt (Berthelot, Alch. grecs III i 2)
body: The opening vision of the Treatise of Zosimos the Divine concerning the Art: a sacrificer on a bowl-shaped altar with fifteen steps; the voice from above — "I have performed the act of descending the fifteen steps into the darkness, and of ascending the steps into the light... I am Ion, the priest of the inner sanctuaries, and I submit myself to an unendurable torment" (cw13 ¶86). Ion is pierced with the sword, dismembered "in accordance with the rule of harmony," flayed head-first, burnt, "till I perceived by the transformation of the body that I had become spirit" — then changes into "a mutilated anthroparion" that spews its own flesh and tears it with its own teeth.

Jung: the homunculus concept "appears here for the first time in alchemical literature" (fn7); the self-devouring anthroparion stands for the uroboros. Ion = Yunan ben Merqūtilus, son of Mercury, of Sabaean tradition (fn4).

occurrences.title: King boiled, dismembered and revived — Allegoria Merlini
occurrences.label: King boiled, dismembered and revived
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The 'Allegoria Merlini': a king drinks 'the water which is closest to my heart', swells, and appears dead; Egyptian and Alexandrian physicians dispute — the Egyptians dismember and triturate him with moist medicines, the Alexandrians wash, dry, powder him again with sal ammoniac and nitre, and melt the mass, 'whereupon the king rose up from death and cried in a loud voice: "Where are my enemies?"' (cw14 ¶357-358). Jung: 'the primitive motif of the murder or sacrifice of the king for the purpose of renewing his kingly power and increasing the fertility of the land' (¶358); the dismemberment's 'original may be the dismemberment of Osiris and Dionysus' (¶365). The medical quarrel 'may hark back to pre-Islamic times' (¶367).

occurrences.title: The Lord of Death's dismemberment of the Bardo body — Chönyid Bardo
occurrences.label: The Lord of Death's dismemberment…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: Then the Lord of Death will place round thy neck a rope and drag thee along; he will cut off thy head, tear out thy heart, pull out thy intestines, lick up thy brain, drink thy blood, eat thy flesh, and gnaw thy bones; but thou wilt be incapable of dying.
body: The hellish torments of the Chönyid state, quoted by Jung as the measure of yoga's real danger:

Jung's reading: the tortures describe "a disintegration of the wholeness of the Bardo body, which is a kind of 'subtle body' constituting the visible envelope of the psychic self in the after-death state" — its psychological equivalent is psychic dissociation, in deleterious form schizophrenia (¶848). The deliberately induced psychotic state of kundalini yoga risks exactly this (¶847).

occurrences.title: Pentheus torn to pieces by the Maenads (Dionysus myth, Thebes)
occurrences.label: Pentheus torn to pieces by the Maenads
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "Pentheus, curious to see the orgies of the Maenads, climbed up into a pine-tree but was spotted by his mother; the Maenads cut down the tree, and Pentheus, taken for a wild animal, was torn to pieces by them in their frenzy, his own mother being the first to hurl herself upon him" (¶662).

Jung reads it as a "striking counterpart to the death of Attis and the subsequent lamentation": the phallic meaning of the tree (felling = castration), its maternal nature ("the tree 'bears' Pentheus"), and its identity with the son (felling = slaying) are all present at once — and in the mother-led sparagmos "we have here the counterpart and complement of the Pietà, namely the Terrible Mother." The Pietà mourns the dead son on the mother's lap; the Maenads' fury is the same mother in her devouring aspect.
Verbatim: "his own mother being the first to hurl herself upon him" (¶662).

occurrences.title: Rosinus' vision of the dismembered white man with the golden head — Splendor solis, sixth parable
occurrences.label: Rosinus' vision of the dismembered white man…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The sixth parable of the Splendor solis portrays the separatio as a dismembered corpse: "Rosinus says that he would like to make plain a vision that he has seen of a man who was dead, whose body was yet all white like a salt, and whose limbs were divided, and his head was of fine gold but separated from the body" (¶530).

Jung traces the golden head to Osiris, "who is described in a Greek papyrus as 'headless,'" and notes that "the Greek alchemists styled themselves 'Children of the Golden Head'" — the severed, gold apex of the separated body as the alchemist's own badge.

occurrences.title: The spiritus phantasticus and the divine punishment of dismemberment — Synesius, De Insomniis
occurrences.label: The spiritus phantasticus and the divine…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: And being divine, as such he has to undergo the divine punishment.
body: Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373-c. 414), Neoplatonist and Christian bishop (Jung says "Edessa" — probably in error), on the creative imagination: there is a spiritus phantasticus in man that can descend into unspeakable depths or ascend almost to the gods — and thereby becomes divine. Jung's citations make it the earliest examination of creative fantasy (CW6 par. 175). In the seminar it grounds his whole reading of the patient's sun-deification: had her experiences been felt in the body she "would have been divine — of course, divine in the human category."

The sting is the corollary: divinity incurs the divine punishment — dismemberment, sacrifice on the altar like the god-animal. "In these words he gives away the secret of the transition from paganism to Christianity."

occurrences.title: Synesius' spiritus phantasticus and the divine punishment (De Insomniis)
occurrences.label: Synesius' spiritus phantasticus…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Jung's patristic authority for the price of identification with the creative spirit: "An old father of the church, the Bishop Synesius, said that the spiritus phantasticus, man's creative spirit, can penetrate the depths or the heights of the universe like God or like a great demon, but on account of that he will also have to undergo the divine punishment". Jung: "That would be the dismemberment of Dionysos or the crucifixion of Christ. We shall come presently to the same problem in Zarathustra."

The context is his law of possession: "man does not possess creative powers, he is possessed by them", and "anybody identified with God will be dismembered" — the anticipation of Zarathustra's own fate, "prophecy of his own life" through the rope-dancer. Editor cites CW6 ¶171 on Synesius assigning the spiritus phantasticus the role Schiller gives the play instinct.

occurrences.title: A man disputes with his Ba — 'The Conversation of a Life-Weary Man with his Soul'
occurrences.label: A man disputes with his Ba
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: Cf. the remarkable account of developing consciousness in an ancient Egyptian text, translated, with commentary, by Jacobsohn, entitled \"Das Gespräch eines Lebensmüden mit seinem Ba.\
body: Jung's oldest witness for the dialogue that begets consciousness, cited in Answer to Job's discussion of reflection:

A man contemplating suicide argues with his Ba — the bird-souled double who threatens to leave him — and in the quarrel a reflected, self-relating consciousness is born. The Ba here is not a belief but an opponent with its own will: the psyche's second voice, two millennia before Job's dialogue with his God.

occurrences.title: Divination bowl of Patricius and Hilarius — the name 'Theodorus' (Rome, 371)
occurrences.label: Divination bowl of Patricius and Hilarius
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung's classical witness that "Experiments in divination are known from the grey dawn of history": a metal bowl with the alphabet engraved round the rim; over it, amid fearful oaths, a ring on a thread "began to swing, and spelt out the name Theodorus" — the successor to Emperor Valens. When the magic was divulged, Patricius and Hilarius were arrested and put to death (¶703).

Jung's reading: the same automatic-movement mechanism as table-turning and the pendulum, in which "intended tremors" guided by unconscious ideas produce apparent alien intelligence (¶729–730). The political lethality of a reading is the historical price of taking the oracle literally.

occurrences.title: Divine birth and coronation of Amenhotep III — Theban birth cycle
occurrences.label: Divine birth and coronation of Amenhotep III
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Thou art reborn in the renewal of the Sed festival.
body: The Luxor reliefs depict Amon uniting with Queen Mutemwiya and begetting the divine child Amenhotep III; the Coronation "advanced him a step further than birth in the divine scale of life" (Colin Campbell), and its anniversary was held as a Sed festival, the king regarded as Osiris on earth — his complete "Osirification."

Jung's reading (with Jacobsohn): the god-king trinity of father, son, and ka/ka-mutef; the divine marriage of god and queen as hierosgamos generating the god-man; the Sed festival as periodic royal rejuvenation ("reborn in the renewal of the Sed festival"). Parallels: heb-sed-festival-egypt-new-kingdom, ka-mutef material, cantilena-riplaei-sterile-king-15c.

occurrences.title: Zarathustra pregnant under the mantle — the anima with child ('Old and Young Women')
occurrences.label: Zarathustra pregnant under the mantle
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "Is it a treasure that hath been given thee? Or a child that hath been born thee?" — Zarathustra steals along in the twilight hiding something under his mantle: a little truth "naughty, like a young child," screaming if not held.

Jung's reading: Nietzsche/Zarathustra is identical with the anima, and "his anima is with child" (Mrs. Sigg); the child is illegitimate, its father the animus of the anima — the wise old man: "the old wise man is forever the Holy Ghost... He is the inspiring archetype that holds the secret of the self". "Expressed in Christian symbolism, that passage would be the conceptio immaculata through the Word" — the anima heard the Word, as Mary conceived by the ear. The jewel-woman "pure and fine like the precious stone" carries it: "The jewel being a symbol of the self, the anima is really pregnant with the self" — buried "in the worst kind of sentimentality".

occurrences.title: The Logos as a small boy — vision of Valentinus
occurrences.label: The Logos as a small boy — vision of Valentinus
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung: Ripley's rejuvenated king may derive from 'the conception of the Ancient of Days and his youthful son the Logos, who in the visions of Valentinus the Gnostic and of Meister Eckhart was a small boy' (cw14 ¶379). The boy-Logos belongs with 'Dionysus, youngest of the gods, and of the Horus-child, Harpocrates, Aion' — 'All naturally imply the renewal of the ageing god' (¶380). Valentinus' vision gives the senex-puer pair its Gnostic form: the eternal son appears as a child to the visionary, the new dominant as a birth.

occurrences.title: Birth of the Buddha beneath the plaksa tree — Lalita-Vistara
occurrences.label: Birth of the Buddha beneath the plaksa tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: At his feet there grew up an immense lotus, and standing in the lotus he scanned the world. Hence the Tibetan prayer: Om mani padme hum (Om! Behold the jewel in the lotus).
body: Jung cites the Lalita-Vistara birth narrative as the exact mythological counter-form to Pandora's jewel: "So Maya, when her hour was come, bore her child beneath the plaksa tree, which bowed its crown shelteringly to earth" (¶298). "From the incarnate Bodhisattva an immeasurable radiance spread through the world; gods and all nature took part in the birth. At his feet there grew up an immense lotus, and standing in the lotus he scanned the world. Hence the Tibetan prayer: Om mani padme hum." The same light-phenomena and prodigies of nature attend his later rebirth beneath the bodhi tree. Jung uses the parallel to show Spitteler drew "on the same depths from which prophets and creative artists call up the redeeming symbol" (¶440), not on conscious borrowing.

occurrences.title: Demeter holding Demophon over the fire — immortality forfeited by the mother's cry
occurrences.label: Demeter holding Demophon over the fire
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: Isis holds the little son of the king of Phoenicia over the fire at night to make him immortal. But once the mother happens on this, she cries out loud; Isis quickly has to draw the child out of the fire, and immortality is lost. / Mr.
body: Amplifying the dream's staff-in-fire scene, Jung cites the fire-baptism legends of the divine child:

The pattern: the goddess secretly hardening the mortal child in fire until the natural mother's cry interrupts the making of immortality. Against it stands the dream's outcome: the girl stuck on the iron staff "for ever and ever" — fire without rebirth — until the water-gush releases her. "There are many mythological images of this... transformation of the ego into spiritual, immortal man".

occurrences.title: The dream of Brother Eustachius (medieval German mysticism)
occurrences.label: The dream of Brother Eustachius
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: I would mention Meister Eckhart's vision of the 'naked boy' and the dream of Brother Eustachius.
body: Paired by Jung with Eckhart's naked boy as a medieval spontaneous experience of the child archetype (¶267). Brother Eustachius' dream appears in the same Dominican-mysticism collection — evidence that the divine child "was not merely a traditional figure, but a vision spontaneously experienced (as a so-called 'irruption of the unconscious')". The pair grounds Jung's claim that archetypal images arrive "autochthonously", independent of tradition.

occurrences.title: Meister Eckhart — the divine child born in the soul ('Gott ist selig in der Seele')
occurrences.label: Meister Eckhart — the divine child born…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: The dark God's invasion of John "engendered in him the image of the divine child, of a future saviour, born of the divine consort whose reflection (the anima) lives in every man — that child whom Meister Eckhart also saw in a vision. It was he who knew that God alone in his Godhead is not in a state of bliss, but must be born in the human soul ('Gott ist selig in der Seele')" (¶741).

Eckhart stands in the lineage John began: the apocalyptist "anticipated the alchemists and Jakob Böhme… the possibility of God's birth in man, which the alchemists, Meister Eckhart, and Angelus Silesius also intuited" (¶733). The birth in the creaturely soul is the continuation of the Incarnation through the Holy Ghost.

occurrences.title: God born in me, the mother — Angelus Silesius
occurrences.label: God born in me, the mother — Angelus Silesius
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: 'Psychology of the Transference' §7 n.10 (pdf p425); §10 n.29 (pdf p431)

occurrences.quote: God is made man and now is born—rejoice! / Where then? In me, the mother of his choice. / How should that be? My soul that Virgin Maid, / My heart the manger and my limbs the shed.…
body: Jung cites Silesius three times across the last sections of the transference essay for the mystical birth of God in the soul — the soul as Christ's mother:
The new birth of §10 and the return-of-the-soul in its feminine aspect, in German mysticism.

occurrences.title: Wyndham's golden-eyed sun children of Midwich — parthenogenesis and participation mystique (novel, 1957)
occurrences.label: Wyndham's golden-eyed sun children of Midwich
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Midwich, England (fiction); sister villages in Siberia, Arctic, Africa
occurrences.quote: children are born with golden eyes.
body: A Ufo-like "thing" seals an English village in a circle of sleep for twenty-four hours; every fecundable woman is found pregnant, and "children are born with golden eyes," learning collectively — "if one of the boys has learnt something new... all the boys know it." Recognized as "a superior type of Homo sapiens" with "complete realization of their potential power for world domination," they are killed everywhere: the Africans immediately, the Eskimos by exposure, the Russians by bombardment, the English by the teacher's dynamite.

Jung's reading: "The peculiar parthenogenesis and the golden eyes denote kinship with the sun and characterize the children as divine progeny. Their fathers seem to have been angels of the annunciation" (¶823). The story repeats "the hero's threatened childhood and his early death through treachery" — but the children "live in a permanent state of participation mystique, or unconscious identity, that precludes individual differentiation," their uniform society "the very ideal of a Marxist state" (¶824).

occurrences.title: Homunculi in swarms — the Schreber case
occurrences.label: Homunculi in swarms — the Schreber case
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The 'imaginary' child is common among women with mental disorders and is usually interpreted in a Christian sense. Homunculi also appear, as in the famous Schreber case, where they come in swarms and plague the sufferer.
body: In the psychopathology of the child motif Jung cites the famous Schreber case: "Homunculi also appear, as in the famous Schreber case, where they come in swarms and plague the sufferer" (¶268). This is the plurality-form of the child: numerous homunculi, dwarfs, boys with no individual characteristics signal dissociation, "the products of its dissolution" (¶278) — schizophrenia as fragmentation of personality. (Schreber's Memoirs already serve c01 as the classic anima-possession document; this note pins the homunculus episode specifically.)

occurrences.title: The virgin shall conceive: Immanuel prophecy — Isaiah
occurrences.label: The virgin shall conceive — Immanuel prophecy
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given; and the government shall be on his shoulder; and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, the Prince of Peace.
body: The Isaian complex is Jung's scriptural paradigm of the redeeming symbol's genesis and fate.
