"Because the solution is irrational, the coming of the Saviour is associated with an irrational and impossible condition: the pregnancy of a virgin (Isaiah 7:14)" (¶438); "Immanuel... means 'God with us,' i.e., union with the latent dynamis of the unconscious" (¶447). Unto us a child is born — "Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God" (¶442); the wolf dwells with the lamb and "a little child shall lead them" — "The coming of the Saviour signifies a union of opposites" (¶441). Hard on the birth follow the Assyrian flood-waters, leviathan to be slain (¶444-445), the birth of the god "threatened by the dragon, by the danger of inundation, and infanticide" (¶448).

occurrences.title: The Magi follow the star to the philosophical infant — Introitus apertus
occurrences.label: The Magi follow the star to the philosophical…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The birth of the lapis told as an Adoration of the Magi: 'The Almighty has made him known by a most notable sign, whose birth is declared throughout the East on the horizon of his hemisphere. The wise Magi saw it at the beginning of the era, and were astonished, and straightway they knew that the most serene King was born in the world. Do you, when you see his star, follow it to the cradle, and there you shall behold the fair infant. Cast aside your defilements, honour the royal child, open your treasure, offer a gift of gold; and after death he will give you flesh and blood, the supreme Medicine in the three monarchies of the earth' (cw14 ¶460). The apotheosis of the filius regius; the dead child-king gives eucharistic flesh and blood.

Verbatim: Viderunt Sapientes in Evo Magi et obstupuerunt statimque agnoverunt Regem serenissimum in mundo natum. Tu, cum eius Astra conspexeris, sequere ad usque cunabula, ibi videbis infantem pulcrum

occurrences.title: 'My son is the coming Messiah' — a woman's hero-projection on her son (case, early 20th c.)
occurrences.label: My son is the coming Messiah
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Closer investigation, however, revealed the existence of an unconscious dogma that said: My son is the coming Messiah. This is a very ordinary instance of the widespread hero-archetype in women
body: A woman Jung knew "surrounded her son with the most solemn care and lent him an importance he in no way deserved, with the result that soon after puberty he became neurotic." Analysis uncovered the unconscious dogma regulating her behaviour: "My son is the coming Messiah." Jung reads it as "a very ordinary instance of the widespread hero-archetype in women, which is projected on the father or the husband or the son, in the form of an opinion which then unconsciously regulates the woman's behaviour" — and cites "a well-known example... Annie Besant, who also discovered a saviour" (Krishnamurti).
The animus here is not an argument but a myth: an a priori assumption with divine content, living the boy's life for him until it sickened him.

occurrences.title: Meister Eckhart's vision of the 'naked boy'
occurrences.label: Meister Eckhart's vision of the 'naked boy
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: I would mention Meister Eckhart's vision of the 'naked boy' and the dream of Brother Eustachius.
body: In "The Psychology of the Child Archetype" Jung cites Meister Eckhart's vision of the "naked boy" (with the dream of Brother Eustachius) as evidence that in the Middle Ages the "child" was not merely a traditional figure "but a vision spontaneously experienced (as a so-called 'irruption of the unconscious')" (¶267). He returns to it in "Phenomenology of the Spirit in Fairytales" (¶407 n8, trans. Evans I, p. 438) as the vision-form of the boy who means the self or filius regius. Source: Spamer, Texte aus der deutschen Mystik des 14. und 15. Jahrhunderts, pp. 143, 150.

occurrences.title: Pandora's jewel born beneath the walnut tree — Spitteler's Pandora interlude
occurrences.label: Pandora's jewel born beneath the walnut tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In the midnight shade beneath the tree it glows and sparkles and flames evermore, and, like the morning star in the dark sky, its diamond lightning flashes afar.
body: In the Pandora interlude — "an account of what goes on in the unconscious during the sufferings of Prometheus" (¶295) — the sick God circles the midpoint of a still meadow like Prometheus himself, whose whole libido has flowed inwards (¶295–296). The equivalent prepared in the unconscious is Pandora's gift: a precious jewel, laid beneath a walnut tree in deliberate mirror of the Buddha's birth ("a God-redeemer, a renewal of the sun," ¶297). Bees, butterflies and larks pay it homage; the tree spreads "his kingly hands protectingly" over the "wonder-child" (¶297). Jung's long commentary: the jewel is the new God-image, the redeeming symbol of the inferior function, rejected by conscience, priests, professors and police, to be picked up at last by Ahasuerus (¶450–454).

occurrences.title: The puer aeternus 'Fa' and his unholy boys — Bruno Goetz, Das Reich ohne Raum
occurrences.label: The puer aeternus 'Fa' and his unholy boys
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: a puer aeternus named Fa (= Buddha) appears with whole troops of 'unholy' boys of evil significance.
body: In Bruno Goetz's strange novel Das Reich ohne Raum a puer aeternus named Fa (= Buddha) appears "with whole troops of 'unholy' boys of evil significance. (Contemporary parallels are better let alone.)" Jung cites it twice (¶268; ¶407 n9, where the "boys" figure as negative spirit-boys beside Eckhart's positive naked boy) "only to demonstrate the enduring vitality of the child archetype". The boys' troops shadow the Hitlerjugend years in which Jung wrote.

occurrences.title: The boy with changing countenance — Faust's transformation (Goethe, Faust II)
occurrences.label: The boy with changing countenance
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: The higher, "complete" (teleios) man "is begotten by the 'unknown' father and born from Wisdom, and it is he who, in the figure of the puer aeternus — 'vultu mutabilis albus et ater' — represents our totality, which transcends consciousness. It was this boy into whom Faust had to change, abandoning his inflated one-sidedness which saw the devil only outside" (¶742).

Christ's "Except ye become as little children" prefigures the change — "but what is meant is the boy who is born from the maturity of the adult man, and not the unconscious child we would like to remain." The black-and-white countenance names the union of opposites the whole book drives toward.

occurrences.title: The 'Radiant Boy' seen where Roman remains lie — English ghost-lore
occurrences.label: The 'Radiant Boy' seen where Roman remains lie
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: we read of the vision of a 'Radiant Boy' said to have been seen in a place where there are Roman remains. This apparition was supposed to be of evil omen.
body: From English ghost-stories (Ingram, The Haunted Homes and Family Traditions of Great Britain, pp. 43ff): a "Radiant Boy" seen in a place where there are Roman remains, of evil omen. Jung reads it as a puer aeternus become inauspicious through "metamorphosis" — sharing the fate of the classical and Germanic gods, "who have all become bugbears" (¶267). A radiant child at Roman ruins: the archetype surfacing where an old order lies buried, now numinous-dark.

occurrences.title: Divine child — Riklin's singer psychosis: katabasis, twins, healing substitute (Burghölzli, ~1904)
occurrences.label: Divine child — Riklin's singer psychosis
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: At first she looked upon her internment and everything that went on around her as a descent into the underworld. She got this idea from her teacher's latest composition, 'Charon.
body: A 26-year-old educated singer fell in love with her composition teacher; the passion turned morbid and brought her to Burghölzli. She read her internment as "a descent into the underworld," taking the myth from her teacher's latest piece, "Charon." After the purifying katabasis she reinterpreted the ward as the ordeal-path to union with the beloved, went nightly to a fellow patient she took for him, then felt twins in her womb — "a girl that looked like her and a boy that looked like the 'father'" — gave birth, hallucinated the child beside her, and "with that the psychosis came to an end. She had discovered a healing substitute for reality."

Jung cites the case (from Riklin) as the type of schizophrenic delirium that heals by autochthonous myth-formation — the same structure he would later name the child archetype (CW9i, 1940) and the "healing substitute" anticipates his reading of psychosis as self-healing symbol-making.

occurrences.title: The heavenly ones breathe fatelessly, like a sleeping infant — Hölderlin's Schicksalslied
occurrences.label: The heavenly ones breathe fatelessly, like…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Jung quotes "Hyperion's Song of Fate" in German: "Schicksallos, wieder schlafende / Saugling, atmen die Himmlischen; / Keusch bewahrt in bescheidener Knospe, / Bluhet ewig ihnen der Geist" — the heavenly ones breathe fatelessly like a sleeping infant, their spirit blooming eternally, chastely preserved in the modest bud.

It is his closest parallel to the lotus: "like the flower in the bud protected by the brown leaves, and so the birth of the spirit is sheltered against the cold north wind of the winter... the lotus bud grows under the water and opens when it reaches the surface; then the god is revealed". Footnote: Hölderlin was a favorite poet of Nietzsche's — "linked as geniuses who ended in madness."
Verbatim: "You see, that is like the flower in the bud protected by the brown leaves, and so the birth of the spirit is sheltered against the cold north wind of the winter".

occurrences.title: The golden child on the square table — dream of 21 October 1938
occurrences.label: The golden child on the square table
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The square table is the quaternity, the classical basis of the 'special' child, for the child is a symbol of the self and the quaternity is a symbolical expression of this.
body: Dream of a woman patient over sixty: "A beautiful little child, a girl of six months old, is playing in the kitchen with her grandparents and myself, her mother. The grandparents are on the left of the room and the child stands on the square table in the middle of the kitchen... The old woman says she can hardly believe we have known the child for only six months. I say that it is not so strange because we knew and loved the child long before she was born."

Jung's exegesis (¶378): the child is "something special, i.e., a child hero or divine child"; the father's absence is part of the picture; the kitchen points to the unconscious; "the square table is the quaternity, the classical basis of the 'special' child, for the child is a symbol of the self and the quaternity is a symbolical expression of this. The self as such is timeless and existed before any birth." The dreamer knew the Upanishads but not the medieval Christian symbolism in question. The child's exact age opened Jung's nine-month/six-month backward reconstruction through the April tree dream to the July 1937 painting.

occurrences.title: Dream of 'Tom Thumb' before the arson — Schwarzwald's twilight-state case (Lausanne, ~1909)
occurrences.label: Dream of 'Tom Thumb' before the arson
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Lausanne (case; patient set fire to his house)
body: A psychogenic twilight state in which the patient set fire to his own house. Jung's abstract corrects the author: the patient's childhood matters "at least as great as the situation at the moment, if not greater", and "The dream of 'Tom Thumb' which the patient had the day before the incendiarism is very significant and clearly indicates that the act was determined by infantile reminiscences. This has escaped the attention of the author" (¶1025).

The fairy-tale child (dwarf-of-the-hearth motif) appearing on the eve of the fire — the child-motif as the infantile determinant that fires the deed; Jung's demonstration of dream-teleology over pure trauma theory.

occurrences.title: God as an ignorant adolescent youth — H. G. Wells, God the Invisible King (1917)
occurrences.label: God as an ignorant adolescent youth
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: God is a sort of ignorant youth who tries to improve the world and who has need of our support.
body: The third modern apparition of the Puer in Jung's historical row (after Goethe's Faust boys and Bruno Goetz's brown-capped boys): "In the book of Wells, God the Invisible King, God is a sort of ignorant youth who tries to improve the world and who has need of our support. Wells' description of God is that of an adolescent boy who tries to do his level best with great enthusiasm."

"Wells has been severely reproached for writing that book but I have seen a young boy in this country, a gifted boy of sixteen, who had a religious revelation and who gave me his idea of God, which was just like this one of Wells; it was his dearest revelation." Hence the conclusion of the whole lecture: "The symbol of the 'Boy' seems to be an archetypal image, still very much alive in our time" — the collective unconscious compensating an aging culture with youth.

occurrences.title: Father and Mother of God vision pair — Brother Klaus (Stoeckli fragment)
occurrences.label: Father and Mother of God vision pair
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: In pagan form they are unmistakably God and Goddess, as their absolute parallelism shows.
body: Two parallel vision reports set side by side: a handsome majestic man in a white garment, and a beautiful majestic woman likewise in white, each pressing a figure to the heart "with an overflowing love, because he had stood so faithfully by her son in his need." The palace is heaven, where "God the Father" dwells — and also "God the Mother"; in pagan form, unmistakably God and Goddess.

Jung's reading: "The androgyny of the divine Ground is characteristic of mystic experience." The Trinity in this vision — Father, Mother, and Son — is "very undogmatic indeed"; its nearest parallel is the exceedingly unorthodox Gnostic Trinity God–Sophia–Christ. "The Church, however, has expunged the feminine nature of the Holy Ghost, though it is still suggested by the symbolic dove" (¶486).

occurrences.title: Obatala and Odudua — world-parents pressed together in a calabash (Yoruba)
occurrences.label: Obatala and Odudua
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: recorded by Frobenius (early 20th c.); myth undated
body: Yoruba cosmogonic image: "In the beginning, Obatala the Sky and Odudua the Earth, his wife, lay pressed close together in a calabash" (¶620). Jung cites it immediately after the Big Snake legend as the second African witness to the mating-in-the-mother motif — the closed primordial round in which the opposites (Sky/Earth, male/female) are still contained undifferentiated, the condition that must be broken for a world of discriminated things to appear.

It thus instantiates the same "dawn state" Jung attributes to Purusha: an all-enfolding container that is at once womb, vessel, and cosmic egg. The calabash as half-gourd container keeps the family resemblance to the krater and the vessels of the horse-sacrifice.
Verbatim: "Obatala the Sky and Odudua the Earth, his wife, lay pressed close together in a calabash" (¶620).

occurrences.title: Osiris with Isis and Nephthys in the womb of Nut — Egyptian myth
occurrences.label: Osiris with Isis and Nephthys in the womb of Nut
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: The episode as Jung tells it: "Osiris was in the womb of his mother Nut together with Isis the queen of the day and Nephthys the queen of night, and while in the womb he had sexual intercourse with his two sisters" (sem-1925). Two sisters, day and night, in conflict over the love of the hero — "an everrecurring motive."

Jung's reading: this is "the archetype aroused in Haggard by Africa" — the Ayesha/Amenartis conflict of She repeats Isis vs Nephthys, and in Ayesha, or the Return of She (1895) Ayesha impersonates Isis against a Nephthys-figure, "the conflict between day and night." He frames it with the Osiris→Horus succession: "Osiris fades into a ghost who rules over the dead, and his son Horus becomes the rising sun. It is an eternal theme" — the father must fade when the hero comes.

occurrences.title: Dream: the planetarium — white and red star, tree-birth of Adonis (young woman)
occurrences.label: Dream — the planetarium
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: In the sky two stars were shining; a white one, which was Mercury, but the other star emitted warm red waves of light and was unknown to her
body: A young woman's initial dream concerned a grotesque, repulsive baptizing ceremony in a Protestant sect — "a precipitate of all the dreamer's disappointments with religion." The dream immediately after: "She was in a planetarium, a very impressive place overhung by the vault of the sky. In the sky two stars were shining; a white one, which was Mercury, but the other star emitted warm red waves of light and was unknown to her." On the walls, frescoes — she recognized only "an antique picture of the tree-birth of Adonis."

Jung: the two dreams should be read with the preface "on the contrary" — violent criticism of Church religion, then a mandala vision of a world clock (a planetarium "in the fullest sense") in which "the divine pair stands united, he white, she red," reversing the alchemical pair Beya (the White One) and Gabricius the "servus rubeus" (¶164). Adonis as dying-and-resurgent god of rebirth; Guillaume's King-and-Queen allegory the Christian analogue. The case proves the patient's series no fluke: modern unconscious production independently repeats the old syzygy speculation.

occurrences.title: Divinity student's dream: the black horse from the virgin's tomb, the keys of Paradise
occurrences.label: Divinity student's dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The workmen who opened it found bones inside, but no sooner had the air and light touched them than they suddenly crumbled and transformed into a black horse that galloped away into the desert.
body: A frequently-cited Jung dream (CW7 ¶287-88; CW9i ¶70-76, 398; CW14 ¶79-80): a young theology student, knowing nothing of analysis, dreams of a white and a black sorcerer. The black one tells the legend: a dying old king seeks a burial place and opens the oldest, untouched tomb, where a legendary virgin is buried.

The sorcerer follows the hoofprints beyond the desert to green pasture — "And there he found the keys of Paradise." Jung's reading: "That virgin who had been buried since time immemorial is the anima; and the old king is the ruling idea, the old god... The old form of religion is going to die... the king recedes into the underworld and up comes the anima, who first manifests in the form of a black horse" (p179). Told here to amplify the patient's black horse.

occurrences.title: Docetism: the white bird descends at the Jordan and abandons Jesus in Gethsemane
occurrences.label: Docetism — the white bird descends…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: And when he began to waver in the garden before his arrest by the soldiers, the bird took the god-man or the ghost-man with him again up into the lap of God and left the human husk, the ordinary man Jesus who was crucified.
body: Jung reconstructs the Docetic doctrine as psychology of the seized soul: Christ was an ordinary individual until his baptism in the Jordan, "when the bird descended upon him, a superior ghost-man seized him and transformed him into the great teacher of mankind."

The cry of dereliction — "My God, why hast thou forsaken me" — is read as abandonment by the eternal spirit; "no god was ever sacrificed... he was abandoned by the white bird." Jung: "An entirely psychological viewpoint, and like most of those early heresies, beautifully human." Cited beside the vision in which the Indian kills the white bird and beside H. G. Wells's Mr. Preenby: the Holy Ghost as a real danger — "it can transform people in one instant for a whole lifetime."

occurrences.title: The 'doctor' coyotes of the Achomawi — animal medicine-men
occurrences.label: The 'doctor' coyotes of the Achomawi
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Thus the Achomawi of northern California speak of ordinary coyotes and of 'doctor' coyotes.
body: Ethnographic report in a footnote to Jung's medicine-man discussion (Part 1, Ch. 7, indexed 'coyotes, "doctor," 96n'): "The idea of the medicine-man who communes with spirits and wields magical powers is so deeply ingrained in many primitives that they even believe 'doctors' are to be found among animals."

Jung's reading: the doctor/magician figure is an archetypal role so autonomous that the role itself is attributed to animals — the healing-and-magic function precedes its human holders. The coyote doubling (ordinary coyotes vs "doctor" coyotes) splits the animal into profane and numinous bearer, the same split Jung finds between patient and doctor when the doctor is "as demon" or "as God" (¶¶64, 70, 130-135).

occurrences.title: The Corascene dog and the Armenian bitch — Kalid's Liber secretorum
occurrences.label: The Corascene dog and the Armenian bitch
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: take a Corascene dog and an Armenian bitch, join them together, and they will beget a dog of celestial hue
body: The passage through which "the 'symbolizatio' by the dog entered Western alchemy": "Hermes said, My son, take a Corascene dog and an Armenian bitch, join them together, and they will beget a dog of celestial hue, and if ever he is thirsty, give him sea water to drink: for he will guard your friend, and he will guard you from your enemy... And by dog and bitch, Hermes meant things which preserve bodies from burning and from the heat of the fire" (¶174). Rosarium variant: "Hali, philosopher and king of Arabia, says in his Secret."

Jung: the filius canis "is the same as the much extolled 'son of the philosophers'... it is at once bright as day and dark as night, a perfect coincidentia oppositorum expressing the divine nature of the self" (¶176). Parallel: the poodle in Faust, Mephistopheles as the familiar of Faust the alchemist (¶177).

occurrences.title: The murderess whose lame dog forced the confession — anonymous Zurich case
occurrences.label: The murderess whose lame dog forced…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: A woman doctor committed a murder about twenty years earlier, "very cleverly done," undiscovered — and was nevertheless destroyed. "Her unconscious made a contract with the whole world to give her no shelter": every human being was removed from her, until she could deal only with animals. She came to Jung "when her dog got lame, then she had to confess it to the world, so she confessed it to me. I did not even ask her name; it was an anonymous business."

Jung's reading: "She forgot that her ego is not her totality; it is not the self... For we are the whole world in ourselves." The case grounds his exegesis of "I have drawn the conclusion;... now, however, doth it draw me": what Nietzsche denied as God took him by the neck from behind; her universe accused her as his conclusion possessed him.

Verbatim: "there was somebody else in her, the thing that is much greater than herself that said: you have committed murder; there is no place for you in the whole world because the whole world knows it".

occurrences.title: Dog and wolf — maid subject 31 after the dog attack (Burghölzli, ~1904-05)
occurrences.label: Dog and wolf — maid subject 31…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The reaction wolf is also repeated twice. To the stimulusword cunning the subject reacts with wolf, volunteering that actually fox had occurred to her first.
body: Subject 31, a religious housemaid of about 27, was "attacked by a large dog, which greatly frightened her" shortly before the experiment. The fright organizes the protocol: dog repeated four times; to growl / dog; knot / the knots (lumps) on the paws of the dog; and to cunning / wolf — the subject volunteering that fox had occurred to her first. Jung reads the repetitions and the perseveration of the dog-image as "feeling-toned complexes and therefore a strong personal participation"; her many failures cluster on heart, custom, flatterer, faithful, rich, revenge. A clean demonstration that a recent real event, not a symbol-system, can constellate animal-images in the test.

occurrences.title: 'Through the mind of the dog the world exists'
occurrences.label: Through the mind of the dog the world exists
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Avestan oral tradition; Sasanian redaction (~5th c. CE)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: Through the mind of the dog the world exists,' it says in the Vendidad, the oldest part of the Zendavesta. Since primeval times, man has been unthinkable without the dog, and this all over the world.
body: Dr. Pitsch's header quotation for the man-with-the-dog scene of the school dream:

The paper assembles Brehm ("Man and dog complement each other a hundred and thousand times over... He is part of man himself") and Friedrich Cuvier ("the most remarkable, perfect, and useful conquest that man has ever made"), then the mythic responsibilities: the dog as gravedigger of ancient Persia; the dog led to the dying man's bed for the appeasing bite; Cerberus calmed by Heracles' honey cake; the dog springing at the bull in the Mithras reliefs; Anubis gathering the dismembered Osiris. "The dog helps with dying, and consequently also helps with rebirth". Jung: in the man-dog pair "the unconscious (the consciously domesticated dog) is, so to speak, bound, and so the miracle can happen".

occurrences.title: The rabid Corascene dog and the doves of Diana — Philaletha's Introitus apertus
occurrences.label: The rabid Corascene dog and the doves of Diana
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: who is infected from his very cradle by the bite of the rabid Corascene dog
body: Philaletha's mad-dog drama: "This Chamaeleon is the infant hermaphrodite, who is infected from his very cradle by the bite of the rabid Corascene dog, whereby he is maddened and rages with perpetual hydrophobia... Yet in the grove of Diana there is a pair of doves, which assuage his raving madness.... When the moon is at the full, give him wings and he will fly away as an eagle, leaving Diana's birds dead behind him" (¶182).

Jung's reading: "the dark, dangerous, rabid dog changes into an eagle at the time of the plenilunium. His darkness disappears and he becomes a solar animal... this refers to a psychic disturbance" whose worst stage "occurred at the novilunium, i.e., the stage of nigredo" (¶183). The doves are "a love pair, for doves are the birds of Astarte," spirits/souls = the extracted aqua; their appearance "points to the imminent marriage of the filius regius" (¶185). Companion text (¶186): the winged youth espoused to Diana's central Water, beset by the thief armed "with the malignity of arsenic," whose darkness is scattered "by the spirit moving over the waters" (¶¶186-211, Jung's full dream-translation).

occurrences.title: The wild dogs in the cellar — Zarathustra, 'On the Tree on the Hill'
occurrences.label: The wild dogs in the cellar
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: the kennel under the heights (Zarathustra I)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Zarathustra assumes the depths of the young man are evil instincts: "Thy wild dogs want liberty; they bark for joy in their cellar when thy spirit endeavoureth to open all prison doors".

Jung's critique is double. First, the diagnosis itself is hysterical: "It might be horses and asses and cows, quite lovely things, perhaps some pigs too, and the whole makes a perfectly workable farm… Why just wild dogs?" — the assumption is "late Christian psychology, or ordinary Protestant psychology… To him the body is of course evil". Second, the moralism makes the instinct evil: "they get evil because we put the devil into them. We say they are devils and cannot be touched, and naturally they will be bad because we send them to hell. Nature is neither good nor bad". The normal man keeps his dogs on the surface, "an inner relationship between man and dog".

occurrences.title: The sister's doll dressed again, and the monster on the stairs — dream of a girl of not yet six
occurrences.label: The sister's doll dressed again…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: girl ≤6, recurred as a young girl (session of 22 Nov 1938)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: I undressed the doll of my eldest sister and put it into the doll bed. On coming up again, the doll is sitting fully dressed in its chair." — thrice repeated, until: "in turning around I'm seeing a monster that did that, and which is now following me on the stairs.
body: Presented by Dr. Liliane Frey (the presenter's own childhood dream, first dreamt "definitely not older than six").

Frey: Puppe = doll and pupa; the doll as receptacle of the child's psyche-butterfly (homunculus parallel); playing with the eldest sister's doll = living the sister's anticipations; thrice-repeated process = magic conjuration (Faust's thrice "Come in!", Peter's denial): "The number three triggers the number four, causes something that should establish the wholeness of the person". The monster: behemoth, Faust's hippopotamus-poodle, the whale of Frobenius, Lamia — "the monster as the terrible mother, a symbol of death, which has to be overcome"; the child must descend, meet the split-off complex, regain bodily consciousness; possibly a prefiguration of individuation (CW6 §773 quoted). Jung: putting the sister's doll to bed is sabotage — "When the child puts to bed the doll of her eldest sister, she insults her".

occurrences.title: 'I could make the summer' — golliwog dream of the child 'Anna'
occurrences.label: I could make the summer
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Two scenes in one dream, split by "then": making the summer, and a golliwog thrown down the toilet. The golliwog is a wished-for masculine doll — "just as Mama has a little boy" (¶38); the toilet is where things come out.

Jung's reading: "seeing the spring, how all the little flowers come out" (her words the previous night, ¶35) means making flowers come out = making a child; the second scene renders birth as defecation, "an analogy to the Lumpf-theory of Little Hans" (¶38). "Here we put our finger on the egoistic wish which lies behind the seemingly objective interest."
Quote. "I dreamt I could make the summer and then someone threw a golliwog down the toilet."

occurrences.title: King Domaldi killed for failure of the crops — Ynglinga saga 18
occurrences.label: King Domaldi killed for failure of the crops
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Swedish king Domaldi was actually killed as a result of the failure of the crops — the king's body given to secure the land's fertility.
Jung's reading: at accession "Princes... had to guarantee a good harvest" (¶306) — the king as husband of the land whose fruitlessness unmakes him; the sacrificial logic of the sacred marriage.
Verbatim: The Swedish king Domaldi was actually killed as a result of failure of the crops (Ynglinga Saga, 18). (cw05 ¶306).

occurrences.title: 'Adam, who bore his invisible Eve hidden in his body' — Dorn
occurrences.label: Adam, who bore his invisible Eve hidden…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Adam, who bore his invisible Eve hidden in his body.
body: Dorn says the lapis was called "Adam, who bore his invisible Eve hidden in his body" — and Jung adds: "This archaic idea occasionally turns up in the products of the insane today" (cw14 ¶545). At ¶587 Dorn calls the "fiery and perfect Mercurius" the "true hermaphroditic Adam."

Adam thus joins the hermaphroditic synonyms of the arcane substance (lead, Azoch, aqua permanens — Ruland; John Dee's "Mercurius of the Philosophers, that most renowned Microcosm and Adam"), the beginning that already contains its end.

occurrences.title: Dorn's recipe for the caelum: wine, honey, herbs, and human blood
occurrences.label: Dorn's recipe for the caelum
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Will the unbelievers... marvel that we handle in our hands the heaven and the stars?
body: Dorn's production of the quintessence: the philosophic wine distilled until "you will see the pureness floating to the top, transparent, shining, and of the colour of purest air... You will see the heretofore spagyric heaven, which you can bedeck with the lower stars." The mixture: heaven of red or white wine or Tartarus, honey, Chelidonia, rosemary, Mercurialis, red lily, and human blood — joined "by the artifice of generation" and reduced by "assiduous rotary movements."

Jung at cw14 ¶681-704: the caelum is the celestial substance, the "truth," the imago Dei; each ingredient chosen for its symbolic value (honey = joy of life and poison; Chelidonia = the golden quaternity of the self; Mercurialis = sexuality; rosemary = binding; blood = the whole soul). Psychologically "a representation of the individuation process by means of chemical substances... or what we today call active imagination."

occurrences.title: Self-knowledge passages — Dorn, Speculativa philosophiae
occurrences.label: Self-knowledge passages
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the greatest treasure of a man exists within the man, and not outside him.
body: Dorn's Speculativa philosophiae carries the opus' psychological charter: "man, heaven and earth are one thing, likewise air and water... the greatest treasure of a man exists within the man, and not outside him" (p. 307); "Learn from within thyself to know all that is in heaven and earth... Thou wilt never make from others the One which thou seekest, except first there be made one thing of thyself" (p. 276). The 'Physica Trithemii' gives the ascent's stages: devotion to the faith, knowledge of God by faith, love from the knowledge of God.

Jung's reading: self-knowledge as the real magnet of the work — with the quis/quid note ("Quis refers to the ego, quid to the self", Aion 252). Parallels: morienus-thing-extracted-from-thee-7c, angelus-silesius lapis-inwardness, ascent-descent-dorn-physica-genesis-frankfurt-1583.

occurrences.title: Dorn's three unions: unio mentalis, the body, and the unus mundus
occurrences.label: Dorn's three unions
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: May He be one in All.
body: Dorn's scheme: "meditative philosophy consists in the overcoming of the body by mental union [unio mentalis]. This first union does not as yet make the wise man, but only the mental disciple of wisdom. The second union of the mind with the body shows forth the wise man, hoping for and expecting that blessed third union with the first unity [i.e., the unus mundus, the latent unity of the world]. May Almighty God grant that all men be made such, and may He be one in All."

Jung at cw14 ¶663-679: the first stage = unio mentalis of spirit and soul ("what I call coming to terms with the unconscious the alchemists called 'meditation'"); the second = making real, union with the body; the third = union with the unus mundus. Dorn "correctly recognized that the entity in which the union took place is the psychological authority which I have called the self," and understood the chymical marriage "as what we today would call the individuation process."

occurrences.title: Gerhard Dorn — 'Transmutemini in vivos lapides philosophicos!' (Transform yourselves into living philosophical stones!)
occurrences.label: Gerhard Dorn — Transmutemini…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)
Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

occurrences.quote: the stone is man
body: Dorn, Jung's clearest alchemical psychologist: the Veritas is a 'metaphysical substance' hidden in things and in the human body — 'it is to be sought not in us, but in the image of God which is in us' (cw09ii ¶248, ¶265); 'nothing exists beside that One' (¶265). 'See, therefore, that thou goest forth such as thou desirest the work to be which thou seekest'; the experiment is best made 'on ourselves' (¶250). His quis/quid distinction — 'No one can know himself unless he knows what, and not who, he is' (¶252) — separates ego-knowledge from knowledge of the self. The vessel 'should be made from a kind of squaring of the circle' (cw09ii ¶378).

The exclamation Jung quotes across both alchemy summations. "To do them justice, one should not overlook the fact that there is more than a little evidence in the literature that they realized it was a matter of their own transformation. For instance, Gerhard Dorn exclaims: 'Transmutemini in vivos lapides philosophicos!' (Transform yourselves into living philosophical stones!)" (cw12 ¶187).

Jung returns to it at the end of the projection argument: "But again, the stone is man. Thus Dorn exclaims… 'Transform yourselves from dead stones into living philosophical stones!' Here he is expressing in the clearest possible way the identity of something in man with something concealed in matter" (cw12 ¶378). And in Aion the same passage crowns the Dorn survey: "'Transmute yourselves from dead stones into living philosophical stones!' (¶264)." The imperative mood (transmutemini, passive) makes the operator the substance to be transformed.

Merged locus (reconciliation batch 2: absorbed the parallel note dorn-transmutemini-vivos-lapides-16c, same exclamation cited in cw12 ¶187/¶378 and cw09ii ¶264). Distinct from ascent-descent-dorn-physica-genesis-frankfurt-1583 (same author, different locus: the ascending elements fetching celestial seed, cw09ii pdf p281).

occurrences.title: 'I and me in conversation' — the anchorite's friend as third, Zarathustra 'On the Friend'
occurrences.label: I and me in conversation
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "'One, is always too many about me'-thinketh the anchorite. 'Always once one-that maketh two in the long run!' I and me are always too earnestly in conversation… The friend of the anchorite is always the third one: the third one is the cork which preventeth the conversation of the two sinking into the depth".

Jung decodes the hermit's duality as Nietzsche and Zarathustra: "the self being greater than his consciousness, he is naturally drawn into the eternal abyss of that which is greater than man… The self would draw him into the abyss of eternity whereas a friend would keep him in the surface reality". Because the rejected relation to the anima is heterosexual, "what remains is homosexuality, so he discovers the friend". The chapter ends by projecting the problem into woman ("a slave and a tyrant concealed in woman") — for Jung, "we must discover the anima for him… The anima is the trouble".

occurrences.title: The treasure-seeker's better self appears at night — Carl Hauptmann, Die Bergschmiede (1902)
occurrences.label: The treasure-seeker's better self appears…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: where the treasure-seeker is confronted one gloomy night by the hallucination of his entire better self
body: In Carl Hauptmann's drama Die Bergschmiede (1902), a treasure-seeker is confronted "one gloomy night by the hallucination of his entire better self" — the inner other stepping out as a visible figure. Jung's use of it in a footnote is theoretically loaded: he names the device "objectivation of associated complexes" (fn 113), i.e. the mechanism he had just spent the occult monograph documenting in S.W.'s visions, here deliberately staged by a naturalist playwright. The passage shows Jung already reading literary hallucinations as complexes made external — the same move later systematized as projection. Note the polarity: this double is the better self (ideal/monitoring counterpart), not the inferior shadow-double — the family spans both.

occurrences.title: The drunken prostitute in the gutter — society lady's dream
occurrences.label: The drunken prostitute in the gutter
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The 'other' person we dream of is not our friend and neighbour, but the other in us.
body: The second of the "two instructive cases" told together at cw10 ¶321: a "distinguished lady in high society" dreamed "of a drunken prostitute who rolled about in the gutter" and, like the theologian of the parallel dream, refused to own the figure as herself. Jung advised her to consider "in what ways [she was] not much better than… their drunken sister in the gutter."

Jung's reading: the gutter-prostitute is the lady's own compensated other — the instinctual, undignified underside of the social persona, refused as "the other in us, of whom we prefer to say: 'I thank thee, Lord, that I am not as this publican and sinner'" (¶321). The pairing with the theologian's tramp (clergy/laity, male/female) makes the two dreams a matched amplificatory row on one law: one dreams "almost to the exclusion of all else, of oneself."

occurrences.title: The drunken tramp in the ditch — theologian patient's dream
occurrences.label: The drunken tramp in the ditch
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The subtle process of selfknowledge often begins with a bomb-shell like this.
body: One of "two instructive cases": a theologian among Jung's patients "dreamed of a drunken tramp who lay in a ditch," and was "outraged and horrified, and absolutely refused to admit that he had dreamed of himself" (cw10 ¶321). Jung's prescription: an hour of devout self-reflection on the ways he was "not much better than his drunken brother in the ditch."

Jung's reading: the dream as bomb-shell opening the process of self-knowledge — "The 'other' person we dream of is not our friend and neighbour, but the other in us" (¶321). The dream "being a child of nature, has no moralizing intention; it merely exemplifies the well-known law that no trees reach up to heaven." The degraded double is the compensated underside of the spiritual persona.

occurrences.title: The gods create Enkidu as Gilgamesh's counterpart — Babylonian Gilgamesh epic
occurrences.label: The gods create Enkidu as Gilgamesh's…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: they create a man equal in strength to Gilgamesh in order to check the hero’s unlawful ambition
body: When Gilgamesh's arrogance and hybris defy the gods, they create a man equal in strength to the hero to check his unlawful ambition — Enkidu, the earthy counterpart who becomes his companion.

Jung's reading is clinical, not philological: "The very same thing has happened to our patient" — a thinker who forced everything under the law of his reason; "somewhere nature escaped and came back with a vengeance in the form of an unassailable bit of nonsense, the cancer idea. This was the clever device of the unconscious to keep him on a merciless and cruel leash" (¶27). The episode is his paradigm of the autonomous counter-move of the unconscious against one-sided hybris. Gilgamesh escaped the gods' vengeance because "He had warning dreams to which he paid attention" — the modern patient, in an age of extinct gods, ignored his (¶28).

occurrences.title: Faust's two souls — 'Two souls, alas, are housed within my breast'
occurrences.label: Faust's two souls — 'Two souls, alas, are…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Two souls, alas, are housed within my breast, / And each will wrestle for the mastery there.
body: Jung sets Faust's confession beside the Taoist division of the psyche into shen (hwan) and kwei (p'o) souls and calls the Chinese conception "a great psychological truth. This Chinese conception is echoed in the well-known passage from Faust" (¶368). The two antagonistic tendencies dragging man toward the material and the spiritual demand a counterweight — "the 'irrational third,' tao" (¶369). The locus anchors his claim that East and West formulate the same intrapsychic dualism.

occurrences.title: Fylgja and hamingja: the caul as guardian spirit (Iceland, per Frazer)
occurrences.label: Fylgja and hamingja: the caul as guardian spirit
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This is a very primitive concept, and it shows how the soul... is derived from the idea of the double.
body: Frazer's report, adduced to substantiate the patient's white-placenta birth: in Iceland the child's guardian spirit, or part of its soul, has its seat in the chorion — the caul, part of the afterbirth — "so the caul is designated as the fylgja or guardian spirit." The fylgja (German folgen; Greek synopados, "the one that follows after") becomes visible shortly before death, entering an animal's skin; as shape-changer she is the hamingja (hamr = hood; the Gluckshaube, the lucky caul). The belief in the placenta as living brother or double is also found among the Aborigines of Queensland, the Bataks of Sumatra, and the Norsemen.
Jung's reading: "the soul, which in other parts of the world is called the bush soul, is derived from the idea of the double" — a detachable complex that can project even into animals.

occurrences.title: Ivenes, the 'higher ego' — S.W.'s second personality (Zurich, 1899–1900)
occurrences.label: Ivenes, the 'higher ego'
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: One cannot say that she deludes herself into the higher ideal state, rather she dreams herself into it.
body: Ivenes is the second personality Jung names at the patient's own baptism: "the patient herself christened her higher ego" (¶113). Calm, dignified, pious, "no longer quite human" (¶116), she appears as a small black-haired woman of Jewish type in white and a turban, freed from the body (¶59); she instructs black spirits, walks on Wednesdays in the gardens of the Beyond, and reincarnates every two hundred years (Swedenborg and Florence Cook as siblings). Jung's two readings stand side by side and must not be reconciled: she is a "dream of sexual wish-fulfilment... spread over months and years" (¶120, the reductive 1902 key) — and she is what the patient "dreams herself into" as her ideal of twenty years hence (¶116), an "attempt of the future personality to break through" (¶136).

occurrences.title: The other ego of the persécuteur persécuté (Zurich, ~1900s)
occurrences.label: The other ego of the persécuteur persécuté
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Jung's model of the "simplest form of schizophrenia": a normal-seeming, jovial man in a good position — until the word "Freemason" falls and "a piercing look full of abysmal mistrust and inhuman fanaticism meets us from his eye... the other ego has risen to the surface" (¶499). The genesis (¶502): as a sensitive, intellectual youth he loved his sister-in-law; his brother's harsh interpretation destroyed the "moonshine" dream, and then "his intellect then took over the role of the brother and, with inquisitorial sternness, destroyed every trace of feeling." When waiters began smiling knowingly — they took him for a homosexual — "the paranoid idea had now become autonomous" (¶502/p199). "That is psychic causality, psychogenesis."

Jung's reading: neither subject can fully experience the other; half the affectivity passes to the double, whence schizophrenic "apathy" (¶500) — contrasted there with the many-subjects case god-image-banknote-monopoly-dressmaker-burgholzli-1886.

occurrences.title: The Student of Prague — the shadow-double who acts alone (film, 1913)
occurrences.label: The Student of Prague
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: The first German expressionist film: a student pledges his mirror-image, which then lives a life of its own. Jung, unprompted, calls it "the best movie I ever saw". He retells the duel scene: the man "pledged himself on his honour not to kill his adversary," then "meets his double coming away, wiping blood from its sword on the grass" — "The shadow, disregarding the intention of the conscious man, had killed his adversary."

Jung's reading: the separation of conscious man and shadow "so that the shadow moves by itself" — the same figure-family as Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (raised by Dr Schmitz in the same exchange), and as the spontaneous shadow-blunder of his introverted friend before Virchow.

occurrences.title: The Student of Prague — the detached shadow on film
occurrences.label: The Student of Prague
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "That excellent film The Student of Prague is an illustration. You remember, he detached from his shadow which then committed awful crimes. The man himself kept his word, he was a man of honor; but his shadow broke his word, and that led to a terrible entanglement and a catastrophic denouement." (Editors: the devil gives the student a fortune and takes his mirror-reflection; the first horror film, a Faust-double combination.)

Jung uses it as "a demonstration of a certain psychological condition" — consciousness merely persona-like, "painted on the wall as two-dimensional," so that the separated shadow "always has body, reality: it is a spontaneous and active agency."
Verbatim: "That excellent film The Student of Prague is an illustration. You remember, he detached from his shadow which then committed awful crimes."

occurrences.title: Twin sister 'Anna' — Margaret's second personality
occurrences.label: Twin sister 'Anna'
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: New York (St. Agatha's School / Frances Wickes case)
body: Margaret, eight, brain-injured at birth and shielded into incapacity, announced in the middle of her lessons: "I have a twin sister. She is called Anna. She is just like me except that she always wears lovely pink clothes and has glasses." Anna was invited in; thereafter Margaret went out, conferred, and returned with the verdict — "Anna says it's my fault and I had better do some work."

Jung's reading: the more developed unconscious personality confronting the regressive ego; "for a while [Anna] represented her moral reason. Later the two merged into one, and this signified a tremendous advance" (¶227). He cites his 1902 dissociation study as the same structure. The psychic double is "a commoner phenomenon than one would expect."
Quote. "I have a twin sister. She is called Anna. She is just like me except that she always wears lovely pink clothes and has glasses."

occurrences.title: Ulrich von Gerbenstein — the comic male control-personality (Zurich, 1899–1900)
occurrences.label: Ulrich von Gerbenstein
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Ulrich von Gerbenstein is simply a silly schoolgirl, with nothing masculine about him except his name.
body: A North-German-accented gentleman with a noble name, "a gossip, a wag, and an idler, a great admirer of the ladies", who guards the medium's body during her journeys, jokes with the sitters, and gradually displaces the solemn grandfather until the séances collapse into his chatter (¶51, ¶57). Jung's key: "Ulrich von Gerbenstein is simply a silly schoolgirl, with nothing masculine about him except his name" (¶132) — the boisterous, "often too far" half of the girl's own character, split off and costumed as a man.

Retro-lens (inferred, not Jung's 1902 claim): a male figure acted within a girl's psyche — proto-animus material six decades before the concept; here strictly the persona-half Jung assigns it. Parallels: double-ivenes-higher-ego-zurich-1899 · senex-figure-grandfather-control-spirit-zurich-1899 · medium-trance-personalities-helene-preiswerk-basel-1896.

occurrences.title: Danish becomes English: vindue -> window — linguistic dream, 1 Oct 1954
occurrences.label: Danish becomes English — vindue -> window
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: The dreams and their images are 'Windaugen' for me... it produces in these dreams and images a new type of visual faculty.
body: Bohr explains that the difference between the dreamer and an unnamed other "corresponds to the difference between Danish and English," urges him on from Danish to English, and invites him to a party in his newly refurbished institute. Waking, the word vindue arrives: Danish v becomes English w — "a new, single sound... forming a unity that contains both conscious (v) and unconscious (w) elements, with neither dominating the other". A long real-life postlude follows: the Anglicist Straumann at the Kronenhalle derives window from Old Norse windauge ("wind-eye"); two years later the Swede Källen confirms vindoga "beyond all doubt" — a synchronistic chain.

Jung on the king-dream sequel: "the double vision... is a distinctive characteristic of the human being who is at one with himself"; v = 5 the natural person, w = 2 x 5 = 10 = 1, the One and the Whole. England as synthesis of Latin and German = coniunctio symbolism on the "chthonic mandala of countries."

occurrences.title: The double in Poe's 'William Wilson'
occurrences.label: The double in Poe's 'William Wilson
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: the self-created thing that becomes more powerful than the creator.
body: Mr. Bash offers Poe's tale in the seminar discussion of created figures that turn on their makers: "the hero of the story is accompanied by his double, who leads him into disgrace after disgrace. He is finally killed by the hero, but at the moment of being killed he tells the hero that it is he who has created him — the double."

Jung's reading: "That would be similar, the self-created thing that becomes more powerful than the creator". The exchange sits in a row with Pirandello's Six Characters ("You have created us but we do as we like"), the Golem motif, and Dorian Gray — "it is really a very frequent occurrence that something which one assumes one has created... is not one's thought really... Then there is the possibility that it overgrows one" — which is exactly what Zarathustra's dwarf does to its author.

occurrences.title: The young major on parade — the old general's dream of the definition of the beautiful
occurrences.label: The young major on parade
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: dining car of a continental train
body: A stranger — an old general, "crusty old disciplinarian" — told Jung (unasked) a dream: on parade, the commander-in-chief, instead of a technical question, demands a definition of the beautiful. The general fails; a very young major answers "just the one I would have given if only I could have found it." Asked what the major looked like: "He looked like me, when I was a young major."

Jung's reading: "you had forgotten or lost something which you were still able to do when you were a young major" — the artistic interest swamped by routine (¶187–188). The adjutant confirmed the sore spot. A textbook compensation dream needing no personal knowledge of the dreamer.
Quote. "Did you notice anything peculiar about this young major? What did he look like?" "He looked like me, when I was a young major."

occurrences.title: 'Come, compassionate mother' — invocations of the Church as virgin mother-wife, Acts of Thomas
occurrences.label: Come, compassionate mother
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: come, holy dove which hath brought forth twin nestlings; come, secret mother
body: In the apocryphal Acts of Thomas the apostle invokes the Church as the virgin mother-wife of Christ: "Come, compassionate mother; come, thou that hast charge of the male child," and again — "come, spouse of [lit. 'communion with'] man... come, woman who knowest the mystery of the chosen one... come, holy dove which hath brought forth twin nestlings; come, secret mother."

Jung notes that "the connection of the Church with the mother is beyond all doubt" and the mother is read as spouse: the "communion with man" points to continuous cohabitation, while the "twin nestlings" carry the old legend that Jesus and Thomas were twins, "based on the Coptic idea of Jesus and his ka" (Pistis Sophia).

occurrences.title: Christ amid a garland of doves — Coptic Apocalypse of Sophonias
occurrences.label: Christ amid a garland of doves
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: In the Apocalypse of Sophonias [Zephaniah], Christ appears surrounded by a garland of doves
body: The text-passage sibling of the two dove-mosaics: in the Coptic apocalypse, Christ appears encircled by doves — the Spirit-flock as a mandala garland around the central figure.

occurrences.title: The white dove in the lead of the philosophers — Grasseus, Area arcani
occurrences.label: The white dove in the lead of the philosophers
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Johannes Grasseus quotes: "The gift of the Holy Spirit, that is the lead of the philosophers which they call the lead of the air, wherein is a resplendent white dove which is called the salt of the metals, in which consists the magistery of the work" (cw11 ¶? pdf p699).

A complete short circuit of alchemy and pneumatology: the dove of the Spirit hidden inside the base metal — Mercurius imprisoned in matter "identified with the Holy Ghost" (the index's own summary of the passage, s.v. Mercurius). The redeemer-image buried in the lead of the world.

occurrences.title: The dove, the emerald table and the twelve dead — Jung's dream (Christmas 1912)
occurrences.label: The dove, the emerald table and the twelve dead
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

occurrences.quote: I am allowed to transform into a human form only in the first hours of the night, while the male dove is busy with the twelve dead.
body: Dreamed at the end of 1912, the turning point when "the idea of the archetypes began to formulate itself" and Jung saw "there was something living down there." On a marble loggia atop a castle tower he sits in a golden Renaissance chair before a table of green stone like emerald; his children are with him. A white bird like a small gull alights, transforms into a little girl with golden hair who plays with the children and embraces him, then reverts to the dove, which speaks with a human voice:

The strange word Tauber, the emerald table flashing the Tabula smaragdina of Hermes Trismegistus to mind, the twelve (Apostles, months, signs of the Zodiac — he had just written on the zodiac in Wandlungen) — none of it could be interpreted yet: "there was a tremendous animation of the unconscious... all I could do was just wait, keep on living, and watch the fantasies".

occurrences.title: Down feather held above the abyss — ritual lysis of the Indians of southern Mexico
occurrences.label: Down feather held above the abyss
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Jung's ritual parallel to the burning of the wedding carriage as lysis: "The same idea is also found in the Indians of the southern states in Mexico: a down feather is held above the abyss, and is carried upward at the rocks by the breeze. The event in the dream can be compared to a ritual action in which God is killed and eaten. These are rites leading to a lysis".
The context is the freeing, relieving effect of fire (Goethe's "The God and the Bayadere," sacrifice consigned to the flame) — dissolution in the rising flame as a religious lysis "for all present."

occurrences.title: Draco — the sky serpent rotating around the pole
occurrences.label: Draco — the sky serpent rotating around the pole
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: Our deepest inner layers are hidden in the stars.
body: The horned serpent of the evil-animal dream carries on its head, "like a diadem or a crown," either the hebdomas (seven planets) or the dodekas (twelve zodiac). In antiquity the image was projected onto the sky as Draco, meandering "as a shining ribbon of stars" between the Great and Little Bear, always visible, rotating around the pole — where "the world fire burns... therefore it is also called the fire pole." The world axis runs through it: center of the world and center of the unconscious.

Jung's crucial gloss: the ancients did not "see" bears and snakes in the sky — Aratus did not interpret; "this sky serpent, the Draco, is the reproduction of a primeval image within ourselves"; Gnostics later drew the projection back into man: serpent-body = spinal cord, serpent-head = brain.

occurrences.title: The sleepless Dragon of the Pole who sees all things — Hippolytus, Elenchos IV, 47
occurrences.label: The sleepless Dragon of the Pole…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

occurrences.quote: who from the height of the Pole looks down upon all things and sees all things, so that nothing that happens shall be hidden from him
body: Hippolytus, citing the Aratus tradition: the Dragon is set "under the Pole", the one "who from the height of the Pole looks down upon all things and sees all things, so that nothing that happens shall be hidden from him" — sleepless because the Pole never sets. Sometimes confused with the sun's serpentine path: "on dispose parfois les signes du zodiaque entre les circonvolutions du reptile" (Cumont); the serpent bears six signs of the zodiac on his back (Philo, via Eisler).

Jung's reading: the all-seeing quality passes to Chronos ("the All-Seeing Time" of Sophocles); the identification of the All-Seeing with Time "probably explains the eyes on the wheels in Ezekiel's vision" and "indicates the relation between the mundus archetypus of the unconscious and the 'phenomenon' of Time... it points to the synchronicity of archetypal events" (¶394).

occurrences.title: Andromeda chained for the sea monster, rescued by Perseus
occurrences.label: Andromeda chained for the sea monster, rescued…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: classical Greek myth (dates of mythic setting and literary record both archaic)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: So a very frequent myth is the virgin sacrificed to the dragon or guarded by him, and rescued by the hero, as in the story of Perseus and Andromeda.
body: Jung's type-myth for the dragon-guarded treasure: "a very frequent myth is the virgin sacrificed to the dragon or guarded by him, and rescued by the hero, as in the story of Perseus and Andromeda." The editorial footnote supplies the episode: "Tied by her father to a rock as a sacrifice to a female sea monster, Andromeda was rescued from on high by Perseus, who beheaded the monster and married the girl."

Jung's reading is explicit: "The treasure, like the virgin, is a symbol for value and life. And the virgin would be an anima symbol, meaning that the anima is caught by a system of values incorporated in the dragon; she has lost her freedom." The same formula covers the jewel — "the symbol of the innermost value of man, individuality or the self" — that Nietzsche's lion must tear from the dragon 'thou-shalt'.

occurrences.title: The basilisk of Basel and the trial of the rooster's egg
occurrences.label: The basilisk of Basel and the trial…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Nietzsche's "immediate background was my good town of Basel, and there it is the basilisk, a sort of winged dragon with a scorpion's tail... with a very poisonous sting" — Basel's totem animal, whose sting Jung hears in the town's medisance.

Legend: when a rooster was found to have produced an egg, "the police arrested the rooster. They had a trial and the judge issued a sentence: the rooster was condemned to death, given to the executioner, and burned like a heretic. For if a rooster produces an egg in the country where the basilisk is the totem animal, it is quite possible that a toad will discover that egg and hatch it; and when a toad hatches a rooster's egg, a basilisk will creep out." The totem must not become real — "That this case happened in Basel is of course the expression of their fear of the totem animal. So the totem animal is a reality in Switzerland" (cf. Berne's bears, bear-goddess-artio-berne-gallic-roman).

occurrences.title: Book of nineteen concentrated pictures: 'A dragon that bites its tail' (Allemann)
occurrences.label: Book of nineteen concentrated pictures
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: A picture-book lent by Mr. Allemann whose images Jung found "tremendously concentrated": "Those pictures are very difficult, I have analyzed about nineteen of them... For instance, the title 'A dragon that bites its tail' can mean God knows what, but if you have a series of superficial visions about the same thing, you can see pretty well what it means."

Its function in the seminar: counter-image to the patient's superficial vision-series, which develops one thought in many pictures and so permits understanding — where the concentrated alchemical series remains hermetically sealed.

occurrences.title: The cold dragon wraps the woman in her grave — Maier, Scrutinium chymicum, Emblem L
occurrences.label: The cold dragon wraps the woman in her grave
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the secret poisoning that otherwise emanates from the coldness and moisture of the moon is occasionally attributed to the 'cold dragon
body: The "cold dragon" who "contains a 'volatile fiery spirit' and 'spits flames'" given "a masculine role: he wraps the woman in the grave in a deadly embrace" (¶30). Companion Emblem V: "a toad is laid on the breast of the woman so that she, suckling it, may die as it grows. The toad is a cold and damp animal like the dragon. It 'empties' the woman as though the moon were pouring herself into the sun."

Jung reads the pair as the secret poisoning of the moon (and of the woman = Luna) by her own cold, wet daemonism — the dark half of the Sol-Luna embrace that the Church allegory suppressed. Sister locus to mercurius-salamander-maier-1687.md (same emblem book, different plate).

image.title: Michael Maier Atalanta Fugiens Emblem 50

occurrences.title: The dragon barring the gate — Hypnerotomachia Poliphili (Venice, 1499)
occurrences.label: The dragon barring the gate
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Venice (Aldine printing; Jung: author a Christian monk of a famous Roman family)

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: ...now there is a dragon sitting behind him that bars the way, and he cannot go back; he simply must go forward. The dragon is Kundalini.
body: Poliphilo, lost in the Black Forest (for Italians "still the ultima Thule where the unicorn still lived"), follows a wolf to a spring — an allusion to baptism — enters the ruins of a Roman town with symbolic inscriptions, is seized by fear, turns back, and finds a dragon sitting behind him blocking the gate. Jung's equation: "The dragon is Kundalini... that which makes you go on the greatest adventures... this is the divine urge."

occurrences.title: Hannibal's dream — the dragon devastating Italy (Livy XXI.22)
occurrences.label: Hannibal's dream — the dragon devastating Italy
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The historical dream Jung cites for the dragon as crowd-soul: "Hannibal, as a young man had a prophetic dream of conquering Italy; he saw that a huge dragon was on his trail, following him and devastating the whole country, which meant of course his army that followed him and devastated the country".

Livy's fuller version: a god-like youth sent by Jupiter leads Hannibal into Italy and forbids him to look back; curiosity wins — "he saw behind him a serpent of monstrous size, that moved along with vast destruction of trees and underbrush, and a storm-cloud coming after, with loud claps of thunder," and is told "it was the devastation of Italy."

The dream grounds Jung's equation: "the dragon is of course the symbol for the collective unconscious; the state is simply the outside appearance of the thousand-headed monster… It also means the crowd within, the collective unconscious; it is the crowd soul, the collective soul of man".

occurrences.title: The dragon whose head is Christ — the eight circles of the 'Scriptum Alberti'
occurrences.label: The dragon whose head is Christ
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The pseudo-Albertine "Scriptum Alberti" describes a picture of heaven in eight concentric circles: the fourth holds "a raging dragon issuing from the seven planets"; the fifth, "the head and the death" of the dragon — the caput draconis "lives in eternity", is named "vita gloriosa", and "the angels serve it" (Matt. 4:11). Jung: "But if the dragon's head is identified with Christ, then the dragon's tail must be identical with Antichrist or the devil... the whole of the dragon's body is absorbed by the head, so that the devil is integrated with Christ... 'The whole body obeys the head, and the head hates the body, and slays it beginning from the tail, gnawing it with its teeth, until the whole body enters in to the head and remains there for ever'" (cw13 ¶416).

The sixth circle holds two storks (vas circulatorium, like the Pelican); the eighth the golden tree shining "like lightning" with the stork as pia avis — "the stork is its spiritual principle and thus a symbol of the Anthropos" (cw13 ¶417). Sibling locus for Alexander's tree and stork: tree-alexander-hermes-tomb-stork-14c (cw12).
Verbatim: the devil is integrated with Christ. (cw13 ¶416)

occurrences.title: The dragon in the fire — Lambspringk's Symbols, Fig. X (Musaeum hermeticum)
occurrences.label: The dragon in the fire
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Figure 50 of Concerning Mandala Symbolism = Figure X of Lambspringk's Symbols in the Musaeum hermeticum (Waite trans., I, p. 295): the dragon glowing in the fire, becoming volatilized — "illumination comes through the fiery torment." Jung introduces it through the fiery-demon drawing of Fig. 49 (a patient's shadow-figure wrapped in flames like a salamander): "the prima materia in alchemy was symbolized by the salamander in the fire, as the next picture shows." Everything the fire consumes rises up to the seat of the gods.
Distinct from the filius regis figure of the same series.

occurrences.title: Lao-tse 'an expert at riding dragons' — Confucius' testimony
occurrences.label: Lao-tse 'an expert at riding dragons'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Asked what he thought of Lao-tse, whom he never met, Confucius replied that he did not know whether the man was expert at weapons or at driving carts, "but however that might be, he knew he was an expert at riding dragons. He knew how to deal with the monster, that is".

Jung sets this as the image of the man who does not sell his soul to the collective: "The only trace of freedom and the only hope is, of course, in the one who is not devoured by the monster, who can deal with it, who can ride the monster" — where the dragon "is of course the symbol for the collective unconscious." The sage rides the state-monster rather than being ridden by it; the footnote adds that the introverted Lao-tse was a great favorite of Jung's, Confucius rarely quoted.

occurrences.title: Leviathan and Behemoth — Yahweh's big exhibits (Job 40-41)
occurrences.label: Leviathan and Behemoth — Yahweh's big exhibits
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: The climactic boasts of the theophany: "Behold, Behemoth, which I made as I made you… He is the first of the works of God" (¶635); and of Leviathan (the crocodile): "He beholds everything that is high: He is king over all proud beasts" (¶599). Jung's sting: Job's God is "just what Yahweh himself says of Leviatham" — unconscious, "not a man" (¶599-600); even in Job's day Yahweh is "still intoxicated with the tremendous power and grandeur of his creation" (¶636).
In Enoch's eschatology the two exhibits are "carved up and eaten" (¶681) — Leviathan and Behemoth forced to succumb before the Son of Man's judgment.

occurrences.title: Ltn the seven-headed serpent — Ugarit text, Ras Shamra
occurrences.label: Ltn the seven-headed serpent
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: "Quand tu frapperas Ltn, le serpent brh / Tu acheveras le serpent 'qltn, / Le puissant aux sept tetes" — for Jung the earliest authentication of Leviathan (he dates the Ugarit texts c. 2000 B.C.; Virolleaud notes the two adjectives recur in Isaiah 27:1). Contemporary pictures show Baal fighting the serpent — a god against a monster, not yet monster against monster.

His frame (pars. 183-185): the great "fish" was first the opposite of the highest God, hence his shadow; its later doubling into Leviathan/Behemoth "relieves God of his own inner conflict, which now appears outside him in the form of a hostile pair of brother monsters."

occurrences.title: The regia Lindensis altar — inhabitants of the water region (near Lake Thun)
occurrences.label: The regia Lindensis altar
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Etymological anchor of Jung's dragon-lecture: "the dragon is the Lindwurm, lind being originally a Celtic word which meant 'soft, flowing like water.' The name of our river Limmat comes from lind, and the upper part of the river is called the Linth."

"There is a Roman inscription found near the lake of Thun in Switzerland which says the inhabitants of the regia Lindensis, meaning the Lind region, devote this altar to the gods; the Lind being the water region, they were inhabitants of the lake."
The dragon is a water-worm; rivers meander as snakes move; Lindau on Lake Constance shares the root; the Chinese Tao likewise "is of the nature of water — it moves like a snake."

occurrences.title: Makara, the devouring water-monster of the svadhisthana — Leviathan parallel (via Avalon)
occurrences.label: Makara, the devouring water-monster…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: traditional doctrine (via Avalon, The Serpent Power, 1931)
body: The svadhisthana (bladder/sexual) centre's subsidiary symbols: "the sickle moon as the feminine principle, and a devouring water-monster called makara, which corresponds to the biblical and cabalistic Leviathan" (¶560; the chunk OCR joins "watermonster"). Jung immediately universalizes: "The mythological whale-dragon is, as you know, a symbol for the devouring and birth-giving womb, which in its turn symbolizes certain reciprocal actions between consciousness and the unconscious." The patient's bladder and uterine symptoms localize to this centre. Makara here joins the Leviathan/whale-dragon family — the womb's double face.

occurrences.title: The mechanical dragon that slew the sacrificed girls — De promissionibus
occurrences.label: The mechanical dragon that slew the sacrificed…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: It is a convenient rationalistic conceit to say that the dragon is only “artificial,” thus banishing the mysterious gods with a word.
body: Girls "consecrated and adorned with flowers" given yearly to the dragon are pierced by its springing sword; a monk examines the steps with a rod, exposes the mechanism, and cuts the dragon to pieces — "thus showing that they are not true gods who are made by the hands of men" (¶574). Jung pairs this rationalizing with the schizophrenic apotropaism "It's all a fake" (¶576).

occurrences.title: The mechanical dragon with the sword, and the monk who split it — Rome
occurrences.label: The mechanical dragon with the sword…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: in quo draco mirae magnitudinis mechanica arte formatus, gladium ore gestans, oculis rutilantibus gemmis metuendus ac terribilis apparebat
body: Near Rome was a cave where a dragon of wondrous size, "formed by mechanical art," brandished a sword in its mouth and appeared terrible with eyes of ruddy gems. Each year flower-crowned virgins, unknowing gift-bearers, were sent down to it in sacrifice; touching the stair they met the spring of the sword and shed innocent blood. A monk famous for holiness — well known to the patrician Stilicho — feels his way down step by step with his staff, uncovers the fraud, crosses the threshold, splits the dragon in two, and shows "that the gods made by hand are not gods."
The devouring mother here exposed as human artifice: the two tales (with the Tarpeian dragon) form the Christian demystification of the cave-beast.

occurrences.title: The dragon chasing the pearl — sun and serpent with the values reversed (China)
occurrences.label: The dragon chasing the pearl
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "In China it is really the pearl and the dragon, and the strange thing is that the pearl there is the moon, the Yin, and the dragon is Yang. The symbolism is just reversed... Everywhere else the dragon is a malevolent and dangerous beast, but in China it is a friendly thing; the Chinaman is a friend of the dragon. The only friend of the serpent we know is the woman; no man ever was the friend of the serpent unless he was a sorcerer and taught by a woman."

The dragon forever chasing the pearl "a little bit ahead... in all eternity the dragon [is] not quite capable of catching that pearl." Hence Jung's quip that in China "it is as if the real teacher there had been a woman." Chinese dragons fly; the Chinese horoscope runs on twenty-eight moon-houses and the currency on silver (p830–831).

occurrences.title: Dragon Poine and the Linus lament — Argos
occurrences.label: Dragon Poine and the Linus lament — Argos
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: mythic; annual lament attested from Homer to Herodotus (II, 79)
occurrences.quote: All these motifs are to be found in Revelation 12: 1f., where the child of the sun-woman was threatened by a dragon and afterwards 'caught up' to God.
