Parallels: dream-jellyfish-round-pool-student-1951c, fish-round-fish-allegoriae-turba-11c.

occurrences.title: Dream: Sophocles sees the theft of the golden temple vessel
occurrences.label: Dream: Sophocles sees the theft…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: when it came a second and a third time, he thought that the gods were insisting and it might be true
body: Jung's classical case of the institutionally received dream: "a famous poet dreamt that a certain man had stolen a precious golden vessel from the temple of Hermes [Herakles, per the editor] and had hidden it in a certain place." Disbelieving, he dismissed it twice; on the third coming he took it as divine insistence, announced it to the Areopagus, the thief was found and the vessel restored.

Told beside the Roman senator's daughter whose dream rebuilt the goddess's temple, it evidences the dream's former "social and political function, the leader getting his thoughts straight from heaven" — the background against which the seminar's "ordinary" dreams still carry "the same guiding function and attempt at a solution."

occurrences.title: Gorgeous apples for the brother — ninth dream of the heat-head hysteric (Burghölzli, Dec 12, 1905)
occurrences.label: Gorgeous apples for the brother
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: A basket full of gorgeous apples is standing there. One of my brothers says: 'This also is something for me.
body: NINTH DREAM (Dec 12): a sad-faced policeman (the "dried-up policeman", i.e. the thin, half-masculine rival Miss L.) talks to an indistinct man; false fire-alarm; then she is home in the kitchen with her mother and two brothers, where "a basket full of gorgeous apples is standing there" and a brother says: "This also is something for me." Jung reads the dinner-table/kitchen scene sexually and grounds the fruit in scripture: the apples resemble the washed "lovely stones" of dream VIII, and "secondly they are something edible (cf. Eve's apple)". The brother's claim on the fruit carries the suspicion that "there is something about the brother that goes beyond a sibling relation" — the defended secret the analysis never opens.

occurrences.title: Dream: the Gothic cathedral burst open by sunlight and bulls
occurrences.label: Dream: the Gothic cathedral burst open…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Blinding sunlight bursts into the interior together with a large herd of bulls and cows.
body: "Again, a man who was much occupied with religious problems had the following dream: An immense Gothic cathedral, almost completely dark. High Mass is being celebrated. Suddenly the whole wall of the aisle collapses. Blinding sunlight bursts into the interior together with a large herd of bulls and cows."

Jung's one-line reading: "This setting is evidently more Mithraic, but Mithras is associated with the early Church in much the same way Dionysos is" (¶180) — the bull-herd as Mithraic irruption paralleling the Dionysian vines of the clergyman's dream (¶179). Recorded as evidence for the pattern of pre-Christian contents breaking back into the Christian temenos (cf. ¶178's "systematic descent ad inferos").

occurrences.title: Dream — the grandmother at the tropical garden gate (businessman, 16 October 1929)
occurrences.label: Dream — the grandmother at the tropical garden…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: dreamer's home town (north); told in Zurich

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: A man "with doubtful qualities as to his business conduct" dreams: on an ordinary street "a very dignified and refined old lady" beckons, leads him to a gate, and "he saw that it was a tropical garden, full of trees and beauty"; seized with fear, unable to resist, "she lured him in. It was a nightmare" (pp335-336). He associated her with his beloved grandmother — so why the nightmare?

Jung's reading: the garden is "a garden of Paradise, the garden of desire" — a psychic world. And the grandmother, not the mother, follows "the old primitive idea": a father who becomes a grandfather is "no longer an ordinary ghost but a sort of duke in ghostland." So "grand-mother refers to the 'great' unconscious, while the mother refers to the 'little' unconscious... as an ocean to a little bay." "Shortly after this dream, he committed a terrible mistake that led him into prison" — read as inviting, it would have helped him to disaster; the tropical garden belongs inner, not outer, life (p336).

occurrences.title: The grey snake and the scarab road — dream of a Swiss girl, 13
occurrences.label: The grey snake and the scarab road
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: The snake said, follow me... in spite of the fact that she was afraid, she followed the snake.
body: A "contribution" read after the shepherd-and-serpent lectures: a girl of thirteen dreams she walks a road with adults; at the crossroads a huge grey snake, "looking as long as the road they were on", says "follow me". The adults refuse and take a path bordered by scarabs that swell "until they were as large as human beings — horrible animals". Frightened, the girl obeys the snake, and it "became more and more benevolent and less and less dangerous."

Jung's reading: scarabs (like worms) "stand for the sympathetic system" and, as Khepra, are "the symbol of resurrection in Egypt... buried in the ball of dung, and then he rises as the sun". Those who refuse the serpent are "devoured by the unconscious... hollowed out from within, a loss of libido". At puberty one meets "the whole force of the instinctive being": "the snake is the mediator between the conscious and the unconscious worlds. Therefore, the snake is the symbol of the savior, the agathodaimon". The dream "is most typical. This is a normal child and it shows what the normal solution would be" — against Nietzsche, who is "at variance" even with the cerebro-spinal system, so his snake is the black poisonous one.

occurrences.title: Dream [22]: the grinding machine with cylinders and rotules
occurrences.label: Dream [22] — the grinding machine…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: After the world-vision, the unconscious drops the dreamer back to "his most personal problem": a grinding machine drawn by horses or motor, its main cylinder surrounded by small globular cylinders fitting into its indentations "like the action of a cog-wheel". The dreamer repositions the rotules himself, speaking French with the mechanic. Associations: the treadmill of his business; the cylinders as units of time (the year, the days), teeth filling gaps. Jung: the machine's ground plan is the flower-mandala (like the earlier steamroller dream); the constituents are the functions, and the dreamer "establishes a consciousness which is aware of the main value of the constituents of his personality". The mechanic figure: the conscious says it is Dr. Jung, the unconscious says it is an unknown man (the autonomous complex) — finally the dreamer mends the machine himself.

occurrences.title: Dream: the 'House of the Gathering' — religion is no substitute (dream 54)
occurrences.label: Dream — the 'House of the Gathering'
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Out of the fulness of life shall you bring forth your religion; only then shall you be blessed!
body: A solemn house — "the 'House of the Gathering'" — with candles arranged in "a peculiar pattern with four points running upward"; an old man at the door: "When they come out again they are cleansed." A voice thunders: "Religion is not a tax to be paid so that you can rid yourself of the woman's image… Religion is no substitute; it is to be added to the other activities of the soul as the ultimate completion." Leaving, the dreamer sees a burning mountain: "The fire that is not put out is a holy fire" (Shaw, St. Joan); distant organ chords recall Wagner's Fire Music.

Jung treats this numinous dream as "a new climax of insight": the square is a "gathering place"; wholeness requires the anima-image of the fourth function; and "man as a whole being casts a shadow" (¶297).

occurrences.title: Dream 20 — the hut-mosque with crocodile and kettle of crosses and crescents (patient-anon, 16 October 1929)
occurrences.label: Dream 20 — the hut-mosque with crocodile…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: In "a hut in Africa, somewhere in the upper part of Egypt" the dreamer finds a crocodile ("a remnant of prehuman, prehistoric times"); his youngest son brings a kettle holding "a whole bundle of small scythes made, not of steel, but of sheet iron — simulacra, not the real thing," sword-handles with blades broken off, and "a statue of Christ, made of sheet iron, with a sword as long as the figure"; a native explains the lamps — "the hut is by no means ordinary but a kind of mosque, and the scythes are crescent moons, and... the handles of the swords are Coptic cross symbols" (pp343-344).

Jung: upper Egypt = his spiritual "upper region"; the crocodile is the totem-ancestral, instinctual saurian in the holy place ("Where there is a church, the devil is not far away," p350); the hut is womb and anchorite-cell; the kettle is the cauldron — Celtic symbol, alembic, "vase of sin" — in which "the irreconcilable nature of Christianity and Islam must be reconciled" (pp354-363). The broken, discarded religious symbols cook in the belly (plexus solaris) toward a new symbol.

occurrences.title: Girl of three — dream of Jack Frost pinching her belly
occurrences.label: Girl of three — dream of Jack Frost pinching…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
jung.locator: session 23 Jan 1940, presented by Dr. Waller (paper missing) (pdf p359-365)

occurrences.quote: Jack Frost is coming. She is scared. He pinches her everywhere in the belly. She awakens and realizes that she has pinched herself.
body: The earliest remembered dream of a three-year-old girl with hereditary taint (a schizophrenic aunt): Jack Frost comes and pinches her everywhere in the belly; she wakes having pinched herself. Connected with early masturbation. The dream has no lysis and is conspicuously meager — both unfavorable prognostic signs. Jung reads Jack Frost through St. Nicholas and Knecht Ruprecht (who carries children into the forest, the place of the dead): the white ghost in the snow-shroud is a memento mori, "the one who freezes all life," a judge of the dead like Osiris.

The belly is the stove, the embryo's shelter, the liver "he who lives," seat of the solar plexus where psychical and physical are one. Masturbation was apotropaic magic, "a stress on life in aspectu mortis." The dreamer's obsessional neurosis masked a latent psychosis; she took her own life at thirty-six in a mental institution — "she herself intervened in her life with a cold hand."

occurrences.title: Dream — the jelly-fish in the round pool (20-year-old student)
occurrences.label: Dream — the jelly-fish in the round pool
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: A student in professional confusion walks into a darkening primeval forest and finds a circular pool of crystal-clear water, in the middle of which floats a pearly, faintly luminous organism about eighteen inches in diameter — a jelly-fish. He wakes 'with a violent emotion' and decides to study science (¶208). Jung: a 'big' dream, archetypal, in no way suggested; the round pool with the medusa is 'a three-dimensional mandala, the self: wholeness as the goal to which the "archetic appetite" points, the magnetic north which gives the traveller his bearings on the "sea of the world"' (¶208). Parallels the fish-symbolism of the alchemists.

occurrences.title: Jung's Kaiser Wilhelm dream-interviews (Zurich, 1914–1916)
occurrences.label: Jung's Kaiser Wilhelm dream-interviews
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Jung's own report: "In the beginning of the war I was always dreaming of having interviews with Kaiser Wilhelm, and I always tried to convince him that he should retire with all his royalties, but he never would listen. We knew each other quite well; when I appeared, he used to wave to me... It stopped in the end of 1916."
Occasion: Mrs. Sigg's note that the supposedly mad Nietzsche wrote advising the rulers of Bavaria and Baden to retire into private life. Jung: "It is quite possible that he saw things ahead."
The dream-figure: the sacral head of the world-order as god-image that must abdicate. Recorded here as dream-material, subject jung.

occurrences.title: Jung's Negro-barber dream — the curling tongs ('going black')
occurrences.label: Jung's Negro-barber dream — the curling tongs
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.place: East Africa (the barber was from Chattanooga, Tennessee)
occurrences.quote: I dreamed that a Negro barber was trying to curl my hair with curling tongs
body: Jung's own dream, offered as evidence that "the anima becomes evident as a peculiar mental nuance" and that the soil of a country gets into it: "I was there fully three months before I discovered the black taint, and then it was in a dream".

"you see, that would make my hair kinky… the tongs were long iron bars, very thick and glowing hot — that black blue heat — and I felt that if he only approached my head, I would be lost… Hair is of course an emanation of the head, so it meant that my natural emanation was going to get kinky". The barber "was not an African barber, he was the barber to whom I usually went when I was in Chattanooga" — the American Negro complex operating on the American sojourner. "Going black" is Jung's technical term for the taint; he pairs the dream with the shifty-eyed District Commissioner of Uganda and the evil-eye caution of primitives.

occurrences.title: The dream-led migration: Eskimo medicine man crossing Baffin's Bay
occurrences.label: The dream-led migration
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Greenland -> Baffin Bay -> North American shore
occurrences.yearDisplay: undated traditional episode (told to Knud Rasmussen; publ. 1927)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: The whole tribe believed him and they started out over the ice.
body: From Rasmussen's Across Arctic America: with the tribe starving in Greenland, an old medicine man dreamt of "a further country with an abundance of seals, whales, walruses... a land of plenty," and led the tribe out over the ice. Halfway, doubters turned back "only to perish," while his half reached the North American shore.

Jung's exhibit of the big dream (ota) as a social instrument — guidance "straight from heaven" — now broken: "African primitives now depend on the English to guide them, no longer on the medicine man's dream." The dreamt land-of-plenty is the paradise image functioning as tribal itinerary.

occurrences.title: Dream: hotel lift, the note of salvation, the eight-spoked wheel (dream 22)
occurrences.label: Dream: hotel lift, the note of salvation,…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Salvation comes from complete surrender, with one's eyes always turned to the centre.
body: In an American hotel the lift stops "about the third or fourth floor"; a friend reproaches the dreamer for keeping "the dark unknown woman waiting so long below," and hands him an unsealed note: "Salvation does not come from refusing to take part or from running away… Salvation comes from complete surrender, with one's eyes always turned to the centre." On the margin, a drawing: "a wheel or wreath with eight spokes." Soldiers with ramrods prepare to shoot at the centre — but do not shoot.

Jung: the lift rises as something comes "up" from the subconscious; the mandala of the number four waits at the fourth floor because the fourth function is taboo; the "red-haired man" (= Mephisto, the man with the pointed beard) commands "completely throttling the left" (¶201, ¶211).

occurrences.title: Dream 16 — machine with yellow labels becoming the little daughter (patient-anon, 12 June 1929)
occurrences.label: Dream 16 — machine with yellow labels becoming…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: The scientist-dreamer sees a machine with defective parts "marked with little yellow labels"; in the dream Dr Jung advises him to attend to them; as he looks closer "the machine disappears and I see my little daughter in a skirt with big holes torn in front" (p285). The machine (his standing symbol for automatic sexuality/will-power) vanishes when inspected — "what it expresses is now exhausted and we need a new symbol" (p286).

Jung's reading: the dream hands the incest warning the dreamer's respectability refuses — the libido arrested from the wife "creeps out" into daughter, dog, furniture, even "the central heating" (p291); the torn skirt touches the neighborhood of sexual murder (pp292-293). The dream addressing "Dr. Jung" is information for the doctor: the unconscious "addresses me and says, 'Now listen Dr. Jung'" (p293). Yellow — quarantine, prostitution — is "the anima flag!" (p294).

occurrences.title: Mice with glowing hot eyes jumping from dog-kennels — second dream of the heat-head hysteric (Burghölzli, Nov 30, 1905)
occurrences.label: Mice with glowing hot eyes jumping…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: they have peculiar glowing hot eyes.
body: SECOND DREAM (Nov 30): the room full of cats is replaced by mice that "are jumping all over the place", not proper mice but bigger-headed, rat-like, with "big black ears" and "peculiar glowing hot eyes" (a fragment of the fire dreams), leaping out of little wooden huts "like dog-kennels". Jung's reconstruction: mouse is the current association to cat, the two substitute in the dream; the black ears come from the two black setters behind her house, one of which "stood up against the maid". "The analysis points to a very ambiguous situation... it is mating again, as in the previous dream" — and the dog on the maid is "a subtle indication as to what sort of person the thought of sexual intercourse refers to".

occurrences.title: Miss X — dream of removing the black fleck from the animus's eye (Nov 1928)
occurrences.label: Miss X — dream of removing the black fleck…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: A little golden lamp then became visible in the centre of the puPil.
body: Four days before Picture 8: she draws a young man to the window and, with a brush dipped in white oil, removes a black fleck from his cornea; a little golden lamp becomes visible in the pupil; he is relieved; she wakes saying "If therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light" (Matt. 6:22). The young man is her animus, now become her patient, who "has seen things too blackly" (¶592). The dream marks the change: the mandala is an "eye," the structure symbolizing the centre of order in the unconscious; the eye is also a symbol for God (Boehme's "Eye of Eternity").

occurrences.title: Miss X — dream of the golden snake demanding sacrifice (~early 1920s)
occurrences.label: Miss X — dream of the golden snake demanding…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: It demanded the sacrifice... of a young man... The dream was repeated a little later, but this time the snake picked on the dreamer herself.
body: The second "big" dream, a year before the narcosis dream: a golden snake in the sky demands, from a great crowd, the sacrifice of a young man, who obeys with sorrow; the assembled people regard him compassionately. Repeated shortly after — this time the snake picks the dreamer herself, who takes her fate "proudly" upon her. The golden snake is the direct ancestor of the golden lightning-snake of Pictures 2-3 (the Nous-serpent, Mercurius Philosophorum). Jung connects the mood to her birth "at the twelfth hour" and to the birth of the self as distinct from the ego (¶548).

occurrences.title: Miss X — dream of the mother sleeping in the father's-room bed (Nov 1928)
occurrences.label: Miss X — dream of the mother sleeping…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: my mother had moved my bed away from the wall into the middle of the room and had slept in it
body: Two days before Picture 7 (four days before Picture 8's eye-dream): the mother has moved Miss X's bed from the wall into the middle of the father's room and slept in it; furious, she pushes it back. The red bed-cover is "exactly the red reproduced in the picture." Jung: her sphere is the father's spiritual sphere, usurped as she usurped his room — identification with the "spirit." The mother (physis vs spirit) intrudes and installs herself in the centre, so the dark chthonic principle penetrates to the mandala's centre — "e tenebris lux!" (¶586). The collision of paternal and maternal principles works like a shock.

occurrences.title: Miss X — narcosis dream of the world-globe with vibrating silver band (~mid-1920s)
occurrences.label: Miss X — narcosis dream of the world-globe…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: She saw a grey globe of the world. A silver band rotated about the equator
body: One of the two "big" dreams of Miss X's life, dreamed under narcosis during an operation. A grey globe of the world; a silver band rotating about the equator forms zones of condensation and evaporation; in the condensation-zones appear numbers 1 to 3, tending to increase to 12 — "nodal points" or "great personalities" of historical development; 12 = the culminating point still to come. The dream is one of the two components amalgamated in Picture 3, where the band becomes the quicksilver girdle of the sphere (¶549: cosmic analogy of the birth of the self). It matches the 1916 world-creation picture (Fig. 2).

occurrences.title: Miss X — dream of the tree growing in the workroom (Nov 1928)
occurrences.label: Miss X — dream of the tree growing…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: To her astonishment she found a tree growing in the middle of the room where she worked.
body: Days before Picture 6: returning from holiday she finds a tree growing in the middle of the room where she works — "with its thick bark this tree can withstand the heat of an apartment." Associations led to the tree's maternal significance; it explains the plant motif of the swastika-mandala and represents "the higher level or freeing of consciousness induced by the movement to the right." The "thick bark" anticipates the protective cortices/skins of Pictures 7-8 (¶572, ¶576). Jung: "the 'philosophical' tree is a symbol of the alchemical opus, which as we know is an individuation process" (¶570).

occurrences.title: Dream 15: the mother pours the water of life into the sister's basin
occurrences.label: Dream 15 — the mother pours the water…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: same series as dream 1 (dreamer a Roman Catholic)
body: "The dreamer's mother is pouring water from one basin into another… This action is performed with great solemnity: it is of the highest significance for the outside world. Then the dreamer is rejected by his father." (cw12 ¶91).

Jung: the father = collective consciousness, traditional spirit; the mother = the collective unconscious, "the source of the water of life"; the sister later proves "the carrier of the anima-image" — "the mother has been replaced by the anima" (¶92). The father's rejection amounts to excommunication. The alchemists' water-synonyms (aqua nostra, mercurius vivus, succus lunariae, acetum fontis) frame it (¶94).

occurrences.title: Mandala dream 9: the pendulum clock that goes forever
occurrences.label: Mandala dream 9 — the pendulum clock…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "A pendulum clock that goes forever without the weights running down." (cw12 ¶134).

"This is a species of clock whose hands move unceasingly, and, since there is obviously no loss due to friction, it is a perpetuum mobile, an everlasting movement in a circle" (¶135). 'Metaphysical' — eternity as a quality predicated by the unconscious: "the other centre of personality lies on a different plane from the ego since, unlike this, it has the quality of 'eternity' or relative timelessness." Precursor of the world-clock vision treated later in the same chapter.

occurrences.title: Mandala dream 10: four figures in the Peterhofstatt, Zurich — the four functions round the self
occurrences.label: Mandala dream 10 — four figures…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "The dreamer is in the Peterhofstatt in Zurich with the doctor, the man with the pointed beard, and the 'doll woman.'… Question: To which of the three does the woman belong?" (cw12 ¶136).

The church precinct is "a temenos in the truest sense of the word"; St. Peter's clock dial "is divided into four quarters, like the horizon." The four persons read as the four functions: dreamer = ego, pointed beard = the 'employed' Mephisto-intellect, doll woman = anima, doctor = non-ego ("he probably contains a faint allusion to myself," Jung notes). "Therefore the centre of the circle which expresses such a totality would correspond not to the ego but to the self as the summation of the total personality." (¶137).

occurrences.title: Dream of the poisoned Paradise tree — young woman patient
occurrences.label: Dream of the poisoned Paradise tree
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Dream: in a garden she finds an exotic tree with strange red fleshy flowers or fruits, picks and eats them, then feels to her horror that she is poisoned.

Jung's reading: after sexual difficulties in marriage, "The tree is the same tree that stood in Paradise... It is the tree of libido, which here represents the feminine as well as the masculine side, because it simply expresses the relationship of the two to one another" (¶326).

Verbatim: She was in a garden, where she found an exotic-looking tree with strange red fleshy flowers or fruits. She picked and ate them. Then, to her horror, she felt that she was poisoned. (cw05 ¶325).

occurrences.title: Dream: discovering the Pole under guidance of the unknown woman (dream 40)
occurrences.label: Dream: discovering the Pole under guidance…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The Pole is the point round which everything turns—hence another symbol of the self.
body: "Under the guidance of the unknown woman the dreamer has to discover the Pole at the risk of his life." Jung: "The Pole is the point round which everything turns—hence another symbol of the self." Alchemy had already taken up the analogy: "In the Pole is the heart of Mercurius, who is the true fire, wherein his master rests… he sets his course by the aspect of the North star" (¶265). "Mercurius is the world-soul, and the Pole is its heart. The idea of the anima mundi coincides with that of the collective unconscious whose centre is the self. The symbol of the sea is another synonym for the unconscious."
Dreams 42–43 (the old master's red-illuminated spot; the murky yellow sun with eight rays) continue the place-and-time determination toward the centre.

occurrences.title: Dream: the portrait that becomes four-colour clovers; the wheel drawings (dream 23)
occurrences.label: Dream — the wheel drawings
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: what the dream represents in personified form the dreamer reproduces as an abstract ideogram
body: In the square space the dreamer sits opposite the unknown woman, commissioned to draw her portrait; what appears instead are "three-leaved clovers or distorted crosses in four different colours: red, yellow, green, and blue." He then spontaneously draws the wheel with eight spokes and a four-petalled blue flower, and "a great many drawings now followed at short intervals, all dealing with the curious structure of the 'centre'" (¶213).

Jung: what the dream personifies the dreamer "reproduces as an abstract ideogram" (¶220); the Trinity symbol is "overshadowed or 'coloured' by the alchemical quaternity" — the four colours as concretization of the tetraktys, the transition from trinity to quaternity, preliminary stage of the lapis that unites omnes colores.

occurrences.title: Dream: the prince gives the diamond ring on the fourth finger of the left hand (dream 37)
occurrences.label: Dream: the prince gives the diamond ring…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The self is made manifest in the opposites and in the conflict between them; it is a coincidentia oppositorum. Hence the way to the self begins with conflict.
body: Curves of light around a dark centre; a dark cave where good and evil battle; "a prince who knows everything" gives the dreamer a ring set with a diamond "and places it on the fourth finger of his left hand." Jung: the gift "means nothing less than the dreamer's vow to the self—for as a rule the wedding ring is worn on the fourth finger of the left hand"; the left hand marks the unconscious situation; the prince is "the representative of the aenigma regis." The dark cave "corresponds to the vessel containing the warring opposites."
Dream 38 confirms it: a circular table with four empty chairs — "The mandala is not yet 'in use'" (¶261).

occurrences.title: Boy of five-six — recurrent vision of the pyramid with a glass house on top
occurrences.label: Boy of five-six — recurrent vision…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Switzerland (dream of childhood; reported to Jung in adulthood)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
jung.locator: session 28 Nov 1939, paper by Aniela Jaffé (pdf p300-320)

occurrences.quote: I see a pyramid in front of me. On its top there is a house made of glass. There is somebody in it. As I come nearer, I realize that it's me.
body: A boy of five-six sees a pyramid crowned by a glass house with someone inside; approaching, he realizes "it's me." The dreamer was a man Jung knew at 45-50, a judge who had been on the inner "quest" all his life; telling the dream "more or less as a curiosity," he received the core of his life back. Jung calls it "a pure product of the prenatal psyche," from a "virginal layer" untouched by the world.

Jaffé's amplifications: the pyramid as archetypal image and body mandala (Cheops, Borobudur, Meru), the vitrum aureum of Revelation's golden city, Snow White's glass casket, the Visio Arislei. Jung adds the Maya turquoise-snake mandala, the Navajo sweat lodge, the benedictio fontis, the Zosimos kratér, the Grail — vessels of transformation — and reads the double in the glass house as the corpus subtile, "a vision of what we have to call the Self". When the meaning was told him, "both currents flowed together... He had found his soul".

occurrences.title: Dream of the fourth chair and the laurel (patient-anon, ~1930s)
occurrences.label: Dream of the fourth chair and the laurel
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: For this purpose she fetched a fourth chair that stood fw,ther off.
body: A patient dreams: a drawing-room, a table with three chairs; an unknown man invites her to sit; she fetches a fourth chair from further off; she turns the pages of a book with pictures of blue and red cubes, as for a building game; leaving for a yellow house, she shelters from torrential rain under a green laurel tree. Jung: table, three-plus-fourth chairs, cubes, building game = a process of composition in stages; the four colours = four qualities; the green laurel = the inferior (sensation) function, "contaminated with the collective unconscious and... used as a bridge." The laurel, like the alchemical tree, is a symbol of the self (¶583).

occurrences.title: Dream [21]: the great vision — multicoloured stripes on the river of fate, all permeated with fluid light
occurrences.label: Dream [21] — the great vision
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: he becomes aware that it is all transparent and luminous, that not only the mass itself but the atmosphere and the people and he himself are all permeated with something that he compares to fluid light
body: The "great philosophical vision" following the union-of-opposites dream: a vast grey plain dissolves into multicoloured stripes moving through each other; people try to shape them ("Cause and effect"); the stripes prove the surface of a huge mass flowing like a lava stream, a river — and everything, the mass, the people, the dreamer himself, is permeated with "fluid light". His own words in the dream: "The Fate of Man, the Fate of People, the Fate of Worlds". Jung reads it with the identity of energy and time prepared in the preceding lectures: each stripe an individual life (cf. the threads of the Parcae), the river the flow of time seen "in space" from a high standpoint — "in the fourth dimension, man is a worm" (cf. the zodiacal Christ-serpent). Association: Kunkel's Das grosse Jahr.

occurrences.title: Dream — saurians bursting from mountain-like molehills (artist patient, told 23 October 1929)
occurrences.label: Dream — saurians bursting from mountain-like…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: An artist "who went all to pieces, got in a terrible turmoil" — Jung feared a psychosis. "Then after a number of unsatisfactory and confused dreams, he had a remarkable dream of a wide plain where big mountain-like molehills appeared. They burst open and out came a number of saurians, dinosaurs and so forth. I took that as a sign of the beginning of a new epoch in that man's life. And so it was" (p353): "he started an entirely new style of creative work... a man of no education, an ordinary painter, but he then started to read, and the whole world of knowledge began to pour down upon him."

Jung's rule: when such a monstrous animal appears, "something is coming up from the unconscious which is not to be influenced by will-power. It is like a fate that cannot be twisted" — the level where life "can no longer be arranged arbitrarily" (p353).

occurrences.title: Dream: stepping on a snake that bites the heel (Swiss infantry lieutenant)
occurrences.label: Dream: stepping on a snake that bites the heel
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: I suggested a metaphorical snake and he said: 'Oh, you mean a woman?' and showed emotion.
body: The case that opens the seminar's methodological discussion: a simple-minded Swiss officer with pains in his heels and heart "as if stabbed," resistant to all treatment, produced one dream — "I was walking in the open somewhere and stepped on a snake that bit me on the heel, and I felt poisoned. I woke up frightened." The snake led straight to his repressed grief at being jilted; when he wept, the heel-pains vanished.

Jung's amplification is the locus of the formula "A snake for a man is eternally a woman" — the serpent of Paradise shown with a woman's head, Genesis 3:15, and Isis sending the serpent to poison Ra "that she might be able to cure him again... the psychology of women poisoners." The dream as key when associations fail: dreams "leak out."

occurrences.title: Girl of ten — recurrent dream of sinking in the water between Bellevue and Quaibrücke
occurrences.label: Girl of ten — recurrent dream of sinking…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
jung.locator: session 21 Nov 1939, paper by Margret Sachs (pdf p284-299)

occurrences.quote: Suddenly, between Bauschänzli and Quaibrücke, I fall into the water in an upright position. Slowly I am sinking deeper and deeper, until I reach the bottom. I nearly drown.
body: A ten-year-old Zurich girl — the same dreamer whose snake vision was discussed the week before — repeatedly dreams she falls upright into the Limmat between Bauschänzli and the quay bridge, sinks slowly, and "nearly drown[s]." Sachs reads the route from Bellevue ("beautiful view" = past childhood) across the bridge (puberty, transition) into the water (the unconscious); bridge amplifications run from the Qur'an hell-bridge and the Chinvat bridge to the Argei dolls of Rome.

Jung: a "simple" dream that must be made "complicated" — even the mundane quay bridge is "the bridge." The upright, feet-first sinking is a retrogressive birth, a return into the womb, a figurative death of the transformation process; Rank's birth-trauma doctrine is cited and refused. The split dreamer will blunder into split situations until an ultimate experience "hits them in their innermost being, where they are still at one with themselves".

occurrences.title: The six mandalas worked out by the dreamer (between dreams 53 and 54)
occurrences.label: The six mandalas worked out by the dreamer
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: the dreamer worked out six mandalas in which he tried to determine the right length of the vertical
body: "After this dream the dreamer worked out six mandalas in which he tried to determine the right length of the vertical, the form of 'circulation,' and the distribution of colour. At the end of this work came the following dream (given unabridged)" — the House of the Gathering (dream 54, ¶293).

The patient's own drawing series is the synthetic opus in miniature: correcting the "disturbed" mandala of dream 51 (oblong, missing blue) toward the squared, right-circulating, four-coloured form — and the work is immediately answered by the series' most numinous dream. It is the clearest documentation in the chunk of the patient as co-worker, not merely dreamer.

occurrences.title: Dream 1: the stranger's hat — first mandala allusion of the 1930s dream series
occurrences.label: Dream 1 — the stranger's hat
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: observed via Jung's woman-doctor pupil (355 of 400 dreams away from Jung)
body: Opening dream of the series: "The dreamer is at a social gathering. On leaving, he puts on a stranger's hat instead of his own." (cw12 ¶52).

Jung: the hat, covering the head, is "a sort of leading idea" covering the whole personality — "a stranger's hat imparts a strange personality." He amplifies with Meyrink's Golem (the hat of Athanasius Pernath) and concludes: "Encircling the head, the hat is round like the sun-disc of a crown and therefore contains the first allusion to the mandala" (¶53). The exchange of hats inaugurates the emergence of the unconscious.

occurrences.title: Girl of five (raised in India) — dream of the tiger torn in two
occurrences.label: Girl of five — dream of the tiger torn in two
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
jung.locator: session 5 Nov 1940, paper by Walter Huber (pdf p417-420; discussion continues beyond this chunk)

occurrences.quote: Then a tiger jumps over the balustrade and wants to attack me, but he gets caught in the jump and is torn into two pieces (like in The Adventures of Baron Munchhausen).
body: A five-year-old girl who grew up in India stands on the porch of a pile house; a tiger leaps over the balustrade to attack her, catches in the jump, and is torn in two — "like in The Adventures of Baron Munchhausen." Huber's amplifications: Brehm on the tiger's power; the Batak tondi (a mana-self inhabiting head, blood, and liver, strongest in the tiger); wer-tiger beliefs of the Sakai and Mantra; and Lévy-Bruhl's Naga, for whom humans and tigers have a common origin — the Angami mourn a killed tiger as an elder brother.
The Munchhausen association marks the magical, incredible lysis characteristic of persecutory dreams. The chunk breaks off mid-presentation (Jung's discussion falls to c04).

occurrences.title: Dream: transformation of animals into men, snakes in the four corners (dream 18)
occurrences.label: Dream: transformation of animals…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: we have to expose ourselves to the animal impulses of the unconscious without identifying with them and without 'running away
body: In a square space, animals are to be transformed into men. Two snakes fleeing in opposite directions are removed at once; the people circumambulate and are bitten in the calf at each of the four corners; four snakes then settle into the corners; sacrificial priests touch a shapeless "life-mass" with a huge reptile, "and out of it there instantly rises a human head, transfigured. A voice proclaims: 'These are attempts at being.'"

Jung reads the life-mass as the inherited unconscious (alchemical chaos, massa informis; midrashic Adam), the serpent rite as the "well-substantiated archetype" of renewal by serpent (Sabazius, Ophites, Kundalini), and the circumambulatio as exclusive concentration on the centre while being "bitten" — exposing oneself to animal impulses without running away. The four-corner arrangement reveals "an order in the unconscious… a kind of Pythagorean tetraktys" (¶189).

occurrences.title: Girl of ten — 'The Transparent Mouse' (worms, snakes, fish, humans)
occurrences.label: Girl of ten — 'The Transparent Mouse'
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: unknown (Zurich circle; presented by Cornelia Brunner)
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1939; session 30 Jan 1940; the girl died one year later

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
jung.locator: sessions 30 Jan & 5 Feb 1940, paper by Cornelia Brunner (pdf p365-388)

occurrences.quote: Then people, and it turned into a human being itself. That's how all men and women develop.
body: From a series of twelve dreams: a mouse — worms enter it, it turns gray; snakes, it turns red; fish, it turns blue; then people, "and it turned into a human being itself. That's how all men and women develop." Brunner's amplifications map the stages onto Tantric lotuses (Muladhara to the thousand-petaled lotus), the astrological ages (Taurus, Aries, Pisces, Aquarius), alchemy's color stages, and soul-animal mouse lore; she calls it "a reversed Bardo Thödol."

Jung: meager but purely archetypal — "the simpler a dream is, the more we are confronted with general and fundamental problems." It is a philosophical answer to a philosophical, pre-mortal question; the girl "is standing in the shadow cast by a future" the unconscious already anticipates. Transparency marks the subtle body, "a criterion for the spirituality of matter"; the four stages enact the quaternity as "the emergence of human consciousness." The soul-mouse never turns toward her; a year later she was dead.

occurrences.title: Dream: treasure in the sea, the walled garden with fountain (second dream series, dream 13)
occurrences.label: Dream: treasure in the sea, the walled garden…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The 'treasure hard to attain' lies hidden in the ocean of the unconscious, and only the brave can reach it.
body: The dreamer must dive through a narrow, dangerous opening to reach a treasure lying in the sea; below he finds "a beautiful garden in the depths, symmetrically laid out, with a fountain in the centre." Jung reads the treasure as the "treasure hard to attain" hidden in the ocean of the unconscious, and conjectures that treasure, companion, and garden-fountain "are all one and the same thing: the self" — the lonely ego finding its mate in the self, "at first the strange non-ego" (¶155).
The garden is "another temenos"; the fountain the source of "living water" (John 7:38); centre and circle are "analogues of the lapis."

occurrences.title: Woman patient's dream: two dogs copulating, the male disappears into the female
occurrences.label: Woman patient's dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The male went head first into the female and disappeared in her belly.
body: The incest dream: "Two dogs were copulating. The male went head first into the female and disappeared in her belly." Jung: "Theriomorphic symbolism is always an indication of a psychic process occurring on an animal level, i.e., in the instinctual sphere. The dream depicts a reversed birth as the goal of a sexual act" (¶178).

It anchors the chapter's thesis on incest: "The archetype of incest is also at the back of the primitive notion that the father is reborn in the son, and of the heirosgamos of mother and son in its pagan and Christian form; it signifies the highest and the lowest, the brightest and the darkest, the best and the most detestable. It represents the pattern of renewal and rebirth" (¶178).

occurrences.title: Dream: the universal Catholic Church (Hagia Sophia, 'Soldiers!' proclamation) (dream 17)
occurrences.label: Dream: the universal Catholic Church
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: it does not lose its sacramental character
body: Given unabridged: a future-dated stage-set church, "This is the universal Catholic Church… founded by Jesus and Paul"; a proclamation forbidding direct address to the ineffable Lord; interior like the Hagia Sophia, only framed texts on the walls; a Bach fugue whose original text is omitted ("Everything else is paper"); then the "gemütlich" part — wine, ragtime, "Charles is also with us now" — an "anti-ascetic" American-flavoured church.

Jung: the temenos "has become a sacred building"; the grotesque-humorous side is Dionysian (cf. the shrine inscription μόνον μὴ ὕδωρ); the regression is "not a relapse but a kind of systematic descent ad inferos, a psychological nekyia" (¶178) that retreads the historical path to the pre-Christian level, joining Church and Dionysian sanctuary without destroying either (¶181).

occurrences.title: Dream: letter from the unknown woman — the uterus drawing, spiral, glaciers (dream 32)
occurrences.label: Dream — letter from the unknown woman
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: the uterus… is a synonym frequently employed for the alchemical vessel
body: The dreamer receives a letter from an unknown woman complaining of pains "in the uterus," with an attached drawing: a spiral line through primeval forest full of monkeys, opening onto "a panorama of white glaciers." Jung reads the life-creating centre now designated "uterus" — "a synonym frequently employed for the alchemical vessel, just as it is one of the basic meanings of the Eastern mandala" (¶246). The serpentine line recalls the healing serpent of Aesculapius and Shiva bindu encircled three and a half times by the Kundalini serpent.

The dream ends by returning the cosmic aspect with "interest and compound interest": the glaciers recall an earlier Milky Way dream and "a conversation about immortality. Immortality is a clock that never runs down, a mandala that revolves eternally like the heavens" (¶246).

occurrences.title: Dunne's nightmare of the exploding mountain — the Martinique catastrophe dreamt with its printing error
occurrences.label: Dunne's nightmare of the exploding mountain
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: a remote place in South Africa (news of St. Pierre, Martinique)
occurrences.quote: And in the paper, through a mistake in printing, the number of people killed was really put at four thousand, the number he saw in his dream; he dreamt the mistake.
body: In a remote South African station Dunne had a terrible nightmare: a mountain exploding, and the knowledge that four thousand people had been killed. The next mail brought the Daily Telegraph with the news of St. Pierre, Martinique, destroyed by Mont Pelee with some forty thousand dead — but the paper, through a printing error, put the dead at four thousand. "He dreamt the mistake." The decisive detail for Jung: the dream came not when the disaster happened but only when the papers carrying the news had already reached the post office — we receive what is approaching us.
Jung retells the case later in "Synchronicity" (CW 8, par. 852).

occurrences.title: The colossal worm drawn from her mouth — recurring phallic worm dream (Burghölzli, recalled Dec 6, 1905)
occurrences.label: The colossal worm drawn from her mouth
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: it was as if a colossal worm was being drawn out of my mouth.
body: Directly after finishing the dinner-table dream analysis, the patient says out of context: "I am reminded of a dream that I used to have very often. I always used to dream of worms, reddish and whitish ones, the floor and the whole room were full of them (just like the blood, the fire, the cats, etc.). Very often, too, it was as if a colossal worm was being drawn out of my mouth." Jung: "This dream in this context can be nothing but one of those penis dreams" — with the neologisms of dementia praecox patients listed alongside ("snakes, the stalk of a lily, staff of life"), and the mouth marking the displacement from below upwards.

occurrences.title: Dream: the evil deity as yellow ball that becomes a gold coin
occurrences.label: Dream: the evil deity as yellow ball…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: what should have been a yellow god came out like a piece of money, a gold coin
body: A later dream of the same businessman: "he was in the presence of a peculiar evil deity, a yellow ball, and he was doing some magic with it" — but when he paints it, "what should have been a yellow god came out like a piece of money, a gold coin." He wants to burn the yellow ball but someone has cut the wires; enraged, he seeks a weapon and finds only a horseshoe, then escapes boyishly down the banisters.

Jung uses it to show what the anima does when she works unaided — switches a man "to an entirely different sphere where he forgets his ordinary life" — and how near the pairs of opposites had come: "a close fight." The merchant's hand degrades the numinous round into currency (our reading: a degraded rotundum; Jung leaves the family implicit).

occurrences.title: The Druid's cutting of the mistletoe — Pliny, Natural History
occurrences.label: The Druid's cutting of the mistletoe
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: After sacrifice, the Druid climbs the sacred oak on the sixth day of the moon and cuts the mistletoe with a golden sickle; two white bulls are sacrificed; the plant is a sovereign remedy against barrenness.

Jung's reading: "when the Druid cuts it, he kills it and by this act symbolically repeats the fatal self-castration of Attis and the wounding of Adonis by the boar's tusk" (¶392) — the matriarchal dream of the son killed by separation from the tree-mother.
Verbatim: In Gaul, it was only after offering sacrifice that the Druid was allowed, amid solemn ceremonies, to climb the sacred oak and cut the ritual branch of mistletoe. (cw05 ¶392).

image.title: Motte Druide coupant le gui au 6e jour de la lune

occurrences.title: The toddler's 'two Mamas' (Karl Abraham's case, Berlin)
occurrences.label: The toddler's 'two Mamas'
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: fn 27 to ch. IV, The Hymn of Creation (pdf p677)

body: Abraham's girl of three and a half, watching her baby brother suckle, told her mother: "You are two Mamas. You are my Mama, and your breast is little brother's Mama." Jung appends the philological sting: "Mamma is Latin for 'breast'" — "characteristic of the archaic thinking of the child to call the breast 'Mama.'" The dual-mother formula appears here from the child's mouth, the analytic observation confirming the mythologem (cf. index: "mother: two, 295n, 317ff").
Verbatim (fn 27): "You are two Mamas. You are my Mama, and your breast is little brother’s Mama."

occurrences.title: Leonardo's two mothers — Freud's dual-mother argument (1910)
occurrences.label: Leonardo's two mothers
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: it is a widespread “primordial” image belonging not to the domain of personal memory but to the secrets of the mental history of mankind.
body: Freud's 1910 essay argued that Leonardo's illegitimate birth — two mothers in his early childhood — shaped his later life and art. Jung cites it as his lead example that certain fantasies have no personal occasion: "Generally speaking it is a mythological motif. Many heroes in legend have two mothers."

Jung's reading: the dual-mother fantasy "does not arise from the actual fact that the heroes have two mothers"; it is "a widespread 'primordial' image belonging not to the domain of personal memory but to the secrets of the mental history of mankind" (cw07 ¶100). The personal reduction is here explicitly inverted — the biographical fact is the hook, not the source. This paragraph is one of the bridge-points between the personalistic and collective phases of the psychology.

occurrences.title: The Oedipus legend — Thebes (Greek myth)
occurrences.label: The Oedipus legend — Thebes (Greek myth)
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The monumental drama of the ancient world at whose root Freud placed "an individual conflict... the incest fantasy" (¶1). Jung opens the whole volume with it: to meet the Oedipus material in one's own psyche is to bridge the gulf to antiquity and learn "that there is an identity of fundamental human conflicts which is independent of time and place" — "Oedipus is still alive for us" (¶1).

Later in the volume the legend becomes the paradigm of the dual-mother motif (the unknowing marriage with the mother); here it already carries the Sphinx as its monster-riddle wing. Burckhardt's word, quoted by Jung: "every Greek of the classical period carries in himself a little bit of Oedipus, and every German a little bit of Faust" (¶45). Jung adds that Faust formulates the same problem for the German sphere that Oedipus did for the Greek (¶121).

image.title: Michael Maier Atalanta Fugiens Emblem 39

occurrences.title: Besenbein, the broom-leg spirit of Barlach's Der Tote Tag (Germany, 1912)
occurrences.label: Besenbein, the broom-leg spirit…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Germany (Ernst Barlach, Der Tote Tag, Berlin 1912; 2nd ed. 1918)
occurrences.quote: he calls the ones who go about in the night and clean the house Besenbein, which means broom-leg.
body: "There is a beautiful drama called Der Tote Tag, written by a German artist named Barlach — he is not a writer, he is a sculptor or painter — about the spirits of things. He gives them names, he calls the ones who go about in the night and clean the house Besenbein, which means broom-leg". Jung cites it as the artistic survival of the Heinzelmanner/brownie complex: the dwarfs who did the housework for the kind woman who set out milk and did not spy — the "innate spirit in things" that has moved from the objects into the unconscious. The editor notes the book's many similarities with Morgan's own visions.

occurrences.title: The Cabiri of Samothrace — hooded dwarf gods in pointed caps
occurrences.label: The Cabiri of Samothrace
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: The Greek Cabiri were adorned with pointed caps... they were kept hidden in cases.
body: The Greek Cabiri, "miniature hooded gods" whose chief shrine was Samothrace and who were also called "the great gods": they wear the pointed cap shared by the pileus of Mithras or Apollo and the Phrygian cap of Attis or Adonis; Pausanias, Jung reports, set two Cabiri statues on the rocks at a particularly dangerous spot to protect navigators. "Ordinarily the Cabiri were little things, and were kept hidden in cases, and always wrapped up carefully."

They anchor the cap-row of the brown-cap dream: "small ones yet so great in power" (Cabiri from Arabic el kabir, "the great one" — Jung's etymology), kin to the Dactyl or thumbling and to Purusha, "smaller than small, yet greater than great." The monks "took on the brown hood of the Cabiri": when the patient is lowered into the earth-brown cap, "he is really being lifted up."

occurrences.title: The dwarfs spring from the earth and tear her clothes from her (patient vision, 11 November 1931)
occurrences.label: The dwarfs spring from the earth…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: While he laughed many dwarfs sprang up from the earth and tore my clothes from me and I was left naked.
body: While the giant laughs, "many dwarfs sprang up from the earth and tore my clothes from me and I was left naked." Jung's two-beat reading: mythologically, the thumbling against the giant — Goliath and David — the old motif of the small one overcoming the great; psychologically, the dwarfs are "the innate spirit in things," the wisdom buried in the earth, keepers of the secret treasures — originally teachers of the crafts, like Bes educating Horus and Mimir bringing up Siegfried. They strip her because she has kept up appearances to ingratiate public opinion; naked, she is nature, and the giant's power collapses when she throws away what is made of the same stuff as he.

occurrences.title: Gnomes torturing the analyst in the flashing cave — Prince's patient, dream 6 (Boston, ~1905–06)
occurrences.label: Gnomes torturing the analyst…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: and all over you there were just hundreds of little gnomes or pigmies or brownies, and they were torturing you. Some of them had axes, and were chopping on your legs and arms, and some were sawing you.
body: Dream 6, twice repeated on succeeding nights, again on Watts's path: a figure rushes past warning "Don't look, you will be blinded"; at the entrance of a great cave it flashes light, and in the cave lies the analyst (metamorphosed with her son) — bound round and round, clothes torn, face bloody — covered by "hundreds of little gnomes or pigmies or brownies" torturing him with axes, saws, and red-hot joss-sticks; "It was something like Gulliver and the little creatures running over him." The dreamer cries "O Dr. Prince, I am coming," but is rooted to the spot; all goes black, flashes again, three or four times; she wakes blind and paralysed. Jung: the cave as the future she "must not look" into is Prince's unargued equation; the real crux is that "the analyst himself suffers hellish tortures" — "a hellish fantasy of revenge" answering the stone-pounding of dream 3 (¶190).

occurrences.title: Bes, the grotesque chthonic dwarf who teaches Horus
occurrences.label: Bes, the grotesque chthonic dwarf…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the chthonic god Bes is really an archetypal figure. He is an exceedingly grotesque little dwarf, but on the other side he is the teacher of Horus, as Mimir is the teacher of Siegfried.
body: In the discussion of the gargoyle clutching the priest in the patient's Gothic-cathedral vision, Jung generalizes: "the most grotesque appearance is associated with wisdom" — Socrates' Silenus face, the king's jester, the deformed medicine man —

Bes is the bandy-legged, mask-faced dwarf god of the Egyptian household, guardian of childbirth and sleep; Jung makes him the type of the chthonic wisdom-figure: "Such figures are also to be seen in Egypt" beside the Gothic choir-stall grotesques. The pairing with Mimir sets Bes inside the dwarf-teacher series that runs through the chunk — the dwarf as "a subordinate creative power in the unconscious that may either be helpful… or it may steal things away" (pdf p690, the patient's snatching dwarf).

occurrences.title: The bearded little man who 'wanted to put the blame on me' — nine-year-old boy (~1930)
occurrences.label: The bearded little man who wanted…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1930 (boy aged 7 at first interview, 9 at the crime; inferred)
body: A nine-year-old boy stabbed his little sister above the eye with scissors, "Had it gone half a millimetre deeper the child would have died instantly" (¶802). Since the age of seven a "little man with a beard" had appeared to him, winking, "each time the little man came nearer and nearer to him, and last time he had come quite close, and that was why he, the boy, stabbed his sister" (¶810–814). Asked what the man wanted: "He wanted to put the blame on me."

Jung's reading: "The appearance of the little man was none other than the personification of the criminal instinct, and what the boy described as 'blame' was a symbol of the second self that was driving him to destruction" (¶814). After the crime, epileptic fits — "an evasion of the crime, a repression of the criminal instinct" (¶815). The shrunk bearded other as the shadow's personification in a child.

occurrences.title: The little man with the pointed cap springs from the furrow — Kerner's old report
occurrences.label: The little man with the pointed cap springs…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: old report in a book ~120 years old in 1936

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: A report "much older" than the book of Justinus Kerner that preserves it: a peasant was plowing and "suddenly out of the furrow came a little man with a pointed cap — the characteristic covering of the cabiri — who gave him a message. He prophesied something which I don't remember, and the peasant naively believed him."

Jung offers it as the living folk continuation of the Tages legend — the Etruscan boylike god who sprang from the furrow behind the plowman and taught arts and crafts — and as "one of the forms in which the Puer Aeternus can appear": the child of the wise old man, alongside Oannes rising daily from the water as a fish.
Verbatim: "out of the furrow came a little man with a pointed cap-the characteristic covering of the cabiri-who gave him a message".

occurrences.title: Schreber's 'little fellows' — the multitude walking on his eyelids
occurrences.label: Schreber's 'little fellows'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: President Daniel Paul Schreber's Memoirs of My Nervous Illness — "the Schreber of whom I am speaking was a lawyer living in Leipzig who became a schizophrenic", the book Freud later "wrote up… in a very unsatisfactory manner after I had drawn his attention to it" (footnote, CW5 ¶458).

His description of the splitting: "at times a multitude of little fellows were all over him-tiny creatures were walking on his eyelids for instance; or they were flying about and setting down upon his skin like mosquitos. And sometimes they disappeared into it shouting, 'Damn it, I go in!'" — parts of the split mind "which still were capable of integration… like splinters of ice which freeze together in the night, and then split again when the wind comes".

Jung cites the memoir as his clearest document of the turba — the pre-schizophrenic multitude (ants, gnats, little animals in dreams) — the "archetype of the many" that inflated consciousness decays into.

occurrences.title: The eagle of brass renewing itself in the spring — Ostanes in Zosimos
occurrences.label: The eagle of brass renewing itself in the spring
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: an “eagle of brass, who descends into the pure spring and bathes there every day, thus renewing himself.
body: Zosimos (Berthelot, Alch. grecs III, vi, 5) quotes Ostanes on an "eagle of brass, who descends into the pure spring and bathes there every day, thus renewing himself." Jung flags it as "Probably the earliest reference to the phoenix" — the self-renewing metal-bird before the phoenix vocabulary is fixed.

Jung's reading: the renewal-bird of the arcane substance in its oldest attested form; metallic (brass) yet self-bathing and self-renewing — the resurrection-motif native to alchemy from the Greek corpus onward. Parallels: phoenix family, eagle-toad-avicenna-emblem-maier-1617, mercurius-nine-eagles-vision-senior-950.

occurrences.title: Double-headed eagle covered with eyes, crowned by Pope and Emperor — Codex Palatinus Latinus 412
occurrences.label: Double-headed eagle covered with eyes, crowned…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Vatican, Biblioteca (Wynandi de Stega, 'Adamas colluctancium aquilarum')
body: "266. Double-headed eagle with crowns of Pope and Emperor, symbolizing the kingdoms of both worlds. The eagle is covered with eyes (enlightenment!)" (fig. 266; verified on plate p0452). The imperial-ecclesiastical two-headed bird of the two worlds, its plumage an eyelike field — Jung's own parenthetical gloss "(enlightenment!)" marks his reading of the many-eyed body as vision, consciousness multiplied across the whole animal.

Jung sets it in the chapter's closing series of figures (figs. 265–266) where the unicorn's reflection ("De moy je m'epouvante") and the two-worlds eagle frame the transition to the Epilogue's psychology of enlightenment and inflation.

occurrences.title: Enkidu's eagle dream — carried by iron claws and dropped, Tablet VII
occurrences.label: Enkidu's eagle dream
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Uruk (text from Assur-bani-pal's library, Nineveh; British Museum tablets)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: After their greatest triumph, Enkidu — the inferior counterpart created by the gods against Gilgamesh — dreams: "An eagle took me with iron claws and flew upward for four hours... Look down upon the earth, what seest thou?... And again for four hours he flew higher... then he dropped me and I fell and fell and finally I lay upon the earth crushed." He wakes "hot with terror"; an evil spirit of fever takes him and he dies on the twelfth day.

Jung's reading closes the eagle-serpent sequence: "The lower inferior man is taken by the iron claws of the spiritlike consciousness which is detached from the ordinary corporeal human being, and is carried up into the air very high, but in the end he is dropped and killed. This is exactly the fate of Zarathustra, or Nietzsche... this is the rope-dancer." Enkidu is "a more developed form of the serpent" — the vertebral psyche.

Verbatim: "An eagle took me with iron claws and flew upward for four hours... then he dropped me and I fell and fell and finally I lay upon the earth crushed. This is the dream, and hot with terror I woke up."

occurrences.title: Ganymede carried off by the eagle of Zeus
occurrences.label: Ganymede carried off by the eagle of Zeus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The classical parallel Jung is sure Nietzsche the philologist knew: Zeus' eagle fetches the beautiful boy Ganymede to serve at the table of the gods.

Jung: "that beautiful boy who was fetched by the eagle of Zeus to serve at the table of the gods — a homosexual interlude, one of the little scandals of Olympus." In the seminar's reading the eagle is the wise-old-man bird lifting a mortal out of his element — the same configuration as the serpent hanging on Zarathustra's eagle: the Hamsa comes "with soft wings and lifts one up and one doesn't notice it and then one is gone".
Verbatim: "Yes, that beautiful boy who was fetched by the eagle of Zeus to serve at the table of the gods-a homosexual interlude, one of the little scandals of Olympus."

occurrences.title: Garuda and the Naga — the surviving serpent worn as neck ornament
occurrences.label: Garuda and the Naga
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Mrs. Zinno's parallel to Zarathustra's eagle-serpent: "the myth of the Garuda and the Naga, and I have here a picture of Vishnu enthroned upon the Garuda, the snake-killing bird. The Garuda is the mind bird, a sort of demoniacal eagle."

Jung: "The Garuda is said to have extinguished all the Nagas except one, which he put round his neck and wore as a neck ornament... It would simply be a sign of his victory over the serpent" — not friendliness, not encumbrance. He adds the historical layer: the Nagas "may also have represented the snake worshippers, a lower stratum of the population, probably of Dravidian origin" — the Aryans "would be the eagles, the air, heaven people."
Verbatim: "The Garuda is said to have extinguished all the Nagas except one, which he put round his neck and wore as a neck ornament."

occurrences.title: Klinger's Nietzsche bust — the eagle holding the serpent
occurrences.label: Klinger's Nietzsche bust
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "The artist Klinger made a bust of Nietzsche, using this symbol of the eagle and the serpent; the four corners of the bust were shaped like the claws of the eagle, and the eagle holds the snake in its claws."

Jung: "You see he corrected Zarathustra's vision, as the artist does; he insisted that the snake was overcome by the eagle because they are eternal enemies." Klinger restores the classical formula (cf. the eagle lecterns) that Zarathustra's coiled-friend version violates — the artistic instinct for "the rules" against the possession-image.

Verbatim: "The artist Klinger made a bust of Nietzsche, using this symbol of the eagle and the serpent; the four corners of the bust were shaped like the claws of the eagle, and the eagle holds the snake in its claws."

occurrences.title: The eagle lecterns — St John's eagle bearing the Gospel
occurrences.label: The eagle lecterns
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The familiar church bird: "the so-called lecterns in churches, sort of reading-desks on which the Bible is supported by an eagle. The eagle is the symbol of St. John the Evangelist, whose philosophy is the idea of the Logos, the word, or the light that comes from God and shines into the darkness of man."

"Antique fantasy ascribed the eagle to John because the eagle was the messenger of Zeus." The lectern is the classical eagle-over-serpent formula: "the eagle has the snake in its claws... the eagle, personifying the light, has overcome the powers of darkness" — the norm against which Zarathustra's coiled serpent is the deviation.
Verbatim: "you remember having seen the so-called lecterns in churches, sort of reading-desks on which the Bible is supported by an eagle."

occurrences.title: The eagle making obeisance to Miriai — Mandaean Book of John
occurrences.label: The eagle making obeisance to Miriai
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Mrs. Crowley's contribution: "In the Mandaean Book of John there is a very definite picture of the eagle coming down as the messenger of God, but making obeisance to Myria; he becomes her messenger, so he is really the messenger of earth there."

Jung: "That is the Gnostic idea, but this is a further development of the Gnostic symbolism" — the divine bird deflected into the service of the earthly feminine (Miriai/Miriam), the reverse of Zeus' eagle. He declines to press it further: "Nietzsche had no knowledge of Gnosticism nor of medieval philosophy."

Verbatim: "In the Mandaean Book of John there is a very definite picture of the eagle coming down as the messenger of God, but making obeisance to Myria; he becomes her messenger, so he is really the messenger of earth there."

occurrences.title: Prometheus — the eagle eating the liver, chained to the rock
occurrences.label: Prometheus — the eagle eating the liver…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "The classical case" (Mrs. Jung) of the bird of prey that finds its prey: Zeus' eagle eats the liver of Prometheus, "chained to a rock, chained to earth". Jung deploys it for the liberated shadow of 'The Spirit of Gravity': Nietzsche's shadow has become a bird — "an independent, autonomous thing, and it swoops down on Nietzsche and takes him up into another world. Eventually, the eagle will eat out his life exactly as the eagle of Zeus ate the liver of Prometheus".
The liver, die Leber, "the life and soul according to primitive ideas" (pdf p1483, on the hero in the whale-dragon's belly) — what the shadow-bird feeds on.

occurrences.title: The eagle with the serpent round its neck — Zarathustra at noon
occurrences.label: The eagle with the serpent round its neck
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Section 10: at noontide an eagle sweeps overhead "in wide circles, and on it hung a serpent, not like a prey, but like a friend: for it kept itself coiled round the eagle's neck." "They are mine animals," says Zarathustra.

Jung's long reading (7 + 14 Nov): eagle = thought, spirit, "a messenger of the highest god"; serpent = earth, chthonic, the spinal cord's psyche. The coiled arrangement is "very unusual... not at all classical" (usually the snake is in the claws — Klinger's bust corrects it): Nietzsche is the serpent "lifted out of the ground... in the power of that enormous bird," voluntarily, as a union — "an attempt at the reconciliation of the pairs of opposites" — yet precarious, "a premonitory picture." "'Beyond good and evil' means beyond eagle and serpent and their moral meanings."
Verbatim: "an eagle swept through the air in wide circles, and on it hung a serpent, not like a prey, but like a friend: for it kept itself coiled round the eagle's neck."
The animals as instinct-symbols in the mountain cave (Prologue 1) are the sibling-locus eagle-serpent-zarathustra-animals-1883, whose pin ('the intertwined passage') this noon vision fulfils.

occurrences.title: Zarathustra's eagle and serpent (Zarathustra, Prologue 1)
occurrences.label: Zarathustra's eagle and serpent
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Zarathustra addresses the sun "mine eagle, and my serpent" — the two animals who waited with him for ten years. Jung's reading: the eagle is "the spirit," "a son of the sun... the bird of light, it is the very high thought, the great enthusiasm" — amplifying with Ganymede carried to Olympus by Zeus's eagle. The serpent is "the body," "the age-old representative of the lower worlds, of the belly with its contents"; "it is the peristaltic movement, it is the personification of the sympathetic system"; "la force terrestre" — everything chthonic, banal, real.

That the animals accompany him means, as in dreams, "that he is going parallel with his instincts" — he is right "from a spiritual as well as a chthonic point of view." Jung promises: "later on we shall come across a passage where the eagle and the serpent are intertwined, meaning a reconciliation of opposites."

occurrences.title: Eagle and toad of Avicenna — Maier, Symbola aureae mensae
occurrences.label: Eagle and toad of Avicenna
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: I would mention the eagle and toad ('the eagle flying through the air and the toad crawling on the ground'), which are the 'emblem' of Avicenna in Michael Maier
body: The emblem pair Avicenna hands the alchemists through Michael Maier: the eagle "flying through the air" and the toad "crawling on the ground" — the volatile and the fixed as theriomorphic opposites. The eagle is Luna "or Juno, Venus, Beya, who is fugitive and winged like the eagle, which flies up to the clouds and receives the rays of the sun in his eyes"; the toad is the contrary element, earth, "which cannot fly [i.e., cannot be sublimated]," the philosophic earth on which "the golden house is to be built" (¶2).

Jung opens Mysterium Coniunctionis with this pair as the classic case of opposites personified in animals: "Theriomorphic symbols are equally common." The toad recurs at ¶30 (Scrutinium Emblem V, suckled by the woman until she dies) and in ¶172's list of the union's poisonous progeny.

occurrences.title: The nourishing earth-mother — Limburg Cathedral vault painting
occurrences.label: The nourishing earth-mother
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Limburg an der Lahn, Germany (vault painting)
body: Pl. XIVa: the nursing earth-mother of the Limburg vault (with the classical Gaia-type streaming water/milk motif).

Jung's reading: "The ideal example of such an object is the nurturing earth-mother" (¶226) — the object invested by desexualized, regressed libido; "the psychology of the presexual stage accounts for her nourishing character, and sexuality for her most typical form of worship, the hieros gamos."
Verbatim: The ideal example of such an object is the nurturing earth-mother. (cw05 ¶226).

occurrences.title: The new fire struck from the firestone — first Collect for Easter Eve
occurrences.label: The new fire struck from the firestone
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The first Collect for the blessing of the new fire on Easter Eve: "O God, who through thy Son, who is called the cornerstone, hast brought the fire of thy light to the faithful, make holy for our future use this new fire struck from the firestone".

Jung's apparatus welds stone and spark: the "stone with seven eyes" read as foundation stone rather than keystone, the lapis angularis whose ritual parallel is the silex from which the spark springs — Christ-cornerstone, firestone, and the light born from stone in one rite. The liturgical sibling of the stone-born light (Mithras petra genetrix, n.87).

occurrences.title: Ebers papyrus - naming the disease; Isis wounds Ra, the snake-bite cure (Egypt, ~1550 B.C.)
occurrences.label: Ebers papyrus - naming the disease
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: A snake bite was cured, for instance, by reading to the patient the story of Isis wounding Ra by a poisonous snake and then curing him again; they gave the facts a symbolic expression.
body: "Therefore old Egyptian medicine consisted in giving the thing the right name. A papyrus has been published by a German named Ebers, in which medical instructions were given to the doctors for dealing with patients". The carbuncle case: "The doctor reads the text to the man: 'Thy neck is red and hot and swollen,' and then he repeats it" - every symptom named as if the patient did not know them.

"A snake bite was cured, for instance, by reading to the patient the story of Isis wounding Ra by a poisonous snake and then curing him again; they gave the facts a symbolic expression." Jung's bridge from the lived to the symbolic archetype - and to the modern clinic: "I have been paid many hundred dollars in America for uttering a strange word, what they call giving an opinion."

occurrences.title: The seven coloured walls of Ecbatana — Herodotus
occurrences.label: The seven coloured walls of Ecbatana — Herodotus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The walls obviously represented the concentric circles of the planets, each characterized by a special colour.
body: Herodotus describes the seven circular walls of Ecbatana, "the ramparts... all painted in different colours; of the two innermost and highest walls one was silvered and the other gilded." Jung at cw14 ¶577: the walls obviously represented the concentric circles of the planets, each characterized by a special colour — the architectural ancestor of the planetary mandala.

occurrences.title: Echidna, mother of monsters — Hesiodic genealogy
occurrences.label: Echidna, mother of monsters — Hesiodic genealogy
occurrences.subject: n/a
