body: Echidna, lovely maiden above and hideous serpent below, daughter of Gaia and Tartarus; mother of Chimera, Scylla, the Gorgon, Cerberus, the Nemean lion, Prometheus' eagle and "a number of dragons"; with her own son Orthrus she incestuously begets the Sphinx.

Jung's reading: "This double being corresponds to the mother-imago: above, the lovely and attractive human half; below, the horrible animal half, changed into a fear-animal by the incest prohibition" (¶265). Revelation's woman-on-dragon revives her: "In this primordial image of the woman on the dragon we recognize Echidna" (¶315).

Verbatim: Echidna herself was the mother of all terrors, of the Chimera, Scylla, the Gorgon (pl. XIVb), of frightful Cerberus, of the Nemean lion, and of the eagle that devoured the liver of Prometheus. (cw05 ¶265).

occurrences.title: Meister Eckhart — the Godhead 'of forms formless'; the poor in spirit
occurrences.label: Meister Eckhart — the poor in spirit
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Eckhart's Godhead 'of which no qualities, except unity and being, can be predicated' — 'of forms formless; of becoming becomingless; of beings beingless; of things thingless' — an 'absolute coincidence of opposites', hence unconscious: 'Union of opposites is equivalent to unconsciousness' (¶301). The poor man 'is so quit and empty of all knowing that no knowledge of God is alive in him'; love God 'as a not-God... a sheer, pure, clear One... sundered from all secondness' (¶301). Jung: Eckhart knew 'the primordial mystical experience of India as well as of the Gnostics', finest flower of the Free Spirit (¶302). His God is the Godhead as agnosia.

occurrences.title: Dream of the whitish foamy face issuing from the neck (borderline patient, pre-WWI)
occurrences.label: Dream of the whitish foamy face issuing…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: 'many years before I ever heard of ectoplasm, before the war' (~1912-13)
occurrences.quote: she dreamt that a whitish mass, like foam, issued from her neck, and gradually formed into a face which was as if plastered or stuck onto that foamy mass, exactly like the photographs in the books by Schrenck-Notzing. She had never seen such things, because they were then not known.
body: A dream Jung reports from "many years before I ever heard of ectoplasm, before the war," from a borderline schizophrenia case with high libido withdrawal:

Jung: instead of projecting the duplication of life into objects, "in her dream it came out of her own body." He understood it psychologically, not parapsychologically, yet records the uncanny timing. The same phenomenon appears, he says, in Picasso's borderline figures with duplicated forms and in the schizophrenic exteriorization of the Kundalini snake as rods.

occurrences.title: Edem: virgin above, serpent below — the Gnosis of Justin
occurrences.label: Edem — virgin above, serpent below
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The Justinian Gnosis depicts her as Edem, virgin above, serpent below.
body: In the Justinian Gnosis, Edem — the body of the world — is "virgin above, serpent below": the upper half the pneumatic virgin, the lower a serpent. She longs for the embrace of the Monad; the demiurge, her faithless lover, abandons her; she strives vengefully against the pneuma. She is "the divine soul imprisoned in the elements, whom it is the task of alchemy to redeem."

Jung's frame: the pagan projection goes beyond man into the unknown substance of the material world, where the Godhead hides "in the uncomely stone" as in Christianity it hides in the man of low degree. Edem names the feminine, matter-pole of the Nous-Physis drama.

occurrences.title: The Egg of Granite: snakes at the base, the crowd's 'It is only granite' (18 January 1933)
occurrences.label: The Egg of Granite
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: It is as if she were received by the egg, as if she became the living germ inside, and would eventually be reborn from it.
body: After the wheel, by enantiodromia, the extreme of stability: "I passed the wheel and came to a great egg. Snakes guarded the base of it." A crowd presses in, threatening — "It is only granite" — and nearly crushes her against it, trying to put out the flame on her breast. She seizes one of the egg's whip-threads, strikes at the crowd, commands "Open unto me": the egg divides into four parts, the yolk pours forth and envelops her, and she turns to the people "without any anger."

Jung's reading: the egg = a latent condition, possible but not accomplished rebirth (Orphic world egg; kundalini's serpent-coiled lingam); a plurality of serpents means disintegration — too much libido in the unconscious, too little in the egg. The crowd is the collective unconscious projected into public opinion; the yolk-womb is the twice-born state, the walls of the church, protection bought at the price of being "stiff and cold and inhuman" from outside.

occurrences.title: Patient grown fast to the rock among egg-boulders (Eranos 1933 case)
occurrences.label: Patient grown fast to the rock among…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: painting ~1930s; lecture 1933; shown in seminar 16 Nov 1938

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The first of the two originals Jung shows of the case behind "A Study in the Process of Individuation": "The patient herself is represented as grown fast to the rock — in other words, identical with the unconscious which is the earth. The boulders are egg-shaped and really mean eggs, or the seed substance that is to be transformed".

Next stage: rotundum-incandescent-sphere-lightning-zurich-1933 — the lightning strike and the round globe cut loose from chaos, "separated from the participation mystique with chaos, or, as we would say, with the collective unconscious".

occurrences.title: Rig-Veda X,129 (Nasadiya hymn) — the One hidden in the shell
occurrences.label: Rig-Veda X,129 — the One hidden in the shell
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Quoted under Fig. 21 (a patient's picture of a fish making a whirlpool in the sea of the unconscious, the precious pearl forming in its midst): "Darkness there was, concealed in darkness, A lightless ocean lost in night. Then the One, that was hidden in the shell, was born through the power of fiery torment. From it arose in the beginning love, Which is the germ and the seed of knowledge." The creation-hymn of the Rig-Veda gives the oldest text-form of the germ-in-the-shell — the world-egg of the mandala centre — arising from the dark watery beginning.

occurrences.title: Seven pictures: the egg divides to the circle — equinox dream, mid-March 1957
occurrences.label: Seven pictures — the egg divides to the circle
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: mid-March 1957 (four days after the H-atom dream)

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: The imaginary unit i... has the irrational function of uniting the pairs of opposites and thus producing wholeness.
body: Second of the two "equinox dreams" given "by way of summing up and looking ahead" in Pauli's unpublished Background Physics essay. Seven wordless pictures: (1) a woman brings a bird, which lays a large egg; (2) the egg divides in two; (4) the dreamer divides the last egg — "Miraculously, they remain whole, and I now have two eggs with blue shells"; (5) the four eggs turn into cos(alpha/2), sin(beta/2) expressions; (6) the compound formula; (7) "The whole thing gives e^{i alpha}, and that is the circle. The formula vanishes, and a circle appears."

Pauli: the H-atom dream beside it is "cosmogonical" ("proton... means 'the first'"), the metal plate the stable physis, the brass tones — "with their connection to the music of the spheres" — symbols uniting physis and psyche, "exactly what is meant by 'archetypes'"; the change in splitting is "an intervention of consciousness." Cf. Jung on eggs, Psychology and Alchemy pars. 384-391.

occurrences.title: Adam first of eight incarnations of the True Prophet — Clementine Homilies
occurrences.label: Adam first of eight incarnations…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Adam is the first of a series of eight incarnations of the 'true prophet.' The last is Jesus.
body: In the Clementine Homilies Adam is the first of a series of eight incarnations of the "true prophet"; the last is Jesus. "The eighth prophet is not merely the last in the series; he corresponds to the first and is at the same time the fulfilment of the seven, and signifies the entry into a new order."
Jung at cw14 ¶573-574: the same 7+1 structure shown with a modern dream in Psychology and Alchemy ¶200ff — hesitation at the eighth as with three and four (Axiom of Maria).

occurrences.title: The eight-petalled flower — 'Recueil de figures astrologiques' (MS., 18th c.)
occurrences.label: The eight-petalled flower
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the eighth or the first of seven
body: Plate 85: "The eight-petalled flower as the eighth or the first of seven." It illustrates visual impression 29, where the dreamer sees "a bunch of roses, then the sign… but it should be [the eightfold flower]" — a mistake corrected "which somehow impaired the wholeness of the rose. The aim of the reconstruction is to bring the problem of the mandala—the correct valuation and interpretation of the 'centre'—once more into the field of consciousness" (¶237).

The historical figure certifies the spontaneous drawing: the eightfold flower as "the eighth or the first of seven" is the same number-structure as the Cabiri scene's eighth-on-Olympus and the world clock's eight spokes.

occurrences.title: Moses and El-Khidr at the source of life (Koran, Sura 18)
occurrences.label: Moses and El-Khidr at the source of life
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the ground round about El-Khidr blossomed with spring flowers, although it was desert
body: Third companion-example: in Sura 18 Moses seeks the place "where the two seas meet" and meets "one of Our servants whom We had endowed with Our grace and wisdom" — El-Khidr, the Green One. "And the legend has it that the ground round about El-Khidr blossomed with spring flowers, although it was desert" (¶155). Jung notes Moses "found to his cost" that the source of life "is not without its dangers" (¶157).

El-Khidr doubles the companion with the well-spring: "The source of life is, like El-Khidr, a good companion" — the eternally renewing life-force, "the clock that never runs down," sought underground: "only down below can we find the fiery source of life" (¶157).

occurrences.title: The Franciscan exorcist heals the Circus Knie elephant (Rapperswil)
occurrences.label: The Franciscan exorcist heals the Circus Knie…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Rapperswil, Switzerland (Franciscan monastery below the castle)
occurrences.quote: All the vets had done their best and all the medicine they could provide had been used, but the elephant simply would not be cured.
body: The Circus Knie animals winter at Rapperswil; a young elephant suffered from diarrhea and resisted every veterinary remedy. The Franciscan father — "really a medicine man... he knew how to deal with ghosts and evil spirits, using the church magic, exorcism" — talked to the animal for an hour and a half, stroked its back, looked long into its eyes, told it to give up being sick and submit; then: "Now he wants to be cured, he will be all right tomorrow, you must do nothing to him, he has submitted." The next day it was well. Jung's frame: the priest's exceedingly limited consciousness lived in participation mystique with all he touched — "he puts something into people... This little elephant merely reacted like any sensible human being would react."

occurrences.title: The elephants whispering at night, sad not to have pleased man — Philostratus on Apollonius
occurrences.label: The elephants whispering at night, sad not…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: On the animals who live with man (the dogs and horses the ordinary person keeps on the surface), Jung adduces Philostratus: "in his book about Apollonius of Tyana… says that elephants like man very much; he heard them whispering among themselves in the night, and they were very sad because they were afraid they had not pleased man during the day. They were ambitious to be appreciated by him".

"This is a very precious piece of animal psychology, inasmuch as our own psychology is similar; many people worry for hours in the night lest they have not lived up to the expectations of others." The locus serves the reading of Nietzsche's "many-too-many": the normal individual "lives together with his animals and therefore he cannot and will not overreach himself." Editorial note: Apollonius — traveller, miracle worker, Pythagorean ascetic, born 3 BCE — "did not know of Jesus but was a kind of rival."

occurrences.title: The sacred white elephant of the muladhara lotus — Tantric chakra symbolism (via Avalon)
occurrences.label: The sacred white elephant of the muladhara lotus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: traditional doctrine (via Avalon, The Serpent Power, 1931)
body: Jung's exposition of the chakra system: "The nethermost chakra, called mulādhāra, is the perineal lotus and corresponds to the cloacal zone in Freud's sexual theory. This centre, like all the others, is represented in the shape of a flower, with a circle in the middle... Thus, the perineal chakra contains as its main symbol the sacred white elephant" (¶560). The white elephant reappeared, unbidden, in his Java-born patient's dream (¶551) — the case's hinge between symptom and doctrine. The elephant carries the living shakti before her ascent; cf. the Bodhisattva-elephant of Queen Maya's dream (cw05 ¶490-492).

occurrences.title: White elephant emerging from her genitals — dream of the Java-born patient (Zurich, ~1931)
occurrences.label: White elephant emerging from her genitals
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: At the start of the real neurosis, the patient "dreamt that a white elephant was coming out of her genitals. She was so impressed by this that she tried to carve the elephant out of ivory" (¶551). Jung at the time had "no idea what it meant." The Serpent Power later supplied the key: "the perineal chakra contains as its main symbol the sacred white elephant" (¶560) — the dream image precisely at the muladhara, root of the kundalini system her symptoms were climbing. The ivory carving is a spontaneous attempt to give the psychosomatic image a body. Cf. Queen Maya's elephant-conception (cw05 ¶490-492).

occurrences.title: Eleusinian mysteries — 'The Mistress has borne the divine boy, Brimo has borne Brimos!'
occurrences.label: Eleusinian mysteries
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Proteus is likened to the green ear of corn of the Eleusinian mysteries; to him the celebrants cry: 'The Mistress has borne the divine boy, Brimo has borne Brimos!' (¶339). The 'lower' correspondence is 'the dark path of Persephone... to the grove of adored Aphrodite, who rouses the sickness of love'; initiates become bridegrooms 'robbed of their virility by the virgin spirit' (Rev. 14:4 motif) (¶339). Jung's footnote records his interview at Turukalukundram on why erotic sculptures guard the path to the adyton — see turukalukundram-erotic-temple-pundit-1937.

occurrences.title: 'Blessed is he among men who has seen these mysteries' — Homeric Hymn to Demeter 480-82
occurrences.label: Blessed is he among men who has seen these…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: The testimonium of the Eleusinian initiate quoted from the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, vv. 480-82 (Evelyn-White trans.): "Blessed is he among men who has seen these mysteries; but he who is uninitiate and has no part in them, never has lot of like good things once he is dead, down in the darkness and gloom." Joined to an Eleusinian epitaph: "Truly the blessed gods have proclaimed a most beautiful secret: Death comes not as a curse, but as a blessing to men" (fn 2).

Jung's reading: exemplar of the fifth form of rebirth — participation in a transformation rite outside oneself; through witnessed mystery "the hope of immortality" is conferred as grace (cf. ¶208 on Osiris and the phoenix).

occurrences.title: The mistake of the eleven thousand virgins — St. Ursula and her company (Cologne)
occurrences.label: The mistake of the eleven thousand virgins
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~11th c. legend (legendary massacre dated 4th c.; 11,000 in medieval tradition)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: The Cologne legend of St. Ursula and the eleven thousand virgins. Jung invokes it sardonically as "the mistake of the eleven thousand virgins": the girls with "a little something repressed" become neurotic, go to the doctor, and are told "that is all repressed sex, you should have a friend or you should marry" — whereupon the parents "take the thing in hand and put her in the marriage box. But then there is a hell of a trouble, and it does not work at all".
The locus serves his critique of reductive sexual explanation — solving a human problem "on the cow-bull level" — against the background of the anima as amoral Nature misunderstood.

occurrences.title: The imp in objects — F. T. Vischer's Auch Einer (1884)
occurrences.label: The imp in objects — F. T. Vischer's Auch Einer
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: Yes, a German book about one of those who know about things, that is, the imp in objects.
body: Vischer's novel of the Tücke des Objekts — the malice of objects: spectacles lost in the impossible place, buttered toast falling buttered side down, the coffeepot spout threading the milk-jug handle. Jung seizes it as literature's testimony to the psychogenic factor: "he gets the psychic factor all right, because it is in a way our doing, and yet it is not our doing; it happens in an impish way" — the psyche manifesting against us, announcing (in grotesque form) the puruṣa.

occurrences.title: The 'maker of fear' of the Elgonyi
occurrences.label: The 'maker of fear' of the Elgonyi
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: He comes to you," they said, "like acold gust of wind, and you shudder, or he goes whistling round in the tall grass
body: Jung's field datum from the Elgonyi elders in Kenya: their nocturnal god, the "maker of fear", comes "like a cold gust of wind, and you shudder, or he goes whistling round in the tall grass" — "an African Pan who glides among the reeds in the haunted noontide hour, playing on his pipes and frightening the shepherds" (¶33).

Jung's reading: exact parallel to the pneuma rushing over the dark water in the theologian's dream — the numen's unseen presence, "like everything whose cause we do not know — since it is not ourselves"; the erstwhile fiery spirit has descended into "the trees and rocks and the waters of the psyche".

occurrences.title: Elgonyi sunrise libation — spitting at the rising sun, Mt Elgon
occurrences.label: Elgonyi sunrise libation
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: southern slopes of Mt Elgon, East Africa (Kenya)

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)
The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

occurrences.quote: At sunrise they spit on their hands and then hold the palms towards the sun as it comes over the horizon.
body: At sunrise the Elgonyi step from their huts, spit or blow vigorously into their hands, and hold the palms toward the rising sun ("We are happy that the night is past"). The same gesture at the new moon. Asked why, neither the people nor the medicine-man knew — only "the moment when the sun or the new moon appeared was mungu" (= mana, mulungu), translated by missionaries as "God"; adhista means both sun and God, yet the sun itself "is not God".

Jung's reading: "Spittle and breath mean soul-substance. Hence they offer their soul to God, but do not know what they are doing and never have known" (¶411) — ritual motivated by a preconscious archetype, identical in kind to the sun-worshipping dog-headed baboon on Egyptian monuments and to the Westerner's equally uncomprehended Christmas tree. His prime exhibit that archetypes act without ever having been conscious (¶412).

occurrences.title: Elijah — the 'light crumpled throwaway' drifting down the Liffey (Ulysses)
occurrences.label: Elijah — the 'light crumpled throwaway'…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Spirit in Man, Art and Literature (CW15)

occurrences.quote: Elijah, skiff, light crumpled throwaway, sailed eastward by flanks of ships and trawlers, amid an archipelago of corks, beyond new Wapping street past Benson's ferry
body: A throwaway protest note, flung from Conmee's and the Viceroy's passing cavalcade, drifts down the Liffey toward the sea — three times recurring in the book, "each time mysteriously connected with Elijah" (cw15 ¶190).

Jung's reading. The scrap is his emblem for the detachment of consciousness that Ulysses practises: "detachment of consciousness can be expressed in the Homeric image of Odysseus sailing the straits between Scylla and Charybdis, between the Symplegades, the clashing rocks of the world and the spirit; or, in the imagery of the Dublin inferno, between Father John Conmee and the Viceroy of Ireland" (cw15 ¶186). The note "drifts towards the East" (¶190) — toward the detached, cosmic, post-ego consciousness Jung finds in the book; its brothel-side fulfilment is Elijah preaching "the higher self" in Nighttown.

occurrences.title: Elijah, Salome and the black serpent in the crater — Jung's vision (December 1913)
occurrences.label: Elijah, Salome and the black serpent…
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: The second, deeper descent — "not a thousand feet but a cosmic depth... like going to the moon": a crater ring of mountains, the mood of the land of the hereafter. Two figures: an old man with a white beard who names himself Elijah, and a beautiful young girl who is Salome — "Elijah assured me that he and Salome had been together since eternity." With them a black snake "who had an affinity for me".

The 1925 seminars unfold the figures across three lectures: Elijah = "the personification of the cognitional element... filled with wisdom," the wise old man, "the medicine man, the mana man"; Salome = the anima, "blind because, though connecting the conscious and the unconscious, she does not see the operation of the unconscious", the historical Salome of the incestuous dance; the serpent = "the introverting libido," intuition-sensation axis of the function-quaternion. "Whenever you take journeys like this you find a young girl with an old man" — Simon Magus's Helen, Kundry, the Hypnerotomachia, Haggard, Melville. This Elijah is the seed of Philemon.

occurrences.title: Elohim and the half-snake virgin Eden — Justinos via Hippolytus
occurrences.label: Elohim and the half-snake virgin Eden
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: "Justinos recounts that on his journey west, Heracles had united with a virgin, half snake, half human (cf. Herodotus), in order to regain his stolen horse. Elohim likewise is said to have united with a virgin half-snake and half-human, called Eden or Israel, and to have procreated with her twelve paternal angels and twelve maternal ones. He then leaves her and returns to the upper, good god. Out of her sorrow at having been left, she then becomes that evil power, hostile toward God".

"Her servant, the angel Naas (snake), later brings about the crucifixion of Christ; Christ, however, left Eden his body on the cross, with the words: 'Woman, behold thy son!'" — hence John, in medieval art, carries the snake's features (the Matsys cup). At the bottom of the Gnostic cosmos: Leviathan, the ouroboros, reappearing in alchemy.

occurrences.title: 'I know the tree of emerald green' — Book of the Dead
occurrences.label: I know the tree of emerald green
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Egypt ('Gate of Knowledge of the Souls of the East')
body: "I am the pilot in the holy keel... I know the tree of emerald green from whose midst Ra rises to the height of the clouds."

Jung's reading: "Ship and tree (i.e., the ship of death and tree of death) are closely related here... The idea is that Ra rises up, born from the tree" (¶368) — Mithras half-risen from a tree (Heddernheim) is the same conglomeration.
Verbatim: I know the tree of emerald green from whose midst Ra rises to the height of the clouds. (cw05 ¶367).

occurrences.title: The disciples on the road to Emmaus — the unrecognized companion
occurrences.label: The disciples on the road to Emmaus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This is the theme of the magical travelling companion, of whom I will give three famous examples: the disciples on the road to Emmaus…
body: First of Jung's three "famous examples" of "the theme of the magical travelling companion": the risen Christ joins the disciples on the road to Emmaus, unrecognized until the breaking of bread (Luke 24). Jung lists it with Krishna–Arjuna and Moses–El-Khidr as analogues of the dream-companion found in the depths of the sea — "a close analogy to the lonely ego who finds a mate in the self, for at first the self is the strange non-ego" (¶155).
The unrecognized-then-vanishing companion precisely figures the self as "strange non-ego": present beside the ego, known only in retrospect.

image.title: The Road to Emmaus title QS:P1476,en:"The Road to Emmaus " label QS:Len,"The Road to Emmaus "

occurrences.title: Empedocles leaps into the crater of Aetna
occurrences.label: Empedocles leaps into the crater of Aetna
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: There is a Latin verse about him which says that he threw himself in to the fire of Aetna because he wanted to become immortal.
body: Jung's second Greek witness to the double meaning of the crater:

Empedocles, "one of the very early Greek philosophers and a sort of savior" — "it is said that when he traveled from town to town about ten thousand people accompanied him" — "when he was old he climbed Mount Aetna and threw himself down into the crater in order to be reborn. There we see the double meaning of the crater again in Greek legend". The crater as fire of destruction and vessel of immortalization is the same ambiguity Jung finds in the patient's volcano (psychosis-threat and crater-of-life) and in Zosimos' krater; cf. Heraclitus' pur aeizoon, "fire always living", the creative time of Chronos-Proclus.

occurrences.title: The legendary emperor pleased that the peasant did not know whether there was an emperor (wu wei)
occurrences.label: The legendary emperor pleased…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: There was a legendary emperor of China who heard a peasant saying he didn't even know whether there was an emperor. The emperor quoted that with particular satisfaction, for it proved his government to be most excellent in that it was invisible. That is the Eastern principle of wu wei.
body: The anecdote carries the Apollonian check on the Dionysian animus in the patient's vision: the old man in the turban who does nothing but gaze at the earth while flowers spring up. "The Eastern way is to sit still and give things a chance to grow... You see, the people who do not know whether they are governed, who are really not governed, govern themselves." Wu wei as "an extraordinary self-restraint" — the political mirror of contemplation without fore-judging.

occurrences.title: The girl who dreamed herself an empress — Pick's pathological daydream (Prague, ~1896)
occurrences.label: The girl who dreamed herself an empress
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: He tells the story of a young girl who flirted with the idea that she was an empress. She painted her role in ever more glowing colours, got so absorbed in it that in the end it turned into an hysterical twilight state with complete splitting of consciousness
body: A young girl "flirted with the idea that she was an empress," painted the role in ever more glowing colours, and got so absorbed that it "turned into an hysterical twilight state with complete splitting of consciousness" (¶304). Jung sets it beside a Breslau girl who staged her own engagement (self-sent letters and flowers in disguised handwriting) and his own somnambulic case, to prove a gradient: "from fanciful exaggerations to genuine twilight states," all beginning with "a feeling-toned idea which develops on the basis of suggestibility into an automatism" (¶304). The imperial mask that starts as play and ends by replacing the player is the persona mechanism in miniature — Jung's explicit persona-theory comes two decades later; the tie is inferred.

occurrences.title: Empusa — Hecate's blood-bladder hobgoblin
occurrences.label: Empusa — Hecate's blood-bladder hobgoblin
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the triskelos-Medusa discussion of the terrible mother: "Another figure connected with the terrible mother was called Empusa, a sort of hobgoblin sent by Hecate, which was nothing but a bladder filled with blood; in that case the mother was only symbolized in the shape of the uterus". Jung adds the parallel: "Negroes have a similar idea: a certain witch is supposed to have the form of a pear."

Within the svadhisthana argument: the makara, Empusa, and Lilith are the devouring negative aspect of the life-giving mother. Cf. Kuan Yin's hell form — the Buddhist gods' three forms (celestial, wrathful, destructive).

occurrences.title: Ephrem the Syrian — Christ 'clothed in figures'
occurrences.label: Ephrem the Syrian — Christ clothed in figures
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The principle of 'outward uncomeliness' said of the lead and the lapis is applied to Christ by Ephrem (d. 373): 'He is clothed in figures, he is the bearer of types.... His treasure is hidden and of small account, but when it is laid open, it is wonderful to look upon' (¶216). Jung cites this in the sequence draconite–lapis–Christ to show that the alchemical fish symbol 'points ultimately to an archetype of the order of magnitude of the self' and that the lapis-Christ parallel (Psychology and Alchemy) is an old, living equation.

occurrences.title: The equinoctical cross and the visible cross in the sky
occurrences.label: The equinoctical cross and the visible cross…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: the cross was a very important time symbol already in antiquity; it has always been explained as the position of the spring equinox, the intersection of the equator with the so-called ecliptic.
body: The cross as time-symbol: intersection of equator and ecliptic in the ancient horoscope (drawn as square or circle). Jung doubts the chi-X of Platonism and proposes instead 'the visible cross in the sky... the intersection of the Milky Way with the zodiacal line,' which he himself saw in the North African desert (Prof. Fierz: also visible in Rhodes). Parallels: quaternity-timaeus-opening-athens-360bce · cross-two-thieves-paradise-hell-luke-23-golgotha-30ce.

occurrences.title: Wotan consults Erda — the war god's recourse to the earth goddess (Wagner's Ring)
occurrences.label: Wotan consults Erda
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: In Wagner's Ring the war god Wotan again and again seeks the counsel of Erda, the primordial earth goddess, wisdom's mother. Jung adduces the pair in one breath with the witch of Endor as proof that "there are many other examples in mythology where men had to go back to women's advice".

The function in dream 30: the dreamer "has used up all the masculine means at his disposition... it is obviously a case which cannot be decided by the masculine mind, and therefore Mother Nature, the great-grandmother, as a last resort has to be called in, and she is very old and very young, like eternal nature".

occurrences.title: Goethe's Erlkönig — the elf-king who summons the child
occurrences.label: Goethe's Erlkönig — the elf-king…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939
Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: Du liebes Kind, komm, geh mit mir!
body: Jung's name for the elves who entice children: "That motif is like one you certainly know which occurs in a famous poem of Goethe. Mrs. Fierz: Der Erlkonig. Prof. Jung: Yes. Du liebes Kind, komm, geh mit mir!". The boy with the white maidens' airship and Nietzsche's dancing maidens belong to the same society: "the Erlkönig and his daughters... those wonderful spirits whose playmate he once been".

The darker register: "in Goethe's poem, Die Erlkonig, it is the archetypal images very often in dreams that anticipate death" — keyed to the dream-seminar girl who died at nine, her archetypal dreams running a year and a half ahead of her illness.

occurrences.title: Eros and Psyche — the entremets of Apuleius' Golden Ass
occurrences.label: Eros and Psyche — the entremets…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: where Psyche lost Eros because she was too curious.
body: Asked what Cupid chasing butterflies means, Miss Wolff names Apuleius: "Yes, in his book The Golden Ass, a Roman novel. You see, when he is chasing butterflies he is Amor and Psyche, and presumably Nietzsche, being a classical philologist, knew all about that. The story of Eros and Psyche is a sort of entremets in The Golden Ass, where Psyche lost Eros because she was too curious".

Psyche's forbidden lamp — wanting to see whether her night-visitor was monster or god — loses her the union; the butterfly (psyche = soul) pursued by the sleeping god is Eros that "never reaches the surface, never reaches the woman." Footnote: Apuleius of Madaura, near St. Augustine's birthplace "who of course hated Apuleius"; the tale "much discussed by Jung and Jungians, notably Erich Neumann in Amor and Psyche."

occurrences.title: The eternal Jerusalem — gold like transparent glass (Revelation 21)
occurrences.label: The eternal Jerusalem
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: and the street of the city was pure gold, as it were, transparent glass
body: The eternal Jerusalem, "lying quadratically on top of the mountain": "and the street of the city was pure gold, as it were, transparent glass" (21:21); "the city was pure gold, like unto clear glass" (21:18). Jaffé: this corresponds to the alchemical vitrum aureum, the golden glass, by which the lapis, the eternal stone, was meant — and "a child's unconscious puts the glass house of the eternal city at the one and only correct place," on the pyramid's summit.

Jung: the wondrous thing about glass is the diaphanitas — the spiritual nature of stone or vessel expressed by transparency; hence lapis spiritualis, lapis invisibilitatis, lapis aethereus, "the diamond stone light as water."

occurrences.title: The Ethiopian treatise: watching the Creation in rainwater (Ch. VIII 'The Creation')
occurrences.label: The Ethiopian treatise
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: treatise 'translated from Ethiopian into Latin and German'
occurrences.quote: you will see with your own eyes… how God created all things in six days
body: Rainwater sealed ten days in glass; poured into a round wooden vessel cut through the middle, one-third full, set in the noon sun; a drop of consecrated red wine falls in — "you will instantly perceive a fog and thick darkness on top of the water, such as also was at the first creation." Drop by drop: "you will see with your own eyes one thing after another… how God created all things in six days… Fall on your knees before you undertake this operation." Chapter IX: seven planetary metals melted in a darkened chamber; a flame lights it "more brightly than sun and moon, and over your heads you shall behold the whole firmament as it is in the starry heavens above" (¶348).
Jung's key witness that "in point of fact there are one or two unmistakable accounts" of the alchemists' own visionary experiences in the work (¶347).

occurrences.title: Vision: the Europa-girl on the white bull, the star-marked child, the satyr (9 Dec 1930)
occurrences.label: Vision — the Europa-girl…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: The bull picks up an infant and lays it at the feet of an antique statue of a woman; then "A naked young girl, her hair crowned with flowers, came riding on the back of a white bull; she seized the child, tossing it up in the air and catching it again" — Jung: like the picture of Europa on the bull-god, an anticipation of what the newborn personality might become on the antique level, and a warning: before the collective unconscious "they become as helpless as children; such visions can play with them, tossing them about like balls" (p226-227). In a Greek temple a ray of sunlight through the roof imprints a star on the child's forehead (the dawn of consciousness — filed separately as star-ray-forehead-child-vision-zurich-1930).
She changes into a youth in a sacred grove; a satyr asks "Why are you here?" — "I have no place to go." Her decent withdrawal sends the animus ahead into the quest that follows.

occurrences.title: The bey of Tunis and the marabou's ring: 'Everything passes'
occurrences.label: The bey of Tunis and the marabou's ring
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: The story told beside the geese dream: the bey of Tunis demands from his vizier the word that changes pleasure to pain and pain to pleasure, on pain of death. Doctors, sages, and the Koran fail; at last the desert marabou gives a mere ring: "The vizier in turn brought the ring to the bey, and there was written on it: 'Everything passes.' Time itself is passing, life as movement is passing".

Paired with the inscription on an old wooden bridge in the St. Gallen hills — "Everything is transition," with its double meaning of crossing and transience — the ring anchors Jung's reading of the geese-locomotive pair: the vision that "everything passes," time as the going-by itself.

occurrences.title: The removal of the Evil Urge — Talmud Yoma 69b and the legend of the Spirit of Passion
occurrences.label: The removal of the Evil Urge
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~500 CE (Talmud; Jung told an expanded folktale version)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: he begged him: 'Couldn't you send back the Evil Spirit of Passion?
body: Jung tells it as "a Jewish legend, beautiful and shameful": a pious old man begs God to remove the demon of passion from the world; God complies — and the roses lose their perfume, the wine its taste, the beautiful wife's kiss is flat. Back on the roof, the old man begs the Evil Spirit of Passion to be sent back, and the world tastes marvellous again. (Scholem, consulted by the editor: the base is Yoma 69b, where after the capture of the evil urge "no fresh egg was to be found in the whole land of Israel.")

Its work in the lecture: trespass against "the eternal laws of the Old Man" takes something out of the world; the devil as the salt of existence — "It is wise, it is vital that we are convinced of certain irrational facts."

occurrences.title: Exorcism of the salt and incense — blessing of holy water (Roman Missal)
occurrences.label: Exorcism of the salt and incense
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Rome (Ordo ad faciendam aquam benedictam, sacristy rite)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: they even exorcize the salt that is to be mixed with the baptismal water, and the incense
body: In the rite for blessing holy water the salt to be mixed into the baptismal water — and the incense — are themselves exorcized, "because everything is supposed to be contaminated by the devil. The smoke at the altar is in order to disinfect it spiritually. 'So may be absent all diabolical fraud,' the Latin text expresses it."

Jung's frame: whatever consciousness man has was stolen from the gods, so man feels sinful and "we have to purify ourselves from the diabolic admixture of nature". Circumcision, likewise, "is a rite of exorcism, to enable one to escape from impure natural elemental influences" — until the ceremonials are undergone we are "impure and contaminated and unacceptable to the grace of God."

occurrences.title: 'The All-Seeing Chronos' and the pantepiskopos daemon of Chaeronea
occurrences.label: The All-Seeing Chronos' and the pantepiskopos…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

occurrences.quote: while in the memorial tablet for those who fell at Chaeronea he is called "ττανί-πίσκottos δαίμων.
body: Sophocles names Chronos "ho pantoptin Chronon" (the All-Seeing Time); on the memorial tablet for those who fell at Chaeronea he is called "pantepiskopos daimon" — the all-beholding daemon (both via Robert Eisler). The all-seeing quality of the Pole-dragon is thus transferred to Time itself.

Jung's reading: "The identification of the All-Seeing with Time probably explains the eyes on the wheels in Ezekiel's vision... it indicates the relation between the mundus archetypus of the unconscious and the 'phenomenon' of Time — in other words, it points to the synchronicity of archetypal events" (¶394). The Uroboros has the meaning of eternity (aion) and cosmos in Horapollo — same complex.

occurrences.title: Argus Panoptes, the all-seeing — eyes in the peacock's tail
occurrences.label: Argus Panoptes, the all-seeing
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

occurrences.quote: Hera transferred the eyes of Argus Panoptes to the peacock's tail.
body: The many-eyed giant Argus, nicknamed Panoptes ("the All-Seeing"), "is supposed to symbolize the starry heavens. Sometimes he is one-eyed, sometimes four-eyed, sometimes hundred-eyed, and even myriad-eyed. Besides which he never sleeps. Hera transferred the eyes of Argus Panoptes to the peacock's tail."

Jung's reading: the same all-seeing motif that stands behind the seven planetary eyes of God; the editors' footnote adds that "this mythologem is of importance in interpreting the 'cauda pavonis'" — the peacock's tail of alchemy carries Argus's hundred eyes. Together with the sleepless Dragon of the Pole (Hippolytus) and all-seeing Chronos, Argus feeds Jung's identification of the All-Seeing with Time, hence with the synchronicity of archetypal events (¶394).

occurrences.title: Horus gives his eye to Osiris blinded by the black pig (Set) — Egypt
occurrences.label: Horus gives his eye to Osiris blinded…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: "It happened once, when Osiris was very old, that as he was walking over the earth, he suddenly complained of a pain in his eye. When his son Horus asked him what he had seen, he said, 'I saw a black pig.' 'Then,' said Horus, 'you have seen Set.' Horus took out his own eye and gave it to Osiris to restore his sight, with the fatal result, however, that Osiris became the judge of the dead in the underworld and Horus was the rising god. This is all symbolic of the second part of human existence" (p311).

Jung's Christian bridge: "While we have no actual texts about it, it is quite clear that the eye of Horus leads directly to Christ. Early Catholic teaching mentioned Isis and Horus as anticipations of Mary and Christ. Horus is the 'healer'... the eye always means vision, view, teaching." Horus, god of the Mysteries, with his four sons (three animal-headed, one human) makes the Egyptian mandala beside the Evangelists' Christian one.

occurrences.title: Indha-Indra in the right eye, viraj in the left (Upanishads)
occurrences.label: Indha-Indra in the right eye, viraj in the left
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Furthermore the human figure in the left eye is his wife, the viraj, the shining one.
body: The passage Jung reads to open the eye-symbolism session: "The man that is here in the right eye is called by the name Indha, the kindler of fire — yet, although he is Indha really, they call him also in a veiled way Indra... because the gods love that which is concealed." In the left eye dwells his wife, the viraj, the shining one. The male eye is identified with the sun, the female left eye with the moon. Jung maps the pair directly onto the patient's black wall: the star that emanates and the eye that receives — Yang and Yin, two eyes of one face.

occurrences.title: Indra's yonis changed into eyes — Indian legend
occurrences.label: Indra's yonis changed into eyes — Indian legend
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The little image reflected in the eye, the “pupilla,” is a “child.
body: The eye stands for the female genitals; the "pupilla" reflected in the eye is a "child": "The great god becomes a child again: he enters into the mother's womb for self-renewal" (¶408). The pun that carries Jung's whole eye–womb–child chain.

occurrences.title: Creeping through the aperture into a huge eye (other patient, ~1931)
occurrences.label: Creeping through the aperture into a huge eye
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich (sensation-type patient, contemporary of the visions patient)
occurrences.quote: then she had the fantasy of creeping, squeezing into that hole, and once inside she became aware that she was in a huge eye.
body: A second patient, a sensation type "wedded to tangible facts," had been unable to find any access to the unconscious: "She always felt as if she were staring at a wall on which was nothing." Once she discovered a tiny aperture, had the fantasy of squeezing through it — and found herself inside a huge eye, after which the vision unfolded in images. Jung adduces her as proof that "that idea of penetrating the eye has occurred to more than one individual," and reads the motif through the eye of Horus and the Egyptian day in autumn when the left eye of the goddess is "prepared for the reception of the god": the eye as entrance of the dark underworld, the mandala's center.

occurrences.title: The left eye of the goddess prepared to receive Ra — 15 September, Egyptian calendar
occurrences.label: The left eye of the goddess prepared…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Egyptian calendar tradition (Brugsch; via CW5 par. 408)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: In Jung's seasonal reading of Virgo: "at that time of the year, the 15th of September in the Egyptian calendar, the left eye of the goddess is prepared to receive the god Ra, who is to walk into it. The eye is a womb symbol. The female element takes the lead. The god enters the womb of darkness, Yang is under Yin. Woman is on top." Footnote quotes Brugsch: "the goddess Nehmit completes her work, so that the god Osiris may enter the left eye" — the passage Jung had already used in Symbols of Transformation (par. 408).

occurrences.title: The Seeress of Prevost perceives the optic chiasma
occurrences.label: The Seeress of Prevost perceives the optic…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "The Visionary of Prevost who has been described by Kerner, perceived by introspection the crossing of the optical nerve, the so-called chiasma which is behind the eyes."

Jung's exemplar for the claim that "many of these symbols are due to introspection" — that "inner anatomical formations... can be perceived by sensitive people." It grounds his somatic readings of the animals: the serpent as spinal cord, the eagle as the brain's unified commissure — "Such symbolism is always peculiarly apt and expressive."
Verbatim: "the Visionary of Prevost who has been described by Kerner, perceived by introspection the crossing of the optical nerve, the so-called chiasma which is behind the eyes."

occurrences.title: The sacrifice of the eye to the earth mother (Visions Seminar, 2 November 1932)
occurrences.label: The sacrifice of the eye to the earth mother
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The child is the tree and the tree is the child.
body: Completion of the two-gold-rings vision: the patient cannot cross the apotropaic rings to reach the child; snakes feed it; a blind old man circumambulates the circle and says "Woman, you must lose one of your eyes." The wind blows a seed into her left eye; the earth mother plucks the eye out — "This eye will I put into my bosom where all things perish and die and are reborn" — the rings break, and she lifts the child: "Now grow as the tree groweth."

Jung's reading: the one-eyed god situation repeating — Horus for Osiris, Wotan for Mimir; the seed-eye is conception, and the child will be sukshma (visionary), not sthula. The earth mother is Hecate, "the mother of fate, which is actual life" — when she appears, things happen in reality: the eye-seed grows into the tree, the impersonal way of fate.

occurrences.title: 'Septem isti oculi sunt Domini' — the seven eyes motto of the Flamel edition (Eirenaeus Orandus, 1624)
occurrences.label: Septem isti oculi sunt Domini
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

occurrences.quote: These seven eyes are evidently the seven planets which, like the sun and moon, are the eyes of God, never resting, ubiquitous and all-seeing.
body: A 17th-century alchemist (Eirenaeus Orandus) prefaced his edition of Nicholas Flamel's Hieroglyphicall Figures with Zacharias 4:10: "Et videbunt lapidem stanneum in manu Zorobabel. Septem isti oculi sunt Domini, qui discurrunt in universam terram" — they shall see the tin plummet in the hand of Zorobabel; these are the seven eyes of the Lord that run to and fro through the whole earth (cf. Zach 3:9: seven eyes upon one stone).

Jung's reading: "These seven eyes are evidently the seven planets which, like the sun and moon, are the eyes of God, never resting, ubiquitous and all-seeing" (¶394) — the stone in the hand of Zorobabel makes the passage a lapis-testimony; the never-resting eyes open the line Argus → Pole-dragon → Chronos → synchronicity.

occurrences.title: siddhaśila, the spiritual eye of the Jain universe
occurrences.label: siddhaśila, the spiritual eye…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: may be called the spiritual eye of the universe
body: Jain cosmography's world-shape: "The loka [world] is held in the middle of the aloka [void], in the form of the trunk of a man, with siddhaśila at the top, the place where the head should be. This siddhaśila is the abode of the omniscient souls, and may be called the spiritual eye of the universe" (¶46).

Jung adduces it as the non-Western twin of the alchemists' fishes' eyes and the one eye of God: "a similar nexus of ideas" to the "particles of light imprisoned in the dark Physis, whose reconstitution was one of the chief aims of Gnosticism and Manichaeism." The universe as Anthropos whose crown is the eye where all souls converge.

occurrences.title: Wotan sacrifices one eye to Mimir's well (Norse myth)
occurrences.label: Wotan sacrifices one eye to Mimir's well
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: Wotan has to sacrifice his one eye to the well of Mimir, the well of wisdom, which is the unconscious.
body: Asked whether touching a higher cakra is like Wotan losing one eye, Jung: "Exactly. And like Osiris, the god of the underworld, who also loses one eye. Wotan has to sacrifice his one eye to the well of Mimir, the well of wisdom, which is the unconscious... one eye will remain in the depths or turned toward it." He adds Jakob Boehme, "enchanted into the center of nature," writing of the "reversed eye" — one eye turned inward into the underworld: the permanent cost of the crossing, and why "when you have actually entered a higher cakra you never really turn back."

occurrences.title: 'I walk upon faces' — the enamel steps where the Self vanishes (Visions, 14 Feb. 1934)
occurrences.label: I walk upon faces
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Opening of the series "The Red Pyramid": "The woman said: 'Descend now with me.' She led me down many steps and I felt dizzy and afraid. I saw that the steps were faces made of small pieces of enamel of different colors... I said to the woman: 'I walk upon faces.' She answered: 'Yes, that must be so.'". Later: "I saw that the faces were broken and I wanted to stop to piece them together, but the woman went on ahead of me and I could not stop. We came to a circle in the rocks. All was bare and barren. The woman vanished.".

Jung: humanity as painted oval disks seen from the height of her swing — "which is a complete depreciation of the surroundings-it means that the whole thing is unreal"; cf. Socrates showing Alcibiades that the Athenians "are nothing but faces." The vanished Self leaves her "only the ego, as naked as an ego can be... restricted and full of fear" — the precondition for the red pyramid.

occurrences.title: Five-year-old girl: the good fairy steps into the circle of three snakes and burns
occurrences.label: Five-year-old girl
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: age five, remembered in adulthood; presented 14 Feb 1939

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: A good fairy, all-powerful, leads the child through a big house of endless corridors to a room where "there are three snakes in the center, coiling around in a circle. The fairy steps into the center, and a fire flares up, into which she disappears." The child escapes, meets a playmate, and the fairy stands there again, taking her under protection. Presented by Walter Huber.

Jung: the dream says "fairy," not "mother" — "archetypes are stronger than outer reality" (p215); the archetype belongs to the child and must not be taken from her. The fairy is the female counterpart of Hermes, the psychopompos (p217), whose burning in the circle parallels the visions of Zosimos, Isis holding the child over the fire, and the phoenix: transformation to immortality. The circle is "the oldest symbol of mankind" — wholeness; the three snakes the hell of instincts and time. The playmate "reestablishes the connection to her age" (p227).

occurrences.title: The Graeae, three sisters with one eye and one tooth
occurrences.label: The Graeae, three sisters with one eye…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Greece (cited via Goethe's 'Classical Walpurgis Night' and Roscher's Lexikon)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: Here one would also have to mention the Graeae, the three of whom have only one eye and one tooth (female and male genitalia).
body: The dark sister of the Fates-parallels for the dream's three young women:

Jung takes them seriously as the archaic floor of the triad: "The Graeae are goddesses of the underworld out of the darkest reaches of mythology... we have to view this one tooth as an exquisitely phallic symbol and the eye as the corresponding female symbol". The German counterpart: the three spinners of Grimm, with big thumb, big lip, big toe. The triad reaches back so far ("father, mother, son"; Brahma-Vishnu-Shiva; Osiris between Isis and Nephtys) that "the triad or the Ternarium" in itself is "plain 'three-ness,' which can be filled with any content".

occurrences.title: The three ladies of The Magic Flute handing over flute and picture (Mozart/Schikaneder, 1791)
occurrences.label: The three ladies of The Magic Flute handing…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: Worthy of consideration as a further parallel are also the three ladies in the Magic Flute (Mozart) who, as we know, hand over the magic flute and the enchantingly beautiful picture to the young man.
body: For the three young women in the underground store, Dr. Fierz adduces Mozart's three ladies:

"The three ladies of the Magic Flute are servants of the Queen of the Night; they appear as huntresses and can justly be equated, therefore, with Diana. The Magic Flute also shows further curious parallels to our dream series: persecution by the snake; the bird-catcher; the three ladies; and fire and baptism with water — these are the images of the libretto. In the dream series, this corresponds to the persecution by the dog; the fisherman; the three ladies; the fire in the hospital; and water".

occurrences.title: Artemidorus: the man who saw his father in a burning house and died days later
occurrences.label: Artemidorus — the man who saw his father…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: A dream reported in Artemidorus of Daldis's dream book, cited by Jung beside his own fatal child-dreams: "He mentions the dream of a man in which he sees his father in a burning house. A few days later, the dreamer himself died from a feverish illness".

Jung invokes it for the ancient precedent of diagnostic dream-observation: "In times of old, therefore, the doctors observed dreams and made their diagnoses accordingly" (p179). The case anchors his claim that dreams without lysis permit a prognosis — here catastrophic — and that "we do not dream, but rather we are dreamt."

occurrences.title: Patient dreams the father dividing the globe into East and West halves
occurrences.label: Patient dreams the father dividing the globe…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Jung's example of interpreting through amplification and verifying in a series: "a dream in which the patient's father holds a globe, trying to divide it into two halves, such that there would be exactly the same number of people in the East as in the West."

The dream reminded Jung of the creation in Genesis, "when on the second day He divided the waters that were under the firmament from the waters that were above the firmament" — from which he concluded "that a process of growing consciousness had occurred in the dreamer, that he had started to think consciously and autonomously". Verification: the patient had already dreamed the night before that God created a world with lightning and thunder, unknown to Jung.

occurrences.title: Asmodeus and the seven bridegrooms of Sara — Book of Tobit (Ecbatana)
occurrences.label: Asmodeus and the seven bridegrooms of Sara
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~3rd-2nd c. BCE (tale set in the 8th c. BCE Assyrian exile)
occurrences.quote: But her evil fate willed it that seven times, one after the other, she chose a husband who died on the wedding-night. It was the evil spirit Asmodeus, by whom she was persecuted, that killed these men.
body: Sara, daughter of Raguel of Ecbatana, married seven times; seven times the bridegroom dies on the wedding night, killed by the demon Asmodeus. Her prayer (Tobit 3) answered, the eighth bridegroom Tobias — her cousin, sent by God — survives, protected by the fish-organ burned to drive the demon to Egypt; Raguel, who had "only pretended to go to bed," thoughtfully digs his son-in-law's grave overnight and sends a maid to check whether he is dead.

Jung's reading (1949 stratum): "an instructive and well-known example of the ambivalent behaviour of the father-imago" (¶742). Raguel is the father in two roles — inconsolable father of the bride, provident grave-digger; Asmodeus is the jealous father split off into a demon, "the negative aspect of the father archetype" (¶743). "He, significantly enough, is the eighth: the last and highest stage" — cross-referenced by Jung to the axiom of Maria and the 3/4, 7/8 problem (n.24). The 1909 stratum read Sara's split father-complex as sublimation into God-worship plus demon (orig. n.26).

occurrences.title: The father at the bedside — 'abominable vision' of the two-sisters case (1912)
occurrences.label: The father at the bedside
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: In bed at night, she suddenly felt herself once again a child of two or three years old, and she saw her father standing by her bed in an obscene attitude.
body: Under analysis the patient reproduces early reminiscences of watching her father undressing, then arrives "terribly embarrassed and shaken" with an "abominable vision, absolutely distinct": at night she feels herself again a child of two or three and sees her father by her bed in an obscene attitude, told "bit by bit, obviously with the greatest internal struggle" (¶388). Jung's verdict is the hinge of his break with the seduction-theory residue: "Nothing is less probable than that the father really did this. It is only a fantasy" — a construction of the same "need for causality" that once misled the analysts (¶389). The fantasy is regressed libido elaborating "everything that is touched by the libido" (¶394): "Even so has it ever been thought that the golden age of Paradise lay in the past!"

occurrences.title: The all-powerful 'big brother' fantasy of Anna and Sophie
occurrences.label: The all-powerful 'big brother' fantasy…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: For three months Anna and her sister Sophie spun a shared fantasy-figure: a "big brother" who knew everything, could do everything, had been everywhere and owned enormous animals — "My brother is in Italy and has a house made of cloth and glass and it doesn't fall down" (¶28).

Jung's reading: the model is the father, who "seems to be rather like a brother to Mama" (¶29); the children claim an equally powerful sibling. The fragile unbreakable house in earthquake-torn Italy is a wish-fulfilment that banished the Messina phobia at a stroke — the volcano pictures left Anna cold ("Dead people! I've seen all that before").
Quote. "For some three months the children had been spinning a stereotyped fantasy of a 'big brother' who knew everything, could do everything, and had everything."

occurrences.title: Case 2: the man who married his brother's wife as mother-substitute
occurrences.label: Case 2 — the man who married his brother's wife…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: This patient, too, moved all through his life in the magic circle of the family constellation.
body: Man of 34, "of small build," nervous stomach trouble, depressions with suicidal thoughts. Father: a big red-haired ex-soldier of the Swiss Guard at the Vatican, later policeman, who "issued commands, did not call them by name, but whistled for them" (¶709). The son's life re-enacts the bond: the school whipping-boy; a homosexual assault at fifteen; impotence in brothels; the eldest brother as "the replica of his father"; then marriage to the brother's divorced wife — "which amounted to marrying his mother" (¶715) — who was also mother-substitute for the woman dead in childbed whom he had promised to provide for.

Jung's reading: "the strongest and most fateful factor was the relationship to the father; its masochistic-homosexual colouring is clearly apparent in everything he did" (¶715). The neurosis began at the first individually directed love — "the family constellation proved to be by far the stronger."

occurrences.title: The father's chastising hand — psychotic hysteria in a woman of twenty (Zurich, ~1907)
occurrences.label: The father's chastising hand
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: In particular, she could not see her father's hands without feeling sexual excitement; for the same reason she could no longer bear to touch his right hand.
body: Jung's one extended case in the 1908 essay, chosen because "a concrete example... will illustrate the meaning of Freud's teachings better than any theoretical formulations" (¶52). An intelligent young woman of twenty: from the third or fourth year she withholds stool, crouching with the heel pressed to the anus (Freud's "anal eroticism," ¶53); at seven the perversion gives way to masturbation; a smack from the father on the bare buttocks produces "distinct sexual excitement," later re-evoked by her brother's punishments. From puberty the fantasies turn obsessive — defecation at every meal, her father's hands unbearable to see or touch — until she alternates depression and convulsive laughter, sticking out her tongue at all contact. Jung derives from it, step by step, Freud's schema (a)–(f) of precocious sexual activity, repression by shame and disgust, blocked libido-transference, and the symptom as substitute sexual activity (¶61).

occurrences.title: Case 3: 'in the devil's clutches' — the peasant woman's hell-terror
occurrences.label: Case 3 — 'in the devil's clutches'
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: she suddenly remembered that the last words she had heard her father say were: 'I am one of those who have got into the devil's clutches.
body: Peasant woman of 36, favourite of a "quarrelsome, foul-mouthed old drunkard" of a father whom she fetched home against her husband's protests. After his sudden stroke-death she remembers his last words — "I am one of those who have got into the devil's clutches" — and, reading tracts that swearers go to hell, falls into a terror neurosis: she must die "so that she could be with her father" in hell (¶721). The father had even tried to marry her to a foundling oaf with suppurating neck-ulcers (¶723-725).

Jung's reading: the husband "must bow down before this bogey" (¶726); the case shows a demonic power controlling destiny — "the power which shapes the life of the psyche has the character of an autonomous personality" (¶727). In the 1949 stratum this daemon is the father archetype; the devil's clutches are its negative aspect.

occurrences.title: The father in the husband's dressing-gown — Prince's patient, dream 1 (Boston, ~1905–06)
occurrences.label: The father in the husband's dressing-gown
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: then the door opened and her father appeared. He had on her husband's dressing-gown, and he was holding two sticks of wood in his hand.
body: Dream 1 of the six Prince analysed and Jung re-analysed: the dream-ego sees an old Jewess drinking whiskey, who changes into her own mother drinking likewise; "then the door opened and her father appeared. He had on her husband's dressing-gown, and he was holding two sticks of wood in his hand." Prince finds a justification of her own tippling and stops before the sticks ("she had ordered firewood the evening before"). Jung: eight pages of print and "the dream has not been analysed" — the father condensed with the husband, the sticks and the whiskey "temptations" of an erotic wish: "If I were this poor Jewess, whom I saw on the previous day, I would not resist temptation... and then a man would come into my room with firewood — naturally to warm me up" (¶165).

occurrences.title: The unjust master's verdict on Jung's essay (gymnasium, Basel, ~1887)
occurrences.label: The unjust master's verdict on Jung's essay
occurrences.subject: jung
body: Twelve-year-old Jung wrote his best essay of the term; the master read every other first, then pronounced: "Jung's essay is by far the best, but he has composed it frivolously and dashed it off without taking any trouble. Therefore it merits no attention whatever." When Jung protested, he shouted "That's a lie!" and held up the worst pupil as the model: "he took trouble over his. He will get on in life, but you won't." "I was silent. From that moment I never did a stroke of work during German lessons" (¶233).

Jung's late reading: the master enacted the noble precept (help the weak) as caricature; yet he was "an instrument of fate," the first to teach him "that the gifts of the gods have two sides, a bright and a dark" (¶246).
Quote. "Jung's essay is by far the best, but he has composed it frivolously and dashed it off without taking any trouble. Therefore it merits no attention whatever."

occurrences.title: The man in the grey suit — exhibitionist dream, two-sisters case (1912)
occurrences.label: The man in the grey suit
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The night after the patient told me about this, she dreamt of a man in a grey suit, who started to do in front of her what the exhibitionist had done.
body: Elder of two sisters, broken off in engagement, sunk in hysteria; analysis meets "numerous perverse fantasies" and traces them to a childhood scene: at eight, confronted in the street by an exhibitionist, "rooted to the spot by fright," the ugly image long pursuing her dreams (¶387). The night after she tells it, the dream repeats the scene with a man in a grey suit; her first association is to a suit of her father's from an excursion at six — "This dream, without any doubt, connects the father with the exhibitionist" (¶388). Jung's point is not the Oedipal content but its regressive manufacture: the "obscene" father scene that then surfaced is "only a fantasy," constructed by the libido's backward movement (¶389, ¶394).

occurrences.title: Case 1: the widow who lived out her father's cult (climacteric neurosis, woman 55)
occurrences.label: Case 1 — the widow…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: She informed me, blushing and dropping her eyes, that she was the divorced wife of a common peasant.
body: Woman of 55, divorced wife of a peasant, with depression, night terrors and climacteric neurosis. Her widowed mother preserved the dead father's memory "like a religious cult" (¶704) and taught the children the same. The patient then married two father-substitutes in succession — both "fine, stately, rather corpulent men of imposing appearance," both dead of stroke — and at 46, driven by the "exacerbation of sexuality at the climacteric," took a brutal peasant "an even worse edition of the father-substitute" (¶706).

Jung's reading: "up to her forty-sixth year the patient did nothing but live out a faithful copy of the milieu of her early youth" (¶706); the neurosis broke out exactly when libido first turned toward an individually chosen goal (¶715). A 1949-stratum illustration of the parental constellation as fate.

occurrences.title: The fauna on the marble wall — dream of the professor of canon law
occurrences.label: The fauna on the marble wall
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: He is on a mountain-pass road, winding along a precipice. Below there is a canyon. The road is secured against the canyon by a wall. The wall is made of Parian marble with its antique yellowish tinge, as he notices at once.
body: A dignified elderly professor of canon law at a Catholic university, "like the old Mommsen," consulted Jung on business and then confessed a single dream dreamt many years before that had preoccupied him ever since and that he had told to many people. Jung: "I sensed that his soul was consumed by a dream."

Jung cites it uninterpreted as an example of a category-4 "great dream" — a spontaneous, overwhelming product of the unconscious before the outbreak of illness or in persons seized by a destiny. The antique marble already suggests the classical stratum the figure steps out of.

occurrences.title: The faun's goblet in the woods and the white bird at the giant's throat (patient vision, 18 November 1931)
occurrences.label: The faun's goblet in the woods…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: A white bird flew at the giant's throat, sucking the blood therefrom until he sank into the ground. Then I stepped over the body and walked into the white city.
body: All her own devices fail — stones, dagger, even the crescent moon of the self-made moon-goddess ("it is just bunk... mere inflation," pdf p519). Then "a faun who beckoned me into the woods and gave me a goblet to drink": a regression into the Dionysian mentality, the antique goblet of blood-or-wine. That single touch of the earth (the miracle of Antaeus, cf. antaeus-mother-earth-strength-greece) summons the white bird, the natural spirit which is also the Holy Ghost, to suck the giant's blood until public opinion sinks into the ground. "Les extremes se touchent": at the furthest pagan point the turn comes, as at Damascus.

occurrences.title: Faust II: the Cabiri scene — 'the fourth refused to call'
occurrences.label: Faust II — the Cabiri scene
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Though they have the Fleece of Gold, / Ye have the Cabiri.
body: In the Classical Walpurgis Night, Nereids and Tritons carry the Cabiri over the sea in Chelone's giant shell: "In Chelone's giant shield / Gleams a form severe revealed." Three Cabiri "followed where we led, / But the fourth refused to call; / He the rightful seer, he said, / His to think for one and all." The Sirens sing the Cabiris' prize over the Argonauts': "Though they have the Fleece of Gold, / Ye have the Cabiri."

Jung: Goethe's feeling-toned nature made thinking the fourth, taboo function — "Because of its contamination with the unconscious it takes on the grotesque form of the Cabiri, for the Cabiri, as dwarfs, are chthonic gods and misshapen accordingly" (¶204). They strive "from the depths to the heights and are therefore always to be found both below and above"; the "severe image" is "the treasure hard to attain" (¶205). The tortoise (Chelone) "symbolizes the instinctual side of the unconscious" (¶203).

occurrences.title: Feast of Fools: the boy bishop and the mock mass (spring carnival)
occurrences.label: Feast of Fools: the boy bishop and the mock mass
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~12th-13th c. (suppressed by papal decree in the 13th c.)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: the abbot and elder monks serving the young lay brothers
body: Jung on the carnival reversals inside the churches: at the spring carnival monasteries reversed abbot and youngest lay brother; at the feast the abbot and elders served the young; "a mock mass was celebrated, the youngest lay brother officiating, at which the songs and jokes were obscene," drunken orgies followed into the street — and the jeu de paume itself was played in churches until the Pope stopped "these revels" in the thirteenth century.

Presented as the historical body behind dream 1's ritual game — the central symbolic game as communion ("These games were communions, the people turned their faces to one another") — and cross-referenced by the editor to Jung's trickster chapter (CW9i pars. 458ff), where the same revels reappear.

occurrences.title: Anima in compedibus — the fettered soul in Dorn's speculations
occurrences.label: Anima in compedibus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: "This idea was formulated in the conception of the 'anima in compedibus,' the fettered or imprisoned soul. (Cf. Dorn, 'Speculativa philosophia,' Theatr. chem., I, pp. 272, 298; 'De spagirico artificio,' etc., ibid., I, pp. 457, 497.)" (cw11 ¶? pdf p697). Jung: "So far, I have found no evidence that the medieval natural philosophers based themselves consciously on any heretical traditions. But the parallels are astonishing" — those "enchained in Hades" already in the 1st-century Comarius text (Berthelot IV, xx, 8), the spark in the darkness of the Gnostics (Leisegang).

With it goes Dorn's natura abscondita: "In the body of man there is hidden a certain substance of heavenly nature known to very few" — "a certain truth not seen by the outward eye but perceived by the mind alone"; already in Pseudo-Democritus.

occurrences.title: The cataleptic suitor of 'Emma C.' — half a face weeping, one eye open (Burghölzli, ~1906)
occurrences.label: The cataleptic suitor of 'Emma C.'
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A catatonic patient, psychotic after four years of wooing a rich cousin "completely ignoring the impossibility", lies in catalepsy: "underlying the catalepsy is a powerful tendency to sleep, to 'be a dead man'" — sleep as repression, "a wish to forget" (¶1014). Through it, thought perseverates "I am going to marry Emma C." against the cousin's verdict "Don't expect anything of the future" (¶1016). Affect leaks through the frost: "The two components were sometimes divided into the two halves of the face: one side weeping, one eye open" — open eye = rapport, closed eye = the victory of sleep (¶1015). He embraces substitutes "through the veil of cataleptic sleep" (¶1017).
The soul bound in an impossible relation — fettered not in Hades but in a clinic; the split face as the visible seam between the two personalities.

occurrences.title: 'Figurarum Aegyptiorum Secretarum' — anonymous Latin alchemical MS in Jung's collection
occurrences.label: Figurarum Aegyptiorum Secretarum
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: An 18th-century Latin manuscript of alchemical pictures, "Incipit: Figurarum Aegyptiorum Secretarum," in Jung's own possession; he cites it four times across the Mysterium footnotes (ch. I nn.19, 85; ch. II n.72; ch. III n.74). Its text-passage of note is the fugitive man: "There was a certain man, who was of use for nothing, and could not be kept under guard: for he broke out of all prisons... yet a certain simple, humble, and sincere man was found, who well understood his nature, and counselled that he be deprived of all his garments and made naked" — the undressing signifying putrefaction (fol. 21r).
This is the servus fugitivus / Mercurius in his aspect of the unusable, uncontainable man who must be stripped: the escaped arcane substance recaptured only by stripping (solutio).

occurrences.title: The filius macrocosmi correlated with Christ — Aquarium sapientum
occurrences.label: The filius macrocosmi correlated with Christ
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The "Aquarium sapientum " (Siebmacher's Hydrolithus sophicus) correlates the "son of the great world" (filius macrocosmi, the lapis) with Christ, "who is the filius microcosm i", his blood the quintessence, the red tincture: "the true and authentic duplex Mercurius or Giant of twofold substance... God by nature, man, hero" (cw13 ¶384). The author adds that since the stone has "almost a thousand" names, all these titles apply "much more properly... to Almighty God and the Supreme Good" (¶385).

Jung: "It obviously never occurred to the author... that he had simply transferred God's attributes to the stone" (cw13 ¶385) — the stone as "a primordial religious experience" (¶386). The 'giant of twofold substance' (gigas geminae substantiae) goes back to Ambrose's hymn (n.5).
Verbatim: the “son of the great world” (filius macrocosmi, the lapis) is correlated with Christ, who is the filius microcosm i, and his blood is the quintessence, the red tincture. (cw13 ¶384ocr)

occurrences.title: The filius macrocosmi as symbol of Christ — Khunrath's Amphitheatrum
occurrences.label: The filius macrocosmi as symbol of Christ
occurrences.subject: n/a
