occurrences.quote: Without blasphemy I say: In the Book or Mirror of Nature, the Stone of the Philosophers, the Preserver of the Macrocosm, is the symbol of Christ Jesus Crucified.
body: Khunrath's "confession without blasphemy": the filius philosophorum is "the Son of the Macrocosm... God and creature," just as Christ is the son of God, the θεάνθρωπος — "the one conceived in the womb of the Macrocosm, the other in the womb of the Microcosm, and both of a virginal womb." The Stone of the Philosophers is "the symbol of Christ Jesus Crucified, Saviour of the whole race of men": "From the stone you shall know in natural wise Christ, and from Christ the stone."

Jung: Khunrath was as unconscious of the full implications as Paracelsus — yet in this equation "Medieval alchemy prepared the way for the greatest intervention in the divine world order that man has ever attempted" (¶163); whereas in Christ God became man, the filius philosophorum is "extracted from matter by human art" — "I under God" versus "God under me."

occurrences.title: The King's Son and the mystagogue Hermes on the mountain — Lambspringk fig. XII
occurrences.label: The King's Son and the mystagogue Hermes…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Th eKing's Son (filius regis) and the mystagogue Hermes on a mountain, an obvious allusion to the Temptation (Luke, ch. 4).
body: Plate B6 of CW13: the King's Son (filius regis) together with the mystagogue Hermes standing on a mountain — "an obvious allusion to the Temptation (Luke, ch. 4)." The accompanying text: "Another mountain of India lies in the vessel, which the Spirit and Soul, as son and guide, have together ascended." The two are called spirit and soul because they represent volatile substances rising up during the heating of the prima materia.

Jung's reading: Hermes/Mercurius as psychopomp and "mystagogue, as in the Corpus Hermeticum or the visions of Zosimos" (¶273); Maier found on his mystic peregrination "a statue of Mercurius pointing the way to paradise" (¶278).

occurrences.title: The filius regius crying from the depths — Maier's Symbola aureae mensae
occurrences.label: The filius regius crying from the depths
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: He lives and calls from the depths: Who shall deliver me from the waters and lead me to dry land?
body: Michael Maier's lament of the kingly substance hidden in the sea: "Who shall deliver me from the waters and lead me to dry land?" Few believe the cry; most take it for "the crashing and roaring of Scylla and Charybdis" and stay at home. In Maier's usage filius regius / Rex marinus means antimony — but only the name, Jung stresses: in reality it is "the secret transformative substance, which fell from the highest place into the darkest depths of matter where it awaits deliverance" (¶183). "The sea (mare nostrum) of the alchemists is their own darkness, the unconscious."

Jung lines the passage up with the Naassene king in the flood (Hippolytus, Elenchos V, 8) and with the Rosarium's promise: "At the end of the work the king will go forth for thee, crowned with his diadem... constant in the fire" (¶183).

occurrences.title: Finna, Geir and Ingeborg — the cross-marriage in an Icelandic fairytale
occurrences.label: Finna, Geir and Ingeborg
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: ...unless he found a wife who knew everything and held her peace, he would be changed into a snake and his sister into a filly.
body: Icelandic fairytale retold by Jung for the archetype of the cross-marriage ("marriage quaternio"): Finna, a girl with mysterious powers, makes her father refuse all suitors at the Althing; the stranger Geir forces the betrothal at sword-point. Each Christmas Geir disappears to an island with a beautiful woman; each year a child appears in Finna's bed, and three times she accepts it. The woman is Ingeborg, his sister — a stepmother-witch had cursed him ("he was to have three children by his sister, and unless he found a wife who knew everything and held her peace, he would be changed into a snake and his sister into a filly"). Finna's silent knowing releases him; Ingeborg is then married to Sigurd, Finna's brother — completing the crossed pair.

Jung (¶431-433): the schema matches the Russian tale and the cross-cousin marriage — the hero wins a bride connected with magic, the carrier of the anima-image marked by magical characteristics; the incest is an evil fate, the endogamous libido held in check by the exogamous order.

occurrences.title: The glowing fire and the trapped phoenix in the cavern beneath the earth (patient vision, 10 June 1931)
occurrences.label: The glowing fire and the trapped phoenix…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Above the fire I saw a phoenix bird which continually flew up and beat its head against the top of the cavern.
body: Following the stream of blood "down and down" she reaches a rocky cavern, dark, with a glowing fire (not blazing — smoldering under ashes), and above it a phoenix beating its head against the roof of the cave, unable to rise. The fire creates small snakes and then men and women — the creator-fire of Tantric philosophy, muladhara and the solar plexus as "the sun of the abdominal cave". The bird commands "Stand in the fire, woman"; her robe burns and she stands naked. Jung: the phoenix cannot rise because consciousness makes no hole for it; through acceptance, not suppression, purification takes place — she becomes the bird herself, the higher consciousness of the Self.

occurrences.title: Fire-boring with a Priapus simulacrum against cattle plague — Fentone, Lotharingia
occurrences.label: Fire-boring with a Priapus simulacrum…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: docebant idiotas patriae ignem confrictione de lignis educere et simulacrum Priapi statuere, et per haec bestiis succurrere
body: A plague-year rite among cattle, performed by a Cistercian lay brother "cloistered in habit, not in mind": fire kindled by friction from wood, a simulacrum of Priapus set up, and a dog's testicles dipped in holy water and sprinkled over the sick beasts.

Jung cites it beside Charlemagne's ban on the niedfyr (need-fire) as proof that the fire-boring magic of the pramantha — sexual generation by friction — lived on inside Christendom, practiced by and against the Church. The Priest's blessing and the phallic fire-drill operate in one gesture.

occurrences.title: Brünnhilde asleep behind the wall of fire — Wagner's Ring
occurrences.label: Brünnhilde asleep behind the wall of fire
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the fiery longing of the hero for the forbidden goal
body: The fire-maiden on the mountain: the ring of fire as the barrier and the lure at once — the forbidden mother behind flame. Siegfried's terror before the sleeping armour ("Mother! Mother!", ¶602) breaks against it; the kiss "Even though I die in a kiss!" consummates the love-death (¶602, ¶610–611).

image.title: Brünnhilde slowly and silently leads her horse down the path to the cave

occurrences.title: Buddha's fire sermon at Benares
occurrences.label: Buddha's fire sermon at Benares
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: The whole world is in flames... that is the fire of illusion because you desire things which are futile.
body: Jung's text for the maṇipūra fire as desire and illusion: "The whole world is in flames, your ears, your eyes, everywhere you pour out the fire of desire, and that is the fire of illusion because you desire things which are futile." Below the diaphragm "there is only the fire of passion, of wishes, of illusions" — yet precisely there lies "the great treasure of the released emotional energy": the fullness of jewels paradox announced two pages earlier.

occurrences.title: Burning house and the rising sun dream — 11-year-old girl (Zurich, 1912)
occurrences.label: Burning house and the rising sun dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I saw that the stones of our house were burning, but the wood remained untouched.
body: The family stands on the roof; the rising sun blazes in the opposite windows; the corner house is really aflame and the fire takes their own — yet "the stones of our house were burning, but the wood remained untouched." "It is queer, like in a fairytale," says the child (¶493), and in defending the fairytale-ness she produces, unprompted, Sleeping Beauty and then Snow White (¶493–496) — Jung reads both as her own complex of expectation, the winter-bound virgin awaiting delivery (¶497). The doll caught in the apron recalls a stork picture — girls holding out aprons for a baby (¶498); the fantasy of a bicycle passing over her stomach (a paramnesia) feeds the trampling motif (¶499–502). The whole dream orbits the awakening reproductive instinct (¶501).

occurrences.title: 'Whoever is close to me is close to the fire' — uncanonical saying of Jesus (Origen)
occurrences.label: Whoever is close to me is close to the fire
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: Whoever is close to me is close to the fire. That means that whoever is close to Christ, is close to Christ's passio, and is apt to have Christ's own psychology and the same fate.
body: Jung cites "another saying of Jesus, similar to those found at Oxyrhynchus, which is not in the Canon": closeness to Christ means closeness to his passio — "and is apt to have Christ's own psychology and the same fate."

His aside is characteristic: the saying is "exceedingly intelligent and exceedingly true, and would therefore have been abolished if the father of the church who quoted it had not been too stupid to understand it." The fire is the passio-flame that turns man to ashes (Leidenschaft ist das was Leid schafft, same page) — the same fire Nietzsche declined to enter.

occurrences.title: 'He who is near me is near the fire' — non-canonical logion
occurrences.label: He who is near me is near the fire
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: For he is the fire, the greatest intensity, and whoever touches upon this intensity is subtilized, made pneumatic
body: A Gnostic-sounding logion preserved "because the Fathers of the church quoted them as being particularly foolish or blasphemous, not understanding what they really meant": "He who is near me is near the fire, and he who is far from me is far from the kingdom." "That is extraordinarily revealing".

Jung returns to it in the Geist discussion of 12 May 1937 and gives it an alchemical reading: Christ "is the fire, the greatest intensity, and whoever touches upon this intensity is subtilized, made pneumatic, made into a volatile body" — the fire that sublimates or destroys, kin to Heraclitus' dry soul and the baptism "with the Holy Ghost and with fire" already in Komarios.

occurrences.title: The patient's dream: the doctor perishing in a great fire (three weeks before his death)
occurrences.label: The patient's dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1930s (dream three weeks before the doctor's death)
occurrences.quote: A former patient of his, who had no knowledge of the nature of the doctor’s illness, dreamt that the doctor was perishing in a great fire.
body: Jung's modern parallel to Artemidorus: a colleague of his lay dying of "a deadly gangrenous fever — in fact, a phlegmone." A former patient, knowing only that the doctor was ill and in hospital, "dreamt that the doctor was perishing in a great fire. The dream occurred three weeks before the doctor died" (¶544).

Jung's reading: the unconscious had "submitted the case to a careful prognostic examination" from subliminal perceptions, but expressed it archetypally — "the dream describes the diseased body as a man's earthly house, and the fever as the heat of a conflagration that is destroying the house and its inhabitant" (¶545). The same treatment as Artemidorus' burning-house dream eighteen centuries earlier shows "the archetypal mind has handled the situation in the same way" (¶546).

occurrences.title: The second fire-dog: the heart of the earth is of gold
occurrences.label: The second fire-dog
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: the heart of the earth is of gold.
body: After belittling the first fire-dog as "the ventriloquist of the earth," Nietzsche invents a second that "speaketh actually out of the heart of the earth": "Gold doth his breath exhale, and golden rain... for, that thou mayest know it, - the heart of the earth is of gold." Jung: "This is an old mythological idea, but Nietzsche did not know it. It is also an alchemical idea that the core of the earth is gold which originated through the movement of the sun round the earth. Since the sun is identical with gold, its continual revolution round the earth has spun the gold in the center and has created its image in the heart of the earth".

So the volcano holds not only the fire-dog but "a kernel of gold" — the unconscious's value, joined to Nietzsche's preaching that man is "a son of the earth" against the Christian devaluation of the flesh; yet the catastrophic character of the picture is evaded.

occurrences.title: The Vedic fire-drill: female wood and male stick produce the spark
occurrences.label: The Vedic fire-drill
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: "Fire is always a coniunctio. Something spiritual and male, the oxygen, combines with something visible and female, the wood. In the act of this combination in fire—for example, in the Vedic tradition—the underlying piece of wood is female; the rotating wooden stick is the corresponding male part. Together they produce a spark. When the marriage takes place, the fire flares up. The eruption of the fire is the actual union, the union of two opposites".

Cited again in the fairy-dream discussion as "fire is an emotional outbreak, an outbreak of the libido. That is why the libido is always compared to fire" (p221). The twinning of the copulating sticks and the wedding carriage's blazing pair carries the seminar's whole fire-bridge between instinct and spirit.

occurrences.title: Empedocles leaps into the crater of Aetna to be reborn a god (Sicily, legend of c. 433 BCE)
occurrences.label: Empedocles leaps into the crater of Aetna…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: c. 433 BCE (legend; the editor notes the death story is apocryphal)
occurrences.quote: to be reborn out of the crater of death as a god.
body: "Empedocles, a Greek philosopher, was said to have ended his life in the crater of Aetna; when he became old he threw himself into the flames of the crater in order to be united with the gods, to be reborn out of the crater of death as a god". Jung cites the legend beside the Mithraic krater — the vessel of fire in which "magic transformation took place... a sort of alchemistic melting pot," with the lion of the reliefs precipitating himself into its flame for rebirth. The old idea of plunging into the crater of death as the price of apotheosis.

occurrences.title: Vision: the flame that entered her mouth — initiation by fire
occurrences.label: Vision — the flame that entered her mouth
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: And the fourth vision was a flame, which she saw right in front of her face, and then it suddenly went into her mouth.
body: Fourth of the fragmentary "hieroglyph" visions (upraised hand; haloed head; fiery globe pierced by a black bar; this flame): a flame before her face suddenly goes into her mouth. Jung reads it as an initiation vision of the prophetic-call type: "like some that are reported in the Old Testament-the fiery coals, or the book brought down by angels, which the prophet has to swallow when he is initiated. It simply means that fire, the creative principle, is entering her, either to devour things in her which must be devoured, or that she is filled with the divine fire, a sort of inspiration" (p118) — "exactly the same meaning as those visions which always occur at the beginning of a prophetic trance or an ekstasis." The sign that the resistances (petrol-anxiety, brain storm, lunatic-asylum fear) were overcome and the development would take its course.

occurrences.title: Hearth-spirit Chi, the fire as lovely maiden — Chuang-tzu commentary
occurrences.label: Hearth-spirit Chi, the fire as lovely maiden
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: commentary on Chuang-tzu (c. 350 BCE); Book of Rites older
body: "Like the sacrificial bull, fire... has a feminine nature in Chinese philosophy, according to one of the commentators on the Chuang-tzu (350 B.C.): 'The hearth spirit is called Chi. He is dressed in bright red, resembling fire, and in appearance is like a lovely, attractive maiden.' The Book of Rites says: 'Wood is burnt in the flames for the Au spirit. This sacrifice to Au is a sacrifice to the old women who are dead'" (¶663).

Jung reads these hearth- and fire-spirits as "the souls of departed cooks" — "old women" — from whom the god of kitchens later grew, who "as a man, became the ruler of the family and the link between it and heaven. In this way the original female fire-spirit became a sort of Logos and mediator" (¶663). A small but exact witness for his claim that sacrificial fire belongs to the maternal-feminine pole, paralleling the bull's hidden femininity (Gosh) in the Gayomart myth (¶662).
Verbatim: "in appearance is like a lovely, attractive maiden" (¶663).

occurrences.title: Heraclitus — 'A dry glowing best and wisest soul' (fr. 118)
occurrences.label: Heraclitus — A dry glowing best…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "And there is an authentic logion of Heraclitus which says: A dry glowing best and wisest soul." (pdf p750; editor: fragment 118, followed by "Souls take pleasure in becoming moist.")

Jung cites it as the Greek anchor of the same fire-psychology as the Christ-logion and Pentecost: the soul nearest the fire-principle is the driest and most blazing — the conflagration in which whoever seeks the self, meeting his own negation, "becomes ashes."
Heraclitus is the seminar's standing Greek ("war is the father of all things," pdf p746; the editor notes Nietzsche too "set apart with high reverence the name of Heraclitus").

occurrences.title: Hotel-fire dream of the sceptical woman (Zurich, ~1916)
occurrences.label: Hotel-fire dream of the sceptical woman
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: She was in a hotel in a strange city. Suddenly a fire broke out. Her husband and her father, who were with her, helped her in the rescue work.
body: An "intelligent, extraordinarily sceptical" patient, "absolutely convinced that dream-analysis was nonsense," dreams early in treatment of a fire in a hotel in a strange city, her husband and father helping the rescue. Jung starts from the most conspicuous image only: her association runs to a real burnt-down Zurich hotel where she once stayed — and to the questionable love-affair begun there, then to "quite a number of similar adventures, all of them decidedly frivolous" (¶538). He deliberately leaves the dream's obvious meaning unpressed: with such a frivolous attitude the interpretation "would have coldly repelled" her; the association route first demonstrates the attitude from her own material (¶538). Cautionary exhibit for beginning analysts against "arbitrary translation" (¶539).

occurrences.title: Dream: the house is on fire — Agni in the framework of the attitude
occurrences.label: Dream — the house is on fire
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I am in a bedroom. A woman enters through the window and says, \"This building is on fire, did you not know it?\" I say, \"No, all is quiet in my room.\
body: A woman enters through the bedroom window and announces the building is burning; the dreamer answers that all is quiet in her room. The house = "a symbol of a most complete system of adaptation... our whole situation in life," cellar and bird-perched roof included (p87). The entering figure is thief or ghost — an alarm from a level she does not inhabit ("people who live only a secluded life up in the attic, in the intellect", p91). Fire specifically: the old idea that "a god was lying dormant in the wood and was brought into existence by the fire" (p91), the Vedic Agni ("Agnis is the Sanskrit word, and in Latin it is ignis", p92) — a latent outburst possibility in the very structure of her house. Fire's double face: "utter destruction... and on the other side a marvelous display of color and light; and on the primitive level, also the apparition of the divine" (p94).

occurrences.title: Hildegard of Bingen's hymn 'O ignis Spiritus paracliti' — the earth sweats out greenness
occurrences.label: Hildegard of Bingen's hymn 'O ignis Spiritus…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: the earth sweats out greenness
body: The hymn to the Holy Ghost beginning "O ignis Spiritus paraclite": "From you the clouds rain down, the heavens move, the stones have their moisture, the waters give forth streams, and the earth sweats out greenness." Jung cites it in the lineage of the alchemical benedicta viriditas — "God has breathed into created things … a kind of germination, which is the viridescence" (Mylius).

His argument: this "water of the Holy Ghost" played a role in alchemy "since the remotest times" as the aqua permanens, "a symbol of the spirit assimilated to matter, which according to Heraclitus turned to water"; the Christian parallel was Christ's blood, whence the philosophers' water was named "spiritualis sanguis." Hildegard's hymn shows the pneumatic water-fire-greenness complex already fully formed in the twelfth century, inside the Church, before the Latin alchemists take it over.

occurrences.title: Izanagi lights his comb and loses Izanami — the Japanese Orpheus
occurrences.label: Izanagi lights his comb and loses Izanami
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: For 'wife' read 'mother,' 'anima,' 'unconscious.' Instead of the mother, the hero brings back fire, just as Hiawatha produced the corn, Odin the runes, etc.
body: Izanagi, the Japanese Orpheus, follows his dead wife to the underworld and begs her to return; she consents but forbids him to look. Impatient, he kindles a light "with one of the 'masculine' prongs of his comb and immediately lost his wife."

Jung's gloss does the work of the image tier: "For 'wife' read 'mother,' 'anima,' 'unconscious.'" What the hero retrieves instead of the woman is fire — "just as Hiawatha produced the corn, Odin the runes, etc." — the beloved's place taken by the boon of culture.

image.title: Illustration of (Izanami and Izanagi) exploring the blue sea with the heavenly spear.

occurrences.title: Fire-sticks as bride and bridegroom — Rig-Veda Agni hymn
occurrences.label: Fire-sticks as bride and bridegroom
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The friction-hymn: "Bring the mistress of the people: we will rub Agni in ancient fashion forth"; Jatavedas lies in the fire-sticks "safe as the seed in pregnant women"; the staff enters the outstretched (wood) and "Straightway she conceives, has given birth to the fructifier... With his red pillar lighting his path, the son of Ila is born."
Jung's reading: "the pramantha is also Agni, the begotten son: the phallus is the son, or the son is the phallus" (¶212) — the sexual symbolism of fire-making "unmistakable".
Verbatim: Let this (staff) enter into her as she lies there outstretched, O you skilled ones; Straightway she conceives, has given birth to the fructifier: (cw05 ¶211).

occurrences.title: Logion — 'Whoever is near to me is near to the fire' (Origen)
occurrences.label: Logion — Whoever is near to me is near…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The apocryphal word of Christ: "There is an apocryphal word of Christ, a logion, which says. 'Whoever is near to me is near to the fire and whoever is far away from me is far from the kingdom.' So the kingdom is the kingdom of fire. Christ himself is the flame."

Jung arrays it for the self-seeker's conflagration with the shadow: whoever unites with the self "will see his other side... it will be a conflagration, a flame in which he is burned up" — together with the Pentecostal tongues of fire and Heraclitus's dry glowing soul, against the Gnostic spinther that falls into matter.

occurrences.title: Uncanonical logion 'Who is near to me is near to the fire' — Origen's Homilies
occurrences.label: Uncanonical logion Who is near…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: Whoever is near to me is near to the fire; whoever is far from me is far from the kingdom
body: An agraphon cited by Origen: "Ait ipse salvator: qui iuxta me est, iuxta ignem est, qui longe est a me, longe est a regno" — the Saviour himself says: whoever is near to me is near to the fire; whoever is far from me is far from the kingdom.

Jung deploys it as patristic warrant for reading the "holy fire" of the patient's House-of-the-Gathering dream ("The fire that is not put out is a holy fire," Shaw's Saint Joan): the unquenchable fire is "a well-known attribute of the Deity, not only in the Old Testament, but also as an allegoria Christi." Since Heraclitus life has been conceived as an ever-living fire; as Christ calls himself "The Life," the saying is "quite understandable" — fire = life = the fulness of life that is "the only legitimate source of religion" (¶60). The four fiery candle-points of the dream "function almost as an icon denoting the presence of the Deity."

occurrences.title: The new fire struck from flint — Holy Saturday blessing, Roman rite
occurrences.label: The new fire struck from flint
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

occurrences.quote: By the analogy of Christ with the cornerstone, the firestone is raised to the level of Christ himself, who again kindles a new fire.
body: On Holy Saturday the new fire was struck from the stone (earlier: bored from wood, a prerogative of the Church), while the priest prays: "Deus, qui per Filium tuum, angularem scilicet lapidem... productum ex silice... novum hunc ignem sanctifica" — O God, who through thy Son, the cornerstone, hast brought the fire of thy light to the faithful, sanctify this new fire struck from the flint.

Jung's reading: a living specimen of magic by analogy, "sicut"-logic surviving in the Mass — by the analogy of Christ with the cornerstone the firestone is raised to the level of Christ himself, who kindles the new fire. The rationalist laughs, "but something deep in us is stirred... that faraway background, those immemorial patterns of the human mind, which we have not acquired but have inherited" (¶315). Same liturgical complex as the benediction of the font.

occurrences.title: The circle of old men around the fire in the dark cellar beneath New York (patient vision, 25 October 1933)
occurrences.label: The circle of old men around the fire…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Sitting around a fire was a circle of old men. They said to me: 'Have you seen the birds?' I said: 'Yes, they wounded me but I was healed. Is there no healing fire in the city? All seems blood and destruction.
body: Under the black-sun panic she enters a house and descends into a dark cellar — the mandala re-entered, the primitive house built round its central fire. There "sitting around a fire was a circle of old men," an animus court of justice holding its meeting in the depths: "the mandala represents the greater circle, the unconscious included; it is the Self, not the conscious only. Therefore the animus is there." They ask whether she has seen the birds (animus thought-birds that wounded her); the fire heals — "In many caves beneath the earth there are fires such as this... The fires are fed by lumps of blood brought in from the market place."
She leaves them impatiently ("You are old and you do nothing but wait") — Jung: the young must live their nonsense.

occurrences.title: Patient standing in the flames (Visions Seminar, 9 March 1932)
occurrences.label: Patient standing in the flames
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)
jung.locator: Lecture 2 (pdf p82) and Lecture 4 (pdf p116, fn5)

occurrences.quote: ...the patient came to the place where she had to stand the fire, and then the stars fell down.
body: Mrs. Sawyer recalls the vision series: "the patient came to the place where she had to stand the fire, and then the stars fell down. So the impersonal things began." Jung treats it as the maṇipūra station in Western material: "the symbol of water and fire, a picture in which the patient stood in flames... the diving down into the unconscious, into the baptismal font of svvdhiü°hvna, and the suffering of the fire of maõipÖra" — a descent that is really an ascent.

occurrences.title: Pillar of cloud by day, pillar of fire by night (Exodus)
occurrences.label: Pillar of cloud by day, pillar of fire by night
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Mrs. Sigg names the source and Jung elaborates: "Jahveh leading his people in the desert, in the day a pillar of cloud, in the night a pillar of fire. Jahveh is a fiery god, a devouring fire. This is a very Protestant vision, absolutely in the style of the Old Testament". Nietzsche's "pillar of fire" before the great noontide wishes "that Jahveh's fire would fall upon the heads of the crowd, as in Sodom and Gomorrah" — "it would be the holocaust," and "he himself would be consumed of course," because the curse works "directly against his body, against the banal human creature in himself upon which he lives."
"The fire of madness, the outburst of mad passion... The fear of God is just as important as the love of God."

occurrences.title: Swedenborg's vision of the great fire in Stockholm (1759)
occurrences.label: Swedenborg's vision of the great fire…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1759 (fn. 15: report in Kant's Dreams of a Spirit-Seer)

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: The classic distant-clairvoyance case Jung uses to open the collective-unconscious argument: "When, for instance, the vision arose in Swedenborg's mind of a fire in Stockholm, there was a real fire raging there at the same time, without there being any demonstrable or even thinkable connection between the two" (¶913). "This case is well authenticated" — documented, as the footnote notes, in Kant's Dreams of a Spirit-Seer.

Jung's reading: Swedenborg's biographical psychic state shows "a lowering of the threshold of consciousness which gave him access to 'absolute knowledge.' The fire in Stockholm was, in a sense, burning in him too." His paradigm of synchronicity category 2 — coincidence with an event outside the observer's field of perception, verifiable afterward (¶984).

occurrences.title: The stove that burned the floor — fire-complex caught by the galvanometer (Zurich, ~1907)
occurrences.label: The stove that burned the floor
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: recently a stove in his dwelling had become defective and burned the floor to such an extent that he had not only to pay for a new stove, but also for an entire new floor which was a hardship for him
body: Case 3 of the word-association + galvanometer series: an uneducated man of 28, lively and excitable, entirely normal and well practised in the experiments. His highest galvanic curve in Series I (51.5 mm) answered the harmless association the sun / burns, with floor, warm, and pay disturbed identically in all three series. Questioned, he denied any complex; distracted, "he said with surprise and embarrassment that recently a stove in his dwelling had become defective and burned the floor" — he had to pay for a new stove and an entire new floor, "which was a hardship for him," after great danger from fire. Jung's lesson: "the galvanic phenomenon, like reaction-time and alteration of reproductions, may give evidence of the existence of an unconscious complex" (¶1136). An everyday fire, not a symbol — a marginal case for the fire family: the image-content is prosaic, the diagnostic mechanism archetypal (the autonomous complex betraying itself involuntarily).

occurrences.title: The Abercius inscription — the 'giant' fish of the Christian aeon (c. AD 200)
occurrences.label: The Abercius inscription
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Cited as the concrete locus of the "great" Fish of the Christian aeon: in Jung's run of world-period images — Parsee world periods, the yugas and avatars of Hinduism, the Platonic months with their bull and ram deities — the fish is the Christian aeon's animal, "born through the power of fiery torment" of the age. The Abercius epitaph (c. AD 200), with Christ as the great fish caught by the holy virgin, is the classic early witness (cf. Aion, par. 127, n. 4). Here it anchors the claim that the patient's number-symbolism (3, 12) is not merely individual but aeon-conditioned: the aeon of the Fishes is drawing to its end and is at the same time the twelfth house of the zodiac (¶552).

image.title: XV01 - Roma, Museo civiltà romana - Iscrizione di Abercio - Foto Giovanni Dall'Orto 12-Apr-2008

occurrences.title: Abercius inscription — the great pure fish caught by a virgin
occurrences.label: Abercius inscription
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The epitaph of Abercius of Hierapolis, the most-discussed early Christian(?) fish text: "everywhere he set before me for food a fish from the source, exceeding great and pure, which a holy virgin had caught". Jung returns to it at pars. 145, 149, 162, 179-180, where — with Scheftelowitz — he identifies the great pure fish with Leviathan.
Jung stresses its doubleness: Dieterich argued the "holy shepherd" is Attis and the inscription commemorates the hieros gamos journey to Rome after A.D. 216; Christian origin is doubtful.

image.title: Cippo di Abercio, fine II - inizi III sec. -FG2

occurrences.title: The April fish run — six fish coincidences in 24 hours (Zurich, 1949)
occurrences.label: The April fish run
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.yearDisplay: April 1-2, 1949 (+ the seventh lake fish months later)

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: The run Jung recorded while working on the fish symbol in history: on the morning of April 1, 1949 he notes the inscription "Est homo totus medius piscis ab imo"; fish for lunch; someone mentions the "April fish" custom; a former patient shows fish paintings; in the evening, embroidery with fish-like sea-monsters; next morning a patient of ten years' absence reports a dream of a large fish swimming to her feet. Only one person knew of his fish studies. Months later, as he finished writing the series down, a foot-long fish lay on the sea-wall — the seventh.

Jung's reading: judged a chance grouping ("fish on Friday is the usual thing"), yet "It seemed to me to have a certain numinous quality" — numinosity growing with the number of terms, constellating "probably archetypal" contents (¶827 & fn. 10). The locus became his standing exhibit for the border between run-of-chance and meaningful coincidence.

occurrences.title: Zarathustra's 'fine catch of fish' — the corpse as companion
occurrences.label: Zarathustra's 'fine catch of fish'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: After the rope-dancer's fall, Zarathustra sits with the corpse through the night and addresses his heart: he has caught no man but a corpse.

Jung: the rope-dancer is "the human form of Zarathustra, Nietzsche himself as the human being," which is why Zarathustra cannot leave the body but must carry it — "Nietzsche being dragged along by that figure of Zarathustra... the gloomy aspect of the whole book." Since the corpse is himself, Zarathustra is dead in his humanity and must replace himself "by other corpses" — handing over to others "his human life which he should have lived."
Verbatim: "Verily, a fine catch of fish hath Zarathustra made to-day! It is not a man he hath caught, but a corpse."

occurrences.title: Denderah zodiac: both fishes facing the same way
occurrences.label: Denderah zodiac: both fishes facing the same way
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The zodiac of the temple of Hathor at Denderah "shows the fishes, but they both face the same way" — evidence for Jung that the contrary movement of the two fishes, so emphasized in Christian astrological speculation, is not ancient: the planisphere of Timochares even shows only one fish where Pisces should be.
Coins and gems of the emperors and Mithraic monuments show fishes either facing the same way or moving oppositely — polarity cannot be demonstrated for pre-Christian times.

occurrences.title: The fish disappear from the waters of the kingdom — 'The Tale of the Otter' (Schmitz)
occurrences.label: The fish disappear from the waters…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1932 (posthumous publication of Schmitz's tale; author d. 1931)
occurrences.quote: The King stands for the ruling principle of consciousness, which strays further and further away from the unconscious. (The fish disappear from the waters of the kingdom.)
body: The opening omen of Schmitz's tale: the fish vanish from the kingdom's waters. Jung decodes it allegorically but psychologically — the King stands for "the ruling principle of consciousness, which strays further and further away from the unconscious"; the vanishing fish figure the life of the unconscious withdrawing from a one-sided attitude. The stagnation that follows "finally compels the King to make contact with the unconscious again" (the King's pilgrimage), and the otter — "the unconscious partner of the ego," named by Jung a Gilgamesh-Eabani motif — mediates the reconciliation.

The sequence (fish-omen → pilgrimage → animal-brother → old king's death → nephew's reign) makes the tale a compact individuation drama ending, deliberately, with the inferior personality on the throne.

occurrences.title: The substance of the dried sea that 'glitters like a fish's eye' — Sir George Ripley
occurrences.label: The substance of the dried sea…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 15th c.; cited from Opera omnia chemica 1649

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

occurrences.quote: on the "desiccation of the sea" a substance is left behind […] which "glitters like a fish's eye
body: A variant of the Morienus fish's-eyes motif in Sir George Ripley: on the "desiccation of the sea" (the nigredo-stage drying of the massa confusa) a substance is left behind which "glitters like a fish's eye" — "an obvious allusion to the gold and the sun (God's eye)".

Jung's reading: the fish's-eye glitter belongs to the same optical family as the scintillae, the sparks in the arcane substance; the eye of the fish = the eye of God = the sun, linking the spark-motif to the all-seeing-eye complex (seven eyes of Zacharias, Argus, the Pole-dragon) through which Jung connects the mundus archetypus with Time and synchronicity (¶394).

occurrences.title: Farnese Atlas globe: the two fishes of Pisces
occurrences.label: Farnese Atlas globe: the two fishes of Pisces
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Naples, Museo Archeologico (Roman copy of Hellenistic original)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The globe of the heavens carried by the Farnese Atlas — for Jung one representation of the fishes "near the beginning of our era... certainly free from Christian influence": "The first fish, depicted north of the equator, is vertical, with its head pointing to the celestial Pole; the second fish, south of the equator, is horizontal, with its head pointing West". Naturalistic, following the astronomical configuration.

Later pictorial polarity of the fishes — "They move almost at right angles to one another and hence form a cross" — was "much emphasized in Christian times," which "leads one to suspect a certain tendentiousness."

image.title: MAN Atlante fronte 1040572

occurrences.title: The Pope's fisher ring with the miraculous draft of fishes — Rome
occurrences.label: The Pope's fisher ring with the miraculous…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: papal fisher ring (medieval institution; date inferred)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: And the Pope's attribute is the fisher ring upon which is carved the miraculous draft of fishes with the nets.
body: Completing the Logos-net chain of 12 Dec 1934: "Then the Pope, as the head of the church, is the living impersonation of the Logos, the church being the body of Christ. He is in the place of Peter who is the representative of Christ, endowed with the apostolic blessing, the grace or the mana that has emanated from the Lord himself. And the Pope's attribute is the fisher ring upon which is carved the miraculous draft of fishes with the nets."
The ring is the institutional tip of the same archetype Jung traces from Thoth's temple and Marduk's net: the word as the net that "gathered in mankind like a swarm of fishes."

occurrences.title: The golden fish and the sun-disk on the cave wall (Visions Seminar, 29 June 1932)
occurrences.label: The golden fish and the sun-disk…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Christ as Ichthys has now descended to the underworld. That is the old animus form, and it is still golden, still luminous, and it points to the new sun.
body: After the Dionysus-figure demonstrates the emptiness of the cathedral (the body-soul and spirit-soul separated, ka from ba), the animus descends into a dark cave floored with water, where tentacled monsters pull his head down. A golden fish cries: "Behold the wall of the cave," and he sees a golden disk and ascends.

Jung's reading: the disk on the abdominal wall is the plexus solaris — "nature's first attempt at a brain... from which ultimately consciousness arises". The fish is Christ-Ichthys, the old animus form, "still golden, still luminous, and it points to the new sun" — the Jonah motif: the sun in the fish's belly, the hero cut out as the new day rises. The new symbol is born in complete darkness, under the sea, where no human eye can see it.

occurrences.title: Life fishing the fish with the golden hook (Dance-Song)
occurrences.label: Life fishing the fish with the golden hook
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: He is like a fish caught with a golden hook. And who is pulling him out of that well?
body: Zarathustra's song to Life: "Of late did I gaze into thine eye, O Life! And into the unfathomable did I there seem to sink. But thou pulledst me out with a golden angle; derisively didst thou laugh when I called thee unfathomable. 'Such is the language of all fish,' saidst thou; 'what they do not fathom is unfathomable.'"

Jung works the amplification hard: the well as the eye of life (the Meeraugen of the Eifel), the fisher as the archetypal figure — Christ and Peter fishing men, Orpheus (Eisler), the Pope's fisher ring, Vishnu's fish of Manu, Dionysos Bakcheus — and the resolution through the sorites: "Nietzsche equals Zarathustra equals anima." Since Zarathustra is the fisher, Life's fishing him out is his own projection: "one never heard that the anima was a fisherman... this is an unheard of abnormality".

occurrences.title: Jonah in the belly of the great fish (Bible, cited cw4 1912)
occurrences.label: Jonah in the belly of the great fish
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This motif is found in countless myths all over the world, and is the motif of the Bible story of Jonah.
body: The prophet swallowed by the sea monster and given up alive on the third day — Jung cites it as the biblical member of the devouring-and-deliverance motif "found in countless myths all over the world," the same motif as the hunter cutting open the wolf in Little Red Riding-hood (¶476). The meaning "immediately lying behind it is astro-mythological: the sun is swallowed by the sea monster and is born again in the morning" (¶477) — but astro-mythology is itself "nothing but psychology—unconscious psychology—projected into the heavens." Here (1912) the motif is read through infantile birth-theories; in Aion it will return as Christ-sign and self-symbol.

occurrences.title: Man with fish's tail, 'Est homo non totus medius sed piscis ab imo' — Pesaro cathedral mosaic
occurrences.label: Man with fish's tail, 'Est homo non totus…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This man is not complete, but half fish from the deep.
body: Sixth-century floor mosaic in Pesaro cathedral showing a man whose lower half is a fish, inscribed "Est homo non totus medius sed piscis ab imo" — this man is not complete, but half fish from the deep. Jung cites it via Becker's study of Christ-under-the-form-of-a-fish, in the context of the half-animal constitution of the primordial or not-yet-complete man.

Jung's reading: the fish-man as incomplete anthropos, ichthys-adjacent; cross-references "The Spirit Mercurius" pars. 267ff. and Paracelsus' arcane teaching. Parallels: christ-figure-alexamenos-graffito-palatine-rome-200, Oannes tradition (Elenchos V, 7, 6), fish-round-fish-allegoriae-turba-11c.

occurrences.title: The fish of Manu — Vishnu as the redeemer-fish
occurrences.label: The fish of Manu — Vishnu as the redeemer-fish
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Vishnu, "in the form of a small goldfish," begs Manu to take him home for fear of the water monsters; "He then grows mightily, fairytale fashion, and in the end rescues Manu from the great flood" (cw09ii par. 176; "I will save thee," Shatapatha Brahmana). Jung also cites the ritual echo: a golden fish placed in a bowl of water on the twelfth day of the first month — "As thou, O God, in the form of a fish, hast saved the Vedas... so save me also, O Keshava!"
Jung rejects de Gubernatis' derivation of the Christian fish from India: Western fish symbolism is "so rich and at the same time so archaic that we may safely regard it as autochthonous."

image.title: Matsya avatar

occurrences.title: Roman marriage vase: couples united by trident, mandrake, and fish (2nd c.)
occurrences.label: Roman marriage vase
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: Then a couple with hands united through a fish. The fish stands for Christ.
body: A Roman vase of the second century, "probably made by a Christian, since it has a Christian marriage scene on it," carrying several scenes of union between men and women: "There is a couple united through a trident—through Neptune! A man is using a mandrake root to charm a woman—seduction, witchcraft. Then a couple with hands united through a fish. The fish stands for Christ."

Produced in the argument that marriage needs the third, the thing from above: in the Catholic Church two people "are married in Christo, Christ holds them together... human beings cannot be connected except through God." For the moderns, says Jung, "the fish stands for a content of the unconscious" — the same tertium comparationis the naked boy of dream 12 was to supply.

occurrences.title: The forgotten fish of Moses and Joshua ben Nun at the meeting of the two seas — Qur'an 18
occurrences.label: The forgotten fish of Moses and Joshua ben Nun…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Arabia (Qur'anic recension); isthmus of Suez per commentators

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: But when they had reached the place where the two seas meet, they forgot their fish, and it took its way through a stream to the sea.
body: In Sura 18 Moses travels with his servant Joshua ben Nun to "the place where the two seas meet"; there they forget their breakfast-fish, which slips back to the sea alive. Where it vanished, the sea turns to solid ground, Khidr sits enthroned "between the upper and the lower sea", and Moses takes him for a teacher, enduring three incomprehensible deeds (the scuttled ship, the slain youth, the rebuilt wall). Jung reads the fish as the unconscious instinctual basis — Joshua is "son of Nun", "fish" — whose loss is the primitive "loss of soul", abaissement du niveau mental (¶244-245). The reanimated fish is identified with the Second Adam; Khidr's birthplace is exactly where the fish disappeared (¶247-248). Alchemical parallels: the "round fish lacking bones and skin", aqua permanens, nigredo after the coniunctio, and the Stone appearing "like fish's eyes".

occurrences.title: 'Purus laton... donec veluti oculi piscium elucescat' — fish's eyes of the lapis, Morienus Romanus
occurrences.label: Purus laton... donec veluti oculi piscium…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Latin translation 1144; printed Artis auriferae, Basel 1593

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

occurrences.quote: ... Purus laton tamdiu decoquitur, donee veluti oculi piscium elucescat...
body: The Morienus passage the later authors themselves cite as the source of the "doctrine" of the scintillae actually reads: "The pure laton is cooked until it has the lustre of fish's eyes" — "Here too the saying seems to be a citation from a still earlier source." The fish's eyes keep cropping up in later authors with the same significance as the sparks.

Jung's reading: "Thus, by the authors themselves, the oculi piscium are interpreted as scintillae" — the luminosity of the arcane substance and the luminosity of the archetypes are one family; the eye-motif feeds directly into the all-seeing eyes of God, Argus, the dragon of the Pole, and the monadic "solitary eye in the depths of the sea or earth" of modern fantasy (¶396).

occurrences.title: Pectorios inscription, Autun: 'divine descendants of the heavenly fish'
occurrences.label: Pectorios inscription, Autun
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: In the Pectorios inscription the believers are "the divine descendants of the heavenly fish": "holding the fish in the hands... Nourish now with the fish, I yearn, Lord Saviour" — the first three distichs make the acrostic Ichthys (Doelger I; Pohl, Das Ichthysmonument von Autun).
Like the Abercius inscription, its Christianity is doubted. Jung reads the family of fish-inscriptions against the question whether Ichthys derived from the zodiac — which he denies (par. 177).

image.title: Pectorios Inscription

occurrences.title: The ring of Polycrates returned by the fish
occurrences.label: The ring of Polycrates returned by the fish
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The classical parallel for the patient's fish: after her volcanic experience, the village normals "blotted out" it — "What they have gained is lost in the ocean, like the ring of Polycrates, which would have been lost had the fish not brought it back". Ed. note: the tyrant of Samos, advised to throw away something he valued to avert the gods' jealousy, cast his seal-ring into the ocean and "retrieved it a few days later in the belly of a fish" — the omen that, in Herodotus, foretells not safety but his doom. In the vision the fish brings back not a ring but "a black rough stone" that becomes beating amber: the treasure lost to collective unconsciousness restored to consciousness — though now in opaque, suffering-bearing form.

occurrences.title: The round fish 'lacking bones and cortex' — Allegoriae super librum Turbae
occurrences.label: The round fish 'lacking bones and cortex'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Latin West (Artis auriferae I, pp. 139ff.; Harran-Alexandrian ancestry)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: "Est in mari piscis rotundus, ossibus et corticibus carens": "There is in the sea a round fish, lacking bones and cortex, and having in itself a fatness, a wondrous virtue" — cooked slowly till it shines, yielding at the citrinitas the ironic "collyrium of the philosophers". Our earliest source for alchemical fish symbolism; nothing suggests Christian origin.

Through the transformation of the arcane substance the fish became "a symbol of the lapis" — prima materia and end product (lapis philosophorum, elixir vitae, filius philosophorum, Hermaphroditus); Jung adds: "The filius philosophorum (or macrocosmi), otherwise the lapis, means nothing other than the self" (par. 194).
Jung identifies the creature as a scyphomedusa of radial construction, "divided into eight sections by means of four perradials and four interradials" (par. 196).

occurrences.title: Fish as soul-symbol — late Hellenistic Egyptian sarcophagus
occurrences.label: Fish as soul-symbol
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: On a late Hellenistic sarcophagus painting the mummy "lies on a lion-shaped bier," the four Canopic jars below (four sons of Horus, three animal-headed, one human), and "over the mummy there floats a fish, instead of the usual soul-bird" — an oxyrhynchus or barbel, one of the three most abominated fishes, said to have devoured the phallus of Osiris after Typhon dismembered him.

Jung: the fish as Egyptian soul-symbol is "all the more remarkable" given the ambivalence — barbels sacred to Typhon, "that part of the soul which is passionate, impulsive, irrational, and truculent"; in the Middle Ages fishes allegorized the damned.

occurrences.title: Sibylline acrostic ICHTHYS — 'Iudicii signum'
occurrences.label: Sibylline acrostic ICHTHYS — Iudicii signum
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Rome (book of the Erythraean Sibyl shown by Flaccianus to Augustine)
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~2nd c.? (via Augustine, City of God XVIII)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Augustine (City of God XVIII.23) reports the ex-proconsul Flaccianus producing the songs of the Erythraean Sibyl, whose verses form the acrostic ICHTHYS (Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour): "Iudicii signum tellus sudore madescet, / E coelo Rex adveniet per saecla futurus".

Jung cites it while arguing ICHTHYS is unlikely to be "simply an anagrammatic abbreviation" — the fish was "the symbolical designation for something far more complex" with a long Near-Eastern prehistory.

occurrences.title: Talmudic prophecy of the war of the tanninim — Rashi: the fishes
occurrences.label: Talmudic prophecy of the war of the tanninim
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Babylon (Sanhedrin 97b; prophecy of R. Hanan ben Tahlifa, 2nd c.)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: "Four thousand two hundred and ninety-one years after the Creation [A.D. 530], the world will be orphaned. There will follow the war of the tanninim [sea-monsters], the war of Gog and Magog, and then the Messianic era". Rashi (1039-1105) remarks that the tanninim are fishes, evidently on older authority.

Jung: "probably the oldest testimony to the antithetical nature of the fishes," an eschatological battle like Behemoth vs Leviathan; the date matches the founding era of Monte Cassino and Joachim's calculations. Gog and Magog likewise antithetical (tectum / de tecto, Augustine).

occurrences.title: Vishnu becomes the fish and recaptures the Vedas — Indian myth
occurrences.label: Vishnu becomes the fish and recaptures the Vedas
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This is a primitive way of describing the libido’s entry into the interior world of the psyche, the unconscious.
body: Vishnu's trance brings forth Brahma on the lotus of his navel — "Birth of creative thought from introversion" — but the ecstatic absorption unleashes the world-flood ("Devouring and destruction of the world through introversion"), and the fish-avatar dives to rescue the Vedas from the demon (¶449, pls. XLVIa–XLVII, plates at pdf pp292–293).

image.title: Matsya Avatar of Vishnu
image.credit: Image: http://collections.lacma.org/sites/default/files/remote_images/piction/ma-31965721-O3.jpg Gallery: http://collections.lacma.org/node/242261 archive copy at the Wayback Machine

occurrences.title: Zohar: the fish that swallowed Jonah dies and revives after three days
occurrences.label: Zohar: the fish that swallowed Jonah dies…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: "According to the Zohar, the fish that swallowed Jonah died, but revived after three days and then spewed him out again. 'Through the fish we shall find a medicament for the whole world'".

Jung's frame: "Always the hope of a Messiah is connected with the appearance of a star" (Balaam, Num. 24:17); Scheftelowitz identifies the Abercius inscription's "very great and pure fish" with Leviathan — the biggest fish, held to be pure.

occurrences.title: The flaming sword and the self-begetting pneuma — Simon Magus in Hippolytus
occurrences.label: The flaming sword and the self-begetting pneuma
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Samaria (teaching); Rome (Hippolytus); MS found on Mount Athos 19th c.

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: For if the flaming sword turned not, then would that fair Tree be destroyed, and perish utterly.
body: Hippolytus reports Simon's doctrine of an incorruptible pneuma present potentially in everyone, "stationed above and below in the stream of water": "I and thou, thou before me. I, who am after thee." It is "a force that generates itself, that causes itself to grow; it is its own mother, sister, bride, daughter; its own son, mother, father; a unity, a root of the whole" — the procreative urge of fiery origin, blood turning into semen and milk.

Jung's reading: the flaming sword "which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life" is the transformation itself — "the seventh power which begets itself," growing from the littlest spark into an unchanging Aeon. The description "corresponds in every detail to the uroboros or serpens mercurialis of the Latinists"; it means the transformation of the vital spirit in man into the Divine, as in the vision of Zosimos (¶359).

occurrences.title: Flaying the young woman to renew the moon-goddess — Aztec rite
occurrences.label: Flaying the young woman to renew…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: The best examples are to be found in the religion of ancient Mexico.
body: "In order to renew the moon-goddess a young woman was decapitated and skinned, and a youth then put the skin round him to represent the risen goddess" — the best example Jung offers of flaying as transformation from a worse state to a better, renewal and rebirth (the Aztec Ochpaniztli/Toci complex; Jung cites the Mexico literature in his footnote).

Jung's reading: "The prototype of this renewal is the snake casting its skin every year, a phenomenon round which primitive fantasy has always played." In the Zosimos vision the skinning is restricted to the head — spiritual transformation; shaving the head since olden times means consecration and initiation (Isis priests bald, the tonsure, the neophyte as a newborn quasimodogenitus, hair loss in the night sea journey).

occurrences.title: Europe sinking under a sea of blood — Jung's vision (October 1913)
occurrences.label: Europe sinking under a sea of blood
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: On a train journey in October 1913, carried away while reading, Jung fantasized looking down on the map of Europe in relief: the North Sea and then floods rolling over Europe; England sinking, the sea coming up to Switzerland while the mountains grew higher to protect it; towns and people destroyed, wrecks and dead bodies on the water — "Then the whole sea turned to blood." The fantasy held him bound for two hours; it returned in three or four weeks with the blood intensified.

Jung's 1925 seminar reading is double: personally, "I could be taken as Switzerland fenced in by mountains, and the submergence of the world could be the debris of my former relationships"; but "the more normal the individual, the more it can be assumed from such fantasies that some profound social disturbance actually is in progress". He felt like "an over-compensated psychosis" and "was not released till August 1st, 1914" — the day war began. He had thought of revolution, "curiously enough never of a war."

occurrences.title: The wish-fish flounder — Grimm, 'The Fisherman and His Wife'
occurrences.label: The wish-fish flounder
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: It fulfills all the wishes of Ilsebill. But when she wants to be God Himself, she plunges back into her old misery.
body: In the fairy tale, the flounder appears as wish-fish, fulfilling all of Ilsebill's wishes; when she wants to be God Himself, she plunges back into her old misery. Cited among the fish-soul parallels (Hofmannsthal's seven fish-souls of unborn children; the Icelandic trout-conception; Mary fetching water or eating a fish at the Annunciation) as the blue stage of the dream: the unborn potentialities, wishes and ideas swimming in the water-element — with the tale's ceiling: the wish that overreaches the human.

occurrences.title: Fountain of life as fons mercurialis — Rosarium philosophorum (1550)
occurrences.label: Fountain of life as fons mercurialis
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Rosarium's fountain-of-life cut, captioned by Jung "The fountain of life as fons mercurialis".

It illustrates ¶92: "the mother stands for the collective unconscious, the source of the water of life (fig. 25)." Jung adds the maternal πηγή and the fons signatus of the Virgin Mary as parallels, and reads the dream's transfer of the water to the sister as "the mother has been replaced by the anima."

image.title: Rosarium Philosophorum

occurrences.title: The foundation stone (shethiyah) cast into the abyss — Zohar I, 231a
occurrences.label: The foundation stone cast into the abyss
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: from it the world was planted. This is the central point of the universe, and on this point stands the Holy of Holies.
body: The Zohar (I, 231a; Eng. trans. II, 339): the world did not come into being until God took "the foundationstone" and cast it into the abyss, where it held fast, and from it the world was planted — "the central point of the universe," on which the Holy of Holies stands; compounded of fire, water, and air, resting on the abyss, bearing seven eyes (Zech 3:9); the rock of Moriah; "the navel of the world."

Jung's reading: the stone as central axiom of the world's manifestation — Jewish lapis-parallel in the Adam-and-Eve chapter's stone-ladder (Malchuth as the stone on which the upper edifice is built, Kabbala denudata). Parallels: lapis as "stone which the builders rejected," ullikummi-stone-kumarbi-boghazkoy-1200bce, ostanes-nile-stone-zosimos-3c.

occurrences.title: Fountain of youth — Codex de Sphaera (Modena, 15th c.)
occurrences.label: Fountain of youth — Codex de Sphaera
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the symbol of the life force that eternally renews itself
body: Plate 56: a walled garden in which bathers crowd round a great many-tiered fountain — the Fountain of youth (plate verified against p0144.jpg). Jung sets it opposite dream 13, where the crash into the sea-deeps lands the dreamer in "a beautiful garden in the depths, symmetrically laid out, with a fountain in the centre": "The source of life… is the symbol of the life force that eternally renews itself… and of the clock that never runs down" (¶157).
The fountain stands "underground and therefore the way leads underneath: only down below can we find the fiery source of life" (¶157) — rejuvenation through descent into the unconscious.

image.title: La Fontaine de jouvence, miniature extraite du De Sphaera
image.credit: Formerly attributed to Cristoforo de Predis

occurrences.title: The four female figures of the Gnostic underworld — Eve, Helen, Mary, Sophia
occurrences.label: The four female figures of the Gnostic…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Spirit in Man, Art and Literature (CW15)

occurrences.quote: the four female figures of the Gnostic underworld, Eve, Helen, Mary, and Sophia.
body: The Gnostic quartet of the anima's faces: "In Faust's metamorphosis, Gretchen, Helen, Mary, and the abstract 'Eternal Feminine' correspond to the four female figures of the Gnostic underworld, Eve, Helen, Mary, and Sophia" (cw15 ¶211).

Jung's reading. The mapping is his bridge between Goethe and Gnosticism: each Faust-woman is a station of the one psychic feminine — the seduced innocence (Gretchen/Eve), the mythic beloved (Helen/Helen), the holy mother-bride (Mary/Mary), and the transcendent wisdom (Eternal Feminine/Sophia). In Psychology and Literature the same ladder is spelled out from the other end: the Eternal Feminine is "the maternal Sophia... the highest manifestation of the anima, stripped of the pagan savagery of the nymph Polia" (cw15 ¶154). The immediate context in ¶211 is the neurotic's encounter with the unconscious "in the form of the 'Dark One,' a Kundry of horribly grotesque, primeval ugliness or else of infernal beauty" — the same field the quartet orders.

occurrences.title: Diagram of the four functions of consciousness — Jung's own diagram (via Jacobi, The Psychology of Jung)
occurrences.label: Diagram of the four functions of consciousness
occurrences.subject: jung
body: Jung's diagram: "Thinking, the superior function in this case, occupies the centre of the light half of the circle, whereas feeling, the inferior function, occupies the dark half. The two auxiliary functions are partly in the light and partly in the dark."

It is brought in at ¶137 to gloss the Peterhofstatt dream's four persons: ego, doctor, pointed-beard (Mephisto-intellect), doll-woman (anima) — "the four persons in the dream to represent the four functions as components of the total personality."

occurrences.title: Four season-goddesses around the round table — Stolcius, Viridarium chymicum
occurrences.label: Four season-goddesses around the round table
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1624 (fig. XLII; also Mylius, Philosophia reformata 1622, p.117)
occurrences.quote: The arrangement of the opposites in a quaternity is shown in an interesting illustration in Stolcenberg's Viridarium chymicum (Fig. XLII).
body: Stolcius von Stolcenberg's engraving of four goddesses seated around a circular table: "The goddesses represent the four seasons of the sun in the circle of the Zodiac (Aries, Cancer, Libra, Capricorn) and at the same time the four degrees of heating, as well as the four elements 'combined' around the circular table" (¶5).

Jung reads it as the quaternio of opposites arranged spatially, whose synthesis is "effected by means of the circular movement in time (circulatio, rota) of the sun through the houses of the Zodiac," the aim being "the production (or rather, reproduction) of the Original Man, who was a sphere." It anchors the book's opening argument that dualities default to fourfold structure.

image.title: Four elements in Viridarium chymicum

occurrences.title: The four strongholds of truth — Dorn, Speculativa philosophiae p. 279
occurrences.label: The four strongholds of truth
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The lowest is of crystal and shelters “philosophical love”; the second is of silver and contains Sophia.
body: Dorn's four-storeyed citadel of truth ("Seest thou that gleaming and impregnable stronghold?"): the lowest stronghold of crystal shelters "philosophical love"; the second, of silver, contains Sophia; the third, of diamond (adamantina), is reached only by a few "taken up by the will of God"; the fourth is golden but "not perceptible to the senses" — "a place of eternal felicity, free from care and filled with every manner of eternal joy." Truth itself is "the supreme virtue and an impregnable stronghold."

Jung's reading: a quaternio of ascending stages — he parallels it to the four stages of transformation in the Liber Platonis quartorum (Psychology and Alchemy 366ff); the castle was also a Mary-allegory (Godefridus). Parallels: joachim-trinity-diagram-zurich-ms, temenos family.

occurrences.title: The fourth man in the fiery furnace — Daniel 3 / Biblia pauperum
occurrences.label: The fourth man in the fiery furnace
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Nebuchadnezzar sees "four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire... and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God." The Biblia pauperum comments: "The three signify for us the Holy Trinity of the person, and the fourth the unity of being."

Jung's reading: the legend is "a magical procedure during which a 'fourth' is produced" (¶245); the fiery furnace is a mother-symbol (like Faust's tripod), the Hermetic vessel a uterus, and the fourth "a son of God made visible in the fire".
Verbatim: The three signify for us the Holy Trinity of the person, and the fourth the unity of being. (cw05 ¶244).

occurrences.title: The Chinese girl possessed by a visible fox spirit (Richard Wilhelm's case)
occurrences.label: The Chinese girl possessed by a visible fox…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: It confirms absolutely what primitives say, that certain individuals have a connection with certain animals, either a friendly or a hostile connection. Such experiences are really the basis for the totemic beliefs.
body: A girl believed possessed by a fox spirit — "a sort of witchlike spirit... able to revive the dead body of a woman"; there is even a Chinese love story of a man enamored of a fox woman, and Garnett's Lady into Fox carries the same idea. What made Wilhelm investigate was that the fox was visible, coming almost daily; he walked to the village, saw the real fox on the courtyard wall, and it moved away only when he came quite near — and whenever it approached, the girl in the house had hysterical attacks.

occurrences.title: Byzantine fractio — the IS XS NI KA quaternity
occurrences.label: Byzantine fractio — the IS XS NI KA quaternity
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: This quaternity, as the letters show, refers to Christ glorified, king of glory and Pantokrator.
body: In the Byzantine rite the altar bread is divided into four pieces marked with the letters IS XS NI KA — "Jesus Christ is victorious." Jung notes the arrangement of the letters "obviously represents a quaternity, which as we know always has the character of wholeness" and refers it to Christ glorified, king of glory and Pantokrator (¶331).

The fractio itself is symbolic of Christ's death; the Libera nos alludes to the descent into hell and the breaking of the infernal power. Read against the Roman single-particule fractio, the Byzantine division makes the quaternary structure of the glorified body explicit.

occurrences.title: Mozarabic fractio — five and four parts
occurrences.label: Mozarabic fractio — five and four parts
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: According to the old view, five is the number of the natural ("hylical") man, whose outstretched arms and legs form, with the head, a pentagram.
body: The Mozarabic breaking of the Host is more complicated than the Roman: the bread is first broken in two, then the left half into five parts, the right into four. The five — corporatio (incarnatio), nativitas, circumcisio, apparitio, passio — refer to the human life of the Lord; the four — mors, resurrectio, gloria, regnum — to his existence beyond this world (¶332).

Jung's reading: five is the number of the natural ("hylical") man, whose outstretched arms and legs form with the head a pentagram; four signifies eternity and totality, as shown by the Gnostic name "Barbelo," translated "fourness is God." The symbol suggests that extension in space signifies God's suffering (on the cross) and his dominion over the universe.

occurrences.title: Frau Welt — Basel Minster
occurrences.label: Frau Welt — Basel Minster
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The famous Frau Welt relief: a smiling young woman in front, devils, apes and toads gnawing her behind. A medieval memento of the world's fair face and rotten back. Nietzsche, who lived in Basel, "must have known" it.

Mrs. Fierz offers it as the picture under Nietzsche's vision of the world: "After having looked only at the devils and apes for such a long time, it is as if Nietzsche finally could see 'Frau Welt' smiling. Anyhow, the picture of a woman is always underneath" — the anima-face of the world he had been reviling, now carried to him by "delicate hands" as a casket.

occurrences.title: Frey drives through Sweden in a wagon with his priestess (the 'light one')
occurrences.label: Frey drives through Sweden in a wagon…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Brunner's companion locus to Nerthus: "In Sweden, the god Frey takes her place, called the 'light one' in the Edda. In winter he drives through the country in a wagon with his priestess. People believed that he was being married to her.... In Frey's case, the return of the light" is anticipated.

The frame is the ritual logic that "the high-spirited frenzy, reigning in winter and spring festivals up to this day, is meant to call on life, frozen in ice, to new procreation." For the dream, the carriage as ritual vehicle of the divine couple — the gods walk — prepares Jung's whole discussion of the transitus of the gods (barque, procession, the roaming totemistic ancestors; the devil as heir of the aljira half-animals).

occurrences.title: The frog-song rain charm of the Rig-Veda priests
occurrences.label: The frog-song rain charm of the Rig-Veda priests
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung's example of primitive magical logic, deployed to explain what the red pyramid would "do" to the patient: "In India, according to the Rig-Veda, the priests sang the frog songs in the time of drought as a rain charm; when the frogs sing it means that rain has fallen, so when the priests sing rain will fall. That is the way the primitive mind works".

The principle: the magic effect works by likeness — water against dropsy, milk sprinkled for rain, imitated wind and raindrops; eagle's wings for the chief's soaring, lion's teeth and mane for his power, "Indians used to eat the heart of the enemy or the brains, in order to integrate either the courage of the enemy which is in the heart, or his cunning which is in the head." Hence the pyramid bursting through the earth suggests "a powerful uplift."

occurrences.title: Three frontier-crossing dreams under three analysts — customs-house and twin beds (patient-anon)
occurrences.label: Three frontier-crossing dreams…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: But the customs official dives into my bag and, to my astonishment, pulls out a pair of twin beds.
body: A female patient's three initial dreams, each dreamt at the beginning of treatment under a different analyst. First: "I have to cross the frontier into another country, but cannot find the frontier and nobody can tell me where it is" — that treatment failed and was broken off. Second: pitch-black night, no customs-house, a tiny light far off, a valley and a dark wood in which she loses her way — then someone clings to her "like a madman" and she wakes in terror; the analyst had unconsciously identified with the patient, total disorientation on both sides (¶309). Third, under Jung: the frontier already crossed, a Swiss customs-house, a handbag with "nothing to declare" — the official dives in and pulls out a pair of twin beds; she married during this treatment and first resisted the marriage violently.

Jung's point (¶311–312): the aetiology appears nowhere in these dreams; "they are without exception anticipations of the difficulties she is to have with the doctors concerned" — dream as prognostic of the analytic situation, evidence that dreams are often anticipatory, not merely causal.

occurrences.title: Indian funeral prayer at the cremation: 'assume a new body, aglow in beauty'
occurrences.label: Indian funeral prayer at the cremation
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Quoted in Dr. Nothmann's paper on the ash-pyramid dream: "This concept is very clearly expressed in an Indian prayer, which the man conducting the funeral addresses to the dead person during cremation: '[... ] move on, on the old paths on which our forebears passed away. [... ] Join the fathers there in the highest heaven [... ] leaving behind all that is imperfect, assume a new body, aglow in beauty'".

The prayer documents the cremation cults' shared idea: to assist the dead to the hereafter "by freeing the soul through destruction of the mortal remains," with the simultaneous cremation of possessions — even the wife. It stands in the paper's series ash → phoenix → pyramid as resurrection symbols from different cultural environments.

occurrences.title: Palissy burns his furniture — the last leg of the last chair
occurrences.label: Palissy burns his furniture
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The potter Bernard Palissy spent years and every cent hunting the enamel glaze; when the kiln's wood gave out "he burned his furniture, every stick in his house, and when he had pushed the last leg of the last chair into the stove, the enamel was there."

Jung's exemplar of creative incarnation: the creator "will repress everything... only that idea remains" — the suspended idea eats the sacrificed body. "The last leg of the last chair must be pushed into the oven before the desired result is reached. But of course one has sacrificed a lot; one has sacrificed perhaps the happiness of one's life."
Verbatim: "So he burned his furniture, every stick in his house, and when he had pushed the last leg of the last chair into the stove, the enamel was there."

occurrences.title: The Galloi: castrated priests of Astarte
occurrences.label: The Galloi: castrated priests of Astarte
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: Christ speaks of those who have castrated themselves for the kingdom of heaven. He probably alludes to the Galloi, the priests of Astarte, who used to castrate themselves officially
