body: The self-castrating Galloi, whose 'not very savory symbols were carried at the head of a special parade' — public knowledge all over the Near East, and Christ's likely reference (Mt 19:12). Exhibit A of the late-Christian 'persecution of the body, the glorification of the spirit through the mortification of the body.' Parallels: origen-self-castration-alexandria-206 · sacrifice-attis-pine-effigy-annual-rite-4c.

occurrences.title: Gandhi's lump of salt and spinning wheel — new collective cakras (Dandi, 1930)
occurrences.label: Gandhi's lump of salt and spinning wheel
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

body: Jung's example of a living symbol being born: Gandhi at the sea "shows a lump of salt to his people, it is as good as a cakra. They need no cakra. Take the spinning wheel. Why should they concentrate on a cakra when they see Gandhi with a spinning wheel? They contemplate it and are carried to a higher plane of thought—the idea of sacrifice, and so on. That is a new 'tantric yoga,' if you like" (sem-kundalini pdf p146).

Context: Jung's law of psychic adaptation — tantric yoga itself was once "an adaptation of the thousand-year-old yoga to a new psychic situation, and that situation has disappeared from India"; new epochs require new community-valid symbols, "and Gandhi is the man who, with a quite new method, has created those symbols out of the new psychic and spiritual state."

occurrences.title: Gardeners making water against the trees — dream of the child 'Anna'
occurrences.label: Gardeners making water against the trees
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Weeks after the seed-theory enlightenment (mother as soil, father as gardener who sows — ¶60), Anna dreamed she was "in the garden and several gardeners stood making wee-wee against the trees, and Papa was also doing it."

Jung's reading: "This recalls the earlier unsolved problem: what does the father do?" (¶64). The enlightenment silenced the questions, but "the unconscious did not lose sight of the riddle of human creation"; the dream fuses the gardener-sower image with urination — the father's role pictured in the only imagery available.
Quote. "She was 'in the garden and several gardeners stood making wee-wee against the trees, and Papa was also doing it.'"

occurrences.title: Sancta Maria, closed gate, sealed fountain — the Melk hymn
occurrences.label: Sancta Maria, closed gate, sealed fountain
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Sancta Maria, / Closed gate / Opened at God's command— / Sealed fountain, / Locked garden, / Gate of Paradise.
body: The 12th-century Melk hymn to Mary folds Song of Solomon 4:12 into liturgy: "Sancta Maria, / Closed gate / Opened at God's command— / Sealed fountain, / Locked garden, / Gate of Paradise."

Jung sets it immediately beside the erotic verse — "Maiden, let me enter with you / Into your rose garden / Where the red rosebuds grow... / And the deep cool well / That lies below" — to show that the same symbolism (enclosed garden, sealed fountain, low door) serves mystic and profane love alike: the hymn to Mary and the seduction song are one vocabulary.

occurrences.title: 'Tear off this garment... this tomb you carry about with you' — Corpus Hermeticum XIII (rebirth)
occurrences.label: Tear off this garment... this tomb you carry…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The rebirth discourse's stripping command: "But first you must tear off this garment which you wear—this cloak of darkness, this web of ignorance, this [prop] of evil, this bond of corruption—this living death, this conscious corpse, this tomb you carry about with you".

Jung gathers the parallel strippings: the Song of Songs' "I have put off my coat, how shall I put it on?", the Aurora Consurgens' "He shall not deride my garment," Madathanus' "Her garments, which were rancid, ill-savoured, and poisonous, lay at her feet" — "the nigredo is also represented as the 'garment of darkness'." Undressing the materia = extractio animae; the corpse-tomb garment is the nigredo-state itself.

occurrences.title: Garuda steals the soma from the snakes — Indian epic
occurrences.label: Garuda steals the soma from the snakes
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: "In Indian mythology and in fairy tales, the races of the snakes and eagles are eternal enemies, and seek to destroy each other. Once, the snakes outwitted the eagles, which then had to serve them, but the eagle Garuda, Vishnu's mount, stole the soma, the drink of immortality that he was supposed to obtain for them".

The eagle is the sun-bird and spiritual principle, the snake's standing opponent: "an eagle sits on top of the Germanic world tree, but a dragon dwells below, while the squirrel Ratatwiskr (bearer of discord) transmits mutual insults" — the vertical antagonism that the Mithraic monuments spatialize as lion vs snake around the Kratér.

occurrences.title: The book of gate-names laid in the king's coffin
occurrences.label: The book of gate-names laid in the king's coffin
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: the Egyptians always put a book in the coffin of a dead king, containing the names of the gates and doors of the underworld, for they were only opened if he could call them by the right name.
body: Jung's exhibit of name-magic: knowing the right name gives power — 'as by giving a name to a demon, one has power over the demon' — deployed in his reading of Zarathustra's 'name not thy virtue.' Parallels: rumpelstiltskin-name-power-grimm-khm55 · ape-judgment-balance-book-of-the-dead-egypt.

occurrences.title: Gayomart — the metals grow from the Original Man's blood
occurrences.label: Gayomart — the metals grow…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'The metals grow from Gayomart's blood' (¶389). Gayomart is the Original Man of the theosophical Zarathustra system; Yima ('the shining Yima') the Original Man of ancient Aryan legend, whose body, per the Bundahishn, consisted of metals (¶389 n.77). Jung uses this to close the uroboros of his four quaternios: 'the heavy darkness of the earth, metal, has a secret relationship to the Anthropos' — the lowest, most material thing identical with the highest and most spiritual (¶389). Parallels: ostanes-nile-stone-zosimos-3c, uroboros-codex-marcianus-venice-11c.

occurrences.title: The gazelle of the heart lotus — fugitive mind to be fettered (Haṭhayogapradīpikā, India, ~15th c.)
occurrences.label: The gazelle of the heart lotus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

body: The antelope/gazelle seated in the anāhata (heart) lotus of the cakra iconography — the black antelope mount of the vāyu bīja in Śaṭcakranirūpaṇa v.23. Hauer, citing the Haṭhayogapradīpikā: "the meaning of it is the versatile and fugitive mind. There always is, in that creative region, a tendency in the intellect to run away; you have to fetter the gazelle of the heart lotus, and there is the danger of just making jumps in any direction" (sem-kundalini pdf p154).

A member of the fettered-soul family in Indian dress: the intellect as skittish beast that must be bound before the heart-center's creative life can hold. Jung received the exposition gratefully but built his own anāhata psychology on breath and expressed feeling.

occurrences.title: The natal Genius, 'changeful of countenance, white and black' — Horace, Epistles II.2
occurrences.label: The natal Genius, changeful…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the god of human nature, changeful of countenance, white and black.
body: Horace's epistolary sketch of the personal Genius: "Scit Genius, natale comes qui temperat astrum, / naturae deus humanae, mortalis in unum / quodque caput vultu mutabilis, albus et ater" — the birth-star's ruling companion, "the god of human nature, mortal in each single life, and changeful of countenance, white and black."

Jung quotes it twice, in both strata of the Father essay: in the 1909 footnote on the daemon of destiny (n.3, "only the Genius knows why this should be so") and in the 1949 definition of the archetype as "the genius and daemon of the personal human being" (¶743). The Roman natal daimon becomes Jung's classical warrant for the archetype's two-sidedness — the same figure that puts Asmodeus behind Raguel.

occurrences.title: Geryon's three bodies and the three Churches — the Naassenes
occurrences.label: Geryon's three bodies and the three Churches
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The beginning of wholeness is the knowledge of man, but the knowledge of God is perfect wholeness.
body: The Naassenes divided the hermaphroditic Adam into three parts as they did Geryon: "one part is spiritual, one psychic, and one earthly"; all three came down into one man, Jesus born of Mary; there are three Churches, angelic, psychic, earthly — the Chosen, the Called, the Captive. "The beginning of wholeness is the knowledge of man, but the knowledge of God is perfect wholeness."

Jung at cw14 ¶652-653: Geryon corresponds to the cosmogonic Adam Kadmon, "the masculo-feminine Man in all things, whom the Greeks call the heavenly horn of the moon"; the unutterable generation of perfect men.

occurrences.title: The sixth circle — ghosts whirling, the Self dismembered and re-wholed (Visions, 7 Feb. 1934)
occurrences.label: The sixth circle — ghosts whirling, the Self…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: First of the "Circles" series discussed: "We emerged into a great circle in the rocks" — "They are really attempts at mandalas. It is as if she were drawing for each variation of mood a different mandala". The mandala as protective circle for ghost-conjuring (ETH lectures), as Ulysses standing over the blood with his sword (pp1347-1348).

"I saw ghosts and phantoms whirling round and round making great moan. Some were like harpies with great claws which reached down to clutch us. Others were beautiful and voluptuous, making sweet sound, while others with pinched and haggard faces screamed and rent the air. The woman at my side said: 'I will show you.' She walked to the center of the circle. Here the phantoms caught at her, clutched her, tore at her. I cried out in fear.".

Dismemberment by hostility or by attraction (harpies, sirens, hags — the anima/anima as dismembering powers, p1357-1358); psychologically schizophrenia, "a sort of explosion" (p1348). Then: "by some strange magic she became whole again... 'Because I was with you there was a way out. Had you entered alone you would have been lost'" — the Self in the center as "a Titan against Titans".

occurrences.title: Corpse and skeleton visions of Miss E. — somnambulistic delirium (Zurich, 1897)
occurrences.label: Corpse and skeleton visions of Miss E.
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: cemetery at C. → asylum at Zurich (case from Dr. L. von Muralt)

jung.locator: ¶150 (pdf p86) — acknowledged as von Muralt's case

occurrences.quote: During the night of the 17th/18th she spoke to the attendant and said she saw the whole room full of dead people looking like skeletons.
body: A 40-year-old book-keeper, exhausted by overwork and claret, tore up flowers and scratched at graves in a somnambulistic state she wholly forgot. Nights afterwards she dealt with the dead: skeletons filling the room, dead children crying from the neighbouring cemetery that they had been buried alive, callers she must "make room" for. Jung reads the cemetery walk as the auto-suggestive seed — "The walk in the cemetery induced the vision of the skeletons" (¶26) — impressions received in somnambulism working on "to form independent growths" that return as hallucination. A "second state" with its own memory, amnesically sealed from waking life (¶15).

occurrences.title: Freud as customs official and the twelfth-century Crusader — Jung's dream (1912)
occurrences.label: Freud as customs official…
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

occurrences.quote: Did you notice him?' my shadow asked me. 'He has been dead since the twelfth century, but he is not yet properly dead. He always walks here among the people, but they don't see him.
body: While still writing Psychology of the Unconscious, Jung dreamed he walked at a country crossing with an unknown companion ("today I would say it was my shadow"). First he passed an old man in the uniform of an Austrian customs official — Freud, "dead for thirty years, but he can't die properly." The scene shifted to a southern medieval town at blazing noon: among the crowd walked a tall Crusader in chain mail with the red Maltese cross, unseen by the people — "dead since the twelfth century... not yet properly dead."

Jung's 1925 reading: the dream's meaning lies "in the principle of the ancestral figure." The customs officer = the Freudian theory of censorship; the Crusader = "an archetypal figure, a Christian symbol living from the twelfth century," from the age of Meister Eckhart and the culture of the Knights, not dead but not yet alive again — the form in which the break with Freud was being prepared.

occurrences.title: The dead mother's veto — Russian-Jewish student's conversion dream (Burghölzli, ~1900s)
occurrences.label: The dead mother's veto
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: That night his mother again appeared before him in a dream and said, 'If you go over I will choke you.
body: Driven by starvation, an orthodox Russian-Jewish student resolves to convert to Christianity; that night his dead mother appears in a dream with a warning. He wrestles for weeks; the night before he means to apply for baptism she returns: "If you go over I will choke you." He abandons conversion for good and emigrates. Jung classes this among his "teleological hallucinations" (¶304): the repressed religious scruples "made use of the strongest possible symbolic argument, his piety towards his dead mother, and in this way overrode the ego-complex" (¶307). The student later fell ill with a paranoid form of dementia praecox. The ancestor as vetoing power — read strictly psychologically in 1907.

occurrences.title: 'Fahre hin und fadere' — dismissing the soul, Canton Aargau
occurrences.label: Fahre hin und fadere
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: A Swiss death-custom still current in the 19th century: when somebody died, the windows were opened and the soul addressed — Fahre hin und fadere, "Farewell and flutter away" — an invitation not to return.

Jung sets it in the register of customs that keep the dead in the hole: stones heaped on graves, bodies nailed to the ground "in order that the body should not rise again," the South Sea boat that politely carries the soul off. Burial in the hollow tree means "to lock him in somewhere so that he cannot get out" — Zarathustra's burial as primitive precaution against the spirit of heaviness.

Verbatim: "in Canton Aargau, in the 1gth century the custom still prevailed that when somebody died one opened the windows and said to the soul of the dead, Fahre hin undfiadere, 'Farewell and flutter away,' thus inviting it not to return." (pdf p209, OCR as in text)

occurrences.title: Dead Alexandros fetches Glaphyra to Hades — dream at the fall of Archelaos (Judea, A.D. 6)
occurrences.label: Dead Alexandros fetches Glaphyra to Hades
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This former husband, Alexandros, appeared to her in the dream and blamed her for her conduct and told her that he was going to take her back into his household.
body: Glaphyra — thrice married, her first husband Alexandros murdered (Archelaos "most probably the murderer") — dreams after her husband's deposition that Alexandros appears, blames her conduct, and says he will take her back into his household. In the ancient reading, to be fetched by the dead = fetched to Hades. "And indeed, a few days later she committed suicide" (¶243).

Jung declines to interpret: "Simon did not interpret this dream, so the analysis is left to our discretion" — but fixes the datum: the dead husband in the dream means the ghost, and the ghost means death. Second of the two Josephus dream-evidence pieces at Tavistock.

occurrences.title: The haunted farmhouse — half-faced old woman (Buckinghamshire, 1920)
occurrences.label: The haunted farmhouse — half-faced old woman
occurrences.subject: jung
body: Jung's own five-weekend haunting in a cheap Buckinghamshire cottage: a sickly smell "unmistakably the same sickly smell" as a carcinoma room (¶766), dripping water with no source (¶767), a panic-stricken dog-sized rush (¶770), muffled hammer-blows on walls (¶771) — then the apparition: "There, beside me on the pillow, I saw the head of an old woman, and the right eye, wide open, glared at me. The left half of the face was missing below the eye" (¶774). Dr. X, left alone with a shotgun, heard footsteps pushing against the bolted door and gave up the cottage (¶776); the owner later pulled the house down as unsaleable (¶777).

Jung's reading: the vision "had the character of a hypnagogic hallucination and was probably a reconstruction of the memory of the old woman with carcinoma" (¶778); the "psychic smells" were subliminal intuitions — "Primitive medicinemen... also 'smell' spirits and ghosts" (¶779–780).

occurrences.title: The legend of Henrico von Brunnen at the Casa di Ferro (Castello di Ferro, Minusio)
occurrences.label: The legend of Henrico von Brunnen…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: A 15th-century stronghold on Lake Maggiore (editors identify the Castello di Ferro, Minusio, citing the Swiss Kunstdenkmaeler) carrying a legend of murder: Henrico von Brunnen, killer of his unfaithful wife and her lover — "a suitable figure for the unconscious fantasy material of Mary, who thinks of herself as the prisoner of an ogre."

Jung, who knows the place ("it is in fact very extraordinary; one wonders what it was, and feels the truth of the legends about it"), describes the possession: arriving there, Latimer says to himself, "This is the place, and I am that man Henrico von Brunnen." — "There is the immediate conviction that always follows when an archetype is struck, it is an extraordinary experience... He was no longer himself, but his unconscious. So he died when he committed the murder. He had not done it himself, nature had brought it about" (sem-1925).

occurrences.title: Ghost-house healing — witch-doctor smells out the grandfather's spirit (East Africa, 1925/26)
occurrences.label: Ghost-house healing
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: East Africa, water-hole near Jung's expedition camp

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: An observed healing: a young woman collapsed by a water-hole "with a septic abortion," feverish; the local medicine-man was passed over for "a foreigner, a witch-doctor from another village. The great man is always abroad." He "was trying to smell out the ghost by behaving like a dog on the scent of something. He went in spirals around the hut — nearer and nearer — till he suddenly stopped and said: Here! It was the spirit of her grandfather," bored and lonely in ghostland, who "came down the trail at night to get the girl" (p346).

The prescription: "building a ghost-house... made one very neatly of stone, quite the opposite of their own wattle huts, and they put in a bed and food and water." The ghost slept late, hurried off at sunrise — "As a matter of fact, the girl's fever went down and in three days she had quite recovered. Funny things in Africa!" (p347).

Jung's use: evidence that primitives "put everything down to the action of ghosts, with the perfectly logical recognition that we are tremendously influenced by ancestral facts" — all children are reincarnations of ancestors until reborn at puberty.

occurrences.title: The Hydesville knockings — Fox sisters, origin of spiritualism (1848)
occurrences.label: The Hydesville knockings
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The founding locus of the spiritualist tradition Jung treats as a religious movement: two daughters of the Methodist Fox family frightened by nightly knockings, from which a "knocking alphabet" was developed; the raps named a man murdered and buried in the cellar, "and Investigations were said to have confirmed this" (¶698). "At first a great scandal arose, because the neighbours suspected that the devil was up to his usual tricks."

Jung's reading (1905): the sect born here swept Europe as a table-turning epidemic, its ground prepared by Romantic occultism (¶700). Later he reads spiritualism itself as compensatory to nineteenth-century materialism (¶750, 1948). The spirits here are, for Jung, unconscious contents that "assume the character of personalities" (¶746).

occurrences.title: The Imperator group — Mrs. Piper's board of invisible directors (Hyslop, James)
occurrences.label: The Imperator group
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Boston, Massachusetts (sittings with the medium Leonora Piper)
occurrences.quote: They were a sort of board of invisible directors who, from the other side, were running the most important jobs in the land
body: Modern form of the spirit-leader: "In Hyslop's book about his own and William James's experiences with their medium Mrs. Piper, he describes her having a whole group of leaders, called the Imperator group. They were a sort of board of invisible directors who, from the other side, were running the most important jobs in the land for the spiritual guidance of the people" (p107). Jung's use: the spirit-teacher archetype appears now as "an important person, a doctor or a professor or a managing director or even a board of directors" (p107) — the contemporary costume of the poimen. In normal circumstances people do not know of these figures; analysis of dreams brings them up (the man in the patient's boat is one).

occurrences.title: The king who carries the corpse — Indian vetala tale
occurrences.label: The king who carries the corpse
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: India (vetala cycle; Zimmer, The King and the Corpse, 1956)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: Nietzsche says 'Thou! Or I!' as if one of them must die, while the king in the Indian tale is very patient and carries the corpse, accepting it in order that the ghost shall teach him.
body: A virtuous king is ordered to cut down a hanged man and carry the corpse to the palace; the corpse-vetala flies back to its scaffold after asking the king one moral question each time, and the conscientious king answers — twenty-four times — until he is transformed. Mrs. Sigg offers it against Nietzsche's dwarf: the king "was so very patient and had not such a negative attitude as Nietzsche has to the dwarf... while the king in the Indian tale is very patient and carries the corpse, accepting it in order that the ghost shall teach him."

Jung's reading: "Yes, that is also a very good example". Against Zarathustra's "Thou! Or I!" — the stance that one of the two must die — the tale models acceptance of the uncanny ghost-teacher: patient carrying of the infernal other until it transforms the carrier. It counters the possession-panic of the dwarf episode with disciplined hospitality to the dead.

occurrences.title: Odysseus' Nekyia — the ghosts drink the blood
occurrences.label: Odysseus' Nekyia — the ghosts drink the blood
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Odysseus kills the sheep and fills the trench with blood; only the shades he wishes to question may drink — the rest he wards off with the sword. Having drunk, the ghosts regain voice and substance.

Jung's point in the Zarathustra reading: "all spirits want bodies; they are crazy without bodies" — Zarathustra, a disembodied spirit after burying the body, craves the communion's "material substance in order to communicate with people." The dim shadow-people of Hades "as soon as there is blood anywhere... go like vultures and drink it in order to get substance, to have a body again".

Verbatim: "Therefore, in Homer, Ulysses kills the sheep and pours out the blood for the ghosts; and only those to whom he wants to talk does he allow to drink of it-the others he wards off with his sword."

occurrences.title: Polar Eskimo sorcerer's ghost-driving incantation — explorer's report (prob. Rasmussen)
occurrences.label: Polar Eskimo sorcerer's ghost-driving…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: An explorer came to a Polar Eskimo hut "where incantations were going on over a sick man for the purpose of driving away the ghosts or evil spirits that were making him sick" — the sorcerer "jumping and running about like mad," then, seeing the visitor: "As soon as he saw the explorer he became very quiet and said: 'This is all a nonsense.'" He had taken him for another medicine man (sem-1925).

Jung's reading: the joke is apotropaic — "not because they think it is, but because they use it as a sort of apotropaic joke. It is in the nature of a euphemism that should protect them against their own fear." The story exemplifies the primitive's awe of what we call the collective unconscious, "to him the ghost world" — an instinctive fear "very strong indeed in us" too.

occurrences.title: The Procession of the Dead: hooded mourners, empty bier, and the volcanic eruption of wild beasts (patient vision, 8 November 1933)
occurrences.label: The Procession of the Dead
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Suddenly the paving stones cracked and burst and a great fire rushed up from the earth with volcanic fury. It cast forth wild beasts and strange half-human forms.
body: The deserted market place, then a great wind — the sukshma aspect, which Jung compares on the spot to Germany under the storm of 1933. The wind takes visible shape: a burial procession of men in black hoods with torches carrying a bier; beneath the pall there is nothing. "Behold we are the dead" — the old convictions going to their own funeral before a rebirth. The ground beneath their feet is hot; at her command they dig, the paving bursts, and a volcanic fire rushes up casting out wild beasts and "strange half-human forms" that prowl the silent streets: everything the Victorian age of respectability repressed, the monstrosities produced by the intellect's "illicit intercourse with matter" — machines, Paracelsus' succubi, the Gnostic serpent-monster.

occurrences.title: Ecstatic visions of a servant girl — Schiller, spirit processions (Zurich, ~1900)
occurrences.label: Ecstatic visions of a servant girl
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A 24-year-old servant girl, alcoholic father and neurotic mother, falls into states in which "the images keep changing with breathtaking speed and lifelikeness"; "her features become transfigured, her movements flow with grace." "Schiller appears to her in person and plays with her. He recites his poems to her" (¶712). In the sombre phases: "She sees ghostly figures prophesying disaster, processions of spirits, caravans of strange and terrifying beastlike forms, her own body being buried."

Jung's reading: the type-form of "visionary ecstasies" (¶713) — the same dissociated second personality he had analysed in his 1902 medium dissertation (cf. ¶951). The procession of beasts and her own burial anticipate the Zurich Black Book visions of processions of the dead.

occurrences.title: Uttering 'selelteni' (ghosts) at the palaver — Mount Elgon (1925–26)
occurrences.label: Uttering 'selelteni' at the palaver
occurrences.subject: jung
body: During a palaver with a tribe on Mount Elgon "most of whom had never come into contact with the white man", Jung incautiously said selelteni — "ghosts". "Suddenly a deathly silence fell on the assembly. The men glanced away, looked in all directions, and some of them made off." His Somali headman whispered: "What did you say that for? Now you'll have to break up the palaver" (¶759).

Jung's reading: "This taught me that one must never mention ghosts on any account. The same primitive fear of ghosts is still deep in our bones, but it is unconscious"; rationalism is "in large measure an apotropaic defence against superstition" — "the brighter the light, the blacker the shadow" (¶759). The name of the ghost acts: speech itself constellates the daemonic.

occurrences.title: The nganga's ghost-trap with clay figure — Mount Elgon
occurrences.label: The nganga's ghost-trap with clay figure
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: Jung's own field observation, given as footnote 2 to the ancestor-worship discussion. A young water-carrier living near the expedition camp fell ill with what looked like septic abortion; the family sent for a nganga (medicine-man), who "walked round and round the hut in ever-widening circles, snuffing the air", then halted on a mountain track and diagnosed: the girl's dead parents, up in the bamboo forest, came down every night to make her die and join them.

"On the instructions of the medicine-man a 'ghost-trap' was then built on the mountain path, in the form of a little hut, and a clay figure of the sick girl was placed inside it together with some food. During the night the ghosts went in there, thinking to be with their daughter. To our boundless astonishment the girl recovered within two days. Was our diagnosis wrong? The puzzle remained unsolved."
The locus gives Jung's essay its sharpest datum for "the wide incidence of ancestor-worship, which is primarily a protection against the malice of the dead" (¶575).

occurrences.title: Two grandfathers arm-in-arm in an open carriage — S.W.'s vision (Zurich, 1899)
occurrences.label: Two grandfathers arm-in-arm in an open carriage
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The proposition “they do not hate one another, but are friends” is expressed in a picture of the two grandfathers arm-in-arm.
body: In the second sitting, as darkness fell and the psychographic communication was brusquely interrupted by a new "spirit", S.W. fell into a waking trance and saw the medium's own grandfather arm-in-arm with Jung's grandfather driving past in an open carriage. Jung's analysis makes this the dissertation's model of symbol-formation: a split-off complex "seized upon the nearest available material" — Jung's family associations — and the unconscious explanation "is no longer given in words, but as an allegorical vision": the two complexes "do not hate one another, but are friends" (¶97–98).

The doctrine that somnambulistic thinking "proceeds in plastic images" (¶98) grows from this one locus. Parallels: vision-swedenborg-man-in-purple-coat-1744 · medium-trance-personalities-helene-preiswerk-basel-1896.

occurrences.title: The ghost of William James identified by the pink pajamas (Hyslop's best case)
occurrences.label: The ghost of William James identified…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: New York / a spiritualist circle in England
occurrences.quote: So a circle with which Hyslop was not acquainted received the same message upon the same evening. This was the best proof that he ever got.
body: James and Hyslop had agreed that whoever died first would send an identifying message. One of Hyslop's mediums relayed a man calling himself William James: "he reminds him of the pink pajamas" — a fact from their student days in Paris that Hyslop himself had forgotten. Ten days later an English circle unknown to Hyslop reported that on the same evening, at the same hour, a spirit gave their medium a message for Professor Hyslop, Columbia University: William James reminds him of the pink pajamas.
Jung's epistemology stays open: telepathic exteriorization by a "good wireless receiving set" of a medium explains it as well as survival — "one proof is as good as another."

occurrences.title: Christophorus: the child growing too heavy for the giant carrying the king of the universe
occurrences.label: Christophorus — the child growing too heavy…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: In the Christophorus legend the little child gradually becomes too heavy for the giant, because he is carrying the king of the universe. Similarly, in a legend of the Mahabharata the (unrecognized) Hanuman makes himself so heavy that not even a god can lift him.
body: For the boy's swelling watch:

Jung is reading the growing weight of the tiny wristwatch: what swells in the hand is a matter becoming "weighty" (gravis — heavy, significant, pregnant) — "an image describing how an unimportant matter becomes 'weighty'" (cf. Faust: "It's growing in my hand! It shines and glows!"). Behind it stands the problem of time the boy is meeting for the first time — the watch as the Self's instrument: "It is the watch we carry within ourselves, the Self... It is a mandala and represents the dynamism of fate".

occurrences.title: The gigantic Man and the dwarf — 'Logos from the Gospel of Eve' (Mead)
occurrences.label: The gigantic Man and the dwarf
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: fragments preserved by Epiphanius (~376 CE); Jung cites via Mead

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: I stood on a lofty mountain, and saw a gigantic Man and another, a dwarf, and I heard, as it were a voice of thunder, and drew nigh for to hear; and he spake unto me and said: I am thou and thou art I
body: Reichstein quotes "the so-called 'Logos from the gospel of Eve'" as the compressed formula of the teaching: the visionary on the mountain sees "a gigantic Man and another, a dwarf," hears the thunder-voice, and receives the identity-saying: "I am thou and thou art I; and wheresoever thou mayest be I am there. In all I am scattered, and whencesoever thou willest, thou gatherest Me, and gathering Me, thou gatherest Thyself."

Jung returns to it twice. First as cosmogony-as-teaching (the transformation process repeats the creation). Then, in Allemann's question, as the pupil-master formula he carefully separates from experience: "For thou art I and I am thou… is a magic incantation" within an already-ritualized situation — "But the original experience… is just the reverse. Therefore, one should always say, 'I am not thou'".

occurrences.title: Six dreams of a boy, ages 3;10–7;9 — fishing giants, iron woman, airship (Appendix)
occurrences.label: Six dreams of a boy, ages 3;10–7;9
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: n/a (all dreams told by the boy to his mother)
occurrences.yearDisplay: six dreams between ages 3;10 and 7;9 (~1930s, before the 1940/41 seminar)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: Two big men—I think giants—are there. They go on the roof and [from there] let a basket down into the water. Then they plop into the water themselves.
body: The Appendix prints six dreams of one boy, told to his mother: (1) aged 3;10 — night-flight "to the maidens," who sent for him; washing in a tub; flying "not with wings, like the Christ Child, but like in an airship" one boards on a pole; (2) 3;11 — a woman with a child and a snow house; the evil "Stuttgarter" doll looks in the window, taken for "an evil daddy"; (3) 4;11 — reaching into a hedge for a little bird, he grasps "an animal that pinched, like a crawfish"; (4) 5;4 — an evil old woman "all made of iron," with long scissors driven by a little iron machine making kicking motions; (5) 5;4 — a dog jumps on the cornice, teased, locked out of the parlor; (6) 7;9 — a house on a river, two giants on the roof letting a basket down into the water, fishing with it, the waves rising because the giants are so big. The series is printed without seminar discussion — a raw instance-set of the child's early archetypal imagery (divine-child flight, the terrible iron mother, the paired giants at the water).

occurrences.title: The serpent steals the herb of immortality — Gilgamesh epic
occurrences.label: The serpent steals the herb of immortality
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Gilgamesh crosses the waters of death to Utnapishtim, dives to the sea-bottom for the magic herb, and on the return journey — escorted by the banished immortal mariner — a serpent steals it and sloughs its skin.

Jung's reading: "a serpent steals the magic herb from him (i.e., the fish slips back into the sea)" — the treasure regained and lost; the mariner is Jensen's prototype of Ahasuerus (¶293). Plate XIX: Gilgamesh with the herb of immortality, relief from the palace of Assurnasirpal II, Nimrud.
Verbatim: But when Gilgamesh arrives home, a serpent steals the magic herb from him (i.e., the fish slips back into the sea). (cw05 ¶293).

occurrences.title: Gilgamesh's journey to the Westland — through the Scorpio gates, across the waters of death
occurrences.label: Gilgamesh's journey to the Westland
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Three facets from the 1929 lectures: (1) "Gilgamesh travels toward the Westland, to the land of the setting sun" seeking the medicine of immortality; the myth of Utnapishtim, flood-survivor, "antedates the Noah legend by a thousand years... They both cross over a great flood and are removed to the Westland to live an eternal life" — anything from death protects from death. (2) The sun's autumnal suicide in Scorpio: "The hero Gilgamesh passes through the autumn gates guarded by the Scorpio giants in going to the Westland." (3) "the hero was two-thirds divine but one-third human, and in order to be wholly divine and gain immortality he must cross the great sea to the Westland" — immortality (pre-Christian) vs eternity (Christian) as the hero's prize.

occurrences.title: Christ as Anthropos on the globe — Glanville, Le Propriétaire des choses (1482)
occurrences.label: Christ as Anthropos on the globe
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the Gnostic quadripartite original man… as well as Christ Pantokrator is an imago lapidis
body: Plate 64: "Christ as Anthropos, standing on the globe, flanked by the four elements." Jung reads it beside the Gnostic quadripartite original man: "Consequently the Gnostic quadripartite original man (fig. 64) as well as Christ Pantokrator is an imago lapidis" (¶173) — the original-man figure and the philosopher's stone are one archetype in different theologies.

The plate shows the translation chain Jung traces in the ape commentary: Thoth → Hermes Trismegistus → Mercurius → the transforming substance as totality of four, culminating in the mystical homo maximus (¶173).

occurrences.title: Glaucus and Polyeides: the snake's herb revives the dead
occurrences.label: Glaucus and Polyeides
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: "A Greek saga recounts that the hero Glaucus, sitting next to the corpse of his murdered friend Polyeides, catches sight of a snake, which he slays. Thereafter a second snake appears, fetches an herb, returns, and reanimates its dead friend. At this they disappear together and leave the herb for Glaucus, who revives his friend Polyeides with it".

"This motif emerges in identical form in the Grimm fairy tale 'The Three Snake Leaves,' and in numerous other fairy tales." The snake is not only the guardian of the herb of life but essentially identical with it — as with Gilgamesh's stolen plant, which the snake "takes back what is hers."

occurrences.title: 'In this fire God himself glows in divine love' — Gloria mundi
occurrences.label: In this fire God himself glows in divine love
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The anonymous Gloria mundi describes the philosophers' unquenchable fire in which 'God himself glows in divine love' together with the sun — fire that 'purifies, as purgatory does in the lower regions' (¶201). 'The Philosophers call this fire the fire of the Holy Ghost'; it unites Mercurius with the sun 'so that all three make but one thing', just as the Trinity is three Persons in one God (¶202). The same fire is 'the dragon that burns furiously like hell-fire' (¶203). Jung: God glows in the subterranean fire — the unity of the symbol implies the identity of the opposites (¶199).

occurrences.title: Justin's gnosis — Elohim and Edem, twelve and twelve angels, Baruch and Naas (Elenchos V, 26)
occurrences.label: Justin's gnosis — Elohim and Edem, twelve…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: The passage of Justin's gnosis Jung mines in the Miss X commentary: the "Father" (Elohim) begets with Edem — half woman, half snake — twelve "fatherly" angels; Edem bears besides twelve "motherly" angels, the shadows of the fatherly ones; the motherly divide into four categories of three, corresponding to the four rivers of Paradise, and dance round in a circle (¶552). Third of the fatherly angels is Baruch, the tree of life; his counterpart Naas (the serpent), the tree of knowledge, torments the pneuma left by Elohim in man (¶560). Edem is the soul, Elohim the spirit; "Naas is the same as the snakelike Nous and mercurial serpent of alchemy"; her snake-maiden figure became the androgynous Mercurius of medieval alchemy.

occurrences.title: The laughing goat, the two white snakes, and the swallowed black snake (patient visions, 3-18 Mar 1931)
occurrences.label: The laughing goat, the two white snakes…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Then I suddenly stood up in anger and seized the black snake. I swallowed it.
body: A laughing goat — instinct, not opinion, leading ("instead of the animus who usually appears... it is a goat") — takes her down many steps into a black cavern: the abdomen, the "snake cellar," below the tree-mandala's roots. Two large white snakes and a small black snake with green eyes await her. The white pair announces the opposites at peace — "We are night and day, we are good and evil, we are your two eyes, your two hands, your two feet" — interchangeable, symmetrical like the body. The black snake coils round her left leg (the unconscious, ill-omened side): the new, unknown disturbing element, the Kundalini-analog, "the psychical tail of man reaching down into history."

When she stops struggling it speaks: "While you walk we are coiled about you, while you rest we are beside you." Then in anger she seizes and swallows it — assimilation, as at Eleusis and in the Sabazios rite.

occurrences.title: Goclenius, Uranoscopiae... contemplatio (Frankfurt 1608) — the doctors' astrology textbook
occurrences.label: Goclenius, Uranoscopiae... contemplatio
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: "I have a little text-book of medicine written by a famous Wurzburg professor towards the end of the sixteenth century. It deals with astrology, phrenology, palmistry, and physiognomy, and was especially for the use of doctors. The author was practically the last of the official professors of astrology." Editorial note identifies it: Rodolphus Goclenius, Uranoscopiae, chiroscopiae, metoposcopiae et ophthalmoscopiae contemplatio (Frankfurt, 1608), cited again in Jung's foreword to Julius Spier, The Hands of Children (CW 18, par. 1818). Exhibit for astrology as "our psychology in its oldest form", university-legitimate until the seventeenth century.

occurrences.title: Indian god-carriages: eight-wheeled mandalas with the divine couple under the baldachin
occurrences.label: Indian god-carriages
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: "In India, for example, the gods are drawn in big rectangular carriages with eight wheels, built in the form of a mandala. On each of these carriages full of woodcarvings there stands a pagoda, in which the god or the divine couple is sitting under a baldachin. So the deity is at the center of the mandala".

"The form of the mandala indicates perfection... The fourness stands in relation to the four horizon points and the four seasons. The roundness is complete fulfillment. The divine couple in the carriage is also a symbol of completeness: the feminine and the masculine are together." From here Jung unfolds the transitus of the gods — Egypt's barque, processions of god-images, the roaming totemistic ancestors — against which the dream's devil-driven carriage is the negative transitus.

occurrences.title: Jewish legend: God the cloud contracts — lightning as the first ray of light
occurrences.label: Jewish legend — God the cloud contracts
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: There is a similar Jewish legend that God was originally a cloud or a gas and entirely alone, whatever he touched he found to be himself, and he could stand it no longer; so he contracted and became a sort of thunder cloud, whereupon something like lightning suddenly burst out of him as the first ray of light.
body: The contraction-creation schema (structurally the Lurianic tzimtzum): solitude becomes intolerable; self-contraction makes room; the first light — the sun — is the first "other". For Jung the legend maps the analysand's position: consciousness that admits it makes nothing is "all alone in one's psyche, like the creator before the creation"; the training of the initiations consists in letting something un-created happen — "then one is no longer alone."

occurrences.title: Unas lives on his fathers and feeds on his mothers — Pyramid Texts
occurrences.label: Unas lives on his fathers and feeds…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Unas rising as a soul, like a god who liveth upon his fathers and feedeth upon his mothers.
body: The oldest Egyptian god-eating text, cited by Jung as parallel to the Aztec teoqualo and to the Consilium coniugii's "the parents are the food of the son": "Unas rising as a soul, like a god who liveth upon his fathers and feedeth upon his mothers" (¶22).

Jung's point is typological: the same archetypal structure — the new thing born from the consumed opposites — appears in a funerary liturgy of the third millennium BCE, in Aztec ritual, and in the 15th-century Latin alchemical allegory, without historical filiation. Distinct from the existing Unas locus (the ladder to heaven in god-image-unas-ladder-pyramid-texts-2350-bce.md); this is the cannibalistic Unas of Utterance 217ff.

occurrences.title: The radiating eye in the triangle — church decoration
occurrences.label: The radiating eye in the triangle
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: in every Catholic church and even in Protestant churches, the deity is represented as the radiating eye in the center of a triangle, the mirroring image of human consciousness.
body: The eye-in-triangle of church decoration read psychologically: 'By that we declare God as an eye, and that our consciousness is that eye; in other words, God has made man so that he might see in the darkness.' Jung's compaction of his doctrine that human consciousness is metaphysically of enormous importance. Parallels: diogenes-lantern-seeking-man-athens-4cbce · comma-johanneum-heavenly-witnesses-vulgate-800.

occurrences.title: Cabalistic legend: God's headache and the birth of the Son as first light
occurrences.label: Cabalistic legend — God's headache…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: and grew to such an extent that he got a terrible headache from it, and realized that there should be something that was not himself.
body: The legend Jung "told you before": in the beginning God was all alone; his loneliness grew "to such an extent that he got a terrible headache from it, and realized that there should be something that was not himself." The vaporous cloud of all-that-is was condensed, "and suddenly a light burnt through, and that was the Son, the first ray of Light" (cf. John 1:9).

Jung's frame: man is indispensable to God — "Without man, God could do nothing... God finds himself in a very helpless condition." Dr Baynes' parallel, endorsed by Jung, is Prajapati: "Exactly the same idea — the extraordinary loneliness of God and his helplessness." With it goes Meister Eckhart: God "must be born through the soul of man again and again".

occurrences.title: A gifted boy of sixteen's revelation: God like an adolescent (Switzerland, ~mid-1920s)
occurrences.label: A gifted boy of sixteen's revelation
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: It was his dearest revelation.
body: Jung's spontaneous modern confirmation of Wells' boy-God: "I have seen a young boy in this country, a gifted boy of sixteen, who had a religious revelation and who gave me his idea of God, which was just like this one of Wells; it was his dearest revelation."

The evidence-value lies in its independence: the boy presumably did not derive his God-image from Wells' much-reproached book — the adolescent God is produced afresh by the religious function of the unconscious, matching what Goethe put into Faust, Goetz into his brown-capped boys, and the patient's own dream of the flying boy. One row of the Boy-symbol's living presence "in our time."

occurrences.title: R. Ishmael's vision: Akathriel Jah Yahweh Zebaoth asks for man's blessing
occurrences.label: R. Ishmael's vision
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Palestine (setting of R. Ishmael b. Elisha, 2nd c.); redacted in Bavli, Berakoth 7a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: "I once entered the innermost sanctuary to offer incense, and there I saw Akathriel Jah Yahweh Zebaoth seated upon a high and exalted throne. He said to me, Ishmael, my son, bless me!". Ishmael blesses God: "May it be Thy will that Thy mercy may suppress Thy anger."

Jung sets this at the end of a midrash chain showing the effect of Job's contradictory God-image: Yahweh's justice and love as his two hands, the destroyer who "even begins with the righteous," God praying to himself that his mercy prevail, sinners hidden under his throne (pars. 106-111).

occurrences.title: Amitābha, Buddha of the setting sun, with the vessel of immortality-food
occurrences.label: Amitābha, Buddha of the setting sun…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Central Asia → China, Japan (sutra highly valued in Japan)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: The theistic-Buddhist God-image of the sutra: one of the five Dhyāni-Buddhas brought forth by the Ādi-Buddha or Mahābuddha, the Primordial Buddha — "Amitābha, 'the Buddha of the setting sun of immeasurable light,' the Lord of Sukhāvatī, land of supreme bliss" — protector of the present world-period as Shākyamuni is its teacher (cw11 ¶912).

Jung notes with surprise the eucharistic element: "In the cult of Amitābha there is, oddly enough, a kind of Eucharistic feast with consecrated bread. He is sometimes depicted holding in his hand the vessel of the life-giving food of immortality, or the vessel of holy water" (¶912). He is "the dispenser of the water of immortality" (¶916).

occurrences.title: Anselm's ontological proof (Bec/Canterbury, ~1077–78)
occurrences.label: Anselm's ontological proof
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The ontological argument is neither argument nor proof, but merely the psychological demonstration of the fact that there is a class of men for whom a definite idea has efficacy and reality — a reality that even rivals the world of perception.
body: For Jung the ontological argument is the great document of the realist type: Anselm, "a true Platonist," locates the universals in the divine Logos, and the proof that God exists because he is thought is "merely the psychological demonstration of the fact that there is a class of men for whom a definite idea has efficacy and reality — a reality that even rivals the world of perception" (¶61). Its "logical weakness" needs a psychological explanation: for the realist "it seemed simply impossible to suppose that what to them was most valuable and significant should not really exist" (¶59). Kant's hundred-thalers refutation (¶63–65) is itself the "power of illusion" of word-magic at work; the true tertium is neither intellectus nor res but esse in anima (¶66).

occurrences.title: 'Before Christ was imagined in us, God was more terrible' — Aquarium sapientum
occurrences.label: Before Christ was imagined in us, God was more…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Deus, antequam Christus filius eius in nobis formatus imaginatusque fuit, nobis potius terribilis Deus
body: The Aquarium sapientum states the alchemical psychology of the God-image with startling economy: "Deus, antequam Christus filius eius in nobis formatus imaginatusque fuit, nobis potius terribilis Deus" — before Christ his son was formed and imagined in us, God was more terrible to us. The divine image is not given ready-made; it must be formed and imagined in the soul, and until then the numen is pure terror.

Jung cites this in the chapter on the mental prerequisites of the work: it is the alchemists' version of his thesis that God-image contents undergo projection and must be consciously realized (cf. cw12 Part I on the God-image in the psyche). The phrase "in nobis formatus imaginatusque fuit" also grounds his later active-imagination vocabulary: imagination as opus.

occurrences.title: The Arian controversy: homoousia vs homoiousia (Eastern Roman Empire, ~320)
occurrences.label: The Arian controversy: homoousia vs homoiousia
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The conflict came to light again in an altered form — which, though doctrinally attenuated, had an even graver effect on Church politics — about the year 320 in the Arian heresy.
body: The archetype of Jung's historical type-conflicts: the substance-formula of the Godhead as battleground of psychological attitudes. Arius denied the orthodox homoousia (of one substance with the Father) in favour of homoiousia (of like substance). Jung reads the pair as accent-markers: "homoiousia definitely puts the accent on the sensuous and humanly perceptible, in contrast to the purely conceptual and abstract standpoint of homoousia" (¶31). Beneath it lie the older Ebionite (purely human Christ) vs Docetist (purely divine Christ) creeds, and ahead the Monophysite–Dyophysite quarrel of Chalcedon — "the same psychology concealed" under new forms (¶35). He adds the sober caveat that for the masses the dogma was mere catchword; only "for those who kindled the quarrel" was it "a very serious matter" (¶32).

occurrences.title: Triumphal song of the ascending soul — 'I am the god Atum' (Egypt)
occurrences.label: Triumphal song of the ascending soul
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Egyptian funerary text (New Kingdom?, dating inferred)
body: An ancient Egyptian funerary text cited by Jung as representing deification "very beautifully, as the triumphal song of the ascending soul": "I am the god Atum, I who alone was. I am the god Ra at his first appearing. I am the great god who created himself... I was yesterday and know tomorrow; the battle-ground of the gods was made when I spoke" (¶133).

The dead soul washes in the two great pools of Heracleopolis, enters "the land of the glorified," and joins the fathers: "I am daily together with my father Atum... I am become one of you." Jung reads the refrain through the parental-imago lens: religious feeling is rooted in "memories of archetypal intuitions" of earliest infancy — "I am in my country, I come into my city. I am daily together with my father Atum" (¶¶134, 139... the hymn recurs in the discussion of regressive reactivation, ¶134).

occurrences.title: Ascension of Isaiah: Sammael and the graded seven heavens
occurrences.label: Ascension of Isaiah
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Isaiah's rapture through the seven heavens: first "Sammael and his hosts, against whom a 'great battle' was raging in the firmament"; then thrones whose right-hand angels sing more beautifully than the left, splendour rising heaven by heaven.

Jung's reading: the devil, like the Gnostic archons, dwells in the firmament (astrological gods); his sphere interpenetrates the divine sphere, "complementary opposites balancing one another like right and left hands" — "a genuine yang-yin relationship... which the Jesuits quite logically translated as 'God'" (Tao). Pre-Manichaean, hence free of defensive dualism.

occurrences.title: 'The Bank-note Monopoly, Queen of the Orphans' — the dressmaker's cosmic self-exaltation (Burghölzli, 1886-1908)
occurrences.label: The Bank-note Monopoly, Queen of the Orphans
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A Zurich dressmaker, born 1845, industrious and secluded, fell ill in 1886 "on the threshold of the age when so many dreams are brought to naught." For twenty years "the absurdity of her delusions exceeded anything the boldest imagination could devise" — the classic demonstration-case of "meaningless" dementia praecox (¶364, ¶368). Decoded: "The Bank-note Monopoly, Queen of the Orphans, Proprietress of Burghölzli Asylum," supplying the world with macaroni from Naples (¶365); "I am Noah's Ark, the boat of salvation and respect" (¶366); "triple owner of the world," owner of the "key of heaven," Queen of Heaven, Mother of God, "and at the same time the Godhead," with three husbands and the Emperor Francis, two phantom children, a Czar son (¶380-382). She identified with Socrates, Mary Stuart, the Lorelei, "a crane" (Cranes of Ibycus), Schiller's Bell, Hufeland, the master-key (¶370-379).

Jung's reading: compensatory wish-fulfilment of a life of "poverty and wretchedness" (¶380), parallel to Hauptmann's Hannele (¶381); a fairy-tale world with "tables... ever laden" (¶383); "even the most absurd things are nothing other than symbols" (¶387). Restated 1928 as the paradigm of "countless subjects and no central ego" (¶500).

occurrences.title: Christ and Barabbas — the year-god exchange (Passover, Jerusalem)
occurrences.label: Christ and Barabbas — the year-god exchange
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939
Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "That is expressed in the Christian mystery where Christ is chosen instead of the criminal Barabbas. (That name also means 'the son of the father.')... To the church, the better man is the worse."

The January 1936 engagement completes it: "It was like putting to death the god of the past year, as Christ was put to death instead of Barabbas whom the people wanted to have released as the god of the coming year. Christ was condemned as the criminal representing the god of the past year, according to the old Babylonian custom. And... Barabbas means 'son of the father,' just as Christ was the son of the Father; so it is one and the same — the god in its going down and in its coming up."
Row: the child-pelote sacrifice rumor, the Easter burial of the Hallelujah, the jeu de pelote.

occurrences.title: The brother as Bismarck, Napoleon, Caesar — arrogant businessman's dreams (Zurich, ~1900s)
occurrences.label: The brother as Bismarck, Napoleon, Caesar
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The brother frequently came into his dreams, always in the role of a Bismarck, Napoleon, or Julius Caesar. His house looked like the Vatican or Yildiz Kiosk.
body: A "somewhat arrogant gentleman" in partnership with his younger brother dreamed of the brother repeatedly — "always in the role of a Bismarck, Napoleon, or Julius Caesar," while the brother's house "looked like the Vatican or Yildiz Kiosk" (¶279).

Jung's reading: since the figures are "universally recognized heroes" — "of a definitely collective nature" (¶283) — the dream does not flatter the brother but corrects the dreamer: "he was setting himself too high and his brother too low." The compensation had to be collective because the arrogance radiated "not only... [to] himself, but [to] a far wider social group" (¶283). Inflation checked by collective hero-images, the exact inverse of the witch-mother dreams of his next case.

occurrences.title: God in the flaming bush — Jahveh's theophany, Exodus 3
occurrences.label: God in the flaming bush
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The burning bush from which Jahveh speaks to Moses — the classic Old Testament theophany in fire.

In Jung's reading of Nietzsche's dithyrambic outburst it anchors the thesis that God is "the unknown partner, the real partner of man": the book "begins, practically, with the statement that God is dead, but you can see throughout the book that Nietzsche never gets rid of him." In any former age "they would have said a god possessed him and was speaking out of him. In Nietzsche the god for the time being is Zarathustra."

Verbatim: "You can name God what you like but he always appears in the fire. In the Old Testament he appears in the flaming bush, which is simply the dithyrambic enthusiasm of God breaking out anew in ecstasy; he was then called 'Jahveh' and here it is 'Zarathustra' but it is the same thing".

occurrences.title: Clementine Homilies: good and evil as the two hands of God
occurrences.label: Clementine Homilies
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The unknown author of the Clementine Homilies "understands good and evil as the right and left hand of God, and views the whole of creation in terms of syzygies, or pairs of opposites". God appointed two kingdoms and two ages; he kills with the left hand and saves with the right (Deut. 32:39); body and spirit are "two triads," and the mixing of the four elements begot choice "as a child" (pars. 100-101).
For Jung this pre-Manichaean, reflective God-image "guarantees that unity on a plane beyond" the Yahweh/Christian split and comes "closer to the actual truth than the privatio boni."

occurrences.title: Maximum cui nihil opponitur — Nicholas of Cusa's coincidentia oppositorum
occurrences.label: Maximum cui nihil opponitur
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Maximum autem est, cui nihil opponitur, ubi et Minimum est Maximum.
body: The Cusanus block at the close of the New Birth notes: the Maximum as that to which nothing is opposed, where Minimum and Maximum coincide; man as contracted God and contracted world; the coincidence of contradictoria as the goal of learned ignorance.
Jung notes that Cusanus "regarded antinomial thought as the highest form of reasoning" — the philosophical charter for the essay's own antinomian method.

occurrences.title: The girl's dream: Jung as god of the cornfields (Zurich, ~early 1900s)
occurrences.label: The girl's dream: Jung as god of the cornfields
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~early 1900s ('quite at the beginning of my career')
occurrences.quote: I appeared, for instance, the size of a god, standing in the fields and holding her in my arms as if she were a baby, and the wind was blowing over the corn and the fields were waving like waves of water, and in the same way I rocked her in my arms.
body: A student of philosophy developed a "terrific father-transference" to the young Jung: "I was her father, brother, son, lover, husband — and, of course, also her hero and saviour — every thinkable thing!" Reasoning failed ("But I can't live without it"). Watching her dreams seriously, he saw Jung-figure grow "much bigger than an ordinary human being," then take divine form:

His conclusion — "that girl needs a god; at least, her unconscious needs a god" — and his admission of the need rather than its depreciation changed everything: "I cured that case, because I fulfilled the need of the unconscious." (¶634)

occurrences.title: Psalm 89 — Yahweh's covenant with David and its breach
occurrences.label: Psalm 89 — Yahweh's covenant with David…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: The divine oath "I will not lie to David" (¶569) followed by its manifest breach — David's answer quoted at ¶571 ("Lord, where are thy former lovingkindnesses?"). For Jung this broken contract is the literary deposit that "grieved some few of the devout, who upon reading it became reflective", and "it is historically possible that these considerations influenced the author of the Book of Job" (¶578).
A later document tells of a pious sage who could never read the Psalm 89 "because he could not bear it" (¶685) — evidence of the wound the passage leaves in the religious consciousness.

occurrences.title: The Goddess of Reason enthroned in Notre-Dame (1793)
occurrences.label: The Goddess of Reason enthroned in Notre-Dame
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The Festival of Reason: Notre-Dame desecrated, la deesse Raison enthroned and worshipped in place of the Christian god; wholesale slaughter, a king killed — "simply unheard of."

Jung: "It was the first time in history that the Christian god was dethroned... values began rattling down like anything, as they are today." The dethronement broke the church's magic system that had "settled once and forever" the shadow-domain — and the problem of the opposites reappeared "in the psychology of man," first in Schiller, then Schopenhauer, then Nietzsche.

Verbatim: "It was the first time in history that the Christian god was dethroned. l'otre Dame was desecrated and la deesse Raison put upon the throne and worshipped instead of the Christian god." (pdf p146, OCR as in text)

occurrences.title: 'I disinfected the whole heavens… but I found no God' — mental patient's saying (Zurich, c.1900s)
occurrences.label: I disinfected the whole heavens… but I found no…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Doctor, last night I disinfected the whole heavens with bichloride of mercury, but I found no God.
body: One of Jung's favourite patient utterances, dropped into the argument on the God-function: "As a mental patient once told me: 'Doctor, last night I disinfected the whole heavens with bichloride of mercury, but I found no God.'"

Jung's reading: "Something of the sort has happened to us as well" (¶110) — the culture-wide rationalist sterilization of the sky. It caps his claim that the idea of God is "an absolutely necessary psychological function of an irrational nature", and that the Enlightenment's disposal of the gods only drove the function underground, poisoning the modern psyche with its surplus libido (¶¶110–111, 150–151). A diagnosis of disenchantment in one psychotic sentence.

occurrences.title: 'Since the English are in the country we have no dreams any more' — Elgon medicine man
occurrences.label: Since the English are in the country we have no…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: southern slopes of Mount Elgon, East Africa (Kenya)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: dreams were formerly the supreme political guide, the voice of Mungu, ‘God.’
body: Jung's field datum from the Elgon palaver. Asking about the ghost-houses (little temples in the woods), he pronounced the word selelteni ('ghost') aloud — "Instantly everybody was silent and painfully embarrassed": a carefully hushed-up word whose utterance invites dangerous consequences. The tribesmen claimed never to dream: dreams "were the prerogative of the chief and of the medicine man." The medicine man then confessed that he no longer dreamed either — they had the District Commissioner instead: "Since the English are in the country we have no dreams any more… The District Commissioner knows everything about war and diseases, and about where we have got to live."

Jung's reading: "This strange statement is based on the fact that dreams were formerly the supreme political guide, the voice of Mungu, 'God'" — so divine-voiced dreams devolved, under colonial rule, onto the worldly authority. One of Jung's clearest ethnographic loci for the dream as vox Dei.

occurrences.title: Meister Eckhart — the godhead must be born in the soul
occurrences.label: Meister Eckhart — the godhead must be born…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "The godhead in itself is not blissful, but must be born in the soul of man again and again: only then does it become God... God is forced to go through that narrow doorway, the gate of man, in order to become God. That is the teaching of Master Eckhart, and that is also the meaning of the Christian mystery, that God first became man and underwent the most miserable fate in order to become God."

Told against Nietzsche's "a God wilt thou create for thyself out of thy seven devils": "It is not he who is creating a god... but the god is creating himself" — like Ptah, builder of his own egg, potter of his own mold; it is the Phoenix myth.
Editor: Jung elsewhere credits Eckhart as, in Europe, the first for whom "the self begins to play a noticeable role."

occurrences.title: 'Fear first made gods in the world' — Statius, Thebaid 3.661
occurrences.label: Fear first made gods in the world
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: ch.7 fn 9 (pdf p605; main text ch.7, Worringer's argument ~¶289-91)

occurrences.quote: Primus in orbe deos fecit timor (fear was what first brought gods into the world).
body: In the aesthetics chapter Jung quotes Worringer's dictum "Primus in orbe deos fecit timor" — fear was what first brought gods into the world — as the formulation of the introverting, abstracting relation to a terrifying object-world. The editors' footnote quietly corrects the source: "Worringer was mistaken about both the author and the quotation. The above words cannot be traced in Tibullus. But the following may be found in Statius (Thebaid, Book 3, line 661)." (The CW6 index still carries the wrong attribution: "Tibullus, 291&n".)

Jung's reading: the gods as projections of affect — dread objectified into numen — the genesis-myth of the God-image out of fear that Worringer, and Jung after him, set against the empathetic (extraverted) deification of the world.

occurrences.title: The giant wind-father in the wheat-fields — woman patient's dream (Zurich, c.1910s)
occurrences.label: The giant wind-father in the wheat-fields
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The wind swept over the wheat-fields, and as the wheat swayed in the wind, he rocked her in his arms.
body: In the transference deadlock of the father-complex case (c.1910), the patient's dreams swell the doctor "to ever vaster proportions". In one: her small-statured father stands with her on a hill of wheat-fields, a giant; he lifts her like a little child and rocks her as the wind sweeps the wheat.

Jung's reading: the dreams disintegrate the personal doctor and build a "transpersonal control-point" — "a gigantic primordial father who is at the same time the wind" (¶217). The god-image is archaic, "a naturedaemon, something like Wotan", matching pneuma = wind and Hebrew ruach — not the Christian old-man-on-a-throne. Here Jung first watches the unconscious reach past the human person "towards a god" (¶214) — the founding observation of Essay II.

occurrences.title: God and devil's wager over Faust (Prologue in Heaven, Faust I)
occurrences.label: God and devil's wager over Faust
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Another case was the meeting between God and the devil, when they agreed what should be done to that miserable creature Faust.
body: Goethe's Prologue in Heaven, where the Lord and Mephistopheles agree on what shall be done to "that miserable creature Faust" — Jung's second example, beside the heavenly wager over Job, of God and devil conferring over a human victim.

Jung's reading: "when a great personality is to be created, integrated in other words, then the four come together. For other people it is not necessary; they are decided by the Trinity alone or by the devil alone." The wager-scene stages the integration of Satan into the Trinity — the quaternity that consciousness must reach in its own psychology ("you are not three but four").

occurrences.title: 'God works in me like a clock' — patient at St. Elizabeth Hospital, Washington (1911)
occurrences.label: God works in me like a clock
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: (pdf p950; cf. CW5 par. 154, CW6 par. 747, CW18 pars. 81ff)

occurrences.quote: God is inside, God works in me like a clock, funny and serious.
body: A "mad old Negro woman" Jung examined in the insane asylum in Washington during his 1911 Fordham trip, speaking of her religious experiences: "God is not up there, that is what they say but I know better, God is inside, God works in me like a clock, funny and serious."

Jung's use (25 January 1933): the sthula aspect of the greatest religious experience — rebirth and renewal. The God within sounds grotesque from outside, "very dark, and it might look very ridiculous," just as the disciples at Pentecost were taken for men "full of sweet wine." To know what a thing is worth one must know both aspects; the patient strikes down her own veiled "indifference" figure for exactly such an outer-aspect humiliation.

occurrences.title: Vision: the dark head with the cross-nimbus — the poimen announced
occurrences.label: Vision — the dark head with the cross-nimbus
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Then another figure appeared-a human head but dark as if in shadow, and around it a halo.
body: On the afternoon after the four-valleys dream was analyzed, she saw "a human head but dark as if in shadow, and around it a halo." Jung: a head one might find in the catacombs — "It is like the sun halo of the gods of the Mithraic cult" (p111); the nimbus of saints and old emperors (blue or green for emperors, gold for saints, p111). He had told her nothing of the poimen: "That the poimen interpretation is right is confirmed by the visions that follow" (p111). The patient saw only a wheel: "she had never heard of a sun-wheel, which is one of the most ancient forms of sun symbol" (p111). Of the whole anticipatory series: "It is the first picture and it sums up all that is to come, it is the whole truth in a nutshell-an amazing fact" (p110). Followed by the double goblet, the wigwam (the seer's dwelling), and the spear shot at the moon.

occurrences.title: The Hasidic girl who forsook the mystery of her race (Zurich, ~1930s)
occurrences.label: The Hasidic girl who forsook the mystery…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A pretty, "murderously" intelligent Jewish girl with years of intractable anxiety neurosis. The night before she first came, Jung dreamt of a young girl whose case he could not fathom until the thought struck: "Hasn't she an extraordinary father complex!" — a hunch that led him to ask about her family: "she came from a Hasidic family — you know, those great mystics. Her grandfather had been a sort of wonder-rabbi — he had second sight"; her father had broken from the mystic community (¶635).

Jung told her: "you have been untrue to your God... you have forsaken the mystery of your race... No wonder that you fear God." "Within one week I had cured that anxiety neurosis" — she had tried "to live with her miserable intellect alone in a perfectly banal world, when in fact she was a child of God and should have lived the symbolic life" (¶636).

occurrences.title: Hitler's picture on Christian altars — Germany
occurrences.label: Hitler's picture on Christian altars — Germany
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: There are people who confess on their tombstones that they died in peace since their eyes had beheld not the Lord but the Führer.
body: The God-image displaced onto the Führer, reported as observed fact: "Hitler's picture has been erected upon Christian altars," with tombstone confessions of dying "in peace since their eyes had beheld not the Lord but the Führer" (cw18 ¶1329). Jung reads it as the State-ghost incarnating itself (¶1325) — the archetypal material of paranoid schizophrenia at national scale — and returns to it in 1945: a "poorly gifted housepainter" placed "quite literally on the altar of totalitarianism, otherwise reserved for a theocracy" (¶1372).

occurrences.title: The Communion controversy: Luther vs Zwingli (1520s)
occurrences.label: The Communion controversy: Luther vs Zwingli
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In the last resort, both points of view are mutually exclusive.
body: Jung's closing case-study of the type problem in church history: Luther "was unable to perceive in [bread and wine] a mere sign; the sensuous reality and the immediate experience of it were for him an indispensable religious necessity," claiming the actual presence of Christ's body "in and beneath" the bread (consubstantiation, later volipresence), while Zwingli "championed a purely symbolic conception" — a "spiritual" partaking (¶96–98). Jung resists reading Luther as mere traditionalist: it was "an acknowledgement, demanded by Luther's own psychology, of the fact of feeling grounded upon the immediate sense-impression" (¶97). "Luther's formulation favours the extraverted conception of things, while Zwingli's favours the ideal standpoint" (¶99). The chapter closes having "done no more than pose the question" (¶100).

occurrences.title: 'Glory to God' dream poem — Miss Frank Miller (at sea, 1898)
occurrences.label: Glory to God' dream poem — Miss Frank Miller
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The founding locus of Symbols of Transformation: the dream that ended with a three-stanza hymn in which the Creator makes Sound, then Light, then Love, each answered by "All glory to the God of Sound/Light/Love!" Its prelude: "when the morning stars sang together" (Job 38:7), mixed with Paradise Lost and Handel's Creation (¶¶60-61).

Jung's reading: after a deliberate introversion on the voyage, the erotic impression of the night-watching singer — underappreciated, half-repressed — regressed to the father-imago and produced the Creator-God: "by the devious route of the father-imago relationship, the night-watching singer becomes the Creator, the God of Sound, of Light and of Love" (¶83). Hence the chain "the singer — the singing morning star — the God of Sound — the Creator — the God of Light — of the sun — of fire — and of Love" (¶65). Her parting "Only this, and nothing more!" quotes Poe's raven of lost Lenore (¶¶81-83).

occurrences.title: 'God is not good' — Meister Eckhart on the divine freedom
occurrences.label: God is not good' — Meister Eckhart…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: In the discussion of Nietzsche's "in sublimity there is malice," Jung produces his authority: "Therefore I always fight against it when the theologians say God is good. Meister Eckhart says God is not good because if he were good he could be better. That is true. Moreover I would say he loses his freedom because he is then bound to be good, can do nothing but good, which would be a very grave restriction to his omnipotence and is surely not meant".
