The thought ties the passage together: anyone who is nothing but good "is a victim of it"; "all the shadow and evil is suppressed and naturally pours forth somewhere else." Hence the compensation law: "Children of very good people must become morally defective in order to compensate for that goodness" — and the same holds for sublimity, whose partners pay for it. Nietzsche's Superman "beyond good and evil" is, for Jung, the self, of which responsibility and irresponsibility are both aspects.

occurrences.title: White face of God, sun, pool of gold — the highest value descends into the earth (patient vision, 25 Feb 1931)
occurrences.label: White face of God, sun, pool of gold
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I passed the white face of God, I saw the sun, and I saw a pool of gold. Then I was in a great dark forest.
body: Carried in the blood-spiral she passes three "secondary visions, like visualized thoughts": the white face of God — "that late Christian bloodless figure" — then the sun, "deeper, more primitive... more real," then a pool of gold embedded in the earth at her feet. Jung reads the sequence through the theory of the highest value: God, then sun, then gold — the god-image sinking chthonic ward, "her God lived in the earth... in the safe or the bank," the yellow god people really fear to lose. Miss Wolff adds the alchemical equation: sun and gold are identical, gold the terrestrial sun. Dr. Reichstein's suggestion — "the first indication of the Self" — Jung takes up: perhaps the pool of gold is her Self, "a tremendous treasure in the earth."

occurrences.title: Light, wind, and the visited heart — Riklin's paranoid megalomania case (Zürich)
occurrences.label: Light, wind, and the visited heart
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: fn 51 to ch. V, The Song of the Moth (pdf p692); index 'Riklin ... megalomanic phase, 102n'

body: Jung records a case from "my late colleague Dr. Franz Riklin": a paranoid woman passing into manifest megalomania. "She suddenly saw a strong light, a wind blew upon her, she felt as if her 'heart turned over,' and from that moment she knew that God had visited her and was in her." The pneuma-formula — light plus wind as divine insemination — the same equation Jung traces through Anaxagoras, the Stoic primal warmth, and the Mithraic liturgy in the surrounding footnotes.
Verbatim (fn 51): "She suddenly saw a strong light, a wind blew upon her, she felt as if her “heart turned over,” and from that moment she knew that God had visited her and was in her."

occurrences.title: The invisible sun / imago Dei within — Dorn, Philosophia meditativa
occurrences.label: The invisible sun / imago Dei within
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 16th c. Dorn; cited from Theatr. chem. I (1602)

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

occurrences.quote: the truth is to be sought not in ourselves, but in the image of God which is within us
body: Dorn on the light "of men" shining dimly in us: "He has implanted that light in us that we may see in its light the light of Him Who dwells in inaccessible light... He has given us a spark of His light. Thus the truth is to be sought not in ourselves, but in the image of God which is within us." "The one archetype emphasized by Khunrath is known also to Dorn as the sol invisibilis or imago Dei" (¶390) — the invisible sun in man, of one and the same sun as the visible one.

Jung's reading: the alchemical One Scintilla, Monad and sol invisibilis converge on the symbol of the self (¶388); Dorn's implanted spark is the theological dress of the lumen naturae that illuminates consciousness (¶389).

occurrences.title: Teresa of Avila's coach mishap — 'That's how I treat my friends' (Spain, ~1570s)
occurrences.label: Teresa of Avila's coach mishap
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Lord, how can you permit such things?” “Well, that’s how I treat my friends.” “Aha, that’s why you have so few!
body: In the discussion following "Good and Evil in Analytical Psychology" (1959) Jung tells of Teresa of Avila whose coach broke down crossing a small river and who "fell into the icy water." Her complaint and the reply she receives — "Lord, how can you permit such things?" / "Well, that's how I treat my friends." / "Aha, that's why you have so few!" — form one of Jung's favorite God-as-prankster texts (cf. his use of the Book of Job material).

Jung's reading: Teresa "had got into a situation where evil — in this case physical evil — was done to her; she did not know how to integrate it, but nevertheless felt God's immediate presence" (¶883). It instances the "closed" situation, the aporia "where whatever we choose is not good," surrounded "on all sides by God, who can bring about either the one or the other" — the Old Testament logic of a God who does evil, standing against the privatio boni Jung doubts in the same discussion (¶879).

occurrences.title: Clement of Rome — God rules with right and left hand (Christ and Satan)
occurrences.label: Clement of Rome — God rules with right…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Pre-Manichaean monotheism of the opposites: before the privatio boni entered the Church, Clement taught that God governs the world with a right and a left hand — the right being Christ, the left Satan. Jung makes this the historical baseline of Answer to Job: "Clement's view is clearly monotheistic, as it unites the opposites in one God", whereas later Christianity "is dualistic, inasmuch as it splits off one half of the opposites, personified in Satan" (Prefatory Note).
The passage anchors Jung's genealogy: whence evil (πόθεν τὸ κακόν) is "the point of departure for the Christian theory of Redemption", and the Job problem is its historical crux.

occurrences.title: Pyramid Texts of Unas: Horus and Set lead the dead up the ladder
occurrences.label: Pyramid Texts of Unas
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Saqqara (pyramid of Unas; via Budge, Gods of the Egyptians II)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: "Unas cometh forth upon the Ladder which his father Ra hath made for him, and Horus and Set take the hand of Unas, and they lead him into the Tuat". Heaven's floor is an iron plate resting on four pillars at the cardinal points; Pepi I's texts praise "the ladder of the twin gods."

Jung (par. 188): Horus/Set "represent the latent opposites contained in Osiris... just as Behemoth and Leviathan do in relation to Yahweh" — and the opposites cooperate to bring the one god to "the heavenly quaternity," personified by the four sons of Horus behind the thigh of the northern heaven, analogues of Ezekiel's cherubim and the evangelists' symbols.

occurrences.title: The Lord commends the unjust steward — Luke 16
occurrences.label: The Lord commends the unjust steward — Luke 16
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: Now isn't that extraordinary? The Lord is glad that mortal man has just muddled through.
body: The steward about to be dismissed cuts his lord's debtors' bills in half — and the lord "commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely." Jung: "you hardly ever hear a sermon preached about the unjust steward," yet the parable "contains a precious piece of Nietzschean morality."

His reading is God-image work: the Lord "is not a fool," so his pleasure must mean that he "is merely a loving father who knows that his child cannot be good" and is "quite satisfied that the vessel he has made is not entirely broken" — "it really was a very poor work on the part of the creator-there is a bit of Gnosticism here." Man's best is to muddle through and save face — the Lord's and his own.
Like the Oxyrhynchus logia, this runs against the herd-edit: "if it had been understood really, it would have been wiped out as other passages were wiped out."

occurrences.title: 'I know that my Vindicator lives' — Job 19:25
occurrences.label: I know that my Vindicator lives' — Job 19:25
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Job's declaration amid his protestations: "Behold, my witness is in heaven, and he that vouches for me is on high" and "For I know that my Vindicator lives, and at last he will stand upon the earth" (¶566). Jung: Job is "quite certain of finding in God a helper and an 'advocate' against God" (¶567) — Yahweh is both persecutor and helper in one.

The traditional Christian reading of 19:25 as anticipating Christ is "correct in so far as Yahweh's benevolent aspect incarnates itself, as its own hypostasis, in the Son of Man"; "Just as Satan plays the role of accuser and slanderer, so Christ, God's other son, plays the role of advocate and defender" (¶684).

occurrences.title: Voice of God and blue-eyed Christ — the converted peasant girl's psychosis (Burghölzli, ~1900s)
occurrences.label: Voice of God and blue-eyed Christ
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A quiet, retiring peasant's daughter, a trained teacher, suddenly psychotic: one night "she heard the voice of God speaking to her, about war and peace and the sins of man," and "Jesus also appeared to her" — "quite like an ordinary man with blue eyes." Of it all she kept only a calendar sheet "with only a cross on it, which she had marked on the date when she heard the voice of God for the first time" (¶482). She stood all day by the stove, rocking, perfectly indifferent.

Jung excavates the aetiology (¶486-491): falling suddenly in love with "Mr. M." frightened her "by the extraordinary intensity of her feelings"; she read the feeling as a sin against God, professed conversion at a revival meeting — and the repressed love, rooted in a shaming sexual episode at sixteen (provoking an imbecile woman to obscene behaviour, ¶490), turned inward. "Her 'fonction du réel' created a world within herself... psychosis is a mental condition in which formerly unconscious elements take the place of reality" (¶491).

occurrences.title: The whirlwind theophany — Yahweh's speeches to Job (Job 38-42)
occurrences.label: The whirlwind theophany
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: God answers the lawsuit not with justice but with power: "he comes riding along on the tempest of his almightiness and thunders reproaches at the half-crushed human worm: Who is this that darkens counsel by words without insight?" (¶584). For seventy-one verses he proclaims his world-creating might (¶587) — to a listener Jung identifies as Satan's phantom projected onto Job (¶591).

The involuntary self-revelation: "This is I, the creator of all the ungovernable, ruthless forces of Nature… I, too, am an amoral force of Nature, a purely phenomenal personality that cannot see its own back" (¶605). Job's answer — "I had heard of thee by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees thee" (¶598) — registers what God did not intend to show: a Moira or Dike rules over Yahweh, who pronounces judgment on himself (¶606).

occurrences.title: The tall man with the beautiful white beard — father-God dream (Zurich, ~1897; reported Clark 1909)
occurrences.label: The tall man with the beautiful white beard
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: as if she were experiencing the presence of God himself.
body: In "The Family Constellation", Jung's patient — favourite daughter of an "impressive" father — at 17, with her first love-affair, twice dreamed the same dream: "she saw a tall masculine figure with a very beautiful white beard, at the sight of which she was filled with a feeling of awe and delight as if she were experiencing the presence of God himself." She "imputed a mystical meaning to it and often remembered it with religious awe". Asked who the bearded man was, "she immediately recognized the image. It was, of course, her father. Every time the patient began to fall in love, the image of her father arose disturbingly" and wrecked the match; married life was judged by the standard "My father would have done all this differently and better", until the neurosis and the psychotic pregnancy-fantasy broke out. The God-presence and the paternal imago are one image here, explicitly.

occurrences.title: The world as picture-book — locksmith's apprentice with megalomania (Zurich, c.1900s)
occurrences.label: The world as picture-book
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich? (case Jung knew personally; published by Maeder)
occurrences.quote: the world was his picture-book, the pages of which he could turn at will.
body: A nineteen-year-old locksmith's apprentice, "never... blessed with intelligence", incurably insane with paranoid dementia and megalomania, "in telephonic communication with the Mother of God and other great ones", "hit upon the magnificent idea that the world was his picture-book, the pages of which he could turn at will" — he need only turn round for a new page.

Jung's reading: "This is Schopenhauer's 'world as will and idea' in unadorned, primitive concreteness of vision" (¶229). The difference between the madman and the philosopher: the philosopher transmutes the vision "into an abstract idea belonging to the common stock of consciousness"; the patient is swallowed by it — "it is truer to say that the undoubted grandeur of his vision blew him up to pathological proportions". The golden apples "drop from the same tree" for both (¶229). Jung's cleanest demonstration of inflation by transpersonal content.

occurrences.title: The gods have come down — Barnabas and Paul as Zeus and Hermes at Lystra (Acts 14)
occurrences.label: The gods have come down
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: "Symptomatic of this is the significant fact that Barnabas and Paul were identified in Lystra with Zeus and Hermes: 'The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men.'" (¶656). For Jung this pagan perception of the Christian transmutation "convinces" precisely because it is naive — the deifying effect of the indwelling Holy Ghost seen from outside.

Tertullian is then adduced describing the "sublimiorem Deum" as a sort of lender of divinity "who has made gods of men"; the apostles as momentary avatars of the old gods mark the broadening incarnation ("you are gods", Ps 82, quoted ¶692).

occurrences.title: The god-representative sacrificed at sunset (Mexico, Babylonia)
occurrences.label: The god-representative sacrificed at sunset
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: they were worshipped as the gods, they themselves being very poor devils.
body: Jung's image for Nietzsche as the irrational type who involuntarily plays the god and is destroyed by the part: "those criminals or prisoners of war who were chosen to represent the gods, in Mexico and also in Babylonia. They were allowed every freedom, until the sun went down, and then they were sacrificed to the gods. In Babylonia they had the chance to escape if they could get out of town before sunset, but in Mexico there was no escape-they were simply sacrificed, but they were worshipped as the gods, they themselves being very poor devils. That is Nietzsche all over".

The instrumental man — "the puppet man," "a figure on the chess board" — gives a living account through his confession: "an unrealized and undigested experience" with "all the advantages... of an immediate and living experience."

occurrences.title: 'Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani' — the god leaves Christ on the cross (Docetic reading)
occurrences.label: Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the sequence after the hermaphrodite: "It is the moment when the god leaves Christ. According to the old idea, Christ had only a sort of apparent body, and the god had already left his body in the garden, but according to the Docetic tradition the god left him on the cross; therefore he cried: 'Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani.'"

Jung places this moment within the crucifixion symbolism that follows the hermaphroditic stage: the cross divides into opposites right/left (the two criminals — "They are very much oneself," Miss Wolff) and above/below — the four, the mandala; the four streams of Eden, the four gates of the heavenly Jerusalem, the city of Brahman on Meru.

occurrences.title: The 'rays of God' that longingly seek to enter — Schreber's Memoirs
occurrences.label: The 'rays of God' that longingly seek to enter
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung's footnote parallel to a Zohar passage on Malchuth: "There is a parallel to this in the psychotic experiences of Schreber (Memoirs of My Nervous Illness), where the 'rays of God' longingly seek to enter into him."

Schreber's 'God-nerves'/'rays of God' — fragmented divine emanations that reach toward the human — are used by Jung exactly as the Cabalistic rays of Malchuth/the Shekinah: the feminine-divine effluence seeking union with the human vessel. Psychosis here parallels the kabbalistic hierosgamos imagery.

occurrences.title: God's telephone: the B. St. case at the Burgholzli
occurrences.label: God's telephone — the B. St. case…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: nearly every day God sent her special messages
body: The old tailoress of the Burgholzli ("B. St.", the paradigm case of Jung's 1907 Dementia Praecox study) who greeted one with "Oh, I have just had a telephone" — fixed through the wall, she knew not how, "nearly every day God sent her special messages". She might say "she was empress of the whole world, or that she possessed an island that consisted of pure silver."

Jung cites her for the minor personalities that speak in dreams and in madness: fragmentary figures without realization of their surroundings; in insanity "there are always favourable and unfavourable voices — employees who are working for your interests and against your interests, pairs of opposites."

occurrences.title: God as a youth — H. G. Wells, God the Invisible King
occurrences.label: God as a youth — H. G. Wells, God the Invisible…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: So that would be the divine child. And what is the divine child? The honest attempt of man.
body: Jung cheerfully "brings in H. G. Wells": in God the Invisible King, God is a youth — "and I know that figure from innumerable dreams. We have often spoken of it, the Puer Aeternus who represents the more or less heroic attempt of man, which becomes or, in a way, takes the place of a deity."

The chapter defines the divine child for this dream-series: "What is the divine child? The honest attempt of man" — weak, embryonic, "that has to become", yet forced upon the dreamer by "a superior factor in himself, Deus ex machina". The one living triplet of dream 26 is this figure.

occurrences.title: Goethe to Lavater, 1780 — acuminate the pyramid of my existence
occurrences.label: Goethe to Lavater, 1780
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
jung.locator: pyramid amplification, paper by Aniela Jaffé (pdf p303)

occurrences.quote: the desire to acuminate the pyramid of my existence, whose base was given to me as a foundation, as high up into the air as possible, prevails over everything else
body: In Jaffé's amplification of the pyramid dream, Goethe (then thirty-one) writes to Lavater: with great aplomb he desires "to acuminate the pyramid of my existence... as high up into the air as possible," fearing only that fate may break him in two and "the Babylonian Tower will remain blunt and unfinished. At least it should be said: He was of audacious design."

The letter carries the dream's structure in reverse — man's pyramid-tower of striving from a given base toward a point — and joins the seminar's axis: base = the given body and family, apex = the dimensionless, gilded summit where the Ka is glorified.

occurrences.title: The Frog King's golden ball (Grimm)
occurrences.label: The Frog King's golden ball (Grimm)
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "Then besides the star and the wheel, there is the symbol of the golden ball. Perhaps you know the German fairy tale about the princess who lost her golden ball in a deep well where the frog prince was watching it... but when he crept into her bed, she threw him out against the wall, and then he transformed into a beautiful prince" (pdf p135–136; editor: Grimm, "The Frog King").

Jung reads it beside the star and the wheel as an individuation symbol: "Verily, Zarathustra had a goal, he threw his ball, now ye others, I throw the golden ball to you" — "meaning: I, Zarathustra, have accomplished individuation and I now throw the golden ball to you; this is the idea of the Superman again". The golden ball (wholeness, the Self) is lost to the chthonic frog and won back through the ugly encounter — the same movement Jung will trace in the shepherd and the black snake.

occurrences.title: Hiranyagarbha — the golden germ / golden child (Upanishads)
occurrences.label: Hiranyagarbha — the golden germ / golden child
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939
Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "the sun, the golden germ, the Hiranyagarbha as it is called in the Upanishads, is another symbol of the self; it is also called the golden child, the precious, perfect substance that is made by man or born out of man; and it is of course the alchemistic gold."

The second engagement names it the gold born of the opposites: "The idea of the self under the aspect of a thing born out of man or out of the world is called in the Upanishads the Hiranyagarbha, which means the golden child or the golden germ; that is the philosophical gold which comes from the union of opposites."
If the lonely Zarathustra unites with a circle of human beings, "the golden child, the god, is born, Hiranyagarbha; then the golden ball appears with the serpent."

occurrences.title: Jeu de pelote — the ritual ball game played in the church
occurrences.label: Jeu de pelote — the ritual ball game played…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "It was a symbolic game with a peculiar meaning and it was played in the church. It was a system of relatedness among the figures of the Chapter, the bishop and the deacons and so on. In the way in which they threw the ball to each other they made a certain pattern; it was generally played standing in a circle and it had to do with the making of a mandala where the center moves from one to the other. The center, that ball which moves from the one to the other, is also a god, the god as a function of relationship."

The ball is the sun, gold, perfection; the rite stages the self as the moving center of a circle of people "according to a preexistent pattern" — the exact picture of Zarathustra's thrown golden ball. Jung adds the antiquity calumny that Gnostics, Christians and Jews played pelote with a child "until it was dead. The child represented the god" — sacrifice of the year-god, Christ for Barabbas; and the Easter burial of the Hallelujah stands beside it.

occurrences.title: 'To you throw I the golden ball' — Zarathustra's goal and heirs
occurrences.label: To you throw I the golden ball
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939
Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "Verily, a goal had Zarathustra; he threw his ball. Now be ye friends the heirs of my goal; to you throw I the golden ball."

Jung's January 1936 exegesis: the golden ball is the sun, gold, "an entirely round thing which expresses the state of perfection"; the self as "a center of personality, a center of gravity that does not coincide with the ego" — thrown among the disciples as Buddha sets the wheel of the law in motion. It is the compensating positive symbol at the end of the "Voluntary Death" chapter, and what the disciples return as the staff with the serpent twined round the sun.
The self "is not identical with one particular individual... there is only the self that can boast of having many individuals."

occurrences.title: The golden bough of Diana at Aricia — rex Nemorensis
occurrences.label: The golden bough of Diana at Aricia
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: cult attested classical era (recorded 1st c. BCE-CE)
body: Only the runaway slave who could pluck the golden bough from the sacred grove of Diana and kill the reigning priest became her priest-king at Nemi.

Jung's reading: grouped with the robbery motifs of the "treasure hard to attain" — sun-cattle of Geryon, apples of the Hesperides, herb of immortality (¶250) — the stolen branch as regressive treasure torn from the goddess.
Verbatim: in the cult of Diana at Aricia only he could become her priest who plucked the golden bough from the sacred grove of the goddess. (cw05 ¶250).

image.title: (Barcelona) The Golden Bough - Joseph Mallord William Turner - Tate Britain

occurrences.title: Red-and-white rose, the 'golden flower' of alchemy — Ripley Scrowle (1588)
occurrences.label: Red-and-white rose, the 'golden flower'…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: London, British Museum (MS Add. 5025, No. 1 detail)
body: Caption: "The red-and-white rose, the 'golden flower' of alchemy, as birthplace of the filius philosophorum.". The Western twin of the Chinese golden flower: the solar essence descended into the flower.

Jung at ¶101: "For the 'golden flower of alchemy' (fig. 30) can sometimes be a blue flower: 'The sapphire blue flower of the hermaphrodite.'" — binding the dreamer's blue flower (dream 17) to the alchemical rose and hermaphrodite.

image.title: WMS 693, Ripley Scroll, Golden winged bird

occurrences.title: Pope Sylvester II's oracular golden head
occurrences.label: Pope Sylvester II's oracular golden head
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Possessed a golden head that imparted oracles.
body: "According to legend, Pope Sylvester II (d. 1003), famed as the transmitter of Arabian science, possessed a golden head that imparted oracles. This legend may perhaps date back to the Harranite ceremony of the oracular head."

Jung at cw14 ¶626: the golden-head tradition — Greek "children of the golden head," the oracular statue, the brain as arcane substance — converging on the head as seat of the "spirit of the supracelestial waters."

occurrences.title: Gerbert's golden speaking head — Pope Sylvester II
occurrences.label: Gerbert's golden speaking head
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: He was believed to have possessed a golden head which spoke to him in oracles.
body: Gerbert of Rheims, Archbishop and afterwards Pope Sylvester II (d. 1003), "was believed to have possessed a golden head which spoke to him in oracles." One of the greatest savants of his time and a well-known transmitter of Arabic science, he fits the chain by which Harranite material — including the Liber quartorum with its brain-pan vessel — entered the Latin West; Jung asks whether that treatise's translation "goes back to this author. Unfortunately there is little prospect of our being able to prove this" (¶367).

With Zosimos' "children of the golden head," the omega-shaped "round element," and the "whitest stone... in the head," this legend anchors the mysterious-head motif in the alchemical lineage running back to the severed head of Osiris (¶366).

occurrences.title: Circle of bluish figures with red seed-pods and the word 'Henoch' (Meyrink, Der Golem, 1915)
occurrences.label: Circle of bluish figures with red seed-pods…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: The vision-series that closes Der Golem: the hero, fallen to the bottom of the depths, sees "a group of bluish figures who form a ring around him. They all wear golden hieroglyphs on their breasts and each one of the figures holds a red seed-pod in its hand" (p319) — the seed-pods he had refused and scattered. A voice: "It is the Night of Protection"; then "He whom you seek is not here" (said of Christ at the tomb); the word "Henoch"; reading the hieroglyphs ends the vision.

Jung's reading: "Obviously these visions are a series of mandalas, not such as you would draw, but they could be danced or acted. Forming a magic circle means individuation" (p320). The seeds are "his various parts. We consist of a lot of particles which must come together as in the magic cauldron"; refusing them, they stand against him — Meyrink's Cabbalist Messiah: "The one that unites, that makes perfect, is not here." The seed-offering is a fatal question, like the quaestio crocodilina (p320).

occurrences.title: The Golem — clay man of the Jewish legends, brought to life by the holy name
occurrences.label: The Golem — clay man…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: "The Golem is an entirely negative figure, the complete shadow of the immortal one. He began as a lump of clay and was brought to life by black magic, by writing the holy name on his brow. So he is a living being that has no soul, a mechanism which can be killed only by wiping out the holy name. The figure occurs in many ancient Jewish legends, and Meyrink used it as a personification of the horrible troubles which befall the hero through those visions." Shadow of Athanasius, the immortal one — the soulless automaton against the diamond body.

occurrences.title: Gate of vision — the hermaphrodite Osiris-gate with hare's head (Meyrink, Der Golem, 1915)
occurrences.label: Gate of vision — the hermaphrodite Osiris-gate…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: The closing vision of Meyrink's novel, translated aloud by Jung (he cites the same passage in Psychology and Alchemy ¶53): the road up to the castle, lilac in bloom, a garden wall "covered with mosaics, with a beautiful turquoise-blue background... which represent the cult of Osiris. The gate is the god himself, a hermaphrodite, the two parts forming a double gate, the right side the female, the left the male... His golden head is the head of a hare" (p306). Pernath hands in the hat of Athanasius; within, "Athanasius Pernath and leaning against him Miriam (the heroine, anima)"; his face is the dreamer's own — "as one sees oneself in a mirror."

Jung: Meyrink invented the hare-headed Osiris, but "Osiris is never represented with the head of a hare... his adversary, Set... is represented with the head of an animal with long ears" — so the gate "makes a union of opposites," Osiris and Set together (pp310-312). The story of a man "who inadvertently got into the role of himself" (p307).

occurrences.title: The Golem: the rabbi's man of clay that grew and killed its maker
occurrences.label: The Golem — the rabbi's man of clay…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: that thing had a tendency to grow and grow and finally it fell on him and killed him
body: Raised against Baynes' churinga comparison in the discussion of whether man can make archetypes: "The old rabbi was capable of making a living thing, the Golem, from a clod of earth by black magic, but that thing had a tendency to grow and grow and finally it fell on him and killed him."

Jung's point: man-made things — churinga, idol, machine, institution — once made, become "the abode of divine power" and can overgrow their maker: "So the churinga is made by man, yet because it is a symbol, it is also the abode of divine power." The Golem is the cautionary Jewish form of the autonomous creation.

occurrences.title: Gospel according to the Egyptians — 'the two shall be one, neither male nor female'
occurrences.label: Gospel according to the Egyptians
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: when ye shall tread upon the vesture of shame, and when the two shall be one, and the male with the female neither male nor female.
body: Salome asks Jesus when the prophecies will be fulfilled, and he answers:

Jung reads the logion as the grammar of the transcendent: "when a thing is yea and nay, then it is neither yea nor nay, it is both and therefore beyond. The unrecognizable and incomprehensible thing can only be expressed by a paradox". It decodes the vision-figure of the reborn Osiris-man holding staff and bowl — "the bowl would be the female and the staff the male form, which means a union of opposites; the male and female are together in this poimen. It also means neither male nor female": the natural mind "beyond sex… that accounts for its divinity". Parallels he gives: nirvana as "positive non-being, or being, non-being"; the creative point as "a completely empty fullness"; Boehme's longing Nichts. Ed. note: the logion is quoted again at CW9i ¶295 and CW14 ¶¶18n, 528.

occurrences.title: Christ as light-bringer — Gospel of Truth (Jung Codex)
occurrences.label: Christ as light-bringer — Gospel of Truth
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Egypt (codex acquired for the C. G. Jung Institute, presented 1953)
occurrences.quote: For him Christ was primarily a light-bringer, who went forth from the Father in order to illuminate the stupidity, darkness, and unconsciousness of mankind.
body: One of the three treatises Jung knew from the Jung Codex at its presentation in 1953: an early Valentinian text, "The Gospel of Truth" — "less a gospel than a treatise explaining the Christian message", assimilating it to "the Hellenistic-Egyptian world of thought" (¶1515). For its author "Christ was primarily a light-bringer, who went forth from the Father in order to illuminate the stupidity, darkness, and unconsciousness of mankind" — deliverance from agnosia, related to Hippolytus' accounts of the Naassenes and Peratics.

Jung's reading: the text shows "in what way the Christian message was taken up by the unconscious of that age" (¶1515) — a "phenomenon of assimilation"; confronting the patient with his own dark side "is a continuation of the Christian development of consciousness" producing assimilations like those "in Gnosticism, the Kabbala, and Hermetic philosophy" (¶1517).

occurrences.title: Amfortas' wound and the restored spear — Wagner's Parsifal (Bayreuth, 1882)
occurrences.label: Amfortas' wound and the restored spear
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Just as the enslavement of the masses was the open wound of the ancient world, so the enslavement of the inferior functions is an ever-bleeding wound in the psyche of modern man.
body: Jung names the division of the psychic functions "a veritable Amfortas' wound" — "an ever open and never healing wound" inflicted by culture's differentiation of one function (¶105). He then reads Wagner's opera as the artistic statement of what Schiller laboured philosophically: "This idea is also the leit-motif of Wagner's Parsifal, and it is given symbolic expression in the restoration of the missing spear and the healing of the wound" (¶114) — the deliverance of the suppressed functions languishing in servitude.
Jung notes Schiller passed over the Christian answer in silence; both Wagner and Schiller seek deliverance from the same inner laceration of modern man.

occurrences.title: Wolfram's Grail as stone — 'lapsit exillis' read as lapis exilis
occurrences.label: Wolfram's Grail as stone
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: In my view, however, this 'lapsit exillis' could refer to the lapis.
body: For Wolfram von Eschenbach the Grail is a stone; his strange expression lapsit exillis is "bungled Latin; he himself did not understand Latin." Philologists proposed "ex illis" (from those eternal stars) or "ex coelis" (from the heavens); Jung: "this 'lapsit exillis' could refer to the lapis." Evidence: Arnoldus de Villanova (a doctor living around 1250, per the seminar) calls the stone "lapis exilis" in a hexameter — had cheaply, vili pretio, found everywhere, in the streets, in dung, in toilets; Petrus Bonus in 1330 first declared the stone an allegory of Christ; the Easter fire is struck from the cornerstone, lapis angularis.
The worthless-that-is-priceless joins the Grail to the kratér of Zosimos and the benedictio fontis in the seminar's vessel series.

occurrences.title: The Grail held suspended by angels between heaven and earth
occurrences.label: The Grail held suspended by angels…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "The swan also figures in the legend of the Holy Grail, and the Holy Grail itself is held in a state of suspension. It is held by angels suspended between heaven and earth."

For Jung suspension is a distinct symbol-state: "Suspension is also an aspect of crucifixion, the unconscious aspect of transfiguration. It is the state of transformation, but it is the fate of the body while transfiguration is the fate of the subtle body... a state of suspension which precedes birth or creation" — the same tormented hanging in which Odin hatched the runes.
Verbatim: "The swan also figures in the legend of the Holy Grail, and the Holy Grail itself is held in a state of suspension. It is held by angels suspended between heaven and earth."

occurrences.title: The Holy Grail as 'Vase of Sin' — C. W. King's Gnostic vessel (1864)
occurrences.label: The Holy Grail as 'Vase of Sin'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: reported in C. W. King, The Gnostics and Their Remains (London, 1864)

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: At the crest of the Mithraic-vessel passage: the amphora with the flame, lion and serpent straining toward the fire, is "the famous symbolism of the vessel, a symbolism that survives till 1925—see Parsifal. It is the Holy Grail, called the Vase of Sin (see King: The Gnostics [footnote block interrupts at the page break] and Their Remains1*). Also it is a symbol of the early Gnostics." And: "It is of course a man's symbol, a symbol of the womb—the creative womb of the man out of which rises the fire". King's 1864 compendium — in Jung's library — carried the Gnostic gems and vessel symbolism into his working vocabulary years before the alchemical Grail literature of the late 1920s-30s. The vessel row runs: Mithraic amphora → Gnostic Vase of Sin → the Grail of Parsifal → "in this deification mystery you make yourself into the vessel, and are a vessel of creation in which the opposites reconcile".

occurrences.title: Vision of the Holy Grail — Roman de Lancelot du lac (Paris MS, 15th c.)
occurrences.label: Vision of the Holy Grail
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Paris MS (Roman de Lancelot du lac)
occurrences.quote: a bewildering profusion of semblances for that obscure thing we call the mandala or 'self
body: Plate 88: "Vision of the Holy Grail" from the Roman de Lancelot du lac. Jung sets it at the head of the passage where the unconscious "puts forth a bewildering profusion of semblances for that obscure thing we call the mandala or 'self'" (¶247) — grail, lapis, and mandala as one family of the treasure hard to attain.
The plate belongs with the Grail-stone lore Jung cites later in the series: "According to the legend the Grail-stone comes from the east and must return there again" (¶263).

image.title: Holy-grail-round-table-bnf-ms-120-f524v-14th
image.credit: Attributed to Maître des cleres femmes.

occurrences.title: The youngest son rides to the grandfather's cellar (Russian fairy tale)
occurrences.label: The youngest son rides to the grandfather's…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: the grandfather really sets the task. He is the origin, because he is the representative of the altjiranga, which means psychologically, the representative of the collective unconscious.
body: Mrs. von Roques' counter-example to Nietzsche's sneering "he who is of the populace, his thoughts go back to his grandfather": a Czar's three sons are told to seek his traces and pick his flowers. The two elders fail on the best horses; the youngest, on a horse he has killed and magically transformed into the best of stallions, rides backwards down to his dead grandfather's cellar, drinks his wine, and takes saddle and head-harness from there. Von Roques: regression "pour mieux sauter," the grandfather "pars pro toto for all the other side." Jung agrees and generalizes:

The tale's positive regression to the origin — the hero "embodied in the grandfather" — against Nietzsche's "all depreciation." Parallels: ancestor-rice-man-transformation-alcheringa-australia · horse-three-legged-witch-german-fairytale · aljira-ancestors-sink-earth-aranda-australia.

occurrences.title: Dream: grapevines overgrowing the altar, crescent moon shining into the church (clergyman)
occurrences.label: Dream: grapevines overgrowing the altar…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The altar with the crucifix was still there, but it was completely overgrown with grapevines. Moreover, the walls had fallen away behind and the crescent moon was shining into the church. He woke up with a tremendous start.
body: A clergyman — liberal, modern, but "absolutely bound by the ecclesiastical prejudice" that the world belongs in one universal church — dreams he enters his church and finds the choir section has fallen down:

Jung's reading: "It is again the vine, the Dionysian principle, the fruit of the earth, that is growing into the church. The altar is where one drinks the wine, the spirit of the earth"; and the moon is "the feminine principle, which is repressed by the church... In the Protestant church everything is masculine; since the feminine principle is connected with the earth, it is considered wrong, and it is therefore completely repressed" (p237-238). Same psychology as the visions then under discussion.

occurrences.title: The white dove hidden in lead is the Queen of Sheba — Grasseus
occurrences.label: The white dove hidden in lead is the Queen…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This is the chaste, wise, and rich Queen of Sheba, veiled in white, who was willing to give herself to none but King Solomon.
body: In the Arca arcanorum Grasseus identifies the white dove hidden in lead with "the chaste, wise, and rich Queen of Sheba, veiled in white, who was willing to give herself to none but King Solomon. No human heart can sufficiently investigate all this."

Jung cites it at cw14 ¶533 as the prototype of the alchemical Minne: the queen's fidelity to Solomon alone prefigures the paired apotheosis of Luna and filius regius in the Cantilena-Ripley tradition.

occurrences.title: The grave-island, the silent isle (Grave-Song)
occurrences.label: The grave-island, the silent isle (Grave-Song)
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939
Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: he himself is a sort of ghost landing there.
body: "Yonder is the grave-island, the silent isle, yonder also are the graves of my youth. Thither will I carry an evergreen wreath of life." Jung reads the island as Nietzsche's "absolute loneliness" — "An island means isolation, insulation, being one thing only... he is a lost island somewhere in the sea" — and, at the next lecture, as the projected ghostland: the descent to the unconscious "has always been thought of as a descent into that other world, a reestablishment of the lost connections with the dead". Nietzsche is both the seafarer in Charon's boat and the island to which the dead (reminiscences with affect) come; the katabasis meets first "his reminiscences that came with affect."
Type-image: the land of the dead as island — Böcklin's Toteninsel, Ulysses' Nekyia, Elgon's bamboo belt.

occurrences.title: Under the sea: the snake-encircled goddess, the old men, the chaos-pit and the crystal man (patient vision, 25 Mar 1931)
occurrences.label: Under the sea — the snake-encircled goddess…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: While we stood a man of crystal was created from the formless mass. She breathed life into him and he became flesh and blood.
body: Inside the eye's liquid (under the sea) a giant animus lifts his hair to the fertilizing rain, sets her on his head like Zeus birthing Pallas, and brings her to "the big woman, this Etruscan type, clearly a goddess": asleep, surrounded by writhing snakes (the exclamation-mark: Look out!), dark-faced, full red lips — "the chthonic woman par excellence." She kisses the little initiate, leads her through a room of young men, then a room of old men with eyes fixed on the ground: "I bring you a gift" — sacrificial prostitution, the hierodule's submission to fate against the patient's headstrong knowing-best. Sorrowing women flee or are touched on the brow — "Know me" — and stand filled with new strength (plate 13). Down many steps: "a pit of seething inchoate chaos," and from the formless mass a man of crystal is created; she breathes life into him, and ascends with him into the day.
Jung: the crystal is "the Chinese term, the diamond body, the center of the mandala" — still projected into another, as transference casts the treasure onto the analyst.

occurrences.title: The Great Spirit's midlife dream — North American Indian warrior chief
occurrences.label: The Great Spirit's midlife dream
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: North America (plains; report in 19th-c. ethnological literature Jung cites without naming)

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: In "The Stages of Life", Jung's exhibit for the psychic revolution at life's noon: "There is an interesting report in the ethnological literature about an Indian warrior chief to whom in middle life the Great Spirit appeared in a dream. The spirit announced to him that from then on he must sit among the women and children, wear women's clothes, and eat the food of women. He obeyed the dream without suffering a loss of prestige" (¶781).

Jung's reading: "This vision is a true expression of the psychic revolution of life's noon, of the beginning of life's decline. Man's values, and even his body, do tend to change into their opposites." The numinous command institutes the contrasexual change that ¶780-783 describes physiologically and psychologically (the leftover "feminine substance" put to use).

occurrences.title: The Green Face — Meyrink's wandering Jew with the cross mark
occurrences.label: The Green Face — Meyrink's wandering Jew…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Dr. Reichstein's pointer: "a German book by Meyrink called The Green Face. It is the face of the wandering Jew, and he is said to have always worn a sort of bandage over his forehead in order to cover the mark of the cross which he bore there."

Jung: "The old man in this vision has a cross upon his forehead, the mark of sacrifice, and that wandering Jew bears the same sign because he is the one that is marked or sacrificed; he is the sacrifice yet also the one that is never sacrificed."

occurrences.title: 'Behold!' — the green goddess apotheosis of the Self (Visions, 31 Jan. 1934)
occurrences.label: Behold! — the green goddess apotheosis…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Challenged ("You may be a witch"), the guide answers: "'Behold!' She pulled off her robe. I saw a beautiful woman. She was all green, triumphant, dazzling, standing in a green light. I bowed my head".

Jung: "the green of vegetation... she is a dryad, a tree spirit... And yet she is a witch, that is the interesting thing" — the imp of fascination and the vegetation spirit are one; "the Irish rightly speak of the Green Folk"; the antique gods were vegetation demons beyond human morality. "This woman is paradoxical, which proves that she is the Self, and this is one of the forms in which the Self often appears, as an absolutely unaccountable nature spirit, sometimes positive, sometimes negative" (ibid.). The divine form in a woman is a woman; the hermaphrodite would be a pre-stage. The Self "wants the conflict and not the solution" — "I came not to bring peace but a sword." Then: "She put on the blue robe and changed again into the old woman... 'You enter among the ghosts. Cover your face with the gray veil. They must not see you.'".

occurrences.title: The green lion devouring the sun — Rosarium philosophorum
occurrences.label: The green lion devouring the sun
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 169. The 'green lion' devouring the sun.—Rosarium philosophorum (1550)
body: Rosarium woodcut: the green lion swallowing the sun disc — the most famous single image of the prima materia consuming the perfected substance.

Jung's context: among the versions of the King's Son's death, "in another version he is eaten by his father …, or the Sun is drowned in Mercurius or swallowed by the lion." The green lion is a form of Mercurius (¶498); in the Cantilena the virgin-mother drinks "the blood of the green lion" that lies bleeding in her lap — communion and Pietà symbols at once.

image.title: Lion eating Sun Rosarium philosophorum

occurrences.title: Maier: the earth of chaos as green lion, or the dragon devouring its own tail
occurrences.label: Maier: the earth of chaos as green lion…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Frankfurt (Michael Maier, Symbola aureae mensae, p. 427)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Michael Maier on the initial substance: "Others have called this earth the green lion, strong and valiant in war, or the dragon that devours its own tail. We see that the lion is a synonym of the dragon devouring itself; obviously it represents a similar state".

Jung's reading: "Now, the dragon devouring itself is a form of libido, which runs in a circle within itself and bites into itself. The dragon forms a circle with itself, bites into nothing but itself, and even fertilizes itself in doing so." The lion must devour itself, stewed in its own juice in the sealed vessel — the greatest passion does not seek the other, but itself; what occurs instead is called transference. The same author: "The green lion is the medium to unify the tinctures between the sun and the moon" — the male and female unified in subtle, psychical form.

occurrences.title: Green Osiris bedstead — seed-grown mummy on a frame (Egypt → British Museum)
occurrences.label: Green Osiris bedstead
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: A spring charm for making the green Osiris: a bedstead covered with canvas bearing the outline of Osiris in the mummy case, filled with wet sand and grass seed — "so in a few days the seed came up and formed an entirely green Osiris, expressing the idea of the renewal of life, the resurrection from the dead". Jung adds the companion painting of the mummy case with wheat growing out of the god's body.

Amplifies the patient's grain-of-wheat vision: the row runs Sufi blade-of-grass theophany, Hindu green-leaf god, Eleusinian ear of wheat (Brimo/Brimos, Iacchus in the winnowing fan), the wheat Host ("Christ is the son of the earth"), and this Osiris — the grain as the god who dies and returns.

occurrences.title: Grenzumgang — boundary-riding procession (Switzerland & Tyrol), with the Roman circumambulatio
occurrences.label: Grenzumgang — boundary-riding procession…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Switzerland & Tyrol (Roman precedent: castle near Pfaffikon, Zurich)
occurrences.yearDisplay: custom of medieval origin, still performed (account 27 Nov 1930)
body: Amplifying the two animus figures walking round the black pond: the Roman town-founding rite — "They drew a furrow round it, the circumambulatio, always going round to the right like the sun or the hands of the watch. Then in the center they made a hole in the ground called a fundus, where they buried fruits... as a sacrificial offering to the chthonic gods". Jung points to the almost-complete Roman castle foundation near Pfaffikon with its fundus still extant. The surviving Christian descendant: "in Switzerland and in the Tyrol there are still places where every year in the spring or early summer, the priest and the people go in a procession on horseback... round the estates of the community... That is called the Grenzumgang".

Reading: "psychical concentration means putting creative libido into the ground" — the rite fertilizes the center; walking with the sun, never contrariwise ("it would be working an evil spell"); boundary gods are phallic, "like Priapus".

occurrences.title: God as King and Queen of Heaven on two thrones — Digulleville's Pelerinage de l'ame
occurrences.label: God as King and Queen of Heaven on two thrones
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Chalis, Normandy (Cistercian priory; author prior there)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: In Guillaume de Digulleville's Le Pelerinage de l'ame — three pilgrimage allegories written in the manner of the Divine Comedy but independently of Dante, 1330-1350 — the visionary "saw God in the highest heaven as the King on a shining round throne, and beside him sat the Queen of Heaven on a throne of brown crystal" (¶133).

Jung's reading: "For a monk of the Cistercian Order, which as we know is distinguished for its severity, this vision is exceedingly heretical" — the condition for genuine (untraditional) projection is fulfilled; the vision belongs with Brother Klaus's God-Father-and-God-Mother theophany as an autonomous uprising of the syzygy archetype against dogma that had "eliminated the feminine element from the Trinity".

occurrences.title: Guillaume de Digulleville: the calendar-circle in the golden heaven (Pélerinage de l'âme)
occurrences.label: Guillaume de Digulleville
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Châlis, Normandy (Cistercian priory; author prior there)
occurrences.quote: Cette cercle que tu vois est le calendrier / Qui en faisant son tour entier
body: The last canto of the Pélerinage de l'âme: Paradise as seven large spheres each containing seven smaller spheres, "all the spheres rotate, and this movement is called a siècle (saeculum)." In the highest heaven of pure gold the King sits on a round throne, the Queen on one "made of brown crystal" (¶315). "The pilgrim perceived a marvellous circle… three feet across" — the sapphire calendrier that "spinning round the course entire / Shows the feast day of each saint" (¶316–317). Three crowned spirits enter with it; the angel expounds the Trinity through gold, red, and green — blue, the Virgin's colour, is missing (¶319–320).

Jung offers this as the chief historical parallel to the world-clock vision: rotating spheres + calendar-circle + three mysterious rhythms = "the moment of time in eternity" (¶318). The missing blue = the forgotten reyne, the feminine vertical.

occurrences.title: The young man with the black pointed beard among the philosophers — Parabolae of the Güldenen Tractat vom philosophischen Stein (1625)
occurrences.label: The young man with the black pointed beard…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "the 'man with a pointed beard' also crops up in alchemical literature, in one of the 'Parabolae' contained in the 'Güldenen Tractat vom philosophischen Stein,' written in 1625, which Herbert Silberer has analysed from a psychological point of view. Among the company of old white-bearded philosophers there is a young man with a black pointed beard. Silberer is uncertain whether he should assume this figure to be the devil." (cw12 ¶89).
The dream's Mephisto-employee (¶88) thus has a dated literary double in the alchemical corpus — the ambiguous junior spirit among the senes.

occurrences.title: The man covered with hair rising from the dark basement — dream of a boy of five
occurrences.label: The man covered with hair rising…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: In the dream, there appears a man covered with hair, who suddenly comes up from the dark basement. He wants to seize the little boy and pull him down into the basement. The boy wakes up crying loudly in fear.
body: Opening case of the 1938/39 term, presented by Mrs. Sachs; Jung chose it "because with its help we can discuss the various possibilities of working with a dream in the simplest form."

The paper amplifies: bogeyman figures — Rübezahl, Swiss Böölima, Flemish Biete Bouw, the troll, the "man in the woodpile"; Frazer's hair-taboo (Masai, Frankonian kings, Samson); the bear, the Berserker, the werewolf. Jung then weighs the practical hypotheses: too-virtuous an education ("As a consequence, there comes the Böölima... He can do anything the boy cannot in the house"); too-infantile regression; or the apeman constellated in a parent, for "the apeman can enter into the little child". Both aspects are always present: destructive anxiety-dream or the child's instinct recognizing "this is 'he'!" — "Here we must trust nature." The dream may "anticipate a later emotional outbreak... The dream would then anticipate the future".

occurrences.title: Hammurabi declares himself the Ram
occurrences.label: Hammurabi declares himself the Ram
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Jung's earliest verifiable datum of the precession reading of history: "About 2000 B.C. Hammurabi announced himself as the great lawgiver. He declared himself the Ram. It was the time when the sun was just coming into Aries." The gods change their horns with the signs — bull horns in Taurus, ram horns in Aries, the Fish at Christianity's dawn — "Probably we are dealing here with unconscious laws of creative energy, of how things develop, which we only now begin dimly to divine."

occurrences.title: The Haṃsa like a steady flame in a windless place — Śaṭcakranirūpaṇa v.26 (Bengal, 1577)
occurrences.label: The Haṃsa like a steady flame…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1577 (Pūrṇānanda, Śrī-tattva-cintāmaṇi ch. 6; trans. Woodroffe, The Serpent Power, 1919)

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

body: The anāhata (heart) lotus closes with the gander-spirit: "This Lotus is like the celestial wishing-tree, the abode and seat of åarva. It is beautified by the Ham˙ sa, which is like unto the steady tapering flame of a lamp in a windless place" (v.26, sem-kundalini pdf p165).

Around it: twelve vermilion petals, the kalpataru wishing-tree (v.22), Kākinī with noose and skull (v.24), the Bāṇa liṅga "like shining gold" that houses Lakṣmī (v.25), and the meditator's promised powers of speech and protection (vv.26–27). The Haṃsa-flame — motionless light in the breath-region — is the Indian still-point of Jung's anāhata psychology, where feeling becomes conscious breath and "the self is only beginning to be visible".

occurrences.title: The enormous hand that gripped him by the chest (Burghölzli, ~1900s)
occurrences.label: The enormous hand that gripped him by the chest
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: he suddenly felt an enormous hand grasp him by the chest and throw him to the floor
body: Second "teleological hallucination" (¶304-307): a psychopath weary of life begins inhaling gas from an open jet — "he suddenly felt an enormous hand grasp him by the chest and throw him to the floor, where he gradually recovered from his fright. The hallucination was so distinct that the next day he could still show me the place where the five fingers had gripped him" (¶306). The arresting, five-fingered hand — in 1907 only the act of an autonomous complex; in Jung's later work the same image carries the invisible hand of God. This note is the earliest clinical witness of the hand-family in the corpus.

occurrences.title: Hanuman swallowed by the mother of Rahu — Ramayana
occurrences.label: Hanuman swallowed by the mother of Rahu
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The sun travelling with Hanuman casts a shadow on the sea; a sea-monster seizes it; Hanuman shrinks, enters the body, and passes through. A second monster — "the mother of Rahu, the sun-devouring demon" — draws him down; he swells inside and bursts her.

Jung's reading: Frobenius' devouring-and-birth sequence, with conquest of the devouring mother; "We now understand why the Indian fire-bringer Matarisvan is called 'he who swells in the mother'" (¶311).

Verbatim: Once more he had recourse to his earlier stratagem, made himself small, and slipped into her body; but scarcely was he inside than he swelled up to gigantic size, burst her, and killed her, and so made his escape. (cw05 ¶311).

occurrences.title: 'Happy Neurosis Island' — washing ceremonials and the provisional life (compulsion neurosis)
occurrences.label: Happy Neurosis Island
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "A patient who called his way of living the provisional life, the man with a compulsion neurosis who said he was living on Happy Neurosis Island" — the worst compulsion neurosis Jung ever saw. Washing ceremonials "for spiritual disinfection... It had nothing to do with germs, it was a magical idea of a completely uncontaminated condition... He disinfected himself from all contact with time, as the altar is spiritually disinfected by the smoke of the incense".

The system: no clock in the room (time = death); no handshake with doctors; a woman in black met at nine in the morning undoes the whole day's acts — necktie returned, tax if are re claimed and re-gifted — and he waits until five for the flower-seller to leave; fifteen hundred sterilized towels; all-white clothes.

Cited under the earth-visions: "The trend of our whole civilization is toward the provisional life... As long as it is a provisional life, your unconscious will be in a state of continuous irritation against you" (p258). Living here-and-now is what the ancient mother's lap demands.

occurrences.title: Three hares in rotation — Gothic window, Paderborn cathedral
occurrences.label: Three hares in rotation
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Fig. 39 of Concerning Mandala Symbolism: the same motif as the three-dogs mandala (Fig. 38) "but represented by hares. From a Gothic window in the cathedral at Paderborn. There is no recognizable centre though the rotation presupposes one." The triad circling an implicit centre embodies the sesquitertian proportion (3:4) — the incomplete, triadic state turning around the complete, tetradic one — known in alchemy as the axiom of Maria. The famous three-hares motif of German church windows, harvested by Jung directly into the sesquitertian series.

image.title: Paderborner Dom Dreihasenfenster

occurrences.title: Picasso's Harlequin — the tragic chthonic god of the underworld journey
occurrences.label: Picasso's Harlequin
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Spirit in Man, Art and Literature (CW15)

occurrences.quote: so Picasso changes shape and reappears in the underworld form of the tragic Harlequin—a motif that runs through numerous paintings.
body: The Harlequin motif that "runs through numerous paintings" of Picasso, in which, "just as Faust is embroiled in murderous happenings and reappears in changed form... Picasso changes shape and reappears in the underworld form of the tragic Harlequin" (cw15 ¶211).

Jung's reading. "It may be remarked in passing that Harlequin is an ancient chthonic god" (cw15 ¶211). Harlequin "wanders like Faust through all these forms, though sometimes nothing betrays his presence but his wine, his lute, or the bright lozenges of his jester's costume" (cw15 ¶212). The essay's last word is deliberately open: "Harlequin is a tragically ambiguous figure... He is indeed the hero who must pass through the perils of Hades, but will he succeed? That is a question I cannot answer. Harlequin gives me the creeps" (cw15 ¶214) — too reminiscent of Zarathustra's buffoon over the rope-dancer, "the greater personality who bursts the shell, and this shell is sometimes—the brain."

occurrences.title: Harmonices mundi — Kepler's Trinitarian cosmic harmony against Fludd's quaternio (Augsburg, 1619)
occurrences.label: Harmonices mundi — Kepler's Trinitarian cosmic…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: Harmonices mundi. 5 books. Augsburg, 1619.
body: Kepler's harmony of the world — five books deriving the planetary motions as archetypal musical ratios — and, with Fludd's reply, the standing type-case of Pauli's thesis that archetypal images steer scientific theory: Kepler's harmony of three (Trinitarian) against Robert Fludd's cosmological monad of four. The controversy is fully catalogued in this volume's bibliography: Fludd's Utriusque Cosmi Maioris (Oppenheim 1621), Demonstratio analytica and Replicatio (Frankfurt 1621–22), Kepler's "Apologia contra Fludd"; the index points to the debate in the letters ("Fludd v. Kepler opposition, 55").
Jung stages the same 3-vs-4 quarrel as the drama of alchemical number (triad vs quaternio, e.g. cw12 ¶449); Pauli's essay makes it the hinge between Renaissance symbol and modern law.

occurrences.title: The cow-headed Hathor — bronze, Serapeum of Sakkara
occurrences.label: The cow-headed Hathor
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Pl. XXXb: bronze cow-headed Hathor.

Jung's reading: "The cow as a mother-symbol (cf. pl. Ia) appears in all the innumerable forms and variations of Hathor-Isis" (¶358); she it is who receives the wounded Ra: "the cow was the cow-headed mother-goddess, just as Osiris was the bull Apis" (¶351) — the mother who wounds and heals.
Verbatim: But the cow was the cow-headed mother-goddess (pl. XXXb), just as Osiris was the bull Apis. (cw05 ¶351).

occurrences.title: Vision: the hawk snatches the egg; woman in blue with the grain of wheat (27 Nov 1930)
occurrences.label: Vision — the hawk snatches the egg
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The egg as well as the grain symbolize the Self that is yet to be born.
body: A great white bird changes into a dark hawk, swoops, snatches an egg from the earth, and flies up as the white bird again; then it descends to a woman in blue "sitting like an ancient statue", lights on her hands, takes the single grain of wheat she holds, and rises into the sky. Jung's reading spans three sessions: the spirit is ambivalent — the hawk is Horus, "the Egyptian Christ", and "it needs a bird of prey" to steal the germ of life; the white Holy Ghost itself must take a dark form to fetch what is below (p199-204). The scene of the bird descending on the mother is "an unmistakable parallel to the conceptio immaculata".

The woman in blue mixes the Christian celestial mother with Demeter and Isis (the Host must be wheat because "Christ is the son of the earth"); a pregnancy begins "in which the patient is her own child. This is the mystical child, another symbol of the Self" (p206).

occurrences.title: The antique black head in the egg, kissed despite the fire (patient vision, plate 16, 27 May 1931)
occurrences.label: The antique black head in the egg, kissed…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: As I did so, tongues of fire leapt from the lips and the face said. 'Kiss me, woman.' I said, 'I cannot, I will be burned.'... Then I felt the fire going all through me.
body: Out of the blinding egg (which replaced the world-giant, cf. world-giant-boiling-blood-egg-vision-zurich-1931) comes an antique black marble head covered with the dust of ages; tongues of fire leap from its lips, it commands "Kiss me, woman," and when she accepts the kiss the fire goes all through her, the head falls and breaks into fragments. Jung reads it as the germ of the new attitude hidden in the old world now coming to life: the primitive mind, the black Messiah, whose fiery words are the tongues of Pentecost rising from below, not descending from heaven. Breaking of the form because its mana has been accepted.

occurrences.title: 'Aufer caput, corpus ne tangiot' — treasure inscription of the Hypnerotomachia
occurrences.label: Aufer caput, corpus ne tangiot
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: foreword to Schmid-Guisan, Tag und Nacht (pdf p1043); linked forward to Fierz-David foreword, pars. 1751ff (pdf p1052)

body: The warning carved over the treasure in Colonna's dream-romance, quoted (with the Latin preserved) in Jung's 1931 foreword to Schmid-Guisan's Tag und Nacht — from the introduction to Béroalde de Verville's 1600 French Hypnerotomachia, the reading that made Poliphilo an alchemical initiation: "Quisquis es quantumque libuerit, huius thesauri sume: at moneo, aufer caput, corpus ne tangiot" ("Whoever you are... take of this treasure: but I warn you, take the head, touch not the body" — cf. The Dream of Poliphilo, p. 39). Head without body: the separatio motif that alchemy and Jung both stage before reunion (caput/corpus as spirit/soul or sol/luna). OCR variant "tangiot" (for tangito) preserved verbatim.

occurrences.title: Rock paintings: humans with long bodies and tiny heads (Frobenius, Erythräa)
occurrences.label: Rock paintings — humans with long bodies…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Africa / Red Sea region (reproduced in Frobenius, Erythräa, Berlin 1931)

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: ...images there of humans with extraordinarily long bodies on which... very small... human or animal heads are placed.
body: Frobenius's plates of prehistoric rock art show "humans with extraordinarily long bodies on which, to some extent very small, or by way of suggestion, human or animal heads are placed" — Jung's documentary image for the historical priority of body-consciousness: the head was once "no more than a button on a feeling body," and only the contemporary person can say "Now I am thinking." Evidence for his belly → diaphragm → head history of psychic localization.

occurrences.title: Misery as a walking head — Cabell, Figures of Earth
occurrences.label: Misery as a walking head
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: Misery is simply a head which moves about, so it may be considered as having feet.
body: Mr. Bash offers a literary parallel to Nietzsche's grotesque image of the will as "your head and your feet" surpassing the man between them: in Cabell's Figures of Earth, Dom Manuel serves Misery for thirty days in the forest —
Each day counts as a year; Manuel stays to win back from Misery the soul of the woman he loves. Jung accepts the symbolism exactly because it is dissociative:

The walking head is the same figure as Jung's "head on two feet, constantly marching about" — will without heart, consciousness without ancestors. Indexed by the volume as a myth: "misery in the forest, 1540."

occurrences.title: Birth of Pallas Athene from Zeus's head (Greek myth, cited cw4 1912)
occurrences.label: Birth of Pallas Athene from Zeus's head
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: I need only remind you of the birth of Pallas Athene, who came out of her father's head.
body: Jung's mythological warrant for an archaic child-theory of birth: his 11-year-old patient held that the child grows in the father's head, the head is split open to let it out, hats conceal the scar — and drew it, a childbirth-through-the-head (¶511). "This idea is archaic and highly mythological. I need only remind you of the birth of Pallas Athene, who came out of her father's head." The mother corroborated a prior fantasy — a jack-in-a-box dancing on the baby brother's head — as the possible seed (¶511). The same child drew the affinity with the Batak serpent columns (¶512): head-birth, incest-punishment, and ancestor-figure forming one archaic constellation.

occurrences.title: Human heads in relief on triassic rock; columns with carved heads in living rock — recurring dreams
occurrences.label: Human heads in relief on triassic rock
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: c. 1950; repeated several times at long intervals (inferred)

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: Two dream versions of nature picturing the human form: (1) "The dreamer was in a wild mountain region where he found contiguous layers of triassic rock. He loosened the slabs and discovered to his boundless astonishment that they had human heads on them in low relief" — repeated at long intervals. (2) A little brown man (an Anthroparion, "metallic man") busily hollowed out a cave at the back of which stood columns in the living rock, each crowned with a carefully carved dark-brown human head with large eyes; the columns "were continued far back into the living rock," the rock "at least half a million years old."

Jung's reading: not lusus naturae but evidence of a formal factor in nature (¶946); the recurrence expresses "the persistent attempt of the unconscious to bring the dream content before the conscious mind" (fn. 74); cf. Kepler's pictured stones (fn. 76).

occurrences.title: Crossing the diaphragm: heart-pain at the sight of a young couple (case)
occurrences.label: Crossing the diaphragm
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: Then suddenly the pain vanished, and for a moment he had an absolutely clear vision.
body: An extreme extrovert, perpetually convinced that "the world was best wherever he was not," chasing the ever-elusive ultimate woman. In the street a young couple passes talking intimately: instant pain in the heart — then the pain vanishes and "for a moment he had an absolutely clear vision": they will do it, life continues, "the thing is taken care of." Jung: in maṇipūra he was identical with the man; here "he breaks through the veil of illusion... his substance is not only his personal self but the substance of that young man, too" — psychical substance enters the game; nothing visible has changed.

occurrences.title: 'We think in the heart' — Pueblo chief of religious ceremonies (New Mexico, 1925)
occurrences.label: We think in the heart
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)
The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)
jung.locator: pdf p84 (print p34, earlier telling in Hauer session)

body: Jung's friend among the Pueblo Indians, "the chief of religious ceremonies" (Mountain Lake / Ochwiay Biano of Memories, Dreams, Reflections), confessed: "they believed all Americans were crazy because they said they thought in the head, whereas the Indians knew that the normal thing was to think in the heart" (sem-kundalini pdf p156).

Jung deploys the remark as ethnographic anchor for his historical ladders of consciousness: Homeric Greeks thought in the diaphragm (phren — root of "schizophrenia"), "certain Negroes put the seat of their emotions and thoughts in the belly," and only "in relatively late periods of civilization that the head was discovered to be the seat of the mind" — i.e. the cakra levels are stages of where consciousness is localized.

occurrences.title: Heaven and earth lying in the calabash — the hermaphrodite son (African myth)
occurrences.label: Heaven and earth lying in the calabash
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "the old Negro myth that heaven is a man and earth a woman: for eternities, they were lying upon each other in a calabash and nothing happened. Then once, in a perfectly unaccountable moment, they felt pushed apart so that the calabash opened, and they found a child in between them, a son. It was the original man who pushed them apart... And the son was supposed to be a hermaphrodite."

Jung: "Plato's philosophic idea was really the result, or later philosophic product, of a most primitive notion" — from a time of such participation mystique with the wife that man could not distinguish himself from her; the church's "one heart and one soul" and the marriage-ideal novel ending carry the same perfect-being myth.

occurrences.title: 'Heaven's way is round, earth's way is square' — Lü Pu-wei
occurrences.label: Heaven's way is round, earth's way is square'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: In Plato the quaternity takes the form of a cube, which he correlates with earth. Lü Pu-wei (Frühling und Herbst, trans. into German by Wilhelm, p. 38) says: \"Heaven's way is round, earth's way is square.\
body: Jung's footnote to the Plato-quaternity discussion (the Timaeus correlates the cube with earth): the same round-square pairing of heaven and earth in Chinese cosmology.

He returns to the formula in the Answer to Job footnotes on Revelation: "In China, heaven is round and the earth square" — the squared New Jerusalem standing to the round heaven of God as earth to heaven. The circle-square pair is one of Jung's most stable cross-cultural constants (cf. the Golden Flower's square-inch field).

occurrences.title: Heb-Sed festival — the king turns to the four cardinal points
occurrences.label: Heb-Sed festival — the king turns…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: New Kingdom (~14th c. BC; Amenhotep III)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The royal renewal rite: the king comes from the sanctuary and 'ascends into a pavilion open at the four sides, with four staircases leading up to it. Carrying the emblems of Osiris, he takes his seat on a throne, and turns to the four cardinal points in succession... he acts as a priest, making offerings to himself... the climax of the deification of the king' (¶309). Jung: 'all kingship is rooted in this psychology' — every king, for his subjects, carries the symbol of the self as cosmic Anthropos, homo maximus (¶310). Parallels: mandala-hasjelti-dailjis-navaho-sand-painting-1887, mandala-madura-temple-floor-1938.

occurrences.title: Helen of the brothel — Simon Magus's companion (Gnostic tradition)
occurrences.label: Helen of the brothel — Simon Magus's companion
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1st c. CE (Simon); reported by the heresiologists, 2nd c.

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar
The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Amplifying his Elijah-Salome vision, Jung cites the Gnostic pair: "In the Gnostic tradition it is said that Simon Magus always went about with a young girl whom he had found in a brothel. She was named Helen and was supposed to be a reincarnation of Helen of Troy". The Samaritan magician's Helen — the fallen thought of God, the lost sheep, in the accounts of Justin, Irenaeus and Hippolytus — is for Jung the standing proof that "whenever you take journeys like this you find a young girl with an old man": the wise-old-man/anima syzygy that his own December 1913 vision produced unbidden. He returned to Simon and Helen at length in "Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious" (CW9i ¶64 and context) and in Aion.

occurrences.title: Same girl's further dream: she opens a door and sees hell burning
occurrences.label: Same girl's further dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
