body: The fairy-dream child's further dream, quoted by Jung mid-discussion: "She opens a door and sees the glow of a fire in the room. She knows: 'This is hell.' Then she leaves."

Jung: "She looked for the way to heaven, and saw hell! She was absorbed by it. This hell is the hell of instincts. The child had a premonition of the instinctual hell into which she will enter". He equates this state with the alchemical three-headed serpens mercurii, "identical with the Gnostic Nous" — the divine spirit present even in the instinctual hell, which through the agony of fire becomes the corpus glorificationis.

occurrences.title: Adoption of Heracles by Hera — Ferrara court painting (Jung's description)
occurrences.label: Adoption of Heracles by Hera
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: It shows the duke as Heracles, lying under the skirts of Hera.
body: In the discussion of second birth Jung cites the two mothers of Heracles — Alkmene who bore him and Hera who adopts him, offering her breast ("He sucks so hard that the milk spurts out, thus creating the milky way") — and then a painting he knows: "a painting by an Italian painter of the adoption of Heracles, on the occasion of the birthday of a duke of Ferrara, in the sycophantic, Byzantine style of the tyrannical courts. It shows the duke as Heracles, lying under the skirts of Hera." Long misread as an Aphroditian amorous play, it is really the adoption by the second mother — who "stands for the great destiny, which can be favorable or unfavorable, just as in our case" (the unborn boy of the grids dream). Godparents ("Gotte" and "Götti" — gods) and baptism realize the same idea of the second, divine begetting; in Egypt the kings were born twice in temple birth chambers.

occurrences.title: Hera's annual disappearance into the lygos-tree — Samos
occurrences.label: Hera's annual disappearance into the lygos-tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Each year Hera's image vanishes from the temple, attaches itself to a lygos (willow) tree on the seashore, is entwined, then "found" and regaled with wedding-cakes; wedding processions at Plataea and Argos; Argive Hera renews her virginity in the fountain of Kanathos.
Jung's reading: the hieros gamos as rejuvenation magic — "its twining-about by the lygos-tree... all this points to death and rebirth" (¶363).
Verbatim: Every year her image “disappeared” from the temple, attached itself to a lygos-tree somewhere on the seashore, and was entwined in its branches. (cw05 ¶363).

occurrences.title: Heracles threatens Helios and wins the sun-ship — journey to Geryon
occurrences.label: Heracles threatens Helios and wins the sun-ship
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: On the way to the sun-cattle of Geryon the burning sun so provokes Heracles that he draws his invincible arrows; Helios yields and lends him the golden sun-ship for crossing Ocean.
Jung's reading: the hero's "bold attitude" toward the sun parallels Mithras as patron of Helios and Peter's investiture as Miles of Christ (¶288-289) — the mortal who commands the luminary.
Verbatim: on his way to fight the monster Geryon the sun burned too fiercely, so Heracles wrathfully threatened him with his invincible arrows. (cw05 ¶288).

occurrences.title: Heraclitus' enantiodromia fragments — bow and lyre (Ephesus, ~500 BCE)
occurrences.label: Heraclitus' enantiodromia fragments
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Men do not know how what is at variance agrees with itself. It is an attunement of opposite tensions, like that of the bow and the lyre.
body: Jung takes the term enantiodromia ("running counter to") directly from Heraclitus, and quotes the founding fragments at length in the Definitions chapter of Psychological Types: "From the living comes death and from the dead life"; souls becoming water, water earth, and back again; "All things are an exchange for fire, and fire for all things, like goods for gold"; "The way up and the way down are the same" (¶708). The bow fragment carries the image in nuce — the bow (bios, "life") whose work is death, an attunement of opposite tensions like the lyre. Jung reads this as the philosophical source of his own law that every extreme one-sidedness of consciousness builds "an equally powerful counterposition" which breaks through in time (¶709), and instances it in the conversions of Paul and Lully, Nietzsche's Christ-identification and turn against Wagner, Swedenborg's passage from scholar to seer.

occurrences.title: Hercules on the night sea journey in the vessel of the sun — Attic vase base
occurrences.label: Hercules on the night sea journey…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 171. Hercules on the night sea journey in the vessel of the sun.—Base of an Attic vase (5th cent. B.C.)
body: Vase-base relief of Herakles riding the sun-barque through the night — the Greek hero assimilated to the sun's nocturnal voyage.

Jung gathers this with the labours of Herakles as one of the journey-forms of the quaternity-cross motif (¶457) and with the sun-hero who "submits to arduous labours and to the passion of self-cremation, like Herakles" (¶469). Hercules is "a favourite symbol because of his opera" even inside the alchemical Mutus liber (fig. 215).

image.title: Heracles on the sea in the bowl of Helios

occurrences.title: The Adamic hermaphrodite carrying hidden Eve — Gnosius' commentary on the Tractatus aureus
occurrences.label: The Adamic hermaphrodite carrying hidden Eve
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: printed 1610; repr. Manget, Bibliotheca chemica curiosa I (1702)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Dominicus Gnosius, commenting on the Tractatus aureus (which Jung insists "is of Arabic origin and does not belong to the Corpus Hermeticum"), writes: "As a shadow continually follows the body of one who walks in the sun … so our Adamic hermaphrodite, though he appears in masculine form, nevertheless always carries about with him Eve, or his feminine part, hidden in his body" (cw11 ¶? pdf p688).

The Eve-within-Adam formula: the feminine as permanent invisible companion of the masculine — precisely the structure Jung will give the anima. Compare Dorn's "invisible Eve" and the Gnostic intra-masculine Sophia.

occurrences.title: Aphrodite and the androgynous number six — Joannes Lydus, De mensibus II, 11
occurrences.label: Aphrodite and the androgynous number six
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: footnote to the Rosarium 'Naked Truth' section (pdf p419)

body: Footnote gem (to the Naked Truth pictures): Lydus on the sixth day of the week — Phosphorus the morning star, "perhaps the son of Aphrodite, like Hesperus the evening star." The number six is "the only number perfect in all its parts"; the ancients "named it marriage and harmony... And they say also that it is both male and female, like Aphrodite herself, who is of male and female nature and is accordingly called hermaphroditic by the theologians," and that it multiplies itself into the worldsphere. Jung uses it for the bareness/androgyny of the Luna figure — even and uneven at once.

occurrences.title: Hermaphroditic symbols — Codex Germanicus Monacensis 598
occurrences.label: Hermaphroditic symbols
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)
Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: The earliest Western hermaphrodite images Jung can document: "But before that date we have the hermaphroditic symbols from the Codex Germanicus Monacensis 598, dated 1417" (cw11 ¶? pdf p687) — i.e. before Ficino's 1471 Poimander printing could have transmitted the Corpus Hermeticum's bisexual first Mind. From this manuscript and Reusner's Pandora come the "pictures of the Hermetic redemption in the form of a tetrad with symbols of the four evangelists" reproduced as Psychology and Alchemy figs. 231–232.

Jung argues the hermaphrodite symbol more probably "derives from Arabic or Syriac MSS. translated in the 11th or 12th century" than from Greek hermetic sources, since "the hermaphrodite figure was practically unknown in the West" before 1471 and there are no Poimandres codices older than the 14th century.

occurrences.title: 'The composite brings itself forth' — Turba philosophorum, Sermo LXV
occurrences.label: The composite brings itself forth
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: "The Turba philosophorum, Sermo LXV, a Latin text of Arabic origin, makes the same allusion: 'The composite brings itself forth.' (Ruska, Turba philosophorum, 1931, p. 165.)" (cw11 ¶? pdf p687).

Third witness (with the Tractatulus Avicennae and Rosinus ad Sarratantam) in Jung's chain of texts in which the arcane substance engenders itself — the textual backbone of the alchemical hermaphrodite as self-begetting uroboric entity, independent of the Greek hermetic corpus.

occurrences.title: Epigram of the Hermaphrodite — Mathieu de Vendôme
occurrences.label: Epigram of the Hermaphrodite
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: And I—male, female, and neither—suffered by water, weapon, and cross.
body: The schoolman's riddling epitaph: "When my pregnant mother bore me in her womb, they said she asked the gods what she would bear. A boy, said Phoebus, a girl, said Mars, neither, said Juno. And when I was born, I was a hermaphrodite. Asked how I was to meet my end, the goddess replied: By arms; Mars: On the cross; Phoebus: By water. All were right. A tree overshadowed the waters, I climbed it; the sword I had with me slipped, and I with it. My foot caught in the branches, my head hung down in the stream; And I — male, female, and neither — suffered by water, weapon, and cross" (¶89).

Jung treats it as the serious relative of the Aelia inscription — "the most important item" of the triple-death motif (Vita Merlini and its 15th-century imitations) — and notes the alchemists strangely never took it up, "though it might have been a more suitable subject for exegesis." Also kin: the Platonic riddle of the one-eyed eunuch and the bat (¶90), and the Hindu paradox "Awakener to Myself is my name."

occurrences.title: The hermaphroditic gate-god with the hare's head — final vision of Meyrink's Der Golem
occurrences.label: The hermaphroditic gate-god with the hare's head
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: But it caused a tremendous headache!
body: Jung translates the novel's ending at length: the hero returns the hat of Athanasius Pernath at a golden gate flanked by yew trees, the garden wall covered with "a beautiful mosaic made of lapis lazuli"; "The god himself, a hermaphrodite, forms the two wings of the gate, the left side male, the right side female. The god is seated on a precious throne of mother-of-pearl, and his golden head is the head of a hare; the ears are erect and close together, looking like the two pages of an open book." Inside, Athanasius with Miriam on his arm, his face the hero's own mirror. The dreamer's church-dream hermaphrodite sang from here; Jung reads the condensation (Athanasius + Miriam + god) as Trinity-structured Godhead — Father, Son, and female Holy Ghost/Sophia.

occurrences.title: The hermaphroditic idol of formless gold (Visions Seminar, 22 February 1933)
occurrences.label: The hermaphroditic idol of formless gold
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: money, for instance, is coined energy, which can be exchanged against any other form of energy-food, motors, electricity, coal. This formless mass of gold, then, simply means a formless mass of libido
body: The narrow path widens and the next series begins: "I beheld a great idol. It had the head of a woman-the hands of a man reaching up. The lower part was a formless mass of gold."

Jung's reading: the male and female separated in the phallic demon are now united — a divine hermaphroditism, "a superior being that is beyond the male and the female," a condition liberated from the prejudice of sex. Woman's head = mind; man's hands = action (Handeln); the gold is "coined energy," a condensed mass of libido, hence of the greatest value. Hermes (phallic hermai) plus Aphrodite is the mythological formula. Decided progress: the gold that was once a pool or disk in the earth is now heaped above it, an unconscious attempt "at forming a new religion" — not made, just happening to her.

occurrences.title: The Evolution of the Soul — lion and wolf vomiting into the alchemical furnace (Reichstein manuscript)
occurrences.label: The Evolution of the Soul
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: A medieval alchemical picture-book, "called The Evolution of the Soul," belonging to Dr. Reichstein, brought to the seminar to show the hermaphrodite's part in alchemy. "A lion and a wolf vomiting a liquid into the alchemistic furnace, where the opposing elements are boiled or melted together. Out of the mixture is born a symbolic being that appears in two forms, a man and a woman; then they also are melted together, thus making the hermaphrodite, which is often represented with both male and female heads."
Jung: "a complete demonstration of the attempt at the union of opposites" — alchemy as psychology of the unconscious under fear of the church.

occurrences.title: Symbolical drawings of Opicinus de Canistris (Pavia/Vercelli)
occurrences.label: Symbolical drawings of Opicinus de Canistris
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: the symbolical drawings of Opicinus de Canistris afford us an interesting glimpse of the way in which this primordial image was instrumental in uniting opposites, even in a pathological state.
body: The priest Opicinus de Canistris left symbolical drawings (Salomon, Opicinus de Canistris, fn40) in which, Jung says, the primordial image of the male-female union was "instrumental in uniting opposites, even in a pathological state" (¶295). Opicinus' visionary diagrams — cartographic body-mandalas in which his own figure, Europe, and the divine interpenetrate — show the hermaphrodite as uniting symbol at work under psychic strain: the medieval coniunctio performed not in glass but in ink and suffering.

image.title: Cathedral of Pavia

occurrences.title: Phanes in the egg — Orphic relief, Modena Museum
occurrences.label: Phanes in the egg — Orphic relief, Modena Museum
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Roman relief, ~2nd c. AD (Orphic, Hellenistic original?)
body: The Orphic Phanes reproduced as Plate XII: "The Shining One, the First-Created, the 'Father of Eros.'" Jung lists him among the "mythological and philosophical attempts... to formulate and visualize the creative force which man knows only by subjective experience" (¶198), beside the cosmogonic Eros of Hesiod.

His attributes per Jung: Orphically he has "the significance of Priapus; he is bisexual and equated with the Theban Dionysus Lysius" — and "the Orphic significance of Phanes is akin to that of the Indian Kama, the god of love, who is likewise a cosmogonic principle" (¶198). The egg-birth makes him a first-form of the philosophic egg; the bisexuality a first-form of the rebis.

image.title: Arte romana, rilievo con aion-phanes entro lo zodiaco, 150 dc ca., probabilmente da un mitreo

occurrences.title: Fish meal with hermaphrodite statue — British Museum MS Add. 15268
occurrences.label: Fish meal with hermaphrodite statue
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The significance of the hermaphrodite in this context is unknown to me.
body: Plate B1 of CW13: "A fish meal, with accompanying statue of the hermaphrodite. Though the picture is undoubtedly secular, it contains echoes of early Christian motifs. The significance of the hermaphrodite in this context is unknown to me."

Jung's caption is a documented refusal: he reproduces the locus and expressly leaves its meaning open — worth preserving as a marker of where the field still needs work (the fish meal belongs to the early Christian ichthys/eucharist complex he treats in Aion). The hermaphrodite statue co-manifests the rebis family in a secular 13th-century context.

occurrences.title: Hermaphrodite figures on Knights Templar tombstones
occurrences.label: Hermaphrodite figures on Knights Templar…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: It appeared in the Eleusinian mysteries, for instance, and in the mysteries of the Templars,4 as we know from tombstones that have been found
body: Jung's evidence that the hermaphrodite "played a very great role in the past": alongside Plato's primordial round beings and the Eleusinian mysteries, the hermaphroditic figure appears "in the mysteries of the Templars, as we know from tombstones that have been found", and again in the medieval Hermetic philosophy, where the daimon-idea also lived.

This is the tradition behind the dreamer's hermaphrodite dream (dream 23, sung in the wrong tune): "a very interesting religious symbol which we did not elucidate very satisfactorily because it is still a twilight figure" — a divine being "in the ancient sense of the word... the quality of the tremendum or daimon; or... the mana figure" (p604). Dating of the tombstone corpus is inferred from the order's floruit.

occurrences.title: Hermaphrodite with three serpents and one serpent; the three-headed Mercurial dragon — Rosarium philosophorum (Artis auriferae, 1593)
occurrences.label: Hermaphrodite with three serpents…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The rebis of the Rosarium: hermaphrodite with three serpents and one serpent, above the three-headed Mercurial dragon — the ternary/quaternary uncertainty in a single image.

Jung cites it at ¶142 for the aenigma regis: "the final production of the lapis in the form of the crowned hermaphrodite is called the aenigma regis," with the German verse: "Here now is born the emperor of all honour / Than whom there cannot be born any higher."

occurrences.title: The hermaphroditic-mother drawings of the castration-complex patient
occurrences.label: The hermaphroditic-mother drawings…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: A man with a still-unresolved high-grade mother and castration complex, "without any hint from me", made drawings showing the mother first "as a superhuman being", then as a figure of woe with bloody mutilations — before her genitals lay the cut-off male organ: a castration obviously performed on the mother (¶138).

Jung's reading: "the mother was a divine hermaphrodite, who then, through the son's disappointing experience of reality, was robbed of her androgynous, Platonic perfection and changed into the woeful figure of an ordinary old woman" (fn 26: conforms to the bisexual Original Man of Plato's Symposium and hermaphroditic Primal Beings generally). The "castration complex" was really the fall from the childhood Olympus of the syzygy-mother — fear of real life, a "godless" existence.

occurrences.title: 'Here is born the Empress of all honour' — the Hermaphroditus poem, Rosarium 1550
occurrences.label: Here is born the Empress of all honour
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: I became a mother yet remained a maid / And in my nature was establishèd. / Therefore my son was also my father / As God ordained in accordance with nature.
body: A long German poem printed with Figure 10 of the 1550 Rosarium, explaining the Hermaphroditus: the Empress, "daughter of the philosophers," who becomes a mother yet remains a maid; her son is also her father; she bears the mother who gave her birth. Four come together in one, six seen as trinity brought to unity; two eagles rise with feathers aflame and fall naked to earth; a fountain branching east and west is "Lord of sun and moon."

Jung (¶529) calls it "of considerable psychological interest": the "unblessedness" of the first body corresponds to the daemonic, unconscious anima; at its second birth she becomes fruitful and is born together with her son as the Hermaphroditus, "the product of mother-son incest" — virginity unimpaired, a Christian paradox connected with the timelessness of the unconscious, "the mother as well as the daughter... and her son was her father."

occurrences.title: Prayer of Astrampsychos — 'Come to me, Lord Hermes... I am thou and thou art I'
occurrences.label: Prayer of Astrampsychos
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Come to me, Lord Hermes... I am thou and thou art I.
body: Jung closes the footnote on Hermes-as-inner-friend (¶238) with "the beautiful prayer of Astrampsychos", which begins "Come to me, Lord Hermes" and ends "I am thou and thou art I" (Reitzenstein, Poimandres, p. 21). It is the purest formula of the identity-colloquy: the invoker takes the god as the partner within, the voice that answers in one's own heart. In Jung's frame this is the "inner friend of the soul" before its alchemical projection into the Stone — the devotional twin of the alchemist's meditatio with aliquem alium internum.

occurrences.title: Hymn to Hermes 'ruler of the world' — Magic Papyrus
occurrences.label: Hymn to Hermes 'ruler of the world'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: (Hermes, ruler of the world, dweller in the heart, circle of the moon, Round and square...
body: The epigraph Jung chose for the entire Spirit Mercurius monograph: "Hermes, ruler of the world, dweller in the heart, circle of the moon, Round and square, inventor of the words of the tongue, Obedient to justice, wearer of the chlamys, shod in winged sandals, Guardian of the many-sounding tongue, prophet to mortals."

Every theme of the essay is prefigured: Hermes as world-ruler and psychopomp ("dweller in the heart" — cf. the centre ¶186-189), and above all the paradoxical "circle of the moon, Round and square" — a mandala-like self-description uniting the opposites in one figure.

occurrences.title: Hermes finds Adam's seven stone tables in the vale of Hebron — Trevisanus
occurrences.label: Hermes finds Adam's seven stone tables…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: On them was a description of the seven liberal arts. Adam had put these tables there after his expulsion from paradise.
body: Trevisanus reports that Hermes Trismegistus found seven stone tables in the vale of Hebron, left from antediluvian times, describing the seven liberal arts; "Adam had put these tables there after his expulsion from paradise" — deriving from Rabbi Eliezer's tables of the law.

Jung at cw14 ¶571 collects the first-adept legends: Dorn makes Adam the first "practitioner and inventor of the arts" whose descendants engraved the natural arts in hieroglyphs on two stone tables, one found by Noah at Ararat.

occurrences.title: Hermes conjuring the winged soul out of an urn — Attic funeral lekythos
occurrences.label: Hermes conjuring the winged soul out of an urn
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 139. Hermes conjuring the winged soul out of an urn.—Attic funeral lekythos
body: White-ground funeral lekythos showing Hermes Psychopompos drawing the winged soul — a small bird — up out of the burial urn.

Jung uses it as the Greek counterpart of the alchemical soul-release: the pneuma or soul hidden in matter (in the vessel, the stone, the body) that the opus must "draw out," as Ostanes draws the heart from the Nile stone (¶405) and as the fig-tree of the artifex's imaginatio releases spirits (¶394-396). The soul-bird is the representable form of what the alchemists called the spiritus in materia.

occurrences.title: 'Take his brain, powder it with very strong vinegar' — Rosarium
occurrences.label: Take his brain, powder it with very strong…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Take his brain, powder it with very strong vinegar... until it turns dark.
body: A Hermes recipe cited in the Rosarium: "Take his brain, powder it with very strong vinegar... until it turns dark" (at ¶733: "grind it up with very strong vinegar, or with boys' urine, until it turns black").

Jung at cw14 ¶626, 733: the brain was of interest as seat of the "spirit of the supracelestial waters" (Genesis 1:7); in the nigredo "the brain turns black" — the darkening is at once a psychic state, melancholia.

occurrences.title: I Ching hexagram 23 (Splitting Apart): the legs of the bed split
occurrences.label: I Ching hexagram 23: the legs of the bed split
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: traditional compilation King Wen/Prince Chou ~1190 BCE (per seminar)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: A participant's parallel to the parents' beds in the death-mask dreams: "In the I Ching, too, the bed stands for the intimate situation. It says in one oracle (number 23, Splitting Apart): 'The leg of the bed is split—the bed is split at the edge—the bed is split up to the skin'".

Jung: "This is a very good parallel: the bed as a symbol of the inner situation. The oracle points to the fact that the dissolution reaches the unconscious. There are signs of a complete dissolution of consciousness." He adds the seminar's dating — the I Ching as "a work of Chinese philosophy from the second millennium b.c.," its present version written around 1190 by King Wen and Prince Chou while imprisoned, "observing how outer events corresponded with psychical situations."

occurrences.title: Hexastichon on the figures of the evangelists — Sebastian Brant, 1502
occurrences.label: Hexastichon on the figures of the evangelists
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Hexastichon Sebastiani Brant in memorabiles evangelistarum figuras (1502). See our Pls. 1 and 2.
body: Sebastian Brant's 1502 hexastichon verses on the memorable figures of the four evangelists — reproduced as Plates 1 and 2 of CW14 itself (Jung: "See our Pls. 1 and 2"). Cited in the queen-virgin context, where Ripley's stanza crowns the virgin "in quinto circulo" between the arms of the four elements.

Jung's reading: the evangelist-quaternity as the Christian tetramorph enclosing the feminine wisdom-figure — the structural frame the alchemists borrowed for their crowned virgin. Parallels: tetramorph family, dream-portrait-four-colours-cw12-1933, horse-quarter visions.

occurrences.title: Babylonian temple prostitution: the bride and the stranger from afar (Babylon)
occurrences.label: Babylonian temple prostitution
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In that Babylonian rite this archetypal image is lived concretely in order to detach the woman from the parental images which are real archetypal images and therefore exceedingly powerful.
body: A marriage rite whose point, for Jung, is prophylactic: girls of good family gave themselves for a night to a stranger visiting the temple — a man presumably never to be seen again. The impressive image thus implanted collides with the husband-image; when marriage trouble comes, the regressive pull falls not back on the father-image but on "the lover who came from unknown lands," a figure suited to the woman's age (¶365).

Jung generalizes: "there is an archetypal image in women of a lover in a remote, unknown land, a man coming over the seas who meets her once and then goes away again" — Wagner's Flying Dutchman, Ibsen's Lady from the Sea (¶366). Compare jus primae noctis (¶365).

occurrences.title: The celestial marriage of St Catherine of Siena (vision, ~14th c.)
occurrences.label: The celestial marriage of St Catherine of Siena
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: One can understand without difficulty the nature of the feelings repressed by St. Catherine of Siena, which reappeared indirectly in the vision of her celestial marriage
body: Jung's bridge-example that the visions of the saints behave exactly like dreams: "One can understand without difficulty the nature of the feelings repressed by St. Catherine of Siena, which reappeared indirectly in the vision of her celestial marriage" (¶72). The repressed erotic-affected content of the mystic returns symbolized and exalted — the same mechanism by which the hysteric's twilight consciousness produces its compensations, "as there is as little difference between the somnambulistic consciousness of the hysteric and the normal dream as there is between the intellectual life of hysterics and that of normal people" (¶35).

occurrences.title: The Chymische Hochzeit C. R. — Andreae (1616)
occurrences.label: The Chymische Hochzeit C. R. — Andreae (1616)
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The Chymische Hochzeit represents the opus Alchymicum under the aspect of the hierosgamos of brother and sister (Venus gives birth to a hermaphrodite).
body: "One of the latest and most perfect examples" of the alchemical source-cluster of the Faust drama: the Chymische Hochzeit of Christian Rosencreutz (1616), actually by Johann Valentin Andreae (1586–1634), who also wrote the Latin comedy Turbo. "The Chymische Hochzeit represents the opus Alchymicum under the aspect of the hierosgamos of brother and sister (Venus gives birth to a hermaphrodite)"; because the royal children are "too infantile (identification with the parents, incest with the mother), they are slain, purified, and put together again, by being subjected to every alchemical procedure"; the bridal pair is taken over the sea, "a kind of Aegean festival... with nymphs and sea-goddesses", and "Rosencreutz is revealed as the father of the young king or, respectively, the royal couple" (¶1692).

occurrences.title: Intercourse in the furrow to fertilize the field — peasant rite, southern Germany (19th c.)
occurrences.label: Intercourse in the furrow to fertilize the field
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In southern Germany as late as the nineteenth century, in order to increase the fertility of the soil, the peasant used to take his wife to his fields and have intercourse with her in a furrow. This is called sympathetic magic.
body: "In southern Germany as late as the nineteenth century, in order to increase the fertility of the soil, the peasant used to take his wife to his fields and have intercourse with her in a furrow. This is called sympathetic magic" (¶264). Jung sets it at the end of the fertility-rite row: the hierosgamos of the priest of Apollo and the priestess of Demeter at Eleusis (Bishop Asterios' report), the aischrologia of the Athenian ladies, the women of the Isis barges at Bubastis exposing themselves (Herodotus).
The value of the locus: a living, dated folk survival proving the sacred-nuptials image did not die with the mysteries.

occurrences.title: Aegean Festival: hierosgamos of Homunculus and Galatea — Faust II
occurrences.label: Aegean Festival — Faust II
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The Aegean Festival is the hierosgamos of Homunculus and Galatea (both are 'stones brought to life') in the sea.
body: In the Classical Walpurgisnacht, Faust is carried to the "classic 'world of fable' (collective unconscious) for 'healing'"; "The 'water' heals (aqua permanens, mare nostrum). From it emerges the mountain (rebirth of the personality, alch. arising of the terra firma out of the sea)" (¶1698). "The Aegean Festival is the hierosgamos of Homunculus and Galatea (both are 'stones brought to life') in the sea" — a union that, with the touching of the tripod by the key, "prefigure[s] the 'chymical' marriage of Faust to Helen, the sister anima".

Jung's reading: the alchemical opus under the aspect of sea-water and rising land — projection, healing, and the sister-bride union, one stage in the Mercurius renewal-chain (Mephisto-poodle → Boy Charioteer → Homunculus → Euphorion).

occurrences.title: Jesod the faithful Friend uniting Tifereth and Malchuth — Steeb, Coelum Sephiroticum
occurrences.label: Jesod the faithful Friend uniting Tifereth…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: Adam and Eve ch. footnotes; appendix V.288-301, 322 (pdf p460-461, 462)

body: The Kabbalistic love-machine in Steeb's Latin compilation: in naturalibus Jesod contains quicksilver, foundation of the whole art of transmutation; in personibus Jesod denotes the genital member of both sexes — 'this firm rung between Him (Tifereth) and Her (Malchuth)', called angel of redemption, fountain of living waters, tree of the knowledge of good and evil, Leviathan, Solomon, and Messiah son of Joseph; the two olives above it are Nezach and Hod, the two masculine testicles (cw14 appendix V.290-291). In the Zohar, in the story of the Boy, the Just One (Jesod) is called the FAITHFUL FRIEND of Cant. 7:10 — 'Jesod is called Friend because he unites the two lovers: for through him comes the union of Tifereth and Malchuth' (V.301). Malchuth is 'the place destined for the cooking of the influence sent down by her husband, as the woman by her heat cooks the seed for generation' (V.322); the covenant of peace (Foedus Pacis) because through Jesod heaven and earth are joined (V.295).

occurrences.title: 'When the two shall be one' — logion of the Gospel according to the Egyptians (2 Clement)
occurrences.label: When the two shall be one
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~2nd c. logion; quoted by Clement of Alexandria

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: When the two shall be one, the outside as the inside, and the male with the female neither male nor female.
body: In ¶295 Jung traces the coniunctio of male and female through Gnosticism's mysterium iniquitatis back to the Old Testament "divine marriage" (Hosea), and forward through the logion Clement of Alexandria quotes from the Gospel according to the Egyptians: "When the two shall be one, the outside as the inside, and the male with the female neither male nor female." Clement introduces it with "When ye have trampled on the garment of shame" — the body. Clement, Cassian, and pseudo-Clement read it spiritually; the Gnostics "would seem to have taken the coniunctio all too literally" (practising abortion and other restrictions to keep the biological meaning from swamping the religious rite).

occurrences.title: 'Now you are wedded to me' — the Negro opens the cavern (patient vision, 24 June 1931)
occurrences.label: Now you are wedded to me
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: He laughed when he saw me. He said: 'Now you are wedded to me.' We ascended the steps into the daylight. He said again: 'Now you are wedded to me.
body: Caught in the muladhara cave, she hears the vegetation-god Negro descending, singing "I sing to you of darkness and of flaming fields." He opens the door of the cavern — he is the power of the serpent fire she could not stand, projected and lived by him, the psychopompos who opens the way. Twice he says "Now you are wedded to me": absolute, unbreakable union with the black savior. Jung reads the phrase against the Christian "Christ became my brother and my brother is myself": an assumption the world calls insane, but for Jung it means only what Christ did — living one's own way against all traditions, "and he paid for it".

occurrences.title: Marie's honeymoon-and-birth dream — the dream that detonated a school rumour (N., Switzerland, ~1910)
occurrences.label: Marie's honeymoon-and-birth dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: N. (Switzerland): school bathing-place → lake → K. → Andermatt
occurrences.quote: We came to Andermatt, and there was no more room in the hotel so we had to spend the night in a barn. There the woman got a child and the teacher became the godfather.
body: Marie X., thirteen, leader of her class and "almost fully developed sexually," dreamt on the night after a bad report and an outburst of vengeful fantasies against the class teacher (pushing him under a train): the class at the bathing-place, no room, swimming far out in the lake with the teacher, a steamer offering a ride, a wedding at K., a honeymoon journey, and at Andermatt — no room at the hotel, a barn, a birth, the teacher as godfather. Jung: the gaps and abrupt transitions prove a genuine dream, not invention; the lack of room at the bathing-place and at the hotel both abolish the segregation of the sexes (¶99). The dream "gave suitable expression to something that was already in the air" — "the spark which fell into the powder-barrel" (¶126) — and its telling detonated the rumour analysed in the rest of the essay.

occurrences.title: The widow Malchuth awaiting Tifereth — Zohar hierosgamos
occurrences.label: The widow Malchuth awaiting Tifereth
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~13th c. (Zohar; via Knorr von Rosenroth, Kabbala denudata 1677)
occurrences.quote: the coming Messiah will reunite the King with the Queen, and this mating will restore to God his original unity
body: The Cabala's widow: "[Almanah] Widow. This is Malchuth, when Tifereth is not with her" (Knorr von Rosenroth). Malchuth is Domina, the Shekinah, the virago; Tifereth is the King, the Microcosm; Yesod "signifies the genital region of the Original Man, whose head is Kether" (¶18). "In this wicked world ruled by evil Tifereth is not united with Malchuth. But the coming Messiah will reunite the King with the Queen, and this mating will restore to God his original unity" (¶18).

Jung: "The Cabala develops an elaborate hierosgamos fantasy which expatiates on the union of the soul with the Sefiroth of the worlds of light and darkness"; the Shekinah is present in the sexual act, the absconditus sponsus joined with the abscondita sponsa, "neither male nor female" (¶18); Yesod acts as paranymphus at the nuptial canopy (¶19). Vigenerus' alchemical citation of the Zohar (Malchuth = Luna) forms "a link with alchemy" (¶19).

occurrences.title: Creator, macrocosm, and microcosm in human form — Hildegard of Bingen, Liber divinorum operum
occurrences.label: Creator, macrocosm, and microcosm in human form
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 195. Creator, macrocosm, and microcosm in human form, the microcosm surrounded by the elements.—St. Hildegarde of Bingen, 'Liber divinorum operum' (MS., 12th cent.)
body: Visionary illumination from Hildegard's Liber divinorum operum: the Creator enthroned within the cosmic man, the microcosm surrounded by the elements and the zones of the world.

Jung reproduces it beside the Zosimos passages on the Anthropos — the first man, symbolized by the four elements, whose body is the whole heavenly sphere. Hildegard's Christian visionary microcosm shows the same figure the alchemists would call the homo philosophicus, the Microcosm (¶476).

image.title: Liber Divinorum Operum

occurrences.title: The Shilluk address to the slain hippopotamus — 'we killed you for love' (Sudan)
occurrences.label: The Shilluk address to the slain hippopotamus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "It is exactly like the Shilluks when they have killed a hippopotamus. They cut out its intestines and a man creeps into its belly and prays to the spinal cord where its soul is supposed to be: 'My dear hippopotamus, don't think we hate you because your flesh is good to us; don't tell the other hippopotami that we have killed you for hatred; we killed you for love because we love your meat.'" (pdf p714; editor: Lévy-Bruhl, Primitives and the Supernatural)
Jung's use: the exact primitive parallel to the "Who is loving?" question — the Christian says "We love" as the Shilluk says "we killed you for love," both covering self-interest with the word love.

occurrences.title: Hoghelande's iridescent colours on the decoctio (1594) — 'Ut vidi, ut perii'
occurrences.label: Hoghelande's iridescent colours on the decoctio
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Ut vidi, ut perii, ut me malus abstulit error
body: "In his biographical notes (1594), Hoghelande describes how, on the third day of the decoctio, he saw the surface of the substance cover itself with colours, 'chiefly green, red, grey, and for the rest iridescent.' Whenever he remembered that day a verse of Virgil's came into his mind: 'Ut vidi, ut perii, ut me malus abstulit error.'… he had believed that he was on the point of attaining the nigredo. But a few days later his fire went out in the night, which led to an irreparabile damnum" (¶353).

Jung's reading: not necessarily hallucination, but "a remarkable willingness on the part of the author to suspect something of the sort" — projection in the laboratory, the opus mirroring the operator's psyche.

occurrences.title: 'We are now exactly in the beginning of the holocaust' — Zarathustra Seminar (30 Nov 1938)
occurrences.label: We are now exactly in the beginning…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: I rather insist upon these passages, because we are now exactly in the beginning of the holocaust.
body: Jung's historical aside on Nietzsche's curse-chapter: Zarathustra wishes Jahveh's pillar of fire on the crowd, "the consuming fire" as the sign of the great noontide — and Jung reads the wish psychoanalytically: "he thinks that this pillar of fire precedes the great noontide, but it would be the holocaust. If that fire comes it will be a terrible conflagration." Then, instantiating the text against his own time: "I rather insist upon these passages, because we are now exactly in the beginning of the holocaust." The god of fire, madness-as-outburst ("a fire in the house always means an outburst of passion or a panic"), and the prophet consumed by his own flame — Nietzsche as the botched counter-figure whose private fire scales to the age's.

Honesty note (see the-turn): "holocaust" here is the sacrificial-conflagration sense in seminar speech — fifteen months before the war, and before the word's later historical instantiation. Dated, verbatim, no predictive weight added beyond what Jung said. Sits on the arc between the 1936 Wotan essay and the 1940 Aquarius-threshold scheme.

occurrences.title: The Albigenses: the descent of the Holy Ghost as active religious principle
occurrences.label: The Albigenses — the descent…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: Yes, the Albigenses assumed that the descent of the Holy Ghost was the active religious principle, but that standpoint was not elaborated by the church.
body: Where did the idea of the Holy Ghost "play a very great role" in the Middle Ages? Mrs. Flower answers: the Albigenses —

Editor's footnote: "members of a Catharistic sect of southern France (Albi) in the eleventh to thirteenth centuries." Jung sets this beside the Joachimite three-age scheme — Father/Old Testament, Son/New Testament, and the third Reich of the Holy Ghost — "the mystical hook in that term which catches on" in 1930s Germany; the Ghost's "wind quality" cuts both ways, external storm-god or spirit within, "the one is a reaction against the other".

occurrences.title: The sculptor who dug for the Holy Ghost and found a demon god — seminar case (Lecture 9)
occurrences.label: The sculptor who dug for the Holy Ghost…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: A sculptor, for a time Jung's patient, entered his neurosis through a Pentecost fresco: having grouped the apostles well, he left the middle space open for the Holy Ghost, "rejected the conventional symbol of the fire, and fell to speculating on what the Holy Ghost was like after all. While he was digging in his mind for the Holy Ghost, he stirred up the collective unconscious and then began to have wild nightmares". In treatment his sculptures passed from "gods with mouths open and dead eyes" (the libido sucked back) through increasingly complicated figures to one endpoint: "an extraordinarily demoniacal figure closely paralleling one of the demon gods of Java. This then was the Holy Ghost to him". For the patient these contacts with the collective unconscious were his religious experiences. Jung sets the case beside Luther's manifest/concealed God — the negative side of the deity preserved.

occurrences.title: The Holy Ghost as Christ's double — Pistis Sophia ch. 61
occurrences.label: The Holy Ghost as Christ's double
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: When Jesus came in, he recognized and embraced him, and they became one.
body: In Pistis Sophia ch. 61 the Holy Ghost appears as Christ's double — "a proper ka," as Jung puts it via Jacobsohn. He enters Mary's house; she mistakes him for Jesus and binds him to the foot of the bed as a phantom; when Jesus arrives he recognizes and embraces him, "and they became one."

Jung's reading: the Egyptian ka-theology (homoousia of father, son, ka, ka-mutef — Jacobsohn) resurfacing in Gnosticism; the Holy Ghost as the counterpart-double of the god-man (cf. Aion, par. 131). Parallels: ka material, christ-figure-pistis-sophia-vineyard-egypt-3c.

occurrences.title: Invocation of the Holy Spirit as Mother — Acts of Thomas
occurrences.label: Invocation of the Holy Spirit as Mother
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The "famous invocation to the Holy Spirit as the mother" which Jung says "has also played a great role almost within the church": "Come Holy Dove, mother of two young twins. Come Hidden Mother, revealed in deeds alone" (footnoteafter Mead).

Offered in the seminar as the Gnostic interpretation behind Nietzsche's sign of the laughing lion surrounded by a flock of doves: the dove as the feminine bird of Astarte/Aphrodite and as Holy Ghost whose "nature... is exceedingly feminine" — Sophia; ample evidence also in the Pistis Sophia, where "the Holy Ghost was supposed to be the wife of God and the mother of Christ, and Mary was herself the Holy Ghost."

occurrences.title: Joachim of Flora: the third aeon of the Holy Ghost
occurrences.label: Joachim of Flora — the third aeon…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Joachim expected "the opening of the seventh seal... the advent of the 'everlasting gospel' and the reign of the 'intellectus spiritualis,' the age of the Holy Ghost" — secretly begun with St. Benedict (~529), the year the Talmud had prophesied as critical. Gerard of Borgo San Donnino proclaimed 1260 as its public inauguration (Paris, 1254).

Jung's psychological re-reading (par. 142): "Joachim could have been seized by the archetype of the spirit," an ambivalent dualistic figure whose era coincided with the beginning of the second Fish — Holy Ghost movement and antichristian dawning in one. The spirit degenerated into rationalism and doctrinairism, "the most unspiritual of all the spirit's manifestations."

occurrences.title: 'Come, secret mother' — the Holy Ghost in feminine form
occurrences.label: Come, secret mother
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: in the Acts of Thomas the Holy Ghost is addressed as the mother, and it is always the mother-imago which proves to be the hero’s greatest danger but is for that very reason the prime source of his deeds and of his ascent.
body: The Third Person invoked as mother: against the Ophite "first word," "Mother of All Living," and the Valentinian "Word of the Mother from Above" (¶563). With the Acts of Thomas addressing the Holy Ghost as the mother (¶558), the Logos-cow of the Rig-Veda, and the Kore-hymn, the feminine spirit trinity within the godhead.

occurrences.title: The anchorite in the forest — das Licht, bread and wine
occurrences.label: The anchorite in the forest
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The same old man whom Zarathustra met on his descent (ch. 2) receives him again at night, gives bread and wine to the living man and bids the dead companion eat too.

Jung (17 Oct + 24 Oct): the old man is "the old Christian spirit," the wise old man incarnated in the church — the soul-side Zarathustra lacks. The decisive point is linguistic: the German says Er trug das Licht, "he carried THE light," "the definite, revealed light." The bread and wine are the communion, "the central mystery of late Christianity," sought in regression after the marketplace failure: "he naturally approaches a former point of view."

Verbatim: "the English text says he carried a light, but the German text says: Er trug das Licht, 'He carried the light,' and that of course makes a great difference; it is not just any light, it is the light."
First meeting (Prologue 2, 'not yet heard that God is dead') is the sibling-locus senex-figure-anchorite-forest-zarathustra-1883; this note is the chapter-8 re-encounter.

occurrences.title: Brother Klaus's twenty-year fast — Ranft
occurrences.label: Brother Klaus's twenty-year fast — Ranft
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: mid-15th c. (~20 years without sustenance; d. 1487)
occurrences.quote: The fact that Brother Klaus, on his own admission and according to the reports of reliable witnesses, lived without material sustenance for twenty years is something that cannot be brushed aside however uncomfortable it may be.
body: Nicholas of Flue (Bruder Klaus), Swiss hermit at the Ranft, reported — "on his own admission and according to the reports of reliable witnesses" — to have lived "without material sustenance for twenty years". Jung refuses to brush the fact aside: such things "naturally cannot be understood with our present knowledge of physiology" but should not be dismissed as impossible; he looks for the explanation "in the realm of parapsychology" (¶1497), comparing Therese of Konnersreuth's reported life "simply and solely on holy wafers".

His conjecture: nourishment "effected by the passage of living molecules of albumen from one body to another", on the model of the medium investigation he witnessed (ionization sixty times normal near the medium's right thorax; weight losses on scales, ¶1498). Companion locus: the vision work at trinity-vision-brother-klaus-sachseln-1480.

occurrences.title: "I have no more dreams since the English are in the country" — the Elgonyi medicine man
occurrences.label: I have no more dreams since the English are…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: his own political function, the spirit-leading of the tribe, had come to an end
body: Jung's firsthand anthropology for the spirit-leader archetype: "The medicine man of the Elgonyis told us that he had no more dreams since the English were in the country. I asked him why, and he said it was because the chief man in power knew everything; he was in charge of the whole country and knew exactly what to do, and since then, his own political function, the spirit-leading of the tribe, had come to an end" (p107). Dreams here are a political function of the medicine man — the tribe's unconscious guidance in embodied form; colonial authority abolishes the office. Set beside Rasmussen's Baffin-Bay migration-leader, it shows the poimen/seer as the tribe's farsight, and grounds the claim that "such an archetype still exists in us in the form of dream-pictures" (p107).

occurrences.title: Elijah's Carmel — the Carmelite foundation (Mount Carmel, 12th c.)
occurrences.label: Elijah's Carmel — the Carmelite foundation
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~12th c. (first Carmelite convent); numinous site far older
occurrences.quote: According to the empirical rule, an archetype becomes active and chooses itself when a certain lack in the conscious sphere calls for a compensation on the part of the unconscious.
body: The longest continuous numinous site in Jung's Elijah demonstration: a pagan sanctuary on Carmel in Roman days ("tantum ara et reverentia" — Tacitus, Hist. II, 78; Vespasian took an oracle there; Iamblichus has Pythagoras dwell in its sacred solitude, ¶1521); "long... a numinous place as the seat of the Canaanite deities Baal and Astarte", where "YHWH supplants them as inhabitant of the sacred place (Eli-yah... a kind of personification of YHWH or Allah)" (¶1529). "One of these phenomena was the choice of Carmel for the foundation of the first convent in the twelfth century" — the Carmelites adopt the numinous inhabitant as patron.

Jung's reading: "an archetype becomes active and chooses itself when a certain lack in the conscious sphere calls for a compensation on the part of the unconscious" — what is lacking is "the immediate relation with God"; Elijah is "the typical [Anthropos], more human than Christ inasmuch as he is begotten and born in peccatum originale", including "even the pre-Yahwist pagan deities like Baal, El-Elyon, Mithras, Mercurius" (¶1529). The Druses may preserve the altar's place.

occurrences.title: Elijah's chair at circumcision and goblet at Passover (Judaism)
occurrences.label: Elijah's chair at circumcision and goblet…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Jewish diaspora (custom attested from antiquity, ongoing today)
occurrences.quote: A special chair is reserved for Elijah at the rite of circumcision, and at the feast of the Passover... the head of the family opens the door to invite Elijah to enter and share the feast.
body: The living ritual assimilations of Elijah, from Pirkê de-Rabbi Eliezer 29, 31: "It was his spirit that called up the ram which was substituted for Isaac. He wears the ram's skin as a girdle or apron. He is present at the circumcision as the 'Angel of the Covenant'". The ritual practice continues: "Even in our own day, a special chair is reserved for Elijah at the rite of circumcision, and at the feast of the Passover a goblet of wine is placed on the table and the head of the family opens the door to invite Elijah to enter and share the feast" (¶1522).

Jung's reading: these are "phenomena of assimilation" (¶1520) accumulating on a probably historical person and proving "a living archetype"; in Hasidic tradition every male child "receives a part of the soul of Elijah", who appears to him once the soul is developed — Elijah "represents both the collective unconscious and the 'self', atman, purusha, of man" (¶1526).

occurrences.title: Vision series: the Indian tribe and the chief facing the desert (Catholic patient)
occurrences.label: Vision series — the Indian tribe…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich (Jung's Catholic patient, 55, after six years of analysis)

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: Here you see the world of citta—figures which the patient has not made and that live their own lives 'willfully,' according to their own laws.
body: Instructed to watch for images before sleep, the patient sees a dark wall; concentrating (dhāraṇā — "impregnate it"), the wall becomes jungle, then a New Mexico Indian tribe: "The Indian archetype of the American had been animated in her." A lake (the unconscious); canoes cross; desert camp under a motionless sun; only the chief remains, face to the sand desert, immovable for a year of living with the image — until "something had finally moved": humidity in the air. The dogmatic wall had been reached; then the Indian faded and the white serpent appeared.

occurrences.title: Entering the city with bliss-bestowing hands — the Ten Cow-Herding Pictures (Suzuki)
occurrences.label: Entering the city with bliss-bestowing hands
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Japan/China (Zen ox-herding sequence; cited from Suzuki's Essays in Zen Buddhism)

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: Carrying a gourd he goes out into the market, leaning against a stick he comes home.
body: Hauer's Japanese parallel for the return of the awakened Kundalini: the disciple finds the ox (his innermost reality), then "no longer cares for her... he lets it drop into the subconscious again as if there were nothing in it," and finally returns to the marketplace: "Bare-chested and barefooted... Daubed with mud and ashes, how broadly he smiles!... For he touches, and lo! the dead trees come into full bloom." Jung's response: the yoga agrees with his earth-value — "it is right in the body, not in the air."

occurrences.title: Angelus Silesius — the introvert's fate in the monastery
occurrences.label: Angelus Silesius — the introvert's fate…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "Angelus Silesius was such a man; he lived in a time when he simply could not find his equal" — an anachronistic overintensity of consciousness with no understanding contemporaries.

His fate is the introvert's version of Nietzsche's problem: "he locked himself away with his complex. He locked himself up literally in a monastery where he died. He lost all his beautiful poetry completely, and produced fifty-six awful pamphlets against Protestantism... That is something horrible, really satanic." The Cherubic Wanderer's soul "became a terrible, poisonous demon"; his body died before his soul — the exact reversal of Nietzsche's fate. Jung's wry remedy: the monastery cellar and a thousand bottles of old wine.
Verbatim: "his body died before his soul, and his soul became a terrible, poisonous demon-the soul of that man who had produced 'Der Cherubinische Wandersmann,' that sweet mystic verse."

occurrences.title: Simeon Stylites on his pillar (Syria, 5th c.)
occurrences.label: Simeon Stylites on his pillar (Syria, 5th c.)
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: That was the psychology of the early saints, like St. Simeon Stylites.
body: Jung's exemplar of "the psychology of the early saints": St. Simeon Stylites "stood on one leg upon a pillar for seven years... his entire occupation consisted of standing upon one leg, and thousands of people made pilgrimages to see him on his pillar and to marvel at the power of the spirit."

Jung's reading: like the fakirs of India, the saint acquires merit "by their demonstrating the power of the spirit" — it is "tremendously important for humanity to be impressed by the power of the spirit, to believe in it; otherwise they cannot live their lives completely, they degenerate into animals." The same economy explains Lourdes cures (people "it pays to be cured for the glory of the church") and Jung's own first hypnotic miracle, worked on him by a woman who adopted him as the promising son.

occurrences.title: Jung's encounter with a disciple of the Maharshi — Trivandrum, Travancore
occurrences.label: Jung's encounter with a disciple of the Maharshi
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: in Trivandrum, the capital of Travancore, I ran across a disciple of the Maharshi.
body: Having declined to visit Ramana Maharshi at Tiruvannamalai ("he is of a type which always was and will be," ¶952), Jung met the holy man anyway, "in a form that was more congenial to me, without my seeking him out":

An unassuming man of primary-school-teacher status with children to feed — like Anatole France's shoemaker of Alexandria, presented to St. Anthony as the greater saint. He "had absorbed the wisdom of the Maharshi with utter devotion, and at the same time had surpassed his master because... he had 'eaten' the world." Jung: "nothing better could have happened to me" — wisdom, holiness and humanity together, "freedom in bondage, victory in defeat."

occurrences.title: Homo maximus — Swedenborg's Greatest Man, in whose body we are cells
occurrences.label: Homo maximus — Swedenborg's Greatest Man…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Swedenborg's teaching of "the greatest man, the Homo maximus, in whose body we are all like cells. Some of us inhabit his soul, some his eyes, some his brain... People with good brains would live in his brain, those with good eyesight would be hunters... making his eyes. Even the genitalia were not left out, by which he explains certain peculiar temperaments" (p313). This is "Swedenborg's doctrine of the correspondentia" — the classical "sympathy of all things," which the editors note Jung regarded as a forerunner of synchronicity (cf. CW8 ¶924; also "Paracelsus," CW15 ¶12).

Jung's critique: "these ideas remained in a metaphysical concretization. They were never fully evolved psychologically. They got stuck on the way to consciousness." He invokes it to gloss the dream's impersonal public building: the self is not the ego but "a collective institution" (pp312-313).

occurrences.title: Souls of the calcined prima materia escaping as homunculi — Codex Rhenoviensis (15th c.)
occurrences.label: Souls of the calcined prima materia escaping…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Fig. 54 of Concerning Mandala Symbolism: from the Codex Rhenoviensis (fifteenth century), Zurich — the souls of the calcined prima materia escape as vapours, in the form of human figures looking like children (homunculi); in the fire is the dragon, "the chthonic form of the anima mundi, which is being transmuted."

Jung's astonishing caveat (¶708): the parallel patient pictures (Figs 52-53, a woman painting flames with a soul rising from them) were made when neither patient knew alchemy nor he himself the alchemical picture material — evidence that "similar psychological situations make use of the same symbols, which on their side rest on archetypal foundations."

occurrences.title: Homunculus flying in his retort — Goethe, Faust II (Weimar, 1832)
occurrences.label: Homunculus flying in his retort
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

body: The artificial little man created in the alchemist's vessel who flies about in his retort. In the 1932 Kundalini seminar Jung names him the Western anticipation of the ājñā stage: "the idea of the winged egg, or the homunculus in the second part of Faust, the artificial little man that flies about in his retort, is really the anticipation of such a possibility—a man who has created himself again in a new form, as the old alchemist produced a little man in his retort. That, again, I take as a symbol for the vjñv center" (sem-kundalini pdf p158).

Ājñā as "the mandala with the two petals, which looks like the winged seed of certain trees... quite purely white light" — beyond the winged word, touching the Logos-possibility ("become a word, like Jesus").

occurrences.title: Hopi emergence myth — the four cave-worlds, sun, moon and stars (Cushing)
occurrences.label: Hopi emergence myth
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Hopi, Arizona (recorded by Frank H. Cushing)
body: Quoted at length as the closest parallel to the patient's emergence from the cavern: men originally "below... There were four worlds: this world, the top of the earth, and three cave-worlds, one below the other." The Two (divine brothers) pierce the roofs; a jointed cane grows through as a ladder. In the third world the women "became crazed" (Jung: hysteria anticipating a new age). In the fourth: Spider spins a mantle of white cotton (becomes the moon); a white deerskin shield painted turquoise (becomes the sun); Coyote's stolen jar releases the sparks that become stars; Vulture fans the waters into mountains.

Jung: "This myth shows in a wonderful way how those people felt that human consciousness arose, and how at the same time a world came into existence" — the four cave-worlds a system of stages like the chakras, with the mind's localization history: belly (primitives), diaphragm (Homeric phren), heart (Pueblo), head (us).

occurrences.title: Horace's ever-gliding river — 'labitur et labetur in omne volubilis aevum'
occurrences.label: Horace's ever-gliding river
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: In the lecture on time-words: "There is a wonderful verse in Horace, about the river that is flowing and flowing, fleeing past into all eternity, (aevum). Again we find here the peculiar union of energy and time." Aion (time of life) = Latin aevum (eternity, duration of life, epoch) = old High German ewa ("always"), English ever. The river-of-time image in miniature, kin to the patient's great stripe-vision.

occurrences.title: The vulture conceiving by wind — Horapollo's Hieroglyphica
occurrences.label: The vulture conceiving by wind
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~5th c. CE (much used in Leonardo's time)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Horapollo's Hieroglyphica: "vultures are female only and symbolize the mother. They conceive through the wind (Pneuma)" — a word that took on the meaning of "spirit" chiefly under Christian influence (Pentecost's pneuma still double: wind and spirit). The vulture also symbolizes Athene, who "sprang, unbegotten, directly from the head of Zeus, was a virgin, and knew only spiritual motherhood" (¶96).

Jung's reading: "All this is really an allusion to Mary" — the virgin who conceived through the pneuma, like a vulture; hence "There is not a shadow of evidence that Leonardo meant anything else by his picture" (the vulture of his childhood fantasy) — the mythological dual-mother motif, not personal prehistory.

occurrences.title: The horn as remedy against hereditary disease — Atharva-Veda III, 7
occurrences.label: The horn as remedy against hereditary disease
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Vedic root of the alicorn-as-medicine, a "charm against kshetriya, hereditary disease": "Upon the head of the nimble antelope a remedy grows! He has driven the kshetriya in all directions by means of the horn. … O horn, loosen the kshetriya that is knitted into his heart! … (The horn) that glistens yonder like a roof with four wings (sides), with that do we drive out every kshetriya from thy limbs" (¶532).

Jung follows the track east ("The track of the unicorn in pre-Christian days leads us to the East") to the horned fish of Manu and the one-horned hermit Rishyashringa — the horn as the healing, saving point of an Anthropos-like figure.

occurrences.title: The horned Alexander coin of Lysimachus (~297–281 BCE)
occurrences.label: The horned Alexander coin of Lysimachus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: pl. XXa; index 'Lysimachus, coin of, pl. XXa' (pdf p590)

body: The two-horned head on Lysimachus' tetradrachms — Alexander with the ram-horns of Ammon — is Jung's pl. XXa for the "two-horned" motif: "horns: two-horned, 194n, 198n, pl. XXa" (index p566). It belongs to his solar-hero row (cf. book p227, pdf 260, where c02 recorded the coin at ¶285 beside Khidr "of the two horns", 198n — the homology of Alexander-Dhulqarnayn-Khidr).
Verbatim (index): "horns: two-horned, 194n, 198n, pl. XXa"

image.title: Thrace - king Lysimachos - 297-281 BC - siver tetradrachm - head of Alexander III with ram´s horn - Athena Nikephoros - Berlin MK BM

occurrences.title: The black horse thundering by with the shaggy ape-man rider (patient vision, 15 November 1933)
occurrences.label: The black horse thundering…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Suddenly a black horse thundered by.
body: No sooner is the star back in her breast than "Suddenly a black horse thundered by. Upon him rode a shaggy naked man. From the waist down he had the black fur of an animal" — like Pan, but more an ape; the devil too has hairy legs. The rider-horse is the complete man mastering his libido; here an apelike elemental rides — the imp, Kobold or Waldschratt, soulless trickster that "just cannot do it right." Jung's structural reading (22 Nov.): as individuation differentiates her from the universal ape-man — imitation, tradition, "by birth I am a good Christian" — the archaic man of the past rides past, protesting.

occurrences.title: Ashvamedha — the world as the sacrificial horse (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1,1)
occurrences.label: Ashvamedha — the world as the sacrificial horse
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The horse-sacrifice cosmogony: "Verily, dawn is the head of the sacrificial horse, the sun his eye, the wind his breath, universal fire his open mouth. The year is the body of the sacrificial horse..." Day and night stand before and behind him "as the two sacrificial vessels"; "as a steed he carried the gods, as a charger the Gandharvas, as a racer the demons, as a horse men." In BU 3,3 Yajnavalkya tells where the offerers of the horse-sacrifice go: to the razor-edge gap between the shells of the world-egg, whither Indra as falcon, having stolen the soma, delivered the Parikshitas — the psychopomp saving them from "repeated death" (¶659).

Jung: the horse "signifies a quantum of energy at man's disposal... the libido which has passed into the world" (¶658); horse between two vessels = "the birth-giving and the devouring mother," life in the ovum. With Deussen he reads the ashvamedha as renunciation of the world — the same libido that created the world by sacrifice destroys it by renewed sacrifice (¶658). In the Miller drama the horse is "the animal brother of the hero" dying first (¶659).
Verbatim: "The sacrifice of the horse can only produce another phase of introversion similar to that which prevailed before the creation of the world" (¶658).

occurrences.title: Horses with moustaches over their tails — B.St.'s Emperor Francis dream (Burghölzli, ~1905)
occurrences.label: Horses with moustaches over their tails
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The horses have 'moustaches over their tails.' This symbol probably stands for the male genitals, which would also explain the connection with the Emperor Francis, the symbolic husband.
body: In the "Maria Theresa" analysis B.St. dreams of a table with omelets and dried prunes, a dam (Damm) fitted with speaking-tubes, and four horses with moustaches over their tails; she is both Maria Theresa and the Emperor Francis — "in spite of that I am a female." Jung reads the moustaches as male genitals, the Emperor as symbolic husband, and suspects but cannot confirm the anatomical sense of Damm without suggestive questions (¶289). The analysis was repeatedly interrupted by thought-deprivation and an embracing gesture — signs it hit the most strongly repressed material; the erotic song "My Liesel rises early" and a remembered dream of a man's embrace give it, in Jung's words, "a definite erotic colouring."

occurrences.title: The black stallion that strikes fire from the rocks (patient vision, 11 November 1931)
occurrences.label: The black stallion that strikes fire…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I beheld a black stallion. With his hoofs he struck fire from the rocks. I was in the sea and I called to the stallion asking how I could mount him.
body: After the Dionysian wedding she wakes "in the sea" — an unconscious condition, too low. The black stallion striking fire from the rocks comes to the water's edge and carries her out: the instinct as rescuer, though "according to medieval psychology the devil rides on a black stallion" (pdf p500, with Plato's charioteer as the classical parallel, horse-plato-charioteer-black-white-horses-380bce). Jung's careful discrimination: the unconscious libido is indifferent energy, but here it has taken a strongly sexual male form — "the animus is in possession of her libido, he is identical with it, he is the black stallion". The stallion melts away when they face the giant, because an animus horse is itself an animus opinion.

occurrences.title: The bolting cab and the frozen fugitive — acute hysteria in a young woman (1905)
occurrences.label: The bolting cab and the frozen fugitive
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: city street and bridge (Central Europe); anamnesis includes St. Petersburg
occurrences.quote: a cab came up behind them at full trot. The others got out of the way, but she, as though spellbound with terror, kept to the middle of the road and ran along in front of the horses.
body: Jung's exhibit against the trauma theory. A young woman, coming home at midnight, is "as though spellbound with terror" before a cab at full trot: she runs down the middle of the road ahead of the horses, onto a bridge, and has to be restrained from leaping into the river; hysteria with twilight states follows. Yet the same woman had walked calmly through the St. Petersburg volley-fire of Bloody Sunday (22 January 1905) — "people were falling to the ground dead or wounded... These dreadful moments caused her no further agitation" (¶218). The trivial stimulus, not the massacre, was pathogenic; the anamnesis yields a childhood carriage accident (horses bolting to the edge of a river-gorge at seven, ¶220) — and by 1912 Jung is prepared to doubt even that: "perhaps it never happened at all. There is nothing to prevent it from being sheer fantasy" (¶300). The fantasy-world, not the trauma, carries the illness.

occurrences.title: The cab-horse phobia — panic before cab-horses, calm in the St. Petersburg volley (Zurich, ~1900s–10s)
occurrences.label: The cab-horse phobia
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The coachman jumped down and shouted to her to do likewise, but she was in such deadly fear that she could hardly make up her mind. Nevertheless she jumped in the nick of time, while the horses crashed with the carriage into the depths below.
body: A young woman suffered acute hysteria after a trifling shock: walking home from a party at midnight she kept to the middle of the road "as though spellbound with terror" before a trotting cab, ran the whole length of the street "which led across a bridge," and on the bridge had to be restrained from leaping into the river to escape the horses (¶417).

Jung's reading: the same woman had stood in the very street of St. Petersburg "cleared by the volleys of the soldiers" on the bloody 22nd of January [1905], people falling dead around her, "quite calm and clear-headed," and escaped through a yard-gate — "These dreadful moments caused her no further agitation" (¶417). Hence "the intensity of a trauma has very little pathogenic significance in itself" (¶418): the predisposition lay in the horse. Analysis found it — at about seven, out driving with the coachman, the horses bolted "at a wild gallop... for the precipitous bank of a deep river-gorge"; she jumped in the nick of time, the carriage crashed below (¶419). The case walks the reader from trauma theory to the deeper "disturbance in the province of love" that the farewell-party night then uncovered (¶419–420).

occurrences.title: The cosmic sacrificial horse — Brihadaranyaka Upanishad
occurrences.label: The cosmic sacrificial horse
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The ocean is his kinsman, the sea his cradle.
body: The ashvamedha cosmology: the horse as time-symbol and the whole world — "his kinsman and cradle is the sea, the mother, who is the equivalent of the world-soul" (¶426). The libido in the mother, "dying and rising again in the unconscious" (¶426).

occurrences.title: The Spanish city dream — Gothic cathedral and the two cream-coloured horses
occurrences.label: The Spanish city dream
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: dreamt at university; verified in a Spanish city

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: A student friend, promised a trip to Spain if he passed his final examinations, dreamed he walked through a Spanish city; the street led to a square with a Gothic cathedral; turning right at the corner into another street he was met "by an elegant carriage drawn by two cream-coloured horses" — then he woke, and told the dream over beer. In Spain afterwards he recognized the city, the square, the cathedral; remembering the dream's right turn, he took it to test the correspondence: "Hardly had he turned the corner when he saw in reality the carriage with the two cream-coloured horses" (¶973).
Jung's reading: the more foreseen details pile up, "the more improbable does chance become" — foreknowledge in dreams, the objective basis of the sentiment de deja-vu (¶974).

occurrences.title: The black horse and the spear-armed rider — painting exhibited at the Kunsthaus, Zurich
occurrences.label: The black horse and the spear-armed rider
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: Aldrich's second example in the seminar's modern-art discussion: "a painting that was in the Kunsthaus here,2 a great black horse rearing up, wild with demoniac energy. On his back sat a heroic figure of a man armed with a spear, nude except for a helmet, who seemed to look intently ahead into the far distance. He was undisturbed by the ferocity of his horse. This horse, like The Bull, was no particular animal—rather, he was The Horse. Both these pictures stirred me greatly".

The editor identifies it presumably as J. H. Füssli's Huon's Encounter with Sherasmin in the Cave of Lebanon (1804–05), sometimes exhibited at the Kunsthaus. Jung's use of it: like the Lugano Bull-Tamer, it shows the archetypal image — the libido-animal mastered by the hero — appearing autonomously in painting, an argument that modern art draws from the same collective layer the analyst reaches.

occurrences.title: The hoisted horse dream — friend 'X' (Zurich, ~1906)
occurrences.label: The hoisted horse dream — friend 'X'
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I saw horses being hoisted by thick cables to a great height. One of them, a powerful brown horse which was tied up with straps and was hoisted aloft like a package, struck me particularly.
body: A friend's dream: horses hoisted by cables to skyscraper height; the powerful brown horse (tied "like a package") falls when the cable breaks, then gallops off dragging a heavy log — the dreamer's old nickname. A rider on a little horse (his superior) and then a cab-load of children slow it to a safe pace. Jung's full analysis: "By labour one gets to the top" — the ambition-complex (skyscraper = America, given up because of the wife's pregnancy) crossed by the sexual-complex; the horse turns from beast of burden into "the symbol of passionate impulsive desire" (¶130), bridled by pregnancy and children; the rocking-horse/hoops childhood memory explains "little horse" (¶131). An early exhibit of dream as wish-fulfilment read by association, with the dreamer hiding in the image.

occurrences.title: The mad horse that jumps from the window — death-dream of the sixteen-year-old girl with muscular atrophy
occurrences.label: The mad horse that jumps from the window
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: For this was the organic physical libido, one could say, which was threatened or which was going to break loose; the horse was riderless and quite mad, which means self-destructive, as her body naturally was, it was about to stop its functioning.
body: A girl of about sixteen with muscular atrophy of the spine and hysterical overlay; asked for dreams she reported, among "terrible ones," this one: a noise at night, a mad horse galloping through the fourth-story apartment looking for a way out; it finds the open corridor window, jumps; she hears the thud and sees it completely smashed on the pavement below. Confirmation by other dreams: "I knew for certain that it was the end, it meant death."
The riderless horse: libido out of human control, energy changed in quality — the exact counter-image to the patient's ape-man-ridden black horse.

occurrences.title: Plato's charioteer with the white and the black horse (Phaedrus, Athens ~370 BCE)
occurrences.label: Plato's charioteer with the white…
occurrences.subject: n/a
