occurrences.quote: one is a white, docile, pious horse, and the other is black, disobedient, obstinate, rebellious.
body: "In Plato's famous simile, man is compared to a charioteer who has to guide two horses; one is a white, docile, pious horse, and the other is black, disobedient, obstinate, rebellious, and so on. This is obviously the evil horse, because for ages past black stallions have been understood to be bad, not only on account of the color, but because they really are very evil tempered and dangerous". Jung cites it as the classical root of the black-stallion vision and of the medieval "devil rides on a black stallion"; he is careful, though, that the patient's stallion is the animus-force needed to lift her out of the sea, not simply evil.

occurrences.title: The horse rising from the Yellow River bearing the trigrams — the River Map legend (China)
occurrences.label: The horse rising from the Yellow River bearing…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: legendary pre-dynastic (Fu Hsi); undated by Jung

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: Jung's closing image for the lecture on how early philosophers took thought as nature speaking: "The legend says of the I Ching that a horse came up out of the Yellow River bearing on his back the trigrams out of which the symbols are built up. The sages copied it and it was known as the River Map". The sacred animal delivers the primordial diagrams (the Ho Tu or River Map, base of the eight trigrams and sixty-four hexagrams); the sages receive rather than invent. It belongs to Jung's argument that "the brain is also a phenomenon of nature... the fruit of the brain is a natural product and as such must be assumed to contain the general principles of nature" — hence "astonishingly true things in the thought of the ancient sages." Confucius is said to have regretted not spending his whole life on the I Ching.

occurrences.title: Horses with 'half-moons' under their skins — dementia praecox patient, Zurich
occurrences.label: Horses with 'half-moons' under their skins
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: declared that her horses had 'half-moons' under their skins 'like little curls.
body: A schizophrenic patient declared that her horses had "half-moons" under their skins, "like little curls." Jung calls it "a special motif which must have something typical about it" and lines it up with three star-skinned beasts: the horse that carried the "river map" on its coat and so brought the I Ching to China; the Egyptian sky-goddess, the heavenly cow dotted with stars (fig. 25); and the Mithraic Aion bearing the zodiac on his skin (pl. XLIV).
The clinical image and the cult image share one grammar: the animal as carrier of the astral order, the cosmos worn as hide.

occurrences.title: The three-legged and four-legged magic horses — 'The Princess in the Tree' (German fairytale)
occurrences.label: The three-legged and four-legged magic horses
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: the young man, who has hidden himself under the bed, learns that about an hour's journey from the hunting-lodge there dwells a witch who breeds magic horses.
body: From the witch who breeds magic horses the hero wins the four-legged horse by guarding the foals three days, helped by wolf, bear, and lion, and paying tribute of twelve lambs to the twelve wolves. The hunter's own mount is three-legged — a hoof torn off at the border of the witch's realm. The horses talk: "Sister, throw him off!" — and trample the magician. Jung's analysis (¶425-426, 430, 441-445): the horses "represent the unconscious spirit"; "the spirit can be somebody's property"; three-leggedness is "the unconscious masculinity immanent in a female creature" (the bewitched mare-princess, i.e. the animus/shadow), four-leggedness the wholeness of the quaternity. "When the third produces the fourth it at once produces unity" — the axiom of Maria in harness.

occurrences.title: Tishtriya the white horse defeats Apaosha at the rain-lake — Avesta
occurrences.label: Tishtriya the white horse defeats Apaosha…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In this symbolism we can see very clearly how libido fights against libido, instinct against instinct, how the unconscious is in conflict with itself
body: The black horse Apaosha blocks the sources of the rain-lake; the white Tishtriya conquers him at the third attempt. Jung's reading: "libido fights against libido, instinct against instinct, how the unconscious is in conflict with itself" (¶395) — the dragon-horse as guardian of the fertilizing waters.

occurrences.title: Wotan riding the eight-legged Sleipnir — Gotland tombstone
occurrences.label: Wotan riding the eight-legged Sleipnir
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Legend attributes properties to the horse which psychologically belong to the unconscious of man
body: Fig. 28 in the great horse excursus (¶421–428): the god on his steed as god-and-animal unity (Drosselbart, "half man, half horse"); the horse as the unconscious of man — mantic, clairvoyant, path-finding — and as devil's beast (horse's hoof, nightmare), psychopomp (Valkyries, "St. Michael's Horse" as bier, the Persian "wooden horse" coffin).

image.title: Tjängvide bildsten - Historiska museet - 108203 HST - 14081

occurrences.title: Twelve horses in the four quarters — Black Elk's great vision
occurrences.label: Twelve horses in the four quarters
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In Black Elk's vision twelve black horses stand in the west, twelve white horses in the north, twelve bays in the east, and in the south twelve greys.
body: In Black Elk's great vision (Neihardt, Black Elk Speaks, p. 23), twelve black horses stand in the west, twelve white in the north, twelve bays in the east, twelve greys in the south — the spirit-horse hoop of the quarters. Jung cites it as "a remarkable parallel vision" to Zechariah 6:1–3 (four chariots with red, black, white and dappled grey horses, "the four winds of heaven") and to Ezekiel's merkabah wheels.

Jung's reading: spontaneous attestation of the four-fold colour/quarter schema that also structures the alchemical quaternio and the divine-chariot tradition. Parallels: horse-tishtriya-apaosha-rain-lake-persia, Ezekiel 1:16f, joachim-trinity-diagram-zurich-ms.

occurrences.title: Cain and Abel — the prologue in heaven repeated on earth (Genesis 4)
occurrences.label: Cain and Abel — the prologue…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: "it was bound to happen that Adam's first son, like Satan, was an evildoer and murderer before the Lord, so that the prologue in heaven was repeated on earth" (¶618). Cain is "a faithful reproduction of Satan in miniature", the progressive one; Abel, dearer to God, "hasten[ed] away from the evil world" — the imperfect prototype of God's forthcoming son (¶628).

Jung reads the pair through the pleroma: "Cain and Abel, Jacob and Esau, correspond to this prototype, and so, in all ages and in all parts of the world, does the motif of the hostile brothers, which in innumerable modern variants still causes dissension in families and keeps the psychotherapist busy" (¶629). Abel's fate "refers back to a metaphysical event… Egyptian tradition can give us information on this point (Horus and Set)" (¶641).

occurrences.title: Horus and Set — the Egyptian fratricide of light and darkness
occurrences.label: Horus and Set — the Egyptian fratricide…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Cited once but structurally: Abel's fate "refers back to a metaphysical event which was played out between Satan and another son of God with a 'light' nature and more devotion to his father. Egyptian tradition can give us information on this point (Horus and Set)" (¶641). The young dying god and the fratricide motif are "well known in the contemporary pagan religions"; the "short, dramatic course of Abel's fate serves as an excellent paradigm for the life and death of a God become man."

The pair anchors Answer to Job's prehistory of the two sons of God — the dark innovator (Satan/Cain/Set) and the light son well-pleasing to the father (Abel/Horus) — whose final reckoning returns as Christ versus Antichrist (¶654).

occurrences.title: The multi-storey house and prehistoric tomb — Jung's dream on the way home from America (1909)
occurrences.label: The multi-storey house and prehistoric tomb
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.place: at sea, returning from the Clark University trip

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

occurrences.quote: a tomb filled with prehistoric pottery, bones, and skulls; as the dust was undisturbed, I thought I had made a great discovery. There I woke up.
body: The dream Jung called "a kind of prelude to my book" (Wandlungen und Symbole der Libido): a medieval house — from a fine sitting-room down a staircase to a Gothic vaulted room, then a Roman cellar, then, through a square hole, dusty stairs to a prehistoric cave-tomb with pottery, bones and skulls, the dust undisturbed. Freud read it as death-wishes against acquaintances; Jung felt the meaning lay "entirely elsewhere" — the stratified house was the psyche itself, and beneath the personal cellars lay remains of prehistoric man. In 1925 he presents it as the pre-history of the collective unconscious: "In those times I had no idea of the collective unconscious; I thought of the conscious as of a room above, with the unconscious as a cellar underneath".

It drove him to the excavations literature — Babylon, then Creuzer's Symbolik — and so into mythology. Parallels: cave-descent-scarab-sun-serpents-jung-1913 (the imagined descent that enacted what this dream showed) · ghost-crusader-freud-dream-jung-1912.

occurrences.title: Tram #5 to the new ETH: ferry dues 568 and red cherries — dream, 11 Aug 1954
occurrences.label: Tram #5 to the new ETH — dream, 11 Aug 1954
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: dream, Zurich (tram #5, hill path, new ETH premises)

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: The final total is 568 Swi.. franc., which I have to pay.
body: The dreamer rides tram #5 up a winding footpath to "a large new house; it is the ETH in new premises" — public, reformed, where he is apparently to teach. Two letters wait on his office table: a long bill from Pallmann (the "master," formerly the stranger) for "ferry dues settlement," total 568 Swiss francs; and an envelope marked "philosophical choral society" containing beautiful red cherries, some of which he eats.

Jung on the numbers: 5 + 6 + 8 = 19 = 1 + 9 = 10 = 1 — "ars requirit totum hominem, in that 1 is the One and the Whole, hen to pan... the microcosmos corresponding to the macrocosmos". The cherries "are definitely concrete eroticism," with their "prelude in the apple in Paradise"; religere, "to conscientiously and meticulously put into practice," is the payment owed. Eating the cherries has serious consequences — the Wallenstein and isomorphy dreams follow.

occurrences.title: The unknown wing of Jung's house: fish-laboratory, ghost hostelry, old library (recurrent dream)
occurrences.label: The unknown wing of Jung's house
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.yearDisplay: recurrent over years, ending ~1930/31 ('thirty years ago')
occurrences.quote: Several weeks after my dream a parcel arrived containing a parchment volume of the sixteenth century with many most fascinating symbolic pictures.
body: For years Jung dreamt of discovering a wing of his house he never knew: often a historical annex several centuries old, holding old furniture, his long-dead father's laboratory ("comparative anatomy of fishes"), his mother's "hostelry for ghostly visitors," and finally an old library whose unknown volumes opened on "a profusion of the most marvellous symbolic pictures." Weeks after the last dream, a parcel arrived from an antiquarian bookseller: a sixteenth-century parchment volume of alchemical pictures, instantly recognized from the dream (¶478-479).
Jung's reading: "the motif of the unknown annex of my house can easily be understood as an anticipation of a new field of interest and research" — the rediscovery of alchemy, from that moment onward.

occurrences.title: Hui Ming Ching, stage 4 — the centre amid the spirit-fire multiplication (China)
occurrences.label: Hui Ming Ching, stage 4
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Hui Ming Ching (Book of Consciousness and Life)
body: The fourth meditation picture (reproduced pdf p47): "a sage sunk in contemplation, his head surrounded by tongues of fire, out of which five human figures emerge; these five again split up into twenty-five smaller figures" (cw13 ¶46). Jung: "This would be a schizophrenic process if it were to become a permanent state." The Hui Ming Ching warns: "The shapes formed by the spirit-fire are only empty colours and forms. The light of human nature (hsing) shines back on the primordial, the true" (¶46); footnote — the figures are recollections of earlier incarnations.
Jung's reading: the protective circle (mandala) exists to prevent the "outflowing" and to keep the unity of consciousness from being burst asunder by the autonomous figures (¶47).

occurrences.title: Hymn of Hibis: the ram of Mendes, 'the phallus, lord of the gods'
occurrences.label: Hymn of Hibis — the ram of Mendes, the…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Amon-Ra invoked: "Thy Ram dwelleth in Mendes... He is the phallus, lord of the gods. The bull of his mother rejoiceth in the cow, and the husband maketh fruitful through his seed."
Jung's reading: Khnum-Ra as ram, consort of Hatmehit ("mother of Mendes", fish on her head) — divine fecundation as phallic godhead (¶357-358).
Verbatim: He is the phallus, lord of the gods. (cw05 ¶358).

occurrences.title: Hymn of the Pearl — the Gnostic song of the soul
occurrences.label: Hymn of the Pearl — the Gnostic song of the soul
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Syria/Edessa? (preserved in the Acts of Thomas)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: It lies at the bottom of a deep well, guarded by a dragon, in the land of the Egyptians
body: The Gnostic hymn to the soul (James, Apocryphal New Testament, pp. 411-15), ascribed to Bardesanes: the son is sent by his parents to seek the pearl that fell from the King's crown; it lies at the bottom of a deep well, guarded by a dragon, in Egypt — "that land of fleshpots and drunkenness". The heir forgets himself in Egyptian worldliness until a letter from his father reminds him; he plunges into the dark depths, finds the pearl, and offers it to the highest divinity.

Jung's reading: an age "that resembled ours" — the way of the waters that raises up "the treasure, the precious heritage of the father"; from this same matrix "it was a fish — 'levatus de profundo' — that became the symbol of the saviour, the bringer of healing" (¶38).

occurrences.title: Poliphilo meets his anima Polia at the court of Queen Venus — Hypnerotomachia Poliphili (1499)
occurrences.label: Poliphilo meets his anima Polia at the court…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1499 (French version 1600 used by Jung: Le Songe de Poliphile)
body: Francesco Colonna's Hypnerotomachia: "Poliphilo meets his anima, the lady Polia, at the court of Queen Venus, quite untouched by Christianity and graced with all the 'virtues' of antiquity. The book was rightly regarded as a mystery text." (cw12 ¶112).

Jung reads it as Renaissance evidence that scholastic intellectualism "drove the anima to regress to the ancient world" — the same regression his dreamer's sun-worshipping anima displays. Seductive maidens also open the Poliphilo's nekyia (¶61; fig. 33).

image.title: Hypnerotomachia Polifili 00104

occurrences.title: Poliphilo's conjuring of Queen Venus (Hypnerotomachia Poliphili)
occurrences.label: Poliphilo's conjuring of Queen Venus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Poliphilo conjured up Queen Venus; Goethe, Helen of Tray.
body: The Renaissance dream-romance Hypnerotomachia of Poliphilo — with Goethe's Faust — "reach deep into antiquity in order to find 'le vrai mot' for the situation. Poliphilo conjured up Queen Venus; Goethe, Helen of Troy" (¶60). Linda Fierz-David's study is cited in the footnote; a kindred Aldrovandus passage on the anima-dryad appears later in the Rebirth essay (¶224 fn).

Jung's reading: the anima "is conservative and clings in the most exasperating fashion to the ways of earlier humanity. She likes to appear in historic dress, with a predilection for Greece and Egypt" — the classic anima stories of Rider Haggard and Pierre Benoit stand in the same row.

occurrences.title: Hexagram 26, Ta Ch'u — the great accumulating power of the mountain
occurrences.label: Hexagram 26, Ta Ch'u
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: I Ching, King Wen tradition (early Zhou, inferred)
body: The hexagram Jung reads over Germany: "Above is the whole weight of the mountain, and below is Chen [Ch'ien], the Yang principle, the masculine creative principle which is held under. The text begins: 'It is good not to eat at home.' That means, it is good to expand... 'And it is advantageous to cross the great river.'" The lines: axle-trees taken from the cart; a good horse, weapons, "it is advantageous to possess a place to which to go"; the protective board of the young bull; the tooth of the castrated boar; and the last line, "One obtains the way of heaven, success" — Tao.

Jung: "that is the condition which actually prevails in Germany. The people are held under the mountain, and so are forced to revivify... the past"; the patient in the belly of the rock-earth-mother is in the same sign. Learning to unite the remains of ancestral lives to one's conscious purposes is the way to attain Tao.

occurrences.title: I Ching hexagram 29, K'an THE ABYSMAL (water) → 48 Ching THE WELL — Jung's second consultation
occurrences.label: I Ching hexagram 29, K'an THE ABYSMAL → 48…
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: The answer was hexagram 29, K'an, THE ABYSMAL.
body: After writing his analysis of the first answer, Jung asked the oracle about his own action — now himself the acting subject:

The emphasized six in the third place: "Forward and backward, abyss on abyss. In danger like this, pause at first and wait" (¶1002) — which Jung reads as the exact portrait of his feelings writing the foreword, "floating in the thin air of unproven possibilities, not knowing whether what one sees is truth or illusion." K'an also stands for water: "I have found that K'an often turned up with patients who were too much under the sway of the unconscious (water) and hence threatened with the possible occurrence of psychotic phenomena" (¶1005). The changing line produces hexagram 48, Ching THE WELL: the dangerous water-hole proves "an old, ruined well, buried in mud, but capable of being restored to use" — "it contains the waters of life" (¶1013-1014).

occurrences.title: Hexagram 34, 'The Power of the Great' — the goat that butts against the hedge
occurrences.label: Hexagram 34, 'The Power of the Great'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Zhou dynasty text; Wilhelm/Baynes version quoted

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: The hedge opens; there is no entanglement.
body: Quoted at the close of the cherry-tree discussion to picture a hopeless-seeming impasse and its natural resolution: "a goat butts against a hedge and gets its horns entangled." But the next line: "The hedge opens; there is no entanglement. Power depends upon the axle of a big cart."

Jung's use: if the dreamer stopped butting against the fence he would not get his horns entangled, "and presently you would have the power of a cart with four wheels. There is another way in nature, the way of a tree... The tree stands still and grows and makes roots, and eventually overgrows the obstacle." Rationalism and "the impatience of the animal man" leap like a tiger; the I Ching, like the dream, prescribes growth.

occurrences.title: I Ching hexagram 50, Ting THE CAULDRON — Jung's consultation for the English edition
occurrences.label: I Ching hexagram 50, Ting THE CAULDRON
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: For the foreword Jung "personified the book in a sense, asking its judgment about its present situation," i.e. its introduction to the English-speaking public: "I made use of the coin method, and the answer obtained was hexagram 50, Ting, THE CAULDRON" (cw11 ¶976).

The answering subject "looks upon itself as a vessel in which sacrificial offerings are brought to the gods, ritual food for their nourishment" (¶982) — for Jung the original sense of religio, "a careful observation and taking account of... the numinous." The salient nines: "There is food in the ting. My comrades are envious, / But they cannot harm me" (¶979); and of the altered handle, "One is impeded in his way of life... Once rain falls, remorse is spent" (¶980-981). The changing lines yield hexagram 35, PROGRESS — "one obtains great happiness from one's ancestress": the ancestress being the unconscious (¶997).

occurrences.title: Kun the Receptive: 'straight, right-angled, large' — the square earth (I Ching, Wilhelm commentary)
occurrences.label: Kun the Receptive — the square earth
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: hexagram text ~King Wen era (~11th-12th c. BCE); Wilhelm's commentary 1920s

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: Heaven has a circle for its symbol, and the earth a right-angled quadrangle. Thus right-angledness is an original attribute of the earth.
body: Mrs. Baynes contributes "a curious parallel between the last verse in the chapter on the Backworldsmen and one of Wilhelm's commentaries on the I Ching": Nietzsche's "perfect and square-built" healthy body speaking "of the meaning of the earth" against Kun, the absolute yin hexagram. Wilhelm's commentary: "Heaven has a circle for its symbol, and the earth a right-angled quadrangle. Thus right-angledness is an original attribute of the earth."

Jung walks the lines — frost and ice, "straight, right-angled, large," the hidden king dormant in the earth, the tied-up sack, the yellow undergarment as "the desired middle way" — then the cosmological diagram: from Kian (heaven) four elementary forces emanate into the square earth, the Yin-Yang qualities forming "a sort of vortex; the whole system is rotating," straight line → square → cube. His conclusion makes the locus archetypal: "the idea that the earth is four-square has been found at a tremendous depth in the collective unconscious, here as well as in China, and probably all over the world."

occurrences.title: Wilhelm's I Ching demonstration and prognosis — Psychological Club, Zurich
occurrences.label: Wilhelm's I Ching demonstration and prognosis
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Spirit in Man, Art and Literature (CW15)

occurrences.quote: whatever is born or done at this particular moment of time has the quality of this moment of time.
body: Richard Wilhelm's first lecture at the Psychological Club in Zurich, at which "Wilhelm, at my request, demonstrated the use of the I Ching and at the same time made a prognosis which, in less than two years, was fulfilled to the letter and with the utmost clarity" (cw15 ¶84). Jung adds: "Predictions of this kind could be further confirmed by numerous parallel experiences."

Jung's reading. He is "not concerned with establishing objectively the validity of the I Ching's statements" but with "the astonishing fact that the hidden qualities of the moment become legible in the hexagram" — coins and yarrow stalks falling "into the pattern of the moment" (cw15 ¶83-84). The event is his standing analogy between divination and horoscopy: "the moment of birth corresponds to the fall of the coins, the constellation to the hexagram, and the astrological interpretation of the birth data corresponds to the text assigned to the hexagram" (cw15 ¶84). It anchors the synchronistic principle as defined in ¶81-82 of the same memorial.

occurrences.title: The hexagrams of the I Ching in the King Wen arrangement — China
occurrences.label: The hexagrams of the I Ching…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~11th–10th c. BCE (traditional King Wen / Duke Chou recension)

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: Jung's furthest reach in the pairs-of-opposites lecture: "if we treated it properly, we should have to go back to the earliest sources of Chinese philosophy, that is to the I Ching oracle." In it the opposites "appear as an ever-recurring enantiodromia, through the action of which one state of mind leads inevitably to its opposite. This is the essential idea of Taoism, and the writings of both Lao-tse and Confucius are permeated with this principle". The arrangement "in the form given it by King Wen and the Duke Chou, who employed a prison term, so it is said, in working out an intuitive interpretation of the I Ching oracle," is hexagrams "symbolizing the enantiodromia to be expressed... a contradiction psychology." He notes the seminar's good fortune: the English translator of the Wilhelm I Ching (Gary de Angulo/Baynes) is the seminar's own recorder, and Wilhelm is "his master in the art of the I Ching."

occurrences.title: The I Ching oracle method of King Wen and the Duke of Chou
occurrences.label: The I Ching oracle method of King Wen…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: The divinatory technique that made the limitless mantic experiment answerable: forty-nine yarrow stalks divided at random and counted by threes and fives (or three coins thrown six times, heads 3, tails 2), yielding odd and even numbers — representatives of Yin and Yang, "the 'mother' and 'father' of everything that happens" and hence the tertium comparationis between psychic inner world and physical outer. Sixty-four hexagram-interpretations, traditionally ascribed to King Wen and the Duke of Chou, "basing themselves on the hypothesis of the unity of nature... sought to explain the simultaneous occurrence of a psychic state with a physical process as an equivalence of meaning."

Jung's reading: the method, "like all divinatory or intuitive techniques, is based on an acausal or synchronistic connective principle"; he first named that principle in the Wilhelm memorial of 1930 (¶866 fn. 59; ¶986).

occurrences.title: Quantum Physics and I Ching — C. H. Hsieh's lost Shanghai synthesis (Shanghai, 1937)
occurrences.label: Quantum Physics and I Ching
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters
jung.locator: bibliography (pdf p296); discussion at print p.188 (index pdf p310, c02)

occurrences.quote: Hsieh, C. H. [Quantum Phy.ics and I ChingJ, Shanghai, 1937. No known European translation.
body: A Chinese book joining quantum physics to the I Ching, published in Shanghai in 1937 — fifteen years before Jung and Pauli pooled their disciplines in Naturerklärung und Psyche (1952). It stands in this volume's bibliography with the quietly astonishing note "No known European translation", and the index shows the Jung–Pauli circle discussing it in the letters (print p.188).

Whether Pauli knew it before the letters or was told of it mid-correspondence, the locus is the Sino-modern anticipation of the synchronicity programme: an acausal physics and an oracle book converging on one ordering of chance. Content unverified in the vault until a translation or the c02 discussion is pinned.

occurrences.title: The I Ching brought on the shells of one hundred tortoises (Chinese legend)
occurrences.label: The I Ching brought on the shells…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: Remember that the / Ching was brought to land on the shells of one hundred tortoises" (4 June 1930; OCR: the italic I dropped to "/
body: Among the tortoise's marks of rank — armoured house, amphibiousness, apathy, long life, "highly mythological and mysterious" — Jung adduces: "Remember that the I Ching was brought to land on the shells of one hundred tortoises." The editors flag the source as untraceable; the legend is Jung's own rendering of the tortoise-oracle tradition behind the ho-t'u and lo-shu diagrams.

It grounds his claim that these are "the qualities of a particular psychological factor in man — age-old, very wise, and manifesting in the conscious as well as the unconscious": the tortoise as carrier of the archaic wisdom that becomes, in the dreamer, the transcendent function.

occurrences.title: Ignatius Loyola — the Foundation of the Spiritual Exercises
occurrences.label: Ignatius Loyola — the Foundation…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'Man was created to praise, do reverence to, and serve God our Lord, and thereby to save his soul.' Jung sets this beside Dorn's quis/quid: man's end is the 'what' not the 'who'. Stripped of theology: 'Man's consciousness was created to the end that it may (1) recognize its descent from a higher unity (Deum); (2) pay due and careful regard to this source; (3) execute its commands intelligently and responsibly; and (4) thereby afford the psyche as a whole the optimum degree of life and development' (¶253). A quaternity of function, transposing dogma into psychological terms.

occurrences.title: White flames and fields of wheat; the dead child and the jewelled heart (patient vision, 6 May 1931)
occurrences.label: White flames and fields of wheat
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: About my head played white flames. I walked through waving fields of wheat... The heart burned into the flesh of my breast.
body: After the old man's vanishing, her robe turns from green (vegetation) to white and white flames play about her head — enlightenment, "typically Eastern symbolism": unconscious life become light, the power of discrimination. She walks through waving fields of ripe wheat — Eckhart's "innermost nature of all grain," Iacchus, Osiris' wheat-grown sarcophagus, Christ as Host: "the highest illumination within and the highest fertility without... complete Tao." Then the counterstroke: a face of suffering in the ground changes into the dead body of a child — the corpse of her new enterprise. She lays it in the stream; it comes alive, puts round her neck a chain with a jewelled heart that burns into the flesh of her breast (where the earlier ring had marked only her forehead, intellect — now feeling is reached), and walks away growing into a man. A flame shoots from the water bearing a laughing face, and she laughs with it in communion.

occurrences.title: Incubation-dreams in the temples of Aesculapius
occurrences.label: Incubation-dreams in the temples of Aesculapius
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: Temple sleep in the Asclepieia: the sick slept in the temple precinct and the god appeared in a dream that was reported to indicate the appropriate method of healing — the classic institution of the healing dream as vox Dei.

Jung invokes it in "On the Nature of Dreams" as the counter-instance to modern compensatory dreams: "I do not mean that the dreams of modern people indicate the appropriate method of healing, as was reported of the incubation-dreams dreamt in the temples of Aesculapius. They do, however, illuminate the patient's situation in a way that can be exceedingly beneficial to health" (¶549). The god's direct therapeutic instruction belongs to the ancient frame; compensation is the modern functional equivalent.

occurrences.title: The dead Indian on the altar guarded by two iron men (Visions Seminar, 10 May 1933)
occurrences.label: The dead Indian on the altar guarded…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Inside the dark cavern of the belly of the ancestors: "Upon the altar lay an Indian guarded on each side by two iron men... They answered: 'We are the great will of a nation. The Indian is dead. We stand here that he may not live again.'"

Jung: the collective will of her (American) nation has crushed the primitive — "the great will of the nation in her that her primitive or her chthonic side should be suppressed." She turns the iron men's heads and kicks them down; the Indian arises, sees the light upon her breast — she demands his "blood and your sinews and believe in me": Messianic inflation, a reversed, anti-Christian communion assimilating the lower instead of the higher. The Indian = the red Indian animus-psychopompos who has gone ahead since the series began.

occurrences.title: 'I am an infirm and weak old man, surnamed the dragon' — Aurelia occulta
occurrences.label: I am an infirm and weak old man, surnamed…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: That out of Three may come One.
body: The transformative substance speaks in the nigredo: "I am an infirm and weak old man, surnamed the dragon; therefore am I shut up in a cave, that I may be ransomed by the kingly crown... A fiery sword inflicts great torments upon me; death makes weak my flesh and bones... a terrible poison, I am likened to the black raven, for that is the wages of sin; in dust and earth I lie, that out of Three may come One. O soul and spirit, leave me not... that the hero of peace whom the whole world shall behold may arise from me."
Jung at cw14 ¶733: the nigredo monologue — cave, fiery sword, raven, and the coming "hero of peace."

occurrences.title: The inner heaven — 'heaven is man and man is heaven' (Paracelsus)
occurrences.label: The inner heaven — heaven is man…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Spirit in Man, Art and Literature (CW15)

occurrences.quote: For heaven is man and man is heaven, and all men are one heaven, and heaven is only one man.
body: The Paracelsan doctrine of the endosomatic heaven: the firmament located "in man's body," the astrum or Sydus keyed to the individual nativity, the corpus sydereum as "the representative of the homo maximus in the individual" (cw15 ¶22; ¶31).

Jung's reading. He treats it as the Hermetic "heaven above, heaven below" surfacing as an eternal image — "In his conception of the inner heaven he glimpsed an eternal primordial image, which was implanted in him and in all men, and recurs at all times and places" (cw15 ¶31), comparing Kant's categorical imperative as the heir of the Stoic Heimarmene. The lumen naturae shines from it: the corpus sydereum is "the source of illumination by the lumen naturae... Its full development is reserved for the future" (cw15 ¶29). Diagnostically the heavenly Father "can also fall sick" (¶32); therapeutically the planets direct the remedies — brain by Luna, spleen by Saturn, heart by Sol (¶33).

occurrences.title: Instructio de arbore solari — catching the Echeneis in the world-sea
occurrences.label: Instructio de arbore solari
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The anonymous French father teaches his son to catch the Echeneis-remora, 'shut up in that deep mid region of the great universal sea', using the 'magnet of the wise'; caught, it becomes first water then earth, dissolving and purifying all bodies (¶217). Jung: the ocean is the 'spirit of the world', a projection of the unconscious; 'our sea' is the unconscious 'just as it is in dreams'; the extremely small fish in its centre is the self as unconscious content, catchable only because a 'magnet' — the theoria — exists in the conscious subject (¶218). The treatise marks alchemy's turn from laboratory to philosophy.

occurrences.title: Interrogationes maiores Mariae — Christ produces a woman from his side on the mountain
occurrences.label: Interrogationes maiores Mariae
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Christ takes Mary up a mountain, 'produced a woman from his side and began to have intercourse with her... partaking of his flowing seed he showed that this was to be done, that we might live' (¶314). Mary falls to the ground in shock; Christ: 'Wherefore do you doubt me, O you of little faith?' Jung's symbol-by-symbol reading (¶316-320): the mountain = spiritual ascent; Christ = Archanthropos and 'squared circle of the self'; the woman from the side = second Adam playing the Creator-god, androgyny ('I am both, man and woman'); the splitting = 'an act of nascent consciousness'. The counterpart vision: mechthild-rocky-mountain-child-13c.

occurrences.title: Roman castellum of Irgenhausen — the fundus at the centre
occurrences.label: Roman castellum of Irgenhausen
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Jung's exhibit of the rotating ground plan made stone, a bus ride from the seminar room: "Not far from Zurich, at Irgenhausen, near Pfaffikon, are the remains of an old Roman castle with the fundus right in the centre; it has been excavated and repaired to a certain extent. It is always a good idea to see these things in reality." The fort around its central plot enacts the same sulcus primigenius geometry as the foundation rite and the patient's revolving machine.

occurrences.title: Ishtar and Tammuz — the two-fold moon goddess of Babylon
occurrences.label: Ishtar and Tammuz — the two-fold moon goddess…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Dr Harding's report takes Ishtar as the typical moon-woman: "both the moon that rises in the sky and increases to fullness and the dark moon that creeps upon the full moon and overcomes it utterly. She has many lovers, but is always virgin." Her son Tammuz, "a sun-hero... also the vegetation of the whole earth... is condemned by her to a yearly death. There was a religious fast of lamentation when the annual death of Tammuz was celebrated" (p395). Gilgamesh reproached her fickleness — Tammuz, a bird, a lion, a horse, a shepherd, a gardener, himself.

Bright phase: Great Mother, "Queen of the dust, and Mistress of the Field," goddess of wedlock and maternity; dark phase: "Goddess of the Terrors of the Night... the Terrible Mother, goddess of storms and war" — "She is invoked as 'Virgin Mother, Daughter of thy Son'" (p395). Her rites orgiastic, served by sacred harlots; she is the "Ship of Life," the crescent resting on the water; the Chaldean Nuah carried the seeds of all living things in an ark (arka = crescent). The summary line: "She is the divine Astarte, the strength, the life, the health of men and gods; and at the same time she is Evil, Death, and Destruction" (p403).

occurrences.title: Isis invoked as 'the One, who art All' — aretalogy inscription
occurrences.label: Isis invoked as 'the One, who art All'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Hellenistic-Roman Isis aretalogy (~2nd c. BCE–2nd c. CE)
occurrences.quote: All these statements apply just as well to the prima materia in its feminine aspect: it is the moon, the mother of all things, the vessel, it consists of opposites, has a thousand names
body: An inscription of the Isis cult invokes her as "the One, who art All" — the same hen-to-pan formula the Greek alchemists give the uroboros and the arcane substance. Jung assembles the aretalogy's evidence for Isis as the feminine prima materia: the Black One ([Kemet], with Apuleius' palla nigerrima), healer of Ra, "redemptrix," "thousand-named," "the nature of the Aeon, whence all things grew and by which all things are" (Athenagoras), whore in Tyre (Epiphanius), teacher of alchemy in "Isis the Prophetess to her Son Horus" (cross-link water-isis-amnael-vessel-egypt-1c.md), collector of Osiris' scattered limbs, "bathed... with her tears and laid... in a secret grave beneath the bank of the Nile" (¶14).

occurrences.title: Isis' lament for the drowned one — daily temple ritual
occurrences.label: Isis' lament for the drowned one
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: New Kingdom ritual texts (Moret, Mystères égyptiens)
occurrences.quote: I have found the drowned one of the earth of aforetime
body: The lament of Isis for her son(consort) in the daily ritual: "I have crossed the seas to the bounds of the earth, seeking the place where my Lord was; I have traversed Nadit in the night; I have sought... him who is in the water... in that night of the great affliction. I have found the drowned one of the earth of aforetime" (Moret, Mystères égyptiens, p. 24).

Jung's reading: "The motif of the drowned king goes back to Osiris" — the alchemical rex marinus (the king imprisoned in the sea, crying for a deliverer in Maier) descends from the searching goddess and the drowned god. Parallels: filius-regius-lament-maier-symbola-frankfurt-1617, rex-marinus-splendor-solis-1582, night-sea-journey family.

occurrences.title: Isis as nanny holds the royal child over the fire — Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride
occurrences.label: Isis as nanny holds the royal child…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Phoenician setting (Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Jung's first parallel to the fairy's self-burning: "for example, in a story of Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride. Isis got herself employed as a nanny by the king of Phoenicia. The child's mother catches her holding the child right above the fire until it burns. The queen shrieks with fright. Isis takes the child out of the fire and says: 'Now everything is in vain. If you had not shrieked, I could have given the child immortality'".
With the phoenix, Heracles' self-burning on the pyre, and Thetis dipping Achilles (his vulnerable heel the trace of interruption), the locus shows: "burning oneself means immortalization."

occurrences.title: Isis conceives Harpocrates from the spirit of dead Osiris
occurrences.label: Isis conceives Harpocrates from the spirit…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Isis copulated with the spirit of the dead Osiris.
body: "We may recall the myth of Isis and Osiris: Isis copulated with the spirit of the dead Osiris, and from this union sprang the god of the mysteries, Harpocrates."

Jung at cw14 ¶726: Osiris' long alchemical career — lead and principle of moisture in Olympiodorus, life-principle in Firmicus, compared to Hermes by the Naassenes, represented ithyphallically; blackish, therefore called Aithiops ("in Christian usage the devil, and in alchemical language the prima materia"); wine as his blood; sun-and-moon nature, hermaphroditic like Mercurius.

occurrences.title: Isis wounds Ra with the serpent — Egyptian hymn
occurrences.label: Isis wounds Ra with the serpent — Egyptian hymn
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Isis fashions a poisonous snake and sets it in the sun-god's path; from the bite "he never recovered", and must retire on the back of the heavenly cow. In the parallel tradition she also frees Set, whom Horus has bound, and loses her diadem for a cow's head (¶374).

Jung's reading: the mother both wounds and cures — "the real cause of the wound is the incest-taboo, which cuts a man off from the security of childhood" (¶351); the son flees to the mother from the wound she herself inflicted.
Verbatim: The hymn describes how Isis fashioned a poisonous snake and set it in his path, and how the snake wounded the sun-god with its bite. (cw05 ¶351).

occurrences.title: TE TIBI UNA QUAE ES OMNIA DEA ISIS — Capuan votive inscription of Arrius Balbinus
occurrences.label: TE TIBI UNA QUAE ES OMNIA DEA ISIS
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Latin votive inscription from Capua, set up by the vir clarissimus Arrius Balbinus to Isis: "TE TIBI / UNA QUAE / ES OMNIA / DEA ISIS" — 'To thee, to thyself, the One who art all things, the goddess Isis' (CIL X, No. 3800 = 3580; now in the Naples Museum). Cited by Jung in a footnote chain on Isis as the all-containing One.

The inscription condenses the aretalogical formula Isis = the All; Jung quotes it amid Isis material (dew, situla, hierosgamos, 'body of Isis') that feeds his reading of Luna/Malchuth as the unconscious feminine totality.

occurrences.title: The Isles of the Great Green — Egyptian ocean-underworld
occurrences.label: The Isles of the Great Green
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "In Egypt we have the Isles of the Great Green, the ocean, which was also the underworld, the land of the dead" — the destination of Osiris' nightly way under the sea.

Jung's key to Nietzsche's Happy Isles: the blessed-island motif is "a very ancient idea... out in the West, outside the gate of the ocean or the pillars of Hercules"; the Western land of the Gilgamesh epic is likewise the place where the dead dwell in eternal bliss. "Therefore Osiris as the judge of the underworld was always painted a blueish green, the color of the sea". Applied to the man Nietzsche: "Everybody will one day go down to the Isles of the Great Green whether happy or not" — his friends and his enemies alike.
Verbatim: "the movement of the spirit is making for that underground existence, like the way of the sun Osiris that goes under the sea and comes upon the Isles of the Great Green".

occurrences.title: Manidvipa, the jewel island in the sea of nectar
occurrences.label: Manidvipa, the jewel island in the sea of nectar
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: The Hindus call them the 'jewel world' or 'manidvipa,' the jewel island in the sea of nectar.
body: The "jewel world" of the Hindus: children's retained memories of the collective unconscious "continue to live in symbols" and are named, from Hindu cosmology, manidvipa, "the jewel island in the sea of nectar." The same image returns in Appendix 1 for the beyond-death cakras — "the 'house without foundation,' on the 'island in the ocean of nectar'" — and for the child's pre-ego paradise it must leave when it first cries.

occurrences.title: Böcklin's Island of the Dead
occurrences.label: Böcklin's Island of the Dead
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: it is practically everywhere in the form of picture postal cards and such horrors.
body: Jung's modern type-image for Nietzsche's grave-island: "You have probably seen the picture called 'The Island of the Dead' by our famous Swiss painter Böcklin; it is practically everywhere in the form of picture postal cards and such horrors". The sarcastic note on its reproduction is itself evidence: the land-of-the-dead-as-island was alive in the 19th-century imagination, closer to folk reality than to academic allegory — the same geography as the haunted Swiss glaciers and Elgon's bamboo belt.

Introduced in the lecture where the unconscious "is the ghostland, the land of the dead," and the approach to it "has always been thought of as... a reestablishment of the lost connections with the dead."

occurrences.title: Sinbad's island that is a whale — the church as slumbering monster
occurrences.label: Sinbad's island that is a whale
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: then you see the church as an island of refuge, which turns out to be Sin bad's monster
body: Sinbad's sailors land on a green island, light a fire to cook — and the island, an enormous whale, plunges and drowns them. Jung deploys it as the gloss on Zarathustra's priests-chapter verse: "On an isle they once thought they had landed, when the sea tossed them about; but behold, it was a slumbering monster!" — the church as refuge that, fired upon by reformers and enlighteners, sinks with those aboard.

His irony cuts both ways: the man outside the walls is "a fish on dry land" mocking "those poor fishes inside" for drowning, "and you don't see that you yourselves, thrown out on the dry land, are the ones who are really left to perdition". Yet the monster-image stands: what carried you can also carry you down.

occurrences.title: Jacob wrestling with the angel: the hip put out of joint (Genesis 32:24-25)
occurrences.label: Jacob wrestling with the angel
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: where he was wrestling with the angel of the Lord all night, and the angel twisted his hip.s That is the destruction of man's selfish power, and that is inevitable.
body: The injured right hand of dream 25 leads Jung to the motif (worked already in Psychology of the Unconscious) of twisting the arm out of action: "the legend of Jacob in the Old Testament, where he was wrestling with the angel of the Lord all night, and the angel twisted his hip. That is the destruction of man's selfish power, and that is inevitable."

The differentiated function "is nearly always misused for one's own selfish power"; the unconscious's compensation disarms — "in the hero myth, in the supreme struggle, the hero has to fight with his bare hands... finds his arm twisted. He is deprived of his superior function for the sake of the next function which is waiting for differentiation."

occurrences.title: Jahve from 'Ehwe': Schure's hermaphroditic etymology (Les Grands Initie's)
occurrences.label: Jahve from 'Ehwe' — Schure's hermaphroditic…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: this name derives from the eternally female Ehwe, to which was added the masculine or phallic "I.
body: The dreamer's association to the dream-name "Jalaubout": in Schure he had read "about the name Jahve (meaning Jehovah) and that this name derives from the eternally female Ehwe, to which was added the masculine or phallic 'I'" — the masculine and feminine mixed in one figure, "so here we see the relation to the hermaphrodite."

Prof. Hooke corrects the philology: Hebrew hawah (existence), whence Jahve, has no connection with haweh (to live). Jung: "Schure had a wild fantasy here, he is not very careful. He is a poet... He has some very good psychological ideas but they are not his own." Yet the association feeds the dream's reading: Jahve + jalon/phallus → "the divine hermaphrodite and the phallic symbol... two sides of one and the same thing."

occurrences.title: Janet's somnambulic personalities — the four graded states of consciousness (L'Automatisme psychologique, 1889)
occurrences.label: Janet's somnambulic personalities
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Jung draws Janet's somnambulists on the blackboard as four nested circles of increasing scope: No. 1, the waking state, "an exceedingly restricted consciousness" with anesthesia and paralysis; No. 2 a semitrance with wider field; No. 3 deeper; "In No. 4 the anesthesia is entirely gone, there is full sensation of pain and warmth and position... the intelligence is more mature and brighter, more vital". Reciprocal amnesias: No. 4 remembers all; No. 1 remembers none.

Applied to normality: "There are many more people than we think living in No. 1 or No. 2 who are capable of the third state or perhaps even more, but they prefer not to rise... It is really an economic, not a moral question, it is a question of economy of force". The unspent energy of the unreached states consolidates into a personified animus/anima "that lives in no-man's-land and eats up all the libido which is left unoccupied."

occurrences.title: The family tree of Adam — roots in sleeping Adam, Christ crowning the top
occurrences.label: The family tree of Adam
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: "It is also a medieval idea, like the family tree of Adam, with the roots in the sleeping Adam, the Kings of Israel in the branches, and Christ crowning the top as the last descendant—again the lightbearing tree." A medieval variant of the Jesse-tree (Isaiah 11:1) cited in the series tree -> birth of the sun from the tree-top -> Christmas tree, the upward anatomy: roots/Adam (or Ka/body), branches/history, light at the crown (mind or spirit).

occurrences.title: Jesus ben Pandira — the illegitimate son of Miriam and the soldier Pandira
occurrences.label: Jesus ben Pandira — the illegitimate son…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: The legendary Jesus behind the seminar's ambivalent Christ: "Christ as the illegitimate son of a woman named Miriam, by an Egyptian soldier, Pandira. Therefore Jesus was called 'Jesu ben Pandira.'" Jung's psychological continuation: an outcast of Galilee with "a tremendous feeling of inferiority", his first temptation a fight with "his own power-devil, his worldly ambition"; trained among the Therapeutae ("teachers and healers... also well-known for their dream interpretation"), initiated by John the Baptist in the Jordan. (Ed. fn: Klausner 1925; CW 5, par. 594 names another Jesus ben Pandira, putative founder of the Essenes c. 100 BC.)

occurrences.title: Leaden amulet from Egypt: 'I conjure thee in the name of Jesus, the god of the Hebrews'
occurrences.label: Leaden amulet from Egypt
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: That shows the confusion of Jesus with Yahweh, and the mock crucifix was of the same origin. We see there how a new manifestation of God is accepted.
body: A leaden tablet amulet against disease opening: "I conjure thee, (the name of the disease) in the name of Jesus, the god of the Hebrews." Together with the Palatine mock-crucifix (ass-headed Christ, "Alexandros worships his god") it documents for Jung the popular confusion of Jesus with Yahweh — "It was a legend in Rome that the Jews worshipped an ass in the temple at Jerusalem" — and so how a new manifestation of God is actually received: ridiculed, persecuted, assimilated to the old.

occurrences.title: The red jewel in the block of ice — the witch's wedding with fire (Visions)
occurrences.label: The red jewel in the block of ice
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: vision read 3 February 1932 (painted late 1929/early 1930 for Jung)
occurrences.quote: We walked on and soon came to a block of ice. I said: 'Within that ice is a beautiful red jewel. How shall we melt the ice to obtain the jewel?' The man answered: 'Only your body will melt it.' So I lay on the ice which melted away.
body: Animus-soldiers throw away their helmets ("Wear this helmet if you would shield yourself from the world"); one dismounts before the ghost of an old woman whose cauldron seethes with fire: "I will wed you with fire" — flames burst from his head (Logos) and her breast (Eros). In the forest the dragon's knife-tongue is wrenched out, its teeth thrown behind (gossip disarmed; Deucalion/Jason motif). Then:

Jung: the jewel = "the treasure or the jewel of life… here surrounded by a block of ice" — animus-spirituality freezes the heart; only body-warmth and "a drop of hellfire" (Yetzer Hara legend) melt it. Wedding with fire = "a sort of smelting procedure" union of animus and feeling, Yang and Yin, "the beginning-or the anticipation at least-of Tao"; the witch's cauldron "is muladhara". Ends in the aurora borealis: "an enlightenment which is only possible when one is in the depths of darkness".

occurrences.title: Indra pulls up the serpent with the seven treasures, among them the Mani
occurrences.label: Indra pulls up the serpent with the seven…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: part of the creation of the world consists of Indra pulling up the big serpent that is deep down in the sea, and with it he pulls up the seven great treasures, enumerated as seven gods, among whom is Mani, which means the jewel in Sanskrit.
body: Jung's first example of the "rapid enantiodromia" that follows every great achievement — the law enacted in the patient's volcano vision:

"When these treasures are brought to the surface, one would assume that things would be all right, but a most destructive poison wells up from the sea, which threatens to destroy the whole world". Mani is "a title of Buddha in Mahayana Buddhism", and the Tibetan formula "Om mani padme hum, means: Oh, the jewel in the Lotus" — the jewel pulled from the deep as the Self-jewel at the center. The same law: "As soon as the redeemer appears, all the devils crowd together to suppress him".

occurrences.title: The red jewel thrown into the pool - hands reach from the water (Visions, 16 Mar 1932)
occurrences.label: The red jewel thrown into the pool - hands…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Here I pulled a red jewel off the necklace hoping that the water in the pool would cool the jewel which still burned my hand. I threw the single stone into the pool. Instantly hands reached up from the water and sought to pull me in.
body: Inside the ring of fire of the garden-mandala she comes to the central pool - the mother-symbol, "a symbol of rebirth-like the baptismal font, or the washing-house in the center of the mosque". Instead of bathing she cheats: she pulls a single red jewel off the necklace to cool it, and hands reach up from the water and tear at her clothes as she flees.

Jung's reading: the jewel should be endured burning "through and through"; offering one stone instead of the whole necklace "shows a certain hesitation or doubt, a reservation; it is not a complete surrender". Because she makes conditions, "the unconscious wants her completely and unconditionally just because she prefers to make conditions" - hence the demoniacal hands. The pool is the equivalent of the white city; "She simply cannot stand the mandala".

occurrences.title: 'Jezoth le Juste', the fils de l'homme with sixteen points — Paris MS Fr. 14765
occurrences.label: Jezoth le Juste', the fils de l'homme…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: There is an illustration of the 'fils de l'homme' (= Mercurius)... bearing the name 'Jezoth le Juste.
body: An illustration of the "fils de l'homme" (= Mercurius) named "Jezoth le Juste," assigned "the significant number 4 × 4 in the form of sixteen points" — the four cherubim of Ezekiel with four faces each. "In unorthodox fashion he is dressed like a woman, as is often the case with the hermaphroditic Mercurius."

Jung at cw14 ¶634-636: Jezoth = Yesod, ninth Sefira of the lowest triad, the Zaddik or "Just One" — the organ of generation, "spout of the waters," creative and procreative power; alchemically the spiritus vegetativus, Mercurius; the Kabbala denudata's Kamea of 8×8 = 64 numbers represents "the sum of the name of the golden water."

occurrences.title: Joachim of Flora — Trinity diagram (Zurich manuscript)
occurrences.label: Joachim of Flora — Trinity diagram
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Plate II of Aion: the Trinity figure from a Joachimite manuscript, which Jung reads as 'a similar motif' to the stacked quaternities of his own diagrams (¶399, cf. ¶390). Footnote 81: Sabellius' 'silent and unacting God' with three prosopa bequeathed 'the first beginnings of a quaternary view of the Deity' — the basis of Joachim's accusation at Lateran IV (1215) that Peter Lombard posited 'not Trinity, but Quaternity... three persons, and that common Something as a fourth'. The 3+1 dilemma of the God-image in an actual medieval diagram.

occurrences.title: The Zohar on Job: the one-sided offering of exaltation
occurrences.label: The Zohar on Job — the one-sided offering…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Mr. Allemann's contribution, translated by Jung at length. Job "brought no other offering than that of exaltation, which rises... If the evil side had obtained a part of the nourishment of the sacrifice, then that other side would have left the sanctuary... And thus the all-holy one himself woke up that accuser, Satan."

Jung's use: "The collective idea of being good is the reason why our patient is caught by the earth; the dark side is neglected and therefore takes its share all the more" — the exact logic of the earth-mother's seizure. "The great drama of man, as described in Faust, is preceded by the same betting in heaven between the creator and the devil as in the Book of Job."

occurrences.title: St. John consecrating the cup with the small dragon — Quentin Matsys
occurrences.label: St. John consecrating the cup…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: "Strangely enough, in medieval art John, too, has the characteristics of a snake. In a picture of Quentin Matsys, he holds a communion cup containing a small dragon, which he consecrates" (pdf p269; the picture also reproduced in Jung's Transformations and Symbols of the Libido).

The reading follows the Justinos myth: Christ left Eden his body on the cross — "So John is, as it were, the body, the mortal part of Christ!" The beloved disciple carries the serpent-dragon in his chalice: the logos present under the species of the snake, the eucharistic snake of the Ophites and Perates made iconography.

occurrences.title: Jonah in the whale — early Christian earthenware lamp
occurrences.label: Jonah in the whale
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 174. Jonah in the whale.—Early Christian earthenware lamp
body: Early Christian lamp with Jonah cast up in the sea-monster — among the oldest Christian images, from the catacomb repertoire Jung surveys.

In the hero myth, writes Jung, the swallowed state "is known as being swallowed up in the belly of the whale or dragon. The heat there is usually so intense that the hero loses his hair, i.e., he is reborn bald as a babe." Jonah is the canonical Christian form of the alchemical mortificatio: three days in the dark belly as the precondition of emission and mission.

occurrences.title: Joyce, Ulysses Nighttown - 'Kitty Christ, Florry Christ': everyone a Christ (1922)
occurrences.label: Joyce, Ulysses Nighttown - Kitty Christ…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: \"Rush on! Join on right here for Eternity Junction!\" or: \"Now you rub shoulders with Christ and Satan!\
body: Jung, on the leading idea of the religion after the Christian age: "the leading idea of a new religion following the Christian age would be that everybody would be Christ, that Christ had been merely the projection of an entirely human mystery... I am not the only one to have had this idea, others have thought of it too, one person whom you would not expect, Mr. James Joyce in Ulysses. In the brothel scene, the prophet preaches in American slang, most outrageous, blasphemous language... 'Rush on! Join on right here for Eternity Junction!'... There are six people, three whores and three men, and he addresses each by his or her name, Kitty Christ, Florry Christ, and so on. He makes everyone a Christ".

"Everybody is now a Christ, and inasmuch as he is a Christ he is crucified" - the vision's star-spear. Ed. note: Joyce lived in Zurich and met Jung; Jung's essay "Ulysses: A Monologue" followed that fall (CW15, pars. 163-203).

occurrences.title: The cook's chicken-saviour — Jung family kitchen, Basel
occurrences.label: The cook's chicken-saviour
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: When the Saviour of men came down to earth, the chicken saviour also came to the chickens.
body: Jung's childhood anecdote: the Swabian cook, returning with the decapitated bantam cock, consoles the household — "He died like a Christian, although he was so wicked … so now he'll go to heaven." Challenged by Jung's mother, she insists animals have souls and their special heavens, "because when the Saviour of men came down to earth, the chicken saviour also came to the chickens, and that's why they must repent of their sins before they die if they want to go to heaven."

Jung's point: "The theology of our cook is a remnant of that folklore mentality which saw the drama of redemption going on at all levels and could therefore discover it even in the mysterious and incomprehensible transformations of matter" (¶495) — the living substrate beneath the alchemical lapis-Christ parallel.

occurrences.title: Jung in the 'haunted' cave - the phosphorescent corpse in the black water (~1925-26)
occurrences.label: Jung in the 'haunted' cave - the phosphorescent…
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: That white phosphorescent body rising out of the black water was a sight that gave one the creeps, particularly as in climbing over the boulders and along the crevasses, one became awfully nervous and could well understand why such a place had a bad reputation.
body: A cave of "particularly ill repute" at almost eight thousand feet, "which they said was inhabited by devils... and if anyone entered it, he was instantly killed" - devils that "put out the light and strangled the man." Suspecting carbon-dioxide pockets in the volcanic mountains, Jung's party descends with lanterns and ropes - and finds the locals keep their salt there: "You see, it was a place that only in the distance had that evil reputation... not even the ghosts work at home, they are only devils abroad".

Inside, in a water-filled crevasse: "we came upon a very ghastly corpse of a Negro... He suddenly shone out in the light of our lanterns as a white body, his skin looking white on account of a certain phosphorescent fungus which was growing on it. That white phosphorescent body rising out of the black water was a sight that gave one the creeps". Also the bamboo forest at 9000 ft, where the trembling soldier whispers: "Yes, thousands and thousands" of ghosts. The empirical nucleus of the place-spell - "the expression of the particular spell of a place".

occurrences.title: The owl-like face in the jungle - Jung's lived archetype in Africa (~1925-26)
occurrences.label: The owl-like face in the jungle - Jung's lived…
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: As we stood there gazing I suddenly saw the most peculiar owl-like face staring up at me from the jungle, and I instantly realized that the face in reality would be huge, many times over life-size.
body: From a house-high rock in the primeval forest, "I suddenly saw the most peculiar owl-like face staring up at me from the jungle, and I instantly realized that the face in reality would be huge, many times over life-size" - eyes "at least one yard in diameter." Field glasses resolve it into "the peculiar contour of the foliage," but "instead of putting my mind or heart at rest, it had the contrary effect. I had the feeling, now something is soon going to drive me mad and it has to do with that thing down there". He stands an hour "in a state between rage and panic... like a cornered animal."

Jung's definition piece of the lived archetype: "Now that is the lived archetype. If I had been a primitive I would have said: 'Ah, here is the devil, a tremendous owl monster is living in that wood, an old witch or a medicine man having taken on the form of a were-owl'". Naming it - the symbolic archetype - is what relieves: "The moment you can designate the lived archetype by its symbol, you feel relieved." Ed. note: in MDR (ch. IX) Jung places the experience in his own psyche - the "going black."

occurrences.title: Little ladders for the Ka and the twelve portrait statues before the Ramses temple
occurrences.label: Little ladders for the Ka and the twelve…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Jung's Egyptian parallel to the death masks of the dream: "the idea of the burial chambers, above which there is the Ka, the semimaterial soul of the Egyptian. This Ka keeps the likeness, not to be lost, so that the dead person, when looking for his body, is reminded of what he actually looked like. The dead person was, for instance, also given little ladders into the grave, so that the Ka could climb up into heaven; or there stood twelve identical portrait statues in front of the Ramses temple, so that the king would not lose his identity".

"For when he dies and becomes a spirit, he might possibly forget who he was." Hence: "The dreamer has made a quite correct burial according to the archetype. She has seen to it that the parents do not lose their identity" — the masks as "a provision for a possible rebirth."

occurrences.title: The living ka of Thutmosis III — 'the victorious bull which shines in Thebes'
occurrences.label: The living ka of Thutmosis III
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: The ka of the king even has an individual name. Thus \"the living ka of the Lord of the Two Lands,\" Thutmosis III, was called the \"victorious bull which shines in Thebes.\
body: In the Trinity essay's argument on divine sonship and the king's ka, Jung notes that the ka is not a generic force but a named individual:

The divine double with its own epithet — bull of the mother-goddess, shining one — a personified "second self" attached to the living king, older brother of the Christian paraclete-argument Jung is building.

occurrences.title: The omen-day in the Kabras forest — mamba, puff-adder, hyenas (Elgon, 1925–26)
occurrences.label: The omen-day in the Kabras forest
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Kitoshi region, Kabras forest, south of Mount Elgon, East Africa
occurrences.quote: He dreamed he was hunting in Africa, and was suddenly attacked by a huge mamba, so that he woke up with a cry of terror.
body: An expedition day that stacked omen on omen: Jung all but stepped on a puff-adder in the thick grass; that afternoon his companion returned "deathly pale," having barely shot a seven-foot mamba that darted at him from behind a termite hill; at nine that night the camp was attacked by hyenas that had torn a man to pieces the day before. Then no more accidents for the whole journey. The key: the companion had had a nightmare in Zurich just before leaving — "he dreamed he was hunting in Africa, and was suddenly attacked by a huge mamba, so that he woke up with a cry of terror" (¶128) — which he had taken as portending one of their deaths; he later nearly died of malarial fever.

Jung's reading: for the African porters the day was "the inevitable fulfilment of an omen" from the first-day Ford-in-the-stream calamity; "for us it was a simple multiplication of chance events." The sequence is his prime exhibit for the primitive science of chance-series.

occurrences.title: Kathakali — god-impersonation dance-drama of Kerala
occurrences.label: Kathakali — god-impersonation dance-drama…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: if one carefully observes the tremendously impressive impersonations of the gods performed by the Kathakali dancers of southern India, there is not a single natural gesture to be seen. Everything is bizarre, subhuman and superhuman at once.
body: The dancers "do not walk like human beings — they glide; they do not think with their heads but with their hands"; their faces vanish behind blue-enamelled masks. Jung: they are no nocturnal phantoms but "intensely dynamic figures, consistent in every detail... more like realities which have not yet been, potential realities which might at any moment step over the threshold" — and to the Indian they are real: "our sense-world fades into a dream, and we seem to wake up in a world of gods" (¶909).

occurrences.title: 'I am the master-key' — the key of heaven in the B.St. case (Burghölzli, ~1905)
occurrences.label: I am the master-key
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: it is a key that unlocks all doors—therefore it includes the house—it is a keystone—monopoly—Schiller's Bell.
body: Stereotypy: "I am the master-key." In continuous association the key wobbles between the doctors' pass key that unlocks every asylum door and the patient herself: "I am not the house-key but the house — the house belongs to me — yes, I am the master-key" (¶230). Jung: by it "she solves the complex of her internment"; the same key that unlocks all doors "prompts the analogy with the key of heaven, which opens for her the door to bliss" (¶231). In the neighbouring crown-analysis the key is "necessary for incontrovertible justice," bolts the door of heaven, and admits her to her coronation as Queen of Heaven (¶229). Asylum incarceration transfigured into Petrine office.

occurrences.title: The theological student's dream of the two magicians and the keys of paradise
occurrences.label: The theological student's dream…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: sent to Jung (student unknown to him personally)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
jung.locator: reused in 'Phenomenology of the Spirit in Fairytales' ¶398 — pin tbd

occurrences.quote: But there lie the keys o.f paradise.
body: A young theological student, "in great straits because of his religious beliefs", dreamt (¶70-71): a handsome old man dressed entirely in black — the white magician — whose closing words were "And for this we need the help of the black magician"; then a double in white; then the black magician's tale of an old king who chose for his tomb the grave of a buried virgin — the bones took on life and changed into a black horse which fled into the desert; pursuing it, the magician found the lost keys of paradise. Dreamer woke at the climax.

Jung's reading (¶72-79): the old king is the ruling symbol seeking its rest in the grave of the anima-Sleeping-Beauty; the black horse is Plato's unruly passions; paradise — Eden and the apocalyptic city — "is conceived as a mandala... the mandala is a symbol of individuation"; the dream paraphrases the Oxyrhynchus sayings and the Ophitic serpent-Saviour; the two magicians are two aspects of the wise old man, "the archetype of the spirit" (¶74), going back in direct line to the medicine man; good and evil work together (nirdvandva).

occurrences.title: Khidr as white light at the door — dream of Jung's Somali headman (Kenya)
occurrences.label: Khidr as white light at the door
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: One 'night, while he slept, he dreamt he saw a bright white light near the door and he knew it was Khidr.
body: During the 1925-26 safari through Kenya the headman, a Somali raised in the Sufi faith, told Jung that Khidr was for him a living person who might be met in the street, as pure white light in the night, or even as a blade of grass. Out of want after the war he dreamt of a bright white light near the door, knew it was Khidr, rose in the dream and saluted him salem aleikum — and a few days later was offered the post of safari headman in Nairobi (¶250). Jung's point: the self-symbol still functions as "friend, adviser, comforter, and teacher of revealed wisdom", dogmatically ranked as maleika kwanza-yamungu, "First Angel of God" (¶251).

occurrences.title: Khidr the Verdant One — Qur'an, Sura 18
occurrences.label: Khidr the Verdant One — Qur'an, Sura 18
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Khidr may well be a symbol of the self. His qualities signalize him as such: he is said to have been born in a cave, Le., in darkness.
body: Khidr, "the Verdant One", appears in Sura 18 as the mysterious servant of Allah whom Moses begs to teach him: he scuttles a fishing-boat, kills a youth, rebuilds a falling wall, then explains the hidden mercy of each act. Jung treats the whole Sura as a rebirth mystery and Khidr as a symbol of the self: born in a cave (darkness), the "Long-lived One" who continually renews himself like Elijah, dismembered at the end of time by Antichrist like Osiris yet restoring himself to life, counsellor and Paraclete (¶247). Khidr stands for "not only the higher wisdom but also a way of acting which is in accord with this wisdom and transcends reason" (¶247); he is paired with Dhulqarnein like the Dioscuri, and still lives in popular religion as "First Angel of God" (¶251) — as Jung's Somali headman attested.

occurrences.title: Khunrath: the Circumrotation of the Quaternarius into the Catholic Monad
occurrences.label: Khunrath — the Circumrotation…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the basic mandala of alchemy
body: "Through Circumrotation or a Circular Philosophical revolving of the Quaternarius, it is brought back to the highest and purest Simplicity of the plusquamperfect Catholic Monad. … Out of the gross and impure One there cometh an exceeding pure and subtile One" (¶165). Khunrath adds the Pauline "Cupio dissolvi, et esse cum Christo" and the command to "catch the Spirit and Soul of the Magnesia."

Jung: spirit (ternarius) must be separated from body (the fourth) and re-infused; Khunrath's Pseudo-Aristotle passage has "the circle re-emerges from a triangle set in a square. This circular figure, together with the Uroboros—the dragon devouring itself tail first—is the basic mandala of alchemy" (¶165).

occurrences.title: Kihe Wahine, goddess of goblins and lizards — Hawaiian wood figure
occurrences.label: Kihe Wahine, goddess of goblins and lizards
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Pl. XVI: kou-wood figure with human teeth, "goddess of goblins and lizards" — the devouring mother of Polynesia.

Jung's reading: cited (¶254) as visual embodiment of the Terrible Mother, "the mother of innumerable evils", whose stagnant-pool phantasmagorias veil reality; cf. the lamias and Frobenius' devouring whale-dragon (¶365, 369).
Verbatim: This dangerous passion is what lies hidden beneath the hazardous mask of incest. It confronts us in the guise of the Terrible Mother (pl. XVI...) (cw05 ¶254).

occurrences.title: Kilkor mandala: cock, snake and pig — lust, envy, ignorance as the roots of the world
occurrences.label: Kilkor mandala — cock, snake and pig
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Jung's Buddhist instance of the meaningful Three: "In Mahayana Buddhism, you will find the Three as the center of the carnal world: a cock, a snake, and a pig. The cock is lust, the snake envy, and the pig ignorance. These three are the roots of the world, these are the three causes of what happens in the world. This can be found in the so-called Kilkor Mandala, which has these three figures at its center".

Said against reducing the three snakes of the girl's dream to sexuality: "This is about emotionality, not only about sex. The other seven devils are implied too: wrath, concupiscentia, avarice, envy, hate, in short, all the devilish things. That's what the Three is!" Companion: Mahasukha's three eyes for past, present, and future.

occurrences.title: Copper as earthly sun, a king upon earth — Zosimos, True Book of Sophe
occurrences.label: Copper as earthly sun, a king upon earth
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: From Zosimos' 'True Book of Sophe the Egyptian and Divine Lord of the Hebrews, and of the Powers of Sabaoth': 'as the sun is the blossom of fire, and the heavenly sun is the right eye of the world, so also the copper, when purification makes it to blossom, is an earthly sun, a king upon earth, like the sun in heaven' (cw14 ¶353).
