Jung: 'the above passage from Zosimos is, to my knowledge, the earliest reference to the king in alchemy' (¶354). The king-gold is born only through liberation of the divine soul or pneuma 'chained in the elements'; chrysopoeia runs as a psychic operation parallel to the chemical one, 'actually... its causa efficiens' (¶354).

occurrences.title: King and Lord of Lords reborn from his glassy sepulchre — Khunrath
occurrences.label: King and Lord of Lords reborn…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Khunrath (Amphitheatrum, 1595): 'When at last... the ash-colour, the whitening, and the yellowing are over, you will see the Philosophical Stone, our King and Lord of Lords, come forth from the couch and throne of his glassy sepulchre onto the stage of this world, in his glorified body, regenerated and more than perfect, shining like a carbuncle, and crying out, Behold, I make all things new' (cw14 ¶355). Jung unfolds the mystic birth: Ruach Elohim penetrates 'the meditullium of the virginal massa confusa'; the son of the Macrocosm and the son of God are 'a mysterium typicum' — 'the one in the womb of the Macrocosm, the other in the womb of the Microcosm', both virginal (¶355). The triune stone: 'earthly, heavenly, and divine... Sal-Mercurius-Sulphur' — the Egyptian sequence Pharaoh, ka, God.

occurrences.title: The King of Glory, 'a worm and no man' — Naassene psalm exegesis in Hippolytus
occurrences.label: The King of Glory, 'a worm and no man'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: But who, say the Naassenes, is this King of Glory? A worm and no man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people.
body: Hippolytus, reporting the mysteries of the Naassenes: the form that "comes down from above, from the Uncharacterized" is found in earthly clay and none recognize it; "that is the god who dwells in the great flood," calling and crying out from the many waters (identified with the multitude of mortal men). To the Uncharacterized Man: "Save mine Only-Begotten from the lions" (a feminine μονογενη, read as the soul). Psalm 23's "King of Glory" gates-of-ascent passage is referred to Adam's regeneration (αναγεννησις), and the King is "A worm and no man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people."
Jung: Maier can have had no access to the long-lost Philosophumena, "and yet it might well have served him as a model for the king's lament" (¶182) — an amplificatio row across thirteen centuries.

occurrences.title: King and Queen immersed in the bath — Rosarium philosophorum, Figure 4
occurrences.label: King and Queen immersed in the bath
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The immersion in the 'sea' signifies the solutio— 'dissolution' in the physical sense of the word and at the same time, according to Dorn, the solution of a problem.
body: The fourth Rosarium woodcut: the royal pair descend together into a bath — the risen mercurial fountain now reaching them from below, counterpart of the dove descending from above.

Jung (¶453-456): the motif has countless alchemical variants (the king drowning in the sea, the sun drowning in the mercurial fountain, the green lion swallowing the sun, Gabricus dissolved into atoms in the body of Beya). The immersion is the solutio — physical dissolution and, per Dorn, "the solution of a problem"; a return to the dark initial state, the amniotic fluid of the gravid uterus (the vas hermeticum as uterus gestating the foetus spagyricus). It is "another night sea journey," as the Visio Arislei proves; a descensus ad inferos into the unconscious. The soul emerges as anima media natura — hermaphroditic vinculum between body (queen) and spirit (king): "Wholeness is a combination of I and You" (¶454). The stage recapitulates the Original Man (Nous) bent down to earth into the embrace of Physis.

occurrences.title: King and Queen joined by the dove — Rosarium philosophorum, Figure 2
occurrences.label: King and Queen joined by the dove
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The gesture points to a closely guarded secret, to the 'left-hand path,' as the Indian Tantrists call their Shiva and Shakti worship. The left-hand (sinister) side is the dark, the unconscious side.
body: The second woodcut of the Rosarium series: the royal bridegroom and bride (brother-sister as Apollo and Diana, standing on sun and moon) give each other their left hands while their right hands hold a device of five (4+1) flowers on three branches; the fifth flower is brought down by the dove of the Holy Ghost from the quintessential star.

Jung's reading (¶410-411): the left-hand contact is the "left-hand path" — the dark, unconscious, incestuous side of the relationship; the right-hand union is mediated from above by the donum Spiritus Sancti, an ogdoad (5 flowers + 3 branches) recapitulating the Mercurial Fountain. Crucially, king and queen are not the adept and his soror mystica but their projected contrasexual components — the man's anima appears as the queen, the woman's animus as the king (¶421). The incest that is taboo for men is the prerogative of kings and gods: "Incest symbolizes union with one's own being, it means individuation or becoming a self" (¶419).

occurrences.title: Death of the royal pair — putrefactio and conceptio — Rosarium, Figure 6
occurrences.label: Death of the royal pair — Rosarium, Figure 6
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Vas hermeticum, fountain, and sea have here become sarcophagus and tomb. King and queen are dead and have melted into a single being with two heads.
body: The sixth Rosarium woodcut: fountain, sea, and vas hermeticum have become sarcophagus and tomb; king and queen lie dead, melted into a single being with two heads. The legend calls it the putrefactio — yet the picture is also entitled "Conceptio": corruptio unius generatio est alterius.

Jung (¶467-474): when the opposites unite, all energy ceases — the waterfall of nuptial joy is a stagnant pool. Like Gabricus after union with Beya, and the son-lover of the Near-Eastern mother-goddess, the pair die after the hierosgamos; the death carries a tacit punishment for the sin of incest ("the wages of sin is death"), its blackness the immunditia needing the later ablutio. But the corpse is already the anticipated hermaphroditus (Hermes-Mercurius + Aphrodite-Venus), the rebis or lapis not yet alive. Psychologically: death-archetype (Linus, Tammuz, Adonis, Good Friday), ego-dissolution, the "royal game" between anima and animus, and — translated — the union of ego and anima producing a transcendent "self" (¶474).

occurrences.title: King and queen perish in the fiery bath — Abraham Eleazar
occurrences.label: King and queen perish in the fiery bath
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Nor is the queen freed; she must perish in this fiery bath.
body: Eleazar on the king's bath: "For in this fiery sea the king cannot endure; it robs the old Albaon of all his strength and consumes his body and turns it to blood-red blood. Nor is the queen freed; she must perish in this fiery bath."

Jung at cw14 ¶537: the close connection of king and queen rests on their shared fate — she is dissolved with him in the bath (in another version she is the bath itself); the pair form a unity because they are forerunners of it.

occurrences.title: 'You need me as the cock needs the hen' — Senior, De chemia
occurrences.label: You need me as the cock needs the hen
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung flags "the classical passage" for the coniunctio's reciprocal need: Senior's "Tu mei indiges, sicut gallus gallinae indiget" (You need me as the cock needs the hen) — De chemia, p. 8. The barnyard image carries the natural-necessity argument Jung builds on for the king-queen pair: the opposites' union as instinctual complement, not moral choice. Senior's treatise recurs through the volume (secrecy oath at p416 n7; "Tria et Tria sunt unum" at p414 n6).

occurrences.title: The King of Thule and his dying mistress' golden beaker (Gretchen's song, Faust I)
occurrences.label: The King of Thule and his dying mistress…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: There was a king in Thule, True even to his grave— To him his dying mistress A golden beaker gave.
body: Gretchen's song in Faust I: a king in Thule faithful unto death, whose dying mistress gives him a golden beaker he treasures and finally hurls into the sea before his own death. Jung uses it in 1909 as the model instance of how a dream works: one does not need to know Gretchen to find the complex that sets her singing — "the hidden thought is Gretchen's doubt about Faust's fidelity" (¶69). Supposed she had dreamt the romance instead of singing it: the far-off king is "an association by analogy, a symbol for Faust, and the 'mistress' for Gretchen" (¶71), the song the manifest content, a "beneficent veil drawn over her grief" (¶70).

occurrences.title: The sunken king renewed with three crowns and seven stars — Splendor Solis
occurrences.label: The sunken king renewed with three crowns…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Trismosin's Splendor Solis narrative: philosophers 'saw a Fog rise... the impetuosity of the Sea... and how these same became foul and stinking in the darkness. They further saw the king of the Earth sink, and heard him cry out with eager voice, "Whoever saves me shall live and reign with me for ever in my brightness on my royal throne," and Night enveloped all things'; next morning a star appears, the sun clears the clouds, and the king is 'released and renewed', crowned 'with three costly crowns, the one of Iron, the other of Silver, and the third of pure Gold', sceptre with seven stars (cw14 ¶465). Jung: 'The king sinking in the sea is the arcane substance... The arcane substance corresponds to the Christian dominant, which was originally alive and present in consciousness but then sank into the unconscious and must now be restored in renewed form' (¶466).

image.title: Splendor Solis 07 drowning king

occurrences.title: Kircher — the four monads of the Arithmologia
occurrences.label: Kircher — the four monads of the Arithmologia
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Kircher's quaternity: Unum = Monas monadike = Deus = Radix omnium; the tenth (1+2+3+4) = mundus intellectualis, 'composition from opposites'; the hundredth = Anima; the thousandth = omnia sensibilia, Corpus (¶416). When the senses are raised through reason to intelligence and 'absolute unity', 'then the Stone too is not so much a Stone as no Stone, but everything is the simplest unity' (¶417); the lapis 'is the arcanum that contains God or that part of God which is hidden in matter' (¶417). Kircher's cycle — God unfolding and returning through human understanding — is another opus circulare (¶418). Communication from M.-L. von Franz.

occurrences.title: Kleist's faith destroyed by Kant's Critique of Pure Reason — suicide
occurrences.label: Kleist's faith destroyed by Kant's Critique…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Heinrich von Kleist (1777-1811), Romantic poet, read Kant's Critique of Pure Reason — the demonstration that man is locked into his own mental categories and can know nothing of God or a world beyond — and wrote that his highest ideal had been destroyed: "he had lost everything, and then he shot himself" (pdf p1419; double suicide with Henriette Vogel).

For Jung this is "a classical case" of the sacrifice entailed by every return from the world of eternal ideas to real life: Kleist "had lived in the magical world of childhood in which the whole Middle Ages lived... he could not give up the paradise of childhood". The same structure reappears in the patient's vision: what is destroyed by the discriminating mind crumbles. Kleist killing a woman with himself is read as putting the anima to death at the same time (Dr. Escher's suggestion, endorsed).

occurrences.title: The Gensha koan — 'Do you hear the murmuring of the brook?'
occurrences.label: The Gensha koan — Do you hear the murmuring…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: A monk once went to Gensha, and wanted to learn where the entrance to the path of truth was. Gensha asked him, 'Do you hear the murmuring of the brook?' 'Yes, I hear it,' answered the monk. 'There is the entrance,' the Master instructed him.
body: Jung returns to the anecdote to define the transformation of consciousness it points to: "It is not that something different is seen, but that one sees differently. It is as though the spatial act of seeing were changed by a new dimension." When the Master asks his question "he obviously means something quite different from ordinary 'hearing'" (¶891).

occurrences.title: The Wu koan — 'Has a dog a Buddha nature too?'
occurrences.label: The Wu koan — Has a dog a Buddha nature too?
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~9th c. (Master traditionally Chao-chou, 778–897; chunk names no master)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)
Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: A monk once asked the Master: 'Has a dog a Buddha nature too?' Whereupon the Master replied: 'Wu!
body: The classic example of the koan in Jung's Suzuki foreword:

Suzuki's gloss, endorsed with relish: "'Wu' means quite simply 'bow-wow' — obviously just what the dog himself would have said in answer to such a question." Jung: the koans are so paradoxical that no rational connection to the enlightenment-experience can be discovered; the answer that comes is "an answer of Nature, who has succeeded in conveying her reaction direct to the conscious mind" (¶895). "How much wisdom there is in the Master's 'Wu'!" (¶901)

occurrences.title: Christ and Church as androgyne — Koepgen, Die Gnosis des Christentums
occurrences.label: Christ and Church as androgyne
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Christianity is neither male nor female, it is male-female in the sense that the male paired with the female in Jesus's soul.
body: A Catholic theology of the androgyne: "in the person of Jesus the male is united with the female"; the Church, his heir, is "hierarchically masculine, yet her soul is thoroughly feminine"; the virgin priest "fulfils in his soul the androgynous unity of male and female."

Jung reads it at cw14 ¶527-528 as modern testimony that the androgyny of Christ — a Gnostic inheritance (the hermaphroditic Primordial Man) — survives in doctrine: the androgyne "has everything it needs" and is already a complexio oppositorum, which "certainly forestalls the marriage of the Lamb." Koepgen's John-14 motto ("greater works than these") makes the believer the bearer of the mystery — the opus Christi transferred to the individual, the very development alchemy anticipated unconsciously (¶531).

occurrences.title: The hero in the belly of Kombili the King Fish — Polynesian myth
occurrences.label: The hero in the belly of Kombili the King Fish
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Swallowed by the King Fish, the hero lights a fire in its belly, cuts out a piece of the heart, then cuts the belly open with his obsidian knife, slips out and beholds a splendour: "Then the sun rose up with a bound."

Jung's reading: one of Frobenius' devouring/sea-journey/opening/slipping-out sequences — rebirth from the whale-dragon (¶310-311); the fire in the belly "kills" the dark state of union with the mother.
Verbatim: the hero, in the belly of Kombili, the King Fish, seized his obsidian knife and cut open the fish’s belly. (cw05 ¶311).

occurrences.title: Case X — Kore vision series (blue mother, golden pig, youth with cymbals, Earth Mother in the snake den)
occurrences.label: Case X — Kore vision series
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: I saw a white bird with outstretched wings. It alighted on the figure of a woman, clad in blue, who sat there like an antique statue. The bird perched on her hand, and in it she held a grain of wheat.
body: A series of spontaneous visual impressions (with X's paintings), presented in the Kore essay as the clearest modern Demeter-Kore material: a white bird alights on a blue-clad archaic mother holding a grain of wheat; a bull lifts a child like Europa; a golden pig on a pedestal; a man in a golden carriage leaps from a hole, rapes the girl and begets a child; a beautiful youth with golden cymbals dances, dissolves into a swarm of bees, sinks exhausted into the lap of a very old mother, sports like a dolphin and falls into a gorge; sacrifice of sheep with a ball-game and blood-bath; X transformed into a plant; a den of snakes; and in the den beneath the sea a sleeping divine woman in a blood-red garment — the Earth Mother — who kisses X and hands her to the men. Emergence brings illumination: white flames playing about her head in waving fields of grain (¶333). Jung: "not the slightest trace of any known myth being repeated", yet every motif familiar from mythology (¶334).

occurrences.title: Case Y iv — the dancer who becomes bees, leopard, octopus; the lily and the white lady
occurrences.label: Case Y iv — the lily and the white lady
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Jung's practice (dream-space: magician's show for an Indian prince)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: During the dance she dissolves with the music into aswarm of bees. Then she changes into a leopard, then into a jet of water, then into an octopus that has twined itself about a young pearl-fisher.
body: Part dream, part visual imagination: a magician demonstrates his tricks to an Indian prince, producing from under a cloth a beautiful dancer. During the dance "she dissolves with the music into a swarm of bees. Then she changes into a leopard, then into a jet of water, then into an octopus that has twined itself about a young pearl-fisher"; again human; then a she-ass with baskets of wonderful fruits; a many-coloured peacock; naked, she tears the skin from her body and falls down — a naked skeleton. Buried by night, "a lily grows out of the grave, and from its cup there rises a white lady, who floats slowly up to the sky". Jung reads the series as "the successive transformations of the illusionist... until she becomes a transfigured personality" (¶350) — artistry in illusion as "a specifically feminine talent".

occurrences.title: Case Y iii — two pictures by 'Hermann Christian Lund': the witchlike humpback and the faceless girl in the dragon's power
occurrences.label: Case Y iii — two pictures…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Jung's practice (dream-space: gallery of invented paintings)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The second picture shows a dragon with its neck stretched out over the whole picture and especially over a girl, who is in the dragon's power and cannot move... Strangely enough, the girl has no face, at least I couldn't see it.
body: Y sees two pictures by the Scandinavian painter Hermann Christian Lund — an invention of the dream. In the first, peasant girls walk arm in arm, the middle one smaller, humpbacked, "keeps turning her head back... gives her a witchlike look". In the second, "a dragon with its neck stretched out over the whole picture and especially over a girl, who is in the dragon's power and cannot move... Strangely enough, the girl has no face, at least I couldn't see it" (¶349). Jung reads the painter motif through the animus as projection apparatus, and the two pictures as the maiden demonic (evil glance — hence amulets worn on the nape) and the maiden as innocent victim of the monster, the girl-dragon relation of identity "which in practical life is often rather more than just a bad joke".

occurrences.title: Case Y v — the girl in the red dress hanging on the stone cross
occurrences.label: Case Y v — the girl in the red dress hanging…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Near the tabernacle a girl in a red dress is hanging on the stone cross of the window. (Suicide?)
body: "I am in a church made of grey sandstone. The apse is built rather high. Near the tabernacle a girl in a red dress is hanging on the stone cross of the window. (Suicide?)" (¶351). Jung reads it with the sacrifice of children and sheep in the earlier material: "the sacrifice of the maiden hanging on the 'cross'" — the doomed maiden whose exclusive domination of the feminine psyche hinders the maturation of personality. The Kore crucified in the church's own architecture: the maiden fixed where the redeemer belongs.

occurrences.title: The maiden-goddess in purest white carrying a black monkey (case vision)
occurrences.label: The maiden-goddess in purest white carrying…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: I remember a case, in fact, where a maiden-goddess appears clad all in purest white, but carrying a black monkey in her arms.
body: Among "very few cases where Demeter's own noble figure in its pure form breaks through as an image rising spontaneously from the unconscious" Jung recalls one where "a maiden-goddess appears clad all in purest white, but carrying a black monkey in her arms" (¶311). Kore in her celestial purity, with the chthonic animal tucked in her arm — the maiden-mother ambivalence in a single image, kin to the white-bird/black-monster alternations of the other Kore material.

occurrences.title: Koschei the Deathless and Queen Maria Morevna — Russian variant of the spirit-fairytale
occurrences.label: Koschei the Deathless and Queen Maria Morevna
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 19th c. collection ('Maria Morevna', 'daughter of the sea')

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The evil spirit is an old man who is often shown naked and is called Koschei the Deathless. The corresponding witch is the well-known Baba Yaga.
body: Jung's postscript (¶435) adds the Russian variant found only after completing the essay: Czarevitch Ivan, his three sisters married to bird-men ("a species of angel" = auxiliary unconscious functions), the evil spirit as Koschei the Deathless — an old man often shown naked, chained with twelve chains in the forbidden room — and the witch Baba Yaga. Ivan, unlike the German swineherd, is killed and dismembered: "The old man puts the dismembered body into a barrel which he throws into the sea. This is reminiscent of the fate of Osiris (head and phallus)" (n55). The princess is Queen Maria Morevna, a martial leader — "Mary the queen of heaven is lauded in the Russian Orthodox hymnal as 'leader of hosts!'". "This Russian story has a distinctly more primitive character."

occurrences.title: The krater filled with nous — Poimandres (Corpus Hermeticum IV)
occurrences.label: The krater filled with nous — Poimandres
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)
Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: This interpretation comes very close to the baptismal krater of Poimandres and to the Hermetic basin filled with nous which God gave to those seeking ἔννοια.
body: In the Hermetic dialogue God sets a krater before the craftsman's world, filled with nous, into which those seeking ennoia (understanding) are baptized — mind given as a cup to be plunged into. Jung links it to the water chalice of the Church Order of Hippolytus and the baptismal font "where the inner man is renewed as well as the body" (¶313), and again to the "divine water" of the alchemists, since "nous is identical with the alchemical Mercurius" (¶355).
Zosimos was probably an adherent of the Poimandres sect, so the krater stands behind his visions' production of divine water by sacrificial transformation.

occurrences.title: Krishna and Arjuna on the chariot — the divine companion
occurrences.label: Krishna and Arjuna on the chariot
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~2nd c. BCE–2nd c. CE (Gita layers, inferred)
occurrences.quote: the disciples on the road to Emmaus, Krishna and Arjuna in the Bhagavad Gita, Moses and El-Khidr in Sura 18 of the Koran
body: Second of the three companion-examples: Krishna as charioteer guiding Arjuna in the Bhagavad Gita — the divine companion who drives while the hero fights, then reveals himself as the Lord "whose body is the whole universe."

Jung's use is typological rather than exegetical: the companion "who goes through life at our side" is "in all probability a close analogy to the lonely ego who finds a mate in the self" (¶155). The Gita supplies the Indian branch of the companion motif alongside the Christian (Emmaus) and Islamic (El-Khidr) ones.

image.title: Sri Krishna preaching Gita Upadesh to Arjun

occurrences.title: Krishna and Rhada: the mandala dance (nritya)
occurrences.label: Krishna and Rhada: the mandala dance (nritya)
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: That dance figures express the same meanings as the drawings
body: Jung's amplification of Nietzsche's ring of dancing maidens: Krishna comes to a society of indistinct milkmaids, "perfectly indistinct, all alike of course, and he chooses one who becomes his favorite, but he also married seven or eight others. Rhada is chiefly chosen to join him in the mandala dance, the nrityia, that circular dance which forms a mandala; Krishna and Rhada are in the center, of course representing the god and his shakti."

The choice that makes one figure distinct is the whole psychological point: the plural maidens are the multiplicity of the unconscious anima; choosing gives a woman a name. Jung notes elsewhere "some of his women patients have preferred dancing a mandala to drawing one" (footnote, CW 13 ¶32), and pairs the couple with Shiva and his Shakti.

occurrences.title: Kubin's Die andere Seite — Patera's dream town dissolving into jungle (1909)
occurrences.label: Kubin's Die andere Seite
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung's literary analogue for the patient's enantiodromia: "Alfred Kubin was an artist not a writer, but he suddenly wrote a book, which was really a representation of an attack of the collective unconscious... He describes the life in the unconscious in the form of a town, and it is an exceedingly original and funny description". Its culmination is "the discovery of a peculiar figure, Patera, who is a sort of ruling principle of the unconscious" (name from Latin pater); "after that culmination the whole atmosphere changes, strange signs are observed and wild animals appear, lions and snakes... finally the town dissolves into the jungle again... and Patera himself is substituted by a Mr. Bell, an American" (pp1372-1373).
Read against Meyrink's Golem and Das grüne Gesicht (both previously discussed in the seminar). The transformation "when the unconscious loses the lead and the conscious takes it on."

occurrences.title: The mad white horse galloping through the cellars of the dream city — Kubin's Die andere Seite
occurrences.label: The mad white horse galloping…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Germany / Austria (the fictional city of Pearl)
occurrences.quote: In the ghostly town where he is living, which is the collective unconscious, there is a peculiar uncanny feeling, and he discovers the reason to be that a mad white horse is galloping through the underground cellars of the town, never finding its way out.
body: Kubin's novel (Jung called it "a classic example of the direct perception of unconscious processes," Letters 1, 19 Nov 1932) supplied Jung with two parallels in one term. (1) The unconscious city slowly invaded by wild animals creeping out of nowhere, "preparatory to an absolute change in the unconscious" — a prophetic anticipation, Jung says, of the volcanic outburst of 1933. (2) The nightmare horse: a mad white horse gallops through the underground cellars of the ghostly town, never finding its way out — "a life that got lost in the tombs of the collective unconscious and went mad".
Riderless = out of control; white in men's material, black in women's — hence the patient's black horse.

occurrences.title: St. Kümmernis — the bearded crucified virgin of Bavaria
occurrences.label: St. Kümmernis — the bearded crucified virgin…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Bavaria (images seen by Miss de Witt)
body: Miss de Witt's contribution, endorsed by Jung: "Is St. Kümmernis in Catholic theology, the saint with a beard, a last vestige of this?... I have seen images of her in Bavaria... Dr. Jung: That is extraordinary. I never heard of her. But it is quite possible." Jung adds the parallel of St. Phalle, "who is worshipped in a chapel on the French Riviera; he is simply the old Priapus taken over into the Catholic church. So such an old androgynous god might also have been smuggled into the church."
The bearded crucified virgin (Kümmernis/Wilgefortis) continues the androgynous deity at the far end of the tradition that runs from Aphroditos through the alchemical hermaphrodite.

occurrences.title: The woman who refused the proposal - receiving in the sign Kun (clinical case, 16 Mar 1932)
occurrences.label: The woman who refused the proposal - receiving…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The situation was that that woman was more or less in love with the man, and he behaved like a man and tried to go a bit further, because life always wants to amplify itself. And then she could have received that proposition in the sign Kun, in Yin. But she said no.
body: Practical parallel to the refused pool, told in the seminar: a gifted, extremely extraverted woman with a nervous breakdown - palatial home, "ideal marriage," an adopted boy of sixteen who looks like the uncle she has loved for seven years and who once proposed intimacy and was refused. "So she has been desperate for four years, and the boy reminds her day and night of the uncle".

Jung: "she could have received that proposition in the sign Kun, in Yin. But she said no" - the pool she did not enter. Refusing in the right moment drops her into hell, where the white Yang column tortures her: "She is now playing the man herself, she persecutes that man, woos him... she was not a woman, she was an opinionated animus, she became a woman too late. And now to play the role of a persecuted man makes her neurotic". Kun, the receptive earth: "yielding, dark, and primal in the I Ching."

occurrences.title: The black serpent in the belly ascends with golden head (post-war case)
occurrences.label: The black serpent in the belly ascends…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: Then the serpent moved slowly upward, coming finally out of her mouth, and she saw that its head was golden.
body: A twenty-eight-year-old who "wanted to be cured within ten hours" declared she had a black serpent in her belly "and thought that it should be awakened." She was not on earth: intuitive, dreaming herself in balloons "from which I had to shoot her down." One day the serpent moved, turned, ascended, and came out of her mouth — "and she saw that its head was golden. This is the shortest Kundalini path of which I have heard... not experienced but only intuited; but already this had a curing effect for the time being. This case is a simple example of the spontaneous appearance of the Kundalini."

occurrences.title: The sleeping Kuṇḍalinī coiled three and a half times round the liṅga — Śaṭcakranirūpaṇa vv.10–11 (Bengal, 1577)
occurrences.label: The sleeping Kuṇḍalinī coiled three…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1577 (Pūrṇānanda, Śrī-tattva-cintāmaṇi ch. 6; trans. Woodroffe, The Serpent Power, 1919)

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

body: The emblematic locus of the whole seminar — Appendix 4 prints Woodroffe's full translation of the Śaṭcakranirūpaṇa: "Over it shines the sleeping Kuõìalinz, fine as the fibre of the lotusstalk. She is the world-bewilderer... Like the spiral of the conch-shell, Her shining snakelike form goes three and a half times round åiva" (vv.10–11, sem-kundalini pdf p162).

Same locus: the mūlādhāra lotus's four crimson petals, the King of Elephants bearing the child Creator (v.6), the Ḍākinī (v.7), and Svayambhū in liṅga-form "beautiful like molten gold, with His head downwards" (v.9) whom She envelops. Jung's clinical parallel is the Java patient's white-elephant dream; his own term for the awakening process is "psychic objectivity".

occurrences.title: The musician who crawled on the lawn like a beast after the dance (Zurich, Jung's early practice)
occurrences.label: The musician who crawled on the lawn like…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: Jung's early practice (case followed twenty years)

jung.locator: 24 June 1931 (pdf p486-488); cf. Dream Analysis p. 705

occurrences.quote: He just escaped by making the immense sacrifice of his whole personality, and the sacrifice of his hard-won artistic achievement as well, because that was associated with it.
body: A very introverted, gifted young musician, refused a dance by the girl he loved, went home in despair, and in the garden "was seized by such a terrible wave of emotion that he rolled on the grass, biting the ground and crawling about like a beast." Jung uses the case to define the danger of the roots: "that moment was enough to kindle the fire" — the dynamite dormant in him, the serpent leaping and catching him in muladhara. The man escaped by the immense sacrifice of his whole personality: he gave up music because it was associated with emotion, became "the most commonplace individual," and for twenty years lived in fear of the emotion that might detach the Kundalini a second time.

occurrences.title: The recumbent female figure dormant in the roots (picture in The Secret of the Golden Flower, 1929)
occurrences.label: The recumbent female figure dormant in the roots
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: picture in Wilhelm/Jung, The Secret of the Golden Flower (1929)
occurrences.yearDisplay: German ed. 1929 (pictures painted by patients 'independently from any Eastern influence')
occurrences.quote: there is one in The Secret of the Golden Flower, a recumbent female figure dormant in the roots, in muladhara.
body: In explaining the danger of the muladhara cave — being "caught in the roots" — Jung points to a picture in The Secret of the Golden Flower: "a recumbent female figure dormant in the roots, in muladhara," painted by a Westerner "who ha[s] not the faintest knowledge of Eastern philosophy". The editor's note adds Jung's postscript: the mandala paintings were done "independently from any Eastern influence... to illustrate clearly the parallelism between Eastern philosophy and the unconscious mental processes in the West"; fig. 9 is by Christiana Morgan. The picture anchors the seminar's recurring claim that the patient's cave-fire visions reproduce Tantric symbolism spontaneously.

occurrences.title: Kuṇḍalinī returns to mūlādhāra with the red nectar — Śaṭcakranirūpaṇa v.53 (Bengal, 1577)
occurrences.label: Kuṇḍalinī returns to mūlādhāra…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1577 (Pūrṇānanda, Śrī-tattva-cintāmaṇi ch. 6; trans. Woodroffe, The Serpent Power, 1919)

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

body: The return that defines tantric against classical yoga: "The beautiful Kuõìalz drinks the excellent red nectar issuing from Para-çiva, and returns from there where shines Eternal and Transcendent Bliss in all its glory along the path of Kula, and again enters the Mulvdhvra" (v.53, sem-kundalini pdf p170).

Preceded by the awakening mechanics — the guru-taught process, Hūṃ-kāra, the piercing of the three liṅgas, leading Kula-Kuṇḍalinī with Jīva to Para-śiva (vv.50–52) — and followed by the offering of the nectar to Ḍākinī and the devatās of the six centers (v.53), with liberation-from-rebirth promised (v.54). Hauer opened the session on exactly this: tantric yoga demands the return "to mÖlvdhvra"; Jung's Western echo is the ego-not-center doctrine — "It is a mistake to think that we are the center".

occurrences.title: Serpent creeping up her back, head divided into a crotch (Burghölzli, 1906)
occurrences.label: Serpent creeping up her back, head divided…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: ...for the first time the image of a serpent, creeping up on her back, its head divided into a crotch.
body: Jung's earliest retrospective Kundalini find: "In 1906 I found in a mentally ill patient for the first time the image of a serpent, creeping up her back, its head divided into a crotch. In 1909 I even gave a lecture on this case without being aware of its general signification." Only the 1932 encounter with the cakra system let him recognize what the spontaneous image had been — his standing argument that Western material produces the symbolism independently, before any knowledge of tantra.

occurrences.title: Serpent rising to the golden star — painting of Jung's patient (July 1937)
occurrences.label: Serpent rising to the golden star
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The serpent represents the hissing ascent of Kundalini, and in the corresponding yoga this marks the first moment in a process which ends with deification in the divine Self, the syzygy of Shiva and Shakti.
body: A picture painted by a woman patient of Jung ("a lady of over sixty," at home in the Upanishads but not in medieval Christian symbolism): on the left a heap of polished precious stones surmounted by a winged, crowned silver serpent; in the middle a naked female figure from whose genital region the serpent rears up towards the heart, bursting there into a five-pointed flashing golden star; on the right a coloured bird flies down with a twig bearing five flowers in a quaternio — "obviously a mandala structure."

Jung (¶380): the serpent is "the hissing ascent of Kundalini," the first moment of the yogic process ending in deification in the divine Self, the syzygy of Shiva and Shakti; yet the bird contaminates the symbolism of the Annunciation with Noah's dove and the sprig of olive. He reads the whole as the moment of symbolical conception — "the first, anticipatory stage of an as-yet-unfulfilled programme that culminates in the union of opposites... analogous to the 'royal marriage' in alchemy," marking the onset of the transference. Nine months later followed the tree dream and the golden-child vision; six months after that, the child-on-the-square-table dream.

occurrences.title: Shiva, the unextended point, encircled by Shakti as serpent — Tantric/Kundalini Yoga
occurrences.label: Shiva, the unextended point, encircled…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Shiva is the eternally unextended point, and he is encircled by the female principle, Shakti, in the form of a serpent.
body: In the Toledo-dream lecture, Jung reaches the layer of "complete unconsciousness... represented as the greatest treasure" and gives the Tantric image for it: "you find in Tantric Yoga or Kundalini Yoga an attempt to reach the condition where Shiva is in eternal union with Shakti. Shiva is the eternally unextended point, and he is encircled by the female principle, Shakti, in the form of a serpent" (¶263).

It is the Eastern member of the union-of-opposites row that runs: Parsifal's spear restored to the Grail (¶263) — Sol and Luna pictures in the alchemical texts (¶264) — the hierosgamos at Eleusis (¶264). The serpent that encircles the point is the same serpent that guards the treasure in the cistern.

occurrences.title: Exploded self and the Kundalini snake — woman's two pictures (Zurich)
occurrences.label: Exploded self and the Kundalini snake
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: A neurotic woman (not insane, though her sister was) drew a picture full of "breaking lines": "a human figure, herself, but completely dissolved or exploded by breaking lines, an eye here, a hand there and a foot somewhere else, like a corpse that had been exploded into many parts by a shell". Jung's diagnosis of the split proved right when she explained the picture as made "in a moment of terrible emotion."

Asked to paint the emotion, she "represented herself as whole but confronted with a terrible snake, and that snake was the cause of her emotion: it was the Kundalini snake." In Tantric terms, "when the snake raises its head, the hissing… has the effect of a tremendous shock," shattering in delicate constitutions. The second, composed picture showed she "could bridge the gap, could strengthen the breaking lines." Jung uses the case to gloss the lightning that destroys Zarathustra's youth: the sudden archetype-contact that splits the mind like ice or a mirror.

occurrences.title: The way of the snake: vertical black line on the woman's body (German seminar plate, 1930)
occurrences.label: The way of the snake
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich (visions seminar patient; plate in Bericht über das Deutsche Seminar 1930, fig. 30)

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: This strip depicts the way of the snake, the Kundalini
body: A naked woman stands on a ridge with outstretched arms under a stream of light and a crescent moon; a vertical black line runs from her genitals to the top of her body. Jung's comment on the plate: "This strip depicts the way of the snake, the Kundalini" — the suṣumṇā of the nāḍī system appearing spontaneously in Western visionary material, cited in the 1930 'Indian Parallels' lecture as evidence for the parallelism claim.

occurrences.title: Kwan Yin's wrathful aspect
occurrences.label: Kwan Yin's wrathful aspect
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: even Kwan Yin, the goddess of boundless kindness, had also a wrathful and infernal aspect.
body: Against reading Zarathustra's unknown presence as the shadow, Jung adduces the eastern law of the two aspects: "Zarathustra also has the aspect of death. In the East, you remember, the deities always had two aspects, the positive and the negative; even Kwan Yin, the goddess of boundless kindness, had also a wrathful and infernal aspect. And so the archetypes have always a positive and a negative aspect".

The goddess of mercy with her infernal double is his compact evidence that the unknown presence is "another aspect of Zarathustra, or another aspect of Wisdom" — the same figure seen from the dark side, not a fourth person added to the trinity of Nietzsche, Life and Wisdom.

occurrences.title: The double adze (labrys) on Cretan monuments (Crete, Minoan)
occurrences.label: The double adze on Cretan monuments
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: We know the object, but we do not know its specific meaning.
body: Jung's opening exhibit for the sign/symbol distinction: a familiar object whose specific meaning is lost. "Take as an example the image of the double adze that occurs frequently on Cretan monuments. We know the object, but we do not know its specific meaning." Unlike a sign (UN, NATO, a trademark), which "is always less than the thing it points to," the double adze once meant more than it showed — its connotations are now beyond recovery, "a matter for controversial speculation" like the wheel and the cross (¶416-417).
For the vault: the instance preserves the locus as an archaeological image family whose symbolism Jung deliberately leaves open — no express tie to any archetype is claimed.

occurrences.title: Ariadne on Naxos — Dionysos, 'Ich bind ein Labyrinth'
occurrences.label: Ariadne on Naxos — Dionysos, Ich bind ein…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: In the myth, Ariadne wakes to find Theseus gone. In Nietzsche's late poem — Jung quotes it in German — Dionysos takes her by the ear: small ears, MY ears, "put a clever word into them — I am thy labyrinth." Ariadne was Nietzsche's name for Cosima Wagner.

Jung reads the poem as a self-definition of the god who is Zarathustra: the labyrinth is not a place the hero escapes but the god's own being, into which the clever word is whispered. "Now that is Zarathustra."
Verbatim: "Ariadne, Du hast kleine Ohren, / Du hast meine Ohren, / Steck ein kluges Wort hinein, / Ich bind ein Labyrinth."

occurrences.title: Easter ball-dance round the cathedral labyrinth (Auxerre)
occurrences.label: Easter ball-dance round the cathedral labyrinth
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 12th-13th c. (survived at Auxerre to the 16th c.)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: the pilota was thrown by the dean alternately to the dancers, one by one
body: From the mediaeval Latin MSS Jung "dug up" (via Mead's Quest paper) for the seminar: at Easter the dean, "supporting the ball with his left hand, danced, and the rest joined hands and, chanting, executed a choral dance round the labyrinth" of the cathedral, the pilota thrown alternately to the dancers — followed by the communal repast with white and red wine.

Jung's reading: the church ball-game is the surviving ritual game — "a sort of theatre and dining-room," communion as played game; the ball is the sun, the god of the past year dismembered (kicked or torn to pieces) so that everybody participates; king-dismemberment and anthropophagy stand behind it. Companion rites: the Narbonne archbishop's Easter ball, the Naples ball games "for the consolation and recreation of the soul," the bride-ball, the "burial of Alleluia."

occurrences.title: 'Mon seul désir' — the Lady and the Unicorn tapestry with crescent standards (Cluny)
occurrences.label: Mon seul désir' — the Lady…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Paris, Musée de Cluny (woven in Flanders)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Harding passes round "a reproduction of one of the Cluny tapestries. There we see the Virgin or Diana with her animals all around and the two animals who attend her with their crescent standards. The tapestries represent the senses, hearing, seeing, tasting, feeling, and smelling, and this one of which I show you the picture. It is called 'Mon seul désir' and obviously refers to the sixth sense, sexuality" (p403).

Compared in the same breath with "a sketch of a Phoenician sacred moon-tree with its animal worshippers and its legend, 'There is the home of the mighty mother who passes across the sky'" — the moon-goddess flanked by her pair of animals, worshippers or combatants, the old picture of the dual (bright/dark) moon.

occurrences.title: The Lamb on Mount Zion and the 144,000 male virgins (Revelation 14)
occurrences.label: The Lamb on Mount Zion and the 144,000 male…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: "a vision of the Lamb on Mount Zion, where the hundred and forty-four thousand elect and redeemed are gathered round the Lamb. They are the παρθάνοι, the male virgins, 'which were not defiled with women'" (¶718). Jung's critique is withering: they follow the young dying god in having "never become complete human beings, but have voluntarily renounced their share in the human lot and have said no to the continuance of life on earth… This is rank pessimism", answered by Mephisto's "Everything created / Is worth being liquidated."
The vision marks the anti-life pole of the Apocalypse against which the sun-woman's child-bearing stands.

occurrences.title: St. Brendan's sacrifice of the immaculate lamb on the island of sheep
occurrences.label: St. Brendan's sacrifice of the immaculate lamb…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Atlantic island of the navigatio (Land of Sheep); legend from Irish monastic tradition
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~11th–13th c. MSS (La Légende latine de S. Brandaines)
occurrences.quote: Faciamus hic opus divinum, et sacrificemus Deo agnum immaculatum, quia hodie cena Domini est.
body: In the Latin legend of St. Brendan's voyage, the monks land on an island covered with flocks of white sheep so numerous "they could not see the ground," and Brendan commands a Mass: "Let us perform here the divine work and sacrifice to God an immaculate lamb, for today is the supper of the Lord." A ewe follows the brothers "as if it were a domestic animal"; the chosen lamb is sacrificed and its blood taken "for life eternal."

Jung quotes the passage (Part II ch. 2, n. 42) as a naive survival of the archaic identification of god, sacrificial animal, and meal — the same structure the alchemical Mass analogies (Melchior Cibinensis, the opus as missa) transpose into the laboratory. The sheep/land-of-sheep motif also belongs to the biblical vision-material of the Book of Enoch (cw12 Part I ch. 2, nn. 14–15).

occurrences.title: The wrathful Lamb — seven horns and seven eyes (Revelation 5-6)
occurrences.label: The wrathful Lamb — seven horns and seven eyes
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: The Lamb that opens the seven seals "has put off the human features of the 'Ancient of Days' and now appears in purely theriomorphic but monstrous form… It has seven eyes and seven horns, and is therefore more like a ram than a lamb. Altogether it must have looked pretty awful" (¶708). It looses the four sinister horsemen; the martyrs cry for vengeance; everything hides "from the wrath of the Lamb… for the great day of his wrath is come".

"We no longer recognize the meek Lamb… there is only the aggressive and irascible ram whose rage can at last be vented" — for Jung less a metaphysical mystery than "the outburst of long pent-up negative feelings such as can frequently be observed in people who strive for perfection". The self as complexio oppositorum appears dark and menacing exactly in proportion to conscious luminousness (¶716).

occurrences.title: Lambspringk — two reversed fishes swimming in our sea
occurrences.label: Lambspringk — two reversed fishes swimming…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Lambspringk's emblem shows two fishes swimming in opposite directions in the sea — 'nostro mari', the aqua permanens or arcane substance — designated 'spiritus et anima' (¶224 n.82, ¶231). With the stag and unicorn, the two lions, the dog and wolf, and the two fighting birds, they indicate the double nature of Mercurius (¶231). Jung dates the symbol to the end of the sixteenth century, 'a revitalization of the archetype', and declines to prove Catharist descent: the reversed fishes visualize 'the antithetical nature of the self'. Parallels: cathar-two-fishes-osob-revelation-1111, fish-round-fish-allegoriae-turba-11c.

occurrences.title: Lao-tze at the western gate - the writing of the book of five thousand words (legend, 11 May 1932)
occurrences.label: Lao-tze at the western gate - the writing…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: It is said that Lao-tze then wrote the book of five thousand words, the Tao-teh-king. Then he disappeared into the western land.
body: The legend Jung tells to gloss the old man's book in the hold: Lao-tze withdrew from his public position "and went to the western slope of the mountain with a dancer"; feeling death approach he left to disappear, and the officer at the western gate would let him pass only if he wrote down his wisdom. He wrote the book of five thousand words, "and then he disappeared into the western land."

Jung: the book "symbolizes formulated wisdom, coined wisdom, the wisdom that can be transmitted". "A book is a great symbol in the West as well as in the East; the sage always writes a book, all the secrets of life are contained in it" - as the writings of Hermes Trismegistus, "a book of lost wisdom which had to be rediscovered," and the tabula smaragdina: "As above, so below." Being told of Tao is the greatest error - yet "if she can ever come anywhere near it, it will be through Lao-tze".

occurrences.title: Lao-tzu writing the Tao Te Ching at the gate of the Great Wall — Chinese legend
occurrences.label: Lao-tzu writing the Tao Te Ching at the gate…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: a pass in the Great Wall, western China

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: The legend Jung tells to mark the Tao Te Ching's audience: "Lao-tse is said to have left his home on the slope of the mountain and to have wandered west. When he reached the gate in the Great Wall, the guard recognized him at once and would not let him pass through the gate until he had written down his wisdom. He wrote it then in the book of five thousand words, the Tao Te Ching. This legend would show that the book was meant for the generally learned, not just for a priest class". The point of the telling: Lao-tse stresses the opposites and "the way between the two, Tao," whereas the Brahman pupil of the Upanishads — born into the wisdom of his caste — could go straight to "the thing between the pairs of opposites," Atman. "We are really in the position of Lao-tse's pupils and need to say of the Tao, 'It is so still.'"

occurrences.title: Spanish Jesuit's case: the lapdog snatches the host; the Inquisition burns the dog
occurrences.label: Spanish Jesuit's case
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Jung's seventeenth-century case history of the host's taboo: "A donna came to church with a little lapdog. When the priest offered her the host, the dog snatched the host away from her. The church was closed; the case was brought before the Holy Inquisition. The women got off with a fine of two hundred Dubloons. The dog was confiscated and consigned to death by fire because of its obscene, blasphemous behavior".

"Here you see the taboo surrounding the holy meal. This is the other, the very dangerous meal, which is more than just eating bread." The case amplifies the robbers'-den boy's clay-eating: the symbolic meal that incorporates the strange and different — the world one has to swallow to grow up.

occurrences.title: The Andalusian prince who desires the torment of the seekers — 'Book of Ostanes'
occurrences.label: The Andalusian prince who desires the torment…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: m edieval Arabic (Berthelot, Chimie au moyen age III, p. 117)
body: The Arabic "Book of Ostanes" (Kitab el-Ful) describes the arcane substance in its forms — water white, black, red, then fire struck from stones — and then: "It is a tree that grows on the tops of the mountains, a young man born in Egypt, a prince from Andalusia, who desires the torment of the seekers. He has slain their leaders... The sages are powerless to oppose him. I can see no weapon against him save resignation, no charger but knowledge, no buckler but understanding" (cw13 ¶424). Slain with these three weapons, "he will come to life again after his death... and will give the seeker the highest power".

Jung reads the hostile prince with Enkidu — "the chthonic man and shadow of Gilgamesh, created by the gods... so that he may kill the hero" (cw13 ¶425) — and with the Khidr legend: at first meeting the self appears negative (cw13 ¶428). 'Unless thy stone shall be an enemy, thou wilt not attain to thy desire' (cw13 ¶426).
Verbatim: a young man born in Egypt, a prince from Andalusia, who desires the torment of the seekers. (cw13 ¶424ocr)

occurrences.title: 'The stone is the saviour' — Codex Rhenovacensis (Zurich)
occurrences.label: The stone is the saviour' — Codex Rhenovacensis
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: There it is openly said that the stone is the savior
body: An alchemical codex from a monastery library, held in Zurich, in which — Jung told the seminar — "it is openly said that the stone is the savior, and the whole alchemical procedure is expressed in the analogy of the Song of Songs." The claim anchors his argument that for the old philosophers "the philosopher's stone, the gold, or the child was really the savior. They called it the savior": alchemy continuing the buried-god thought after the Mass's transubstantiation "did not hold life" for them.

The Song-of-Songs framing makes the opus a sensuous, even obscene wedding — Arabic and Syrian parallels of the same character exist, and the antique obscenity "had a sort of fertilizing power" (pdf p987, and the Eleusis Aischrologia).
Sibling locus in the same codex: homunculi-souls-codex-rhenoviensis-15c.

occurrences.title: Orthelius: the earthly saviour of two natures, parallel to Christ the Mediator
occurrences.label: Orthelius — the earthly saviour…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: so likewise is that earthly saviour composed of two parts, the heavenly and the earthly
body: Of the "mediator," the wonderful stone, Orthelius writes: "For as … the supernatural and eternal good, Christ Jesus our Mediator and Saviour, who delivers us from eternal death, from the devil, and from all evil, partakes of two natures, the divine and the human, so likewise is that earthly saviour composed of two parts, the heavenly and the earthly. With these he has restored us to health, and delivers us from diseases heavenly and earthly, spiritual and corporeal, visible and invisible."

Jung's gloss fixes the direction of the symbolism: "Here the 'saviour' does not come down from heaven but out of the depths of the earth, i.e., from that which lies below consciousness. These philosophers suspected that a 'spirit' was imprisoned there, in the vessel of matter" — the white dove comparable to the Nous in the krater of Hermes. The lapis-Christ parallel completes the series Petrus Bonus (allegoria Christi, ¶93) and the Aurea hora's rating of the stone above the Christian mysteries.

occurrences.title: 'Within the stone slumbereth an image' — Zarathustra's lapis intuition
occurrences.label: Within the stone slumbereth an image
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "But to man doth it ever impel me anew, my fervent creative will; thus impelleth it the hammer to the stone... within the stone slumbereth an image for me, the image of my visions! Ah, that it should slumber in the hardest, ugliest stone!"

The seminar's identifications: the Gnostic soul sleeping in prison (Reichstein); "that has to do with the philosopher's stone... the thing that has been rejected, the thing you find ejected in the road; you tread it under your feet or you find it on the dung heaps cast away, vilis et vilissimus, cheap and the cheapest" — like Isaiah 53's Messiah who "hath no form nor comeliness" (not of Christian origin: "a very pagan origin... an archetypal idea"; Pygmalion contrasted). The rejected raw material "is the past and all the values of the past... out of the stone rejected by the builders must he work that precious image. In other words, just out of the anima, out of that feeling that seems to be a mere nuisance" to his creative will.
Verbatim: "Ah, yemen, within the stone slumbereth an image for me, the image of my visions! Ah, that it should slumber in the hardest, ugliest stone!".

occurrences.title: 'Hic lapis exilis extat' — despised-stone verse, Rosarium preface (1550)
occurrences.label: Hic lapis exilis extat
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Hic lapis exilis extat, precio quoque vilis, Spernitur a stultis, amatur plus ab edoctis. (Here stands the mean, uncomely stone, ’Tis very cheap in price!
body: The Rosarium's preface verses on the mean, uncomely, cheap stone "despised by fools, loved by the wise" — the worthlessness-of-the-prima-materia topos in hexameters. Jung quotes it in full (¶1782) and immediately draws the medieval correlation: "The 'lapis exilis' may correspond to the 'lapsit exillis,' Wolfram von Eschenbach's name for the Grail" (¶1783) — knotting the alchemical stone to the Grail-stone tradition.

The verse supplies the despised/cheap pole of the lapis paradox (found everywhere, dung-heap stone, yet panacea and redeemer) that runs from the Turba through Arnaldus de Villanova's "lapis exilis" to Wolfram.

occurrences.title: 'That little circle… a mediator making peace between enemies' — commentary to the Tractatus aureus
occurrences.label: That little circle… a mediator making peace…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Latin West (commentary printed with the tract; Ars chemica 1566 / later editions)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: It is a mediator making peace between enemies or the elements, that they may love one another in a meet embrace
body: In the commentary to the Tractatus aureus, the elements must be reduced to "that little circle holding the place of the centre in this squared figure. It is a mediator making peace between enemies or the elements, that they may love one another in a meet embrace. He alone brings about the squaring of the circle, which many hitherto have sought, but few have found."

Jung reads this as the Reformation-era formulation of the mandala: "speculative ideas, symptomatic of an activated archetype," appearing in alchemical treatises as "symbolic geometrical figures which sought to express the nature of the Deus terrenus, the philosophers' stone" (¶150). The little circle in the square is the lapis as union-of-opposites — the exact functional definition he gives the modern mandala ("a union of opposites, or of mediation"), and the schematic ancestor of the patient's world clock with its empty mathematical centre.

occurrences.title: The magistery revealed in a dream — Sendivogius, 'Parabola'
occurrences.label: The magistery revealed in a dream
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: "Revelation of the magistery in a dream in Sendivogius, 'Parabola' (Bibliotheca chemica curiosa, II, 1702, p. 475)" (cw11 ¶? pdf p698) — named by Jung beside the Visio Arislei and the visions of Zosimos as "classical examples" of the arcanum disclosed in dream/vision rather than by laboratory work.
The dream as authority in alchemy itself: Jung's license, in the Mass essay, for taking the dream-series of his own patient as modern equivalent of the alchemical revelation.

occurrences.title: Ostanes to Cleopatra: 'In you is hidden the whole terrible and marvellous secret' (Greek alchemy)
occurrences.label: Ostanes to Cleopatra
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: text ~1st c. A.D. (Ostanes legendary, possibly 4th c. BCE)
body: Jung quotes the saying again in the stone-symbolism chapter: "Thus the legendary Ostanes, speaking of the secret of the 'philosophy,' says to his pupil Cleopatra: 'In you is hidden the whole terrible and marvellous secret... Make known to us how the highest descends to the lowest, and how the lowest ascends to the highest, and how the midmost draws near to the highest, and is made one with it'" (cw13 ¶131).

His comment: "This 'midmost' is the stone, the mediator which unites the opposites. Such sayings have no meaning unless they are understood in a profoundly psychological sense" (¶131) — the stone hidden in man, quoted here against the anima-figure of the turquoise goddess who "contains the secret of the precious stone."

occurrences.title: The scala Unitatis: Yod — anima mundi — sol — lapis — cor — Lucifer (Agrippa)
occurrences.label: The scala Unitatis — Yod
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: From Agrippa's correspondence tables (based on the numbers 1 to 12): "Yod [the first letter of the tetragrammaton, the divine name]—anima mundi—sol—lapis philosophorum—cor—Lucifer" — a rung-ladder from God's letter, through World Soul, Sun, Philosophers' Stone and heart, down to the light-bearer.

Jung's reading: "I must content myself with saying that this is an attempt to set up a hierarchy of archetypes, and that tendencies in this direction can be shown to exist in the unconscious" (¶931) — citing Jaffe on E. T. A. Hoffmann and von Franz's Passio Perpetuae. Around it Jung reads Agrippa's spiritus mundi / quinta essentia as "what we would call the unconscious," and the World Soul as that whose presence makes things "beget their like," i.e. correspondences.

occurrences.title: The Yellow Man and the Red Man — dialogue of the Cardinal of Brixen (Aureum vellus)
occurrences.label: The Yellow Man and the Red Man
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Aureum vellus printing (attrib. Melchior, Cardinal of Brixen, d. 1459)
body: An alchemical folk-tale of personified metals, quoted at length: the seeker goes to the house with two shut doors, until one comes out — "that will be a Yellow Man, and is not pretty to look upon, but you should not fear him, because he is unshapely, but he is sweet of word" — who asks what he seeks; the answer: "I have come here and seek the Lapidem Philosophorum." Deeper in, at a running fountain, meets the Red Man, "he is Fiery Red and has Red eyes," equally gentle of word (cw13 ¶123).

Footnote 5: "After the Red Man he finds the Black Raven, and from this comes the White Dove." Jung's frame: alchemical projections "are only a special instance of the mode of thinking typified by the idea of the microcosm" (¶123) — personification as participation mystique (¶122).

occurrences.title: The last man (Zarathustra, Prologue 5)
occurrences.label: The last man (Zarathustra, Prologue 5)
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "We have discovered happiness"-say the last men, and blink thereby. Jung reads the sermon as Zarathustra's second attempt to reach his audience: "he thinks that he might reach them if he speaks of the most contemptible of all things", but "what he describes is simply the ideal man, an ideal rationalist or the ideal opportunist... He describes the collective man of his day". The last man "is not able to individuate, who has no chaos in himself and therefore no motive to give birth to a star".

Yet Jung's verdict is double-edged — recall over simple agreement with Zarathustra's contempt: "So that last man is a very ordinary and quite reasonable individual, with nothing particularly excessive... he is cursing a fairly normal human being, and if Nietzsche had accepted that man in himself as an indispensable fragment, at least, of his make-up, he would have been better perhaps. He would not have been so excessive, and he would not have injured himself". The sermon's failure — "There is ice in their laughter" — is what triggers the rope-dancer.

occurrences.title: 'When the statue shall come' — Manichaean eschaton (Hegemonius, Acta Archelai)
occurrences.label: When the statue shall come
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Manichaean end-state as reported by Hegemonius: the world will be consumed with a great fire and the soul thrown into it, the souls of sinners chained for all eternity — 'then shall these things be, when the statue shall come' (cw14 ¶567). The recently discovered Kephalaia of Mani confirms: 'The fourth time, when they shall weep, is the time when the statue shall raise itself on the last day... At that same hour, when the last statue shall rise, they shall weep.' Jung would not venture whether the Manichaeans influenced the alchemists, 'but it is worth noting that in both cases the statue is connected with the end-state' (¶567).
Verbatim: Tunc autem haec fient, cum statua venerit. (cw14 appendix V.70; also quoted at II.219with 'corpus inanime in statuam viventem confingere')

occurrences.title: The statue that shall raise itself on the last day — Manichaean Kephalaia
occurrences.label: The statue that shall raise itself…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The fourth time, when they shall weep, is the time when the statue shall raise itself on the last day.
body: The Kephalaia (Mani's original work, confirming Hegemonius): "the statue shall raise itself on the last day." The Pillar of Glory is "the perfect man, who has been summoned by the glorious messenger... He bore the whole world and became the first of all bearers"; the five intellectual elements perfect its body as the Great Garments.

Jung at cw14 ¶567: the statue or pillar is either the perfect Primordial Man or at least his body, "both at the beginning of creation and at the end of time" — statue connected with the end-state, as in alchemy.

occurrences.title: The black Isis with child, kept as a Madonna — Lateran museum, Rome
occurrences.label: The black Isis with child, kept as a Madonna
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: From the black-Artemis discussion: "In early Christianity she was sometimes confused with the Madonna. In the Lateran museum there is a statue of a black Isis with the child, which was preserved because it was once understood to be a Madonna. There are a number of such Artemis, or Ishtar, or Isis heads of black basalt, which are supposed to be Christian".

The frame: black = fertile earth — "Black soil is the best to grow wheat, the black Egyptian soil is exceedingly fertile" — as with the black Artemis of Ephesus and the Black Madonna of Einsiedeln, whose fire-blackening story Jung doubts.

occurrences.title: The coffin that bursts into laughter — Zarathustra's dream (The Soothsayer)
occurrences.label: The coffin that bursts into laughter
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939
jung.locator: Spring Term wrap-up + 11 May lecture (pdf p1261-1264)

occurrences.quote: Verily, like a thousand peals of children's laughter cometh Zarathustra into all sepulchres, laughing at those night-watchmen and grave-guardians, and whoever else rattleth with sinister keys.
body: Zarathustra's dream told to his disciples after the soothsayer's prophecy: he guards the fortress of Death at night, coffins burst open, and out rush wind and "a thousand peals of children's laughter". The beloved disciple interprets: "Art thou not thyself the wind with shrill whistling, which bursteth open the gates of the fortress of Death?" — Zarathustra is the laugher, the wind, the coffin.

Jung's reading: the disciple's interpretation "is of course a desperate attempt to twist it into a favorable statement". The coffin full of laughter "is the paradoxical pair of opposites that are mixed up together and form the grotesque and horrible aspects of the unconscious"; to identify with it is to be annihilated, "because your consciousness is the only element of order". He "has dreamt himself; that is his own case, his own insanity" — the dream "where Nietzsche's imminent madness was portrayed". The laughter returns transfigured in the shepherd vision and in the legend of the prophet born laughing.

occurrences.title: The prophet born laughing — Zarathustra's birth (Bundahishn)
occurrences.label: The prophet born laughing — Zarathustra's birth
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: the real prophet was born, not with a cry, but with laughter.
body: Prof. Reichstein recalls "the legend that Professor Abegg told here about the real Zarathustra, the legend that the real prophet was born, not with a cry, but with laughter" — the story preserved in the Bundahish, the Persian scripture compiled 226-640 CE (seminar footnote).

Jung's reading: he does not know "in how far Nietzsche was informed about the legend... and it is possible that laughter plays such a role with him just because he knew that story about the Persian founder of the religion". The laughing birth answers the shepherd's inhuman laughter after the serpent-bite: "There is a connection here because this is a kind of rebirth." But Jung darkens it at once: "the laughter here has to do with the thousand peals of mad laughter when the coffin was split open. The shepherd went mad — that is perfectly clear. That is the inevitable outcome when one integrates one of the performers of the divine play." The savior's laughter at birth and the madman's laughter after god-identification are one motif at two temperatures.

occurrences.title: Leonardo's St. Anne with the Virgin and Child (the dual-mother picture)
occurrences.label: Leonardo's St. Anne with the Virgin and Child
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

jung.year: Leonardo da Vinci and a Memory of His Childhood

occurrences.quote: Surely not all of them had two mothers?
body: Leonardo's St. Anne with the Virgin Mary and the Christ-child — the picture Freud interpreted through Leonardo's two mothers. Jung's counter-reading: "interwoven with the apparently personal psychology there is an impersonal motif well known to us from other fields. This is the motif of the dual mother)" (¶94) — an archetype "to be found in many variants in the field of mythology and comparative religion", whatever Leonardo's biography; the vulture symbol (Freud's other plank) comes from Horapollo's Hieroglyphica, current among educated artists of the day.
The fn to ¶140 adds: Freud assimilated the painting to his theory — "the 'religious inhibition of thought'... proved true of the author himself".

occurrences.title: The Leontocephalus of Arles (and the British Museum): snake-lion unity
occurrences.label: The Leontocephalus of Arles: snake-lion unity
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Jung, on the lion/snake competition of the herb dream: "In the Aion leontocephalus, snake and lion are also depicted together... Yes, but there they form a unity.... It is the statue of a human body with the hands resting on it. In the museum of Arles there is a wonderful Leontocephalus, also in the British Museum. He is lion-headed; a snake entwines him completely and lays its head on his head. Here lion and snake are identical".

The reading: "this is man in the state of his spinal cord: it is unconscious man." Where the Mithraic monuments show lion and snake fighting over the Kratér, the leontocephalus has already unified the cold-blooded and the warm-blooded stages — but still below consciousness.

occurrences.title: Behemoth and Leviathan — Jahveh's lap-dogs (Book of Job 40–41)
occurrences.label: Behemoth and Leviathan — Jahveh's lap-dogs
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Book of Job (final form ~6th–4th c. BCE; inferred)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939
Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "In the Book of Job God is accompanied by two monsters, the leviathan and the behemoth, and those are the pair of opposites. The behemoth is the warm-blooded, land animal, and the leviathan is the great sea monster that fills two thirds of the ocean." — like the makara of the svadhisthana chakra, and the Brahman's two monsters of the Upanishads.

The second engagement is Jung's torrent: "Look at what Jahveh did to old man Job... Jahveh was betting with the devil... there was no judge above Jahveh, he was a lawless individual — it was not even fair play... Look at my power — here is my Behemoth, here is my Leviathan, my two monsters are my lap-dogs, such a fellow am I!" — and therefore "such a God needs rebuilding, and that is the reason he was crucified."
Pre-echo of Answer to Job (editor points to CW11).

occurrences.title: Leviathan pair: slant and tortuous serpent — Baba Bathra 74b
occurrences.label: Leviathan pair — slant and tortuous serpent
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: He castrated the male and killed the female, preserving it in salt for the righteous in the world to come.
body: The Talmud (Baba Bathra 74b, Slotki trans.) reports that God created the male and female Leviathan — the slant serpent and the tortuous serpent — and, had they mated, they would have destroyed the world; so He castrated the male and killed the female, preserving her in salt for the righteous in the world to come (Isaiah 27:1). The same for Behemoth.

Jung's reading: "the two prehistoric animals, Leviathan (water) and Behemoth (land), together with their females, form a quaternio of opposites. The coniunctio oppositorum on the animal level, i.e., in the unconscious state, is prevented by God as being dangerous" — it would keep consciousness on the animal level. The salting of the female underlines salt's feminine affiliation. Parallels: dragon-leviathan-ltn-ras-shamra-2000-bce, ophite-diagram-origen-contra-celsum-6c.

occurrences.title: Diagram of the stages of the opus — Libavius, Alchymia (1606)
occurrences.label: Diagram of the stages of the opus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Q A vision of heaven, where a dragon lies on his back and devours his own tail: he is an image of the second coagulation.
body: A full synoptic picture of the opus with Libavius' own lettered explicatio: two Atlases; a four-headed dragon of the four fires; Mercurius with a silver chain; green lion and one-headed dragon (both the mercurial materia prima); a three-headed eagle spitting the white water; black stream of putrefactio; the black-white mountain; ravens in the sea; silver rain; the dragon in heaven "that lies on his back and devours his own tail"; the Ethiopian pair as nigredo; the swan as white elixir; eclipses of sun and moon each flanked by rainbows (the peacock's tail); the king with red lily and golden lion beside the queen with white lily and silver eagle; and the phoenix cremating itself with birds flying from the ashes.

One plate carrying nearly the whole image-inventory of the spagyric process; Jung reproduces it to show the method's density. Parallels: uroboros-codex-marcianus-venice-11c · sol-luna-allegory-rosarium-1550.

occurrences.title: Mercurius made equal to the Virgin Mary — Liber de arte chymica
occurrences.label: Mercurius made equal to the Virgin Mary
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: it is not without good reason that Mercurius is made equal [non immerito … aequiparatur] to the most glorious and worshipful Virgin Mary.
body: The anonymous Liber de arte chymica sets an aequiparatio of Mercurius with the Virgin Mary: Christ unlocked the gate of the ethereal Olympus; correspondingly the virginal Mercurius — who "has never increased any kind of metallic body" — opens the gold, leads out the soul (a divinity), carries it in his belly, and brings forth the puer, the lapis, by whose blood the lower bodies are tinctured.

Jung: as anima mundi, Mercurius can be compared with the Gnostic parthenos tou photos (virgin of light) and with the Virgin Mary; the puer is then the filius macrocosmi, an analogy of Christ. The author also argues Christ's body would never have died had he not sought death freely — the same incorruptibility the stone derives from the alliance of its elements.

occurrences.title: Ammonius the anchorite of the Libyan desert — the many meanings of the word (Cap. iv, Dies I, Dec 30, 1913)
occurrences.label: Ammonius the anchorite of the Libyan desert
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.yearDisplay: December 30, 1913 (anchorite dated to the 3rd c. by Jung)
occurrences.quote: I am with an anchorite of the Libyan desert.
