body: Following footprints in the sand Jung reaches a mud-brick hut with a red-painted cross: "I am with an anchorite of the Libyan desert" — Ammonius, ex-rhetorician of Alexandria, once ensnared in Philo's word-webs, now reading his Greek gospel by daily rounds. His teaching: "a succession of words does not have only one meaning"; John gave the Logos to living men where Philo "gave AOrOL as the dead concept that usurped life." Religions differ only in their expressions: "it's always one and the same religion. Every subsequent form of religion is the meaning of the antecedent." Jung's doubt will make him appear to Ammonius as Satan ("I recognize you-give way, adversary!") — the solitary meets the devil of his own desire.

PLATE (p0046.jpg = LS p.15): "Der Anachoret. Cap. IV. Dies. I." — the great illuminated D set inside a square panel of Ravenna-like mosaic: interlaced red-orange-purple maze bands around a blue field; the eye-opening page of the desert cycle.

occurrences.title: Atmavictu the kabir manikin, with Telesphorus (Liber Novus ms p. 117, image 117)
occurrences.label: Atmavictu the kabir manikin, with Telesphorus
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.place: Zurich; sculpture later in Jung's Kusnacht garden; Bollingen stone 1950

jung.locator: liber-novus ms p. 117, image 117 (pdf p334, Nox Quarta)
'Basically, the manikin is a kabir' (editor n.222)

body: The dwarf-god of Nox Quarta. Legend in Jung's hand: "Der Drache will die Sonne fress / der Jüngling beschwört ihn / es nicht zu thun · er frisst sie ab·do·" — "The dragon wants to eat the sun and the youth beseeches him not to. But he eats it nevertheless." The page names four figures: ATMAVICTV (the dragon), iuvenis adiutor, TEΛΕΣΦΟΡΟΣ, spiritus malus in hominibus quibusdam. Editor n.222: Atmavictu was "first an old man... a bear... an otter... a newt... the serpent," from whom Philemon transformed; Jung carved two such figures in England in 1920, "It called the figure Atmavictu — the 'breath of life'... Basically, the manikin is a kabir." Telesphorus, child-daimon of Asclepius, was carved on the Bollingen stone in 1950.

Plate (p0148.jpg = ms p. 117). Left half: a tall vertical serpent-dragon in scaled greens, small human arms sprouting in tiers along its body, a black eye and red fanged open mouth at the top, labelled "ATMAVICTV"; a pale sun disc floats above. Right half: a dense blackletter text block; beneath it the three small figures with Latin labels; the blackletter legend runs across the foot. Corner-marked "117".

occurrences.title: The Cabiri as casters of holy water (Liber Novus ms p. 123, image 123)
occurrences.label: The Cabiri as casters of holy water
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.locator: liber-novus ms p. 123, image 123 (pdf p337, The Three Prophecies)

body: Image legend (in Jung's hand): "Dies ist der heil. Wasserspender. Aus dem Blüten des Leibes des Drachen entspringen / wachsen die Cabiren. u. Ist der Tempel" — "This is the caster of holy water. The Cabiri grow out of the flowers which spring from the body of the dragon. Above is the temple". It belongs with the prose Cabiri dialogue of The Magician: elemental spirits rising from the devil's shredded body, "dwarfish, shriveled, unspectacular bearers of secret arts, possessors of ridiculous wisdom, first formations of the unformed gold, worms that crawl from the liberated egg of the Gods" — "We carry what is not to be carried from below to above... We know the unknown ways and the inexplicable laws of living matter." Editor n.310: Samothracian mysteries; Creuzer and Schelling's primal deities; the Cabiri scene in Faust II; CW11 §244 — "the mysterious creative powers, the gnomes who work under the earth."

Plate (p0154.jpg = ms p. 123). Gold ground. Upper left: a white domed temple on a small cloud. Upper right: a dark-haired man in a green-and-white striped robe stands on a wide blue-and-white disc beneath a red sun disc, pouring a zigzag stream of holy water from a vessel. Below, dark red-tipped flowers rise from a black earthen band in which the prone dragon's body lies traced with lightning squiggles; water drips onto the blossoms. Corner-marked "123".

occurrences.title: The castle in the forest — the pale maiden bewitched by the banal (Cap. ii, Dec 28, 1913)
occurrences.label: The castle in the forest
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: Where she stood something shadowy lies-it is a profusion of red roses.
body: Lost in a dark forest, Jung lodges in a small castle whose aged scholar-owner is "squashed to nothing by the abundance of knowledge." At midnight a girl "pale as death" enters his room — a pulp-fiction scene Jung despises until she asks whether he too takes her "for a fantasy." Accepting the banal releases her: "Know then: I was bewitched by the banal." Layer two: the adventure re-plays the Mysterium "as a distorted likeness" — Elijah and Salome became "the old scholar and his pale, locked-up daughter"; the maiden sends "greetings from Salome" and dissolves into "a profusion of red roses." The chapter states the anima doctrine outright: "the most masculine man has a feminine soul... As a man you have no soul, since it is in the woman."
PLATE (p0036.jpg = LS p.5): illuminated D of "Das Schloß im Walde. Cap. II" — a night-blue castle with lit windows and moon above dark water, painted inside the initial.

occurrences.title: The conception of the God — the spirit's proclamation panel (Cap. viii, after Dec 18, 1913)
occurrences.label: The conception of the God
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: I have received your sprout, you who are to come! I have received it in deepest need and lowliness.
body: Once the hero falls, the spirit of the depths erupts "with intoxication and mist" and proclaims the conceived God: received "in deepest need and lowliness," covered "in shabby patchwork," whose constellation "is an ill and changing star," whose believers must speak of his glory "in tongues that are atrocious to them." Jung's layer-two gloss: "I understood that the new God would be in the relative" — the God of the encompassing ambiguity (hateful-beautiful, evil-good), not the absolute idea. Christ must first become "his Antichrist, his underworldly brother."

PLATE (p0026.jpg = RB fol. iv(v)/v(r)): a full illuminated page — the proclamation set in white script on a deep red-blue diagonally striped frame, a compass/wind-rose star at the head, a chalice at the foot; opposite, a painted border of red flowers on orange ground.

occurrences.title: Communion of the dead: the Last Supper inverted (Scrutinies, 1915/16)
occurrences.label: Communion of the dead: the Last Supper inverted
occurrences.subject: jung
body: The dead woman — the shade who had shown him "the red sun disk and the golden wings" of Egypt — teaches the cult of the dead that issues in the Sermones. She drinks Jung's blood to speak, demands his dog's body as her dwelling ("If possible, yes... I would even like to be your dog"), and finally evokes the dead in his name: "You dead, I call you... My blood, the juice of my life, will be your meal and your drink... Take, eat, this is my body, that lives for you. Take, eat, drink, this is my blood, whose desire flows for you. Come, celebrate a Last Supper with me for your redemption and mine". The Eucharist is turned toward the dead: "Community with the dead is what both you and the dead need... The dead demand your expiatory prayers... Only recently have men begun to forget the dead and to think that they have now begun the real life."

The doctrine is prepared across the whole second half of the book: "The number of the unredeemed dead has become greater than the number of living Christians; therefore it is time that we accept the dead"; the dead are "the thronging dead of human history" behind the soul's "quiet place"; and in Appendix C: "The dead who besiege us are souls who have not fulfilled the principium individuationis, or else they would have become distant stars". Jung to Jaffe: the dead are "the voices of the unanswered, unresolved and unredeemed".

occurrences.title: Jung crucified with lion countenance — Salome's eyes opened (Cap. xi close, Dec 25, 1913)
occurrences.label: Jung crucified with lion countenance
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: The serpent has wound itself around my whole body, and my countenance is that of a lion.
body: The climax of the Mysterium cycle and the deification scene of Liber Primus: at the foot of the cross on the green mountain the black serpent coils around Jung's feet and body, he spreads his arms "like someone crucified," blood streams down the mountainside, "and my countenance is that of a lion." Salome wraps her black hair around his feet, then cries "I see light!" — her blindness healed by the sight of the crucified; the serpent falls; Elijah transfigures into "a huge flame of white light." Jung: "I became a Christ... I am made into Christ, I must suffer it." The redemption is not through the hero but by becoming the Christ oneself — imitation is ended.

PLATE (p0031.jpg, initial painting, RB fol. vi(v)): tiny figures in white and red within the Auflösung initial; the full scene is text-borne — the only surviving image evidence of the mystery in this range.

occurrences.title: The dead serpent, umbilical cord of a new birth (Liber Novus ms p. 111, image 111)
occurrences.label: The dead serpent, umbilical cord of a new birth
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.locator: liber-novus ms p. 111, image 111 (pdf p330, Nox Tertia)

body: Image legend (in Jung's hand above the painting): "Die Schlange fiel tot auf die Erde. Das war die Nabelschnur einer Neugeburt" — "The serpent fell dead unto the earth. And that was the umbilical cord of a new birth" (pdf p330, n.201). It follows image 109, in which "the man of matter rises up too far in the world of the spirits, but there the spirit of the heart bores through him with a golden ray. He falls with joy and disintegrates" — the serpent "who is evil, could not remain in the world of spirits." In Black Book 7 (27 Jan 1922) Jung's soul describes the giant cloud of eternal night, the yellow lightning-stroke, the dead black serpent with the spear in its head, and concludes: "It is an image of your self."

Plate (p0142.jpg = ms p. 111). Full-page painting: a black serpent patterned with white eye-spots winds up from lower left, head at upper right above a cluster of red cloud-blossoms ringed in red, over a swirling purple-red-and-olive vegetal ground. Blackletter legend above; corner-marked "111".

occurrences.title: Death — the dark one on the last dune and the sea of the dead (Cap. vi, Jan 2, 1914)
occurrences.label: Death — the dark one on the last dune…
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.yearDisplay: night of January 2, 1914 (second night of the year)
occurrences.quote: a new sun escapes from the bloody sea, and rolls gleamingly toward the uttermost depths-it disappears under my feet.
body: Wandering northward to where rivers lose themselves in the sea, Jung meets on the last dune a gaunt figure in a black wrinkled coat — "you are ice and the end; you are the cold silence of the stones." Past them flows the enormous stream of the dead: "densely pressed multitudes of men, old men, women, and children... a forest swims near, innumerable faded flowers, an utterly dead summer" — wave after wave dissolving into black mist. Then the dark sea breaks: "a sea of blood foams at my feet... a new sun escapes from the bloody sea, and rolls gleamingly toward the uttermost depths." The war-vision of 1913 returns as cosmology; layer two: "virtues and vices are brothers," and "If I accept death, then my tree greens, since dying increases life."
PLATE (p0061.jpg = LS p.30): text page with small red-and-green initial at "Ich schreite um..." — the sea-of-blood passage and the note "es war die zweite Nacht des Jahres 1914" are text-borne here.

occurrences.title: Descent into Hell in the Future — the cave, the red crystal, the slain head, scarab and sun of the depths (Cap. v, Dec 12, 1913)
occurrences.label: Descent into Hell in the Future
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: I see a large black scarab floating past on the dark stream. In the deepest reach of the stream shines a red sun, radiating through the dark water.
body: The first deliberate descent — the founding katabasis of the Red Book. Voices fill the air ("I am falling"); Jung sinks along a gray rock face into a cave with black water, seizes a luminous red stone (the six-sided crystal of the Corrected Draft), lays his ear to the opening and hears underground waters: the bloody head of a slain man floats past, then "a large black scarab," and in the deepest reach "shines a red sun, radiating through the dark water," which a thousand serpents strive to veil. Blood surges up. Read backward from the war: "in the depths of what is to come lay murder."

PLATES (p0024.jpg = RB fol. iii(v)/iv(r)): two paintings — above, a small dark panel with a glowing red sun-disc in a cavernous field; below, a larger blue-gray cave scene with a white-robed figure bending toward a red radiant form. The chapter initial "Höllenfahrt in die Zukunft Cap V" shows a horned red goggle-face (lion-serpent countenance).

occurrences.title: The desert of the self — twenty-five nights of waiting (Cap. iv-v, Nov 28 - Dec 11, 1913)
occurrences.label: The desert of the self
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: My soul leads me into the desert, into the desert of my own self I did not think that my soul is a desert, a barren, hot desert, dusty and without drink.
body: "My soul leads me into the desert, into the desert of my own self" — the place of the soul turns out to be "a barren, hot desert, dusty and without drink," and the torment is waiting: "Torment belongs to the desert." Over twenty-five nights the soul wakes "from a shadowy being to her own life," teaching scorn of one's own cleverness and "the vow of poverty of spirit." Layer two anchors the archetype: "to find their soul, the ancients went into the desert... the place of the soul is a lonely desert" — the desert fathers lived in advance what Jung now lives inwardly. When the desert begins to bloom, "it brings forth strange plants" and madness: "madness is divine" (Cap. v).
PLATE (p0021.jpg = RB fol. ii(v)/iii(r)): illuminated D of "Die Wüste Cap. IV" — a small human figure standing within the initial on deep color grounds.

occurrences.title: Mysterium. Encounter — Elijah and blind Salome with the black serpent (Cap. ix, Dec 1913)
occurrences.label: Mysterium. Encounter
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: Consider this: her blindness and my sight have made us companions through eternity.
body: The original of the Elijah-Salome vision, later retold anonymously as "case Z" (CW9i): in a dark depth before a columned house, the old prophet Elijah ("I am Elijah and this is my daughter Salome") and blind Salome, who loves Jung and is refused. "Her blindness and my sight have made us companions through eternity." The crystal reflects Eve, the serpent, Odysseus. Jung's reading: Elijah = forethinking (Logos), Salome = pleasure (Eros), and "apart from Elijah and Salome I found the serpent as a third principle... the earthly essence of man of which he is not conscious." When Jung protests "you are symbols," Elijah answers: "We are real and not symbols" — the doctrine of psychic objectivity in nuce.

PLATE (p0028.jpg = RB fol. v(v)/vi(r)): the famous painting atop the chapter — night-blue mountains, a white-domed columned house at right, Elijah in white-blue robe leading red-robed Salome toward the door, a white bird on the ground before them, and red serpents writhing around all four sides of the frame; above, "MYSTERIUM" in gold Gothic on a red-gold chevron band over the great B initial "Begegnung. Cap. IX."

occurrences.title: Epilogue, 1959 — the last written page of Liber Novus (ms p. 190)
occurrences.label: Epilogue, 1959 — the last written page…
occurrences.subject: jung
body: Jung's own closing of the Red Book, written in ordinary hand (not calligraphy) on ms p. 190, headed "1959," and cut off mid-sentence like the transcription it follows: "I worked on this book for 16 years. My acquaintance with alchemy in 1930 took me away from it. The beginning of the end came in 1928, when Wilhelm sent me the text of the 'Golden Flower,' an alchemical treatise. There the contents of this book found their way into actuality and I could no longer continue working on it. To the superficial observer, it will appear like madness. It would also have developed into one, had I not been able to absorb the overpowering force of the original experiences. With the help of alchemy, I could finally arrange them into a whole. I always knew that these experiences contained something precious, and therefore I knew of nothing better than to write them down in a 'precious,' that is to say, costly book and to paint the images that emerged through reliving it all — as well as I could. I knew how frightfully inadequate this undertaking was, but despite much work and many distractions I remained true to it...".
Plate (p0221.jpg = ms p. 190). Plain cream page, dense blue ink in Jung's everyday script within a ruled margin, "1959" at top left. The final plate of the facsimile (p0223) is a blank endpaper.
This is the document that fixes the Red Book's place in the corpus timeline: 1913–1930 composition, alchemy as the hermeneut that made it survivable, the Golden Flower as its exit into "actuality."

occurrences.title: The flood and the sea of blood over the northern lands — Jung's founding visions (October 1913)
occurrences.label: The flood and the sea of blood…
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: I saw a terrible flood that covered all the northern and low-lying lands between the North Sea and the Alps.
body: The episode that triggered the whole self-experiment: a daylight vision of a flood covering all lands between North Sea and Alps, "yellow waves, swimming rubble, and the death of countless thousands," repeated two weeks later "still more violent," with the inner voice: "look at it, it is completely real, and it will come to pass. You cannot doubt this." Then a sea of blood over the northern lands; in June-July 1914 the thrice-repeated icy-cold dream with the barren tree whose leaves turn to sweet grapes, given to "a great waiting throng." When war broke out while Jung travelled from Scotland, the visions were read as collective precognitions — the reason Liber Novus was written at all. No painting of this episode in the present folio range.

occurrences.title: The God in the Egg — Incantations illumination (Liber Novus ms p. 50)
occurrences.label: The God in the Egg — Incantations illumination
occurrences.subject: jung
body: Cap. X of Liber Secundus opens the incubation of the sick God (Izdubar), lamed and shrunk in Liber Primus, now sealed "in his beginning": "Set the egg before you, the God in his beginning. / And behold it. / And incubate it with the magical warmth of your gaze". Jung sings himself into mother, father, shepherd, magus, holy animal, and egg; the God's attributes ("eternal emptiness and the eternal fullness... Freedom in bondage... Yes in no") are the seed of Abraxas, elaborated in Sermones II–III (editor n.125).

Plate (p0081.jpg = ms p. 50, image 50). Full-page illumination on a dense red ground: bold blue, white and ochre totemic meander-ornament frames a central blackletter text column opening "Weihnacht ist gekommen: der Gott ist im Ei..." — under a blue cloud-arc holding a many-domed temple and a lotus; at the base, a golden egg rests in a dark vessel-niche. Corner-marked "50".

occurrences.title: Helios and the four winged white horses — dawn dream in the desert gorge (Dies II, Jan 1, 1914)
occurrences.label: Helios and the four winged white horses
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: There were four white horses, each with golden wings. They led the carriage of the sun, on which Helios stood with flaring mane.
body: New Year's dawn in the gorge below Ammonius's cell. Jung dreams of a white horse on the eastern sky that says: "Hail him who is in darkness since the day is over him." Then: "There were four white horses, each with golden wings. They led the carriage of the sun, on which Helios stood with flaring mane" — while a thousand black serpents plunge into their holes. Jung kneels and prays the heathen prayer: "Give us your light, you are flame-curled, entwined, crucified and revived." The second layer drinks the sun ("I drank fire in this night"), and the desert day animates itself: the scarab rolling its ball becomes "my father," the stones line up "like a troop transport," and Jung prays to the mother stone — the desert demanding prayers.

PLATE (p0052.jpg = LS p.21): the great Gothic display page of Dies II — "Wenn du schläfst, so ruhst du, wie all das was je war..." in large black and red textura — the sleep through the millennia and the temple chants; no figurative painting.

occurrences.title: Instruction — the crystal visions: Madonna, Peter, Pope, Buddha in flames, Kali (Cap. x, Dec 22, 1913)
occurrences.label: Instruction — the crystal visions
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: a Buddha sitting rigidly in a circle of fire-a many-armed bloody Goddess-it is Salome desperately wringing her hands
body: Second visit to the house of Elijah. In the burning crystal Jung sees the series of transformations: the mother of God with the child, Peter adoring, Peter alone with the key, the Pope with the triple crown, "a Buddha sitting rigidly in a circle of fire," and "a many-armed bloody Goddess" — "it is Salome desperately wringing her hands" — she "takes hold of me, she is my own soul," and Elijah appears in the stone. Then Salome's shattering claim: "You are his son, and I am your sister... Mary" — the Virgin as mother of Elijah, Salome and Jung; Christ's logion from the gospel of the Egyptians is quoted ("when the two become one, and the male with the female, neither male nor female"). The layer-two reading: forethinking rests on the lion (Elijah leaning on the marble lion), pleasure is the tormented tormentor Kali.
PLATE (p0027.jpg = RB fol. v(r)/v(v)): "Die Belehrung Cap X" — great blue B initial hung with red flame-spikes (the Buddha in the circle of fire) in a dense text spread.

occurrences.title: First Day — Izdubar the bull-man lamed by science (Cap. viii, Jan 8, 1914)
occurrences.label: First Day — Izdubar the bull-man lamed…
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: this is Izdubar, the mighty, the bull-man. He stands and looks at me: his face speal<:s of consuming inner fear, and his hands and knees tremble.
body: On the pass between burning-black and freezing-white rock Jung meets "an enormous man" coming from the East: "Two bull horns rise from his great head, and a rattling suit of armor covers his chest... The giant is carrying a sparkling double axe in his hand, like those used to strike bulls." It is Izdubar (the mistranscribed Gilgamesh), seeking the western lands where the sun sinks to be reborn — and Jung's science kills the myth in one sentence ("the earth is round and moreover it turns around the sun"). The bull-man collapses, poisoned: "No monster has ever resisted my strength. But your poison, worm... has lamed me to the marrow." Their fire dialogue sets "two sorts of truth": outer knowledge and inner truth — Jung's confession that "we are all somewhat poisoned."

PLATE (p0068.jpg = LS p.37): "Erster Tag. Cap. VIII." — the great E initial on deep-blue starfield with a golden rayed sun-disc at its center and a red-orange serpent coiling down the panel's right edge; the meeting scene itself is text-borne.

occurrences.title: Second Day — Izdubar carried as a fantasy, squeezed into an egg (Cap. ix, Jan 9, 1914)
occurrences.label: Second Day — Izdubar carried…
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: with no difficulty squeeze Izdubar into the size of an egg and put him in my pocket.
body: Izdubar lies paralyzed through the night. Jung's saving thought: the giant is "not at all real, but only a fantasy" — and by accepting the new name he becomes "lighter than a feather." Jung carries him down toward the Western lands — "I was as small as a child and bore a giant, and yet my burden lifted me up" (the inverted St Christopher) — and, since a fantasy takes up no space, squeezes him "into the size of an egg" and pockets him into the house of healing. Layer two draws the theological point: the God declared a fantasy is not murdered but interiorized — "This tangible and apparent world is one reality, but fantasy is the other reality... if we turn the God into fantasy, he is in us and is easy to bear." "How completely one are the serpent and the God! The word which was our deliverer has become a deadly weapon."

PLATES: p0072.jpg (LS p.41) — "Der mächtige fiel, er liegt am Boden" set in a Ravenna-style red mosaic border of tiny blue figure-tiles, beneath the great apostrophe "Ach, herrlich äußerlich schöner Freund... wie ganz eins sind Schlange und Gott"; p0075.jpg (LS p.44) — the wide night painting: star-filled sky between two dark brick pillars over blue mountains, a band of glowing fire-colored light at the horizon, a tiny dark figure with raised arms before it (Images 44/45; Atharva-veda 4,1,4 virility charm cited in legend — the healing of the wounded bull-god).

occurrences.title: Izdubar reborn from the egg as the sun — The Opening of the Egg (Liber Novus ms p. 65)
occurrences.label: Izdubar reborn from the egg as the sun
occurrences.subject: jung
body: Cap. XI: on "the evening of the third day" Jung kneels and opens the egg; "suddenly Izdubar is standing before me, enormous, transformed, and complete" — healed of the wounds Jung's laming had given him. "Where was I?... I was completely sun," he says, and an inexpressible light breaks from him: "He who had been pressed into the core of the beginning rose up... he was the sun itself". Editor n.136 reads the incubation as the classic solar-myth pattern (Roscher, Frobenius); n.137 quotes CW6 §301: the renewed God = a renewed attitude, the greatest libido-value. While the God rises, Jung, his "nocturnal mother," sinks: "Woe betide the mother who gives birth to a God!... a thousand times more difficult is the hellish afterbirth".

Plate (p0096.jpg = ms p. 65). Rubricated title "die eröffnung des eies · Cap. XI"; a square gold block holding a red-and-black interlaced fantastic animal initial A opens the blackletter text: "Am Abend des dritten tages kniete ich auf dem Teppich nieder u öffnete behutsam das Ei. Wie ein Rauch stieg es daraus empor u plötzlich steht Izdubar vor mir / riesengroß u verwandelt u vollkommen..." — followed by the sun-monologue in verse lines.

occurrences.title: Image 36 — the Izdubar plate: horned giant in the weave of serpents and dragons (Liber Secundus p. 36)
occurrences.label: Image 36 — the Izdubar plate
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.yearDisplay: painted around Christmas 1913 (per margin inscription); printed legend: 'Christmas 1915'
occurrences.quote: This image was printed on Christmas 1915. The depiction of Izdubar strongly resembles an illustration of him in Wilhelm Roscher's...
body: The one fully worked painting of the Izdubar cycle, inserted at the end of the "great wandering" before First Day. PLATE (p0067.jpg = LS p.36): a frontal standing giant filling the page — black-bearded, crowned with bull horns, eyes wide, wearing a blue-black scale corselet and a red kilt patterned with cuneiform-like ornament; his right hand plants a double-axe (the bull-slaying labrys) point-down. The entire ground is a tiled textile of pale-blue serpents interlaced with brown winged dragons on blue; stepped ziggurat-like brick flanks descend at both sides, rows of dark serpents crawling on them; at the bottom, behind a fence, a tiny white-robed human figure with raised arms faces the colossus. Jung's margin inscription records that the image was painted around Christmas 1913 — i.e. BEFORE the Jan 8, 1914 fantasy it "illustrates": the painting led the text.

occurrences.title: Lapis Philosophorum as Atmavictu's stone face, four Aquarius streams (Liber Novus ms p. 122, image 122)
occurrences.label: Lapis Philosophorum as Atmavictu's stone face…
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.locator: liber-novus ms p. 122, image 122 (pdf p336, The Three Prophecies)

body: Image inscription: "This stone, set so beautifully, is certainly the Lapis Philosophorum. It is harder than diamond. But it expands into space through four distinct qualities, namely breadth, height, depth, and time. It is hence invisible and you can pass through it without noticing it. The four streams of Aquarius flow from the stone. This is the incorruptible seed that lies between the father and the mother and prevents the heads of both cones from touching: it is the monad which countervails the Pleroma." The page legend: "In Gestalt Izdubar hater den Menschen überwachsen u aus ihm ΦΙΛΗΜΩΝ u Ka befreit. ΦΙΛΗΜΩΝ gab den Stein, Ka das ☉" — in Izdubar's form he outgrew man and freed Philemon and Ka; Philemon gave the stone, Ka the sun. (A rare dated use of "Aquarius" in the corpus — the coming aeon read alchemically.)

Plate (p0153.jpg = ms p. 122). A monumental horned mask-face fills the sheet: orange-red speckled skin, large eyes with blue lids and rayed irises, shaggy black mane and long pointed beard, small dark horns. The ground is cracked cream-and-rose stone strewn with dark fossils — an ammonite, a crinoid frond, bone fragments, a trilobite-like shell, a horn. Inscription "a der MCMXIX" at lower left; legend in blackletter across the foot.

occurrences.title: Mandala of the four cardinal figures (Liber Novus ms p. 105, image 105)
occurrences.label: Mandala of the four cardinal figures
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.locator: liber-novus ms p. 105, image 105 (pdf p328, Nox Secunda)
A6 (published anonymously as a patient's mandala)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: The mandala Jung painted at the close of Nox Secunda (the chapter of "accepting the dead") and later published twice anonymously as the picture of "a male patient," first in the Golden Flower commentary (1930) as CW13 A6, then in "Concerning mandala symbolism" (1952) at CW9i §682: "In the center is a star... At the four cardinal points we see human figures: at the top, an old man in the attitude of contemplation; at the bottom, Loki or Hephaestus with red, flaming hair... To the right and left are a light and dark female figure... the two aspects of the anima".

Plate (p0136.jpg = ms p. 105). A four-lobed black-outlined mandala: at center a blue eight-pointed star on a brown-black ring segmented like a zodiac with red/white counter-chips; around it eight scroll-filled lobes in blue, yellow and white beneath red bands; at the cardinal points four small roundels — top: white-robed old man seated in contemplation; left: woman in red robe; right: woman in blue robe; bottom: dark chthonic figure against purple. Corner-marked "105".

occurrences.title: One of the Lowly — the one-eyed tramp dies at the inn (Cap. iii, Dec 29, 1913)
occurrences.label: One of the Lowly — the one-eyed tramp dies…
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: A dark stream of blood is flowing from his mouth and forming a puddle on the floor.
body: In a snow-covered country Jung walks with a tramp — one eye lost in a brawl, ex-convict, locksmith out of work, lungs failing, full of cinema wonder-workers and regicide talk ("at least they got one of them"). Jung feeds him at the inn; at night the man dies hemorrhaging, and Jung stands with bloody hands "as if I were a murderer... Is it not the blood of my brother that sticks to my hands?" Layer two turns the death into doctrine of the depths: without the bottommost there are no heights — "you also climb into the holy stream of common life, where you are no longer an individual on a high mountain, but a fish among fish, a frog among frogs." "The knowledge of death came to me that night, from the dying that engulfs the world."
PLATES (p0043.jpg = LS p.12; p0044.jpg = LS p.13): text pages in Jung's brown-black hand with red rubrics for the tramp's speeches — the Kiniematograph dialogue; no painting in this chapter.

occurrences.title: HAP the Phallos given to the dead; Sermon V's superhuman daimons (1915/16)
occurrences.label: HAP the Phallos given to the dead
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.locator: Scrutinies, pdf p370-371 and pdf p383-384
childhood phallus dream in the underground temple (editor n.49)

body: Two linked loci of the phallic daimon. (1) The first of the three dead — a woman who in life "recovered the mysteries of the Egyptians for me, the red sun disk and the song of the golden wings" — demands a symbol: "The symbol, the mediator, we need the symbol, we hunger for it." "At this moment the sign was placed in my hand": "That is it, that is HAP, the symbol that we desired... naturally godlike, the God's other pole". Editor n.44: Black Book 5 reads "Phallus?" here; n.49: Black Book 5 has "The Phallus," and Budge, "The Phallus of his Pepi is Hap" — HAP is the phallic son of Horus; the note cross-refers to Jung's childhood dream of the ritual phallus enthroned in the underground temple. Later: "HAP is not the foundation but the summit of the church that still lies sunken"; the soul: "Matter is stronger than HAP, since HAP is the son of the earth."

(2) Sermon V makes it doctrine: "Man shall call spirituality mother, and set her between Heaven and earth. He shall call sexuality Phallos, and set him between himself and earth. For the mother and the Phallos are superhuman daimons that reveal the world of the Gods". Black Book 6 adds: "The mother is the grail. / The phallus is the spear" (editor n.116).

occurrences.title: Philemon and Baucis, pensioned magicians — The Magician (Liber Novus ms p. 139ff)
occurrences.label: Philemon and Baucis, pensioned magicians
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.place: a far country (fantasy); Ovid's Phrygia / Faust II as anchors

jung.locator: liber-novus Cap. XXI, ms p. 139ff (pdf p343-357)

body: Cap. XXI, the longest chapter of Liber Secundus. Jung seeks a magician who can teach "magic to compel inner fate" and finds Philemon retired in a small house behind tulip beds with Baucis: "PHILEMON is one of those magicians who has not yet managed to banish old age, but who lives it with dignity... The magical rod lies in a cupboard together with the sixth and seventh books of Moses and the wisdom of HERMES TRISMEGISTUS". The lesson: "magic is the negative of what one can know... Magic is a way of living. If one has done one's best to steer the chariot, and one then notices that a greater other is actually steering it, then magical operation takes place". Philemon is then hymned: "you are a lover of your soul... Such a one is PHILEMON, the host of the Gods"; "you are a teacher and friend of the dead"; "your wisdom is the wisdom of serpents, cold, with a grain of poison, yet healing in small doses".

Jung's later gloss (editor n.264): the Bollingen tower bears the hidden inscription "Philemon sacrum Fausti poenitentia"; "When I first encountered the archetype of the old wise man, he called himself Philemon" — Philemon and Baucis as artifex and soror mystica (Zosimos–Theosebeia, Flamel–Peronelle).

occurrences.title: The Red One — red knight on the tower road, 'I am joy' (Liber Secundus Cap. i, Dec 26, 1913)
occurrences.label: The Red One — red knight…
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: The red of the rider transforms itself into a tender reddish flesh color. And behold-Oh miracle-my green garments everywhere burst into leaf
body: Liber Secundus opens with Jung as tower guard in a green garment, watching a red point wind toward his castle: "there stands the Red One, his long shape wholly shrouded in red, even his hair is red." The dialogue ranges over Christianity, sophistry and "the black school of Salerno," until the Red One doffs his mask at the mention of dancing: "Don't you recognize me, brother, I am joy!" — and Jung's green garments "everywhere burst into leaf." Layer two: "Surely this red one was the devil, but my devil... he was my joy"; the devil as "your own other standpoint," whose seriousness must be earned. The episode founds the rule of the whole book: "to take seriously every unknown wanderer who personally inhabits the inner world, since they are real because they are effectual."

PLATES: p0032.jpg (LS p.1) — the Liber Secundus title "DIE BILDER DES IRRENDEN" beneath a great D containing a single red EYE on mosaic-tile ground, a red-blue serpent zigzagging down its edge; p0033.jpg (LS p.2) — "Der Rote Cap I" initial painting: tiny green-clad Jung on a red tower, a huge red wing-like shape sweeping the blue sky over water.

occurrences.title: The remains of earlier temples — the greening man meets Ammonius and the aged Red One (Cap. vii, Jan 5, 1914)
occurrences.label: The remains of earlier temples
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: Ammonius exclaims horrified: \"Apage, Satanas!\" The Red One: \"Damned pagan riffraff!\
body: Ammonius (now a paunched monk) and the Red One (aged, gray, shabby) meet on the road and both cross themselves in horror at Jung — "I am fully covered in green leaves, which spring from my body." Each tells his fall: the anchorite founded a wealthy monastery near Alexandria and drowned in life; the Red One became a dancing abbot and could not stop dancing. Both call Jung devil and pagan; he passes on to the East. Layer two: the two ruins were "the sad remains of earlier temples and rose gardens" — his own ideals, temple-solitude and devil-joy, "the most laughable place in the world"; within himself he has become "a laughing being of the forest, a leaf green daimon... not man but nature," the greening tree that grows from the temple's ruins.

PLATE (p0065.jpg = LS p.34): display page of ch. vii — "Nach Flucht kommt das Licht, damit die Ferne errettet werde von dem Tod" in large textura with A initials; the greening is text-borne in this range.

occurrences.title: Satan hauled up: the devil defends personal life against the absolute (Liber Novus ms pp. 162–163)
occurrences.label: Satan hauled up — the devil defends personal…
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.place: empty space, the hauled-up order of heaven

jung.locator: liber-novus Cap. XXI, ms p. 162 (pdf p350-351)

body: After uniting the opposites ("we have bonded you with God"), everything stands still; life stalls. The serpent dives and hauls up "the throne of the God... the holy trinity; all of Heaven, and finally Satan himself," who resists: "The upperworld is too chilly for him." Asked for counsel, Satan refuses to endorse the union of opposites — "This smells of monism" (Haeckel, editor n.305) — and defends himself: "I am utterly restless, quickly hurrying life. I am never contented, never unperturbed. I pull everything down and hastily rebuild. I am ambition, greed for fame, lust for action; I am the fizz of new thoughts and action. The absolute is boring and vegetative". Jung takes the point and lets him go: "You are personal life, but the apparent standstill is the forbearing life of eternity, the life of divinity!" Satan "crawls deftly like a mole back into his hole."

Plate (p0193.jpg = ms p. 162). Full page of blackletter dialogue in red ("I:") and green (the devil's initial) alternating — the page ends "ich glaube / du wirst bald am aussterben" ("I believe [the dead] will soon become extinct," pdf p353). Corner-marked "162".

occurrences.title: The Abraxas hymn — Septem Sermones II–III (1916)
occurrences.label: The Abraxas hymn — Septem Sermones II–III (1916)
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
jung.locator: Abraxas-type God of the year (Visions seminar, editor n.93)

body: Sermon II: "God is not dead. He is as alive as ever" — but "Effectiveness, therefore, stands above both [God and devil], and is a God above God... We call him by his name ABRAXAS... He is improbable probability, that which takes unreal effect". The Christian dead "raised a great tumult." Sermon III is the hymn: "Abraxas is the sun, and at the same time the eternally sucking gorge of emptiness, of the diminisher and dismemberer, of the devil... He is the great and the small Pan alike. He is Priapos. He is the monster of the underworld, a thousand-armed polyp, a coiled knot of winged serpents, frenzy. He is the hermaphrodite of the earliest beginning. He is the lord of toads and frogs... To look upon him, is blindness. To recognize him is sickness. To worship him is death. To fear him is wisdom. Not to resist him is redemption". Philemon's gloss: "This God is to be known but not understood."

Editor n.93: Abraxas = the Gnostic year-god (365); Jung studied Dieterich's Abraxas closely in early 1913; in the Visions seminar he equated Abraxas with the Demiurgos, Purusha, Shiva. n.100: the God of the frogs is "the union of the Christian God with Satan" — the start of the anti-privatio-boni line that runs to Answer to Job.

occurrences.title: Man is a gateway; the lonely star — Septem Sermones VII (1916)
occurrences.label: Man is a gateway — the lonely star
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.locator: to Joan Corrie, 29 Feb 1919: the divine child, 'the beginning of individuation' (editor n.123)

body: The seventh and last instruction: "Man is a gateway, through which you pass from the outer world of Gods, daimons, and souls into the inner world, out of the greater, into the smaller world... At immeasurable distance a lonely star stands in the zenith. This is the one God of this one man, this is his world, his Pleroma, his divinity. In this world, man is Abraxas, the creator and destroyer of his own world. This star is the God and the goal of man". The dead, released, "ascended like smoke above the shepherd's fire." Philemon's commentary: "man is a gateway through which crowds the train of the Gods and the coming and passing of all times... he is the moment of the world, the eternal moment... What is time? Time is the fire that flares up, consumes, and dies down. I saved being from time."

Jung to Joan Corrie (29 Feb 1919, editor n.123): the blind creative libido "becomes transformed in man through individuation... out of this process... arises a divine child, a reborn God... In the last sermon you find the beginning of individuation." The star reappears in Appendix C: "the wonderfully beautiful and kind, the solitary, starlike, unmoving" one God within every man — each man himself "a God who lives in faraway realms."

occurrences.title: Philemon in the white robe of a priest preaches the dead — Septem Sermones I (1916)
occurrences.label: Philemon in the white robe of a priest preaches…
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.place: Zurich, Jung's garden door; pseudographically 'Basilides in Alexandria, where the East touches the West'

jung.locator: p. 217 (the dead as 'the voices of the unanswered, unresolved and unredeemed')

body: The frame-scene of the Septem Sermones ad Mortuos. At night "a dark crowd knocked at my door"; Philemon comes to him "dressed in the white robe of a priest". The dead — the same Anabaptist pilgrims who in Nox Secunda (Jan 1914) refused him because "you have a body. But we are dead" — have returned: "We have come back from Jerusalem, where we did not find what we sought. We implore you to let us in. You have what we desire. Not your blood, but your light." Philemon lifts his voice and teaches them (Sermon I): "Now hear: I begin with nothingness. Nothingness is the same as the fullness... We call this nothingness or fullness the Pleroma". Afterward he tells Jung the dead "ended their lives too early. These were seekers and therefore still hover over their graves... since no one teaches them, I must do so. That is what love demands" — because "their Christian faith once discarded and persecuted precisely this teaching," the Gnostic one.

Editor nn.78–81: Jung told Jaffe the discussions with the dead "formed the prelude" to all his later work, and that "he grasped Philemon in the Sermones. It was here that Philemon lost his autonomy"; the printed Sermones bear the pseudonymous subheading "The seven instructions of the dead. Written by Basilides in Alexandria."

occurrences.title: Resolution — duel of the black and white serpents and the temple of the sun (Cap. xi, Dec 25, 1913)
occurrences.label: Resolution — duel of the black…
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: the black one withdrew and its head and the top part of its body had turned white.
body: On a mountain ridge the rock divides day and night: on the dark side a big black serpent, on the bright side a white one; they fight, and the black serpent's head and foreparts turn white — the daimonic principles of forethinking and love transforming each other. Elijah (dwindling into the dwarf Mime) shows the "temple of the sun" on the summit — "This place is a vessel, that collects the light of the sun" — with wisdom-wells Jung cannot reach. The crystal then shows the giant's foot crushing a city, the cross, the dying Christ — and Jung himself crucified, coiled by the serpent, his countenance a lion's, until Salome cries "I see light!" and is healed. In 1925 Jung identified the lion face as the Deus Leontocephalus of the Mithraic mysteries.

PLATE (p0031.jpg = RB fol. vi(r)/vi(v)): "Die Auflösung Cap XI" — illuminated initial inset with a miniature painting of white- and red-robed figures (the serpents' meeting), red marginalia; the book's own "finis partis primi" follows at fol. vii(r) (plate p0029).

occurrences.title: Murder of the Hero — Siegfried shot on the chariot of dead men's bones (Cap. vii, Dec 18, 1913)
occurrences.label: Murder of the Hero
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: Oh that Siegfried, blond and blue-eyed, the German hero, had to fall by my hand, the most loyal and courageous!
body: With a younger companion (a rejuvenated self) Jung ambushes Siegfried, who comes over the mountains "on a chariot made of the bones of the dead," and they shoot him at the turn of the path. A terrible rain falls — "the great stream of tears... after the constriction of death." Jung passes through torment unto death, saved only by the spirit's word: "The highest truth is one and the same with the absurd." A second vision follows: a merry garden of forms "clad in white silk, all covered in colored light." The killing of the superior function — "I had killed my intellect" (1925) — makes room for the coming God.

PLATE (p0025.jpg = RB fol. iv(r)/iv(v)): top left, framed illumination of a radiant golden sun-star flanked by two robed figures (the white-silk garden); mid-page the heading "Heldenmord. Cap VII"; lower left, a framed mountain landscape at dawn with a tiny chariot-figure on the pass (the murder scene); below, "Des Gottes Empfängnis Cap VIII" with flowering border panel.

occurrences.title: Sigg memorial mandala — the 'Liverpool dream' rose (Liber Novus ms p. 159, image 159)
occurrences.label: Sigg memorial mandala
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.locator: liber-novus ms p. 159, image 159 (pdf p349, The Magician)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Image inscription in Jung's hand: "D IX Januarii Anno 1927 obiit Hermannus Sigg aet. suae 52 amicus meus" — painted for his friend Hermann Sigg, dead at 52. Legend in Jung's own description (editor n.296): "A luminous flower in the center, with stars rotating about it. Around the flower, walls with eight gates. The whole conceived as a transparent window." Published anonymously as a male patient's mandala (CW9i §654–55): "The mandala thus combines the classic motifs of flower, star, circle, precinct (temenos), and plan of city divided into quarters with citadel... 'a window opening on to eternity.'" The related dream ("Liverpool is the center of life") corrected his "Western prejudice that I was the center of the mandala — that I am everything, the whole show... I am not the center; I am one of those little side lights."

Plate (p0190.jpg = ms p. 159). Square black frame enclosing an orange-red lattice of interlocking triangles; white star-points glint at the lattice crossings. At the center a dark-green eight-pointed star/rose-window holds a white-and-rose layered rosette "like ruby-colored glass." Blackletter dedication beneath. Corner-marked "159".

occurrences.title: Refinding the soul — the white bird and the almost-forgotten soul (Liber Primus Cap. i, Nov 12, 1913)
occurrences.label: Refinding the soul
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: the wealth of the soul exists in images
body: The opening act of Liber Novus. After the flood vision of October 1913 the spirit of the depths drives Jung to call his soul "as a living and self-existing being" — against the spirit of the time, for whom the soul "is a thing dependent on man." The address is Am heraldic: "Give me your hand, my almost forgotten soul. How warm the joy at seeing you again, you long disavowed soul." The soul is "a child and... my God in my soul is a child" (fol. ii(v)); "The God is where you are not."

PLATE (p0019.jpg = RB fol. i(v)/ii(r) spread): illuminated initial D of "Die Wiederfindung der Seele Cap I" — a white bird (the soul) on a dark blue ground — heading the chapter; lower right the S initial of "Seele und Gott Cap II."

occurrences.title: The three prophecies: war, magic, religion — 22 Jan 1914, seven months before the war
occurrences.label: The three prophecies — war, magic, religion
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.locator: Scrutinies, pdf p366 (May-June 1914 blood visions; 'Then the war broke out')

body: Jung sends his soul "down into the floods, whose distant roaring I could hear" on 22 January 1914 (Black Book 4). She surfaces with the dead world in her hands — war-gear, "superstitions hatched by dark prehistory," fratricide and child sacrifice, "the treasures of all past cultures" — and he accepts all of it, then trims his greed: "Be content and cultivate your garden with modesty" (Voltaire, editor n.235). Then the prophecy: "From the flooding darkness the son of the earth had brought, my soul gave me ancient things that pointed to the future. She gave me three things: The misery of war, the darkness of magic, and the gift of religion... These three mean the unleashing of chaos and its power, just as they also mean the binding of chaos. War is obvious and everybody sees it. Magic is dark and no one sees it. Religion is still to come". The Draft goes further: "How can I fathom what will happen during the next eight hundred years, up to the time when the One begins his rule?" (editor n.236).

Confirmed in Scrutinies: in May–June 1914 the risen soul drinks "red blood," the hermit speaks oracular nonsense ("The worst comes last. The hand that strikes first, strikes best"), sadness lasts until 24 June — "And then the war broke out. This opened my eyes about what I had experienced before". In the Sermones frame the same doctrine returns as the reckoning: "things rise and number and weigh and apportion and devour millions of men".

occurrences.title: Liber Platonis quartorum: the occiput as vessel of transformation
occurrences.label: Liber Platonis quartorum
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the use of the occiput… as the vessel of transformation
body: "The 'Liber Platonis quartorum' accordingly recommends the use of the occiput as the vessel of transformation, because it is the container of thought and intellect. For we need the brain as the seat of the 'divine part.'… on account of its proximity to the anima rationalis the brain had to be assimilated to the amalgam" (¶376).

The recommendation makes literal the treatise's premise of "an unconscious identity between the psyche of the alchemist and the arcane substance, i.e., the spirit imprisoned in matter" (¶376): the container of the opus is the operator's own head, the skull as vas (cf. fig. 135, the skull of Eve with the tree growing from it).

occurrences.title: 'Res ex qua sunt res, est Deus invisibilis' — Liber Platonis quartorum
occurrences.label: Res ex qua sunt res, est Deus invisibilis
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Res ex qua sunt res, est Deus invisibilis et immobilis.
body: The Arabic-derived Liber Platonis quartorum states the terminus of the prima materia speculations: "That from which things arise is the invisible and immovable God." Jung quotes it after the Aquarium sapientum had applied Micah 5:2 and John 8:58 ("Before Abraham was made, I am") to the stone.

His reading: "the alchemists came to project even the highest value—God—into matter," which gave the starting-point for genuine chemistry and, later, philosophical materialism. Psychologically the identification is compelled because unconscious contents, "lacking all recognizable qualities," are indiscriminable from one another.

occurrences.title: The baptismal candle: 'Dono tibi lucem eternam' (Catholic rite)
occurrences.label: The baptismal candle: 'Dono tibi lucem eternam'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Roman Catholic church (rite described by Jung)

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: Dono tibi lucem eternam
body: The godfather holds the child; the priest approaches with the burning candle: "Dono tibi lucem eternam — I give thee the eternal light — which means, I give you relatedness to the sun, to the God." The baptized receives the immortal soul it did not before possess and becomes "twice-born" — as Christ becomes Christus, the anointed one, only after the Jordan: "a nonpersonal or symbolic personality... He belongs to the whole world." Maṇipūra (sun-rise center) is fed by this rite.

occurrences.title: 'Brighter than a thousand suns' — Oppenheimer's Gita flash at Trinity (New Mexico, 1945)
occurrences.label: Brighter than a thousand suns
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Trinity test site, Alamogordo, New Mexico
occurrences.quote: When Oppenheimer saw the first test of an atomic bomb the words of the Bhagavad Gita flashed into his mind: “Brighter than a thousand suns.
body: In the discussion on "Good and Evil in Analytical Psychology" (1959), Jung reports: "When Oppenheimer saw the first test of an atomic bomb the words of the Bhagavad Gita flashed into his mind: 'Brighter than a thousand suns.'" The context is his answer to the editors' question about "the devil and his special reality today, since every epoch has its own peculiar devil" (¶878 — cross-link wotan for the previous epoch's possession).

Jung's reading: "Through nuclear fission something tremendous has happened, tremendous power has been given to man… God's powers have passed into our hands, our fallible human hands"; the forces that hold the world's fabric together may yet make "an artificial sun." The involuntary Gita quotation is the archetype supplying the only adequate language for the technological sacrum — the theophany-vocabulary of Krishna's cosmic form erupting at the instant of the man-made sun. It grounds Jung's refusal of the privatio boni: "Evil is terribly real, for each and every individual" (¶879).

occurrences.title: Sun vision in the cell — Benvenuto Cellini at Sant'Angelo (Rome, ~1538–39)
occurrences.label: Sun vision in the cell
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The sun vision of Benvenuto Cellini in Sant’ Angelo probably belongs to the same category.
body: One line in Jung's roster of visionary light-phenomena: "The sun vision of Benvenuto Cellini in Sant' Angelo probably belongs to the same category" — the imprisoned goldsmith's overwhelming apparition of the sun in his cell, which he reported as leaving a visible mark on him. Jung groups it with the retinal-light mechanism (sparks, spheres, flames) that precedes figure-hallucination in Joan of Arc and Swedenborg, i.e. a physiological matrix later dressed as numinous event.

occurrences.title: Cosmic rays on the photographic plate — 'spin factor' as circumambulatio (dream 7 Oct 1949)
occurrences.label: Cosmic rays on the photographic plate
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters
jung.locator: Pauli's handwritten note 'Observations on Cosmic Rays as Dream Symbol' (pdf p272)

occurrences.quote: The 'cosmic rays' in the dreams are not the real cosmic rays of physics. They are actually suprapersonal (archetypal) contents but not yet made more specific.
body: The dated example in Pauli's undated handwritten note recording 10-15 years of "cosmic rays" dreams: the physicist H. says his father is experimenting with cosmic rays, made visible by obstacles in their way; on a photographic plate lines appear, with "the 'fine structure' of the second line"; the wife finds it "very interesting." Comment made at the time: "It is as if 'contents' had been sent to me but ricochet off me (scattering), possibly to reappear elsewhere."

The rays "can all cause 'burn wounds' (like radioactive rays)"; against them the dream physicists deploy "asbestos sheets" or a "'spin factor' ('spin' meaning 'rotating on its own axis'; 'spin factor' here being similar in meaning to 'circum-ambulatio')" — one of the corpus' rare explicit equations between physics dream-language and an alchemical ritual term. The fine structure marks "the beginning of an assimilation of an unconscious content into consciousness."

occurrences.title: Buddha steps into the lotus — the light of the dharmakaya fills the universe
occurrences.label: Buddha steps into the lotus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Light is always a symbol of consciousness; light enables you to see, light helps your vision, and that seems to be the purpose.
body: The newborn Buddha, three days after his birth, steps into the lotus and pronounces the first words of the law, and the light of the dharmakaya fills the universe. Jung cites the episode in a triad with the Prologue of St. John ("the true Light which lighteth every man," John 1:9) and the light-phenomenon of Moses descending from Sinai, as evidence that illumination characterizes religions themselves:
The seminar's editorial note glosses dharmakaya as the Truth Body, "the innate, nondual, radiant essence of pure mind... profound, clear emptiness."

occurrences.title: The Ericipaeus hymn dream (patient, ~50 miles from Jung, Christmas 1918)
occurrences.label: The Ericipaeus hymn dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: During Christmas 1918, while Jung labored on the Orphic fragment in Malalas, a patient he had not seen for a month — who knew nothing of his studies — dreamed an unknown man handed her a paper bearing a "Latin" hymn to a god called Ericipaeus. On waking she wrote the hymn down: "a peculiar mixture of Latin, French, and Italian." The name was completely unknown to her.

Jung's reading: "I can only suppose that she unconsciously 'read' not my mistake but the text in which the Latin transliteration 'Ericepaeus' occurs" — her variant (i fore) misread the same vowel his had (a fore). The case parallels Dunne's Martinique misreading (¶853-854): unconscious "reading" of a remote text, evidence for the a priori knowledge later named "absolute knowledge" (¶913).

occurrences.title: Cloud of light and the three saints — Joan of Arc's first visions (Domrémy, ~1425)
occurrences.label: Cloud of light and the three saints
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Joan of Arc saw first a cloud of light, then out of it, a little later, stepped St. Michael, St. Catharine, and St. Margaret.
body: Jung's exhibit that visionary figures are preceded by light-phenomena: Joan first saw a cloud of light, and out of it, a little later, stepped St. Michael, St. Catharine and St. Margaret — the same sequence as S.W.'s sparks-then-figures and Swedenborg's luminous spheres (¶99–101). Twice cited: as psychophysiology (retinal light as hallucination-matrix) and, at ¶136, as the paradigm of "teleological hallucinations" — the somnambulism that "gives the individual, who would otherwise inevitably succumb, the means of victory".

occurrences.title: 'A luminosity surrounds the world of spirit' — Hui Ming Ching
occurrences.label: A luminosity surrounds the world of spirit
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: late imperial text (via Wilhelm's ed., 1929; inferred)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Quoted as the Chinese parallel to the "detached consciousness" state of the Great Liberation: "A luminosity surrounds the world of spirit. We forget one another when, still and pure, we draw strength from the Void. The Void is filled with the light of the Heart of Heaven … Consciousness dissolves in vision" (¶816).

The passage belongs to Jung's light-symbolism complex: enlightenment "aptly symbolized by Light in most of the numerous forms of mysticism… the usual enantiodromia per tenebras ad lucem"; rebirth symbolism — katabasis into the cave, the baptismal depths, return to the womb — "simply describes the union of opposites", with the transcendent function underlying all of it (¶828).

occurrences.title: Moses' radiant face — Exodus 34
occurrences.label: Moses' radiant face — Exodus 34
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Descending from the mountain, Moses' face shone so that the people could not bear it; he veiled it (Exodus 34:29–35).

Jung sets it as the bright counter-face to the mirror-dream's devil's grimace: Zarathustra-Nietzsche should have asked "How is it that I appear before the people like Moses, with a face radiant like the sun, when behind that mask I have a devil's face?" — for "his face was like Jahve." The radiance belongs to the spirit's epiphany ("This light which is now shining out of him like the rising sun is a sort of ekstasis"), while the black face belongs to the human being identified with it.
Verbatim: "He is now like Moses who came down from the mountain with his face so luminous and shining that they could not stand the light of it: he had to cover it because his face was like J ahve".

occurrences.title: The light that hurled him back from the window (Burghölzli, ~1900s)
occurrences.label: The light that hurled him back from the window
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: He jumped on to the window-sill, but at that moment a tremendous light appeared in front of the window, hurling him back into the room.
body: The first of Jung's three "teleological hallucinations" (¶304-307): a patient in the first stages of progressive paralysis, desperate to die, jumps for the window — "at that moment a tremendous light appeared in front of the window, hurling him back into the room." Jung's 1907 reading is strictly psychological: a split-off complex acts with apparent purpose, vetoing the ego's intention. He asserts nothing metaphysical; the protective light stands here at the boundary where the autonomization of complexes begins to look like grace. The same series supplies the arresting hand (¶306) and the dead mother's threat (¶307).

occurrences.title: Luminous spheres and flames, then angels — Swedenborg's light-crisis (1744–45)
occurrences.label: Luminous spheres and flames, then angels
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Swedenborg saw nothing for a whole hour but luminous spheres and brilliant flames.
body: During the crisis that opened his spiritual seeing, Swedenborg "saw nothing for a whole hour but luminous spheres and brilliant flames", feeling "a tremendous change going on in his brain, which seemed to him like a 'release of light'"; an hour later real figures appeared whom he took to be angels and spirits. Jung files him with Joan of Arc and Cellini: light first, figures after — and, in the dissertation's closing economy, ranks him with the Clairvoyante of Prevorst as a "Magnesor medium" (¶70) and, in S.W.'s romance, as one of the three beings who must embody every two hundred years (¶63).

occurrences.title: 'Trinitarian Metis, Phanes, Ericepaeus' — Orphic fragment in Malalas
occurrences.label: Trinitarian Metis, Phanes, Ericepaeus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: The Orphic fragment in Malalas describing the Primordial Light as "the trinitarian Metis, Phanes, Ericepaeus" — the first-born light-god under his three names (mind/meti, appearing/phanes, and the Ericepaeus of the theogonies).

Jung's reading: over Christmas 1918 he consistently misread Ericepaeus as "Ericapaeus" (both readings occur in the tradition), and the misreading froze into a thirty-year paramnesia. The locus matters as the anchor of his synchronistic test case: a patient fifty miles away, unaware of his studies, dreamed an unknown man handed her a "Latin" hymn to "Ericipaeus" — her variant misreading affecting the same vowel. See light-ericipaeus-hymn-dream-patient-1918.

occurrences.title: Yajñavalkya and the king — the light of the self (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upanishad)
occurrences.label: Yajñavalkya and the king — the light of the self
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "A particularly beautiful example of that philosophy is the dialogue between Yajñavalkya and the king... the king asks: But when the light of the sun is extinct, by what light shall they live?, and Yajñavalkya says by the light of the moon. Finally every light, every fire, comes to an end, and there would be utter darkness, but there is still left the light of the self, which is the supreme light." (pdf p826; OCR 'Yajftavalkya')
Jung: "That is the exact parallel of the idea of the golden ball" — his proof that "in the west we have no philosophy of the self, but in the Upanishads you will find all these attributes."

occurrences.title: Lilith, Adam's demon-wife — Jewish legend
occurrences.label: Lilith, Adam's demon-wife — Jewish legend
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Adam's first wife Lilith strives with him for supremacy, rises into the air by the magic of God's name and hides in the sea; forced back by three angels, she becomes the lamia who haunts pregnant women and kidnaps infants.

Jung's reading: the Terrible Mother betrayed into nightmare — cf. Lamia, whom jealous Hera cursed to bear only dead children; "a well-known German paradigm is the story of Hansel and Gretel" (¶369); Lamia is also "a large, voracious fish", the whale-dragon.
Verbatim: whereupon Lilith changed into a nightmare or lamia (pl. XXXVIIIa) who haunted pregnant women and kidnapped new-born infants. (cw05 ¶369).

image.title: Lady Lilith

occurrences.title: The lily between angel and Mary — Annunciation pictures
occurrences.label: The lily between angel and Mary
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Mr. Baumann's observation, endorsed by Jung: in pictures of the Annunciation "Always between the angel and Mary there is a flower, usually a lily. I think it is the same archetype" — the flower that comes up by the impregnation of the Holy Ghost; sometimes a bunch of flowers, elsewhere alchemy's three roses or the Rosenlilie.

The underlying archetypal idea: "flowers are really the mirror images of the sun. They are matter that forms into the shape of the sun, receive the sun's image and the sun's rays and represent it. The sun of course is the god that descends into matter, fertilizing and vivifying it".
Verbatim: "Always between the angel and Mary there is a flower, usually a lily. I think it is the same archetype".

occurrences.title: Lingam with yoni — Angkor Wat
occurrences.label: Lingam with yoni — Angkor Wat
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Pl. XXV: the aniconic lingam standing within its spouted yoni-base, "found everywhere in Indian temples" (cf. also the 'Goddess in the Lingam', Cambodia 14th c.).

Jung's reading: form of the motif of "continuous cohabitation" of Shiva and Parvati — "the base is a female symbol, and within it stands the phallus" (¶306); akin to the Greek phallic baskets and chests.

Verbatim: The motif of continuous cohabitation is expressed in the wellknown lingam symbol found everywhere in Indian temples: the base is a female symbol, and within it stands the phallus. (cw05 ¶306).

occurrences.title: The anointed lingam in the oil press (Indian phallic worship)
occurrences.label: The anointed lingam in the oil press
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: lingam worship, ancient to present (Jung: the form 'often... in India, they sell them to tourists')
occurrences.quote: sterile women still anoint the lingam... it is anointed with butter by women in order to obtain fertility.
body: Presenting the animus scale (phallus — husband — lover — Hermes) on 9 December 1931, Jung takes the phallus-stage's symbol from Indian worship: "sterile women still anoint the lingam. The most usual form is a sort of reddish stone of an oblong shape in an olive-oil press; there is a round mold with a little canal out of which the oil flows... it is anointed with butter by women in order to obtain fertility. It is a remnant of the old phallic worship, the worship of the generative powers". He draws plan and elevation in the seminar. The lowest stage of the animus: the man "exists only inasmuch as he is a generative factor."

occurrences.title: Jung's 1938 conversation with the rimpoche Lingdam Gomchen on the khilkor (mandala)
occurrences.label: Jung's 1938 conversation with the rimpoche…
occurrences.subject: jung
body: "In 1938, I had the opportunity, in the monastery of Bhutia Busty, near Darjeeling, of talking with a Lamaic rimpoche, Lingdam Gomchen by name, about the khilkor or mandala." (cw12 ¶123).

The lama explained the khilkor as a dmigs-pa ("migpa"), a mental image built up only by a fully instructed lama through the power of imagination: "The true mandala is always an inner image… at such times when psychic equilibrium is disturbed or when a thought cannot be found… because it is not contained in holy doctrine." Jung's caveat: Lamaic mandalas nonetheless share "a quaternary system, a quadratura circuli," with contents from dogma; the khilkor is strictly distinct from the sidpe-korlo World Wheel with its ternary centre.

occurrences.title: The lion, the loaf of bread, and the magic mirror — dream of a girl of eight and a half
occurrences.label: The lion, the loaf of bread…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich area (lower-middle-class family; Wesemlin church, Lucerne, in her associations)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: The term's centerpiece, presented by Margret Sachs. The girl had to repeat second grade; teacher complained of absent-mindedness. She goes into the forest; a lion comes; she strokes it, rides, falls, is eaten; the mother lays the dead child in bed. In her apron pocket she finds a magic mirror, enchants herself awake; the whole house is transformed, people walk slantwise; below is a store. She buys a loaf of bread, lets it fall despite the woman's warning — worms crawl out; a second loaf falls into a hole in the stairs with the money; she brings her mother stones instead of bread and is beaten. On the mirror's reverse: a burning house with tiny people, and a skull with four horn-legs hanging on a tree; the mirror turns its light on her, she vomits, clings to the skull; arms and legs fall off, then return — the body stays down.

Jung: forest = Muladhara, dark place of fantasy; lion = instinctual fire, Leo as domicilium solis, deus leontocephalus; "she has become an invisible lion child." Mirror = the double, Ka, self-restoring identity — and inflation. Bread = body (Laib/Leib), nutritive regression of libido. Skull on tree = solificatio, the hanged god (Odin, Attis, Christ), dismemberment into the four functions: "Whenever four things appear in a dream, I 'see my chance'". Had an adult dreamed it: the Myste's descent, sunrise, "a child of the golden head" (Zosimos); in a child, a prophylactic warning against being devoured by fantasy.

occurrences.title: Circle of lions around the fiery pit — dream of the lady 'in the upper stories'
occurrences.label: Circle of lions around the fiery pit
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: There was a very dangerous-looking circle of lions. In the middle there was a pit that was filled with something hot. She knew that she had to go down into the pit and dive into it. So she went in and was somehow burned in the fire. Just one shoulder of her jutted out.
body: A lady who had "settled too much in the upper stories, living too much in the head, and on a poor footing with the underworld" brought this dream the very day of the session. With it she mentioned — as a mere fragment — that St. Eustache was said to be her patron saint.

The legend of sacrifice-eustache-lions-brazen-bull-rome-118ad fits exactly — martyred by lions who would not devour the holy family, then roasted in the brazen bull — something the patient did not know. Jung weighs cryptomnesia but keeps the case under dreams that reproduce historical material from archetypal contents.

occurrences.title: Crouching lions carrying the porch columns — St. Zeno, Verona
occurrences.label: Crouching lions carrying the porch columns
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "In the former vision the lion under the feet of the primordial man was in the position of the lion in old Lombard churches, in St. Zeno in Verona, for instance; at the entrance crouching lions carry on their backs the two columns that support the porch of the church, or sometimes they are under the pillars supporting the pulpit. They symbolize paganism, or heathen Rome, overcome by Christianity."

Also: the lion holding a shield in knights' coats-of-arms; the little lion at the feet of the recumbent knight on his sarcophagus — "that position symbolizes the instinctive form of energy overcome by the human mind or by human power." In the patient's mark, the order is reversed: the animal energy streams up from below and crowns the cross.

occurrences.title: Dionysus captured by pirates transforms into a lion and tears them apart
occurrences.label: Dionysus captured by pirates transforms…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~7th–6th c. BCE (Homeric Hymn to Dionysus, type scene)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: Dionysus also has something to do with the lion: about to cross the sea, he is captured by sailors, whereupon he transforms himself into a lion and tears them apart. The lion is the animal that overpowers the dreamer. So Dionysus is that enigmatic instinctual being that causes the agitation.
body: Reading the lion-dream against the Dionysus stratum:

Jung had just compared Wotan to Dionysus: "similar gods of emotionality, ecstasy, prophecy, the mystical... with Dionysus we find the Maenads, with Wotan the Berserkers," and found "peculiar relations to mythological ideas in the Wotan religion, and also in the Dionysus cult" in the child's dream — deeper layers of the unconscious set in motion. "In the language of the dream, this lion is the sun animal. The sun has attacked her and wants to devour her. This is the god. Wotan seizes her. Unfortunately, this very much corresponds to our present situation" (1936).

occurrences.title: The lion and the doves of the Piazza San Marco, Venice
occurrences.label: The lion and the doves of the Piazza San Marco…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Mrs. Sigg's memory: "this connection of the lion and the doves is a remembrance of the Piazza di St. Marco in Venice." Jung confirms: "the Baroque lion is often laughing. That combination of doves and the laughing lion in the Piazza di St. Marco is surely the external origin; it is most impressive and Nietzsche was of course under that impression" — Nietzsche often visited Venice to see Peter Gast.

The pigeons swarm all over the lion "as the lovebirds would make a circle round him"; the internal meaning is carried by lion-laughing-lion-doves-zarathustra-1883 — the sun-lion at fulfillment, ringed by the feminine.

occurrences.title: Green lion bleeding in the queen's lap — Ripley
occurrences.label: Green lion bleeding in the queen's lap — Ripley
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: green lion lying in the queen’s lap with blood flowing from his side
body: Ripley's image of the "green lion lying in the queen's lap with blood flowing from his side." Jung reads it as a double allusion: "on the one hand to the Pieta, on the other to the unicorn wounded by the hunter and caught in the lap of a virgin (figs. 241, 242), a frequent theme in medieval pictures." That the green lion replaces the unicorn "did not present any difficulty to the alchemist since the lion is likewise a symbol of Mercurius"; the virgin is Mercurius' "passive, feminine aspect," while the beast is "the wild, rampant, masculine, penetrating force of the spiritus mercurialis" (¶519). The side-wound ties the image to the lance-wound of Christ.

occurrences.title: Deus leontocephalus (Aion) with the serpent — statue in the Saalburg mithraeum
occurrences.label: Deus leontocephalus with the serpent
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Saalburg near Frankfurt am Main (underground Mithras grotto)
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~2nd–3rd c. CE (Mithraic cult at the Saalburg limes)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: In these mythraeums, most often there stood a strange statue near the altar, a man's figure with a lion's head, with a snake coiled around it that laid its head on that of the lion. This is the deus leontocephalus, that is, Aion, meaning infinitely long time, the god of time who combines the opposites.
body: Amplifying the lion of the girl's dream, Jung describes the mithraea's cult image:

Context in Jung's reading: the Mithraic lion grade (fourth grade of initiation) whose officiants "roared like lions"; the lion as fire; the zodiacal Lion as domicilium solis; the deus leontocephalus at the climax of the zodiacal circle, end of July. Distinct locus from the Vatican Aion (lion-headed-god-mithraic-aion-vatican-2c-3c), here witnessed at the Saalburg grotto near Frankfurt, which Jung cites as an actual site ("for example, at the Saalburg near Frankfurt-on-Main").

occurrences.title: Mithraic god Aion (leontocephalic) — Vatican
occurrences.label: Mithraic god Aion (leontocephalic) — Vatican
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The leontocephalic Aion — lion-headed, winged, entwined by a serpent, often holding keys — is the frontispiece and namesake of Aion: the volume on the phenomenology of the self takes its title from this figure of eternal time. Jung's working of the leontocephalic god lies in "A Psychological Approach to the Dogma of the Trinity" and later Aion chapters (ch. XIV falls outside chunk c01).
Caption (OCR-damaged): "The Mithraic god Aion / Roman,:nd-jrd century."

The figure condenses time, fire, and the pole: cf. cw09ii par. 190, where the Mithraic Liturgy's bull-shoulder Bear turns the heavens from the fiery north. Parallels: god-image-unas-ladder-pyramid-texts-2350-bce, fish-farnese-atlas-pisces-naples.

image.credit: Unknown artist Unknown artist , perhaps Félix Lajard

occurrences.title: The laughing lion and the flock of doves — the sign of the hour (Zarathustra)
occurrences.label: The laughing lion and the flock of doves
occurrences.subject: n/a
