occurrences.yearDisplay: Also sprach Zarathustra III (1883); discussed 25 Jan 1939

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The sign Zarathustra waits for before going down to men once more: "for first must the signs come unto me that it is mine hour — namely, the laughing lion with the flock of doves".

Jung's reading: the lion is "the age-old symbol of the sun... the domicilium solis... the flashing sun itself" — the animal god in Nietzsche; the doves the birds of Astarte/Aphrodite/Venus and of the feminine Holy Ghost (Sophia); "completion is a circle and here it is a circle of lovebirds. That is the Shakti circling round Shiva". External origin: the laughing Baroque lion and doves of the Piazza San Marco (lion-doves-piazza-san-marco-venice). Miss Wolff's astrological key: Leo followed by Virgo — "the lion, or sun, or hero, is confronted with the feminine principle, and that leads to the decline"; Jung: "The hour of descent is the hour of the coming-up of Yin".

occurrences.title: Lion hunt of Marchos — lion swallowed by the woman-stone (Senior)
occurrences.label: Lion hunt of Marchos
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In Senior's 'lion hunt' the lion takes the king's place: lured by a sweet-smelling eye-charm stone, it falls into a trap under a 'glass roof' — 'the "cucurbita," is here called the "thalamus" (bridal chamber)' — and is swallowed (transglutit) by the stone: 'And this stone, which the lion loves, is a woman' (cw14 ¶409). Jung: 'This is a parallel of the Arisleus vision, where Beya causes Gabricus to disappear into her body' (¶409). The royal incest is 'projected on the lion, the animal nature or "accrescent soul" of the king... it is enacted in his unconscious' (¶410) — the sacral act performed 'outside oneself' in the glasshouse.

occurrences.title: Norman church columns standing on crouching lions (Romanesque portals, ~11th-12th c.)
occurrences.label: Norman church columns standing…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: on top of crouching lions, signify the Christian church built upon, or victorious over, the power of paganism.
body: Closing the lion discussion: "Those columns at the entrance of Norman churches, on top of crouching lions, signify the Christian church built upon, or victorious over, the power of paganism. All the Italian guides will tell you that the lion is the symbol of pagan days, the power of imperial Rome". The lion's power-meaning is astrologically grounded (the sign of the year's greatest heat, when the sun god's power is at its height), psychologically "the kingly, royal animal," and apotropaic before temples and pyramids — with the juju door and the hand of Fatimah as its primitive cousins.

occurrences.title: The roaring lion wakes its dead children — Consilium coniugii (Ars chemica)
occurrences.label: The roaring lion wakes its dead children
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: "It further says in this source: 'This is the reason why our ore, the enigmatic substance, is called lion, because—just like the roaring lion wakes the dead children by breathing life into them—the dead body of the ore is resurrected'" (pdf p251; Ars chemica, p. 139).

Jung's gloss: "In this connection we have to know that there is an ancient legend according to which the lion gives birth only to dead children, which it then brings to life by roaring at them. This idea of the lion with its four children, whom it had brought to life by roaring, is a portrayal of transformation, of the resurrection of the dead.... In the original matter, the prima materia, the dark chaotic substance, there lie sleeping seeds of life, which are brought to life by intense desire, that is, by the lion's roar."

occurrences.title: The lion lured from the Saturnine mountain with rose-coloured blood — Khunrath
occurrences.label: The lion lured from the Saturnine mountain…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Khunrath's Hyl. Chaos gives the "lion lured forth from the Saturnine mountain" rose-coloured blood: "the costly Catholick Rosy-Coloured Blood and Aetheric Water that flows forth Azothically from the side of the innate Son of the Great World when opened by the power of the Art" (cw13 ¶383).

Jung: the lion "signifying 'all and conquering all,' corresponds to the pan or panta of Zosimos, i.e., totality" (cw13 ¶383) — the blood of the lion equated elsewhere with the lion of the tribe of Judah, i.e., Christ (n.18 on ¶390).
Verbatim: the “lion lured forth from the Saturnine mountain” had rose-coloured blood. (cw13 ¶383ocr)

occurrences.title: The marching men 'We are the way,' the snow mountain and the lion (patient vision, 2 December 1931)
occurrences.label: The marching men 'We are the way,' the snow…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: A lion appeared to me and I asked: 'Why am I here, oh lion?' The lion answered: 'Because you have taken the way.
body: The many birds of the tree return as many men — the animus as multitude — marching and crying "We are the way": a system of collective opinion that accepts her rather than being accepted. They lead her up a high mountain and dissolve, leaving her alone in the snow, "deprived of animal warmth". The lion appears and answers her question: "Because you have taken the way." Jung reads the lion through Mithraic leontes and the taurobolium contrast, astrologically the blazing heat after the summer solstice — the Yang principle, fiery, strong, royal, "the instincts" returning as compensation once the collective thought-system collapses.

occurrences.title: The man who saddled the lion — pseudo-Aristotle in the Book of Ostanes
occurrences.label: The man who saddled the lion
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Arab world (Book of Ostanes, Kitâb el Foçoul; Berthelot, Chimie au moyen-âge III)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: "That the lion is a dynamic phenomenon is evident from The Book of Ostanes. It is an Arab text going back to an ancient Greek-Persian source. An Aristotle is quoted in the book—a pseudo Aristotle... He tells the story of a man who wanted to put saddle and reins on a lion, but the lion did not obey, so he took a whip and humiliated the lion. This worked, and he was able to ride it. This is an allegory for the transformation process".

"It follows that this is the stage of unbridled instinct or untamed power, which is called lion in the alchemical process because of its inherent instinctual force." Jung translates into the chemistry: acids that bite into bases, the lime "bitten into," "the most acidic vinegar" — the lion as devouring, penetrating affinity.

occurrences.title: Lion and unicorn together — Chymical Wedding and the royal arms
occurrences.label: Lion and unicorn together
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "In the Chymical Wedding, as in the royal arms of England, lion and unicorn are combined (fig. 258); both are symbols of Mercurius in alchemy, just as they are allegories of Christ in the Church" (¶547). The pairing is not decorative: "Lion and unicorn stand for the inner tension of opposites in Mercurius. The lion, being a dangerous animal, is akin to the dragon; the dragon must be slain and the lion at least have his paws cut off. The unicorn too must be tamed; as a monster he has a higher symbolical significance and is of a more spiritual nature than the lion" (¶547).
The English royal arms make the same heraldic pair — church and state both holding the two beasts of the one substance.

occurrences.title: Same girl, second dream: bathroom mirror, wings grow — the little angel
occurrences.label: Same girl, second dream — the little angel
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: age four, remembered in adulthood; presented 31 Jan 1939

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Dream 2 of the wedding-carriage girl: "The dreamer stands in the bathroom of her parents' house and looks at herself in the mirror. In the mirror image she sees that, very slowly, wings grow out of her shoulders, so that she looks like a little angel."

Jung: the bathroom is the ablutio, which in alchemy "regularly follows the so-called blackening, the nigredo" (p210); the mirror is self-reflection, the answer to the preceding archetype's dangerous intrusion — "When a person is in danger of dissolution, it is necessary that he look at himself, in order to reestablish identity with himself" (p212). But the wings cut both ways: she could as well have grown bat's wings. The report on the dreamer, now 23-24, delicate, shy, in the Oxford movement, shows her "still in the egg" — the little angel is one "who has not yet become a human being... not completely born yet" (p213).

occurrences.title: Man the 'little heaven' of the intelligible world — Philo, De mundi opificio
occurrences.label: Man the 'little heaven' of the intelligible…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: A 'little heaven' that 'bears in itself the reflections of many natures similar to the stars.
body: Philo says the Creator made in the intelligible world "an incorporeal heaven, an invisible earth, and the idea of the air and the void. Last of all he created man, a 'little heaven' that 'bears in itself the reflections of many natures similar to the stars.'" The relation of Creator to mundus intelligibilis is the "imago" or "archetypus" of the relation of mind to body.
Jung at cw14 ¶761: "I conjecture that the immediate model for Dorn's idea [of the unus mundus] is to be found in Philo Judaeus."

occurrences.title: Clay liver-models with omen readings (Babylonia and Assyria)
occurrences.label: Clay liver-models with omen readings
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the entrails, and particularly the liver, were supposed to contain the imprint of destiny.
body: Clay tablets illustrating every variation of the liver with its interpretation — "they look like the pictures in a book about palmistry" (source: Morris Jastrow, Religious Belief in Babylonia and Assyria). The entrails, especially the liver, "were supposed to contain the imprint of destiny": the liver is "that which lives" (German Leber), the original seat of life, so one went to the sources of life to read fate — as oracles sat over wells and holes in the earth like Delphi, or Mimir drank wisdom from his spring. The seminar's platform for the "abdominal soul": Homer's psychic centre in the phren (diaphragm), the abdomen of primitive peoples, and the patient's entrails-turned-jewels.

occurrences.title: 'To mould the lifeless body into a living statue' — Mylius
occurrences.label: To mould the lifeless body into a living statue
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: To mould the lifeless body into a living statue.
body: Mylius on the second part of the philosophical practice: "it is more difficult to make a man live again, than to slay him. Here is God's work besought: for it is a great mystery to create souls, and to mould the lifeless body into a living statue."

Jung at cw14 ¶567: the living statue is the end-result; the work is at once a repetition of the creation and a process of redemption — for which reason the lapis was paraphrased as the risen Christ; the texts strike chiliastic notes of a golden age.

occurrences.title: Lizard ancestor of the Unmatjera — multiplying by watching, becoming man
occurrences.label: Lizard ancestor of the Unmatjera
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
jung.locator: Brunner's parallels to the transparent mouse (pdf p374)

occurrences.quote: And as he was again lying still, he became a man.
body: Parallel to the transparent-mouse development: the ancestor of the Unmatjera tribe was a lizard; lying in the sun he stretched his legs, looked around, and found a second lizard beside him — "But this is my spitting image!" New lizards kept emerging as he watched, all out of his body; and as he lay still again, he became a man. Cited (from the Handwörterbuch des deutschen Aberglaubens) with the Zuni cave worlds and the Tantric lotuses as racial-dream parallels to "that's how all men and women develop."

occurrences.title: The locked door opened by contemplation - the eye in the background (pictures, 11 May 1932)
occurrences.label: The locked door opened by contemplation -…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: (In the second picture the door was open, and the conventional symbol of an eye was the most conspicuous thing in the background.)
body: Two pictures "made by a woman who is not in analysis," shown to demonstrate the fertilizing effect of contemplation (betrachten): first, a woman standing before a door she cannot open - the blank-wall moment, "such a locked situation where nothing moves"; then the door open with a great eye in the background.

Jung: "the mere looking at it causes the background to reflect her gaze, and then the door opens." The eye "is her own eye really, but the eye... is the place where things begin, the place of rebirth" - as of the Egyptian autumn festival in which "the left eye of the goddess is prepared for the god to enter in order to be reborn," the mystical eye of Horus. At the impasse one should contemplate the wall so that "all the invisible germs of possibilities... are warmed up and brought to life."

occurrences.title: Companion dream: the locomotive kills merely by going past
occurrences.label: Companion dream — the locomotive kills merely…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Dream 2 of the geese-girl: "A locomotive comes down the street. It kills, not by running people down, but merely by going past them."

Jung reads the pair as one vision of transience: "the geese form a line. Anything passing with a certain rhythm is a train, something going by.... It is the nature of time to go by". The geese are nature, animal life; "The locomotive is cultural life, spiritual life, man's invention. It also passes by. And everything passes, and the people drop dead" (p254). The child, "coming from timelessness" — the aljira — is told: "You are coming from timelessness. Here, however, in this world, there is time" (p255).

occurrences.title: Oxyrhynchus logion: know yourselves, ye are the City of God
occurrences.label: Oxyrhynchus logion
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: 27 May 1931 (pdf p433); 11 November 1931 (pdf p508-509, quoted in full by Allemann)

occurrences.quote: and ye shall know that ye are in the city of God, and ye are the city.
body: The sayings fragment Jung quotes twice in the seminar, reading the patient's egg-head and white-city through it: "The Kingdom of Heaven is within you; and whosoever shall know himself shall find it. Strive therefore to know yourselves, and ye shall be aware that ye are the sons of the Father; ye shall know that ye are the City of God"; fuller at pdf p511 with the animals that draw one to the kingdom. Jung's reading: "when the Self is asserted through pain, it means that the Kingdom of Heaven is established"; the city-logion makes the Self's paradox explicit — the inmost unique thing is the most collective, "ye are the city". "The Kingdom of Heaven is in between people — like cement — is degenerate theology."

occurrences.title: 'Man, if indeed thou knowest what thou doest…' — the Codex Bezae logion (Luke 6:5 addition)
occurrences.label: Man, if indeed thou knowest what thou doest…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: The Western-noninterpolation logion, quoted by Jung in full: "Man, if indeed thou knowest what thou doest, thou art blessed: but if thou knowest not, thou art cursed, and a transgressor of the law" (¶745). Paired with the parable of the unjust steward, it shows "an ethical standard very different from what is expected. Here the moral criterion is consciousness, and not law or convention" (¶696).

The logion underwrites Jung's differential morality of evil — "it is good if evil is sensibly covered up, but to act unconsciously is evil" — and returns at the book's climax: "Before the bar of nature and fate, unconsciousness is never accepted as an excuse; on the contrary there are very severe penalties for it" (¶745).

occurrences.title: 'When there is one alone I am with him' — Oxyrhynchus logion
occurrences.label: When there is one alone I am with him
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Jung's specimen of what the Church did with the tradition: the Gospel text "When two or three are gathered together in my name" (Matthew 18:20) against the original rendering: "When there are two together they are not without God, but when there is one alone I am with him. There, you see what the Church has done." (Ed. fn: Oxyrhynchus Papyrus 1; the full logion in the Coptic Gospel of Thomas, sayings 30, differs again.) The God who is with the solitary underwrites the whole seminar's defense of the individual voice against the gregarious.

occurrences.title: 'Raise the stone and there thou shalt find me' — Oxyrhynchos Fragment 5
occurrences.label: Raise the stone and there thou shalt find me
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Raise the stone, and there thou shalt find me; cleave the wood, and there am I.
body: Oxyrhynchos Fragment 5 (Grenfell and Hunt, New Sayings of Jesus, p. 38): "Jesus saith, Wherever there are (two), they are not without God, and wherever there is one alone, I say, I am with him. Raise the stone, and there thou shalt find me; cleave the wood, and there am I." Jung notes the text is fragmentary (cf. Preuschen, Antilegomena p. 43).

Jung's reading: the split-material logion — divinity present in the sundered halves of matter, the deus in rebus of alchemy; cited in the Rex-and-Regina chapter's discussion of the god hidden in matter. Parallels: oxyrhynchus-sayings-fishes-fowls-2c, Gospel of Thomas 77/30, lapis as God in matter.

occurrences.title: 'When there are two together, they are not without God' — Oxyrhynchus papyrus logion
occurrences.label: When there are two together, they are not…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Oxyrhynchus, Egypt (P. Oxy. I, x; ed. M. R. James 1924)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: The original form, which was found in an Egyptian papyrus, was: "When there are two together, they are not without God, but when there is one alone, I say I am with him.
body: The original form of "Where two or three are gathered together in my name" (Matt 18:20), recovered from an Egyptian papyrus: "When there are two together, they are not without God, but when there is one alone, I say I am with him."

Jung: "The Church interfered and separated man from grace when alone" — outside the Church, no redemption; the single man counts for nothing against the three. This is the dogmatic portrait of "three against one", the relation of relatively primitive man's conscious to his unconscious, which the Trinity formula expresses (gods of tremendous size and power, man "just nothing"). He had cited the logion on 5 Mar 1930 (c04).

occurrences.title: The Logos is a dog: Kyon the Begetter — Aratus via Hippolytus
occurrences.label: The Logos is a dog — Kyon the Begetter
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: For the Logos is a dog... and begets all things. For Cyon, they say, means the Begetter.
body: The Naassene-Aratus astronomy: "Cynosura is the [little] Bear, the Second Creation, the small, narrow way... For the Logos is a dog who guards and protects the sheep against the wiles of the wolves, and chases the wild beasts from Creation and slays them, and begets all things. For Cyon, they say, means the Begetter." The Dog-star rises "judge of the quick and the dead," star of the plants; "between the two Creations stretches the Dragon, hindering anything of the Great Creation from entering the lesser" (¶176).
Jung sets it beside Kalid's filius canis: the dog as divine Logos-Begetter is the archetype's most startling form, millennia before the alchemists' puppy "of celestial hue."

occurrences.title: The Buddha in the lotus — 'thy mind that is indeed the Buddha'
occurrences.label: The Buddha in the lotus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: In fine, it is your mind that becomes the Buddha, nay, it is your mind that is indeed the Buddha.
body: The sequence culminating in the meditation on Amitābha himself: a lotus "on a ground of seven jewels," the flower with 84,000 petals, each petal 84,000 veins, each vein 84,000 rays "of which each can clearly be seen" — and then the Buddha, seated on the flower "like to Jambunada gold in colour." The sutra's decisive formula:

The meditator is next to imagine himself "born in the World of Highest Happiness in the western quarter, and to be seated, cross-legged, on a lotus-flower there" that shuts him in and unfolds (¶923). Jung: the inmost being "is bodied forth in the vision and revealed as the true self of the meditator" (¶932).

occurrences.title: The eight-leafed lotus of the heart — Hamsa Upanishad
occurrences.label: The eight-leafed lotus of the heart
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: ...in the heart region there is an eight-leafed lotus... At the center lives Vairagya, passionlessness
body: "In the heart region there is an eight-leafed lotus. The eight leaves correspond to the compass and portray both moral and psychic states. At the center lives Vairagya, passionlessness, disinterest, and detachment (cf. Meister Eckhart)." Jung's Upanishadic warrant for anāhata as heart-center, with the Eckhart cross-reference typical of his comparative chain; the oldest Upanishads already make the four-chambered heart the seat of soul and waking consciousness.

occurrences.title: The Flower Sermon — Buddha holds up a flower, Mahakasyapa smiles
occurrences.label: The Flower Sermon — Buddha holds up a flower…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: India (traditional site: Vulture Peak); transmission via China/Japan
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~6th–5th c. BCE (attested later; cited via Suzuki)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)
jung.locator: ¶? (pdf p578 index; main text print p. 538n)

body: "Flower Sermon, Buddha's, 538n" (cw11 index; Kasyapa pinned at 538n, Ohazama/Suzuki at 538n, 540). The wordless transmission of the dharma: the Buddha holds up a single flower; Mahakasyapa alone smiles, and receives the mind-to-mind transmission outside the scriptures — the founding legend of Zen cited by Jung in his Suzuki-based exposition.

For Jung's argument it is the type-case of meaning conveyed without signification — the immediate numinous fact that Zen's koan technique then systematizes (cf. satori, "a natural occurrence," print pp. 539ff).

occurrences.title: Om mani padme hum — the gem in the lotus
occurrences.label: Om mani padme hum — the gem in the lotus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: To this relate the mystical syllables Om mani padme hum... They mean the highest perfection and the first beginning at the same time.
body: In the 1930 lecture Jung links the mantra to the śiva-bindu mandala: "they mean the highest perfection and the first beginning at the same time. Contained therein is everything that can be said. For us such speculations are the ultimate point at which one may arrive, whereas for the Indian they are simply the starting point." The gem-in-lotus is the liṅga-in-yoni, center of the primal mandala.

occurrences.title: Louse planted on the newborn — soul transfer rite of the Caucasus
occurrences.label: Louse planted on the newborn
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: they take a louse from the grandfather's head and plant it on the head of the grandchild. By this the soul has been transferred
body: Amplifying the lice of the pigs-and-lice dream, Jung gives the ethnographic locus: "When a child is born in the Caucasus Mountains, they take a louse from the grandfather's head and plant it on the head of the grandchild. By this the soul has been transferred, because in the primitive view the spirits always accompany us, buzz around us like bats or like vampires; they suck the blood from us." Hence the dream-logic: "The lice are the familiares of the pig. If we concern ourselves too much with them, we take over the familiares and get the animal spirits ourselves."

occurrences.title: Love God: seven incarnations; hate him: three
occurrences.label: Love God: seven incarnations; hate him: three
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: they have the saying that if a man loves God he needs seven incarnations in order to reach him, but when he hates him he only needs three.
body: Jung's proof-text that 'to the self it does not matter whether you love or despise; it is only important that you are concerned' — for the East the love and the hatred of God 'are essentially the same.' Used to vindicate Zarathustra's despisers of the body, who at least concern the self. Parallels: atman-brahman-kena-upanishad · prajapati-consults-own-greatness-upanishads-india.

occurrences.title: 'New occasions teach new duties' — Lowell's The Present Crisis stanza
occurrences.label: New occasions teach new duties
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Boston, USA (J. R. Lowell, 1845; dreamer found it in an American finance paper)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: New occasions teach new duties: Time makes ancient good uncouth
body: The dreamer's spontaneous association to dream 25: verses that "suddenly... I were hearing" — Lowell's "New occasions teach new duties: Time makes ancient good uncouth... We ourselves must Pilgrims be, / Launch our Mayflower, and steer boldly through the desperate winter sea, / Nor attempt the Future's portal with the past's blood-rusted key."

Jung, amused that an American finance paper carried them: the verses "really do apply to the last dreams" — the old Christianity is outgrown, the new truth demands the Pilgrim's crossing, and the "blood-rust" names the cost of every step out of unconsciousness (the Inquisition's hundred thousand burned). The dreamer had assimilated the new element.

occurrences.title: Luddite machine-breaking as fear of the dragon in machines
occurrences.label: Luddite machine-breaking as fear…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: perhaps those riots in England arose from the fear of the dragon in machines
body: Mr Holdsworth asks whether the farm labourers who broke machinery in the industrial riots "were working under the fear of the dragon". Jung, wary ("too near to us"), allows: "perhaps those riots in England arose from the fear of the dragon in machines."

The exchange belongs to the lecture's thesis that machines, big guns and trusts are the archetypes of today — the dragon transformed, not abolished: "we are actually in the stage of inventing the machine... After a while, when we have invested all our energy in rational forms, they will strangle us. They are the dragons now."

occurrences.title: The lapis-Christ parallel of Raymond Lully's Codicillus
occurrences.label: The lapis-Christ parallel of Raymond Lully's…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: And as Jesus Christ, of the house of David, took on human nature for the deliverance and redemption of mankind, who were in the bonds of sin on account of Adam's disobedience, so likewise in our art that which has been wrongfully defiled by one thing is absolved by its opposite; cleansed, and delivered from that stain.
body: The oldest lapis-Christ testimony Jung could discover: chapter IX of the Codicillus ascribed to Raymond Lully (1235–1315) — against A. E. Waite's claim that Khunrath (Amphitheatrum, 1598) first identified stone with Christ.

Jung's frame: the roots of the parallel are pagan-Gnostic, not ecclesiastical — "it is far truer to say that Christianity was assimilated through Gnosticism" (¶453) — and a mid-2nd-century Chinese text shows the same ideas where Christian influence is impossible.

occurrences.title: 'A man is made perfect by numen and lumen' — Paracelsus, Philosophia sagax
occurrences.label: A man is made perfect by numen and lumen
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

occurrences.quote: A man is made perfect by numen and lumen and these two alone.
body: "And as little as aught can exist in man without the divine numen, so little can aught exist in man without the natural lumen. A man is made perfect by numen and lumen and these two alone. Everything springs from these two, and these two are in man, but without them man is nothing, though they can be without man."

Jung's reading: Paracelsus "seems to have had an inkling" that the archetypes are luminous — numinosity entails luminosity (¶388). Around this passage Jung assembles Paracelsus's whole lumen naturae doctrine: the light from the astrum or "star" in man; the inner man / inner body (corpus subtile) to whom the light is given, all inner bodies being "one light, and one reason"; the "fiery longing to enkindle"; and the claim that man "learns" the lumen naturae through dreams: "As the light of nature cannot speak, it buildeth shapes in sleep from the power of the word" (¶391).

occurrences.title: Der Wasserstein der Weysen: the inner light that cannot be placed in man from without (1619)
occurrences.label: Der Wasserstein der Weysen
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Germany (German treatise, trans. R. T. Llewellyn)
body: The passage Jung quotes to illustrate the medieval doctrine of the inner man: "Behold, the kingdom of God is within you — from which it is clearly seen that knowledge of the light in man must emerge in the first place from within and cannot be placed there from without" (cw13 ¶141). The boards example: knowledge of white and black "does not come from the boards themselves (for they are mute and inanimate), but originates in and flows forth from your innate faculties." And the flint: "likewise hidden in man, there exists such a heavenly and divine light which... cannot be placed in man from without, but must emerge from within".
Jung's frame: the alchemists' inner light = the divine water as corpus mysticum; the withdrawal of projection as "an extremely difficult affair from the very beginning".

occurrences.title: The luminous room and the three split glasses — hysterical woman patient
occurrences.label: The luminous room and the three split glasses
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: case earlier; published CW 10 ¶123; retold 30 June 1937

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: So it happened three times-three glasses were split, and all in the same regular way.
body: Jung's exemplary case that "the approach to the unconscious... really looks like ghosts." A hysterical woman at an impasse dreams she wakes in a room filled with a strange diffused light, "round luminous accretions" in the drawn curtains — "It was a psychic phenomenon-what is called an exteriorization." The next morning, at about seven, a cracking and trickling: "the whole of the rim of the glass had been split off in a perfectly clean-cut regular fashion" — three glasses on three mornings, always the same clean rim. "I have another glass in my possession which was split in exactly the same way".
Jung stays agnostic in theory but firm on fact: such things "show the peculiar reality of certain psychological events" — the substantiality the descent to the unconscious still carries.

occurrences.title: The kenosis of Ecclesia-Luna — Augustine, Epistola 55 (with the Manichaean light-ships)
occurrences.label: The kenosis of Ecclesia-Luna
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The more the inward man draws nigh to the sun, the more is the outward man destroyed, but the inward man is renewed from day to day
body: Augustine's Epistola 55 builds the patristic parallel Luna = Ecclesia: the Church-Luna wanes as she approaches Christ the sun, and at the new-moon conjunction "all her light is 'emptied' into Christ, the sun" — her kenosis, on Ps. 71:7 "until the moon shall fail" (interficiatur/tollatur/auferatur). The holy man "continueth in wisdom as the sun, but a fool is changed as the moon" — and the fool is Adam. Jung quotes Rahner's full exposition, including Augustine's report of the Manichaean "two light-ships": "the ship of Luna pours out its light into the ship of the sun" (Epist. 55, iv, 6).

Jung's working: the Ecclesia-Luna doctrine is the Church's version of Luna's death at the coniunctio — the feminine unconscious extinguished into the solar Christ, the paradox "darkest when nearest the sun."

occurrences.title: The lunaria/lunatica on mountain Mambracus — Aurora consurgens
occurrences.label: The lunaria/lunatica on mountain Mambracus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Europe (Aurora consurgens, in Artis auriferae, vol. 1, p. 198)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: The alchemical herb named in the same discussion: "This magic herb also plays a role in the Epic of Gilgamesh.... The herb is called lunaria or lunatica; it grows on the mountain Mambracus or Mambraces, like the stone for which one should also always look on high mountains" (pdf p241; Aurora consurgens, in Artis auriferae, vol. 1, p. 198).

Around it: the fairy-tale herb that brings the dead back to life, the alchemical alexipharmakon (antidote), and the proverb "There's no herb for it." For the dreamer, "the quality of healing already appeared with the boa, which actually is a snake of salvation or healing" — the herb is the medicine he can eat himself, where the snake could devour him.

occurrences.title: Alphidius' lux moderna — 'to which no light is like in all the world'
occurrences.label: Alphidius' lux moderna
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: Alphidius (12th cent.?): \"Of them is born the modern light (lux moderna), to which no light is like in all the world.\
body: The Terry Lectures footnote on the lumen naturae: Alphidius, one of the pseudo-ancients of the Turba cycle, names the product of the work a "modern light" without peer in the world.

The same title-family recurs in the Tibetan-commentary footnotes: "In alchemy the philosophers' stone was called, among other things, lux moderna, lux lucis, lumen luminum, etc." — the stone as a light born of matter, cousin of the Golden Flower's inner light.

occurrences.title: White dogs with red noses and eyes in the underworld — Mabinogion
occurrences.label: White dogs with red noses and eyes…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: In the Mabinogion, there are white dogs with red noses and eyes in the underworld.
body: In the dead-girl dream's color analysis: white and red "are also the colors of the underworld, as we know from the so-called Apocalypse of Peter. In the Mabinogion, there are white dogs with red noses and eyes in the underworld." Like the uterus, the underworld symbolizes the unconscious — a state of unconsciousness that is simultaneously a potential state, in utero, before birth.

The red-white checkered apron of the dead girl thus unites femina alba and servus rubeus; as her white skin dissolves and red flesh appears, "the whole girl herself becomes that apron," returning to the state of dissolution.

occurrences.title: The clashing skyscrapers of New York and the mangled red birds (patient vision, 4 October 1933)
occurrences.label: The clashing skyscrapers of New York…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: 4 October 1933 session (vision had on the steamer to New York, c. 1926/27)
occurrences.quote: Every time the buildings crashed together, a great red bird flew screaming into the sky.
body: Returning to America after her European analysis she leaves the mandala through the "fatal gate" and finds the New York streets animated by a most unnatural life: "Great buildings rose above me, bent over me, towered and swayed and hit with thundering crashes." Fear has descended her into manipura, where dead objects assume life; whenever the buildings crash together a great red bird flies screaming skyward, mangled and dripping blood — her anahata contents (thoughts and feelings, "air beings") wounded by the descent.
The vision anticipates life in the collective world outside analysis — "the real fight begins."

occurrences.title: The artist enters the Mürren poster: chapel, Madonna, pointed ears (Zurich, 1935)
occurrences.label: The artist enters the Mürren poster
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: small railway station near Küsnacht, Zurich (fantasy set in the Bernese Alps)
occurrences.quote: He looked up at her face, and in that exact moment something with pointed ears disappeared behind the altar.
body: A young artist who "could not think" could not grasp active imagination until he began to fantasize himself into the Mürren travel poster on his station wall: up the hill among the cows, over the stile, round the rock — to a small chapel, door ajar, on whose flower-decked altar stood a wooden Mother of God. "In that exact moment something with pointed ears disappeared behind the altar." The fantasy collapsed ("that's all nonsense") until he re-entered it as a test and the thing jumped down again on cue; "from then on he had the key" (¶393-395).
Jung's point: images "have a life of their own and... develop according to their own logic" — and prove their autonomy by repeatable, unmanipulated coincidence (¶397).

occurrences.title: Adolescent dream 3: the magic herb under the transparent stone, the lion, the mother's bicycle
occurrences.label: Adolescent dream 3
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Third adolescent dream: on the greening prairie the dreamer seeks a herb that grows under a nearly transparent stone; "a mighty lion appears before me that also eagerly heads for that stone and the magic herb." A spell-word puzzles the lion; in ultimate despair he calls his mother, who rescues him with a bicycle.

Jung: the herb is the panacea of Gilgamesh and of the lunaria of the alchemists; the stone's diaphanitas is the philosopher's stone, the diamond, vitrum aureum — "a consciousness has crystallized that is imperturbable" (p243). The lion is the snake on a higher, warm-blooded level, the green lion of the alchemists, the roaring desire born of melancholia. The bicycle rescue is regression: the collective formula of the dear mother's darling — "One forgoes becoming what one is oneself" (p253).

occurrences.title: The child with the mirror — Zarathustra's devil's-face dream
occurrences.label: The child with the mirror
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Opening Zarathustra Part II: woken before dawn, Zarathustra recounts the dream — "Did not a child come to me, carrying a mirror?... But when I looked into the mirror, I shrieked... for not myself did I see therein, but a devil's grimace and derision" — and concludes his doctrine is in danger.

Jung: "I am quite convinced that he really had this dream just then"; it came in the withdrawal after Part I's creative flood, when "one comes to oneself, everything is quiet, and then... one sees one's own face". "The mirror is the intellect or the mind, and the child carrying the mirror means... the child's mind" — children and fools tell the truth. Nietzsche's "awful mistake": assuming someone blackened his doctrine instead of seeing the devil in himself — the shadow side, the reverse of the Moses-radiance (cf. pdf p885–886), and in the wrathful aspect "he is like Wotan". Wagner's death on the day Part I was finished darkens the same face.
Verbatim: "he has a devil's face because he mirrors himself in the mind of a child".

occurrences.title: Aztec bowl-of-water-and-knife mirror magic — killing through the reflection
occurrences.label: Aztec bowl-of-water-and-knife mirror magic
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: A magic used by the Aztecs consisted in filling a bowl with water, and then putting a knife into it. Then they had the person whom they wanted to harm look into his mirror image in this water. He would be killed by this, because there is a knife in his mirror image.
body: Amplifying the murderous power of the mirror in the girl's dream, Jung cites an Aztec practice:

The row Jung assembles: the Greeks found dream-mirrors uncanny — seeing one's double means death; the Egyptian Ka; primitives refusing to be photographed lest the soul-image be carried off; Narcissus drowning in his image; the Student from Prague selling his reflection; Chamisso's Schlemihl and Wilde's Dorian Gray. Against this the child's magic mirror is ambivalent: it removes her into a mythological situation (inflation) yet also restores identity — Jung's patient: "I am all confused, and cannot start speaking unless I know again how I look".

occurrences.title: Adolphus' vision: the crowned psychopomp of the Aurelia occulta (late medieval)
occurrences.label: Adolphus' vision — the crowned psychopomp…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The "Declaratio et Explanatio Adolphi" reports a dream-vision Jung judges genuine ("certain features that are not traditional but are entirely original"): "a shining male figure wearing a crown of stars. His robe is of white linen, dotted with many-coloured flowers, those of green predominating. He assuages the anxious doubts of the adept, saying: 'Adolphus, follow me. I shall show thee what is prepared for thee, so that thou canst pass out of the darkness into the light'" (cw13 ¶106).

"This figure, therefore, is a true Hermes Psychopompos and initiator, who directs the spiritual transitus of the adept"; the book shown with the "parabolic figure" of the Old Adam indicates "the psychopomp is the second Adam, a parallel figure to Christ" (¶106).

occurrences.title: 'Myself philosopher, demon, hero, god and all things' — Agrippa's motto
occurrences.label: Myself philosopher, demon, hero, god…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The motto of Agrippa von Nettesheim's De incertitudine et vanitate scientiarum (1527): "Agrippa spares no man... being, himself philosopher, demon, hero, god and all things" (quoted by Jung in his Paracelsus article, CW15 ¶9, footnote pdf p942).

Jung reads it as the confession of the first modern individuals for whom authority had completely collapsed: "he himself became the authority: he was then identical with the absolutely divine uncertainty, with the creative uncertainty." A certain megalomania of the 16th century "is the God that came into man" — with inflation's consequences following: war, the peasants' revolt after Luther, and eventually Protestantism's four hundred denominations.
Verbatim: "That was such an individualistic confession by a man for whom authority had completely collapsed, so that he himself became the authority".

occurrences.title: The doctor as sinister magician-demon — transference projection (Zurich, c.1920s)
occurrences.label: The doctor as sinister magician-demon
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: When I am by myself... the picture I have of you changes in a remarkable way.
body: The same crab-dream patient, asked how the doctor seems outside the consulting hour: "Sometimes you seem rather dangerous, sinister, like an evil magician or a demon." Jung recognizes that he has been "contaminated (identified) with the artist" of her Mrs. X fantasy — he now is the crab, the obstacle at the crossing (¶144).

Jung's reading: "magician" and "demon" are not personal qualities but mythological ones; the projection marks contents of the collective unconscious (¶150). Raised to the subjective level, "I became an image for the figure of the magician in the collective unconscious" (¶158). The case anchors his account of the "magic demon" — the medicine-man stratum of the God-conception, dark twin of the wise old man (¶¶153–154).

occurrences.title: Megissogwon the Pearl-Feather magician, guarded by fiery serpents — Song of Hiawatha
occurrences.label: Megissogwon the Pearl-Feather magician, guarded…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The magician, we are told, had killed the father of Nokomis. Now she sends her son forth to avenge her father.
body: The danger in the West: snake and water are "mother attributes"; the black Stygian water "is the place where the sun sinks down for rebirth, the maternal sea of death and night" (¶541). The woodpecker "Mama" reveals the one vulnerable spot under the topknot — "the point where the mythical 'head-birth' takes place" (¶547) — and the wampum belt passes to the hero.

occurrences.title: 'The Stranger' — Pauli's Mercurius dream-figure (Zurich, 1946-1950)
occurrences.label: The Stranger' — Pauli's Mercurius dream-figure
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: This 'stranger' is something that did not accept the scientific world picture about 300 years ago...
body: Pauli's Philemon: the figure appearing since 1946 as "The Blond" and "The Persian" (light and dark aspects, "never appear together"), merged by 1948 into one man "blond, but in a dark robe, or vice versa" — younger than Pauli, not white-haired. Pauli's portrait (letter 44P): "It is evidently the archetype of the 'mana personality' or the 'magician'... Everything that Prof. Jung says about the 'spirit Mercurius' fits him perfectly"; dual-layered "half Christian-human, half devilish-pagan" like Merlin (Robert de Boron), "in need of redemption." He treats ancient magic as "a popular preliminary stage," makes "no distinction whatsoever between 'physical' and 'psychic'", uses the terminology of modern science (radioactivity, spin, prime numbers) unconventionally, and — the "really odd bit" — is "not an Antichrist, but in a certain sense an 'Antiscientist'": what "did not accept the scientific world picture about 300 years ago and is now running around autonomously in the collective unconscious like a loose cannon," loaded with mana whenever physics stalls.

In the dream language he "would be identified with the 'radioactive nucleus'"; his hypothesis-form: "'The stranger' is the archetypal background constellated by the system of scientific concepts of our time."

occurrences.title: The rope-trick and the headless officer — sorcerer's projection in an Indian garrison
occurrences.label: The rope-trick and the headless officer
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Jung's own experience stands behind the story: "A sorcerer tried that once with me and I stepped into the trap; he had such amazing intuition that he was able to twist a cell in my brain". Then the garrison tale: an officer arrives late to a rope-trick performance and "saw nothing there. He only saw the boy standing beside the sorcerer and the rope lying on the ground, and he was just about to shout when the sorcerer caught him, saying, 'Look at that man, he has no head!' And he looked and the man had no head, and then he was all in-and there was the rope and the boy climbing up it."

The locus illustrates Jung's theory of intuition as invasive: "Intuition seems to work through the sympathetic system… intuitions also bring out an unconscious effect in the object of the intuition" — one of "the important sources of mental infections and there is no defence against it."

occurrences.title: White magician in black, black magician in white — theological student's dream (Zurich, ~1900s–10s)
occurrences.label: White magician in black, black magician in white
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The black magician appeared, but clad in a white robe. He declared that he had found the keys of paradise, but needed the wisdom of the white magician in order to understand how to use them.
body: A young theological student "involved in all sorts of difficulties of belief" dreamed he was the pupil of the "white magician," "who, however, was dressed in black." Instructed up to a point, the white magician said they now needed the "black magician" — who appeared "clad in a white robe," declaring "that he had found the keys of paradise, but needed the wisdom of the white magician in order to understand how to use them" (¶287).

Jung's reading: the dream stages the problem of opposites in impersonal collective figures, "in contrast to the Christian view... stresses the relativity of good and evil in a way that immediately calls to mind the Taoist symbol of Yin and Yang" (¶287). The crossed robes make each carrier of the opposites incomplete without the other; the keys without wisdom are inert. Jung notes the dream "cannot... be an intellectual problem, but is profoundly emotional" (¶289).

occurrences.title: Meister Eckhart's 'daughter': neither virgin nor spouse
occurrences.label: Meister Eckhart's 'daughter'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~14th c. (anecdote attached to Meister Eckhart, d. 1327)
occurrences.quote: Of all these things I am no single one, and am the one thing and the other running thither.
body: A daughter comes to the convent asking for Meister Eckhart and answers the porter: "I am neither virgin nor spouse, nor man nor wife nor widow nor lady nor lord nor wench nor thrall." To the Master she explains each refusal — virgin, "I were in my first innocence"; spouse, "bearing the eternal word within my soul unceasingly"; widow, "ever yearning for my one and only love" — until: "Of all these things I am no single one, and am the one thing and the other running thither." Eckhart: "I have been listening to the most perfect person I ween I ever met" (¶102).

Jung reads her as "the divine maiden (anima)," paired with Eckhart's vision of the naked boy as "the divine child (the self)": "these primordial images can rise up anywhere at any time quite spontaneously, without the least evidence of any external tradition" (¶103). She is the Aelia Laelia Crispis figure two centuries before Bologna — the paradoxical one beyond every predicate.

occurrences.title: Erythraean Sibyl as feminine psychopomp — Maier's peregrinatio
occurrences.label: Erythraean Sibyl as feminine psychopomp
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Arabia Felix (Maier's narrative); cave of the Sibyl
body: Near the Red Sea Maier 'heard a rumour' of the Erythraean Sibyl dwelling in a cave — the sibyl who foretold Christ (via Augustine, De civitate dei, and the Sibylline acrostic IHΣOYΣ XPEIΣTOΣ ΘEOY YIOΣ ΣΩTHP ΣTAYPOΣ) (cw14 ¶277-278). Jung: 'by the Red Sea, he met the animal soul... and, at the same time and in the same place, the meeting with the anima, a feminine psychopomp who showed him the way to Mercurius' (¶282). Where Hermas' maiden meant the Church, Maier's means the sibyl: 'the newer is the older' (¶303). The scandal: at the start of the 17th c. he asks the sibyl not for Christ but for Mercurius — 'striking proof of the parallelism between Mercurius and Christ' (¶285).

occurrences.title: Prisoner-of-the-ogre fantasy (young deliverer, little bird in the gilded cage) — recurring clinical material
occurrences.label: Prisoner-of-the-ogre fantasy
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: The recurring fantasy Jung reports from his practice, describing what happens when a woman's libido, denied outlet, "goes into the unconscious in a lump... It becomes an egg that she broods over and hatches out. What is in this egg? Feminine instinctiveness." Then: "Fantasies begin to form around the figure of a young man who will come and free her from this tyrant... her being a prisoner of a cruel tyrant," and — "Often I have seen this fantasy material about the young man, and the old man who has put the little bird into a gilded cage" (sem-1925).

Jung's reading: the woman is usually unconscious of it until forty or forty-five; the material begins in the personal unconscious and makes "wonderful material out of which an unconscious complex can form"; brutal sexuality opens the deeper layers, "right back to the monkey age."

occurrences.title: Maier — the four elements as four stages of fire (Scrutinium chymicum, Emblem XVII)
occurrences.label: Maier — the four elements as four stages of fire
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Four spheres filled with fire: 'Imus Vulcanum referat... Mercurium, Lunam tertius orbis habet: Quartus, Apollo' — the lowest is Vulcan's earthly fire, the second Mercurius the vegetative life-spirit, the third the moon, female psychic principle, the fourth the sun, male spiritual principle (¶393). Jung tabulates the Vigenère, Ripley and Maier fire-series against the states of aggregation — solid, liquid, gas, flame — and reads the whole as an adumbrated phlogiston theory: 'fire is peculiar to all the states of aggregation' (¶394-395). The alchemical lapis-quaternity as proto-physics. Cf. mercurius-salamander-maier-1687 (same work).

image.title: Michael Maier Atalanta Fugiens Emblem 17

occurrences.title: Edward Maitland's vision of the dual God
occurrences.label: Edward Maitland's vision of the dual God
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1870s-80s (published in Maitland's biography of Anna Kingsford, I, pp. 130)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Edward Maitland — biographer and collaborator of Anna Kingsford — described his own experience of God, "which, like that of Brother Klaus, consisted in a vision of light": "This was... God as the Lord, proving by His duality that God is Substance as well as Force, Love as well as Will, feminine as well as masculine, Mother as well a Father" (¶134).

Jung's reading: another "impressive account of the syzygy vision" whose dual God cannot be derived from tradition (the footnote compares the male-female light of the Poimandres, adding "I do not know whether Maitland was acquainted with the Poimandres; probably not") — spontaneous projection of the divine pair.

occurrences.title: Malchuth's cognomens — moon, earth, bride, queen of heaven, fish-pool, hind of loves (Kabbala denudata)
occurrences.label: Malchuth's cognomens
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Knorr von Rosenroth's digested list of Malchuth's names: "She is called moon, earth, bride, matron, queen of heaven, fish-pool, sea, well, tree of knowledge of good and evil, hind of loves ('so is Malchuth especially called because of the mystery of the new moon'), belly, etc."; Gikatila (Shaare Ora, via S. Hurwitz) adds fountain, stone, sapphire, land of life; Malchuth is the Kenesseth Israel, "the mystical archetype of the community of Israel".
For Jung this is the complete feminine-symbol catalogue attached to one figure — the Hebrew sister of Luna, the sponsa, and the widowed/altered feminine through which the King's unity is restored.

occurrences.title: Malchuth called the 'statue' when united with Tifereth — Zohar, Haye Sarah
occurrences.label: Malchuth called the 'statue' when united…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Malchuth is called the 'statue' when she is united with Tifereth.
body: The Zohar on Genesis 28:22 ("And this stone, which I have set for a pillar, shall be God's house"): Malchuth is called the "statue" when she is united with Tifereth. The stone reminds that "here the upper (Tifereth) has united with the lower (Malchuth): Tifereth the son has come together with the 'Matrona' in the hierosgamos."
Jung at cw14 ¶568: if his conjecture is right, the statue could be the Cabalistic equivalent of the lapis Philosophorum, which is likewise a union of male and female.

occurrences.title: The man from the sea — Apocalypse of Ezra (II Esdras), fifth and sixth visions
occurrences.label: The man from the sea
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In a footnote on the alchemical sea (Pernety: their sea is "in general the four elements, in particular... their mercury"), Jung points to "the 'man from the sea' cf. II Esdras (Apoc.) 11 and 13, fifth and sixth visions". After the eagle-vision (the world-power's dissolution), the man flying from the sea with the cloud-hosts judges and destroys the eagle: the saving Anthropos rising from the waters.
The locus anchors Jung's chain sea = prima materia = origin of the hero/Anthropos who rises from the unconscious.

occurrences.title: Every human being a ray of sunlight — Jorge Guillén's Cántico
occurrences.label: Every human being a ray of sunlight
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)
jung.locator: 'Transformation Symbolism in the Mass' n.37 (pdf p730)

occurrences.quote: Another idea of the kind is that every human being is a ray of sunlight. This image occurs in the Spanish poet Jorge Guillen, Cántico: Fe de Vida, pp. 24–25 ('Más allá,' VI)
body: Jung's footnote on the human being as a ray of the one sun — modern poetry's version of the scintilla:
The individual as an emission of a central light — the same structure as Khunrath's scintillae and Schreber's sun-rays, arrived at by lyric reason.

occurrences.title: The man, his son, and the ass
occurrences.label: The man, his son, and the ass
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: finally you are in the situation of that famous old parable of the man, his son, and the ass.
body: Jung's emblem for the conflict of virtues: whatever arrangement the man tries, someone criticizes — as whichever named virtue you serve, its rival "will keep on grumbling." A battle between two goods "is worse" than good against evil: "you can slay the devil by the aid of all sorts of helpful ideas and institutions... But to slay another virtue is harder: there you gain no recognition."

occurrences.title: The royal touch — Most Christian King cures epilepsy by laying on of hands
occurrences.label: The royal touch — Most Christian King cures…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the Most Christian King could cure epilepsy with his mana by the laying on of hands.
body: Footnote to Jung's definition of mana in the mana-personality chapter (index: "mana: definition of, 233"): "According to popular belief, the Most Christian King could cure epilepsy with his mana by the laying on of hands." The French royal touch — the sovereign's healing of scrofula ("the King's evil") and, in this strain of belief, epilepsy — as a lived mana-institution of Christian kingship, cited alongside Lehmann's Mana (1922).

Jung's reading: mana is "an efficiency that comes from..." — a dynamic, transmissible effect residing in persons and offices (¶¶233ff); the king, the medicine-man, and the doctor share the same dynamic status, which is why the doctor is "as God" to the patient (¶¶70, 130-135). The royal touch shows mana historically vested in an office, not merely in primitives — the same projection that Jung warns the analyst inherits.

occurrences.title: The dispute of John and Jesu ben Miriam 'the deceiver' — Mandaean Book of John
occurrences.label: The dispute of John and Jesu ben Miriam the…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: "Now, happily enough, the writings of John have been discovered... In the book of Johanna we find the whole discussion between Johanna and Jesu ben Miriam, the deceiver. That is the title under which he is introduced, because he betrayed the mysteries according to their point of view. John reproaches him for having handed out the great mysteries of life to the people, and Jesus defends himself, saying that he is right in doing so. Curiously enough that discussion ends without any final agreement... the scales remain in complete balance—John is right and Jesus is right." The community itself: ~3,000 silversmiths who eat only drowned meat, with averted faces. Jung's lever for the law-vs-freedom reading of the church-dream's son.

occurrences.title: 1916 patient — world-creation picture: sun, twelve-part halo, four lines (Fig. 2)
occurrences.label: 1916 patient — world-creation picture
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The nodes are "great personalities and founders of religions," as my erstwhile patient told me.
body: In 1916 Jung observed a similar individuation process, illustrated by pictures, in another woman patient: a world creation. Fig. 2: at the top the sun, surrounded by a rainbow-coloured halo divided into twelve parts like the zodiac; to the left, three drops fall from an unknown source, dissolve into four lines (two pairs, painted in the classical four colours), which move, form four paths, and unite periodically in a node — building a system of vibrations. The nodes are "great personalities and founders of religions." The same conception as Miss X's narcosis dream; archetypal, grounded in world-period ideas (Parsees, yugas, Platonic months).

occurrences.title: Akbar's hall of private audience — the Mogul in the centre of his mandala (Diwan-i-Khas, Fatehpur Sikri)
occurrences.label: Akbar's hall of private audience
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: The Mogul sits in a sort of saucer of red sandstone supported by a slender pillar.
body: Mr. Gibb's example, brought by Jung alongside the patient's mandala dream-hall: the Mogul Emperor Akbar the Great in his hall of private audience, where "the pattern of the building quite clearly forms a mandala, the Mogul sits in a sort of saucer of red sandstone supported by a slender pillar, so that the saucer appears almost to be suspended from heaven."

Jung's reading: "It is a fine idea for the old man to sit in that manner in the middle of his mandala, so that wisdom should come to him from all four corners of the world." The architecture realizes in stone what the patient's dream realized in vision — the central seat in the quaternary structure (compare the four-cornered gallery of the dream hall).

occurrences.title: Black Pagoda of Konarak — the ruin covered with obscenities (Odisha, ~1250)
occurrences.label: Black Pagoda of Konarak
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1250 CE (built under Narasimhadeva I; ruined by the 17th c.)
occurrences.quote: go to the Black Pagoda of Konarak, sit down in the shadow of the mighty ruin that is still covered with the most amazing collection of obscenities
body: The Black Pagoda: Jung's name for the ruined Sun temple of Konarak, "still covered with the most amazing collection of obscenities" — the celebrated erotic (maithuna) sculpture of the temple walls.

Jung's reading: not a sight but an exercise in projection-withdrawal, the practical test of "What India Can Teach Us." The European is to "wrap yourself in the cloak of your moral superiority," sit in the shadow of the ruin, read Murray's Handbook "which tells you how to be properly shocked," and "then analyse carefully and with the utmost honesty all your reactions, feelings, and thoughts" — the payoff being knowledge "about yourself, and about the white man in general." The obscenities are the hierosgamos imagery that white consciousness suppresses and therefore meets as filth; the exercise concretizes the essay's thesis that India civilizes "without suppression" (¶1011).

occurrences.title: Jakob Boehme's mandala — XL Questions concerning the Soule (1620)
occurrences.label: Jakob Boehme's mandala
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Gorlitz, Germany (picture from the 1647 English edition)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Boehme's diagram of the divine quaternity in the XL (=Forty) Questions concerning the Soule: Father, H. Ghost, Sonne, and Earth or Earthly Man — with the two semicircles turned back to back instead of closing. Jung uses it twice: as the anticipation of Miss X's divided mandalas (cross, quaternity, lower hell-half, upper "Salniter" realm, ¶535), and in Concerning Mandala Symbolism as "un-united opposites, which presumably should be bound together by the heart standing between them" (¶704). The outermost ring is labelled "will of ye Devill Lucifer," "Abysse (of) Eternity," "Hell of Devills" (¶578). The soul is "an Eye in the Eternal Abyss... a fiery Eye."
Jung: Boehme "was the first to try to organize the Christian cosmos, as a total reality, into a mandala" — and failed, unable to unite the halves (¶601).

occurrences.title: Mandala of opposites in Boehme's XL Questions concerning the Soule
occurrences.label: Mandala of opposites in Boehme's XL Questions…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: London (1647 English printing of Boehme's treatise)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The mandala is divided into a dark and alight half, and the semicircles that are drawn round them, instead of joining up to form a ring, are turned back to back.
body: Jakob Boehme knew a God of the "Wrath-fire", a real Deus absconditus; he bridged the agonizing contradiction through the Christian formula of Father and Son and — "undoubtedly alchemy, long brewing the union of opposites in secret" (¶21). The mandala appended to his XL Questions concerning the Soule (London, 1647; CW9i Fig. 1, anchored at ¶297) shows the nature of the divinity with the opposites still visible.

Jung's reading: the semicircles turned back to back record the un-reconciled opposites in Boehme's God-image — had they formed a ring, the union would be achieved. Otherwise Boehme "would have become a dualist".

occurrences.title: Borobudur — the mandala-temple walked in a spiral
occurrences.label: Borobudur — the mandala-temple walked…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: "Certain temples have the form of typical mandalas, like the famous temple of Borobudur in Java, which is a circle in a square" — built, Jung notes, on the Terrace of Life scheme shared with the Mayan temples and (in raised terraces) Zoser's pyramid at Sakkara. Its psychological meaning: "a pyramidal mass consisting of circular corridors decreasing in size, like a spiral... It is a pilgrimage of initiation", the walls bearing bas-reliefs of the 576 former incarnations of the Buddha — "he lived as a plant and as a locust and as a monkey" — so that circumambulation completes the whole extension of life. The rotating movement: "if one covers the whole ground one cannot fail to complete oneself."

occurrences.title: Mandalas round the bed — boy of seven against nameless fears
occurrences.label: Mandalas round the bed
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: He only feels safe when they are around him. His fantasy tells him that they protect him against nameless fears assailing him in the night.
body: Fourth in Jung's run of mandala cases (cw18 ¶1265), each showing that "the underlying reason for producing a mandala seems to be a certain definable mental state" (¶1265). A boy of seven papered the corner where his bed stood with mandalas and could not sleep without them; his fantasy said they protected him against nameless fears of the night. Jung names the confusion driving the compensation: his parents were contemplating divorce. The mandala here is a self-made apotropaion — circle as temenos against dissolution of the family field.

occurrences.title: Buddha sets the wheel of the law in motion (Sarnath)
occurrences.label: Buddha sets the wheel of the law in motion
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "there is a clear connection between this idea and the idea of the wheel in motion in Buddhistic literature; the teaching of the law is compared to a moving wheel... As Zarathustra has thrown a ball, so Buddha brings a wheel among men and sets it in motion, a process which will eventually lead up to the Buddhistic idea of the most perfect condition — the condition of complete detachment, of nirvana."

"It is also characteristic of Buddhism that it is considered to be a spiritual merit to depict such a wheel, to make a drawing of it... Of course a mandala is such a wheel, though that is again a somewhat different aspect."
Zarathustra's thrown golden ball and the dharma-wheel are one gesture: instigating the self, setting the center moving among men.

occurrences.title: The Aztec Calendar Stone as mandala (Mexico City)
occurrences.label: The Aztec Calendar Stone as mandala
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: a face in the centre with four tower-like forms grouped about it
body: "There is a Mexican mandala, the famous Calendar Stone, which has a face in the centre with four tower-like forms grouped about it. The whole is surrounded by a circle and the calendar reckonings are in the intersections of the circle."

One exhibit in Jung's world-mandala survey (Norman MSS — Cologne — Mexico — Pueblo sand-paintings — Wilhelm's Taoist monastery example), summoned to prove the fourfold circular centre is autochthonous, not borrowed: "Scientists like to think that symbols have migrated. This is not true." The sun-face at the centre makes it simultaneously a sun locus (editor cross-references CW12 fig. 41, where Jung reproduces it in the sacrifice-context).

occurrences.title: Patient case with mandala drawings — Hauer's Kundalini Yoga seminar (autumn 1932)
occurrences.label: Patient case with mandala drawings
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: [This case is discussed by Jung in Prof. J. W. Hauer's Seminar on Kundalini Yoga (privately multigraphed, Zurich, autumn 1932, pp. 91 ff.). … Examples of this patient's drawings are reproduced and discussed in 'Concerning Mandala Symbolism,' figs. 7–9, and pars. 656 ff.]
body: The anonymous patient of the Appendix essay "The Realities of Practical Psychotherapy" (lecture, Bern, May 28, 1937; previously unpublished). The editors' notes identify the case's twin records:

Also cross-referenced: pars. 307–10 supra and Two Essays ¶189. A seminar-documented case whose drawings entered the CW9i mandala corpus — the junction of clinical record, kundalini comparison, and mandala symbolism.

occurrences.title: The celestial hierarchies as mandala — pseudo-Dionysius and medieval diagrams
occurrences.label: The celestial hierarchies as mandala
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: these are simply self-representations of the unconscious structure
body: Answering Dr. Harding's question whether the one Holy Spirit is split into many selves, Jung adduces "those old hierarchies like the one of Dionysius the Areopagite, father of scholastic philosophy, or the ideas of the Gnostics, or of Paul": the world with "a peculiar hierarchic structure," groups under one angel, angels under archangels, "and so on, up to the throne of God. You find such representations quite often in the Middle Ages where the heavenly hierarchies were represented even in the form of mandalas."

The interpretive point: "Now, these are simply self-representations of the unconscious structure" — the many-selves-in-one-self question diagrammed centuries before psychology. India says the same "the other way round," from the one being splitting into "the millions of forms of Maya."

occurrences.title: Symmetrical flower drawings of the chakra patient (Zurich, ~1931)
occurrences.label: Symmetrical flower drawings of the chakra…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: To "ex-press" the bladder symptom, Jung set the patient the task of drawing whatever her hand suggested. "Symmetrical flowers took shape under her hand, vividly coloured and arranged in symbolic patterns. She made these pictures with great care and with a concentration I can only call devout" (¶553). Later understood as spontaneous renderings of the chakra lotuses — each centre "represented in the shape of a flower, with a circle in the middle" (¶560) — drawn by a woman with no conceivable knowledge of the system (¶559). A key case of collective symbolism emerging under active-imagination-like technique.

occurrences.title: Chaos-mandala frontispiece: metal fragments, flames and tears, the Happy Island, the tree
occurrences.label: Chaos-mandala frontispiece
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: in the center is one little magic circle which is the Happy Island... here the flame and the tear are held together exactly as in the Lamaistic mandala.
body: A medieval mandala Jung showed the seminar, from the frontispiece of a book containing "the secret psychology of the Cinquecento." At the bottom a pool holds irregular polygonal fragments of rock and ore bearing the planetary signs of metals (Saturn/lead, Venus, Mercury, moon, sun) — "constituents of the self." All is in wild turmoil: flames of passion and drops of water like tears of repentance. In the center one little magic circle — "the Happy Island, this is nirvana" — where flame and tear are held together; from the central tear a tube or root leads up past the flames into the tree above: "Thus the tree takes root." Jung stresses that no Eastern iconography of the tree-mandala is known to him: "a thoroughly Western idea," drawn with "no possibility of any direct influence from the East."

occurrences.title: Mosaic mandala of eight in the limestone jar — Temple of the Warrior, Chichen Itza
occurrences.label: Mosaic mandala of eight in the limestone jar
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: It was a mandala based on the principle of eight.
body: An American explorer broke through the outer wall of the pyramid and found an older, smaller temple within; knowing the custom of burying ritual treasure under the floor, he dug up a cylindrical limestone jar about a foot high. Inside, a wooden plate fixed with a mosaic: "a mandala based on the principle of eight, a circle inside of green and turquoise-blue fields... filled with reptile heads, lizard claws." Jung had read of the find in the Illustrated London News of 26 Jan 1929.

For Jung this is "the earliest [mandala] I know" — evidence that the figures are "naively produced by the unconscious and therefore you can find them all over the world." One of his own patients had made "a similar mandala with the same sort of divisions but filled in with plant designs, not animals."

occurrences.title: Mandala vision: the male child in the double gold ring (Zurich, 29 June 1932)
occurrences.label: Mandala vision — the male child…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)
jung.locator: Lecture 1 opening (pdf p53, fn3); Interpretation of Visions vol 6, 127-28

occurrences.quote: I saw two rings of gold upon the black ground. One ring was smaller and was encircled by the larger ring. Within the small ring lay a male child as though in the womb.
body: The bridge-vision with which Jung opened the Kundalini seminar: two gold rings on black ground, a male child lying as in the womb within the inner ring, surrounded by amniotic fluid; the dreamer cannot step over the outer rim. Jung's commentary: "Here the mandala psychology begins" — the moment the Visions Seminar's spontaneous imagery starts to run parallel to tantric cakra symbolism, and "the patient's attempts to unite with the child... is entering the mandala."

occurrences.title: Chinese yogi with ten Self-figures — picture from Wilhelm's Golden Flower
occurrences.label: Chinese yogi with ten Self-figures
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Spirit in Man, Art and Literature (CW15)

occurrences.quote: a Chinese picture, published by Richard Wilhelm,17 of a yogi in meditation, with five human figures growing out of the top of his head and five more figures growing out of the top of each of their heads.
body: A Chinese picture "of a yogi in meditation, with five human figures growing out of the top of his head and five more figures growing out of the top of each of their heads," published by Richard Wilhelm and kept in Jung's mind whenever he reads Ulysses (cw15 ¶189).

Jung's reading. The picture "portrays the spiritual state of the yogi who is about to rid himself of his ego and to pass over into the more complete, more objective state of the self" — the exact structure he attributes to Joyce's detached consciousness: Joyce's figures "talk and go about as in a collective dream... and yet the ego that embraces them all appears nowhere" (cw15 ¶188). It is the iconographic counterpart of the "moon-disk, at rest and alone," of satchit-ananda, "the ultimate goal of the Eastern way of redemption, the priceless pearl of Indian and Chinese wisdom" (cw15 ¶189).

occurrences.title: The Chönyid Bardo deities in their mandalas — Bardo Thödol
occurrences.label: The Chönyid Bardo deities in their mandalas
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Reading the Chönyid Bardo backwards, the karmic thought-forms emerge from chaos into order: companies of gods and goddesses "arranged according to the four directions and are distinguished by typical mystic colours" — the twenty-eight "power-holding" goddesses, the fifty-eight "blood-drinking" goddesses, and before them the all-destroying God of Death (cw11 ¶850).

Jung's reading: "all these deities are organized into mandalas, or circles, containing a cross of the four colours" — white (mirror-like wisdom), yellow (equality), red (discrimination), green (all-performing) (¶850). The ascent culminates in the Four Great Ones — "the green Amogha-Siddhi, the red Amitābha, the yellow RatnaSambhava, and the white Vajra-Sattva" — and the "effulgent blue light of the Dharmadhātu... from the heart of Vairochana" (¶852). This "takes us straight to the psychology of the lamaistic mandala" of the Golden Flower (¶851).

occurrences.title: Circle in a square — the epileptic prodrome and the raw material of mandalas (America, 1950s)
occurrences.label: Circle in a square
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Jung's late physiological crossover: "two American investigators succeeded in evoking an hallucinatory vision of coloured squares and circles by stimulating the occipital cortex. It was the case of an epileptic who, as a prodromal symptom of the attack, always had a vision of a circle in a square" (¶582; fn 6 = Penfield & Jasper, Epilepsy and the Functional Anatomy of the Human Brain, 1954, listed in the CW3 bibliography). "This imagery, probably related to the well-known Purkinje figures, suggests that we are dealing with the raw material from which mandala symbols originate" (¶582).
