occurrences.title: The grave of Sahafa and Māriyah — Marqūsh/Safanjā dialogue in Muhammad ibn Umail's Arabic commentary
occurrences.label: The grave of Sahafa and Māriyah
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Arabic text behind a long Mysterium footnote sequence: a dialogue between Marqūsh, king of Egypt, and Safanjā, king of Saīd, concerning "a house, which is called the grave (qabr) of Sahafa," where the woman Māriyah works the mystery (cw14 ch. II nn.205-219). Its imagery: the "reptile" whose Arabic name means witches "who consume the livers of children and drink the milk of black goats" (n.209); the goat's blood that feeds the shades as in the Nekyia (n.211); the egg-laying birds, the love-birds of Astarte (n.218); marble as the female substance that dissolves the sun (n.219).
Jung reads the dialogue as a Sol-Luna coniunctio text: the grave-house is the vas, Māriyah the feminine arcane substance — the Arabic root of the Latin king-queen allegories.

occurrences.title: The Marriage of the Lamb — Revelation 19:6-10
occurrences.label: The Marriage of the Lamb — Revelation 19:6-10
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: for the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready.
body: Jung quotes the Apocalyptic marriage of the Lamb in full: "for the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready... Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb." Union with the feminine personification of the unconscious "is a well-nigh eschatological experience, a reflection of which is to be found in the Apocalyptic Marriage of the Lamb, the Christian form of the hierosgamos" (¶225).

The angel who refuses John's worship — "I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren" — is read through Paracelsus: "in the language of Paracelsus, he is the homo maior, Adech.... Adech is not my self, he is also that of my brothers" (¶226). The participants' virginity (Rev 14:4) parallels "the year Aniadin," when the One Man reigns for ever (¶227, ¶235).

occurrences.title: Martian-invasion radio panic — H. G. Wells broadcast, USA
occurrences.label: Martian-invasion radio panic
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1938 (inferred from 'just before the second World War')
occurrences.quote: The play evidently hit the latent emotion connected with the imminence of war.
body: "a radio play, based on a novel by H. G. Wells, about Martians invading New York, caused a regular stampede and numerous car accidents." Jung links it into the genealogy of the saucer rumour: "The play evidently hit the latent emotion connected with the imminence of war" (¶599) — the same emotional foundation of collective distress on which the later visionary rumour runs (¶608).

occurrences.title: Barrie's Mary Rose: the island that wants to be visited
occurrences.label: Barrie's Mary Rose
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: those nice maidens who seem to be always ready in the unconscious to entice lonely wanderers or children.
body: Barrie's play in the amplification of the dancing maidens: "that most suggestive play by Barrie, Mary Rose, about the 'Island that wants to be visited,' where the child hears the voices of the elves who want to play with him, the Green Folk, presumably those nice maidens who seem to be always ready in the unconscious to entice lonely wanderers or children". Like Peter Pan, the title character "exists off and on in a world where there is no growing old and dying" (footnote).

A literary parallel to Nietzsche's ring of maidens and Jung's boy with the airship-maidens: the lure of the unconscious island that claims its visitor — also the geography of the grave-island two chapters later.

occurrences.title: Masked dancers — griffin, lion and wild man landing on a raft (Basel, 13 January)
occurrences.label: Masked dancers — griffin, lion…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: annual custom, pre-modern origin (Jung's childhood memory)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: "In my native town Basel, every year on January 13th, three masked dancers, a griffin, a lion, and a wild man, come down the Rhine on a raft; they land and dance around the town, and no one knows why. It is an amazing thing in a modern town" (p357).

Jung's exhibit for symbols preceding mind: "These things originate before mind and consciousness. In the beginning there was action, and only afterwards did people invent opinions about them, or a dogma, an explanation for what they were doing" — set beside the unexplainable Christmas tree and the Elgonyi sunrise offering. The wild man (Wilder Mann) belongs to the Basel carnival complex; the trio figures the animal-masked ancestors still walking the city.

occurrences.title: The Roman Mass — Canon and transformation rite
occurrences.label: The Roman Mass — Canon and transformation rite
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Rome (rite celebrated throughout the Latin Church)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)
Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: The Mass thus contains, as its essential core, the mystery and miracle of God's transformation taking place in the human sphere, his becoming Man, and his return to his absolute existence in and for himself.
body: The Latin rite Jung dissects step by step: oblation of bread, preparation and elevation of the chalice, censing, epiclesis, consecration, greater elevation, fractio, consignatio, commixtio. Two ideas blend — deipnon (sacred meal) and thysia (sacrifice) — around the mysterium fidei, the transubstantiation "vere, realiter, substantialiter" (¶302–307). The sequence condenses the whole life of Christ, from Benedictus qui venit to resurrection hinted in the commixtio (¶336).

Jung's reading: Christ is simultaneously sacrificer and sacrificed; the words of consecration are the sword (Lessius) that consummates the thysia; the priest is only causa ministerialis of an act of grace (¶323–324). The two substances — masculine wine, feminine bread — signify "the androgynous nature of the mystical Christ" (¶337). Psychologically the Mass "tries to effect a participation mystique... of priest and congregation with Christ" and is "the rite of the individuation process" (¶413–414).

occurrences.title: Materialization photographed with medium Florence Cook (London, 1873)
occurrences.label: Materialization photographed…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In 1873 the physicist William Crookes and the Royal Society member Varley, in Crookes's London laboratory, produced with the medium Florence Cook a spirit manifestation and repeatedly photographed it under electric light together with the medium — the founding case of instrumented psychical research (Crookes's "classical report" to the Royal Society, ¶108).

The 21-year-old medical student cites it as prime evidence for the "intelligent organizational activity of the soul" (¶116–117): every sense-perceptible representation of the soul is a materialization, and man himself is "the most wondrous and incredible materialization which has ever occurred" (¶116).

Verbatim: "In 1873 Crookes and Varley, a member of the Royal Society, succeeded, with the aid of the medium Florence Cook, in producing a manifestation in their London laboratory and in repeatedly photographing it, under electric light, together with the medium."

occurrences.title: Paraffin molds of materialized hands — William Denton (New Guinea, 1875)
occurrences.label: Paraffin molds of materialized hands
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: New Guinea (per Jung's text; historically doubtful)
body: The first paraffin molds "of hands that spontaneously materialized in space" (1875), attributed by Jung to William Denton, geology professor at Wellesley College, Massachusetts († 1883), "while he was on a geological expedition in New Guinea." The New Guinea setting is Jung's own (or his source's) and sits oddly with the standard history of the Dentons' American experiments — flag for verification.

Jung cites the molds as repeatable, contoured evidence of the soul's formative intelligence: "Since that time these experiments have been repeated, with great success, in England and on the continent" (¶118), and volunteers: "I myself have in my possession photographs of such phenomena, and anyone who would like to see them may do so at any time" (p66).

Verbatim: "In 1875, for the first time, paraffin molds were taken of hands that spontaneously materialized in space. This feat was achieved by William Denton, a geology professor at Wellesley College in Massachusetts (t 1883)" [=(† 1883), OCR].

occurrences.title: Materialized hand photographed above the medium (St. Petersburg, ~1875)
occurrences.label: Materialized hand photographed above the medium
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The zoology professor Wagner (Jung's Russian spiritualist authority, ¶108) succeeded — "after countless failures" and with the assistance of Frau von Pribitkov — in photographing a hand floating above the medium's head in a room at the University of St. Petersburg. The classic "third hand" photograph of the Aksakov circle.

Jung uses it, with the Crookes photographs, to document the soul's organizational power: the materialized hand is the soul's "power of organization... manifested in the phenomenon of materialization" (¶116–117). Its isolation of the hand makes visible what Jung generalizes: the soul assuming spatial, i.e. material, form (¶117).

Verbatim: "After countless failures Professor Wagner, with the assistance of Frau von Pribitkov, succeeded in photographing a hand above the medium's head in a room at the University of St. Petersburg."

occurrences.title: Hand- and footprints with medium 'Dr. Stack' [Slade] (Leipzig, 1877–1879)
occurrences.label: Hand- and footprints with medium 'Dr. Stack'…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Zöllner (astrophysicist), Wilhelm Weber (physicist) and Fechner (psychophysicist) conducted joint experiments, 1877–1879, with the medium Jung's text calls "Dr. Stack" — the American medium Henry Slade, Zöllner's celebrated Leipzig subject. They produced "a series of handprints and footprints on soot-blackened paper laid between two pieces of slate": material imprints with no bodily agent.

Jung reads the prints as the soul's intelligent organizing activity again — form appearing where no body is (¶116–118) — and recommends Zöllner's Abhandlungen and Aksakov's Animismus und Spiritismus as follow-up reading (¶118). The case is also the martyrdom emblem of his roll-call: Zöllner died 1882 "broken in body and spirit" (¶109, p62).

Verbatim: "Zollner, Wilhelm Weber, and Fechner, who from 1877-1879 conducted joint experiments with the medium Dr. Stack, did not take any photographs, but did obtain a series of handprints and footprints on soot-blackened paper laid between two pieces of slate."

occurrences.title: Queen Maya's delivery beneath the sala tree — Buddha's birth
occurrences.label: Queen Maya's delivery beneath the sala tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "The conscious tree bent down its boughs to make / A bower about Queen Maya's majesty"; the rock gives forth a stream for the bath, and she brings forth her child.

Jung's reading: the embracing-entwining motif — tree as birth-giving mother (¶362, pl. XXXIX); the same motif in Sleeping Beauty, the sun-hero freed from a creeping plant, Ra's barge entwined by the nocturnal serpent.
Verbatim: And, knowing the time come—for all things knew— The conscious tree bent down its boughs to make A bower about Queen Maya’s majesty (cw05 ¶362).

image.title: Birth of Siddhartha Sakyamuni with Queen Maya as a Shalabhanjika circa 2nd century CE, Gandhara School of Art, Lahore Museum, Pakistan

occurrences.title: Maya, weaver, encircled by the Uroboros — Brahminic vignette
occurrences.label: Maya, weaver, encircled by the Uroboros
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the centre is (in other cases) often pictured as a spider in its web
body: Plate 108: "Maya, eternal weaver of the illusory world of the senses, encircled by the Uroboros.—Damaged vignette from a collection of Brahminic sayings."

Jung cites it for the image of the centre "often pictured as a spider in its web, especially when the conscious attitude is still dominated by fear of unconscious processes" (¶325) — Maya weaving the world at the centre of the encircling serpent, the self's creativity seen from the frightened ego's side as illusion and trap.

occurrences.title: Mayan ritual tree with serpent — Dresden Codex
occurrences.label: Mayan ritual tree with serpent — Dresden Codex
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 190. Mayan ritual tree with serpent.—Dresden Codex
body: Page of the Maya Dresden Codex showing the ritual tree with the serpent — the world-tree and snake in an American tradition wholly outside the Western alchemical line.

Jung prints it in the series of tree-pictures (coral tree, Hesperides tree with dragon, tree of the philosophers) that amplify the fructus arboris immortalis of the Visio Arislei: the food of life hanging on a tree guarded by a serpent. Its presence argues the complex is archetypal rather than transmitted.
