occurrences.title: Mechthild of Magdeburg — the bearded-less Lord and the birth on the rocky mountain
occurrences.label: Mechthild of Magdeburg
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The soul remarks that when the Lord kissed her 'he had, contrary to expectation, no beard' — the tokens of masculinity lacking (¶320). In a vision Mechthild is transported to a 'rocky mountain' (allegory of the spiritualis habitus) where the Virgin awaits the birth of the divine child; she embraces and kisses it three times; the Son is 'the innermost core [medulla] of the Father's heart' (¶320). Jung: 'that sweetest thing' is the self, indistinguishable from the God-image; the daughter-bride has become a mother who bears the Father as Son — a new millennium speaking, where 'God is born from the soul' (¶321). Counterpart: interrogationes-mary-mountain-vision-2c.

occurrences.title: The medicine man torn asunder in the four directions of space
occurrences.label: The medicine man torn asunder…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: North America (per an American paper Jung read)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: A medicine man who has misused his powers, failed or neglected to do the right thing, is put to death by being torn asunder in the four directions of space, and the torn-out parts are left in the distance.
body: From an American newspaper article: execution of a failed medicine man by four-way dismemberment. Jung's comment fuses quaternity and individuation: 'a medicine man is made by the drawing together of the four into one, a process of individuation; therefore, when he is killed he will be torn asunder into those four directions.' Parallels: dismemberment-lord-of-death-chonyid-bardo-bardo-thodol · christ-crucified-by-virtues-besancon-13c.

occurrences.title: Polar Eskimo medicine man's vision of the land of food — migration over Baffin Bay ice
occurrences.label: Polar Eskimo medicine man's vision…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Baffin Bay / Polar Eskimos (Rasmussen, Neue Menschen)
occurrences.yearDisplay: as told to Rasmussen (publ. 1937); event older (inferred)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Jung's example of what the medicine man can be, from Knut Rasmussen's book on the Polar Eskimos: "a medicine man who, when his tribe suffered great hardship because of a lack of food, had a vision of a land offering food. He persuaded his tribe to go with him over the ice of Baffin Bay. They came to the shores of North America, where they found plenty of food. One half of the tribe turned back before that, and perished. The other half went with him, and was able to be saved by him".

"He had the inner certainty of a sleepwalker, with the help of which he led his people to the right place. This is what the medicine man can do. It need not always be cunning; the idea that will save the situation can also come from the heart." Context: the archetypal pair of chief (power) and medicine man (ruse).

occurrences.title: Swazi medicine murder of the chief's half-brother — van der Post's 1951 report
occurrences.label: Swazi medicine murder of the chief's…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: All are agreed that at the end of nine months this fat, normal, healthy boy was like an animal and quite white-skinned.
body: A Bantu tribe related to the Swazi, needing "the strongest medicine of all" to strengthen a weak young chief, chose the chief's twelve-year-old half-brother. A sorcerer blew powder into the boy's ears and nostrils; he was tied in a river bed for nine months, kept from all food but earth and roots, repeatedly caged in the stream "so that the water should flow over him and make his skin white." Witnesses: "His eyes were white and the whole of his body was white as white paper." He was then killed; the witch doctor cooked the nose, ears and lips over a fire and the twelve participants inhaled the steam; the body was kneaded into a bread for doctoring the tribe's crops.

Jung's reading: not a head-mystery but sharing its features — maceration, transformation by long immersion, a rebirth after nine months' incubation in water; the whitening (van der Post: assimilating the white man's mana) parallels white-clay transformation into ancestral spirits (¶371).

occurrences.title: 'Meditation': an internal talk with an invisible other — Ruland
occurrences.label: Meditation' — Ruland
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The name of an Internal Talk of one person with another who is invisible.
body: Ruland's definition: "Meditation: The name of an Internal Talk of one person with another who is invisible, as in the invocation of the Deity, or communion with one's self, or with one's good angel."

Jung at cw14 ¶707: "What I call coming to terms with the unconscious the alchemists called 'meditation'" — though the somewhat optimistic definition must be qualified by the adept's relations with his spiritus familiaris, since "Mercurius is a rather unreliable companion, as the testimony of the alchemists agrees."

occurrences.title: Trance personalities of Helene Preiswerk — the Basel medium (1896)
occurrences.label: Trance personalities of Helene Preiswerk
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

jung.locator: 'On the Psychology and Pathology of So-called Occult Phenomena'

occurrences.quote: During the trance several personalities would manifest themselves; and, little by little, I found I could call up by suggestion one personality or another.
body: Jung's first case, told to the 1925 seminar as "the impetus for my future life": his fifteen-and-a-half-year-old cousin, a somnambulist medium in whom trance personalities could be summoned by suggestion. Her seances ran from ~1896 until the medium "ran out" and began to cheat. Out of them Jung took the personification tendency of the unconscious, the mediatory symbol (the "older woman of great spiritual beauty" she became in trance), and the law that advance often requires a seemingly ruinous mistake — her cheating forced her back into reality; she became a successful dressmaker in Paris, regressed to two years old before her death (~1910s). Jung names her case an illustration of enantiodromia.

The unconscious hierarchy (grandfather → Goethe → "the important personality") is the germ of the collective-unconscious idea. Parallels: anima-voice-art-dialogue-jung-1913 (the inner woman with "a deep cunning") · zarathustra-figure (the analogy Jung felt at 24).

occurrences.title: Melchior Cibinensis: the alchemical paraphrase of the Mass
occurrences.label: Melchior Cibinensis
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Buda, Hungarian court (Nicholas Melchior of Hermannstadt/Szebeny; addressed to King Ladislaus II)
occurrences.yearDisplay: early 16th c. (before 1516; author executed 1531; Maier's print 1617)
occurrences.quote: Behold a wondrous restoration and renewal of the Ethiopian! Because of the bath of rebirth he takes a new name, which the philosophers call the natural sulphur and their son.
body: The Hungarian alchemist Nicolaus Melchior (Szebeny/Cibinensis, of Hermannstadt), court astrologer to King Ladislaus II (1471-1516), sent the king a chemical process "in the form of a Mass" (Addam et processum sub forma missae; printed in Maier's Symbola aureae mensae, 1617, and Theatrum Chemicum III, 1659, pp. 758ff): Introitus ("Fundamentum vero artis est corporum solutio"), a Kyrie to the "blessed stone of the art of the science … for the extirpation of the Turk," the Graduale's south wind, an Ave Praeclara to the Virgin, and the paraphrase of the hymn: the lamp of heaven united with the moon, the band of Mars, the conjunction of Mercury; from the three, in mercurial water, "the strong giant whom a thousand times a thousand seek"; the mighty Ethiopian dead in the vessel, then raised by the bath of rebirth and renamed the philosophers' son — the stone. The author was condemned to death under Ferdinand I and executed in Prague, May 2, 1531.

Jung (cw12 ¶480, ¶484): the Consecration is conspicuously missing — "a conflict of conscience," the rite acting from without set against the individual experience acting from within; yet "the alchemical process [is] the equivalent of the transubstantiation in the Mass." Jung (cw13) cites it twice more: as proof that the opus alchymicum "was always understood as a kind of rite after the manner of an opus divinum" (¶158), and as the "bold attempt" showing how far the nature-mystery of alchemy was at odds with the Church "despite the superficial analogies" (¶195). The Mass-form presupposes the long-standing equation of the filius / lapis philosophorum with Christ: "If the opus alchymicum claimed equality with the opus divinum of the Mass, the reason... was not grotesque presumption but the fact that a vast, unknown Nature... was imperiously demanding recognition" (¶196).

occurrences.title: Melchisedec's offering of bread and wine
occurrences.label: Melchisedec's offering of bread and wine
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Genesis 14 (~6th–5th c. BCE text); liturgical use from antiquity

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)
Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: The manifestation of an order outside time involves the idea of a miracle which takes place 'vere, realiter, substantialiter' at the moment of transubstantiation.
body: After Abraham's victory, Melchisedec ("teacher of righteousness"), king of Salem and "priest of the most high God" El 'Elyon, meets Abraham with bread and wine and blesses him; Abraham pays him a tenth of all. Hebrews 7 declares him "without father, without mother, without descent, having neither beginning of days, nor end of life, but made like unto the Son of God" — a pre-Christian incarnation of the Logos grounding the eternal priesthood "after the order of Melchisedec."

Jung's reading: in the Canon's Supra quae the Old Testament prefigurations form a crescendo — Abel (son, animal), Abraham (tribal father, only son), Melchisedec (symbolical bread and wine, self-offering). "Melchisedec's offering is thus a prefiguration of Christ's sacrifice of himself" (¶328).

occurrences.title: The melon as holy food — Manichaean communion
occurrences.label: The melon as holy food — Manichaean communion
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: In the Manichaean mysteries the communion table "was laden with gorgeous fruits, especially the melon, which was the sacrificial fruit because it demanded the sun in order to ripen and therefore contained the most particles of light." Eating it assimilates light: "when man ate the melon, he was likely to assimilate an enormous amount of light, and then the black substance, the devil, was overgrown." Jung sets it beside the Christian insistence on intoxicating wine — both communions handling the same death-conquering, light-bearing substance under a taboo frame.

occurrences.title: Melothesia figure — Hildegard of Bingen, Liber Divinorum Operum (Lucca codex)
occurrences.label: Melothesia figure — Hildegard…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: It is always a naked figure because it shows man as he is without any veils, the true man.
body: The melothesia of the Middle Ages — "a certain position of the limbs" — as Jung knows it from the famous Lucca manuscript of Hildegard von Bingen (Liber Divinorum Operum; English treatment by Charles Singer). The naked human figure, often five-rayed as "the star of man, the pentagram," is ringed by the phases of the zodiac or of the moon: "the microcosm within the macrocosm," man placed among the elementary powers.

Jung's use: mandala figures put a naked figure in the center "because you are there exactly what you are," while the patient still wears garments — veils of illusion, the subtlest persona, "the convictions one has about oneself." Hildegard's cosmic man is the counter-image: the true man without any veils.

occurrences.title: The anima as Melusina embracing the man from the sea — Ripley Scrowle variant
occurrences.label: The anima as Melusina embracing the man…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The anima as Melusina, embracing a man rising out of the sea (= unconscious): a coniunctio animae cum corpore.
body: Plate B5 of CW13, from a variant of the Ripley Scrowle: "The anima as Melusina, embracing a man rising out of the sea (= unconscious): a coniunctio animae cum corpore. The gnomes are the planetary spirits in the form of paredroi (familiars)."

Jung's reading: Melusina belongs to the Aquaster, the watery realm of the "Nymphidida"; she is "clearly an anima figure" and a variant of the mercurial serpent (¶181). The picture states pictorially what ¶223 formulates: union with the feminine personification of the unconscious as "a well-nigh eschatological experience." Mercurius in the form of Lilith or Melusina also appears in the tree of the Ripley Scrowle (¶247 n.1).

occurrences.title: Melusina's transmutation — final chapter of De vita longa
occurrences.label: Melusina's transmutation
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: And in this manner, through the intervention of the Scaiolae, Melosine departs from her nymphididic nature, to remain in another transmutation if that difficult Adech permit, who rules over both the death and life of the Scaiolae.
body: The deliberately obscure closing chapter of Paracelsus's treatise on longevity, given by Jung in the original Latin with his English translation, followed by Gerard Dorn's commentary of 1583. Through the "intervening" Scaiolae (the four spiritual powers of the homo maximus), Melusina departs from her "nymphididic nature" into another transmutation — if "that difficult Adech" (the inner man, ruler of the death and life of the Scaiolae) permits. The adept then takes the "characters of Venus" to attain the "year Aniadin" of immortality.

Jung reads the whole chapter as a coded account of the ego's problematic relation to the self (¶214, ¶221) and of the anima's assimilation: the "gesta Melusinae" are a "veritable veil of Maya" from which the "supermonic" elements must be distilled (¶221).

occurrences.title: 'Desinit in piscem mulier formosa superne' — the woman who ends in a fish (Horace)
occurrences.label: Desinit in piscem mulier formosa superne
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "there is a Latin verse about it, not exactly a snake in this case but another cold blooded animal, a fish: Desinit in piscem mulier formosa superne, which means that the woman who is beautiful above ends with a fish's tail."

Jung's anima-formula: "the anima is a semihuman function on one side; through her head she denotes that she has connection with human consciousness, but below she extends into the spinal cord and into the body" — woman above, serpent (or fish) below, as the Paradise serpent is drawn with a woman's head.

occurrences.title: Melusina with the snake's tail — Drivaltigkeitsbuch, Codex Germanicus Monacensis 598
occurrences.label: Melusina with the snake's tail
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung identifies the picture prototype of the Melusina-like figure in the Ripley Scrowle roll as this 15th-century German manuscript, the Drivaltigkeitsbuch (Codex Germanicus Monacensis 598, fol. 2r): "There she has a proper snake's tail". A 16th-century variant stands in the Codex Germanicus Alchemicus Vadensis; the printed Scrowle version (1588) softens the tail into an odd trailing form — water? steam?
The picture fixes the alchemical Melusina as serpent-woman composite, matter's feminine half turning serpentine — the same roll family Jung analysed in Psychology and Alchemy.

occurrences.title: Melusina dwelling in the blood as anima vegetativa — Paracelsus, Paragranum
occurrences.label: Melusina dwelling in the blood…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Spirit in Man, Art and Literature (CW15)

occurrences.quote: According to him, Melusines dwell in the blood, and, since blood is the ancient seat of the soul, we may conjecture that Melusina is a kind of anima vegetativa.
body: In the Paragranum's great catalogue of the physician's knowledge — "what Melosina is, and what Syrena, what permutatio, transplantatio and transmutatio are" (cw15 ¶24) — Paracelsus makes the water-sprite an arcanum of bodily process.

Jung's reading. In the 1942 Zurich lecture he takes the locus into depth-psychology: "Melusina is a magical creature belonging half to folklore and half to the alchemical doctrine of Paracelsus, as her connection with the permutatio and transmutatio shows."

She is "in essence, a variant of the mercurial spirit, which in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries was depicted as a female monster" — Jung declines to go further, "as it would lead us into the depths of alchemical speculation."

occurrences.title: Melusina, ancestress of the counts of Lusignan
occurrences.label: Melusina, ancestress of the counts of Lusignan
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: When her husband once surprised her in her fish-tail, which she had to wear only on Saturdays, her secret was out and she was forced to disappear again into the watery realm.
body: The water-nymph with the fish- or snake-tail, forced to disappear into the watery realm when her husband surprised her secret (the tail she wore only on Saturdays); she reappears only as a presage of disaster. In the Raymond-of-Poitiers episode she appears to a man whose whole life-form has collapsed — the classic situation, Jung says, in which "the harbinger of fate, the anima, an archetype of the collective unconscious, appears" (¶217).

Jung's reading: Melusina is "clearly an anima figure," a variant of the mercurial serpent sometimes shown as a snake-woman; her birthplace "is the womb of the mysteries, obviously what we today would call the unconscious" (¶180). She dwells in the blood, has no genitals (paradisal being), and was seduced by Beelzebub into witchcraft.

image.title: Jean d'Arras - Histoire de la belle Mélusine - Dutch version - 1491 - Illustration page 12

occurrences.title: Melusina with the lance of Longinus — Pandora woodcut
occurrences.label: Melusina with the lance of Longinus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Melusina as the aqua permanens, opening the side of the {tlius (an allegory of Christ) with the lance of Longinus.
body: Plate B4 of CW13: Melusina as the aqua permanens opening the side of the filius (an allegory of Christ) with the lance of Longinus; Eve (earth) in the middle is reunited with Adam (Christ) in the coniunctio, and from their union is born the hermaphrodite, "the incarnate Primordial Man." To the right the athanor with the vessel in the centre from which the lapis will arise; the vessels on either side contain Sol and Luna.

Jung's reading (¶181): the snake-woman form expresses "the monstrous, double nature of Mercurius," and "the redemption of this monstrosity was depicted as the assumption and coronation of the Virgin Mary." His posthumous note on Pandora (¶181 n.52) values its eighteen symbolic pictures, one of them the Echidna symbol of Mercurius.

occurrences.title: Melusina in Paracelsus's De vita longa (fig. B5)
occurrences.label: Melusina in Paracelsus's De vita longa (fig. B5)
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: Paracelsus as a Spiritual Phenomenon — ¶ pin tbd (print 138–183)

body: In Paracelsus's treatise on longevity the water-spirit Melusina appears "in the mind" as an animating figure of the Aquaster region; Jung's commentary (1942) makes her the central exhibit of the Paracelsan anima: "Melusina as anima, fig. B5, 144", "vision appearing in mind, 144, 174", "psychic reality of, 176", "transformation of, 179", "as tree-numen, 315". Illustration CW13 fig. B5.

Verbatim: Melusina, 138, 142/f, 145, fig. B5, 163, 173-80, 182, 183, 199, 240, 303, 315, 317, 321; as anima, fig. B5, 144; Isis has form of, 318; psychic reality of, 176 — Isis has form of Melusina (318); counts of Lusignan (143); the Melusinian Ares (138, 142).

occurrences.title: Men-an-Tol: the rebirth hole of Cornwall
occurrences.label: Men-an-Tol: the rebirth hole of Cornwall
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Near Penzance / Madron, Cornwall (Men-an-Tol, also Menetol)
occurrences.yearDisplay: prehistoric holed stone; ritual use into modern times

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: I myself went through the hole.
body: "There was a prehistoric clinic in Cornwall, the Menanthole, a huge slab of stone with a hole through which the fathers pulled their children, and sick people were supposed to be cured in that way. I myself went through the hole." Jung adduces it to unpack the everyday metaphor of treatment — Latin trahere, to pull: "the doctor is pulling you through the hole of rebirth... 'The doctor pulled me through.'"

The German nineteenth-century parallel (a hole made in the wall behind the sick man's bed, pulling him out into the garden for rebirth) extends the family: cure as passage through the hole of rebirth — frontier-crossing in stone.

occurrences.title: Rubbing stones for cattle erected ceremonially — the menhirs of Cornwall
occurrences.label: Rubbing stones for cattle erected ceremonially
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Dr. Baynes: "In England they used to erect the rubbing stones in a ceremonial way for the cattle to rub against. There are any amount in Cornwall." Jung: "Exactly. Those menhirs were no doubt for that purpose and for nothing else." The passage roots the yantra-meditation in animal rubbing (the cow against the tree, butter on the lingam): worship as the transformation of an instinctual movement into rite — the churinga chain of the same lecture.

occurrences.title: Mephistopheles: 'Scorn reason and science'
occurrences.label: Mephistopheles: Scorn reason and science
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Weimar (Goethe, Faust II.ii; tr. Alice Raphael 1932)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: Scorn reason and science if you can, The highest powers yet bestowed on man!
body: Mephistopheles in Faust's robe, advising the student. Jung quotes the devil in order to refuse him: 'Science is the highest power of man, for we can do just what we can do' — the subtle body is a transcendental concept, and overstepping competence into it is the devil's ground. Parallels: homunculus-faust-retort-flight-weimar-1832 · mothers-of-faust.

occurrences.title: The Boy Charioteer (Mercurius juvenis) — Faust II fire magic
occurrences.label: The Boy Charioteer — Faust II fire magic
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The Boy Charioteer, a Mercurius juvenis, on the one hand hermaphrodite like his preform, the Devil, a kyllenios, and on the other an analogy to Christ and the Holy Spirit.
body: Second renewal-form of Mercurius in Goethe's drama: "In the fire magic and the gold swindle there appears the Boy Charioteer, a Mercurius juvenis, on the one hand hermaphrodite like his preform, the Devil, a kyllenios, and on the other an analogy to Christ and the Holy Spirit; at the same time he brings the wild host (Wotan!)" (¶1696). "The Homunculus corresponds to the Boy Charioteer. His father is Wagner (Rosencreutz); his cousin is the Devil, hence Mercurius in a younger shape" (¶1698).

Jung's reading: Goethe's Mercury-chain — Mephistopheles-poodle (filius canis) → Boy Charioteer → Homunculus → Euphorion, "the third renewal form of Mercurius" (¶1698) — with the 3+1 of the axiom of Maria "pervading the whole work" (¶1695). The wild host marks the Wotan-Mercurius chthonic underside (¶1693).

occurrences.title: Spiritus Mercurialis as monstrous dragon-quaternion — German alchemical ms. c. 1600
occurrences.label: Spiritus Mercurialis as monstrous…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Germany (Mellon Collection, now Yale University Library)
body: The CW13 frontispiece: the spiritus mercurialis and his transformations as a monstrous dragon, "a quaternity, in which the fourth is at the same time the unity of the three, the unity being symbolized by the mystagogue Hermes. The three (above) are (left to right): Luna, Sol, and coniunctio Solis et Lunae in Taurus, the House of Venus. Together they form ~ = Mercurius." The editors note it replaces an almost identical woodcut from Nazari, Della tramutatione metallica sogni tre (Brescia, 1599) which Jung had published in Paracelsica (1942); the ms. replica was found in the Mellon Collection.
Hermes as mystagogue uniting the three: the dragon as the many-in-one body of Mercurius — the same mercurial monster Jung analyzes in "The Spirit Mercurius" (¶191ff).

occurrences.title: 'I am the poison-dripping dragon' — the Aurelia occulta monologue
occurrences.label: I am the poison-dripping dragon
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: I am the egg of nature, known only to the wise, who in piety and modesty bring forth from me the microcosm
body: The most complete self-description of Mercurius in the literature, quoted entire by Jung: "I am the poison-dripping dragon, who is everywhere and can be cheaply had... My water and fire destroy and put together; from my body you may extract the green lion and the red... I am the egg of nature... By the philosophers I am named Mercurius; my spouse is the [philosophic] gold; I am the old dragon, found everywhere on the globe of the earth, father and mother, young and old, very strong and very weak, death and resurrection, visible and invisible, hard and soft... I contain the light of nature; I am dark and light... I am the carbuncle of the sun."
Jung uses it as exhibit A for Mercurius's antinomian dual nature (¶266-267), for the egg of nature (¶268), and for the whole six-point summary (¶285).

occurrences.title: Mercurius as Mephistopheles the poodle — Faust I (1808)
occurrences.label: Mercurius as Mephistopheles the poodle — Faust I
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Mercurius enters in the shape of Mephistopheles (Devil and Satan), as a dog to begin with, son of Chaos, and fire (alch. filius canis, arises out of chaos, natura ignea).
body: Faust is "introduced like Job", and the dark companion enters in the alchemical dog-shape: "Mercurius enters in the shape of Mephistopheles (Devil and Satan), as a dog to begin with, son of Chaos, and fire (alch. filius canis, arises out of chaos, natura ignea). He becomes the servant of Faust (familiaris, servus fugitivus)" (¶1694). He has "two ravens (cf. Wotan)", is "the 'northern phantom'"; unlike Faust, "the Devil knows who he himself is; he does not lie to himself, he has humour and the small kind of love (insects)" (¶1699).

Jung's reading: the central figure of transformation — "a chthonic spirit, related to Wotan and the Devil" (¶1693) — wears the poodle's skin as filius canis; through him comes the anima projection with its tragic end, and the Walpurgisnacht is "overpowering by the shadow" (¶1696).

occurrences.title: Fourfold Hermes of the four quarters — invocation of Astrampsychos (PGM)
occurrences.label: Fourfold Hermes of the four quarters
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the love-magic of Astrampsychos the invocation to Hermes catalogues the god's four forms at the four corners of heaven: ibis (East), dog-headed baboon (West), serpent (North), wolf (South); his plant is the grape (elsewhere the olive), his wood ebony (cw13 ¶359).

Jung uses it to show the fourfold Mercurius: "The fourfold Mercurius is also the tree or its spiritus vegetativus" (cw13 ¶360), the four forms derived from the four sons of Horus (see osiris-four-sons-horus-lotus). A sibling locus holds the same prayer's identity-formula "I am thou and thou art I" (hermes-astrampsychos-prayer-egypt-hellenistic, cw9i ¶238n31).

Verbatim: in the East you have the form of an ibis, in the West you have the form of a dog-headed baboon, in the North you have the form of a serpent, but in the South you have the form of a wolf. (cw13 ¶359)

occurrences.title: Elijah as 'Helyas Artista' — Dorn, Theatrum chemicum (1602)
occurrences.label: Elijah as 'Helyas Artista'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Frankfurt (Theatr. chem. print); text-phrase via Paracelsus, 'De tinctura physicorum'
occurrences.quote: Elijah should become 'Helyas Artista' in medieval alchemy (e.g., Dorn... 1602: 'usque in adventum Heliae Artistae quo tempore nihil tam occultum quod non revelabitur').
body: The alchemical assimilation of the prophet: Elijah becomes "Helyas Artista" in medieval alchemy — the coming artist-revealer before whom "nihil tam occultum quod non revelabitur". Dorn, "De transmutatione metallorum," Theatrum chemicum, 1602, I, p. 610: "usque in adventum Heliae Artistae quo tempore nihil tam occultum quod non revelabitur" — a passage, Jung notes, originating in Paracelsus' "De tinctura physicorum"; echoed in Helvetius, Vitulus aureus (1667), and Glauber, De Elia Artista (1668) (¶1528).

Jung's reading: one terminus of the assimilation chain running Baal–Astarte → YHWH → Gospel → Kabbala → Islam → alchemy: the prophet fused with Idrīs/Hermes/Mercurius (¶1527) emerges as the Deus absconditus of the opus, "the same compensating function as the figure of Elijah" (¶1531) — the archetype "gets itself chosen" where consciousness lacks the immediate relation with God.

occurrences.title: 'Hermes omnia solus et ter unus' — the hermetic confession formula (Greco-Egyptian, ~2nd–3rd c.?)
occurrences.label: Hermes omnia solus et ter unus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: (Cf. the Trinity and the two mystic formulae of confession: 'Isis una quae es omnia,' 'Hermes omnia solus et ter unus.')
body: The second of the two "mystic formulae of confession" Jung cites for the multiplication of personality: Hermes omnia solus et ter unus — "Hermes, all things alone and thrice one." The thrice-one god is the one who is also the many: an ancient witness to the same logic Jung has just extracted from the schoolgirls' rumour — that significance expresses itself by duplication and multiplication — and, in the vault's longer arc, an early appearance of the figure who will become mercurius, "sol et luna" compressed into a single thrice-named god. Cited in the same breath as "Isis una quae es omnia" and the Trinity.

occurrences.title: Humidum radicale as serpens mercurialis / dragon's blood — Clavis sapientiae (attrib. Alfonso X)
occurrences.label: Humidum radicale as serpens mercurialis /…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Castile (attributed to Alfonso X's court; said to be a translation from the Arabic)
occurrences.quote: The humidum radicale is identical with the serpens mercurialis, the dragon, hence is also named “dragon’s blood.
body: In the Rosarium's second chapter, on the secret of the aqua nostra, Jung anchors the doctrine of the humidum radicale in the Clavis sapientiae attributed to Alfonso X of Castile ("sapo sapientum," 'soap of the wise,' a play on words): the radical moisture is identical with the serpens mercurialis, "the dragon," hence "dragon's blood." The body to be transformed must be dissolved in its own liquid, its "blood" — the tincture, elixir, lapis, all one with the aqua nostra.

Jung's reading (¶1788): the texts' apparent confusion dissolves once one sees that "the 'water' is either extracted by sublimation from a body... or the elixir already extracted is used for dissolving the body" — synonyms pinguedo, unctuositas, vapor unctuosus all name the same Agent.

occurrences.title: Quicksilver the self-impregnating serpent and Monocolus — Albertus Magnus
occurrences.label: Quicksilver the self-impregnating serpent…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: One is the stone, one the medicine, and therein lies the whole magistery.
body: On philosophical quicksilver: "It is the perennial water, the water of life, the virgin's milk, the fount... It is the serpent that rejoices in itself, impregnates itself, and gives birth in a single day, and slays all metals with its venom... As it is transmuted, so it transmutes." The quicksilver is like the "Monocalus," of "immense weight" and "fortissimae compositionis," indivisible — the cause of perfection.

Jung at cw14 ¶712-719: more than three hundred years before Dorn, the transcendental substance described by antinomies; the uroboros as "symbol of the union of opposites par excellence" that "symbolizes the goal of the process but not the beginning"; the "son of one day" = light (Genesis 1:5), lux moderna; the monocolus/uniped and the middle disposition (the cross) point to Mercurius quadratus, the quinta essentia = anima mundi.

occurrences.title: Mercurius bound to his mother's breast — Septem tractatus aurei (1566)
occurrences.label: Mercurius bound to his mother's breast
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Ego vinctus ulnis et pectori meae matris... et invisibile ex visibili compono.
body: The arcane substance speaks: "Ego vinctus ulnis et pectori meae matris et substantiae eius continere et quiescere meam substantiam facio, et invisibile ex visibili compono" — "Bound to the arms and breast of my mother, and of her substance, I make my substance to contain itself and rest, and I compose the invisible from the visible."

Jung opens the Dual Mother chapter with it: the subject of the sentence (Mercurius, the arcane substance) "can be interpreted as inner fantasy activity," while the original text's anagogic meaning "naturally has a much more comprehensive... meaning... while making use of the primordial image of relationship to the mother" (cf. Psychology and Alchemy, par. 141). The alchemical opus speaking the mother-bond as its engine.

occurrences.title: Nine eagles shooting arrows at Hermes Trismegistus — Senior's vision
occurrences.label: Nine eagles shooting arrows at Hermes…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: 'This image occurs again in Senior's vision of Hermes Trismegistus, at whom nine eagles shot their arrows. Mercurius is the archer who, chemically, dissolves the gold, and, morally, pierces the soul with the dart of passion' (cw14 ¶416). The vision parallels the Book of Krates, where Venus appears surrounded by Indians shooting arrows at him; as Kyllenios, Mercurius is Cupid, who also shoots arrows in the Chymical Wedding (¶416). The god of the stone appears in vision as the target-and-source of the piercing arrow — the dart of passion that both wounds and tinctures.

occurrences.title: Oil from the hearts of statues, called Mediator — Lully (ascribed), Codicillus
occurrences.label: Oil from the hearts of statues, called Mediator
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In Raymond Lully (Ramon Llull) there is 'an oil that is extracted from the heart of statues,' and moreover 'by the washing of water and the drying of fire' — 'an extremely paradoxical operation in which the oil evidently serves as a mediating and uniting agent' (cw14 ¶561). The oil is the tincture, gold and soul, the philosophers' unguent, the divine water called MEDIATOR. Jung sets it in the statue-cluster: Senior's water from the hearts of statues (Egyptian sarcophagi as portrait-statues), Maier's oracle-statue of Hermes, the Mercurius-statues with the god hidden inside (Pseudo-Dionysius), and the living statue of Mylius (¶559-567).

Verbatim: Et ideo per ablutionem aquae et desiccationem ignis semper extrahis oleum a corde statuarum. / Hoc oleum est tinctura, aurum et anima, ac philosophorum unguentum. / Illud oleum seu aqua divina... et vocatur Mediator.

occurrences.title: The Blond, the Cosmic-Ray Casket and the Eight Keys — Pauli dream (25.10.1946)
occurrences.label: The Blond, the Cosmic-Ray Casket…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: The figure has an extremely 'psychopompos' character and has a similar function to Mercury with the alchemists.
body: First dream in Pauli's postwar series introducing "The Blond": "Through the post I receive a casket. Inside it is apparatus for the experimental investigation of cosmic rays. Next to it is a tall, blond man" who commands: "You must force the water up higher than the houses in the city so that the city dwellers will believe you." In the box "a bunch of keys, 8 in all, arranged in a circle with the key-bits hanging down". The water and city allude to earlier dreams; behind the figure stands a rejected "Persian" student of the Institute of Technology — the one who contradicts "the prevailing scientific collective opinion."

Pauli: The Blond and the Persian "may be dual aspects of one and the same figure (they never appear together)" with "an extremely 'psychopompos' character... a similar function to Mercury with the alchemists", distinct from the wise old man only in age. Three days later the figure returns in the Inquisition-trial dream.

occurrences.title: 'That I may be reborn a king' — Mercurius transformation poem, Verus Hermes
occurrences.label: That I may be reborn a king
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: That I may be reborn a king.
body: The poem Jung quotes entire ("A rather deplorable but picturesque poem") in which Mercurius describes his own transformation: "A weakling babe, a greybeard old, / Surnamed the Dragon: me they hold / In darkest dungeon languishing / That I may be reborn a king... To a black crow am I akin... In deepest dust I lie alone, / O that the Three would make the One!... Hero of peace, come forth from me, / Whom the whole world would like to see!"

Jung: "Mercurius is describing his own transformation, which at the same time signifies the mystic transformation of the artifex; for not only Mercurius but also what happens to him is a projection of the collective unconscious... the projection of the individuation process" (¶277).

occurrences.title: The Mercurial spirit of the prima materia as a salamander in the fire
occurrences.label: The Mercurial spirit of the prima materia…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 138. The Mercurial spirit of the prima materia, in the shape of a salamander, frolicking in the fire.—Maier, Scrutinium chymicum (1687)
body: Emblem from Michael Maier's Scrutinium chymicum pictura XXI: the spirit of the prima materia as a salamander frolicking in the flames — fire as its element rather than its destroyer.

Jung sets it beside a French alchemist's vision of the Sacerdotes Aegyptiorum revealing "the Hermetic vessel, the salamander, the full moon and the rising sun" (¶391), and beside the hidden elemental fire of the hyle (¶433): the salamander shows the spirit dwelling IN the burning matter of the opus, not consumed by it.

image.title: Michael Maier Atalanta Fugiens Emblem 29

occurrences.title: Six planets united in the seventh, Mercury, as Uroboros — pseudo-Aquinas, De alchimia (Codex Vossianus 29)
occurrences.label: Six planets united in the seventh, Mercury…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Caption: "The six planets united in the seventh, Mercury, depicted as the Uroboros, and the red-and-white (hermaphroditic) double eagle.". The seven planetary gods gathered into Mercurius — the dream's "That is the seventh!" made pictorial.

Jung's commentary at ¶84: "In the alchemical hierarchy of gods Mercurius comes lowest as prima materia and highest as lapis philosophorum… His dual nature enables him to be not only the seventh but also the eighth."

occurrences.title: The Spirit in the Bottle — Grimm, KHM 99 ('Der Geist im Glas')
occurrences.label: The Spirit in the Bottle — Grimm, KHM 99
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Fairy tale: a spirit shut in a bottle under an oak (its roots wrapped around the flask) proves to be the dangerous, ambivalent Mercurius — a "spellbound spirit" whom the boy outwits rather than a wish-fulfilling genie. Jung makes it the opening exhibit of "The Spirit Mercurius" (1943/48), retelling it across print pp. 193–201 and returning to it at 239n and 258, where the motif "spellbound spirit, 198" anchors his argument that the alchemist's quicksilver-spirit is the same autonomous complex the tale knows.
Verbatim: bottle, spirit in (tale), 193, 194*2, 195, 197. i99> 2 0 a> 239/^ 258 — and the Grimm entry: "fairy tale of spirit in bottle, 193, 194n, 258."

occurrences.title: Mercurius allegorized as the stag — Manget, Bibliotheca Chemica, Tab. IX, fig. XIII
occurrences.label: Mercurius allegorized as the stag
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1702 (Bibliotheca Chemica Curiosa; Jung cites 'Manget, Bibl. chem., Tab. IX, fig. XIII')

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: The alchemical emblem in which Mercurius appears as the stag: "In alchemy, Mercurius is allegorized as the stag (Manget, Bibl. chem,, Tab. IX, fig. XIII, and elsewhere) because the stag can renew itself" (¶559 n. 9, ocr).

Jung places it as the third station of the stag-dossier: Christ-allegory (Honorius), Christophany (Saint-Graal), then Mercurius — the self-renewing, transforming substance. The same footnote also carries the Cyranides line on the stag's heart ("Les os du cuer du serf vault moult pour conforter Ie cuer humain", Delatte, p. 346) — the stag-heart as medicine.

occurrences.title: Quadriga Aminadab — Suger's window, Abbey of Saint-Denis
occurrences.label: Quadriga Aminadab — Suger's window, Abbey…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: A stained-glass medallion by Abbot Suger (Saint-Denis, ~1140-44): God the Father standing on a four-wheeled chariot, crucifix before him, the four evangelist emblems in the corners; inscription 'QUADRIGE AMINADAB' after Song of Songs 6:11 (cw14 ¶267). Jung reads it with Ezekiel's Merkabah and the Christian tetramorph: 'The four gospels form, as it were, a quaternary podium on which the Redeemer stands' (¶267). Alongside the Tractatus Aristotelis chariot and Puri it shows the quadriga as vehicle of divinity — the functions carrying the god-image.

occurrences.title: Serpent of Hermes in the four-wheeled chariot — Tractatus Aristotelis
occurrences.label: Serpent of Hermes in the four-wheeled chariot
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: A recipe in the Tractatus Aristotelis ad Alexandrum Magnum: 'Take the serpent, and place it in the chariot with four wheels... until it is immersed in the depths of the sea, and nothing more is visible but the blackest dead sea' (cw14 ¶260); the goal is the Red Sea, 'running without running, moving without motion' (¶260). Jung glosses: the Serpens Hermetis / Agathodaimon, 'the Nous that animates the cold part of nature — that is, the unconscious — is enclosed in the spherical vessel of diaphanous glass which... represents the world and the soul' (¶261). The four wheels are the four elements or functions; incubation (tapas) spins the mandala of the total personality (¶262). 'The "chariot of Aristotle" can be understood in this sense as a symbol of the self' (¶261).

occurrences.title: Zohar — Metatron, the central column of the Sephiroth
occurrences.label: Zohar — Metatron, the central column…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: In the Zohar the Messiah is the 'central column' of the Sephiroth system: 'The column of the centre is Metatron, whose name is like that of the Lord. It is created and constituted to be his image and likeness, and it includes all gradations from Above to Below and from Below to Above, and binds them together in the centre' (¶335). Jung cites it as the cabalistic counterpart of the Paracelsian Mumia and the Naassene Protanthropos — the Original Man as mediator-column running through all gradations of the self. Parallels: paracelsus-mumia-de-vita-longa-1562, naassene-hymn-polymorphous-attis-2c.

occurrences.title: The great Mexican image in the sky — river to blood, black mountains (Visions Seminar, 24 May 1933)
occurrences.label: The great Mexican image in the sky
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: From her raised standpoint: "Suddenly I beheld in the sky a great Mexican image... The river turned to blood, the houses vanished and great black mountains arose where the valley had been, and towered about me." Then a narrow path descends between black rocks, and she begins the descent with decision.

Jung: the old Mexicans, a gentle people, embodied their cruelty in their gods; the image's "exaggerated cruelty" now casts its shadow over the lovely valley. Appearing in the sky (the old ghost-world of breath beings) means the content has left the body: unrealized mythological images are performed in mimicry as neurotic or even physiological symptoms, and "the moment you are conscious of them, the neurosis disappears". Against Freud: making the incest fantasy conscious does not settle it.

occurrences.title: Meyrink's privy alchemy experiment — the 'peculiar juice' in the sealed pot
occurrences.label: Meyrink's privy alchemy experiment
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: For this purpose he had bought an old privy, had it emptied, and put the base, the 'peculiar juice,' into an alchemical pot.
body: In the discussion of the toilet as the place of the prima materia: Meyrink reports, in his translation of a tract attributed to Thomas Aquinas, an experiment of his own — he bought an old privy, had it emptied, put the base, the "peculiar juice," into an alchemical pot, coated it with clay and sealed it "hermetically" (well enough that the lid blew up under heating); a strange yellowish matter had formed. "The experiment still did not convince him that one couldn't make gold out of the sediment of a sterquilinium after all!"

Jung's point: the claim that the prima materia, "that earth of paradise, that primordial chaos, is hidden in the fecal matter" is a significant contribution to the psychology of the place — the thesaurus thesaurorum in the lowest.

occurrences.title: Michelspacher: the Mountain of the Adepts (Cabala, 1654)
occurrences.label: Michelspacher: the Mountain of the Adepts
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Augsburg (Stephan Michelspacher, Cabala, spec. ed. cited 1654)
occurrences.quote: the philosophers' stone lies buried in the earth and must be extracted and cleansed
body: Plate 93: "The Mountain of the Adepts. The temple of the wise ('House of the Gathering' or of 'Self-Collection'), lit by sun and moon, stands on the seven stages, surmounted by the phoenix. The temple is hidden in the mountain—a hint that the philosophers' stone lies buried in the earth and must be extracted and cleansed. The zodiac in the background symbolizes the duration of the opus, while the four elements indicate wholeness. In foreground, blindfolded man and the investigator who follows his natural instinct."
Jung pairs it with dream 54's "House of the Gathering": the square as "'gathering place'"; the temple hidden in the mountain is the centre buried in the natural man, reached only by the gathered.

occurrences.title: 'Heaven above, heaven below…' — the old mystic saying applied to love (New Paths appendix)
occurrences.label: Heaven above, heaven below…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Tabula Smaragdina family of sayings (attrib. ~1st–9th c.; Latin text known by medieval era)
occurrences.quote: Heaven above, heaven below, sky above, sky below, all above, all below, accept this and rejoice.
body: Footnote to the 'New Paths in Psychology' appendix (1912): "We may apply to love the old mystic saying: 'Heaven above, heaven below, sky above, sky below, all above, all below, accept this and rejoice.'" The same note adds: "Mephistopheles expresses the same idea when he speaks of the 'power that produces good whilst ever scheming evil.'"

Jung's reading: Eros is the within-below correspondence — the same above/below analogy that structures the Tabula Smaragdina's macrocosm-microcosm ("Quod est inferius est sicut quod est superius") here grounded in the feeling-life; and the Faustian unity of good and evil powers says the same thing morally. The editors' gloss: giving love cosmic rank in the 1912/1917 revaluation of sexuality-as-energy. Attribution of the wording to the Tabula Smaragdina family is our inference; Jung says only "the old mystic saying."

occurrences.title: Tabula Smaragdina — creation through adaptation, the world as image of God
occurrences.label: Tabula Smaragdina — creation…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 'a classical text of the time of Alexandria'; Arabic ~8th-9th c.

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: The story is that in the grave of Hermes the Thrice Greatest, a tablet of emerald was found, upon which a text was engraved saying that the world was created in the beginning through adaptation.
body: Jung's bridge from totemic creation-by-transformation to the Hermetic world-picture: the legend of the emerald tablet found in the grave of Hermes Trismegistus —
"Adaptation" means God shaped the world into his own image; a living image of the deity is the deity — "the face of the deity, the Angel of the Face. That is man". Hence:

Round because God is round; split only on Genesis' second day, the binarius God "never quite pleased him" — the same doubt that split Ormazd and Ahriman. Distinct passage from the ascent-descent reading: ascent-descent-tabula-smaragdina-arabic-latin-9c. Parallels: grandfather-cellar-youngest-son-russian-fairy-tale · anthropos-first-man-five-elements-armor-acta-archelai-340.

occurrences.title: Midrash: Adam fashioned from the shapeless mass in hourly stages
occurrences.label: Midrash — Adam fashioned…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: in the first hour God collected the dust, in the second made a shapeless mass out of it, in the third fashioned the limbs
body: "According to a midrashic view, Adam was created in much the same way: in the first hour God collected the dust, in the second made a shapeless mass out of it, in the third fashioned the limbs, and so on" (¶185) — illustrated by fig. 71, Schedel's Buch der Chroniken (1493): the creation of Adam from the clay of the prima materia.

Jung uses it to gloss dream 18's "shapeless life-mass": the human form rises from the massa informis "which has contained the divine seeds of life ever since the Creation." The anthropogony from chaos is the same pattern the alchemists projected into the vessel.

occurrences.title: The 'Mill of the Host' — high altar, Tribsees, Pomerania
occurrences.label: The 'Mill of the Host'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The Word, in the form of scrolls, is poured into a mill by the four evangelists, to reappear as the Infant Christ in the chalice.
body: Fifteenth-century altar painting: the four evangelists pour the Word — as scrolls — into a mill; from the mill issues the Infant Christ in the chalice. The caption Jung supplies: John 1:14, "And the word was made flesh."

His use: a churchly transformation-machine standing exactly where the alchemists set their opus — mechanical processing of a sacred substance into the God-man, with the quaternity of the evangelists as millers. It opens Jung's comparison of the Mass's transubstantiation with the alchemical transmutation (¶417).

image.title: Tribsees church interior 004

occurrences.title: Minerva's crumbling temple — the senator's daughter's dream (late Roman Republic)
occurrences.label: Minerva's crumbling temple
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "The daughter of a Roman Senator appeared before the Senate and said she had dreamed that Minerva came to her complaining that her temple was crumbling, and that the Senate should vote some money for its repair; and the Senate really had that temple repaired."

Jung's frame: under primitive circumstances "the unconscious can still see; it functions like an eye or like consciousness... dreams have a sort of social function" — traces surviving into the last years of the Roman Republic. He retells the story later in the Tavistock Lectures (CW 18 ¶250).

occurrences.title: The Dark Woman and the mirror-image secret — dream, 7 Nov 1954
occurrences.label: The Dark Woman and the mirror-image secret
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: Afterward, the Dark Woman and I walk alone down a steep mountainside.
body: Dreamt immediately after Pauli finished his 1954 theoretical paper on mirror-image symmetries — work that struck him as "a thoroughly straightforward activity": in a room with the "dark woman," experiments produce "reflections" which the others take for "real objects"; the Dark Woman and the dreamer alone know they are mere mirror images. "This secret fills us with apprehension"; the two then walk down a steep mountainside alone.

Pauli, after the January 1957 parity experiments ("God is a weak left-hander"): "all multiple manifestations of an archetype can very well be described as 'reflections,' whereupon that which reflects itself remains in the background as an invisible reflector" — regarded by rationalistic opinion as nonexistent, "whereas the 'Dark Woman' knows all about it." Jung: "Your dream about the 'Chinese woman' seems to have anticipated this; i.e., your anima already had scent of asymmetry".

occurrences.title: 'Director Spiegler, please!' — Krishna drives to the mirror — dreams, 11 & 14/15 Mar 1957
occurrences.label: Director Spiegler, please!
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: 11 and 14/15 March 1957 (dates per van Erkelens' collation)

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: Spiegler' [Reflector] is a dominant archetype, the producer of the mirror image.
body: First dream: a youngish dark-haired man "enveloped in faint light" hands the dreamer a manuscript and is shouted at — conventional fear losing, as always, to the unconscious. Three days later the same man, "now a policeman," bolts into the passenger seat: "Come with me!" A sudden thought: "the car driver Krishna." At the police station a brusque voice addresses the counter's "unfamiliar dark woman": "Director Spiegler [Reflector], please!" — at which the dreamer wakes, taken aback, then dreams on and explains parity violation to a Jung-like psychologist.

Jung: the haloed man "is certainly the shadow, but he has a halo, making him the unacknowledged hero. Hence the idea of 'Krishna'" — the secret cooperation of hero and dark woman around the one invisible reflector, the unus mundus.

occurrences.title: Mithraeum at the sacred spring (Provence; Saalburg)
occurrences.label: Mithraeum at the sacred spring
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Provence (unnamed by Jung); Saalburg near Frankfurt
occurrences.quote: There is such a place in Provence-I have forgotten the name-where a beautiful clear spring comes out of the green under a wall of rock, on the surface of which the Romans carved a huge altar picture of Mithra slaying the bull.
body: The antique locus of the conflict between nature spirit and Christian spirit that opens the 17 Feb 1932 lecture:

"Then they made holes in the rock into which they inserted beams, and so erected the temple right beside the spring. The spring was always outside for the sacred ablutions, and there the mystery of rebirth was performed" — the same arrangement "at Saalburg near Frankfurt; the mithraeum has been reconstructed, and the mystical spring is just as it was". "The spirit of late antiquity was expressed in the worship of the deity inter nemora et fontes… there Christianity met its most formidable enemy": mithraea sited at springs and grottoes, nature worship as such — against which the early Christians repudiated nature itself.

occurrences.title: The Mithraic sacrifice creating fruitfulness — Heddernheim relief
occurrences.label: The Mithraic sacrifice creating fruitfulness
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Rotating stone slab (pl. XXXIII): tauroctony on one side; on the other Sol with grapes, Mithras with cornucopia, dadophors bearing fruits, Silvanus above. From the dead bull "comes all fruitfulness: fruits from his horns, wine from his blood, corn from his tail, cattle from his semen, garlic from his nostrils".

Jung's reading: the sacrifice "should be conceived as the moment of supreme fruitfulness"; the dog leaping on the bull as compensatory sign of the dog-star at solstice, death equated with the sun's highest point (Creuzer, ¶354).
Verbatim: In the light of the Persian legend, and on the evidence of the monuments themselves, this sacrifice should be conceived as the moment of supreme fruitfulness. (cw05 ¶354).

image.title: Tauroctony Heddernheim

occurrences.title: The Mithraic cave - communicants drinking the bull's blood (Visions, 18 May 1932)
occurrences.label: The Mithraic cave - communicants drinking…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: They prayed in a loud voice while they dipped their hands in the blood: \"Give us of your blood, Oh bull, that we also may live.\
body: After the white light an enantiodromia-test: a dark jungle where "the trees parted to let me pass and many wild animals followed behind me" - "the problem, what shall we do with the animals?" She emerges at the entrance of a Mithraic cave - "a place where death may be avoided by sacrifice" - and enters: "I entered and beheld the communicants who had just killed the bull." Their prayer: "Give us of your blood, Oh bull, that we also may live."

Jung: "she naturally turns to the Mithraic solution, which, mind you, has worked in the past" - killing, eating, drinking the blood: integrating the animals "in a form that is not dangerous". She criticizes: "Your faces are encrusted with blood. You are too heavy with the blood of the bull" - "too heavy, too earthbound," like the taurobolium and "a horrible idea underlies our Christian communion; taken literally, it is a feast of cannibals". All the communicants arise and follow her; she leads them past the deserted temples of Rome, Greece and Egypt to the sea, where the past cannot follow: "there the past cannot understand the future, so it simply drops away from her".

occurrences.title: Mithraic initiation grades — milites, leones, heliodromi (Roman empire, ~1st–4th c.)
occurrences.label: Mithraic initiation grades
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

body: The Mithraic congregation's ladder of consecration grades — soldier (miles), lion (leo), sun-runner (heliodromus) among the seven — cited by Jung (cf. his 1925 Analytical Psychology, 98–99; fn6) as his Western exhibit of staged impersonal experience: "in the initiations, people were changed into milites, the soldiers of the god, and lions, and the heliodromoi, the sun runners of the god. These were simply different stages of impersonal experience" (sem-kundalini pdf p144).

His gloss: a Roman innkeeper made a miles is not afterwards only that — "he has experienced himself on a higher level that was not identical with the three-dimensional world: an impersonal level where he was allowed to look out the window into another dimensional way, onto psychical reality."

occurrences.title: The Mithraic ladder of seven doors and an eighth — Celsus
occurrences.label: The Mithraic ladder of seven doors and an eighth
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The stairway represents the 'passage of the soul' (animae transitus).
body: Celsus reports the idea "found among the Persians and in the Mithraic mysteries, of a stairway with seven doors and an eighth door at the top. The first door was Saturn and was correlated with lead... The seventh door was gold and signified the sun." The colours are also mentioned; the stairway represents the "passage of the soul" (animae transitus); the eighth door corresponds to the sphere of the fixed stars.
Jung at cw14 ¶578: the soul-ladder through the planetary spheres, with the eighth beyond them.

occurrences.title: Mithras swinging the cow's shoulder (the Great Bear) — Mithraic Liturgy
occurrences.label: Mithras swinging the cow's shoulder
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Amplifying the boy's North Pole dream, a participant cites the Mithraic liturgy: "Mithras appears as a fiery god, as an adolescent deity. In his right hand he swings a cow's shoulder. This is the Great Bear, rotating around the North Pole" (pdf p154; Dieterich's Eine Mithraslithurgie, cf. Cumont).

Jung: "The cow's shoulder thus represents the connection with the Pole. With it, the god holds the whole sky and from there rotates the world. The Pole is therefore a very important symbol, something transcendent. It is the place where the world axis goes through, it is the center of the world" (p154). The Cheops pyramid's northern exit, extended, pointed to the polestar.

occurrences.title: Mithras crowning Helios — Klagenfurt relief
occurrences.label: Mithras crowning Helios — Klagenfurt relief
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Marble relief (pl. XXIVa): Mithras crowns the kneeling Helios with a ray-crown, shakes his hand in farewell, and mounts his chariot for the ascension; the Osterburken monument shows the bull's shoulder held over Helios' head with a crown on the ground.

Jung's reading: "the divine prototype of initiation into the degree of Miles" (Cumont, ¶288) — the setting sun invests a successor with solar power, the pattern of Khidr-Dhulqarnein and Peter-Christ; "the Pope is a symbolical 'solis invicti comes'" (¶289).
Verbatim: On the marble relief at Klagenfurt, Mithras is shown crowning Helios with a crown of rays, as he kneels before him or floats up to him from below. (cw05 ¶288).

occurrences.title: Mithras with three heads rising out of the tree
occurrences.label: Mithras with three heads rising out of the tree
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: "Then there was the idea of the birth of the sun out of the top of the tree; Mithras and Ra have both been represented in that way. Mithras is sometimes shown with three heads, a trinity, rising out of a tree." The light-bearer born from the tree-top — the same image-family as the winged disk on the Babylonian seals, the Christmas tree ("the light of the new year"), and the Jesse tree with Christ crowning it.

occurrences.title: Monas hieroglyphica — Dee's glyph of sun, moon and their union
occurrences.label: Monas hieroglyphica
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: there was evening and there was morning, one day. Be that (day) therefore the first, on which was made the light of the Philosophers.
body: Dee's Monas: "when the semi-circle of the moon was brought to be the complement of the sun, there was evening and there was morning, one day. Be that (day) therefore the first, on which was made the light of the Philosophers." The union of the sun and moon signs produces the sign for Taurus, ruler of the house of Venus.

Jung's reading: the marriage of day and night in the glyph grounds the rare designation of the lapis as "filius unius diei" (son of one day) — cross-referenced forward to the ch. VI discussion (pars. 472ff. in the main text). Parallels: king-queen-pair family, alchemical-prayer-horridas-nostrae-mentis, eagle-double-headed-eyes-palatinus-412-15c.

occurrences.title: Monoïmos — the Monad that wars with itself; the jot of the iota
occurrences.label: Monoïmos — the Monad that wars with itself
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'This Man is a single Monad, uncompounded and indivisible, yet compounded and divisible; loving and at peace with all things, yet warring with all things and at war with itself in all things... as it were a musical harmony containing all things... It is its own mother, its own father' (¶340). Its emblem is 'the jot or tittle' — the many-faced, thousand-eyed jot of the iota; the Son of the Man is 'the one iota flowing from on high' (¶340). Jung: this 2nd-c. Monad 'describes the psychological nature of the self' (¶341); footnote links iota to the Hebrew Yod of the lapis, Adam as the hook of the Yod. 'Seek him from out thyself... thou wilt find Him in thyself, the One and the Many' (¶347).

occurrences.title: Crab-lizard monster killed by magic wand — crucial dream of the mountain-sickness case
occurrences.label: Crab-lizard monster killed by magic wand
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: told 1935 (Jung dates the analysis 'before the war')
occurrences.quote: In the background appears a monstrously big crab-lizard. It moves first to the left and then to the right so that I find myself standing in the angle between them as if in an open pair of scissors.
body: Third and crucial dream of the ~40-year-old director of a public school (peasant origin, "mountain sickness" vertigo): in a peasant house that is "the lazar-house of St. Jacob near Basel," after boasting of a walk to Leipzig, a "monstrously big crab-lizard" appears moving left then right, trapping the dreamer in an open-scissors angle; he touches its head with a little rod — a magical wand — and kills it, then contemplates it long (¶180, 183).

Jung reads the St. Jacob setting (1,300 Swiss who rushed ahead against orders and died, 1444) and the engine-driver dream as one warning against head-only rushing; the crab-lizard is not personal but "an archetype" (¶190), the hero-dragon conflict (¶191–192) whose monster is also the mother dragon / "mother sarcophaga" (¶193). Organically: serpent/lizard = cerebro-spinal system, crab = sympathetic/abdominal system — the body's rebellion against his conscious attitude (¶194). The wand kills by thinking-things-away (¶197–199). The patient rejected the warning and lost his position within three months (¶201). NOTE a real contradiction to keep: cw16's 1934 version of the same case (mountain-derailment-train-dream-zurich-1931) implies analysis ~1930/31, while cw18 ¶186 says "before the war."

occurrences.title: Four-coloured beast and the maiden — Shepherd of Hermas
occurrences.label: Four-coloured beast and the maiden
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the Shepherd of Hermas (Vision IV) the hero travelling the Via Campana meets 'a monster resembling a dragon of the sea': 'the beast had on its head four colours, black, then the colour of flame and blood, then golden, then white. After I had passed the beast by... lo! a maiden met me, "adorned as if coming forth from the bridal chamber," all in white... but her hair was white' (cw14 ¶301). 'The similarity between the two stories is so complete' with Maier's Ortus-Sibyl sequence that Jung suspects a shared archetypal source rather than literary dependence (¶302). Hermas' mistress decodes the colours: black = this world, fire and blood = its destruction, gold = the tried soul, white = the world to come (¶303).

occurrences.title: Leviathan and behemoth — God's two acolyte monsters (Book of Job 40-41)
occurrences.label: Leviathan and behemoth
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "Even the God of Job, as you remember, had not only one monster but two with which to rule the world, the leviathan and the behemoth; the leviathan fills one third of the ocean and is the ruler of the seas, and the behemoth rules the earth. Now, if God himself cannot do without two monsters-acolytes-how can man do without them?".

Jung's point is structural, in the middle of the New Idol chapters: the state-monster cannot be abolished, only answered by another monster. "That great monster, the people, can only be kept in order by another monster, just as a wild elephant cannot be dealt with alone, but only with the aid of other elephants". The monsters are amoral — "Good and evil are considerations for the individual but not for a monster" — and the individual's task is to ride rather than worship them.

occurrences.title: The many-headed, many-horned beast = the nations (Revelation 13)
occurrences.label: The many-headed, many-horned beast = the nations
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: One sentence, in passing, gives Jung's political reading of the apocalyptic beast: "In the Book of Revelations, the monster with the many heads and the many horns means the nations, the Romans for instance".

The gloss belongs to his equation of organized bodies with the dragon: "Any organized body of men is a huge snake; one dreams of such things in that form, and one finds it in historical dreams." The Revelation beast is thus the same crowd-soul as Hannibal's devastating dragon (Livy) and the "thousand-headed monster" whose outside appearance is the state. The whole sequence answers Zarathustra's "New Idol": the collective appears in dream and vision as one many-headed animal, and only the man who can ride it — Lao-tse fashion — keeps his soul.

occurrences.title: The state, coldest of all cold monsters — Zarathustra, 'On the New Idol'
occurrences.label: The state, coldest of all cold monsters
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "A state is called the coldest of all cold monsters. Coldly lieth it also; and this lie creepeth from its mouth: 'I, the state, am the people'". Nietzsche's chapter against the state, read by Jung across four lectures as a prophecy of the totalitarian claim moving from church to science to state — "first in Russia to the horror of the world, then in Italy, then in Germany".

The analytical core: "An idol is a symbol which possesses authority, which is mana. In the individual case, if it is a question of individuation, the symbol creates order; but if it is a question of collective events, it must be an organization, and then it is no longer a symbol. Then the symbol becomes an idol". The state itself "doesn't even stink, because it does not exist… The state is a convention, an abstraction"; what stinks is humanity, the herd. Against the monster only the man who has not sold his soul stands: "the dragon is of course the symbol for the collective unconscious; the state is simply the outside appearance of the thousand-headed monster".

occurrences.title: Dream of the two fighting elephants — the monsters of good and evil (Zurich, 1935)
occurrences.label: Dream of the two fighting elephants
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: A patient dreamt she woke as if from unconsciousness, lids like lead, standing under something like two columns — then saw with terror that she stood between the legs of an enormous elephant, an equally huge one opposite, about to fight with her in between. She jumped free and woke terrified.

Jung: "Those are the two monsters of good and evil" — the opposites that were always there, but "now man has come in between them — consciousness has come — and the moment my patient saw those two creatures, they had instantly to fight."

His amplificatory row: the Behemoth and Leviathan beside Jahveh, the makara in the svadhisthana chakra, the Brahman's two monsters of the Upanishads. The dreamer should "assert her humanity above the animal fight" — she would be the reconciling symbol.

occurrences.title: Vidarr's fight with the Fenris-Wolf — Gosforth cross relief
occurrences.label: Vidarr's fight with the Fenris-Wolf
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The rescue of the hero is at the same time a sunrise, the triumph of consciousness.
body: Fig. 33 beside the "rescue of the hero … at the same time a sunrise, the triumph of consciousness" (¶539): the Norse monster-slaying carved on an English cross — Christ sphere and Norse myth fused on the same stone, the monster of death overcome at the world's end.

image.title: Vidar by Collingwood

occurrences.title: The moon, author of mortal bodies — Macrobius
occurrences.label: The moon, author of mortal bodies — Macrobius
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: There is no doubt that the moon is the author and contriver of mortal bodies.
body: Macrobius on the lunar border: "The realm of the perishable begins with the moon and goes downwards. Souls coming into this region begin to be subject to the numbering of days and to time.... There is no doubt that the moon is the author and contriver of mortal bodies" (¶173).

Jung uses it to fix the ancient psychology of the moon's position: "Because of her moist nature, the moon is also the cause of decay. The loveliness of the new moon, hymned by the poets and Church Fathers, veils her dark side, which however could not remain hidden from the fact-finding eye of the empiricist.... She partakes not only of the earth's sufferings but of its daemonic darkness as well" (¶173).

occurrences.title: The moon as eye of the basilisk of heaven — Paracelsus, De pestilitate
occurrences.label: The moon as eye of the basilisk of heaven
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the moon in the sky is the eye of the basilisk of heaven
body: Paracelsus' lunar pathology: "the moon in heaven is the corpus to bring this about" for the timid man's imagination, which makes his eyes basilisk-like and poisons "the speculum venenosum magnum naturae [great poisonous mirror of nature]"; conversely "the sidereal spirit and body draw poison out of the mirror of the moon into which you have looked." The clinching clause: "Quia ex menstruo et venenoso sanguine mulieris causatur et nascitur basiliscus, ita luna in coelo est oculus basilisci coeli [Because as the basilisk is caused and born from the menstrual and poisonous blood of a woman, thus the moon in the sky is the eye of the basilisk of heaven]" (¶215). "Menstruating women do poison the moon and the stars much more readily and also more intensely than any man."
Jung: the passage "catches very aptly the atmosphere which hangs round the pale moonlight" — imagination and mirror poisoning each other, magnetic reciprocity of sidereal body and sky.

occurrences.title: 'The disc of the moon is filled with souls' — Epiphanius, Firmicus, Lydus
occurrences.label: The disc of the moon is filled with souls
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the disc of the moon is filled with souls
body: A standing late-antique doctrine of the lunar gate: Firmicus — "The soul is believed to descend through the disc of the sun, but its ascent is prepared through the disc of the moon"; Lydus reports the hierophant Praetextus saying Janus "sends the diviner souls to the lunar throng"; Epiphanius — "the disc of the moon is filled with souls." Jung adds "It is the same in exotic myths" (Frobenius) and, in ch. V, reads the Egyptian "left eye" as the moon, "the gathering-place of souls" (fig. 31).
The moon as the collecting vessel of the dead between death and rebirth — the counter-gate to the sun's.

occurrences.title: The fool changed as the moon is Adam — Augustine's moon exegesis
occurrences.label: The fool changed as the moon is Adam
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The moon and death significantly reveal their affinity.
body: Augustine on the unfavourable aspect of the moon: "The wise man remaineth stable as the sun, but a fool is changed as the moon" — "Who then is that fool who changeth as the moon, but Adam, in whom all have sinned?" (¶20). He attaches the Church as Luna (Ep. LV, 10), the arrows "to shoot in the darkness of the moon at the upright of heart," and Psalm 71's "until the moon shall be destroyed," glossed: "the abundance of peace shall grow until it consumes all changefulness of mortality... the last enemy, death, shall be destroyed" (¶20).

Jung reads a disguised fear here: "the destruction of the moon is manifestly equivalent to the destruction of death... To eliminate the moon from Creation is therefore as desirable as the elimination of death" — Augustine's "cautious and perhaps not altogether unconscious disguising of the sinister aspect of the moon" (¶20, p34). Alchemy, "all the more ruthlessly," insists on the dangerousness of the new moon (¶21).

occurrences.title: 'Luna is diminished that she may fill the elements' — Ambrose's kenosis
occurrences.label: Luna is diminished that she may fill…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Thus has Luna proclaimed the mystery of Christ.
body: Ambrose's lunar kenosis, the heart of Hugo Rahner's "Mysterium Lunae": "Luna is diminished that she may fill the elements. Therefore is this a great mystery.... He emptied her that he might fill her, as he also emptied himself that he might fill all things. He emptied himself that he might come down to us. He came down to us that he might rise again for all.... Thus has Luna proclaimed the mystery of Christ" (¶28).

Jung reads the changefulness of the moon as causally dependent on the transformation of the bridegroom (Philippians 2:6), the patristic root of the Sol-Luna allegory's darkening: the sponsa is "black but comely" because she reflects his kenosis. St. Hilary's lapidary paradox follows — "Deus homo, immortalis mortuus, aeternus sepultus" — and Ephraem Syrus' image of creation unburdened of "the prefigurations of his glory" (¶29).

occurrences.title: The lovesick Moon shrinking to the dot of the yod — Zohar III, 191
occurrences.label: The lovesick Moon shrinking to the dot…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: she shrinks to nothing until only a dot is left of her... “I am black,” like the letter Yod, in which there is no white space
body: Zohar III, 191 (on "I am black, but comely"): when the Moon "is very lovesick for her Beloved, she shrinks to nothing until only a dot is left of her, and she is hidden from all her hosts and camps" — she says "I am black, like the letter Yod, in which there is no white space," having no room to shelter anyone under her wings.

Jung's reading: the Luna-kenosis — the feminine light diminished to the single point (yod) from which all renewal begins; read alongside the Kabbala denudata's yod-speculation (point→line vau, yod as vas of the fount). Parallels: moon-kenosis-luna-ambrose-milan-4c, moon-author-of-mortal-bodies-macrobius-rome-5c, point image family.

occurrences.title: Luna's sudden intervention with the child — Mutus liber
occurrences.label: Luna's sudden intervention with the child
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the Mutus liber (1702) the goddess 'who suddenly intervenes in the opus... appears equally suddenly during the procedure, as a naked female figure crowned with the sign of the moon and bearing a child in her arms' (cw14 ¶436). 'The miracle is there described as an intervention of the gods, who, like god-parents, take the place of the earthly parents and arrange for the spiritual procreation of the foetus spagyricus' (¶436); there follows adoption by Sol and a coniunctio Solis et Lunae including the adoptive child (¶436). The Cantilena's Luna who takes the dissolved king into her own solution repeats the same motif: the matrix itself becomes the divine mother.

occurrences.title: Nokomis falls from the moon and bears Wenonah — Song of Hiawatha
occurrences.label: Nokomis falls from the moon and bears Wenonah
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the moon is the gathering-place of departed souls (fig. 31) a guardian of the seed, and hence a source of life with a feminine significance.
body: The moon as "the gathering-place of departed souls … a guardian of the seed, and hence a source of life with a feminine significance" (¶487); the plucking of the grape-vine branch as infringement of the incest-taboo.
