Nokomis' fall and birth-pangs are "something altogether typical"; the rejuvenated mother is to be thrown up to the sky to bear a daughter-wife for the sun-god, "the 'father of his mother'" (¶496).

occurrences.title: The blood-bearing moon-sponge of the lunar sea — Allegoriae super librum Turbae
occurrences.label: The blood-bearing moon-sponge of the lunar sea
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: a sponge planted, having blood and sentience [sensum], in the manner of a tree that is rooted in the sea
body: The moon-plant in the lunar sea: "In the lunar sea there is a sponge planted, having blood and sentience [sensum], in the manner of a tree that is rooted in the sea and moveth not from its place. If thou wouldst handle the plant, take a sickle to cut it with, but have good care that the blood floweth not out, for it is the poison of the Philosophers" (¶157).

Jung: "it would seem that the moon-plant is a kind of mandrake and has nothing to do with the botanical Lunaria (honesty)," though kin to Galen's arbor philosophica Lunatica/Berissa (thirty flowers for the moon's age) and Khunrath's "red and white coral-tree of our sea." Ruland: the sponge "has understanding." It belongs to the family of the tree of the sea in Arabian alchemy and the arbor philosophica, "which in turn has parallels with the Cabalistic tree of the Sefiroth and with the tree of Christian mysticism and Hindu philosophy" (¶158).

occurrences.title: The crescent moon lifts her from the erupting volcano (Visions)
occurrences.label: The crescent moon lifts her from the erupting…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: vision read 24 February 1932 (painted late 1929/early 1930 for Jung)
occurrences.quote: Then I called out that I was lost and would be burned alive. The crescent moon swung down low to me. I caught it with my hands and it lifted me out.
body: Ascending from the well, skeletons on horseback gallop by, the eruption begins again, and no way leads to the rim:

Jung: "That Luna herself descends to take her out of danger is very fantastic symbolism, but psychologically it means that through her complete surrender to the unconscious powers she made them into friends; the unconscious then develops a helpful function and produces a miracle in her favor". The connection is earned in the well: Cybele "is the moon, the crescent is her emblem" — "she received divine help down below, she made friends with the gods". In the valley village the mountain is only "The Great Mother… She only smokes" to normal people; she alone must "know a bit more about the inside of that mountain".

occurrences.title: The moon slays the sun: the Tyriac serpent — Consilium coniugii
occurrences.label: The moon slays the sun — the Tyriac serpent
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the two opposites cancel each other out, their impact resulting—in accordance with the laws of energetics—in the birth of a third and new thing
body: The Consilium coniugii's darkest Sol-Luna text: the lion, the lower sun, "grows corrupt through the flesh... For the moon is the shadow of the sun, and with corruptible bodies she is consumed, and through her corruption is the lion eclipsed." The substance "is named the Tyriac of the Philosophers, and it is also called the poisonous serpent, because, like this, it bites off the head of the male in the lustful heat of conception, and giving birth it dies and is divided through the midst. So also the moisture of the moon, when she receives his light, slays the sun, and at the birth of the child of the Philosophers she dies likewise, and at death the two parents yield up their souls to the son... And the parents are the food of the son" (¶21).

Jung: "In this psychologem all the implications of the Sol-Luna allegory are carried to their logical conclusion" — the parents cancel out, the son is "a united double nature" — and the god-eating ending (teoqualo, Unas) shows it was never conscious of its kinship with transubstantiation (¶22).

occurrences.title: Manichaean myth: the moon as receptacle of souls
occurrences.label: Manichaean myth: the moon as receptacle of souls
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: She first gets quite full of dead souls—that is the pregnant full moon—and then she gives them to the sun, where the souls attain new life (a Manichean myth).
body: Souls migrate to the moon after death; the moon fills with them — the pregnant full moon — then gives them to the sun, where they attain new life. Jung cites it while arguing the moon below in svādhiṣṭhāna is "like a cup from which flows the offering of souls to the cakras above, maõipura and anvhata. You see, there is the sun myth again." The moon is thus a symbol of rebirth, whatever the Eastern crescent-Shiva reading.

occurrences.title: The moon as vessel of souls poured into the sun — Manichaean doctrine
occurrences.label: The moon as vessel of souls poured into the sun
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Manichaean dogma of the dead: "The spirits of the dead are received by the moon which thereby increases until it is quite full and then it begins to approach the sun... finally pours all the souls back into the sun." Emptied, the moon reappears on the other side, sucking up souls again; from the sun they pass "into the pillar of life or of souls, which apparently carries them back to the origin of life, to the divine father."

Jung cites it amid the wind-sun complex (rising sun = spirit; morning wind = pneuma emanating from the father), beside the Neoplatonist idea that the animus descends from the sun and is gathered up by the female moon. "This idea of the pillar of life occurs in She, though I don't know how it got there" (Rider Haggard).

Verbatim: "When the moon is quite close to the sun it is completely empty, and then it appears again on the other side slowly increasing, sucking up souls from the earth in order to bring them back to the sun".

occurrences.title: Chinese sage realizing he lacks the wisdom of the moon — picture, 5th c. BC (Jung's library)
occurrences.label: Chinese sage realizing he lacks the wisdom…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: "We have here a picture of a Chinese sage from the fifth century B.C. He is shown as a learned doctor, with his bundle of scientific remedies, minerals, and herbs which he has gathered from all over the earth. But still men die and his wisdom is not sufficient to save them. In the picture he is seen struck by the sudden realization that if he could only obtain the wisdom of the moon also, he would be able to cure all disease and bring immortality to mankind" (p397).

Harding's report offers it under the full-moon phase (on the Buddha's left hand while the sun is on the right, in Indian pictures): Logos-wisdom completed only by Eros-wisdom — the whole argument of the crescent report in one image. Jung returns to it at p403: "man is not complete without that other side that is represented by the moon."

occurrences.title: The Moor's head boiled and poured into a golden ball — Chymical Wedding
occurrences.label: The Moor's head boiled and poured…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The head was boiled in a pot and the broth poured into a golden ball.
body: In the Chymical Wedding the caput mortuum appears as "the 'Moor'... The head was boiled in a pot and the broth poured into a golden ball. This gives us the connection with the 'golden head' of the Greek alchemy." The Moor is probably identical with the black executioner who decapitates the royal personages, until his own head is struck off; later a black bird is beheaded.

Jung at cw14 ¶730: beheading = "the separation of the 'understanding' from the 'great suffering and grief' which nature inflicts on the soul," an emancipation of the cogitatio — a unio mentalis "in the overcoming of the body." Mylius' Schema XXIV shows king and queen as two ravens fighting.

occurrences.title: Morienus on alchemy as God's gift to the elect
occurrences.label: Morienus on alchemy as God's gift to the elect
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: For the Lord selects of his servants those whom he wills and chooses, to seek after this divine science which is concealed from man, and having sought it to keep it with them.
body: In the testament-dialogue Morienus declares the art a matter of election, not merit: "God vouchsafes this divine and pure science to his faithful and his servants... The Lord selects of his servants those whom he wills and chooses, to seek after this divine science which is concealed from man."

Jung cites it at cw14 ¶529 beside Dorn's "some are chosen, when much knocking, many prayers, and diligent enquiry have gone before" — both prefiguring Koepgen's dedication "Renatis praedestinatione." The motif of election binds alchemy to the charismatic religion of the Holy Ghost Jung sees brewing in it (¶531).

occurrences.title: Morienus to Kalid: the introduction to the art — 'none may enter save through affliction of the soul'
occurrences.label: Morienus to Kalid — the introduction to the art
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Jerusalem? (Morienus the hermit) → Latin transl. by Robert of Chester, 1144
occurrences.quote: Exceeding narrow is the gateway to peace, and none may enter save through affliction of the soul
body: "Particularly instructive is the introduction to the art given by Morienus to Kalid: 'This thing for which you have sought so long is not to be acquired or accomplished by force or passion. It is to be won only by patience and humility and by a determined and most perfect love. For God bestows this divine and immaculate science on his faithful servants…'" Asked why he lives in mountains and deserts rather than hermitages, Morienus answers: "no one reaps who does not sow.… Exceeding narrow is the gateway to peace, and none may enter save through affliction of the soul" (¶386).
Jung's capstone to the "mental attitude" chapter: the divine science "draws its master away from the suffering of this world and leads to the knowledge of future good" — the opus as via purgativa.

occurrences.title: Morienus — the stone extracted from man, 'thou art its ore'
occurrences.label: Morienus — the stone extracted…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Morienus (7th-8th c.), writing on the rim of the Hermetic vessel 'All those who have all things with them have no need of outside aid' — not chemistry but a moral matter (¶256). 'This thing is extracted from thee, for thou art its ore; in thee they find it, and... from thee they take it.' The lapis contains the four elements and is likened to the cosmos; the procedure 'cannot be performed with hands' but is a 'human attitude' (dispositio hominum), accomplished through the coniunctio which forms the essence of the work (¶256). Jung: self-knowledge as the oldest layer of the opus. Parallels: rosinus-ad-sarratantam-lapis-animalis.

occurrences.title: Apotropaic mosaic against the evil eye — Moknine, Tunis (Roman)
occurrences.label: Apotropaic mosaic against the evil eye
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Moknine, Tunis (floor mosaic of a house)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Fig. 44 of Concerning Mandala Symbolism: a motif from a Roman mosaic on the floor of a house in Moknine, Tunis, which Jung himself photographed — "It represents an apotropaism against the evil eye." Placed among the eye-mandala parallels (eye motif, polyophthalmia, observing consciousness), it shows the apotropaic, magical-protective function that patient mandalas spontaneously reproduce.

occurrences.title: Moses lifts up the serpent — John 3:14
occurrences.label: Moses lifts up the serpent — John 3:14
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: "Moses lifted up the serpent and Christ said that so he must be lifted up to draw all men unto him." In Jung's chain: the serpent was the original form of the physician's god (Aesculapius himself a serpent; the caduceus the symbol "of Hermes the Sorcerer"); "so it conveyed the idea of healing, as Christ was the healing one. Saviour and serpent are used interchangeably." The bridge to the Gnostic Christ-serpent of Eden (ophites-christ-serpent-2c).

occurrences.title: The mother's broken leg: dream and next-day telegram (doctor with mother complex)
occurrences.label: The mother's broken leg
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: Next day, in reality, a telegram came: "Your mother has broken her leg.
body: A doctor, "by no means a fool", an alienist living in his mother's house as "a little husband", writing her daily letters on his own analysis. Six months of mother-complex dreams passed before he could hear the interpretation. The moment he finally realized he must detach, he dreamt he climbed a slippery hill, saw his mother below, shouted "For heaven's sake, don't try to come up!" — she slipped and broke her leg. Next day a telegram: "Your mother has broken her leg."
"That explained his stupidity, why he was so deaf. His unconscious knew that it might kill his mother. Those old bonds, cases of participation mystique, are exceedingly dangerous."

occurrences.title: Slippery-grass dream — the doctor with a mother complex (Zurich, ~1930s)
occurrences.label: Slippery-grass dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: He climbs on slippery grass, climbs up; the mother also wants to go up... She slips and fractures the femur.
body: A thirty-five-year-old doctor with a mother complex; Jung fought two months to convince him he would not get out of the mother by staying at home. When he finally resolved to leave, the mother fractured her femur — and he dreamt: "He climbs on slippery grass, climbs up; the mother also wants to go up, she also wants to reach the top of the hill, as stubborn as ever. She slips and fractures the femur." The mother had demanded he write down every word of the analysis ("she always had him in her grip"). Jung: separation risked the mother's life — sons then feel responsible; it takes "a desecrating move backward, a look away from the mother's Medusa head." Even her death would not free him: "As the mother of God, she will always crouch there and brood over the child."

occurrences.title: The mother-demon's last word: 'God is his father' — Barlach, Der Tote Tag
occurrences.label: The mother-demon's last word
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In Ernst Barlach's tragedy The Dead Day, the mother-demon says at the end: 'The strange thing is that man will not learn that God is his father.
body: The closing line of Ernst Barlach's expressionist drama Der Tote Tag (The Dead Day, 1912), spoken by the mother-demon: "The strange thing is that man will not learn that God is his father." Jung sets it against Faust's reproach — "Thou art conscious only of the single urge" — as the voice of the spirit against the fleshly bond of family romance: "That is what Freud would never learn, and what all those who share his outlook forbid themselves to learn."

For the vault this is the counter-locus to the demonized father of the neuroses: the mother-demon herself must announce the divine father before the play can end. (Seminars on the same play produced steissbart-gnome-mother-barlach-der-tote-tag-1912 and dwarf-barlach-besenbein-toter-tag-1912 — Barlach's figures as archetypal field.)

occurrences.title: Fionn carries his mother — the two fishes and the thumb of wisdom (Fenian cycle)
occurrences.label: Fionn carries his mother
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Mrs. von Roques' "very clear example" of carrying-the-burden: the hero Fionn goes out with his mother; first she carries him, then they change, "but he gradually loses parts of her until he has only her feet, and those he throws into a lake belonging to a witch." The witch sends him to fish; he catches two fishes — the mother's feet — and must cook them without spots from a too-hot fire. They get spots, he presses his thumb on them and burns it, "and from that day, he is wise when he sucks his thumb".

Jung: "part of such a mystery, the integration and disintegration. Being carried by the mother means being carried by the unconscious, and carrying the mother would of course mean carrying the unconscious" — as Christ carried the cross, "his whole ancestral heaven and hell".

occurrences.title: The all-devouring mother in a depressive psychosis (patient: mother, Zürich)
occurrences.label: The all-devouring mother in a depressive…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: case-index [20], ref. book p328 ≈ pdf p295 (harvested from index, pdf p579)

body: A depressed mother "became symbol of the all-devouring mother in her depressive psychosis" (case [20], book p328) — the Terrible Mother manifesting as diagnosis. The index cross-files it under psychoses: "mother as symbol of all-devouring mother, 328", and under "Terrible Mother: as death-symbol, 328".
Verbatim (case-index): "Mother who became symbol of the all-devouring mother in her depressive psychosis. — 328"

occurrences.title: The Ancient Mother with the grain of wheat taken by the bird (Visions plate 2)
occurrences.label: The Ancient Mother with the grain…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich (patient's painting; plate following p. 272 of the edition)
occurrences.yearDisplay: painted late 1929/early 1930 for Jung; vision from the 1926-32 series

jung.locator: plate 2 caption (pdf p3); discussion in later sessions

occurrences.quote: The Ancient Mother \"held one grain of wheat which the bird took\
body: Plate 2 of the patient's painted series: the Ancient Mother "held one grain of wheat which the bird took" — the archaic Great Mother with the seed of the corn-god and the bird that carries it off. The constellation is nearly identical to the opening image the same visioner produced for the Kore essay (Case X: "a white bird... alighted on the figure of a woman, clad in blue... in it she held a grain of wheat", CW9i ¶320), which Jung adduced as the clearest modern Demeter material — the same patient, later material. In the early seminars Jung reads her descents through this chthonic feminine (muladhara/svadhisthana levels); the introduction notes his reading of the wheat-tree energy conduits via Kundalini.

occurrences.title: The mater sarcophaga — Etruscan urn-mother (Florence)
occurrences.label: The mater sarcophaga — Etruscan urn-mother
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: A terra-cotta Etruscan figure in Florence (Jung's OCR garbles the name: Dea Matuta / "Dea Matula"): hollow, liftable, made to hold the ashes of the dead in her belly.

Jung had cited it already in The Psychology of the Unconscious as the mater sarcophaga — "the mother that eats the dead." In the seminar it glosses the hollow tree: the corpse placed in wood awaits rebirth, "for the dead were buried again in the mother." The cross too is "the mother of the dead, the Dea Matuta".
Verbatim: "It is made of terra cotta and is hollow-one can lift it apart-and the ashes of the dead were put inside, into her belly: so the dead were buried again in the mother."

occurrences.title: The king's daughter buried in a gilded wooden cow — Mykerinos
occurrences.label: The king's daughter buried in a gilded wooden…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the Egyptian king Men-kau-Re (Mykerinos) had his daughter buried in a gilded wooden cow, as a guarantee of rebirth.
body: Herodotus (II, 129) records that the Egyptian king Men-kau-Re — Mykerinos — had his daughter buried in a gilded wooden cow, "as a guarantee of rebirth": the cow stood in a gorgeous apartment with offerings made to it, and in an adjoining room stood the images of the king's concubines.

Jung cites it under "Death is a re-entry into the mother": the hollow cow as the womb-tomb of royalty, the gilded beast both mourning monument and rebirth machine. It is the monumental form of the cow-rebirth rites (Ra's retreat on the heavenly cow; the Hindu crawl through the artificial cow).

occurrences.title: Hecate of Samothrace with cross on her head — Gnostic gem
occurrences.label: Hecate of Samothrace with cross on her head
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Where the roads cross and enter into one another, thereby symbolizing the union of opposites, there is the “mother,” the object and epitome of all union.
body: Fig. 34: the triple-bodied goddess of dogs and gate of Hades, "more or less identical with Cerberus" — Heracles bringing up Cerberus "was really bringing the vanquished mother of death to the upper world" (¶577). She is kourotrophos and birth-goddess, "the patron goddess of Medea, because the power of the Terrible Mother is irresistible, coming as it does from the unconscious" (¶577); in Orphic cosmogony she occupies the centre of the world as Aphrodite, Gaia, or the world-soul itself.

occurrences.title: 'Isis una quae es omnia' — the goddess's self-revelation (Apuleius, Metamorphoses XI, ~2nd c.)
occurrences.label: Isis una quae es omnia
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Rome (Apuleius writing in Latin; cult imagines Egypt)
occurrences.quote: (Cf. the Trinity and the two mystic formulae of confession: 'Isis una quae es omnia,' 'Hermes omnia solus et ter unus.')
body: One of the two "mystic formulae of confession" Jung cites at the climax of the rumour essay's analysis of multiplication: duplication and multiplication of persons express libido-investment, "the significance of this multiplication is especially clear in religion and mythology" — and his first witness is the goddess who is all: Isis una quae es omnia ("Isis, the one who is all"). The formula is the goddess's own self-revelation to Lucius in Apuleius — the many-named plenitude (Persephone, Venus, Diana, Proserpina) gathered into one being — the clearest ancient statement of deity as multiplicity-in-unity, cited here alongside "Hermes omnia solus et ter unus" and the Christian Trinity.

occurrences.title: Kali in her fury and Shiva lying among the corpses — recognition scene
occurrences.label: Kali in her fury and Shiva lying among…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: The Indian goddess Kali has got teeth like a wild animal; she has drunk wine and blood and is dripping with blood and grease. She is a raving lioness. In most pictorial images, she is riding on a lion, or goes over the bodies of her male victims. When she went into a fury, her husband Shiva was called.
body: Amplifying the overwhelming instinct that devours the eight-and-a-half-year-old dreamer:

Jung's frame: examples of states of inexorable desire — Malaysians running amok, the Maenads tearing and eating raw kids in Dionysian orgy, Kali as raving lioness. The recognizing of the god-husband lying among the corpses is the mythic formula for what the child's dream enacts dangerously (being devoured by the lion = devoured by fantasy) and what analysis teaches: let it come, recognize it, and the fury comes to its senses.

occurrences.title: Kuan Yin feeding the devils of hell
occurrences.label: Kuan Yin feeding the devils of hell
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: There is a beautiful traditional painting, where she is represented as a devil among the devils in hell, giving them food; but a fine thread goes from her head up to the heavenly being above, and there she is in all her fine splendour.
body: Jung's image for love with feeling-consideration, in contrast to the patient's reckless maenad march into the world: in the East, "where they know as little about that kind of love as we do, they have a beautiful symbol for it in Kuan Yin, the goddess of kindness. She gives nourishment to all living beings, even to the evil spirits of hell".

She "transforms herself into an evil spirit and in that guise takes the food down to hell — having such an extraordinary regard for the feelings of the devils. That is the psychological attitude which is suggested by real love". The double figure — hellish disguise below, splendour above, joined by the thread — is the exact complement of the patient's two-flame wedding: Logos-fire from the man's head, Eros-fire from her heart.

occurrences.title: Matuta, the Etruscan Pietà — ossuary vessel of the death-mother
occurrences.label: Matuta, the Etruscan Pietà
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Matuta is the mother. Her chair is adorned with sphinxes, a fitting symbol of the mother of death.
body: An Etruscan ossuary that is at once statue and urn (pl. LIV, plate at pdf p301): the goddess of death as hollow mother receiving the dead, "her chair … adorned with sphinxes, a fitting symbol of the mother of death. (Cf. the Oedipus myth.)" (¶536). The Pietà iconography a millennium early.

image.title: Mater Matuta Chianciano

occurrences.title: Maui creeps into the jaws of Hine-nui-te-po — Maori myth
occurrences.label: Maui creeps into the jaws of Hine-nui-te-po
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: My little friends, when I creep into the jaws of the old woman, you must not laugh...
body: The monster to be overcome is Grandmother Hine-nui-te-po, the great-woman-of-night. Maui instructs the birds who accompany him: "when I creep into the jaws of the old woman, you must not laugh, but once I have been in and have come out of her mouth again, you may welcome me with shouts of laughter." Then Maui creeps into the mouth of the old woman as she sleeps.

The hero's victory consists in a voluntary re-entry into, and exit from, the devouring mother's body — the night-side of rebirth, with laughter as the fatal boundary (in the full myth, the birds' laughter wakes her and Maui dies: the venture's shadow Jung leaves unspoken in this footnote).

occurrences.title: The moon-lady at the landing-stage — recurrent childhood dream
occurrences.label: The moon-lady at the landing-stage
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The moon-lady was always waiting for me down by the water at the landing-stage, to take me to her island.
body: A girl who grew up in peculiarly difficult psychic circumstances had a recurrent dream between her seventh and tenth years: "The moon-lady was always waiting for me down by the water at the landing-stage, to take me to her island." She never remembered what happened there, "but it was so beautiful that she often prayed she might have this dream again" (¶344). Jung: "The moon-goddess also appears in children's dreams." Thirty years later the same figure returned in a dramatic fantasy — proof of the image's persistence across a lifetime (¶345-346).

occurrences.title: The horned moon-lady, the nine suns, and the Earth Mother of clay — fantasy thirty years later
occurrences.label: The horned moon-lady, the nine suns…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: same dreamer as moon-lady childhood dream

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: I see a black tentacle like that of an octopus groping towards me from underneath the sun. I step back in fright and plunge into the abyss. But instead of being dashed to pieces I lie in the arms of the Earth Mother. When I try to look into her face, she turns to clay
body: Thirty years after the moon-lady dream, the same woman, climbing a steep dark mountain in fantasy, finds a domed castle; within, a woman with a head-dress of cow's horns whom she recognizes as the moon-lady of her childhood. At her behest she crosses a narrow transparent bridge toward a dazzling sun — "If you can approach me nine times without being burned, all will be well" — but looking down sees "a black tentacle like that of an octopus groping towards me from underneath the sun", steps back and plunges into the abyss. "But instead of being dashed to pieces I lie in the arms of the Earth Mother. When I try to look into her face, she turns to clay, and I find myself lying on the earth." Jung: moon-lady above, Earth Mother below; the dreamer is in the role of the Kore (¶347).

occurrences.title: Racial-mother fantasy of the fifteen-year-old girl (clinical case, ~1899)
occurrences.label: Racial-mother fantasy of the fifteen-year-old…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Jung's own clinical precedent for the Miller material, observed "during the latter part of my medical studies": a fifteen-year-old girl whose outward demeanour gave no hint of the contents of her unconscious fantasy. "They were far-reaching fantasies of a positively mythical nature: the girl saw herself, in her split-off fantasy, as the racial mother of uncounted generations of men" (¶75).

Jung's generalization: elements of this fantasy are "probably common to all girls of her age," for "the unconscious is infinitely more common to all men than are the contents of their individual consciousnesses" — indeed "the unconscious is, in fact, the condensation of the average run of historical experience" (¶75). It anchors the volume's argument that individual fantasy draws on the collective creative substratum.

occurrences.title: Case Y i — the sky-woman and the bear (Diana / Dea Artio)
occurrences.label: Case Y i — the sky-woman and the bear
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: A woman comes down from the sky to accompany and help me. She is all bright with light hair and shining eyes... at her look the bear lies down quietly and lets us pass.
body: Case Y's first dream: on a lonely wild mountain the dreamer meets a bear-monster she must pass twice; a radiant woman "comes down from the sky to accompany and help me", vanishes, and returns — "at her look the bear lies down quietly and lets us pass". Jung: "a maternally protective goddess related to bears, a kind of Diana or the Gallo-Roman Dea Artio"; the sky-woman the positive, the bear the negative aspect of the supraordinate personality, extending the human being "upwards into the celestial and downwards into the animal regions" (¶340).

occurrences.title: The Sleeper of Hal Saflieni — hypogeum figurine, Malta
occurrences.label: The Sleeper of Hal Saflieni
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: In form she not infrequently resembles the neolithic ideal of the 'Venus' of Brassempouy or that of Willendorf, or again the sleeper of Hal Saflieni.
body: Jung names the corporeal ideal of the modern Earth Mother as she appears in women's unconscious: "In form she not infrequently resembles the neolithic ideal of the 'Venus' of Brassempouy or that of Willendorf, or again the sleeper of Hal Saflieni" (¶311, fn6 → Neumann, The Great Mother, pls. 1a, 1b). The Hal Saflieni "Sleeping Lady" — the obese reclining terracotta from the Maltese underground sanctuary — stands for Jung (with the two Venuses, mentioned only) as the a-temporal, purely somatic figure of the chthonic Great Mother.

image.title: Sleeping Lady, front view

occurrences.title: Case Y ii — the shrine of Ursanna: red stone temple, moon-bowl, 'Vis ut sis'
occurrences.label: Case Y ii — the shrine of Ursanna
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: It is the shrine of Ursanna, the bear-goddess and Mother of God in one. The temple is of red stone.
body: Case Y's second dream climbs a tower of steps inscribed "Vis ut sis" ("wish to be" / "may you be as...") to a temple on a wooded crest: the shrine of Ursanna, "the bear-goddess and Mother of God in one". Red stone; bloody sacrifices; entry only by transformation into a beast of the forest. The temple has "the form of a cross with equal arms and a circular space in the middle, which is not roofed, so that one can look straight up at the sky and the constellation of the Bear", with the moon-bowl steaming on the altar. Jung: the relation to the self is shown "not only by the oracle 'Vis ut sis' but by the quaternity and the circular central precinct of the temple"; stars symbolize eternity, the soul coming "from the stars" and returning (¶343); the bear-goddess expresses itself also in Cybele-Artemis.

occurrences.title: The Great Whore of Babylon — Revelation 17-18
occurrences.label: The Great Whore of Babylon — Revelation 17-18
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: "The piece de résistance is the destruction of the Great Whore of Babylon, the counterpart of the heavenly Jerusalem. The Whore is the chthonic equivalent of the sun-woman Sophia, with, however, a reversal in moral character" (¶721). The compensatory law: "If the elect turn themselves into 'virgins' in honour of the Great Mother Sophia, a gruesome fantasy of fornication is spawned in the unconscious by way of compensation."

Her fall silences "harpers and minstrels… the light of a lamp… the voice of bridegroom and bride" (18:22-23) — "the utter eradication of all life's joys and pleasures", which Jung pointedly connects with "the doom that has overtaken our modern art" at the end of the aeon Pisces (¶722). Against the vengeful rejoicing (¶724) stands the sun-woman's birth.

occurrences.title: The mother who became wolf and pig in psychosis — clinical case
occurrences.label: The mother who became wolf and pig in psychosis
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: In her psychosis she had herself become the symbol of the all-devouring mother.
body: A mother who "kept her children tied to her with unnatural love and devotion" breaks into the devouring-mother identity at the climacteric: "In her psychosis she had herself become the symbol of the all-devouring mother" (¶504). The clinical root of Jung's animal-as-Terrible-Mother reading of the bear, the roebuck, and the dragon.

occurrences.title: The mother on the chandelier and the horse through the window — prognostic dreams of a 17-year-old girl
occurrences.label: The mother on the chandelier…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: We must therefore look more closely into the meaning of the two main symbols, 'mother' and 'horse.' They must be equivalents, for they both do the same thing: they commit suicide.
body: Two dreams by which a seventeen-year-old girl, consulted over the differential diagnosis of progressive muscular atrophy vs hysteria, answered Jung's request for dreams: (1) coming home at night, "I see my mother hanging from the chandelier, swinging to and fro in the cold wind that blows in through the open windows"; (2) a frightened horse tears through the rooms of the house and "jumps through the hall window from the fourth floor into the street below... I was terrified when I saw it lying there, all mangled."

Jung's reading: "Mother" and "horse" must be equivalents — both commit suicide. Mother: place of origin, nature, matter, the womb, the vessel, the unconscious, the Yin idea; horse: the non-human, subhuman animal side, the unconscious body-life (Valkyries' horses, the Trojan horse, black night-horses that herald death). Interpretation: "The unconscious life is destroying itself... The animal life is destroying itself" (¶346, ¶348). The dreams pointed to a fatal organic outcome — "There is no mention of the death of the individual... When it is really a question of death, the dream speaks another language" — and the prognosis "was soon confirmed" (¶350). The classic locus for Jung's statements that "'Mother' is an archetype" and "'Horse' is an archetype."

occurrences.title: 'I am Isis, named dew' — magic papyrus of the night-spirit
occurrences.label: I am Isis, named dew
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: I am the mother of the gods, named heaven; I am Osiris, named water; I am Isis, named dew.
body: A papyrus text: "I am the mother of the gods, named heaven; I am Osiris, named water; I am Isis, named dew;... I am Eidolos, likened to the true spirits." Thus speaks a magician who wishes to conjure up his familiar — he himself is a spirit, akin to the bird of the night.
Jung at cw14 ¶727 under the bird-of-Hermes material: the cloud-rain-dew cycle behind the alchemical "water" that is at once sea, rain, and heaven.

occurrences.title: The Mothers and the fiery tripod — Goethe, Faust II
occurrences.label: The Mothers and the fiery tripod
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Mephistopheles sends Faust down "To the untrodden, / Untreadable regions" to the Mothers, throned "in no place, still less in any time", around a fiery tripod: "Formation, transformation, / Eternal Mind's eternal recreation."

Jung's reading: the fiery tripod is a mother-symbol from which Paris and Helen arise (the alchemical royal pair, ¶245); the Mothers are "thronged round with images of all creation" (¶373) — the primordial image of the mother as matrix of all forms.
Verbatim: They are the Mothers!... Formation, transformation, Eternal Mind's eternal recreation. (cw05 ¶245 / 373).

occurrences.title: The realm of the Mothers — Faust II, the key and the Mothers
occurrences.label: The realm of the Mothers
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Mephistopheles presses the key on Faust: "Here, take this key... The key will smell the right place from all others: Follow it down, it leads you to the Mothers!" (¶180). Jung reads the key as libido's "intuitive faculty, a strange power to 'smell the right place,' almost as if it were a live creature with an independent life of its own (which is why it is so easily personified)" (¶182) — "the dark creative power of the unconscious."

His reading of the realm: "The 'realm of the Mothers' has not a few connections with the womb (fig. 12), with the matrix, which frequently symbolizes the creative aspect of the unconscious" (¶182). There Faust finds the tripod, "the Hermetic vessel in which the 'royal marriage' is consummated," and with the phallic wand works "the greatest wonder of all — the creation of Paris and Helen" (¶182). The devil, as ever, is "part of that power which would / Ever work evil, but engenders good" (¶181).

occurrences.title: Mothers suffocating their infants during an Abyssinian slave raid (East Africa)
occurrences.label: Mothers suffocating their infants during…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: A tribe hidden in dense jungle while experienced slave-traders search close by: "the mothers held their little children by the throat, and in the moment when a child began to cry they just suffocated it, killed it on the spot. The mothers did it."

Jung uses the story for the terrible mother's fierceness, "all the more unexpected because it comes from the mother" — the maternal instinct continuous with destructiveness (the sow eating her litter, the hedgehog nest, the tiger turning on her grown young). From the child's side of the experience the archaic mother image is born. Dr. Schlegel adds that neonaticide was punished far more leniently.

occurrences.title: 'Don't you think all life is coming from the mountain?' — speech at Taos Pueblo (January 1925)
occurrences.label: Don't you think all life is coming…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: Three months before opening the seminar, Jung had visited the Taos Pueblo for a day or two. In Lecture 3 he uses this memory to characterize Freud: "When Freud talked of sexuality it was as though he were talking of God—as a man would talk who had undergone a conversion. It was like the Indians talking of the sun with tears in their eyes. I remember one Indian coming up softly behind me while I was looking at the mountain over the pueblo, and saying quite suddenly in my ear, 'Don't you think all life is coming from the mountain?'". The mountain as source of all life — the numinous locus the Pueblo people ritually serve — is Jung's touchstone for Freud's unconscious God-image in sexuality, and a first fruit of the America trip that also produced the seminar's Radin connection.

occurrences.title: 'I created the highest mountain-peak' — B.St.'s Finsteraarhorn summit (Burghölzli, ~1905)
occurrences.label: I created the highest mountain-peak
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: It was obviously an unusually vivid concretization of a fantasy-image such as otherwise occurs only in dreams.
body: Stereotypy: "I created the highest mountain-peak" — the Finsteraarhorn. In continuous association the peak is spun out of her linen-mending: enough mended linen to make a mountain, white as a sugar-cone, "white on top and blue below, hence Finsteraarhorn" (¶246). Within the same analysis an intermezzo surfaces: a mountain with big hotels where distinguished inhabitants live, "you had to descend the mountain for meals" — Jung thinks involuntarily of the Rigi, and the patient says she "only dreamt of it," though she spoke of it "as if it were something real, or at least a vision." The summit is the spatial form of her grandeur complex — the neologism "summit" collects all her titles (Socrates, Lorelei, Mary the mother of God, key of heaven, ¶224).

occurrences.title: Castle on the cliff — Jung's compensatory dream of the undervalued patient (Zurich, ~1900s)
occurrences.label: Castle on the cliff
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: In a dream I saw a castle perched on a high cliff, and on the topmost tower was a balcony, and there sat my patient.
body: Jung reports a dream of his own in the compensation chapter: "I myself once happened to put too low a value on a patient, both intellectually and morally. In a dream I saw a castle perched on a high cliff, and on the topmost tower was a balcony, and there sat my patient" (¶281).

Jung's reading: he "did not hesitate to tell her this dream at once, naturally with the best results" — the height-exaltation of the patient repairs the analyst's unconscious depreciation. It is the analyst-side twin of the brother-as-Caesar dream: where the conscious attitude pushes a person down, the unconscious enthrones them ("We all know how apt we are to make fools of ourselves in front of the very people we have unjustly underrated," ¶282).

occurrences.title: Initial dream pair: the village and the derailed train — the mountain-sickness case (patient-anon)
occurrences.label: Initial dream pair — the mountain-sickness case
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: It describes the patient's frantic haste to advance himself still further. But since the engine-driver in front steams relentlessly ahead, the neurosis happens at the back: the coaches rock and the train is derailed.
body: A self-made man, son of a poor peasant risen "to the spring-board" of further advancement, consults Jung with anxiety, dizziness, nausea and constriction of breath — "a state that might easily be confused with mountain sickness." Two initial dreams from the preceding night: (1) back in his birth village, schoolfellows in the street, one saying "He doesn't often come back to our village" — the dream says "You forgot how far down you began" (¶298); (2) a frantic packing-and-missing-the-train dream ending in catastrophe: the long train runs in a curious S-shaped curve, the engine-driver puts on steam, and "the rear coaches give a frightful lurch and are thrown off the rails" (¶299).

Jung's reading: the neurosis is a warning at the highest point of the climb — "the strain of the long ascent from his lowly origin has exhausted his strength" (¶301). The patient rejected the view, exploited the openings his ambition tempted him with, and "ran so violently off the rails that the catastrophe was realized in actual life" (¶302). The mountain sickness was "a symbolical representation of the patient's inability to climb any further" (¶303); the dreams gave aetiology, prognosis, and the point at which treatment should begin (¶305).

occurrences.title: Murder of the mother on the mountain, the barn of skulls and the 120 cows — dream of a girl
occurrences.label: Murder of the mother on the mountain, the barn…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Lucerne area (Glacier Garden in the dream imagery)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: But I got very angry at her and beat her to death with an ax that was lying around there, and the flesh was all hanging down.
body: Presented by Ilse Berg in three phases. On a high mountain walk the mother slaps the girl for nearing the precipice:

The board-bridge breaks; below, a barn "filled up" with dead persons and skulls — and a living man with 120 cows; the brothers milk, all drink. A bell summons an elevator; its cable breaks; she falls down a glass tube (Glacier Garden glacial mills) onto burning ground, where she sticks an unbreakable iron staff (crosier) into the fire and must sit on it "for ever and ever," until water gushes down and puts the fire out. With long fingernails she climbs to a house full of cakes and eats them all.

Jung: the normal world feels like a high mountain because part of her is stuck in the primal collective world; the bridge = continuity of consciousness (islands of consciousness, Chinvat); the barn-charnel-house = "the second mother," warm and fecund — the cow-barn for the cow, India's cow culture; 120 = rebirth-time numbers (four Babylonian months of 120 days; Abraxas 365; Prajapati the year; "time is a psychological function, identical with living as such," pdf p122). The staff-into-fire: procreation in the womb of the world; sitting in the soul-fire "until we are burned up... the transformation of the ego into spiritual, immortal man". With Isis/Demeter holding the divine child over fire — here without rebirth. "A child is always nearer the collective unconscious".

occurrences.title: Petrarch's ascent of Mont Ventoux
occurrences.label: Petrarch's ascent of Mont Ventoux
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Jung's landmark for the end of the medieval contempt of nature: "It was then that the poet Petrarch climbed a mountain for the first time to enjoy a beautiful view; he climbed Mont Ventoux in Provence, and the expedition was surrounded by all sorts of anticipations and fears because it was then supposed that mountain tops were inhabited by particular nature devils, so it amounted to an almost blasphemous boldness to climb to the heights".

He sets it within the arc he draws from the benedictio cerei — "the admixtio diabolicae fraudis" purged from all natural things — to the Renaissance "resurrection of the spirit of antiquity, and of the old feeling of connection with nature," culminating for Nietzsche's generation in the recognition "that the Christian principle was dead". The mountain that was devil-inhabited becomes the sage's place of enlarged consciousness.

occurrences.title: Stepping out into space from a mountain top — dream of Jung's acquaintance (~1916)
occurrences.label: Stepping out into space from a mountain top
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: Jung's most compact prospective-dream case in "The Transcendent Function": "An acquaintance of mine once told me a dream in which he stepped out into space from the top of a mountain. I explained to him something of the influence of the unconscious and warned him against dangerous mountaineering expeditions, for which he had a regular passion. But he laughed at such ideas. A few months later while climbing a mountain he actually did step off into space and was killed" (cw08 ¶164).

The dream is the counter-position announcing itself: the mountaineer's one-sided conscious passion is met by an inner image of exactly the fatal step. Disregarded, the compensatory warning was enacted. Jung draws the moral at ¶165: knowledge of the unconscious regulating influences renders much bad experience unnecessary.
Distinguish from Jung's own mountain dream, ascent-descent-mountain-dream-jung-pre-1940 (cw09i ¶335).

occurrences.title: The climber who stepped off the summit (dream six months before his death)
occurrences.label: The climber who stepped off the summit
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1930s (dream c. six months before the fatal fall)
occurrences.quote: In one dream he saw himself stepping off the summit of a high mountain into the air.
body: A man inextricably involved in shady affairs developed "an almost morbid passion for dangerous mountain-climbing as a sort of compensation: he was trying to 'get above himself.'" In one dream "he saw himself stepping off the summit of a high mountain into the air." Jung read it as meaning his death in a mountain accident and warned in vain: six months later, roping down a difficult place, "he let go of the rope 'as if he were jumping into the air,'" taking his young friend down with him (¶471).
The locus anchors Jung's rule that high-place dreams — vertiginous heights, flying, falling — accompany grandiose inflation, and that unheeded warnings are replaced by real accidents.

occurrences.title: Mountains are mountains — the three stages of Zen perception
occurrences.label: Mountains are mountains
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~9th c. tradition (Master Ch'ing-yüan Wei-hsin; saying transmitted via Suzuki)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: Before a man studies Zen, to him mountains are mountains and waters are waters; after he gets an insight into the truth of Zen … mountains are once more mountains and waters are waters.
body: The classic formulation of the satori transformation of perception, quoted by Jung in the Suzuki foreword as evidence that Zen aims not at regression but at a second naivety — the world regained after being de-absolutized:

Stage one: unconscious identity with the world. Stage two: detachment (the dissociation of the vision-quest). Stage three: return — the same mountains, now seen. Jung's parallel instinct draws him beside it to Eckhart, Silesius and the Theologia Germanica in the same footnote apparatus.

occurrences.title: Phoebus Smintheus — the Mouse-Apollo with mice under the altar
occurrences.label: Phoebus Smintheus — the Mouse-Apollo…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: The Greeks worshipped Phoebus Smintheus, that is, the Mouse-Apollo, in whose temple mice were kept under the altar.
body: In the transparent-mouse discussion: the Greeks worshipped Phoebus Smintheus, the Mouse-Apollo, in whose temple mice were kept under the altar, tended — an apotropaic magic. Apollo is not only the god of light but the bearer of death: his arrows bring the plague, the illness spread by mice and rats. The mouse is "an uncanny, deathly messenger"; a great mouse plague is an evil omen, bringing famine.
The cult condenses the dream's paradox: the deathly chthonic animal housed within the temple of light — mouse and god, exactly the mouse-to-human transformation the child dreamed.

occurrences.title: 'Some Suggestions about the Dream-Mouse' — the mice's conciliatory proposals (Linda Fierz-David)
occurrences.label: Some Suggestions about the Dream-Mouse
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: March 1930 (read aloud 26 Mar 1930; author identified in the 1939 index)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: As Parsifal before the Holy Grail, so man stands before woman's Eros.
body: An unsigned, brilliant jeu d'esprit laid on Jung's desk: "the mice have taken the liberty to send in the following conciliatory proposals" after the seminar's slighting discussion. The mouse is small, shy, nocturnal, greedy — and extraordinarily fertile: "an animal of darkness, of night, and of fertility", moon-life. A girl not afraid of mice has lost her virginity; woman's scream at a mouse means "Please ask now! — ask a question!": the mouse is "a symbol of woman's wish for fecundity", the Yin principle in its readiness to conceive; man's fear is "a pious fear", Logos afraid of Eros. And "the cat which eats the dream-mice is called Anima."

Jung: "This is excellent. I congratulate the unknown writer. That the anima is the cat that eats the dream-mice is decidedly a new consideration" (p581). The paper weaves Parsifal and the Grail question, and the French law "La recherche de la paternite est interdite".

occurrences.title: Bishop Hatto and the Mouse-Tower (Mäuseturm), Rhine near Bingen
occurrences.label: Bishop Hatto and the Mouse-Tower, Rhine near…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~10th c. (legend; tower destroyed by the Swedes, 1635)
occurrences.quote: But then the real mice came and attacked him, so he had to take refuge in that tower, and the mice followed him there and ate him alive.
body: Dr. Escher's medieval parallel to the ants that stamp out the patient's thread of fire: Bishop Hatto of Mainz, "a very bad man," locks hungry people into a barn during a famine and burns it, asking the onlookers whether they can hear the mice peeping. The real mice then come, swim the Rhine, and eat him alive in his tower — the Mäuseturm, destroyed by the Swedes in 1635.

Jung uses it diagnostically: visions that break up "into many analogous but smaller objects" signal the disintegration of a synthetic vision — the logic of delirium tremens, chronic intoxication, fever and dementia praecox — against which the patient's ants mark a dangerous regression at height ("the higher one builds, the more dangerous the fall").

occurrences.title: Girl's dream 4 — the mouse penetrated by worms, snakes, fishes, and humans (origin of mankind)
occurrences.label: Girl's dream 4 — the mouse penetrated…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1938-39 (dreams dreamt at age eight; presented at ten; died of an infectious disease about a year later)
occurrences.quote: A small mouse is penetrated by worms, snakes, fishes, and human beings. Thus the mouse becomes human. This is the origin of mankind in four stages.
body: Dream 4 of the Christmas booklet: "A small mouse is penetrated by worms, snakes, fishes, and human beings. Thus the mouse becomes human. This is the origin of mankind in four stages."

Jung's reading: with dream 5 (the water-drop world), this is one of "the cosmogonic myth[s] of the creation of the world and of man" — material "more analogous with primitive tales" than with anything Christian (¶529). The four-stage succession of invaders echoes initiation instruction about how the world and man were made (¶536), and the girl, he notes, "was rather surprised at finding them" — she did not seek these images, she came upon them (¶550).

occurrences.title: MS 'Figurarum aegyptiorum secretarum' — Jung's own 18th-century alchemical manuscript
occurrences.label: MS 'Figurarum aegyptiorum secretarum'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Sic fit, ut quod latuit, pateat.
body: An 18th-century Latin manuscript of 'Figures of the secret Egyptians' in Jung's own possession ("author's possession," noted twice). Fol. 19: "Duo tantum sunt coadjutores qui hic perficiuntur" (Only two are the helpers who are perfected here); fol. 27: "Sic fit, ut quod latuit, pateat" (So it comes to pass that what was hidden becomes manifest). Plate 4 of CW14 is reproduced from its fol. 20, similar to the Paris Codex pictures.

Jung's reading: manuscript evidence for the two-helper and hidden-made-manifest formulas of the conjunction stage. A physical locus of Jung's scholarly engagement. Parallels: ethiopian-treatise-creation-rainwater-17c, lapis "quod latuit" motifs.

occurrences.title: Mucius Scaevola's hand in the fire — Roman exemplar of endurance (Rome, legendary ~508 BCE)
occurrences.label: Mucius Scaevola's hand in the fire
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Rome (legend: siege by Lars Porsena of Clusium; Livy II.12–13)
occurrences.quote: which would be to credit them with the energy of a Mucius Scaevola—but with subconscious mechanisms which far exceed the strength of the initial conscious impulse
body: The youth Gaius Mucius, captured while assassinating an enemy of Rome, thrusts his right hand into the sacrificial fire and holds it there until it burns away — "Scaevola," the left-handed one, ever after. Jung reaches for the figure as the upper limit of conscious endurance: when a hysteric burns her own feet with sulphuric acid for a hospital stay, "we no longer have to reckon with the possibilities of normal psychology — which would be to credit them with the energy of a Mucius Scaevola — but with subconscious mechanisms which far exceed the strength of the initial conscious impulse" (¶305). The heroic fire-ordeal becomes the yardstick that hysterical automatism overtops.

occurrences.title: The mummy of the ancient king in the black cavern (Visions)
occurrences.label: The mummy of the ancient king…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: vision read 16 December 1931 (painted late 1929/early 1930 for Jung)
occurrences.quote: There I beheld the mummy of an ancient king encrusted with gold.
body: Led by the snake "down to a black cavern deep in the earth" — much deeper than the bull sacrifice — the patient finds the dead divine father her Great-Mother initiation lacked:

The voice: "Unwrap the linen winding sheet" — and out steps "a strange creature, half animal, half man": "I am he who dwells beneath the sphinx itself. Though you wind me with linen you cannot kill me for I am within you where I grow". Jung: Osiris "attained his greatest power only through his death"; the gold marks royal character like Tutankhamen's sarcophagus; the half-animal Osiris-man is "an entirely new idea… a representation of the spirit, as it appears to a woman in its genuine living form" — an animus "undergoing a resurrection or a rebirth ritual".

occurrences.title: Lenin's mummy — Mausoleum pilgrimage, Red Square
occurrences.label: Lenin's mummy — Mausoleum pilgrimage, Red Square
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: instead of the sacred body a place of pilgrimage with the mummy of the first witness.
body: Jung's compressed analogy for the totalitarian transposition of Christian symbols (cw18 ¶1328): as the star of Bethlehem announced God's incarnation, Soviet Russia has the red star; as Christianity had Dove and Lamb, the revolution has hammer and sickle; and "instead of the sacred body a place of pilgrimage with the mummy of the first witness" — Lenin's embalmed body in the Mausoleum, the State-religion's relic and shrine. The ancient mummy-image recurring as the sacralised corpse of a political godhead.

occurrences.title: The murderer under the bed — simulated psychosis of the millhand I.G. (Zurich, 1903)
occurrences.label: The murderer under the bed
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: maintained that he had killed his wife and that there was a murderer under the bed with a knife.
body: I.G., a vagrant millhand awaiting trial for bicycle theft, fills his cell nights with an unseen adversary: someone "always trying to get in," food "poisoned," "a murderer under the bed with a knife" — and he "maintained that he had killed his wife" (¶324). The tableau is repeated almost verbatim in the later medical-opinion version, adding poisonous spiders on the wall "as a sign that he was being poisoned" and a plaster rose on the ceiling that "would fall on top of him" (¶367–368). The prison doctor took him for a catatonic; Jung's opinion: mostly conscious simulation riding on an hysterical disposition, the role slipping by auto-suggestion into real disturbance (¶419–423). The under-bed murderer is the unseen nocturnal assailant — black-man family — staged, yet effective.

occurrences.title: The opus of adept and soror mystica — Mutus liber figs. 11–13
occurrences.label: The opus of adept and soror mystica
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: 'Psychology of the Transference' Epilogue n.1 (pdf p437)

occurrences.quote: Birds, being volatile creatures, stand for thoughts or the pluralistic animus, and the nixie corresponds to the anima.
body: Jung's Epilogue reading of the wordless book's picture-series, "where the adept and his soror mystica are shown performing the opus":

Fig. 11 — an angel wakes the sleeper with a trumpet. Fig. 12 — "the pair of alchemists kneel on either side of the Athanor (furnace) with the sealed phial inside it, and above them are two angels holding the same phial, which now contains Sol and Luna, the spiritual equivalents of the two adepts." Fig. 13 — the soror catches birds in a net while the adept hooks a nixie with rod and line.
"The undisguisedly psychic character of this portrayal of the opus is probably due to the fact that the book was written comparatively late — 1677."

occurrences.title: Mutus liber plate — angels presenting the vessel with the regenerated king (CW16 fig. 12)
occurrences.label: Mutus liber plate — angels presenting…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: La Rochelle (1677) → Geneva, Bibliotheca chemica curiosa (1702)
body: Second of the closing Mutus liber plates of the Psychology of the Transference (caption in chunk: "Figure 12"; description from the plate image). Upper register: a radiant sun and two angels holding up a glass vessel in which stands a naked bearded kingly man in a mandorla of rays — the manifestation of the perfected human within the vas. Lower register: the furnace/athanor tended by a kneeling adept and his wife, sea behind — the labouring couple below, the revelation above. The plate condenses the Rosarium series' death-resurrection sequence into one image: vessel as matrix (cf. cw16 p414 n2, "Per matricem, intendit fundum cucurbitae").

occurrences.title: Mutus liber final plate — cosmic sphere with God, sun and moon, and the fishing couple (CW16 fig. 13)
occurrences.label: Mutus liber final plate
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: La Rochelle (1677) → Geneva, Bibliotheca chemica curiosa (1702)
body: Third closing Mutus liber plate of the Psychology of the Transference (caption in chunk: "Figure 13"; description from the plate image). A great concentric world-sphere: God/angel enthroned on clouds at its summit, sun and moon flanking; within its rings, landscapes and seas, a couple drawing a net / angling from the waters (an erotic fishing scene), sea-creatures below. The opus displayed as a cosmic mandala with the coniunctio hidden as fishing in the mare — catching the lapis from the unconscious-sea; cf. Jung's fish material (Aion; cw16 p415 n7, lapis as al-shaitan).

occurrences.title: Mutus liber frontispiece — ladder, descending angel and sleeper (CW16 fig. 11)
occurrences.label: Mutus liber frontispiece
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: La Rochelle (1677) → Geneva, Bibliotheca chemica curiosa (1702)
body: One of the three textless Mutus liber plates with which the Psychology of the Transference closes (figs 11-13; reproduced from Bibliotheca chemica curiosa iii per the CW16 bibliography). The plate (described from the image; the chunk carries only the bare caption "Figure 11") shows an oval wreath framing a night scene: a ladder set from earth to a starry sky with crescent moon, an angel descending and scattering dew/seed from a sack, and a sleeper at the foot — Jacob's ladder as the opus's descent of heavenly dew upon the sleeping adept. Jung prints it without commentary here; his extended Mutus liber reading is in cw14 (¶436ff).

occurrences.title: Naassene hymn — the polymorphous Attis, 'dark rumour of Rhea'
occurrences.label: Naassene hymn — the polymorphous Attis, dark…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The Naassenes call the central figure the 'polymorphous Attis', young dying son of the Great Mother, 'the dark rumour of Rhea'; in the hymn his synonyms are Adonis, Osiris, Adam, Korybas, Pan, Bacchus, and 'shepherd of white stars' (¶311). He is the 'undivided point', 'present in the body' (¶310), the Naas as moist substance that 'contains within itself, like the horn of the one-horned bull, the beauty of all things' (¶311). Hippolytus objects that a point cannot have human form — precisely the objection the transcendent self always provokes. Parallels: monoimos-monad-iota-2c, naassene-water-above-firmament-2c.

occurrences.title: Naassene triad — the 'kingless race': Moses, Sephora, Mariam, Jothor
occurrences.label: Naassene triad — the 'kingless race'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The Naassenes derive all things from a triad: the 'blessed nature of the blessed Man on high, Adamas'; the mortal lower man; and 'the kingless race begotten from above' — 'Mariam the sought-for one, and Jothor the great wise one, and Sephora the seer, and Moses whose generation was not in Egypt' (¶328). Jung reads a marriage quaternio (husband Moses / wife Sephora / sister Mariam / brother Jethro) whose synonyms are mother-queen-anima and father-king-animus; its senarius extension gives the Shadow Quaternio (Ethiopian woman, Miriam the 'white' leper) (¶328-330). Basis of Jung's Moses Quaternio schema (¶359ff.).

occurrences.title: Naassenes — the water above the firmament and the Heracleian stone
occurrences.label: Naassenes — the water above the firmament…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The Naassenes map the four rivers of Paradise onto the senses — Pison = sight, Gihon = hearing, Tigris = smell, and the Euphrates = the mouth, 'through which prayers go out and food goes in' (¶288, ¶311). This fourth is the 'water above the firmament' of which the Saviour spoke: 'To this water comes every nature to choose its own substances... more certainly than iron to the Heracleian stone' (¶288). Jung: the water is the aqua doctrinae which 'perfects every nature in its individuality and thus makes man whole too', a magnetic power of integration — 'the doctrine is the magnet' (¶289). Eden is 'the brain' (¶311).

occurrences.title: The Birth of the Ganga — naga in the rock cleft, Mamallapuram
occurrences.label: The Birth of the Ganga
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram), Bay of Bengal, east-coast India

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: the naga is in a cleft of the huge boulder, and that is the source, the origin, of the heavenly river Ganges.
body: Enumerating snake rituals that assimilate the chthonic mana, Jung turns to India: "one finds those stone nagas nearly everywhere; they are supposed to be sort of goddesses or demons that come up from the ground. The river Ganges is represented as such a naga, woman above and serpent below." At Mamallapuram stands the great carved boulder "called The Birth of the Ganga; the naga is in a cleft of the huge boulder, and that is the source, the origin, of the heavenly river Ganges."

Jung's reading: the Ganges "spreads fertility over the greater part of the country, in contradistinction to the Indus which... flows through vast deserts" — the serpent-guarded cleft is the origin of the fertile water, the earth power made river. Like the Hopi dance and the Ophite bread-rite, the image binds serpent, earth, and the flow of life: "the chthonic powers bring fertility, health, duration, strength."

occurrences.title: 'He who is near me, is near the fire' — apocryphal word of the Lord
occurrences.label: He who is near me, is near the fire
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: The apocryphal saying with which Brunner's paper crowns its fire-amplification: "And Jesus Christ says, according to an apocryphal word of the Lord: 'He who is near me, is near the fire.' So the savior is of a fiery nature".

It stands at the end of a chain: Heraclitus' world created and perishing in fire, whose fire "is the power of God"; Simon Magus seeing "the dynamis of the fire at the origin of the cosmos... It is logos; it is the primeval unity and it is the root of the cosmos" (cf. CW11 §359, CW13 §408); and the alchemical "In this fire, which God created in the earth, just as he created the Purgatory in hell, God Himself is glowing in divine love." Through fire the soul "becomes the pure image, godlike and immortal."

occurrences.title: The Dream of Nebuchadnezzar — Speculum humanae salvationis, Codex Palatinus Latinus 413
occurrences.label: The Dream of Nebuchadnezzar
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: Frontispiece of CW8: a woodcut from the Speculum humanae salvationis ("mirror of human salvation"), a typological picture-book of the 14th–15th c., here from Codex Palatinus Latinus 413 in the Vatican. It shows Nebuchadnezzar's dream-madness from Daniel 4 — the king who, "at the height of his power," dreamt of the great tree and, suppressing the dream's warning, "was degraded to an animal" (cw08 ¶163).

Jung uses Nebuchadnezzar as "the classic case of megalomania": Daniel's expert interpretation got no hearing, the unconscious regulating influence was suppressed, and the counteraction broke through as psychosis. The volume's caption cross-references ¶163, ¶484f. and ¶559 (later essays in the same volume).
The dream locus itself: tree-nebuchadnezzar-dream-babylon-6cbce (also cited via cw13).

occurrences.title: The necklace before the great Chinese statue (Visions, 16 Mar 1932)
occurrences.label: The necklace before the great Chinese statue
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I walked away and as I walked trees swayed down towards the necklace and animals followed me. I beheld a great Chinese statue. Taking the necklace from my neck I placed it before the statue. Then I lay down to sleep for I was very weary.
body: Fleeing the pool she throws the whole necklace into the ocean; the waves cast it up cooler, and now "trees swayed down towards the necklace and animals followed me... like a cortege royal." She sets the necklace before a great Chinese statue and lies down to sleep.

Jung: cooled in the collective, she is dissolved - "it is participation mystique again. The trees want her jewels... There is a participation mystique between the jewel and nature which she has not fully accepted". The statue is "a petrified animus," a petrified historical Hermes or psychopompos - and specifically Chinese philosophy: "She probably shields herself behind the Tao-teh-king, taking the wisdom of the East to substitute for her own foolishness or incapability", a mitigated version of throwing the burden on the church. Lying down to sleep = fading into unconsciousness; the enantiodromia of the white temple follows.

occurrences.title: Nodfyr need-fire with Priapus image — Chronicle of Lanercost
occurrences.label: Nodfyr need-fire with Priapus image
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: To stop cattle murrain, monastery folk taught rustics to kindle fire by rubbing wood and to set up an image of Priapus; a Cistercian lay brother dipped a dog's testicles in holy water and sprinkled the herd.

Jung's reading: the rite "plainly reveals the sexual symbolism of the ceremonies" (¶212) — fire-making and sexuality are one symbolic act across cultures (with the Indian pramantha and the Wachandi dance).

Verbatim: certain cattle-breeders, monastery folk by habit or dress but not by disposition, taught the ignorant rustics to make fire by rubbing pieces of wood together, and to set up an image of Priapus (cw05 ¶212).

occurrences.title: Neith, 'Father of Fathers, Mother of Mothers' — Esne invocation
occurrences.label: Neith, 'Father of Fathers, Mother of Mothers'
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Invocations to Nit/Neith: "the mother who bore Ra... who, brought forth when there was nothing which brought forth. The Cow, the Ancient, who bore the sun and set the seeds of gods and men."
Jung's reading: Neith as feminine aspect of Nun-Amon, the primordial water "which was in the beginning" — "father of fathers, the mother of mothers" — the androgynous primary substance (¶358).
Verbatim: Nit, the Ancient, the Mother of God, Mistress of Esne, Father of Fathers, Mother of Mothers, who is the Scarab and the Vulture, who was in the beginning. (cw05 ¶358).

occurrences.title: Picasso's Blue Period as Nekyia — descent into the Tuat-blue underworld
occurrences.label: Picasso's Blue Period as Nekyia
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Spirit in Man, Art and Literature (CW15)

occurrences.quote: the blue of night, of moonlight and water, the Tuat-blue of the Egyptian underworld. He dies, and his soul rides on horseback into the beyond.
body: The opening phase of Picasso's oeuvre as read by Jung in 1932: "Picasso starts with the still objective pictures of the Blue Period—the blue of night, of moonlight and water, the Tuat-blue of the Egyptian underworld" (cw15 ¶210).

Jung's reading. It is the first movement of the symbolic series every patient's work begins with — "the symbol of the Nekyia—the journey to Hades, the descent into the unconscious, and the leave-taking from the upper world" (cw15 ¶210). "He dies, and his soul rides on horseback into the beyond. The day-life clings to him, and a woman with a child steps up to him warningly" — the light and the dark soul (anima). "The motif of the prostitute begins with the entry into the beyond, where he, as a departed soul, encounters a number of others of his kind." The descent continues through Harlequin to the union of opposites (¶213), though Jung refuses to prophesy the outcome (¶214).

occurrences.title: Nerthus, Mother Earth, drawn in a cow-carriage to the humans (Tacitus)
occurrences.label: Nerthus, Mother Earth, drawn…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: From Cornelia Brunner's paper on the wedding carriage: "Tacitus relates the journey of Nerthus: each year in winter a priest leads the goddess Nerthus—Mother Earth—to the humans in a carriage drawn by cows. Then come peaceful times and happy days. Nerthus is the Ur-mother of humankind".

"The wagon journey and the marriage of the divine couple anticipate, in the form of a ritual, future events. In Nerthus's case, the fertility of the approaching spring should be furthered." Related ritual survivals named: the Sechseläuten procession, the carnival parade, the Walpurgis-night King Lenz (King Lucifer) freeing life from the winter giant (after De Coster). The wedding carriage of the dream belongs to this family of divine wagons.

occurrences.title: Dissolved human body as spiders' webs — chaos picture (second patient)
occurrences.label: Dissolved human body as spiders' webs
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: First of two photographs of pictures "made by another patient": "one gets the impression of a terribly cut-up condition: it looks like sort-of spiders' webs. This is a state of complete chaos... a close analysis shows that it is a dissolved human body; one can discern an eye in it, and in the original... other organs and blood".

"This would point to a schizophrenic condition, but it is a liquid schizophrenia, not a congealed case — a latent psychosis... as if those sharp splits, like splitting wood or ice with sharp edges, might eventually cut the whole human being into fragments". Next move: serpent-chaos-coils-patient-picture-zurich-1930s — from one day to the next the chaos "lost its multitudinous quality and became... personified" in the great serpent.

occurrences.title: The 'house of the net' — temple of Thoth
occurrences.label: The 'house of the net' — temple of Thoth
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Egyptian temple (date not given by Jung; inferred New Kingdom era)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: Then peculiarly enough, the temple of Thoth is called the house of the net-the fisherman's net-and the Babylonian Marduk is the Logos and his attribute is also the net.
body: "Now peculiarly enough, the temple of Thoth is called the house of the net — the fisherman's net — and the Babylonian Marduk is the Logos and his attribute is also the net." Jung builds the Logos-net chain across three traditions in a single breath: Thoth (anticipation of the Logos, hence of Christ), Marduk (Logos with the net), and the Pope with his fisher ring.

The interpretive point is the net itself: "the Logos worked like a net which gathered in mankind like a swarm of fishes; the power of the word, a concept, an idea, a point of view, is really like a net. It constellates, it brings together, it unites. You learn once that two things are the same and they will remain the same forever. This is the creative power of the mind." The temple-name makes the word's catching function sacred space.

occurrences.title: Nietzsche's dream: the father rises from the grave with a child
occurrences.label: Nietzsche's dream — the father rises…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1849 (just after the father's death, before the brother's)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: He hurried into the church and in a moment or two reappeared with a small child in his arms.
body: The childhood dream Jung quotes as evidence that Nietzsche was "concerned with an archetypal memory" the theologian-father's wisdom could not explain: "A grave suddenly opened and my father in his shroud arose out of it. He hurried into the church and in a moment or two reappeared with a small child in his arms" (pdf p1240, footnote — recorded by the sister just after the father's death and just before that of the young brother, who dies in the dream's arms).

Jung pairs it with "the howling dog, remembered from his sixth year, in Thus Spake Zarathustra, ch. 46, 'The Vision and the Enigma'" — the same complex of forebodings as the Wotan dream at fifteen and the awful cry.

occurrences.title: 'Rather a professor in Basel than God' — Nietzsche's letter to Burckhardt, Turin
occurrences.label: Rather a professor in Basel than God
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939
jung.locator: Lecture VII, read from Salin (pdf p1351)

occurrences.quote: Alas, I would have much preferred to be a professor in Basel rather than God.
body: Jung opens Lecture VII by translating from Edgar Salin's Burckhardt und Nietzsche the letter of 6 January 1889, written in Turin at the threshold of Nietzsche's psychosis: "Alas, I would have much preferred to be a professor in Basel rather than God, but I did not dare to push my private egotism so far as to omit the creation of the world on account of that professorship. You see one has to sacrifice something — where and how one lives."

Jung's reading: "This was in the beginning of his disease and it shows how he understood his role: he really believed he had become God, or something like God, and had to create a new world, and therefore could not be an ordinary human being". It confirms the thesis stated the week before: "by denying the existence of god, in declaring God to be dead, he himself became God; and he realized that it would have been better to have remained a professor in Basel".
