Jung adds the human frame: "I was a boy when he was a professor at the university... I saw his friend Jakob Burckhardt very often, and also Bachofen... we were not separated by cosmic distances".

occurrences.title: Nietzsche's Noontide Vision at Surlei
occurrences.label: Nietzsche's Noontide Vision at Surlei
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Surlei, Engadine, Switzerland ('6000 feet beyond man and time')

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

jung.year: Nietzsches Lehre von der ewigen Wiederkehr

body: Nietzsche's "classic example" of an immediate (ritual-less) experience of the transcendence of life: standing by the pyramid-shaped rock at Surlei, he suddenly saw. Zarathustra's Noontide Vision: "Hath time flown away? Do I not fall? Have I not fallen — hark! — into the well of eternity?"; even the "golden ring", the "ring of return", appears "as a promise of resurrection and life" (¶211).

Jung's reading: Nietzsche substitutes for the Christian mystery the myth of Dionysus-Zagreus, dismembered and come to life again; the Deity appears in the garb of Nature as antiquity saw it, the moment of eternity is the noonday hour sacred to Pan — "It is just as if Nietzsche had been present at a performance of the mysteries."

occurrences.title: Nietzsche's psychosis — identification with the Crucified and the dismembered Dionysus (Turin, 1889)
occurrences.label: Nietzsche's psychosis
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: The terminal event of Nietzsche's breakdown as Jung reads it in "The Transcendent Function": "As is well known, Nietzsche's psychosis first produced an identification with the 'Crucified Christ' and then with the dismembered Dionysus. With this catastrophe the counteraction at last broke through to the surface" (cw08 ¶162).

The sequence is diagnostic for Jung: years of suppressed unconscious regulation in Zarathustra (the "higher men" and the "ugliest man" forced back into the cave by the lion of moral conviction) did not neutralize the counterposition but charged it, until it erupted as psychosis with archaic mythological content — the crucified god and the torn-apart god. A paradigm case of the compensatory counteraction overwhelming a one-sided consciousness.

occurrences.title: Joseph in the cistern, Christ in the sepulchre, Jonah in the whale — Biblia pauperum
occurrences.label: Joseph in the cistern, Christ…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 170. The night sea journey. Joseph in the cistern, Christ in the sepulchre, Jonah swallowed by the whale.
body: Typological blockbook page setting the three descents side by side: Joseph thrown in the cistern, Christ laid in the sepulchre, Jonah swallowed by the whale — the night sea journey as prefiguration-chain.

Jung's reading: the "ritual katabasis eis antron, the perilous adventure of the night sea journey," images the descent of the conscious mind into the unconscious, "whose end and aim is the restoration of life, resurrection, and the triumph over death" (¶436). The belly-heat is the ignis gehennalis, the hell Christ entered "in order to conquer death as part of his opus" (¶440).

image.title: Biblia Pauperum - British Library manuscript King's 5 - Folio 20 - Jonah
image.credit: The Master of the Hours of Margaret of Cleves (Lisbon, Museum Calouste Gulbenkian, Ms. LA 148)

occurrences.title: Hiawatha swallowed by Mishe-Nahma the fish-king — Song of Hiawatha
occurrences.label: Hiawatha swallowed by Mishe-Nahma the fish-king
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Often the monster is killed by the hero lighting a fire inside him—that is to say, in the very womb of death he secretly creates life, the rising sun.
body: The eighth-canto battle: swallowed with his canoe, the hero smites the heart of Nahma, crosses the canoe for safety, and the fish dies and drifts ashore, where a bird helps him out. Jung's worldwide formula: "in the very womb of death he secretly creates life, the rising sun"; the rescue "is at the same time a sunrise, the triumph of consciousness" (¶538–539).

occurrences.title: Ishtar's descent to free Tammuz from Ereshkigal — water of life over the dead lovers
occurrences.label: Ishtar's descent to free Tammuz from Ereshkigal
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~2nd millennium BCE tradition (Semitic countries, 'since prehistoric times')

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: His death induces her to go on a journey through the underworld. In doing so, she falls into the hands of Ereshkigal, goddess of the underworld, who wants to keep Tammuz for herself and takes Ishtar prisoner.
body: Told by Ilse Berg as the closing amplification of the mountain-murder dream. Ishtar, Asian goddess of love and war whose animal is the lion, transforms the men she desires into animals (against Gilgamesh she unleashes the heavenly bull); the only one she truly loves is the young Tammuz, the dying-and-rising shepherd.

"This myth ends in the same way as that part of the dream just discussed. A gush of water pours down on the dreamer, too, the fire goes out, and she can again reach a higher level... This myth confirms anew that this is about a rebirthing process". For the presenter the archetype of Ishtar is "of special significance for this girl."

occurrences.title: Nganaoa in the whale's belly with his parents — the Rata cycle, Polynesia
occurrences.label: Nganaoa in the whale's belly with his parents
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: oral tradition (published Frobenius, Zeitalter des Sonnengottes, 1904)
occurrences.quote: Then Nganaoa leapt into the maw of the great whale (devouring of the hero) and peered down into his belly... There sat his two parents
body: The watchful Nganaoa defeats a giant clam, an octopus, and finally a great whale whose jaws close around the boat. Leaping into the maw, he finds his two parents — swallowed long before while fishing — sitting alive in the belly. He breaks his spear into fire-sticks, kindles fire inside the monster with his father's help, heats the heart-fat, and the dying whale swims to land, where father, mother, and son step out through the open gullet.

Jung prints the tale whole in the dual-mother chapter: devouring, discovery of the parents within, fire-boring inside the monster, and release — the dragon-whale mythogram complete, with the hero's rebirth achieved as a family delivery.

occurrences.title: Zarathustra's ship over the sleeping sea — night sea-journey
occurrences.label: Zarathustra's ship over the sleeping sea
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Zarathustra III, 'The Wanderer' → 'On the Vision and the Riddle'

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: he descends again to the sea where he takes a boat. That is the old symbol of the night sea-journey, navigating on the sea of the unconscious to reach the new country, and that is the transitus.
body: After crossing the mountain divide, Zarathustra descends to the sea and takes ship ("Ah, this sombre, sad sea, below me! Ah fate and sea! To you must I now go down!"), sails two days silent among sailors "who make distant voyages", and on board tells the enigma of the shepherd and the serpent.

Jung's reading: "That is the old symbol of the night sea-journey, navigating on the sea of the unconscious to reach the new country, and that is the transitus". "The sea is, of course, the unconscious to which he has to descend, and it means fate also, because the unconscious is fate. There the roots are, and whatever your roots are, is what you will get". The sea sleeps and dreams on "hard pillows", groaning "with evil recollections! Or evil expectations?" — Nietzsche's projection; "Those dreams are divine, creative thoughts — the very life of nature".

occurrences.title: The Night-Song — the light that cannot receive
occurrences.label: The Night-Song — the light that cannot receive
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: Nacht ist es: nun reden lauter alle springenden Brunnen. Und auch meine Seele ist ein springender Brunnen.
body: The chapter Jung calls "the substance and the immortal merit of the book" — the first place where Nietzsche's language "becomes truly musical... a descriptive quality from the unconscious which the intellect can never produce." Zarathustra, all light, drinks "the flames into himself," knows "the happiness of the taking one" not at all, and discovers the hunger of the bestower: giving that turns into robbery, "I should like to rob those I have gifted: -thus do I hunger for wickedness."

Jung reads it as confrontation with the spirit's two sides — "its superhuman light and its cosmic coldness" — pride and humility, heat and ice, the encounter with the deity that antiquity would have called a rencontre; suns "cold, despite all heat... the image or the allegory of the hunger of the spirit." Nietzsche recited both the German opening and close in seminar.

occurrences.title: Zarathustra's dream: night-watchman in the mountain-fortress of Death
occurrences.label: Zarathustra's dream
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: Night-watchman and grave-guardian had I become, aloft, in the lonely mountain-fortress of Death.
body: The text-dream that answers the volcano: after three days without meat or drink, Zarathustra dreams he has renounced all life and become "Night-watchman and grave-guardian... aloft, in the lonely mountain-fortress of Death" — "full stood the musty vaults of those trophies of victory. Out of glass coffins did vanquished life gaze upon me." He carries "the rustiest of all keys"; the creaking gate gives way to silence, "that malignant silence" — "the stillest hour" — and then: "a roaring wind... a merciless wind is tearing out with a thousand laughters."

Jung: "the wind is a spirit... That is insanity very clearly-those distorted figures. Insanity is the secret, the utter destruction of his mind". The wind that is Zarathustra throughout now tears out of the grave-castle — the honest report, "an impartial, unadulterated voice which has not been twisted," where one's feeling can follow at last.

occurrences.title: 'Accipe hominem, tonde eum' — the torture of the anthropos in the Allegoriae
occurrences.label: Accipe hominem, tonde eum
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Accipe hominem, tonde eum, et trahe super lapidem … donec corpus eius moriatur …
body: The rawest formulation of the opus as torture of the human substance: "Take a man, shave him, and drag him over a stone … until his body dies …" — the anthropos himself is the material of the mortification. The same note preserves the Rosarium's admission: "Nonnulli perierunt in opere nostro" (not a few have perished in our work).

Jung adduces it (Part II ch. 4, n. 46) where the Visio Arislei's Thabritius is killed and reborn in Beya's womb: the alchemical suffering of the king's son is not metaphor but a ritual dismemberment of the ego-figure, the psychic danger the dreams of the "perishing" seeker echo. Fear of ghosts here means "the overpowering of consciousness by the autonomous contents of the unconscious" (n. 43).

occurrences.title: Hoyle's 'The Black Cloud' — the globulus nigredo and the fatal encounter (novel, 1957)
occurrences.label: Hoyle's 'The Black Cloud'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: a nigredo like that described in the Aurora consurgens, a treatise ascribed to St. Thomas Aquinas
body: Fred Hoyle's science-fiction "frolic": a dark gas cloud (globulus) the size of the earth's orbit swings into the solar system, feeds on the sun, kills much of earthly life with heat, then brings "a total extinction of light and a more than Egyptian darkness lasting for about a month." Its nervous system communicates by radio; the two scientists who receive its knowledge directly die — the genius-mathematician hero in delirium.

Jung reads it as the Ufo problem again: the darkness is "a nigredo like that described in the Aurora consurgens... 'Beholding from afar I saw a great cloud looming black over all the earth, which had absorbed the earth and covered my soul'" (¶811). The collision is psychic: consciousness "perceives the totality only in projected form, outside itself, and cannot integrate it as a subjective phenomenon" (¶814); the political analogue is "National Socialism and... the Communist inundation" (¶818). "The encounter with the unconscious ends bootlessly" (¶819).

occurrences.title: 'I am black and swarthy' — Aurora Consurgens, Parable VII
occurrences.label: I am black and swarthy
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Aurora Consurgens, Parable VII: 'Be turned to me with all your heart and do not cast me aside because I am black and swarthy, because the sun hath changed my colour and the waters have covered my face... for I stick fast in the mire of the deep and my substance is not disclosed. Wherefore out of the depths have I cried... if any shall find one like unto me, I will give into his hand the morning star' (cw14 ¶468). Jung: 'the sunken king forms a parallel to Parable VII of Aurora Consurgens' (¶468). Sophia-as-nigredo speaks in the first person — the despised substance crying from the depths, promising the morning star to her finder.

occurrences.title: Disaster from a technical blunder — Wei Po-yang's opus
occurrences.label: Disaster from a technical blunder
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Wei Po-yang (Ts'an t'ung ch'i, ~142 CE), 'quite uninfluenced by Western alchemy', on a technical blunder in the opus: 'Disaster will come to the black mass... The right essence will be exhaled and the evil one inhaled. Days and nights will be passed without sleep, moon after moon. The body will then be tired out, giving rise to an appearance of insanity. The hundred pulses will stir and boil so violently as to drive away peace of mind and body... Ghostly things will make their appearance... all of a sudden he is seized by an untimely death' (cw14 ¶495). The Chinese parallel proves the nigredo's psychic dangers are archetypal, not a medieval Latin fantasy — the same 'appearance of insanity' Dorn's vesania names.

occurrences.title: The secret laboratory and the radioactive isotope — dream, Sweden, 15 Jul 1954
occurrences.label: The secret laboratory and the radioactive…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters
jung.locator: 'Statements by the Psyche' + Jung's Letter 71 (pdf pp196-197, 215)

occurrences.quote: What occurred to me at once about the laboratory is that the unconscious is a laboratory in which the individuation process takes place.
body: Opening dream of the 1954 series dedicated to Jung with Mysterium Coniunctionis I–II. Gustafson of Lund shows the dreamer a secret laboratory where "a radioactive isotope has been isolated"; he knew nothing of it. Weeks earlier the dreamer had stood under the total solar eclipse of 30 June 1954 in southern Sweden — darkness at noon without visible corona.

Jung: "the eclipse is to be understood as nigredo — i.e., as a darkening of consciousness, which always occurs when crucial things are going on in the unconscious"; the isolated radioactive isotope is "an essential content of the unconscious," the Self "still a very unusual, a familiar element" not yet central; "radioactive" = numinous. The secret lab "immediately upset me, and I determined to work on bringing it out into the open — i.e., making it conscious." Continues directly in trinity-three-popes-house-dream-copenhagen-1954.

occurrences.title: The nigredo standing on the rotundum, i.e. sol niger — Mylius, Philosophia reformata (1622)
occurrences.label: The nigredo standing on the rotundum, i.e. sol…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Mylius's blackened figure standing on the round chaos — Jung's caption: "The nigredo standing on the rotundum, i.e., sol niger.".

Cited at ¶140 where Jung links gnostic and alchemical black suns: "the Monogenes is called the 'dark light,' a reminder of the sol niger, the black sun of alchemy (fig. 34)." The nigredo is "the first stage of the work, which was felt as 'melancholia' in alchemy and corresponds to the encounter with the shadow in psychology" (¶41).

occurrences.title: Noah in the Ark — enamelled altar of Nicholas of Verdun
occurrences.label: Noah in the Ark — enamelled altar…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Fig. 21: Noah's ark on the enamelled altar (1186) — the chest floating on the Flood that kills all living things, saving one family and the animals for a new creation.

Jung's reading: the ark is "an analogy of the womb, like the sea into which the sun sinks for rebirth" (¶311); a close parallel to the Frobenian night-sea-journey — the chest/barrel floating on the water as the sun's course.
Verbatim: The ark (fig. 21), chest, casket, barrel, ship, etc. is an analogy of the womb, like the sea into which the sun sinks for rebirth. (cw05 ¶311).

occurrences.title: Noah's Ark with the lid underneath — dream of the child 'Anna'
occurrences.label: Noah's Ark with the lid underneath
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Days after being told that children never grow in fathers, Anna announced at lunch: "I had a dream last night about Noah's Ark." Only on the third telling did the decisive image come: a lid underneath that opened, and all the little animals fell out.

Jung's reading: the children's real toy ark opened on the roof, "but the opening, a lid, was in the roof and not underneath" (¶32) — the dream quietly corrects the mouth/chest birth theories she had been given: the animals (babies) come out "from underneath." Child symbolism preserving the cloacal theory the adults' enlightenment was meant to replace.
Quote. "I had a dream last night about Noah's Ark and there were lots of little animals in it and underneath there was a lid which opened and all the little animals fell out."

occurrences.title: Nous caught by his reflection in the chaotic waters (Gnostic myth)
occurrences.label: Nous caught by his reflection…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: instantly the Physis leapt up and took him in and he dissolved in matter.
body: The myth Jung sets under Nietzsche's sinking into the Yin: "the Nous of the Gnosis was attracted by his own reflection in the chaotic waters, and instantly the Physis leapt up and took him in and he dissolved in matter. Now the result of it was the creation of man, the ordinary man. The anthropos was the second man, who was born from that embrace".

Two standpoints are held apart, never reconciled: from Nietzsche's side it is an ordinary human depression into Yin; from Zarathustra's it is the eternal four-dimensional spirit entering space and matter — "the eternal myth of the descent of the spirit is repeated once more." Zarathustra is thereby "something like the first man, the Adam Cadmon of the Cabalists or the Primus Adam of medieval philosophers. And we are the second Adam."

occurrences.title: The analyst's bill: 315 francs, 1 franc interest (extramarital-affair patient, Zurich, ~1910)
occurrences.label: The analyst's bill: 315 francs, 1 franc interest
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: He received a bill from the analyst charging him interest of 1 franc on a sum of 315 francs for delay in payment from the 3rd to the 29th September.
body: Third dream of the same series: "He received a bill from the analyst charging him interest of 1 franc on a sum of 315 francs." The reproach of meanness covers "a strong unconscious envy": the analyst has just had another child, the patient's marriage permits none. The numbers do the envy's arithmetic: 315 = 3 children + 1 new; the patient "would have had 5 children if all were living," has 2 (3 stillborn, 2 miscarriages); the 26 days' delay = the lost months of pregnancy, added to the two successful 9-month pregnancies makes 44; 315 and 342 "added crosswise, each gives a total of 9. Now 9 − 8 = 1." Jung follows the patient's own number game to the edge of play and warns against despising it: "1 franc may therefore mean 1 child" (¶142).

occurrences.title: 'Aucker': 206 becomes 306 — number dream, Sweden, 11 Aug 1954
occurrences.label: Aucker' — 206 becomes 306
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: The transformation from 2 to 3 seems positive, indicating some sort of realisation.
body: An important letter found in Sweden says the dreamer differs from C. G. Jung in that "the number 206 has changed to 306," signed "Aucker" — a puzzle Pauli could do little with; he suspected repression (the letter's beginning unremembered) and camouflage. His factorisations: 206 = 2·103; 306 = 2·3·3·17; digit sums 2+0+6 = 8 = 2, 3+0+6 = 9 = 3. Jung: "The name Aucker could also be auctor."

Pauli's working hypothesis: analytical psychology "has remained in the dependent relationship of the younger brother" on natural science, whereas it "should represent the Fourth and hence the whole — i.e., 4:3 instead of 2:3 — proportio sesquitertia instead of sesquialtera". The dream that "took place in Sweden indicates that the transformation 2->3 has already 'secretly' begun there."

occurrences.title: Gambling on 152 — 'You are sadly cheated' (extramarital-affair patient, Zurich, ~1910)
occurrences.label: Gambling on 152 — 'You are sadly cheated'
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The patient said he gambled, and always on a very high number: 152. The analyst remarked: 'You are sadly cheated.
body: Second dream of the same patient: the analyst asks what he does with his mistress; he gambles, "always on a very high number: 152," and the analyst remarks, "You are sadly cheated." Analysis: 152 francs ≈ the affair's monthly cost; and the reproach of being cheated is the defloration dispute — she claims he deflowered her, he is "quite convinced that she was not a virgin." The word "number" slides to glove size, calibre, "a remarkable width of the opening instead of the expected resistance of the hymen" (¶135). The number also sums the mistress's successive house numbers (17 + 129 + 48 − 48 + 6 = 152). Sexual suspicion, accounting, and topography converge on one integer.

occurrences.title: 'Luke 137' — the Annunciation as number dream (analyst's wife, Zurich, ~1910)
occurrences.label: Luke 137' — the Annunciation as number dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: His wife had the following dream: she dreamt–and this is the whole dream–Luke 137.
body: The patient's wife — "not at all well up in the Bible... not in the least religious" — dreams a single item: "Luke 137." The number splits into her conflict: analyst 1 more child (had 3); she counts miscarriages and wishes 1+3+7 = 11 children "a twin number, 1 and 1," her mother having had twins; "finished" at 44 like her dead father. Seeking the reference she opens the Bible at random — Acts 1:7, "It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power" — but the true address is Luke 1:35–37, the Annunciation: Elizabeth "conceived a son in her old age... For with God nothing shall be impossible." The chain completes with Luke 13:7 (the unfruitful fig tree — "since ancient times a symbol of the male genitals" — cut down: the impotent husband) and Luke 7:13 (the widow's only son raised: his cure). Jung: "Since the dreamer was totally ignorant of the Bible, 'Luke 137' must be regarded as a cryptomnesia" (¶152).

occurrences.title: The season-ticket number 2477 (extramarital-affair patient, Zurich, ~1910)
occurrences.label: The season-ticket number 2477
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: the dreamer shows his season ticket to the conductor. The conductor protests at the high number on the ticket. It was 2477.
body: First of the number dreams from a middle-aged man in conflict over an extramarital love-affair: "the dreamer shows his season ticket to the conductor. The conductor protests at the high number on the ticket. It was 2477." Free association builds the number out of the family's dates and ages — his own and his mother's birthday (26.II), his mistress (28.VIII), his wife (1.III), his two children, the years of birth, his 36 and her 25 — whose sum is exactly 2477. The conductor's appearance pointed to the analyst, "from whom the patient both feared and wished firm control as well as sharp censure of his dependent state" (¶133). An ungentlemanly unconscious reckoning-up of the affair's costs turns into a portrait of the whole family constellation.

occurrences.title: 'God can also appear to you like this' — the Somali headman's blade of grass (1925 expedition)
occurrences.label: God can also appear to you like this
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung's often-repeated anecdote: "my Somali head man in Africa, who picked up a blade of grass and said: 'God can also appear to you like this.' In a drop of dew, in a flower, in a shooting star, in any humble animal that crosses your path, even in a ray of sun on a tin dish, as it happened to Jakob Boehme."

In the seminar it anchors the religious attitude — "an attitude of great totality, so that you receive the next leaf that falls from the tree as a message from God, and it works" — against the aesthetic attitude that multiplies telegraphic visions without being changed by any of them.

occurrences.title: Nut the heavenly cow giving birth to the sun — tomb of Seti I
occurrences.label: Nut the heavenly cow giving birth to the sun
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Valley of the Kings, Thebes (tomb of Seti I); Dendera-type reliefs
body: Figs. 24-25: Nut with starry body as the heavenly cow dotted with stars, swallowing and bearing the sun daily; from Naunet of the primordial flood-waters (nun).

Jung's reading: "when the sun-god Ra retires on the back of the heavenly cow, it means that he is going back into the mother in order to rise again as Horus. In the morning the goddess is the mother, at noon she is the sister-wife, and at evening once more the mother" (¶360).
Verbatim: From her sprang Nut, the sky-goddess, who is represented with a starry body or as a heavenly cow dotted with stars (figs. 24, 25). (cw05 ¶359).

occurrences.title: The King's bath in the hollow oak — Bernard Trevisan's parable
occurrences.label: The King's bath in the hollow oak
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the oak, as the feminine numen, has taken the place of the Queen
body: Trevisan's parable of the adept who finds "a clear spring set about with the finest stone and 'secured to the trunk of an oak-tree,' the whole surrounded by a wall." Hermes the mystagogue explains that the King had his renewal-bath built by placing in it "an old oak, 'cloven in the midst'... first it was enclosed in hard, bright stone, then in a hollow oak" (¶74).

Jung's reading is delicate: the Queen is missing from the nuptial bath, so "the oak, as the feminine numen, has taken the place of the Queen" (¶75). The tree is at once "stock" (source of the fountain), "trough" (vessel) and "protecting tree" (mother); "From ancient times the tree was man's birthplace... The alchemists called both the vessel and the bath the 'womb.'" In the Ripley Scrowle the tree stands in the bath with a snake-tailed mermaid = anima; the Dodonian oak houses the oracle.

occurrences.title: Priest with fish-mask representing Oannes — Nimrud relief
occurrences.label: Priest with fish-mask representing Oannes
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Fig. 18: the fish-cloaked priest as Oannes-Ea, who "daily came out of the sea as a fish to teach the people wisdom".

Jung's reading: Khidr born "as a 'son of the watery deep'... like the Babylonian Oannes-Ea" (¶291); Oannes' name "brought into connection with John's" — the Baptist's water-and-fire baptism (Matthew 3:11) (¶292).
Verbatim: who was represented in fish form and daily came out of the sea as a fish to teach the people wisdom. (cw05 ¶291).

occurrences.title: 'Oculatus abis' — Hermes united with artifex and soror — Mutus liber finale
occurrences.label: Oculatus abis' — Mutus liber finale
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Hermes as Anthropos, united with the artifex and soror through the threefold cord.
body: The final plate of the wordless book: Hermes as Anthropos united with the artifex and his soror mystica by the threefold cord; Hercules below (a favourite symbol "because of his opera"); the ladder in the background, no longer needed. Inscription: "oculatus abis" — provided with eyes, thou goest thy way.

Jung reads the Mutus liber as the opus stripped to pure image: the ladder of ascent discarded once the threefold cord (body, soul, spirit of the transforming substance) holds the union — the filius philosophorum comparable to the mystical body of the Church.

occurrences.title: Odin on an equal-armed cross — the window in Bremen (1933)
occurrences.label: Odin on an equal-armed cross
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "Then I am told that in a house in Bremen, a huge window is decorated with the figure of a man on a cross, but the cross has equal branches, it is by no means a crucifix, and the figure is Odin. A metaphysical fate very similar to that of Christ befell Odin, he also had a symbolic relation to the cross-the tree."

Jung sets beside it the medieval iconography of Christ hanging on the living, leafed tree, the Edda verse of Odin nine nights on the windswept tree ("I myself to myself"), and the legend that the wood of the tree of life became the cross: an "early parallel that is beginning to live again."

occurrences.title: Odin hanging on the tree, wounded by the spear — Hovamol (Edda)
occurrences.label: Odin hanging on the tree, wounded by the spear
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Cited within the initiation complex (ghost-house, skull-pole, dagger-licking): "The Greek word for cross is pole; the primitive victim was hanging on the cross. And in an old Germanic ritual Odin was represented hanging on a tree, pierced with a spear" (p352). The footnote gives the Hovamol strophe: "I ween that I hung on the windy tree, / Hung there for nights full nine; / With the spear I was wounded, and offered I was / To Odin, myself to myself."

Jung's context: the sacrificial death that opens the community of spirits — comparable to communion's tasting of blood and "the spear-thrust when Christ is on the pole"; self-sacrifice to oneself as the pattern of the hanged, reborn god (cf. Barrett's cross report at pdf p377: Attis, Marsyas, Odin as "hanged gods... reborn after their ordeal").

occurrences.title: Odin feast with bloody sheep sacrifices on the mountaintops (Germany, summer solstice 1933)
occurrences.label: Odin feast with bloody sheep sacrifices…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: A symptom of the German revolution read by Jung as regression: "The National Socialist movement began with very strange proceedings, the Jugend Bewegung, for instance. And at the summer solstice they celebrated the feast of Odin on top of the mountains, they really sacrificed sheep-bloody sacrifices. That was ridiculous sentimentality, but it was also a symptom, it was an attempt toward the past."
With it: the Berlin exhibition of Nordic religion remains and the "Deutsche Christen" seeking to abolish the Old Testament. Footnote cross-references Jung's later essay "Wotan" (CW 10 ¶371-99).

occurrences.title: Oedipus and the Sphinx of Thebes
occurrences.label: Oedipus and the Sphinx of Thebes
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Hera sends the Sphinx against Thebes; whoever solves her riddle wins the throne and the widowed queen. Oedipus solves it "merely because he had solved her childishly simple riddle", marries Jocasta, and falls into matriarchal incest.

Jung's reading: "The riddle of the Sphinx was herself—the terrible mother-imago" (¶265); overestimating his intellect "in a typically masculine way", Oedipus walks into the trap; the riddle "can never be solved merely by the wit of man" (¶264).
Verbatim: The riddle was, in fact, the trap which the Sphinx laid for the unwary wanderer. (cw05 ¶265).

image.title: Oedipus and the Sphinx

occurrences.title: The old man reading the illuminated book, chained Negroes and the cat in the hold (Visions, 11 May 1932)
occurrences.label: The old man reading the illuminated book…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: There (in the darkness of the hold) I saw many negroes in chains. In their midst sat an old man with a beard reading from a great book. At his feet lay a cat.
body: Deepest descent of the ship series: below the tablet-trapdoor, "in the darkness of the hold... many negroes in chains. In their midst sat an old man with a beard reading from a great book. At his feet lay a cat."

Jung: the descent goes from the snake-Tao through the tablet (navigation with the head) to the medicine man - Lao-tze, "old man," a title; "It is the greatest error to think one can be told of Tao; one must experience it to understand". The instincts must be chained for the stillness of "It is so still, so still": "the animus mind must be chained; otherwise she couldn't understand or even hear what the old man says". Asked why he does not free the Negroes, he answers only: "I am reading the illuminated book which shows the way" - the book of illumination, "pictures which demonstrate things... revelations of nature," parallel to the book of her own visions "the old man within her" is writing. The cat = female instinct, unchained, "absolutely at peace with the old man".

occurrences.title: The eye turns inward; the growing tree; the old man with the river of souls (patient vision, 25 Mar - 6 May 1931)
occurrences.label: The eye turns inward — the growing tree
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The water cast a few souls upon the bank. Then the men who stood there lifted them up and showed them a star and a sun.
body: Before the same black wall, the eye "turned inward on itself"; imitating it she turns her own eye inward and sees a growing tree — then outside, a real tree that gathers her up and lifts her over the wall without an act of will. Beyond it sits an old man "of legendary age... the personification of the collective unconscious"; in his eyes she sees a great river full of writhing bodies — the river of life, individual lives twisting into patterns that dissolve and reform — while a few men on the bank call the strugglers out of the water and show the saved a star (individual fate) and a sun (the deity). "You have perceived," says the old man, and sinks into the earth; small animals and flowers growing in blood appear where he stood.

Jung: the archetypal wise old man, "the acquired wisdom which is the common inheritance of man," speaking the proverbial truth of the consensus gentium; consciousness as redemption from the wheel of death and rebirth — the Buddhist teaching coming "directly out of the kitchen of the unconscious."

occurrences.title: Whether all individuals are merely one soul — Plotinus, Ennead IV.9
occurrences.label: Whether all individuals are merely one soul
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Whether all individuals are merely one soul.
body: In his fourth Ennead (9, 1ff.) "Plotinus discusses the problem of whether all individuals are merely one soul, and he believes he has good grounds for affirming this question."

Jung at cw14 ¶761: Plotinus as an earlier witness to the idea of the unus mundus; the "unity of the soul" rests empirically "on the basic psychic structure common to all souls, which, though not visible and tangible like the anatomical structure, is just as evident as it."

occurrences.title: The One Mind and its Trikaya — Obeisance of the 'Tibetan Book of the Great Liberation'
occurrences.label: The One Mind and its Trikaya
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: The text's opening obeisance, translated by Jung into psychological language: "The unconscious is the root of all experience of oneness (dharmakāya), the matrix of all archetypes or structural patterns (sambhogakāya), and the conditio sine qua non of the phenomenal world (nirmānakāya)" (¶790). The One Mind is "characterized as 'eternal, unknown, not visible, not recognized'" — hence identical with the unconscious (¶793) — and as the Clear Light that "those fettered by desires cannot perceive" (¶796).

The commentary's running equation: the Mind's innumerable names make it "something as vague and indefinite as the philosophers' stone… the Eastern equivalent of our concept of the unconscious, more particularly of the collective unconscious" (¶806-807); the "Mental Self" of the East vs the Western self that "comprises instincts, physiological and semi-physiological phenomena" (¶808).

occurrences.title: The pit of onyx: old Indian woman holding the living Mexican image in fire (Visions Seminar, 7 / 14 June 1933)
occurrences.label: The pit of onyx — old Indian woman holding…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: The narrow path opens into a circle: "I saw a round pit of onyx which went down into the earth like a cone... At the bottom I beheld an old Indian woman holding in her arms the Mexican image which seemed alive... Every now and then she would hold it in a fire and take it out unharmed."

Jung: after the lion-heat chaos, enantiodromia brings the picture of duration — the circle is a mandala, protective against the flames of desire; the conical onyx pit is the amphora, the hard imperishable vessel in which one is caught and preserved. The Indian squaw (chthonic Eros, the American soil) holds the germ of the spirit proper to that soil, strengthening the idol in fire as primitives charge a fetish with blood or dance — the accumulator-principle of the churinga. Logos and earth-mother, two principles held together.

occurrences.title: 'A street which consists of nothing but deep holes' — multiplicity dream from psychopathology
occurrences.label: A street which consists of nothing but deep…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: A dream thanked to Dr. Meier, quoted by Dr. Nothmann as the farthest-reaching analogy to the crater landscape of the death-mask dreams: "I am on a street which, however, consists of nothing but deep holes. They are open manholes... I have the impression that the holes communicate down below, and in a way form an underground street. Perhaps, to make progress, I will have to go down after all."

Nothmann's reading: "The motif of multiplicity indicates a splitting of the soul. We find this motif particularly often in the dreams of schizophrenics." Companion images from psychopathology: a room full of mice or cats, a pool of corked bottles each with a message, nothing but broken window panes.

occurrences.title: The Ophite diagram: circles, Leviathan, seven animal-formed archons
occurrences.label: The Ophite diagram
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Alexandria? (known to Celsus and Origen; Origen ~248)
occurrences.quote: The outermost circle was labelled 'Leviathan' and the innermost 'Behemoth.
body: Celsus's Ophite diagram — "what I would call a mandala, an ordering pattern or pattern of order" — ten circles, presumably concentric; the outermost labelled Leviathan, the innermost Behemoth, the two apparently coinciding ("Leviathan was the name for the centre as well as the circumference"; "the soul that has permeated the universe"). The seven archons bear animal forms (lion Michael, bull Suriel, snake Raphael, eagle Gabriel, bear Thauthabaoth, dog Erataoth, ass Onoël); their prince is the "accursed God," Yahweh; a power flows from the virgin Prunicus.

Jung at cw14 ¶574-577: concentric structure confirmed by "circles included in circles," parallel to Ecbatana's seven walls; Ialdabaoth the lion-headed "child of chaos" is first son and last of the series, like Adam and Leviathan.

occurrences.title: The Ophites' diagram of ten circles with Leviathan — Origen, Contra Celsum VI
occurrences.label: The Ophites' diagram of ten circles…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: ten circles, which were separated from one another and held together by a single circle, which was said to be the soul of the universe and was called Leviathan.
body: Origen (Contra Celsum VI, 25–31) describes the Ophite diagram he saw: ten circles separated from one another and held together by a single circle "said to be the soul of the universe and... called Leviathan" — the name entered twice, on the circumference and at the centre; Behemoth fixed below the lowest circle; the lion-like Archon in sympathy with Saturn; prayers addressed to Ialdabaoth "first and seventh"; the fallen Prounikos.

Jung's reading: a Gnostic mandala avant la lettre — concentric world-system with the world-soul serpent as enclosing and centring figure; he compares Leisegang's reconstruction and the seven spheres of the archons. Parallels: adam-kadmon-kabbala-denudata-1677 (Luria's concentric circles), leviathan-male-female-baba-bathra-6c, mandala-navaho-mountain-chant-rainbow.

occurrences.title: The Ophites: Christ as the serpent
occurrences.label: The Ophites: Christ as the serpent
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Egypt/Syria (Ophite sect; reported by Hippolytus, Rome)
occurrences.quote: Among the Ophites, Christ was the serpent.
body: "Among the Ophites, Christ was the serpent." Jung gives this one line in the dream-18 commentary, ranking serpent-renewal developments: the healing serpent of the mysteries, the Ophite identification of Christ with the serpent, and "Probably the most significant development of serpent symbolism as regards renewal of personality… in Kundalini yoga" (¶184).
The Ophite equation belongs with the corpus's Christ–serpent–lapis cluster: the redeeming principle taking the form of the despised chthonic animal (cf. Mercurius' devil-attributes, ¶173).

occurrences.title: Ophites — eucharistic feast with a live snake
occurrences.label: Ophites — eucharistic feast with a live snake
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'The emphasis falls so much on the "serpent" that the Ophites celebrated their eucharistic feast with a live snake, no less realistic than the Aesculapian snake at Epidaurus' (¶294). Jung's point is the degree of hypostatization: real water in ritual, a real snake on the table, real fish-monuments — the symbols of the incarnate God were not metaphors but numinous presences (¶294). The Gnostic tier of Christ's serpent-form, 'an old-established symbol for the "good" genius loci, the Agathodaimon' (¶291).

occurrences.title: Archonides' head in the honey jar — Cleomenes of Sparta
occurrences.label: Archonides' head in the honey jar
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Cleomenes I (r. 519–490 BCE); Aelian ~3rd c. CE

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: Cleomenes of Sparta had the head of his friend Archonides preserved in a jar of honey, and... he consulted it as an oracle.
body: Aelian reports that king Cleomenes had the head of his friend Archonides preserved in a jar of honey and consulted it as an oracle; the same was said of the head of Orpheus. Jung cites this as the Greek member of the oracle-head family that runs from Harran through the teraphim to Gerbert's golden head, and connects it with skull worship in Melanesia and Polynesia, where ancestor skulls serve as tutelary deities "like the head of Osiris in Egypt" (¶372–373).

He then takes up Onians' finding that the psyche, seated in the head, "corresponds to the modern 'unconscious'" — consciousness then being localized in the chest (thymos, phrenes) — so that Pindar's soul as "image of Aion" becomes extraordinarily apt: the collective unconscious both imparts oracles and forever represents the microcosm.

occurrences.title: The Harranite oracle head — Ghaya al-hakim
occurrences.label: The Harranite oracle head — Ghaya al-hakim
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: events of 765 and 830 CE; compilation ~11th c.

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: The head would thereupon predict famines or good harvests, changes of dynasty, and other future events.
body: The Ghaya records the "people of the head": a fair-haired man with dark-blue eyes was lured into a temple chamber and immersed to the neck in a jar of sesame oil for forty days, fed only figs soaked in oil, fumigated with incense while magical formulae were pronounced. His head was then torn off at the neck and set on a niche of burnt-olive ashes packed with cotton; it predicted famines and harvests, dynastic changes, revealed people's inmost thoughts — "Its eyes could see, though the lids did not move." The Jacobite patriarch Dionysius I set the rite on record (765); caliph Mamun taxed the Harranite envoys with it (830).

Jung's reading: taken with the Liber quartorum's round vessel generated "from the brain-pan... of the element Man," the ceremony "seems to point to an original human sacrifice" (¶366) behind the oracle-head idea.

occurrences.title: Girl's dream 10 — the luminous ball, the vapours, the killing man
occurrences.label: Girl's dream 10 — the luminous ball,…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1938-39 (dreams dreamt at age eight; presented at ten; died of an infectious disease about a year later)
occurrences.quote: She touches a luminous ball seen in a vision. Vapours come out of it. Then a man comes and kills her.
body: Dream 10 of the Christmas booklet: "She touches a luminous ball seen in a vision. Vapours come out of it. Then a man comes and kills her."

One of the darkest links in the death-omen chain Jung traces through the series: touch, emanation, and a fatal male figure — the approach of the girl's own death from an infectious disease "about a year after that Christmas" (¶526). Within his reading, "the unknown approach of death casts an adumbratio, an anticipatory shadow, over the life and dreams of the victim" (¶537); the luminous ball belongs with the series' destruction-and-restoration imagery, its numinosity touched at first hand.

occurrences.title: Reichsapfel — the imperial orb of the Emperor's coronation
occurrences.label: Reichsapfel — the imperial orb…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Mrs. Wolff names it and Jung elaborates (30 Nov 1938): "the apple that represents the world in the hand of the Emperor. It was not an apple really, but a golden globe which the Emperor held in his hand at the coronation, denoting that he was in loco Dei, that he was God's lieutenant".

The whole regalia is a cosmos: "his head was the sun, and his crown expressed the celestial rays... the pallium, the coronation tunic, symbolized the firmament, decorated with stars and with the zodiacal signs," like the old Babylonian and Assyrian kings whose star-covered bodies meant they were gods — the king as incarnation of the deity, "able to carry the earth in the hollow of his hand." In the vision, "Nietzsche has here unwittingly slipped into the role of the deity."

occurrences.title: Origen — 'thou thyself art even another little world': sun, moon and stars within (In Leviticum, Hom. V,2)
occurrences.label: Origen — sun, moon and stars within
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Origen on the sacrificial animals, quoted by Jung after the ten-year-old girl's animal-quaternity dream: "Seek these sacrifices within thyself... Understand that thou hast within thyself flocks of cattle... flocks of sheep and flocks of goats.... Understand that the birds of the sky are also within thee. Marvel not if we say that these are within thee, but understand that thou thyself art even another little world, and hast within thee the sun and the moon, and also the stars." Jung: the many animals are the affective states; individuation subordinates the many to the One — the imago Dei, which "expresses itself in the mandala" (¶626).
The companion passage (In libros Regnorum I,4): "Each of us is not one, but many" — man "changed as the moon" until the unus et ipse.

occurrences.title: Origen's self-castration for the kingdom of heaven
occurrences.label: Origen's self-castration for the kingdom…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: we know that later on Origen did castrate himself for the kingdom of heaven, and probably such a case occasionally happened.
body: The one attested Christian case behind Christ's word about eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven. Jung sets it in the late-Christian despising of the body — saints rotting alive "a sign of the glory of God," hermits and fakirs drying up in the desert — against which Nietzsche's identification of the self with the body is the counter-move.

occurrences.title: 'Show me your original face before you were born' — Hui-neng
occurrences.label: Show me your original face before you were born
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: When a monk asked Hui-neng for instruction, the Master told him: \"Show me your original face before you were born\
body: The fourth Zen maxim — "Seeing into one's nature and the attainment of Buddhahood" — condensed into Hui-neng's demand, which Jung quotes among the "original man" sayings:

And again: "Think not of good, think not of evil, but see what at the moment your own original features are, which you had even before coming into existence" (II, p. 42). The face before birth is the archetype's own countenance — the original man behind the ego's acquired features, Zen's answer to "that which sees" in every age.

occurrences.title: The 'orphan' stone — Albertus Magnus
occurrences.label: The 'orphan' stone — Albertus Magnus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Orphan' as the name of a precious stone is found in Albertus Magnus.
body: "Orphan" as the name of a precious stone in Albertus Magnus: called orphan "because of its uniqueness — 'it was never seen elsewhere'" — said to be set in the Emperor's crown, wine-coloured, and once luminous at night, "but nowadays it does not shine [any more] in the darkness" (¶13). Jung glosses it as the medieval "solitaire" — "a very apt name for the unique lapis Philosophorum" — and traces Dorn's and Petrus Bonus' use of the name to this source; in the Carmina Heliodori the orphan is the [parentless one] "slain at the beginning of the work for purposes of transformation."

The orphan's absent father opens the whole son-of-the-widow complex of ¶¶13-35: Mani sold as a child to a rich widow, the Manichaeans as "children of the widow," Beya marrying her son Gabritius, and the Cabala's Malchuth widowed when Tifereth is not with her.

occurrences.title: Orpheus in the cathedral - the skeleton at the altar, the walls crumbled (Visions, 22 June 1932)
occurrences.label: Orpheus in the cathedral - the skeleton…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Then raising the flute to his lips he blew a loud and savage note. The walls of the cathedral crumbled and fell about him and nothing was left but the altar and the skeleton at his feet.
body: After the leopard drops the flute at his feet, a man walks toward the tree: "His robe was dark blue, his face was very beautiful. He said: 'I have heard my own voice speaking to me.'" Jung: "it might be Orpheus, who would be a more spiritual figure. Yet he is a parallel to Dionysus. Orpheus is the psychopompos par excellence" - the animus "who anticipates the things to come."

He comes - against expectation - not to a pagan temple but "to a great cathedral which he entered. It was empty save for a black hooded figure kneeling before the altar... he beheld a skeleton." Then: "raising the flute to his lips he blew a loud and savage note. The walls of the cathedral crumbled and fell about him and nothing was left but the altar and the skeleton at his feet" - "like the walls of Jericho falling before the blast of Joshua's trumpets of rams' horns." He lays the cross on the skeleton and kicks over the altar: "This is the psychopompos... he demonstrates to her that the Christian point of view is empty and dead... therefore she walked away from her own body".

occurrences.title: Orpheus dismembered by the maenads — the charmer of his own unconscious
occurrences.label: Orpheus dismembered by the maenads
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Mr. Baumann's question ("Why does Eurydice disappear when Orpheus looks at her?") draws Jung's reading: "Orpheus symbolizes the faculty of man to charm his unconscious powers; he made such sweet music that all the wild animals became tame and gathered round him... we can charm all our instincts and impulses". But this self-taming by imagination "is black magic in a way: you can only do it when you have enough imagination to deceive yourself into thinking that you are wholly good... until something black occurs, and then the imagination snaps and up come all the devils. That is the reason why Orpheus was dismembered by the maenads, and Zagreus by the Titans".
"By doing the right things in the right way and having the right imagination, he lost his soul... And the soul contains the mystery of individuation" — Eurydice preferred Hades, "like Mrs. Lot."

occurrences.title: Night, the black-winged bird, bears the silver egg — Orphic hymn
occurrences.label: Night, the black-winged bird, bears the silver…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The product of this union was the silver egg.
body: The Orphic hymn names the creative night "a bird with black wings that was fertilized by the wind (pneuma). The product of this union was the silver egg, which in the Orphic view contained heaven above and earth below, and was therefore a cosmos in itself, i.e., the Microcosm. In alchemy it is the philosophical egg."
Jung at cw14 ¶734: the night-bird raven parallel, with Uranos and Gaia as the primordial image behind the uniped-king pictures.

occurrences.title: Orthelius: verbum scriptum and verbum factum, the spiritus mundi
occurrences.label: Orthelius — verbum scriptum…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The spirit of God filled the whole world.
body: Orthelius' theology of the lapis: "There are said to be two treasures: one is the written word and the other is the word become fact. In the verbum scriptum Christ is still in swaddling clothes in his cradle; but in the verbum dictum et factum the word is incarnate in God's creatures, and there … we may touch it with our hands." The spiritus mundi that brooded on the waters, impregnated them, and "hatched a seed within them, like a hen upon the egg," dwells in the inward parts of the earth, above all in the metals; the task of the art is to separate the Archaeus and produce a quintessence "whose action may be compared with that of Christ upon mankind." Some, he notes, made this world-spirit the third person of the Godhead — forgetting that "Elohim" is plural.

Jung: "Once more the Gnostic vision of Nous entangled in the embrace of Physis flashes forth in the work of this latecomer" — but the philosopher-Hercules has become a laboratory worker seeking a tonic.

occurrences.title: The dripping bull-skin that yields up Osiris' soul — tomb of Sen-nezem
occurrences.label: The dripping bull-skin that yields up Osiris…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~13th c. BCE (19th-Dynasty tomb painting, reproduced by Campbell)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)
jung.locator: 'Transformation Symbolism in the Mass' n.11 (pdf p722)

occurrences.quote: In this scene the god is usually represented enthroned. Before and behind him, hanging from a pole, is the dripping skin of a slain bull that was slaughtered to yield up the soul of Osiris at his reconstruction, with the vase underneath to catch the blood.
body: Jung's Egyptian parallel for the blood-rebirth of the Mass and of Zosimos' visions: in the judgment-scene painting, Osiris sits enthroned with the flayed skin of a slaughtered bull hanging beside him — the skin in which the god's soul is reconstructed.
The vase under the dripping skin is the vessel that catches the rebirth-fluid — the same logic as the Eucharist's chalice under the blood of the god.

occurrences.title: Osiris in the cedar-coffin at Byblos — Dendera relief
occurrences.label: Osiris in the cedar-coffin at Byblos
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The coffer with Osiris floats to Byblos; a cedar shoots up enclosing it; the king fells the tree for a roof-pillar. His absence = winter solstice, lament for the dead god; his heuresis (finding) a feast of joy. Fig. 23: Osiris in the cedar-coffin, Dendera.

Jung's reading: "he enters into the mother's womb, into the coffer, the sea, the tree, the Astarte column; is dismembered, put together again, and reappears in his son Horpichrud" (¶361) — the tree as maternal container.
Verbatim: the coffer containing Osiris was cast ashore at Byblos and came to rest in the branches of a cedar-tree, which shot up and enclosed the coffer in its trunk (cw05 ¶353).

occurrences.title: The ritual enactment of the slaying, dismemberment, and resurrection of Osiris
occurrences.label: The ritual enactment of the slaying…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: "The initiate who ritually enacts the slaying, dismemberment, and scattering of Osiris, and afterwards his resurrection in the green wheat, experiences in this way the permanence and continuity of life, which outlasts all changes of form and, phoenix-like, continually rises anew from its own ashes" (¶208).

Jung's reading: ritual-induced transcendence of life — the transformation occurs objectively, in the god, while the initiate is "influenced, impressed, 'consecrated', or granted 'divine grace' on the mere ground of his presence". Later (¶229): the Osiris cult's democratization — first only Pharaoh "had an Osiris", then the nobles of the Empire, finally "the Christian idea that everyone has an immortal soul and shares directly in the Godhead"; the totem-meal logic of the One eaten in many (one Christ-child, one Santa Claus) anticipates it.

occurrences.title: Osiris enters Selene at the new moon of Phamenoth — Plutarch
occurrences.label: Osiris enters Selene at the new moon…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Egypt (calendar rite, reported by Plutarch of Chaeronea)
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1st–2nd c. CE (De Iside et Osiride); Egyptian festival far older
occurrences.quote: the unconscious is pregnant with consciousness and gives birth to it
body: The synodos rite: "On the first day of the month of Phamenoth, Osiris enters into Selene, and this is evidently equivalent to the synodos in the spring. 'Thus they make the power of Osiris to be fixed in the moon.' Selene, Plutarch says, is male-female and is impregnated by Helios" (¶219).

Jung draws the consequence for his lunar psychology: the moon has "a double light, outside a feminine one but inside a masculine one which is hidden in it as a fire. Luna is really the mother of the sun, which means, psychologically, that the unconscious is pregnant with consciousness and gives birth to it. It is the night, which is older than the day" — capped with Shelley's "Part of the darkness which gave birth to light."

occurrences.title: The reborn Osiris-man with staff and bowl — the black face with the white halo (Visions)
occurrences.label: The reborn Osiris-man with staff and bowl
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: vision read 20 January 1932 (painted late 1929/early 1930 for Jung)
occurrences.quote: I saw that in one hand he held a staff and in the other hand a bowl. I looked into the bowl and saw reflected my own face. It was black and about my head was a white halo.
body: Continuation of the mummy vision: the faun-like Osiris-man now bears attributes —

Jung reads staff = the poimen, the shepherd's guidance; bowl = mirror of self-knowledge, Schopenhauer's intellect mirroring the blind will; staff+bowl = "neither male nor female", the Gospel-of-the-Egyptians paradox. Her black face = the earth/Yin she has become — cf. St. Ambrose, "thy face is black" — and the white halo = the saintliness of the extreme, "the light comes out of the darkness" as paradox. The creature dashes the bowl and vanishes; a goat leads her up (instincts, Capricorn); lying in the desert she feels him growing within her: "the great moment of rebirth when she assimilates the animus… For the first time in history the animus appears as a human function".

occurrences.title: Osiris with the four sons of Horus on the lotus (Book of the Dead)
occurrences.label: Osiris with the four sons of Horus on the lotus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Father Horus with his four sons, or Osiris with the four sons of Horus
body: Plate 102: "Osiris, with the four sons of Horus on the lotus.—The Book of the Dead." Jung sets it parallel to Christ with the evangelists in the world-clock commentary: the Egyptian quaternity of Amset, Hapi, Duamutef, Qebehsenuf around the enthroned Osiris is the oldest documented form of the deity-with-four arrangement that reappears in the Christian mandorla and, transformed, in the modern patient's world clock.
Horus is also "the ἣλιος ἀνατολῆς (rising sun), and Christ was still worshipped as such by the early Christians" (¶314).

image.title: BD Ani before Osiris
image.credit: Published by James Wasserman; facsimile made by E. A. Wallis Budge; original artist unknown

occurrences.title: Osiris sprouting as grass — grain-mummy in the British Museum
occurrences.label: Osiris sprouting as grass
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: grain-mummy rite of the 1st millennium BCE (as seen by Jung)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: then Osiris sprang up in the form of grass. Thus, every year Osiris sprang up again from the earth.
body: Amplifying the cold frame full of seedlings in a girl's devil-dream, Jung recalls the British Museum figure: "the figure of Osiris stretched on a canvas, covered by wet sand in which grass was planted; then Osiris sprang up in the form of grass. Thus, every year Osiris sprang up again from the earth." He was also depicted as wheat springing up from his sarcophagus — the god reappearing as young corn, its first green seedlings. Osiris as vegetation god and master of the underworld "actually bears a certain resemblance to our god of the underworld, the devil"; his brother Seth-Typhon, born with him in the same pregnancy as his opposite, "is simply the shadow of Osiris," a chthonios. The dream's modified devil is "the life demon of the budding, future life, quite like an old Osiris."

occurrences.title: The head of Osiris washed ashore at Byblos, venerated by the women
occurrences.label: The head of Osiris washed ashore…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Byblos, Levant coast (Osiris myth; classical account)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: "It is symbolized as the head of Osiris that was washed ashore from the sea and venerated by the women of Byblos. This severed head, the so-called round element, is the epitome of perfection. A consciousness has crystallized that is imperturbable, a detached consciousness, characterized by wholeness (represented by roundness)".

The head continues into the alchemical series: "that round thing, originally hidden in matter, that Zosimos called the Omega element... That's why the ancient philosophers called themselves 'children of the golden head'" — the caput aureum against the caput mortuum, the nigredo's sediment. The existing vault locus osiris-cedar-coffin-byblos-egypt covers the Byblos coffin episode; this note holds Jung's specific head-roundness reading.

occurrences.title: Ostanes' stone with a spirit in the Nile — quoted by Zosimos
occurrences.label: Ostanes' stone with a spirit in the Nile
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Egypt (Nile; via Zosimos; Berthelot, Alch. grecs III, vi, 5)
occurrences.yearDisplay: Ostanes ~4th c. B.C.?; Zosimos ~3rd c. A.D. (Jung: 'of considerable antiquity, possibly pre-Christian')
occurrences.quote: Go to the waters of the Nile and there you will find a stone that has a spirit. Take this, divide it, thrust in your hand and draw out its heart: for its soul is in its heart.
body: The saying of Ostanes — "known even to Pliny," among the dawn-figures of alchemy — preserved in Zosimos: go to the Nile, find the stone that has a spirit (pneuma), divide it, thrust in the hand, draw out its heart: its soul is in its heart. An interpolator glosses it as the expulsion of quicksilver.

Jung's reading (cw12): the pneumatic stone is the carrier of projected psychic content — the divine slumbering in matter which the opus must liberate. Nietzsche's Zarathustra image, "an image slumbers for me in the stone," "says much the same thing, but the other way round" (¶406). The Easter fire-rite's spark struck from the stone is "yet again an imago Christi" — the same extraction (¶451).

Jung's reading (cw13): the saying — which he calls "of considerable antiquity (possibly pre-Christian)" — grounds the whole doctrine of the animated lapis, spirit in matter, that The Spirit Mercurius builds to: "the lapis is none other than the figure of light veiled in matter" (¶299). Cited twice there: among the oldest witnesses that the arcane substance is spirit (¶264, beside the Isis-to-Horus divine water and Zosimos's incorporeal Mercurius), and again at the essay's climax where Mercurius as φωσφόρος brings "the light of nature, the light of the moon and the stars" (¶299 n.10).

occurrences.title: 'Whereof was Adam made? Of VIII thingis' — Oxford master-and-scholar riddles
occurrences.label: Whereof was Adam made? Of VIII thingis
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Of VIII thingis: the first of earthe, the second of fire, the IIId of wynde...
body: A 15th-century English riddle-dialogue: "Whereof was Adam made? Of VIII thingis: the first of earthe, the second of fire, the IIId of wynde, the IIIIth of clowdys, the Vth of aire where thorough he speketh and thinketh, the Vlth of dewe whereby hi sweteth, the Vllth of flowres wherof Adam hath his ien, the VIIIth is salte wherof Adam hath salt teres."
Jung at cw14 ¶552-553: the ogdoadic Adam — tetradic and ogdoadic natures coexist with the characteristic uncertainty between three and seven.

occurrences.title: Oxyrhynchus sayings — fishes and fowls pointing to the kingdom
occurrences.label: Oxyrhynchus sayings
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The logion: 'the fowls of the air and the fishes of the sea and whatsoever is upon or beneath the earth' point the way to the kingdom of heaven — the motif of the helpful animals (¶224). Jung reads the 'kingdom of heaven' or conjectural 'city' like the alchemical arcane substance: it refers to the self, and the cooperation of birds and fishes illustrates that 'wholeness is perforce paradoxical in its manifestations' (¶225). Ripley's fishes and birds that 'bring the storie' continue the same messianic role (¶224). Parallels: ripley-lapis-everywhere-birds-fishes-15c, lambspringk-two-reversed-fishes-1678.

occurrences.title: 'The bottom of a pail is broken through' — Zen image of Buddhahood
occurrences.label: The bottom of a pail is broken through
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: When a Master was asked what Buddhahood consisted in, he answered, \"The bottom of a pail is broken through\" (Suzuki, Essays, I, p. 229). Another analogy is the \"bursting of the bag\" (Essays, II, p. 117).
body: Asked what Buddhahood consists in, a Master answers with a broken container:

The vessel that held the waters of the psyche loses its floor — the ego-container ruptures and the divided contents are one water again. The Zen image matches the alchemical vas and the Christian "bursting wine-skins" without borrowing from either.

occurrences.title: The monk who fell at the inn of Alexandria — Paradise of Palladius
occurrences.label: The monk who fell at the inn of Alexandria
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: out came the pig as fresh as on the first day.
body: A monk of twenty years in the desert, "advanced in age and perfectly fortified against all devilish temptations," travels to visit a friend made bishop of Alexandria. At an inn at the suburbs the smell of "wine and garlic and oil" undoes him: "they discovered him in the depths of slime; he forgot all about his twenty years in the desert and his saintliness, and out came the pig as fresh as on the first day".

Jung cites it "in order to show how great was the power of the devil" — but his reading cuts deeper: the desert was a fence against temptation because the tempter was carried within; the devils the saint meets are his own inferior function. Nobody "is so gorgeously tempted as the saint," and Flaubert's Tentation merely records what the hagiographers knew.

occurrences.title: The voice proclaiming the birth of Osiris — Pamyles at Thebes
occurrences.label: The voice proclaiming the birth of Osiris
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Pamyles, drawing water, hears a voice from the temple proclaim that Osiris, "the great and beneficent king", is born; the Pamylia festival resembles the Phallophoria.

Jung's reading: "Pamyles seems, therefore, to have been originally a phallic daimon, like Dionysus. In his phallic form he represents the creative power which 'draws' things out of the unconscious (i.e., the water)" (¶349) — the archetype "drawing up from the depths"; the type recurs in the baptism in the Jordan.
Verbatim: This type of experience recurs in the baptism in the Jordan, Matthew 3:17. (cw05 ¶349).

occurrences.title: P'an Ku and the Holy Mother of the First Cause — Taoist China
occurrences.label: P'an Ku and the Holy Mother of the First Cause
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: He was hermaphroditic, the embodiment of both yang and yin.
body: P'an Ku, a dwarf in bear-skin or leaves with two horns, "proceeded from yang and yin, fashioned the chaos, and created heaven and earth," helped by unicorn, phoenix, tortoise and dragon, sun in one hand and moon in the other; he changed himself into the earth with all its creatures — "a real homo maximus and Anthropos." Reborn as Yüan-shih T'ien-tsun, he entered a hermaphroditic holy virgin as a ray of light; after a twelve-year pregnancy birth took place from the spinal column, and she was called T'ai-yüan Sheng-mu, "Holy Mother of the First Cause."
Jung at cw14 ¶573: the late date leaves Christian influence open, but analogy does not prove dependence.

occurrences.title: 'Pan megistos ethneken' — the death of Great Pan, reported at Ostia
occurrences.label: Pan megistos ethneken
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Aegean island of Paxos → Ostia → Rome
occurrences.quote: The people were all shouting: Pan megistos ethneken, Pan the Greatest is dead.
body: Jung's telling of the legend: a ship's captain lands at Ostia and begs audience with the emperor — sailing among the Aegean islands he heard "a tremendous lamentation":

"Everybody was so impressed that it was recorded in the official history of the time as a most remarkable but inexplicable fact." Read as symptom: "the unconscious felt the necessity of informing the people that Pan the Greatest had died, which would mean that that principle had come to an end" — the end of the nature deity. And "in our time again, after the reign of the spirit, something similar is happening": Nietzsche's "God is dead" in Thus Spake Zarathustra "is exactly the same cry as Pan megistos ethneken, but now it means the spiritual God has come to an end. Then instantly the unconscious reacts and brings up the symbols of Pan once more" — as in the patient's Pan-painting and Dionysian self-image.

occurrences.title: 'Pan megistos ethneken' — the death of Pan (Plutarch)
occurrences.label: Pan megistos ethneken' — the death of Pan
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: an island in the Archipelago; reported to the emperor at Rome (harbor of Ostia)
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~2nd c. CE (Jung's dating of the rumor)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The story Jung tells behind "God is dead": a ship's captain sailing "from the Grecian islands to Ostia, the harbour of Rome" is hailed at night from an island — "he heard people shouting: Pan megistos ethneken, Pan the greatest is dead," and hurries to report it to the emperor. Jung: Pan "had been a Latin local god of the fields and the woods, a sort of midday demon," elevated by folk-etymology (pan = all) into "the god of the world" — "the last conception of a nature god created by antiquity."

Jung's reading: "when the god is dead, it means the end of an epoch; therefore, the great emphasis laid upon that story." He sets it behind Nietzsche's announcement and behind the old anchorite's receding: "One reads in old Latin literature that two thousand years ago..." Editor notes Jung later extends the theme to Bacchus (CW14 ¶510n) — the dirge echoed in Zarathustra.

occurrences.title: Starving Pan under the tree - the leopard seizes the flute (Visions, 22 June 1932)
occurrences.label: Starving Pan under the tree - the leopard…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I beheld a man sitting under a tree playing a long flute. His eyes were turned inwards so that only the whites showed. His face was long and thin, the skin tightly drawn. He seemed to be suffering.
body: After the dissociation-end of the crucifixion series, the reaction Jung predicted (satyrs and nymphs after medieval mortification): "I beheld a man sitting under a tree playing a long flute. His eyes were turned inwards so that only the whites showed. His face was long and thin, the skin tightly drawn. He seemed to be suffering."

Jung: "Having been treated to a Christian monastery, Pan is thin, his skin is tightly drawn over his bones and he is suffering... Pan always represents the life of the body and of natural things, trees and animals and so on" - the neglected body. "While he played a leopard leapt down from the tree and seizing the flute in his mouth climbed up to the topmost branches. The man fell over dead." The leopard = "the first form of the new animus, the animus in animal disguise; that was a were-leopard... It points to the fact that the leopard is really god. Dr. Jung: Yes, Dionysus himself". The sky darkens with birds crying "Behold he cometh" - "a Dionysus-Orpheus miracle" - leading to orpheus-cathedral-skeleton-vision-zurich-1932.

occurrences.title: Pandora (1588) — three alembics in the cooking-pot, Christ bleeding beside them
occurrences.label: Pandora — three alembics…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Aurora consurgens (Part II) calls the vas naturale the matrix: 'the One in which there are three things, namely water, air, and fire. They are three glass alembics, in which the son of the Philosophers is begotten. Therefore they have named it tincture, blood, and egg' (¶380). The Pandora illustration confirms the Trinitarian allusion: beside the three alembics in the great cooking-pot stands Christ 'with blood pouring from the lance wound in his breast — flumina de ventre Christi!' (¶380). The round Hermetic vessel 'is God himself, the (Platonic) world-soul and man's own wholeness... the universe in its smallest and most material form' (¶380).

occurrences.title: The club-battle of Papremis — Herodotus II.63
occurrences.label: The club-battle of Papremis — Herodotus II.63
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: At sunset, votaries armed with clubs storm the temple gate against the priests defending the god's shrine; "heads are broken and not a few actually die of the wounds". The local aition: Ares came as a man to visit his mother in the temple, was refused, and forced his way in by violence.
Jung's reading: "It is clear that the votaries fight and even kill each other for their share in the mystery of divine incest" (¶392) — participation in the god's action.
Verbatim: the votaries fight and even kill each other for their share in the mystery of divine incest. (cw05 ¶392).

occurrences.title: Hermes identity and womb prayers — London magical papyrus CXXII
occurrences.label: Hermes identity and womb prayers
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: for I am your image
body: A Greek prayer to Hermes from the British Museum papyri, cited twice in CW5 for two different doors it opens. (1) The identity formula — "For you are I and I am you; your name is mine and my name is yours; for I am your image" — Jung's evidence that in the mystery religions "there is no doubt about the identity of the divine hero with the celebrant" (ch. IV n. 20). (2) "Come to me, O Hermes, as children come into the womb of women" (ch. VII n. 76) — the god as the one who enters the womb, the reverse of the hero born from it.

occurrences.title: Papyri Graecae Magicae V: Hermes 'round and square' (line 401)
occurrences.label: Papyri Graecae Magicae V
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: this is round and square, i.e., a totality consisting of four parts
body: "Hermes is associated with the idea of roundness and also of squareness, as can be seen particularly in Papyrus V (line 401) of the Papyri Graecae Magicae, where he is named [Greek lost to OCR], 'round and square.' He is also called [—], 'quadrangular.' He is in general connected with the number four; hence there is a [—], a 'four-headed Hermes'" (¶172; the Greek terms are eaten by OCR in the chunk).

This squareness of Hermes, glossed by Cartari's reading of the square herms ("the Sun is the head of the world… the four quarters of the world or the four seasons"), makes Mercurius "an eminently suitable symbol for the mysterious transforming substance of alchemy; for this is round and square, i.e., a totality consisting of four parts" (¶173).

occurrences.title: The unica materia increata — Paracelsus, Philosophia ad Athenienses
occurrences.label: The unica materia increata
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This uncreated mystery was prepared (praeparatum) by God in such a way that nothing will ever be like it in the future nor will it ever return to what it was.
body: Paracelsus teaches that the unique materia of the work is increatum — uncreated: a great secret with nothing in common with the elements, filling the whole regio aetherea, mother of the elements and of all created things; corrupted beyond reparation (the Fall); prepared by God once and never again.

Jung: such autonomy and everlastingness suggest "a principle equal to the Deity, corresponding to a dea mater"; Dorn, Paracelsus' pupil, renders it the "Adamica," the limbus microcosmicus. The increatum is the psychologicalAbsolute of the prima materia series — the unknown that precedes all opposites.

occurrences.title: Paracelsus — life as an embalmed mummy: the Mumia (De vita longa)
occurrences.label: Paracelsus — life as an embalmed mummy
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)
