body: 'Life, verily, is naught but a kind of embalmed mummy, which preserves the mortal body from the mortal worms' (¶334). The body lives from the Mumia, through which the peregrinus microcosmus — the wandering microcosm corresponding to the macrocosm — rules the body; his synonyms are Adech, Archeus, Protothoma, Ides, 'the door whence all created things have come' (¶334). Jung: the Mumia corresponds 'in every way to the Original Man, who forms the microcosm in the mortal man and, as such, shares all the powers of the macrocosm' (¶335) — the Hippolytan Papa/Attis 'buried in the body like a mummy in a tomb'.

occurrences.title: Paracelsus, De lunaticis — two bodies in man, one of the elements, one of the stars
occurrences.label: Paracelsus, De lunaticis
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: so there are two bodies in man, one composed of the elements, the other of the stars; therefore, these two have to be well distinguished from each other.
body: Quoted in full in the seminar's Doppelgänger series: besides the physical body Paracelsus posits the sidereal body, a half-material reversed image of its counterpart, "subtle flesh" that walks through walls, roams after death simulating the departed, and is slowly consumed by the stars. It stands between the Egyptian Ka (the immortal double with ~14 soul-parts) and the alchemists' incorruptible body extracted in the opus.

Jaffé applies it directly to the dream: "the Ka soul, the sidereal or subtle body of the child, sits on top of the pyramid" — desire for perfection and immortality embodied, while the child still stands on the ground.

occurrences.title: Asenath and the honeycomb of paradise — Joseph and Asenath
occurrences.label: Asenath and the honeycomb of paradise
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Hellenistic Egypt (Joseph in Egypt); midrash preserved in Christian revision
occurrences.quote: a male messenger from heaven (in the recension: Michael)—whom she received as a δαίμων πάρεδρος, spiritus familiaris, in truly pagan fashion—gave her a honeycomb of paradise to eat and thus endowed her with immortality.
body: Asenath, daughter of the priest of On (Heliopolis), loves Joseph and is rejected as an unbeliever; after penance a male messenger from heaven (Michael in the recension) — whom she receives "as a δαίμων πάρεδρος, spiritus familiaris, in truly pagan fashion" — feeds her a honeycomb of paradise, endowing her with immortality, and announces that Joseph will come to court her.

Jung cites the episode (Part II ch. 5, n. 36) in the scholarly apparatus to the Zosimos "men of light" material: the hieros-gamos prepared by heavenly food and the paredros-spirit belong to the same syncretistic complex as the alchemical assessor (πάρεδρος) of Mercurius (cw12 Part I, index s.v. "paredros"). Jung speculates the messenger "was originally Hermes."

occurrences.title: Out-of-body vision of the park, meadow and wrought-iron gate — patient near death in childbirth
occurrences.label: Out-of-body vision of the park, meadow…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Switzerland (hospital; difficult first birth, forceps delivery)

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: After thirty hours of fruitless labour and a forceps delivery under light narcosis, with severe bleeding, the patient sank through the bed "into a bottomless void" — then found herself, without feeling her body, "looking down from a point in the ceiling," seeing herself deadly pale, the nurse, the excited doctor, her relatives. Behind her: "a glorious, park-like landscape shining in the brightest colours," an emerald meadow sloping to a wrought-iron gate, spring flowers never seen before. "I knew that this was the entrance to another world, and that if I turned round to gaze at the picture directly, I should feel tempted to go in at the gate, and thus step out of life." She knew she would turn back. Next day she described the coma scene in detail; the nurse had to admit its accuracy (¶951).
Jung's reading: genuine syncope, not hysteria — consciousness continued when it should have blacked out, evidence for psychic processes independent of the cortex (¶952-953).

occurrences.title: Paradise put into the future — cabalistic lore of Adam and Eve's exile
occurrences.label: Paradise put into the future
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: God put paradise into the future
body: In the explication of the hermaphrodite as pleromatic symbol: "according to old cabalistic lore, when Adam and Eve were exiled, God put paradise into the future, which means that the original condition, an undifferentiated unconscious, becomes a goal, and the things which were separated after the first sin shall come together again."

The original condition — wolf sleeping with lamb, the unity of opposites in the pleroma — is both the mother from which consciousness emerges and the symbol of the future: "the idea of the kingdom of heaven is a repetition of paradise", and in India tat tvam asi restores that identity consciously.

occurrences.title: The two trees of Paradise become Solomon's pillars and the cross (legend)
occurrences.label: The two trees of Paradise become Solomon's…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "there is an old legend that the two trees of Paradise, the tree of knowledge and the tree of life, were removed from Paradise and made into two pillars which Solomon put in front of his temple, and that later on-the pillars having in the meantime been thrown away and discovered again-the cross of Christ was made out of one of them."

Given among the parallels to the ancestral pillar of the vision: stained-glass trees growing from Adam with the fathers of Israel in the branches and Christ on top, the family tree as series of generations.

occurrences.title: Parity violation — the Wu Cobalt-60 experiment and the collapse of mirror symmetry (New York/Washington, 1957)
occurrences.label: Parity violation — the Wu Cobalt-60 experiment…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Pupin Physics Laboratories, Columbia University, New York; National Bureau of Standards, Washington

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: The parity law of physics states that for any atomic or nuclear system no new physical consequence or law should result from the construction of a new system, differing from the original by being a mirror twin.
body: The moment physics discovered that nature is left-handed. Following Lee and Yang's proposal, Chien-Shiung Wu and colleagues oriented Cobalt-60 nuclei at 0.01° above absolute zero ("like small magnets") and found electrons emitted preferentially along one spin direction; Garwin, Lederman and Weinrich found the same handedness in mu-meson decay. "Parity is not conserved — thus destroying one of the basic laws built into all physical theories of the past thirty years". Rabi: a theoretical structure "shattered at the base".

Vault reading: the physis-side twin of the mirror symbolism of the psyche — the reflection ("parity operation") that had stood as an unnamed axiom since 1925 proved a "door painted on the wall". Pauli answered with his last essay, "Die Verletzung von Spiegelungs-Symmetrien in den Gesetzen der Atomphysik" (Experientia, 15 Jan 1958; bib pdf p301), and the volume's "Spiegler"/Reflector letters (c02); the press dubbed it the "'Chinese revolution' in physics" (index pdf p306 → print p.161).

occurrences.title: Parricida kills King Albrecht in the ford of the Reuß — the archetypal situation
occurrences.label: Parricida kills King Albrecht in the ford…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Ford of the river Reuß, Switzerland

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: The 1308 murder of King Albrecht I by his nephew Johann Parricida while crossing the river Reuß, cited by Jung as "a clear example of such an archetypal influence": "Parricida could already have killed him before. But only when they were riding into the ford did he summon his courage... and he drew his sword and killed King Albrecht. 'In the ford' is the archetypal situation in which the murder can be done, in which great danger is threatening and can be overcome".

The theoretical point follows immediately: "The archetypal is a powerful emotion brought into its original form. When someone is able to perform the art of touching on the archetypal, he can play on the souls of people like on the strings of a piano." With it go the helpful images of difficult transitions — the clashing rocks, the fire made in the dragon's body (night-sea journey).

occurrences.title: The parson in the engraving who walked down the stairs (Jung, childhood)
occurrences.label: The parson in the engraving who walked down…
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.place: old aunt's house, rural Basel country (Switzerland)
occurrences.quote: I looked at him very hard because he was such an interesting old chap, and once I discovered that he began to walk down the stairs. I called to my aunt: 'He is walking!
body: Jung's own first datum of the animated image, told to justify the technique of concentrating on vision-figures: every Sunday morning the little boy was allowed to visit an old aunt whose walls hung "beautiful old engravings" — one showing a country vicarage, the parson just shutting the door to go to the service.

"Of course, she said it was impossible... And every Sunday thereafter, that was my great pleasure — to stare at the old parson till he walked down the steps." The law derived from it, matching the patient's swan that begins to speak: "If you look at a picture long enough it will move. If not, it is your mistake, you do not put yourself into it." So too the ancients with answering idols and ladder-whispering worshippers.

occurrences.title: Parvati grieved at her blackness, given a golden skin
occurrences.label: Parvati grieved at her blackness, given…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Parvati, who, saddened by her blackness, was given a golden skin by the gods.
body: Parvati — "mountain dweller," daughter of Himavat (the Himalaya) — was reproached by Shiva for her blackness; grieving, she left him and withdrew to the solitude of the forest, where the gods gave her a golden skin.

Jung at cw14 ¶607-609, 622: Parvati belongs with the black goddesses "whose names mean 'earth'" (Isis, Artemis, Mary, the Shulamite); the difference is that Parvati is transformed outwardly while the Shulamite is transformed inwardly — her blackness "will not come off."

occurrences.title: Patrizi proposes Hermetic philosophy to Pope Gregory XIV
occurrences.label: Patrizi proposes Hermetic philosophy…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: it was a moment of the utmost significance when the humanist Patrizi proposed to Pope Gregory XIV that Hermetic philosophy should take the place of Aristotle in ecclesiastical doctrine.
body: The humanist Francesco Patrizi proposed to Pope Gregory XIV that Hermetic philosophy replace Aristotle in ecclesiastical doctrine. Jung calls it "a moment of the utmost significance... At that moment two worlds came into contact, which—after heaven knows what happenings!—must yet be united in the future. At that time it was obviously impossible. A psychological differentiation of religious as well as scientific views is still needed before a union can begin to be brought about."
The event closes the Mercurius-Hermes section: "Hermes is a god of thieves and cheats, but also a god of revelation who gave his name to a whole philosophy" (¶280).

occurrences.title: St. Paul's Christophany on the road to Damascus
occurrences.label: St. Paul's Christophany on the road to Damascus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: "Another example is St. Paul, who, on his way to Damascus, was suddenly confronted by Christ" (¶217) — given by Jung as a classic case of the enlargement of personality, alongside Nietzsche's encounter with Zarathustra "which made of the critic and aphorist a tragic poet and prophet".

Jung's reading: "True though it may be that this Christ of St. Paul's would hardly have been possible without the historical Jesus, the apparition of Christ came to St. Paul not from the historical Jesus but from the depths of his own unconscious." In the same paragraph-milieu (¶218): the greater figure appears to the lesser personality "with the force of a revelation" — "the long expected friend of his soul, the immortal one... a moment of deadliest peril"; "Christ himself is the perfect symbol of the hidden immortal within the mortal man."

image.title: The Conversion of St. Paul

occurrences.title: Paul's conversion on the road to Damascus
occurrences.label: Paul's conversion on the road to Damascus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939
Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: when the spirit cut into his life
body: Jung's paradigm of the spirit that "cutteth into life": Paul's violent conversion "like many other cases of such violent forms of conversion... It was nothing mental, nor could it be formulated by mental means. It was a sort of autonomous, divine manifestation".

At the later lecture he defends its facticity against the reduction to illusion: "So when Paul experienced Christ on his way to Damascus, we cannot say that was an illusion; he was obviously gripped by that experience and so it is a fact" — the photographic-apparatus objection dismissed as the way "ordinary idiots think." And the stakes: "There would be no Paul if it had not been for his experience on the way to Damascus, and probably a great part of our Christianity".

occurrences.title: First vision: the peacock perched on the man's back, beak at his neck
occurrences.label: First vision — the peacock perched…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: A beautiful peacock was perched on the back of a man, and the beak of the peacock was pointed at the man's neck.
body: The patient's first spontaneous vision (with the hole-in-the-shoe vision): a beautiful peacock perched on a man's back, beak pointed at his neck. Jung amplifies: the peacock = spring, sunrise, resurrection — "In the early Christian church, and in the sermons of St. Augustine and St. Anthony of Padua... the peacock was a symbol of resurrection" (p81); in the East a "proud Lucifer kind of bird" (p81); among the Kurd devil-worshippers the symbol of creative power (p81). The back is the unconscious side — the shadow-side, the Greek synopados ("the one that comes with me and is behind me", p82). So the animus-man is himself possessed: "behind that man is a new principle that possesses him... his genius... like the king's hawk, or the eagle of Zeus" (p83) — "The animus is himself controlled by something much greater, by the spirit of creation, or sunrise, or rebirth" (p83). The menace at the neck: the man is controlled from the unconscious by that powerful being.

occurrences.title: Seed like a peacock's egg — Basilides' threefold sonship
occurrences.label: Seed like a peacock's egg
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Basilides (via Hippolytus): the 'God who is not' cast down a seed which, 'like a grain of mustardseed, contained the whole plant, or, "like a peacock's egg, had in itself a varied multitude of colors"'; in it a 'threefold sonship, consubstantial with the God who is not' (cw14 ¶397). Jung lines this up with alchemy: 'In alchemy, the end of the work announced by the cauda pavonis was the birth of the filius regius. The display of colours in the Basilidian doctrine therefore occurred at the right place. Again one must ask: tradition — or spontaneous generation?' (¶397). The egg-totality of all colours pre-contains the son.

occurrences.title: Osiris' chariot drawn by peacocks — bronze tablets at Meroë
occurrences.label: Osiris' chariot drawn by peacocks
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Meroë (Sudan); reported in late alchemical text
occurrences.yearDisplay: late antique (Meroë); reported in late alchemical text
body: 'According to a late alchemical text, the bronze tablets in the labyrinth at Meroë showed Osiris, after his regeneration by Isis, mounting a chariot drawn by peacocks, in which he drives along triumphing in his resurrection, like the sun' (cw14 ¶395). Jung cites it beside Penotus' Table of Symbols, where the peacock correlates with the mysterium coniugii and Venus, and the coniugium with the dii mortui 'presumably because they need resurrecting' (¶395). The peacock is 'an ancient Christian symbol of resurrection, like the phoenix' — here in an Egyptian, pre-Christian key: the resurrected god rides the bird of 'all colours'.

occurrences.title: Peacock as Phoenix rising from the fire — Codex Alchemicus Rhenoviensis (15th c.)
occurrences.label: Peacock as Phoenix rising from the fire
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Fig. 32 of Concerning Mandala Symbolism, reproduced from the Codex Alchemicus Rhenoviensis (Central Library, Zurich): the peacock as the Phoenix rising newborn from the fire. A similar picture exists in a British Museum manuscript, only there the peacock is enclosed in a flask, the vas hermeticum, like the homunculus (cf. John Read, Prelude to Chemistry, frontispiece). In the vessel beside the peacock the colours of the cauda pavonis appear — sign that the transformation process is nearing its goal. The peacock is an old emblem of rebirth and resurrection, quite frequently found on Christian sarcophagi; in the alchemical process "the serpens mercurialis, the dragon, is changed into the eagle, the peacock, the goose of Hermes, or the Phoenix."

occurrences.title: Peacock standing on the two heads of the Rebis — Khunrath
occurrences.label: Peacock standing on the two heads of the Rebis
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In Khunrath's Amphitheatrum (1595) a peacock stands on the two heads of the Rebis: 'Since the peacock stands for "all colours" (i.e., the integration of all qualities)... it stands on the two heads of the Rebis, whose unity it obviously represents. The inscription calls it the "bird of Hermes" and the "blessed greenness," both of which symbolize the Holy Ghost or the Ruach Elohim' (cw14 ¶391). The cauda pavonis is here 'the soul of the world, nature, the quintessence'; the peacock occupies the highest place, 'in whom the male-female polarity of the hermaphrodite and the Rebis is integrated' (¶391-392). Jung elsewhere: at the hour of conjunction appear 'all the colours in the world... even Iris, the messenger of God, and the peacock's tail' (¶392).

occurrences.title: The peacock-cult of the Kurd devil-worshippers (Yazidi Melek Taus)
occurrences.label: The peacock-cult of the Kurd devil-worshippers
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Jung undated; Yazidi cult attested from ~12th c. (inferred)
occurrences.quote: In the Kurd tribes there were so-called devil worshippers who worshipped the peacock as a symbol of the creative power, again the unfolding of spring.
body: In amplifying the patient's peacock vision, Jung sets the Eastern bird against the Christian one: "In the East, the peacock plays a more unfavorable role. It is a proud Lucifer kind of bird there, self-produced, and disobedient to the creator. In the Kurd tribes there were so-called devil worshippers who worshipped the peacock as a symbol of the creative power, again the unfolding of spring" (p81). This is the Yazidi cult of the Peacock Angel (Melek Taus) — the fallen angel honoured as demiurge of beauty, precisely the ambivalence Jung needs: "Naturally it is the same peacock, spring, the sudden vision of the unfolding of beauty and form" (p82). Paired with the plague-era French devil-worship as evidence that when the bright god fails, the creative power is sought in his opposite.

occurrences.title: Cintāmani, the wishing-pearl — source of Sukhāvatī's eight lakes
occurrences.label: Cintāmani, the wishing-pearl
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: Its source derives from the king of jewels that fulfils every wish [cintāmani, the wishing-pearl].
body: The waters of the Amitābha land's eight lakes arise from a central wishing-jewel; from it stream "golden-coloured rays excessively beautiful," which "transform themselves into birds possessing the colours of a hundred jewels," singing the remembrance of Buddha, Law and Church.

Jung's reading: the cintāmani is "a symbol of the 'treasure hard to attain,' the highest value" — "In Chinese art it appears as a moonlike image, frequently associated with a dragon" (¶931). Its singing waters are "a redeeming water of wisdom, an aqua doctrinae, to use an expression of Origen"; the source of the water, "the pearl without peer, is the Tathāgata, the Buddha himself."

occurrences.title: The pearl of light in the fish's belly — Pirkê de Rabbi Elieser
occurrences.label: The pearl of light in the fish's belly
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In the darkness of the unconscious a treasure lies hidden, the same “treasure hard to attain” which in our text, and in many other places too, is described as the shining pearl
body: Jonah "entered its mouth just as a man enters the great synagogue"; the fish's eyes were windows of glass. Paracelsus says he saw "mighty mysteries" there (¶509) — the treasure hard to attain, the fascinosum, shining in the darkness of the unconscious (¶510).

occurrences.title: Pegasus and the crucified woman - the star on the staff piercing her breast (Visions, 1 June 1932)
occurrences.label: Pegasus and the crucified woman - the star…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: And as I approached I saw that the star was on the end of a staff, and the other end of the staff pierced the breast of a woman who lay crucified upon the ground.
body: "I mounted upon a white winged horse which flew with me through the sky." Pegasus - "the poet's winged libido... the great enthusiasm," but mounting it risks inflation - carries her through black clouds and black vultures ("the shadow of the Holy Ghost," pdf p788) to the white city in the clouds: "the world city on the mountain of Meru... the square center in the Tibetan mandala, with the four gates meaning the four functions. So she is arriving... in the center of the Self, the perfect condition".

There the star: "the star was on the end of a staff, and the other end of the staff pierced the breast of a woman who lay crucified upon the ground" (plate 24) - nailed to a jet-black cross. Jung: "this is the shadow of individuation: on the one side the liberation or the synthesis of a superior being, and on the other side that terrible shadow, the sacrifice of the personal earthly being". "The star forces her to be crucified; in other words, it forces her to become Christ." The star = the individual fate penetrating the heart; the spear like Longinus proving death = "an achievement or an accomplishment, something divine has penetrated". Astrologically the Pegasus square has ruled since ~1900 - "the animal principle," the tetraktys, the fourth added to the Trinity. Cf. Joyce's Nighttown, where everyone is a Christ (joyce-ulysses-nighttown-everyone-christ-1922).

occurrences.title: Pelican vessel uniting superius/inferius, exterius/interius — scholia to the Tractatus aureus
occurrences.label: Pelican vessel uniting superius/inferius…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: early 17th c. (Jung: 'cannot be dated earlier than the beginning of the seventeenth century')
occurrences.quote: For this vessel is the true philosophical Pelican, nor is any other to be sought after in all the world.
body: The scholia's diagram B C D E F G with the central point A: superius/inferius, exterius/interius "united into one thing by means of the circular distillation, named the Pelican." The point A, "as it were the origin and source from which the other letters flow," is the circulus exiguus and "a mediator making peace between the enemies or elements, that they may love one another in a meet embrace" (¶¶8-9).

Jung identifies this little circle with the Mercurial Fountain of the Rosarium (cw12/cw18 cross-ref) and with the vessel of transformation: "the circle and the Hermetic vessel are one and the same, with the result that the mandala, which we find so often in the drawings of our patients, corresponds to the vessel of transformation" (¶12). The Pelican's Christ-allegory (blood that revives, ¶11, p26-27) pulls the text toward Mercurius as Holy Ghost and toward the author's confessed Ecclesia spiritualis scattered "in Turkey, in Persia... and even in farthest India" (¶9-10, p25-26).

occurrences.title: The pelican wounding her breast to revive her young on the third day — Honorius of Autun
occurrences.label: The pelican wounding her breast…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Honorius' bestiary allegory, quoted in full by Jung: "For it is said that the pelican so loves her young that she puts them to death with her claws. But on the third day for grief she wounds herself, and letting the blood from her body drip upon the fledglings she raises them from the dead. The pelican signifies the Lord, who so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son".

Jung adds the apparatus note: "Pelican is also the name of a retort, the spout of which runs back into the belly of the vessel" — the self-wounding bird and the circulating glass are one body; the blood-sacrifice that quickens the dead children is the aqua permanens returning upon itself.

occurrences.title: The Pelican vessel of the circulatory distillation — Rhenanus
occurrences.label: The Pelican vessel of the circulatory…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Picture of the Pelican, the vessel in which the circulatory distillation takes place.
body: Plate B7 of CW13: "Picture of the Pelican, the vessel in which the circulatory distillation takes place," from Rhenanus's Solis e puteo emergentis (1613). The Pelican is the vas hermeticum shaped for the distillatio circulatrix: the distillate runs back into the belly of the retort, endlessly recycling — "By means of the 'thousandfold distillation' they hoped to achieve a particularly 'refined' result" (¶185).

Jung conjectures Paracelsus's retorta distillatio took place in such a vessel: a distillation "turned back upon itself," whose psychological analogue is the work upon the Iliaster starting "from the midst of the centre" (ex medio centri) — "This process was a psychic as well as a physical experience" (¶185). The Pelican also appears in the Rosarium hermaphrodite plate (B2).

occurrences.title: The virgin earth as Queen of Sheba — Penotus
occurrences.label: The virgin earth as Queen of Sheba — Penotus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: She is the Queen of Sheba, hence there is need of a king crowned with a diadem—where shall we find him?
body: Penotus addresses the artifex: "You have the virgin earth, give her a husband who is fitting for her! She is the Queen of Sheba, hence there is need of a king crowned with a diadem." Mercury has "left his own lands and clothed himself with the fairest garment of white, and has given himself to Solomon, and not to any other who is a stranger and impure."
Jung at cw14 ¶533-534: the queen is the "heaven" wherein the (mineral) sun shines — a medium surrounding it with the nature of Mercurius, "whose one definable meaning is the unconscious."

occurrences.title: The Soviet five-rayed red star — pentagram as sign of evil magic
occurrences.label: The Soviet five-rayed red star
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: red star adopted after the 1917 revolution (inferred); Jung discusses 1935

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: The five-rayed star is the pentagram, and because it is the sign of earthly man, it is the sign of evil magic.
body: In the same discussion as the swastika, Jung turns to the other contemporary emblem: "it is as interesting as the fact that the Soviets, who really cannot be accused of spiritual symbolism, have chosen the five-rayed star."

His reading is unhesitating: "The five-rayed star is the pentagram, and because it is the sign of earthly man, it is the sign of evil magic. You see, David's star is six-rayed, but the Soviet star is not only five-rayed, it is also red, the color of blood, so it is an intensely evil sign. Of course, the people who chose it for the Soviet had no idea of that." He explicitly refuses the conspiracy gloss ("a master of the black arts was behind the whole show") — "But I don't believe in such stunts."

occurrences.title: Cloven tongues of fire at Pentecost — Acts 2
occurrences.label: Cloven tongues of fire at Pentecost — Acts 2
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Fire appears as parted tongues on the apostles, who are filled with the Holy Ghost and speak with other tongues: "The γλῶσσα of the fire caused the glossolalia of the apostles."

Jung's reading (cw05): the mouth-fire-speech fusion of ch. III (¶229-233) at its Christian apotheosis — fire "devouring/consuming" recalls the mouth (Deut 4:24, Ezek 15:4), and speech-fire chains run from II Samuel 22:9 through Isaiah to Revelation 11:5.
Verbatim: And there appeared unto them cloven tongues [γλῶσσαι] like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them. (cw05 ¶232).

Jung's reading (sem-visions): Pentecost as his classical example of possession by the collective unconscious — "the apostles when the tongues of fire descended upon them; they were accused of being full of sweet wine because they had just undergone a tremendous experience of the collective unconscious". It returns at the end of the spirit-lecture: "you are filled with the wind of Pentecost; the Holy Ghost is a strong wind that fills the whole house, you pant with excitement... you are drunk with it like the disciples at the descent of the Holy Ghost" — spirit as emotional dynamism of an attitude, with the physiognomy of intoxication (spirits, Dionysus).

image.title: The Pentecost label QS:Les," Pentecostés " label QS:Len," The Pentecost "

occurrences.title: The Perates' evening meal: the snake summoned onto the loaves (Epiphanios)
occurrences.label: The Perates' evening meal
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: "The main ritual of the Perates, the evening meal, proceeded as follows: they piled loaves of bread on the table and summoned the snake that, as a holy animal, was cared for in a container box. The snake came near and slithered on top of the loaves. Through this the breads were consecrated. Each member kissed the snake on the mouth and prostrated himself before it. Thus logos is present in the form of the snake at the Lord's Supper. It is Christ both as logos and as snake".

The Perates' doctrine behind it: "The primeval power originating from the father, the logos, is a snake... This all-encompassing snake is the wise logos of Eva, this is the mystery of Eden, this is the river that flows out of Eden" — read with John 3:14 and John 1:1-3. The evil materia is the other snake: Chronos, the water of Styx encircling the world.

occurrences.title: Peratae — the Serpent who carries the signs of the Father down and back
occurrences.label: Peratae — the Serpent who carries the signs…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'This is the serpent. For it is he who brought the signs of the Father down from above, and it is he who carries them back again after they have been awakened from sleep' — the 'I am the Door'; naphtha draws fire 'more than the Heracleian stone draws iron'. 'Thus the perfect race of men, made in the image of the Father and of the same substance [homoousion], is drawn from the world by the Serpent' (¶290). Jung: here the magnet is the Son himself, Christ as the brazen serpent of John 3:14; the serpent 'is an equivalent of the fish' and its comparison with Christ is 'more authentic' (¶291).

occurrences.title: Pererius on the four causes of dreams — De Magia; De Observatione Somniorum
occurrences.label: Pererius on the four causes of dreams — De Magia
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Benedictus Pererius, S.J., classifies dreams as natural, human, and divine — and demonic. Four causes: bodily affection; vehement commotion of mind; "the power and cunning of the demon, i.e. of a heathen god or the Christian devil"; and dreams sent by God (cw11 ¶? pdf p684). The devil "is able to know natural effects which will needs come about at some future time from fixed causes" and can make them known in dreams — true prophecy from a false source.

Jung quotes him at length as the Church's considered psychology of dreams: the criterion of a divine dream is unshakable conviction, "which the author does not touch on" — Pererius "merely takes it for granted that a dream of this sort would naturally exhibit a character consistent with the 'highest mysteries of our faith', and not perchance with those of another one". Cassian's dream-testing directors and Gregory the Great's discernment-of-spirits quote are folded in.

occurrences.title: Osiris and Isis as sulphur and moisture — Dom Pernety's Egyptian fables
occurrences.label: Osiris and Isis as sulphur and moisture
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Osiris was 'the fire hidden in nature.
body: The French alchemists of the eighteenth century "were familiar with the king, the hot, red sulphur of the gold, and called it Osiris; the moist (aquosum) they called Isis. Osiris was 'the fire hidden in nature, the igneous principle... which animates all things'; Isis was 'the passive and material principle of all things.'" The dismemberment of Osiris corresponds to the solutio; "The solution of the body is the coagulation of the spirit"; the blackness pertains to Isis (Apuleius: a "shining robe of the deepest black").
Jung at cw14 ¶734.

occurrences.title: Perseus and the Gorgon's head — the petrifying face above Taurus
occurrences.label: Perseus and the Gorgon's head
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: "In the stars you find the constellation of Perseus with the Gorgon's head above the sign of Taurus. The great Gorgon's head is the horrible face entwined by snakes; it is the face of the past in front of which we are petrified. The fear it provokes can be traced back to the fear of the devouring mother, the horror of this; for this face can turn you into dead earth again. This danger was averted by Perseus by cutting the Gorgon's throat with a fiery sword, a diamond sword".

"This would mean that the danger is averted by the intervention of consciousness, of thinking; because it was an act of consciousness that detached him from that horror." Paired with the Upanishads: "the knowledge about Atman liberates from the law of the earth."

occurrences.title: The mask that becomes real: I.G.'s simulated insanity turning genuine (Zurich, 1903)
occurrences.label: The mask that becomes real
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: it was an intentionally simulated insanity, but, without his either knowing it or willing it, it succeeded so well that it almost turned into real insanity
body: The millhand I.G., shamed before his "respectable" mother and sisters, decides to look madder than he is — and the role works too well: "without his either knowing it or willing it, it succeeded so well that it almost turned into real insanity," the meticulous imitation of semi-imbecility disturbing attention, retention and perception until the simulated faints and misreadings became his (¶419). Jung's mechanism: strong affect + hysterical dissociability → the mask is "an overmastering suggestion... a genuine auto-hypnosis" (¶422–423). After the faradism threat he suddenly clears and confesses: "I'm not crazy, yet I sometimes feel I'm not quite right in the head" (¶329), then saws at his wrist with a stone — an attempt Jung calls "definitely hysterical" (¶417). The corpus's cleanest early document of a persona taken on becoming a psyche taken over; the persona tie is ours (Jung's term comes later), his own formula being simulation "slipped out of the conscious into the subconscious" (¶320).

occurrences.title: Personified Peruvian cooking-pots — Museum of Natural History, New York
occurrences.label: Personified Peruvian cooking-pots
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Step in Jung's genealogy of the cauldron-symbol: "when they invented cooking-pots, they gave them faces, eyes, ears, human form. There is a marvellous collection of Peruvian pots in the Museum of Natural History in New York, and among them are personified pots, and as soon as they are given human form, one recognizes the analogy to the human body. Then one puts the cauldron into man himself, he becomes the cauldron" (p358).

The sequence: hole in the ground (Wachandi ceremonial hole = female genitals) → kettle → faced pot → the body itself → the abdomen as mental organ (navel-concentration, plexus solaris): "as food is transformed in the cauldron, so it is in the belly" (pp357-359). The homunculus of the alchemists was "the symbol of the transformation of man in his own belly" (p360).

occurrences.title: Peter's inverted crucifixion and the first man — Acts of Peter
occurrences.label: Peter's inverted crucifixion and the first man
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: Learn the mystery of all nature and the beginning of all things, as it was.
body: Crucified upside down at his own request, Peter preaches his valedictory: "O name of the cross, hidden mystery!" The inverted position represents the first man "who fell head downwards and showed forth a manner of birth such as had not existed till then, for it was dead" — the creation turned everything upside down, left made right, above below. Only when the opposites are made one ("Except ye make the things of the right as those of the left...") is the kingdom known. Christ is the word (upright beam), man's nature the crossbeam, and "the nail which holds the centre... is man's conversion and repentance (μετάνοια)."

Jung's reading: symbolical interpretation of the cross coupled with the problem of opposites, uniting them by identification (¶437); the Acts of Peter's predication "Thou art All and All is in thee" anticipates the subject-object paradox of the self (¶426).

occurrences.title: Trimalchio's dog for life after death — Petronius, Satyricon 71
occurrences.label: Trimalchio's dog for life after death
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Trimalchio begs the sculptor: "paint a small dog round the foot of my statue... so that by your kindness I may attain to life after death."

Jung's reading: the dog as companion of healing and rebirth — Hecate dog-headed (Canicula), dog sacrifices to Eileithyia, Aesculapius' dog, Cerberus pacified with honey-cakes; the necrophagous helper who "assists in the reconstitution" (¶354-355).
Verbatim: I earnestly beseech you to paint a small dog round the foot of my statue … so that by your kindness I may attain to life after death. (cw05 ¶355).

occurrences.title: Petrus Bonus of Ferrara, Pretiosa margarita novella (1330–39)
occurrences.label: Petrus Bonus of Ferrara, Pretiosa margarita…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Now, since no creature except man can unite with God, on account of their dissimilarity, God must needs become one with man. And this came to pass in Christ Jesus and his virgin mother.
body: The oldest source treating specifically of the stone's connection with Christ. At the end of sublimation germinates "a shining white soul (anima candida) which flies up to heaven with the spirit … This is clearly and manifestly the stone." The secret stone is grasped only by the intellect through inspiration, divine revelation, or an initiate's teaching. Hermes: "It is needful that at the end of the world heaven and earth be united: which is the philosophic Word." The old philosophers discerned the Last Judgment and the resurrection of the dead in the art; Alphidius says the stone's mother was a virgin; Balgus: "the father has become the son"; Plato "wrote a gospel which was completed long after by John the Evangelist"; God will become man on the Last Day of this art (in novissima die huius artis).
Jung: this text, "at least a century older than Khunrath," proves the mystery of Christ and the mystery of the lapis were felt as parallel — perhaps continuous — by 1330.

occurrences.title: Peucer on divine and diabolical dreams — Commentarius de praecipuis generibus divinationum
occurrences.label: Peucer on divine and diabolical dreams
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Kaspar Peucer (Melanchthon's son-in-law, crypto-Calvinist) restricts God-sent dreams to the Holy Patriarchs and Prophets, matters of "Christ, the governance of the Church, with empires and their well ordering" — while diabolical dreams are "which the devil shows nowadays to Anabaptists, and at all times to Enthusiasts and suchlike fanatics" (cw11 ¶? pdf p686).

Jung sets this "far more definite and restrictive" scheme beside Pererius' more humanly permissive one: Peucer's "hint about 'revelations' refers to certain heretical innovations." The footnote is Jung's miniature history of confessional dream-politics — who is licensed to receive revelation, and how the devil's true predictions police the boundary.

occurrences.title: Phalli and serpent-pastries thrown into the pit — Arrhetophoria
occurrences.label: Phalli and serpent-pastries thrown into the pit
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: pastries shaped like phalli and serpents were thrown into a pit near the Thesmophorion, to invoke the blessing of children and good harvests.
body: Earth-fertilization by the phallus-and-serpent pair thrown back into the mother-pit — the negative of the Gaia-temenos grain offering (¶570–571) and the edible counterpart of Tages' furrow-birth (¶527).

occurrences.title: The phallic demon bound between two women (Visions Seminar, 25 January 1933)
occurrences.label: The phallic demon bound between two women
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The animus should not be left with the shadow, for he then marries the shadow and there are two against one.
body: Immediately after the second birth, the inevitable counterpart: "I came upon a barrier, a man with a woman above him and a woman below him lay across the path. The man had phalli for hands and a hand instead of a phallus." Like one of the grotesque antique statues of Priapus, he begs to be unchained; she unchains him, steps over him, and sends him back to make his peace with the two women.

Jung's reading: sexuality is the power that fastens man to the world — the first problem after becoming immune through rebirth. The figure is the animus standing between ego and shadow (the wrong sequence: ego-animus-shadow instead of ego-shadow-animus), an "obscene animus" that is "an almost unique instance," compensating her Christian conscious and her flirting with the antique gods whose phallic core she has not assimilated. Christ's own rebirth was followed by Satan; hers, being well-born, is followed by the devil of lust.

occurrences.title: The alley of herms at Athens: phallic columns of Hermes the psychopompos (~5th c. BCE)
occurrences.label: The alley of herms at Athens
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: on each was the sign of the phallus because each was a Hermes, a psychopompos, a shepherd of souls.
body: Closing the animus doctrine, Jung turns to Hermes, its highest stage: "His name plays a great role in the history of Greek art; for instance, you all know that Greek style of bust, the head of a man upon a long pedestal tapering at the lower end. It is called a herm because such phallic columns were the original statues of Hermes. First they worshipped a sort of wooden pole with the phallic meaning... In Athens a long alley was flanked by those herms, representing the famous men of old Greece, and on each was the sign of the phallus because each was a Hermes, a psychopompos, a shepherd of souls". The phallic sign is "of a very carnal nature and therefore divine, a chthonic divinity."

occurrences.title: Phales, personified phallos of Dionysus (Athens, ~5th c. BCE)
occurrences.label: Phales, personified phallos of Dionysus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Athens (Dionysian procession; phalles-songs, cf. Aristophanes, Acharnians)
occurrences.quote: A simple example is Dionysus and his companion Phales, Phales (phallos) being the personification of the penis of Dionysus.
body: Jung's "simple example" of the mechanism he calls "the raising of some attribute to a living figure": "Dionysus and his companion Phales, Phales (phallos) being the personification of the penis of Dionysus." The whole Dionysian train — "satyrs, tityrs, Sileni, maenads, Mimallones" — consists of such personified attributes: affect-investment split off the god and walking beside him as a person. In the rumour essay this classical hypostasis stands behind the schoolgirls' multiplication of the teacher ("each of the girls has a teacher") and the schizophrenic's "two Professor N's."

occurrences.title: Priapus figures set up as scarecrows in Egyptian fields (custom observed in the 1930s)
occurrences.label: Priapus figures set up as scarecrows…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Egypt (fields); medieval parallels in Basel and Nuremberg

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: Even today, in Egypt, Priapus figures are put up as scarecrows in the fields. Such a symbol was embedded in the St. Alban Schwibbogen in Basle. In Nuremberg, too, there is such a curbstone, on the Dürer house near the city gate.
body: In the discussion of the three shrines of antiquity dedicated to Hekate that were simultaneously temples of Priapus ("an ithyphallic river god"), Jung adds a living observation:

The apotropaic field-Priapus — fruitfulness and warding-off in one — survives from antiquity into modern folk custom; Jung read the same figure masoned into Basel's St. Alban quarter and at the Dürer house in Nuremberg. Related: Priapus as "simply a post of fig wood," the ithyphallic Hermes, and the megalithic menhir with phallic meaning.

occurrences.title: Priapus with the snake biting his phallus — Verona museum
occurrences.label: Priapus with the snake biting his phallus
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung's pl. LXIb: "a statue of Priapus in the archaeological museum at Verona: Priapus, with a sidelong smile, points with his finger to a snake biting his phallus" (¶680). The god of the erect member calmly presenting the serpent that devours it — phallic libido and its castrating chthonic other in a single ironic figure.

Jung introduces it precisely to image the ambivalence of libido discovered in ch. VIII: the conflict of horse and snake or bull and snake "represents a conflict within the libido itself, a striving forwards and backwards at one and the same time"; like the sun, "the libido also wills its own descent, its own involution" (¶680). The Priapus is the comic-monumental form of that doctrine. The same serpent-castration recurs in Jung's next plate, Rubens' Last Judgment (¶681).
Verbatim: "Priapus, with a sidelong smile, points with his finger to a snake biting his phallus" (¶680).

occurrences.title: The indecent phallus carried in the parade — Dionysian procession, Athens
occurrences.label: The indecent phallus carried in the parade
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Jung on the orgiastic cult: "the Corybantes were a wild, orgiastic band of dancers. They wore animal skins and goats' horns, to be as much like satyrs as possible, and the girls were nymphs in their lovely nakedness, like maenads... In Athens it was rather obscene; a huge indecent phallus was carried in the parade." The point is cult licence: within the taboo frame "man could do what ordinarily he could not do", identified with the heroes or totem ancestors — the frame modern man has lost, so that "now only the intoxicating wine is left".

occurrences.title: Chapels of Saint Phallus in the South of France
occurrences.label: Chapels of Saint Phallus in the South of France
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: And there are still chapels in the South of France which are dedicated to a patron saint called St. Phalle-Saint Phallus.
body: Evidence that the persecuting church absorbs what it overcomes. After Cumont's case (Elijah's ascent copied from Helios' Mithraic sky-flight), Jung adds Usener's demonstration "that [St. Tycho] was really Priapus, the phallic god of fertility", and then:

"So we are quite safe in assuming the possibility that the chalice in the vision is really an antique symbol which originally looked a bit different" — the serpent-and-poison medicine bowl of Aesculapius. The chalice-frogs vision thus carries a double stratification: Christian Eucharist over the antique healing vessel, over the phallic chthon — a layering Jung elsewhere states as law: "always the persecutor cannot help taking into his psychology a part of that which he has overcome" (pdf p605, on the Marcionites).

occurrences.title: Bust of the sotér kosmú — savior of the world in double form, savior and phallus
occurrences.label: Bust of the sotér kosmú
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: There is a (possibly Gnostic) bust called sotér kosmú, the savior of the world; it exists in a double form, sotér, the savior, and the phallus.
body: In the reading of the stable (birthplace among animals) as "the most meaningful: the low, sad human life, beginning in lowness and ending in lowness, as the highest possible symbol":

The savior and the procreative organ in one image condenses Jung's point that descent — being born in the animal stable, dying between thieves — belongs essentially to the highest symbol: "remember that you came from the stable, from the world of animals... Our development begins in the unconscious." The body is an animal, the body-soul an animal soul; from the unconscious animal soul run the stairs by which we ascend.

occurrences.title: The 'sun phallus' hallucination: tube from the sun causing wind (Burghölzli, 1906)
occurrences.label: The 'sun phallus' hallucination
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)
jung.locator: Lecture 3 (pdf p87, fn10); CW B §173; CW8 §§319-21

occurrences.quote: You remember the case of the insane man who saw a sort of tube hanging down from the sun.
body: The psychotic patient who saw a tube hanging from the sun — "he called it the 'sun phallus,' and it caused the wind" — Jung's proof that sun and wind are one (the anāhata ascent), and, matched years later against Dietrich's Mithraic Liturgy (1903, patient hospitalized before its publication), his classic demonstration ruling out cryptomnesia: evidence for the collective unconscious. "That shows that the sun and the wind are the same."

occurrences.title: Anton Unternährer: the devil's communion and the sacred stones — early 19th c. Switzerland
occurrences.label: Anton Unternährer — early 19th c. Switzerland
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: History has numerous examples of how easily the mystery can turn into a sexual orgy just because it grew out of the opposite of the orgy.
body: The blasphemer of the Bernese Oberland: "The communion of the devil is in the brothels … there they have sucked the head of the snake" (¶581); a self-styled priapic divinity preaching nakedness before God, the lap of the daughters of Jerusalem as "the gate of the Lord," and God creating children from stones — "for the seed comes from the stones" (¶583). Jung's exhibit for the enantiodromia by which "the mystery can turn into a sexual orgy just because it grew out of the opposite of the orgy" (¶584).

occurrences.title: Pharaoh's second, divine conception on the temple birth-chamber walls
occurrences.label: Pharaoh's second, divine conception…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Egypt (temple birth chambers / mammisi, e.g. Luxor, Deir el-Bahari)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: "What was a myth in Greece was actually a ritual in Egypt: Pharaoh was both human and divine by nature. In the birth chambers of the Egyptian temples Pharaoh's second, divine conception and birth is depicted on the walls; he is 'twice-born'" (¶94). The Greek parallel given is Heracles, who "received immortality through being unwittingly adopted by Hera".

Jung's reading: the dual-birth motif underlies all rebirth mysteries, Christianity included — Christ "twice-born" through Jordan baptism; in the Roman liturgy the font is the "uterus ecclesiae" (benediction of the font, Holy Saturday); the early Christian-Gnostic dove = Sophia-Sapientia, Mother of Christ; godparents preserve the motif today.

occurrences.title: The King who 'possesses his mothers' — Pyramid Texts
occurrences.label: The King who 'possesses his mothers'
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The dead Pharaoh's fight for supremacy in heaven: "The sky weeps, the stars shake... when they behold the King rising up as a spirit, as a god who lives on his fathers and possesses his mothers."

Jung's reading: divine incest as royal prerogative — "the votaries fight and even kill each other for their share in the mystery of divine incest" (¶392); parallels the Papremis club-battle and Herodotus' aition of Ares forcing his way to his mother (¶390).
Verbatim: as a god who lives on his fathers and possesses his mothers. (cw05 ¶391).

occurrences.title: True names of the gods imparted to the dead Pharaoh — Egyptian royal funerary ritual
occurrences.label: True names of the gods imparted…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: New Kingdom royal funerary practice (Jung gives no source)

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: Name-magic at the highest level: "When the Egyptian Pharaohs were laid in the tomb, the true names of the gods were imparted to them in word and image, so that they could compel the gods to do their bidding" (¶735). Knowledge of the true name is power over the being named — the dead king receives the gods' names as the instrument of his post-mortem authority.

Jung cites it in his genealogy of the name-function (Rumpelstiltskin — tribal chief — Pharaoh — Cabalists — Ptah) to expose what every Weltanschauung does when it claims objective validity: it treats a name as the thing.

occurrences.title: Pharmakon athanasias — the medicine of immortality
occurrences.label: Pharmakon athanasias
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Antioch/Smyrna (Ignatius, Eph. 20:2; term unattributed in seminar)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: you eat the pharmakon athanasias, the medicine of immortality, and are given an immortal soul. For without the sacraments of the church, unless you participate of the God, in other words, you cannot attain to immortality.
body: The Eucharist as the Greek 'medicine of immortality' (Ignatius of Antioch's phrase, not named by Jung): eating the distributed god. Completes the dismemberment row — Osiris, Dionysos, the divided mantle, the Host. Parallels: melon-eucharist-manichaean-communion · captive-blood-licking-rite-celebes-1890s.

occurrences.title: Philalethes' chalybs — the infernal fire, magnet and the royal child (Introitus apertus)
occurrences.label: Philalethes' chalybs
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: In the Introitus apertus the arcane substance is named 'chalybs' (steel), the 'auri minera', a 'secret, infernal, and yet most volatile fire' (¶204). The magnet's hidden centre turns 'with an archetic appetite' towards the Pole, where the heart of Mercurius rests (¶205); the wise man is bidden to follow the star to the cradle and 'honour the royal child' — the filius born in the philosophical East. Jung reads the peregrinatio to the four quarters as a quaternity centred on the Pole, the hidden God who reveals himself through magnetism (¶205, ¶209).

occurrences.title: Philalethes — Mercurius as two-edged sword and hidden vessel
occurrences.label: Philalethes — Mercurius as two-edged sword…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Summing up the synonyms of Mercurius, Philalethes calls him the key of the art, 'that two-edged sword in the hand of the cherub who guards the way to the tree of life', and 'our true, hidden vessel, the Philosophic garden, wherein our Sun rises and sets' (¶379). The vessel is thus identical with its content — the Mercurius non vulgi — and with the guarded way to Paradise; Jung pairs it with Rupescissa's cherub-vessel. Parallels: rupescissa-cherub-vessel-1351, philalethes-chalybs-royal-child-pole-1667.

occurrences.title: Prajapati hatches himself from the world-egg — Rig-Veda and Brahmanas
occurrences.label: Prajapati hatches himself from the world-egg
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Immersion in oneself (introversion) is a penetration into the unconscious and at the same time asceticism.
body: Tapas, "he heated himself with his own heat" — "brooder and brooded being conceived not as separate, but as one and the same thing" (¶589): introversion as cosmogony. "The result, for the philosophy of the Brahmanas, is the creation of the world, and for the mystic the regeneration and spiritual rebirth of the individual" (¶590); "Then the One, that was hidden in the shell, was born through the force of fiery torment" (Rig-Veda X, 129).

occurrences.title: The phoenix sets itself on fire at Heliopolis, to give birth to itself out of its own ashes
occurrences.label: The phoenix sets itself on fire…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: as told in the classical tradition; Egyptian myth older

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: From Nothmann's paper: "The phoenix's ashes have become the epitome of the symbol of the resurrection of the dead; that miraculous bird which, coming from Arabia, flies to Egypt after having lived for five hundred years, where it sets itself on fire after self-laceration, to give birth to itself out of its own ashes. But the flight to Egypt is the flight to Heliopolis, where the old phoenix is buried as a god".

Re-invoked in the fairy dream (p220) as chief parallel to the fairy's self-burning: "the phoenix achieves a new existence by burning itself. Every five hundred years it burns itself with incense and other fragrant wood" — burning oneself means immortalization (with Heracles' pyre and Thetis dipping Achilles).

occurrences.title: The Persian bird Semenda: ashes, serpent, bird again
occurrences.label: The Persian bird Semenda
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This bird is also a phoenix and is said to transform himself into a heap of ashes; then after a while out of the ashes comes a worm, a serpent, and the serpent again transforms into a bird.
body: Jung's second phoenix, "more specific" than the Egyptian: the bird Semenda transforms himself into a heap of ashes; out of the ashes comes a worm, a serpent; and the serpent again transforms into a bird — the caterpillar-butterfly pattern with a transitus through snake-form. Exactly the patient's scene: the black snake burns to ashes on the golden disk, and its spirit drives her on toward further transformation.

occurrences.title: Phoenix reborn as an 'unseemly worm' in one day — Epiphanius, Ancoratus
occurrences.label: Phoenix reborn as an 'unseemly worm' in one day
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Epiphanius (Ancoratus): 'When the bird is dead, indeed utterly consumed... there are left only the crude remnants of the flesh. From this there comes forth in one day an unseemly worm, which puts on wings and becomes as new; but on the third day it matures' (cw14 ¶472). The worm-stage anchors Jung's decoding of Khunrath's 'filius unius (SVI) diei' — the Hermaphrodite of nature, Saturn, 'the ambisexual Philosophic Man', world-egg, green and red lion (¶472-476): the one day of Genesis 1:5, when 'darkness precedes the light and is its mother' (¶476). The phoenix's lowest form is the worm — the renewal beginning from what is most abject.

occurrences.title: Burning starfish of Picinellus — 'Stella maris' (Polyhistor symbolicus)
occurrences.label: Burning starfish of Picinellus — 'Stella maris'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Picinelli's baroque emblem dictionary reads the burning starfish ('stella marina', Pliny) as the fire of the Holy Ghost — Ecclesiasticus 48:1, the Pentecostal tongues, charity that 'many waters cannot quench' (Song of Solomon 8:7). In the next breath he gives the opposite reading: St. Basil's hell-fire, 'fire that has no brightness', the 'scintilla voluptatis' of concupiscence (¶199). Jung's point: the unity of the symbol implies the identity of the opposites, which the medieval symbolists never noticed (¶199). Picinellus even makes the fish man's tongue, 'set on fire by hell' (James 3:6, ¶209).

occurrences.title: Patient's picture: boy in the cross position with sun and sistrum, 'I am the Resurrection'
occurrences.label: Patient's picture — boy in the cross position…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Painting made by the seminar dreamer after Jung explained his Telesphoros dream: a boy in the cross position, a sun in one outstretched hand, the sistrum or crescent in the other — uniting precisely the cross and crescent symbols the seminar was discussing, "mind you, he knows nothing of what is going on here". The robe bears a fleur-de-lys design that is "also a Buddhist symbol for the thunderbolt, or collective energy, which the dreamer did not know". While painting he constantly had the words "I am the Resurrection and the Life" in mind. Jung: the symbols "probably would not have come without our seminar. I think he was stirred from within" — a synchronicity exhibit (the word coined 4 Dec 1929).

occurrences.title: Drawing — cross, crescent, Tau and star (seminar member's son, 17, November 1929)
occurrences.label: Drawing — cross, crescent, Tau and star
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Zurich (family home, within miles of the seminar room)
occurrences.yearDisplay: November 1929, days after the cross-crescent lectures

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: A seminar member, her mind full of the cross and crescent discussions, gave her sick 17-year-old son his toothbrush to mark; "instead of signing his name, he had made the following picture.... Reading it from the bottom up, there is first the cross, then the crescent, then 'Tau,' and he made the remark that it could just as well have been a cross like this X or a human body. The star above we have not spoken of." The mother "had said not a word to the boy about it" (p417).

Jung: "It is from the collective unconscious, yet it is from his own unconscious just as well. This is not merely a thought transference, it is a magic effect, a Hecate dream, the language of the collective unconscious... This also shows you a most precious piece of symbolism, and how things synchronize in a radius of several miles... This is a power centre, and they are within the radius" (p417). Not insinuated by the mother's unconscious — "it was simply released by the mother's attitude. If touched upon, it comes up." The hieroglyph "explains the sequence of our thoughts" — the seminar's own path in one spontaneous image.
A proto-synchronicity record, 23 years before the 1952 essay. Parallels: picture-temple-sacrifice-crescent-star-boy-1929 · fire-stockholm-vision-swedenborg-1759 (distance-synchronisation family).

occurrences.title: Seven painted pictures: Yang above, Yin below, soul-birds and the leap — young American patient (1925)
occurrences.label: Seven painted pictures — young American patient
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: A progressive series of seven pictures by a young American with a badly muddled mind, who "had no knowledge of my theories" — told only to paint his inner condition, uninstructed as to style. Jung reads the series as "a further expression of the transcendent function... a struggle between the pairs of opposites, with an attempt to solve the problem of bringing the two together". Picture 1: clearness above, something snakelike and the weight of earth below, emptiness between — "consciousness above, sex below, nothing in the middle." 2: complete division, "Yang above and Yin below." 3: first growth, a green tree, "Snakes are coming up from below." 4: the two principles "join in a starlike figure." 5: '"Soul-birds" are shown; helpful animals are needed.' 6: the man high up, "looking to see if he can jump down into the depths of the unconscious. The unconscious contents are felt as fishes." 7: the leap — but into air, a desert, skulls, iron balls. Jung: "The production of these pictures is a stimulation of the primitive layers of the mind," and their Eastern cast is "generally characteristic of American psychology."

occurrences.title: Drawing — temple, bloody fleece, cavern 'where no one goes', crescent-and-star (boy of 17, 1929)
occurrences.label: Drawing — temple, bloody fleece, cavern…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: drawn ~1929, after an operation without anaesthetic

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: "Above is a temple. In the middle is the Holy Stone of the Highest, represented by a greenish square. Around it are the inscripions of ancient priests... A sacrifice has just taken place there, and the blood-stained fleece of the sacrificed animal is stretched on the ground before the altar. Below is a dark cavern. 'That is the place where no one goes.' On the floor is the blood-stained dagger... Below this is a river which leads to a deeper, unknown underworld" (p405; OCR 'inscripions'). Drawn naively by a boy of 17 after a painful operation, during his regression to his mother.

Harding's reading: the operation appeared as a sacrifice with himself the lamb — "he, as his mother's little lamb, has been slain. This is his initiation into manhood." After the drawing, the regression ended. In the depths "a crescent moon aris[es], with the star between its horns... the light of Eros... It is as though for him woman was born out of this experience."

occurrences.title: The Pieta with the black Messiah — fire, tree and star (Visions, 24 Jan. 1934)
occurrences.label: The Pieta with the black Messiah
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: The weeping animus complains "You have made me black"; she pities him, picks him up, and "plays the Pieta with her poor black Messiah. In one of her early pictures she was lying upon the knees of the Great Mother. This time she herself is the very grand mother... It is obviously an inflation". While he sleeps — slipping back into the unconscious — "From a gate in the black wall issued many phantoms... I saw before me fire springing up from the earth. The fire took the shape of a strange tree. Above it I saw my star".

Jung's reading: "This vision consists of three elements: the leaping flames [manipura]... the tree with branches [anahata]... And the fruit of this tree is... the light of the star" beyond life, "the center of the mandala... the symbol of the essence of individuation" (pp1324-1325). "So this is the whole way of the Kundalini in a nutshell: the fire below, the tree above, and on top the result, the single eye, ajna... It is the Christmas tree". The animus brings this true vision to end her Great-Mother inflation.

occurrences.title: Pigs in all the trees — the drunkard's delirium on the boulevard
occurrences.label: Pigs in all the trees
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "I have mentioned before that particularly funny case of a very educated man who drank too much. After a very strenuous night he fell into a delirium and when he woke up in the morning he saw that pigs were in all the trees on the boulevard in front of his house. He thought that there had been a stock-market nearby, and that the pigs had run away and climbed up the trees, so he laughed and laughed and shouted to the people in the street to look up at them too. Naturally the police caught hold of him for making too much noise".

The case belongs to Jung's phenomenology of the many: delirium-tremens hallucinations multiply small units of one kind — "they see coins on the floor and try to pick them up; or they see thousands of rats and mice or birds" — the same splitting that dreams render as swarms of ants or gnats.

occurrences.title: Eleusinian pig-sacrifice relief with the two goddesses (Eleusis)
occurrences.label: Eleusinian pig-sacrifice relief…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: There exists a relief in Eleusis with the pictures of the two goddesses and the Eleusinian pig sacrifice.
body: Evidence in the pigs-and-lice amplification that the pig was a chthonic sacrificial animal: "There exists a relief in Eleusis with the pictures of the two goddesses and the Eleusinian pig sacrifice." The two goddesses are Demeter and Persephone; per Roscher the pig was the sacrificial animal "particularly of the chthonic Demeter, in Hermione," and per Preller it was sacrificed to Aphrodite in Greece and Cyprus — the pig symbolizing "a sexual relationship and the idea of rut and lustful fertility." The same chain runs on to the Hyads depicted as a herd of little pigs.

occurrences.title: Cumaeic relief vase with pig sacrifice (Hermitage, St Petersburg)
occurrences.label: Cumaeic relief vase with pig sacrifice
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: In the Hermitage in Leningrad there is a Cumaeic relief vase, on which a priest sacrifices a little pig.
body: The second artifact in the pig-sacrifice amplification: "In the Hermitage in Leningrad there is a Cumaeic relief vase, on which a priest sacrifices a little pig." Together with the Eleusis relief it anchors the pig as ritual victim — the chthonic side of the pig family that the presenter sets against the New Year lucky-pig and the dreamer's sentimental care for her two starved piglets.

occurrences.title: Little pigs and lice in the fenced garden — recurring dream of a girl (10 December 1940)
occurrences.label: Little pigs and lice in the fenced garden
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: session of 10 December 1940; recurring since childhood, ~twice a year into adulthood

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: I step out of the house and see two little pigs in a square, fenced-in little garden. They are very lean. 'Oh, my poor little pigs; they nearly let you starve!'... in the end I'm covered all over with them myself.
body: A woman's recurring dream, dreamt since childhood at least twice a year: she steps out of the house, sees two starved little pigs in a square, fenced-in garden, takes them on her lap and feeds them with a spoon until they grow round — then finds them covered with lice, picks the bugs off, and ends completely covered with lice herself. Presenter's amplification: pig = fertility, voracity, dirt, rut, "the primitive, instinctual world" — sacrificial animal of Aphrodite and the chthonic Demeter (see the Eleusis relief and the Cumae vase); the girl's education starved the pigs. Jung goes deeper: pigs in a garden is "incommensurable... you will have a pigsty" — sentimentality covering a repressed unclean side; and the fenced garden "could really be a temenos... a symbol of the self, that specially fenced-in place" — with the animal still in it, as in the barn of the nativity: "Christ is the symbol of the self and was born in the barn." The two pigs = doubling, the symbol on the point of becoming conscious; the lice are vampires, the familiares of the pig — the cared-for instinct returns as a parasite. An archetypal problem "that can't possibly be addressed in childhood": archetypes constellated at the wrong time.

occurrences.title: The moving pillar of flame in Rider Haggard's She
occurrences.label: The moving pillar of flame in Rider Haggard's…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "A moving pillar of flame passes rhythmically through a cave in the middle of a volcano, a most amazing and grotesque idea. With a great rumbling it appears from time to time, and whoever penetrates its radiance attains an immensely long duration of life, several thousands or perhaps millions of years, not exactly eternal. But if anyone gets into it a second time, they just shrivel up, as She did."

Jung: "later on, in a posthumous edition of Wisdom's Daughter, I found a description of it, which said that one could see faces of living beings in it, that it was teeming with the life of generations. Obviously it is the same idea as the Manichaean pillar of life and the family tree."

occurrences.title: The Manichaean pillar of light — souls carried by moon and sun
occurrences.label: The Manichaean pillar of light
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "Then there is the Manichaean legend about the pillar of light, an unimaginable cosmic pillar consisting of departed spirits. The ghosts travel to the moon, and the moon fills its belly with them, it becomes the full moon, after which it approaches the sun and all the souls are poured back into the sun; then from the sun they somehow get into the pillar of light, and from the pillar of light all those ghosts of dead people rise to heaven."

Jung reads the vision's ancestral pillar through it — a cosmic family tree, the current of the river of life seen as nature sees it, the individual leaf meaning nothing. Cf. the Kephalaia's Pillar of Glory, the perfect man.

occurrences.title: The pillars of the Great Mother broken — ancestor bodies, spears and boiling water (Visions Seminar, 10 May 1933)
occurrences.label: The pillars of the Great Mother broken
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "It is really the belly of an old woman. Perhaps the pillars are her intestines. Destroy them and she may die." The Indian breaks the first pillar: "formless bodies of men and women fell out and heaped up upon the ground." The second issues "sharp spears and boiling water."

Jung's reading: the classic night-sea-journey motif — the hero kills the monster from within. The monster is the past, "death, destruction through time which swallows everything"; in the belly of time are the parents and all the swallowed. Spears and boiling water are speech metaphors: to bring the past back into life means wounds and hot water (try speaking truth for twenty-four hours like a "harmless Canadian"). The release of the buried is the apokatastasis.

occurrences.title: The small pine tree lying in blood — the new world of consciousness (Visions Seminar, 17 May 1933)
occurrences.label: The small pine tree lying in blood
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: The altar destroyed, "We looked within and saw a small pine tree lying in blood. The Indian lifted up the pine tree. The blood changed to clear water... The tree grew and grew. The growing branches lifted up the roof of the cavern (it opens like a sarcophagus) and we emerged onto a beautiful grassy bank lit with sunlight."

Jung: muladhara symbolism — the pine tree is Shiva as the young green leaf, the first shoot still in the blood, i.e. still in the unconscious body (parallels the Attis pine, the Christmas tree's evergreen light-magic). Blood to clear water = more of the nature of consciousness, "light always symbolizes consciousness." The lifting of the roof repeats the Hopi cane piercing the cave-worlds and Mohammed's leap through the rock — a cosmogonic act, the creation of a new conscious world.

occurrences.title: Birth from the white placenta; the iron wolf suckles the child (Visions Seminar, 23 November 1932)
occurrences.label: Birth from the white placenta
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Our last hero birth was the Christ, a very gentle spirit... Whilst our patient's unconscious points to the birth of a most dangerous warlike spirit, fed by a wolf with iron milk.
body: Opening sequence of the post-Abraxas visions: two faces (one utterly white, one red and bloody) gnaw at her veils; clothed in black shot with green she descends a defile of petrified opposites and finds a woman grown into the earth by a stagnant pool. "She was in travail and I stood while she gave birth. From a white placenta emerged a creature in the shape of a child" — four bulging eyes, club hands, clawed feet. Its mother's breasts are dried; it crawls to an iron wolf and is suckled. The patient weeps "with pity and passed on."

Jung's reading: a ghost child, the synopados — the placenta-double (Frazer, Levy-Bruhl collectanea at pdf p903-906) — but born white, a child of the psyche not of the blood, four-eyed = all-round consciousness, a bija-deva; as hero it is fed miraculously (Romulus and Remus), the milk of iron making it "a spirit as strong as iron." Luther's Deus Absconditus: the hidden, warlike side of the new god.

occurrences.title: Journey through the seven mouths of the Nile — Maier's transitus
occurrences.label: Journey through the seven mouths of the Nile
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Maier's transitus: the seven mouths of the Nile = seven planets, beginning at the Canopic Gate where Saturn is 'domiciled' (cw14 ¶287). The ascent runs 'from darkness and cold to light and warmth, from old age to youth, from death to rebirth', but Mercurius is not found in the sun's region; only on returning to Saturn — now a 'domus barbae' where 'the wisest of all, Thrice-Greatest Hermes, imparts wisdom' — is he met (¶298, ¶303). Jung: the ascent sheds the character 'imprinted by the archons' (¶308), the descent carries light back into darkness (¶309); the opus is 'a "transitus"... in the Gnostic sense' (¶288).

occurrences.title: Gates of the planets — Origen on the soul's descent
occurrences.label: Gates of the planets
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Origen describes the soul's descent through 'the gates of the planets': 'the first gate is of lead and is correlated with Saturn' (cw14 ¶299) — the same lead-gate at which Maier begins and ends his Nile journey. Jung sets it beside Priscillian's soul 'imprinted' by the archons with the 'chirographum' (the bill of debt to fate blotted out by Christ, Col. 2:14) and calls the whole a 'heavenly journey of the soul' 'developed more particularly in Persia' (¶299). The planetary gate-series is the descent-side of the ascent-descent that alchemy reverses.

occurrences.title: Plato's spherical primordial man — round, four-armed, cut in two (Symposium)
occurrences.label: Plato's spherical primordial man
