occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Equated with the split tongue of the vision's serpent and the Gospel-of-the-Egyptians logion: "It is the idea of Plato's primordial man, which was a round ball with four arms and four legs; it was both male and female and then God cut the two parts asunder because he took pity on the misshapen thing... they had their backs turned to one another and were cut in two so that they could see each other. So the original state becomes the symbol for the future state".

Jung links it to the kabbalistic legend of paradise "removed into the future," whose totality "was in the form of a mandala. In the center was the tree of life, and out of that Garden of Eden the four rivers flowed... a symbol of the complete man, of man beyond the separation of the sexes" (ibid.), and to the Holy Saturday fertilization of the font.

occurrences.title: The remora that stopped Caligula's ship — Pliny
occurrences.label: The remora that stopped Caligula's ship — Pliny
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Pliny tells how a remora half a foot long 'had sucked fast to the rudder on the return journey from Stura to Entium, and had brought the ship to a standstill'; Caligula was murdered on his return — the fish as omen, the same trick played on Mark Antony before Actium (¶223). This amazement fixed the identification of the 'round fish in our sea' with the remora. Jung: the remora symbolizes 'that extremely small thing in the vastness of the unconscious which is charged with such fateful significance: it is the self, the atman, "smaller than small, greater than great"' (¶223). Parallels: dream-golden-fish-limmat-woman-1951c.

occurrences.title: The snake out of Plotinus's mouth — his death (Porphyry)
occurrences.label: The snake out of Plotinus's mouth — his death
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: "Porphyry writes in the biography of his revered teacher, Plotinus, that the latter's disciples had observed by his bedside, a few days before his death, how a snake came out of Plotinus's mouth and left; the master died shortly thereafter. For these reasons the appearance of a snake at the sickbed can also mean death".

In von Franz's compilation the locus belongs to the snake as carrier of the mysterious vital power: the child who eats with a snake thrives until his mother slays it (Grimm), Asklepios' companion serpent signalling healing in dreams of the sick (Artemidorus) — the same animal announcing life or death.

occurrences.title: Plotinus — the soul circles around a centre (Enneads VI, 9, 8)
occurrences.label: Plotinus — the soul circles around a centre
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'Self-knowledge reveals the fact that the soul's natural movement is not in a straight line... it circles around something interior, around a centre. Now the centre is that from which proceeds the circle, that is, the soul... divinity consists in being attached to the centre.... Anyone who withdraws from it is a man who has remained un-unified, or who is a brute' (¶342). Jung: the point is 'the centre of a circle that is created, so to speak, by the circumambulation of the soul... a God-image. This is an idea that still underlies the mandala-symbols in modern dreams' (¶343). Parallels: monoimos-monad-iota-2c, mandala-modern-man-jung-zurich-1916.

occurrences.title: Six ithyphallic men carrying an ithyphallic plough — vase, Museo Archeologico, Florence
occurrences.label: Six ithyphallic men carrying an ithyphallic…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Florence, Museo Archeologico (vase 'in [or once in]' the collection)
occurrences.quote: it portrays a row of six naked ithyphallic men carrying a plough which is represented ithyphallically (fig. 15).
body: An archaic Greek vase picture: a row of six naked ithyphallic men carrying a plough that is itself represented ithyphallically — the implement and its bearers one continuous phallus, ploughing as ritualized copulation with the earth.

Jung adduces it (via Dieterich, Mutter Erde, pp. 107ff.) as the "excellent picture" capping his etymology of ploughing as libido: IEur. *ueneti "he ploughs" piercing the ground, Lat. arare with its erotic double sense, and the "bridal bed in the field" custom — "as I make this woman fruitful, so I make the earth fruitful" (ch. III n. 22). The phallic plough is the canalization formula made visible.

occurrences.title: Four lines from a single point — John Dee's Monas hieroglyphica
occurrences.label: Four lines from a single point
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Things and beings have their first origin in the point and the monad.
body: Dee's speculation on the monad: "It is not unreasonable to suppose, that by the four straight lines which run in opposite directions from a single, individual point, the mystery of the four elements is indicated.... Things and beings have their first origin in the point and the monad." The centre of nature is "the point originated by God," the "sun-point" in the egg (¶41).

Jung files Dee with the scintilla-doctrine that runs from Heraclitus' "spark of stellar essence" and the Sethian spark in the dark waters to Khunrath's "fiery sparks of the World-Soul": the geometry of the cross-in-circle as the point's own unfolding, a "double quaternio" whose centre is the germ of the egg in the yolk.

occurrences.title: 'Consider the point in nature' — Sendivogius, Novum lumen chemicum
occurrences.label: Consider the point in nature
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: fire is the life of the metals
body: The admonition that opens the doctrine of the point: "But you, dear reader, you will have above all to consider the point in nature... and you need nothing else, but take care lest you seek that point in the vulgar metals, where it is not. For these metals, the common gold more especially, are dead. But our metals are alive, they have a spirit... For know that fire is the life of the metals" (¶40). The point "is identical with the prima materia of the metals, which is a 'fatty water' (aqua pinguis), the latter being a product of the moist and the hot."

Jung's section II.2 ("The Scintilla") treats the point as "the symbol of a mysterious creative centre in nature," whose epilogue passage ("When a man is illuminated by the light of nature... he may behold the point of our magnet, which corresponds to both centres of the rays, that is, those of the sun and the earth") shows the centre as "a conjunction of male and female" (¶43).

occurrences.title: The polymorphous Christ of the Acts of John
occurrences.label: The polymorphous Christ of the Acts of John
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: first half of the 2nd cent. (per Jung, n.32)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)
jung.locator: 'Transformation Symbolism in the Mass' n.39 (pdf p730)

occurrences.quote: Drusiana saw the Lord once \"in the likeness of John\" and another time \"in that of a youth.\" The disciple James saw him as a child, but John as an adult. John saw him first as \"a small man and uncomely,\" and then again as one reaching to heaven
body: Jung's footnote on the shifting shape of the appeared Lord: each disciple sees a different Christ, and the same Christ at different times.

Sometimes the body felt "material and solid," sometimes "the substance was immaterial and as if it existed not at all" (p. 252). "The universality of this figure may explain why its epiphanies take so many different forms" — the docetic fluidity that lets the One wear every face.

occurrences.title: Dinner beside Pope Pius X, and the wedding-urination (bachelor of 31, Europe, ~1908)
occurrences.label: Dinner beside Pope Pius X,…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I found myself in a little room, seated at a table beside Pope Pius X, whose features were far more handsome than they are in reality, which surprised me.
body: An intelligent, well-educated unmarried man of 31 dreams he is seated at table beside Pope Pius X, "whose features were far more handsome than they are in reality" — a "great apartment" laid for a dinner, ladies in evening dress; then a repeated need to urinate that finally wakes him. He defends the dream as bladder irritation; his strong resistance is itself Jung's clue. Free association unpacks the condensation: "The Pope is a celibate, the Moslem a polygamist" — the dreamer as Pope (celibate life), the Pope as transformation of the Sheikh of a Moslem sect in Arabia whose guest he had been, and the ladies at table as the two marriageable women now interesting him (¶85–91). The need to urinate at a wedding ceremony (¶92) anchors the whole in a childhood scene at eleven: he wet his trousers at a relative's marriage.

occurrences.title: The Pope's ring with the miraculous draft of fishes (Vatican, still worn 1932)
occurrences.label: The Pope's ring with the miraculous draft…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The Pope still wears a ring with the picture of the miraculous draft of fishes, meaning that he is pulling all the peoples of the earth into his net.
body: "The Pope still wears a ring with the picture of the miraculous draft of fishes, meaning that he is pulling all the peoples of the earth into his net".

Jung's emblem for the church of the Fishes-age: "the ruling principle of that part of Fishes would be feminine, it was most certainly the church, Ecclesia Mater, or the Virgin Mother, the Heavenly Bride, etc., and that would last up to about the sixteenth century" - the first, vertical half of Pisces, before the horizontal extension of the great voyages.

occurrences.title: Papa pater patrum, Papissa peperit partum — the Pope Joan legend (medieval Rome)
occurrences.label: Papa pater patrum, Papissa peperit partum
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: medieval legend (chronicles from ~13th c.); Jung names 'Pope John XXII'

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: Hence the phrase: Papa pater patrum, Papissa peperit partum.
body: Cited by Jung inside his commentary on the three-popes dream of 20 July 1954: John the Evangelist stands as "the Gnostic, author of the Apocalypse... a herald of love, and there is a legend that Pope John XXII was a woman, became pregnant by a chamberlain, and gave birth to a child during a procession."

In Jung's reading the legend puts femininity and parturition inside the papal office itself, sealing the identity of the three popes with "the lower Trinity" — the triad that the Bohr couple (rex et regina) then complete toward a quaternity in the dreamer's house of coniunctio.

occurrences.title: Popol Vuh — the Quiche 'textbook of their mystery teaching'
occurrences.label: Popol Vuh — the Quiche textbook…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: written shortly after 1519 in Quiche language, Latin script
body: Cited among the transitus parallels: "we have particularly interesting references concerning them from the American and Mexican Indians; there is an old Mexican Indian document, the Papal Vuh [sic — Popol Vuh], which represents such a way of initiation; it is a sort of textbook of their mystery teaching, which was derived from the classical Maya Quiche culture".

Jung's frame: the transitus — "the passing over or the change from one condition to another by carrying out a difficult task" — compares to Hercules' twelve athla and "the ritual acts which the mystai had to perform in order to attain to a higher degree of initiation. In primitive rites these trials were exceedingly painful, the trial of water, of cold, of fire, of starvation" (ibid.). Footnote 3 cites the Goetz/Morley translation (1950) and Maud Oakes, The Two Crosses of Todos Santos.

occurrences.title: John Pordage's letter of instruction to Jane Leade — the inner Mars-Venus opus
occurrences.label: John Pordage's letter of instruction…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This sacred furnace, this Balneum Mariae, this glass phial, this secret furnace, is the place, the matrix or womb, and the centre from which the divine Tincture flows forth from its source and origin.
body: The English theologian-alchemist John Pordage's spiritual instruction to his soror mystica Jane Leade on the opus: the "sacred furnace, this Balneum Mariae" as the matrix from which the divine Tincture flows; the fire is the love-fire of Venus, not the wrath-fire of Mars; the "first marriage or wedding of Galilee" celebrated between Mars and Venus when they return from their fallen state; the magical child (Tincture) that must descend into the Divine Darkness of Saturn, be swallowed by Mars "as happened to Jonah in the belly of hell," be tempted by Lucifer — the black crow / black raven, the "blessed and blissful black" — before the resurrection in the white of Luna and the crowning of the love-fire Tincture: the pearl of the virgin, the seed of the woman trampling the serpent, the Man of Paradise "clear as a transparent glass."

Jung (¶518): this "hymn-like myth of love, virgin, mother, and child" is "an archetypal conception sprung from the masculine unconscious, where the Virgin Sophia corresponds to the anima" — and, in her unclear distinction from the son, also to the self. A woman's compensatory symbolism would instead give "not Sophia but Hecate, Demeter, and Persephone, or the matriarchal Kali."

occurrences.title: John Pordage — Paradise rising from the Heart of the New Earth
occurrences.label: John Pordage — Paradise rising…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The alchemist-mystic Pordage (1607-81): divine Wisdom is 'a New Earth, the heavenly Land.... For from this Earth grew all the Trees of Life.... Thus did Paradise... rise up from the Heart and Centre of this New Earth, and thus did the lost Garden of Eden flourish in greenness' (¶373). Jung cites it with the alchemical equation of Paradise = albedo, the regained innocence, whose rivers' source is the aqua permanens; for the Fathers Christ himself is the source, Paradise the 'ground of the soul' (¶373). Parallels: tree-ripley-scrowle-bm-sloane-5025-london-1588, golden-flower-ripley-scrowle-1588.

occurrences.title: Signs of possession — the exorcism section of the Rituale Romanum
occurrences.label: Signs of possession
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Rituale Romanum promulgated 1614 (1952 edn cited by Jung)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: any autonomous complex not subject to the conscious will exerts a possessive effect on consciousness proportional to its strength and limits the latter's freedom
body: The Church's official criteria for distinguishing possession from disease: the exorcist must know the signs separating the possessed from "those suffering from melancholy or any morbid condition" — fluency in unknown tongues, knowledge of distant or secret things, unnatural strength. Jung notes the Church confines possession to "extremely rare cases," while he uses the word "in a much wider sense as designating a frequently occurring psychic phenomenon."

Jung's widening is the bridge between demonology and complex psychology: whatever autonomy consciousness cannot assimilate acts on it from outside, "proportional to its strength." The Rite's own diagnostic list reads, psychologically, as a catalogue of autonomous-complex symptoms.

occurrences.title: Possession of Gottliebin Dittus — Blumhardt's deliverance at Möttlingen
occurrences.label: Possession of Gottliebin Dittus
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: The celebrated possession case of Gottliebin Dittus, a young woman of Möttlingen whose two-year torment — apparitions, poltergeist phenomena, trance states — ended with pastor Johann Christoph Blumhardt's exorcistic struggle and cry "Jesus ist Sieger!" (1843). In the history of German psychology of religion it stands as the last great public deliverance-case, bridging demonic possession and clinical psychiatry.

Jung names it once, in the 1936 typology paper, as an example of the "holistic" observation of the psyche as a whole — the genre of "curious lives": "the case of the elder Blumhardt and his medium Gottliebin Dittus" (cw6 ¶966), paired with Justinus Kerner and his Seeress of Prevorst (see eye-prevorst-optic-chiasma-weinsberg-1826) and, "to be historically fair," the medieval Acta Sanctorum. Jung's point: before experimental psychology dismantled the psyche into mechanisms, single whole lives were the field on which the unconscious psyche showed itself entire.

occurrences.title: Sewing shoes for thirty-five years — the shoemaker-lover catatonic (Burghölzli)
occurrences.label: Sewing shoes for thirty-five years
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: 35-year illness; died ~2 years before the 1908/13 lecture
body: For decades a Burghölzli inmate lay speechless and unreacting, head bowed, making rubbing movements with her hands until "thick horny patches developed on the palms," thumb and forefinger held "as if sewing." Earlier she had made "rapid sweeping movements of the arms across her right knee; she was said to be 'sewing shoes' and, later, 'polishing shoes'" (¶358). The records held nothing; only the seventy-year-old brother at her funeral supplied the key: her love-affair had come to nothing, and the girl had become melancholic. "I asked who her lover was: he was a shoemaker" (¶358).

Jung's reading: "Unless we choose to see here some very strange play of chance, we must assume that the patient had kept the memory-image of her lover unaltered in her heart for thirty-five years" (¶359) — the autonomous complex living itself out through the body as a lifelong ritual of fidelity, behind an impenetrable silence.

occurrences.title: Possession epidemic of the Ursulines (1632)
occurrences.label: Possession epidemic of the Ursulines (1632)
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: London (per CW18 text; the famous Ursuline epidemic is usually Loudun, France, 1632–34)
occurrences.quote: One of the most celebrated epidemics of the Middle Ages was the possession of the Ursulines of London, 1632.
body: In "The Definition of Demonism" (1945) Jung cites as "one of the most celebrated epidemics of the Middle Ages" the "possession of the Ursulines of London, 1632". The celebrated convent possession of that year is that of the Ursulines of Loudun (Jeanne des Anges, exorcisms of 1632–34, Urbain Grandier's trial); the CW18 text as printed says "London" — kept verbatim, flagged for verification.

Jung's reading: demonism = daemonomania = possession — complexes taking over control of the total personality in place of the ego, "at least temporarily, to such a degree that the free will of the ego is suspended" (¶1473). The epidemic form includes "the induced collective psychoses of a religious or political nature, such as those of the twentieth century" (¶1474).

occurrences.title: Prajapati consulting his own greatness
occurrences.label: Prajapati consulting his own greatness
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: when Prajapati is deliberating about the creation of certain parts of the world, he usually consults with his own greatness, as if his own greatness were something different from himself
body: 'So even Prajapati, the Atman of the world, has a self, something greater than himself; then his own greatness speaks to him.' Jung's Vedic warrant for the virtue that must not be named and pocketed — a super-quality beyond the nameable. Parallels: atman-brahman-kena-upanishad · love-god-seven-incarnations-hate-three-india.

occurrences.title: Prajapati's loneliness — the creator brings forth the universe for company
occurrences.label: Prajapati's loneliness
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: It is like Prajapati... the extraordinary loneliness of God and his helplessness in that condition.
body: Dr Baynes names Prajapati when Jung tells the cabalistic legend of God's loneliness, and Jung confirms: "Exactly the same idea — the extraordinary loneliness of God and his helplessness in that condition." Prajapati, the Vedic creator, "felt lonely... and so he brought forth the universe to surround himself with company" (Zimmer, Philosophies of India, cited editorially).

The parallel carries Jung's whole argument of the lecture: God's helplessness explains why man is "the indispensable means of God's becoming" — Eckhart's God who must be born through the soul, the angelus Silesius couplet "Without me God cannot live".

occurrences.title: Prayer for Ruach-Hokhmah-El as laboratory familiar — Khunrath's Amphitheatrum
occurrences.label: Prayer for Ruach-Hokhmah-El as laboratory…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: send me from thy holy heavens Ruach-Hokhmah-El, the Spirit of thy Wisdom, that it may ever be beside me as a familiar
body: Khunrath's naive prayer at Amphitheatrum sapientiae p. 221 asks God to send Ruach-Hokhmah-El, the Spirit of Wisdom, "that it may ever be beside me as a familiar, may skilfully govern me, wisely admonish me and teach me; may be with me and pray with me and work with me" — even granting "right will and knowledge and experience and ability in physical and physico-medical matters."

Jung's dry comment: "The learned Dr. Khunrath would no doubt have been delighted to have the Holy Ghost as a laboratory assistant" — the alchemists' religion of the Holy Ghost in its most concrete form. Parallels: khunrath material, adech-scaiolae-de-vita-longa-1562.

occurrences.title: Mr. Preenby filled with the Holy Ghost as the great Sargon — H. G. Wells, Christina Alberta's Father
occurrences.label: Mr. Preenby filled with the Holy Ghost…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Wells's comic-serious case of possession by the spirit: "Mr. Preenby, a charming man of the smallest size, was suddenly filled with the Holy Ghost and understood that he was the great Sargon, which practically settled him forever. He would have been a lunatic had it not been for a wonderfully clever doctor; as it was, his poor little head got so swelled up that, although it did not snap, it remained in a liquid condition". The book's idea originated in a conversation between Jung and Wells (CW7 ¶270n).

Jung's frame: the initial vision of the daimonion can overwhelm — "I have seen many cases of people who have had such an initial vision; they become so inarticulate... they have seen things that were simply too big, and they are carried away." The bird comes and takes the soul away in the night, "a lost soul, or a part of the soul"; the Docetae made Christ exactly such a case.

occurrences.title: Cazotte's prophecy of the French Revolution (Paris, 1788)
occurrences.label: Cazotte's prophecy of the French Revolution
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The celebrated dinner prophecy: Jacques Cazotte, in 1788 — before the Revolution — is said to have told each guest at the table the manner of his death in every detail, princes and poets alike, himself included. Jung cites it, "according to the account of a witness, Francois de la Harpe of the Academy," as a canonical case of "long-range effects in time" (¶131): premonition, prophecy, second sight, strict clairvoyance.

The theory he only hints at (¶131–132) is Schopenhauer's: since the Ding an sich knows nothing of past, present and future, the barrier between now and later "show themselves not to be absolute" — proto-synchronicity ground twenty years before the word (inferred).

Verbatim: "the case of Cazotte, who in the year 1788, according to the account of a witness, Francois de la Harpe of the Academy, prophesied the terrors of the French Revolution, telling each person present the manner of his death in every detail."

occurrences.title: Hysteric patient's prophecy of the Münchenstein rail disaster (Basel, 1875)
occurrences.label: Hysteric patient's prophecy of the Münchenstein…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Münchenstein nr. Basel (percipient in upper Switzerland)
body: "A case close to home": a female patient suffering from hysteria prophesied, in obscure words, the Münchenstein railway disaster several months before it occurred; when it happened she was in upper Switzerland and "clairvoyantly perceived the catastrophe at the same moment that it took place." "An inquiry dispatched immediately by telegram confirmed the accuracy of this clairvoyant vision" (¶133). Jung learned it "from a thoroughly reliable source, namely the attending physician."

This is the local, medicalized prophecy case of the 20-year-old student — the direct ancestor of the medium experiments with his cousin Hélène Preiswerk and of the dissertation (CW1). It carries both halves of his time-phenomena taxonomy at once: premonition (months ahead) and simultaneous distance-perception (co-manifest clairvoyance).
Verbatim: "a female patient suffering from hysteria prophesied, in obscure words, the disaster of Munchenstein, several months before it occurred."

occurrences.title: Priapus with the infant Dionysus and the bunch of grapes — statue from Herculaneum (copy in Jung's collection)
occurrences.label: Priapus with the infant Dionysus…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Herculaneum → copy in Jung's collection, Zurich
occurrences.quote: I have a copy of that wonderful statue which was excavated in Herculaneum, Priapus as the educator, one might say, of the bambino. The little god is seated upon his shoulder as a baby, and Priapus is holding up a bunch of grapes to him, and looking at him with an indescribable smile, that marvelous archaic smile…
body: Called up by the patient's divine laugh as she steps into the golden boat: "It is the laughter of the Greek gods, the laugh of Priapus... That goes with the animals very well, that is excellent, there is no trouble." The phallic god as benign educator of the divine child — the chthonic and the childish-solar in one image, exactly the "divine above and the animal below" structure Jung finds in her satyr-god vision of the Self.

occurrences.title: Horace's fig-wood Priapus poem
occurrences.label: Horace's fig-wood Priapus poem
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the hermaphrodite lecture's Priapus excursus: "There is a poem by Horatius with an exceedingly funny description of such a Priapus carved from the wood of the fig tree." Jung notes the fig was "supposed to be very fertile on account of the many seeds," that the figure "was represented with a huge phallus" and "designated the borderline of the fields; instead of putting a stone there as we do, they put a figure of Priapus."

Even "that unmistakably phallic god is represented at times in hermaphroditic form, meaning the intuitive awareness of the fact that in sexuality there is an unconscious element of both the male and the female."

occurrences.title: Priapus as Pulcinello in the Roman carnival — witnessed by Goethe
occurrences.label: Priapus as Pulcinello in the Roman carnival
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Rome, carnival in the ecclesiastical state

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: "Even in Rome as Goethe saw it, during the carnival in the ecclesiastical state, the old Priapus god, in the form of Pulcinello, walked about disturbing the women. This was in the eighteenth century, in the very heart of Christendom, and that symbol was intended to suggest animal increase, animal sexuality." For Jung a survival of the old religious festivals "of course no longer connected with the church" — evidence that the orgiastic licence never died out but lost its sacred frame.

occurrences.title: Zosimos' vision: Agathodaimon transformed into a pillar of fire, the leaden man (Egypt, ~3rd c.)
occurrences.label: Zosimos' vision — Agathodaimon transformed…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Third ascent: "I saw an old man whitened by years, who had become wholly white, with a blinding whiteness. His name was Agathodaimon" — who at the place of punishments "was transformed by the flame into a pillar of fire," groaning: "I am the leaden man, and I submit myself to an unendurable torment" (cw13 ¶86). Zosimos wakes and interprets: "the lead is to be rejected, and in truth the vision refers to the composition of the liquids."

Jung's footnote: "In our text (III, v, 3) it is the Agathodaimon itself that suffers transformation" (pdf p91 n4) — the good daimon as arcane substance imprisoned in lead, the anima media natura in matter. Lead = "the sealed tomb of Osiris".

occurrences.title: Chaos of planetary fragments — frontispiece of the Songe de Poliphile
occurrences.label: Chaos of planetary fragments
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1499 (Jung cites the French title Songe de Poliphile)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Jung's first "classical representation" of the alchemical chaos (16 Nov 1938): at the bottom of the frontispiece page, chaos as a circle containing irregular fragments characterized by the planetary signs — "a company of the gods," since iron is Mars, tin Jupiter, silver the moon, copper Venus. Sometimes, he adds, the gods are shown as a collection of minerals or metals in the subterranean cave, "as if they had degenerated into terrestrial bodies."
The massa confusa of the alchemical opus in its Renaissance emblematic form: the multitudinous unconscious gathered into one round beginning, the state the Ripley Scroll renders as the dark sphere.

occurrences.title: God, prima materia and nous the same — David of Dinant's heresy
occurrences.label: God, prima materia and nous the same
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Sunt quidem haeretici dicentes Deum et materiam primam et [nous] sive mentem idem esse.
body: In the New Birth section Jung traces the identification of prima materia with God from Aristotle, "its first appearance in alchemy" being the Harranite "Liber Platonis quartorum," through Mennens ("Aureum vellus"), to David of Dinant, attacked by Albertus Magnus:

Mennens had already made the materia God's shadow: the four-letter name of God signifies "the Most Holy Trinity and the Materia, which is also called his shadow, and which Moses called his back parts" — the materia as umbra Dei. Cf. Amalrich von Bena (Krönlein cited).

occurrences.title: Hyle, the congealed mass discordant with itself — Bernardus Sylvestris, De mundi universitate
occurrences.label: Hyle, the congealed mass discordant with itself
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Chartres/Tours school (contemporary of William of Champeaux, 1070–1121)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Bernardus Sylvestris' cosmology — "a widespread influence," Jung notes — names the primordial: "the confusion of the primary matter, that is, Hyle" (p. 5); "the congealed mass, formless chaos, refractory matter, the face of being, a discolored mass discordant with itself" (p. 7); "a mass of confusion" (p. 56). And the descensus: "When Jove comes down into the lap of his bride, all the world is moved and would urge the soil to bring forth" (p. 51) (cw11 ¶? pdf p700).

The classic 12th-century statement of massa confusa plus hierosgamos-in-nature — the meeting-point of Timaeus, Chartres Platonism, and later alchemical terminology ("The terms chaos and massa confusa were in general use, according to the testimony of Bernardus").

occurrences.title: Prima materia as the mountain containing all knowledge and all vices — Abu'l Qasim
occurrences.label: Prima materia as the mountain containing all…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Arabic alchemy (ed. Holmyard, Kitab al-'ilm al-muktasab p. 24)
occurrences.quote: And this prime matter is found in a mountain containing an immense collection of created things. In this mountain is every sort of knowledge that is found in the world.
body: Abu'l Qasim locates the prime matter "in a mountain containing an immense collection of created things. In this mountain is every sort of knowledge that is found in the world" — and, in the same breath, "hatred or malevolence or fraud or villainy or deceit or tyranny or oppression … or blood or killing that is not present there." The prima materia as the total mountain: all wisdom and all evil in one substance.

Jung opens the unicorn chapter's footnote apparatus with this text because it states the moral ambivalence of the arcane substance — the same radical ambivalence he predicates of Mercurius (bestia, ascia, and salvator in one) and of the self as union of good and evil. The mountain is the unfolded massa confusa; the unicorn/stone hunted on the mountain is its liberated core.

occurrences.title: Chaotic Matter as panspermia — Kircher, Mundus subterraneus (1678)
occurrences.label: Chaotic Matter as panspermia
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Quoting "the holy words of Moses," Kircher has God create from nothing a Matter "which we not unfittingly call Chaotic … within which something … confused lav hidden as if in a kind of panspermia … as though he brought forth afterward from the underlying material all things which had already been fecundated and incubated by the divine Spirit" (cw11 ¶? pdf p691; OCR 'lav'=lay). The Chaotic Matter is not destroyed but "willed … to endure until the consummation of the world … a panspermia replete with all things."
Jung's bridge-sentence follows at once: "These ideas lead us back to the 'descent' or 'fall of the deity' in the Gnostic systems" — panspermia as dogmatic survival of the fallen divine in matter.

occurrences.title: Primal man as a double-sexed globe, cut in two
occurrences.label: Primal man as a double-sexed globe, cut in two
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: the myth where man was made as a perfect form, a globe with double sex, which had to be cut asunder. In that case, it was cut into only two parts.
body: Jung pairs Aristophanes' spherical androgyne with the Timaeus quaternity: the demiurge cuts the round universe into four, the primal man into two. 'Since the dawn of time it has been assumed that the living unit consisted of four' — Pythagoras to the medieval elements, temperaments, and Jung's four functions. Parallels: quaternity-timaeus-opening-athens-360bce · atman-androgyne-creation-brihadaranyaka-upanishad-india.

occurrences.title: The blind primordial man: cross of blood, yellow robe with Chinese dragons, stone lion (Visions Seminar, 24 May – 7 June 1933)
occurrences.label: The blind primordial man
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: At the bottom of the descent: "a black man lying with his face to the sky. He was blind. Upon his forehead was a cross of blood. His robe was yellow embroidered with Chinese dragons. At his feet was a lion carved in stone... He said: 'In me have the ages come together.'" Asked who he is: "I am the great philosopher of the East. I am a crusader. I am Christ. I am Ahasuerus."

Jung's reading: the sum total of the collective unconscious, the two-million-year-old man — "a fact which you can see in every detail of your anatomical structure." We are his eyes; consciousness is an eye. The cross of blood is the brand of sacrifice (he must be sacrificed for the sake of consciousness); the imperial yellow robe makes him also an Eastern man; the lion under his feet is power over power. He is one of the personifications of the collective unconscious — Adam Kadmon, Purusha, Prajapati, the Demiurge. "Go forward you fool... until you have stepped upon me and gone beyond."

occurrences.title: Prince Danila Govorila and the four dolls — Russian fairytale of prevented incest
occurrences.label: Prince Danila Govorila and the four dolls
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Cuckoo, Prince Danila, / Cuckoo, Govorila, / Cuckoo, he takes his sister, / Cuckoo, for a wife, / Cuckoo, earth open wide, / Cuckoo, sister fall inside.
body: The Russian fairytale "Prince Danila Govorila": a witch's magic ring will fit none but the girl the prince must marry — and it fits his own sister. On the beggars' advice she makes four dolls and sets them in the four corners of the room; as her brother summons her to the bedchamber they sing ("Cuckoo, he takes his sister, Cuckoo, for a wife...") until the earth opens and swallows her. Under the earth she finds the hut of Baba Yaga; the witch's daughter shelters her, and the two escape by putting Baba Yaga in her own oven. Back home the sister is recognized when she throws herself on the "stabbed" prince in the blood-skin test — but the ring also fits the witch's daughter, so the prince marries her and gives his sister to a suitable husband.

Jung (¶430): "The four dolls in the four corners of the room form the marriage quaternio, the aim being to prevent the incest by putting four in place of two... a magic simulacrum which stops the incest by removing the sister to the underworld, where she discovers her alter ego."

occurrences.title: Priscillian — Christ destroying the wheel of generation
occurrences.label: Priscillian — Christ destroying the wheel…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Priscillian, the Gnostic-leaning bishop executed in 385, takes the horoscope as the wheel of birth: 'He alone has the power to join together the Pleiades and to loose the bands of Orion. Knowing the changes of the firmament and destroying the wheel of generation, he has overcome the day of our birth by the renewal of baptism' (¶212). For Jung this proves that in the fourth century the trochos geneseos was 'in fact regarded as the horoscope'; setting fire to the wheel is a catastrophic revolt of the psyche's original components (¶211). Cf. the chirographum of the zodiacal signs on Priscillianist bodies (¶366 n.25).

occurrences.title: Prometheus 'Here I sit creating human beings' — Goethe's Prometheus poem
occurrences.label: Prometheus 'Here I sit creating human beings'
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Goethe's Promethean demigod "sang happily while he worked: / Here I sit creating human beings..." (quoted at ¶268). Jung caps his Ritschl critique with the riposte: "The Ritschlian can claim, among other things: / Here I sit creating gods!" (¶269) — the theology that makes God real only by the feeling of value vested in him is a school of god-manufacture, and "modesty increases with the advance of civilization!" (¶270).

The passage shows the young Jung wielding Prometheus as the emblem of autonomous creation — the same figure as his ¶194 "Man is a Prometheus who steals lightning from heaven in order to bring light into the pervasive darkness of the great riddle" (Lecture IV). Fire/theft/creation: the heroics of cognition he would later have to sacrifice.
Verbatim: "In classical antiquity the demigod Prometheus sang happily while he worked: Here I sit creating human beings"

occurrences.title: Prometheus steals the fire — consciousness stolen from the gods
occurrences.label: Prometheus steals the fire
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: Whatever consciousness man has acquired he had to steal from them.
body: Jung's privileged parallel for the detachment of the first function: "He stole one function from the gods. That is beautifully illustrated by the myth of Prometheus stealing fire from the gods. Whatever consciousness man has acquired he had to steal from them."

Man emerged from "the thick cloud of general unconsciousness" by tearing loose one function; hence his feeling of inferiority and sin — and on 7 May the Promethean act returns as revolution: what was lacking in the Trinity "was the devil, Prometheus, the fourth, Lucifer rebelling against God... It is always man's self-assertion over against the gods, that increases his consciousness." Not to be confused with Spitteler's literary Prometheus.

occurrences.title: The severed man healed: fire from hands and lips, veils descend (Visions patient)
occurrences.label: The severed man healed
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I mixed earth with his blood and fashioned feet and hands for the bleeding stumps. Then he stood erect and he lifted his hands up and fire sprang forth from them and from his lips. He walked forward. Shadowy forms rose up from the earth and followed him... 'Give, that they may live.
body: The culminating gesture of the final vision: the patient severs the earthbound man from the ground, then heals him herself.

Jung reads it as "one of those famous plots, one of the most precious devices of the female mind" — Penelope-weaving: she fashions feet and hands (action and standpoint) and the man becomes "a prophet and a miracle worker, the word of God pours out of his lips like liquid fire," the ordinary woman's fantasy that her child will be a Messiah. But "the plot has obviously not hit the mark... she again stood alone" — an anticipatory gesture with no effect on the world; the veils shut her out and the descent must resume.

occurrences.title: Proteus — the Old Man of the Sea, psychopomp of the fish-giving sea
occurrences.label: Proteus — the Old Man of the Sea, psychopomp…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The Naassenes read Aipolos — 'the Pole that turns the cosmos round' — as Homer's Proteus, 'the Old Man of the Sea, immortal Proteus the Egyptian... who always tells the truth' (¶338). Jung: 'Proteus is evidently a personification of the unconscious'; he must be seized and held, lies among his warm-blooded seals — contents capable of becoming conscious — and teaches the hero the way home 'over the fish-giving sea': 'the Old Man proves to be a psychopomp' (¶338). 'He spins round himself and changes his shape' — the revolving image that cannot be grasped; 'il ne se laisse pas rouler'. Cf. his Faust II role with the Homunculus.

occurrences.title: 'Happy Neurosis Island' — the provisional life of a compulsion neurotic
occurrences.label: Happy Neurosis Island
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: part of the neurosis consists of that suspended life, or rather, the provisional life." (11 June 1930; the patient's own words are quoted in the body, hyphenated "pro- / visional
body: The term "provisional life" — which Jung says he "learned from a patient": "The trouble is, I am living a provisional life, and the name of it is Happy Neurosis Island, where nothing has come off yet. I am now forty-five, and I know I began my provisional life... when I was seventeen. And I cannot be cured because, if I should remember again, I should wake up a boy of seventeen and have to realize that so many years had gone by wasted."

Jung told him at the beginning he would not be cured: the sacrifice of thirty years was too bloody; "Such a case hardly ever does." The neurotic "lives as if there were no time... There is no here and now but an eternity of ten million possibilities."

occurrences.title: Nails through the insteps: the pseudo-saint Sabina S. (Erlangen, 1888)
occurrences.label: Nails through the insteps
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: She abstained apparently from all food, twice drove nails through her insteps to the soles of her feet, and performed all sorts of miracles which fooled the doctors and officials and created a great sensation.
body: A seventeen-year-old girl, "spurred on by reading the life of Katharina Emmerich" (the stigmatic visionary Anne Catherine Emmerich of Dülmen), passes herself off as a saint: apparent total abstinence from food, miracles that fool doctors and officials, induced tonic and clonic spasms of eye, face and throat — and twice she drove nails through her insteps to the soles of her feet: crucifixion wounds made with hardware (¶352). Jung's reading is the essay's sharpest conceptual cut: this is not simulation but hysteria — "the abnormal actions of Sabina S. were precisely what revealed her inner morbidity"; "hysterics do not lie, even though what they say is not true in the objective sense" (¶353). The imitatio Christi passion replayed in an asylum ward: the saint-mold as hysterical role. (No relation to Sabina Spielrein.)

occurrences.title: Pueblo rite of following the sun's course — the mandala in time
occurrences.label: Pueblo rite of following the sun's course
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: "The Pueblo Indians have rites in which they follow the sun's course for five hours, beginning with the rising sun and ending with the contemplation of the North at midday. By doing this, they are purified and become true children of their sun-father. This is not a dance, it is rather a mandala in time" (p330).

Jung introduces it as the third of his typology of mandalas — (1) static design (the magic circle, as in the plow-circle of Roman city foundation with the fundus at centre; in China "the space of the former heavens, the house of the ancestors"), (2) the mandala dance / Mandala nritya / circumambulatio, (3) "the mandala in time, the performance through life." Living it as one dances it = "being the child of God... One becomes the child of God only by carrying the cross" — the whole course of Christian life so symbolized, as Attis' tree and Mithras' bull were carried (pp330-331).

occurrences.title: Euphorion — the Puer born of Faust and Helena (Goethe, Faust II, 1832)
occurrences.label: Euphorion — the Puer born of Faust and Helena
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Dr Schmitz asks whether Euphorion, son of Faust and Helena, is "such a child of the wise man and the anima, such a Puer Aeternus." Jung: "Helena is very clearly the anima, so the child would be the product of the wise man with his anima" (p308) — but that is the hitch: a Puer created from two collective figures, where "the real man" does not come in. "As soon as Euphorion is born he begins to show symptoms of extraordinary desirousness... and eventually he vanishes in flames" (p309).

Jung lines him up with two more of Faust II's self-consuming creations — the Charioteer, and Homunculus who "hurls himself against the throne of Galatea... and is gone": "These three identical fatal occurrences mean that the creation of the Puer Aeternus has had no long duration." The remedy: "Man should not be identified with the 'Great Wise Man,' but he must assimilate his own shadow" (p309).

occurrences.title: The youth on the hill struck by lightning — Zarathustra, 'On the Tree on the Hill'
occurrences.label: The youth on the hill struck by lightning
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Zarathustra's hill (Nietzsche writing in the Engadine)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Zarathustra meets a youth who longs for the heights and is destroyed by the encounter: "My destruction I longed for when I desired to be on the height, and thou art the lightning for which I waited". Jung reads the youth as "the part of Nietzsche which simply cannot join in," a puer drawn toward the spirit.

Zarathustra himself is "not human, but a spirit, a demon full of dangerous energy" — a thundercloud. When the youth reaches the demon's tension, "he is as if struck by lightning. This would be insanity; it is the sudden explosion in the head which many cases of schizophrenia describe". Jung's counterfactual: had Nietzsche treated "this spirit of Zarathustra" as "a tree spirit… an elemental power to which I have fallen a victim", he would never have climbed the hill.
The chapter's whole tragedy rests on "the overvaluation of the spirit" — "as indeed the whole drama of Zarathustra is based on that prejudice".

occurrences.title: The dark-red purse — association diagnosis of the nurses' theft (Burghölzli, February 6, 1908)
occurrences.label: The dark-red purse
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: on the same evening she made a full confession of the theft and thus confirmed the success of the experiment.
body: The Clark-lecture theft case: a nurse robbed of seventy francs kept in a dark-red leather purse hidden in the linen cupboard of a room shared by six nurses; the purse also held a fifty-franc note, a watch-chain, a crockery seal, and a Dosenbach shoe-shop receipt. Jung tests three suspects (A, the charge nurse's friend; B, the charge nurse who knew every detail; C, the cleaning nurse). A shows the longest critical reaction-times, the most complex-characteristics, and the most critical incorrect reproductions: "All these data are pointers to show that in subject A the critical stimulus-words have acted with the greatest intensity... and on the same evening she made a full confession of the theft". Jung's method warning stands beside the triumph: "One must always base one's judgment on calculation, because appearances are most deceptive!". Pursuer-attribution provisional for the reconciliation pass.

occurrences.title: The Culprit — association diagnosis of the protege's theft (Burghölzli, September 1905)
occurrences.label: The Culprit — association diagnosis…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: he suddenly burst into tears and confessed.
body: The founding case of psychological criminal diagnosis: an elderly gentleman (evening of September 1905) reports ~100 francs missing from his strongbox and suspects his 18-year-old protege; Jung hides 37 critical stimulus-words (drawer, watch, sister, key, to steal, police, jail...) among 63 neutral ones. Reaction-times, slips ("frei-freigebig" stammered), failures, and wrong reproductions cluster at the theft-words; "I told the subject point-blank that he was a thief... Thereupon he suddenly burst into tears and confessed". Controls — the Informed and the Uninvolved — show innocents producing almost as many complex-signs ("The result of the control-experiments is depressing"), and Jung appeals to "those imponderables of human contact... innumerable and immeasurable facial expressions" beyond the tables. The pursuer-cluster (police, to catch, to arrest — "To arrest was a direct hit") is the image family carrying the guilty fear; attribution provisional, for reconciliation pass.

occurrences.title: The lawyer persecuted by the waiters — flight from the projected pursuer
occurrences.label: The lawyer persecuted by the waiters
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich; flight via Brugg, Basel, Freiburg to Hamburg

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Illustration for "your enemy shall ye seek… for your enemy": "the patient I mentioned was a lawyer, a highly intelligent man, and he was persecuted by the waiters in cafes; they always stuck their heads together and laughed and he knew they had certain thoughts about him" — in fact homosexual fantasies he could not own.

His flight is the paranoia's geography: a ticket to Brugg near Zurich, over the mountain on foot to another station, a ticket to Basel, "then by crooked ways he ran through the town of Basel to the German station," hiding in Freiburg, then Hamburg — "he had despised his enemies." Within half a year a waiter winked at another: the enemy had travelled with him. His explanatory theory: "an international journal for waiters through which they exchanged news".
"Every neurotic has a bête noire somewhere" — "they carry the enemy within; they can go where they please but the enemy is always in themselves".

occurrences.title: The putissimus homo who sweats rose-coloured blood — Dorn, Congeries Paracelsicae
occurrences.label: The putissimus homo who sweats rose-coloured…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Dorn, "Congeries Paracelsicae chemicae de transmutatione metallorum " (Theatr. chem. I, 1659, pp. 519ff): the Philosophers' material is "a golden tree with seven branches" enclosing the seven metals; at the final operations "a dark red liquid, like blood, sweats out drop by drop from their material and their vessel. And for this reason they have prophesied that in the last days a most pure man, through whom the world will be freed, will come to earth and will sweat bloody drops of a rosy or red hue, whereby the world will be redeemed from its Fall" (cw13 ¶380-381).

Jung: this is not a future Christ but "the alchemical servator cosmi, representing the still unconscious idea of the whole and complete man, who shall bring about what the sacrificial death of Christ has obviously left unfinished" (cw13 ¶390); putus = 'genuine', unalloyed (n.5).
Verbatim: they have prophesied that in the last days a most pure man, through whom the world will be freed, will come to earth and will sweat bloody drops of a rosy or red hue (cw13 ¶381ocr)

occurrences.title: Great pyramid at Giza — gilded apex, benben light-hieroglyph, Ka transformation
occurrences.label: Great pyramid at Giza
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
jung.locator: pyramid amplification, paper by Aniela Jaffé (pdf p302-303)

occurrences.quote: the hieroglyph for certain pyramids, therefore, means source of light, and various inscriptions indicate its light symbolism.
body: The pyramid as tomb of the Pharaoh: polished, reflecting surfaces — gigantic mirrors casting a cone of sunlight by day, showing the stars by night; the hieroglyph for certain pyramids (belbel, a sun disk with three rays) means "source of light"; apexes gilded or made of gleaming stone. After death the Pharaoh's Ka-soul travels through the underworld and is transformed into Osiris, or rises to Atum, god of light, "exactly at this top of his grave." Matter dematerializes upward from the quadratic base to the dimensionless, most sacred point.
Jaffé: "a central edifice is a body mandala... a place in whose center the god is born or has his home"; such perfection leaves no twilight zone for legends.

occurrences.title: The pyramid's sacrificial remains: knife, split face, overgrown man (Visions patient)
occurrences.label: The pyramid's sacrificial remains
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich (seminar); New York in the vision
occurrences.quote: I saw a knife from which dripped blood. On another side was carved the split face of a man, on the third side a man was lying face downward on the ground beating off the green things that grew all about him. I returned to the knife. Blood still dripped from it and the stream of blood covered my feet.
body: Final vision-series episode of the Visions patient, on her descent from the world of images back to her tangible reality in New York. The pyramid — the Self's tomb, "materialized in stone" like the pharaoh's — displays the remains of a slaughter:

Jung: "This sacrificial killing is the slaughter of the things within" — the sacrificed animus (split face, prone man, knife) lying beside the buried Self. Leaving the psychological atmosphere for the collective atmosphere of the world "is a most painful procedure... therefore it is quite justified to symbolize it by a lot of sacrificial blood".

occurrences.title: The women who lunched on the python — flood follows (African myth, Jung's telling)
occurrences.label: The women who lunched on the python
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Amplifying the patient's vision of walking on the serpent's back: "an African or possibly South American myth about the women going out into the bush and sitting on a fine long tree, which was lying on the ground, to eat their lunch. Then the men came along and told them they were sitting on the back of a big snake". The men killed the snake, boiled the flesh and feasted; "Then it began to rain, and it rained until the earth was covered up to the highest mountaintops. That was the great flood, which came upon them because the women made an animus assumption about that python".

The edition's footnote 2 notes Jung bends the myth — the flood follows the men's killing and eating as much as the women's sitting. Jung pairs it with his acquaintance's boa-as-rotting-tree story from the Nandi escarpment.

occurrences.title: Christ between Ahriman and Ormazd — square vision (Mr. Baumann's subject)
occurrences.label: Christ between Ahriman and Ormazd
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: A man with a scholastic mind — no experience of fantasy-drawing — contemplates a simple square for a minute and sees Christ in the center, Ahriman in the upper right corner, Ormazd in the lower left. He had nothing to do with the myth consciously.

Jung: "that is a revelation from the unconscious. The unconscious is several lengths ahead" — it knew the problem before he did: Christ as mediator of the opposites, the god-man paradox dogma could only bind as "real man and real God." Had he thought in historical-Christian terms he would not have chosen Ormazd/Ahriman; "our unconscious is in the world and not in the books about history." The fantasy "absolutely formulates the idea of Christ as the superman."

occurrences.title: The Merkebah — Ezekiel's vision of the four cherubim
occurrences.label: The Merkebah — Ezekiel's vision…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Babylon (exilic setting of the vision; text Judah)
body: Ezekiel's throne-vision (chs. 1 and 10): four cherubim "had 'the likeness of am an'", each with four faces — man, lion, ox, eagle — and a wheel; the four wheels were read as the Merkebah, the chariot, under "a firmament as the colour of terrible crystal" bearing the throne of him who had "the appearance of am an", "the counterpart of Osiris" (cw13 ¶362-363).

Jung: 4x4 faces in all (¶362); the one human head signals consciousness — "Horus as the rising sun is the enlightener"; the apotropaic tau-mark of Ezekiel 9:4 shows God's own quaternity (¶363). The analogy with the Egyptian four sons of Horus "is at once apparent" (¶361).
Verbatim: The analogy with the vision of Ezekiel (chapters 1 and 10) is at once apparent. (cw13 ¶361)

image.title: Ezekiel's Wheels label QS:Len,"Ezekiel's Wheels" label QS:Leo,"Radoj de Jeĥezkelo" label QS:Lhe,"אופני יחזקאל"

occurrences.title: The four beasts of Daniel's night-vision
occurrences.label: The four beasts of Daniel's night-vision
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~6th c. BCE setting (text perhaps 2nd c. BCE)
body: Daniel 7: four beasts — lion with a man's heart, bear, leopard, and the "dreadful and terrible" fourth with iron teeth and ten horns. Jung: "AU four of them are beasts of prey or, in psychological terms, functions that have succumbed to desire, lost their angelic character, and become daemonic in the worst sense" — the negative aspect of the four angels of God (Book of Enoch), "the daemonization of man" (cw13 ¶365).

Daniel reads them as four kings; the fourth beast "shall devour the whole earth" — "a monstrous lust for power will make the human quarter unconscious again... It has recurred countless times in the history of mankind" (cw13 ¶365).
Verbatim: a monstrous lust for power will make the human quarter unconscious again. (cw13 ¶365ocr)

image.title: Daniel's vision of the four beasts from the sea and the Ancient of Days - Silos Apocalypse (1109), f.240 - BL Add MS 11695

occurrences.title: The four faces of God, one fending off the Satans (1 Enoch 40)
occurrences.label: The four faces of God, one fending off…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: "Enoch in his vision sees the four faces of God. Three of them are engaged in praising, praying, and supplicating, but the fourth in 'fending off the Satans and forbidding them to come before the Lord of Spirits to accuse them who dwell on earth'" (¶673) — the angel Phanuel's office (¶690). "God now has four faces, or rather, four angels of his face, who are four hypostases or emanations, of which one is exclusively occupied in keeping his elder son Satan, now changed into many, away from him" (¶674).

An essential differentiation of the God-image: a pneumatic quaternity "presumably the descendants of Ezekiel's four seraphim"; the doubling into upper and lower quaternity betokens the deeper split — "the father wants to become the son… the unconscious wants to become consciously responsible" (¶675).

occurrences.title: The four hollows of Hades — Enoch's chthonic quaternity (1 Enoch 22)
occurrences.label: The four hollows of Hades
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Enoch's underworld "is divided into four hollow places which serve as abodes for the spirits of the dead until the Last Judgment. Three of these hollow places are dark, but one is bright and contains a 'fountain of water'" (¶671). Jung: "With statements of this type we enter into a definitely psychological realm, namely that of mandala symbolism, to which also belong the ratios 1:3 and 3:4."

The quadripartite Hades is a chthonic quaternity "in everlasting contrast to a pneumatic or heavenly one"; the former "corresponds in alchemy to the quaternio of the elements, the latter to a fourfold, or total, aspect of the deity, as for instance Barbelo, Kolorbas, Mercurius quadratus, and the four-faced gods all indicate" (¶672).

occurrences.title: The Ortus — four-coloured beast at the Red Sea (Maier)
occurrences.label: The Ortus — four-coloured beast at the Red Sea
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In Maier's peregrinatio (Symbola aureae mensae, 1617) the adept reaches the Red Sea and finds the animal 'Ortus' (rising): 'a red head with streaks of gold reaching to its neck, black eyes, a white face, white forepaws, and black hindpaws' (cw14 ¶277), after Avicenna: 'That thing whose head is red, its eyes black and its feet white, is the magistery.' Jung: 'The Ortus is the alchemical "animal" which represents the living quaternity in its first synthesis... the prima materia of the self and, as the phoenix, rebirth' (¶282). The beast is met at the 'ford', the critical fourth direction — 'Africa', the inferior function (¶276-280). 'The animal is the symbolic carrier of the self' (¶283).

occurrences.title: Ostanes between two brilliances and two dim lights — Abu'l-Qasim
occurrences.label: Ostanes between two brilliances…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: each of them has reached me and I know not how to save myself from them
body: Ostanes' cry from Abu'l-Qasim: "Save me, O my God, for I stand between two exalted brilliancies known for their wickedness, and between two dim lights; each of them has reached me and I know not how to save myself from them." Sent up to Agathodaimon, he is told of "somewhat of his nature, which will never be corrupted," and receives the "child of the bird which is mixed with redness," to be sealed in its vessel "whence it has no power to come out except when thou desirest" (¶5).

Jung decodes the quaternio: Mars and Saturn (malefici, rulers of Aries and Capricorn) against the moon and Venus (dim lights of Cancer and Libra) — masculine/feminine crossed with good/evil. The adept stands "subject to Heimarmene, the compulsion of the stars" (¶6), while the incorruptible germ — gold, aurum philosophorum, "the son of the bird... the filius philosophorum" — must be heated until the humidum radicale departs. Same text: Hermes makes the Sun "a crown" of its brothers' spirits (¶6, p23).

occurrences.title: Benedictio fontis — the water divided in a cross and sprinkled to the four quarters
occurrences.label: Benedictio fontis — the water divided…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: attested in early medieval sacramentaries; 'even today' (Jung, 1952)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: A living quaternity-rite: "even today, in the rite of the benedictio fontis, the water is divided into a cross by the hand of the priest and then sprinkled to the four quarters" (¶677). Jung's comment makes the font a cosmic diagram: as God sets out to become man, man is correspondingly "immersed in the pleromatic process… made to participate in the divine quaternity (i.e., is crucified with Christ)".
The rite descends from Ezekiel's throne-vision geometry, via Enoch's four quarters, into the liturgy — ritual evidence that the quaternity structure of the God-image was enacted, not merely imagined.

occurrences.title: Serpentine plates with ingrained concentric squares — dream of a lady in Jung's circle
occurrences.label: Serpentine plates with ingrained concentric…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: c. 1950, while the synchronicity essay was being written (inferred)

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: After someone remarked in Jung's circle, "The geometrical square does not occur in nature except in crystals," a lady present dreamed that night: in a garden sandpit, among deposited layers of rubbish, thin slaty plates of green serpentine; one bore black squares "arranged concentrically... not painted on, but... ingrained in the stone, like the markings in an agate" — Mr. A (a slight acquaintance) then took the plates away.

Jung's reading: the dream answers the waking remark with a natural product that carries the form — "These dreams seem to point to the presence of a formal factor in nature... the meaningful coincidence of an absolutely natural product with a human idea apparently independent of it" (¶946). The animus-figure takes the designs back because consciousness treats them as lusus naturae (fn. 73).

occurrences.title: Quaternarius and Ternarius ascend to the Denarius — Gerhard Dorn
occurrences.label: Quaternarius and Ternarius ascend…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Quando quidem ubi Quaternarius et Ternarius ad Denarium ascendunt, eorum fit ad unitatem regressus. In isto concluditur arcano omnis occulta rerum sapientia.
body: Dorn's number-mysticism of the new birth, cited by Jung for the ten-fold perfection of the lapis:

But in "Duellum animi" (ibid., p. 545) Dorn denies 1+2+3+4=10, since 1 is not a number: the denarius comes from 2+3+4=9+1, and he "insists on the elimination of the devilish binarius" (pp. 542ff.) — the two as the devil's number that must fall away for unity.

occurrences.title: Einstein draws the hachured functional figure — physicist dream (~1934)
occurrences.label: Einstein draws the hachured functional figure
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: A man resembling Einstein is drawing the following figure on a board
body: A dream "which preoccupied me for years": a man resembling Einstein draws a board figure — a hachured surface crossed by a graph, the hachured sections the "less differentiated (more unconscious, inferior) functions," the opposites problem between left and right halves. The dreamer read it as the unconscious' answer to the Einstein–Bohr controversy: quantum mechanics as a one-dimensional special case of a two-dimensional, more meaningful world whose second dimension "could be only the unconscious and the archetypal."

Reading: "Einstein played the role of the shadow but that the dream showed me how the 'Self' was also contained in the shadow". From this period dates the quaternio Einstein / Jung / Bohr / Pauli, "in which the people stand for mental attitudes".

occurrences.title: Dream: the four valleys converge, the lame sheep and the pregnant lamb
occurrences.label: Dream: the four valleys converge, the lame…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: We must go to the very end of the lake where the four valleys converge, where they bring down the flocks of sheep to the water.
body: The "great dream" of the series: in a boat with an unknown man she must go "to the very end of the lake where the four valleys converge," where flocks come down to drink; he finds a lame sheep, she a pregnant lamb too young to carry. Jung: the symmetric fourfold structure marks an archetypal pattern ("When dreams have that symmetrical character, one can be sure that they refer to an archetypal pattern", p103) — the dream of a "great vision," announcing fate. Amplifications: the Argonauts and the night-sea journey (p99); the lake = the unconscious (p99); the fourth-magi legend; the four rivers of Paradise; the heavenly Jerusalem of Revelations where all peoples stream together like sheep (p100); the universal fourfold symbol "among the American Indians, in China, in India" (p100). The man = the poimen/good shepherd (Hermas, Poimandres, p105-106); the sick sheep = her inherited Christian attitude dying out; the pregnant lamb = "She is still too young to carry, and yet she is pregnant with the future... a general truth for the whole present epoch" (p110).

occurrences.title: The fourth Magus who did not come in time — legend of the four wise men
occurrences.label: The fourth Magus who did not come in time
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Christian legend (Jung cites from memory, no source given)
occurrences.quote: instead of only three wise men, four were supposed to come from the four corners of the world, but the fourth did not come in time
body: First parallel offered for the dream's four streams of sheep: "There is a legend that when Jesus was born, instead of only three wise men, four were supposed to come from the four corners of the world, but the fourth did not come in time" (p99). Jesus as the source of the waters of life and his followers as the sheep — the fourfold gathering of humanity to a living center. Jung immediately complements it with the reverse picture, the four rivers flowing out of Paradise (Garden of Eden), and with the Last Judgment of Revelations, "where all the peoples of the earth stream together like sheep" toward the heavenly Jerusalem at the center (p100). The incomplete fourth (the magus who failed) quietly anticipates the whole later doctrine of the defective quaternity.

occurrences.title: The fourth man in the fiery furnace — Wernher vom Niederrhein's Mary allegory
occurrences.label: The fourth man in the fiery furnace
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Lower Rhine (cited from Salzer, Sinnbilder und Beiworte Mariens, p. 21)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: "A peculiar coincidence of three and four is to be found in Wernher vom Niederrhein's allegory of Mary, where, besides the three men in the burning fiery furnace, a fourth appears who is interpreted as Christ" (cw11 ¶? pdf p695).

Daniel 3's three youths plus the son-of-God fourth (prefiguring Trinity-plus-matter, 3+1) absorbed into Marian symbolism: Jung's medieval exhibit for the quaternity secretly completing the triad — the same move he reads into Ezekiel, Enoch, and the Atman doctrine.

occurrences.title: Gitche Manito painted as an egg with points to the four winds — Hiawatha's pictographs
occurrences.label: Gitche Manito painted as an egg with points…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The hieroglyph is at the same time a quaternity-symbol, which psychologically always points to the self.
body: Hiawatha invents writing: the egg with four points is the world enclosed in the egg, "the cosmic birth-giver, a symbol used by Plato and by the Vedas"; "this 'mother' is omnipresent, like the air … so the world-mother is a spirit, the anima mundi. The hieroglyph is at the same time a quaternity-symbol, which psychologically always points to the self" (¶550) — with the atman "no bigger than a thumb" as the centre. The second glyph paints the evil spirit as the serpent Kenabeek (¶550–551).

occurrences.title: Four sons of Horus — three animal-headed, one human-headed (Egyptian representations)
occurrences.label: Four sons of Horus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Egypt (canopic amulets and vignettes of Amset, Hapi, Duamutef, Qebehsenuf)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: there are occasionally representations in which three of the sons have animals' heads and only one a human head, in keeping with the Old Testament visions as well as with the emblems of the seraphim which were transferred to the evangelists
body: Egyptian representations of the four sons of Horus (Amset, Hapi, Duamutef, Qebehsenuf) in which three have animals' heads (man, ape, jackal, falcon — one variant human) and only one a human head. Jung uses this zoomorphic/anthropomorphic differentiation of the divine four as an "interesting differentiation" inside the quaternity-of-the-One schema, and lines it up with the Old Testament throne-visions, the seraphim emblems transferred to the evangelists, and the gospels themselves ("three of which are synoptic and one 'Gnostic'").

Jung's reading: the four sons are an early, materially dated form of the deity-with-four arrangement that runs Ezekiel → seraphim → evangelists → alchemical quaternity; the animal/human head ratio marks the chthonic-natural versus human-spiritual quarter. Index concordance: "Horus... four sons of, 234n, 319, 346n, 366, 388".

image.title: The Four Sons of Horus (deity)

occurrences.title: The mystic quadriga of four horses — Dio Chrysostom
occurrences.label: The mystic quadriga of four horses
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The horses represent the four elements.
body: The highest god drives his chariot in a circle with four horses — the four elements; when the fiery one consumes the others, "the division of God into Many ceases, and the divine One is restored." Jung reads the quadriga as "an astronomical symbol of Time" with the same libido symbolism as fate-as-fire (¶423).

occurrences.title: 'One arcanum, four-square, like a tower facing the four winds' — Paracelsus, Paragranum
occurrences.label: One arcanum, four-square, like a tower facing…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: The Paragranum on the physician's philosophy: he must make heaven and earth a microcosm, "so that the philosopher does not find anything in heaven and earth which he does not also find in man." Of the four pillars of medicine: "not four, but one arcanum, which is, however, four-square, like a tower facing the four winds. And as little as a tower may lack a corner, so little may the physician lack one of the parts." The world is "an egg in its shell," the chick hidden within; alchemy broods the arcana to maturity in the physician.

Jung's reading: Paracelsus "steeped in the idea of correspondence" through Agrippa's influence (¶932) — the one-and-four tower standing in the line Jung traces from the axiom of Maria to Dorn's Trinity-vs-quaternity decision (¶962).

occurrences.title: Three (of Four) Children and the I Ching Book — Pauli dream (1949)
occurrences.label: Three Children and the I Ching Book
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: It seems fairly obvious that the children — there are supposed to be four actually — should be linked with your function schema.
body: Two dreams sent to Jung on 4 June 1950, "that occurred last year after I had read your manuscript on the phenomenon of synchronicity." Dream 1 turns on the "dark anima's" time concept; dream 2 presents the stranger, "the light maiden" holding a book in gothic lettering that on waking resolves into the Wilhelm translation of the I Ching ("he also says that he gave her the book"), and "there are only three children here and not four" — which for Pauli "means that the" feeling-intuitive side is not yet lived; other dreams with four children came in autumn 1949.

Jung's schema-reading (letter 39J): mother = wholeness, predominantly maternal; "Older boy probably = ego; younger boy = shadow"; daughter = the anima who must "transplant herself into consciousness in order to be able to define time". Pauli: "the children — there are supposed to be four actually, and sometimes there were — should be linked with your function schema", and the stranger "makes it a sort of long-term task that she should learn" mathematics.

occurrences.title: The preacher preaches the four quantities — church dream, 24 Oct 1955
occurrences.label: The preacher preaches the four quantities
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: 24 October 1955 (preceded by the last-train dream, same night-series)

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: Le sujet demon sermon sera ces formules de M. le prof. Pauli. Ily a ici une expression de quatre quantites.
body: Started the night after reading Mysterium Coniunctionis. A deviation around an obstacle; a timetable for a very last train at 17:00; then wife, a conventional friend, and the dreamer enter a church where strangers wait. On the blackboard the dreamer writes lengthy formulas — magnetic field theory, "+ and - signs," "Il H N/V." The "major unknown figure," the famous preacher, the "master," arrives, examines the formulas, is satisfied, and announces in French:

The strangers shout "portez, portez" — the dreamer's heart races and he wakes. Pauli: "After the upper and lower Trinity, there now appears the quaternity"; French is "the language of the country of feeling (mandala of countries)," matching the eaten cherries; "In the church — the new house — I was free from the pairs of opposites, at one with myself." Jung interprets the magnet as Self (Mysterium, CW 14ii par. 360) and the magnetic field as producer of "magic" effects.

occurrences.title: The physics teacher and the H-atom doublet — physical dream in three languages (1948)
occurrences.label: The physics teacher and the H-atom doublet
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: The 'Self' that appears here in the form of the physics teacher states that the physis carries permanently with it the image (eidolon) of the tones (ideai), so that there is a consubstantial unity (homousia) of both.
body: Pauli's exemplary "physical dream," retold in 1953 in three parallel languages: (a) physical-symbolic — the first physics teacher (A. Sommerfeld) announces that the change in the splitting of the ground state of the H atom is fundamental; bronze tones are engraved on a metal plate; then the journey to Göttingen, city of mathematics; (b) theological-metaphysical — God as complexio oppositorum shining into the dark world, perceived "in a minor key" (Fludd), God become man; (c) analytical psychology — the individuation process after Plato's Timaeus, dyad reflected into a quaternio, metal plate = physis/feminine, tones = flying-spiritual/masculine.

The dream recurred, with "brass" instead of "bronze," as Dream 1 of the mid-March 1957 equinox pair, where the change in splitting = intervention of consciousness and the tones = archetypes stamping matter (aes perennium).

occurrences.title: The Tetraktys of Pythagoras — the four as mystical principle
occurrences.label: The Tetraktys of Pythagoras
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Even the Tetraktys of Pythagoras, where the four is a mystical principle, must refer to the same basic symbol of orientation.
body: Amplifying the four-valleys dream, Jung runs the quaternity through its historical forms and names the Greek one: "Even the Tetraktys of Pythagoras, where the four is a mystical principle, must refer to the same basic symbol of orientation" (p100). The editor notes the figure: 1+2+3+4 = 10, the pyramidal arrangement held mystical by the Pythagoreans (6th c. BCE).
