The claim it serves: "the four cardinal points do not exist in reality, so it is an entirely man-made projection, the projection of an inner sense of orientation which consists of four points, and why that is so I do not know" (p100) — the honest agnosticism that keeps the quaternity empirical.

occurrences.title: Plato's Timaeus opening — 'One, two, three... but where is the fourth?'
occurrences.label: Plato's Timaeus opening
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: ever since the opening of Plato's Timaeus ('One, two, three... but where, my dear Socrates, is the fourth?') and right up to the Cabiri scene in Faust) the motif of four as three and one was the ever-recurring preoccupation of alchemy.
body: The opening of Plato's Timaeus: Socrates counts his guests of the day before — "One, two, three" — and asks where the fourth has gone (the missing fourth is Timaeus, who supplies the missing speech). Jung cites this as the fountainhead of the "four as three and one" motif: "ever since the opening of Plato's Timaeus... and right up to the Cabiri scene in Faust, the motif of four as three and one was the ever-recurring preoccupation of alchemy."

Jung's reading: the counting-scene is a literary vestige of the archetypal quaternity problem — the conspicuous absence of the fourth — which the appendix sets as the schema behind the visions of Ezekiel, Daniel, and Enoch, Horus with his four sons, the seraphim-evangelist emblems, and the three synoptic gospels plus one "Gnostic." (CW9i Appendix; OCR ¶ markers on the appendix pages are truncated — likely ~¶717 in continuous CW9i numbering.)

occurrences.title: The 'secret square of the sages' with the mediating circle — Tractatus aureus (Gnosius scholium)
occurrences.label: The 'secret square of the sages'…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Tractatus aureus … cum Scholiis Dominici Gnosii (1610), pp. 43–44, 262f.
occurrences.quote: the mediator, making peace between enemies, or [the four] elements; nay rather he alone effects the squaring of the circle
body: A drawing of the "secret square of the sages": in the centre of the square a circle surrounded by rays of light. The scholium explains: "Divide lapidem tuum in quatuor elementa … et coniunge in unum et totum habebis magisterium," and names the central circle "the mediator, making peace between enemies, or [the four] elements; nay rather he alone effects the squaring of the circle." An accompanying drawing of the circulatio shows four rivers flowing in and out of the inner "ocean" — "for this vessel is the true philosophical Pelican, and there is no other to be sought for in all the world."

Jung uses it (Part I ch. 3, n. 44) as the alchemical twin of his dream-mandalas: the centre as mediator making peace among the four, and the circumambulatio/circulatio as the movement in which "all would be one thing in one circle or vessel."

occurrences.title: The triad as unity, the quaternity standing on the binarius — Valentinus, Duodecim claves
occurrences.label: The triad as unity, the quaternity standing…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 185. Below, the triad as unity; above, the quaternity standing on the binarius.—Valentinus, 'Duodecim claves,' in Mus. herm. (1678)
body: Diagram from the Duodecim claves of Basilius Valentinus: below, the triad fused as unity; above, the quaternity standing upon the binarius — the arithmetic of 3-and-4 that Jung made central to his alchemical structural analysis.

His context: the stone is "trinus et unus"; the fourth, "absent and yet present," appears in the fiery furnace (Daniel 3:25) as the completion of the three (¶449). The same figure underlies Böhme's quaternity of the cross in the zodiac (fig. 192).

occurrences.title: 'Vultur in cacumine montis' — the vulture that is black, white, red and citron
occurrences.label: Vultur in cacumine montis
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: antique material in Latin pseudo-Hermetica (printing era)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Quoted from "one of the Latin pseudo-Hermetic writings," where the vulture is "the spiritus volatilis rising from the black mother": "Vultur in cacumine montis magna voce clamet: ego sum ater et albus, rubens et citrinus — 'The vulture upon the top of the mountain cries with loud voice, I am white and black and red and citron'" (pdf p576; OCR noise in chunk).

Jung's gloss runs through the four functions: the bird "is the one that unites the four qualities, being above the temperaments… With us it would mean the one that is neither thinking, feeling, sensation, nor intuition, but above the four functions." The colors coincide with the church's original four colors (white, black, yellow, red) — "they must have to do with some original conception" — and the one they unite into is named "lapis philosophorum, aurum nostrum… It was very clearly not a chemical body… It was symbolic".

occurrences.title: The queen's discourse at her apotheosis — Tractatus aureus
occurrences.label: The queen's discourse at her apotheosis
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: After death is life restored to me. To me, poor as I am, were entrusted the treasures of the wise and mighty.
body: At her apotheosis the queen holds a discourse: "After death is life restored to me. To me, poor as I am, were entrusted the treasures of the wise and mighty... But I am not yet equal to my most beloved brother, the mighty king, who has yet to be raised from the dead. But when he comes, he will verily show that my words are the truth."

Jung at cw14 ¶534-535: in this "soror et sponsa" we discern the analogy with the Church, corpus mysticum and vessel of the anima Christi — the queen entrusted with treasures answers to Honorius' queen of the south who gives body and blood.

occurrences.title: Queen of Heaven — B.St.'s ascension fantasy (Burghölzli, ~1905)
occurrences.label: Queen of Heaven — B.St.s ascension fantasy
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: This seems to be nothing but an analogy, giving promise of her own ascension, when she will become the (sexually not inactive) Queen of Heaven, Mary the mother of God.
body: In the "Stuart" analysis B.St. sets beside "the Roman Mr. St., our all-highest deity in heaven" the head of her dead sister — "an image that reminds one of the two pagan divinities, Jupiter and Juno." She thus "more or less marries her sister to the divine Mr. St.," an analogy "giving promise of her own ascension, when she will become the (sexually not inactive) Queen of Heaven, Mary the mother of God" (¶279). She already styles herself "Lord God" and "Mary the mother of God" (¶224), and the crown-analysis crowns her in heaven by "incontrovertible justice" (¶229). Jung sets the fantasy in the millennial row of Christian spiritual marriage — the Song of Songs interpretation, Catherine of Siena, Hauptmann's Hannele: "the prologue in heaven to the earthly comedy."

occurrences.title: The Queen of the South gives body and blood — Honorius of Autun
occurrences.label: The Queen of the South gives body and blood
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: For while the Queen of the South gave her body and her blood to the disciples, John lay in the bosom of Jesus.
body: On the queen of the south (Matt 12:42): "John abandoned his bride and, himself a virgin, followed the son of a virgin... For while the Queen of the South gave her body and her blood to the disciples, John lay in the bosom of Jesus and drank from that fount of wisdom."

Jung at cw14 ¶535-536: in both this passage and the Tractatus aureus the queen "seems to be identified with Jesus" — the thought of Christ's androgyny shows how nearly queen and king are one, as body and soul, spirit and soul.

occurrences.title: Birkhäuser's 'The Fourth Dimension' — quincunx of animal-human faces above the city
occurrences.label: Birkhäuser's 'The Fourth Dimension'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This is a symbol of the quinta essentia, which is identical with the Philosophers' Stone.
body: A contemporary painting on two incommensurable planes: a dark-red three-dimensional city on the horizontal, and a watery greenish-blue "fourth dimension" behind it, holding fourteen circles — ten forming the eyes of shadowy half-animal, half-human faces, four being dark haloed objects. From the mouth of the great face flows a stream of water down through the city; "Neither touches the other." The ground structure is a quincunx; the eye-quaternity has a 3+1 structure (one human face among three animal-daemonic).

Jung's reading: the quincunx "is a symbol of the quinta essentia, which is identical with the Philosophers' Stone... the four functions of consciousness with their unitary substrate, the self" (¶738); the 3+1 runs through alchemy (Axiom of Maria), Ezekiel, the sons of Horus, the evangelists and "the four Persons of Christian metaphysics: the Trinity and the devil" (¶738); "Our mandala seems to be complementary to the Christian totality" (¶741). Conclusion: "the Ufos are subliminal contents that have become visible; that they are, in a word, archetypal figures" (¶747).

occurrences.title: Yves Tanguy's painting of 1927 — quincunx, whirls and cigar-form over a night city
occurrences.label: Yves Tanguy's painting of 1927
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Thus we arrive at an apparently fortuitous picture of a hierosgamos taking place in the heavens, followed by the birth of a saviour and his epiphany on earth.
body: Yves Tanguy's 1927 painting, "thus anticipating by more than a decade the great bombings of cities": five shadow-casting forms on a black-and-white plane (sea-ice, fog, planet surface, or a night city by the sea), over which hangs a quincunx — a daemonic central face flanked by four figures (a quaternity with 3+1 structure), while in the sky two faint luminous whirls with dark centres, a cigar-shaped cloud bank and a connecting flame-line appear.

Jung ran an informal Rorschach with many viewers (¶748). His own amplification finds "a cylinder... aimed straight at the topmost luminous whirl" — cohabitation — and concludes: "Thus we arrive at an apparently fortuitous picture of a hierosgamos taking place in the heavens, followed by the birth of a saviour and his epiphany on earth" (¶751). Modern art here "evokes complexes which have sloughed off their usual personal aspect and appear as what they originally were, namely primordial forms of the instincts" (¶755).

occurrences.title: 'Our heaven' — the quintessence of the microcosm — Christopher of Paris, Elucidarius
occurrences.label: Our heaven' — the quintessence of the microcosm
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Christopher of Paris on the Chaos: "In this Chaos the said precious substance and nature truly exists potentially, in a single confused mass of the elements. Human reason ought therefore to apply itself to bringing our heaven into actuality" (cw11 ¶? pdf p699). "Our heaven" is the microcosm, "also called the 'quintessence' … 'incorruptible' and 'immaculate'"; Rupescissa calls it "le ciel humain."
The work of art becomes the raising of one's inner heaven from potentiality to act — the psychological reading Jung draws from the whole chain (Hortulanus' massa confusa → Rupescissa → Christopher).

occurrences.title: Graveyard rabbit's left hind foot, caught in moonlight — charm of the American South
occurrences.label: Graveyard rabbit's left hind foot, caught…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Dr. Draper's example: "The North American Negro is not happy unless he has a razor in one pocket and in the other the left hind foot of a graveyard rabbit, caught in the light of the moon." Jung's reading: the foot carries the animal instinct; from the graveyard it is "impregnated with the qualities, or the mana, of the dead, so it is a charm that has to do with the whole complex of questions... under the heading of moon symbolism. It is an apotropaic charm because it comes from the dead" — whatever comes from death protects from death, the same logic as soma and the Eucharist.

occurrences.title: Rabi'a — 'I have made Thee the Companion of my heart' (Sufi mystic, 8th c. Iraq)
occurrences.label: Rabi'a — 'I have made Thee the Companion…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: The woman mystic of Islam on the third stage of love (Uns, intimacy): "I have made Thee (God) the Companion of my heart, / But my body is available for those who desire its company, / And my body is friendly towards its guests, / But the Beloved of my heart is the guest of my soul." (p404)

Harding's frame: the Islamic mystics took the stages of love — Rida (Satisfaction), Shavq (Longing), Uns (Fellowship/Intimacy) — "as the outwardly lived dramatic representation of Union with God," exactly as Christian sacraments dramatize initiation. The quote marks the transformation "from the concrete, the material, into the unseen, the spiritual" — by the downward-going road of the crescent, as the I Ching homily on the Cauldron puts the same move ("All that is visible must grow beyond itself").

occurrences.title: Ragnarök — the Völuspá's doom of the gods
occurrences.label: Ragnarök — the Völuspás doom of the gods
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Iceland (Codex Regius copy; mythic material older)
occurrences.quote: The myth has been fulfilled, and the greater part of Europe lies in ruins.
body: The Eddic prophecy of the gods' twilight, quoted in long verse blocks at the end of Jung's "Wotan" essay: Garm howls at Gnipahellir, the fetters burst, Yggdrasil shivers, Wotan "murmurs with Mimir's head," the serpent writhes over the waves, Naglfar sails with the people of Hel at whose helm stands Loki.

Jung's reading is two-staged. In 1936 the quotation is prognosis: the re-dammed water of the archetype leaps its old channel, and what Wotan will say when he "murmurs with Mimir's head" is still to be heard (cw10 ¶399). In 1945, opening "After the Catastrophe," he declares the omen fulfilled: "The myth has been fulfilled, and the greater part of Europe lies in ruins" (cw10 ¶400). The Ragnarök script is thus the one myth Jung claims as a literally accurate forecast of a historical event — expresses_inferred shadow: the apocalyptic form taken by an archetype erupting unintegrated (cf. ¶461 on the bipolarity of archetypes).

occurrences.title: The rain-maker of Kiaochau — Wilhelm's story of being back in Tao
occurrences.label: The rain-maker of Kiaochau
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: told by Wilhelm ~1928; printed in seminar 1939
occurrences.quote: So I had to wait three days until I was back in Tao and then naturally the rain came.
body: Wilhelm's story, retold by Jung as "an example of 'being in Tao' and its synchronistic accompaniments": during a catastrophic drought, processions and prayers having failed, the fetched rain-maker locks himself alone in a hut for three days — then the unprecedented snow falls. Asked how, he answers that he came from a country in order; here everything is out of order, "not as they should be by the ordinance of heaven," so he too was out of Tao and had to wait three days until he was back in it — "and then naturally the rain came."

Jung's canonical anecdote for the individuated person's non-agential cooperation with the totality. Source: "Interpretation of Visions," Vol. 3 of the English seminars (new edn., 1939), p. 7. Parallels: synchronicity concept, mandala-university-trained-woman-golden-flower-fig-a4-1928.

occurrences.title: Six-year-old girl climbs the rainbow to heaven — 'Children's Dreams' seminar
occurrences.label: Six-year-old girl climbs the rainbow to heaven
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: age six, remembered in adulthood; presented 29 Nov 1938

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: A remembered childhood dream: a beautiful rainbow rises before the dreamer; she climbs it into heaven, calls her friend Marietta to follow, and when Marietta hesitates the rainbow disintegrates and she falls. Presented by Dr. Emma Steiner; amplified with Noah's covenant rainbow, the rainbow-bridge of Traumsymbole des Individuationsprozesses (CW12 §§44ff), rainbow cups of folklore, and Gallic gold bracteates.

Jung's reading: Marietta is the earth-bound friend carrying the dreamer's shadow ("in psychology we call the shadow the inferior figure, bound to the earth," pdf p149). The ascent is the child's development of consciousness at school age — "it is a 'reculer pour mieux sauter'" — carried too far, so the unconscious ends the splitting by letting her fall: "the dream aims at keeping consciousness and shadow together". The rainbow itself is "a numinosum... a bridge leading into the hereafter".

occurrences.title: Rainbow after long storms — redemption from revenge (Zarathustra)
occurrences.label: Rainbow after long storms
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939
Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: that would be a rainbow bridge; that is the thing to be hoped for-that he could accept his inferior side.
body: Zarathustra: "Because, for man to be redeemed from revenge — that is for me the bridge to the highest hope, and a rainbow after long storms." Jung reads it as the hope of reunion with the projected shadow: "if the shadow could be redeemed from its spirit of revenge, there would be a chance of reunion and that would be a rainbow bridge".

At the next lecture Mrs. Sigg recalls Jahveh's rainbow after the flood (the folk play Green Pastures); Jung endorses with reserve: "I am sure that archetypal image of the great flood is behind this particular passage, but I would not attach too much importance to it". The rainbow covenant folded into Nietzsche's psychology of revenge — the two time axes kept distinct: 1883 text, Genesis myth behind it.

occurrences.title: Rainbow cups: Gallic gold bracteates explained as found where the rainbow touches earth
occurrences.label: Rainbow cups — Gallic gold bracteates explained…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 5th-6th c. (time of the migration of peoples)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: In the rainbow-dream discussion Jung adduces the folk belief that "rainbow cups are found where the rainbow touches the earth. The Gallic gold bracteates have been explained in this way". The bracteates — flat gold medallions imitating Roman imperial coins, with runes — are thus folk-etymologically tied to the treasure at the rainbow's end.

His point: "Here the rainbow is just the bridge to an Above, set in opposition to a Below. Which psychological figure would correspond to this Below? — The shadow" (pp149-150). The rainbow joins the series of numinous bridge-images (Noah's covenant token, the rainbow-bridge of CW12 §§44ff, where mortals must pass under, not over).

occurrences.title: The Noahic covenant — rainbow as token (Genesis 9)
occurrences.label: The Noahic covenant — rainbow as token
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Yahweh's contract with Noah, his children, and all their animals "both tame and wild", sealed by a sign: "In order to strengthen this contract and keep it fresh in the memory, he instituted the rainbow as a token of the covenant" (¶577). Jung reads the arrangement darkly — the temptation to use the assembled thunder-clouds for "an experimental deluge was no small one", so a timely warning-sign was prudent.
Within Answer to Job's sequence of covenants, this contract too "had gone to pieces with David" (¶578), preparing the Job catastrophe.

occurrences.title: The shofar that reminds YHWH of his injustice — Midrash
occurrences.label: The shofar that reminds YHWH of his injustice
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The Shofar is still sounded on the Day of Atonement to remind YHWH of his act of injustice towards Abraham... and to prevent him from repeating it.
body: In the Letter to Père Lachat: "A Midrash says that the Shofar is still sounded on the Day of Atonement to remind YHWH of his act of injustice towards Abraham (by compelling him to slay Isaac) and to prevent him from repeating it" (¶1551). The ram's horn — the ram that replaced Isaac — becomes an annual instrument of divine self-restraint.

Jung's reading: a stunning rabbinic acknowledgement that YHWH is "moral and immoral at the same time" (¶1593), needing liturgical guarding against his own wrath — exactly the "divine antinomy" that Answer to Job unfolds; it grounds his claim that "a conscientious clarification of the idea of God would have consequences as upsetting as they are necessary" (¶1551).

occurrences.title: Vision: the ram met by the Indian's spear; black horse, black pond, the Chinaman (19 Nov 1930)
occurrences.label: Vision — the ram met by the Indian's spear
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I beheld the head of a ram. Swiftly and with fearful strength the ram charged and was met full on the forehead by the spear of an Indian.
body: The first dynamic vision of the American patient's series, after eight static hypnogogic fragments (peacock, sun-man — earlier chunk): the ram charges and is stopped by the Indian's spear; the Indian gallops off on a black horse to a black pond ringed by black mountains; the horse dies; the Indian turns into a Chinaman who bows his forehead to the ground three times. Jung: movement means "energy has entered the images" and the sequence becomes drama — a mystery play that will catch and transform the patient.

Reading: ram = Aries, the first green shoot of autonomous creative impulse; spear = "la qualite tranchante of the intellect", the animus opinion that kills it (p176); the killer inherits the victim's spirit — the Indian takes over the ram's dynamism (p177); black horse = chthonic power (Plato's black horse, the Yin side, p178); the pond = womb of the earth, entrance to the underworld; the Chinaman = her sensation function, "the philosophy of the earth" (p180).

occurrences.title: Rama marries Sita the furrow — Ramayana
occurrences.label: Rama marries Sita the furrow — Ramayana
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Sita means "furrow": the hero-king marries the ploughed earth; Indra likewise is husband of Urvara, "the fertile land"; Chinese emperors ploughed a furrow on accession.
Jung's reading: "the seizure of a country by the king was regarded as his marriage with the land" (¶306) — the hieros gamos of king and soil; its failure kills the king (Domaldi).
Verbatim: In the Hindu Ramayana, the hero Rama marries Sita, the furrow. (cw05 ¶306).

occurrences.title: Dhulqarnein's iron-and-brass rampart against Gog and Magog — Qur'an 18
occurrences.label: Dhulqarnein's iron-and-brass rampart…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: He dammed up the valley between the Two Mountains, and said: 'Ply your bellows.' And when the iron blocks were red with heat, he said: 'Bring me molten brass to pour on them.
body: Dhulqarnein ("the Two-horned One", Alexander the Great) journeys to the sun's setting in a pool of black mud and to its rising, then dams the valley between the Two Mountains with blocks of iron poured over with molten brass — an unscalable rampart against Gog and Magog, destined to fall to dust when the Lord's promise is fulfilled (¶252-255; cf. Revelation 20:7). Jung reads the rampart as protection thrown around "the place in the middle": "the self, enthroned in the place of the middle... the beloved city (Jerusalem, the centre of the earth). The self is the hero... the jewel... the god who is dismembered" (¶256). Individuation here is opus contra naturam, its wall provisional — it falls "when consciousness sinks back into the darkness... the moment of death" (¶256-256a).

occurrences.title: The raven nailed with three nails on the world-tree — 'The Princess in the Tree' (German fairytale)
occurrences.label: The raven nailed with three nails…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Germany ('The Princess in the Tree', Deutsche Marchen seit Grimm, pp. 1ff)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: there in the room he finds a raven fixed to the wall with three nails. One nail goes through his throat, the two others through the wings.
body: A swineherd climbs a tree whose branches lose themselves in the clouds; in a castle atop it a king's daughter is held by a wicked magician. In the one forbidden room he finds "a raven fixed to the wall with three nails. One nail goes through his throat, the two others through the wings." Out of pity he gives the raven water — at each sip a nail falls out, and the raven flies free. The raven is the hunter-devil who stole the princess (an anima mundi "bewitched up there"); the three nails are "the triune name". Jung reads the whole as an inverted Christian image: "The Saviour who freed the soul of humanity from the dominion of the prince of this world was nailed to a cross down below on earth, just as the thieving raven is nailed to the wall in the celestial branches of the world-tree" (¶427). The raven's release, the theft of the four-legged horse from the witch, and the trampling of the hunter carry the triad-quaternion drama to the hieros-gamos ending.

occurrences.title: Elijah fed by ravens at the brook Cherith — I Kings 17
occurrences.label: Elijah fed by ravens at the brook Cherith
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: It is a raven that brings the food to Elijah but of course it is much more distinguished to have an eagle
body: "Eagles shall bring us lone ones food in their beaks!" — and Jung locates the source: "from the Old Testament-the Protestant comes out in Nietzsche again. It is a raven that brings the food to Elijah but of course it is much more distinguished to have an eagle-a raven would not quite do. So he is in the place of Elijah the prophet; Zarathustra is a prophet as good as any."

The upgrade is telling: the black raven of the desert episode must become the eagle, "the bird of light, the cousin of the Phoenix," when Nietzsche identifies with the spirit — yet in alchemy it is precisely the raven (caput corvi, the head lost with Osiris in the dark waters of Set's dismemberment) that "later on... becomes a golden head," the alchemists of a Greek text calling themselves "children of the gold head".

occurrences.title: Raymond Lodge's after-death communications — houses, vaguely
occurrences.label: Raymond Lodge's after-death communications
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: He answered as if he were in a dream. It is the psychology of a very fragmentary person
body: Sir Oliver Lodge's book about his dead son Raymond: asked all sorts of questions, "the replies were peculiarly meagre". Do you live in houses? — "Yes, we have houses... as if he didn't realize that they lived in them. He answered as if he were in a dream."

Jung: "It is the psychology of a very fragmentary person" — either a mere psychical phenomenon, or ghosts live in fragmentary forms; the same fragmentariness appears in the insane. The point serves the employees reading: split-off partial personalities have "only a very partial realization of their own existence".

occurrences.title: The angel Raziel brings Adam the book of 72 kinds of wisdom — Zohar
occurrences.label: The angel Raziel brings Adam the book…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: But when he sinned and transgressed the command of the Lord, this book fled from him.
body: When Adam was in paradise, God sent the angel Raziel, keeper of the higher secrets, with a book in which "two and seventy kinds of wisdom were described in six hundred and seventy sections," with fifteen hundred keys. "When he sinned and transgressed the command of the Lord, this book fled from him... He bequeathed it to his son Seth. And from Seth it came to Enoch, and from him... to Abraham."
Jung at cw14 ¶572: the legend behind the alchemical Adam-as-first-adept and the chain of Philosophers.

occurrences.title: Re poisoned by the worm of his own saliva — the secret of the name
occurrences.label: Re poisoned by the worm of his own saliva
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Egypt (Tale of Isis and Re; cf. CW5 §451)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: From von Franz's snake survey: "In a very similar way, the son god Re is poisoned, according to an Egyptian hymn, by a venerable worm, formed out of his own saliva and laid in his way by Isis, who is enraged at him. She then heals him only after he discloses his name to her, but his power remains broken" (pdf p263; cf. CW5 §451).

The worm formed of the god's own spittle — the autonomous bite from within oneself — takes its place among the snake's attacks on the bright upper world: Hera's serpents in Heracles' crib, the python before Apollo's Delphi, the Midgard snake, Leviathan. It is simultaneously the pattern of the healing serpent: poison and remedy, name and secret held together.

occurrences.title: Hottentot initiation: the son proves his mother is 'just a woman' (South West Africa)
occurrences.label: Hottentot initiation
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Formerly, with the Hottentots, the boy had occasionally even to perform incest once with his mother in order to prove that she was not his mother any more, but just a woman like the rest.
body: In the puberty rites Jung sketches — night, bull-roarers, the bush-house, the boys told they are dead and then reborn with new names — he reports the Hottentot extreme: after initiation the mothers may not speak to their sons, for the young men are no longer their children; and "formerly" a boy might have to perform incest once with his mother to prove "that she was not his mother any more, but just a woman like the rest."
Jung's reading: the rites detach the boy from "original biological participation with the parents," the work baptism performs in Christian form by substituting godfather and godmother (¶361-363).

occurrences.title: Rebirth of water and spirit — the Nicodemus dialogue, John 3
occurrences.label: Rebirth of water and spirit
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Nicodemus asks literally: "Can he enter the second time into his mother's womb?" Jesus answers: "Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit..." — πνεῦμα meaning both spirit and wind.

Jung's reading: "to be born of water simply means to be born of the mother's womb; to be born of the Spirit means to be born of the fructifying breath of the wind" (¶334); symbolical truth "puts water in place of the mother and spirit or fire in place of the father, frees the libido from the channel of the incest tendency" (¶335); the Church becomes the mother (¶335).
Verbatim: Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God. (cw05 ¶333).

occurrences.title: The Rebis — Book of the Holy Trinity, Codex Germanicus 598
occurrences.label: The Rebis — Book of the Holy Trinity, Codex…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The Rebis: from "Book of the Holy Trinity and Description of the Secret of the Transmutation of Metals" (1420)
body: Plate B3 of CW13: the Rebis from the "Book of the Holy Trinity" (Dreifaltigkeitsbuch) of 1420, Munich Codex Germanicus 598, fol. 105v. Jung notes it "may have served as a model for the hermaphrodite in the Rosarium (pl. B2)."

The same 1420 manuscript was mined again by Reusner's Pandora (1588) for several of its eighteen pictures (¶181 n.52), making this codex a documented hub of the hermaphrodite iconography that Jung reads as "the monstrous, double nature of Mercurius" (¶181) and as the filius's "rounded perfection" (¶157). The picture series of the Rosarium and its kin is the pool from which his rebis instances aggregate.

occurrences.title: The filius as hermaphrodite with bat's wings — Rosarium 1550, fol. X
occurrences.label: The filius as hermaphrodite with bat's wings
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The axiom of Maria is represented by 1 + 3 snakes: the filius, as mediator, unites the one with the three.
body: Plate B2 of CW13: "The filius or rex in the form of a hermaphrodite. The axiom of Maria is represented by 1 + 3 snakes: the filius, as mediator, unites the one with the three. Characteristically, he has bat's wings. To the right is the Pelican, symbol of the distillatio circularia; to the left, the arbor philosophica with golden flowers; underneath, the chthonic triad as a three-headed serpent."

A compressed synthesis of the essay's whole symbolic field: rebis (hermaphroditic Mercurius, ¶268), the quaternity problem of three and four (the axiom of Maria Prophetissa, ¶272-273), the arbor philosophica, the Pelican vessel (¶185), and the chthonic serpent triad.

image.title: Fig.17

occurrences.title: Red ball, Trinity devalued, and the green-faced spirit — dream of a boy of ten (January 1940)
occurrences.label: Red ball, Trinity devalued, and the green-faced…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: wartime Europe (city under bombardment; dreamer has a brother Meinrad)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: When the ball had come into the house, it opened and 'God' came out. It was a shining triangle with rays, and in the middle there was a figure that looked like 'God.' But it was someone young, not an old man, and also not the Savior.
body: A ten-year-old Catholic boy, raised religiously in a city under wartime bombardment, dreams (in two parts): a red ball approaches from the sky and enters the house; it opens and "God" comes out — a shining triangle with rays, but the figure within is young, "not an old man, and also not the Savior," a stranger. Then the end of the world: moon and stars fall (Apocalypse, the angel of destruction), Jesus alone in an empty sky, heaven a theater with the Trinity on a throne — and God gone. A "spirit" with a green face comes; it is winter; the boy lunges at the devil and dumps him into the snow. Jung reads the ball as the deity, "the world soul, the rotundum, the round one" (red = blood, emotion; cf. Ignatius's globe visions and Buber's nun); the devaluation of the dogmatic images is compensatory, and the green-faced one is Al-Khidr, the Green One — "the angel of the face, the visible Allah, the deuteros theos" — a natural spirit appearing where the dogma no longer contains the pneuma zoés. The boy's terror and snow-dumping repeat St. Anthony's rejection of the enlightening spirits. A war dream with collective significance: "similar dreams have been dreamed in many other places."

occurrences.title: Pursued by the drunk old woman in the red corset — childhood dream (girl 4)
occurrences.label: Pursued by the drunk old woman in the red corset
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: She is being pursued by a drunk old woman wearing a red corset.
body: A middle-aged woman (45–50), "leading a spiritual existence," who only at forty-five discovered she possessed something called sexuality, reported this as her first impressive dream. Nothing of the sort existed in her environment.

At seven followed the second dream — "She has to wash white linen, in a tub filled with blood" ("Here you have the red color again") — and from seven a stereotyped anxiety dream of a small side-door and a dark basement staircase with a ghost. Jung's reading: "A persecutory dream always means: this wants to come to me... The urge of what had been split off to unite with you becomes all the stronger." She should have said to the ghost: "Oh here you are, come and show yourself!" — the way to totality through the underworld she evaded.

occurrences.title: The red Indian in the catacomb — teeth transformed into blood-red jewels (Visions)
occurrences.label: The red Indian in the catacomb
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: vision read 2 March 1932 (painted late 1929/early 1930 for Jung)
occurrences.quote: I passed them by until I came to a dead man whose flesh was red. He was very beautiful and I thought he was an Indian.
body: A descent "many steps into the black earth" to a catacomb of the dead — the psychopomp leading to the land of the Hereafter:

The Indian of the first visions, now a beautiful corpse with living flesh: the animus "that would make her adapted to the American soil" — "he really demonstrates the American soil". "From his neck I took a necklace of teeth" — amulets, "the power of the animus"; a dwarf — "a subordinate creative power in the unconscious… or it may steal things away", like the snake robbing Gilgamesh — tries to snatch it. In a fire of blue flame: "The teeth changed to blood-red jewels which burned my hand". The teeth (aggression, negative feeling) become the heart-jewel — "An animus attack is usually a substitute for a positive feeling"; the red crystal "points to the center of the mandala… the Self which appears in the feeling", so hot it breaks the living taboo of the animus.

occurrences.title: Circumambulatio and the red pyramid with the dripping knife (Visions, 21 Feb. 1934)
occurrences.label: Circumambulatio and the red pyramid…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Alone in the barren rock-circle: "I walked around and around" — the circumambulatio, "as the sacred place-the stupas in Buddhism-are circumambulated, and always clockwise"; betrachten, "making a thing pregnant... She is impregnating the earth by the circumambulatio, because in that way the object of worship is filled with mana". "At last I saw the earth move in the center of the circle... And the earth cracked and then slowly there towered up a great pyramid of red." (pp1385-1386).

"Blue and white rays went out from it along the ground and turned to marble. I stood in wonder. Then I walked to the pyramid. I saw a knife from which dripped blood.". The American-flag colors (Mrs. Baumann's reading, accepted: "the most amazing condensation of associations," p1390). Jung: the pyramid is "a mandala, the symbol of individuation, the four functions which come to the oneness of realization" — the buried king, "the equivalent of the vanished Self... what has been female is now male": her forcing her way up out of the ground into conscious life. The blood-knife postponed to the next session (end of chunk).

occurrences.title: Red Teacher and Yellow Teacher — Chinese Buddhist cosmology painting (Escher)
occurrences.label: Red Teacher and Yellow Teacher
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: China → Zurich (shown in seminar by Dr. Escher)
body: A Chinese Buddhist painting brought to the Visions seminar by Dr. Escher: an assembly of gods beneath which opens the typical hell of Mahayana Buddhism — scales weighing the merits and demerits of the soul, demons torturing, "blood pouring out like wine". Two presiding figures, the Red Teacher and the Yellow Teacher, are designations from Lamaistic Buddhism.

Jung reads the pair as the two principles: yellow, colour of the Chinese Emperor ("son of heaven"), indicates a Yang teaching — the original Mahayana; dark red the chthonic Yin teaching of the Bon religion, Tibet's primitive substrate. The Red Teacher's jade weapon is the magic dagger, an equivalent of the vajra/thunderbolt — for Jung the medicine man's icicle, a "witch's shot": "the Yellow Teacher has nothing in his hands, there is no vajra because he himself is the vajra; the diamond body is in his bosom, in his heart". White magician and black magician sit peaceably together — "the Yin and Yang always cooperate in a very friendly way".

occurrences.title: Judas the Galilean's insurrection — political redeemer (Josephus)
occurrences.label: Judas the Galilean's insurrection
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 6 CE (after Herod the Great's death; Quirinus census era)
occurrences.quote: above all Judas of Galilee, whose insurrection is reported by Flavius Josephus,2 and who, boldly but quite logically, entangles the eponymous hero of this drama in a similar task.
body: In the 1938 foreword to Gertrud Gilli's verse drama Der dunkle Bruder, Jung gives the historical matrix of the redemption mystery: after Herod the Great, "all hope of an independent sacerdotal order or kingdom had vanished, and the country had become a Roman province lacking any form of autonomy," so Messianic expectation "was bound to rise to fever pitch" and fixed on a political redeemer. Foremost of the patriots: Judas of Galilee, whose insurrection Flavius Josephus reports and whom Gilli's play entangles with her eponymous hero.

Jung's reading: the redeemer figure "invariably emerges from the unconscious of the individual or the people when an intolerable situation cries out for a solution that cannot be implemented by conscious means alone" (¶1744). Judas of Galilee is the political twin of the dark-brother Judas — the human drama that "at all times... accompanied the divine drama and often eclipsed it" (¶1747).

occurrences.title: Manda d'hayye, 'understanding of life' — the Mandaean Saviour near Kut-el-Amara
occurrences.label: Manda d'hayye, 'understanding of life'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: texts ~3rd-7th c. CE; sect still living in 1929 (~3000, silversmiths)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: manda = 'gnosis' or 'understanding,' and hayye = 'life.
body: "One of the last Gnostic groups, the so-called Mandaeans, have a concept for the Saviour which means 'understanding of life,' manda d'hayye; manda = 'gnosis' or 'understanding,' and hayye = 'life.'" Some three thousand still lived near Kut-el-Amara, famous silversmiths, eating only drowned animals; their books (Lidzbarski's Book of John; Mead's John the Baptizer) were known but hard to translate.

Jung uses them at the end of the worm-lecture: the Gnostics made the serpent the Messiah who "teaches people how to escape the curse of unconsciousness," and "the Gnosis therefore remained a bud that never unfolded" — while the Mandaeans' John-Book stages the introvert/extravert quarrel: "John the introvert said, 'Don't give it away, they will spoil it.' Christ as the extravert said, 'But I can work miracles with it.'" The Book of John called Christ the "Deceiver" for betraying the mysteries.

occurrences.title: Manda d'haje, the impersonal savior of the Mandeans (Book of John)
occurrences.label: Manda d'haje, the impersonal savior…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Mesopotamia (Mandean Book of John; Mead, The Gnostic John the Baptizer, 1924)
occurrences.quote: Manda d 'haje, meaning understanding of life; that is an impersonal figure, a sort of poimen
body: On St. John's day 1931 Jung introduces the Mandean Book of John (via Mead's extract): John accuses Jesus of having given out the mysteries — "the betrayer of the truth" defends himself by his miracles, "and to this day it remains undecided who really was right". The Mandeans know no personal savior: "the savior there is called by a name which is of particular interest for us: Manda d'haje, meaning understanding of life; that is an impersonal figure, a sort of poimen, representing the wisdom or the consciousness of life, an exceedingly modern conception" — the shepherd-figure that returns in the patient's psychopompos.

occurrences.title: The Negro beneath the tree, singing, blood from his heart (patient vision, plate 17, 10 June 1931)
occurrences.label: The Negro beneath the tree, singing, blood…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: 10 June 1931 session (picture: plate 17, first shown 27 May)
occurrences.quote: While he sang blood poured from his heart in slow and rhythmic beats. It flowed along in a stream covering my feet. I followed the stream of blood.
body: The black head of the egg now has its whole body: a Negro lying beneath a tree, fruits in his hands, singing "with a full throaty voice" to darkness, to flaming fields and to the children in her womb — an incantation like the Australian singing of the kangaroo. Blood pours from his heart in slow rhythmic beats and covers her feet. Jung reads the figure in the archetypal role of the vegetation god — Attis, Adonis, Osiris, Tammuz, Mondamin — whose blood is the wine, and as mediator between her intellect and her instinctive life: "the black Messiah". Nature demands a death; no inflicted sacrifice but the Dionysian abandon of amor fati.

occurrences.title: Manda d'hayye, the Gnosis of Life — 'victorious was Life' refrain of the Book of John
occurrences.label: Manda d'hayye, the Gnosis of Life
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~3rd-7th c. CE (translated only recently in Jung's day)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The Mandaean Gnosis of John the Baptizer, "the initiator of Christ," keeps a refrain Jung finds astonishing: "In the Book of John one is astonished to find at the end of each chapter that almost epical phrase: 'And the Life be praised, victorious was Life'".

"Their savior was that Manda d'hayye, the Gnosis of life. They believed that the understanding of life was the supreme knowledge-that the ultimate decision about human action was given through life itself." Jung offers it as the pre-modern precedent for his own criterion against Nietzsche's "highest thought" placed above life: "the vital" as the measure of morality. The same refrain surfaces, uncannily, in Zola's Fécondité — "And victorious was life" — which Zola could not have known, the Book of John being written in "a lost language which even existing adherents of that belief were unable to read."

occurrences.title: The insurance clerk with the secret savior fantasy — seminar case (Lecture 11)
occurrences.label: The insurance clerk with the secret savior…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: Jung's case for the law that "Dissolving an image means that you become that image": a man whose mother "had repeatedly told him, as he was growing up, that he would some day be a savior of mankind." He slumped consciously — a post in an insurance company amounting "to little more than licking stamps" — while living the secret role of the despised-of-men. Intellectual insight alone changed nothing; he was "still drawing satisfaction out of being an unrecognized savior." When the unrealized emotional values drove him to apply for a factory directorship he was unfitted for, he collapsed utterly. "His fantasy was really nothing but a power fantasy, and his desire to be a savior was based on a power motive". The lesson: a fantasy system can be seen through and yet persist in the unconscious, because its emotional value was never realized.

occurrences.title: Buddhist candleholder as a pine tree with Buddhas — the vertical mandala (Berlin museum)
occurrences.label: Buddhist candleholder as a pine tree…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Dr. Adler's question: "I saw in the museum at Berlin a buddhistic candleholder in the form of a pine tree. In its top was sitting a great Buddha and at the ends of its branches there were many small Buddhas. I thought it to be a vertical mandala instead of the horizontal one that we know ordinarily." (The footnote identifies a Tibetan refuge tree; Jung notes a more elaborate specimen in Paris.)

Jung affirms the reading: the chakra system itself "is a sequence of mandalas [that] forms a tree"; the lotus (padma) rises on its stem from the mud bearing the flower of light above the surface; Ra's falcon nest and Mithra born from the tree carry the same sun-from-tree symbolism. Seen from above, a tree is a mandala; from the side, a spiral of layers.

occurrences.title: Eirenaeus Philalethes — the Queen as the King's sister, mother, or wife (~1645)
occurrences.label: Eirenaeus Philalethes
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: "The English alchemist Eirenaeus Philalethes ('lover of truth'), writing about 1645, remarks that the 'Queen' was the King's 'sister, mother, or wife.'" Jung cites this as the alchemical form of the anima's "distinctly 'historical' aspect and her condensation with the figures of the sister, wife, mother, and daughter, plus the associated incest motif" — the same constellation he finds in Goethe ("You were in times gone by my wife or sister") and in the regina / femina alba of Latin alchemy. Published in Ripley Reviv'd (1678), translated into German in 1741 and possibly known to Goethe.

occurrences.title: Appearances after death — Luke 24
occurrences.label: Appearances after death — Luke 24
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Easter appearances — the risen Christ on the road to Emmaus, among the disciples, eating broiled fish — close Jung's anthology as its final section heading, in his own words: "Appearances after death." The phrasing is telling: the 23-year-old describes the resurrection narratives in the vocabulary of the apparition research (Doppelgänger, hallucination vs reality) that structures his whole lecture cycle, and on the same notebook page he is outlining Ritschl's reduction of Christ's presence to remembered value.

The tension stands unreconciled in the document: ¶289-291 both demystifies the "miracle" of conversion as autosuggestion and insists that only the substantial presence of Christ would make it "a great miracle".
Verbatim: "Appearances after death. [Luke 24]"

occurrences.title: Ashes turning into a man; dismembered children in glass coffins — Spielrein's patient, Zurich
occurrences.label: Ashes turning into a man
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The ashes can turn into a man... and she also saw 'dismembered children in glass coffins.
body: The schizophrenic woman in Spielrein's material: fragments of different things and materials "cooked" or "burnt" — "The ashes can turn into a man" — and the vision of "dismembered children in glass coffins."

Jung sets this beside the mythic parallel of Demeter collecting the limbs of the dismembered Dionysus and putting him together again: incineration-dismemberment as the negative face of rebirth, the destroyed body re-collected in the vessel (glass coffin = alchemical vas). One of several loci from this patient recorded in CW5's apparatus (sun-sunbeam-pierces-earth-spielrein-patient-zurich, serpent-gods-animal-spielrein-patient-zurich, arrow-three-wounds-god-spielrein-patient-zurich, water-spermatic-communion-spielrein-patient-zurich).

occurrences.title: 'Cheer up, initiates of the saved god' — the Attis night-liturgy, Rome
occurrences.label: Cheer up, initiates of the saved god
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~4th c. CE (Firmicus Maternus, De errore profanarum religionum)
occurrences.quote: Θαρρεīτε μὑσται τοῡ θεοῡ σεσωσμένου, ἒαται ϒὰρ ήμīν ἐκ πóνων σωτηρíα
body: The nocturnal rite Firmicus reports: an image of the god laid supine on a bier is mourned with measured wailing; then, when the feigned lamentation is sated, a light is brought in, the mouths of all the mourners are anointed by the priest, and he whispers over them the consoling formula — "Cheer up, initiates of the saved god: for salvation from our toils shall come to us."
The movement from lament to light is the ritual kernel of the resurrected-god: grief ritually timed, then answered by illumination and the whispered promise.

occurrences.title: Faust's suicide night and the Easter mood (Faust I)
occurrences.label: Faust's suicide night and the Easter mood
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Prof. Fierz names the literary case of despair-turning-to-life: Faust. Jung: "he also maneuvered himself into complete loneliness, and then comes the moment of suicide, and then suddenly a new mood surges up, the Easter mood, resurrection... The evidence that it is really a Christian mood in Faust is that he identifies with another famous personage of religious importance, Luther. And he translates the Evangel of John."

The law drawn from it (enantiodromia): after extreme isolation, one returns "to the earth... and there is nothing to believe except what was there before" — possibly with a Gotteserlebnis, a vision of Christ (Paul's Damascus mood is wondered about). Applied to Zarathustra leaving the town called "The Pied Cow": his heart was attached to it, love for humanity surges up — "the question is... to be in the herd and alone."

occurrences.title: 'Take courage, the god is saved' — Attis lament and light, Firmicus Maternus
occurrences.label: Take courage, the god is saved
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the priest whispers softly: “Take courage, ye initiates, for the god is saved
body: The night-liturgy of Attis: the image laid on its back in a litter, rhythmical laments, then the light brought in and the whispered consolatio — the mystery-formula of dying-and-rising that Jung sets beside the Eleusinian epitaph and Preiswerk's wheat hymn (¶532–535).

occurrences.title: The stone 'daily born anew' yet existing 'from the beginning of the world' — Gloria mundi
occurrences.label: The stone 'daily born anew' yet existing…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Et quamvis cottidie denuo nascatur, nihilominus tamen ab initio mundi ille fuit. …
body: The Gloria mundi describes the lapis begotten by sun and moon: born on earth, broken, destroyed, mortified, generated again through vapour, coming with the wind to the sea and from the sea back to the land, vanishing and re-arising. Then the paradox that defines it: "Et quamvis cottidie denuo nascatur, nihilominus tamen ab initio mundi ille fuit. …" — and though it is daily born anew, yet it existed from the beginning of the world. Jung notes the formula of the Fourth Gospel standing behind it (John 1: 1, 14).

This is the alchemical statement of the two time-axes the vault itself insists on: the eternally latent (the self existing from the beginning, cw12 Part In. 34) and its repeated empirical births — renewal of life through the sea-crossing and return.

occurrences.title: Dead infant in a reed basket laid in an opened nobleman's tomb — Aswan
occurrences.label: Dead infant in a reed basket laid…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Just behind the entrance-door was a little basket made of reeds, containing the withered body of a new-born infant, wrapped in rags.
body: Jung's own field observation (return leg of the 1925-26 East Africa journey): an ancient Egyptian tomb just opened near Aswan held, just behind the entrance door, a little reed basket with the withered body of a new-born infant wrapped in rags — hastily laid there by a workman's wife so that, when the nobleman entered the sun-barge to rise anew, her dead child might "share in his salvation" from within the holy precinct. A living folk-practice piggy-backing on the funerary solar theology Jung cites for the alchemists' transformation: the transformation of the mortal into the immortal "mounts the sun-barge and may take me with it" (¶238).

occurrences.title: 'I approached the very gates of death' — Lucius' initiation, Metamorphoses XI, 23
occurrences.label: I approached the very gates of death
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: I approached the very gates of death and set one foot on Proserpine's threshold, yet was permitted to return, rapt through all the elements.
body: Lucius describes his initiation into the Isis mysteries as a willed death: "I approached the very gates of death and set one foot on Proserpine's threshold, yet was permitted to return, rapt through all the elements." The rites "approximate to a voluntary death" from which he was "born again" (p. 284).

Jung generalizes: "This was the real purpose of all the mystery religions. They created symbols of death and rebirth" — with Frazer's primitive initiation mysteries as the lower register of the same pattern. The locus complements the existing note on the initiate elected Helios (the solar apotheosis that follows this night-descent).

occurrences.title: Death enters the world: the old woman who put on her old skin — African myth
occurrences.label: Death enters the world — African myth
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: people renewed themselves by casting their skins like snakes
body: The etiology of death through failed skin-casting — the snake's renewal mechanism withheld from mankind. Pairs with the snake as renewal symbol (¶410) and the snake stealing Gilgamesh's herb of immortality (¶457).

occurrences.title: Osiris as crucified god mourned by Isis and Nephthys — effigy from Philae
occurrences.label: Osiris as crucified god mourned by Isis…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: represents Osiris in the form of a crucified god, mourned by Isis and Nephthys
body: An Osiris effigy in crucified form, flanked by the two mourning sister-wives — the Egyptian dying god on the tree of life, the figure behind Jung's "crucified God" typology of ¶398 and the lamenting-mother motif of ¶415.

occurrences.title: Osiris — the dying and resurrecting god-man of Egypt
occurrences.label: Osiris — the dying and resurrecting god-man…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: New Kingdom temple reliefs (discussion range 4000-100 BCE)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Osiris, "an original god of Egypt, just as old as Ra, yet he was always different from Ra, the sun god. He was a sort of god-man, the dying and resurrecting hero god. He was first understood to be a god and then he became the soul, the Osiris, of the Pharaoh" — mediator between gods and men.

Jung's reading of the temple walls: outside, the king's worldly feats with soldier-figures; inside, "the god-man who converses with the gods," exchanging the ankh. "This figure of Osiris is very clearly an anticipation of Jesus or of the Christus idea" — even the Church permits Isis-Horus as anticipation of Mary and the Christ Child. Osiris then banalizes: the Osiris of the vizier, the treasurer, "Mr. Smith" — and the symbol is replaced by the new man, the god of disreputable birth.
Verbatim: "He was a sort of god-man, the dying and resurrecting hero god. He was first understood to be a god and then he became the soul, the Osiris, of the Pharaoh."

occurrences.title: Vision of his own sarcophagus, soul arising — J. S., memorial (1927)
occurrences.label: Vision of his own sarcophagus, soul arising
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1927 (vision c. 3 weeks before J. S.'s death)

jung.locator: Memorial to J. S., vision passage (pdf p701)

occurrences.quote: how finally, three weeks before his death, he beheld the vision of his own sarcophagus from which his living soul arose.
body: Jung's memorial (1927) for "J. S.", an anonymized pupil, closes with a terminal vision sequence: the eternal image of the soul appeared to J. S. "first dimly, then slowly taking shape in the vision of his dreams," culminating three weeks before his death in the vision of his own sarcophagus, from which his living soul arose. The passage is the physical tail of the essay continuing from pdf p700 (¶1708); the chunk carries ¶1709–10, where Jung refuses commentary — "Who am I that I should dare say one word beyond this vision?" — and turns to I Corinthians 13; 15:31–55.

Jung's reading: the death-preparation symbolism ("the four-petaled flower of the immortal light," ¶1707) consummated in an anticipated resurrection — the soul as something that rises alive from the tomb it has already seen. Locus joins the funeral-vision row of antiquity and of Liber Novus.

occurrences.title: Rex marinus crying from the sea, renewed with the columba spiritus sancti — Splendor Solis
occurrences.label: Rex marinus crying from the sea, renewed…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Whosoever will free me from the waters and lead me to dry land, him will I prosper with everlasting riches.
body: Splendor Solis plate: in the background the sea-king cries for help from the water; in the foreground his renewed form stands with the rotundum (golden globe) and the dove of the Holy Spirit.

Jung's reading: the Rex marinus of the Visio Arislei — whose land is sterile because "only like mates with like" — is the projected content in its hidden, latent state; his cry from the deep is the fascination by which the projected content summons the conscious mind. The same MS (fig. 219) shows the "mighty Ethiopian, burned, calcined, altogether dead and lifeless" — the nigredo awaiting the bath of rebirth.

image.title: Splendor Solis 07 drowning king

occurrences.title: The ring flung through the window — the unconscious courtship (Zurich, ~1900s)
occurrences.label: The ring flung through the window
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Overcome by a strange and irresistible feeling, she tore the ring from her finger and flung it through the open window.
body: The cab-horse patient's history, dug out "bit by bit": a tomboy since childhood, she had evaded "all those little adventures, hopes, and expectations which ordinarily move a girl's heart" until two men — Mr. A (her best friend's husband) and Mr. B (the suitor) — broke through the thorny hedge. At a party, dreamily playing with her ring, "it suddenly slipped off her finger and rolled under the table"; Mr. B restored it "with an arch smile" — "You know what that means!" — and "Overcome by a strange and irresistible feeling, she tore the ring from her finger and flung it through the open window" (¶420). Then the health resort with Mr. and Mrs. A: the walk alone, the boating accident — "So boisterous was she in her merriment that she suddenly fell overboard" — Mr. A hauling her out half-unconscious, "and then it was that he kissed her. With this romantic episode the bonds were tied fast" (¶425). At the farewell party "the evil spirit stepped up to our patient and whispered in her ear, ‘Tonight he is alone. Something must happen to you so that you can go to his house.’" And so it happened (¶425).

Jung's reading: "only the pose should be conscious, while the patient's real passion remained hidden from her" (¶425); the whole chain was directed to this end "while the conscious mind was struggling to bring about the engagement to Mr. B" (¶421). The case is the demonstration-piece that the trauma is "no more than an occasion" and the pathogenic agent is an unconscious erotic conflict (¶422).

occurrences.title: 'Birds and fishes bring us the lapis … it is in every place' — Ripley
occurrences.label: Birds and fishes bring us the lapis … it is…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The philosophers tell the inquirer that birds and fishes bring us the lapis, every man has it, it is in every place, in you, in me, in everything, in time and space.
body: Sir George Ripley's formula of the stone's ubiquity: birds and fishes bring it, every man has it, it is in you, in me, in everything, in time and space; it "offers itself in lowly form (vili figura)," and from it springs the aqua permanens.

Jung: "The prima materia has the quality of ubiquity: it can be found always and everywhere, which is to say that projection can take place always and everywhere." The passage continues into Ripley's water-hyle, the dark sphere of creation, and the round stone of Empedokles' sphairos, "the most serene God."

occurrences.title: The Risen Christ as filius philosophorum — Rosarium philosophorum
occurrences.label: The Risen Christ as filius philosophorum
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: After my many sufferings and great martyry / I rise again transfigured, of all blemish free.
body: The closing picture of the 1550 Rosarium series: the Risen Christ, with the inscription "After my many sufferings and great martyry / I rise again transfigured, of all blemish free."

Jung cites it as the plainest statement of the lapis-Christ parallel: the filius philosophorum appears in the figure of the resurrected God-man; Ripley's king — "a supreme victor triumphant, a great healer of the sick and a redeemer of all sins" — stands on the same axis (¶501). The stone's passion, death, and glorification re-enact the Christian drama inside matter.

occurrences.title: Fire-boring for the streams of rta — Vedic Agni worship
occurrences.label: Fire-boring for the streams of rta
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In the worship of Agni, the fire obtained by boring is used as a magic symbol of the regeneration of life.
body: Agni, "the red bull of rta," is drawn forth by the ritual fire-drill: "Boring for the streams of rta obviously has the same significance; the streams of life rise to the surface again, libido is freed from its bonds" (¶350). Believers credit the object; Jung re-reads the efficacy as "an 'enchantment' of the subject, an intensification of vital feeling, an increase and release of life force, a restoration of psychic potential" (¶350). The hymns image the release as milch-cows overflowing, rivers breaking through rock, rain-clouds bursting, Agni as lightning "swollen with the milk of rta" born from the womb of the waters (¶351–353) — energic tension, damming up, discharge.

occurrences.title: Aischrologia at Eleusis: Baubo's obscenity that makes Demeter laugh
occurrences.label: Aischrologia at Eleusis
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: The obscenities in antique cults had a sort of fertilizing power
body: The ritual ribaldry of the Mysteries: "the rich ladies of Athens after a very good meal with wine started making obscene jokes, because it was supposed to have a favorable effect on the crops of the next season. Mother Earth likes to hear such jokes, it makes her smile, she brings forth rich crops". The editors add the Baubo ("belly") figure whose obscene dances made the mourning Demeter laugh (Kerenyi, Eleusis).

Jung raises it from the Song-of-Songs analogy of the Codex Rhenovacensis: "the obscenity then had not the evil connotation which it has now. The obscenities in antique cults had a sort of fertilizing power" — the psychoid link between the earth-mother's humor, sexuality, and the field's fertility.

occurrences.title: Confession, penance, and absolution — Catholic pastoral technique
occurrences.label: Confession, penance, and absolution
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: historically sanctioned form; annual confession mandated 1215 (inferred frame)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: "The Catholics possess a ready-made pastoral technique in the historically sanctioned form of confession, penance, and absolution… a rich and palpably ritualistic symbolism which fully satisfies the demands as well as the obscure passions of simpler minds" (¶548). Jung's functional reading of the rite: "Any sacral action, in whatever form, works like a vessel for receiving the contents of the unconscious" (¶543) — the priest hears and asks, and "can ask about things which would otherwise only come to the ears of the doctor" (¶542), then absolves what he provokes.

The essay's contrast: Protestantism, stripped of ritual forms, "cannot translate the fundamental problem of the transference into something impersonal, as the Catholic can" (¶549) — hence its hunger for analytical psychology.

occurrences.title: The grandmother eaten out of love (north Kenya)
occurrences.label: The grandmother eaten out of love (north Kenya)
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Just recently there was a case in north Kenya. They ate a grandmother who was particularly beloved.
body: After the mummy vision Jung glosses the Great Mother as sarcophagus — flesh-eater — with a living case of sympathetic magic:

The family "had a grandmother… whom they worshipped, so they gave her very good food, they fed her well till she grew quite fat, and when she died the family ate her… they ate her in the end out of sheer love in order to give her continuation of life. It was a supreme act of devotion; they continued her life by embodying her body in theirs". "They did not kill her… they gave her a very decent burial in their stomachs." Jung's moral: "One should not disturb people in such acts of devotion, it is very foolish, it destroys their morality completely" — the devouring mother as fertility rite, the sarcophagus etymology (sarx + phagos) made flesh.

occurrences.title: Winnowing basket (liknon) on the bride's head — Greek marriage custom
occurrences.label: Winnowing basket on the bride's head
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: classical Greek custom (date not given by Jung; inferred)
occurrences.quote: There used to be a Greek marriage ceremony in which a winnowing basket filled with fruit was placed on the head of the bride, an obvious fertility charm.
body: Beside the Gnostic "vase of sins" gems and the Egyptian water-wheel pots, Jung adduces the winnowing basket, λίκνον, "the mystical winnowing basket of Iakchos... the figurative birthplace of the grain of wheat, symbolizing fertility" (¶396): "There used to be a Greek marriage ceremony in which a winnowing basket filled with fruit was placed on the head of the bride, an obvious fertility charm." The cluster grounds his derivation of the ecclesiastical vessel symbol (vas spirituale, vas Sapientiae) from the archaic uterus idea rather than from Scripture.

occurrences.title: The Marabout's dancing dam-builders (south of Tunis)
occurrences.label: The Marabout's dancing dam-builders
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Jung's witnessed example of dance as original work and magic efficiency: the Marabout — a saintly man "who is usually in charge of the poor" — has voluntary village laborers work his estate "as a sort of ritual." "I saw them assembling the evening before with their camels, hundreds of them with green banners, and then in the morning a wild druming and singing started and the whole crowd began to dance." Carrying hundred-pound sacks of sand "in dancing step," "in a few hours they had built a huge dam."

Jung's point: "they dance until they are completely exhausted"; rhythm produces "a sort of ekstasis in which the effect takes place" — "it was originally a magic ritual by which something was produced, it was the original idea of work even". "But I am perfectly certain that if I had hired that crowd for three or four shillings they would hardly have moved." Setting for the dancer-motif in Zarathustra (God "dances the world," pdf p80).

occurrences.title: Shouting the prayer into the god's ear — the numen as the god's nod
occurrences.label: Shouting the prayer into the god's ear
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: This was an abbreviated method of active imagination, concentrating upon the image until it moved
body: Jung's etiological vignette for Rudolf Otto's numinosum (Latin numen, "hint, or sign"): the worshipper "stepped upon a stone that was erected at its side to enable people to shout their prayer into the ear so that the god would hear them; and then he stared at the image until the god nodded his head or opened or shut his eyes or answered in some way."

His psychological point makes the locus a missing link between cult and method: "this was an abbreviated method of active imagination, concentrating upon the image until it moved; in that moment the god gave a hint... and that is the numinosum." God-image as psychical fact, "a psychological fact that happens to people," against Nietzsche's treating "God is dead" as the deletion of an opinion.

occurrences.title: Uterus taken for rain and fertility charms — southern Egypt
occurrences.label: Uterus taken for rain and fertility charms
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: reported early 20th c. (via Wallis Budge; date inferred)
occurrences.quote: the uterus symbolism exists today in the southern hinterland of Egypt in the form of rain and fertility charms
body: Jung's evidence that the vessel symbol is no dead antiquarian survival: "Wallis Budge drew my attention to the fact that the uterus symbolism exists today in the southern hinterland of Egypt in the form of rain and fertility charms. Occasionally it still happens that the natives in the bush kill a woman and take out her uterus for use in magical rites" (¶397). The report anchors his chain from the Egyptian primal water Nu (written with three pots) through the Gnostic pitcher-gems to the Church's vas spirituale — the uterus idea at the living root of the vessel symbol.

occurrences.title: The River Map (Ho-t'u) — dragon dredges the magical signs from the river (legendary, ~12th c. BCE)
occurrences.label: The River Map — dragon dredges the magical…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: "According to the legend, a dragon dredged the magical signs of the 'River Map' from a river. On it the sages discovered the drawing, and in the drawing the laws of the world-order." The River Map is one of the legendary foundations of the I Ching, whose present form derives partly from the twelfth century BC; in accordance with its extreme age it shows the knotted cords that signify numbers — with the usual primitive character of qualities: all uneven numbers masculine, even numbers feminine. Jung asks whether this primitive conception influenced the much younger Tantric mandala; Wilhelm held no direct connection was assumable — the ideas "arise autochthonously... out of a psychic matrix that seems to be ubiquitous" (¶643).

occurrences.title: 'When I recover from long illness I have the life of the roaring lion' — Senior's stone
occurrences.label: When I recover from long illness I have…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Europe (Senior; quoted in Aurora consurgens, Artis auriferae vol. 1, p. 219)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: "Another ancient author is Senior Filius Hamuelis... In this source there is a passage where the stone speaks: 'It is through me that the secret of secrets is generated. When I recover from long illness I have the life of the roaring lion'" (pdf p248; Aurora consurgens, in Artis auriferae, vol. 1, p. 219).

Jung: "So this expresses the fact that after a longer process, in which the prima materia suffers, the lion—that is, a wild desire—is the result. Psychologically this would mean: there is a state of suffering, and out of this suffering comes roaring passion." With it, "the philosopher's work begins with melancholia and ends in pleasure and joy" (Maier) — the nigredo/tenebrositas called melancholia, out of which the libido surfaces as desire.

occurrences.title: Boy of four to five in the robbers' den: fire, two robbers, clay to eat
occurrences.label: Boy of four to five in the robbers' den
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: age four to five, remembered in adulthood; presented 6 Dec 1938

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: A dark robbers' den lit by a fire; a strong giant and a thin "hop pole" who laughs mischievously. The hungry boy asks for bread; the thin robber slices clay from a lump and makes him eat it. Dream of a boy of four to five, presented by Dr. Hans Wespi.

Jung's reading: the two robbers are the "world powers" of ruse and power — archetypal ideas found "everywhere," paired as Odysseus/Ajax, chief/medicine-man (pp162-163). The fire is a positive centre of life, "the sacred hearth" (p164). Eating clay is no regression but anticipation: clay is the food of the dead in the Gilgamesh epic, and "he who eats the heavy clay will become heavy himself... we become mortal" (p168). The dream is "an adhortatio, that is, a preview of the world now unfolding, which approaches the boy and which he has to swallow in God's name" (p171).

occurrences.title: The rock shaped as an old hag with green eyes — 'I will destroy you and the flame upon your breast' (Visions Seminar, 3 May 1933)
occurrences.label: The rock shaped as an old hag with green eyes
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: The second circle: pressed back against a great wall of rock, she looks up and sees "the rock in the shape of an old hag with green eyes. She said: 'At last I have you. You shall go no further into the valley. I will destroy you and the flame upon your breast.'" She answers "I am not afraid, I will enter into you" — the rock opens and closes around her.

Jung: the earth mother herself, the same goddess she passed and neglected — those who disregard the chthonic factor are injured by it (illness of the abdomen, the intuitive's ulcers). Green = vegetation in its negative, demoniacal aspect. The flame on her breast is the Purusha, the little flame in the anahata triangle; the earth mother is muladhara, and if she drags the patient down, the flame goes out.

occurrences.title: Rohita the red sun as one-footed goat, Rohini the steed in the waters — Atharva-veda
occurrences.label: Rohita the red sun as one-footed goat, Rohini…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The one-footed goat.
body: The sun-god Rohita (red sun) is called the "one-footed goat" (agá ékapada). Hymn XIII, i of the Atharva-veda praises him together with his wife Rohini: "Rise up, O steed, that art within the waters... The steed that is within the waters is risen up" — Rohini united with Rohita after he has climbed to his highest place in heaven.

Jung at cw14 ¶735: "The parallel with our French text is so striking that one would have to infer its literary dependence if there were any way of proving that the author was acquainted with the Atharva-veda" — impossible, since Indian literature reached the West only with Anquetil du Perron's Oupnek'hat; hence "we have to infer an archetypal connection."

occurrences.title: 'O blessed greenness, which generatest all things' — Rosarium
occurrences.label: O blessed greenness, which generatest all…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: O blessed greenness, which generatest all things!
body: The Rosarium author cries: "O blessed greenness, which generatest all things!" Jung at cw14 ¶623-624: viriditas signifies on the one hand the "leprosy of the metals" (verdigris), on the other "the secret immanence of the divine spirit of life in all things." Mylius: God breathed "a certain germination or greenness, by which all things should multiply... the Soul of the World"; Arnaldus de Villanova: "the green which is in this substance signifies its total perfection." Green = hope and the future — the hidden joy of the imperfect transformation.

occurrences.title: The lapis speaks: 'I beget the light, but the darkness too is of my nature' — Hermes quotation in the Rosarium philosophorum (1550)
occurrences.label: The lapis speaks — I beget the light, but…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Two Rosarium speeches of the stone ascribed to Hermes. (1) From a treatise ascribed to Hermes: "And my light conquers every light, and my virtues are more excellent than all virtues.… I beget the light, but the darkness too is of my nature." (cw12 ¶99).
