(2) "therefore nothing better or more worthy of veneration can come to pass in the world than the conjunction of myself and my son" (¶140).

The same folio gives the killing-and-quickening stone: "For our stone, namely the living western quicksilver which has placed itself above the gold and vanquished it, is that which kills and quickens." Jung: "the transformer is above the transformed."

occurrences.title: Rosarium: the lapis speaks — 'Protege me, protegam te'
occurrences.label: Rosarium — the lapis speaks
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Protege me, protegam te. Largire mihi ius meum, ut te adiuvem
body: "In the Rosarium the lapis says: 'Protege me, protegam te. Largire mihi ius meum, ut te adiuvem' (Protect me and I will protect you. Give me my due that I may help you)" (¶155).

Jung reads the speaking stone as "nothing less than a good friend and helper who helps those that help him, and this points to a compensatory relationship" — the alchemical analogue of dream 13's companion in the depths. The stone that demands its due and promises aid is the self as reciprocal partner, not object.

Distinct locus within the same work: this is the ¶155 speech of the lapis as reciprocal friend/helper (dream 13's companion); rosarium-lapis-hermes-light-darkness-1550 covers the ¶99/¶140 Hermes speeches (light-and-darkness nature; conjunction of stone and son). Kept as separate loci (batch 2).

Same formula in the earlier work: the Tractatus aureus has the Stone cry "Protect me and I will protect thee. Give me what is mine that I may help thee" (cw09i ¶238) — stone-tractatus-aureus-protect-me-voice; there the scholiast's "one mouth" makes the Stone identical with Mercurius, the Latin Hermes.

occurrences.title: Rosarium: 'Out of man and woman make a round circle' — the squaring recipe
occurrences.label: Rosarium — the squaring recipe
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Make a round circle and you will have the philosophers' stone
body: "The Rosarium says: 'Out of man and woman make a round circle and extract the quadrangle from this and from the quadrangle the triangle. Make a round circle and you will have the philosophers' stone'" (¶167, with figs. 59, 60 — Jamsthaler's Viatorium spagyricum 1625 and Maier's Scrutinium chymicum 1687).

Jung introduces it as the medieval counterpart of dream 16's leftward circumambulation of the square: the squaring of the circle as "a stage on the way to the unconscious, a point of transition leading to a goal lying as yet unformulated beyond it… one of those paths to the centre of the non-ego which were also trodden by the medieval investigators when producing the lapis" (¶167). Circle → square → triangle → circle: the coniunctio of man and woman sublimated into the rotundum.

occurrences.title: 'I am the only daughter of the wise' — Queen of the South in the Rosarium
occurrences.label: I am the only daughter of the wise
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: I am the only daughter of the wise, utterly unknown to the foolish.
body: The Rosarium reports King Solomon: "This is my daughter, for whose sake men say that the Queen of the South came out of the east, like the rising dawn... she wears the royal crown of seven glittering stars, like a bride adorned for her husband, and on her robe is written in golden lettering, in Greek, Arabic, and Latin: 'I am the only daughter of the wise, utterly unknown to the foolish.'"

Jung at cw14 ¶542-543: Queen of Sheba, Wisdom, the royal art and the "daughter of the philosophers" are interfused — "the art is queen of the alchemist's heart, she is at once his mother, his daughter, and his beloved," the drama of his individuation. The marriage must remain the "mystery of the queen": the union of opposites is transconscious, not amenable to scientific explanation.

occurrences.title: Rosarium: the secret concealed in the mind ('in ipsa sola')
occurrences.label: Rosarium: the secret concealed in the mind
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the essential secret of the art lies hidden in the human mind—or, to put it in modern terms, in the unconscious
body: "Who therefore knows the salt and its solution knows the hidden secret of the wise men of old. Therefore turn your mind upon the salt and think not of other things; for in it alone [i.e., the mind] is the science concealed and the most excellent and most hidden secret of all the ancient philosophers" (¶359).

Jung's philological move: the Latin reads "in ipsa sola," referring to mens — "One would have to assume a double misprint were the secret after all concealed in the salt. But as a matter of fact 'mind' and 'salt' are close cousins—cum grano salis!" Khunrath's sal sapientiae confirms the pun. Conclusion: "the essential secret of the art lies hidden in the human mind—or, to put it in modern terms, in the unconscious" (¶361).

occurrences.title: Rose and Cross — union of Dionysus and Christ in Goethe's 'Geheimnisse'
occurrences.label: Rose and Cross — union of Dionysus…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Here the Rosicrucian solution is attempted: the union of Dionysus and Christ, rose and cross. The poem leaves one cold.
body: Jung's footnote to the Spitteler chapter (the failure of the two-brother reconciliation): "Goethe's 'Geheimnisse'… Here the Rosicrucian solution is attempted: the union of Dionysus and Christ, rose and cross." The poem's monastery of twelve brothers under a rose-cross dome is the Rosicrucian allegory of reconciled opposites — the wild (Dionysian) and the Christian-ethical.

Jung's verdict is famously cold: "The poem leaves one cold. One cannot pour new wine into old bottles." The rose-cross union fails as live symbol in 1786 because the opposites were not yet felt — the same diagnosis he brings to Spitteler's Pandora. A dated negative instance: the redeeming symbol attempted and stillborn.

occurrences.title: Christ hidden in the flos maris like a water bird — medieval Marian hymn
occurrences.label: Christ hidden in the flos maris like a water…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: In one of his hymns to Mary, a medieval poet says "that Christ has hidden himself in the flower of the sea, not in the stella maris but in the fios maris, like a water bird."

Jung: "that is the spirit, the water bird descending upon the flower that rises above the sea; and that is based upon the four pillars, the quality of four in the earth." The hymn belongs to his rosa mystica series — "the rosa mystica is of course a mandala; our Western idea of the rosa mystica is the absolute parallel to the Eastern Padma lotus" — with alchemy's three roses and the Rosenlilie, "a rose and a lily at the same time".
Verbatim: "Christ has hidden himself in the flower of the sea, not in the stella maris but in the fios maris, like a water bird".

occurrences.title: The five-petalled rose on Christ's breast — Mechthild of Magdeburg
occurrences.label: The five-petalled rose on Christ's breast
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Lord speaks to Mechthild: "Look at my heart, and see! A most beautiful rose with five petals covered his whole breast, and the Lord said: 'Praise me in my five senses, which are indicated by this rose'" (cw13 ¶388; Liber gratiae spiritualis).

Jung reads the rose as mandala and as "a projection of her own feminine Eros up on Christ" (cw13 ¶389), and makes this rose-mysticism the bridge by which "the mystique of the Rose entered in to alchemy" (¶387) — surfacing as the rose-coloured blood of the lapis. A sibling locus holds Mechthild's bridal coniunctio (coniunctio-mechthild-flowing-light-magdeburg-13c, cw9i ¶295).
Verbatim: A most beautiful rose with five petals covered his whole breast (cw13 ¶388ocr)

occurrences.title: Rosinus ad Sarratantam — the living stone 'below thee... above thee... from thee... about thee'
occurrences.label: Rosinus ad Sarratantam
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Arabic-style compilation; 'Rosinus' = Zosimos via Arabic transcription

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The oldest Arabic-style alchemical text: 'This stone is below thee, as to obedience; above thee, as to dominion; therefore from thee, as to knowledge; about thee, as to equals' (¶257) — which Jung says 'fits the paradoxical situation of the self', older than the ego yet needing to be built up by consciousness. The same treatise gives the lapis animalis, the animate stone 'sensible... to the presence and influence of the magnesia and the magnet' (¶243), and the stone 'fixed more in thee... created of God, and thou art its ore... so the end looks to the beginning, and contrariwise' (¶258). Parallels: morienus-thing-extracted-from-thee-7c, dorn-transmutemini-living-stones-16c.

occurrences.title: 'As the heaven … so is the Gold' — Maier, De circulo physico quadrato (1616)
occurrences.label: As the heaven … so is the Gold
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Maier's circle-treatise, Jung's main source on the round: "The circle is a symbol of eternity or an indivisible point" (p. 27); and "For as the heaven which is visible is round in form and motion … so is the Gold" (p. 39) (cw11 ¶? pdf p691–692). The aurum philosophicum "was named the 'rotundum'" (p. 15) — onto which "the philosophers projected the vision of the golden and blue circle … and onto the blue quintessence".
The gold as heaven-body: the metal's roundness identical with the visible cosmos's — matter carrying the shape of eternity.

occurrences.title: Lightning and the incandescent sphere (Eranos 1933 case)
occurrences.label: Lightning and the incandescent sphere
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: painting ~1930s; lecture 1933; shown in seminar 16 Nov 1938

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Second stage of the Eranos-1933 series: "instead of the human being there is a perfectly round incandescent sphere, like the earth in a primeval incandescent condition, split off from the surrounding chaos — a bit of chaos is now cut loose from the surrounding chaos, as on the frontispiece of the Songe de Poliphile".

"The lightning means an influence which suddenly starts the individuation process: namely, that separation of a certain area of chaos... through this lightning she suddenly appears as a whole, a circle or a globe, separated from the participation mystique with chaos, or, as we would say, with the collective unconscious. She is still a piece of chaos... every piece contains chaos, is chaos".

occurrences.title: Zosimos' round element / omega element — 'he himself describes it as round'
occurrences.label: Zosimos' round element / omega element
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Panopolis, Egypt (Berthelot, Alch. grecs, III, xlix, 1)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Against Ruska's claim that the Turba's "rotundum which turns copper into four" has no Greek parallel, Jung corrects: "This is not quite correct" — Zosimos has a round element (stoicheion) in Berthelot III, xlix, 1, Berthelot's "objet circulaire" being doubtful; and "A better parallel might be Zosimos' 'omega element.' He himself describes it as 'round' (Berthelot, III, xlix, 1)" (cw11 ¶? pdf p691).
The Greek ancestry of the Latin alchemical rotundum — the round first-thing that transforms what it touches into four, i.e. into totality.

occurrences.title: The sphairos, 'most blissful God' — Empedocles fragment 28
occurrences.label: The sphairos, 'most blissful God'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Empedocles of Acragas: the all-round being, the sphairos, is the eudaimonestatos theos, the most blissful God — "equal in all directions to himself and altogether eternal, a rounded sphere enjoying a circular solitude" (fragment 28, quoted in footnote pdf p939).

Jung cites it in the self-symbol series: "it must be one that is filled with the most blissful spirit and all-round like the Platonic primordial being, which is also the idea of the self" — alongside the Kingdom-of-Heaven-within (fortified city, pearl, stone, gold) and the Upanishadic/Tantric formulations Hauer traced at Eranos 1934. The Superman-as-self transmigration has ancient precedent.
Verbatim: "Empedocles, for example, had the conception that the all-round being, the sphairos, was the eudaimonestatos the6s, the most blissful God".

occurrences.title: Sanchi stupa — Buddha's rice-bowl hemisphere (India, ~3rd–1st c. BCE)
occurrences.label: Sanchi stupa — Buddha's rice-bowl hemisphere
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Sanchi hill (near Vidisha), Madhya Pradesh, India
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~3rd–1st c. BCE (Ashokan core, enlarged 2nd–1st c. BCE)
occurrences.quote: you behold a huge globe of masonry, half-buried in the earth.
body: The Great Stupa on the hill of Sanchi, "not very far from Agra and Delhi," visited by Jung "on a brisk morning" during the 1938 India journey ("The Dreamlike World of India"). Jung anchors its form in the MahaParinibbana-Sutta (run-on as printed): the dying Buddha covered one rice bowl with another to show how his remains should be enshrined — "The visible stupa is just the bowl on top. One has to imagine the lower one, buried in the earth."

Jung's reading: the hemisphere "half-buried in the earth" is the rotundum — "The roundness, a symbol of perfection since olden days, seems a suitable as well as an expressive monument for a Tathagata" — its "immense simplicity, austerity, and lucidity" matching Buddha's teaching. With its silence and "forgetfulness of human emotions" the place is "as much the 'secret' of India as the Taj Mahal is the secret of Islam" (¶992); Buddha lives on in Hinduism as an avatar of Vishnu.

occurrences.title: The round dance hymn — Acts of John
occurrences.label: The round dance hymn — Acts of John
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: Who joins not the dance mistakes the event, Amen.
body: Before his crucifixion (in place of the synoptic Last Supper) Christ institutes a mystical round dance: disciples hold hands in a ring, the Lord stands in the centre, and the hymn runs in antithetical couplets — "I will be saved and I will save... I will be wounded and I will wound... I will eat and I will be eaten." "The Eight [ogdoad] sings praises with us"; "Who joins not the dance mistakes the event."

Jung's reading: the circle with centre is, "psychologically... equivalent to a mandala and is thus a symbol of the self" (¶419); the rite parallels the Eucharist on the Johannine pattern (vine and branches). The antithetical predications formulate Christ as God and man, sacrificer and sacrificed — and "could be interpreted as referring just as well to Mercurius, if not better" (¶420). The ogdoad is a double quaternity; the Twelve the zodiacal archetype.

occurrences.title: Zosimos — the cinnabar of the philosophers and the copper man turned to gold
occurrences.label: Zosimos — the cinnabar of the philosophers…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Berthelot (Alch. grecs, III, xxix, 24), quoted by Jung in the cinnabar discussion around Miss X's Picture 2: "(After the preceding process) you will find the gold coloured fiery red like blood. That is the cinnabar of the philosophers and the copper man (chalkanthropos), turned to gold." The kinnabari ton philosophon stood for the rubedo stage of the transforming substance; cinnabar was also supposed identical with the uroboros dragon, and Pliny already calls it sanguis draconis, 'dragon's blood' — a term that lasted all through the Middle Ages. The copper man anticipates the Anthropos-chalkanthropos of later alchemy.

occurrences.title: Ruland — 'Imagination is the star in man, the celestial or supercelestial body'
occurrences.label: Ruland — Imagination is the star…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
jung.locator: quoted via Jung, 'Representations of Redemption in Alchemy' (pdf p308)

occurrences.quote: Imagination is the star in man, the celestial or supercelestial body.
body: Quoted in the seminar from Jung's own CW12 §394: Ruland defines imagination as "the star in man, the celestial or supercelestial body" — an astounding definition casting the opus's fantasy-processes as something corporeal, a semi-spiritual "subtle body," not immaterial phantoms. The accompanying alchemical text says the greater part of divine wisdom is outside the body of the world and "imagines far higher things than the body of the world could conceive."

Jung's gloss (quoted here): imagination actualizes contents "outside nature... a priori of archetypal character," in "that intermediate realm of subtle reality that can be adequately expressed [only] by the symbol" — a psychoid statement delivered inside the children's-dream seminar.

occurrences.title: Rumpelstiltskin blasted by his right name — Grimm KHM 55
occurrences.label: Rumpelstiltskin blasted by his right name
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: fairytale; Grimm KHM 55 (1812, older oral tradition)

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: Jung's fairytale exhibit for name-magic in the Weltanschauung essay: "In the fairytale you can blast Rumpelstiltskin to fragments if you call him by his right name" (¶735). The manikin who spins gold and demands the queen's first-born falls apart the moment his secret name is spoken.

Jung's frame is the critique of Weltanschauungen as magic names — the belief that naming the world aright conjures the thing: "for the primitive mind the thing itself is posited by the name" (¶735). The same paragraph arrays the tribal chief's hidden name, the Pharaohs' tomb-names of the gods, the Cabalists' true name of God, and the Ptah saying.

occurrences.title: Rupescissa — the vessel made after the manner of a cherub
occurrences.label: Rupescissa — the vessel made…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'Have a vessel made after the manner of a cherub, which is the figure of God, and have six wings, after the fashion of six arms, turning back on themselves; and above, a round head... and put within this vessel the said burning water' (¶379). Jung reads the cherub as Ezekiel's vision, whose horizontal section 'would produce a mandala divided into four parts... equivalent to the squaring of the circle'; psychologically: 'make the Hermetic vessel out of your psychic wholeness and pour into it the aqua permanens' (¶379). Parallels: pelican-vessel-rhenanus-frankfurt-1613, philalethes-chalybs-royal-child-pole-1667.

occurrences.title: Sabaoth Adamas, ruler of the Aeons, fights the light — Pistis Sophia
occurrences.label: Sabaoth Adamas, ruler of the Aeons, fights…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: A Sabaoth Adamas, the ruler of the Aeons, who fights against the light of Pistis Sophia.
body: In the Pistis Sophia we meet "a Sabaoth Adamas, the ruler of the Aeons, who fights against the light of Pistis Sophia and is thus wholly on the side of evil."

Jung at cw14 ¶589: the dark pole of the Adam-figure — Gnostic Adamas equated with the ithyphallic Hermes, Korybas and the Cabiri; the Bogomils' Satanaël and the Rabbinic Adam-on-Satan's-throne belong to the same field.

occurrences.title: Mysteries of Sabazius: the golden snake let into the lap of the initiated
occurrences.label: Mysteries of Sabazius
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: A golden snake is let down into the lap of the initiated and taken away again from the lower parts
body: "It is reported of the mysteries of Sabazius: 'Aureus coluber in sinum demittitur consecratis et eximitur rursus ab inferioribus partibus atque imis' (A golden snake is let down into the lap of the initiated and taken away again from the lower parts)."

Jung cites it in dream 18's commentary as a classical parallel for the ceremonial use of the reptile in transformation: "The idea of transformation and renewal by means of a serpent is a well-substantiated archetype… It is the healing serpent, representing the god" (¶184). The snake passing down into the lap and up from "the lower parts" enacts renewal through the body's depths.

occurrences.title: The pine felled, the youth's effigy tied to its trunk — annual Attis rite
occurrences.label: The pine felled, the youth's effigy tied…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Per annos singulos arbor pinea caeditur, et in media arbore simulacrum iuvenis subligatur
body: "Each year a pine-tree is felled, and an effigy of a youth is tied to the middle of the tree" — the dendritic core of the March Passover of Attis: the sacred tree cut down as the young god dies, his image bound to the trunk he embraces in the myth.
Jung quotes it in the sacrifice chapter as the ritual fixation of the myth (the hanged youth beneath the mother-tree), the cultic twin of the self-castration under the pine recorded in the main text.

occurrences.title: Spring sacrifice to Cinteotl — youth nailed to the cross
occurrences.label: Spring sacrifice to Cinteotl
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: by nailing a youth or maiden to the cross every spring and shooting the victim with arrows
body: Aztec spring rite for the grain-goddess Cinteotl: crucifixion plus arrow-death — the martyr-god complex of the sacrificial father (cf. ¶445, "the martyred and sacrificed god whom we have already met in the Aztec crucifixions and in the sacrifice of Odin"). The cross-name signifies "Tree of our life or flesh" (¶400).

occurrences.title: The Dionysian satyr festival as totem feast (Greece, archaic–classical)
occurrences.label: The Dionysian satyr festival as totem feast
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: archaic–classical Greece (no date given by Jung)
occurrences.quote: The Dionysian satyr festival, to judge by all the analogies, was a kind of totem feast involving a regressive identification with the mythical ancestors or directly with the totem animal.
body: Jung corrects Nietzsche's aestheticism: "Because of this, Nietzsche quite forgets that in the struggle between Apollo and Dionysus and in their ultimate reconciliation the problem for the Greeks was never an aesthetic one, but was essentially religious" (¶231). The Dionysian rout — where "man appears as a satyr, god above and goat below" (¶227) — he reads as "a kind of totem feast involving a regressive identification with the mythical ancestors or directly with the totem animal" (¶231), in which the Greek, "robbed of his individuality, dissolved into his collective components, made one with the collective unconscious" (¶230). In the festivals' "exuberant sexual licence... the most savage bestialities of nature were unleashed, including that atrocious amalgam of lust and cruelty" (¶227, quoting Nietzsche).

occurrences.title: Hölderlin's Empedocles — pearls dissolved in the krater of rebirth (~1799)
occurrences.label: Hölderlin's Empedocles
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In Hölderlin's Empedocles fragment Jung finds the poet's "secret longing for the maternal depths and for the regenerating womb": "You seek life, and a godly fire / Gushes and gleams for you out of the deeps of earth, / As, with shuddering longing, you / Hurl yourself down to the flames of Etna... / And I would follow the hero into the depths / Did not love hold me" (¶625).

Jung: "He would like to be melted like pearls in wine, to be sacrificed in the chalice, the 'krater' of rebirth. He longs to imitate Empedocles, of whom Horace says: 'Empedocles, eager to be thought a god immortal, coolly leapt into burning Aetna'" (¶626). The leap into the volcano — the same fire that later swallows Chiwantopel — figures self-sacrifice into the maternal container: dissolution in the krater as the price of renewal. The accompanying fig. 40 shows the "womb of the World Mother," a wooden bowl from the Congo.
Verbatim: "to be sacrificed in the chalice, the 'krater' of rebirth" (¶626).

occurrences.title: St. Eustache and his family martyred by lions and the brazen bull (Rome, ~a.d. 118)
occurrences.label: St. Eustache and his family martyred…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: He was thrown to the lions. The lions, however, did not want to devour the holy family. So they heated a brazen bull until it was red hot, and roasted them to death in it. This is something the patient did not know.
body: The legend of St. Eustache (Eustachius), told by Jung as the objective parallel to a patient's dream of a circle of lions around a fiery pit. Eustache and his family converted to Christianity and died the martyr's death around a.d. 118:

Jung's point: the dream motif (dangerous lions, hot pit, descent demanded — "Not out, but through it!") is fitted exactly by the legend of which the patient knew nothing, as a mere "fragment" she attached. He seriously entertains cryptomnesia ("as if this patient had hunted out the calendar of saints in my library") but frames the case under the reproduction of historical material by archetypal contents: "It belongs to the nature of the archetype that it is capable of reproducing again exactly the same images in an identical way".

occurrences.title: 'Give up what thou hast, and then thou wilt receive' — saying of the Greek mysteries
occurrences.label: Give up what thou hast, and then thou wilt…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Give up what thou hast, and then thou wilt receive.
body: An apophthegm Jung quotes without source as "a saying from the Greek mysteries": the relinquishment-conditioned receiving that he takes as the motto of the confession stage — and as evidence that "the beginnings of psychoanalysis are... nothing else than the scientific rediscovery of an ancient truth," catharsis being "a familiar term in the classical rites of initiation" (¶134). The saying condenses his whole theory of the secret: the private secret isolates, the shared surrender re-admits to community.

Jung's use: confession is "the firm bridge" across the gulf that secrets dig; whoever cannot "cease to defend and assert himself, and instead confess himself fallible and human" is shut off "from the vital feeling that he is a man among other men" (¶132).

occurrences.title: Beloved suspended by the genitals — hanging fantasies of two patients (1911)
occurrences.label: Beloved suspended by the genitals
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "The case of a 34-year-old female neurotic": "The patient's fantasy deals with a man she loves unrequitedly who is suspended by the genitals" — a fantasy "also found in a 9-year-old boy as a symbolic expression of his unfulfilled libido ('Hanging and fearing, suspended in pain')" (¶1083).

Jung's reading: taken with "ethnological traditions and mythological parallels of the sacrifice of the god of spring by hanging or flaying", the fantasy "signifies a sacrifice of sexuality which one hangs on to and cannot get rid of and which in ancient cults was offered to the Great Mother as a sacrifice of the phallus" (¶1083). The unquittable libido hangs its own god — demonstration piece of historical amplification against sexual concretism (cf. ¶1058).

occurrences.title: The eucharist of Huitzilopochtli — Aztec god eaten (Sahagún)
occurrences.label: The eucharist of Huitzilopochtli
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Christ is a divinity who is eaten in the Lord’s Supper. His death transforms him into bread and wine, which we relish as mystical food.
body: The ethnographic anchor of the edible-god complex: the independently attested Aztec ceremonial eating of the god beside the Christian Lord's Supper ("Christ is a divinity who is eaten in the Lord's Supper", ¶526), Agni and soma, Dionysus and wine.

occurrences.title: Tertullian's sacrificium intellectus — Carthage (~200 CE)
occurrences.label: Tertullian's sacrificium intellectus — Carthage
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Through the sacrificium intellectus the way of purely intellectual development was closed to him; it forced him to recognize the irrational dynamism of his soul as the foundation of his being.
body: Jung's paradigm case of the introverted thinking type under the Christian process (¶20): Tertullian, "a classic example of introverted thinking," renounces the intellect — "the amputation, of the most valuable function — a mythical idea that is also found in the great and exemplary symbol of the sacrifice of the Son of God" (¶20). He attacks Gnosis and philosophy with "unrelenting fanaticism," crystallizing his religious necessity in the formula anima naturaliter christiana (¶19). The sacrifice closes the way of purely intellectual development and forces recognition of "the irrational dynamism of his soul as the foundation of his being" (¶20). In the Christian process the type reverses: the acute thinker becomes the man of feeling (¶27). Later a Montanist, assailing Pope Calixtus I (¶19).

occurrences.title: Kavirondo puberty initiation — symbolic death and transformation
occurrences.label: Kavirondo puberty initiation
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: Among the Kavirondos, a tribe in East Africa, the young men in the puberty initiations, for instance, are told that they are now going to die, or that they are already dead and have transformed into new beings, sort-of spirits
body: Jung's ethnographic example for "any sacrificial death has that meaning": among the Kavirondo, puberty initiates are told they are dying, or already dead —

They receive a new name and lose their family — "their mother is no longer their mother." Those who refuse initiation are held "not human... nothing but animals," lacking "the spiritual quality which can only be acquired through the sacrificial death." Jung opposes the officials and missionaries who suppress initiation ("stupidly enough"), and reads the rite as the model Christianity realizes blindly when a whole nation turns itself into sacrifice.

occurrences.title: The Pharaoh devours the gods — the Cannibal Hymn, Pyramid Texts
occurrences.label: The Pharaoh devours the gods
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: He devours the great gods for breakfast, the middle gods for dinner, and the little gods for supper … The king devours everything that comes his way.
body: The dead Pharaoh arrives in heaven and overpowers the gods to assimilate their nature: "His servants have caught the gods with lassoes... they have cut them up and cooked them in hot cooking-pots." The king "devours the great gods for breakfast, the middle gods for dinner, and the little gods for supper," consumes the crowns and bracelets, "eats the wisdom of all the gods," and becomes lord of heaven.

Jung reads this "ravenous hunger (boulimia)" as the image of "man's repressive instinctuality at the stage where the parents have a predominantly nutritive significance" — the gods eaten as the primordial parents consumed.

occurrences.title: 'A lamb is a substitute for a man' — Sumerian-Assyrian fragment, library of Assurbanipal
occurrences.label: A lamb is a substitute for a man
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~7th c. BCE (library of Assurbanipal; text far older)
occurrences.quote: A lamb is a substitute for a man. He gives the lamb for his life, he gives the head of a lamb for the head of a man.
body: The substitution formula at the root of sacrificial religion: "To the wise man he said: A lamb is a substitute for a man. He gives the lamb for his life, he gives the head of a lamb for the head of a man." Jung prints it mid-chapter VIII as the baudierte Urform of the sacrifice argument — the surrogate victim standing in the place of the human.
The text gives the logical grammar that Christological and ram/lamb typologies (Melito's ram in the thicket, the Manichaean ram-serpent) elaborate.

occurrences.title: The man who wounds his own breast: 'Blood will give us strength' (patient vision, 11 October 1933)
occurrences.label: The man who wounds his own breast
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: If one wounds the abdominal region in order to create the anahata psychology, it is right; but if one wounds the heart region in order to be in anahata, it is a mistake.
body: The wounded man of the market: "We must be strong. There is much to seek. Blood will give us strength... I have put my head in the fire and behold it is without wounds. To destroy the body is strength." Jung reads the suppression of feeling for the sake of strength and argument ("a strong man is of iron") — the Anglo-Saxon ideal; Mountain Lake's Pueblos thought all Americans crazy "because they believe that they think in the head; we think in the heart." Wounding the abdominal region to reach anahata is right; wounding the heart region there is "a vital mistake" — that wound belongs to the next sacrifice, vishuddha: "the traditional image of the wounded god" — Christ's opened breast, Odin pierced by the spear, Amfortas.

occurrences.title: Mithras' tauroctony sequence — Heddernheim Relief
occurrences.label: Mithras' tauroctony sequence
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: First we see the birth of Mithras from the top of the tree; the next picture shows him carrying the conquered bull
body: Four-picture relief series (pl. XL, plate at pdf p285): Mithras born from the top of the tree, carrying the conquered bull, reaching for Sol's nimbus (¶397), Sol kneeling before him (¶398). Jung reads the bull as both father-monster and Mithras' own animal nature: "Mithras has thus sacrificed his animal nature" (¶398) — conquest of instinct no longer by overpowering the mother but by renouncing one's own instinctive desire, the anticipation of the crucified God. The bull is killed by taurokathapsis on its back, itself a life-giving deity (¶421).

occurrences.title: Eating raw the flesh of Zagreus — the Cretan initiates' confession
occurrences.label: Eating raw the flesh of Zagreus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: have eaten raw the flesh of Zagreus, the night-roaming shepherd
body: The initiate's credo in Euripides' Cretans: "Leading a holy life since I have been initiated into the mysteries of Idaean Zeus, and have eaten raw the flesh of Zagreus, the night-roaming shepherd." Through the omophagia the initiates assimilated the essence of the god — the dismembered Dionysus-Zagreus eaten raw, his death made the eater's life.

Jung pairs it with the Mexican rite of Teoqualo, "god-eating," as the trans-cultural theophagy that the Eucharist formalizes; and the sacrifice of Dionysus-Zagreus produced the neos Dionysos, the god's resurrection.

occurrences.title: Agni turns on Prajapati with gaping maw — Shatapatha Brahmana 2.2.4
occurrences.label: Agni turns on Prajapati with gaping maw
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Then Agni turned upon him with gaping maw. His own greatness spoke to him: Sacrifice! Then Prajapati knew: My own greatness has spoken to me. And he sacrificed.
body: Prajapati alone in the beginning begets Agni from his mouth; Agni, a devourer with nothing else to eat, "turned upon him with gaping maw." Prajapati's own greatness advises "Sacrifice!" — and through the offering he both propagates himself and escapes being devoured: "Thereupon that rose up which shines yonder (the sun); thereupon that rose up which purifies all things here (the wind)." Jung's reading: "Sacrifice always means the renunciation of a valuable part of oneself, and through it the sacrificer escapes being devoured... there is no transformation into the opposite, but rather equilibration and union, from which arises a new form of libido: sun and wind" (¶339). Half of Prajapati is mortal, half immortal (¶339).

occurrences.title: Sheep sacrificed on the stone altar; entrails become red jewels (patient vision, 18 Feb 1931)
occurrences.label: Sheep sacrificed on the stone altar
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: They tore out the entrails and hung them about their necks. The entrails changed into great red jewels. I appeared dressed in white.
body: The Christian lamb-sacrifice returns in primitive dress: North American Indians — "a whole tribe of animi" — slaughter a sheep on a stone altar, toss it into the air, smear their faces with its blood (birth magic, "to help the sun to rise," cf. the taurobolium), tear out the entrails and wear them; the entrails change into great red jewels. Jung reads it as the sacrifice of her gregarious, sheep-like collective side: the entrails — the abdominal seat of the primitive mind — become precious when made conscious, "the priceless jewel of life."

She appears "dressed in white" (quasi modo geniti, rebirth innocence) and begs for the red jewel — the inferior feeling-function, "a rough diamond but full of promise." But the Indians flee and their speaker pronounces the verdict "You have violated the blood": her idealistic, above-the-earth standpoint violates the law of the blood; the instincts (animals standing behind the Indian) back the animus up.

occurrences.title: The Tantalus Club emblem — man hanged by penis and nose
occurrences.label: The Tantalus Club emblem
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: unknown (discussed at the Vienna psychoanalytic meetings)
body: "As a contribution from child psychology to the significance of sacrifice, C. G. Jung tells about the 'Tantalus Club' which was founded by some youngsters for the celebration of sexual mysteries. Their emblem depicted a man who hung from a gallows by a rope tied to his penis and his nose" (¶1081). "The sacrificed and tormented were the youngsters themselves, just like Tantalus whose torment consists in constantly being denied satisfaction of his most ardent desires."

The self-hanged phallus: boys rediscovering, in club ritual, the pattern Jung two paragraphs later reads as the "sacrifice of the god of spring by hanging or flaying... offered to the Great Mother as a sacrifice of the phallus" (¶1083) — and the pattern of Odin's self-hanging on the tree.

occurrences.title: The old sage dwelling in the heart — Wang Yang-ming
occurrences.label: The old sage dwelling in the heart
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: If thou thinketh thou art alone and canst do what thou pleaseth, thou art forgetting the old sage that dwelleth in thy heart and knoweth of all thou dost.
body: Jung's Eastern parallel to Zarathustra's 'mighty lord, an unknown sage' (Z I.4): the Neo-Confucian sejin (sage) in every heart, cited from CW6 par. 370. He places it in the anahata chakra — 'it would of course be the archetype of the old wise man,' which at that level 'still covers the symbol of the self.' Parallels: hamsa-steady-flame-anahata-shat-cakra-nirupana-16c (anahata) · eagle-serpent-noon-zarathustra-1883.

occurrences.title: The thousand-petalled Lotus, the hare-less Moon and the Great Void — Śaṭcakranirūpaṇa vv.40–49 (Bengal, 1577)
occurrences.label: The thousand-petalled Lotus, the hare-less Moon…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1577 (Pūrṇānanda, Śrī-tattva-cintāmaṇi ch. 6; trans. Woodroffe, The Serpent Power, 1919)

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

body: The sahasrāra, crown of the system: "the Lotus of a thousand petals. This Lotus, lustrous and whiter than the full moon, has its head turned downward... and it is the absolute bliss" (v.40). Within it the full Moon "without the mark of the hare," the lightning Triangle, "the Great Void which is served by all the Suras" (v.41), the subtle Bindu-Śūnya and Parama-śiva (v.42), and the nectar-stream instructing the yogin in the oneness of Jīvātman and Paramātman as Ham˙ sah Parama (v.43).

V.44 catalogues its sectarian names — "The åaivas call it the abode of åiva; the Vaiüõavas call it Parama Puruüa" — down to "the pure place of Prakùti-Puruüa." Vv.46–49 nest Amā-Kalā, Nirvāṇa-kalā and Nirvāṇa-śakti, "the Mother of the three worlds," around the abode Nityānanda. Jung's equivalent: patient mandala series "wind up with analogies to the vjñv center, or even the sahasrvra... they are really an equivalent in a way".

occurrences.title: The 'salmon of wisdom' — he who eats it becomes the wisest seer
occurrences.label: The 'salmon of wisdom'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: He who eats it will become the wisest seer in the world.
body: From the fish-material of the transparent-mouse dream: in Irish myth the "salmon of wisdom" — he who eats it will become the wisest seer in the world; Irish peasants still say of a cause "they will not be able to do justice to it unless they have eaten from the 'salmon of wisdom.'" Set beside the Aberkios epitaph (belief as a woman giving the fish from the well with wine and bread), Friday's fish-meal once dedicated to Venus/Ishtar/a Babylonian fish goddess, the Babylonian god called both fish and "writing stone of Bel," and Orpheus whose name Eisler translates "fisherman."
In the dream's logic, the fish bring the blue, cool flood of thought: "one idea devours another."

occurrences.title: Salome, the incestuous dance and the head of John the Baptist — Judea (~1st c. CE)
occurrences.label: Salome, the incestuous dance and the head…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1st c. CE (named by Josephus, Antiquities XVIII.5)

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: The historical-biblical figure behind the second person of Jung's December 1913 vision. In Lecture 12 he gives the legend: "the real Salome was involved in incestuous relations with Herod, her stepfather, and it was because of the latter's love for her that she was able to get the head of John the Baptist.^" (pdf p112; footnote marker as printed) — the dance, the demand, the Baptist's head on the platter (Matthew 14:6ff., Mark 6:22ff.; the name supplied by Josephus, whose works Jung's family owned). In Jung's reading of the vision: "Salome is an anima figure, blind because, though connecting the conscious and the unconscious, she does not see the operation of the unconscious" — blind, and blind since the beheading of the prophet in her presence; her eyes are healed only in the deification episode. "Salome is the anima and Elijah the wise old man... she being instinctive and quite blind, needs the foreseeing eyes of wisdom".

occurrences.title: 'When the two become one' — Christ and Salome in the Evangel of the Egyptians
occurrences.label: When the two become one
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "it was in the Evangel of the Egyptians which still existed and was seen by Origen, the old Greek father. In that Evangel is a conversation between Christ and a certain woman called Salome of whom we know nothing-she is not the daughter of Herod. She asks him when the things she was asking about would come true. And he says: 'When ye tread underfoot the husks of shame. When the two become one, and the male with the female. Neither male nor female.'"

Jung: "the same symbolism... meaning a condition above or beyond the mere sex condition. Then the millennium, the Kingdom of Heaven, the perfect all-round condition, the most precious form of existence, the gold state, will be fulfilled. Above, it appears like a hermaphrodite, and below it is gold."

occurrences.title: Salt, the oldest mystery, hidden in the denarius — Khunrath
occurrences.label: Salt, the oldest mystery, hidden in the denarius
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Audi atque attende: Sal antiquissimum Mysterium! Cuius nucleum in Denario, Harpocrate, sile.
body: In the New Birth section of the transference essay Jung cites Khunrath's address to Harpocrates, the boy-god of silence with his finger on his lips:

Jung: "The salt is the salt of wisdom. Harpocrates is the genius of the secret mysteries" (cf. Psychology and Alchemy, figs. 52 and 253). The salt's core is guarded by silence and by the number ten — the denarius structure of the completed opus.

occurrences.title: Sethian light imprisoned as 'the salt of all created things' — Hippolytus
occurrences.label: Sethian light imprisoned as the salt…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Hippolytus' Sethians: when the wave raised from the water by the wind 'has received within itself the reproductive power of the feminine, it retains the light scattered from on high... It is engendered from the water and commingled and mixed with the bodies as if it were the salt of all created things, and a light of the darkness struggling to be freed from the bodies' (cw14 ¶327). Jung: 'this strangely beautiful passage contains pretty well everything that the alchemists endeavoured to say about salt: it is the spirit, the turning of the body into light (albedo), the spark of the anima mundi, imprisoned in the dark depths of the sea' (¶328). Since the Philosophumena surfaced only in the 19th c., the affinity is not transmission but archetypal kinship (¶328).

occurrences.title: Solomon seeks the chaste virgin — Aurora Consurgens, the heavenly pair
occurrences.label: Solomon seeks the chaste virgin
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: O Queen of the heights, arise, make haste, my love, my spouse, speak, beloved, to thy lover, who and of what kind and how great thou art.
body: The Aurora's bridal mysticism: the speaker (Solomon, the Wisdom-seeker) will "rise and go into the city, seeking in the streets and the broad ways a chaste virgin to espouse... that she may roll back the stone from the door of my sepulchre and give me wings like a dove." The Queen in gilded clothing (Ps 45), the flower of the field and lily of the valleys, mother of fair love (Ecclus 24) — Sapientia as the heavenly bride.
Jung at cw14 ¶532 sets this pair against gold-and-silver: Sol and Luna form "the classic alchemical syzygy," here spiritualized into the language of the Song of Songs.

occurrences.title: The sapphire stone that administers good and evil — Kabbala denudata
occurrences.label: The sapphire stone that administers good…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Administering at times good, at others evil, now life, now death.
body: On the lapis in the Cabala: the stone is the "capital-stone, from which all the upper and lower hosts in the work of creation are brought into being," called "the sapphirestone, because it takes on divers colours from the highest powers, and works in created things now in one wise, now in the contrary, administering at times good, at others evil, now life, now death, now sickness, now healing, now poverty, now riches."

Jung at cw14 ¶640-641: "The stone appears here as the power of fate; indeed, as the reference to Deuteronomy 32:39 shows, it is God himself." Knorr "was himself an alchemist, and his words here are written with deliberate intent"; the stone which the builders rejected; Paracelsus introduced the sapphire into alchemy from the Cabala.

occurrences.title: Adam created by Satanaël out of mud — the Bogomils
occurrences.label: Adam created by Satanaël out of mud
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Satanael was unable to bring him to life, so God did it for him.
body: "According to the teachings of the Bogomils, Adam was created by Satanaël, God's first son and the fallen angel, out of mud. But Satanael was unable to bring him to life, so God did it for him."
Jung at cw14 ¶589: Adam's inner connection with Satan (Rabbinic tradition: Adam will one day sit on Satan's throne) — the Anthropos' shadow-side.

occurrences.title: Meister Eckhart's breakthrough (Durchbruch) — 'I am the unmoved mover'
occurrences.label: Meister Eckhart's breakthrough
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: By this thrust I become so rich that God cannot suffice me, despite all that he is as God and all his godly works; for in this breakthrough I receive what God and I have in common. I am what I was, I neither increase nor diminish, for I am the unmoved mover that moves all things.
body: The longest quotation in the Suzuki foreword, from Eckhart's breakthrough sermon:

Jung's reading: "Here the Master may actually be describing a satori experience, a supersession of the ego by the self, which is endued with the 'Buddha nature' or divine universality" (¶888). In the breakthrough man stands "empty in the will of God, and empty also of God's will, and of all his works, even of God himself" — then "I am neither God nor creature."

occurrences.title: 'Do you smell it?' — the Zen master and the wild laurel
occurrences.label: Do you smell it? — the Zen master…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: There, I have told you everything, I have kept nothing back.
body: A Chinese statesman, a follower of Confucius, asks a Zen master for initiation. The master answers with Confucius' own words, "I have told you everything, I have kept nothing back." Days later, walking in the hills while the wild laurel is in bloom, he asks, "Do you smell it?" — and then: "There, I have told you everything, I have kept nothing back." "And the statesman was enlightened. He realized. It broke through into consciousness."

Jung's reading: the story answers his question "How would you define realization?". Zen (Jap. for dhyana, "enlightenment"; also satori, sambodhi) is "nothing but the education of consciousness, the faculty of realizing things" — the tradition Jung contrasts with the West, where "we always start with the idea that our consciousness is perfect. It never occurs to us that it could be dim, or that it might develop." Buddha began "the extraordinary attempt to educate consciousness"; Nietzsche stands at the opposite pole, "in an impasse with his faculty of realization."

occurrences.title: Invoking Saturn 'dressed in the manner of the Jews' — Ghāyat al-hakīm
occurrences.label: Invoking Saturn dressed in the manner…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)
jung.locator: 'Transformation Symbolism in the Mass' n.18 (pdf p723)

occurrences.quote: In a text named \"Ghāya al-hakīm,\" ascribed to Maslama al-Madjrītī, the following instructions are given when invoking Saturn: \"Arrive vêtu à la manière des Juifs, car il est leur patron.\
body: The Picatrix's ritual dress-code for Saturn evocation, cited by Jung in the Mass essay's Saturn/Kronos footnote chain (with Plutarch and Diogenes Laertius; Origen, Contra Celsum VI, 31):

Saturn is the patron god of the Jews — the planetary god carries an ethnic affiliation, and the adept must become his people to reach him. Jung uses the passage for the identity of Saturn with the Old-Testament God (cf. Yahweh as Saturn-Ialdabaoth, Aion ¶128).

occurrences.title: 'Blessed the man to whom the providence of Saturn flows' — Aurora Consurgens
occurrences.label: Blessed the man to whom the providence…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)
jung.locator: 'Transformation Symbolism in the Mass' n.22 (pdf p723)

occurrences.quote: \"Beatus homo qui invenerit hanc scientiam et cui affluit providentia Saturni.\" [Ed. von Franz, pp. 37f.]
body: The benediction of the malefic planet, quoted in the Mass essay's Saturn chain (with Aion ¶128f on Ialdabaoth):

Blessed is the man who finds this science and on whom the providence of Saturn flows — the dark, leaden god as bestower of the art. Saturn's ambivalence (Yahweh-Ialdabaoth for the gnostics, patron of the Jews in the Picatrix, source of genius for Steeb) is the great ambivalent father-image of the opus.

occurrences.title: Vision: the satyr — 'I am the immortal one, I am the past, I am also the future' (9 Dec 1930)
occurrences.label: Vision — the satyr
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: 9 Dec 1930, discussed through 21 Jan 1931 (Visions Seminar vol 1)
occurrences.quote: Then he spoke to me saying: 'I am the immortal one, I am the past, I am also the future. You shall know me.' He made the sign of the cross upon my face and breast.
body: After the animus's fire-sacrifice, the patient must face what she fled: a satyr under a tree playing a reed. Great stars fall upon him; a band of streaming light crosses his face (only his green eyes visible); hair torn from his breast turns to little flames; he blows a fire; he robes her in blue and puts pearls around her neck; she kneels.

Jung (21 Jan): "the patient meets the god Pan" — "it has the characteristics of an ancient Dionysian image", the god of early Greece, sixth-seventh century BCE, exactly compensating her puritanical God-concept (p235-236). She expected something sexual; instead "the spirit of the animal puts a celestial mantle upon her, the blue mantle of Mary, and he gives her a necklace of pearls, which means tears, the sadness and divinity. He is crowning her in the mysteries" (p232). In her painting the satyr is without genitals — the animal's spirit, not its lust.

occurrences.title: The schizophrenic girl who became savior of the moon people
occurrences.label: The schizophrenic girl who became savior…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A schizophrenic girl "so caught by that redemption mystery which was going on in her that she could no longer speak to people", locked up about sixteen months. Jung "got behind her screen": "She went to the moon and became the savior of the moon people... she built temples and did all sorts of wonderful things, it was a most amazing story".

The betrayal-bond of telling: "in telling me that story, she cut the thread to the moon and could not go back; she had to be sane, she was caught to the earth because she had betrayed the mystery. She wanted to kill me because I had cured her... 'Oh, it was so much more beautiful, I hate to live on this earth.'" She "had no idea that the moon was a symbol... she got stuck in the moon, she became the prisoner of the moon spirit" — whence "lunatics". Referred to again at p219 against the patient who touched the earth-secret: telling cuts both ways; since then Jung is "not so compassionate about insane people; it may not be so bad, it only looks so."

occurrences.title: The Spindles Become a Pair of Scales — Pauli dream (mid-November 1950)
occurrences.label: The Spindles Become a Pair of Scales
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: the arrangement of the 'fusaux' described in your letter is transformed into a pair of scales.
body: After Emma Jung's letter describing the arrangement of the three fusaux ("One of them was attached to the front side of the bed... the second... to the back side... the third lay crosswise over the whole width of the bed"), Pauli found the non-rotating mechanism odd — "a mechanism to prevent the spindles from rotating" — and learned from C. A. Meier that folklore forbids spindle rotation at harvest as magically harmful. "A couple of nights later, I had the dream... in it, surprisingly, the arrangement of the 'fusaux' described in your letter is transformed into a pair of scales".

Pauli is explicit about method: "The meaning of the dream certainly has a lot to do with the problems discussed by Prof. Jung in his latest treatise on synchronicity. However... it is impossible for the dream to have been influenced by Prof. Jung's new writings... The dream occurred quite a while earlier and is thus to be interpreted as a consequence of reading your letter" — a disciplined observation for the synchronicity problem (spindles ↔ scales: fate weighing, the compensatory image following the letter's affect).

occurrences.title: The Old Testament scapegoat sent to Azazel — Leviticus 16
occurrences.label: The Old Testament scapegoat sent to Azazel
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: like the Old Testament scapegoat, which was supposed to carry the evil into the wilderness.
body: The Day of Atonement rite of Leviticus 16: one goat sacrificed to YHWH, one — the scapegoat — sent alive into the wilderness "for Azazel," carrying the people's evil away from the camp. Jung invokes it in The Undiscovered Self as the type of the "apotropaic attitude towards evil": "We should, so we are told, eschew evil and, if possible, neither touch nor mention it… like the Old Testament scapegoat, which was supposed to carry the evil into the wilderness" (cw10 ¶573).

Jung's reading: the ritual flatters "the primitive tendency in us to shut our eyes to evil and drive it over some frontier" — a frontier that, in the nuclear age, is the political one beyond which the shadow is projected (¶572). His counter-claim: "evil, without man's ever having chosen it, is lodged in human nature itself" and must be met as "the equal and opposite partner of good" (¶573). expresses_inferred shadow: the goat as collective carrier of the refused shadow; Jung names the mechanism (projection, apotropaism) without here naming the archetype.

occurrences.title: Changing a dog into a golden scarab — Case D's transfiguration claim (penitentiary, 1895)
occurrences.label: Changing a dog into a golden scarab
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: he could “change a dog into the most beautiful golden scarab in the twinkling of an eye.
body: From the penitentiary report on the manic painter: he claimed to have known for 25 years how, "by means of a certain substance, as with a breath, everything could be decked in the most gorgeous, dazzling colours" and "change a dog into the most beautiful golden scarab in the twinkling of an eye." Jung files the fantasies under manic self-exaltation (he "gave more or less logical reasons," gilding by the right brush-colour); the image itself is a transformation rite in alchemical-Egyptian dress — base animal transfigured into golden scarab by a breath-substance.

occurrences.title: The golden scarab dream and the rose-chafer at the window (Zurich)
occurrences.label: The golden scarab dream and the rose-chafer…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: A young patient, armored in "a highly polished Cartesian rationalism with an impeccably 'geometrical' idea of reality" that three doctors could not crack, dreams at the critical moment of treatment that someone gives her a golden scarab — a costly piece of jewellery. As she reports it, Jung (back to the closed window) hears a gentle tapping: a scarabaeid beetle, the rose-chafer (Cetonia aurata), "the nearest analogy to a golden scarab that one finds in our latitudes," strives to enter the dark room. He hands it over: "Here is your scarab" (¶982).

Jung's reading: the event "punctured the desired hole in her rationalism"; the animus possession broke and transformation began — "Any essential change of attitude signifies a psychic renewal... The scarab is a classic example of a rebirth symbol" (¶845). His paradigm of synchronicity category 1 (¶984); unique in his experience.

occurrences.title: The green scarab over the grave of the dwarfs (Visions, 16 Mar 1932)
occurrences.label: The green scarab over the grave of the dwarfs
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The men wounded themselves with knives and let the blood fall upon the earth. When they had done this the earth parted and a great green scarab appeared over the grave of the dwarfs.
body: Climax of the temple vision: the young men wound themselves with knives and let the blood fall on the buried dwarfs; the earth parts and a great green scarab appears. Jung: "Here again the sacrificial blood is wanted... The blood falling to the earth is more than just a loss, it is also a charm-then something grows". "This is like a mystery play, it is an anticipation of what should happen" - the animus performing the rite d'entree she has refused.

The scarab, "the kheper-ra, has always symbolized the rebirth of the sun"; green = vegetation, spring, spiritual rebirth; "rebirth symbolism always means a new uniting of opposites in the process of transformation" - valid only when "the opposites grow together in a living progress," unlike the static compromise "Alas, yes, black is white and white is black". Like the phoenix burning its father's body, "that is the renewal of the libido".

occurrences.title: The dead sun-god becomes Khepri at the tenth station — Book of What Is in the Netherworld
occurrences.label: The dead sun-god becomes Khepri…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: The tenth and twelfth stations of the sun-god's twelfth-hour night-journey through the Netherworld: at the tenth station the dead sun transforms into Khepri, the scarab; at the twelfth he mounts the barge that carries the rejuvenated sun into the morning sky.

Jung's reading, in the scarab case: "Any essential change of attitude signifies a psychic renewal which is usually accompanied by symbols of rebirth in the patient's dreams and fantasies. The scarab is a classic example of a rebirth symbol" (¶845). He adds the caveat that with educated patients cryptomnesia cannot always be ruled out — though his scarab patient did not know the symbol. The passage supplies the archetypal pedigree for the synchronistic scarab: rebirth at the decisive turning of the solstice-like night journey.

occurrences.title: Vision: the scarab opens — man and woman; the ring sunk into her forehead (21 Jan 1931)
occurrences.label: Vision — the scarab opens
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "I beheld a scarab which opened. A man and a woman emerged. They walked down some steps to a pond and gazed there at their own images. Then the man dove into the pond and emerged holding in his hand a ring. This ring he held to the forehead of the woman and the ring sank into the flesh of her forehead and remained there."

Following the god Pan vision, the relationship between man and woman is itself regenerated: the scarab is the kheper-ra, "the chthonic form of the sun god... forming his own egg" — the pair coming out of it is like the sun rising (p240-242). The ring grown into the flesh marks a union "far more penetrating than the conventional relationship" — anything on the exalted level "burns itself into the flesh... If the ring is removed, the scar will be forever visible" (p245).

The spot is the ajna centre, "the center of supreme knowledge, supreme consciousness" of Tantric theory, the birthplace of the diamond body in Chinese yoga, the branded criminal's spot, the caste mark, the Buddha's sign: "supreme consciousness and individuation are identical" (p245-246).

occurrences.title: The unicorned scarab, sacred to Mercurius — Horapollo
occurrences.label: The unicorned scarab, sacred to Mercurius
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "An important source of information concerning the unicorn symbolism of Mercurius": Horapollo says "the third genus of the scarab is unicorned (μονόκερως) and, on account of this peculiarity, sacred to Mercurius, like the ibis. Moreover the scarab is a μονογενής (only-begotten, unigena) in so far as it is an [αὐτογενές] (a creature born of itself)" (¶530). Hence the chain: self-born → unicus filius = "the filius philosophorum, i.e., the stone." The scarab shares the dragon's fate of dismemberment ("the sun-beetle … was beheaded and dismembered" — Greek papyrus), and the alchemists' self-name "Children of the Golden Head" points back to the golden head of Osiris.

occurrences.title: Elixir from the scarabs of our water — Consilium coniugii
occurrences.label: Elixir from the scarabs of our water
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The rare alchemical scarab, from the Consilium coniugii de massa solis et lunae: "Nulla aqua fit [elixir], nisi illa que fit de scarabaeis aquae nostrae — No water will become the elixir save that which comes from the scarabs of our water" (¶531; "fit quelles" in the chunk is an OCR garble). Jung: "The aqua nostra is nothing other than the aqua divina, i.e., Mercurius."
The scarab thus appears inside the water of the work — the self-born, unicorned beetle swimming in the divine water that is itself the transforming substance.

occurrences.title: Scheuchzer's 'witness of the flood' — fossil salamander read as human skeleton
occurrences.label: Scheuchzer's 'witness of the flood'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Betriibtes Beingeriist van einem alten Sunder / Erweiche Stein und Herz der heut'gen Bosheit Kinder.
body: Johann Jakob Scheuchzer (1672-1733), Zurich physician and naturalist, wrote a natural history proving the Flood: petrified shells on mountains four to five thousand feet up, petrified fishes ("the flood must have been so great that even the fish died"), and a huge fossil salamander of a species now extinct except in Japan — taken for a human skeleton, "one of the witnesses of the great flood." Jung quotes his verse:

Cited as the pre-Kantian state of science — "Science was in those days only a means to prove the existence of God" — the intellectual world whose collapse destroyed Kleist. The fossil (later named Andrias scheuchzeri) is a locus of proto-geology bending facts to scripture.

occurrences.title: Schlemihl: the mirror-reflection sold — Chamisso's Peter Schlemihl and Der Student von Prag
occurrences.label: Schlemihl — the mirror-reflection sold
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: One sees the man and his reflection in the mirror, and the devil stands behind and beckons to the reflection of the student in the glass
body: Jung screens the motif for the seminar from the film (Der Student von Prag, 1926, after Chamisso's 1814 novella): the devil buys "just something you have in this room" — and beckons the student's reflection out of the mirror; the reflection follows the devil, and the hero becomes a man without reflection or shadow, pretending at the barber's, losing his lady at the ball.

Read as the shadow doctrine made image: "the situation of a man who has split off all consciousness of his shadow, who has lost it" — exactly the patient whose brother-in-law (the follower, synopados) invites him to dinner. Kracauer (editor's note): the film "seemed to make the Germans realize their own duality."

occurrences.title: Babylonian seal cylinders — Maltese cross, crescent, and the sacred tree (Berlin Museum)
occurrences.label: Babylonian seal cylinders
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Photographs and plaster impressions of Babylonian cylinders of amethyst and jade that Jung retrieved "in looking through the cellars of the East Asiatic department of the Museum in Berlin": a Maltese cross with the crescent in one corner and the sun below; two male figures flanking the sacred tree, its segmented trunk carrying the winged disk divided in four by the cross; a segmented tree with an amphora on top out of which the winged disk appears; another with human heads equivalent to the winged sun. The sacred tree "played a great role in the Babylonian cult... sometimes like a date palm, usually with two priests in adoration, or giving water to the tree" — the cross-crescent symbolism millennia before the seminar's dreamer drew it.

occurrences.title: Seasonal dream-cycle of the woman confined twenty years (Zurich, ~1930)
occurrences.label: Seasonal dream-cycle of the woman confined…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: But she does not see it, she cannot grasp it, and it passes by as a sort of miracle, a lovely vision which happens I don't know where, on another star, and she is not touched by it. The pillar of life passes her by and then comes the winter again... a regular cycle.
body: A psychotic woman, confined for twenty years, willingly told Jung her dreams; he "simply took down the series. There was an absolutely rhythmical development in them" — winter dreams of an emptied world, then spring symbols, the rising sun, "a beautiful symbol of individuation or of rebirth".

Like the lame man waiting by the healing water, and Ayesha passing through the pillar of fire in Rider Haggard's She, the cycle is "the eternal cycle of death and rebirth which is always revolving in the unconscious" — but she cannot catch it: "she has lost her hands". Cited in the saint discussion: the unconscious both produces and cannot take up its own redemption symbol.

occurrences.title: 'Secret Inscription' — Great Magic Papyrus of Paris
occurrences.label: Secret Inscription
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: O great, greatest, incomprehensible fabric of the world, formed in a circle!
body: The prayer Jung quotes entire as "the continuation of that religious feeling for nature, so alien to Christianity": "Greetings, entire edifice of the Spirit of the air... greetings, beginning and end of irremovable Nature... O great, greatest, incomprehensible fabric of the world, formed in a circle!... having the form of water, of earth, of fire, of wind, of light, of darkness, star-glittering, damp-fiery-cold Spirit! I praise thee, God of gods, who hast fashioned the world... Destroyer, Begetter of living things, God of the Aeons, great art thou, Lord, God, Ruler of All!"

Jung: just as this prayer survives "embedded in a mass of magical recipes, so does the lumen naturae rise up from a world of kobolds and other creatures of darkness" (¶199). The passage carries his apologia for the symbol as the paradoxical "tertium" that "in reality is the living truth" (¶199).

occurrences.title: Sekhmet — the black basalt lioness-headed goddess at Luxor
occurrences.label: Sekhmet — the black basalt lioness-headed…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "those of you who have been in Luxor remember that great statue of the goddess Sekhmet. It is made of the most beautiful black basalt, and she has the head of a lioness. She personified the terrible destructive power of Ra, or the sun at its height, at the hottest time of the year."

Invoked in reading the lion's head above the cross on the patient's sole: the sun in its animal, fiercest aspect — power of a special kind, "not of a powerful man" — against the sun as enlightened man (Moses' radiating face) or as mind (the crown of Helios on the Caesars' coins).

occurrences.title: 'When thou knowest thyself, thou knowest God' — Zosimos to Theosebeia
occurrences.label: When thou knowest thyself, thou knowest God
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Olympiodorus preserves Zosimos's exhortation to his disciple Theosebeia: "If thou wilt calmly humble thyself in relation to thy body... thou wilt summon the divine to thyself, and in truth the divine, which is everywhere, will come to thee. But when thou know est thyself, thou know est also the God who is truly one" (cw13 ¶372).

Jung's footnote draws the theologic: God's attribute is infinity, the daemon's is spatial limit — the ego "separated and split off from God, is likely to become daemonic as soon as it accentuates its independence of God by its egocentricity" (cw13 ¶372 n5), the dynamism of the self "placed at the service of the ego" — Burckhardt's "great despoilers".
Verbatim: But when thou know est thyself, thou know est also the God who is truly one. (cw13 ¶372ocr)

occurrences.title: The self-rolling wheel (das aus sich rollende Rad) — Zarathustra, 'On the Three Metamorphoses'
occurrences.label: The self-rolling wheel
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Sils Maria / Basel (writing; Jung's Basel seminar reading)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: Now, the symbolism of the wheel suggests of course a mandala. In other words, this argument-the camel, the lion, and the child-is obviously the expression of the process of individuation, for which the universal dragon is killed.
body: Nietzsche's child of the third metamorphosis is "a new beginning, a game, a self-rolling wheel, a first movement, a holy Yea." Jung pauses on the strange symbol: das aus sich rollende Rad — a wheel whose center of impetus lies in itself, hence self-creative, like the child who "played with world fantasies until they became."

Jung's reading: "the symbolism of the wheel suggests of course a mandala" — the camel-lion-child argument is "obviously the expression of the process of individuation, for which the universal dragon is killed," and the wheel "is the sun symbolism… the sun has forever been a symbol of individuation, a symbol of the man who can stand by himself and move out of himself without being pushed."

occurrences.title: The dirty old man and the stepdaughter — Estonian tale of the moral test
occurrences.label: The dirty old man and the stepdaughter
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Pretty maid, pretty maid, wash me, do, it is hard for me to be so dirty!
body: The obedient stepdaughter jumps into a well after her distaff, meets cow, ram, and apple-tree, then a washhouse where "a dirty old man is sitting who wants her to wash him": fuel of "wooden pegs and crows' dung", bath-water the white mare's piss, a switch of the mare's tail, pumice for soap — she refuses each cruelty and substitutes the humane thing. Rewarded with "a bag full of gold and precious stones"; the jealous real daughter obeys every monstrous instruction and is rewarded accordingly. Jung's point: the old man "even tests the moral qualities of others and makes his gifts dependent on this test" (¶412) — spirit giving only what mercy, not obedience to sadism, draws forth.

occurrences.title: Father-God with 550 membra, shrunk to a five-ton lump — Nelken case
occurrences.label: Father-God with 550 membra, shrunk…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Nelken's patient, a primary-school teacher suffering paranoia, 'developed a theory about a Father-God with immense procreative powers. Originally he had 550 membra virilia, but in the course of time they were reduced to three... His colossal sperm production weakened him in the end, and finally he shrank to a five-ton lump and was found chained up in a ravine' (cw14 ¶378). Jung: 'This psychologem contains the motif of ageing and loss of procreative power. The patient was the rejuvenated Father-God or his avatar'; the embellishment 'is completely original, so that we can safely take it as an autochthonous product' of the collective unconscious (¶378) — the same mythologem Ripley clothed as the 'Ancient of Days'.

occurrences.title: The anchorite in the forest (Zarathustra, Prologue 2)
occurrences.label: The anchorite in the forest
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "there suddenly stood before him an old man, who had left his holy cot to seek roots" — who praises God by hymns in which he "laugh[s] and weep[s] and mumble[s]" (Jung: "brummt," like a bear — a regression to animal-voice imitation, as in the Mithras and Bakcheus cults). Zarathustra tells him: "This old saint in his wood has not yet heard that God is dead!"

Jung's reading: "He is an anchorite, he represents the early Christian spirit that does not know yet that its God is dead." He is "the paraclete; he is the remaining spirit of Christianity and is about to recede into nature" — a "pensioned paraclete" who advises Zarathustra to stay with the animals, "a bear amongst bears, a bird amongst birds." He knew Zarathustra of old ("many years ago passed he by") because "the greater part of the Christian dogma is Persian in origin." When the god is dead "it means the end of an epoch"; the same old spirit is renewed "in a new figure with a new message."

occurrences.title: Grandfather as control spirit — the pietistic guide of S.W. (Zurich, 1899–1900)
occurrences.label: Grandfather as control spirit
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The grandfather was the medium’s guide and protector.
body: The medium's dead grandfather, a clergyman, opens the séance series and acts as guide, protector and speech-automatism ("he loved her more than anyone in this world"). Jung splits the figure in two: Grandfather I, the banal automaton of the table, and Grandfather II, Ivenes' teacher in the ecstasies — never both present at once — before resolving the dualism in the "one and indivisible" basis of the patient's personality (¶129). The 1902 reading is reductive and biographical: "The grandfather represents this side of her past... the compulsorily educated bigot" (¶132).

Retro-lens (inferred, not Jung's 1902 claim): the sanctimonious old-man guide is the earliest documented appearance of what he later calls the wise old man / mana-personality behind spirit-controls. Parallels: medium-trance-personalities-helene-preiswerk-basel-1896 · senex-figure-anchorite-forest-zarathustra-1883 · grandfather-cellar-youngest-son-russian-fairy-tale.

occurrences.title: The Wise Man Decodes the Seven of Diamonds (M = Mother and Mary) — Pauli dream (~1935)
occurrences.label: The Wise Man Decodes the Seven of Diamonds
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: the step from the personified Mary to the 7 of diamonds went much further than Catholicism.
body: Pauli's counter-reading to Jung's interpretation of the seven and the ace of clubs in the published series: "In my seventh year my sister was born. So the 7 is an indication of the birth of the anima". In this later dream the 7 of diamonds "came up, and it looked like this" — seven pips drawn — "And then the 'wise man' in the dream explained to me that this also meant Mand referred to Mother and Mary. And he said that the step from the personified Mary to the 7 of diamonds went much further than Catholicism." The diamond card is also "a reference to the color of the sun."

The dream carries Pauli's persisting numerological line: 7 = anima-birth, attached to the Marian dogma sphere a decade and a half before the 1950 assumpsit Jung links to the reinstatement of the Goddess.

occurrences.title: The murder of Philemon and Baucis — Goethe's Faust II
occurrences.label: The murder of Philemon and Baucis
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "In his blind urge for superhuman power, Faust brought about the murder of Philemon and Baucis. Who are these two humble old people? When the world had become godless and no longer offered a hospitable retreat to the divine strangers Jupiter and Mercury, it was Philemon and Baucis who received the superhuman guests. And when Baucis was about to sacrifice her last goose for them, the metamorphosis came to pass: the gods made themselves known, the humble cottage was changed into a temple, and the old couple became immortal servitors at the shrine" (¶561).
Goethe's aged couple keep the gods in a godless world — and Faust's development requires their liquidation. (Cf. Jung's own inner figure Philemon, later painted at Bollingen.)

occurrences.title: The old man of Les Tableaux des Riches Inventions — frontispiece, Paris 1600
occurrences.label: The old man of Les Tableaux des Riches…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Paris; parallel: German book printed at Basel, 1588

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: In both, you find the lion with its paws cut off, for instance. We don't know where they originated, but one thing seems to be certain: there is hardly a trace of these symbols before the 15th century.
