body: Jung displays a picture-book: "it is a curious fact that the same figure occurs in an entirely different book, Les Tableaux des Riches Inventions" — the bearded old man as image of God, the Word, matching the German Basel book of 1588 and, "peculiarly enough," the alchemical book of tears and flames he showed earlier. "In both, you find the lion with its paws cut off, for instance. We don't know where they originated, but one thing seems to be certain: there is hardly a trace of these symbols before the 15th century. As a rule, they date from the time of the Reformation."

His hypothesis: the wise old man "was again teaching symbols, having appeared in a time when there was particular need of him" — the loss of confession and absolution created "an intolerable tension," the church became introverted, and the picture series answered with "the priesthood within." "They are exactly what you can observe in your own drawings; we have such picture-series again in our days."

occurrences.title: The little hooded man on the glacier — collective vision after a mountaineering accident
occurrences.label: The little hooded man on the glacier
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: after the catastrophe two of the climbers had the collective vision, in broad daylight, of a little hooded man who scrambled out of an inaccessible crevasse in the ice face and passed across the glacier, creating a regular panic in the two beholders.
body: Jung's strongest evidence that the gnomes and metal-men of fairy-tale are "real": "on the occasion of a serious mountaineering accident... after the catastrophe two of the climbers had the collective vision, in broad daylight, of a little hooded man who scrambled out of an inaccessible crevasse in the ice face and passed across the glacier, creating a regular panic in the two beholders" (¶410). The cucullatus — the hooded, invisible one, genius of the departed (¶298) — crossing the ice in daylight before two witnesses at once. Jung draws no "rational" conclusion beyond noting the uncanny fit of the diminutive to "the world of the infinitesimally small" (¶411).

occurrences.title: Winged senex ithyphallicus reliefs — Padmanabhapura temple
occurrences.label: Winged senex ithyphallicus reliefs
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In the royal temple of Padmanabhapura in Travancore (c. fifteenth century) I found two reliefs representing an entirely non-Indian senex ithyphallicus with wings.
body: Two temple reliefs Jung personally inspected: "an entirely non-Indian senex ithyphallicus with wings. In one of them he stands up to his waist in the bowl of the moon." He compares them with the winged ithyphallic old man who pursues the "blue" or "doglike" woman in Hippolytus's Naassene report (Elenchos V), where Kyllenios is "identical on the one hand with the Logos and on the other with the wicked Korybas, the phallus, and the demiurgic principle in general."

The reliefs support his claim of East-West traffic behind the erotic Mercurius: "Mercurius represents the 'continuous cohabitation' which is found in unalloyed form in the Tantric Shiva-Shakti concept"; Indian religious influences were at work in Mesopotamia from the first centuries AD.

occurrences.title: Krates' vision of Hermes as the old man with the book — Book of Krates
occurrences.label: Krates' vision of Hermes as the old man…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Greek original → Arabic transmission (Berthelot, La Chimie au moyen âge III)
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~9th c. (Arabic copy); Greek material considerably older
occurrences.quote: Then I saw an old man, the handsomest of men, sitting in a chair. He was dressed in white, and was holding in his hand a board from the chair, on which rested a book.…
body: The oldest extant vision of the Hermetic wise old man. In the Book of Krates — Greek in origin, handed down in Arabic, the present form ~9th century — the narrator sees Hermes enthroned, white-robed, holding a book containing "the explanation of the secret things he has hidden from men."

Jung cites it (Part II ch. 2, n. 7) as the prototype of the vision reported in Senior's Tabula chymica and reused on the frontispiece of Béroalde de Verville's Songe de Poliphile (fig. 4): the senex holding the book of secrets on his knees — the revealer who both hides and gives the arcanum.

occurrences.title: The little grey man as the Lord God — German tale of the soldier and the black princess
occurrences.label: The little grey man as the Lord God
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Suddenly a little man stood before him with along grey beard, but it was none other than the Lord God himself, who could no longer go on looking at all the mischief the devil wrought every night.
body: A princess under curse creeps from her iron coffin nightly and devours the soldier guarding the tomb. One escapes — and "suddenly a little man stood before him with a long grey beard, but it was none other than the Lord God himself, who could no longer go on looking at all the mischief the devil wrought every night. 'Whither away?' said the little grey man, 'may I come with you?'" Good advice follows, as always. Jung: the old man is taken for God "in the same naive way that the English alchemist, Sir George Ripley, describes the 'old king' as 'antiquus dierum' — 'the Ancient of Days'" (¶412, Cantilena, 15th c.). The fairy-tale senex shading directly into the God-image.

occurrences.title: The mad monk of Mipam — wisdom from the husk (David-Néel & Lama Yongden)
occurrences.label: The mad monk of Mipam — wisdom from the husk
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Mrs. Fierz reports the novel: "The hero is a so-called tulku, an incarnation, though he does not know it, and he learns all his wisdom from a monk in a monastery whom all the other monks think completely mad. But when he talks to him, he always learns the essential thing. It is just as you say, he is just a husk."

Jung: "Such peculiar things do happen" — and adds the counter-story of a drunken "lunatic" who talked to a man "from another dimension, and everything he described came off. So keep an open mind for these things."

The locus matters for the wise-old-man family: the senex appears as the mad husk whose words carry the essential — the same figure Nietzsche's "removed" state raises (only the husk remained; the soul "crossed the dark waters").

occurrences.title: The Masai medicine man who bet £4,000 on the Great War
occurrences.label: The Masai medicine man who bet £4,000…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Then the Masai, a very warlike tribe in East Africa, have a famous medicine man-a short man with a peculiarly big head-who made a lot of trouble for the English administration.
body: The living proof that "chthonic wisdom has always been associated with grotesque form":

"It is told as a fact that he prophesied that there would be war in the country before the Great War broke out" — the English assumed revolution; "he said, no, it would be among the white people". The colonial government wagered: "they promised to pay him four thousand pounds if there should be a war among the white people, and if nothing of the kind occurred, they would shoot him". "Then came the Great War, and they paid him the four thousand pounds. That fellow was still in existence when I was in Africa". Standing beside Rider Haggard's Zulu dwarf ("The thing that never should have been born"), Wieland, Vulcan, blind Melampus: the crippled, grotesque body as vessel of the seer's compensation.

occurrences.title: Milarepa's self-song — 'Yet an old man am I, forlorn and naked' (Tibet)
occurrences.label: Milarepa's self-song
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: I am Milarepa, great in fame, the direct offspring of Memory and Wisdom; Yet an old man am I, forlorn and naked.
body: Reichstein closes his survey of the old wise man with Milarepa's self-description, quoted "without commentary" as the Eastern analogue to the Iranian and Hermetic material: "I am Milarepa, great in fame, the direct offspring of Memory and Wisdom; Yet an old man am I, forlorn and naked."

The song gathers the old-man marks Jung and Reichstein have listed: secret knowledge ("all Nature at which I look, serveth me for a book"), the staff as guide "over the Ocean of Changing Life," mastery of "Mind and Light," and independence of powers — "depend not on earthly deities." The forlorn, naked old man in nature is the introverted face of the archetype that in the West appears as guide, magician, or Guru.

occurrences.title: The old man with compass and square and the red star — Kieser, Cabala Chymica (1606)
occurrences.label: The old man with compass and square…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: Praised be God that for once evil is put down and the truth revealed. Rejoice that the darkness has an end, the sun will not set again but will shine eternally.
body: Reichstein's alchemical example of the old wise man (report of 12 Dec 1934): in Kieser's vision-dialogue the pupil meditating on the "supernatural" finds himself in a deep valley; behind him stands "a very old man, with a long snow-white beard, in a black robe, with a compass and square," who grows gigantic, draws the lines of the world and speaks a "magic number spell."

On the quadrangle a dove appears — "the spirit of conjunction and vivification"; a flame shoots down from above, a white star rises from below, and where they meet "a brilliant red star remains… the symbol of the philosopher's stone." Everything burns; a new world arises — emerald earth, sun and moon standing still — and the old man cries that darkness has an end, "the sun will not set again but will shine eternally." Jung: through the old man's magic "the turning of the wheel of the world is stilled."

occurrences.title: 'The One-sided Old Man' — Siberian tale of the one-legged, one-handed, one-eyed greybeard
occurrences.label: The One-sided Old Man
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: In a Siberian tale, he appears as a one-legged, one-handed, and one-eyed greybeard who awakens a dead man with an iron staff.
body: In a Siberian tale the old man appears "as a one-legged, one-handed, and one-eyed greybeard who awakens a dead man with an iron staff"; the revived man, killed and reawakened several times, finally slays his benefactor by mistake — and with him his good fortune. His missing half appears separately "in the shape of a murderer who seeks the hero's life", and only when both are dead is the identity of victims revealed. Jung: "the old man is his own opposite, a life-bringer as well as a death-dealer — 'ad utrumque peritus' (skilled in both), as is said of Hermes" (¶413-414). The archetype's dark side, split off and walking.

occurrences.title: The old man with the milk-flask — Estonian tale of the runaway orphan
occurrences.label: The old man with the milk-flask
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Estonia (collection, 'How an Orphan Boy Unexpectedly Found His Luck')

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Give me some more to drink,' begged the boy. 'You have had enough for today,' replied the old man.
body: An ill-treated orphan boy lets a cow escape and flees, falls asleep exhausted — and wakes to find "a little old man with a long grey beard... in the act of replacing the stopper in his little milk-flask": "If my path had not chanced to lead me to you, that would assuredly have been your last sleep." He refuses to shelter the boy but gives counsel: go eastward; after seven years he will reach the great mountain that betokens his fortune; he gives his scrip and flask (food and drink each day) and a burdock leaf that becomes a boat. Jung uses the tale to define the archetype: the old man appears when insight "cannot be mustered on one's own resources", compensating spiritual deficiency; he is "purposeful reflection and concentration of moral and physical forces... outside consciousness" (¶401-403). The mountain "often has the psychological meaning of the self" (n14, I Ching hexagram 17).

occurrences.title: The dark tower and the sevenfold rope — Christian Rosenkreutz's dream (Chymical Wedding, 1616)
occurrences.label: The dark tower and the sevenfold rope
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1616 (first edition; written ~1602; first day of seven)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: He is with some other people in a dark tower and they are held fast by heavy chains (compare Ormuzd fettered in matter).
body: Reichstein's second example, the first day of the Chymical Wedding: a heavenly virgin brings Rosenkreutz a letter — "this is the divine messenger, the awakening" (cf. the Iranian messenger known by his voice). His dream follows: prisoners "held fast by heavy chains (compare Ormuzd fettered in matter)"; music; the roof opens; "a man hoary with age calls out that his mother (nature, corresponding to the Mother of the Living in some gnostic teachings) had commanded a rope to be lowered seven times."

Most drag each other down; some have their arms torn off rather than let go. The dreamer escapes by chance, then must help pull. Jung's comment: in alchemical writings the old man "often appears only at the beginning," and the striking feature is "the complete helplessness of the imprisoned people — not only is a way shown to them, but they must be literally pulled out of their predicament."

occurrences.title: Ryochi, the true self within — Nakae Toju's teaching
occurrences.label: Ryochi, the true self within
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: We might define this false self as the persona... What one is, is one's individual self, Toju's 'true self' or ryochi.
body: The "sage of Omi" posits ri (world soul) and ki (world stuff), both attributes of God whose union is God. Against the false self — "an acquired personality compounded of perverted beliefs," which Jung equates with the persona — stands ryochi, "God within us," the individual's "heaven," the summum bonum and light pervading the world. Jung: "Ryochi is the self-regulating function, the mediator and uniter of the opposites, ri and ki; it is in fullest accord with the Indian idea of the 'wise old man who dwells in the heart'" (¶370). Wang Yangming: "In every heart there dwells a sejin (sage). Only, we do not believe it firmly enough."

occurrences.title: Wise old man with the book of secrets — Senior's Tabula chymica (fig. 128)
occurrences.label: Wise old man with the book of secrets
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Arabic author (Mohammed ibn Umail) → Latin print tradition

jung.locator: pdf p660 (Part II ch. 2, n. 7); fig. 128

occurrences.quote: The figure as depicted in the treatise, of a wise old man holding the book of secrets on his knees, was taken over in the frontispiece of Béroalde de Verville, Le Songe de Poliphile (see fig. 4).
body: The frontispiece vision of Senior (Zadith), the Latin name of Mohammed ibn Umail: a wise old man seated, the book of secrets on his knees — the alchemist's personified arcanum as revealer. Jung reproduces it as fig. 128 and reads it alongside the vision of the man on the cathedra in the alchemist's own "seeing in the spirit" (cw12 Part II ch. 2, n. 7).

Jung notes the figure was taken over for the frontispiece of Béroalde de Verville's Le Songe de Poliphile (fig. 4), showing the continuity of the senex-revealer motif from 10th-century Arabic alchemy into Renaissance emblematics. The oldest antecedent he knows is the vision of senex-krates-vision-hermes-white-9c.

occurrences.title: The adder bites Zarathustra under the fig tree — 'The Bite of the Adder'
occurrences.label: The adder bites Zarathustra under the fig tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Zarathustra I, ch. 19 ('On the Adder's Bite')

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Zarathustra falls asleep under a fig-tree in the heat, arms over his face; an adder bites him in the neck. He rebukes it — "When did ever a dragon die of a serpent's poison?" — and the adder, unrecognized, licks the wound back.

Jung's exegesis is a chain: the fig tree mobilizes an archetype with "a peculiar fascination which makes you unconscious" (mother-tree, Priapus-wood, womb-fig); the bite lands in the throat because "Zarathustra is very obviously the logos... you can only reach it by the throat where the word comes from" — visuddha, not muladhara; being himself serpent-natured, the bite "cannot" hurt him — "that is the illusory protection which identification with an archetype gives you"; the wound-licking serpent "must have arms to do it!... it is always through a woman that the serpent reaches a man, as it was in Paradise". Lou Salomé, after five months of daily discussions, is named as the serpent Nietzsche met.

occurrences.title: The great serpent of Aesculapius brought to Rome against the pestilence
occurrences.label: The great serpent of Aesculapius brought…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Jung: 'the third century'; historically the plague embassy of 293/291 BCE

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: "The serpent was the original form of the physician's god. There was an enormous serpent in the temple of Aesculapius, and in the third century, the huge beast was brought to Rome to combat the spirit of pestilence. For centuries, there was a serpent in the sanctuary. It was snake worship." (The historical embassy from Epidaurus to Rome during the plague belongs to 293/291 BCE; Jung's "third century" is loose.) From this root: the doctor's staff with the snake, "the caduceus... also the symbol of Hermes the Sorcerer", and "there was originally an idea that Aesculapius himself was a serpent".

occurrences.title: Agathodaimon serpent — antique gem (fig. 37)
occurrences.label: Agathodaimon serpent — antique gem (fig. 37)
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: It is both Agathodaimon (fig. 37) and Cacodaimon.
body: Fig. 37 beside the double aspect of the hero-snake: "It is both Agathodaimon (fig. 37) and Cacodaimon. In German legend we are told that the heroes have snake's eyes" (¶593). Tum of Pithum-Heroopolis "was chiefly worshipped as the Agathodaimon serpent, of whom it was said: 'The sacred Agathodaimon serpent goes forth from the city of Nezi'" (¶410).

occurrences.title: Jung's Gnostic agathodaimon ring
occurrences.label: Jung's Gnostic agathodaimon ring
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: For instance, this ring of mine with the snake engraved on it is two thousand years old; it is the agathodaimon, and it is also the Kundalini serpent
body: Worn on his own hand while teaching the amber-stone vision, Jung's example of the talisman's "magic effect":

"it gives me special satisfaction to wear such a historical ring, it conveys a particular meaning to me. Of course it has artistic quality and that is very interesting, but it appeals to my nocturnal side particularly, it expresses something unconscious, and so it is thoroughly alive and full of mana". Context: the missionaries' argument against idols ("only stone or wood that could be chopped up") holds "in the daytime… but in the night it is different. Then the idol assumes a life of its own". Ed. note: Jung discusses the ring with Miguel Serrano, C.G. Jung Speaking, p. 468. The good-daimon serpent that is "also the Kundalini" ties the ancient gem to the chunk's coiled serpent at the bottom of the well.

occurrences.title: Seven-headed snake of Amente, the Egyptian underworld
occurrences.label: Seven-headed snake of Amente, the Egyptian…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: 'In Amente, the Egyptian underworld, dwells the great seven-headed snake, and in the Christian underworld is the most celebrated snake of all, the devil, "that old serpent"' (cw14 ¶482). Hell's pair of brothers: 'the devil being characterized by the snake and death by worms'; in Old German and Latin 'worm, snake, and dragon coalesce' (vermis, serpens, draco) (¶482). The dragon-slayer 'is therefore always a conqueror of death' (¶482). The seven-headed snake gives the chthonic serpent its maximal, underworld form — counterpart to the Mercurial serpent of the work.

occurrences.title: The ancestral spirit in the hut — East African soul-serpent custom
occurrences.label: The ancestral spirit in the hut
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "In East Africa they generally assume that souls appear in the form of serpents, and whenever a serpent enters a hut the people clear out, not from fear, for they could kill it, but out of sheer politeness; they say an ancestral spirit has honored their hut with his visit and so they leave the hut for its use. They even leave food for it, and then when it has gone, they use the hut again for ordinary purposes."

Standing in Jung's soul-serpent row: Greek heroes' souls as serpents fed through the tomb opening; the first animal seen near a grave carrying the dead man's soul; the hero's serpent-soul of the Northern myth (Grimm's "snake in the eye").

occurrences.title: Ra fighting the serpent in the Seventh Hour of the Night Journey — Egyptian Amduat (~1400 BCE)
occurrences.label: Ra fighting the serpent in the Seventh Hour…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Thebes (Valley of the Kings tomb texts)

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: In the middle of his great serpent lecture, Jung reaches Egypt: "The snake encoils the vessel of Ra. In the Night Journey, in the Seventh Hour, Ra must fight the serpent. Ra is supported by the ritual of the priests: if he kills the serpent, the sun rises, if he should not succeed, the sun would rise no more". The Seventh Hour of the Amduat (the sun's journey through the underworld): Apophis, the great serpent of chaos, attacks the solar barque; the daily battle on which sunrise depends — the ritual of the living keeps it going. The passage stands in his argument that the serpent "leads the psychological movement apparently astray into the kingdom of shadows," connects above and below, and must be fought through nightly.

occurrences.title: Tormented at night by thousands of snakes — B.St. at the Burghölzli (1899)
occurrences.label: Tormented at night by thousands of snakes
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: 1899: Patient is tormented at night by thousands of snakes.
body: A single line of the published case-history of B.St. — the old dressmaker whose paranoid system Jung dissects as his paradigm: "1899: Patient is tormented at night by thousands of snakes." It belongs to the injury side of her psychosis, alongside the bed "stuck full of needles" (¶200) and the voices she explained as invisible telephones. Jung draws no amplification here; within the same case the serpent returns tender rather than persecutory — the little green snake that comes to her mouth "as if it wanted to kiss me" (¶283). Terror and eros in one image-family, ten years before the 1911-12 serpent studies.

occurrences.title: Walking on the back of the great snake — 'We stamp upon it' (Visions, 6 Dec. 1933)
occurrences.label: Walking on the back of the great snake
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: On the black and rocky path down into reality: "Suddenly I felt and saw that we were walking along the back of a great snake. I said to the man: 'We walk upon the back of a great snake.' He answered: 'Yes, we stamp upon it.'".

Jung's amplification: Frobenius' African rock drawings of little men on a great snake; the python myth (see python-women-lunch-flood-myth-africa); the wollunqua-serpent-ancestor-australia; Christ as zodiacal serpent whose back carries the twelve apostles-stars; Tao "symbolized originally as a dragon" (pp1289-1293). The meaning: "what they thought was dead is in reality a living thing... the inevitable path is a thing that is living in itself, autonomously living" — the way itself takes command, the instincts ruling when one is unconscious, the philosopher's Tao when conscious.

occurrences.title: Batak ancestor-columns: the incest family strangled by snakes (Sumatra, cited 1912)
occurrences.label: Batak ancestor-columns
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: artifact undated (ethnographic collection era); cited by Jung 1912
occurrences.quote: They assert that these superimposed figures are members of a family who, because they committed incest, were entwined by a snake while being bitten to death by another snake.
body: Carved columns of human figures standing one on top of another. The Bataks' own explanation — "generally regarded as nonsense" by collectors — is that the superimposed figures are members of a family who, because they committed incest, were entwined by a snake while being bitten to death by another snake (¶512). Jung sets this beside his 11-year-old patient's drawing of birth-through-the-head: the same "infantile bonds," the same primary incest condition (her sexual fantasies "revolved round her father" as the Batak ones round the primal incest) — ethnographic artifact and child's fantasy illuminating each other. Same artifact class as the wand shown in the 1933 seminar, with the snake detail to the fore.

occurrences.title: The Big Snake — twins in the ditch who become dragon-killers (Frobenius)
occurrences.label: The Big Snake — twins in the ditch…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung's fig-40-adjacent African parallel for the twins-in-the-womb motif: "the Big Snake, which grew out of a little snake in a hollow tree ('stretching forth of the serpent'), and which devoured all human beings (devouring mother = death) until only one pregnant woman remained. She dug a ditch, covered it with a stone, and there gave birth to twins who afterwards became dragon-killers" (¶620).

Jung reads the devouring serpent as the devouring mother = death; the hollow tree as the maternal container; the stone-covered ditch as a substitute womb from which the dragon-killer twins are born — the psyche's compensatory counter-figure to the monster that ate everyone else. It stands beside the Hölderlin material as evidence that "guarded in modest bud" (the fateless gods' eternal infancy) and its violent termination are a universal pattern.
Verbatim: "She dug a ditch, covered it with a stone, and there gave birth to twins who afterwards became dragon-killers" (¶620).

occurrences.title: Snake bites the patient in the genital region — Zürich dream
occurrences.label: Snake bites the patient in the genital region
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: the moment he felt the impulse to go forward he also felt the pull of the bond to the mother.
body: The dream struck "at the moment when the patient was convinced of the truth of the analysis and was beginning to free himself from the bonds of his mother-complex" — the pull of the bond striking precisely as he "felt the impulse to go forward." Jung: "Being bitten in the genital region by a snake … reminds us of Attis, whose self-castration was occasioned by his mother's jealousy" (¶585). Companion reports: the woman filled with an enormous snake, the woman with a snake stuck in her throat.

occurrences.title: The snake with the black hood wound upon the cross (Visions plate 20)
occurrences.label: The snake with the black hood wound upon…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich (patient's painting; plate following p. 272 of the edition)
occurrences.yearDisplay: painted late 1929/early 1930 for Jung; vision from the 1926-32 series

jung.locator: plate 20 caption (pdf p12); discussion in later sessions

occurrences.quote: A snake with a black hood... wound itself upon the cross
body: Plate 20: a hooded snake winding itself upon the cross — serpent and cross in one figure, the instinctual spirit climbing the Christian tree of death-and-rebirth. The cobra-hood links the image to the Kundalini serpent the seminar group used "as a map and guide in which to set Morgan's visions"; the cross carries the fourfold-sacrifice symbolism Jung unfolded on 22 Oct 1930 ("the four arms of the cross and the idea of the sacrifice in the center"). Together with plate 26 (snakes gliding over rings feeding the child) it marks the series' movement from the Christian symbols of the early visions toward the chthonic-redeeming serpent.

occurrences.title: The black snake asleep in the abdomen — patient's symbolic statement
occurrences.label: The black snake asleep in the abdomen
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: a girl of about twenty-six once came to me and said: \"Doctor, I have a black snake in my abdomen and it is asleep.\
body: A girl of about twenty-six opens with: "Doctor, I have a black snake in my abdomen and it is asleep." She immediately adds that she means it symbolically — and Jung says that is exactly why she is not mad: "Since she knows that this sounds crazy, I know she is not."

He uses the case to state the rapport-criterion for borderline states ("As long as you can explain yourself and feel the need of explaining yourself to a human being… you are not crazy"), and the image itself — a dormant black serpent in the belly — sits squarely in the kundalini/muladhara field Jung had mapped in the Hauer seminar (cf. the sleeping soul "comparable to the condition of Muladhara," pdf p334).

occurrences.title: The black snake at the sick-bed — Anna O.'s waking vision (Vienna, ~1880)
occurrences.label: The black snake at the sick-bed
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: she saw a black snake coming, apparently out of the wall, towards the sick man as though to bite him.
body: The founding scene of the talking cure: Bertha Pappenheim ("Anna O."), nursing her dying father, falls into a twilight state and sees a black snake come out of the wall toward the sickbed. Paralysed, she tries to pray; no words come until she remembers an English nursery rhyme — whence her systematic aphasia. As she stares at her dead right arm, "the fingers changed into little serpents with death's-heads."

Jung's reading: the narrated scene removed the paralysis and speech disturbance (cw07 ¶7); he uses the case to show how the trauma theory arose and why it had to be surpassed — the trauma is "no more than an occasion" for a deeper erotic conflict (¶13). The snake-hallucination is, structurally, an archetypal appearing at the birth of psychoanalysis itself.

occurrences.title: Black snake attacking the face — dream of the 8-year-old boy (Case 4)
occurrences.label: Black snake attacking the face
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Very often he dreamt of a black snake that wanted to bite his face.
body: An intelligent, delicate 8-year-old with enuresis, clamped to a tender mother against a strict father, dreams "very often" of a black snake that wants to bite his face, until he cries out and his mother comes from the next room (¶732).

Jung's 1949 reading: "'Black' indicates something dark, the unconscious... The threatening agency is represented by the mythological motif of the 'father animal'" — the father as anticipation of the boy's own masculinity against his wish to stay infantile; "The snake's attack on the boy's face, the part that 'sees,' represents the danger to consciousness (blinding)" (¶737). The 1909 stratum read the bed-wetting as sexual substitute (orig. n.20); the revision reads it as premature masculinity compensating the child's inferiority (¶736). Companion dream: black-man-wicked-sword-bed-dream-boy-8-zurich-1909.

occurrences.title: The bronze serpent on the pillar — Sant'Ambrogio, Milan
occurrences.label: The bronze serpent on the pillar
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 9th-11th c.? (Jung: if that old, likely Christ as serpent)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: It is very old and very simple... just opposite a pillar that has a cross on top.
body: Dr. Escher reports: in the old church of St. Ambrogio "there is a huge bronze snake on a pillar in the middle of the church, just opposite a pillar that has a cross on top. It is not the ouroboros. It is very old and very simple" — offered against the rule that the Catholic church counts the snake as evil.

Jung's reading: "They would not represent the devil — that is certain — so it may be the old idea of Christ as the serpent. That figure, or metaphor, was frequently used by the Latin Fathers of the church... well prepared historically in the pre-Christian mediator: the agathodaimon of the Hellenic-Egyptian mysteries was represented as a serpent". Dating decides: "if that serpent in Milan dates from the 9th to the 11th century, or even as late as the 13th, it is quite possible that it represents Christ; if it is later it becomes doubtful. They had to be careful, naturally, on account of the infernal meaning of the serpent."

occurrences.title: Man castrated by a serpent — Rubens' Last Judgment
occurrences.label: Man castrated by a serpent
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "A similar motif can be found in a Rubens' Last Judgment (pl. LXIV), where, in the foreground, a man is being castrated by a serpent. This motif illustrates the meaning of the end of the world" (¶681).

Jung's reading makes the painting's castration-by-serpent the eschatological image of psychological change: "The fantasy of world conflagration, of the cataclysmic end of the world in general, is the projected primordial image of the great transformation, the enantiodromia of life into death, which Rubens represents as emasculation by the serpent" (¶681). The consuming change that dissolves "the phenomenal world of individual psychic existence" originates in the unconscious and announces itself in dreams and premonitions — the more unwilling the ego, the more frightening the symbols. Pair with the Verona Priapus (¶680), the classical twin of the motif.
Verbatim: "a man is being castrated by a serpent. This motif illustrates the meaning of the end of the world" (¶681).

image.title: The Great Last Judgement title QS:P1476,en:"The Great Last Judgement " label QS:Len,"The Great Last Judgement " label QS:Lit,"Grande Giudizio Universale" label

occurrences.title: Cecrops, half snake half man, beneath the Parthenon — Athens
occurrences.label: Cecrops, half snake half man, beneath…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Above his subterranean dwelling rose the Parthenon, the temple of the virgin goddess.
body: "Clear traces of the original identity of hero and snake" (¶594): the buried snake-king under the temple of the virgin goddess; above his subterranean dwelling rose the Parthenon. The flaying of the god (Aztec ceremonies) "is intimately bound up with the snake-like nature of the hero" (¶594).

occurrences.title: Chaos as the great serpent crushing the patient (second patient)
occurrences.label: Chaos as the great serpent crushing the patient
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The next state after the spiders' webs: "She herself is almost crushed in the coils of an enormous serpent. This is again chaos but in the form of the great leviathan, as chaos is often represented in alchemy by the ouroboros, the great dragon". "That change took place practically from one day to the next... the chaos was then in a form and the splits had disappeared; that sort of dead chaos became vivified in the form of the great original serpent."

Diagnostic reading: "the chaos lost its multitudinous quality and became, as it were, personified; it was gathered together and shaped into one being, a representative of the cerebro-spinal system" — a great advance.

occurrences.title: Chnuphis / XNOUMIS serpent, seven- and twelve-rayed — Gnostic gems
occurrences.label: Chnuphis / XNOUMIS serpent, seven…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The Agathodaimon serpent on Gnostic gems also has seven or twelve rays about its head (figs 203–5).
body: Gnostic gems and amulets showing the Agathodaimon serpent: fig. 203 the Chnuphis serpent with a seven-rayed crown; fig. 204 a lion-headed, twelve-rayed XNOUMIS serpent over an altar-stone.

Jung adduces them as the antique serpent-photism behind Sapientia's crown of seven (or twelve) stars in the Aurora-Rosarium line: "The Agathodaimon serpent on Gnostic gems also has seven or twelve rays about its head." Seven answers the seven planets/metals and the seven spirits of God; twelve the zodiac and the apostles. The serpent's ray-crown carries the same sidereal numerology the alchemists transferred to the lapis.
Cf. the seven-headed serpent of fate on the seal of St. Servatius, Maastricht (fig. 205) — the seven-starred Sapientia of aurora-consurgens-sapientia-dei-14c.

occurrences.title: The cobra at the haunted ford (Talbot, In the Shadow of the Bush, Nigeria, reported 1912)
occurrences.label: The cobra at the haunted ford
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Nigeria (P. A. Talbot, In the Shadow of the Bush, London 1912)
occurrences.quote: He tells of a ford which was supposed to be haunted by demons in the form of snakes.
body: The ethnographer Talbot came to a ford "supposed to be haunted by demons in the form of snakes" and "really met a snake, a cobra. It went across the path between himself and his wife, who was preceding him. He shot the beast and it jumped into the air and hit him on the cheek". Jung cites it while interpreting the patient's snake-guide: fords are "a typical danger in folklore; and dragons are supposed to live near the fords, or they are guarded by snakes" — but the Negro myths, Talbot shows, "are suggested by the real character of the situation": the haunted caves and fords were genuinely dangerous places.

occurrences.title: The pair of cobras at the tropical house — dream, 30 Sep 1954
occurrences.label: The pair of cobras at the tropical house
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: dream, house located in the Tropics

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: The union of the two cobras indicates that the real coniunctio is still in the state of the spiritus Mercurialis and is marked out only in the unconscious.
body: With his wife, in a house in the Tropics, the dreamer meets a rising cobra without fear, "friendly toward it"; then a second cobra rears up before the window — "The snakes are a pair, a male and a female." Only afterwards are the voices of two physicist colleagues heard outside the house.

Jung continues: "Nor can it actually come about unless the opposites that are to be united are present in the form that penetrates chthonic depths." Pauli: the dream "seems to be saying that the possibility of PARITY exists also in the psyche" — a pleasing state for the individuation process "outside the ego."

occurrences.title: The crowned serpent coils her at the bottom of the well (Visions)
occurrences.label: The crowned serpent coils her at the bottom…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: vision read 24 February 1932 (painted late 1929/early 1930 for Jung)
occurrences.quote: There upon the ground I saw a man and a woman lying as if in the womb and about them was coiled a snake.
body: In the oasis she meets a woman wearing the Cybele jewel drawing water from a well in the crater, and descends its shaft to the bottom, where:

The serpent approaches her: "You too will I coil about" — "But I am all alone." Yet it coils her as if she were a couple; she sees "a crown upon its head and rings of gold around its body", embraces it — "Serpent you are beautiful to me" — and it falls away. Jung: the bottom of the well "would be muladhara in the terminology of the Kundalini yoga system"; the pair = Shiva and Shakti dormant, the lingam encoiled; the embrace makes her "into a whole, the male and the female… come together". Like the Eleusinian snake-kiss and the golden snake passed through the initiate's garments, the god enters: entheos. Panic is "a misfiring of the conubium of the god"; the crescent moon — Cybele's emblem — then lifts her from the erupting crater.

occurrences.title: Ebony bedstead with serpent-on-cross and pelican — Indian royal palace, Italian master
occurrences.label: Ebony bedstead with serpent-on-cross and pelican
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Jung's eyewitness report: "In an Indian royal palace from the fifteenth century I found a bedstead made of ebony, and there was that symbolic image, with many birds around it, and above there hovered a pelican. This piece was made by an Italian master in the sixteenth century. He depicted alchemical symbols on it, among them that snake, which can also be found in the famous book by Abraham le Juif".

"That snake" is the serpent on the cross — the sotēr snake of Numbers 21 read Christian-alchemically; Abraham le Juif = Abraham Eleazar, Livre des figures hiéroglyphiques, the same figure reproduced in Jung's CW12 fig. 217. The locus: "Just as the one snake in the desert overcame the many, Christ, so to speak, overcame the autonomous instinctual forces."

occurrences.title: Two snakes atop the marble curse-inscription on the Palatine
occurrences.label: Two snakes atop the marble curse-inscription…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: with two snakes on top of it, saying that anybody who soiled that place would be cursed in the name of the twelve gods.
body: On one of the walls of the Palatine a marble plate carries an inscription crowned by two snakes: anyone who soiled the place would be cursed in the name of the twelve gods. Jung's visual proof that the snake functions as a sign — "The figure of a snake is like an exclamation mark on a road... Achtung!" — danger, magic, mana; the same convention recurs in corners of Italian churches. It is why the snake-surrounded goddess of the patient's underworld vision announces: Look out!

occurrences.title: 'Thou risest up like the sacred snake' — Hathor temple, Dendereh
occurrences.label: Thou risest up like the sacred snake
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Inscription on the temple of Hathor at Dendereh: 'The sun, who has existed from the beginning, rises up like a falcon out of the midst of his lotus-bud... Thou risest up like the sacred snake as a living spirit, creating the beginnings and shining in thy glorious form in the barge of the sunrise... Coming as one, he multiplies himself a millionfold when the light goes forth from him in the form of a child' (cw14 ¶483). Jung: 'The comparison of the god to a snake reminds us of his chthonic form in the underworld, just as the rejuvenated phoenix (falcon) first takes the form of a worm' (¶483). The snake as the god's renewing form passed into Christian allegory (John 3:14) and 'was readily seized on by the alchemists' (¶483).

occurrences.title: Zosimos' resume: the dragon guarding the round temple of one stone (Egypt, ~3rd c.)
occurrences.label: Zosimos' resume — the dragon guarding the round…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The resume (prooimion) Jung places at the end of the visions: "build a temple from a single stone... with neither end nor beginning in its construction... Note carefully on what side is the entrance to the temple... A dragon lies at the entrance, guarding the temple. Lay hold upon him; immolate him first; strip him of his skin, and taking his flesh with the bones, separate the limbs; then... make a step of them, mount thereon, and enter, and you will find what you seek" (cw13 ¶87). The priest within, first brazen, then silver, then golden man.

Jung: the sacrificed is the uroboros serpent, "whose circular form is suggested by the shape of the temple, which has 'neither beginning nor end'"; the temple of a single stone paraphrases the lapis; dismembering = dividing the chaos into four. "The dragon, or serpent, represents the initial state of unconsciousness" whose sacrifice opens the way to the head (¶118).

occurrences.title: Baumann's pictures — the eagle, the snake, and the heart in the water
occurrences.label: Baumann's pictures
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Mr. Baumann, seminar member, showed paintings from his own inner process — "Mr. Baumann has looked in through the window and painted some of the pictures presented by the unconscious." First picture: "the eagle with the snake, and the figure of a boy is hovering over the water seeking the heart in the water."

Jung reads a drama interieur, an initiation: "The heart in the water cannot be discovered as long as the snake is also in the water. To enable the boy to find the heart, the snake has to be brought up into the sky or the air... Therefore, Yin must be taken out of its element." Afterwards "a very bad fight takes place between them, for they are like dog and cat" — the domestic miracle of eagle-snake friendship being impossible.
Verbatim: "Here is the eagle with the snake, and the figure of a boy is hovering over the water seeking the heart in the water."

occurrences.title: The Eleusinian kiss of the serpent of Demeter (excavated relief, Greece)
occurrences.label: The Eleusinian kiss of the serpent of Demeter
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the initiate was depicted kissing a serpent that represented Demeter, the goddess of the earth.
body: "In the Eleusinian mysteries, you remember, the initiate had to unite himself with the powers of the earth by kissing the serpent. There is no text which corroborates that ceremonial, but a sort of relief has been excavated where the initiate was depicted kissing a serpent that represented Demeter, the goddess of the earth". Jung cites it in reading the patient's kiss of the black head: the kiss is "the union with it, an acceptance" — a repetition of the swallowing of the black snake in the earlier vision. The earth-powers accepted through the mouth, fire and all.

occurrences.title: Patient who became a snake and crawled into her mother (cw05 ¶676)
occurrences.label: Patient who became a snake and crawled…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: undated patient fantasy (~1911-12 writing period; inferred)
body: Immediately after the Gabricus-Beya legend Jung writes: "Such fantasies are not uncommon among patients. Thus one patient of mine had the fantasy that she was a snake which wound itself round her mother and finally crawled right into her" (¶676).

The clinical twin of the alchemical coniunctio: the patient as serpent (serpens mercurialis in the making) embracing and then entering the mother's body — regression depicted as a voluntary return into the womb, with the snake as the shape of the libido that gets itself swallowed. Jung introduces it to prove that alchemical fantasies of dissolving into the partner's body "are not uncommon among patients," tying the Latin corpus to living psychology. Compare the same chapter's Jonah-and-the-Whale complex (¶54/654): fear of incest turning into fear of being devoured — here turned inside out as desire.
Verbatim: "she was a snake which wound itself round her mother and finally crawled right into her" (¶676).

occurrences.title: The devil as four-horned serpent — Dorn's warlike quaternity
occurrences.label: The devil as four-horned serpent
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Dorn 'saw in the quaternity the absolute opposite of the Trinity, namely the female principle, which seemed to him "of the devil," for which reason he called the devil the "four-horned serpent"' (cw14 ¶238). 'The devil, he thought, was the binarius itself, since it was created on the second day of Creation, on Monday, the day of the moon' (¶238). Later: the battle of copper and quicksilver (Turba Sermo 42) is the vicious quaternity 'which the devil, after his fall from heaven, sought to "infix" in the mind of man'; Dorn 'puts the motif of war on a moral plane and thereby approximates it to the modern concept of psychic dissociation' (cw14 ¶494). Jung: 'This insight must have given him a glimpse into the core of the problem' (¶238).

occurrences.title: Descent of the Ganges — goddess, woman above serpent below (Mamallapuram)
occurrences.label: Descent of the Ganges
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Jung cites the "famous rock sculpture at Mamallipuram, where the birth of the Ganges river is represented as a goddess, female above and serpent below" — the classical type of the half-human, half-cerebro-spinal anima, "the consort of the gods... partially she is a cerebro-spinal animal, half woman, half serpent, being stuck in the lower parts of the nervous system."
Same row as Lilith as the serpent of paradise and the salamander-tailed, frog-footed female of the Ripley Scroll: the feminine as spirit above and reptile below.

occurrences.title: Gilgamesh robbed of the magic herb by the demon-serpent
occurrences.label: Gilgamesh robbed of the magic herb…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Old Babylonian version ~1800 BCE (Sumerian tales older)
body: Returning from the Western Land with the herb of immortality (Jung's pl. XIX), Gilgamesh bathes; the demon-serpent robs the treasure and sloughs its skin — mortality stays with man. Jung uses it as the mythological form of a lament of failure: "as once Gilgamesh... was robbed of his treasure by the demonserpent, so Hölderlin's poem dies away in a painful lament, which tells us that his descent to the shadows will be followed by no resurrection in this world" (¶642). The serpent frustrates the hero's rebirth and keeps the renewal for itself — the chthonic power claiming the treasure hard to attain.

In the same chapter the Epic supplies the hero's shadow-brother: the horse that dies first in the Miller drama corresponds to "the early death of the half-bestial Enkidu, friend and brother of Gilgamesh" (¶659); later "Gilgamesh and Enkidu" name the centaur-unit of ego and shadow (¶678).
Verbatim: "robbed of his treasure by the demonserpent" (¶642).

image.title: Tablet XI or the Flood Tablet of the Epic of Gilgamesh, currently housed in the British Museum in London

occurrences.title: The son in the form of the first snake — Gnostic serpent as bringer of knowledge
occurrences.label: The son in the form of the first snake
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: and he sent his son in the form of the first snake in Paradise to teach the first parents to eat from the tree of knowledge.
body: Jung's retelling of the Gnostic myth of the imperfect creator: the demiurge, "a sort of sub-god… who in his vanity created a world," looks up, sees "a light which he realized he had not created," and ascends to the world of the spiritual father, the real God — understanding his mistake.

The father "took pity on those half-conscious worms, human beings, whom the demiurgos had made without consciousness enough to see their own imperfection; and he sent his son in the form of the first snake in Paradise to teach the first parents to eat from the tree of knowledge." Eating, the first parents learn the difference of good and evil, "and that was the way to salvation." The serpent here is the father's emissary against the demiurge's ignorance — the Naassene-ophite reading Jung knew from the Elenchos material.

occurrences.title: 'It is God's animal' — the green-blue-white snake of Spielrein's patient (Zurich)
occurrences.label: It is God's animal'
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Spielrein's patient on her snake: "It is God's animal, it has such wonderful colours: green, blue, and white. The rattlesnake is green; it is very dangerous.… The snake can have a human mind, it can have divine judgment; it is a friend of children. It would save the children who are needed to preserve human life" (¶677).

Jung cites it in the chapter's final snake-survey: the snake of the same case had also announced "God pierces the earth with his ray" (¶638, see sun-sunbeam-pierces-earth-spielrein-patient-zurich). Here the serpent is explicitly numinous and rational — "divine judgment" — the regenerative instrument: "The significance of the snake as an instrument of regeneration is unmistakable" (¶677, cf. fig. 37). Green, blue, white: life-colour plus the spirit-colours — the same green Jung assigns to Chiwantopel's fatal viper and to the anima (¶678).
Verbatim: "It is God's animal, it has such wonderful colours: green, blue, and white" (¶677).

occurrences.title: Great snake guarding a golden bowl in an underground vault — young man's dream
occurrences.label: Great snake guarding a golden bowl…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: Jung's exhibit for the archetypal dream whose personal context is too meagre to explain it: "a young man dreamed of a great snake that guarded a golden bowl in an underground vault" (¶555). The dreamer could offer only a zoo snake and fairytale reminiscences — yet the dream "produced a very powerful effect" whose emotionality demanded explanation.

Jung's reading: amplification to the hero myth — "we have to go back to mythology, where the combination of snake or dragon with treasure and cave represents an ordeal in the life of the hero" (¶554). "Then it becomes clear that we are dealing with a collective emotion, a typical situation full of affect, which is not primarily a personal experience... Primarily it is a universally human problem which, because it has been overlooked subjectively, forces itself objectively upon the dreamer's consciousness."

occurrences.title: The golden serpent let down into the bosom of the consecrated — Rome / Alexandria
occurrences.label: The golden serpent let down into the bosom…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~2nd c. CE (Clement) and ~4th c. CE (Firmicus), describing one rite-type
occurrences.quote: aureus coluber in sinum demittitur consecratis et eximitur rursus ab inferioribus partibus atque imis.
body: Two independent testimonies to the same rite-type. Clement, mocking the mysteries, says the god "through the womb" is a dragon, dragged through the womb of the initiated; Firmicus describes the golden serpent let down into the bosom of the consecrated and drawn out again "from the lower parts and from below." The serpent-god passes through the initiate's body as through a birth canal — descent into the body and emergence as second birth.
Jung cites both in the mother-chapter's note on entering the womb as the salvific act, immediately beside the Hermes "as children come into the womb of women" papyrus.

occurrences.title: The black snake leaps from her throat onto the golden disk and burns to ashes (patient vision, 18 Mar 1931)
occurrences.label: The black snake leaps from her throat onto…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The black snake which I had swallowed leapt from my throat and fell upon the golden disk... Instantly it was transformed into a handful of ashes.
body: Emerging from the cavern with the goat and a white snake, she comes upon "a brilliant disk of gold lying on the ground" — the pool of gold again, the chthonic equivalent of the sun beneath the tree. The swallowed black snake leaps of its own accord from her throat, falls upon the disk, and is instantly transformed into a handful of ashes: "the phoenix miracle," the utter destruction of the snake's specific life. The snake sought not matter but the fire of the sun in order to transform — Jung's exhibit of real sublimation, as against repression ("one represses it and plays the piano instead"). Its spirit survives in her and drives her on toward the black wall with the star and the eye. The Persian bird Semenda — ashes, serpent, bird again — gives the mythic parallel.

occurrences.title: The golden snake passed through the garment — mysteries of Sabazios
occurrences.label: The golden snake passed through the garment
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: they put a golden snake down through their clothes and pulled it out from under the garment below.
body: In the Orphic mysteries of Sabazios, reported by one of the early Fathers, the celebrants drew a golden snake down through their clothes and pulled it out from below the garment — "a sort of transitus of the snake through the body, meaning its assimilation, obviously." Jung's key parallel for the patient's swallowing of the black snake, and for Nietzsche's shepherd into whose throat the serpent crawls. Companion rite: at Eleusis the initiate kissed the huge snake.

occurrences.title: Coiled granite snake with coin-slit as offering box — Ptolemaïs
occurrences.label: Coiled granite snake with coin-slit…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Fear of the deadly maternal womb has become the guardian of the treasure of life.
body: The Archaeopteryx of the poor-box: the chthonic snake-pit of the Asclepieia (fed with pelanoi, cf. the Cos pit with its square slot) fossilized into a stone serpent guarding a slot for coins. Jung's aphorism over the find: "Here the serpent lies on the treasury as protector of the hoard. Fear of the deadly maternal womb has become the guardian of the treasure of life" (¶578).

occurrences.title: The green snake that wanted to kiss — Jung's patient (cw05 ¶677)
occurrences.label: The green snake that wanted to kiss
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: undated patient report (~1911-12 writing period; inferred)
body: "The snake that killed the hero is green. So was the snake of another patient, who said: 'Then a little green snake came up to my mouth, it had the finest, loveliest feeling—as if it had human reason and wanted to tell me something—just as if it wanted to kiss me'" (¶677).

The exchange with the Chiwantopel viper is exact and unsettling: the same green snake that stings the hero to death here approaches the patient's mouth with "the finest, loveliest feeling" — deadly and tender at once. Jung lets the parallel stand uninterpreted beyond "The significance of the snake as an instrument of regeneration is unmistakable" (¶677): the serpent is the transformative numen, and its affective colour is eros, not only terror. See ¶678 for the identification of the green snake with the anima, "the archetype of life itself."
Verbatim: "as if it had human reason and wanted to tell me something—just as if it wanted to kiss me" (¶677).

occurrences.title: The snake guide, the river of life and the temple absolution (patient vision, 27 May / 3 June 1931)
occurrences.label: The snake guide, the river of life…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Then he took out his sword and struck the walls of the temple so that with a noise of thunder they crumbled to the ground. The man then put his hand upon my forehead and said: 'Woman, you are forgiven.
body: On a great plain with no road the snake appears — Jung's "exclamation mark," the deeply unconscious instinct as guide. It leads her to the river of life, where the beautiful form of a man (the animus as Hermes psychopompos) takes her hand into a temple by the bank. Kneeling at the altar she begs "Expel the fire from me"; the charm-water fails ("The fire within me still burns"), so the psychopompos strikes the temple walls with his sword — the sacred precinct profaned — and lays his hand on her forehead: "Woman, you are forgiven". The animus assuming the gesture of Christ to the adulterous woman: acceptance, not repentance, changes the system.

occurrences.title: Hannibal's dream: the divine guide and the destroying serpent (Coelius Antipater)
occurrences.label: Hannibal's dream — the divine guide…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: Before marching on Rome, Hannibal dreamed he was in an assembly of the gods themselves, where Jupiter ordered him to undertake the war and gave him "a youth of supernatural powers" as guide, with the command not to look back. He looked: "what was following him was a most extraordinary monster, a sort of serpent which was wiping out of existence everything they met—houses, gardens, and woods" (sem-1925). The ancient interpreters read the serpent as the destruction of Italy.

Jung's reading (Addendum 2, quoted from Joan Corrie's ABC of Jung's Psychology, "Jung, Lectures (unpublished)"): god, then man, then monster — "we have a fair representation of the make-up of a great man." The guide "expresses the superhuman element in Hannibal"; the dreamer is called to the gods because "the unconscious knows what it means to follow the command of a god"; greatness is mana-bearing and inevitably destructive.

occurrences.title: The officer's snake-bite heel dream — CW8 'The Structure of the Psyche'
occurrences.label: The officer's snake-bite heel dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

occurrences.quote: The patient now had a dream in which he was bitten in the heel by a snake and instantly paralysed.
body: A 27-year-old officer, jilted two months before, developed heart pain, globus hystericus and an inexplicable pain in the left heel. The heart and throat symptoms yielded when the repressed grief was abreacted — "heartache" and "swallowed tears" — but the heel symptom had no rational source. Then came the dream: bitten in the heel by a snake and instantly paralysed.

Jung's reading: a content from the collective unconscious had translated the patient's disappointments with women into "a regular mythological event" (¶312); Genesis 3:15 ("thou shalt bruise his heel") echoes the far older Egyptian snake-bite hymn; the pampering hysterical mother, too, "had lamed him" (¶307). The symptom is simultaneously an attempt at healing — the personal is raised sub specie aeternitatis into "the sorrow of the world" (¶316).

occurrences.title: Serpent among the roses — Hélène Smith's séance vision (Geneva, ~1895)
occurrences.label: Serpent among the roses
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: April 1 sitting, ~1895 (Flournoy, Des Indes à la planète Mars)
occurrences.quote: Suddenly she sees a small snake come out from underneath the bouquet; it rises up gently, smells the flowers, looks at them.
body: From the sequence Jung quotes as the "classical" genesis of a complex hallucination: on April 1 the medium, shivering and agitated, sees a "grinning, very ugly face, with long red hair" hovering above the table, then a magnificent bouquet — and out from under the bouquet a small snake rises gently, smells the flowers, looks at them. Jung's frame: entoptic light and tense expectation condense into figures that dramatize the medium's inner state (¶99–104); the serpent appears as the uncanny inhabitant of the beautiful, after the grotesque mask — the vision's own compenso of tones.

occurrences.title: Hera's serpents sent against the infant Heracles (Thebes)
occurrences.label: Hera's serpents sent against the infant Heracles
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: pre-literary myth (classical sources ~5th c. BCE, inferred)
occurrences.quote: The serpents sent by Hera to destroy the infant Hercules, the python that tries to strangle Apollo at birth, the massacre of the innocents, all these tell the same story.
body: Hera, hostile to the child of Zeus and Alcmene, sends two serpents to destroy Heracles in his cradle; the infant strangles them. Classical emblem of the hero whose birth is menaced by the powers.

Jung's use (¶321, "The Development of Personality"): the episode stands first in a triad of threatened hero-births — Hera's serpents, the Python that tries to strangle Apollo at birth, the massacre of the innocents — "all these tell the same story." The context is the danger of the inner voice and of vocation: "The hero's birth and the heroic life are always threatened... the daemon of the inner voice is at once our greatest danger and an indispensable help" (¶321). Ties directly to ¶318: the hero's birth coincides with sunrise; most heroes bear solar attributes.

occurrences.title: The Hopi snake dance performed in the Christian church
occurrences.label: The Hopi snake dance performed…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Jung reads the Hopi as autochthonous chthonic worshippers like the Indian Nagas: "the Hopi Pueblo Indians have such a chthonic cult of snakes. They even perform their snake dances in the Christian church, for they are also Christians."

The double naming — Christian Spanish names at baptism, retained Indian names "important on account of their mystical meanings" — enacts the eagle-and-serpent problem in one community: the chthonic cult surviving inside the church of the spirit. The Pueblos are "the forefathers really of the Aztecs" (pueblo = town, from populus).
Verbatim: "They even perform their snake dances in the Christian church, for they are also Christians."

occurrences.title: The initiate kisses the huge snake at Eleusis
occurrences.label: The initiate kisses the huge snake at Eleusis
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: there the initiate had to kiss a huge snake.
body: At Eleusis the initiate had to kiss a huge snake. Kissing means "a very close and intimate acquaintance, and it means also a certain assimilation" — of the snake to the man or the man to the snake, since the snake was supposed to be a heroic soul: many Greek heroes had snakes' souls, appearing after death as the serpent near the tomb (Erechtheus' serpent, Cecrops under the Acropolis). The rite partakes of the serpent's mana, as the communion partakes of the body of the Lord.

occurrences.title: Ra bitten by the snake: Isis heals the poisoned god (Egyptian spell tradition)
occurrences.label: Ra bitten by the snake
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: You remember how Ra was bitten by a snake and what Mother Isis did in order to cure the poisoned god.
body: In explaining the patient's temple rite, Jung describes Egyptian medicine: the cure consisted "in what the doctor said, not what he did" — the priest named the disease and told the story of the ailment (the carbuncle on the neck: "Thy neck is smarting, thy neck is hot..."). For snakebite "you remember how Ra was bitten by a snake and what Mother Isis did in order to cure the poisoned god. That was read to the sufferer, with the assumption that it would help him by speaking the suitable word, reminding him of the holy legend of the god" — exactly as a priest points to the suffering of Mary and Christ. The patient's absolution works the same way, concealed from her consciousness so she cannot destroy it.

occurrences.title: The woman who draws knives, spears and a poisonous black snake from her throat (patient vision, 11 October 1933)
occurrences.label: The woman who draws knives, spears…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: We stab men in the back because they must know us.... She drew from her throat knives, spears, and a poisonous black snake.
body: Seizing one of the stabbing women of the mad market, the patient asks how she can bear so many wounds and still live: "She said: 'I will show you.' She drew from her throat knives, spears, and a poisonous black snake." The throat means speech — "the knives they use are chiefly words, they stab by words. And the black snake is the principle of darkness, of the poisonous evil that stings; it is really a visualized proverbial expression". The women stab men in the back "because they must know us" — the most outrageous projection; the men believe the poison can be destroyed by argument, but "evil cannot be destroyed because it is necessary."

occurrences.title: Kundalinī, the Serpent Power — mahādevishakti rising through the chakras (via Avalon)
occurrences.label: Kundalinī, the Serpent Power
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: traditional doctrine (via Avalon, The Serpent Power, 1931)
body: Jung's definition: "a feminine creative force in the shape of a serpent, named kundalinī, rises up from the perineal centre, where she had been sleeping, and ascends through the chakras, thereby activating them and constellating their symbols. This 'Serpent Power' is personified as the mahādevishakti, the goddess who brings everything into existence by means of māyā, the building material of reality" (¶561). In the patient the ascent reached manipura, where "the bird of thought descending from above" met it (¶562); the shakti's gift proved to be the wish for a real child — "her building material is māyā, 'real illusion.' In other words, she spins fantasies with real things."

occurrences.title: Lilith, the serpent of Eden — Adam's first wife (Talmudic legend)
occurrences.label: Lilith, the serpent of Eden — Adam's first wife
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: "A legend of later origin maintains that the snake in the Garden of Eden was Lilith, Adam's first wife, with whom he begot a horde of demons" (¶619). Jung places the legend in his two-wives scheme: as Yahweh is legitimately united with Israel while keeping Sophia, the feminine pneuma, as eternal playmate, so Adam had first Lilith — "the daughter or emanation of Satan… a Satanic correspondence to Sophia" — with Eve then corresponding to the people of Israel.

The serpent itself was Satan's disguise: a trickster's move against the Creation programme, since the reptiles made before Adam were "common or garden snakes, highly unintelligent" (¶619); later tradition made the snake "the most spiritual animal" and a symbol of the Nous.

occurrences.title: Roman ladies wearing live snakes as neck ornaments
occurrences.label: Roman ladies wearing live snakes…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: A fashion-detail offered in the seminar as an echo of Zarathustra's image: "the ladies of old Rome really used to wear in hot weather a living snake as a neck ornament — of course a harmless snake."

The mutual comfort is the point: "The neck was cooled by the body of the snake, and the snake loved to be coiled round the neck of its mistress because her skin was warm." Against the mythic hostility of eagle and serpent, here the coiled serpent is domestic union — "a sort of fashion," as children carry pets.
Verbatim: "the ladies of old Rome really used to wear in hot weather a living snake as a neck ornament-of course a harmless snake."

occurrences.title: The lizard in the Haoma tree — Bundahishn XVIII
occurrences.label: The lizard in the Haoma tree — Bundahishn XVIII
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Pahlavi cosmology (West, Pahlavi Texts p. 65); Persian
occurrences.quote: The evil spirit has formed therein, among those which enter as opponents, a lizard as an opponent in that deep water, so that it may injure the Hôm
body: In the Zoroastrian Bundahishn, at the crown of the cosmic tree in the deep water grows the Hôm (Haoma), the plant of immortality; the evil spirit "has formed therein, among those which enter as opponents, a lizard as an opponent in that deep water, so that it may injure the Hôm" — the immortalizing tree guarded and gnawed by its built-in serpent-adversary.

Jung's footnote draws the exact alchemical parallel: "In alchemy, the spiritus mercurii that lives in the tree is represented as serpent, salamander, or Melusina," and points to the Ripley Scrowle, where the lizard is half woman celebrating the coniunctio with the filius philosophorum (fig. 257), quoting "The Serpent of Arabia is my name." The lizard/haoma opposition is the mythic template of the alchemical tree with its indwelling, ambivalent Mercurius-serpent.

occurrences.title: Neophyte fondling the serpent of Demeter — Lovatelli urn
occurrences.label: Neophyte fondling the serpent of Demeter
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The fondling or kissing of the “fear-animal” symbolizes the ceremonial conquest of incest.
body: "The fondling or kissing of the 'fear-animal' symbolizes the ceremonial conquest of incest" (¶530) — the neophyte's hand-to-hand truce with the regressive serpent, echoed at Eleusis' Demeter serpent and the Ophite live-snake kiss (¶584).

image.title: Lovatelli drawing 01

occurrences.title: Ignatius Loyola's vision of the many-eyed serpent (Spain)
occurrences.label: Ignatius Loyola's vision of the many-eyed…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: fn 4 to Part II, Introduction (pdf p696); index 'Loyola, St., vision, 122n'

body: In the footnote on wind-gods and creator-gods Jung remarks: "the Persian sun-god Mithras is equipped with an immense number of eyes. It is possible that Loyola's vision of the snake with multiple eyes is a variant of this motif" (cf. "On the Nature of the Psyche," par. 395). The index anchors the vision at book p122n, in the discussion of theriomorphic libido — the serpent bristling with eyes as the all-seeing instinct, kin to the Mithraic many-eyed sun-god.
Verbatim (fn 4): "It is possible that Loyola’s vision of the snake with multiple eyes is a variant of this motif."

occurrences.title: The mercurial serpent generated in the lower world — Steeb, Coelum Sephiroticum (1679)
occurrences.label: The mercurial serpent generated…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Joannes C. Steeb's descensus spiritus: "The spirit of God fertilized the upper waters with a peculiar fostering warmth and made them as it were milky" — and the virtue so generated "combining with light, generated in the mineral kingdom of the lower regions the mercurial serpent … in the vegetable kingdom the blessed greenness [chlorophyll] … so that the supracelestial spirit of the waters united in marriage with light may justly be called the soul of the world" (cw11 ¶? pdf p699; pp. 33, 38).

"The lower waters are darksome, and absorb the outflowings of light in their capacious depths." Jung's verdict: "This doctrine is based on nothing less than the Gnostic legend of the Nous descending from the higher spheres and being caught in the embrace of Physis." Steeb's prima-materia definition (p. 26, "the receptacle and the mother") is drawn from Plato's Timaeus.

occurrences.title: The mile-long snake that meant typhoid fever (woman's dream, told 5 June 1929)
occurrences.label: The mile-long snake that meant typhoid fever
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: Once a woman dreamed of a snake a mile long, as big as an elephant, which meant typhoid fever.
body: A woman Jung met but never analysed reported: "Always before I am ill I dream of a snake, but never of so big a one" — a snake a mile long, as big as an elephant. She then had typhoid fever. Jung had thought on hearing it that it meant a long illness.

The anecdote anchors his rule against fixed symbol-decoding: "A snake in one case may mean something favourable, 'the wisdom of the depths,' in another something unfavourable, such as a physical illness... A snake may have seven thousand meanings." In the language of the unconscious, "whenever the unconscious is on top, whenever it prevails against the present, it grows heavy and important, and is pregnant with the past or the future... the snake can mean the past or the future."

occurrences.title: Miss X, Picture 13 — four snakes, 3 + 1 (Aug 1929)
occurrences.label: Miss X, Picture 13 — four snakes, 3 + 1
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The mandala is laced together by four black and golden snakes, the heads of three of them pointing to the centre, while the fourth rears upwards.
body: After the radiation ceased, the mandala is "laced together by four black and golden snakes, the heads of three of them pointing to the centre, while the fourth rears upwards." Jung: "The breaking down of the quaternity into 3 plus 1 is in accord with the archetype" — an instance of the axiom of Maria, alongside Horus' four (or 3+1) sons, Ezekiel's four figures, the four evangelists, and the three synoptic gospels plus John (¶612 n. 169). The full moon outside radiates rainbow-coloured rings; spermatozoon motifs appear between snakes and centre.

occurrences.title: The Naassene serpent and the horn of the one-horned bull — Hippolytus
occurrences.label: The Naassene serpent and the horn…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Hippolytus' report of the Naassenes: the serpent dwells in all things, "all temples were named after her (ναοὺς ἀπὸ τοῦ ναάς)," every shrine, initiation, and mystery is dedicated to her; she is the moist element (as Thales said) without which nothing exists. And decisively for the unicorn chapter: "all things are subject to her … she is good and has something of everything in herself as in the horn of the one-horned bull [ἐν κέρατι ταύρου μονοκέρωτος]. She imparts beauty and ripeness to all things" (¶528).

Jung: "Like the alicorn, therefore, the serpent is an alexipharmic and the principle that brings all things to maturity and perfection" — the same ripening function alchemy assigns to Mercurius, "the salvator and servator" (¶529). The same primal being is named Osiris ("heavenly horn of the moon"), Sophia, Adam, "many-formed Attis."

occurrences.title: The shepherd who bites off the serpent's head — Nietzsche's vision (Zarathustra)
occurrences.label: The shepherd who bites off the serpent's head
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1884 (Zarathustra Part III, 'On the Vision and the Riddle')
occurrences.quote: No longer a shepherd, no longer a man, but a transfigured being with light all about him, who laughed!
body: Jung's reading: the snake is "the unconscious psyche which, like the snake-god in the Sabazios mysteries, crawls into the mouth of the celebrant" — here Nietzsche himself as poimen, "the shepherd of souls and preacher" — to make him entheos; but "fear was swifter and more violent: it bit off the snake's head and spat it out" (¶586). The compensation dished, the wild hysterical laughter, and the insoluble case where "the compensation appears in a form that cannot be accepted" (¶587).

occurrences.title: Snake-shaped chariot gods — black temple of Puri
occurrences.label: Snake-shaped chariot gods — black temple of Puri
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: 'The chariot-driving, snake-shaped gods of southern India, for instance on the immense black temple at Puri, which is itself a chariot of stone' (cw14 ¶266). Jung adduces it as an eastern parallel to the Nous-serpent enthroned on the chariot in the Tractatus Aristotelis, while denying direct influence: 'another model closer to hand' is Ezekiel's Merkabah (¶266). The stone chariot-temple makes the god's vehicle architectural: the serpent-god rides a totality-symbol built in stone.

image.title: Annual chariot festival 'Jagannath Yatra', Puri Odisha

occurrences.title: Python at the spring of Castalia — Delphi
occurrences.label: Python at the spring of Castalia — Delphi
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: mythic antiquity (Delphic oracle historical ~8th c. BCE on)
