occurrences.quote: The fountain of Castalia at Delphi was originally inhabited by a python. Apollo fought and overcame the python, and from that time Delphi was the seat of the famous oracle
body: The fountain of Castalia was originally inhabited by a python; Apollo fought and overcame it, and from then Delphi was the seat of the oracle — until Apollo "left half his powers to Dionysus, who later came in from the East" (¶258). In the underworld, "snakes and water are always together," as Aristophanes' Frogs shows; the Latin draco simply means snake.

Jung uses Castalia (like the Asklepieion pit and the Sylvester dragon) to build the amplification row for the serpent in the Toledo cistern: serpent + spring + cave = prophecy, wisdom, healing, the underworld. The Tavistock retelling stresses that these caves "contain springs," which ties the row to the Mithraic spring-sanctuaries (¶259).

occurrences.title: The quadricornutus serpens — four-horned serpent of the Latin alchemists (Europe, ~16th-17th c.)
occurrences.label: The quadricornutus serpens
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Europe (Latin alchemical literature; single author per Jung)
occurrences.quote: The horned serpent appears in Latin alchemy as the quadricornutus serpens (four-horned serpent), a symbol of Mercurius and an antagonist of the Christian Trinity.
body: Chasing the sources available to an eight-year-old for the horned monster of her first dream (snakelike, many-horned, slain by the four gods from the four corners), Jung reaches the Latin alchemists: "The horned serpent appears in Latin alchemy as the quadricornutus serpens (four-horned serpent), a symbol of Mercurius and an antagonist of the Christian Trinity. But this is an obscure reference, and, as far as I can discover, it occurs only in one author" (¶533).

The locus is the hinge of his argument for archetypal origin: no middle-class milieu, no catechism, no accessible alchemical folio could have transmitted it — "It seems to have originated outside the historical tradition" (¶538).

occurrences.title: White feathered serpent with diadem — Quetzalcoatl vision (Catholic patient)
occurrences.label: White feathered serpent with diadem
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: ...a white serpent appeared to her in splendor and imperturbable majesty, wearing feathers and a diadem.
body: After the dew fertilized and burst the Indian's wrapping, he dissolved into a second vision: "a white serpent appeared to her in splendor and imperturbable majesty, wearing feathers and a diadem" — Quetzalcoatl, the Plumed Serpent, "the redeemer-god of the Indian, who embodies for the psyche of the American person the unconscious spirit." The patient knew nothing of its meaning; the vision gave her courage for her general confession after ten years — the therapeutic effect. From the church's standpoint, "the appearance of a devil, who had merely assumed the form of the redeemer."

occurrences.title: Ra stung by Isis' serpent and robbed of his true name — Egyptian hymn
occurrences.label: Ra stung by Isis' serpent and robbed…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The poisonous worm is a deadly instead of an animating form of libido. The “true name” is Ra’s soul and magic power (his libido).
body: Isis kneads the god's spittle into a spear-like worm and lays it on Ra's path; the aging sun is poisoned and only the mother can cure him. Ra surrenders his true name — "Ra's soul and magic power (his libido)" — and is "fulfilled to the letter" in the transference: "the aging god returns to the heavenly cow, the symbol of the mother" (¶455). Jung's master-text for the poisonous mother and the treasure of the secret name.

occurrences.title: 'Now, we will let the snake rise up' — the Kundalini rears and opens its mouth (Visions, 13 Dec. 1933)
occurrences.label: Now, we will let the snake rise up
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: She pulls the animus off the living way: "we stood with our backs pressed against the towering rocks, and our feet on a narrow ledge of rock" — a standstill. Then: "I said: 'Now, we will let the snake rise up.' (By stopping.) The man shook with fear... The great snake arched up its back, reared upward into the sky, then brought its head down close to us. It opened a great mouth".

Jung: "If you ask how one can make the Kundalini serpent rise, I can tell you a very simple means: by stopping your analysis" — the stopped movement returns as monster; "it is the Kundalini" in whale-dragon aspect, "a situation for St George." Inside the open mouth she sees golden lungs (anahata "as understood by the animus," a masculine formulation) and the serpent's tongue split into man and woman — vishuddha, union of the opposites, "neither male nor female" (pp1301-1304).

occurrences.title: Dream of the red worm encircling the leg (patient: girl of six, Zürich)
occurrences.label: Dream of the red worm encircling the leg
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: case-index [18], ref. book p245 ≈ pdf p278 (harvested from index, pdf p579)

body: A six-year-old girl dreamed of a red worm encircling her leg. The index files it twice: "worm: red, dream of, 245" and under "entwining, 245" — the worm as serpent-form binding the child's body, in Jung's corpus of child material on the serpent as instinct and the mother's numen.
Verbatim (case-index): "Six-year-old girl who dreamed of red worm encircling leg. — 245"

occurrences.title: Two ring-snakes copulating; snow-white snake with black belly — woman patient's dream pair
occurrences.label: Two ring-snakes copulating
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A woman patient "much concerned with the problem of opposites" dreamt "on the shore of a lake [i.e., the edge of the unconscious] two ring-snakes as thick as an arm, with pale human heads, were copulating." About six months later: "A snow-white snake with a black belly was growing out of my breast. I felt a deep love for it".

Jung's bracketed gloss sets the shore as the edge of the unconscious. The paired dreams move from the serpentine coniunctio observed at the threshold to the birth of the white-black serpent — the united opposite-coloured Mercurius-serpent — out of the dreamer's own breast, with love.

occurrences.title: The god through the lap — golden snake drawn across the initiates (Sabazius mysteries)
occurrences.label: The god through the lap
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the god entered his devotees as if through the female genitals
body: Arnobius: "A golden snake is let down into the lap of the initiates and is drawn out again from below." Orphic hymn 52 invokes Bacchus as hypokolpie, "lying in the lap" — "which suggests that the god entered his devotees as if through the female genitals" (¶530). The mystery-snake that can degenerate into the orgy (¶584).

occurrences.title: Dream: the Saviour on the way to Golgotha turns into a snake (or crocodile)
occurrences.label: Dream: the Saviour on the way…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: n/a (Jung's clinical material, reported in Aion)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: In a footnote to the 7 B.C. conjunction discussion Jung reports: "A characteristic dream of this sort is the following: The dreamer was watching a Passion play in the theatre. On the way to Golgotha, the actor taking the part of the Saviour suddenly changed into a snake or crocodile".

Its frame: "The Cross with a snake on it, instead of the Crucified, is often found in medieval times [Psychology and Alchemy, fig. 217], and also in the dreams and fantasy-images of modern people who know nothing of this tradition" — spontaneous re-emergence of the serpent-for-Redeemer equivalence.

occurrences.title: The serpent-slayer dream before the Spanish flu epidemic (officer's wife, 1918)
occurrences.label: The serpent-slayer dream before the Spanish flu…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Switzerland (camp where Jung was in charge of British interned officers)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: she dreamt of an enormous serpent which killed many people... A few days later... the so-called Spanish flu broke out
body: In the war, among the British interned officers, Jung met the wife of one of them, "a peculiarly clairvoyant person": whenever she dreamt of snakes it meant disease. While he was there she dreamt "of an enormous serpent which killed many people" and predicted a catastrophe; days later the second great Spanish flu epidemic broke out and she herself nearly died.

Jung's frame: "there is an organic threat which calls forth all one's instinctive reactions" — the saurian appears "when life means business"; folk dream-interpretation already knows that snake-dreams herald illness. The dream belongs to the cold-blooded-animal family (crocodile, tortoise) = the instinctual fundament.

occurrences.title: Snake-eyed hero — Scandinavian heroic legend
occurrences.label: Snake-eyed hero — Scandinavian heroic legend
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In Scandinavian mythology the hero is recognized by the fact that he has snake’s eyes. He has snake’s eyes because he is a snake.
body: "In Scandinavian mythology the hero is recognized by the fact that he has snake's eyes. He has snake's eyes because he is a snake." The same ¶ collects the row: Cecrops, man above and serpent below; "the souls of heroes often appear after death in the form of serpents" (¶195). Jung raises it against the simple hero-fights-dragon schema: "the hero is himself the dragon" (¶195).
The locus is a legend-motif rather than one named text — kept as an instance for its clear tradition-place identity, with the specific source owed as a pin.

occurrences.title: Fantasy of the snake crawling into the mother (patient: woman, Zürich)
occurrences.label: Fantasy of the snake crawling into the mother
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: case-index [27], ref. book p436 ≈ pdf p469 (harvested from index, pdf p579)

body: A female patient had a fantasy of a snake crawling into her mother (case [27], book p436). With its companion case [28] (snake into the mouth) it belongs to Jung's material on the serpent as "instrument of sacrifice and regeneration, 436f" — the snake entering the mother's body as insemination and return to the womb at once.
Verbatim (case-index): "Female patient who had fantasy of snake crawling into her mother. — 436"

occurrences.title: The snake that crawled into the mouth (patient: woman, Zürich)
occurrences.label: The snake that crawled into the mouth
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: case-index [28], ref. book p436f ≈ pdf p469-470 (harvested from index, pdf p579)

body: A female patient said a snake had crawled into her mouth (case [28], book p436f). The index ties mouth to re-entry into the mother ("re-entry into mother through, 419") and files "snake in, 378f, 436f" under mouth — the serpent swallowed as ingestion of the numen, kin to the snake-kiss ("snake-kiss, 376, 378").
Verbatim (case-index): "Female patient who said that snake crawled into her mouth. — 436f"

occurrences.title: The snake stuck in the throat (patient: woman, Zürich)
occurrences.label: The snake stuck in the throat
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: case-index [24], ref. book p378 ≈ pdf p411 (harvested from index, pdf p579)

body: A patient complained of a snake stuck in her throat (case [24], book p378). The index files "throat, snake stuck in, 378" under mouth: the serpent lodged at the organ of speech — the instinctual (snake) blocking the word. It is one of the companion snake-cases Jung reports with the genital snake-bite dream of ¶585.
Verbatim (case-index): "Patient who complained of a snake stuck in her throat. — 378"

occurrences.title: De stella no vain pe de serpent ar ii — Kepler on the new star in the Serpent-bearer's foot (Prague, 1606)
occurrences.label: De stella no vain pe de serpent ar ii
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: De stella no vain pe de serpent ar ii. Prague. 1606.
body: Kepler's treatise on the 1604 supernova standing "in the foot of the Serpentarius" (Ophiuchus, the Serpent-bearer) — the serpent and the star laid across the sky at the birth of modern astronomy. Kepler weighs the astrological reading of the new star while dismantling the traditional heavens: the exact knot Pauli's "The Influence of Archetypal Ideas on the Scientific Theories of Kepler" cuts (bound with Jung's synchronicity monograph). This volume's bibliography carries the title, and the index scatters Kepler across the letters.

The serpent that holds the healer's place in the zodiac — Ophiuchus as Asklepios' serpent — makes the nova a serpent-star omen read by the man who would later defend astrology's "synchronicity" of earth and sky as the anima telluris (see stone-facultas-formatrix-anima-telluris-kepler-1610).

occurrences.title: Franz Stuck, 'Sin' (Die Sünde) — Munich, 1893
occurrences.label: Franz Stuck, 'Sin' (Die Sünde) — Munich, 1893
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The famous snake-woman painting, reproduced as Plate X. Jung cites it in his catalogue of the serpent's dream-roles: the snake creeps into the mouth, bites the breast "like Cleopatra's legendary asp," or appears "in the role of the paradisal serpent, or in one of the variations of Franz Stuck, whose snake-pictures bear significant titles like 'Vice,' 'Sin,' or 'Lust'" (¶8).

His reading: "The mixture of anxiety and lust is perfectly expressed in the sultry atmosphere of these pictures" — the serpent as the seductive principle in woman, a coupling Jung finds again in the old painters' feminine Eden-serpent (fig. 8, ¶155) and in the snake-faced maidens of the Mithraic liturgy (¶155). Adjacent in the text: Mörike's "Girl's First Love Song" (eel/snake in the net).

image.title: The Sin label QS:Len,"The Sin" label QS:Lpl,"Grzech" label QS:Lde,"Die Sünde"

occurrences.title: The snake — 'quite definite people' in nurse subject 24's reactions (Burghölzli, ~1904-05)
occurrences.label: The snake — 'quite definite people'…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: pdf p71 (print ¶ 286 area — unmarked in chunk)

occurrences.quote: the snake (quite definite people)
body: In the catalogue of subject 24's masked complex-reactions, the article-plus-noun series runs: the pious one (herself), of love, of expiation (guilt toward her father), the father, the snake (quite definite people), the school-boy / the industrious (the worker friend of her youth), the human being (her father). The serpent-image is here worn at its most literal: Jung does not amplify it — he uses it the other way round, as evidence that a concrete set of people (father, seducer, friend) are constellated behind the reaction. A rare early-vault locus where serpent appears as a live, personal, defensive image in an experimental protocol rather than in myth or alchemy.

occurrences.title: Serpent in the cistern under the cathedral of Toledo — dream of a French patient (~1920s)
occurrences.label: Serpent in the cistern under the cathedral…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Toledo, Spain (dream scene); dreamer: 22-year-old Frenchman, manic-depressive clinic
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1920s (dream after his Spanish trip; sent to Jung years before 1935)
occurrences.quote: In the water there is a huge serpent whose eyes sparkle like jewels. Near it there is a golden bowl containing a golden dagger. This dagger is the key to Toledo, and its owner commands full power over the city.
body: A distinguished, highly aesthetic young Frenchman of 22, back from Spain with a manic-depressive depression, dreams a cistern beneath the great cathedral of Toledo: dark water connected to the Tagus, a huge serpent with eyes "like jewels," and a golden bowl holding a golden dagger — the key to Toledo. The serpent is friend and protector of B—C—, the dreamer's childhood friend, "a child without guile," who plays with it fearlessly; the dreamer fails his descent via the Moorish-descent friend S— and the ancient Phocaean sword, loses Toledo, and some months after his release committed suicide in calm reasoning (¶251–253).

Jung reads the cistern as the crypt/mystery-place beneath the Christian Weltanschauung — Mithraic vault, pagan well (Chartres), baptismal piscina of death-rebirth (¶254–256); the serpent-cave parallels (Asklepieion, Castalia, St. Sylvester) as the healing-wisdom serpent (¶257–259); bowl + dagger as Grail and spear, the union of opposites in the layer where nothing is yet discriminated (¶261–263); the dagger-key via the Mithraic key-god Aion and psychopomp Hecate (¶266–267); the city as self/totality (¶268–270). The child without guile "has the key to Spain and the power over the four gates" (¶272).

occurrences.title: Two-headed Mercurial serpent over the fountain — Rosarium picture 1 (1550)
occurrences.label: Two-headed Mercurial serpent over the fountain
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Surmounting the star is the two-headed Mercurial Serpent, symbolizing the contamination of opposites in the unconscious.
body: Jung's 1937 synopsis "On the Rosarium Philosophorum" opens the picture series with this cut: a fountain from which the aqua permanens flows in three pipes — lac virginis, acetum fontis, aqua vitae — with a star above, sun to the left and moon to the right as opposites, and the two-headed Mercurial serpent surmounting the star. Two columns of cloud flank the picture (the "spiritual," volatile nature of the process); four stars in the corners allude to the quaternity of the elements.

His reading: the doubled serpent heads "symboliz[e] the contamination of opposites in the unconscious," while "the three springs form the material Trinity... Together with inert matter (earth) they constitute the unity which is indicated by the quaternity of the elements (3 + 1 = 4)" (¶1784) — the trinity/quaternion arithmetic in one image.

occurrences.title: The big snake under the bed — dream of the nine-year-old girl
occurrences.label: The big snake under the bed
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: The same girl (see ship-granny-kiss-dream-girl-9-1924) dreamt several times of "a big snake, which came out from under my bed and played with me," and spoke of the snake dream often.

Jung's reading: "the child is in danger of being swallowed by her father's regressive libido. That is why she dreams of the snake; for the snake, since ancient times, has always been the symbol of danger: of being caught in coils, or swallowed, or poisoned" (¶219). The serpent bodying forth the parental unconscious that "seeps into the child's soul like a poisonous vapour" (¶217).
Quote. "Another time she dreamt of 'a big snake, which came out from under my bed and played with me.'"

occurrences.title: The disc of the sun encoiled by the uraeus
occurrences.label: The disc of the sun encoiled by the uraeus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Mrs. Sigg: Egyptian sun symbolism? Jung: "That is the closest analogy, the disc of the sun encoiled by the uraeus."

Read against Zarathustra's staff (golden handle, serpent twined round the sun): "the addition of the serpent is the earth lying in the sunshine, warming its cold body in the rays of the sun; that is the idea of the uraeus". Editor adds Mead's "Books of the Savior": "The disk of the sun... a vast dragon with its tail in its mouth mounted on seven powers."
Row: uraeus — Chinese dragon-and-pearl (values reversed) — Kundalini's bindu coiled by Shakti in the muladhara mandala — the Orphic egg.

occurrences.title: The elixir as self-impregnating serpent — Tractatulus Avicennae
occurrences.label: The elixir as self-impregnating serpent
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Latin West (printed Artis auriferae I, Basel 1593)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: "In the old Latin 'Tractatulus Avicennae,' which is strongly influenced by Arabic tradition, we find: '[The elixir] is a voluptuous serpent impregnating itself' (Artis auriferae, I, 1593, p. 406)" (cw11 ¶? pdf p687). The author is a Pseudo-Avicenna, not Ibn Sina (970–1037) — one of the Arabic-Latin sources of medieval Hermetic literature.

Jung builds his textual genealogy of the self-fecundating hermaphrodite-serpent on this line: the same passage recurs in "Rosinus ad Sarratantam" (Artis aurif. I, p. 303), where "Rosinus" is an Arabic-Latin corruption of Zosimos; and the Turba philosophorum Sermo LXV says likewise "The composite brings itself forth." "Since the history of these texts is still shrouded in darkness, nobody can say who copied from whom."

occurrences.title: The cloud serpent that fertilizes the earth (Vedic)
occurrences.label: The cloud serpent that fertilizes the earth
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Mrs. Crowley offers the Hindu parallel: "there is the Hindu idea of the cloud serpent that fertilizes the earth." Jung: "Yes, that is also usually represented with wings. It is, of course, an attempt at the reconciliation of the pairs of opposites." (The editors' footnote identifies it with the myth of Indra's killing thunderbolt at the cloud serpent, releasing "the flood of life" — Vritra — after Zimmer, Myths.)

A winged, rain-bringing serpent: the chthonic animal become aerial and fertilizing — an organic union of bird and serpent, like Quetzalcoatl and the Chinese dragon, set against the precarious coiled arrangement of Zarathustra's eagle.
Verbatim: "there is the Hindu idea of the cloud serpent that fertilizes the earth."

occurrences.title: Wall of snakes above the onyx pit; the buffalo herd rushes over it (patient vision, 14 June 1933)
occurrences.label: Wall of snakes above the onyx pit
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I heard a distant sound of thunder and saw a great herd of buffalo. As they approached, the onyx pit closed over and the buffalo rushed over the ground where the pit had been and disappeared. I felt afraid and sat down to rest.
body: The finale of the fire-magic sequence: beside the chthonic Indian woman and a buffalo stands a wall of snakes above the alchemical pit in which the idol is hardened in the fire; then thunder, a great herd of buffalo, the pit closes over, and the herd rushes across it. Jung reads the inverted order (serpent above, sun-fire below) as the night-sea-journey situation — Ra's ship caught in the coils of Apophis — and the herd as the collective instinct that tramples whoever attempts individuation. The pit protects: "instinct is never individual, it is always legion."

occurrences.title: The serpent warning-notice at the imperial palace, Rome
occurrences.label: The serpent warning-notice at the imperial…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: A notice was hewn on the stone wall-like a poster-that the man who dared to do anything unclean in that corner was cursed in the names of the twelve gods. All their names were carved there, and the snake also, to make it more impressive
body: A corner of the imperial palace where everybody was warned not to leave any dirt: "A notice was hewn on the stone wall-like a poster-that the man who dared to do anything unclean in that corner was cursed in the names of the twelve gods. All their names were carved there, and the snake also, to make it more impressive".

Jung's example of the symbol wearing out - the serpent "which was to be found everywhere in antiquity, even if only as a warning": "So the snake degenerated to something like an exclamation mark. Exactly as we use the concept of God as an exclamation mark, or as the French expression sacre has degenerated." The form loses its mana while "the contents necessarily remain the same because they are untouchable".

occurrences.title: The winged serpent flying to the sun — Rousselle's Tibetan mandalas
occurrences.label: The winged serpent flying to the sun
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Tibetan series shown at the Zurich Psychology Club
occurrences.yearDisplay: slides shown by Erwin Rousselle (Eranos 1933-35 circle)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Mr. Baumann reports: "Professor Rousselle showed us symbols like that; he had a whole series of small Tibetan mandalas, and one was a serpent with huge wings flying up into the sky. And in the next picture the serpent had disappeared and there were only the wings left flying to the sun."

Jung: "That is a picture of ekstasis" — the serpent sloughed off entirely as the spirit-body flies to the sun. It opens the plumed-serpent discussion: Quetzalcoatl, the Chinese dragon, the Hindu cloud serpent — unions of bird and serpent — against which Zarathustra's non-organic serpent-on-eagle looks precarious.
Verbatim: "And in the next picture the serpent had disappeared and there were only the wings left flying to the sun!"

occurrences.title: The medicine-woman with a twenty-foot boa familiar — Natal
occurrences.label: The medicine-woman with a twenty-foot boa…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: a medicinewoman in Natal who had a twenty-foot boa constrictor as her familiar
body: A medicine-woman in Natal keeps a twenty-foot boa constrictor as her familiar. Jung adduces it to show "how concretely this mythologem is taken on the primitive level" — in the same note complex where the hero must split, bore, or open the earth, and where the wise-woman/serpent union stands at the mythologem's living edge.
The familiar-serpent of the wise woman is the small-scale, social form of the serpent-mother complex the chapter tracks in myth.

occurrences.title: The snake with a woman's head and a bunch of keys — Oselberg, near Dinkelsbühl
occurrences.label: The snake with a woman's head and a bunch…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In Oselberg, near Dinkelsbühl, there is a snake with a woman's head and a bunch of keys round the neck.
body: A local legend-beast: on the Oselberg there dwells a snake with a woman's head and a bunch of keys about its neck. Jung sets it in the row of German legends where "the maiden in distress often appears as a snake or dragon that has to be kissed" — then changes into a beautiful woman; wise women are supposed to have a fish's or serpent's tail; a king's daughter was immured in the Golden Mount as a snake.
His interpretive sentence is the chapter's thesis: "The dragon in the cave is the Terrible Mother" — the serpent-woman as the enchanted, imprisoned, and devouring feminine in one body.

occurrences.title: The white and black serpents duelling on the ridge — Jung's vision (December 1913)
occurrences.label: The white and black serpents duelling…
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.yearDisplay: December 1913 (a few evenings after the Elijah vision)

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: A few evenings after meeting Elijah and Salome, Jung could not descend — "I only felt that two dark principles were fighting each other, two serpents." The fantasy that came instead: a knife-edge mountain ridge, a sunny desert country on one side, darkness on the other; a white snake on the light side, a dark snake on the dark side, meeting in battle on the narrow ridge. "Finally the head of the black snake turned white, and it retired, defeated. I felt, 'Now we can go on.'" Then the old man appeared high on the rock, and the way led up to the cyclopean ring-wall and the Druid altar of the second descent.

His reading: the white snake = movement into the day, the black = "the kingdom of darkness, with moral aspects too"; his own resistance to going down, the stronger tendency to go up — "The mountain was the kingdom of the sun, and the ring-wall was the vessel in which people had gathered the sun". The duel itself is the introverting and extraverting currents of the libido in conflict.

occurrences.title: Snakes and toads on the floor, and the man in the red mantle — Swedenborg's inn vision (London, ~1744)
occurrences.label: Snakes and toads on the floor, and the man…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar
Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Jung's example of the representation that liberates "because of being so objective": Swedenborg, in London, "after having had a very good dinner," suddenly saw the whole floor covered with snakes and toads; then a man appeared before him in a red mantle. One expects weighty words, "but what he said was, 'Don't eat so much!'" — "Thus did Swedenborg's thought take on bodily form, and because of being so objective, it had a tremendous effect on him. He was shaken to the depths by it". Jung's point: the liberating representation "must have an ancient character... It must be organically true, that is, in and of our own being" — the collective image convinces as no mere counsel can. He retold the anecdote differently in the Suzuki foreword of 1939 (CW11 ¶882) — the two versions are preserved unreconciled.

occurrences.title: Sethians — the ray of light mingled with the dark waters; the unmixing
occurrences.label: Sethians — the unmixing
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Sethian theory of 'composition and mixture': the ray of light from above mingles with the dark waters below 'in the form of a minute spark'; at death — or its mystical figure — the two unmix (¶292). The helpful Mercurius appears with the dividing sword ('I came not to send peace, but a sword'), and each substance is drawn 'to its own place... like iron to the magnet'; the spark 'hastens to the Logos' (¶292). Jung deliberately uses the medieval alchemical Latin — divisio, separatio — to mark the identity of Gnostic and alchemical procedure (¶292).

occurrences.title: Lully's seven images: three silver ladies, four gold knights — Norton's Ordinall
occurrences.label: Lully's seven images — Norton's Ordinall
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Three were good Silver, in shape like Ladies bright, Everie each of Foure were Gold and like a Knight.
body: Norton's verse: in a city of Catalonia Raymond Lully "Made in seaven Images the trewth to disclose; Three were good Silver, in shape like Ladies bright, Everie each of Foure were Gold and like a Knight," with letters in the borders of their clothing.

Jung at cw14 ¶562-563: the seven = gods of the planets or the seven metals; the correlation of three with silver and four with gold is "remarkable in that three is usually considered a masculine and four a feminine number" — a concretization of Senior's saying, and a 3+4 structure.

occurrences.title: The seven ravens and their one sister — Grimm KHM 25
occurrences.label: The seven ravens and their one sister
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The parallel to this is Grimm's tale of the seven ravens: there the seven brothers have one sister.
body: Grimm's tale of the seven ravens: "there the seven brothers have one sister." Jung cites it at cw14 ¶574 as the fairy-tale parallel to the Taoist eight immortals — seven great sages, while "the eighth is a girl who sweeps up the fallen flowers at the southern gate of heaven" — and to Sophia, whom the Valentinians call the Ogdoad.

occurrences.title: The Seven Sleepers in the cave — Ephesus (Decius, c. 250)
occurrences.label: The Seven Sleepers in the cave — Ephesus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: c. 250 (sleep begins); woke under Theodosius II (408-450)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The cave is the place of rebirth, that secret cavity in which one is shut up in order to be incubated and renewed.
body: Seven youths flee the persecution of Decius (c. AD 250) into a cave near Ephesus and sleep 309 years, waking under Theodosius II (408-450); the Qur'an recasts them in Sura 18, "The Cave" (eighth companion a dog; versions of 3, 5, or 7 sleepers). Jung reads the cave as the place of rebirth, "that secret cavity in which one is shut up in order to be incubated and renewed", and the "middle" as the centre where the jewel reposes — the same arrangement as Mithraic altarpieces and the alchemical substance between sun and moon (¶240). The sacred number marks them as gods transformed during sleep into eternal youth (¶242); the same seven sleepers reappear in alchemy as "sleepers enchained in Hades" under the seven planetary stars (¶245 n16).

occurrences.title: Girl's dream-vision: seven white geese pass and everything they pass drops dead
occurrences.label: Girl's dream-vision
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Dream 1 of a girl, presented by Hans Baumann: "Seven white geese go along the street; all beings that they pass drop dead to the earth on the spot."

Jung: the dream is really a vision — "The core of the dream is actually a vision. It is as if the child's eyes had been opened. She was shown that picture: 'Everything passes.'" The geese are the animal life that passes; the seven belongs to lunar time ("the number seven goes back to the seven lunar days," p254). Amplified with the St. Gallen bridge inscription "Everything is transition" and the Arab ring inscribed "Everything passes." From such lapidary vision Jung infers the child's health: it contains "a colossal synthesis."

occurrences.title: The seventh day that has no evening — Augustine's Sabbath of rest in God
occurrences.label: The seventh day that has no evening
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~401-415 (De Genesi ad litteram; De Civ. Dei XI)

jung.locator: Paracelsus as a Spiritual Phenomenon ¶301 (pdf p281-82)

body: Augustine's week-symbolism, the theological frame with which "Paracelsus as a Spiritual Phenomenon" ends: the cognitio matutina (scientia Creatoris) darkens into the cognitio vespertina (scientia hominis — "Who is it that knows...? Why, it is myself"), and the Sabbath is "the day on which man returns to God and receives anew the light of the cognitio matutina. And this day has no evening" (cw13 ¶301; City of God XI, viii).
Jung reads the pagan day-names symbolically: darkness peaks on Venus-day, turns Lucifer on Saturn's day, full light on Sun-day — "As Mercurius he is juvenis, as Saturn senex" (cw13 ¶301).
Verbatim: And this day has no evening. (cw13 ¶301)

occurrences.title: Carpocratian exegesis: 'Agree with thine adversary' — the other in me (Irenaeus, Adv. haer. I.25)
occurrences.label: Carpocratian exegesis — the other in me
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Alexandria (Carpocrates' school; reported by Irenaeus, Lyons)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: the soul could only ransom itself from imprisonment in the somatic world of the demiurge by complete fulfilment of all life’s demands
body: Carpocrates, a 2nd-century Neoplatonist "of otherwise legendary personality," taught per Irenaeus that good and evil are merely human opinions, and that the soul must "pass through the whole gamut of human experience to the very end if it is not to fall back into the prison of the body." The Carpocratians read Matthew 5:25f. — "Agree with thine adversary quickly… lest… thou be cast into prison" — of the somatic man, the bodily existence that is "a kind of hostile brother whose conditions must first be known."

Jung: the adversary is "none other than 'the other in me'" — the shadow-side whose reconciliation with the conscious personality is "a major problem" that "even in antiquity… bothered certain minds." He extends their exegesis to the uncanonical saying "Man, if indeed thou knowest what thou doest, thou art blessed…" and the parable of the unjust steward (Luke 16:8, prudenter / φρονίμως), where "practical intelligence functions… as a court of ethical decision." Beside it stands the Gnostic doctrine "that no man can be redeemed from a sin he has not committed."

occurrences.title: The Superman comes as a shadow — Zarathustra, end of 'Upon the Blessed Isles'
occurrences.label: The Superman comes as a shadow
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: for a shadow came unto me-the stillest and lightest of all things once came unto me!
body: The passage Jung calls "one of the most genuine things in Zarathustra": after raging at the stone with his hammer, Nietzsche receives the vision "for a shadow came unto me — the stillest and lightest of all things... The beauty of the Superman came unto me as a shadow."

Jung reads the word double: not yet his technical shadow, but "unsubstantial like a shadow... a foreshadowing, an anticipation". Yet the psychological sense is latent: "Nietzsche's idea of the Superman, which I would express by the term of the self, would naturally appear first under the cloak of the shadow... It appears in what has been rejected" — the lapis philosophorum that is "at the same time the cornerstone first rejected by the builders." It came "instead of the lost God; God is dead but he reappears in the idea of the Superman".

occurrences.title: The church as stable: good shepherd and sheep — Zarathustra, 'The Priests'
occurrences.label: The church as stable — good shepherd and sheep
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: the good shepherd symbolized the Lord
body: Jung's image for what the church is and does: "the church could also be described as a spiritual stable for superior animals with a good shepherd-of course the good shepherd symbolized the Lord. We are all sheep, and there are probably wolves and even bulls, but at all events he knows what is good for them." Shepherd and sheep "are simply two different aspects of one and the same thing" — a priest unfettered by his dogmas "makes no sense".

The ambivalence is the point: the stable is hell to the creative man and salvation to the inferior man, who "wants to go to sleep in the church, to have a safe bed in which to sleep unquestioningly." The Saviour "who is understood to be a liberator, has made a prison, a sort of big hospital for mental diseases, a psychotherapeutic institution in which people are kept and treated and fed".

occurrences.title: The Poimen (Shepherd) — hidden name of Christ in the Shepherd of Hermas (Rome, ~A.D. 140)
occurrences.label: The Poimen — hidden name of Christ…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The spiritual teacher who appears to Hermas is called the Poimen, the Shepherd, and not the Christ.
body: An early Christian document of about A.D. 140, recognized by the Church until ~the fifth century, never once mentions the name of Christ: the mystery attached to the holy name (Christ = Ichthys, the Fish) and the teacher-figure of Hermas's visions is called simply the Poimen, the Shepherd — "and not the Christ." Hermas is supposed to be the brother of the Roman bishop Pius (¶255).

Jung reads this as liturgical secrecy: baptism and communion were mysteria "of which one could not speak directly," inherited from the mystery-religions; the name-taboo is the same mechanism as the crypt under the church. Distinct locus from the tower-of-living-stones vision of the same book already noted.

occurrences.title: 'I am Noah's Ark, the boat of salvation' — B.St. self-title (Burghölzli, 1896)
occurrences.label: I am Noah's Ark, the boat of salvation'
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I am Noah's Ark, the boat of salvation and respect, Mary Stuart, Empress Alexander.
body: From the 1896 entries of the case-record: "I am Noah's Ark, the boat of salvation and respect, Mary Stuart, Empress Alexander." The rescue-vessel of the Flood is welded in one breath to martyred queen and empress — the ark as the vessel that rides out the deluge of her persecutions, carrying the remnant of a respected life. Jung prints the line without comment inside the case-history, but it anchors the grandeur-complex's consistent imagery: salvation, dignity, and survival, later expressed as the banknote factory "seven storeys high" and the "mightiest silver island."

occurrences.title: The ship with black sails and gold rings - Isolde's ship (Visions, 4 May 1932)
occurrences.label: The ship with black sails and gold rings…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The sails of the ship were black and on each sail was a ring of gold.
body: Opening of the spring-term descent series: standing on the shore of the collective unconscious she stares at the horizon - "that looking... brings about the activation of the object" (betrachten = making pregnant) - and a ship appears. Black sails each bearing a gold ring; a wooden woman on the prow; nobody aboard.

Jung: the black sail is Tristan's death portent - "that ship was bringing Isolde, Tristan's anima, only the black sails concealed her"; for a woman it is "the shadow part"; "a ring always means a union. We could go further and say it pointed to a mandala". Climbing into the ship = accepting the shadow form, "like Kuan Yin, the goddess of kindness, who took on the form of an evil spirit herself in order not to frighten the devils when she went down to comfort them in hell" (cf. mother-goddess-kuanyin-feeding-devils-hell-china). Descending into the blue room = the heart of darkness of the I Ching, where the germ of the new Yang waits (snake-fur-rug-blue-room-vision-zurich-1932).

occurrences.title: Granny in the big boat — dream of the nine-year-old girl
occurrences.label: Granny in the big boat
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A nine-year-old with subnormal temperature, sleeping in her father's room, dreamed: "I went with Daddy to see Granny. Granny was in a big boat. She wanted me to kiss her and wanted to put her arms round me, but I was afraid of her. Daddy said, 'Well then, I'll kiss Granny!'"

Jung's reading: "It is he who wishes to kiss his mother, and the child feels forced to kiss her in the dream" (¶219) — the father's unconscious incest fastening on his daughter, his regressive libido toward the mother-imago. Granny "all mouth" (a recurring dream) "suggests swallowing and devouring" (¶219); the boat bears the devouring encounter. The case: parents' concealed marital crisis made the child ill; separation restored her health (¶217).
Quote. "I went with Daddy to see Granny. Granny was in a big boat. She wanted me to kiss her and wanted to put her arms round me, but I was afraid of her."

occurrences.title: Schopenhauer's mariner in his frail barque — principium individuationis (via Nietzsche, Birth of Tragedy)
occurrences.label: Schopenhauer's mariner in his frail barque
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The image Nietzsche borrowed from Schopenhauer to define the Apollinian: "As upon a tumultuous sea, unbounded in every direction, the mariner sits full of confidence in his frail barque, rising and falling amid the raging mountains of waves, so the individual man, in a world of troubles, sits passive and serene, trusting to the principium individuationis" (cw6 ¶876). The barque is the individual self, the raging sea the torrent of the will.

Jung cites it in the 1913 typology paper to root his introversion/extraversion distinction in Nietzsche's Apollo/Dionysus pair: the Apollinian dream-state is "a withdrawal into oneself, or introversion" (¶877), and Apollo himself "the glorious divine image of the principle of individuation" (¶876) — the ship as the image of individuated consciousness riding the Dionysian sea.

occurrences.title: Silvery disk of cloaked figures at the edge of the world — dream of an academic woman
occurrences.label: Silvery disk of cloaked figures at the edge…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The dream, then, uses the symbol of a disk-like Ufo manned by spirits, a space-ship that comes out of the beyond to the edge of our world in order to fetch the souls of the dead.
body: A woman with an academic education dreamt, with no thought of Ufos: two women on "the edge of the world" — the older lame, the younger supporting her — under crescent moon, morning star and rising sun, as "an elliptical, silvery object came flying from the right... peopled around its rim with figures... all silvery white." The dreamer seized a paintbrush at once (Plate I); her ill friend X, whom she had identified with the older woman, died about two years later.

Jung's reading: a borderline situation — beyond lies cosmic space, the land of the dead, or the unconscious; the disk is "a space-ship that comes out of the beyond... to fetch the souls of the dead," and "The idea that the Ufo might be a sort of Charon is certainly one that I have not met in the literature so far" (¶699). The white-robed crew suggests the animus in plurality and "a marital union of opposites... also applies to death as a final realization of wholeness" (¶698).

occurrences.title: Tibetan picture: Śiva in female form dancing on corpses (in Jung's possession)
occurrences.label: Tibetan picture — Śiva in female form dancing…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: ...I have a Tibetan picture at home in which åiva is depicted in the female form, dancing on the corpses in the burial ground.
body: A picture Jung kept at home showing Śiva in female form dancing on corpses in the burial ground — his counter-evidence to Hauer's insistence (from the Sanskrit tradition) that the crescent of svādhiṣṭhāna is Śiva's, i.e. male. "At all events, the moon is always understood as the receptacle of the souls of the dead" — for Jung the second center is "intensely female, for the water is the womb of rebirth."

occurrences.title: Kali dancing on the corpses, Shiva among the dead (Indian legend)
occurrences.label: Kali dancing on the corpses, Shiva among…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Mrs. Crowley raises Shiva's dance; Jung tells the Kali legend: Kali in a fit of rage "danced upon the corpses in the burial-ground and nobody could stop her." The only way Shiva could stop her was "to place himself among the corpses, so she danced on him. But when her foot touched him he looked up, and she saw he was her husband, and then she instantly ceased dancing and shamefacedly hung her head". Sometimes the dancer "looks exactly as if he were a woman... a sort of Kali dancing in the form of Shiva."

Reading: the dancing Shiva is "the cruelty and indifference of nature that destroys with no regret" — reckless, in ecstasy, creating and destroying worlds "with no relationship even to one's own doing"; unchecked intuition, which Nietzsche deploys as dancing over the difficult places.

occurrences.title: Shri-Yantra — traditional Tantric figure (reproduced from Avalon, The Serpent Power)
occurrences.label: Shri-Yantra — traditional Tantric figure
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: traditional form (repr. from Avalon, The Serpent Power, 1913)
body: The Shri-Yantra opens Jung's chapter on mandala symbolism: "this word denotes the ritual or magic circle used in Lamaism and also in Tantric yoga as a yantra or aid to contemplation (fig. 39)." (cw12 ¶122).

Ceremonial mandalas are "figures fixed by tradition… drawn or painted or, in certain special ceremonies, even represented plastically" — against which Jung will set the spontaneous, individually formed mandalas of dreams.

occurrences.title: The Shulamite lapis laments in the nigredo — Abraham Eleazar, Uraltes chymisches Werk
occurrences.label: The Shulamite lapis laments in the nigredo
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: O! Adam Kadmon, how beautiful art thou!... Like Kedar I am black henceforth
body: The arcane substance speaks in the first person through the Egyptian-Hellenistic and Song of Songs masks: "Through Cham, the Egyptian, I must pass.... Noah must wash me... in the deepest sea, that my blackness may depart.... O! Adam Kadmon, how beautiful art thou!... Like Kedar I am black henceforth, ah! how long! O come, my Mesech, and disrobe me, that mine inner beauty may be revealed.... O Shulamite, afflicted within and without, the watchmen of the great city will find thee and wound thee, and rob thee of thy garments" (¶43).

Jung's conclusion: "the 'hidden' thing, the invisible centre, is Adam Kadmon, the Original Man of Jewish gnosis... personified by the black Shulamite of the Song of Songs. He is the product of the conjunction of sun and moon" — "its father is the sun, and its mother the moon" (¶44). At ¶185 the same lapis "says: 'But I must be like a dove.'"

occurrences.title: The Seeress of Prevorst in spirit-communion — Justinus Kerner's patient (Weinsberg, 1826–1829)
occurrences.label: The Seeress of Prevorst in spirit-communion
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: pars. 49–148 (per ed. n. 5: dissertation use of Kerner's Seeress)

body: Friederike Hauffe, the "Seeress of Prevorst," the physician-poet Justinus Kerner's famous somnambulic patient (1826 until her death in 1829): conversations "with blessed or accursed spirits," magnetic cures, and ghostly visions at the Weinsberg house. Jung quotes David Friedrich Strauss's assessment of her as his first authority in Lecture II — a "prophetess who partook of communion with a higher world," whose celestial radiance and musical speech Strauss vindicates against charges of fraud (¶74–75).

This is the direct background of Jung's own family mediumship (his cousin Hélène Preiswerk) and of his 1902 dissertation, which leans on Kerner's Seeress throughout (CW1 pars. 49–148, per the volume's editorial note). In 1897 the point is evidentiary: the seeress's organized, purposeful phenomena prove an intelligence independent of space and time (¶96, ¶116).
Verbatim: "Her face, suffering but with noble and tender features, suffused with a celestial radiance; her speech the purest German; her talk gentle, slow, solemn, musical almost like a recitative."

occurrences.title: Walburga Sibylla — the German household sibyl of a Roman officer (Aswan)
occurrences.label: Walburga Sibylla — the German household sibyl…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: an inscription was discovered which gave the list of the members of the household of a high Roman officer… among the members of the staff was a slave whose name was unusual in that country, Walburga Sibylla.
body: Illustrating the "natural mind" realized by prophetic women (Tacitus' Germanic women "reverenced for their wisdom and their gift of prophecy"), Jung cites an excavation find from "about twenty years ago":

"So she was probably a German woman who had been sold to a powerful man in Egypt for the guidance of his life, a woman analyst for his personal use" — "It seems that the Sibylla was a sort of profession, and this Walburga no doubt provided the household with her prophetic opinions and was consulted in all difficult situations". A first-millennium witness that the prophetess-as-function — the psyche's own guidance figure — was once an institution, projected exactly as the analyst today receives the psychopomp transfer.

occurrences.title: Walburga Sibylla — German slave girl as house-medium (Roman Egypt)
occurrences.label: Walburga Sibylla — German slave girl…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: An excavated list of the servants in the house of a Roman official in imperial Egypt includes a girl with the Greek name Walburga Sibylla — "Walburga is a German name, and the women of Germany were particularly mediumistic; it is known that many German women slaves were sold to be used as mediums and somnambulists". She was the household medium: "in case of emergency could be his medium; he could ask his Sibylla to prophesy what he should do."

Jung produces her while analysing the boy-medium of dream 30, who calls up the great-grandmother from Hades: child-mediums were "a sort of profession" in antiquity, and the modern clairvoyant is the same expedient. The locus documents the historical trade behind mediumship as an archetypal role.

occurrences.title: Initial dream of the sick little girl — the occult studies of a 'normal' patient (patient-anon)
occurrences.label: Initial dream of the sick little girl
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: So the child evidently represented his interest in the psyche — an idea I should never have arrived at of my own accord.
body: A long initial dream of one of Jung's "normal" patients: the illness of his sister's child, a little girl of two, played an important part — although the sister had never had a sick daughter (an earlier boy had died). The image fit no personal fact; the dreamer then remembered that two years earlier he had taken up the study of occultism, through which he discovered psychology. Jung: "the child evidently represented his interest in the psyche — an idea I should never have arrived at of my own accord."

Jung's frame: the dream displays "unconscious metaphysics" (¶90); the only certainty is that "it is always man who interprets, who assigns meaning" — and here "the interpretation works": the implied criticism of his occult studies changed the patient's attitude and overcame the dead point (¶93–94).

Instance_of note: the child here symbolizes a nascent psychic content (the child archetype's forward-looking sense) rather than the divine child of legend — reconciliation pass to weigh against child (archetype).

occurrences.title: The killing of Siegfried — Jung's dream (December 1913)
occurrences.label: The killing of Siegfried — Jung's dream
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: Soon after the cave fantasy, Jung dreamed he climbed an Alpine mountain before dawn with "a curious shortish man with brown skin," both carrying rifles. Siegfried's horn sounded from above; he appeared in the first sunlight, plunging down in a chariot made of bones — "Only Siegfried could do that." Around a bend they fired full into his breast; filled with horror and disgust at the cowardice, Jung fled as his companion moved to knife the heart, and a deluge of rain broke over him; he woke in relief.

The interpretation given in 1925: "Siegfried stands for the ideal, and the killing of the ideal is the killing of the superior function." Jung — who disliked Wagner's "exaggeratedly extraverted" Siegfried — had killed his own ideal of force and efficiency: "I had killed my intellect, helped on to the deed by a personification of the collective unconscious, the little brown man with me". The dream elaborates the slain hero seen floating in the cave. The rain is "a symbol of the release of tension;... as soon as the main function is deposed, there is a chance for other sides of the personality to be born into life".

occurrences.title: Simia Dei: the demon in the shape of a monkey — Speculum humanae salvationis (14th c.)
occurrences.label: Simia Dei — the demon in the shape of a monkey
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the devil is in fact regarded as the 'ape of God
body: Plate 67: "Demon in the shape of a monkey.—'Speculum humanae salvationis' (Cod. Lat. 511, Paris, 14th cent.)." Jung: "Mercurius, however, had several things in common with the devil… and so the ape once more crops up in the vicinity of Mercurius as the simia Dei" (¶173); and later: "the devil is in fact regarded as the 'ape of God'" (¶181).
The medieval ape-of-God completes the triangle Thoth-baboon (divine) / gibbon (archaic) / devil-ape (diabolical): one animal, three valences of the archetypal Other.

occurrences.title: Simon Magus and his Helen, rescued from the Tyrian brothel
occurrences.label: Simon Magus and his Helen, rescued…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Tyre → Samaria? (Simonian legend reported by the Church Fathers)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Helen of Troy, in her reincarnation, is rescued from a Tyrian brothel by the wise Simon Magus
body: Helen of Troy "in her reincarnation" is rescued from a Tyrian brothel by the wise Simon Magus and accompanies him on his travels (¶64). Jung cites her as the anima's hidden-wisdom face: the same figure who was the cause of a war between two worlds now carries, in her Gnostic reincarnation, the "superior knowledge of life's laws".

Jung's reading: behind the anima's cruel sporting with human fate "there lies something like a hidden purpose"; in literature he instances Rider Haggard's She ("Wisdom's Daughter") and Benoit's Queen of Atlantis with her library containing a lost book of Plato — the anima as bearer of secret knowledge, which appears "only to the person who gets to grips with her seriously".

occurrences.title: The Girl and the Skull — Siberian tale (Kunike No. 31)
occurrences.label: The Girl and the Skull — Siberian tale
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: …and the Siberian tale 'The Girl and the Skull,' in Kunike (ed.), Märchen aus Sibirien, No. 31, where a woman marries a skull.
body: A Siberian tale in which a woman marries a skull, cited beside the Alaskan spider-woman tale in the Return of the Soul notes.

The soul-bride's union with the death's-head: love directed to what is already dead — the transference-essay's dark counterpart to the alchemical marriage, the psyche binding itself to its own mortal remainder.

occurrences.title: Ten-year-old girl's recurrent vision: the snake with eyes sparkling like diamonds
occurrences.label: Ten-year-old girl's recurrent vision
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: A recurrent dream of a ten-year-old girl that crosses into waking: "A snake with eyes sparkling like diamonds chases me in a forest or in my bedroom.... even when awake, everywhere in the room I see the glowing eyes of the snake that wants to bite me." Presented by Marie-Louise von Franz, whose paper surveys the snake as chthonic earth-demon, sotēr, and time-symbol (Ophites, Perates, Sabazios, Kundalini, Gilgamesh, Glaucus, the cobra's diamond).

Jung: the general, non-pathological symbol shows the child is normal; the concretism and force point to a split, probably mirroring the parents' conflict. The snake-entity unconscious produces an "artificial personality" that fails precisely at love and marriage (p276). Because snake and child attract each other, "the prognosis of this split is good" (p279). The diamond eyes announce "a light hidden in the brain of the snake" — the brain stone of alchemy, the capability of an extended consciousness, gnosis.

occurrences.title: The snake of the Erechtheion — spirit of Erechtheus fed through the burial hole
occurrences.label: The snake of the Erechtheion
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: The snake that was worshipped in the Erechtheion on the Acropolis was considered to be the spirit of King Erechtheus or Erechthonios, who was buried there.
body: The snake worshipped in the Erechtheion on the Acropolis was considered the spirit of King Erechtheus (Erechthonios), buried there; the living spirit of the dead was fed by sacrificial food offered through burial holes. In Greece generally, snakes creeping from graves were the dead themselves — fed and cared for; if such a snake entered a house, the family moved out, "because the spirit of the dead had taken possession of the house" (the same among certain primitive tribes, Jung adds).
The cult was also apotropaic: snakes appear suddenly out of darkness, cannot be brought into rapport, and are "as enigmatic and frightening as the unconscious."

occurrences.title: The snake on the white fur rug in the blue room - the Yang in the Yin (Visions, 4 May 1932)
occurrences.label: The snake on the white fur rug…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: In the center of the room was a white fur rug on which lay a snake coiled up.
body: In the belly of the black-sailed ship she enters "a room hung with blue" - the heart of darkness - and in its center, on a white fur rug, "lay a snake coiled up."

Jung: the rug is a flayed animal, abgezogen - distilled, abstracted; flaying = "man must be denaturalized in order to attain to the god" (flaying-moon-goddess-renewal-aztec-1500). The snake, usually the Yin, stands in the place of the Yang: "the Yang can be Yin too... philosophical thought, which to us is entirely bright and shining, could in the unconscious darkness be a snake". The snake = "that thing which is Yin as well as Yang" = the transcendent function = Tao, "where yea and nay are the same"; the archaic feminine-serpentine Tao resurfacing. She does not understand - "she pays no attention to the serpent, that most important central symbol" - kicks it away, and must descend through the tablet (torrent-waters-of-life-white-light-vision-zurich-1932 follows later) to the chained hold. Like the dead in the Chikhai Bardo who turn from the Clear Light to lesser lights.

occurrences.title: The old woman who put on the old skin - how death came into the world (African myth, 4 May 1932)
occurrences.label: The old woman who put on the old skin - how…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: They thought that human beings were originally like snakes that shed their skins once a year and thereby got a new skin, a new life; but once an old woman became somewhat distracted and put on the old skin again, and so death came into the world.
body: The Negro tale of the origin of death, told to ground the flayed fur rug of the blue-room vision: humans were once like snakes that shed their skins yearly and so renewed their lives, until a distracted old woman put the old skin back on - "and so death came into the world."

Jung: "The idea of flaying is really archetypal, so the fur rug probably refers to the animal that has been flayed, meaning the animal consciousness that has been transformed into a detached consciousness". Shedding = the renewal of life by denaturalization; putting on the old skin = relapse into participation mystique.

occurrences.title: 'I am Socrates' — B.St.'s martyr identification (Burghölzli, ~1905)
occurrences.label: I am Socrates' — B.St.'s martyr identification
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The explanation of her stereotypy 'I am Socrates' or 'I am Socratic' is that she is the 'best dressmaker' who 'never cut a thread' and 'never left a bit of cloth on the floor.
body: The first neologism Jung subjects to continuous association in the B.St. case: "Socrates" unfolds into wisdom, "the highest ground-pedestal," martyrdom ("had to die because of wicked men—falsely accused"), and finally the crucial phrase: "never cut a thread—I was the best dressmaker." She is Socrates because, like him, she achieved the highest in her line, was slandered, imprisoned, and unrecognized; "she is so identified with Socrates that she can no longer get away from him" (¶217). Jung's general: "The complex functions automatically in accordance with the law of analogy" (¶218) — metaphor lived as reality. The identity propagates: her delusional daughter later becomes the "Socrates deputy" (¶295).

occurrences.title: Silenus figures with gods hidden inside — Plato's Symposium
occurrences.label: Silenus figures with gods hidden inside
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: They are hollow inside, and when they are taken apart you see that they contain little figures of gods.
body: Alcibiades compares Socrates to "those figures of Silenus in statuaries' shops, represented holding pipes or flutes; they are hollow inside, and when they are taken apart you see that they contain little figures of gods."

Jung at cw14 ¶564: Plato is referring to the herms of Mercurius with a simulacrum of the god hidden inside (Pseudo-Dionysius) — the classical witness to the statues that so fired the alchemical imagination: a precious substance hidden in the "statue" is an old tradition.

occurrences.title: 25 December as the feast of Sol Invictus, taken over for Christmas — Rome (274 CE; fixed 4th c.)
occurrences.label: 25 December as the feast of Sol Invictus, taken…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 274 CE (Aurelian's Sol Invictus feast); Christmas on Dec 25 fixed in the 4th c.

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: Jung's answer to Miss Taylor on whether Mithraism might become a living religion again: no — but its assimilations and discardings by Christianity are the interesting part. "In early days, Christmas came on the 8th of January, and was a day taken over from the Egyptians, being the day celebrating the finding of the body of Osiris. It was only in later days, when the Mithraic cult was being overcome, that the Christians took the 25th of December, the day celebrated by the followers of Mithras as the day of Sol invictus, for their Christmas. To the early Christians, Christmas was the resurrection of the sun, and as late as Augustine, Christ was identified with the sun". With the Mass-bells this forms his case for the Mithraic substrate of Christian practice — and the background to his own December 1913 sun/deification visions, "Mithraic symbolism from beginning to end."

occurrences.title: Sol and Luna united — 'as the cock the hen' — Rosarium philosophorum
occurrences.label: Sol and Luna united — 'as the cock the hen'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: O Luna, folded by my embrace, / Be you as strong as I, as fair of face. / O Sol, brightest of all lights known to men, / And yet you need me, as the cock the hen.
body: The Rosarium woodcut of the embraced solar king and lunar queen (with verses on their mutual need), which Jung calls "the allegory of the psychic union of opposites."

His reading: the brother-sister pair (Thabritius and Beya in the Visio Arislei) "stands allegorically for the whole conception of opposites — dry-moist, hot-cold, male-female, sun-moon, gold-silver, mercury-sulphur, round-square, water-fire, volatile-solid, physical-spiritual." The king's son is the masculine spiritual principle of light and Logos which, like the Gnostic Nous, sinks into the embrace of physical nature.

image.title: Woodcut depicting the king & queen standing atop a sun & moon

occurrences.title: Sol and Luna naked — 'Spiritus est qui unificat' — Rosarium, Figure 3
occurrences.label: Sol and Luna naked — 'Spiritus est qui unificat'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Man stands forth as he really is and shows what was hidden under the mask of conventional adaptation: the shadow.
body: The third Rosarium woodcut: the chaste disguises of Figure 2 have fallen away; Sol and Luna confront each other naked, joined now by both hands through a uniting symbol of only three flowers. The dove bears the inscription Spiritus est qui unificat; the accompanying text is taken from the "Tractatus aureus" with its moral exordium (fear God, be devout, righteous, humane).

Jung (¶451-452): the number has shifted from ogdoad to hexad — double quaternity become double triad, the elements having paired off each with its opposite, so that only the masculine-feminine pair (agens-patiens) remains. Psychologically the picture is the stark encounter with reality after convention drops: the shadow comes to light and is integrated with the ego. "Wholeness is not so much perfection as completeness" — assimilation of the shadow "gives a man body" and brings the archaic psyche into consciousness.

occurrences.title: Winged Sol and Luna conjoining in the water — Rosarium, Figure 5a variant
occurrences.label: Winged Sol and Luna conjoining in the water
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: There again Sol and Luna are in the water, but both are winged. They thus represent spirit—they are aerial beings, creatures of thought.
body: A variant of the fifth Rosarium picture: Sol and Luna again unite in the water, but both are winged. Jung (¶459) uses it to correct the impression of pure natural instinct: winged beings are aerial, creatures of thought — spirit mating on or beneath the water. The texts describe the pair as two vapores or fumi rising, as on wings, from the decoctio and digestio of the prima materia; the same opposites appear elsewhere as two birds fighting, or as the winged and wingless dragon.
Water and fire, opposition and identity at once — "a philosophical problem only when taken as a psychological one" (¶455).

occurrences.title: The black sun with fire and two red outstretched arms (Visions plate 36)
occurrences.label: The black sun with fire and two red…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich (patient's painting; plate following p. 1050 of the edition)
occurrences.yearDisplay: painted late 1929/early 1930 for Jung; vision from the 1926-32 series

jung.locator: plate 36 caption (pdf pp27-28); discussion in later sessions

occurrences.quote: A black sun with fire coming out around it and a red outstretched arm on each side
body: Plate 36: "A black sun with fire coming out around it and a red outstretched arm on each side" — a spontaneous sol niger in Western visionary material, the darkened sun of the alchemists flanked by helping/hailing red arms. It stands late in the painted series, after the great wheel and the Mexican image, among the descent pictures (the Ghosts, the hands and feet growing into the earth) — the blackening at the bottom of the opus the patient's sequence performs. Jung's general frame for such blackness belongs to this seminar's central string: "So the blackness of this woman's face means sinfulness from the Christian standpoint, because it is the color of the Yin, of the black soil... For a long time Christianity was exclusively a religion of the light" (quoted in the introduction from pp526-27).

occurrences.title: The solar-phallus vision of the paranoid patient (Burgholzli, 1906)
occurrences.label: The solar-phallus vision of the paranoid patient
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
jung.locator: Wandlungen und Symbole der Libido ¶¶149f., 223 — pin tbd

body: About 1906 Jung found a long-interned, incurable paranoid schizophrenic (state-school educated office clerk) standing at the window, wagging his head and blinking into the sun: "Surely you see the sun's penis — when I move my head to and fro, it moves too, and that is where the wind comes from" (¶105). Four years later Dieterich's Eine Mithrasliturgie (1910) disclosed the close parallel; Jung could not have known the book, and the patient had been committed years before even its first (1903) edition.

Jung's reading: the patient played mystic sage to Jung's neophyte, feeling himself "the sun-god himself, creating the wind by wagging his head" — the ritual transformation into the Deity attested by Apuleius as Helios apotheosis; the "ministering wind" is the procreative pneuma (¶107). The case is his showcase that archetypal visions arise autochthonously.

occurrences.title: Zosimos' vision: the 'Meridian of the Sun' beheaded (Egypt, ~3rd c.)
occurrences.label: Zosimos' vision — the 'Meridian…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the fourth-step vision a figure follows the sword-bearer, "one adorned round about with signs, clad in white and comely to see, who was named the Meridian of the Sun," commanded: "Cut off his head, immolate his body, and cut his flesh into pieces" (cw13 ¶86).

Jung's reading: "The decapitation... therefore signifies the obtaining of the arcane substance" (¶95); the initiate has undergone the solificatio, since "the sun's rays are gathered together in the quicksilver" (Aurelia occulta) — the "Meridian of the Sun" himself represents the arcane substance (¶95). The striking-off of the golden head recurs in the Splendor solis manuscripts and the Rorschach printing of 1598; Apuleius' initiate "dressed like the sun" is the mystery-parallel (fn12, M.-L. von Franz).

occurrences.title: Soma — the revivifying drink of the Rig-Veda, from the moon-tree
occurrences.label: Soma — the revivifying drink…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Rig-Veda (Jung: 'supposed to go back to 5000 B.C.')

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: The oldest of the intoxicating drinks of the gods: "soma is a mythological drink in the Vedic religion, magical like the wine in the Christian sacrament, or in the Dionysian mysteries. It is a revivifying drink which is also intoxicating." Dr. Harding's material: in the moon grew a soma-tree from which the gods extracted the drink of immortality; Varuna, the moon, churned the cosmic ocean and produced the soma. Jung: "The soma drink is an apotropaic drink against death... that medicine comes from the land of the dead, moonland, the moon-tree, it is the medicine of immortality" — and the Eucharist is "exactly the same as the primitive idea of soma": eating the dead god who gives life.

occurrences.title: Son of Man coming in the clouds — Matthew 26:64
occurrences.label: Son of Man coming in the clouds — Matthew 26:64
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Christ before the high priest, quoting Daniel 7:13: the Son of Man "sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven" — the Danielic heavenly anthropos claimed as self-designation. No. 40 in Jung's 1899 research anthology, the climax of a five-strong parousia group he collected (Nos. 17 [Matt 10:23], 28 [16:27], 35 [19:28 — the twelve thrones in "the regeneration"], 38 [24:44], 40 [26:64], plus Luke 9:26).

Jung filed Nos. 26-29 under the heading "Knowledge" and gave the Son of Man sayings no commentary — but their concentration shows him already reading the Gospel figure as the apocalyptic heavenly man his later work will equate with the anthropos/Self line.
Verbatim: "Hereafter shall ye see the Son of Man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven. [26:64]"

occurrences.title: The Son of Man with seven stars and brass feet — Revelation 1:13-16
occurrences.label: The Son of Man with seven stars and brass feet
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: His feet like unto fine brass, as if they burned in a furnace.
body: "His head and his hairs were white like wool, as white as snow, and his eyes were as a flame of fire, and his feet like unto fine brass, as if they burned in a furnace... And he had in his right hand seven stars, and out of his mouth went a sharp two-edged sword, and his countenance was as the sun shineth in his strength."

Jung at cw14 ¶633: "We would hardly recognize the Son of Man, who is the true incarnation of God's love. But actually this image comes nearer to the paradoxes of the alchemists than does the Christ of the gospels, whose inner polarity was reduced to vanishing-point after the 'Get thee behind me, Satan' incident. In the Apocalypse it becomes visible again."

occurrences.title: Sophia-Achamoth's fall and the outstretched Christ — Irenaeus, Adv. haer. I, 4
occurrences.label: Sophia-Achamoth's fall and the outstretched…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Enthymesis [reflection] of the Sophia who dwells above, compelled by necessity, departed with suffering from the Pleroma in to the darkness and empty spaces of the void. Separated from the light of the Pleroma, she was without form or figure, like an untimely birth... But the Christ dwelling on high, outstretched upon the cross, took pity on her, and by his power gave her a form " (cw13 ¶451). From her affects — sadness, fear, bewilderment, longing, laughing and weeping — "arose the entire created world" (cw13 ¶452).

Jung's psychologem: the myth "describes, in the form of acosmic projection, the separation of the feminine anima from a masculine and spiritually oriented consciousness" (cw13 ¶453); the Greek etektathenta "lays particular emphasis on stretching and extension" (cw13 ¶456); neither light nor dark "notices that their suffering is one and the same" (¶456).
Verbatim: departed with suffering from the Pleroma in to the darkness and empty spaces of the void. (cw13 ¶451ocr)

occurrences.title: The mother called Ogdoad, Sophia, Terra, Jerusalem, Holy Spirit — Irenaeus
occurrences.label: The mother called Ogdoad, Sophia, Terra…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This mother they also call the Ogdoad, Sophia, Terra, Jerusalem, Holy Spirit, and, with a masculine reference, Lord.
body: Irenaeus on the Valentinian mother: "This mother they also call the Ogdoad, Sophia, Terra, Jerusalem, Holy Spirit, and, with a masculine reference, Lord." She is "below and outside the Pleroma."
Jung at cw14 ¶574, 579: the feminine eighth is "the mother of a new series" — the archetype of the seven plus one reappearing in the week, the octave, the eighth day.

occurrences.title: Wisdom enthroned in the cloudy pillar — Ecclesiasticus 24
occurrences.label: Wisdom enthroned in the cloudy pillar
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Wisdom's self-praise: "I came out of the mouth of the most High, and covered the earth as a cloud. I dwelt in high places, and my throne is in a cloudy pillar… in Jerusalem was my power" (¶610). Jung's analysis: she describes herself "in effect, as the Logos, the Word of God"; as Ruach she brooded over the waters; she corresponds "in almost every feature to the Logos of St. John" (¶611).

She is "the feminine numen of the 'metropolis' par excellence… a reflection of Ishtar, the pagan city-goddess", confirmed by her tree catalogue — cedar, palm, terebinth, olive — the ancient symbols "of the Semitic love- and mother-goddess", all recurring in the Song of Songs for sponsus and sponsa alike (¶612). Her throne on earth (vs heaven) returns at ¶727 to identify the New Jerusalem with Sophia.

occurrences.title: Sophia, consort of the Trinity — abolished by the Fathers, retained by the Coptic Church
occurrences.label: Sophia, consort of the Trinity
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: she was abolished except in the Coptic Church
body: Miss Wolff having remarked that the triplets of the dream are born of a woman because "the Christian religion leaves out the woman, excepting the Virgin", Jung replies with church history: "when good old Sophia became a member of the Trinity, as the wife of the Lord God, the old Fathers never liked it, and she was abolished except in the Coptic Church; they had only the Virgin Mary as a sort of spiritual midwife in the neighbourhood."

Since then the female element has been absent from the Trinity — "but now she comes back... It is a very remarkable fact that now the woman should bring forth the lost Trinity." The dating is inferred (patristic era); Jung asserts the Coptic retention without source.

occurrences.title: Irenaeus — Sophia as dove begets Saturn, identical with Yahweh
occurrences.label: Irenaeus — Sophia as dove begets Saturn…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'The Gnostics held that Sophia represents the world of the Ogdoad, which is a double quaternity. In the form of a dove, she descended into the water and begot Saturn, who is identical with Yahweh' (¶307). Saturn is the 'other sun', the sol niger of alchemy, and here the 'primus Anthropos' who created the first man that could only crawl like a worm.
