Jung's set-piece for the Gnostic dark side of the God-image: the creator-god is the shadowy demiurge (Saturn/Yahweh), set against the Archanthropos (¶307, ¶367). Her equivalent in the Barbelo-gnosis is Prunicos, 'carrying a burden' and 'lewd'.

occurrences.title: The Kore, 'Mother of Wisdom' — hymn from the Acts of Thomas
occurrences.label: The Kore, 'Mother of Wisdom'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This maiden, according to the Acts of Thomas, is the “Mother of Wisdom.
body: Thomas' song to the maiden who is "the 'Mother of Wisdom'" (¶561) — the feminine agent of the masculine deity, set by Jung beside Brünnhilde, Pallas Athene, the angel of Yahweh, Vohu Manah, Nabu and Hermes as the deity's "split-off" emissary (¶560, ¶563). The Eucharistic feast of the "secret mother" follows the exorcism of an unchaste demon — "the transformation of a sexual obsession into a recognition of the positive qualities of the feminine spirit" (¶562).

occurrences.title: Jeshu ben Mirjam vs John: has the secret wisdom been betrayed to the mob? — Mandaean Book of John
occurrences.label: Jeshu ben Mirjam vs John — Mandaean Book of John
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~2nd-3rd c. text (community persists into modern era)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: if this beautiful truth is given to the inept, they will only destroy it, will make something bad or ugly of it, so one should conceal it.
body: In the dialogue, Christ is called "Jeshu ben Mirjam, the deceiver," and John reproaches him "for having betrayed the secret wisdom to the people." Christ answers with his works — the lame walking, the blind seeing — "And the dialogue never comes to a definite solution, so it is open to doubt whether John was right or Christ."

Jung frames it as the permanent question of the savior-type: whether "the precious fruit of a past civilization should be handed over to the herd." The Gnostic Evangel is also called the Evangel of St. John; John "must have received the Gnostic teaching"; the wisdom at stake is Sophia, whose personification ties the Holy Ghost to the mother.
"You see, that has once to be: the pearls have to be cast before the swine eventually, since the swine are also human".

occurrences.title: Sophia the master workman at the foundations of the earth — Proverbs 8
occurrences.label: Sophia the master workman at the foundations…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Wisdom's self-report at the creation: "The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old… when he marked out the foundations of the earth, then I was by him, as a master workman, and I was daily his delight" (¶609). The Sapientia Dei is "a coeternal and more or less hypostatized pneuma of feminine nature that existed before the Creation" — for Jung the symptom of Greek influence entering the Jewish sphere.

She "already shares certain essential qualities with the Johannine Logos", is close to the Hebrew Chochma, yet "goes so far beyond it that one can hardly fail to think of the Indian Shakti" (¶610). Her anamnesis is Answer to Job's engine: the "friend and playmate from the beginning of the world" whom Yahweh forgets and must remember if he is to become conscious (¶617).

occurrences.title: The New Jerusalem — foursquare bride of the Lamb (Revelation 21)
occurrences.label: The New Jerusalem — foursquare bride of the Lamb
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: The final vision: the bride is "the 'new Jerusalem coming down out of heaven.' Her 'radiance [was] like a most rare jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal'" (¶726). The city is built foursquare, of pure gold clear as glass; river of the water of life; tree of life as "a reminder of paradise and pleromatic pre-existence"; no night. Jung's reading: "The city is Sophia, who was with God before time began, and at the end of time will be reunited with God through the sacred marriage" — following Ecclesiasticus 24, where Wisdom's throne is on earth.

The uniting symbol expresses perfection and wholeness "hence the quaternity, which expresses itself in the city as a quadrangle, in paradise as the four rivers, in Christ as the four evangelists, and in God as the four living creatures" (¶727). KEY: "the four seraphim represent God's consciousness with its four functional aspects"; God and city are "originally one, a single hermaphroditic being, an archetype of the greatest universality" — the hieros gamos restoring the pleromatic state (Shekinah in the Cabala). Yet the solution is severance, not reconciliation of opposites (¶728).

occurrences.title: Sophia the psychopomp — Wisdom of Solomon 7-8
occurrences.label: Sophia the psychopomp — Wisdom of Solomon 7-8
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: The pneumatic Wisdom of Hellenistic Judaism: "a loving spirit", "the breath of the power of God, a pure effluence flowing from the glory of the Almighty", "the brightness of the everlasting light, the unspotted mirror of the power of God", "conversant with God", for "the Lord of all things himself loved her" (¶613). "As a psychopomp she leads the way to God and assures immortality"; she is sent from heaven as a "Holy Spirit".

Her Maya-character and world-building role come out "still more clearly" here (¶613). Jung then notes the book's dark double: the ungodly plotting to torture the righteous man (Wis 2) repeats the Job prologue — "Where did we read but a short while before: 'And the Lord said to Satan, Have you considered my servant Job…'?" (¶615).

occurrences.title: Sophia, 'my wheel within my wheel' — John Pordage
occurrences.label: Sophia, 'my wheel within my wheel'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: She is my divine, eternal, essential self-sufficiency. She is my wheel within my wheel.
body: John Pordage, Oxford theologian, Boehme disciple, "an accomplished alchemist and astrologer"; with Jane Leade he forms the second "pair of alchemists" Jung sets beside the Mutus liber's adept and soror mystica (§9 n.32). "One of the chief figures in his mystical philosophy is Sophia":

Jung's verdict: "Pordage's view is more or less in agreement with woman's conscious psychology, but not with her unconscious psychology" — the Sophia-theosophy as feminine self-description that the unconscious corrects.

occurrences.title: The sorcerer whose hut was burnt down — Powys, Black Laughter
occurrences.label: The sorcerer whose hut was burnt down
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Llewelyn Powys's sketches of life in East Africa include "a case of magic influence... about a sorcerer whose hut had been burnt down". Jung uses it for the law of the returning projectile: "as long as one feels that one's opponent controls his emotion, it is not so dangerous, but if it is really uncontrolled, anything might happen, and one is afraid... nothing is so contagious as uncontrolled emotion."

The episode grounds his psychology of magic: a fascination "only takes place if the person who causes it is a victim himself"; the sorcerer must dodge his own returning spell — exactly what Mother Isis does when, in dream 30, she jumps out of the window before the ape-man she herself generated.

occurrences.title: The soul ascending from the corpse as homunculus — Rosarium, Figure 7
occurrences.label: The soul ascending from the corpse as homunculus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Out of the decay the soul mounts up to heaven. Only one soul departs from the two, for the two have indeed become one.
body: The seventh Rosarium woodcut: out of the decayed, still unified corpse the soul — depicted as a tiny homunculus — mounts up to heaven, while the four elements divide below.

Jung (¶475-482): only one soul departs, "for the two have indeed become one"; the soul is vinculum / ligamentum, a function of relationship, the idea of unity still only a potentiality. Psychologically this is the dark state of disorientation — dissociation analogous to schizophrenia, akin to the primitives' "loss of soul," the moment latent psychoses may become acute ("in cuius investigatione nonnulli perierunt"). The alchemical "torments" of the iterum mori belong here. But after the nadir: the Nile-flood analogy, St John of the Cross's "dark night" as positive, the cauda pavonis as spring. The homunculus-soul is "on the way to becoming the filius regius, the undivided and hermaphroditic First Man, the Anthropos" — ascending, like Basilides' third filiation, only to return as mediator and saviour (Second Coming).

occurrences.title: Souls in feathered garments — the Gilgamesh epic's land of the dead
occurrences.label: Souls in feathered garments
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In the Gilgamesh epic there is a description of that sad place where souls wear feathered garments.
body: Within the shadow amplification of the peacock vision: ghosts are shadows, "Hades is the shadow world, the shadows dwell there. It is also often symbolized as a bird that flies away. The idea is that when we die, we become shadows and put on wings, feathered garments. In the Gilgamesh epic there is a description of that sad place where souls wear feathered garments" (p83). The dead as birds — the soul-bird family at its oldest attested literary appearance; it lets Jung read the peacock on the man's back as "a sort of ghost that possesses the man," the genius/daimonion perched behind him like the king's hawk or the eagle of Zeus (p83).

occurrences.title: Bird piercing the opening fontanelle — somatic vision of the chakra patient (Zurich, ~1931)
occurrences.label: Bird piercing the opening fontanelle
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: After the abdominal symptoms ascended, "the patient had the feeling that the top of her skull was growing soft, that the fontanelle was opening up, and that a bird with a long sharp beak was coming down to pierce through the fontanelle as far as the diaphragm" (¶554). Jung's later reading: "the kundalinī serpent had reached the manipura centre in my patient, it was met by the bird of thought descending from above, which with its sharp beak pierced through the fontanelle (sahasrāra chakra) to the diaphragm (anāhata)" (¶562). The collision of the rising serpent with the descending bird-thought broke out as "a wild storm of affect" and ended the treatment — the shakti's insinuated thought (wanting a real child) proving to be māyā, "real illusion" (¶562).

occurrences.title: The golden-winged bird from Kaineus' tree-pile — Lapith battle
occurrences.label: The golden-winged bird from Kaineus' tree-pile
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Once again we recognize the typical elements of a libido myth: original bisexuality, immortality (invulnerability) through entry into the mother (splitting the mother with the foot), resurrection as a soul-bird, and production of fertility (rain).
body: Kaineus — born the maiden Kainis, made invulnerable by Poseidon, worshipped his lance, "descended into the depths, splitting the earth with a straight foot", and when the Lapiths buried him under trees a bird flew up. Jung's formula of the libido-myth: "original bisexuality, immortality (invulnerability) through entry into the mother (splitting the mother with the foot), resurrection as a soul-bird, and production of fertility (rain)" (¶441).

occurrences.title: Girl's dream 11 — birds come out of her skin and cover her
occurrences.label: Girl's dream 11 — birds come out…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1938-39 (dreams dreamt at age eight; presented at ten; died of an infectious disease about a year later)
occurrences.quote: She is dangerously ill. Suddenly birds come out of her skin and cover her completely.
body: Dream 11 of the Christmas booklet: "She is dangerously ill. Suddenly birds come out of her skin and cover her completely."

In a series nine of whose twelve dreams "are concerned with the theme of destruction and restoration" (¶529), this is the restoration image in its most classical form — the soul-birds released at the point of death, covering the body as a psalm covers a grave. Jung reads the whole booklet as "a preparation for death, expressed through short stories, like the instruction at primitive initiations, or the koans of Zen Buddhism" (¶538); here the instruction is given in birds.

occurrences.title: The soul gathers herself out of every quarter — Gospel of Philip (via Epiphanius, Panarium XXVI)
occurrences.label: The soul gathers herself out of every quarter
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Two allied Gnostic sayings preserved by Epiphanius: from the Gospel of Philip, "I have taken knowledge (saith the soul) of myself, and have gathered myself together out of every quarter and have not begotten (sown) children unto the Ruler, but have rooted out his roots and gathered together the members that were scattered abroad" (Panarium XXVI, 13); and the Naassene "I am thou, and thou art I... and I am scattered in all things, and from wherever thou wilt thou canst gather me, but in gathering me thou gatherest together thyself" (XXVI, 3). Jung cites both in cw14 ch. I n.26 among his 'uniting the Many into One' authorities (Origen, Porphyry).

The self-gathering soul that refuses to bear children for the Ruler (the demiurge) is, for Jung's use here, an image of the self collecting itself from dispersion — the psychological counterpart of the coniunctio.

occurrences.title: The soul as a spherical glass vessel — Caesarius of Heisterbach
occurrences.label: The soul as a spherical glass vessel
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Caesarius of Heisterbach (thirteenth century) mentions a vision in which the soul appeared as a spherical glass vessel.
body: The Cistercian Caesarius of Heisterbach "mentions a vision in which the soul appeared as a spherical glass vessel." Jung adduces it in his analysis of the fairytale bottle: the vas Hermeticum was sealed "with the sign of Hermes" (cf. Rev 20:3), had to be of glass and as round as possible, "since it was meant to represent the cosmos in which the earth was created." Transparent glass is "something like solidified water or air, both of which are synonyms for spirit"; the retort is "equivalent to the anima mundi, which according to an old alchemical conception surrounds the cosmos."
He adds the parallel of the "ethereal" philosophers' stone as a precious vitrum (sometimes malleabile), equated with the gold glass of the heavenly Jerusalem (Rev 21:21).

occurrences.title: Soul as shining globe — nun's vision in Buber's Ecstatic Confessions
occurrences.label: Soul as shining globe
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: Martin Buber mentions the visions of a nun. There the soul was seen as a shining globe.
body: A participant brings Martin Buber's collection of ecstatic confessions: the visions of a nun in which "the soul was seen as a shining globe." Jung affirms at once: "Yes, this is the deity... the all-round, cosmic being, the world soul, the rotundum, the round one" — his gloss on the red ball of the ten-year-old's dream. Ignatius of Loyola's globe visions (including the undogmatic snake with many eyes) are cited in the same breath: primordial images perceived through the religious images one happens to have.

occurrences.title: The soul returning to the purified corpse — Rosarium, Figure 9
occurrences.label: The soul returning to the purified corpse
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Here is the soul descending from on high / To quick the corpse we strove to purify.
body: The ninth Rosarium woodcut: the reconciler — the soul, identical with the dew — dives down from heaven to breathe life into the dead body. At bottom left two birds, fledged and unfledged, carry the allegory of the winged and wingless dragons.

Jung (¶494-504): the divided bird-pair means the conflict of Mercurius duplex is not resolved, only relegated to the left and bottom — the sphere of the unconscious. The Rosarium text quotes Morienus ("Despise not the ash, for it is the diadem of thy heart") and Senior on the white tincture and the son of the moon; the neighbouring Coronatio Mariae picture makes resurrection a glorification. Psychologically the returning soul is the One born of two, essence of relationship; when projections are withdrawn the anima "ceases to act as an autonomous personality and becomes a function of relationship between conscious and unconscious" (¶504). The reanimation is a transmundane event in the psychic non-ego — hence its compulsive projection.

occurrences.title: Tertullian, De testimonio animae — the testimony of the soul
occurrences.label: Tertullian, De testimonio animae
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Tertullian's appeal to the soul's natural knowledge of God, quoted by Jung at length as patristic warrant for his own procedure: "These testimonies of the soul are as simple as they are true, as obvious as they are simple, as common as they are obvious, as natural as they are common, as divine as they are natural" (¶556). "Feel that which causes you to feel; think upon that which is in forebodings your prophet; in omens, your augur."

Jung steps beyond Tertullian: the Holy Scriptures themselves are "utterances of the soul", and these entia "are the archetypes of the collective unconscious, and they precipitate complexes of ideas in the form of mythological motifs" (¶557).

occurrences.title: Nietzsche's spark of the eternal fire — 'Schopenhauer as Educator'
occurrences.label: Nietzsche's spark of the eternal fire
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: In one of his earliest works Nietzsche writes that a single spark fallen from the eternal fire into a truth-seeking soul "suffices to devour his entire life."

Jung: in that sentence Nietzsche "expresses very clearly the descent of the Holy Ghost: that is a fiery spark of the eternal fires, and this most holy ghost is able to devour the whole of a human life... To be devoured by the spirit is just as bad as to be devoured by a wild animal: it is an act of destruction." The spark names the destructive aspect of spirit that Christianity will not see — the same spirit Klages accuses of "strangling life."
Verbatim: "one spark fallen from the eternal fire into the soul of a man searching after truth suffices to devour his entire life."

occurrences.title: 'Radii atque scintillae' of the anima catholica — Khunrath, Von hylealischen Chaos (1597)
occurrences.label: Radii atque scintillae' of the anima catholica
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

occurrences.quote: They were seeds of light broadcast in the chaos, which Khunratli calls "mundi futuri seminarium" (the seed plot of a world to come)
body: Khunrath explains the sparks of the Aurora-quote as "radii atque scintillae" of the "anima catholica", the world-soul identical with the spirit of God (Ruach Elohim) — seeds of light broadcast in the chaos, which he calls "mundi futuri seminarium", the seed-plot of a world to come. The sparks are "formae rerum essentiales", corresponding to the Platonic Ideas. Among them Khunrath singles out the "scintilla perfecta Unici Potentis ac Fortis" — the elixir, the arcane substance itself, described as Monad and Sun, both indicating the Deity.

Jung's reading: "One would have to conclude from these alchemical visions that the archetypes have about them a certain effulgence or quasi-consciousness, and that numinosity entails luminosity" (¶388); and "Psychologically, the One Scintilla or Monad is to be regarded as a symbol of the self."

occurrences.title: 'Terra foetida cito recipit scintillulas albas' — white sparks in the foul earth (Aurora consurgens, Part II)
occurrences.label: Terra foetida cito recipit scintillulas albas
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: early 15th c. ms; printed Artis auriferae 1593

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

occurrences.quote: Scito quod terra foetida cito recipit scintillulas albas" (Know that the foul earth quickly receives white sparks)
body: "Know that the foul earth quickly receives white sparks" — the scintillae appearing as visual illusions in the arcane substance, quoted by Jung as his first alchemical exhibit for the spark-motif (editors: the passage stands in Artis auriferae I, 208, and is said to quote Morienus; Mylius repeats it and adds "scintillas aureas").

Jung's reading: with Khunrath's "radii atque scintillae" this grounds the equation "the archetypes have about them a certain effulgence or quasi-consciousness, and... numinosity entails luminosity" (¶388) — the multiple luminosities surrounding ego-consciousness (¶387) were already divined as psychic by the alchemists.

occurrences.title: Seeds of Light eaten as ritual food (melons) — karpostai, Irenaeus, Adversus haereses I.2.4
occurrences.label: Seeds of Light eaten as ritual food
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

occurrences.quote: the Manichaean doctrine of the light-particles which have to […] be taken into one's body as ritual food, at a sort of Eucharist when melons were eaten
body: In a footnote to the scintillae discussion Jung cites "the Gnostic doctrine of the Seeds of Light harvested by the Virgin of Light, and the Manichaean doctrine of the light-particles which have to be taken into one's body as ritual food, at a sort of Eucharist when melons were eaten. The earliest mention of this idea seems to be the karposts (Irenaeus, Contra haereses, I, 2, 4)" — with reference to M.-L. von Franz, "Der Traum des Descartes", on the melons.

Jung's reading: the Manichaean-Gnostic light-particles are the religious-systematized form of what alchemy saw as scintillae in the arcane substance and analytical psychology as the "multiple luminosities" surrounding ego-consciousness — archetypal sparks with "a certain effulgence or quasi-consciousness" (¶388).

occurrences.title: 'Sparks shining day by day... into a great light' — Dorn, Speculativae philosophiae
occurrences.label: Sparks shining day by day... into a great light
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

occurrences.quote: scintillae are germinal luminosities shining forth from the darkness of the unconscious
body: "Thus little by little he will come to see with his mental eyes a number of sparks shining day by day and more and more and growing into such a great light that thereafter all things needful to him will be made known" — Dorn's promise to the adept who follows the via veritatis.

Jung's reading: "This light is the lumen naturae which illuminates consciousness, and the scintillae are germinal luminosities shining forth from the darkness of the unconscious" (¶389). Dorn, like Khunrath, owes much to Paracelsus, "with whom he concurs when he supposes an 'invisibilem solem plurimis incognitum' in man". Dorn's sparks carry the clear psychological meaning Jung needs for his hypothesis of a multiple consciousness.

occurrences.title: The spinther — the Gnostic soul-spark fallen from the pleroma
occurrences.label: The spinther — the Gnostic soul-spark fallen…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "That is like the Gnostic myth of the soul, the soul being the spinther (the Greek word for spark) which falls from the pleroma or the empyrean into matter; that spark is the soul of man and if it is touched, there will be a fire."

Jung reads Nietzsche's 1874 line — a spark from the fire of justice "sufficient to devour his whole life" — as an unbeknownst repetition of this Gnostic myth: "This idea was in the grain of man, and in the philosophy of the time of Christ."
The spinther is the seminar's bridge between the fire-logion, Pentecost, Heraclitus's dry soul, and the scintilla/spark family of alchemy.

occurrences.title: Wizard's hand-written book of magic opening with the Merseburg incantation (Switzerland, late 19th c.)
occurrences.label: Wizard's hand-written book of magic opening…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: beginning with the Merseburg magic spell in modern High German and an incantation to Venus of unknown age.
body: At the house of one of the Swiss rustic wizards — the so-called "Strudel," whose clientele came from town and country and whose letters of thanks for ghost-laying Jung saw in the hundreds — Jung "once discovered a book of this kind from the end of the nineteenth century, beginning with the Merseburg magic spell in modern High German and an incantation to Venus of unknown age."

His point: the "disreputable relatives" of church symbolism — blood pacts with the devil, pin-stickings, milk-drying spells — are alive "in spite of all education and enlightenment" (¶700), and they legitimize learned amplification: the same village held the wizard who had taken the spell off a dreamer's stable. "Anyone who does not know that 'Wotan's host'—enlightenment or no enlightenment—still roams about our Swiss cantons would accuse me of the greatest whimsicality" (¶701) — the Merseburg charm being the Wodan text par excellence, here continuous with the "Doggeli" and Wotan's nightly cavalcade feared by mountainfolk.

occurrences.title: Plato's spherical primordial man cut in two (Symposium)
occurrences.label: Plato's spherical primordial man cut in two
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "the idea of a primordial being that was entirely round, a globe. The globe was thought to be the most perfect form, so it is simply a symbol, showing that the idea of man originally, the eidos or the eidolon of man, was the most perfect form. Then God cut this globe into two parts, so there was a female and a male side who were forever seeking each other; and that is Eros."

Jung: not mythology but ideology — "a philosophical intuition" of the perfect, all-round being; the same unconscious intuition that in the African calabash myth and the Agdistis cycle knows the son, the hermaphrodite, as union of sky and earth, spirit and matter. The marriage ideal ("one heart and one soul") is its modern residue.

occurrences.title: The sphinx in the desert whose green eyes hold the tree (Visions)
occurrences.label: The sphinx in the desert whose green eyes hold…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: vision read 9 December 1931 (painted late 1929/early 1930 for Jung)
occurrences.quote: The eyes of the sphinx opened. I saw that they were green and I beheld therein a tree. The branches of the tree reached up into the white snow. The roots of the tree reached down into a stream of blood beneath the earth.
body: Alone on the mountain top after the lion ("Because you have chosen the way"), the patient follows a bird — "an intuition of a new possibility" — down to a sphinx in the desert, and boldly demands: "Render unto me your secret." The eyes open:

Jung: the tree is "the soul of the sphinx", the union of opposites (blood and spirit) that animal and human life cannot manage; the sphinx is "a sort of dragon-the animal devouring the animal", the great enigma death, yet also temple and altar; part human, part animal, a "provisional attempt at a reconciliation between animal and man". Asked what the sphinx is psychologically, Jung endorses Mrs. Fierz: "The unconscious".

occurrences.title: Sphinx-head hypnagogic vision — Miss Miller
occurrences.label: Sphinx-head hypnagogic vision — Miss Miller
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: After the prayer "Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth", Miller sees "the head of a sphinx in an Egyptian setting", which vanishes when she is disturbed.

Jung's reading: the Sphinx "propounds riddles, like the Sphinx of Oedipus, and stands on the threshold of man's fate"; "a semi-theriomorphic representation of the mother-imago, or rather of the Terrible Mother" (¶261, 264) — the enigma that precedes the masculine hero-figure (the Aztec) of the next vision.
Verbatim: After the prayer, "the head of a sphinx in an Egyptian setting" appeared, only to disappear again immediately after. (cw05 ¶261).

occurrences.title: Log of the ship 'Sphinx': two men fly into Stromboli (1686)
occurrences.label: Log of the ship 'Sphinx'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1686 (log date); printed in Kerner, Blätter aus Prevorst IV

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: One was dressed in black, the other in grey.
body: The source Jung unearths behind Zarathustra's volcano-descent: "The four captains and a merchant, Mr. Bell, went ashore on the island of Mt. Stromboli to shoot rabbits. At three o'clock they called the crew together to go aboard, when, to their inexpressible astonishment, they saw two men flying rapidly over them through the air. One was dressed in black, the other in grey... they descended amid the burning flames into the crater of the terrible volcano, Mt. Stromboli. They recognized the pair as acquaintances from London".

The rabbit-crew parallel proved cryptomnesia: Nietzsche and his sister read the Blätter in their grandfather Pastor Oehler's library before his eleventh year; Jung had published the case in his 1902 inaugural dissertation — "the first item in CW 1!" The vision itself: death-apparitions, "the only sort of radio they had in those days," read as warning that the spirit asserting itself personally "goes down and ends its life."

occurrences.title: The Black Spider conjured into a box — Jeremias Gotthelf
occurrences.label: The Black Spider conjured into a box
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: If the vessel is opened, the whole process is destroyed and evil is created.
body: The Swiss parson-novelist's tale, which Jung calls "highly symbolic... astonishingly enough, which contains an attempt at a solution": the devil's kiss creates the black spider, which multiplies "till it threatened to destroy everything," and is finally "conjured away by putting the spider into a box, catching that spider in form, in a sort of vas Hermeticus... which is a vessel that must not be opened. If the vessel is opened, the whole process is destroyed and evil is created."

The principle generalized: "nothing is ever so negative that it has not also a positive aspect" — the devil properly bottled is "useful; he has even a beneficient influence." Jung sets beside it Pandora's box and Apollonius of Tyana's jar in which Brahmanic priests kept good and bad weather sealed.

occurrences.title: Flying metal spider with the prayer 'Lead us downwards' — 42-year-old patient
occurrences.label: Flying metal spider with the prayer Lead us…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The gist of the prayer was: 'Lead us downwards and keep us (safe) below... Carry us up to the height!
body: A 42-year-old woman patient, years before the saucer era, dreams a round black metallic object — "a huge flying spider made of metal, with great dark eyes" — circling her garden and past the windows of a building "where international decisions were being taken." From it a solemn voice prays: "Lead us downwards and keep us (safe) below... Carry us up to the height!" — the way to peace is "the way to the inner, secret world."

Jung's reading: the spider is a "profoundly alien psychic world," contents lodged in the sympathetic system (¶672); the prayer names the spider "divine" yet asks it to keep souls below — no spiritual inflation, the ego "not sole master in its own house" (¶673); katabasis before anabasis, krater and Mass (¶674); a regression of religious ideas "to the theriomorphic symbol of supreme power" (¶679).

occurrences.title: Spider as sapphire jewel in the golden web — patient dream
occurrences.label: Spider as sapphire jewel in the golden web
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: And people make pictures like that, not knowing of course what they mean.
body: Jung's positive completion of the tarantula chapter: dreams and patient pictures in which the spider is "a jewel, perhaps a sapphire, a blue resplendent gem in the center of the web which is made of golden threads" — the self-symbol in a condition of complete unconsciousness. Miss Hannah proposes the spider as self-symbol; Jung agrees and adds the law that the unconscious only heaps up such attributes while the meaning is wholly unknown — such dreams occur "never unless the person is completely unconscious of what that symbol could mean."

The positive reading: "there is a central being somewhere that has spread its golden web throughout the world to catch the souls of man." Projected negatively it becomes the analyst as spider sucking people dry — the tarantula quality Nietzsche reviles as collectivism is the fear of individuation.

occurrences.title: The spinning spider — school-poem quotation in nurse subject 26's test (Burghölzli, ~1904-05)
occurrences.label: The spinning spider
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: 19th-c. German school poem; quoted in ~1904-05 experiment

jung.locator: pdf p76 (print ¶ 333 area — unmarked in chunk)

occurrences.quote: An obvious condensation (Freud) of the situation and apparent form into the word trage (lazy) has occurred in the subconscious
body: To the stimulus-word to be lazy, nurse subject 26 reacts with a single is (1.8 s) — the first line of a school poem Jung quotes in full: "The girl came to the spider / And the spider said: Why so late? / I have been spinning threads for three hours / See how finely and delicately they are twisted!" He reads a Freudian condensation: sound of spät (late) and gedreht (twisted) fused into träge (lazy) "in the subconscious" — no time for conscious search — the spider's spinning thread doubling the girl's own dilatory spinning. Jung generalizes: "the subconscious or unconscious likes to associate quotations or complexes... fragments of quotations and songs which happen to have been picked up... are directly connected with the complex." The web-weaver appears here as the masking image of a work-complex (her night-duty grievance against the late-relieving day nurse).

occurrences.title: The tarantula's triangle of black on its back — Zarathustra, 'The Tarantulas'
occurrences.label: The tarantula's triangle of black on its back
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: There cometh the tarantula willingly: Welcome, tarantula! Black on thy back is thy triangle and symbol
body: "Black on thy back is thy triangle and symbol" — though the real tarantula has no triangle ("The European tarantula does have a small triangle on its back," the editors note), and Nietzsche "simply equips the tarantula with the triangle, presumably because he never has seen one," a creativity of the intuitive who attributes the symbol "whether it is so in reality or not".

Jung reads the triangle as the one-sided Christian Trinity — three masculine entities, "the evil is lacking in that symbol" — carried on the back of the chthonic, sympathetic-system animal: "on the back of the tarantula it clearly represents the evil principle of the earth". Joined to the upper triangle it would form the quadrangulum, "that eternal problem, the three and the four"; the tarantula itself is the compensatory feminine that follows the Wotan-wind identification of "The Rabble".

occurrences.title: The Woman Who Became a Spider — Alaskan Eskimo tale
occurrences.label: The Woman Who Became a Spider
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Cf. the Alaskan Eskimo tale 'The Woman Who Became a Spider,' in Rasmussen, Die Gabe des Adlers, pp. 121ff.
body: An Alaskan Eskimo tale of a woman's transformation into a spider, cited by Jung in the Return of the Soul section as an ethnographic parallel to the European soul-bride material (Melusina, the nixie) — the feminine soul-image in its animal-transformation aspect.

Its companion citation is the Siberian "Girl and the Skull" (skull-girl-marries-skull-siberia-kunike-1914): woman weds death. Together they show the soul's marriage-motif operating far outside the alchemical West.

occurrences.title: Bernoulli's spiral tombstone: 'Eadem mutata resurgo' (Basel cathedral)
occurrences.label: Bernoulli's spiral tombstone
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Basel cathedral (grave slab of Jacob Bernoulli, 1654-1705)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: Always changing in the same way, yet I arise.
body: "The man who discovered the mathematics of the spiral lived in my town. On his tombstone is engraved: 'Always changing in the same way, yet I arise'" — Jacob Bernoulli's logarithmic spiral and its motto Eadem mutata resurgo, requested for his grave in Basel cathedral (cross-ref CW12 par. 325).

Jung cites it at the crux of the steamroller-labyrinth dream: "One of the fundamental laws of natural development is that it moves in a spiral... you always come over the same point where you have been before, but it is never exactly the same, it is either above or below." The patient's own spiral footpath at the labyrinth's centre is the subjective twin of the tombstone's emblem.

occurrences.title: Denial of spirits for fear of them — dwellers on Mt Elgon
occurrences.label: Denial of spirits for fear of them
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the fear of spirits is sometimes so great that people will actually deny that there are any spirits to fear.
body: Footnote to Jung's discussion of spirits and the ancestral psyche (Part 2: "In cases of reports to the contrary, it must always be borne in mind that the fear of spirits is sometimes so great that people will actually deny that there are any spirits to fear. I have come across this myself among the dwellers on Mount Elgon.").

Jung's reading: denial is itself a symptom — an apotropaic negation of the numinous; belief in spirits is not credulity to be argued away but a dread-charged relation to the ancestral psyche (index: "spirits, ancestral, 186; dangerous, 186"; "Bataks of Sumatra, 186" — the Batak spirit-cult via Warnecke runs parallel at ¶186). Negative reports about spirit-belief must be read through the defence they serve.

occurrences.title: 'The Spirit in the Bottle' — Grimm fairytale KHM 99
occurrences.label: The Spirit in the Bottle
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: I am the great and mighty spirit Mercurius, and now you shall have your reward. Whoso releases me, him I must strangle.
body: The fairytale that opens The Spirit Mercurius and carries the whole essay: a student finds a spirit crying "Let me out!" from a glass bottle buried among the roots of a mighty oak. The spirit names himself: "I am the great and mighty spirit Mercurius... Whoso releases me, him I must strangle." The boy tricks him back into the bottle, receives a healing and silver-making rag, and becomes a famous doctor.

Jung's reading: the fairytale "contains the quintessence and deepest meaning of the Hermetic mystery" (¶239); the forest = the unconscious, the oak = "the prototype of the self, a symbol of the source and goal of the individuation process" (¶241); the spirit = the principium individuationis imprisoned by a Master (God) since the principle of individuation "is the source of all evil" (¶244); the boy's release of Mercurius is "alchemically incorrect" (¶251). Mercurius here = the pagan god identical with Wotan (¶246).

image.title: Otto Ubbelohde - Der Geist im Glas 3

occurrences.title: St. Anthony sends back the enlightening spirits — tale by Anatole France
occurrences.label: St. Anthony sends back the enlightening spirits
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Paris (Oeuvres complètes, ed. Calman Lévy, vol. 4, pp. 526ff)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: he saw a great light at night, and spirits who said: 'We have come to enlighten you.' But he concluded that they were demons who tested him.
body: The hermeneutic precedent Jung invokes for the boy who dumps the green-faced spirit into the snow: St. Anthony "saw a great light at night, and spirits who said: 'We have come to enlighten you.' But he concluded that they were demons who tested him. So he packed his suitcase and left." Jung is explicit about the source: "This is a story by Anatole France, by the way, not from the Acta Sanctorum." The structure — direct presence of the numinosum rejected as the devil because it does not fit the dogmatic frame — is exactly the boy's: "if it is not the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, it has to be the devil!" What is frightening is "the direct presence of God."

occurrences.title: Spitteler's Prometheus: the rejected jewel picked up by Ahasuerus
occurrences.label: Spitteler's Prometheus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: where Ahasuerus picks it up and puts it into his pocket
body: In Spitteler's Prometheus epic the divine jewel is "despised by the stupid… rejected by everyone from the high priest and the academicians down to the very peasants, and 'in viam eiectus,' flung out into the street, where Ahasuerus picks it up and puts it into his pocket. The treasure has sunk down again into the unconscious" (¶160).

Jung uses the episode as a literary double of the dream's cheap "special water": the water of life, "like the lapis, it is 'pretio quoque vilis,' of little price," prized by no one because "every good thing is always outside and somewhere else, and… the source in their own souls is a 'nothing but.'" A continues an existing line of Spitteler material in the corpus (cf. the Imago figure).

occurrences.title: Spreuer bridge, Lucerne — Dance of Death paintings and the burning sanctuary lamp
occurrences.label: Spreuer bridge, Lucerne
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: On the Spreuer bridge in Lucerne, adorned with pictures of Holbein's Dance of Death, a sanctuary lamp is still burning today in a small altar niche
body: The Spreuer bridge in Lucerne, adorned with paintings of Holbein's Dance of Death (executed by Kaspar Meglinger, 1616-35), still keeps a sanctuary lamp burning in a small altar niche built in a little oriel above the Reuss; passersby raise their hats, cross themselves, or murmur a prayer. Cited as the living relic of the chapels built on bridges' former sacrificial sites — the place where every bridge is "the bridge," and "everything is transition".
With St. Nepomuk, the drowned bridge-saint of Bohemia, it shows the Middle Ages' still-functioning relation to the symbol that the modern "topographical" mind has lost.

occurrences.title: St. Anthony and the shoemaker of Alexandria — the angel who was the devil
occurrences.label: St. Anthony and the shoemaker of Alexandria
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Then it dawned upon St. Anthony that the angel was the devil. The angel must have been wrong because that method did not suit hirn.
body: Desert-father anecdote told for the psychology of saintliness: after twenty years in the desert — three days' journey deeper than any rival, "a competition in saintliness" — Anthony receives a flattering "angel": you are a great saint, but there is one greater, a shoemaker in Alexandria. Anthony tramps off, finds the little man mending shoes to feed his wife and nine children; no method, no sanctity.

Jung's point: the differentiation of a saint is training, technique, conscious ideal — not the natural mana personality of the primitive, who "doesn't want to be a medicine man... usually they kill him in the end". The devil enters as the collector of the saint's vanity, catching him precisely through his competitive asceticism.

occurrences.title: St. George and the dragon
occurrences.label: St. George and the dragon
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Lybia/Cappadocia legend; episode fixed in Europe ~11th-12th c.
occurrences.yearDisplay: legend episode fixed ~11th-12th c. (older cult; inferred)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: as if he were a new St. George who has to kill the dragon first in order to go on
body: Invoked twice as the frame for dream 28: "It is the fight with the dragon who holds the treasure inside, and when the hero has succeeded in beating the dragon down, out will come the father or mother, or he will get at the hidden treasure. In this case, the dragon or tortoise delivers a child" — the dreamer "has to detach [the child] from the unconscious as if he were a new St. George who has to kill the dragon first in order to go on."
On 11 June the whole dream is summed as "mythological, St. George and the dragon... the dragon was a turtle that was giving birth to a child."

occurrences.title: Feeble-minded boy: heaven refused, St. Peter turns him into a rabbit; North Pole dreams
occurrences.label: Feeble-minded boy — North Pole dreams
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Dream of a feeble-minded fourteen-year-old boy, presented by Mr. Kadinsky as an analogue to the rainbow dream: "He dreams that he comes into heaven. St. Peter tells him he should go back to the earth. But he does not want to. So St. Peter turns him into a rabbit." Up to age eleven he could keep up at school; then not. Later he dreamed no longer of heaven but of climbing to the North Pole — after which his school performance improved again.

Jung: the unconscious clips the boy's wings because he drifts too far from earth; the North Pole then compensates rather than warns, for "the archetype of the North Pole has a centering meaning" — it is the centre of the world, that is, of the unconscious. Amplified with the Cheops pyramid's polestar-aligned exit and Mithras swinging the Great Bear's shoulder in the Mithraic liturgy.

occurrences.title: St. Sebastian shot with arrows at the pillar
occurrences.label: St. Sebastian shot with arrows at the pillar
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: He is now a sort of St. Sebastian at the pillar.
body: In the Grave-Song, where "malice ever shot its arrows" at his dearest memories "to hit my heart," Jung fixes Nietzsche's pose: "He is now a sort of St. Sebastian at the pillar, a complete victim of certain enemies who are shooting arrows at him". Footnote: "St. Sebastian, third-century Roman soldier and Christian martyr."

The type of the projected enemy: "Their enemies are called parents or school teachers, and later on, the analyst, or the newspapers, or the Jesuits, or the Freemasons" — the figure who absorbs the murder one dare not see in oneself, since "he has become a shadow... he as his own memory, the man of the past, has been killed."

occurrences.title: Actaeon devoured by his own hounds — Diana at the bath
occurrences.label: Actaeon devoured by his own hounds
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: his own hounds, not recognizing him, thereupon tore him to pieces
body: Diana's dark half: "she is also a goddess of destruction and death, whose arrows never miss. She changed the hunter Actaeon, when he secretly watched her bathing, into a stag, and his own hounds, not recognizing him, thereupon tore him to pieces" (¶188).

Jung derives from it "the designation of the lapis as the cervus fugitivus (fugitive stag), and then the rabid dog, who is none other than the vindictive and treacherous aspect of Diana as the new moon" — the mythic source of Philaletha's hydrophobic dog and of the "surprise in the bath" motif shared with the De sulphure parable, where Helios finds Diana and the brother-sister incest ends with both drowned.

image.title: Diana and Actaeon

occurrences.title: Christ appearing as a white stag with four lions — the Saint-Graal
occurrences.label: Christ appearing as a white stag with four lions
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: From the Grail cycle: "it is related that Christ sometimes appeared to the disciples as a white stag with four lions (= four evangelists)" (¶559 n. 9). A Christophany in stag form, flanked by the four beasts of the evangelists — the same quaternity-structure Jung decodes in the Nebuchadnezzar frontispiece's stag with four animals.

Jung cites it as the second leg of his stag dossier (Honorius of Autun's self-renewal allegory, this Grail apparition, and Mercurius-as-stag in alchemy): the stag as Christ-symbol and, alchemically, as the self-renewing Mercurius.

occurrences.title: The white stag with the crucifix between its antlers — St. Hubert / St. Eustace
occurrences.label: The white stag with the crucifix…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: All of a sudden he perceives a shining crucifix between its antlers.
body: Jung's example of hunting "that went wrong and became serious": on a Sunday the hunter sees a white stag he wants to bag by all means — and suddenly perceives a shining crucifix between its antlers. "This is a prey he hasn't dreamed of: it is the Holy Spirit itself whom he meets in the forest." The same story is told of St. Eustace, "another Hubert, so to speak."

Function in the dream interpretation: many people interact playfully with their unconscious — fishing daily in it, even writing newspaper articles about it — until the catch turns out to be the numinosum: the golden fish, the anima, "the being that has no soul and therefore strives after it."

occurrences.title: Stag renewing itself after swallowing the serpent — Honorius of Autun, Speculum de Mysteriis Ecclesiae
occurrences.label: Stag renewing itself after swallowing…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: The patristic source for the stag-as-Christ allegory: self-renewal through taking in the serpent and casting it out at the water. Jung quotes: "They say that the deer, after he has swallowed a serpent, hastens to the water, that by a draught of water he may eject the poison, and then cast his horns and his hair and so take new" (¶559 n. 9).

Jung's frame: "The stag is an allegory of Christ because legend attributes to it the capacity for self-renewal" — the passage underwrites his reading of the stag in the Nebuchadnezzar frontispiece, and anticipates his later alchemical use of the stag (the cervus fugitivus, Mercurius as stag).

occurrences.title: Stag and unicorn as soul and spirit — Lambspringk's emblems
occurrences.label: Stag and unicorn as soul and spirit
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Emblem plate III of Lambspringk's Figurae et emblemata (fig. 240), captioned by Jung: "Stag and unicorn, symbolizing soul and spirit." The stag (cervus fugitivus) and the unicorn alternate as fleeting forms of the transforming substance — Mercurius as the soul-principle chased, captured, and united.

The accompanying poem makes the unicorn's indivisibility the central riddle: "I am the right true Unicorn. / What man can cleave me hoof from horn / And join my body up again / So that it no more falls in twain?" — the One that cannot be divided without perishing, i.e. the unicum of the stone.

occurrences.title: 'Star / Stern' — the Alice Stern love-complex case (Burghölzli, 1904-05)
occurrences.label: Star / Stern' — the Alice Stern love-complex…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Let us call her Alice Stern: we shall be keeping as near the truth as is necessary for the experiment.
body: The founding case-study of the association technique (subject 19, physician, 25): a young man under "adolescent internal conflict" — strict Christian upbringing, secret attachment to a Jewish girl, pseudonymized Alice Stern. Her name constellates everything: star / Stern / Isaac ("Isaac, the son of Abraham, is a fairly frequent though not a current association"), and at pdf p96 a type-table shows star / Miss Stern (an actual person). The complex works through song-fragments — the Erlkönig's "Come with me, sweet games will I play with you," Weber's Jungfernkranz — and through the perseverating "yesterday", plus the slip to love / Stern (star) / son → Isaac!. Jung: "the complex makes use of a mode of reaction that is not usual in this subject"; failures at to kiss; Lore points to the girl's real first name.

occurrences.title: The star taken from the breast and worshipped; the pale blue star in the mandala (patient vision, 8-15 November 1933)
occurrences.label: The star taken from the breast and worshipped
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Then I saw a new pale blue star grow out from the circle and hold in check the red and black teeth. The circle grew stronger and more distinct.
body: On the inescapable black path she wants to pray: "Then I knew that I could only pray to my star. I took it forth from my breast and laid it on the ground and knelt before it." The star is her uniqueness, the Self as microcosm — the Hiranyagarbha golden germ, the blue flower, the pearl. Objectified, it is at once attacked by jagged red and black bands (the destructive powers of the crowd, the banal opinions of the near surroundings, muladhara-black and manipura-red); then "a new pale blue star grow[s] out from the circle and hold[s] in check the red and black teeth" — the mandala of remoteness, anahata's answer, Mara attacking an empty throne. A rite d'entree before the descent; the star, strengthened, returns to her breast.

occurrences.title: The black wall with a star and an eye (patient vision, 18 Mar - 6 May 1931)
occurrences.label: The black wall with a star and an eye
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Upon the wall I saw a star and an eye. I walked along it seeking for some way to penetrate it and pass beyond.
body: Leaving the animals at the golden disk, she walks alone to a black wall — the obstacle, utter darkness — upon which shine a star and an eye. Jung unpacks the pair exhaustively: the star emits light (primitives: stars are holes in the world-envelope through which the empyreum glows; Lucretius' royal idea of the light-emitting eye), the eye receives; star = Yang, eye = Yin; the eye is the way through. Amplified with Horus' sacrificed eye, Wotan's eye at Mimir's well, the autumn day when the sun returns into the womb through the left eye of the goddess, the Upanishad's Indha/Indra in the right eye, Emerson's "the eye is the first circle," and the Trinity-eye of Catholic churches. Entering the eye = entering the mandala's center — or losing oneself in subjective fantasy: "is it a psychological fantasy or is it substantial life?"

occurrences.title: Girl's dream 12 — gnats hide sun, moon, and stars; one star falls on the dreamer
occurrences.label: Girl's dream 12 — one star falls on the dreamer
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1938-39 (dreams dreamt at age eight; presented at ten; died of an infectious disease about a year later)
occurrences.quote: Swarms of gnats hide the sun, moon, and stars, all except one star which then falls on the dreamer.
body: The last dream in the Christmas booklet: "Swarms of gnats hide the sun, moon, and stars, all except one star which then falls on the dreamer."

The cosmic darkness and the single surviving light falling on the dreamer close the series' movement toward death and restoration: Jung found "the uncanny feeling that they foreboded disaster," the compensation showing "a new and rather terrifying vision of life and death, such as one might expect in someone who looks back upon life rather than forward to its natural continuation" (¶537). The girl died of an infectious disease about a year later (¶526).

occurrences.title: The star and moon as witnesses — Epirus love-song (printed 1902)
occurrences.label: The star and moon as witnesses
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1902 (printed version, Zeitschrift des Vereins für Volkskunde XII, p. 159)

jung.locator: fn 20 to ch. IV, The Hymn of Creation (pdf p682)

body: "O maiden, when we kissed, it was night. Who saw us? — A bright star saw us, and the moon saw us, / And it leaned down to the sea and whispered the tidings, / And the sea told the rudder, and the rudder told the sailor, / The sailor made a song, then the neighbours heard it, / Then the priest heard it too and told it to my mother, / From her my father heard it and was livid with anger." Jung quotes the Epirote song of many variants to show "how collective the elements in such an experience are": the star and moon as watchers whose knowledge travels down a chain of nature and society.

occurrences.title: The star-lovers on the river — suicidal youth's night vision (Zurich, c.1900s)
occurrences.label: The star-lovers on the river
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: he became aware that every star was a face, and that all these pairs were lovers, who were carried along locked in a dreaming embrace.
body: A quiet, sentimental youth, jilted, goes to the river at night to drown himself. The stars gleam up from the dark water: "the stars were swimming two by two down the river... every star was a face, and all these pairs were lovers, who were carried along locked in a dreaming embrace." His despair dissolves into certainty of untold treasure hidden in the neighbouring observatory — he is arrested breaking into it at four in the morning.

Jung's reading: "a Dantesque vision" that "transformed him" — he "crossed 'Proserpine's threshold'"; "He did not drown in the river, but in an eternal image, and its beauty perished with him" (¶232). Exhibit A of inflation by a collective image: the "magical représentations collectives" that englobe a personality and disintegrate it (¶¶233–231), operating through his "primitive participation mystique" (¶231).

occurrences.title: Queen Maya's dream: six-rayed star and white elephant — Gandhara relief
occurrences.label: Queen Maya's dream — Gandhara relief
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: fertilization by a theriomorphic symbol, the elephant, who, as Bodhisattva, begets the Buddha.
body: The Buddha's miraculous conception by star, wind ("A wind blew with unknown freshness over lands and seas", ¶491), and the theriomorphic Bodhisattva-elephant (pl. XLIXb, plate at pdf p296). Jung: "In Christian picture-language the unicorn, as well as the dove, is a symbol of the spermatic Word or Spirit" (¶492); the four genies of the quarters answer the Wise Men.

image.title: Dream Queen Maya BM OA 1932.7-9.1

occurrences.title: 'I am a star wandering together with you' — Mithraic Liturgy, hieros logos
occurrences.label: I am a star wandering together with you
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The hieros logos of the papyrus Dieterich published as Eine Mithrasliturgie, in which the neophyte, filled with religious ecstasy, declares: "I am a star wandering together with you and shining up from the depths" (¶130).

Jung's reading: the idea of becoming a god is age-old — old belief relegated it to the time after death, "but the mystery cults bring it about in this world" (¶133). The Isis mysteries parallel: the neophyte crowned with palm leaves, set on a pedestal and worshipped as Helios (¶130, pl. VI). Christian echoes: Hippolytus' "You have become God" (¶132), Psalm 82:6. The stars that float down from the opened sun-disc after the second prayer (¶¶135, 143) belong to the same visionary sequence.

occurrences.title: 'A star shone in heaven beyond the stars' — Ignatius of Antioch, To the Ephesians XIX
occurrences.label: A star shone in heaven beyond the stars
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Asia Minor (en route to martyrdom, Rome)

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

occurrences.quote: A star shone in heaven beyond the stars, and its light was unspeakable, and its newness caused astonishment
body: Ignatius on the manifestation of Christ: "A star shone in heaven beyond the stars, and its light was unspeakable, and its newness caused astonishment, and all the other stars, with the sun and moon, gathered in chorus round this star."

Jung's reading: Christian assimilation of the One among the many scintillae. Just as Khunrath among the dispersed sparks of the world-soul stresses the single "scintilla perfecta" (the Monad, the Sun, the Deity), so the Ignatian star outshines and gathers the chorus of all other lights. "Psychologically, the One Scintilla or Monad is to be regarded as a symbol of the self" (¶388) — the monadic luminosity that later, in ¶396, "readily assumes the shape of a mandala and must then be interpreted as the self."

occurrences.title: Feeling of relation to the stars as first symptom (patient: male schizophrenic, Zürich)
occurrences.label: Feeling of relation to the stars…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: case-index [25], ref. book p402 ≈ pdf p369 (harvested from index, pdf p580)

body: A male schizophrenic's first symptom was "feeling of relation to the stars" (case [25], book p402n). The index clusters the motif: "star: mystic identification with, 402n", "as brothers, 402", "compulsion by, 67, 415" — the psychotic version of the initiate's kinship with the cosmos ("I am a star wandering with you", Mithraic liturgy).
Verbatim (case-index): "Male schizophrenic whose first symptom was feeling of relation to the stars. — 402n"

occurrences.title: Ray of light imprints a star on a child's forehead (Visions Seminar, 9 Dec 1930)
occurrences.label: Ray of light imprints a star…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: In the vision in question, a ray of light strikes a child on the forehead, imprinting a star.
body: Editor's footnote identifying the Western parallel Jung adduced for the ājñā cakra ("located between the eyebrows... here the command of the leader, the guru, is received from above"): in the patient's vision "a ray of light strikes a child on the forehead, imprinting a star" — cross-referenced to The Secret of the Golden Flower, where the same forehead-point carries the light-circulation.

occurrences.title: 'Extraction of thought' by the Chaldaeans of the Euphrates — Platonis liber quartorum
occurrences.label: Extraction of thought' by the Chaldaeans…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Euphrates (Harran — Sabaeans/Harranites) → Theatrum chemicum V, Strasbourg
occurrences.yearDisplay: printed Theatrum chemicum V, 1622, p. 144 (Harranite material older, ~10th c. Latin)

jung.workTitle: The Spirit in Man, Art and Literature (CW15)
jung.locator: fn 46 to Paracelsus the Physician (pdf p161)

occurrences.quote: they were the first to accomplish the extraction of thought
body: The Harranite treatise spuriously fathered on Plato records the oldest claim of its lineage: "Those seated by the river Euphrates are the Chaldaeans, who are skilled in the stars and in judging them, and they were the first to accomplish the extraction of thought." Its companion line makes the opus astral through and through: "They who sit by the banks of the Euphrates convert gross bodies into a simple appearance, with the help of the movement of the higher bodies" (Theatrum chemicum, 1622, V, p. 144).

Jung's editors add the genealogy: these Euphrates dwellers "were probably the Sabaeans or Harranites, to whose learned activities we owe the transmission of a great many scientific treatises of Alexandrian origin," and "here, as in Paracelsus, alchemical transformation is connected with the influence of the stars." Jung invites the comparison with his saying that the Archasius "attracts science and prudence" — thought itself as a substance drawn down by the stars.

occurrences.title: Van Gogh's Starry Night — stars as shining disks from a dream (Saint-Rémy, 1889)
occurrences.label: Van Gogh's Starry Night
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: There the stars are painted as large shining disks, though the eye never sees them like that.
body: Jung adduces van Gogh's Starry Night as a modern, artistically self-conscious analogue of the round "signs in the heavens": the stars are painted as large shining disks, though the eye never sees them so. Van Gogh himself called the picture's mood a "pantheistic frenzy," a "remnant of an apocalyptic fantasy," and compared the starry disks to "a group of living figures who are like one of us." Jung notes the painting "is supposed to be derived from a dream."

The footnote sits inside Flying Saucers (1958), where the painted disk answers the round Ufo: both are contemporary round-symbol products alongside mandala and rotundum (cf. index print pp.387, 423f). The star that stares like a living being is the Ufo's oldest sibling — archetypal roundness breaking into the sky.

occurrences.title: The two barbarian slaves of the Boboli Gardens, Florence (Roman, Hellenistic type)
occurrences.label: The two barbarian slaves of the Boboli Gardens…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the stone speaks, it is really the stone.
body: "Those two figures of the barbarians are suggested by the stone, the stone speaks, it is really the stone; while in Michelangelo's figures the stone has just nothing to say... I had a feeling of nausea; I said, 'Now this is hysteria'". Jung sends the seminar from the Medici tombs to the Boboli Gardens as a lesson in the animation of matter: the antique sculptor let the marble say what it wanted to become, while the Baroque beginnings (and the Gothic, which "suggested wood into the stone") impose form on the material. One of the seminar's clearest images of the spirit as the inside of things.

occurrences.title: The statue erected, filled with light and divinity — Book of Komarios
occurrences.label: The statue erected, filled with light…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The house was sealed, and the statue was erected, filled with light and divinity.
body: One of the earliest Greek treatises: after the body was hidden in darkness the spirit "found it full of light"; body, soul, and spirit "all became one; in this the mystery is hidden... the house was sealed, and the statue was erected, filled with light and divinity."
Jung at cw14 ¶559: here the statue "evidently denotes the end-product of the process, the lapis Philosophorum or its equivalent" — the oldest stratum of the Adam-as-lifeless-statue tradition.

occurrences.title: Schiller's Juno Ludovisi — beauty against the opposites
occurrences.label: Schiller's Juno Ludovisi
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Schiller's Letters on Aesthetic Education (1795); bust is a Roman copy

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: In the Letters on the Aesthetic Education of Man, Schiller's medicine for the split between civilized and barbarous man is the contemplation of beauty — and "as an example of beauty he chose the Juno Ludovisi, an antique bust."

Jung is half-baffled, half-mocking: "I think he must have had such a bust in his study, and he probably contemplated it and thought it a most marvelous face." The aesthetic solution is "very weak... like trying to put out a great fire with a bottle of lemonade" — but Schiller was "the first German to become aware of the problem of the opposites in human nature," the line that runs through Schopenhauer to Nietzsche.
Verbatim: "Curiously enough, as an example of beauty he chose thejuno Ludovisi, an antique bust that has nothing particularly interesting about it." (pdf p146, OCR as in text)

occurrences.title: The water extracted from the hearts of statues — Senior (Ibn Umail)
occurrences.label: The water extracted from the hearts of statues
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: That is the statue from whose heart the water is extracted.
body: Senior speaks of "the water that is extracted from the hearts of statues." He is reported to have opened tombs and sarcophagi in Egypt and removed the mummies (mumia as medicament); he describes a statue of Hermes Trismegistus in an underground chapel: "in it he has described that whole science, as it were, in the figure, and taught his wisdom in the stone." Maier comments: "That is the statue from whose heart the water is extracted," and mentions an oracular stone statue of Hermes in Achaia Pharis.
Jung at cw14 ¶560-561; Lully's parallel "oil that is extracted from the heart of statues... by the washing of water and the drying of fire."

occurrences.title: Pygmalion and Galatea — Ovid, Metamorphoses X
occurrences.label: Pygmalion and Galatea — Ovid, Metamorphoses X
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: he made a beautiful statue which through the grace of the gods came to life, and since it was a woman, Galatea, he lived with her-she became real.
body: The sculptor-king who, disillusioned with women, carved an ivory woman, named her Galatea, loved her, and — Venus granting — saw her come to life. The type-myth of the image dormant in matter that art wakes.

Jung's reading: the surface metaphor for Nietzsche's "image slumbering in the stone" (Zarathustra's hammer chapter), but "a bit more than a mere mythological metaphor." Every artist feels the material contain life — the empty page's "magnetic charm," the color that "has its own life". "Of course it is a sort of sex allegory one could say, as in the case of Pygmalion, but that doesn't mean that it comes out of sex. It rather means that the creative instinct is so strong that even sex is pulled into it and made serviceable."

occurrences.title: Houdon's bust of Voltaire — foyer of the Comédie-Française
occurrences.label: Houdon's bust of Voltaire
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Discussing Nietzsche coquetting "like an old maid… with his own malice," Jung reaches for the embodiment of the real thing: "Whenever I read such a passage I think of the bust of Voltaire by Houdon in the foyer of the Comédie Française: that exceedingly malicious and ironical look. It needs a Frenchman-it needs just Monsieur Voltaire-to have that malice".

Voltaire's malice stays light to the deathbed: asked by the abbé if he regretted his sins, "Mais oui, je regrette tous mes péchés, surtout ceux que je n'ai pas commis" — "the sublime and the ridiculous in one." Nietzsche by contrast "is pathetisch, an expressive actor of his own tragedy": his Bosheit "weighs about ten tons, it is not light: it has not the sting of a wasp". The marble face of Voltaire is Jung's standing counter-image to German heaviness.

occurrences.title: Steissbart, the dwarfish gnome-mind of the mother (Barlach, Der Tote Tag)
occurrences.label: Steissbart, the dwarfish gnome-mind…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Among Jung's chthonic-animus figures: "If you have read Der Tote Tag by Barlach, a sort of mythological drama, you will remember a figure there with the grotesque name Steissbart, he is also the dwarfish gnomelike mind of the mother."

The cluster: the Syrian-Egyptian Bes in Constantinople — "he is the tutor of Horus, and he is always connected with the mother goddess. In Karnak, at the entrance of the temple of Mut, there are two figures of Bes... he is the animus of the mother" — and the grotesque gods of the Ptolemaic syncretism: "the gods in primitive tribes usually look absurd and paradoxical, because they express the earth element."

occurrences.title: Archetype of the self in mediumistic communications — Stewart E. White's 'Betty' books
occurrences.label: Archetype of the self in mediumistic…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: USA (books published 1940-42; Jung's attention drawn by Fritz Künkel, Los Angeles)

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: The rare positive exception among spiritualistic communications: "a remarkable case Stewart E. White has described in a number of books. Here the communications have a much profounder content than usual. For instance, a great many archetypal ideas were produced, among them the archetype of the self, so that one might almost think there had been borrowings from my writings" (¶599). Jung rules out cryptomnesic reproduction: "It appears to be a case of genuine, spontaneous production of a collective archetype... since the archetype of the self is met with everywhere in mythology as well as in the products of individual fantasy."

He reads spiritualism overall as "a spontaneous attempt of the unconscious to become conscious in a collective form", and calls The Road I Know "an admirable introduction to the method of 'active imagination'". A 1948 bridge-case between mediumship, active imagination, and the self.

occurrences.title: Basuto legend: the hero who became a stone and was thrown across the river (transitus)
occurrences.label: Basuto legend — the hero who became a stone…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "In a Basuto legend reported by Frobenius, the hero is left stranded by his pursuers on the bank of a river. He changes himself into a stone, and his pursuers throw him across to the other side. This is the motif of the transitus: the 'other side' is the same as eternity" (cw13 ¶133).

Jung sets it beside the lapis' incorruptibility: "the ancient idea that the body of a saint becomes stone. Thus the Apocalypse of Elijah says of those who escape persecution by the Anti-Messiah: 'The Lord shall take unto him their spirit and their souls, their flesh shall be made stone, no wild beast shall devour them till the last day of the great judgment'" (¶133). Stone = immortality = the crossing.

occurrences.title: Stone that speaks vs stone whipped to hysteria — Boboli barbarians and Michelangelo's Medici tombs
occurrences.label: Stone that speaks vs stone whipped to hysteria
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: you feel that stone has had the word!
body: Jung's own sight-seeing contrast, offered as evidence that "the projection into matter is... an indispensable quality of art": the antique barbarian figures of the Boboli Gardens "consist of stone, represent the spirit of stone," while Michelangelo's Medici figures show stone "brought to a super-life... hysterical and exaggerated." The same gradient runs Norman → Gothic ("stone behaves like a plant"), Greek temple → Abu Simbel, and culminates in the Indian cave temples where man "makes it jump, fills it with an uncanny sort of life which destroys the peculiar spirit of the stone."

His verdict is aesthetic-metapsychological: "it is always to the detriment of art when matter has no say in the game of the artist" — the law the alchemists obeyed in seeking the stone "which contains a ghost".

occurrences.title: Stone cube with Latin inscription — Bollingen Tower
occurrences.label: Stone cube with Latin inscription
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.locator: editorial note to 'On the Rosarium Philosophorum' (pdf p1060 n.2)

body: The CW18 apparatus to Jung's 1937 Rosarium lectures records, in its own words: "Jung carved the Latin text on a cube of hewn stone at his 'Tower' in Bollingen, in 1950" — the Bollingen stone as Jung's private opus-endpoint, cut and inscribed the year Mysterium Coniunctionis was in progress. Attached here to Rosarium/alchemical material, the "Latin text" is plausibly an alchemical tag; the full inscription (including the 75th-birthday dedication and the Philemon-epigraph lines) is documented in Memories, Dreams, Reflections, pp. 226f./215f. — text to be pinned before this stub goes rich. Subject is Jung himself: the stone as temenos-marker and self-monument (cf. the 1927/1950 'orphan, alone' complex the MDR chapter reads).
Verbatim: Jung carved the Latin text on a cube of hewn stone at his “Tower” in Bollingen, in 1950. Cf. Memories, Dreams, Reflections, pp. 226f./215f.

occurrences.title: The carbuncle under the unicorn's horn — Wolfram von Eschenbach
occurrences.label: The carbuncle under the unicorn's horn
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "According to legend, this stone may be found under the horn of the unicorn, as Wolfram von Eschenbach says: We caught the beast called Unicorn / That knows and loves a maiden best / And falls asleep upon her breast; / We took from underneath his horn / The splendid male carbuncle stone / Sparkling against the white skull-bone" (¶552). "The alchemists attribute the same qualities to their stone, calling it the 'carbuncle'" — the treasure hard to attain hidden at the point of the tamed beast, taken while it sleeps in the virgin's lap.
The white skull-bone under the sparkling male stone: death's field as the ground of the lapis.

occurrences.title: The Eben-ezer stone, 'Up to here God has helped us' — Israel (~11th c. BCE)
occurrences.label: The Eben-ezer stone, Up to here God has helped…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Eben-ezer, between Mizpah and Shen (I Samuel 7:12)

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: Jung's example, in the discussion of Nietzsche, of the universal drive to give symbols permanence: "every symbol seeks to be concretized. With this in mind, when we read in the Old Testament that it was engraved upon the stone, 'Up to here God has helped us,' we know that it was done in the effort to hold on to the faith that had brought them that far". Samuel raises the stone, names it Eben-ezer ("stone of help"), after the Lord's deliverance of Israel from the Philistines. Jung sets it in a row with Egypt's "pyramids and embalming in order to concretize the principle of immortality" and with Nietzsche's need "to materialize his symbol" — the creative mind's urge to get the fantasy "down in some relatively permanent form in order to hold it."

occurrences.title: Estsanatlehi, the turquoise goddess ('the woman who rejuvenates herself') — Navaho
occurrences.label: Estsanatlehi, the turquoise goddess — Navaho
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the days of the great darkness the ancestors saw the Sky Father descending and the Earth Mother rising to meet him; "they united, and on the top of the mountain where the union took place the ancestors found a little figure made of turquoise. This turned into (or in another version gave birth to) Estsanatlehi, 'the woman who rejuvenates or transforms herself'" (cw13 ¶130). Mother of the twin gods who slew the primordial monsters; the sun from the turquoise beads of her right breast, the moon from white shell beads of her left; reborn by rolling a piece of skin from under her left breast; so sacred "that no image may be made of her".

Jung: "This matriarchal goddess is obviously an anima figure who at the same time symbolizes the self. Hence her stone-nature, her immortality, her four daughters born from the body, plus one from the spirit, her duality as sun and moon..." (¶131) — and she "contains the secret of the precious stone."

occurrences.title: The facultas formatrix of the anima telluris — pictured stones in the earth's womb (Kepler)
occurrences.label: The facultas formatrix of the anima telluris
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)
