body: Kepler's proofs that the earth is animated by an anima telluris: constant sub-surface temperature; the production of metals, minerals and fossils; above all "the facultas formatrix, which is similar to that of the womb and can bring forth in the bowels of the earth shapes that are otherwise found only outside—ships, fishes, kings, popes, monks, soldiers, etc."; and the practice of geometry in the five regular bodies and six-cornered crystal figures — all "from an original impulse, independent of the reflection and ratiocination of man."

Jung's reading: "The seat of astrological synchronicity is not in the planets but in the earth; not in matter, but in the anima telluris" (¶936). The pictured stones are the object-world counterpart of the dreams of heads and squares in living rock at ¶945 — nature herself picturing.

occurrences.title: The Flint Man of the Iroquois twin-brothers tale
occurrences.label: The Flint Man of the Iroquois twin-brothers tale
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "Begotten in a miraculous manner in the body of a virgin, a pair of twins were born, one of whom came forth in the normal way, while the other sought an abnormal exit and emerged from the armpit, thereby killing his mother. This twin had a body made of flint. He was wicked and cruel, unlike his normally born brother" (cw13 ¶132).

In the Sioux version "the mother was a tortoise"; among the Wichita "the saviour was the great star in the south, and he performed his work of salvation on earth as the 'flint man.' His son was called the 'young flint.'" Jung: "In this myth, just as in medieval alchemy, the saviour coincides with the stone, the star, the 'son,' who is 'super omnia lumina'" (¶132).

occurrences.title: The analyst hammering her head with a stone — Prince's patient, dream 3 (Boston, ~1905–06)
occurrences.label: The analyst hammering her head with a stone
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: picked up a stone and hammered her head, and with every blow you said, 'I can't be bothered, I can't be bothered.' And every blow sent a weight down into her heart so she felt heavy-hearted.
body: Dream 3, set once more on the rocky path of Watts's "Love and Life": barefoot, stones hurting, the analyst appears, refuses help — "you must help yourself. Let me see if I cannot hammer it into your head" — picks up a stone and hammers her head, saying with every blow "I can't be bothered," each blow dropping a weight into her heart. The material: the previous day's telephone refusal ("I cannot possibly come to see you today... you must not depend on me") and her pre-sleep thought "I must not bother him"; "If my heart was not like a stone, I should weep" (¶172). Jung: Prince takes the manifest content literally and finds no wish; but the torture is the wished-for treatment — "in the dream she is treated, though in a new and remarkable way" (¶173) — and "the wish-fulfilment lies in the greatest disappointment" (¶174).

occurrences.title: 'O stone of the wise, how thou shinest!' — manic ecstasy verse of Case D (St. Pirminsberg, 1886)
occurrences.label: O stone of the wise, how thou shinest!
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: O stone of the wise, how thou shinest! O D—(his own name), what brilliance!
body: In a "real ecstasy" of writing, the vagabond painter of Case D — who styled himself founder of God's kingdom, equal of the pope, a new Messiah — produced: "The greatest artist of all times past and to come shines the shoes of the unfortunate, polishes the floor in St. Pirminsberg... O stone of the wise, how thou shinest! O D—(his own name), what brilliance!" The alchemical lapis-language erupts unbidden in megalomanic rapture: shining stone, brilliance, and the self addressed as the radiant thing.

Jung's frame is clinical (unbounded self-glorification "like a red thread"), not alchemical — but the verse is a dated natural datum for the lapis as self-symbol. Parallels: lapis-image-slumbering-stone-zarathustra-1883 · scarab-golden-dog-transformation-penitentiary-1895.

occurrences.title: Mithras born from the rock (petra genetrix)
occurrences.label: Mithras born from the rock (petra genetrix)
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "The stone as the birthplace of the gods (e.g., the birth of Mithras from a stone) is attested by primitive legends of stone-births which go back to ideas that are even more ancient" (cw13 ¶128) — Jung's bridge from the earliest Greek alchemy's stone-God-image to pre-alchemical ethnology (Australian child-stones follow immediately).
The rock-born Mithras, wearing the Phrygian cap and grasping torch/dagger, is the standard Mithraic image of the god springing adult from stone — the saviour who coincides with the stone.

occurrences.title: Moses as stone — 'stonehorned, stonebearded, heart of stone' (Joyce, Ulysses)
occurrences.label: Moses as stone — stonehorned, stonebearded…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1922 (1st edn.); Jung cites the 10th printing, Paris 1928, pp. 134-35

jung.workTitle: The Spirit in Man, Art and Literature (CW15)

occurrences.quote: that stone effigy in frozen music, horned and terrible, of the human form divine, that eternal symbol of wisdom and prophecy
body: In a passage of Ulysses (pp. 134-35 of the 1928 printing Jung owned) Stephen/Bloom's day sideswipes Moses — "who refused to be cowed by the might of Egypt" — through a run of petrifying epithets: "that stone effigy in frozen music, horned and terrible, of the human form divine, that eternal symbol of wisdom and prophecy... a man supple in combat: stonehorned, stonebearded, heart of stone." The horned stone Moses carries the whole Exodus numinosum in a modernist pile-up.

Jung reports these as "the magic words that sent me to sleep": "The two passages contained the narcotic that switched off my consciousness, activating a still unconscious train of thought which consciousness would only have disturbed. As I later discovered, it dawned on me here for the first time what the author was doing" — his own hypnotic threshold into the book, and the origin of his reading of Joyce's deliberate abaissement.

occurrences.title: The Stone 'near to the fire' — Pseudo-Aristotle in the Rosarium philosophorum
occurrences.label: The Stone 'near to the fire'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Choose for your Stone him through whom kings are honoured in their crowns, and through whom physicians heal their sick, for he is near to the fire.
body: A Pseudo-Aristotle quotation printed in the Rosarium philosophorum (1550, fol. q): the alchemist must choose for his Stone one through whom kings are honoured in their crowns and physicians heal their sick — "for he is near to the fire". Jung cites it in "Concerning Rebirth" (¶238) as the alchemical projection of the inner friend of the soul: the "certain other one within" (aliquem alium internum) of the alchemists' meditatio, exteriorized into a substance. The Stone here is a person to be approached in colloquy, not a reagent — the same grammar as the Tractatus aureus speech and the prayer of Astrampsychos.

occurrences.title: Orestes cured by a stone (Laconia, per Pausanias)
occurrences.label: Orestes cured by a stone
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "For example, the madness of Orestes was cured by a stone in Laconia" (cw13 ¶129; footnote to Pausanias, Descriptio Graeciae).

Jung lists it in the magic-stone cluster: "Zeus found respite from the sorrows of love by sitting on a stone in Leukadia. In India, a young man will tread upon a stone in order to obtain firmness of character, and a bride will do the same to ensure her own faithfulness"; the electors of the king stood on stones "in order to give their vote permanence" (Saxo Grammaticus); "the green stone of Arran was used both for healing and for taking oaths on" (¶129).
The stone heals madness, gives permanence and firmness — the psychically stabilizing function Jung later assigns the lapis.

occurrences.title: Quetzalcoatl, 'priest of the precious stone' (Aztec cycle)
occurrences.label: Quetzalcoatl, 'priest of the precious stone'
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "For instance, the mother of Quetzalcoatl was made pregnant by a precious green stone. He himself had the cognomen 'priest of the precious stone' and wore a mask made of turquoise. The precious green stone was an animating principle and was placed in the mouth of the dead. Man's original home was the 'bowl of precious stone'" (cw13 ¶132).

The Aztec cycle gives Jung the fullest American stone-body complex: among the Taos Pueblos "a virgin was made pregnant by beautiful stones and bore a hero son, who, owing to Spanish influence, assumed the aspect of the Christ child"; the Natchez culture hero "changed himself into a stone statue, from which the priestly chieftains of the Natchez were descended"; petrifaction legends of Peru and Colombia point to a megalithic stone-cult (¶132).

occurrences.title: The rock of the mosque of Omar that wanted to fly up with Mohammed
occurrences.label: The rock of the mosque of Omar that wanted…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the Mohammedan legend of the rock in the mosque of Omar, at Jerusalem, which wanted to fly up with Mohammed when he ascended to heaven.
body: The Mohammedan legend of the sacred rock in the mosque of Omar, which "wanted to fly up with Mohammed when he ascended to heaven" — the stone seized by the same levitation as the ascending prophet, held down (in the fuller legend) only by an iron nail.

Jung cites it (Part II ch. 2, n. 99) beside the alchemists' insistence on meditation and the volatile's longing to rise: the stone that would fly is the folk-religious twin of the volatile alchemical substance and of the "rock" of the philosophers that must be fixed by art. It belongs with the corpus subtile motifs of ascent (Philalethes' pole-star heart of Mercurius, n. 129).
