occurrences.title: The seven eyes of the Lord on the corner-stone — Zechariah
occurrences.label: The seven eyes of the Lord on the corner-stone
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Jerusalem (vision); read as scintillae by the Latin alchemists

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: And they shall rejoice and see the tin plummet in the hand of Zorobabel. These are the seven eyes of the Lord that run to and fro through the whole earth.
body: Zechariah's seventh vision (Zech 4:10): "These are the seven eyes of the Lord that run to and fro through the whole earth"; with 3:9, the seven eyes set on the corner-stone of the new temple. Jung cites the passage (¶245 n16) for the alchemical scintillae — the sparks of light appearing in the dark substance at the end of the nigredo and the beginning of the albedo, where the white stone shows on the vessel's edge "like Oriental gems, like fish's eyes" (Hollandus; Lagneus). The seven eyes connect the Stone with the seven planetary gods the alchemists depict in a cave under the earth (Mylius 1622) — "the sleepers enchained in Hades" (Berthelot), alluding to the legend of the seven sleepers.

occurrences.title: Taj Mahal — 'a heavenly dream crystallized in stone' (Agra, 1632–53)
occurrences.label: Taj Mahal — a heavenly dream crystallized…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In a world of tyranny and cruelty, a heavenly dream crystallized in stone: the Taj Mahal.
body: Shah Jehan's white-marble mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, on the Yamuna at Agra. Jung visited during his 1938 India journey and wrote it up in "The Dreamlike World of India."

Jung's reading: Islam in India is a religion of longing — "an ardent longing and even greed for God; I would not call it love" (¶990) — but in the Moguls that longing crystallized into beauty: "a heavenly dream crystallized in stone," the one place where the hidden "beauty of the Islamic Eros has been revealed by a well-nigh divine miracle." Deliberately anti-symbolic: "It is thoroughly un-Indian… It is Eros in its purest form; there is nothing mysterious, nothing symbolic about it. It is the sublime expression of human love for a human being." He pairs it with rotundum-stupa-sanchi-globe-india-250bce: the Taj as "the secret of Islam," Sanchi as "the secret of India" (¶992).

occurrences.title: The Stone that speaks — 'Protect me and I will protect thee' (Tractatus aureus)
occurrences.label: The Stone that speaks
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Latin West (ed. Ars chemica, 1566; material Hermetic, older)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Protect me and I will protect thee. Give me what is mine that I may help thee.
body: In the Tractatus aureus the Stone cries out to the sons of the wise: "Protect me and I will protect thee. Give me what is mine that I may help thee." A scholiast adds that the seeker after truth "hears both the Stone and the Philosopher speaking as if out of one mouth" — and the Philosopher is Hermes, the Stone identical with Mercurius, the Latin Hermes (cw09i ¶238). Jung uses the passage to show the alchemists' colloquy: a two-way address in which the projected transformation-substance answers back. The Stone is "like a teacher mediating between the stone and the disciple".

Same formula, different work: the Rosarium has the lapis say "Protege me, protegam te. Largire mihi ius meum, ut te adiuvem" (cw12 ¶155) — rosarium-lapis-protege-me-1550. Distinct loci (Tractatus aureus vs Rosarium; colloquy/Mercurius vs companion/self), kept separate, cross-linked (batch 2).

occurrences.title: Twelve-faceted blue crystal of the Cairo museum — the mana number twelve
occurrences.label: Twelve-faceted blue crystal of the Cairo museum
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In the Musee Egyptien at Cairo there is a beautiful blue crystal-well, it is made of glass-that represents the number twelve.
body: In the Egyptian Museum, Cairo, "a beautiful blue crystal — well, it is made of glass — that represents the number twelve": each of its twelve surfaces a triangle, another mana number, so the whole object is mana and "probably used for magic purposes." Exhibit A in Jung's account of holy numbers: numbers were first qualities, not quantities — geometrical designs carrying mana (all primaries one to nine, then constructed numbers like twelve and twenty-one), as with the primitive chief who knows his 650 cattle individually by name.

occurrences.title: Stork in the thunderstorm dream — 11-year-old girl (Zurich, 1912)
occurrences.label: Stork in the thunderstorm dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I was with other children in a clearing in a wood, surrounded by beautiful firtrees. It began to rain, there was thunder and lightning, and it grew dark. Then I suddenly saw a stork in the air.
body: A fragment: children in a clearing ringed by fir-trees; rain, thunder, lightning, darkness; "Then I suddenly saw a stork in the air." Jung pairs it with the Indo-Germanic thunderstorm mythology of Kuhn and Steinthal: the storm as "the cohabitation of Father Heaven and Mother Earth, where the lightning takes over the role of the winged phallus," the stork in flight "just the same thing, a winged phallus" (¶507). The child's associations confirm psychosexual fertilization-ideas: the drowned uncle, "wouldn't the baby drown in the water, too?", the doctor mixing her sent-in urine "like syrup, which babies grow from" (¶508) — drowning symbolism self-interpreted as pregnancy fantasy (¶510). Mythological strata, Jung notes, are "still active in modern individuals" (¶507).

occurrences.title: The Sufi cosmogonic bull: God kills the world-bull, its left horn is the earth
occurrences.label: The Sufi cosmogonic bull
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: It is the same idea, a violent creative impulse, a passion through which creation comes about. Without that nothing happens.
body: "According to the cosmogonic myth of the Sufis, a Mohammedan sect, God created the world in the form of an immense bull; he then killed the bull, transformed him into stone, and threw him into the sea; and the bull sank down till only his left horn was still sticking out of the waters, and that left horn is the earth." Jung's use: creation comes from a violent creative impulse, a passion — kill it and "everything becomes petrified"; keep those powers alive and you continue to create.

occurrences.title: Sufi secret teaching: God appears as man, as pure white light, as a blade of grass
occurrences.label: Sufi secret teaching
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: East Africa (reported by Jung's head man)
occurrences.quote: And to explain the third form, my head man smiled and picked up a blade of grass, saying: 'God can appear like that.
body: Jung reports a "sort of secret teaching" of the Sufis, "who practice a form of Mohammedan mysticism", as told by his head man on the African trip: God appears in three forms. First as an ordinary man, recognizable only to those who can chant the chapters of the Koran — greet him with "Salem Alaikum" and all wishes are granted. Second "as a pure white light, not like a flame, not like a fire or a lantern".

Cited in the row of spring/resurrection symbols around the patient's visions — the divine in its smallest, greenest manifestation, parallel to the Hindu god "in his origin... called the green leaf", Eleusis's wheat, and the green Osiris.

occurrences.title: Sulcus primigenius — the magical furrow of Roman city foundation
occurrences.label: Sulcus primigenius
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: from the founding of Rome (trad. 753 BCE)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: "In the foundation of a Roman city, for instance, they moved in a circle, the sulcus primigenius, around the fundus in the centre, they went with a plough in the way of the sun, making a furrow around that central place." Jung's point in the machine-mandala lecture: "the rotating idea is in fact necessary to bring about the magic circle around the sacred place within" — circumambulation creates the temenos, as the mandala's rotation does. Local field-trip footnote: the excavated castellum of Irgenhausen near Pfaffikon, with its fundus in the centre, an omnibus ride from Zurich (irgenhausen-roman-castellum-fundus). Cited in the Golden Flower commentary, CW 13, par. 36.

occurrences.title: Sulphur the prisoner in the grove of Venus — 'De sulphure' parable
occurrences.label: Sulphur the prisoner in the grove of Venus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Sulphur is not only the 'medicina' but also the 'medicus'—the wounded physician.
body: An alchemist seeking sulphur comes to the grove of Venus and hears Saturn's voice: Sulphur "is held a prisoner at the command of his own mother" — praised as "the 'artificer of a thousand things,' as the heart of all things, as that which endows living things with understanding, as the begetter of every flower and blossom on herb and tree, and finally as the 'painter of all colours'" (¶140). Jung: "This might well be a description of Eros," imprisoned "because... he had shown himself too obliging towards his mother."

The sequel is the allegory's dream-tableau (¶144): Sal wounds Sulphur with an "incurable wound"; the blood flows as "whitest milk," becomes a river; Diana bathes; prince Sol plunges in and both drown; their souls refuse "bodies so polluted"; the adept finds Sulphur's corpse and pieces of it fail in every hand. Conclusion: "Sulphur is not only the 'medicina' but also the 'medicus' — the wounded physician."

occurrences.title: Aten — the disc of the sun rejoicing in its two horizons (Amarna)
occurrences.label: Aten — the disc of the sun rejoicing…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "In Egypt the positive celestial body of the sun is the important thing; therefore in the time of Amenhotep IV the symbol was no longer the disc and the serpent, but was the disc of the sun rejoicing in its two horizons — the worship of the positive principle par excellence."

Jung's counter-case within the sun-and-serpent family: Akhenaten strips the serpent (the earth, the Yin) away and worships the pure positive principle — exactly what Zarathustra does in throwing only the golden ball, leaving his disciples to add the serpent.

occurrences.title: The Aton reform of Amenophis IV — the sun-disc as sole god (Egypt, c. 1350 BCE)
occurrences.label: The Aton reform of Amenophis IV
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The climax of Egyptian solar syncretism. Local gods — "Amon of Thebes, Horus of the East, Horus of Edfu, Khnum of Elephantine, Atum of Heliopolis" — had all been identified with Ra; the composite Amon-Ra-Harmachis-Atum was invoked as "the only god, in truth, the living one." Then "Amenophis IV... replaced all former gods by the 'great living disc of the sun'" (¶147).

Jung's reading, with Erman: "it was not a sun-god who was adored, but the material sun itself, which, by the hands of his beams, bestowed upon living beings that 'eternal life' which was in him" (fig. 5). Psychologically the reform is "a valuable work of interpretation": the bull, ram, crocodile and pile-dwelling gods are united in the sun-disc, their attributes shown compatible with those of the sun (¶148) — the clearest ancient case of libido-symbols being reduced to a common denominator.

image.title: Akhenaten and the his family worshipping the Aten

occurrences.title: The dead Pharaoh embarks in the ship of the sun (Egypt)
occurrences.label: The dead Pharaoh embarks in the ship of the sun
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: The Pharaoh climbs into the sun bark and travels through the night and conquers the serpent, and then rises again with the god.
body: The dead Pharaoh descends to the underworld and boards the sun-bark, "travels through the night and conquers the serpent, and then rises again with the god, and is riding over the heavens for all eternity." Later even nobles friendly with the Pharaoh climbed into the ship of Ra. Jung seals the maṇipūra argument (escape from personal futility to a nontemporal existence) with his excavation memory: a workman tucked his dead baby in a reed basket inside a noble's tomb door, "so that the baby... should rise with the noble on the great day of judgment."

occurrences.title: Hippolytus reproaches Christians who prostrate themselves before the rising sun (Rome, c. 2nd-3rd c.)
occurrences.label: Hippolytus reproaches Christians…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the early Christians saluted the rising sun as if it were Christ himself.
body: "St. Hippolytus wrote that he himself had seen Christians prostrating themselves before the sun, shouting: 'Have pity upon us'; and he reproached them for it". Jung uses the passage to fix the origin of Christian sun symbolism: Christ as the new light was saluted as the rising sun before the church rationalized the image "with a certain purpose... to assimilate the Mithraic cult, just as they usurped the birthday of Mithra (25 December)" — the "new sun of justice with salvation under its wings" of Malachi 4:2 completing the assimilation. The same sun-symbol appears head-for-head in the Autun figure (cf. christ-figure-headless-sun-disk-autun-cathedral-1135).

occurrences.title: Vision: rider, self-baptizer, wheat on the water, the sun city and the fire ordeal (8 Dec 1930)
occurrences.label: Vision — rider, self-baptizer, wheat…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A man on horseback throws grains of wheat onto a mountain stream — "the minute that the wheat fell upon the water it sprang up into fully ripe stalks"; below, a man baptizes himself. Passing a defile, the rider (the Indian) comes out into full sunlight before a white city of many domes where the crowd worships a golden sun; he holds his face over a fire unharmed; arrows fly at him until one strikes his left leg below the knee and blood flows. Weeping on a high hill at being lamed, he cleanses the wound in the fountain, rides toward the sun, and is received by his village: "Lo, he has returned to us." Then the apokatastasis feast: "all the animals came forth from the wood, and shoals of fishes cast themselves upon the dry land."

Reading: after touching the animal, the ascent through the religions begins — sun-worship; the ordeal is "a condition of conflict... hot and cold, fire and water, and arrows from right and left", endured with Indian stoicism; the finale is "a great feast of nature where everything is reconciled again... a sort of Paradise condition" (p221).

occurrences.title: Christ born on the day the sun was created — De Pascha Computus (~243)
occurrences.label: Christ born on the day the sun was created
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: fn 66 to ch. V, The Song of the Moth (pdf p693)

body: The De Pascha Computus (Migne, P.L. 4, col. 964; Usener, Weihnachtsfest, p. 5) marvels: "O quam praeclara... providentia ut in illo die quo factus est sol, in ipso die nasceretur Christus" — Christ born on the fourth day of creation, the very day the sun was made. Jung adds the Malachi text behind it — "the Sun of righteousness [shall] arise, with healing in his wings" — and notes: "This image recalls the winged sun-disc of ancient Egypt. (Pl. IXa; cf. also pl. VII)." The companion fn 67 cites the December-25 natalis Invicti: "ipse est sol iustitiae."
Verbatim (fn 66, Malachi): "But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise, with healing in his wings."

occurrences.title: Christians prostrate before the rising sun: 'Eleeson hemas' (Hippolytus)
occurrences.label: Christians prostrate before the rising sun
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: St. Hippolytus wrote of having seen Christians throw themselves down on their faces before the rising sun, shouting: "eleeson hemas," have pity upon us.
body: Hippolytus reports Christians throwing themselves on their faces before the rising sun, shouting "eleeson hemas" — have pity upon us. The early Christians of Asia Minor (and places in Italy) were still sun-worshippers; Christ was supposed to be the newly risen sun, hence the birthday on 25 December when the old sun rises from its winter coma. Augustine still had to teach that God was not the sun but the creative spirit behind it. For Jung the passage shows how easily the conception of God could change back into the sun — the exact regression his patient's vision performed.

occurrences.title: The setting sun 'like a suspended drum' — First Meditation, Amitāyur-dhyāna Sūtra
occurrences.label: The setting sun 'like a suspended drum'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: gaze upon it more particularly when it is about to set and looks like a suspended drum. After you have thus seen the sun, let that image remain clear and fixed, whether your eyes be shut or open.
body: The Buddha teaches Queen Vaidehi the first of sixteen meditations:

"The setting sun is an allegory of the immortality-dispensing Amitābha" (¶915). Jung's psychological reading: the southern sun's intense after-image works "a similar hypnotic effect" to the fixating of a shining crystal, and — decisively — "the sun's disk serves as a model for the later fantasies of circular structures": the seed of the whole mandala series that follows (¶928).

occurrences.title: Christ bringing the tree of life, 'INTROITUS SOLIS' — Pisa baptistry
occurrences.label: Christ bringing the tree of life, INTROITUS…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the Sol mysticus which was before and will be afterwards
body: The crowning witness to pre-existence: the Baptist's "he was before me" and the Johannine Logos prologue introduce "the annunciation of the Light, of the rising sun — the Sol mysticus which was before and will be afterwards" (¶496). The sun-wheel Christ as the reborn god entering again.

occurrences.title: Second sun and falling spheres, 'you will live till eleven eight' — astrologer's dream, 27 May 1957
occurrences.label: Second sun and falling spheres, you will live…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: And she said in extraordinarily distinct tones: 'J—S—, you will live till eleven eight.
body: An amateur astrologer interested in synchronicity, knowing nothing of Jung's Ufo work, dreamt (and unbidden sent Jung) a whitened, dying sun; then "a second sun... took on the distinctive form of a sphere," which — like Jupiter "in aberration from its proper orbit" — sped toward the earth, followed by sphere after sphere crashing at a distance; fear turned to "awe," night "spoke of majesty, power and beauty." A composed young woman at her work will not flee, and pronounces: "J—S—, you will live till eleven eight."

Jung's reading: the pallor is the daylight world's fear of catastrophe; the approaching Jupiter is God drawing near as in Schreber (¶690); eight is "a double quaternity and, as an individuation symbol in mandalas, plays almost as great a role as the quaternity itself" (¶692); the lady is "a compensating anima figure" who "alludes... to the totality, the self, which is present in the Ufo projection" (¶693) — the real fear is his own death (¶696).

occurrences.title: 'The Moth to the Sun' poem — Miss Frank Miller (train to Paris, 1898)
occurrences.label: The Moth to the Sun' poem — Miss Frank Miller
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The second Miller product: a hypnagogic poem at four in the morning in a hot railway compartment, in which the soul-moth begs one rapturous glance of the sun and dies content. Jung: a condensation "of two things that do not really belong together — firstly the moth which flies round the light till it burns its wings; secondly the image of a tiny ephemeral being... which in pathetic contrast to the eternity of the stars longs for the imperishable light" (¶117).

His amplification digs to the sun-hero, "the 'well-beloved'" (¶146, ¶158), and ends: "For him the dreamer longs with her very soul, for him the 'soul-moth' burns her wings" (¶164). Sources Miller herself named: a philosophical article ("the same passionate longing of the moth for the star, of man for God"), the play The Moth and the Flame, and Byron's "Heaven and Earth" with its flood of unleashed passion (¶¶123, 165-167).

occurrences.title: Sun and moon of oiled paper — schizophrenic dream
occurrences.label: Sun and moon of oiled paper
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Sun and moon, as divine equivalents of the parent archetype, possess a tremendous psychic power that has to be weakened apotropaically
body: The apotropaic trick of the psychosis: "Sun and moon, as divine equivalents of the parent archetype, possess a tremendous psychic power that has to be weakened apotropaically, because the patient is already far too much under the power of the unconscious" (¶576). Same mechanism as the mechanical-dragon rationalization ("It's all a fake", ¶576).

occurrences.title: The trees of the Sun and Moon that declare the future — Old French Prose Alexander Romance
occurrences.label: The trees of the Sun and Moon…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: At the world's edge Alexander consults the two oracular trees: "Perhaps you would like to see the most holy trees of the Sun and Moon, which will declare the future to you". Jung cites them beside the sun-and-moon trees of the alchemical pictures (Psychology and Alchemy figs. 116, 188).

The paired luminaries vegetated as trees — the conscious and unconscious principles rooted in one arboreal body, giving oracular (unconscious) knowledge — a folk-epic sibling of the alchemical arbor philosophica duplex.

occurrences.title: 'He who goes there is our father' — Mountain Lake refutes the Augustinian sun (Taos, 1925)
occurrences.label: He who goes there is our father
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: Pointing to the sun he cried indignantly: “He who goes there is our father. You can see him. From him comes all light, all life—there is nothing that he has not made.
body: Jung tried on Mountain Lake (Ochwiay Biano), the Pueblo chief, "the Augustinian argument: 'Not this sun is our Lord, but he who made this sun.'" The chief called him sharply to account, pointed at the sun and cried: "He who goes there is our father. You can see him. From him comes all light, all life — there is nothing that he has not made," and, struggling for words: "Even a man in the mountains, who goes alone, cannot make his fire without him."

Jung's reading (¶138): "The archaic standpoint could hardly be more beautifully expressed" — the ruling power is outside, in the visible world, and life is permitted through it alone; "religious thought keeps alive the archaic state of mind even today, in a time bereft of gods." It grounds his 1931 question whether the psyche was ever "outside us in the form of arbitrary powers" (¶140).

occurrences.title: Hölderlin's 'Patmos' — the sun shatters its rayed sceptre (1803)
occurrences.label: Hölderlin's 'Patmos'
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The apocalyptic hymn Jung sets at the climax of his Hölderlin series: "Near is God / And hard to apprehend. / But where danger is, there / Arises salvation also" (¶630). The poet identifies with John on Patmos facing the dying Christ: "For now was put out / The day of the sun, the kingly one, / And himself, divinely suffering, / Shattered the straight-rayed sceptre, / For it shall come again / At the proper time" (¶637).

Jung reads the underlying images as "the sacrificial death and resurrection of Christ, conceived as the self-sacrifice of the sun, which voluntarily breaks its rayed sceptre in the certain hope of resurrection" (¶638) — sceptre-breaking = "the sacrifice of power as previously exercised, i.e., of the libido which had been organized in a certain direction." "Wisdom dwells in the depths, the wisdom of the mother" (¶640); the eagle, "the sun-bird, dwells in darkness" (¶633); the vision of Asia blooms as "the mother-city in the land of eternal youth" (¶637). Yet the poem ends in lament — like Gilgamesh, Hölderlin loses the treasure: no resurrection in this world (¶642).
Verbatim: "But where danger is, there Arises salvation also" (¶630).

occurrences.title: Sun = phallus, moon = vessel — late Roman inscription, Verona
occurrences.label: Sun = phallus, moon = vessel
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: An inscription composed of symbols (sun-disc, phallus, moon-vessel); a second monument from the same collection replaces the vessel with a female figure. The Lajard gem (fig. 19) carries the same code: sun-snake/moon-snake around an androgynous deity.
Jung's reading: "The symbolism is plain: sun = phallus, moon = vessel (uterus)" (¶298) — sun and sex as twin symbolic channels of the libido (¶297).
Verbatim: The symbolism is plain: sun = phallus, moon = vessel (uterus). (cw05 ¶298).

occurrences.title: Punctus Solis in medio rubeus — the sun-point germ in the yolk (Consilium coniugii; Codex Berol. Lat. 532)
occurrences.label: Punctus Solis in medio rubeus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: ch. II nn.32-33; ch. III n.22 (pdf p670, 687)

body: The Consilium coniugii: "Punctus Solis in medio rubeus" (the sun-point in the midst of the yolk); "in the midst of the yolk" is the quintum elementum, the quintessence "from which will grow the chick". The Codex Berolinensis Lat. 532 (fol. 154v) repeats: "The sun-point is the germ of the egg, which is in the yolk, and that germ is set in motion by the hen's warmth" (n.33).
The central red point in the yellow of the philosophical egg — the fiery germ of the whole opus: a filius-germ image Jung aligns with the Gnostic iota/point and the scintilla.

occurrences.title: 'We are the children of the sun' — the Pueblo chief's letter to Jung
occurrences.label: We are the children of the sun
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: We are the children of the sun and we are entrusted with that office, and the Americans are mad, they gamble away the sun.
body: The chief of a Pueblo tribe (Jung's Taos informant, the "heart-thinking" chief of the 1925 trip) wrote to Jung threatening, on the tribe's behalf, the collapse of the cosmic order: the Americans "gamble away the sun"; if the Indians stop helping the Great Father rise and wander the heavens, "the sun won't rise any longer." Jung files it beside the Christmas tree and the sheep-tossing Indians as proof that the preoccupation of the primitive mind — keeping the sun rising — is still the operative magic in his patient's sacrificial vision.

occurrences.title: Watching the sun from the roofs — Pueblo rite before the buffalo dances
occurrences.label: Watching the sun from the roofs
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ritual witnessed during Jung's January 1925 journey

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: They turn slowly with the sun until they are in a state of complete identification with it, the sun being their ancestor, their father.
body: The master of religious ceremonies who accompanied Jung to the buffalo dances explained he could not dance that day because he was not purified: at sunrise all the men climb the flat roofs of the pyramid-stacked pueblo houses and watch the sun the whole day, slowly turning with it "until they are in a state of complete identification with it, the sun being their ancestor, their father. Then they are the sons of the sun and as such they can dance."

Jung's reading: rites are valid only under ritual re-identification with the divine ancestor — "if they are not reidentified with the divine ancestor, they cannot perform the rites. Or if they did, it would be merely a theatrical performance and would have no magic effects". He cites it beside the Central Australian Alcheringa rites as evidence that "psychological possession" is known and deliberately used by primitives: they induce the condition in which they "become some one that ordinarily they are not". Possession, he adds, "is the original condition of mankind".

occurrences.title: The sun on the back of his mother the sky — Egyptian hymn
occurrences.label: The sun on the back of his mother the sky
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Thy mother, the sky, Stretches forth her arms to thee.
body: The daily solar hieros gamos: Tum/Atum, "the father of his mother," united each night with the sky-mother; the "pupilla" (child-image reflected in the eye) marks the great god becoming a child again, entering the mother's womb for self-renewal (¶408).

occurrences.title: The staff with the serpent twined round the sun — Zarathustra's parting gift
occurrences.label: The staff with the serpent twined round the sun
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: At the cross-road Zarathustra's disciples present him "a staff, on the golden handle of which a serpent twined round the sun."

Jung: the disciples return the golden ball he threw them — with an addition that is really theirs, the serpent. Zarathustra is "the masculine archetype of the wise old man par excellence... the pneuma, the wind-god, and therefore has to reject the serpent"; his disciples are his earth, and the sun-encoiled-by-serpent is "a symbol of the union of Zarathustra and his disciples." Amplificatory row: the uraeus, the Chinese dragon-and-pearl (values reversed), the bindu coiled by Shakti in the muladhara mandala, the Orphic egg.
Chapter-close echo: "a golden sun, with the serpent of knowledge around it" — the new virtue.

occurrences.title: The sun as 'clear and manifest statue of God' — Vigenerus
occurrences.label: The sun as 'clear and manifest statue of God'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: St. Dionysius called it the 'clear and manifest statue of God.
body: Vigenerus calls the sun "the eye and heart of the sensible world and the image of the invisible God," adding that St. Dionysius called it the "clear and manifest statue of God" — translating agalma by "statua," where the Ficino Latin has "imago." The same treatise shows he knew the Zohar; the sun there appears as bridegroom.
Jung at cw14 ¶568: possibly a recollection of Senior's "hearts of statues"; the statue may thus converge with the Cabalistic Malchuth-statue and the stone of Bethel.

occurrences.title: 'God pierces the earth with his ray' — the solid sunbeam of Spielrein's patient (Zurich)
occurrences.label: God pierces the earth with his ray
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Quoted at the climax of the Patmos analysis — Christ as the sun shattering its rayed sceptre: "Spielrein's patient said that 'God pierces the earth with his ray.' For her the earth was a woman; she also regarded the sunbeam in mythological fashion as something solid: 'Jesus Christ has shown me his love by tapping at the window with a sunbeam.' I have come across the same idea of the solid substance of the sunbeam in other insane patients" (¶638).

The ray as penetrative solid makes visible the libido-symbol chain Jung builds here: sceptre, staff, spear, lance, Thor's hammer that "split the earth and penetrated deep into it" and behaves inside the earth "like the treasure, for in the fulness of time it comes to the surface again, i.e., is born again from the earth" (¶638). The sunbeam-phallus motif returns from above instead of from below — same equation, inverted direction.
Verbatim: "God pierces the earth with his ray" (¶638).

occurrences.title: 'The Night of the Swinging Censer' — first dream of Authentic Dreams of Peter Blobbs (1916)
occurrences.label: The Night of the Swinging Censer
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: The dream Jung sets beside his own midnight-sun discovery: the dreamer is in an old cathedral at sunset that slowly fills with people "clad in the costumes of all times and of all centuries," finally even the primitives. In the middle a censer swings to and fro; the deeper the night, the wider and brighter its oscillations; at midnight the maximum; towards morning it declines, and at sunrise it stands still.

Jung: "This is an extremely fine demonstration of the movement of the unconscious. As day fades the unconscious is activated, and by midnight the censer is in full blaze, but lighting up the past." The flaming censer is "analogous to the midnight sun, which becomes incandescent when the day sun, or superior function, goes out". He had used the book before — it was the subject of his unrecorded Cornwall seminar of summer 1920. The book is A. J. Hubbard's Authentic Dreams of Peter Blobbs and of Certain of His Relatives (London, 1916), then anonymous.

occurrences.title: Symeon the New Theologian's inner sun (Constantinople, c. 1000)
occurrences.label: Symeon the New Theologian's inner sun
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Byzantine mystic's account of the invisible light: his spirit searched "through the air... over the heavens... across the abysses" and found nothing created; then "it came as it was wont, and descending like a luminous cloud, seemed to envelop my whole head... I realized suddenly that it was within me, and in the midst of my heart it shone like the light of a spherical sun" (¶141). Earlier: the Invisible "rises in my poor heart like a sun or circular disc of the sun, like light, for it is a light" (¶140).

Jung's reading: "That the thing perceived as an inner light, as the sun of the other world, is an emotional component of the psyche, is clear from Symeon's words" (¶141) — the mystic's sun as direct perception of one's own libido, undiminished when imparted: "you enkindle fire from fire, and you receive the whole fire" (¶140).

occurrences.title: 'You will see hanging down from the disc of the sun a tube' — Mithraic Liturgy passage
occurrences.label: You will see hanging down from the disc…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: The Greek papyrus edited by Albrecht Dieterich as Eine Mithrasliturgie: a religious prescription for incantations naming Mithras, from the Alexandrian school of mysticism, with affinities to the Leiden papyri and the Corpus Hermeticum. Quoted passage: "Draw breath from the rays, draw in three times as strongly as you can... The path of the visible gods will appear through the disc of the sun, who is God my father. Likewise the so-called tube, the origin of the ministering wind" (¶106).

Jung's reading: the invoked fire-/sun-god has close historical parallels "for instance with the Christ-figure of the Apocalypse"; the text is a "representation collective" — and the exact match, four years after the fact, for his 1906 patient's sun's-penis/wind vision (¶¶105, 108-109).

occurrences.title: The weeping evening sun — Mathilde von Wesendonck, 'Grief'
occurrences.label: The weeping evening sun
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: fn 28 to ch. V, The Song of the Moth (pdf p690); index 'Wesendonck, Mathilde von, 93n'

body: "The sun, every evening weeping, / Reddens its beautiful eyes for you; / When early death seizes you, / Bathing in the mirror of the sea.... You awaken anew in the morning / Like a proud conqueror." Jung uses the poem (with a parallel by Ricarda Huch: the earth fleeing the sun into winter night, then "warmly embraced with rosy light / Leaning against the lost consort") to gloss "the heavenly wanderings of the soul": "It is an image of the wandering sun (fig. 3), which from its rising to its setting travels over the world." The same footnote sends the motif back to the Harranite Platonis liber quartorum and forward into the alchemical peregrinatio.

occurrences.title: Bronze Age sun-wheels — circles with four spokes, Zurich Landesmuseum
occurrences.label: Bronze Age sun-wheels
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Local counterpart to Barrett's cross-report: "Among the prehistoric remains in the Landesmuseum here in Zurich are sun-wheels, dug up in this vicinity, which would date from the Bronze Age. They are just ordinary small wheels, about four inches in diameter, circles with four spokes, the most ancient form of the cross. They were probably worn as a sort of charm" (p380).

Jung then reaches behind all such objects to the Palaeolithic Rhodesia circle-with-double-cross: with no wagon-wheel yet in existence, "we must assume that they have seen that thing, it was a vision" (pp380-381) — "I assume that this cross is really a ghost — a psychic reality in the Paleolithic Age" (p382).

occurrences.title: The winged sun disc of Amenhotep IV (Ikhnaton)
occurrences.label: The winged sun disc of Amenhotep IV (Ikhnaton)
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Mr. Allemann's closing contribution: the bird-form of consciousness is visible in "the famous Egyptian symbol, the winged disc of the sun which was declared by Amenhotep IV to be the supreme symbol of the deity."

Jung has just read the eagle as the brain's oneness (the commissure) and the serpent as the spinal psyche; the winged disc joins the series of bird-forms "symbolizing the supremacy of consciousness" — with the Gilgamesh eagle, the eagle lecterns, the Hamsa. (Editors footnote: Amenhotep = Ikhnaton, Freud's source for Hebrew monotheism.)

Verbatim: "the bird-form symbolizing the supremacy of consciousness is visible in other symbols which have very much the same significance; for instance, in the famous Egyptian symbol, the winged disc of the sun which was declared by Amenhotep IV to be the supreme symbol of the deity."

occurrences.title: Zarathustra's invocation to the great star (Zarathustra, Prologue 1)
occurrences.label: Zarathustra's invocation to the great star
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: the mountain above 'the lake of his home' (composed Riviera/Engadine)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Opening scene of Zarathustra: after ten years on the mountain, the sage "rising one morning with the rosy dawn, went before the sun, and spake thus unto it: Thou great star! What would be thy happiness if thou hadst not those for whom thou shinest!" Jung reads the sun as the personified "great clarity of his lonely consciousness" — the sun is "the symbol of the center of consciousness, it is the principle of consciousness because it is light". A man alone "is always his own speaker and your own listener; you are always looking into your own light."

The invocation opens the Untergang: wearying of pure consciousness, Zarathustra will set like the sun and go down "to the netherworld" — the move Jung reads as descent from abnormal sun-consciousness toward the collective. The lake left behind is "the personal familiar unconscious"; the sea would be the collective.

occurrences.title: Brahmin Sutapas — rebirth chain through the sacred waters of Benares
occurrences.label: Brahmin Sutapas — rebirth chain…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: The Brahmin turned into a girl of a Chandala family
body: Zimmer's Maya supplies the wondrous motif of immersion and re-emergence in new life: the Brahmin Sutapas enters the sacred waters at Benares and emerges as a girl of a Chandala (outcast) family; she marries, bears blind sons and a deaf daughter, weeps at the river, and diving to bathe re-emerges as the Brahmin; the husband too, diving after her, is freed of all stigma and rises heavenward. Sinking through life-dream after life-dream, the Brahmin finally returns as Prince Kamadamana to tell the story.
Quoted for the water's positive aspect: womb and grave of all forms, the palpable element of the divine Maya — "down into the water means down into knowledge."

occurrences.title: Parcival's shooting of the swan — Grail-quest episode (Wolfram von Eschenbach)
occurrences.label: Parcival's shooting of the swan
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: The Grail hero becomes conscious through killing the bird: "In the story of Parcival, the unconscious hero Parcival becomes conscious through the shooting of the swan" (sem-1925).

Jung's reading, prompted by the committee on Rider Haggard's She: the goose shot after the lion-crocodile fight (Harding associated its head-spur to the unicorn) is "surely the same motive as that in the Grail story... It is an omen or presage of coming events. The ancients always thought of coming events as having shadows cast in front of them." A mythological animal is instinct itself; "when it is killed, someone will become conscious" — and "A bird is a mind animal, symbolically, so the unconsciousness is in the mind." The editors note Emma Jung began her Grail study in this same year (1925), leaving the Grail-alchemy links to her.

occurrences.title: Swastika on the robe of Fossor Diogenes — catacomb of Peter and Marcellinus, Rome
occurrences.label: Swastika on the robe of Fossor Diogenes
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Rome (coemeterium SS. Petri et Marcellini, Via Appia)

jung.locator: fn 70 to ch. V, The Song of the Moth (pdf p693); index 'swastika, 107n, 247'

body: Jung's footnote collects the sun-symbolism of the Roman catacombs: "there is a swastika (sun-wheel) on the robe of Fossor Diogenes in the cemetery of Peter and Marcellinus. The symbols of the rising sun—bull and ram—are found in the Orpheus frescoes in the cemetery of Domitilla; also the ram and peacock (a sun-symbol like the phoenix) on an epitaph in the Callistus catacomb." The gravedigger's own portrait wearing the sun-wheel — Christian art carrying the pagan solar repertory.
Verbatim (fn 70): "there is a swastika (sun-wheel) on the robe of Fossor Diogenes in the cemetery of Peter and Marcellinus."
Parallels (sun-wheel row): tauroctony-osterburken-monument-germany, mithraic-bull-sacrifice-heddernheim-relief-2c, world-wheel-ixion-sun-wheel-negro-dream-usa, sun-patmos-hymn-holderlin-1803.

occurrences.title: The Greek mandala cross — swastika as the four-footed sun
occurrences.label: The Greek mandala cross
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: "The Greek mandala cross, for instance, the swastika, is the four-footed sun rolling on four feet. The original form of it was really the disc of the sun with four little legs, as among the red Indians." Context: Western mandalas overwhelmingly take the number four (five and six occur; three signals a missing function) — the rotating quaternity as the sun's own gait.

occurrences.title: The swastika of the German Christians and the German Faith Movement — Germany, 1933–35
occurrences.label: The swastika of the German Christians…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Even a political creed may occasionally revert to mythology, as is proved very clearly by the swastika, the German Christians, and the German Faith Movement.
body: The modern political locus of the gamma-cross: in "Principles of Practical Psychotherapy" Jung cites "the swastika, the German Christians, and the German Faith Movement" as proof that "even a political creed may occasionally revert to mythology." The context is his claim that all religions — and, under modern conditions, political creeds — "are forms of psychotherapy," containing the still-living remains of a mythological age; for patients in whom the mythological remains are alive, referral to a credo (including a political one) is legitimate treatment.

This is the first modern-Western, non-mandala locus for the swastika in the vault; it sits in tension with the mandala-reading of CW9i (see swastika image note) — the contradictions between Jung's phases are preserved, not reconciled.

occurrences.title: Miss X, Picture 6 — right-turning green swastika (Oct 1928)
occurrences.label: Miss X, Picture 6 — right-turning green swastika
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The most striking thing is the appearance of a swastika, undoubtedly wheeling to the right.
body: Bright red-green-blue mandala whose most striking feature is a swastika "undoubtedly wheeling to the right" — painted in 1928, before swastikas were publicly current. Jung's rule: leftward = toward the unconscious, rightward (clockwise) = toward consciousness; in Tibet the leftward swastika belongs to the Bon religion, and stupas are circled clockwise (¶565). The picture is linked to the tree-in-workroom dream: the philosophical tree, symbol of the opus = individuation (¶570). The upward, rightward movement rescues consciousness from the darkening background the black snake has left behind.

occurrences.title: The black left-turning swastika of National Socialism — Germany, 1935
occurrences.label: The black left-turning swastika…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1935 (discussed 13 Feb and 20 Feb 1935; swastika already the German state emblem)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939
Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: So one could say the sun is now transformed into a counter-sun, a sun which is not above but below, which is not bright but dark, which does not go clockwise but counterclockwise. It is a revolution against the old trend of things, and therefore progress is arrested: there is a regression.
body: Jung's live reading of the German emblem, prompted by Mrs. Baumann's question linking it to the Platonic year. Three regressions: the swastika is "an exceedingly archaic sun symbol"; it turns backward — against the sun, the path of the left hand, "the dark unconscious side"; and it is black, "the color of evil." Hence "the sun is now transformed into a counter-sun, a sun which is not above but below, which is not bright but dark, which does not go clockwise but counterclockwise."

He reports asking National Socialists about it: "those rather competent National Socialists to whom I talked in Germany did not know that their swastika was turning the wrong way," and — a most embarrassing moment — "though it moves the wrong way when you look at it, if you put yourself into the National Socialist swastika, it moves the right way." Allemann adds that it ought to be golden, not black. Mrs. Spider-web's later note (p416) reads the black swastika as the earth turning away from the sun.

occurrences.title: Triskelos on Greek coins of Sicily (400-200 BCE)
occurrences.label: Triskelos on Greek coins of Sicily (400-200 BCE)
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: There is the Greek form of the triskelos, but I don't know whether that existed in India.
body: The three-legged triskelos, "found on Greek coins in Sicily, from a period between four hundred and about two hundred B.C.," brought in against Hauer's hypothetical reading of the maṇipūra emblem as a swastika: "I never have seen a swastika symbol that had only three feet." Jung prefers the pot-handles interpretation — maṇipūra as the cooking vessel over the fire, the alchemical kitchen where substances are transformed.

occurrences.title: The Gadarene swine — 'My name is Legion' (Mark 5:2–13)
occurrences.label: The Gadarene swine — 'My name is Legion'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: Jesus sent the unclean spirit of the possessed man—who said, 'My name is Legion'—into a great herd of swine, which then ran violently down a steep place into the sea.
body: The biblical pig locus cited in the pigs-and-lice amplification: Jesus sends the unclean spirit of the possessed man — "My name is Legion" — into a great herd of swine, "which then ran violently down a steep place into the sea" (Mark 5:2–13). It stands in the uncleanness line that begins with the pork taboo of Deuteronomy 14:8 (adopted by the Koran) and ends with Matthew 7:6, pearls before swine — of which the presenter says: "Something similar to this statement of the Bible happened to the dreamer," who ends the dream covered with the lice of what she fed.

occurrences.title: Ostanes' fiery sword and the egg — Tractatus Micreris
occurrences.label: Ostanes' fiery sword and the egg
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Europe (Latin; material attributed to Egypt via Arabic)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: Take an egg, pierce it with the fiery sword, and separate its soul from its body.
body: In this old treatise Ostanes ("Astanus") instructs: "Take an egg, pierce it with the fiery sword, and separate its soul from its body." Jung reads the sword here as dividing body and soul, corresponding to the division between heaven and earth, ring of fire and paradise, or paradise and the first parents (¶361).

Within the sword-family of the essay (¶357–361): the philosophical egg is divided with the sword, the King transfixed, the dragon or corpus dismembered — the solutio/separatio that restores chaos for a new impressio formae. "The sword is therefore that which 'kills and vivifies.'"

occurrences.title: Kill the mother — sacrifice recipes of the Allegoriae super librum Turbae
occurrences.label: Kill the mother — sacrifice recipes…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: Take a man, shave him, and drag him over the stone [i.e., dry him on the hot stone] till his body dies.
body: A sequence of sacrificial recipes: "Kill the mother [the prima materia], tearing off her hands and feet." "Take a viper... cut off its head and tail." "Take a cock... and pluck it alive." "Take a man, shave him, and drag him over the stone... till his body dies." "Take the glass vessel containing bridegroom and bride, throw them into the furnace, and roast them for three days, and they will be two in one flesh." Then: "Take the white man from the vessel." The companion treatise decapitates a fowl with the fiery sword, plucks and cooks it to one colour.

Jung's reading: these are "instructions for magical sacrifices, not unlike the Greek magic papyri," aimed at summoning the paredros; the cookings, pluckings and shavings dramatize the mortificatio of the hylical man preparatory to his transformation into spirit.

occurrences.title: The sword of wrath hung on the tree — Dorn's golden trident
occurrences.label: The sword of wrath hung on the tree
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: And having hung the sword on the tree, he substituted for it a golden trident, and thus was the wrath of God changed into love.
body: In the colloquy between Animus, Anima, and Corpus, Dorn recounts that God took "the sword of wrath from the hand of the angel," hung it on the tree, and "substituted for it a golden trident, and thus was the wrath of God changed into love" — whereon the water of Grace "bathes the whole world." Jung says the passage might have occurred in Rabanus Maurus or Honorius of Autun without discredit (¶357).

Jung's reading: the context identifies the waters with Sophia, the Sapientia of the alchemists, "de cuius fonte scaturiunt aquae" — the nous hidden and bound in matter, the serpens mercurialis or humidum radicale. "The apparent transformation of the God of the Old Testament into the God of the New is in reality the transformation of the deus absconditus... into the medicina catholica" (¶358).

occurrences.title: The old sword with weird ciphers — a dream read constructively (Zurich, ~1913)
occurrences.label: The old sword with weird ciphers
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A man of "extremely feeble will-power, lazy and inactive," cast into despair by a slight physical illness, dreamt: "A certain man gave him a peculiar old sword, ornamented with weird old ciphers" (¶400). Jung stages the dream as his textbook case of the two standpoints. The reductive reading is "entirely satisfactory" — father-complex, wish for "the phallic power of his father (sword)" (¶401) — and perfectly useless: the patient already knew it and "learnt nothing." The constructive reading follows his associations: the giver is the tubercular friend who conquered death by will ("I will not die, I have decided to live"); the sword is "an old heirloom of mankind... a guard against the dangers of life" (¶402). Hence: "The words 'I will' are mankind's oldest heritage and have helped it through innumerable dangers" (¶403) — the dream opens "a way to a more idealistic standpoint."

occurrences.title: Antique sword dug from a tumulus — dream of an unmarried woman patient (~1916)
occurrences.label: Antique sword dug from a tumulus
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: Jung's showcase dream for the constructive (synthetic) method in "The Transcendent Function": "An unmarried woman patient dreamt that someone gave her a wonderful, richly ornamented, antique sword dug up out of a tumulus" (cw08 ¶149). Her associations: her father's dagger that once flashed in the sun before her, and a Celtic bronze sword (she is proud of her Celtic ancestry; the ornamentation suggests "ancient wisdom").

Jung lays the two readings side by side (¶150). Reductively: father complex, wish for the father's "weapon," phallic fantasy. Constructively: "This weapon is a very ancient heritage of mankind, which lay buried in the patient and was brought to light through excavation (analysis). The weapon has to do with insight, with wisdom" — the passionate, unbending will she must learn from her father, against her pampered-child passivity. No supplementary analogies from the analyst were needed; the patient's own associations pointed to the sword's cultural significance.

occurrences.title: 'In habentibus symbolum facilior est transitus' — Hermetic aphorism
occurrences.label: In habentibus symbolum facilior est transitus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: In habentibus symbolum facilior est transitus.
body: Can Nietzsche, situated in the rationalist 1880s, have made the needed submission? "In habentibus symbolum facilior est transitus," which Jung found "quite by chance" in a 16th-century Latin Hermetic author: "For those who have a symbol, the passing from one side to the other, the transmutation, is easier. In other words, those who have no symbol will find it very difficult to make the transition."

Jung's reading: the Hermetics spoke "of beings, but not of human beings — rather, of chemical substances, metals, which... were often understood by the alchemists as homunculi", whose souls transmute more easily when they "had a symbol". Generalized: "This is the condition by which any man in any time can make a transition: with the symbol he can transmute himself." The symbol "functions as a sort of machine... by which the libido is transformed"; the creed is the symbolum "to apply when the soul is in danger". Nietzsche "wiped out his symbol when he declared that God was dead" and so could not make the transitus. Footnote: no idea is more central to Jungian thought.

occurrences.title: 'I am you... I am yourself' — the table-turning communicant (SPR case)
occurrences.label: I am you... I am yourself
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: I am you, you should not ask any more, I am yourself.
body: In the discussion of the dream's "employees" — delegated partial functions — Jung cites "one very important case published in the reports of the Psychical Research Society": a man took immense trouble to interrogate the thing speaking through the table, "and it got quite embarrassed in the end and finally confessed, 'I am you, you should not ask any more, I am yourself.'"

For Jung this is probable: "an unconscious delegate that says things occasionally which the conscious would not say... These are the persons who produce dreams." He is agnostic on ghosts ("whether they get more intelligent I don't know") — the psychology of split-off fragments is what matters.

occurrences.title: 'The dream is its own interpretation' — Talmudic saying
occurrences.label: The dream is its own interpretation
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This assumption is wholly arbitrary. The Talmud says more aptly: “The dream is its own interpretation.
body: Against the hermeneutic assumption "that dreams meant something different from what they said" — the assumptions alike of Greek euhemerism and of modern reductive dream theory — Jung cites the Talmud: "The dream is its own interpretation." He glosses: "Why should dreams mean something different from what appears in them? Is there anything in nature that is other than what it is?" (¶569).

The saying anchors his manifest-dream-first method: symbols "have obviously not only one meaning, but point in different directions and must therefore mean something that is unconscious, or at least not conscious in all its aspects" (¶569).

occurrences.title: T'ang bronze mirror: the pearl of Ch'ien amid the four dragons
occurrences.label: T'ang bronze mirror
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In China it is Ch'ien—heaven—with the four cosmic effluences radiating from it
body: Plate 61: "The pearl as symbol of Ch'ien, surrounded by the four cosmic effluences (dragons).—Chinese bronze mirror of the T'ang Period." Jung uses it in the Holy-of-Holies argument: "in the interior of the Lamaic quadrangle, and again in the Chinese earth-square, there is a Holy of Holies with its magical agent, the cosmic source of energy… In China it is Ch'ien—heaven—with the four cosmic effluences radiating from it" (¶169).
It is the Eastern counterpart of the medieval Western mandalas with the deity enthroned at the centre — and the very centre our dream 16 fills with a gibbon instead of a god (¶169).

image.title: Tang dynasty bronze mirror with dragon and clouds design

occurrences.title: Ritual cohabitation at the centre of the Terrace of Life — Tantric initiation
occurrences.label: Ritual cohabitation at the centre…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: The most striking claim of the mandala lectures: "Much of what goes on in Eastern rituals is hushed up. For instance, in certain Tantric systems, at the crowning moment when the initiant has entered the central place on the Terrace of Life, he performs a ritual cohabitation with a woman. That fact is not known, or it is just whispered. Westerners think the centre is a great void. Only when a man is capable of thinking of that act as a sacred nuptial can he understand the East." The void of the centre and the coniunctio are two readings of one place — totality, not "an artificial two-dimensional being".

occurrences.title: Chuang-tze's wood-carver: 'My Heaven-given faculty and the Heaven-given nature of the wood' (China, ~4th c. BCE)
occurrences.label: Chuang-tze's wood-carver
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: My Heaven-given faculty and the Heaven-given nature of the wood worked together upon it.
body: A wood-carver made a bell frame "which all the people admired as if it were the work of spirits." Asked by the Marquis of Lu, he explains his fasting: three days, no thought of gain or honor; five days, no thought of praise or blame; seven days, "I had forgotten my body and all my limbs." Then "When I came to the right tree, I saw the figure of the bell frame finished before me... My Heaven-given faculty and the Heaven-given nature of the wood worked together upon it". Jung's exhibit for the animation of objects: "the material spoke to them" — the antique relation in which the goblet, the sword, the canoe tells the craftsman what to do, the condition out of which the dwarf-lore grew.

occurrences.title: 'It is not a war, it is an epoch' — House of Exile on the Chinese attitude
occurrences.label: It is not a war, it is an epoch
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: China (American girl travelling with a Chinese family)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: In Nora Wain's House of Exile, a modern American girl accompanies her family's Chinese business friends through a devastated, war-torn region; frightened, she asks what war this is. "The Chinaman calmly explains that this is an epoch, meaning that such a disturbed period would last seventy or ninety years perhaps and then pass by".

For Jung the sentence condenses the Chinese counter-position to the European state: "China is not a state, but a people-well, not even a people-living and feeding on pieces of ground… nobody wanders about to steal and rob and kill, so why have soldiers?". The Chinese "start from the idea that to be human is to be civilized," govern by Wu Wei, and meet disorder (in Jung's no-doubt idealized telling) with edicts and patience rather than "belligerent order." "Nietzsche is terribly excited here; a Chinaman would not understand his language" — though Jung fears "this very old human way of looking at things is fast disappearing in China."

occurrences.title: 'There is something formless yet complete' — Tao Te Ching, ch. XXV
occurrences.label: There is something formless yet complete
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: The chapter Jung quotes entire (Waley's version adjusted to Wilhelm's reading): "There is something formless yet complete / That existed before heaven and earth... One may think of it as the mother of all things under heaven. / I do not know its name, / But I call it 'Meaning.' / If I had to give it a name, I should call it 'The Great.'"

Jung's reading: Tao is what the Jesuits wrongly rendered "God" and makeshifts render "Providence"; "Richard Wilhelm brilliantly interprets it as 'meaning'" (¶917). The chapter grounds Jung's central forerunner-claim: where causality governs the Western picture of nature, Chinese philosophy placed meaning — "Where meaning prevails, order results" (¶922) — the exact position Jung gives to synchronicity as tertium comparationis.

occurrences.title: 'The pivot of Tao' — ego and non-ego no longer opposed (Chuang-tzu)
occurrences.label: The pivot of Tao' — ego and non-ego no longer…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: Chuang-tzu on the psychological premise of Tao: "The state in which ego and non-ego are no longer opposed is called the pivot of Tao." Jung strings further citations: "Tao is obscured when you fix your eye on little segments of existence only"; "Originally words had no fixed meanings. Differences only arose through looking at things subjectively"; the sages started from a state when things had not yet begun — after affirmation and negation arose, "Tao faded."

Jung's reading: "Outward hearing should not penetrate further than the ear... thus the soul can become empty and absorb the whole world"; with the inner eye and inner ear one pierces "to the heart of things" without intellectual knowledge — "obviously an allusion to the absolute knowledge of the unconscious, and to the presence in the microcosm of macrocosmic events" (¶923).

occurrences.title: The rainmaker of Kiau Tschou — sequestering oneself back into Tao
occurrences.label: The rainmaker of Kiau Tschou
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: A drought-stricken village in Wilhelm's region of China summons a rainmaker, who asks only for a quiet house, locks himself in for three days, and on the fourth there is a great snow. He denies any power to make it: the country was out of order, so he himself was out of order — "I had to wait three days until I was back in Tao and then naturally the rain came" (footnote; cf. CW5 ¶604n).

Jung uses it twice in one lecture: for the world experienced as order only when someone experiences its order — "it is a chaos if nobody experiences it as a cosmos" — and for Nietzsche's "Physician, heal thyself": the cure is made "where it is most needed and most immediate." Whoever beholds the healed one "beholds Tao and enters Tao" against the late-Christian cure of the neighbor.
Verbatim: "If that fellow had not gone into Tao it would not have rained, yet there is no causality; the two things simply belong together, the order is only established when order is established".

occurrences.title: The Tao symbol: white and black spiral divisions of a circle (taijitu)
occurrences.label: The Tao symbol — white and black spiral…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~11th c. CE (Song-dynasty taijitu; Jung describes it undated)

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: Jung's emblem of enantiodromia in the same lecture: "This same conception is involved in the symbol of Tao, where the opposing principles are represented by white and black spiral divisions of a circle. They are thought of as the male and female elements respectively. The white portion, or masculine principle, contains within it a black spot, and the black portion, or female principle, contains a white spot. Thus Yang the masculine principle, when at its full, generates Yin the feminine, and vice versa". He connects it through the Tao Te Ching's "High rests upon Low, Great Good and Great Evil" to Nietzsche's "the greater the spread of the tree, the deeper the roots" — nothing exists save by virtue of a balancing opposite. Note the serpent-lecture echo: the Chinese assign the dragon (snake) to Yang, not Yin — Yin's beast is the tiger.

occurrences.title: Tao-te-king ch. 20, 'Away from the crowd' — 'I value the all-giving mother'
occurrences.label: Tao-te-king ch. 20, 'Away from the crowd'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: I alone am different from other men For I value the all-giving mother.
body: Mr. Allemann draws Jung's attention to aphorism 20; Jung reads it aloud in "the most recent translation by Mrs. Sawyer" (the seminar member, later Mrs. Baumann; no published record):

Jung reads the whole aphorism as "the confession of one who broke through taboos, who saw behind the veil". The all-giving mother is Tao; "if you violate the way of which you know, the way of consciousness, you are sinning against the all-giving mother" — and "taboos are ways of living… if they once break through, they can only live by the way of their consciousness". He glosses the sign: "the sign for Tao is written with the sign of the head and the sign for going" — consciously going. The historical warning: Angelus Silesius, who "created an entirely new understanding of the relation to God" and then "turned away from Tao", regressing into Catholicism, neurosis, and fifty-two polemics.

occurrences.title: 'The meaning that you can think out is not the meaning' — Tao Te Ching ch. 1 (China, ~4th c. BCE)
occurrences.label: The meaning that you can think out is not…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~4th–3rd c. BCE (Hauer's rendition; Waley trans. 1934, fn18)

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

body: The opening line of the Tao Te Ching, quoted by Hauer as the hermeneutic caveat over his whole cakra-symbolism lecture: "I may cite here a word of Lao-tzu: 'The meaning that you can think out is not the meaning.' Take all I say in this light. Forget everything I tell you, and begin as you must begin" (sem-kundalini pdf p152). Footnote 18 gives Waley's version ("The way that can be told is not an unvarying way") and notes Jung owned that translation.

Functionally the East's counterpart of Jung's irrepresentability doctrine: the meaning is not exhaustibly thinkable; cakra symbolism "runs into another and is discovered only by deep insight" — one must sink into the movement, "You sink into the color, so to speak, and then you find its meaning".

occurrences.title: 'The utility of the vessel depends on the space where there is nothing' — Tao Te Ching, ch. XI
occurrences.label: The utility of the vessel depends…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: Chapter XI — thirty spokes and the wheel's hub, clay and the vessel, pierced doors and windows and the house: "it is on the space where there is nothing that the utility of the vessel depends. Therefore just as we take advantage of what is, we should recognize the utility of what is not."

Jung's reading: Lao-tzu's "Nothing" is his name for Tao; "'Nothing' is evidently 'meaning' or 'purpose,' and it is only called Nothing because it does not appear in the world of the senses, but is only its organizer" (¶920) — Wilhelm glosses it as mere "contrast with the world of reality." The empty center of the vessel prefigures Jung's reading of the mandala's empty middle and of meaning as the non-appearing organizer of coincident events.

occurrences.title: 'When we can no longer help the sun' — Taos pueblo speech
occurrences.label: When we can no longer help the sun
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: The religious leader of the Taos pueblo (the Loco Tenente Gobernador) to Jung: the Americans should stop meddling with their religion, "for when it dies and we can no longer help the sun our Father to cross the sky, the Americans and the whole world will learn something in ten years' time, for then the sun won't rise any more" (¶48).

Jung's reading: the primitive barriers — rites and dogmas as "dams and walls to keep back the dangers of the unconscious, the 'perils of the soul'" — whose collapse lets night fall and "the dark sea of the unconscious break in". Ritual helping of Father Sun is the collective work that keeps the cosmos running; the speech is his prime exhibit for symbol-protection in the 1934 essay.

occurrences.title: Tarantism — the tarantula dance of Apulia
occurrences.label: Tarantism — the tarantula dance of Apulia
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939
Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: bind me fast, my friends, to this pillar.
body: The folk legend behind Nietzsche's tarantula chapter: the tarantula's bite poisons the soul into giddiness and compulsive dancing — the tarantella as attempted cure. Jung: "This of course refers to the tarantula dance, the madness caused by the tarantula", and again: "The poison of the tarantula is supposed to make people dizzy and to cause madness... it is not true but that is the legend". Nietzsche, "being no zoologist, believed that, so the giddiness is an attack of madness; the recognition of the other side meant a stroke of madness to him."

The bite that arrives just when the reviler of tarantulas becomes one — "Rather will I be a pillar-saint than a whirl of vengeance" — binds Jung's reading of projected shadow to the dance: dancing as suspension over the abyss.

occurrences.title: The hermaphroditic diable of the Tarot
occurrences.label: The hermaphroditic diable of the Tarot
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung introduces the Tarot as "a set of playing cards, such as were originally used by the gypsies... really the origin of our pack of cards, in which the red and the black symbolize the opposites, and the division by four-clubs, spades, diamonds, and hearts-also belongs to the individuation symbolism." Besides the court cards stand twenty-one symbolic cards — sun, hanged man, lightning-struck tower, wheel of fortune — "archetypal ideas, of a differentiated nature."

Key reading: "Now in the Tarot there is a hermaphroditic figure called the diable. That would be in alchemy the gold. In other words, such an attempt as the union of opposites appears to the Christian mentality as devilish." The Tarot reads the flow of life like the I Ching, because the prevailing condition corresponds to the condition of the collective unconscious.

occurrences.title: Taurobolium — the initiate bathed in bull's blood at the Attis cult, Vatican hill, Rome
occurrences.label: Taurobolium — the initiate bathed…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Rome, Vatican hill (site of St. Peter's)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: "In the place where St. Peter's now stands in Rome, the Attis cult celebrated the taurobolium. The initiate was put into a cauldron, a hole in the earth; a grating was put over it and there they killed a bull so that the blood of the sacrificed animal streamed down on him. Then he was pulled out, washed, clothed in white, and fed on milk for eight days, for he was a baby, his own youngest son. The high priest, now the Pope, was called Papas" (pp354-355).

Jung's reading: the cauldron as rebirth-womb — the initiate becomes "his own youngest son," exactly the figure the dreamer's youngest son plays in the kettle-dream ("the wife who brings forth a son has given birth to the husband," p354). The rite grounds the sequence womb → cauldron → baptismal rebirth, in white magic; the same vessel serves black magic depending on "what you cook in the cauldron and with what attitude" (p355).

occurrences.title: The rotating Mithraic altar slabs: from the dead bull the world grows (c. 2nd-3rd c. CE)
occurrences.label: The rotating Mithraic altar slabs
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: By his death the bull gave birth to vegetable life on earth.
body: The Mithraic altarpieces were "usually huge stones, with an axis on which they could be turned round, so probably during the sacred ceremonial the slab was turned and the other picture appeared. On one side was the usual sacrificial scene, Mithra sticking his sword into the bull, and on the other side of the slab the bull was dead but already in a state of transformation. By his death the bull gave birth to vegetable life on earth. Out of his spinal marrow 'grew grain of fifty-five species and twelve species of medicinal herbs'; out of his nose grew garlic; out of his testicles came all species of cattle, out of his horns came fruits, and out of his blood the wine". On the Heddernheim reverse Mithra receives grapes from the sun god. The death of the bull is the condition of the world's fertility — the interpretation Jung gives the patient's golden bull and tree.

occurrences.title: The Mithraeum of Dura-Europos — discovery reported 1934
occurrences.label: The Mithraeum of Dura-Europos
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Jung cites the news of the day: "quite recently a well-preserved Mithraeum has been discovered in the Syrian desert, where the French are making explorations in cooperation with Yale University. They have now asked the connoisseur of Mithraism, Cumont, to help in the excavations."

The French-Yale Dura-Europos expedition uncovered the famous wall-painted Mithraeum in 1934 with Cumont's involvement — identification inferred from Jung's description. Jung's point: Mithraeum sites sit "chiefly near the garrisons" — the religion of the Roman soldiers, "a religion of discipline."
Verbatim: "quite recently a well-preserved Mithraeum has been discovered in the Syrian desert, where the French are making explorations in cooperation with Yale University."

occurrences.title: Mithras carries his own bull — the Mithraic transitus
occurrences.label: Mithras carries his own bull
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Roman imperial era (~2nd c. CE monuments)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Mithras as the world bull (Abudabad, "the white bull of the beginning of the world" in Persian mythology): he sacrifices the bull — himself — and then carries his own corpse. The iconography: the god leaping on the bull's back like a toreador, short sword at the shoulder blade, head averted with a "peculiar face of hysterical sentimentality, like a Guido Reni."

Jung: "That carrying of the bull is really the parallel to Zarathustra carrying the corpse of the rope-dancer." The after-death carrying is "absolutely dark" (after Cumont), but it is the transitus part of the mystery. Mithraism is the religion of the Roman soldiers — "a religion of discipline."
Verbatim: "Mithras was the white bull of the beginning of the world, the world bull, Abudabad, in Persian mythology; so he sacrificed his own bull, himself, and then he carried his own corpse."

occurrences.title: Head of Mithras Tauroctonos — Ostia
occurrences.label: Head of Mithras Tauroctonos — Ostia
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The head (cw05's frontispiece, attributed by Cumont to Mithras Tauroctonos) shows the god at the moment of the bull-sacrifice: "The face... is that of a young man of almost feminine beauty... the contraction of the brows and lips gives a strange expression of sorrow" (Cumont, ¶666). Benndorf: the ideal features "wear an extremely sickly expression" (¶665).

Jung reads the face as the exact psychic signature of the tauroctony: "He slays it willingly and unwillingly at once" (¶665) — "the disunity and split-mindedness of the sacrificer: he wants to, and yet doesn't want to. This conflict tells us that the hero is both the sacrificer and the sacrificed" (¶668). The expression, "which we know all too well from our patients as one of sentimental resignation," belongs with the sentimentality-brutality pair typical of the first-to-third centuries; only the animal nature, the instinctual libido, is sacrificed, "always in close analogy to the course of the sun" (¶668).
Verbatim: "The head from Ostia... certainly wears an expression which we know all too well from our patients as one of sentimental resignation" (¶667).

occurrences.title: Mithraic monument of Osterburken (Germania superior)
occurrences.label: Mithraic monument of Osterburken
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The index lists the Osterburken monument at book p197, in the row of Mithraic monuments Jung discusses between Klagenfurt (196f, pl. XXIVa — instance exists) and Heddernheim (238, 246f, 261, 425 — instances exist). The relief of Mithras tauroctonos from the limes fort at Osterburken completes the set of the German mithraea Jung used for the sacrifice chapters.
Verbatim (index): "Osterburken monument, 197"

occurrences.title: Tefnut, devouring mother at the weighing of the heart — Egyptian Books of the Dead
occurrences.label: Tefnut, devouring mother at the weighing…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Egypt (Book of the Dead, hall of the two truths)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Jung's amplification of the devouring monster in a child's doll-dream: "In Egypt there exists such a monster, a goddess of the underworld, a devouring mother goddess—Tefnut. She is known for always being present in the scene of 'weighing the heart' in the Books of the Dead". Should the dead person's heart be found unworthy, she eats it, and the dead is given over to "the chthonic underworld, the cooking pot of creation, to be dissolved."

So the child's monster "is a devouring mother, a negative mother, who does not give birth, but devours the creatures herself. There is, however, also a positive aspect to this devouring: maybe it is the preparation for a new birth" (p142). Note: Jung's attribution of the heart-devouring role to Tefnut is idiosyncratic — the usual devourer is Ammit; kept as Jung's reading, for reconciliation.

occurrences.title: Telesphoros — hooded child-companion of Aesculapius
occurrences.label: Telesphoros — hooded child-companion…
