occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: The figure Jung used to read the little old man / beautiful boy of Dream [18]: "the Cabiri of Aesculapius, the inspiring familiar spirit of the doctors, who is often represented as holding a scroll and reading wisdom to Aesculapius, and he is always cloaked from head to foot with a hood over his face. His name is Telesphoros, meaning the one that brings completion, perfection, or initiation." He notes the kinship of the type to the Munchner Kindl on the arms of the city of Munich. Telesphoros marks the doctor's god as accompanied — healing wisdom delivered by a hooded child-guide.

occurrences.title: Telesphorus, familiaris of Aesculapius — bronze from Roman Gaul
occurrences.label: Telesphorus, familiaris of Aesculapius
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: as kinsmen of the unconscious, they protect navigation, i.e., the venture into darkness and uncertainty
body: Plate 77: "Telesphorus, one of the Cabiri, the familiaris of Aesculapius: (a) Bronze figure from Roman Gaul; (b) Marble statuette from Austria." The hooded, cloaked manikin standing beside the healing god.

Jung reads the Cabiri-dwarfs as "hooded and cloaked manikins who are kept hidden in the dark cista, but who also appear on the seashore as little figures about a foot high, where, as kinsmen of the unconscious, they protect navigation, i.e., the venture into darkness and uncertainty. In the form of the Dactyls they are also the gods of invention, small and apparently insignificant like the impulses of the unconscious but endowed with the same mighty power" (¶203). "El gabir is 'the great, the mighty one.'" They surface in the dream-series as the four children carrying the ring (dream 56).

image.title: 1948.1.308 Statuette romaine 'telesphore' (Musée de Die)

occurrences.title: The teraphim as speaking head — midrash in Die Sagen der Juden
occurrences.label: The teraphim as speaking head
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: And if any man fell down before it, the head began to speak, and answered all questions that were addressed to it.
body: Rabbinic tradition took the teraphim — which Michal put in David's bed with a pillow of goats' hair to deceive Saul's messengers (I Samuel 19:13f) — to be either a decapitated human head or a dummy head. The midrash gives the recipe: the head of a first-born man, cut off, hair plucked out, sprinkled with salt, anointed with oil; a plaque of copper or gold inscribed with an idol's name placed under the tongue; candles lit; and "if any man fell down before it, the head began to speak, and answered all questions."

Jung's reading: an obvious parallel to the Harranite ritual; the tearing-out of the hair is "an equivalent of scalping or shearing, and is thus a rebirth mystery" (¶369). Teraphim functioned as household lares and penates, plural spirits like the Cabiri.

occurrences.title: The virgin earth from which Adam and Christ were formed — Tertullian
occurrences.label: The virgin earth from which Adam…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: …ilia terra virgo nondum pluviis rigata nec imbribus foecundata, ex qua homo tunc primum plasmatus est, ex qua nunc Christus secundum carnem ex virgine natus est
body: Tertullian's typology cited in Answer to Job's footnote on the earth-woman of Revelation: the unploughed ground as virgin, yielding first Adam and then Christ.
The uncultivated prima materia as maiden — the same equation the alchemists made when they called the moist earth "virgin" and let the son be born in it.

occurrences.title: 'The Son of God is dead, which is worthy of belief because it is absurd' — Tertullian
occurrences.label: The Son of God is dead, which is worthy…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Tertullian's avowal quoted by Jung: "And the Son of God is dead, which is worthy of belief because it is absurd. And when buried He rose again, which is certain because it is impossible." (cw12 ¶18).

Jung sets it as the limit-case of religious paradox: "the paradox is one of our most valuable spiritual possessions, while uniformity of meaning is a sign of weakness… only the paradox comes anywhere near to comprehending the fulness of life." But "the inordinate number of spiritual weaklings makes paradoxes dangerous" — Enlightenment reason cannot endure them (¶19).

occurrences.title: The tetramorphos — the savior riding the four-beast (illuminated manuscripts)
occurrences.label: The tetramorphos — the savior riding…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "it is also called the tetramorphos, but that properly is the sort of monstrous animal with four heads that one sees in old illuminated manuscripts, the head of a lion, an ox, an eagle and an angel — the four Evangelists. And it has one leg of the lion, one of the ox, one of the eagle, and a human leg, and then the savior with a flag or emblem of the church is riding upon that animal."

Jung's bridge: the four Gospel-pillars as animals with Christ in the center are "faintly analogous to the quaternium in Christian iconography," set beside the Orphic Phanes — hermaphroditic, with two bodies and four symbolic animals — as parallel fourfold mounts of the god of the beginning.

occurrences.title: Evangelists with the heads of their symbolic animals — Gellone manuscript
occurrences.label: Evangelists with the heads of their symbolic…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 7th c. per Jung (MS usually dated 8th c.)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: "In a manuscript from the 7th century (Gellone), the evangelists are represented with the heads of their symbolic animals instead of human heads" (cw11 ¶? pdf p695) — cited beside Budge's Osiris and the Egyptian Book of the Dead pl. 5.

Total theriomorphic identification of the four: not men accompanied by beast-symbols but men as beasts — the level Jung elsewhere calls the unconscious identity of participation mystique, here preserved in the copyist's art at the edge of the Carolingian world.

occurrences.title: The four evangelists in rose, circle, and melothesia — Hortus deliciarum of Herrad of Landsberg
occurrences.label: The four evangelists in rose, circle…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: Herrad of Landsberg's encyclopedic manuscript is Jung's first named instance of "the 'four' in Christian iconography": the evangelists and their symbols "arranged in a rose, circle, or melothesia, or as a tetramorph, as for instance in the Hortus deliciarum of Herrad of Landsberg and in works of mystical speculation" (cw11 ¶? pdf p689).

A convent-produced mandala-quaternity a century before Dante: the four fixed around the centre as an image of the ordered whole — the arrangement Hildegard's visions pioneered (cf. her Codex Luccensis fol. 372 and Scivias Codex Heidelbergensis, cited in the same footnote).

occurrences.title: Rex gloriae with the four evangelist symbols — Romanesque Maiestas Domini
occurrences.label: Rex gloriae with the four evangelist symbols
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: the Rex gloriae with the four symbols of the evangelists (three theriomorphic, one anthropomorphic)
body: The Maiestas Domini: Christ enthroned in glory, surrounded by the four living creatures of Ezekiel/Revelation as the evangelists' symbols — angel (Matthew), lion (Mark), ox (Luke), eagle (John). Jung cites it as the prime Western quaternity beside the Gnostic figure of Barbelo ("God is four"): "the Rex gloriae with the four symbols of the evangelists (three theriomorphic, one anthropomorphic)."

Jung's reading: examples like this "bring the quaternity into closest relationship with the Deity, so that... it is impossible to distinguish the self from a God-image. At any rate, I personally have found it impossible to discover a criterion of distinction" (¶281) — a key statement of the self/God-image indistinguishability that Aion will develop.

occurrences.title: Tetramorph on two wheels — Vatopedi Monastery, Mt. Athos (1213)
occurrences.label: Tetramorph on two wheels
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: from the depths to the heights… to the mystical homo maximus
body: Plate 65: "Tetramorph (Anthropos symbol) standing on two wheels, symbols of the Old and New Testaments.—Mosaic, Vatopedi Monastery, Mt. Athos (1213)."

Byzantine witness to the imago-lapidis chain: the fourfold original-man figure (man, lion, ox, eagle) standing on the two wheels of the Testaments, "from the bestially archaic and infantile to the mystical homo maximus" (¶173) — the tetramorph as the transformed totality the alchemists sought in the stone.

occurrences.title: The theologian's dark-lake dream (wind over the water)
occurrences.label: The theologian's dark-lake dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
jung.locator: ¶33 (pdf p28) — ¶ marker lost in OCR, reconstructed

occurrences.quote: the mysterious water. And now there occurs the miracle of the pool of Bethesda: an angel comes down and touches the water, endowing it with healing power.
body: A Protestant theologian's recurring dream: standing on a mountain slope above a deep valley with a dark lake; something had always prevented his approach, this time he resolves to go down to the water. As he nears the shore "everything grew dark and uncanny, and a gust of wind suddenly rushed over the face of the water" — panic, and he awoke.

Jung's reading: the descent to the water is the descent into one's own depths; the wind is the pneuma which bloweth where it listeth — the miracle of the pool of Bethesda re-enacted: "Man's descent to the water is needed in order to evoke the miracle of its coming to life". The breath of spirit over the dark water is numinous, "a spookish thing" — paralleled with the Elgonyi "maker of fear" and with the old man of Nietzsche's Zarathustra withdrawing into the forest.

occurrences.title: The second theologian's Grail-castle dream (chasm before the mountain)
occurrences.label: The second theologian's Grail-castle dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Another theologian (fn 26 notes clergymen's professional stake in the "ascent" motif) dreamed he saw on a mountain "a kind of Castle of the Grail" and took the road that seemed to lead straight up. Nearer, he found a chasm: "a deep, darksome gorge with underworldly water rushing along the bottom"; a steep path led down and toilsomely up the other side — the prospect looked uninviting, and he woke.

Jung's reading: "the dreamer, thirsting for the shining heights, had first to descend into the dark depths, and this proves to be the indispensable condition for climbing any higher" (¶40). The prudent man avoids the danger lurking in the depths and thereby throws away the good of the venture. Sits inside ¶40's water-symbolism: "Water is the commonest symbol for the unconscious".

occurrences.title: Theotokos proclaimed — Council of Ephesus, 431
occurrences.label: Theotokos proclaimed — Council of Ephesus, 431
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the archetypal numen of feminine deity... imperiously announced her claim to the title of 'Theotokos
body: Jung's framing of the Marian dogma-line: "Behind this stands the archetypal numen of feminine deity, who, at the Council of Ephesus in 431, imperiously announced her claim to the title of 'Theotokos' (God-bearer), as distinct from that of a mere 'Anthropotokos' (man-bearer) accorded to her by the Nestorian rationalists" (¶237).

The claim matured into the 1950 dogma of the Assumption — "motivated chiefly by the religious need of the Catholic masses" — which for Jung converts "the medieval representations of the quaternity" (Trinity + Virgin) into dogma: the fourth, feminine term completing the Trinity, just as alchemy's Sulphur-Mercurius-Sal triad hides a quaternity in its androgynous middle figure (¶¶235-237).

occurrences.title: Thoth as cynocephalus — tomb of Amen-her-khopshef, Luxor (XXth dynasty)
occurrences.label: Thoth as cynocephalus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: near Der el-Medina, Luxor (tomb of Amen-her-khopshef)
occurrences.quote: its godlike affinities make it an equally appropriate symbol for that part of the unconscious which transcends the conscious level
body: Plate 68: "Thoth as cynocephalus" from the tomb of Amen-her-khopshef near Der el-Medina. Jung: "we have seen from the cynocephalus or dog-headed baboon associated with Thoth-Hermes, the highest among the apes known to the Egyptians, that its godlike affinities make it an equally appropriate symbol for that part of the unconscious which transcends the conscious level" (¶175).

The baboon closes the ape argument's other end: if the gibbon is man as archaic fact (below), Thoth's cynocephalus is the divine ape (above) — the archetype spanning layers beneath and beyond consciousness. The idea was "visibly preserved all through the numberless editions of the Book of the Dead" (¶173).

occurrences.title: Thoth heals Horus and Seth — arbiter of the wounded opposites (Osiris myth)
occurrences.label: Thoth heals Horus and Seth
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: in the Osiris myth when Horus avenges the death of his father (he overcomes Seth, his evil brother in a dreadful struggle in which both gods are wounded, Horus in one eye and Seth in the testicles), Thoth heals both of the gods again.
body: Reichstein's leading Egyptian example: "in the Osiris myth when Horus avenges the death of his father… in a dreadful struggle in which both gods are wounded, Horus in one eye and Seth in the testicles, Thoth heals both of the gods again."

He quotes Mead on the function: "The names of the God of Light and the God of Darkness change, but what does not change is the name of the arbiter, the mediator, whose duty it was to see that neither god destroyed the other or gained a decisive victory." Thoth — moon-god, ibis-headed, "the heart, or the tongue of Ra," author of the holy writings — becomes Hermes Trismegistos, then (per Reichstein's genealogy) Megistophiel and Mephistopheles, and "rose again from this depth" (compare Faust). Jung adds: Thoth "is the anticipation of the Logos, so he is also the anticipation of Christ."

occurrences.title: Three young women in the underground store handing red sticks — dream of a boy of nine
occurrences.label: Three young women in the underground store…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: Three young women sat at a small table behind the counter. They gave us red sticks that we didn't have to pay for: like sealing-wax that one could smoke. So we put them into our mouths and started to smoke. Then I staggered out of the store; I'd gotten all dizzy and sick.
body: First dream of the seminar's boy series, presented by Dr. Markus Fierz. With his friend Richard (the double) the boy descends from the street — collective consciousness — into a strange store below street level.

Jung: "The boy is here being initiated, for the first time, into sexuality, through women of a mythological nature who replace the mother. Procreation, however, is here still in the stage of nibbling sweets" — nutritive stage of the libido. The three women: Moirae, Nornes, Graeae, Hekate triformis; "When a trinity appears... a fateful point has been reached". The sealing-wax sticks read as phallic; mouth as female organ; "The simultaneous appearance of the male and the female organ is an archetype, that of constant cohabitation" — the ouroboros family. The drunkenness: the unconscious getting out of hand.

occurrences.title: The tigress under the trees — anima's first apparition in Spitteler's Prometheus
occurrences.label: The tigress under the trees
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "Spitteler compares the first apparition of the anima to a tigress walking under the trees with the leaves casting shadows on her fur. That is a very suggestive passage" — from the prose epic Jung had analysed at length in Psychological Types (CW6; footnote pdf p905).

Against Mrs. Jung's "anima wisdom" reading of Zarathustra's pregnant lioness: "the wisdom of the anima is wild because the anima is nature. That is the one thing in man which he cannot rule, the thing by which he is connected with nature; and if he apparently succeeds in cutting that communication, he is done for." In Spitteler's symbolism the lion is the will to power and the little dog the sentimentality, the craving for love.
Verbatim: "So sure enough, the wisdom of the anima is wild because the anima is nature".

occurrences.title: Tiger-headed goddesses of the Chönyid Bardo — Bardo Thödol, days 13–14
occurrences.label: Tiger-headed goddesses of the Chönyid Bardo
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Tibet (Chönyid Bardo of the Bardo Thödol; Evans-Wentz/Houston translation)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: again on the fourteenth day: 'from the south dawns the yellowishblack, tiger-headed Rakshasi, a blood-filled skull in her hand.
body: In the Bardo Thödol the tiger appears twice to the departed during the Bardo existence: on the thirteenth day, among the eight wrathful deities (the kerimas and htamemnas) appearing to one still in samsara, "from the south, [there appears] a red, tiger-headed [goddess], crossing her arms downward, staring hypnotically and gnashing her fangs"; and on the fourteenth day, the tiger-headed Rakshasi "a blood-filled skull in her hand". Huber cites both as the eastern, yin-side pedigree of the tiger of a five-year-old girl's dream in India (the tiger-dream session of the 1940/41 seminar). A sibling amplification: in Shinto the tiger is worshipped as a sacred animal.

occurrences.title: Adolescent dream 1: desert thirst, oasis, the tiger ready to leap
occurrences.label: Adolescent dream 1
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: First of the only three dreams a fifteen-year-old boy recorded in adolescence, presented by Jung for contrast with childhood dreams: lost in the desert under the merciless sun, about to die of thirst, he finds an oasis — and crouching to drink sees "a giant tiger, preparing to leap to kill me. Its eyes have a reddish glow, and I feel paralyzed."

Jung: the desert is the place of horror and loneliness (its wadis "populated by devils called djinns"); the thirst is the alien need of puberty. "The tiger, just like the bull, is always a personification of the instinct that is directed against us" (p230); the well is always guarded by the evil that wants to come to us — the oasis and the tiger are one and the same. Parallel drawn to Virgo's water-serpent with Heracles and Ophiuchos above it.

occurrences.title: The rope-dancer in the marketplace (Zarathustra, Prologue 6)
occurrences.label: The rope-dancer in the marketplace
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: the marketplace; the rope over the abyss between house and church tower
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1883 (Part I; fall at the end of ch. 6)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The Seiltänzer begins his performance while Zarathustra still preaches: "When Zarathustra had thus spoken, one of the people called out: 'We have now heard enough of the rope-dancer; it is time now for us to see him!'". Jung's reading, the pivot of the first term: "the rope-dancer is an equivalent of himself, or himself under a certain aspect-a shadow aspect of himself"; "he represents Nietzsche's inferior side... the shadow figure, the inferior man in himself"; "that quantity of energy which has been in the god before... he is a dancer because God dances the world".

His appearance is "symbolic action" — the sermon "has hit upon something there, he has hurt himself against an invisible snag". It is "the prophecy of his own life, of which he could not have been conscious": the dangerous transitus from collective man to Superman, begun at the very moment "There is ice in their laughter". "It is a drame interieur of the author himself".

occurrences.title: The rope-dancer and the buffoon — Zarathustra's prologue
occurrences.label: The rope-dancer and the buffoon
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The opening "happening" of Zarathustra: a rope-dancer crosses a rope hung between two towers, a gaudily dressed buffoon springs after him, jeers ("thou blockest the way!"), jumps over him, and the dancer falls to his death "like an eddy of arms and legs."

Jung's reading (20 June 1934): the rope stretched between two towers is the pairs of opposites joined by the transcendent function — "man is a bridge between two banks" — but the crossing is "in the air," circuslike, unreal. The rope-dancer is Nietzsche himself as shadow-attempt; the buffoon is the active shadow, "the part of the shadow that holds divine power, the power over death and life." The scene is "a play of shadows... which forecasts the fate that Nietzsche the man will experience": his soul died in 1889 before his body.
Verbatim: "So the fate of that rope-dancer symbolically anticipates the fate that overcame Nietzsche: Nietzsche himself is the rope-dancer and the same fate will befall him."

The performance's beginning (Zarathustra still preaching) is the sibling-locus tightrope-walker-zarathustra-marketplace-1883; this note carries the fall, the death, and the buffoon it hands to c02 (pdf p141+).

occurrences.title: A man and woman devoured by the Terrible Mother — Tlingit shaman's amulet
occurrences.label: A man and woman devoured by the Terrible Mother
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Pl. XXXVIIIb: walrus-ivory shaman's amulet showing a man and woman disappearing into a fanged mouth — the devouring maw.

Jung's reading: the mother as murderess/eater of flesh (Hansel and Gretel, the lamias) and "the voracious maw, the jaws of death in which men are crunched and ground to pieces" (¶374); Frobenius' monster devouring even "an entire country, which are all delivered by the hero to a glorious rebirth" (¶369).
Verbatim: b. A man and woman devoured by the Terrible Mother Shaman’s amulet, walrus ivory, Tlingit Indians, Alaska, 19th century.

occurrences.title: The Frog Prince — the golden ball, the bed, the wall
occurrences.label: The Frog Prince — the golden ball, the bed,…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The golden ball is the sun which represents our libido. The libido of the princess runs away, so the poor girl has a depression, she loses her joy in life.
body: Jung retells the tale to read the frogs leaping from the chalice: the princess loses her golden ball in the well; the frog fetches it for the price of eating from her dish and sleeping in her bed; thrown against the wall, "in that instant the frog fell away and out came the prince."

To recover joy she "must assimilate that cold repulsive thing" — an "eternal truth" Jung says he must preach "three or four times every day". The frog is "a sort of embryonic man in which the beautiful prince is not yet recognizable", "a cold-blooded little man"; the tale is "a sort of initiation myth" sealed by Angelus Silesius' verse — catch the godhead's pearl-dew only by clinging to its humanity. The frog means "man under his chthonic aspect, his 'nothing but' aspect", redeeming exactly when compensatory.

occurrences.title: Nietzsche's toad dream (Basel dinner party)
occurrences.label: Nietzsche's toad dream (Basel dinner party)
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: fn 1 to ch. III, The Miller Fantasies (pdf p679); cf. index 'toad, Nietzsche's dream of, 34n'

body: At a Basel dinner Nietzsche told the young lady beside him a dream: his hand, laid on the table, grew "a skin like glass, shiny and transparent," showing bones, tissues, muscles — and "All at once I saw a fat toad sitting on my hand and I felt at the same time an irresistible compulsion to swallow the creature." The companion felt "an oracle had spoken to her in a parable." Jung (1952 fn) reads the transparent hand and swallowed toad as prophecy of Nietzsche's disease — "a glimpse, as through a narrow crack, into the dark abyss of his inner self" (Bernoulli, Franz Overbeck und Friedrich Nietzsche, I, p. 72).

occurrences.title: Nietzsche's toad dream — the crystal hand that must swallow the toad
occurrences.label: Nietzsche's toad dream
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Basel (told at a dinner; Bernoulli, Overbeck-Nietzsche correspondence, 1908)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Nietzsche suffered a lifelong phobia "that when he saw a toad, he felt that he ought to swallow it". Sitting beside a young woman at dinner he told a dream: his hand seen "with all the anatomical detail, quite translucent, absolutely pure and crystal-like, and then suddenly an ugly toad was sitting upon his hand and he had to swallow it."

Jung reads the toad as "a secret poison hidden in the darkness" — and the dream as the quintessence of Nietzsche's fate: "that exceedingly sensitive nervous man has a syphilitic infection. That is a historical fact-I know the doctor who took care of him. It was when he was twenty-three years old". Telling the dream was unconscious information: "Don't touch me! I am unclean-marked by my fate". The locus reappears a week later as the cue for the chapter "On Chastity."

occurrences.title: Nuremberg fountain — water from the women's breasts into the frogs' mouths
occurrences.label: Nuremberg fountain
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: I remember a fountain in Nuremberg where the water pours from the breasts of women into the mouths of frogs. Also, the toad is a medieval symbol of the womb.
body: The folk-material behind the virgin-toad connection that Dr. Reichstein opens ("The toad drinks her milk"):

Jung sets it in the series virgin ↔ toad/frog: the toad that drinks the Virgin's milk; the virgin as "the vas insigne devotionis, as she is called in the Lorettanian Litany, the excellent vase of devotion" and as the astrological Virgo meaning the earth — "so the earth is the cup, or the receiving or conceiving vessel from which issues the saving symbol"; the virgin "gives birth to, or nourishes, the toad or the frog… it is simply another analogy; it is an animal symbol of the child". The frogs from the chalice in the vision inherit this lineage: the healing substance issuing from the womb of the chalice.

occurrences.title: Standing under the waters of life - the flames of white light (Visions, 18 May 1932)
occurrences.label: Standing under the waters of life - the flames…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I stood under the stream of water which issued from the rock and was afraid lest I also would perish. But I stood firm and lifted up my face to the water which was greatly refreshing.
body: The series after the blasted house opens "immediately with the symbol of the waters of life": a great stream rushing from a rock - "life moving like a river, seeking the deepest place, and that is Lao-tze's definition of Tao". Many souls are "caught" in the foaming torrent; then she stands under the stream, faces the falling water, and is refreshed: "If you can be conscious of the stream of life... you are naturally at variance with things... Nothing is more deadly than to be always in harmony with things". Crossing the great river is "a rebirth symbol."

The reward: "I was filled with a new strength and about me played flames of white light." Jung: no longer the chthonic witchcraft fire but "the pure light of truth" - the Clear Light of the Void, the Dharmakaya of the Chikhai Bardo, "the Divine Body of Truth". "The criterion of a real truth, or of a real symbol, is that it does stand the onslaught of fire and of water." The white city was "the first glimpse of the white light."

occurrences.title: The woman hit when her bush-soul leopard was shot (Talbot, West Africa)
occurrences.label: The woman hit when her bush-soul leopard was…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: West Africa (Ekoi country, per P. Amaury Talbot)
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1900s (Talbot, In the Shadow of the Bush)
occurrences.quote: The interesting thing is that there are still people who are partially identical with certain animals, there is a peculiar attraction between them.
body: Talbot's reported case: a farmer shot a leopard that was after his cattle, and the woman whose bush soul was identical with that leopard "was hit too" by the same bullet. In West Africa generally, to shoot a man's bush-soul animal — crocodile, snake, or leopard — is to wound its owner.

Jung's reading: "this bush soul idea is not only a superstition, it is also a psychological fact." People partially identical with animals attract or provoke strange behavior in them; such cases show "detachable psychological complexes which project themselves to such an extent that even an animal feels influenced by them" — the hamingja/bush-soul lineage of the placenta-double.

occurrences.title: Fire Lakes totem-animal quest — marathon race and the first animal seen (Achumawi, northern California)
occurrences.label: Fire Lakes totem-animal quest
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: northern California (Fire Lakes, reached in sunset light)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: "in northern California there is a sort of marathon race; a man starts early and races up the mountain to the Fire Lakes (so called because they are reached in the sunset light). It is a lonely place and there he must sleep, and in the early morning the first animal he sees is his totem animal. If the animal speaks to him he must be a medicine-man" (p351). On return, the old men sing the animal songs in circle — "when they sing the song of the animal he has conversed with, he cannot help betraying it," sighing audibly, "and then he is in for trouble."

Jung sets this within the archetypal situation of isolation for meeting the ancestors ("North American Indians... go alone into a cave or little tent... supposed to have dreams and intercourse with spirits, chiefly in the form of animals") — the frame for the dreamer's crocodile: "in the place of his origin he meets the ancestral animal, the divine crocodile" (p351).

occurrences.title: 'We are red araras' — South American Indians' parrot identity (South America)
occurrences.label: We are red araras
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Certain South American Indians assure you that they are red araras (parrots), although they are quite aware that they have no feathers and don't look like birds.
body: Amid primitive "fringe of consciousness" phenomena, Jung reports: "Certain South American Indians assure you that they are red araras (parrots), although they are quite aware that they have no feathers and don't look like birds." The assertion is not confusion but psychic identity — participation mystique, "this halo... which gives a colourful and fantastic aspect to the primitive's world" (¶465).

Jung's reading: the civilized mind has stripped such identity off the world of things, keeping it "below the threshold"; when it reappears (visions, involuntary fantasies) moderns panic and diagnose pathology (¶465-466).

occurrences.title: Church-spire, policeman and sword dream — 11-year-old girl (Zurich, 1912)
occurrences.label: Church-spire, policeman and sword dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I am as tall as a church-spire and can see into every house. At my feet are very small children, as small as flowers are.
body: Dream after the third interview: as tall as a church-spire, seeing into every house, tiny children "as small as flowers" at her feet; a policeman approaches and she threatens decapitation with his own sword. Associations: "I would like to be taller than my father, because then he would have to obey me"; policeman = the military father (¶489). Jung's exhibit A for the compensatory, teleological dream function (¶490) — the dream restores the child's "sense of the value of her own personality" after the fear-dream, and its symbols work "through intuition," the same efficacy religious symbols draw on, "no conscious understanding needed" (¶490).

occurrences.title: Tractatus Aristotelis: the drunken serpent of materia hypostatica
occurrences.label: Tractatus Aristotelis
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Matter is thus formed through illusion
body: "The serpent is more cunning than all the beasts of the earth; under the beauty of her skin she shows a harmless face, and she forms herself in the manner of a materia hypostatica, through illusion, when immersed in water. There she gathers together the virtues from the earth, which is her body. Because she is very thirsty she drinks immoderately and becomes drunken, and she causes the nature wherewith she is united to vanish" (¶354).

Jung: "The serpent is Mercurius, who as the fundamental substance (hypostatica) forms himself in the water and swallows the nature to which he is joined (fig. 130). (Cf. sun drowning in the Fountain of Mercurius, lion devouring the sun, Beya dissolving Gabricus in her own body.) Matter is thus formed through illusion, which is necessarily that of the alchemist. This illusion might well be the vera imaginatio possessed of 'informing' power" (¶355).

occurrences.title: The crowned king chained to his mother — Tractatus aureus, ch. 4
occurrences.label: The crowned king chained to his mother
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Chapter 4 of the Tractatus aureus: "But the king reigns, as is witnessed by his brothers, [and] says: 'I am crowned, and I am adorned with the diadem; I am clothed with the royal garment, and I bring joy to the heart; for, being chained to the arms and breast of my mother, and to her substance, I cause my substance to hold together and rest…'" (cw12 ¶141).

Jung: the "king" is the lapis — "an interesting parallel to the Monogenes who dwells in the bosom of the Mother-City and is identical with the crowned and veiled Monad." The Rosarium adds: "the philosopher is not the master of the stone but rather its minister" (¶142). At ¶144 the heresy breaks open: the Son "was something that man could produce out of his own nature—with God's help."

occurrences.title: 'God, in whom is the help of all who are lonely' — Tractatus Aureus passage
occurrences.label: God, in whom is the help of all who are lonely
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Europe (printed Latin text; late-antique attribution to Hermes)
occurrences.quote: (Deus) in quo est adiuvatio cuiuslibet sequestrati” (God, in whom is the help of all who are lonely).
body: Closing his argument that the one "who is going alone and has no guidance... has the somnia a Deo missa; he has no D.C.," Jung cites the alchemical Hermes: "you read in the Tractatus Aureus of Hermes Trismegistus a passage that bears out what I said about isolation. There you read: '(Deus) in quo est adiuvatio cuiuslibet sequestrati' (God, in whom is the help of all who are lonely)."

Hermes, he adds, "was a real leader of souls and the very incarnation of inspiration, thus representing the unconscious manifest in dreams" (¶674). The passage consecrates the alchemists' isolation — "That was the case with the old alchemical philosophers" — as the modern condition of those legitimately extra ecclesiam, guided only by dream and vision.

occurrences.title: 'We marry the crowned king with the red daughter' — Tractatus aureus
occurrences.label: We marry the crowned king with the red daughter
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The king shall come forth from the fire and rejoice in the marriage. The hidden things shall be disclosed, and the virgin's milk be whitened.
body: The Hermetic Tractatus aureus — regarded as of Arabic origin even in the Middle Ages — describes an Easter-drama in other language: the precious stone cast on the dung-heap, altogether vile; the marriage of the crowned king with the red daughter; the son begotten in the gentle fire; death, darkness, and the waters flee away; "our dead son shall live"; the son reigns in the red garment and the purple.

Jung: "We can take this text as a variant of the mythical God-man and his triumph over death, and thus as an analogy of the Christian drama" — with Christian influence probable but undecidable given the text's unknown age.

occurrences.title: Adam the lesser world — Tractatus Micreris
occurrences.label: Adam the lesser world — Tractatus Micreris
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: When the water fell upon the earth, Adam was created, who is the lesser world.
body: Man "is called the lesser world [mundus minor], because in him is the figure of the heavens, of the earth, of the sun and moon, a visible figure upon earth and [at the same time] invisible." Hence the saying of the old Philosophers: "When the water fell upon the earth, Adam was created, who is the lesser world."
Jung at cw14 ¶552 uses it to show why Adam suited the prima materia: composed of the four cosmic principles, he is the Microcosm — the water-and-earth creation myth in alchemical dress.

occurrences.title: The king and the corpse — the Vetala carrying tale (India)
occurrences.label: The king and the corpse
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Mrs. Sigg recalls Zimmer's Die Geschichte vom indischen König mit dem Leichnam; Mrs. Baumann adds the English translation, Vikram and the Vampire (Burton 1870, from the Baital-Pachisi). "Professor Zimmer's interpretation of that myth was that the king had to carry a corpse as a sort of ordeal, and thereby he learned the greatest wisdom. That is a very wonderful myth, an extraordinary piece of psychology".

Jung's reading: the corpse is the corpus, the body — "the same word is used for the living and the dead body" because the body is dead in itself, animated by Prana. "The protection against inflation, against possession through an archetype, is carrying the burden." The integration of the ancestral dead is "the carrying of the corpse of the ancestors, or the burden of the ancestors".

occurrences.title: Kant's treasure in the deep abyss of dim representations
occurrences.label: Kant's treasure in the deep abyss…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: he speaks of the 'treasure lying within the field of dim representations, that deep abyss of human knowledge forever beyond our reach.
body: In his lectures on psychology Kant speaks of "the treasure lying within the field of dim representations, that deep abyss of human knowledge forever beyond our reach." Jung quotes him twice in CW7 — in the 1928 text (Part 2, Part 1, Ch. 4) and again in the 1916 first-version appendix (pdf p417, n13, wording there citing Psychology of the Unconscious).

Jung's reading: "This treasure, as I have demonstrated in my Symbols of Transformation, is the aggregate of all those primordial images in which the libido is invested, or rather, which are self-representations of the libido". Enlightenment's own philosopher already posited the impersonal psyche's riches beneath clear representation — the abyss that "forever" resists reach becomes, for Jung, the fantasy-making stratum the analytic method can actually work.

occurrences.title: 'Take from the head and touch not the body' — warning dream of Poliphilo, Hypnerotomachia preface
occurrences.label: Take from the head and touch not the body
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Venice (1499) → Paris (Béroalde de Verville's Recueil Stéganographique, 1600)
occurrences.quote: Whoever thou mayest be, take of this treasure as much as thou willst. Yet I warn thee, take from the head and touch not the body.
body: In the 1931 foreword to Schmid-Guisan's Tag und Nacht, Jung aligns the book with the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili as "a petal fallen from the unfading mystic rose which the troubadours accused the Church of hiding under a veil of secrecy" (¶1711). From the preface he quotes the Knights-of-the-Rose passage on the secrets of Love, then the "classical warning which the unconscious gave Poliphilo on his journey into the darkness" (¶1712).

His reading: the warning is aimed at literal-minded readers — "Since witless literal-mindedness has not died out in four hundred years" — head (spirit, meaning) may be taken freely; the body (sensuous vehicle, the letter) must not be grasped. The same esoteric-exoteric split governs the whole Poliphilo tradition Jung later mined for alchemy (¶1749).

occurrences.title: The treasure that rises on the ninth day of the ninth month of the ninth year
occurrences.label: The treasure that rises on the ninth day…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: a treasure which is hidden in the ground rises to the surface on the ninth day of the ninth month of the ninth year, and if you are on the spot then it is yours. But if you are not on the spot, the treasure descends with a noise like thunder into the earth, into unfathomable depths. Then slowly it rises again.
body: An "old saying" Jung tells the seminar:

Jung uses it to state the periodicity of the unconscious: "they get into the unconscious where they are subject to the laws, the peculiar slow rhythm of the unconscious." Asked by Mrs. Crowley about the Pindar-Pater legend of Persephone restoring souls every nine years, he answers "it would be the same idea probably — it is typically a period of pregnancy": the treasure is "always symbolized by a child about to be born," and nine-month and nine-year intervals govern dreams and decisive developments in analysis.

occurrences.title: B.St.'s dream of the Predigerkirche filled with silver five-franc pieces (Burgholzli, Jung's early cases)
occurrences.label: B.St.s dream of the Predigerkirche filled…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Burgholzli asylum, Zurich (patient B.St., schizophrenic seamstress)
occurrences.yearDisplay: Jung's Burgholzli years, c. 1902-07 (case published in Dementia Praecox, 1907)
occurrences.quote: She called herself the silver island and the church because she once had a dream in which the Predigerkirche was filled from floor to ceiling with silver five-franc pieces which belonged to her.
body: The schizophrenic B.St. identified herself with institutions and landscape — "I am the double Polytechnikum," the Lorelei, Naples "feeding the nation with macaroni," the silver island, the Predigerkirche. The church-identification rested on a dream: the Predigerkirche filled from floor to ceiling with silver five-franc pieces belonging to her, "Reden ist Silber, Schweigen ist Gold" folded in (she never stopped talking), and her asylum isolation behind the island image. Jung's exhibit of primitive mentality persisting in psychosis: the ego swallowed by collective identifications, the personality living through impersonal places rather than persons.

occurrences.title: Starry couples in a great river; the treasure in the astronomical observatory (Two Essays case)
occurrences.label: Starry couples in a great river
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: He saw those starry couples in a great river, and then had a strong feeling conviction that the treasure was in the astronomical observatory.
body: The young man of the Two Essays who became insane after a disappointment in love saw "starry couples in a great river" and formed the strong feeling-conviction that the treasure was in the astronomical observatory. Jung retells him in the seminar as the type of the person caught in the roots: "He never could ask himself what it meant... they stick to the fact that it has happened and are crazy". Had he been able to say "This is a strange idea which is rising in my mind, what does it mean?" he would have been ready for a supernormal psychology — and "cured in one stroke." The case is the negative foil to the patient's own question "Must I know you?"

occurrences.title: The talisman casket — childhood relics of the runaway neurotic (Clark lecture, 1909)
occurrences.label: The talisman casket
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich (case reported at Clark University, Worcester, Mass.)
occurrences.quote: it was a casket containing his old childhood books, old dried flowers, stones, and even small bottles of water.
body: In "The Family Constellation", after the doctrine that "what most influences him are the unconscious personal affective states of his parents and teachers", Jung gives the case of "a neurotic young man who ran away from home. He was estranged from and almost hostile to his family, but he admitted to me that he possessed a very special talisman; it was a casket containing his old childhood books, old dried flowers, stones, and even small bottles of water from the well at his home and from a river along which he used to walk with his parents". Estrangement on the surface, sacramental bond underneath: the casket is the family constellation made portable — a private relic-cult of place (well-water, river-water) and childhood thing. Image attribution (treasure, with stone co-manifest) provisional for reconciliation.

occurrences.title: The tree with four-coloured blossoms on the sea — Abu 'l-Qasim al-Iraqi
occurrences.label: The tree with four-coloured blossoms on the sea
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Abu 'l-Qasim's Kitab al-'ilm al-muktasab describes the philosophical tree's four kinds of blossom — "red, midway between white and black, black, and midway between white and yellow" — "The four colours refer to the four elements that are combined in the opus" (cw13 ¶402). Its habitat: "The philosophical tree usually grows alone and, according to Abu'l Qasim, 'on the sea' in the Western Land, which presumably means on an island" (cw13 ¶406).
Jung connects the sea-habitat to Persian tradition (Vourukasha) and to the Hesperides' island with its dragon and ambrosia fountain (n.1).
Verbatim: The four colours refer to the four elements that are combined in the opus. (cw13 ¶402ocr)

occurrences.title: Adam's last look into Paradise: the dead tree with a baby in its branches (Jewish legend)
occurrences.label: Adam's last look into Paradise
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Judea (Life of Adam and Eve tradition)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: The tree is dead, but in its branches is lying a little baby.
body: "There is a Jewish legend in which Adam, just before his death, is allowed to look for the last time into Paradise. The tree is dead, but in its branches is lying a little baby."

The final image of the cherry-tree lecture: the tree of life dead at the fall of the first man, yet holding the renewal — the child in the tree. It condenses the whole series of dream 15 (tree, anima-child, growth beyond the father's death) and the Puer row of dream 12, and stands in the Adam-cycle the vault already tracks. Jung gives it without source; it belongs to the Adam-literature (Life of Adam and Eve / Seth legends of the wood of the cross).

occurrences.title: Alexander finds Hermes' tomb: the tree of glorious greenness and the stork
occurrences.label: Alexander finds Hermes' tomb
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: treatise ascribed to Albertus Magnus (Theatr. chem. II p. 527)
occurrences.quote: Alexander invenit sepulcrum Hermetis et quandam arborem sitam ab extra intus tenentem viriditatem gloriosam: super eam ciconia ibi sedebat, quasi se appellans circulum Lunarem: et ibi ipse aedificavit sedes aureas et posuit terminum itineribus suis idoneum.
body: Alexander the Great comes to the tomb of Hermes and finds beside it a tree "green and glorious within"; on it sits a stork "calling itself the circle of the Moon," and there Alexander "built golden seats and put a fitting end to his travels." Jung glosses: the stork is an avis Hermetis, like the goose (fig. 198) and the pelican — the bird as the self-moving, self-renewing aspect of the arcanum.

The locus condenses the alchemical end-goal: the seeker (Alexander = the heroic ego) arrives at the master's grave and the journey ends where the lunar-solar bird sits in the evergreen tree — the arbor philosophica as terminus of the peregrinatio (cw12 Part II, "journeys to the four quarters" ¶452ff).

occurrences.title: The young ash and the two knights — Lower Saxon world-end legend
occurrences.label: The young ash and the two knights
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Each New Year's Eve a white knight riding upon a white horse comes to cut down the young shoot.
body: A young ash grows unnoticed in a wood. Each New Year's Eve a white knight on a white horse comes to cut down the young shoot; each time a black knight arrives and fights him, and after a long battle the white knight wins and fells the tree. "But one day the white knight will be unsuccessful, then the ash will grow, and when it is big enough for a horse to be tethered under it, a mighty king will come and a tremendous battle will begin: i.e., end of the world."
The tree whose fate is the aeon's fate — the apocalyptic growth of the world-tree guarded by an annual duel of light and dark riders.

occurrences.title: Ask and Embla — first and last humans in the world-tree (Edda)
occurrences.label: Ask and Embla — first and last humans…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Germanic myth: the first human beings are born from the ash and alder; before Ragnarok the last human beings "enter the tree again and become a tree, the world ash."

Jung reads the Germanic tree through Nietzsche — "he would naturally use Germanic archetypal material" — as mother and sarcophagus at once: "The tree first gives birth to man, and then it is the sarcophagus, as the earth is the mother that gives birth in the dawn of humanity — and in the evening is the sarcophaga: she eats the dead." Hence the corpse in Zarathustra's hollow tree expects resurrection: "out of a wood the body would rise."
Verbatim: "The first human beings were supposed to be born from the ash and alder, and the last human beings before the world-hell breaks loose enter the tree again and become a tree, the world ash."

occurrences.title: The village aswatha (Ficus religiosa), clothed and pierced — Indian tree worship
occurrences.label: The village aswatha, clothed and pierced
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: he is taking a dangerous step, for he is seeking refuge with the mother whose garment is the garment of death.
body: Tree-anthropomorphism: "every village has its sacred tree (pl. LV), which is clothed and treated exactly like a human being"; trees anointed, garlanded, and pierced through the ear "as an apotropaic charm against death" (¶545). Hiawatha's fungus-coated pine is the death-garment of the same mother-tree (¶546).

occurrences.title: The Attis transitus — the pine carried into the cave
occurrences.label: The Attis transitus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Jung: "The transitus in the cult of Attis is a better analogy, where the fir tree is carried into a cave, into the earth, the cave being a burial place or a mystery place — they are indistinguishably the same."

Of the three transitus figures (Christ's cross, Attis' tree, Mithras' bull) the Attis rite is closest to Zarathustra's corpse-carrying: a god-adjacent body borne into the earth's burial-mystery place. The first Christian cult took place in the catacombs "by no means to escape persecution" — they "simply worshipped in the burial ground," and medieval churches remain burial grounds.

Verbatim: "The transitus in the cult of Attis is a better analogy, where the fir tree is carried into a cave, into the earth, the cave being a burial place or a mystery place-they are indistinguishably the same."

occurrences.title: Attis — self-castration under the pine and the annual tree rite (Attis-Cybele cult)
occurrences.label: Attis — self-castration under the pine…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: cult attested at Rome from 204 BCE; legend older
body: "Attis was the son-lover of Agdistis-Cybele, the mother of the gods. Driven mad by his mother's insane love for him, he castrated himself under a pine-tree" (¶659). Every year a pine was garlanded, an effigy of Attis hung on it and cut down; Cybele carried the tree into her cave and lamented — the son taken back into the maternal womb. Ovid: Attis "put off his human form and stiffened into a tree-trunk" (¶661); on the Coblenz bas-relief Attis grows out of the tree (¶662). The priests were eunuch Galloi; the archigallos was named Atys; arm-scratching replaced annual castration — "arm as substitute for phallus" (¶662).

Jung disentangles the overlappings: tree = mother and son's phallus at once; felling = castration = mother-sacrifice; "the impulse to sacrifice proceeds from the mater saeva cupidinum" (¶660). The feast moved from lamentation to joy — "(Good Friday and Easter)" — the Terrible Mother as "counterpart and complement of the Pietà" (¶662).
Verbatim: "Driven mad by his mother's insane love for him, he castrated himself under a pine-tree" (¶659).

occurrences.title: Baruch the 'wood of life' and the Naas — the Gnosis of Justin
occurrences.label: Baruch the 'wood of life' and the Naas
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the Gnosis of Justin (Hippolytus, Elenchos V, 26): "the trees in the Garden of Eden are angels, while the tree of knowledge of good and evil is the third of the motherly angels, th eN aas" (cw13 ¶420ocr). The angel Baruch, named the "wood of life", is the angel of revelation (cw13 ¶459).

Jung's reading: the Naas is the prima materia of the Naassenes, "a moist substance" like Thales' water, dividing like Eden's river into four (n.10); the division of the tree-soul into a masculine (Baruch) and a feminine figure "corresponds to the alchemical Mercurius as the life principle of the tree, for as an hermaphrodite he is duplex" (cw13 ¶420).
Verbatim: the trees in the Garden of Eden are angels, while the tree of knowledge of good and evil is the third of the motherly angels, th eN aas. (cw13 ¶420ocr)

occurrences.title: The vanity figure of Basel Minster: snakes and toads creeping up her back (Gothic, ~14th-15th c.)
occurrences.label: The vanity figure of Basel Minster
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: she is standing so still that you can almost see the snakes and toads creeping up her back as if she were a tree.
body: In the seminar's Gothic-vs-Romanesque discussion Jung points to "a famous figure in the cathedral in Basel where you can see how still a human being stands in the Gothic style; it is a woman's figure, representing worldly lust or vanity, but she is standing so still that you can almost see the snakes and toads creeping up her back as if she were a tree". In the Gothic "the stone becomes a plant, the feeling of man becomes plantlike" — man becomes a column, a pine cone, part of the upward movement; the human figure assumes the tree quality that the Romanesque had given to fighting animals (St. Zeno in Verona's friezes as the contrast).

occurrences.title: Bata's soul on the acacia blossom — the Egyptian tale of the two brothers
occurrences.label: Bata's soul on the acacia blossom
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the Egyptian tale of Bata (papyrus of the nineteenth dynasty; Flinders Petrie, Egyptian Tales), the hero "placed his soul on the topmost blossom of an acacia-tree. When the tree was cut down with treacherous intent, his soul was found again in the form of a seed. With this the dead Bata was restored to life"; killed again as a bull, two persea trees grow from his blood, and a chip fertilizes the queen, who bears the reborn Bata as Pharaoh (cw13 ¶401).

Jung: "It is evident that the tree here is an instrument of transformation" (¶401); he notes these transformation processes are omitted in Pritchard's recension (n.4) — a parallel to Christ as "tree cut down in his passion" (Cassiodorus) and to the pine of Attis (n.13).
Verbatim: his soul was found again in the form of a seed. With this the dead Bata was restored to life. (cw13 ¶401ocr)

occurrences.title: "I knew I had become a tree and lifted my face to the sun" (Visions plate 12)
occurrences.label: I knew I had become a tree and lifted my face…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich (patient's painting; plate following p. 272 of the edition)
occurrences.yearDisplay: painted late 1929/early 1930 for Jung; vision from the 1926-32 series

jung.locator: plate 12 caption (pdf p8); discussion in later sessions; intro pp44-45

occurrences.quote: I knew I had become a tree and lifted my face to the sun
body: Plate 12: the visioner's transformation into a tree, face lifted to the sun — the human-vegetation metamorphosis at the center of the series. Douglas's introduction records Jung's hermeneutic for this image: "Jung used the yogic view of the circulating and expanding spinal energy as a hermeneutic to inform his psychological understanding of the meaning of the tree in Morgan's visions. Jung described both images as referring to conduits of vitality, energy openings, that mediate between heaven and earth to bring about transformation through the union of the opposites" — the tree read through the Kundalini axis, and the Kundalini read through the tree.

occurrences.title: Das Buch der heiligen Dreifaltigkeit — Codex Germanicus 598 (Munich, 1420)
occurrences.label: Das Buch der heiligen Dreifaltigkeit
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: The Spirit Mercurius, fig. B3 — ¶ pin tbd

body: German alchemical picture-manuscript of 1420 whose central image is the Trinity shown as a tree — the "Holy Trinity" growing as the arbor philosophica — with a famous Rebis (double-being) illustration that Jung reproduces as CW13 fig. B3. In the index Jung cites the manuscript at print p144n, in the Melusina/hermaphrodite region of the Paracelsus commentary.

Verbatim: Munich. Staatsbibliothek. Codex Germanicus 598. 1420. "Das Buch der heiligen Dreifaltigkeit und Beschreibung der Heimlichkeit von Veranderung der Metallen." (OCR noise preserved; "Veranderung" = Verwandlung, "transmutation of metals").
The codex fuses the Christian quaternity-of-God motif ("God is four", cf. Barbelo formula, print 13n) with the philosophical tree — a key Latin-Christian instance of tree as quaternity.

image.title: Engraving and etching - a handbook for the use of students and print collectors (1907) (14774017535)

occurrences.title: Christmas-tree lights as surviving sun-magic (Europe / North America)
occurrences.label: Christmas-tree lights as surviving sun-magic
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: On 25 December we put lights on our Christmas tree in order that the sun may rise.
body: Jung catches the modern festival fossilized in solstice magic: lights on the tree on 25 December "in order that the sun may rise," the evergreen "so that it will bring forth fruit" — a magic ceremonial to produce and increase the sun, now re-read as the festival that "produces Christ again" on the borrowed birthday of Mithra, the invincible sun. Companion exhibit: the Pueblo chief's letter claiming the sun will not rise if the Americans destroy his tribe's religion. All the festivals of that season were magic rituals for the renewal of light and warmth.

occurrences.title: The Christmas tree — a ritual whose meaning its performers never knew
occurrences.label: The Christmas tree
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

occurrences.quote: What the meaning of the Christmas-tree might be our forefathers knew even less than ourselves
body: "The behaviour of the Elgonyi certainly strikes us as exceedingly primitive, but we forget that the educated Westerner behaves no differently. What the meaning of the Christmas-tree might be our forefathers knew even less than ourselves, and it is only quite recently that we have bothered to find out at all."

Jung's reading: the Christmas tree is his counter-example from the reader's own culture for the preconscious archetype — a living ritual performed for centuries without anyone knowing what it means, structurally identical to the Elgonyi sunrise spitting (¶411) and the Egyptian baboon gesture (¶412). Ritual acts precede and outlive their meaning; "a later, more conscious humanity" rationalized such things as vestiges of a Golden Age of men who knew all things (¶412).

occurrences.title: The tree of contemplation, palm with seven birds — Basel MS
occurrences.label: The tree of contemplation, palm with seven birds
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The treatise "De arbore contemplationis" (Basel UB MS AX 128b) shows the tree of contemplation as a palm with seven branches — matching the seven branches of the tree of the metals — each branch bearing a bird ("pavo, [illegible], cignus, [h]arpia, filomena, hyrundo, fenix") and a flower ("viola, gladiola, lilium, rosa, crocus, solsequium "), all of moral significance (cw13 ¶414).
Jung: "These ideas are very much like those of the alchemists. They contemplated their tree in the retort, where, according to the Chymical Wedding, it was held in the hand of an angel" (cw13 ¶414).
Verbatim: so also has the tree of contemplation, as a treatise entitled "De arbore contemplationis" shows. (cw13 ¶414)

occurrences.title: The corpse in the hollow tree — Zarathustra's burial
occurrences.label: The corpse in the hollow tree
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Zarathustra sleeps on the ground beside the hollow tree in which he has placed the rope-dancer's corpse, "for he wanted to protect him from the wolves."

Jung: the wood is "simply another symbol like the sea; it is the darkness" — burial in the unconscious so the heaviness can be forgotten and Zarathustra becomes "light, a dancer." But the burial is also positive: the tree is mother and sarcophagus, a burial "with the idea of resurrection" — "one fertilizes the mother by putting a corpse into her and she will transform it and give it rebirth in time." The body might "suddenly... resurrect from the tree."
Verbatim: "Yes, it is the depths of the unconscious. The wood in this respect is simply another symbol like the sea; it is the darkness."

occurrences.title: The cross of the tree of paradise — Jachin and Boaz legend
occurrences.label: The cross of the tree of paradise
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939
Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "An old legend says that the wood for the cross was taken from the tree of paradise which was cut down and made into the two pillars, Aachim and Boas, in front of Solomon's temple. Then these were thrown away, and discovered again, and made into the cross. So Christ was sacrificed on the original tree of life, and in the transitus he carried it" (pdf p1433; repeated 7 Dec 1938 with the pillars thrown into a pond of the river valley after the temple's destruction).

The analogues: Egyptian obelisks flanking the sun-barque's way (Karnak; one now in Rome, one in Paris); medieval crucifixion pictures with branches, leaves and fruits; Christ crucified "on the tree of life."

occurrences.title: The despairing devata of the tree (Samyutta Nikaya)
occurrences.label: The despairing devata of the tree
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: A story from one of the Buddhistic treatises: a devata — a tree-soul, a semidivine being living in a tree — falls into despair on seeing termites approaching the tree, "because it cannot get away." The tree is the one life that cannot deviate a single inch from the divine law: rooted to the spot, exposed to every enemy.

Jung uses it to mark the tree's specific character against the totem animal: the animal can dodge conditions, man deviates consciously — the tree symbolizes "the kind of life that cannot deviate for one single inch," which is why it is "a more primitive and yet a more advanced symbol," fit to carry divine grace and Yoga alike.

occurrences.title: The metallic tree whose branches are the veins of the earth — Dorn, De genealogia mineralium
occurrences.label: The metallic tree whose branches are the veins…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Dorn, "De genealogia mineralium" (Theatr. chem. I, 1659, p. 574): nature plants "the root of the metallic tree in the midst of her womb, viz., the stone which shall bring forth the metals"; the trunk divides into branches spread "from Germany even as far as Hungary and beyond... as in the human body the veins spread through the different limbs". The fruits drop, the tree dies and vanishes, "afterwards... another new [tree]" (cw13 ¶375).

Jung: "The tree is obviously thought of as a system of blood vessels" whose liquid fruit coagulates — and juxtaposes the Persian Gayomart, whose blood became the seven metals (cw13 ¶376; see gayomart-metals-original-man-persia). The same treatise calls Aristotle, Albertus, Avicenna tares of "that Greek Satan" who "turned the name Sophia in to Philosophia" (cw13 ¶377).
Verbatim: After nature has planted the root of the metallic tree in the midst of her womb, viz., the stone which shall bring forth the metals (cw13 ¶375)

occurrences.title: The tree of faith growing from above downwards, twelve branches — John of Ruysbroeck on Luke 19
occurrences.label: The tree of faith growing from above downwards…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The last footnote of this chunk: "And he must climb up into the tree of faith, which grows from above downwards, for its roots are in the Godhead. This tree has twelve branches, which are the twelve articles of faith. The lower speak of the Divine Humanity" (cw14 ch. III n.210; the chunk breaks off mid-quote).

Zacchaeus climbing the sycamore to see Christ becomes the mystic climbing the inverted tree — roots in the Godhead, branches descending into doctrine and the Divine Humanity. The image pairs with the kabbalistic Tree of the Sefiroth (YHVH the trunk, Ehyeh the root; Kether the source of sap "like the soul in the body" — n.209) as a Christian instance of the inverted world-tree.

occurrences.title: The pine-tree and the white sheet — Heine recitation blocked (Zurich, ~1906)
occurrences.label: The pine-tree and the white sheet
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: he had totally forgotten the words 'mit weisser Decke' (with white sheet).
body: A gentleman reciting Heine's "Ein Fichtenbaum steht einsam" (A pine-tree stands alone) sticks hopelessly at "Ihn schläfert" — he has totally forgotten "mit weisser Decke" (with white sheet). Pressed for associations he runs: white sheet → winding-sheet for the dead → a close friend whose brother just died of a stroke → the friend is corpulent, as I am → our family tends to stoutness → I have begun a reducing course. Jung: "the gentleman at once identified himself unconsciously with the pine-tree enveloped in a white sheet" (¶119); the recitation itself was a symptomatic action discharging the excitation of the death-complex (¶120). His model for the complex "condensing a distant analogy and a person" (¶218: then the patient would say "I am the pine-tree").

occurrences.title: The tree in the sea Vourukasha / tree of life at Ardvi Sura Anahita — Bundahish
occurrences.label: The tree in the sea Vourukasha / tree…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Persian legend of the tree that grows in the sea named Vourukasha, and of the tree of life at the fountain of Ardvi Sura Anahita (Windischmann, Zoroastrische Studien, pp. 90, 171) — the Gaokerena com plex Jung invokes to explain why Abu 'l-Qasim's philosophical tree grows "on the sea" (cw13 ¶406).

The same Iranian field gives the world-tree guarded by a lizard (see serpent-lizard-haoma-tree-bundahishn-9c, cw12) and the three-legged ass standing in Vourukasha (ass-three-legged-ass-bundahish-persia-9c). Gaokerena is the good tree against which the combative powers of Ahrimanic darkness press — the ambrosia-tree guarded, like the Hesperides' tree, by a hostile guardian.
Verbatim: the legend of the tree in the Bundahish that grows in the sea named Vourukasha, or of the tree of life that grows in the fountain of Ardvi Sura Anahita. (cw13 ¶406ocr)

occurrences.title: From Anthropos and gnosis is born the tree — the Barbeliots
occurrences.label: From Anthropos and gnosis is born the tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the Barbeliot system (Irenaeus, Adv. haer. I, 29, 3), the Autogenes creates "the man perfect and true, whom they also called Adam as", and with him perfect knowledge: "From [the perfect] man and gnosis is born the tree, which they also call gnosis" (cw13 ¶419).

Jung: "Here we find the same connection of man with the tree as in the case of Adam and the Buddha" (¶419) — Adam made of "the earth of the tree of life" (¶418), Buddha shaded by the Bodhi tree. Hegemonius's Acta Archelai gives the parallel: "that tree which is in paradise, whereby the good is known, is Jesus and the knowledge of him " (n.7). The fire-tree of Simon Magus "is a similar conception" (¶459 n8).
Verbatim: From [the perfect] man and gnosis is born the tree, which they also call gnosis. (cw13 ¶419)

occurrences.title: Monkey-puzzle tree and the golden child — dream and waking vision (20 April 1938)
occurrences.label: Monkey-puzzle tree and the golden child
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: she suddenly had a vision of a tiny golden child lying at the foot of the tree (tree-birth motif). She had thus gone on dreaming the sense of the dream.
body: Dream of 20 April 1938, found in her notes when Jung asked the patient (the "golden child" case) what had happened in the unconscious six months before the October dream: with other women she looks at a piece of tapestry, "a square with symbolical figures on it," then sits before a marvellous tree — a monkey-puzzle (Araucaria) with branches like candles, confused with Cereus candelabrum — into which a Christmas tree is fitted "in such a way that at first it looks like one tree instead of two." While writing the dream down she suddenly saw, in waking vision, a tiny golden child lying at the foot of the tree.

Jung: "She had thus gone on dreaming the sense of the dream. It undoubtedly depicts the birth of the divine ('golden') child" — the tree-birth motif. Counting backwards another nine months leads to the Kundalini-serpent painting of July 1937: symbolical conception, gestation, birth — an unconscious "time-reckoning" of pregnancy.

occurrences.title: God hangs the sword of wrath on the tree — Dorn, Speculativa philosophia
occurrences.label: God hangs the sword of wrath on the tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Dorn, "Speculativa philosophia" (Theatr. chem. I, 1659, p. 254): "[God] hath determined to snatch the sword of his wrath from the hands of the angel, substituting in place thereof a threepronged hook of gold, hanging the sword on a tree: and so God's wrath is turned in to love" (cw13 ¶447).

Jung: "Christ as Logos is the two-edged sword, which symbolizes God's wrath" (Rev. 1:16); the golden trident alludes to the Trinity, and 'golden' is "an alchemical sous-entendu" (cw13 ¶450). The allegory continues: the hook with which God the Father catches the Leviathan is the crucifix (¶450), of Manichaean origin — see anthropos-bait-manichaean-primordial-man-3c; and the sword-on-the-tree "is almost certainly an analogy of the serpent hanging on the cross" (cw13 ¶448).
Verbatim: substituting in place thereof a threepronged hook of gold, hanging the sword on a tree: and so God’s wrath is turned in to love. (cw13 ¶447ocr)

occurrences.title: The tree-goose Paracelsus claimed to have seen transform — Liber Azoth
occurrences.label: The tree-goose Paracelsus claimed…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Spirit in Man, Art and Literature (CW15)
jung.locator: fn 7 to Paracelsus the Physician (pdf p160)

occurrences.quote: He declares that he witnessed the transformation of the tree-goose himself.
body: The barnacle-goose legend of medieval natural history — geese engendered on trees hanging over water, dropping into the sea full-formed — survives inside alchemy at its highest prestige: in the Liber Azoth Paracelsus "declares that he witnessed the transformation of the tree-goose himself." The empiricist who lectured other physicians on observing nature anchors his authority in an eyewitness claim for spontaneous generation.

Jung's 1941 lecture treats such reports as the wonderful but truthful-to-him sources of Paracelsus's empiricism (body ¶25, in the cw15-c01 range, adds the Spanish tree-goose putrefying into tortoises and the Portuguese wind "which begets mice" in a sheaf of straw). The tree that bears birds is the Philosophical Tree's folk cousin: life arising directly from wood and putrefaction, the opus naturae without human hands.

occurrences.title: The opus as sowing and nurturing the tree — Jodocus Greverus, Secretum (1588)
occurrences.label: The opus as sowing and nurturing the tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jodocus Greverus's "Secretum nobilissimum et verissimum" depicts the whole opus as the sowing and nurturing of a tree in a walled garden: soil = purified Mercurius; Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus form the trunk; sun and moon supply the seeds — "not the common gold, nor the common Mercurius... but [the metals] of the Philosophers" (cw13 ¶355). A wise old man admonishes the adept: "Son, lay aside the snares of worldly appetites" (¶355). The treatise closes with a hymn calling the art "gift of God, containing the secret of the undivided oneness of the Holy Trinity... testimony to the resurrection of the dead" (¶355).

Jung reads the planetary names as "(astrological) temperaments, that is, to psychic factors" (¶355) and the four-trunk union as the coniunctio tetraptiva over the tetrasomia, "a characteristic example of the dilemma of three and four" (¶357-358).
Verbatim: The whole opus is depicted as the sowing and nurturing of the tree in a well-tended garden (cw13 ¶355ocr)

occurrences.title: The white haoma on lake Vouru-Kasha, guarded by the fish Kar-mahi — Persia
occurrences.label: The white haoma on lake Vouru-Kasha, guarded…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Avestan texts (composition redacted late; material older)
occurrences.quote: the white haoma is a celestial tree growing in the lake Vouru-Kasha, while the fish Kar-mahi circles round it and protects it from the frog of Ahriman.
body: The Persian tree of life standing in the lake of rain, Vouru-Kasha: its seeds, mixed with the waters, maintain the fertility of the earth — "Those plants I, Ahura-Mazda, rain down upon the earth, to bring food to the faithful, and fodder to the beneficent cow" (Vendidad, via Darmesteter). The white haoma in the spring Ardvisura, water of life, gives "eternal life, children to women, husbands to girls, and horses to men"; in the Mainyo-i-Khard it is the "preparer of the corpse." The fish Kar-mahi circles it forever, guarding it from the frog of Ahriman.

Jung uses it as another form of the mother-tree motif opening ch. V's symbolism of rebirth — tree and water as one generative complex, and the ever-vigilant guardian against the devil-frog as the shadow-attack on life's source.

occurrences.title: The old man rejuvenated in the hollow oak — Song of Hiawatha
occurrences.label: The old man rejuvenated in the hollow oak
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: an old man is changed back into a youth by crawling through a hollow oak-tree.
body: Re-entry into the tree-mother as cure of age — the hollow tree as womb, with the snake-guarded cave and the skin-casting myth as siblings of the rejuvenation motif (¶410, ¶538).

occurrences.title: The perfect saint who turns into a plant — Jain picture shown in the seminar
occurrences.label: The perfect saint who turns into a plant
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: representing a perfect saint who turns into a plant
body: "Here is a picture from the Jain sect in India, representing a perfect saint who turns into a plant. Mr. Baumann brought it to us as an example of spiritual development being represented by the plant, which we were talking about last week".

The artifact continues the argument of the nest-on-the-tree-of-the-future passage: the tree/plant as symbol "of spiritual development... an almost parasitic kind of development" that extracts and sublimates — "As a tree extracts mineral substances from the earth, the spirit transforms the coarse body... into the subtlety of organic matter". The Jain saint's vegetal apotheosis is the East's diagram of the same sublimatio Jung finds in Nietzsche's fatal flight into the spirit.

occurrences.title: The kalpataru wish-fulfilling tree in anahata (cakra symbolism)
occurrences.label: The kalpataru wish-fulfilling tree in anahata
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: India (epic roots; codified in the cakra descriptions)

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: The accompanying symbol is the kalpataru tree, which fulfills all wishes. Below it is the manipitha altar.
body: In anāhata lives puruṣa; from there the yogi sees the ātman and knows "I am it"; "the prospective spirit is born; it starts becoming conscious. The accompanying symbol is the kalpataru tree, which fulfills all wishes. Below it is the manipitha altar." The wish-tree anchors the tree-family to the fourth center — the place from which values and the "prospective" (teleological) function grow, against mere maṇipūra burning.

occurrences.title: Inverted tree with roots upward — Katha Upanishad II.6.1
occurrences.label: Inverted tree with roots upward
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: There is that ancient tree, whose roots grow upward and whose branches grow downward—that indeed is called the Bright, that is called Brahman, that alone is called the Immortal.
body: The Katha Upanishad describes the eternal asvatta tree whose roots grow upward and branches downward — the cosmic tree inverted relative to the earthly one, "that alone is called the Immortal. All worlds are contained in it, and no one goes beyond." Jung cites it (SBE XV) in the Sol-and-Luna notes, immediately after Ruysbroeck's tree whose highest part is the Godhead — the upward-rooted tree marks the axis of the supernal.

Jung's reading: the tree expresses the atman-Brahman totality that contains all worlds; paired in the same note with the "Adornment of the Spiritual Marriage," where the man must cling to the unity at the top of the tree. Parallels: ashvattha-inverted-tree-bhagavadgita-india, tree-sefiroth-inverted-cabala-1677.

occurrences.title: Tree of life growing from the Father-God's breast — Nelken's schizophrenic patient
occurrences.label: Tree of life growing from the Father-God's…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
