body: Jan Nelken, "Analytische Beobachtungen uber Phantasien eines Schizophrenen" (p. 541): in his patient's cosmic system the Father-God bore a tree of life growing out of his breast, with red and white fruits or spheres "which were worlds" — red for sun, white for moon, the alchemical colour-pair — and on the tree-top sat a dove and an eagle, recalling the stork on the sun-and-moon tree of the "Scriptum Alberti" (cw13 ¶460).

Jung's use: "Any knowledge of the alchemical parallels was quite out of the question in this case" — a rare modern exception to his rule that cosmic tree symbolism recedes when individuation is no longer projected into the cosmos (cw13 ¶459ocr).
Verbatim: It bore red and white fruits, or spheres, which were worlds. (cw13 ¶460ocr)

occurrences.title: Druids cutting a tree into the shape of a man (Caesar's Gaul)
occurrences.label: Druids cutting a tree into the shape of a man
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1st c. BCE (Caesar; via Thomas Maurice, Indian Antiquities, cf. CW5 par. 402)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: The Druids used to cut a tree into the shape of a man with outstretched arms in the form of a cross.
body: Closing the tree-lecture on the cherry-tree dream: "According to Caesar, the Druids used to cut a tree into the shape of a man with outstretched arms in the form of a cross. Christ on the cross is another example, for the cross is also the tree of life."

The row runs: the old Germanic idea that every man has his own tree planted at birth (injure the tree, injure the man), Rider Haggard's People of the Mist where each tribesman's tree falls as he dies, the Druid tree-man, and the crucifix as tree of life — man and tree identified from custom through cult to redemption history. Jung's source for the Druid passage is Thomas Maurice's Indian Antiquities (1796), as in Symbols of Transformation ¶402.

occurrences.title: Man as the inverted tree — Alciati's Emblemata
occurrences.label: Man as the inverted tree — Alciati's Emblemata
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Andrea Alciati (d. 1550), Emblemata cum commentariis: "It pleased the Physicists to see man as a tree standing upside down, for what in the one is the root, trunk, and leaves, in the other is the head and the rest of the body with the arms and feet" (cw13 ¶412). The same volume supplies the birth-tree: "a tree is planted at the birth of a child, and its and the child's fates are identical. 'Therefore the tree is the image and mirror of our condition'" (cw13 ¶350 n1).
Jung's arbor inversa chain runs from the Cabala (Vigenere, Knorr von Rosenroth) through this humanist emblema to the Indian ashvattha (cw13 ¶412-413).
Verbatim: It pleased the Physicists to see man as a tree standing upside down (cw13 ¶412ocr)

occurrences.title: Meschia and Meschiane as trees — the Bundahish
occurrences.label: Meschia and Meschiane as trees — the Bundahish
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: In the Persian holy book the first parents, Meschia and Meschiane, are represented as trees: the first man killed by Ahriman, and from his seed a double plant with a single root whose stems are the primordial man and woman (editors, citing Sacred Books of the East vol. I).
Jung: "That is Indo-Aryan. This idea was in the air generally" — the same mother-tree as the Germanic, here in the tradition of the Persian Zoroaster whose name Nietzsche's prophet carries.
Verbatim: "in the Persian holy book, the Bundahish, the first parents, Meschia and Meschiane, were also represented as trees. That is Indo-Aryan."

occurrences.title: The Nakassa — East Siberian shamans' inverted tree
occurrences.label: The Nakassa — East Siberian shamans' inverted…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: East Siberia; specimen in the Leningrad Museum
body: Kagarow's photograph ("Der umgekehrte Schamanenbaum", p. 183) of a shaman's tree named Nakassa, preserved in the Leningrad Museum: an inverted tree whose roots signify hairs, with a face carved on the trunk near the roots — "showing that the tree represents a man. Presumably this is the shaman himself, or his greater personality" (cw13 ¶462).
Jung's use closes the shamanic row: "The shaman climbs the magic tree in order to find his true self in the upper world" — shamanism read as "a projection of the individuation process" (cw13 ¶462).
Verbatim: The roots signify hairs, and on the trunk, near the roots, a face has been carved, showing that the tree represents a man. (cw13 ¶462ocr)

occurrences.title: Nebuchadnezzar as the tree in his dream — Daniel 4
occurrences.label: Nebuchadnezzar as the tree in his dream
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Daniel 4: the king himself is the tree of the dream — "a tree in the midst of the earth, and the height thereof was great", its heart made beast-like until seven times pass over it (cw13 ¶350 n1: "In the dream of Nebuchadnezzar the king himself is a tree... a tree is planted at the birth of a child, and its and the child's fates are identical").

Jung returns to it for the fruit "not cast in to the fire" (cw13 ¶374) and lists it beside Zarathustra's vision and Bardesanes among "man's relationship to the philosophical tree" (cw13 ¶458): the tree as "an intermediate form of man".
Verbatim: In the dream of Nebuchadnezzar the king himself is a tree. (cw13 ¶350 n1ocr)

occurrences.title: Dream of Nebuchadnezzar picture — CW8 frontispiece (tree from the navel, pelican-quincunx, stag)
occurrences.label: Dream of Nebuchadnezzar picture
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Europe (reproduced as the CW8 frontispiece; artist/provenance not stated by Jung)
occurrences.yearDisplay: late medieval / early modern (inferred; Jung gives no source)

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: The picture of Nebuchadnezzar's dream (Daniel 4) reproduced as the CW8 frontispiece — for Jung a demonstration that "such mythologems get 'condensed' in dreams, and how they modify one another": the artist "has, so to speak, been dreamed over again" (¶559).

The tree grows "in a quite unbiblical manner" out of the king's navel — the genealogical tree of Christ's ancestors growing from the navel of Adam. In its branches the pelican (blood-nourishing Christ allegory) together with four birds forms a quincunx in place of the four evangelists' symbols; below, the stag — "another symbol of Christ" — with four beasts. "Above the volatilia, below the terrena... the alchemical idea of the double quaternity ('superius est sicut quod inferius')". "This contamination shows in the most vivid way how individual dreams make use of archetypes. The archetypes are condensed, interwoven, and blended not only with one another (as here), but also with unique individual elements."

occurrences.title: King Pepi and the tree of life on the isle in the Field of Offerings
occurrences.label: King Pepi and the tree of life on the isle…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~Old Kingdom, c. 2300 BCE (prior to the Osiris faith)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Mrs. Crowley's contribution (7 Dec 1938), quoting the Pyramid Texts: the dead king on his way to Re comes upon a tree of life on the mysterious island in the midst of the Field of Offerings, "over which the gods make the swallows fly. The swallows are the imperishable stars. They give to this king Pepi this tree of Life, whereof they live, and Ye-Pepi and the Morning Star may at the same time live thereof."

Jung: a tree of life rather than the world-tree — the aspect of the tree that gives life, in the oldest stratum of Egyptian religion, "the Solar religion of the old kingdom, about 3000 B.C.". Earliest dated locus of Jung's tree-of-life family in this seminar.

occurrences.title: The old man eats of the white tree and becomes a youth — Turba
occurrences.label: The old man eats of the white tree…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the father is become the son
body: The Turba's rejuvenation recipe in miniature: "Take that white tree and build around it a round dark house covered with dew, and place in it a man of great age, a hundred years old, and close the house upon them and make it fast, so that no wind or dust can get in. Then leave them for one hundred and eighty days in their house.... that old man becomes a youth. O what wondrous natures, which have changed the soul of that old man into a youthful body, and the father is become the son" (¶76).

Sealed vessel as round dark house, dew-covered tree as the white fruit, 180 days of incubation — the senex/puer renewal cycle set inside the opus. Jung cites it between the Trevisan oak-bath and Senior's grave of Sihoka as part of the tree/tomb/womb complex.

occurrences.title: The Market Place: palm tree in the mandala and the little image that springs the iron gate (patient vision, 21 June 1933)
occurrences.label: The Market Place — palm tree in the mandala…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: In the center of the circle where the pit of onyx had been grew a palm tree.... I took it and hurled it against the gate. The gate swung open.
body: After the buffalo onrush the dust cloud holds small snakes with fishes' tails carrying plant germs (half-unconscious fears bearing the possibility of new life — the dove's olive branch). The circle of rock is prison and shelter; an iron gate shuts it; the rocks turn green and a palm tree grows where the onyx pit had been — the pit transformed into "the crater of rebirth," dead stone into plant life, the yoga tree rising from muladhara in spiral stages. At its foot she finds a small image; hurled against the gate, the gate springs open.

Jung amplifies the little image with the mandrake/Springwurzel and its positive aspect: the hero child, the savior treasure at the root of the tree — "the jewel and the child are symbols for the Self... or the Purusha."

occurrences.title: Tree growing from the woman's head — Pandora woodcut (Reusner, p. 211)
occurrences.label: Tree growing from the woman's head
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: A tree is growing out of the head of a naked woman and birds are flying about.
body: The woodcut Jung showed on 9 December 1931 (a book Dr. Reichstein had just given him): a naked woman standing on an alchemical furnace with retort and alembic, a tree growing out of her head, birds about her, an eagle on her crown, sun at left and moon at right — a variant of the tenth Rosarium woodcut, used again by Jung in CW12 (p. 419, ed. fn).

Jung reads the apparatus as a sex analogy — "the alchemistic process that takes place down below in the earth is a sort of sexual process" — the retort/alembic as union of male and female, like the Hindu lingam. The Pandora text he quotes: "The tree comes out of the semen of the man and the woman"; sun-birds die the white death, moon-birds the black death; and the lion — "usually connected with the growth of the tree", his paws cut off — introduces conscious intervention, the ointment "that heals all sickness", the pharmakon athanasias.

occurrences.title: 'Je suis... le vieil Hêtre' — Pelletier's catatonic beech-tree identification (Paris, ~1902)
occurrences.label: Je suis... le vieil Hêtre
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Je suis l'être, l'être ancien, le vieil Hêtre, que l'on peut écrire avec un H. Je suis universel, primordial, divine, catholique, apostolique, Romaine.
body: The association-chain of a dementia-praecox patient, quoted by Jung from Madeleine Pelletier's thesis on ideation in mental debility: "Je suis l'être, l'être ancien, le vieil Hêtre, que l'on peut écrire avec un H. Je suis universel, primordial, divine, catholique, apostolique, Romaine" — I am the being, the ancient being, the old beech (Hêtre, to be written with an H; clang on être); universal, primordial, divine. Jung uses it to show dementia-praecox association sinking from daydream-level to dream-level (¶23), but the image itself is striking: the self as an ancient vegetative being, "eternal, immense, il n'y a ni haut ni bas" — a tree-self with none of the later symbolism worked out.

occurrences.title: The animus daemon and the gambler — Figs. 29-30 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: The animus daemon and the gambler
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: n/a (Jung's patient, born in the East)
body: A masculine daemon wakes "with an air of triumph: he is the animus, the personification of masculine thinking in a woman" (cw13 ¶339). His sentence "I am the Game of the gambler" points to Bhagavadgita X, 36 ("I am the game of dice") — Krishna as self — but Jung warns the animus "has a Janus face" and "is therefore quite unfitted to represent totality": Indian theosophy induced "a kind of psychological short-circuit, to identify the animus at least provisionally with wholeness" (cw13 ¶342ocr).

Fig. 30 restyles him as a gnomelike monk with outstretched arms — "a union of intellect and sexuality, just as the alchemical Mercurius duplex... is a quaternity composed of the four elements" (cw13 ¶343). In Fig. 31 the animus "no longer usurps the place of the self, but has been transcended by it" (¶346).
Verbatim: he is the animus, the personification of masculine thinking in a woman (and of her masculine side in general). (cw13 ¶339ocr)

occurrences.title: Boy in the tree watching two dragons — Fig. 9 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: Boy in the tree watching two dragons
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: An old, huge tree on a tangle of roots; two dragons approach from left and right; a tiny boy has climbed up to watch them. Jung recalls the dragons guarding the tree of the Hesperides and the snakes that guard the hoard: "the modicum of security it [consciousness] has just acquired is liable to be devoured again by the unconscious" (cw13 ¶314).

Yet the tree itself is not threatened — its growth is independent of human consciousness, guarded and dangerous, but protective for whoever "summons up courage enough to climb into the tree despite its guardians" (cw13 ¶314).
Verbatim: Two dragons are approaching from left and right. In the tree there is a boy who has climbed up to watch the dragons. (cw13 ¶314ocr)

occurrences.title: Pueblo corn-goddess fastened to the tree — Fig. 25 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: Pueblo corn-goddess fastened to the tree
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A later, differentiated stage of the Fig. 24 painter: the female figure, marked as a goddess by corn-cobs at the cardinal points (bird, tortoise, lion, grasshopper), is fastened to the tree by a snake — "an analogy to the crucified Christ, who, as the self, was sacrificed for earthly humanity, just as Prometheus was chained to the rock" (cw13 ¶331).

Jung: "Man's efforts to achieve wholeness correspond, as the divine myth shows, to a voluntary sacrifice of the self to the bondage of earthly existence" (cw13 ¶331). The picture's many divine-myth elements let the painter "discriminate between ego and self" — the protection against inflation stressed in ¶332.
Verbatim: She is fastened to the tree by a snake, and thus forms an analogy to the crucified Christ, who, as the self, was sacrificed for earthly humanity (cw13 ¶331ocr)

occurrences.title: Fire-tree growing from water — Fig. 5 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: Fire-tree growing from water
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Leafless tree with red flowers, branches tipped with flame, fire leaping from the water out of which it grows — "something like the jet of a fountain". Jung names the alchemical fontina (medieval town-fountain pictures) and quotes the saying "Our water is fire" (cw13 ¶310).
Verbatim: The branches are tipped with flames, and fire leaps up from the water out of which the tree is growing. (cw13 ¶310ocr)
The union of fire and water here anticipates Jung's later reading of Mercurius as "both water and fire" (cw13 ¶408).

occurrences.title: Tree on the island in the sea — Fig. 1 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: Tree on the island in the sea
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A huge solitary tree on an island, upper crown cut off by the picture edge, buds and white blossoms announcing spring. Jung reads its axial position and solitude as world-tree and world-axis, "a symbol that is universal and alien to the personal consciousness" — evidence that the painter's process has "nothing to do with his personal psychology" (cw13 ¶306). One of 32 pictures, 19 drawn before Jung knew alchemy.
Verbatim: The tree stands by itself on an island in the sea. Its great size is indicated by the fact that the upper part of it is cut off by the edge of the picture. (cw13 ¶306)

occurrences.title: Tree of light as candelabrum — Fig. 3 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: Tree of light as candelabrum
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: An abstract tree of light that is simultaneously a candelabrum, its branch-tips burning candles in a dark enclosed space — "perhaps a cave or vault". The plate caption describes a seven-branched candelabrum or Christmas tree whose "lights symbolize the illumination and expansion of consciousness".
Jung: "The secret and hidden nature of the process is thus emphasized and its function made clear: the illumination of consciousness" (cw13 ¶308).
Verbatim: The picture shows a tree of light that is at the same time a candelabrum. (cw13 ¶308ocr)

occurrences.title: Hollow tree with the locked door — Fig. 13 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: Hollow tree with the locked door
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A stylized tree of 4+1 branches — sun in the central branch, stars on the four — hollow inside and shut by a door in the trunk. A bird representing the painter weeps "because it has forgotten the key to the door"; it "obviously suspects that there is something valuable inside the tree" (cw13 ¶318).
The middle branch is snakelike and bears a luminous body like a sun — tree and mercurial serpent still distinguishable before their union in Fig. 12's haloed snake.
Verbatim: The stylized tree has in its trunk a locked door leading to a hidden recess. (cw13 ¶318)

occurrences.title: God's birth from the archaic plant — Fig. 27 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: God's birth from the archaic plant
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A thoroughly Western picture in "the archetypal category of the god's birth from the tree or lotus blossom": a human figure grows from an archaic carboniferous plant whose calyx bears four human heads — "in agreement with the alchemical view that the lapis is composed of four elements" (cw13 ¶336). The woman's head rises "like the pistil of a flower", compared by Jung with the Mithras relief from Osterburken (cw13 ¶404).

Its companion Fig. 28 localizes the dark principle: "The black earth... is now in her body as a black ball, in the region of the manipura-chakra... (The alchemical parallel to this is the “black sun.”)" (cw13 ¶337) — the shadow integrated as a bodily centre.
Verbatim: The human figure growing out of the archaic plant represents the union and quintessence of the four heads at its base (cw13 ¶336ocr)

occurrences.title: Lotus with the gnome and the corona — Fig. 31 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: Lotus with the gnome and the corona
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: n/a (Jung's patient, born in the East)
body: The tree of the series has "turned into a blossoming lotus plant, with the gnomelike figure sitting in the flower, reminding us that the lotus is the birthplace of the gods" (cw13 ¶345). The figure's head is encircled by a mandala with a flowerlike centre, wreathed by a corona: the alchemists' corona sive diadema cordis tui, "a symbol of perfection" — "the “golden flower” of Chinese and the “sapphirine flower” of Western alchemy" (cw13 ¶346).
Verbatim: The animus no longer usurps the place of the self, but has been transcended by it. (cw13 ¶346ocr)

occurrences.title: Sapphire treasure and the uroboros — Figs. 16-17 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: Sapphire treasure and the uroboros
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Fig. 16: a leafless tree full of birds guarding a dark blue sapphire hidden in its roots — "the sapphirine flower" of the alchemists, linked by Jung (not the painter) to Ezekiel's sapphire and to Grimm's bottle-elf in the oak's roots, "which contained the spirit Mercurius" (cw13 ¶321). Fig. 17, a later and more differentiated version: a blossoming tree grows from a magic circle enclosing the uroboros with the sapphire at its centre — "Hermaphroditi flos saphyricus", the self-devouring dragon that "begot and gave birth to itself" (cw13 ¶322).
Verbatim: They therefore called the sapphirine flower (i.e., the lapis) “Herm aphroditi flos saphyricus.” (cw13 ¶322ocr)

occurrences.title: Sun-quaternity watered by four rivers — Fig. 24 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: Sun-quaternity watered by four rivers
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: The female figure has taken the place of the tree; the sun disk becomes a symbol of individuation "characterized as such by the quaternity fed by four different-coloured rivers flowing down from four mountains, and flanked by four animals. The scene is paradisal". The four "heavenly or metaphysical" mountains already appeared in Fig. 6 and in Psychology and Alchemy figs. 62 and 109 (cw13 ¶329).
Jung's aside on the number four: "there are not three or, for that matter, five directions, but precisely four" (cw13 ¶330).

Verbatim: The quaternary elements in our picture, as well as accentuating the light-symbol, amplify it in such away that... an acceptance of wholeness by the little female figure, an intuitive apprehension of the self. (cw13 ¶330ocr)

occurrences.title: The tree-born woman emerging — Fig. 22 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: The tree-born woman emerging
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: The sleeping figure of Figs. 20-21 awakens and half emerges from the tree-trunk, making contact with the animal world: a snake whispers in her ear, and "bird, lion, lamb, and pig complete the paradisal scene". Jung: the tree-born is "not only as a child of nature but as an autochthonous primordial being" (cw13 ¶327ocr by design).

The tree nymph is "an Eve who, instead of being taken from Adam's side, has come into existence independently" — the symbol compensates "the biblical myth of the secondary creation of Eve" (cw13 ¶327). The same motif recurs ethnographically in the Yakut birth-tree (cw13 ¶461).
Verbatim: The tree nymph is an Eve who, instead of being taken from Adam’s side, has come into existence independently. (cw13 ¶327ocr)

occurrences.title: Dream of being poisoned by the fruit of a tree (patient: young woman, Zürich)
occurrences.label: Dream of being poisoned by the fruit of a tree
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: case-index [17], ref. book p221 ≈ pdf p188 (harvested from index, pdf p579)

body: A young woman with sexual marital difficulties dreamed of being poisoned by the fruit of a tree. Jung's case-index (Cases in Summary, [17]) anchors it at book p221, inside the mother-symbolism chapters: the tree as mother — its fruit poisoned, sexuality turning the nourisher deadly. The index glosses the tree entry directly: "dream of being poisoned by fruit of, 221."
Verbatim (case-index): "Young woman with sexual marital difficulty who dreams of being poisoned by fruit of a tree. — 221"

occurrences.title: The tree in the lands of the West growing on the ocean — Abu'l Qasim al-'Iraqi
occurrences.label: The tree in the lands of the West growing…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "The Arabic alchemists likewise obtain their prima materia from the tree in the western land. We read in the book of Abu'l Qasim: This prime matter which is proper for the form of the Elixir is taken from a single tree which grows in the lands of the West. … And this tree grows on the surface of the ocean as plants grow on the surface of the earth. This is the tree of which whosoever eats, man and jinn obey him; it is also the tree of which Adam (peace be upon him!) was forbidden to eat … And this tree may be changed into every animal shape" (¶537).

Jung pairs it with the ass in the ocean and the tree Gokard ("both are or have mana," ¶537), and with the verse-shifting power of "Mercurius versipellis" (¶538): tree, beast, and monster are one elixir-substance.

occurrences.title: Ring of Nestor — world-tree and underworld judgment (Crete)
occurrences.label: Ring of Nestor — world-tree…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: A gold seal ring whose intaglio shows a tree of life dividing the field into four scenes of the underworld (Mrs. Baumann's contribution): two butterflies and two chrysalises over the Mother Goddess — the souls of a man and woman greeting each other; below, a judgment scene, the goddess behind a table on which a griffin sits, souls brought before her by bird-headed beings.

With it Jung sets the miniature gold scales found in Cretan graves, a butterfly engraved on each balance-disc: "it looks as if the souls were weighed as butterflies, not as hearts as in Egypt". The tree as collectivum (before man and after man) joined to the butterfly-soul and the balance.

occurrences.title: The Ripley Scrowle — 'Four Rolls Drawn in Lubeck' (BM MS Sloane 5025)
occurrences.label: The Ripley Scrowle
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: drawn in Lübeck, 1588 → London, British Museum (MS Sloane 5025)
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1588 (rolls); Ripley d. 1490; scroll variants into the 17th c.

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

jung.locator: The Spirit Mercurius, fig. B5 — ¶ pin tbd

body: Emblematic scroll of the George Ripley tradition: a bird-and-flask picture chain wound around the "tree" of the opus, drawn in Lübeck in 1588 and preserved as British Museum MS Sloane 5025. Jung reproduces it as CW13 fig. B5 and cites it across "The Spirit Mercurius" and "The Philosophical Tree" (index: print 199n, 212, 286n, 303, 306n, 317), reading its beast-and-bird hermaphrodite sequence as a Mercurius transformation series on a tree.

Verbatim: London. British Museum. MS. Sloane 5025. 1588. "Four Rolls Drawn in Lubeck" (The Ripley Scrowle). The verses ("Emblematicall Scrowle") are printed in Ashmole's Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum (1652), ii.

The Scrowle is also Jung's chief example of the opus rendered as pictures: "the stages of transformation have been depicted over and over again, above all in the Ripley 'Scrowle' and its variants. These should be understood as indirect attempts to apprehend the unconscious processes of individuation in the form of pictures" (cw09ii ¶421) — the vertically unrolling stage-sequence from vessel to hermaphrodite read as a pre-psychological individuation map (printed variants: Ripley, Chymische Schrifften, Erfurt 1624; Opera omnia chemica, Kassel 1649).

Panels of the same scroll (kept as separate loci): anthropos-three-forms-ripley-scrowle-1588 · golden-flower-ripley-scrowle-1588 · melusina-anima-ripley-scrowle-bm-sloane-5025-1588 · uroboros-ripley-scroll-dark-sphere-frog-british-museum-16c.

image.title: Ripley alchemical scroll. Leonard Smethley, 1624, after George Ripley. Princeton University Library

occurrences.title: Ruysbroeck's tree of faith — roots in the Godhead, branches below
occurrences.label: Ruysbroeck's tree of faith
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: And he must climb up into the tree of faith, which grows from above downwards, for its roots are in the Godhead.
body: Ruysbroeck's mysticism supplies Jung's closest Western parallel to yoga's emptying of consciousness:

Jung notes the image "was also known to Indian philosophy" — the inverted tree, roots above, branches below. Around it stand Ruysbroeck's yoga-like formulae: "Man must be free and without ideas, released from all attachments and empty of all creatures"; being turned inwards means understanding "the inner working and the inner words of God" — a new state of consciousness in which a non-ego acts in place of the ego, "already formulated by St. Paul" (¶890).

occurrences.title: The tree of the Sefiroth as inverted world-tree — Cabala
occurrences.label: The tree of the Sefiroth as inverted world-tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Sulzbach (Knorr von Rosenroth); via Vigenere, Paris
body: Vigenere quotes "Rabbi, the son of Josephus Carnitolus": "The foundation of every lower structure is affixed above and its summit is here below, like an inverted tree" (cw13 ¶411; De igne et sale). "Vigenere had some knowledge of the Cabala and is here comparing the philosophical tree with the tree of the Sefiroth, which is actually a mystical world-tree. But for him this tree also signifies man" — implanted in paradise by the roots of his hair (Song of Songs 7:5).

Knorr von Rosenroth (Kabbala denudata): the "great tree" refers to Tifereth, bridegroom of Malchuth; the upper Sefira Binah is named "the root of the tree", the linea media through which "it brought life down to earth from Binah" (cw13 ¶411).
Verbatim: comparing the philosophical tree with the tree of the Sefiroth, which is actually a mystical world-tree. But for him this tree also signifies man. (cw13 ¶411ocr)

occurrences.title: Seth at the barkless tree of paradise — the skinless snake and the babe
occurrences.label: Seth at the barkless tree of paradise
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The old English legend of what Seth saw in Eden: a shining fountain with four streams, and over it the tree of the Fall — leafless, without bark, with "a naked snake without a skin" coiled round it; looking again, Seth sees it covered in bark and leaves, and "in its crown lay a little new-born babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, that wailed because of Adam's sin. This was Christ, the second Adam" (cw13 ¶400-401).

Jung's note: "The tree's lack of bark and the snake's lack of skin indicate the identity between them" (n.8) — the dead tree of paradise reviving as the tree of Christ's genealogy, whence the cross-wood legend (cw13 ¶446).
Verbatim: in its crown lay a little new-born babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, that wailed because of Adam's sin. This was Christ, the second Adam. (cw13 ¶401)

occurrences.title: The great tree of supracelestial fire — Simon Magus
occurrences.label: The great tree of supracelestial fire
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Hippolytus preserves Simon Magus's "great tree" that "consists of 'supracelestial fire.' 'From it all flesh is fed'" (cw13 ¶374; Elenchos VI, 9, 8ff). Jung reads it with the ever-living fire of Heraclitus and with Mercurius as fire and spiritus vegetativus, "both animating and destructive" (cw13 ¶374) — and with Nebuchadnezzar's tree, whose fruit ready-formed "is brought in to a barn and not cast in to the fire": the pneumatic man who has stood the test.
The fire-tree recurs as the fire-tree of the patient's picture (Fig. 15, cw13 ¶320) and in the Barbeliots' tree of gnosis (¶419n, ¶459n8).
Verbatim: In Gnosticism we encounter the “great tree” of Simon Magus, which consists of “supracelestial fire.” “From it all flesh is fed.” (cw13 ¶374)

occurrences.title: The catalapa of the dead hearts — Noel Pierre, 'Soleil Noir' (1952)
occurrences.label: The catalapa of the dead hearts
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Literary close of the picture series: Jung cites verses XXVI-XXVII of "Soleil No ir" by Noel Pierre, "a modern French poet who is personally unknown to me", as "an authentic experience of the unconscious" (cw13 ¶348). A spiral vortex sucks the crowd down toward a colossal catalapa "Ou pendaient les coeurs des morts", a little sage winking at each fork, and below, an island where a cube of grey rock rises — "la Capitale des Mondes".

Jung's feature list: universal midpoint, spiral rotation (often shown as a snake), tree of life and death, heart as centre of vitality joined to the tree, natural wisdom as a dwarf, island as seat of the tree, "Cube = philosophers' stone = treasure guarded by the tree" (cw13 ¶348).
Verbatim: Dans l'axe, un catalpa gigantesque / Où pendaient les coeurs des morts (cw13 ¶348)

occurrences.title: The sun-and-moon tree on the island — Mylius's parable
occurrences.label: The sun-and-moon tree on the island
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Mylius's parable: "the sun-and-moon tree stands on an island in the sea and grows out of the wonderful water that is extracted by the power of the magnet from the rays of the sun and moon" (cw13 ¶406). In the same volume's "Symposium Saturni" the seven planet-trees grow in "the 'private garden' of the blessed isles" (cw13 ¶407 n11): two outstand — one bearing sun-fruit with gold leaves, one white fruit with quicksilver leaves, "named by Neptune the tree of the sun and the tree of the moon."
Jung's use: the tree's special connection with water, salt and sea-water — "thus with the aqua permanens, the true arcanum of the adepts. This as we know is Mercurius" (cw13 ¶408).
Verbatim: the sun-and-moon tree stands on an island in the sea and grows out of the wonderful water that is extracted by the power of the magnet (cw13 ¶406ocr)

occurrences.title: Mary's lament against the false tree — Old English lament of the Virgin
occurrences.label: Mary's lament against the false tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Tre unkynde, thou schalt be kud, mi sone step-moder I the calle
body: Mary accuses the cross of being a false tree and step-mother which destroyed "the pure fruit of her body, her gentle birdling"; the Cross answers, calls itself the shining relic that will appear at Doom's-day parliament, and claims its blooming fruit. "Thus the Mother of Death joins the Mother of Life in lamenting the dying god, and, as an outward token of their union, Mary kisses the cross and is reconciled" (¶415) — the dual-mother union of opposite tendencies.

occurrences.title: The wak-wak tree with human fruit — Ta'rikh al-Hind al-Gharbi (11th-c. Munich MS)
occurrences.label: The wak-wak tree with human fruit
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: pl. XXXIX; fn 74 to ch. V (pdf p694); index 'wak-wak tree, pl. XXXIX' (pdf p656)

body: The plate Jung reproduces as XXXIX is the wak-wak tree of the Arabic geography Ta'rikh al-Hind al-Gharbi ("Report on the Happenings in Persia," "from an 11th-cent. MS in Munich: Wirth, ed., Aus orientalischen Chroniken, p. 151"). The index files it among birth-giving trees: "tree(s): birth from, 246f, 248, 425", "with human fruit, pls. XXXIX, XLV", "as birth-giving mother, 246, pl. XXXIX" — the tree that bears human bodies, the vegetable mother of heroes (cf. book p246f, pdf ~279, c02 range).
Verbatim (fn 74): "“Report on the Happenings in Persia,” from an 11th-cent. MS in Munich"

occurrences.title: The tree of wisdom in the Western Land — Ethiopic Book of Enoch
occurrences.label: The tree of wisdom in the Western Land
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the Ethiopic Book of Enoch the tree of knowledge of Genesis becomes the tree of wisdom in the Western Land, standing on a mountain: "it is said that the fruits of the tree in the Western Land will be the food of the elect. This is a clear hint of death and renewal" (cw13 ¶403); its fruits are likened to grapes (n.19) — the vine-complex that medieval alchemy took up in "I am the true vine" (John 15:1).
Jung folds this into the food-of-im mortality chain: Turba fruits that end the old man's hunger until "that old man becomes a youth"; manna, Host, and panacea (cw13 ¶403).
Verbatim: the fruits of the tree in the Western Land will be the food of the elect. (cw13 ¶403)

occurrences.title: Patient picture: woman entangled in the roots of a tree (Zurich, ~1931-32)
occurrences.label: Patient picture — woman entangled…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich (visions seminar patient; 1932 edn note: Golden Flower no. 5; editor suggests Visions vol 2, 25 Feb 1931)

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)
jung.locator: Lecture 1 (pdf p63-64) and Lecture 1 discussion (pdf p69)

occurrences.quote: That woman entangled in the roots is just entangled in her personal life.
body: A woman entangled in the roots of a tree, stretching upward toward the light — Jung's exhibit for what muladhara means psychologically: not the genitals but "her personal life... entangled in the duties of life, in her relations with her family." Asked where the woman is, the seminarians answer "In mÖlvdhvra"; Jung: "the self is then asleep." For her, going into analysis "was surely going up," though it is represented as going down.

occurrences.title: Wotan's self-hanging on the windy tree — Havamal 139
occurrences.label: Wotan's self-hanging on the windy tree
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: I ween that I hung / on the windy tree, Hung there for nights full nine; With the spear I was wounded, and offered I was To Othin, myself to myself
body: Footnote to Jung's analysis of the hunter-God-image: "I ween that I hung / on the windy tree, / Hung there for nights full nine; / With the spear I was wounded, and offered I was / To Othin, myself to myself, / On the tree that none / may ever know / What root beneath it runs." (Havamal 139, trans. H. A. Bellows). Jung cites it as the Germanic deep-structure beneath his fairytale: the swineherd "very nearly made its prisoner, like Wotan" when he climbed the world-tree (¶445); the hunter's suspension in the boughs and the crucified raven are the Christian reflection of this pagan hanged-god. The Wotanic God-image that, "reflected in the ocean of the (Germanic) unconscious", was "the psychological godfather of National Socialism" (¶452).

image.title: Odin's Self-sacrifice by Collingwood

occurrences.title: The eight-branched birth-tree of the first man — Yakut
occurrences.label: The eight-branched birth-tree of the first man
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Among the Yakuts a tree with eight branches is the birthplace of the first man. He is suckled by a woman the top part of whose body grows out of the trunk" (cw13 ¶461; Eliade, Shamanism, p. 272). Jung immediately connects it to his own case material: "This motif is also found among my examples (Figure 22)" — the tree-born woman emerging from the trunk (see tree-picture-tree-born-eve-patient-1935).

The eight branches echo the shamanic ogdoad-world-tree planted with the first shaman (cw13 ¶402), and the birth-tree's maternal numen belongs to the feminine tree-num en row (Melusina, Isis, the Pandora woman-trunk).
Verbatim: He is suckled by a woman the top part of whose body grows out of the trunk. (cw13 ¶461ocr)

occurrences.title: Zarathustra's dream: the tree with four metallic branches (Iran)
occurrences.label: Zarathustra's dream
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "It is said, for instance, that after Zarathustra had received the drink of omniscience from Ahuramazda, he beheld in a dream a tree with four branches of gold, silver, steel, and mixed iron. This tree corresponds to the metallic tree of alchemy, the arbor philosophica, which, if it has any meaning at all, symbolizes spiritual growth and the highest illumination" (cw13 ¶119).

Jung's point: the inner man's spiritual growth symbolized by metals is "not peculiar to alchemy" — nature exploits man's greed for metals, "and there may be hidden in lead either a deadly demon or the dove of the Holy Ghost" (¶119).

occurrences.title: Nest on the tree of the future — Zarathustra, end of 'The Rabble'
occurrences.label: Nest on the tree of the future
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: On the tree of the future build we our nest
body: "On the tree of the future build we our nest" — Nietzsche's "extraordinary metaphor, pretty daring." Jung reads the tree as "a symbol of spiritual development... a sort of sublimation," roots in earth and in air at once, the spirit growing "out of the material, animal man... into a different region above" — the arbor philosophorum "with the immortal fruits," the tree of knowledge with the serpent, the Edda's Yggdrasil "below [which] is a well".

Because Nietzsche has become the winged Zarathustra, the nest-builders are the wise birds: "as the wise man is always a bird... I have wings. I am a bird. I make my nest on that marvelous Yoga tree". Phoenix and Ra's falcon are the myth-kin; the eagles that feed the lone ones transpose Elijah's ravens. The cost is named: "the spiritual development in Nietzsche's case destroyed his brain".

occurrences.title: The transformation as a well-tended tree — Zosimos via Pelagios
occurrences.label: The transformation as a well-tended tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Pelagios's treatise preserves Zosimos's image of the opus: the transformation is "like a well-tended tree, a watered plant, which, beginning to ferment because of the plentiful water, and sprouting in the humidity and warmth of the air, puts forth blossoms and fruits by virtue of the great sweetness and special quality of nature" (cw13 ¶354).

Jung opens the historical half of the essay with this locus: the tree appears in medieval texts "and in general represents the growth of the arcane substance and its transformation into the philosophical gold" (cw13 ¶354) — and its Greek prototype stands already in Zosimos.
Verbatim: Zosimos had said the transformation process was like “a well-tended tree, a watered plant, which, beginning to ferment because of the plentiful water” (cw13 ¶354ocr)

occurrences.title: Teardrop and flame united — frontispiece of the Songe de Poliphile
occurrences.label: Teardrop and flame united
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: it is only a symbol when it expresses opposites; otherwise it has no meaning
body: The emblem Jung cites for the alchemical fire and water triangles (flame /\, water ~): "the union of the teardrop and the flame, called in their interpretation the fires of passions and the tears of repentance. That was an attempt at the union of opposites: namely, a process of life looked at from a static point of view."

He raises it to a definition of the symbol as such: "This is always necessary for the creation of a symbol, because it is only a symbol when it expresses opposites; otherwise it has no meaning. It must be an idea superior to any definite one-sided philosophical or intellectual concept" — the criterion by which the tarantula's triangle fails and the quaternity succeeds.

occurrences.title: The Koshari 'Delight Makers' — sacred clowns of the Pueblos
occurrences.label: The Koshari 'Delight Makers'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The Koshari are a special group within an Indian tribe, whose particular task is to ridicule the gods; they are the clowns of the gods, and they are called the \"Delight-makers. \
body: Answering why the Gothic grotesques are comical, Jung cites the ritualized caricature of the sacred:

Edition note: Kokoyemsin, the Hopi Mudhead Kachinas, and the Koyemshi, Zuni clowns, "upset ceremonial order" (Frank Waters, Book of the Hopi; Adolf Bandelier, The Delight Makers — cited by Jung for the trickster in CW9i ¶255). Same family as the medieval mock mass "in which vulgar and obscene songs were sung as the responses, in order to interrupt once a year the solemn hierarchic structure of the church" and the carnival abbot of the lay brothers: the chthonic-grotesque built into the sacred order itself, interrupting "that wonderful elevation, that uplifting effect" of the Gothic line.

occurrences.title: The Feast of the Ass at Beauvais — priest and congregation braying
occurrences.label: The Feast of the Ass at Beauvais
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~11th-12th c. codex; suppressed by the auctoritas supremi Senatus

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: At the end of the mass, instead of the words 'Ite missa est,' the priest shall bray three times (ter hinhamabit), and instead of the words ' Deo gratias,' the congregation shall answer 'Y-a' (hinham) three times,
body: The festum asinorum, "celebrated mainly in France" as a "harmless festival in memory of Mary's flight into Egypt": the ass procession went right into the church at Beauvais, a girl with the ass stationed by the altar, and at each part of the high mass "the whole congregation brayed". An eleventh-century codex prescribes: "At the end of the mass, instead of the words 'Ite missa est,' the priest shall bray three times (ter hinhamabit), and instead of the words 'Deo gratias,' the congregation shall answer 'Y-a' (hinham) three times." Jung notes the hymn Orientis partibus and the danger that the ass be brought "into symbolic relationship with Christ" — "the god of the Jews was vulgarly conceived to be an ass", as the Palatine mock-crucifixion shows. "The more ridiculous this rite seemed, the greater the enthusiasm with which it was celebrated" (Du Cange).

occurrences.title: The Feast of Fools at Notre Dame, Paris (1198; Fools' Pope, 1444)
occurrences.label: The Feast of Fools at Notre Dame, Paris
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: A report from the year I1g8 says that at the Feast of the Circumcision in Notre Dame, Paris, 'so many abominations and shameful deeds' were committed that the holy place was desecrated 'not only by smutty jokes, but even by the shedding of blood.
body: Medieval church carnival as the trickster at the altar's edge: on Innocents' Day an Episcopus puerorum was elected, vested in pontifical robes, and blessed the city from the archbishop's window; the subdeacons' dance degenerated by the late twelfth century into the festum stultorum. A report of 1198: at the Feast of the Circumcision in Notre Dame "so many abominations and shameful deeds" were committed "not only by smutty jokes, but even by the shedding of blood". In 1444 the Theological Faculty still fulminated against the fatuorum papam: masqueraders "sang indecent songs in the choir, ate their greasy food from a corner of the altar..., got out their games of dice, burned a stinking incense made of old shoe leather". For Jung these customs "demonstrate the role of the trickster to perfection" — the remnant of the collective shadow figure inside the Church itself.

occurrences.title: The table that would not say three — medium experiment (Zurich, ~1905)
occurrences.label: The table that would not say three
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Jung's number-experiments with a medium: thinking a number 0–10 while the tilted table answers, he achieved correct transmission in 77 per cent of trials even after withdrawing his hands (¶733). When everything "went wrong", he told the medium only that the number 3 lay "between 2 and 5": "The numbers it reproduced with iron consistency were 2, 4, and 5, but never 3... the table, or rather the unconscious of the medium, was well aware of the number I was thinking of and avoided it out of mere caprice" (¶734).

Jung's reading: "The capriciousness of the unconscious is something the spiritualists could tell us a good deal about, only in their language it would be said that the good spirits had been supplanted by mischievous mocking spirits" (¶734) — the mocking-spirit, trickster face of the autonomous psyche, caught in the laboratory.

occurrences.title: Trimurti picture: tortoise, skull, and lotus-flower as opus allegory (Indian painting)
occurrences.label: Trimurti picture — tortoise, skull…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the tortoise symbolizing the massa confusa, the skull the vas of transformation, and the flower the 'self' or wholeness
body: Plate 75: "The triangle symbolizes the tendency of the universe to converge towards the point of unity. The tortoise represents Vishnu; the lotus growing out of the skull between two flames, Shiva. The shining sun of Brahma forms the background. The whole picture corresponds to the alchemical opus, the tortoise symbolizing the massa confusa, the skull the vas of transformation, and the flower the 'self' or wholeness."

Jung's caption makes the Trimurti a complete Indian allegory of the alchemical opus: chaos (tortoise), container (skull), goal (flower), with the trimurtic triad converging on unity. Paired with fig. 76 (the tortoise as alchemical distilling instrument, Porta 1609) and the "green womb" of Ishvara (¶199).

occurrences.title: The Athanasian Creed (Quicumque vult): 'one God in Trinity, and Trinity in Unity'
occurrences.label: The Athanasian Creed
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Latin West (origin disputed; falsely ascribed to Athanasius)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)
jung.locator: ¶218–219 (pdf pp122–124); D. F. Strauss cited ¶226 (pdf p128)

occurrences.quote: neither confounding the Persons nor dividing the substance
body: The so-called Athanasian Creed — "the (falsely so-called)" as Jung notes — "insisted in the strongest possible terms on the equality of all three Persons": "we worship one God in Trinity, and Trinity in Unity, neither confounding the Persons nor dividing the substance… And yet not three Eternals, but one Eternal… So the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Ghost is God; and yet there are not three Gods, but one God." The filioque is taken up by the Lateran Creed of 1215 (¶219–220).

Jung: "Here the Trinity is a fully developed conceptual schema in which everything balances, the homoousia binding all three Persons equally" (¶219) — the elaborate version that "shows very clearly what Church doctrine understands by the Trinity" (¶171). He quotes D. F. Strauss against it — "anyone who has sworn to the Symbolum Quicumque has abjured the laws of human thought" — as the inevitable retrograde step once the revelation of holiness no longer impresses; liberalistic humanization "goes back to the rival doctrine of homoiousia and to Arianism" (¶226).

occurrences.title: The Batak trinity: a high god too far away to be useful (Sumatra)
occurrences.label: The Batak trinity — a high god too far away…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Batak religion as documented by Warneck (1909)

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: One finds it among the Bataks,7 for instance; they recognize the existence of such a trinity but they say it is far away
body: Among the Batak of Sumatra (Jung's source J. G. Warneck, Die Religion der Batak, 1909) a trinity of high, spiritual gods is acknowledged — but "they say it is far away, they don't know whether he or they are concerned with them any longer", so the people turn to ghosts, sorcerers and witches, "because that is more practical".

Jung uses the Bataks to show the fate of abstract high gods in primitive religions — faint and insignificant while ghosts and devils do the real work — and to mirror the Christian triangle: "it is now too far away from man... it has become intangible and inefficient" (p605). Jung had discussed the Batak religion since 1912 (CW4 par. 512).

occurrences.title: The Christian Trinity with the Holy Ghost as a winged man — Master of the Berlin Passion
occurrences.label: The Christian Trinity with the Holy Ghost…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: He is often represented as a winged old man, i.e., Mercurius in the form of the god of revelation.
body: Fifteenth-century engraving in which the third person of the Trinity appears as a winged MAN rather than a dove.

Jung's reading: the Holy Ghost is "often represented as a winged old man, i.e., Mercurius in the form of the god of revelation, who is identical with Hermes Trismegistus and, together with the King and the King's Son, forms the alchemical trinity" (fig. 179). The fire extracted from chaos "is the Holy Ghost, who unites father and son" — the model the alchemists copied as Hermes standing between king and son.

occurrences.title: The homoousios decision — Council of Nicaea, 325
occurrences.label: The homoousios decision — Council of Nicaea, 325
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: the development of the Christian idea of the Trinity unconsciously reproduced the archetype of the homoousia of Father, Son, and Ka-mutef which first appeared in Egyptian theology
body: The Council of Nicaea created the creed confessing the Son "begotten not made, consubstantial [ὁμοούσιος] with the Father" and anathematizing those who say "There was a time when He was not." A Spanish bishop, Hosius of Cordoba, proposed the crucial word homoousios (the Greek word itself is dropped by the OCR at this point in the chunk). The word did not occur for the first time there: Tertullian's "unitas substantiae," and Gnostic usage — the Valentinian Aeons "of one substance with their creator, Bythos," per Irenaeus.

Jung's reading is the essay's central historical claim: the Fathers "neither paused in their labours nor rested until they had finally reconstructed the ancient Egyptian archetype" — the homoousia of God, son-king, and Ka-mutef — "much the same sort of thing" as the Theotokos decision at Ephesus, where the archetype likewise "reasserted itself" (¶194, ¶222). The Nicene Creed concentrates on the father-son relationship; the Holy Ghost "receives scant mention" — his turn comes at Constantinople (381) and in the filioque controversy.

occurrences.title: Horus-Hathor-Akori trinity amulet with winged serpent
occurrences.label: Horus-Hathor-Akori trinity amulet…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: A late Egyptian trinity amulet (published by Spiegelberg): 'Horus and Hathor sit facing one another, and between them and over them hovers a winged serpent. The three deities all hold the ankh... "Bait is one, Hathor one, Akori one, one is their power. Greetings, Father of the World, greetings, three-formed God."' (cw14 ¶352). Spiegelberg: despite its Greek form it 'breathes an Egyptian spirit of Hellenistic nature... born of a spirit that made its contribution to the development of the dogma of the Trinity in Christianity.' Jung: 'The illustrations of the coniunctio in the Rosarium, showing King, Queen, and the dove of the Holy Ghost, correspond to the figures on the amulet exactly' (¶352).

occurrences.title: Ka-mutef: the triunity of God, king, and ka in the Egyptian theology of kingship
occurrences.label: Ka-mutef — the triunity of God, king, and ka…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: In it and through it father and son are combined not in a triad but in a triunity
body: Egyptian theology asserts the essential unity (homoousia) of God as father and son, both represented by the king; the third person is Ka-mutef, "the bull of his mother" — the ka, procreative power of the deity, in and through which father and son are combined "not in a triad but in a triunity." "God is the father, the king is the son, and ka the connecting-link between them" (after Jacobsohn, whose concluding chapter draws the credo parallel via Karl Barth: the Holy Ghost as the unity of father and son, the vinculum caritatis).

Jung: Ka-mutef is "exactly the same hypostatization of an attribute" as the Holy Ghost's "spirated" life (¶197) — the archetype behind the Christian formula. Early Christian Egyptians "simply transferred their traditional ideas about the ka to the Holy Ghost"; in the Coptic Pistis Sophia Jesus has the Holy Ghost as his double, "just like a proper ka" (¶177). At Nicaea the Fathers "finally reconstructed the ancient Egyptian archetype" without knowing anything of the Egyptian model (¶222).

occurrences.title: Trinity of mens, sapientia, amor — the Liber de Spiritu et Anima
occurrences.label: Trinity of mens, sapientia, amor
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: thus all three, intellect, wisdom, and love, appear in one
body: A book "well known in the Middle Ages" that attempts a psychological interpretation of the Trinity: by self-knowledge a man may attain knowledge of God, since the mens rationalis is made "expressly after his likeness." "The intellect sees how wisdom (sapientia) proceeds from it and how it loves this wisdom. But, from intellect and wisdom, there proceeds love, and thus all three, intellect, wisdom, and love, appear in one" — mens corresponding to the Father, the begotten wisdom to the Son (Logos), love to the Spirit breathed forth between them.

Jung's comment reverses the arrow: "The medieval mind finds it natural to derive the structure of the psyche from the Trinity, whereas the modern mind reverses the procedure." The passage is his earliest exhibit of psychological Trinity-reading inside the tradition itself — the assimilation stands or falls with his claim that the dogma is "a revelation not only of God but at the same time of man" (Koepgen, ¶127).

occurrences.title: Three Pieces of Wood by the River — Pauli dream (1950)
occurrences.label: Three Pieces of Wood by the River — Pauli dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1950 (before Pauli's summer reading of Boulanger's Table Ronde)

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: there are 3 pieces of wood with an apparently archetypal significance.
body: The dream that "actually led me to write to you about the 3 spindles": "In this dream, there are 3 pieces of wood with an apparently archetypal significance, and when I read about the 3 spindles in Boulanger this summer, I immediately felt myself transported back into the mood of the dream". "The river in the dream evidently corresponds to the mother's lap"; the stranger figure "emerged from the river but had already been there in another form" — the lower-chthonic archetype in "what is so far a definitive form, namely, the above-named 'dual-layered' one."

Pauli's alchemical gloss: "It is always the wood that has been treated by human beings that has a 'magic' effect in my dreams, in contrast to the natural state of the prima materia" — hence "not just an external analogy between my dreams and the Grail myth but... a more far-reaching identification of the relation of the archetype to consciousness".

occurrences.title: Roscellinus' tritheism condemned at Soissons (1092)
occurrences.label: Roscellinus' tritheism condemned at Soissons
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: it dissolved the Trinity into three separate persons, so that Roscellinus arrived at tritheism. This was intolerable to the prevailing realism of the times, and in 1092 his views were condemned by a synod at Soissons.
body: The opening engagement of the medieval universals controversy, in Jung's telling: Roscellinus held universals to be mere nomina rerum, flatus vocis — "For him there were only individual things. He was, as Taylor aptly observes, 'strongly held by the reality of individuals'" (¶58). Applied to the Godhead, nominalism dissolves the one divine substance:

The God-image itself becomes the casualty of a type dispute: logical nominalism applied to the Trinity clashes with the age's realism, for which the universal (the one substance) is the higher reality. The opposing extreme realist was William of Champeaux, Abelard's teacher (¶58).

occurrences.title: The angel explains the Trinity by three colours in the peacock's tail — Digulleville's Pélerinage de l'âme
occurrences.label: The angel explains the Trinity…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: The almighty King who puts three colours in one, cannot he also make one substance to be three?
body: In the last canto of the Pélerinage de l'âme, while Guillaume gazes at the blue calendar circle, three spirits clad in purple appear (the feast of three saints); discourse on the zodiac reaches the sign of the Fishes and the feast of the twelve fishermen that precedes Holy Trinity. Guillaume confesses he never understood the Trinity, and the angel answers: "Well, there are three principal colours: green, red, and golden. One can see them united in the peacock's tail. The almighty King who puts three colours in one, cannot he also make one substance to be three?" Gold belongs to the Father, red to the Son, green to the Holy Ghost — then the angel "warns the poet not to ask any more questions and disappears."

Jung's reading: "Poor old Guillaume has evidently been stumped by the same problem. Three there are, but where is the fourth?" The missing colour is blue — Mary's colour (¶120, ¶123); the patient's world clock has four colours, Guillaume's heaven only three. The angel's hasty exit "before… awkward questions" is itself evidence for the concealed quaternity.

occurrences.title: Forbidden three-headed Trinity — Monastery of St. George, Stein am Rhein
occurrences.label: Forbidden three-headed Trinity
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Chapel of the monastery of St. George, Stein am Rhein
occurrences.quote: A picture of the Trinity with three heads was interdicted by a papal bull in the early seventeenth century... there is still one of those forbidden representations in the chapel of the monastery of St. George at Stein on the Rhine.
body: A painting of the Trinity with three heads — the type interdicted by a papal bull in the early seventeenth century — surviving in the chapel of the monastery of St. George at Stein on the Rhine. Jung adduces it while glossing the patient's monstrous four-eyed child: the fourth is always the devil, so a three-headed godhead begs Faust's question, "There are three and where has remained the fourth?" — "That is the devil, of course."

Jung's reading sits inside his larger claim of these sessions: the Trinity is the three without the fourth, the projected inferior function; hell its distillation apparatus. The forbidden image is the visual shadow of that doctrinal quaternity-deficit.

occurrences.title: Three popes give a house — dream at the Bohrs', Copenhagen, 20 Jul 1954
occurrences.label: Three popes give a house
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: Just as the three popes represent the lower Trinity, Niels Bohr and his wife represent father and mother, Adam and Eve, rex and regina.
body: Continuation of the 15 July secret-laboratory dream. Bohr, "an official announcement": three popes (one named John) have given the dreamer a house; Bohr and his wife present the document and a train ticket to northern Jutland; the wife is absent — "what can I do in a new house without her?" A Catholic Austrian uncle then receives the house. Pauli: the new house "is always the place where a union of pairs of opposites takes place, a coniunctio"; the opposites here are natural science vs Catholic tradition, whose rites preserve "experiences of a 'magical' nature" — the Mass "an 'experiment' that involves the transformation of the person experimenting."

Jung adds the Pope-John legend (pope-pope-joan-papissa-legend-rome), John the Evangelist as the Gnostic, and the alchemist "who does not realize that he himself is part of the process of transformation."

occurrences.title: Sol, luna, mercurius as three snakes in the vas Hermeticus
occurrences.label: Sol, luna, mercurius as three snakes…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: the vessel was number four
body: "The idea of Hermetic philosophy is that the three, the trinity, are represented by three bodies. They call them sol, luna, and mercurius-gold, silver, and mercury-and they are represented as three snakes joined together by their tails, a unit in themselves but with three heads, three persons in one. This is the dogmatic form of the trinity contained in a vessel, in the vas Hermeticus, and the vessel was number four."

Jung's use is the three-four problem: the fourth may be "a basis, or a base, as the earth can be a basis for water, earth, and fire" — "a formula for bringing those four together." But "in the Christian psychology the fourth is the devil, and how can you bring the good and evil together?... that moral valuation creates such a split that you cannot bring those opposites together."

occurrences.title: The Three Spindles of Merlin's Isle — Roman de la Table Ronde (France, ~13th c.)
occurrences.label: The Three Spindles of Merlin's Isle
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: France (Old French prose redaction; Paris ed. Jacques Boulanger 1941)

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: The spindles, one of which is white, one red, and one green, are found on a mysterious revolving island.
body: In Merlin's story of the French Table Ronde (pp. 56-78): "The spindles, one of which is white, one red, and one green, are found on a mysterious revolving island" — the island section opening with the four elements "like so many alchemical treatises." The spindles derive from "a tree that stems from a branch that Eve was allowed to take to Earth from the Tree of Paradise" (first white, then red, then green); "Solomon's wife had the spindles made from it and added them to David's sword"; the ship that carries sword and spindles "is later (p. 364) claimed to be the Church," while the spindles remain "specifically feminine" and chthonic — "they relate to the boat as the Trinity does to the Church." Galahad sleeps with the three spindles before seeing the Grail's secret and dies (p. 379f.).

Pauli's reading: the spindles manifest "the archetype of the lower chthonic Trinity" (cf. the downward-reflected triangle of Fludd, the ace of clubs); their missing spinners "can probably be identified with the Fates" — victims of "a sort of Christian 'censorship'" of the heathen motif — and the revolving island matches Plato's spindle of necessity (Fierz's observation). Emma Jung had connected Grail and quaternity; Pauli supplies the "lower Three".

occurrences.title: 'One, two, three — but where is the fourth?' — opening scene of Plato's Timaeus
occurrences.label: One, two, three — but where is the fourth?
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: One, two, three— but where, my dear Timaeus, is the fourth … ?
body: The dialogue opens with one of the invited four absent "because he was taken ill" — "One, two, three — but where, my dear Timaeus, is the fourth…?" Jung reads the scene as symbolic, not jocose: the missing fourth of the elements out of which reality is composed. Plato first binds fire and earth by one geometrical mean (the plane triad 2:1 thought-structure), then needs two means (water, air) for a solid — "the dilemma of three and four" (¶183).

Jung's psychological translation: the plane triad is "not yet a reality" — thought not become real; the fourth is "the 'adversary'… that resists harmony" (¶188), and biographically "Plato certainly did not lack spirit; the missing element he so much desired was the concrete realization of ideas" (¶185, after Dionysius had him sold as a slave). The same "unconscious spiritus rector" twice impelled him to attempt a tetralogy whose fourth part remained unfinished, and kept him a bachelor "as if affirming the masculinity of his triadic God-image" (¶192). Goethe's Cabiri scene takes up the same words.

occurrences.title: Trinity Vision of Brother Klaus — the Sachseln painting
occurrences.label: Trinity Vision of Brother Klaus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: It is a mandala divided into six parts, and in the centre is the crowned countenance of God.
body: The central religious experience of the Swiss hermit Nicholas of Flue (Bruder Klaus): a terrifying theophany — Woelflin, the oldest source, reports he "had seen a piercing light resembling a human face" and feared his heart would burst "into little pieces" (¶14). He elaborated it for years with an illustrated devotional booklet, and had it painted on his cell wall: a six-part mandala with the crowned countenance of God at the centre, still preserved at Sachseln (¶12-13).

Jung's reading: the dogmatic symbol assimilated a "fatal incursion of an archetypal image" and saved Klaus from being torn asunder (¶20); the mandala/protective circle is "the traditional antidote for chaotic states of mind" (¶19). In the anima essay he adds the initiation visions where God appeared "once as a majestic father and once as a majestic mother" — the syzygy, "heretical" against Trinitarian dogma (¶¶131-132).

occurrences.title: The vision-creed of Gregory Thaumaturgus: the Virgin and St. John dictate the 'Perfect Trinity'
occurrences.label: The vision-creed of Gregory Thaumaturgus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: Perfect Trinity, whose glory and eternity and dominion is not divided and not separate
body: Gregory Thaumaturgus, pupil of Origen until ~238, received in a vision an appearance of the Blessed Virgin and St. John, who "enunciated a creed which he wrote down on the spot." Its close: "And one Holy Spirit, having existence from God and appearing through the Son, Image of the Son and perfect [Image] of the perfect [Father]… Perfect Trinity, whose glory and eternity and dominion is not divided and not separate."

Jung cites it as proof that an explicit trinitarian symbolum stood "in a position of authority long before the appearance of the Apostles' Creed" — against the quibble "that the Trinity was 'invented only long afterwards'" (¶213). In the sequence of the Symbola (¶207–221) it is his earliest fully-formed datum: the archetype already spoken, two centuries before Nicaea, through a Marian vision — the feminine figure standing beside the doctrine she formally cannot enter.

occurrences.title: The triskelos — three-legged symbol on pre-Christian Greek coins
occurrences.label: The triskelos — three-legged symbol…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: "on pre-Christian Greek coins we find a three-legged symbol, which is called a triskelos." Jung's question "Which function did the Greeks leave out?" goes unanswered — "Greece is altogether a puzzle psychologically" — but the frame is his rule that a threefold mandala betokens a missing fourth (his one three-cornered mandala was drawn by a man "almost entirely without the function of sensation").

occurrences.title: Triskelos with Gorgon Medusa center — Sicilian coin inscribed 'Tan Panormos'
occurrences.label: Triskelos with Gorgon Medusa center
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Greek-Sicilian coinage, ~5th-4th c. BCE (brought to seminar 24 Jan. 1934)
body: Reproduction brought by Dr. Escher: a triskelos "in itself a sun symbol" whose center is "the Gorgon-headed Medusa with her hair of snakes"; the inscription reads Tan Panormos, "all-defended, in full armor" — possibly referring to Tanith, the Syrian-Phoenician goddess analogous to Artemis of Ephesus, Ishtar, Atargatis.

Jung's reading: "this Medusa might represent the devouring mother, the terrible side of the goddess of fertility; it would be a kind of threatening sun, the 'black sun.'" The winged head is an attribute of Somnus/Hypnos — "a face which floats in the darkness surrounded by snakes, flying in the night like a bat... such ideas or images probably originated in individual nightmares" (ibid.). Instead of the beneficial sun, "the sun in its own opposition, the midnight sun."

occurrences.title: Tsoavits rescued by the eagle, the witch devoured by her snake-grandfather
occurrences.label: Tsoavits rescued by the eagle, the witch…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: "A North American fairy tale recounts that a child-stealing witch seizes the hero Tsoavits, but an eagle leads him back again. At this, the witch seeks help from her grandfather, the giant snake, but is devoured by him on the spot. 'Ever since all witches have been snakelike'".

A neat two-line instance of the eagle/sercle antagonism: the bright rescuer from above, the chthonic devourer below, and the witch — the negative feminine — squarely on the serpent's side of the ledger.

occurrences.title: 'Out of the four elements were created our Father Adam' — Turba philosophorum
occurrences.label: Out of the four elements were created our…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: For out of the four elements were created our Father Adam and his children.
body: The Turba states plainly: "For out of the four elements were created our Father Adam and his children" — the Philosopher repeats God's work of Genesis 1, and the prima materia called Adam "consisted or was made out of the four elements."

Jung at cw14 ¶552 gathers the family: Jabir's Book of Balances (body of warm, cold, moist, dry; dryness from earth, moisture from water, heat from spirit, cold from soul), the compositio elementorum of the later literature, Adam as Microcosm.

occurrences.title: Turba philosophorum — the punctum solis in the egg-yolk
occurrences.label: Turba philosophorum
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'In the egg therefore are four things: earth, water, air, and fire; but the "punctum solis" is apart from these four, in the midst of the yolk (which) is the chick' (¶345). Ruska reads 'saliens' for 'solis'; Jung is 'not so sure'. In the alchemical tradition the point stands for the arcane substance: Maier's 'purity or homogeneity of the essence', Khunrath's salt-point (Sapientia), the scholiast's circulus exiguus, 'mediator... by persistent rotation changes the angular form of the square into a circular one like itself', Dorn's punctum vix intelligibile, John Dee's monad, Mylius' bird of Hermes (¶345). Parallels: monoimos-monad-iota-2c, egg-rigveda-nasadiya-hidden-one.

occurrences.title: The woman who slays her husbands buried with the dragon — Turba, Sermo LIX
occurrences.label: The woman who slays her husbands buried…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The coniunctio can therefore take more gruesome forms than the relatively harmless one depicted in the Rosarium.
body: Sermo LIX of the Turba: "the Philosophers have put to death the woman who slays her husbands, for the body of that woman is full of weapons and poison. Let a grave be dug for that dragon, and let that woman be buried with him, he being chained fast to that woman; and the more he winds and coils himself about her, the more will he be cut to pieces by the female weapons which are fashioned in the body of the woman" — until he is "changed wholly into blood," the blood dries in the sun, and "What then appears, is the hidden wind" (¶15).

Jung's comment closes the widow/Isis excursus: "The coniunctio can therefore take more gruesome forms than the relatively harmless one depicted in the Rosarium." The water that "gathers together all my divided and scattered limbs" is "my mother who is my enemy."

occurrences.title: Turukalukundram — the erotic temple sculptures and the Tantrist pundit
occurrences.label: Turukalukundram — the erotic temple sculptures…
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Visiting the ancient pagoda, Jung asked a local pundit why the temples are covered 'from top to bottom, with obscene sculptures': to remind ordinary people of their dharma, because Yama 'would instantly carry off' the imperfect who tread the spiritual path unprepared; the two seductresses at the entrance lure visitors to fulfil their dharma before ascending (¶339 n.131). The lingam stands in the garbha griha, the 'house of the womb'. Jung notes the pundit 'was a Tantrist'. A living instance of the same initiation logic as the Eleusinian lower path — the Persephone route before the Brimo-Brimos ascent.

occurrences.title: The two birds on the selfsame tree — Shvetashvatara Upanishad 4, 6ff.
occurrences.label: The two birds on the selfsame tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~6th-5th c. BCE (trans. based on Hume, The Thirteen Principal Upanishads)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: The Indian parallel to the Dioscuri motif of the mortal and immortal twin: "Two birds, fast-bound companions, sit /... / Behold, upon the selfsame tree, / This one enjoys the ripened fruit, / The other looks, but does not eat. // On such a tree my spirit crouched, / Deluded by its powerlessness, / Till seeing with joy how great its Lord, It found from sorrow swift release" (Shvetashvatara Upanishad 4, 6ff.).

Jung's reading: the dual motif symbolizing "the hidden immortal within the mortal man" — "Christ himself is the perfect symbol" of it; when the summit of life is reached, "'One becomes Two', and the greater figure, which one always was but which remained invisible, appears to the lesser personality with the force of a revelation" (¶218). Announces the Moses-Khidr analysis (Koran, 18th Sura) as "another notable parallel" (¶219 — treated later in the essay, beyond this chunk).

occurrences.title: Two dragons devouring each other — Viridarium chymicum
occurrences.label: Two dragons devouring each other
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)
jung.locator: 'Transformation Symbolism in the Mass' n.23 (pdf p723)

occurrences.quote: Mostly the pictures show two lions eating one another. The uroboros, too, is often pictured in the form of two dragons engaged in the same process (Viridarium chymicum, 1624).
body: Jung's footnote on the self-devouring motif in the Mass essay's sacrificial argument: the uroboros is "often pictured in the form of two dragons engaged in the same process."

The doubled form matters: self-devouring split into a pair — the one divided into two who consume each other — the same image Jung uses for the hostile brothers and the coniunctio's mutual mortification.

occurrences.title: Two lions eating one another — Reusner's Pandora
occurrences.label: Two lions eating one another — Reusner's Pandora
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)
jung.locator: 'Transformation Symbolism in the Mass' n.23 (pdf p723)

occurrences.quote: See the illustration in Reusner, Pandora (1588), and in Le Songe de Poliphile, trans. Béroalde de Verville (1600). [Psych. and Alch., fig. 4.] Mostly the pictures show two lions eating one another.
body: The emblem of mutual devouring Jung reproduces as Psychology and Alchemy fig. 4 and cites here for the Mass's sacrificial symbolism: two lions, each eating the other.

In the Mass essay the image anchors the claim that the sacrifice is mutual — Christ and the communicant, sacrificer and sacrificed. The green lion devouring the sun is the single-beast sibling of this doubled form.

occurrences.title: The Superman sermon in the marketplace (Zarathustra, Prologue 3–5)
occurrences.label: The Superman sermon in the marketplace
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: the town adjoining the forest, the marketplace

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "I teach you the Superman. Man is something that is to be surpassed."
