Jung's seminar reading of the sermon: the Superman is "the consequence of the God that is dead" — "when God is dead he appears next in the one who kills him: then the divine creative faculty needs must dwell in man". Hence the inflation: Zarathustra "is now the expression of man plus God," "confronted with the task of creating the Superman" — "We are not creating. We are only instrumental in the creative process: it creates in us, through us".

The Superman is "the meaning of the earth" = the body = the self: "The Superman, the self, is the meaning of the earth; it consists of the fact that we are made of earth". He is the ocean in whom "your great contempt can be submerged", and "that lightning, he is that frenzy" — waking the dormant Yin condition of late-medieval man, "a man who can deal with the darkness in human nature."

occurrences.title: The saucer-man in the desert — Adamski's contact claim
occurrences.label: The saucer-man in the desert
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: California desert (claimed encounter; Desert Center tradition)

jung.locator: Jung's own footnote in the Weltwoche reply on flying saucers, 9 July 1954 (pdf p1015 n.2)

body: The founding contactee story: George Adamski's account (in Flying Saucers Have Landed, with Desmond Leslie, 1953) of meeting a humanoid from a saucer in the California desert. Jung records it in his OWN unbracketed footnote to his 9 July 1954 Weltwoche reply — "In it he tells the story of how he met a saucer-man in the California desert" — four years before Flying Saucers (CW10), and without endorsement: in the same apparatus he files the 1938 War of the Worlds panic and Keyhoe's Pentagon struggle, treating the contactee narrative as mythological material appearing as claimed fact ("the appearance of real objects affords an opportunity for mythological projections", cw10 ¶782).
Verbatim: In it he tells the story of how he met a saucer-man in the California desert.

occurrences.title: Basel broadsheet — black globes fighting before the sun, 7 August 1566
occurrences.label: Basel broadsheet — black globes fighting…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: many large black globes were seen in the air, moving before the sun with great speed, and turning against each other as if fighting.
body: A Basel broadsheet written by Samuel Coccius, "student of the Holy Scripture and of the free arts, at Basel, in the Fatherland," reporting that at sunrise on 7 August 1566 "many large black globes were seen in the air, moving before the sun with great speed, and turning against each other as if fighting. Some of them became red and fiery and afterwards faded and went out."

Jung's reading: the dark colour "may be due to their having been seen against the light of the rising sun"; "Their speed and irregular motion are typical Ufo features" (¶759). Together with the Nuremberg broadsheet of 1561 it shows that the phenomenon and its mythic framing long precede 1947 — and that sunrise, "the Aurora consurgens (Aquinas, Boehme), suggests the revelation of the light" (¶763).

occurrences.title: Deep-sea-fish Ufo and the anima's mission — dream of the 'Fire Sower' painter, 12 Sept 1957
occurrences.label: Deep-sea-fish Ufo and the anima's mission
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: It did not look like a machine but like a deep-sea fish, round and flat, but enormously big (about thirty to forty feet in diameter).
body: The painter of "The Fire Sower," prompted only by Jung's letter about possible links between his picture and the sky-apparitions, dreamt a saucer that "did not look like a machine but like a deep-sea fish, round and flat, but enormously big," speckled blue-grey-white, its undulating edges acting "as oars and rudders." It landed; a semi-human woman came out: "they knew me well in that other world... and were watching how I fulfilled my task (mission?)." The other people fled.

Jung's reading: the figure "belongs to the anima type... she is the Sphinx of Oedipus, a Cassandra, the messenger of the Grail, the 'white lady' who gives warning of death" (¶713); her question is "the question of individuation, the most fateful of all questions" (¶714); "the anima is the quintessence of the Ufo," while the whole is "obscurely alluded to in the deep-sea fish, the 'rotundum'" (¶715). The psychologem "is a reality in its own right" (¶716).

occurrences.title: Drop-shaped Ufo over the empty Champs Elysées — dream 1 of an educated lady
occurrences.label: Drop-shaped Ufo over the empty Champs Elysées
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: instead of the expected bombers I saw a sort of Flying Saucer, a metallic sphere shaped like a drop.
body: An educated lady who had "never seen a Ufo," knew neither the Ufo literature nor Jung's ideas, dreams an air-raid panic on the Champs Elysées: everyone vanishes into houses, doors are locked, and instead of bombers a metallic sphere "shaped like a drop" crawls slowly across the sky while alone woman's heels click on the empty pavement — "The atmosphere was most uncanny."

Jung's reading: the drop-form means the Ufo is conceived as heavenly fluid, rain-like — a conception "similar to that of the alchemical aqua permanens... which was also called 'Heaven' in sixteenth century alchemy and stood for the quinta essentia" — Mercurius himself, who "falls as the aqua coelestis from heaven" (¶628). The dreamer who does not flee meets the phenomenon harmlessly (¶632).

occurrences.title: Circular eye, half blue half white — dream 2 of the same lady (burned face)
occurrences.label: Circular eye, half blue half white
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: From the front, seen close to, it looked like a circular eye, half blue, half white.
body: A month later the same dreamer stands her ground while an interplanetary "machine" — "large steel cigars" — comes straight at her ("Professor Jung says that one should not run away"). Close to, it is "a circular eye, half blue, half white"; she wakes in a hospital with her head bandaged, her whole face "burnt" by the mere sight.

Jung's reading: the plurality of machines splits the one self-symbol (multiplicatio, ¶633–635); at confrontation the round form returns as the "traditional eye of God, which, all-seeing, searches the hearts of men" (¶639); the two colours are the sky's blue and cloud-white — "The psychic totality, the self, is a combination of opposites. Without a shadow even the self is not real" (¶640). The burn is the mark of overwhelming affect, like Moses' radiant face and Brother Klaus (¶641–643) — "dreams sent by God" mistaken for symptoms (¶642).

occurrences.title: Ufo as film projection — dream of a 23-year-old actress (California)
occurrences.label: Ufo as film projection
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: One of the producers was directing this Flying Saucer thing.
body: A young film actress in treatment for "a marked dissociation of personality" dreams a fluorescent circle of light swelling to cover the whole sky, figures pacing its deck — then discovers men with a movie projector projecting the image, and two rival old producers both casting her in the lead of their science-fiction films.

Jung's reading: from a central position (square, centre, circle) the Ufo appears as symbol-carrier, but the dream immediately devalues it — "the apparently cosmic phenomenon is nothing more than a meaningless trick" (¶706). The rival lovers become producers; what she really wants is the chief role in her own drama. Paradigm lesson: "the symbols cannot be interpreted in a uniform manner and... their meaning depends on many different factors" (¶711); the Ufo serves only as "a sort of alarm signal, thanks to the collective excitement occasioned by flying saucers" (¶710).

occurrences.title: Mantell's tear-drop Ufo — Kentucky (1948)
occurrences.label: Mantell's tear-drop Ufo — Kentucky (1948)
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: A report on the case of Captain Mantell, now become a classic, speaks of the Ufo's resemblance to a 'tear drop' and says it behaved like a fluid.
body: Captain Thomas Mantell's fatal pursuit of a large round object near Fort Knox — "now become a classic" of Ufo lore. Jung's footnote keeps two phenomenological details: the object's "resemblance to a 'tear drop'" and that it "behaved like a fluid." The round thing in the sky that moves not like a machine but like a liquid — matter taking the behaviour of the psychic round (rotundum) is exactly the boundary-phenomenon Flying Saucers is about.

Jung cites the case among the sightings that resist the projection-only reduction; elsewhere he insists "Neither is there any proof that they are 'only' psychic!" (cw10n7). Mantell's death gave the myth its martyr, and the tear-drop its fluid physics.

occurrences.title: Nuremberg broadsheet — aerial battle of globes, crosses and tubes, 14 April 1561
occurrences.label: Nuremberg broadsheet
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: They all began to fight one another.' This went on for about an hour.
body: A broadsheet relating a "very frightful spectacle" seen by "numerous men and women" at sunrise: hundreds of blood-red, bluish and black globes and plates near the sun — "some three in a row, now and then four in a square" — with "blood-coloured crosses" among them, and "two great tubes" (three in the woodcut) holding more globes. "They all began to fight one another" for about an hour, then all fell toward the earth "as if everything were on fire," leaving much steam; beneath lay "a long object, shaped like a great black spear." It was read as a divine warning.

Jung's reading: the tubes are the "mother-ships" of modern Ufo language (¶761); "especially important... are the indubitable quaternities, seen sometimes as simple crosses, sometimes as disks in the form of a cross, that is, as regular mandalas," with "a hint of the 3 + 1 motif in the dilemma of three and four" (¶761). The militaristic reading is "as characteristic of the sixteenth century as the technological one is of ours" (¶761); the crossed globes form "the crossed marriage quaternio... also an individuation symbol" (¶762).

occurrences.title: The Ufo rumour as living myth (worldwide, 1947–1958)
occurrences.label: The Ufo rumour as living myth
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: one thing is certain: they have become a living myth.
body: The worldwide rumour of round objects in the sky — "Flying Saucers, soucoupes, disks, and 'Ufos'" — beginning with the American sightings of the late 1940s and running through official Air Force investigation (Ruppelt) into the late 1950s. Jung treats the rumour itself as the locus: "a golden opportunity of seeing how a legend is formed" in a dark time.

His reading: visionary rumours rest on "an emotional tension having its cause in a situation of collective distress or danger, or in a vital psychic need" (¶608); the projections climb "into interstellar space, where the rulers of human fate, the gods, once had their abode in the planets" (¶610); "they have become a living myth" (¶614). Crucially, the age dresses its archetype in technology: the archetype "should now take the form of an object, a technological construction, in order to avoid the odiousness of mythological personification" (¶624).

occurrences.title: 'The Spiritual Pilgrim Discovering Another World' — woodcut with Ezekiel wheels and disks
occurrences.label: The Spiritual Pilgrim Discovering Another World
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 17th c. (text ¶764); plate caption says '19th (?) century' — unresolved
occurrences.quote: In these symbols we have a prototype of the Ufo vision, which is vouchsafed to the illuminati.
body: A woodcut of unknown source which Jung reads as "possibly representing a Rosicrucian illumination": a pilgrim on a pélerinage de l'âme "has broken through the star-strewn rim of his world and beholds another, supernatural universe filled with what look like layers of cloud or mountain ranges. In it appear the wheels of Ezekiel and disks or rainbowlike figures, obviously representing the 'heavenly spheres.'"

Jung's reading: "In these symbols we have a prototype of the Ufo vision, which is vouchsafed to the illuminati. They cannot be heavenly bodies belonging to our empirical world, but are projected 'rotunda' from the inner, four-dimensional world" (¶764) — the sky-realm as projection-surface of the psyche's round forms, centuries before saucers.

occurrences.title: Ullikummi, the diorite stone-son of Kumarbi — Hurrian Song of Ullikummi
occurrences.label: Ullikummi, the diorite stone-son of Kumarbi
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the son of the father-god Kumarbi is the stone Ullikummi, a “terrible” diorite stone that “grew in the water.
body: In the Hurrian texts of Boghazköy the son of the father-god Kumarbi is the stone Ullikummi, a "terrible" diorite stone that "grew in the water" — a Titanic being, implacable enemy of the gods. Jung cites Güterbock's "Kumarbi" and Gurney, The Hittites, in the Conjunction chapter's stone-symbolism note.

Jung's reading: proof of the antiquity of stone symbolism — the stone-son parallels the Greek stone Kronos swallowed and spat out under compulsion from Zeus, later set up as a cult-object in Pytho; the stone as primordial divine-born being that can also be the gods' adversary. Parallels: foundation-stone-shetiyah-zohar-13c, armillus-son-of-stone-midrash-ten-kings-10c.

occurrences.title: Fantastic-underworld picture series — van Helsdingen's patient
occurrences.label: Fantastic-underworld picture series
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Netherlands (patient raised in the Dutch East Indies)
occurrences.quote: They communicate their frightening, daemonic content to the beholder and convince him of the terrors of a fantastic underworld.
body: A picture series by Jung's former patient (published with her permission by van Helsdingen, 1954): an "Indomalaysian phantasmagoria of pullulating vegetation and of fear-haunted, stifling tropical nights" (cw18 ¶1253), compared with the monstrous masters of the patient's mother country, Hieronymus Bosch. Jung reads it as infantile-archaic fear — the unprotected child exposed to the unconscious, plus a European's rejection of everything "the East conjures up". Therapeutically the pictures were an instrument: they fixated floating images to a common denominator and "depotentiate[d]" them (¶1254).

occurrences.title: The unicorn tied to Noah's ark and Og who escaped the flood — Talmud
occurrences.label: The unicorn tied to Noah's ark and Og…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Babylonian Talmud redaction (~5th–6th c.); saga older
occurrences.quote: For it is said [Gen. 14: 13]: 'and there came one that had escaped, and told Abram the Hebrew,' and R. Johanan said: 'That was Og who escaped the flood.
body: Rabbinic flood-saga: the re'em (unicorn) could not enter the ark; Noah tied it by its horn to the vessel and it swam behind — but the flood-water was hot, so it was scalded to death (Zebahim 113b, with Goldschmidt's and Jung's comments on the melting pitch of Gen. 6: 14). The same tractate preserves Og: "'and there came one that had escaped' — R. Johanan said: 'That was Og who escaped the flood'" (Nidda 61a), the last of the giants of Gen. 6: 4 riding out the deluge atop the ark.

Jung's apparatus (Part II ch. 6, nn. 62–69) gathers these as the Jewish monstrous counterpart to the unicorn material of the chapter: the too-much-of-the-body that cannot be brought into the vessel of salvation.

occurrences.title: The captive unicorn in the fenced round garden — Verteuil tapestry
occurrences.label: The captive unicorn in the fenced round garden
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "264. Mandala of the unicorn and the tree of life. — Verteuil tapestry (15th cent.), 'The Hunt of the Unicorn'" — the tamed unicorn lying within a circular fence around the tree of life, in a field of flowers. Jung caption-reads the enclosure as a mandala and uses the plate to close his reading of the horn: "The horn as an emblem of vigour and strength has a masculine character, but at the same time it is a cup, which, as a receptacle, is feminine. So we are dealing here with a 'uniting symbol' that expresses the bipolarity of the archetype" (¶553).
The captive unicorn as the rounded, bounded totality — horticus conclusus, temenos, mandala.

image.title: The Unicorn in Captivity (from the Unicorn Tapestries)
image.credit: This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

occurrences.title: The ch'i-lin announcing the birth and death of Confucius
occurrences.label: The ch'i-lin announcing the birth and death…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~551 BCE (birth omen); death omen 481 BCE; reproduced in Sheng Chi-t'u rubbings
body: The Chinese unicorn as herald of the sage. At Confucius' birth: "a ch'i-lin came to the governor's house in Tsou and spat out a jade tablet, bearing the inscription: 'The son of the mountain crystal [lit. water-essence] will perpetuate the fallen kingdom of Chou and be a king without a crown.' His mother … tied an embroidered bow to the unicorn's horn" (fig. 259). Before his death (481 BCE) "a ch'i-lin was caught on a winter hunt"; Confucius wept: "The ch'i-lin, benevolent beast, appears and dies. My Tao is exhausted" (fig. 260).

By the Li Chi the ch'i-lin is chief of the four spiritual animals (unicorn, phoenix, tortoise, dragon) and "shows itself when perfect rulers [chen-jen] appear and the Tao of the king is accomplished"; the male is ch'i, the female lin — "the unicorn is thus endowed with an androgynous quality" (¶548).

occurrences.title: Ctesias' Indian wild ass: the tri-coloured horn that detoxifies
occurrences.label: Ctesias' Indian wild ass
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: India (as reported in Ctesias' Indika, from Persia)
occurrences.quote: There is a horn on the forehead, nearly one and a half cubits in length; the lower part of the horn is white, the upper part purple, but the middle is pitch black.
body: The West's oldest unicorn report. Ctesias (c. 400 BCE, via McCrindle): a wild ass of India, white-bodied, purple-headed, with "a horn on the forehead, nearly one and a half cubits in length; the lower part of the horn is white, the upper part purple, but the middle is pitch black." Princes drink from horn-cups bound with gold rings and are immune to poison and convulsions.

Jung assembles this in the unicorn chapter's zoological apparatus (n. 30) with Aelian's Kartazonon ("the strength of its horn is invincible. It seeks solitude"), Philostratus' fire-walking cup, and Kosmas' unicorn that leaps into an abyss and lands on its unbreakable horn. The antidote-horn — the poison-warding cornu — is for Jung the natural-magic root of the symbol: the one-horned, solitary, fierce animal as bearer of the "alexipharmic," later allegorized as Christ consecrating the baptismal water (Caesarius, n. 21).

occurrences.title: Cardinal Torquemada's unicorn cup at table — Rome
occurrences.label: Cardinal Torquemada's unicorn cup at table
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "Migne says that Cardinal Torquemada always kept a unicorn cup at table: 'La corne de licorne préserve des sortilèges' (fig. 261)" (¶550). The prince of the Inquisition using the alicorn as an anti-sorcery amulet at his own table — the healing cup standing between medicine, sacrament, and mantic use: "The healing cup is not unconnected with the 'cup of salvation,' the Eucharistic Chalice, and with the vessel used in divination" (¶550). Illustrations: the pope with the unicorn as Holy Ghost (Scaliger 1570, fig. 261) and Pisanello's lunar-unicorn medal (fig. 262).

occurrences.title: David rides the re'em to heaven; the lion makes it crouch — Midrash Tehillim
occurrences.label: David rides the re'em to heaven
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "R. Huna bar Idi said: At the time when David was still tending the sheep, he went and found the unicorn [re'em] asleep in the desert, and thinking it was a mountain he climbed to the top and pastured his flock there. Then the unicorn shook himself and stood up. And David rode on his back and reached up to heaven. … He ordained that a lion should come, and when the unicorn saw the lion, he was afraid and crouched down before him, because the lion is his king" (¶545). David, descending, now fears the lion — hence Ps 22:21: "Save me from the lion's mouth, for thou hast heard [freed] me from the horns of the unicorns."
A second midrash (¶546) has unicorn and lion fight: the unicorn's horn sticks fast in a tree "and then the lion comes and kills the unicorn, but sometimes the matter is reversed."

occurrences.title: The unicorn as demon — St. Basil's warning
occurrences.label: The unicorn as demon — St. Basil's warning
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The unicorn's dark side, from the Physiologus tradition — Basil: "it is a swift-running animal, having one horn, and evilly disposed towards man (μνησίκακον … ἐν ἀνθρώποις)," and: "take heed unto thyself, O man, and beware of the unicorn, who is the Demon [fig. 249]. For he plotteth evil against man, and he is cunning in evil-doing" (¶525).

Jung uses these to establish that the one-horned beast "has more than one meaning. It can also mean evil," concluding (¶526): "Originally a monstrous and fabulous beast, it harbours in itself an inner contradiction, a complexio oppositorum, which makes it a singularly appropriate symbol for the monstrum hermaphroditum of alchemy." Illustrated by the wild unicorn of Bock's Kräuterbuch (fig. 249) and the wild man riding the unicorn (fig. 250, Master E.S.).

occurrences.title: Caesar's unicorn in the Hercynian Forest (Bellum Gallicum 6.26-27)
occurrences.label: Caesar's unicorn in the Hercynian Forest
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: one reads in Caesar, in the Bellum Gallicum, about a unicorn in the Black Forest that could not lie down because its joints were stiff
body: Caesar's report of a huge ox-like beast in the Hercynian forest that could not lie down (its joints were stiff), slept leaning against trees, and was killed by the Germans sawing the trees down — a passage Jung freely renders as "a unicorn in the Black Forest... the people cut the trees down so that it would fall".

Read within Jung's argument that dragon-fears and monstrous animals persist as images after the reality is gone: "That unicorn was undoubtedly a rhinoceros" — and a woolly-rhinoceros carcass had just (1930) been dug from a Silesian oil seep. The elk/unicorn of Caesar shows how a real saurian-grade animal becomes the archetypal beast of memory. Jung later became learned on the subject (CW12, "The Paradigm of the Unicorn").

occurrences.title: Jehovah as unicorn tamed in the virgin's lap — Caussin's compilation
occurrences.label: Jehovah as unicorn tamed in the virgin's lap
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: From Nicolas Caussin, "from whom I have culled these extracts" (Jung): "the unicorn is a fitting symbol for the God of the Old Testament, because in his wrath he reduced the world to confusion like an angry rhinoceros (unicorn) until, made captive by love, he was soothed in the lap of a virgin" (¶522). With Picinelli and Bonaventure: "Christ was tamed and pacified by the most kindly Mary, so that he should not punish the sinner with eternal death."

Jung's point: "This ecclesiastical train of thought has its parallel in the alchemical taming of the lion and the dragon" — the conversion of the wrathful Old-Testament God into the God of Love mirrors the opus' taming of the dangerous beasts of Mercurius (¶522).

occurrences.title: The ch'i-lin — Chinese unicorn of the Confucius legend (figs. 259–260)
occurrences.label: The ch'i-lin — Chinese unicorn…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: China (Tz'u-yuan lexicon; Wilhelm, Kung-Tse, Leben und Werk pp. 189, 60)
occurrences.yearDisplay: Confucius legend (~6th–5th c. BCE); codified in later encyclopedias

jung.locator: pdf p702 (Part II ch. 6, n. 75); figs. 259, 260 (captions trans. E. H. von Tscharner)

occurrences.quote: From the Tz'u-yuan, s.v. 'Ch'i-lin.' The text of the captions for figs. 259 and 260 was specially translated from the Chinese for the Swiss edn. of the present volume by Dr. E. H. von Tscharner.
body: The Chinese unicorn (ch'i-lin, or ki-lin), a hoofed, benevolent chimeric beast that appears only at the birth or death of a sage — in the Confucius legend it heralds the birth of the philosopher and its capture marks his death. Jung closes the unicorn chapter's apparatus with two plates of the ki-lin (figs. 259, 260), their captions specially translated from the Tz'u-yuan for the Swiss edition by E. H. von Tscharner.

Its place in Jung's argument: the unicorn is not a European Christian fantasy but a worldwide image of the singular, wise, gentle-fierce wholeness-beast; the ki-lin ties it to the birth and death of the self-realized man rather than to the virgin's womb.

occurrences.title: The unicorn draws the poison from the water — Physiologus Graecus
occurrences.label: The unicorn draws the poison from the water
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The alexipharmic scene at the water-hole: "when a snake has poisoned their drinking water, the animals, noticing the poison, will wait for the unicorn to come down to the water; 'for his horn is a symbol of the cross,' and by drinking he dissipates the virulence of the poison" (¶549). The horn that detects, absorbs, and neutralizes the serpent's venom — the alicorn as antidote, made material in the rhinoceros-horn poison cups of the Africa–China trade ("even today," ¶549) and in the Campion pendant scraped for medicine (fig. 263).
Same text family as the man-hating unicorn of the Physiologus (¶525): the beast that saves the animals from the serpent is the demon that plots against man.

occurrences.title: Priscillian: 'Unicornis est Deus … nobis lapis angularis Jesus'
occurrences.label: Priscillian — Unicornis est Deus … nobis lapis…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Unicornis est Deus, nobis petra Christus, nobis lapis angularis Jesus, nobis hominum homo Christus.
body: The Gnostic-leaning bishop Priscillian compresses the whole unicorn-Christology into one sentence: "Unicornis est Deus, nobis petra Christus, nobis lapis angularis Jesus, nobis hominum homo Christus" — God is the unicorn; Christ the rock; Jesus the corner-stone; Christ the man of men. The unicorn, the stone, and the anthropos fall together into one identity.

For Jung's argument this is a key patristic witness that the unicorn is a Christ- (hence self-) symbol, not a zoological memory: the horn that crushes all obstacles (Honorius, Speculum; cf. cw12 n. 23) is the same "strong strength of all strength" the alchemists predicate of the lapis. Priscillian is also Jung's source for the wheel of the zodiac-generations (cf. priscillian-wheel-of-generation-385).

occurrences.title: The re'em tied to the outside of the ark — Babylonian Talmud
occurrences.label: The re'em tied to the outside of the ark
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Talmudic legendary zoology of the re'em: too gigantic for the ark, it was tied to the outside — or, per R. Jannai, they took young unicorns in; per Reš Laqiš, "they tied its horns to the ark." Rabba b. Bar Hana "had seen a young unicorn as large as Mount Tabor, which measures forty parasangs, … and that the Jordan was choked with the dirt it voided" (¶540).

Jung links it to Og king of Bashan — also flood-survivor, also gigantic, also mountain-linked — and suggests "an inner connection between Og and the unicorn" (¶545). With Behemoth and Leviathan, "the two manifestations of Jehovah," these beings are "personifications of the daemonic forces of nature. … God is ambivalent so long as man remains bound to nature" (¶547).

occurrences.title: Rishyashringa, the one-horned hermit fetched for the drought — Mahabharata
occurrences.label: Rishyashringa, the one-horned hermit fetched…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "The virgin and unicorn motif is to be found in the Ramayana and in the Mahabharata": the hermit Rishyashringa ("gazelle's horn"), son of Vibhandaka or Ekasringa ("one-horn"), is fetched from his solitary retreat by the king's daughter Shanta, who marries him — "or, in another version, he is seduced by a courtesan. Only by this means can the terrible drought that is scourging the land be broken" (¶534).

The one-horned ascetic whose only weakness is the feminine: the capture-of-the-unicorn plot in Indian dress, with rain-making (fertility) as the fruit of the taming — the same structure as the Chinese ch'i-lin appearing "when the Tao of the king is accomplished."

occurrences.title: Slaying the unicorn in the Virgin's lap — MS Harley 4751
occurrences.label: Slaying the unicorn in the Virgin's lap
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Slaying the unicorn in the Virgin’s lap. (Note the significance of the “wound in his side.”)
body: Bestiary initial (fig. 242): hunters slay the unicorn as it lies in the Virgin's lap. Jung's caption draws out the Christological point: "Note the significance of the 'wound in his side'" — the killing of the captured unicorn repeats the piercing of Christ's side, and the picture belongs to the same family as the Pieta allusion Jung finds in Ripley's green lion (¶519).

image.title: Ashmole unicorn

occurrences.title: Christ the unicorn-bull, his horns the ends of the cross — Tertullian
occurrences.label: Christ the unicorn-bull, his horns the ends…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: His glory is that of a bull, his horn is that of a unicorn.
body: Tertullian's exegesis of the blessing of Moses (Deut 33:13–17), the fountainhead of the ecclesiastical unicorn allegory Jung traces through the Psalms (Ps 29:6, 92:10, 22:21):

And: "Christ was named the bull on account of two qualities: the one hard [ferus, 'wild, untamed'] as a judge, the other gentle [mansuetus, 'tame'] as a saviour. His horns are the ends of the cross" (¶521). The wild/tame polarity inside the one beast is exactly the ambivalence Jung later locates in Mercurius and in the God-image itself (¶547). Justin Martyr reads the same verse: "Cornua unicornis cornu eius" — the horns can only be the cross.

occurrences.title: The virgin catches the unicorn — Honorius of Autun
occurrences.label: The virgin catches the unicorn
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The classic scholastic form of the capture allegory: "The very fierce animal with only one horn is called unicorn. In order to catch it, a virgin is put in a field; the animal then comes to her and is caught, because it lies down in her lap. Christ is represented by this animal, and his insuperable strength by its horn. He, who lay down in the womb of the Virgin, has been caught by the hunters; that is to say, he was found in human shape by those who loved him" (¶523). Jung pairs the passage with the Khludov Psalter miniature (fig. 247, Byzantine, 9th c.).
The "wound in his side" of the hunt pictures and the "insuperable strength" of the horn hold together the same polarity Tertullian named: judge-wild, saviour-tame.

occurrences.title: The virgin and the unicorn — Physiologus Graecus
occurrences.label: The virgin and the unicorn — Physiologus Graecus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Alexandria (Physiologus tradition; Pitra, Spicilegium solesmense III p. 355)
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~2nd c. (tradition possibly reaching Didymus of Alexandria, 4th c.)
occurrences.quote: They cast a sacred virgin before it. And it leaps into the lap of the virgin, and the virgin warms the animal with love and bears it to the palace of the kings.
body: The classic Christian unicorn-hunt: "How is it hunted? They cast a sacred virgin before it. And it leaps into the lap of the virgin, and the virgin warms the animal with love and bears it to the palace of the kings." Medieval allegory (Isidore of Seville, Etymologiarum xii, 62, is the transmitting source) reads the virgin as Mary and the captured unicorn as Christ entering the womb.

Jung's unicorn chapter builds on this locus: the fierce, uncatchable one-horned beast that can only be taken through the virgin is the image of the dangerous, autonomic wholeness (or its masculine fierce aspect) that the feminine — the vessel, the virgin as vas (figs. 241, 242, 245, 247) — alone can render incarnate. The wounded unicorn lying in the virgin's lap (Reusner, Pandora) is its alchemical echo (cw12 pdf p693, n. 186).

occurrences.title: Virgin taming a unicorn — pseudo-Aquinas, 'De alchimia'
occurrences.label: Virgin taming a unicorn
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Leiden, Bibliothek der Rijksuniversiteit, Codex Vossianus 29
occurrences.quote: 241. Virgin taming a unicorn.—Thomas Aquinas (pseud.), “De alchimia” (MS., 16th cent.)
body: Alchemical picture (fig. 241) in the 16th-century MS De alchimia attributed to Thomas Aquinas: a virgin holding/taming the unicorn. In Jung's reading the picture carries the Mercurius-Christ identity: because "the symbol of the unicorn as an allegory of Christ and of the Holy Ghost was current all through the Middle Ages," Ripley and his fellows knew exactly what they meant when they let the tamed beast stand for the spiritus mercurialis (¶519).

occurrences.title: The uniped king and priest — 'Abraham le Juif' manuscript, Plates 4-7
occurrences.label: The uniped king and priest
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: There they make but one.
body: A series of uniped pictures: a crowned man in a yellow robe and a priest in white, "Each of them has only one foot," with the inscription beginning with the sign for Mercurius: "There they make but one" — Mercurius duplex, the two sulphurs. Later: the two separated with two feet, spiritual and temporal crowns, mirror-image colours; then united again, each with one blue foot; finally the (spiritual) king joined to the green-clad queen whose feet are black — the caput corvi. The "Silène endormy" is bound with rainbow garlands: "So say the philosophers that when the blackness appears one must rejoice."

Jung at cw14 ¶720-725: the mythologem of the sun-king descending to earth and uniting with the earth-queen; the king become "sol ni'ger"; the parallel with Rohita and Rohini of the Atharva-veda implies an archetypal connection.

occurrences.title: 'To the Unknown God' — Nietzsche's early storm-god poem
occurrences.label: To the Unknown God
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: And blowest through my life like a storm, Ungraspable, and yet my kinsman!
body: Nietzsche's juvenile poem, written in 1863 or 1864 — two decades before Zarathustra — and quoted at length by Jung in "Wotan": "I shall and will know thee, Unknown One, / Who searchest out the depths of my soul, / And blowest through my life like a storm, / Ungraspable, and yet my kinsman! / I shall and will know thee, and serve thee."

Jung's reading: the poem is the first rustling in the primeval forest. Set beside the "Mistral Song" of 1883 ("Raging storm-wind, how I love thee! Are we not both the first-fruits / Of the same womb") and the "Ariadne's Lament" (the cruel huntsman, the unknown God), it shows Nietzsche seized for twenty years by the same wind-god whom the philologist in him insisted on calling Dionysus (cw10 ¶376–383).

occurrences.title: Anquetil du Perron brings the Upanishads back to Europe (Oupnek'hat, Latin, 1801-02)
occurrences.label: Anquetil du Perron brings the Upanishads back…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "a Frenchman, Anquetil du Perron, traveled to the East and became a Buddhist monk; he studied the sacred books of the East and brought back the first translation of the Upanishads (an Arabic translation which he translated into Latin), and it was that edition which Schopenhauer knew."

Jung's timing-claim: between 1790 and 1805 the French Revolution "actually dethroned Christianity — Diderot and Voltaire having ridiculed it for fifty or sixty years before — and just then... A new crusader pushed through into the East and brought the East back with him, and from that time on, it has filtered in." The old man of the vision is "a crusader," a mediator between West and East.

occurrences.title: Retainer sacrifice in the royal tomb of Ur (~50 killed for the king)
occurrences.label: Retainer sacrifice in the royal tomb of Ur
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: They discovered, in excavating, about fifty corpses of soldiers, women of the court, and slaves, who were killed in order to accompany the soul of the dead king.
body: Excavations of a prehistoric king of Ur brought to light "about fifty corpses of soldiers, women of the court, and slaves, who were killed in order to accompany the soul of the dead king". For Jung this is the terrible outgrowth of the vessel-soul logic: belongings broken or burned to release their souls for the dead - so too persons.

Continuation of the same custom: "The kings of the Huns were always accompanied by soldiers, slain with their horses, and buried near the king. In Egypt human sacrifices were substituted by ushabti" (ushabti-servant-figures-egyptian-tombs).

occurrences.title: Uroboros with 'hen to pan' legend — Codex Marcianus
occurrences.label: Uroboros with 'hen to pan' legend
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: It appears as the ούρο βόρος, the tail-eater, in the Codex Marcianus (fig. 147), which dates from the tenth or eleventh century, together with the legend: νἓ τò πάν (the One, the All).
body: A tail-eating dragon in the Greek alchemical codex Marcianus, tenth or eleventh century, ringed by the legend "hen to pan" (the One, the All). Jung calls the dragon "probably the oldest pictorial symbol in alchemy of which we have documentary evidence."

His reading: the uroboros compresses the whole opus into one figure — "the opus proceeds from the one and leads back to the one, that it is a sort of circle like a dragon biting its own tail." Mercurius as uroboros "devours, fertilizes, begets, slays, and brings itself to life again" (¶460): prima materia, caput corvi, nigredo, and rising lapis in one hermaphroditic body — "a symbol uniting all opposites."

image.title: Chrysopoea of Cleopatra 1

occurrences.title: Harpokrates encircled by the uroboros — gnostic gem
occurrences.label: Harpokrates encircled by the uroboros
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "253. Harpokrates encircled by the Uroboros. — Gnostic gem" (fig. 253): the self-born child-god (Horus the child, finger to lips) ringed by the self-devouring serpent. Jung cites it exactly at the point where alchemy's prima materia is "an increatum … bisexual, capable of self-fertilization and self-parturition" (¶530) — the self-contained circle of generation that needs no other.
The same self-birth the Horapollo scarab carries (unicorned, monogenes, autogenes, sacred to Mercurius).

occurrences.title: Uroboros as symbol of the aeon — Horapollo, Selecta hieroglyphica (1597)
occurrences.label: Uroboros as symbol of the aeon
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Tail-eating serpent as emblem of the aeon, from the Renaissance hieroglyphic manual of Horapollo. Jung places it first in the CW12 illustration sequence, opening the whole volume's uroboros row.
Caption: "7. The Uroboros as symbol of the aeon.—Horapollo, Selecta hieroglyphica (1597)". Jung reads the tail-eater here as a time-symbol of self-contained cyclic totality.

occurrences.title: Kekule's dream of the dancing pairs and the benzol ring
occurrences.label: Kekule's dream of the dancing pairs…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Ghent (Kekule's own account; Jung gives no place/date)
body: "When Kekule had his dream of the dancing pairs and deduced from it the structure of the benzol ring, he accomplished something that Zosimos strove for in vain. His 'composition of the waters' did not fall into as neat a pattern as did the carbon and hydrogen atoms of the benzol ring. Alchemy projected an inner, psychic experience into chemical substances that seemed to hold out mysterious possibilities but nevertheless proved refractory" (cw13 ¶143).

Jung's contrast: the natural-scientific dream worked where the alchemical vision failed — yet both draw on the same archetypal imagery of circling, paired dancers. (The uroboros-family reading is ours: Jung does not name the uroboros here.)

occurrences.title: The tail-eater as prima materia — Reusner, Pandora (1588), p. 257
occurrences.label: The tail-eater as prima materia
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The full plate: "The 'tail-eater' (Uroboros) as the prima materia of the alchemical process, with the red-and-white rose, the flos sapientum. Below, coniunctio solis et lunae, with the lapis philosophorum as the son.". One image compresses Jung's whole reading of alchemy: circular prima materia, rose of wisdom, coniunctio, lapis-son.

Jung uses it at ¶63 to gloss the dreamer's snake-circle vision: "The drawing of a spellbinding circle (fig. 13) is an ancient magical device." The serpens mercurii is "the dragon that creates and destroys itself and represents the prima materia" (¶26).

occurrences.title: Ripley Scroll — chaos as dark sphere, dragon and frog (British Museum)
occurrences.label: Ripley Scroll — chaos as dark sphere, dragon…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939
Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Jung's second picture of the alchemical chaos (16 Nov 1938): not fragments but "a dark sphere... the basis of the alchemical process," from which vaporous exhalations rise — spirits or breath-beings that ascend and transform, revealing themselves "up above as the company of the gods," all contributing to the vase in which the coniunctio yields the divine being, Puer Aeternus or Rebis hermaphrodite. A nyagrodha tree grows from above, roots in heaven; "the round sphere is also often represented by the ouroboros that eats its own tail".

Later he returns to the same scroll for the union with the cerebro-spinal being: the female with salamander's tail and frog's feet, and "the dragon — originally the ouroboros — represents chaos underneath... persecuting a small frog" which "becomes the Puer Aeternus" in the assembly of the gods, i.e. the brain.

Distinct from anthropos-three-forms-ripley-scrowle-1588 (batch-2 picture check): that note is the published plate cw12 fig. 196 — scroll MS Add. 5025 panel No. 2, detail ("three manifestations of the Anthropos... below, dragon and toad as preliminary forms," pdf p360). This note's primary anchor is the dark-sphere/ouroboros description (pdf 1441), which no CW12 plate detail reproduces; the seminar's dragon-and-small-frog motif overlaps panel No. 2's lower register, and the salamander-tailed female on top is the Melusina/Lilith of the tree register (cw12 fig. 257; melusina-anima-ripley-scrowle-bm-sloane-5025-1588). Seminar locus ≠ plate locus — kept as separate loci.

occurrences.title: Ushabti - clay workmen substituted for human sacrifice in Egyptian tombs
occurrences.label: Ushabti - clay workmen substituted…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In Egypt human sacrifices were substituted by ushabti, small clay figures of workmen.
body: The Egyptian sublimation of retainer-killing: "In Egypt human sacrifices were substituted by ushabti, small clay figures of workmen. They assumed that the pharaoh would not suffer from hunger in the land of the hereafter if he had workers for the fields, so they put hundreds of those little clay figures into his tomb; they were usually bluish green, the color of the underworld".
The servant-soul in effigy - the logic of the broken vessel and the killed retainer carried into a magic-technical substitute, colored like the underworld itself.

occurrences.title: Utnapishtim's secret: the hidden magic herb of eternal youth (Gilgamesh)
occurrences.label: Utnapishtim's secret
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Land of the West, beyond the waters of death (Gilgamesh, tablet XI)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: The herb-revelation quoted at length in the herb-dream discussion: "I will tell you a secret, of a hidden magic herb I will talk to you. The herb looks like boxthorn and grows deep down in the sea, its thorn is like the spine of a porcupine, it blossoms in the freshwater sea far away. If you can lay your hands on this herb and eat of it, you will find eternal youth and life".

"So here you have the magic herb. It is an herb with healing powers, a power that will heal forever. It is the so-called panacea, a cure-all, the elixir vitae, the quinta essentia. At the same time it is also the herb that helps the adept to produce the lapis philosophorum." Context: Gilgamesh "takes the path of the sun," through the gate of the Scorpio giant — "the autumnal equinox of the Taurus age"; the epic stems from the end of the Taurus age.

occurrences.title: Valentinian letter — the Autopator in agnosia
occurrences.label: Valentinian letter — the Autopator in agnosia
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'In the beginning the Autopator contained in himself everything that is, in a state of unconsciousness [agnosia]' (¶298). Hippolytus' parallel: the Father 'deprived of consciousness and substance, neither masculine nor feminine' — nirdvandva, without opposites, therefore unknowable: 'This describes the state of the unconscious' (¶298). Ennoia, consciousness, is present only as 'the latent possibility of consciousness'; the differentiated syzygies and tetrads follow after (¶298). Jung links this to Paul's ignorantia (Acts 17:30) and to Eckhart's Godhead — Gnostic agnosia as the earliest psychology of the unconscious God-image.

occurrences.title: Valentinus' hymn — the cosmos hanging from spirit
occurrences.label: Valentinus' hymn — the cosmos hanging…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: All things depending in spirit I see; all things supported in spirit I view; flesh from soul depending; soul by air supported; air from aether hanging; fruits born of the deep; babe born of the womb.
body: A gnostic chain-of-dependence hymn Jung quotes in the Trinity essay's discussion of the "flesh from soul, soul from spirit" ladder of substance (alongside the \u03c0\u03b5\u03c1\u03b9\u03c4\u03c4\u03c9\u03bc\u03b1\u03c4\u03b1 of Isidorus, "outgrowths" of animal qualities on the soul):

The hymn's descending levels (spirit → aether → air → soul → flesh) make the visible world a suspension system whose top hook is spirit — an anima-mundi formula in gnostic dress, ending unexpectedly in the womb: the last link is a birth.

occurrences.title: The black bridal veil — twelve schoolgirl retellings of Marie's dream (N., Switzerland, ~1910)
occurrences.label: The black bridal veil
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1910 (rumour chain within days of the dream)
occurrences.quote: The teacher bought a jacket, and Marie and Lina got a long thick veil, such as is worn only in case of death or at weddings.
body: The teacher makes Marie's schoolmates write down what they had heard of the dream, yielding twelve versions — the rumour "analysed and interpreted the dream" (¶125). In the retellings the veil appears and does the symbolic work: the teacher buys a jacket, the girls get "a long thick veil, such as is worn only in case of death or at weddings" — and "the one who has the veil is the bride!" (¶102). Successive narrators darken it (a black veil "naturally in order to conceal anything indelicate," ¶104), add the undressing scene, the piggyback ride, the night in the barn, each giving the story "an innocent turn." Jung reads the chain as each child's "inner participation" — the dream continued collectively, wish and censor collaborating.

occurrences.title: Dream: the black veil over the back of the head — veiling the unconscious
occurrences.label: Dream — the black veil over the back of the head
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Someone was putting a black veil over my head. It seemed to me that I was meant to wear it always. I said, \"This veil will always show.\" Someone answered, \"No, it is thin, it is worn over the back part of the head, not over the face.\
body: The day after the Madonna and harvest dreams: someone puts a black veil over her head, meant to be worn always; a voice corrects her — thin, worn over the back of the head, not over the face. Amplification runs from the veiled sacred virgins and the early-Christian veiling of the sex element (hair in church, "evil elementals would appear", p133) to the black virgins — black Isis figures, Augustine's Mary as black earth, the black Madonna of Einsiedeln (p132). The rule the voice delivers: "the unconscious aspect should be veiled, but the face should be visible. Whatever one is conscious of may be shown, but what is in the unconscious should not be seen" (p133). People with large unconscious areas "smear it all over the place" (p134). The moral: "Be conscious-or as conscious as possible" (p134), pointing to the Gnostic morality of the Sabbath-worker logion — "be wise as the serpent... the new morality, the Gnostic morality" (p135). The black veil as mourning then bridges to the graveyard dream of 12 Nov (p136-137).

occurrences.title: Vision: the veiled patient in the medieval town; the child becomes two goats (8 Dec 1930)
occurrences.label: Vision — the veiled patient in the medieval town
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: The patient herself enters the mystery play, veiled; the Indian lifts her veil ("In the mysteries, veiling means that the initiate dies, and the unveiling means the resurrection", p212), gives her water from the spring, and leads her into a medieval town. In the square a woman holds her baby up to an erected cross; the Indian walks silently past; in anger the woman throws the baby at him — "Instantly the baby was transformed into two little goats that followed along behind the bull."

Reading: historical regression into the collective past when the way ahead is blocked; the medieval woman sacrifices the future child (progress as "an absolutely modern invention", p213); two alike things mark an unconscious condition still holding yea and nay (p214). The goats put her in the Dionysian suite — satyrs and Pan — confirmed by the Pompeii initiation fresco "where the woman who is to be initiated appears with the two little goats" (p215). The vision continues: Christ in a white robe appears and is left behind for the Indian-shepherd; a castle woman throws the scarlet flower (Hawthorne's scarlet letter); an ostrich (head in the sand) joins the cortege through Rome and past Grecian temples.

occurrences.title: The bedchamber of Venus — Chymical Wedding of Christian Rosencreutz
occurrences.label: The bedchamber of Venus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: they came to the bedchamber of Venus and found the goddess asleep on a couch.
body: The descent episode of the Chymical Wedding: a boy leads the hero down to an underground chamber whose copper door bears a secret inscription (cuprum — the Cyprian, Aphrodite/Venus); within, a three-cornered tomb on three animals (eagle, ox, lion — "the lower triad, corresponding to the upper Trinity... Reversal of moral values," ¶227 n.18) holds a copper cauldron with an angel and a dripping tree; below lies the bedchamber of the sleeping Venus, whose coverlet the boy twitches away.

Jung cites the episode four times: for the hierosgamos of Venus and Mars (¶227), against Dorn's christianized reading of the "characters of Venus" (¶235), as the central mystery of Mercurius's relation to the goddess of love (¶248), and for Mercurius appearing as Cupid who wounds the adept in the hand with the "dart of passion" (¶278).

occurrences.title: Venus turned St. Verena — springs and avalanche chutes of Aargau
occurrences.label: Venus turned St. Verena
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Baden, Canton Aargau, Switzerland; Verenelisgärtli near the Glärnisch; St. Verenakehle, Schafburg (Säntis)
occurrences.yearDisplay: medieval folklore transformation (inferred; toponyms continuous to Jung's day)
body: Jung's showcase of mythological ambivalence-by-succession: "Venus, as the philologists teach us, acquired a good aspect and turned into St. Verena (St. Verena, the patron saint of Baden, Ct. Aargau; watering places, as we know from history, were consecrated and subject to Venus)" (¶1077). Yet the goddess keeps her dangerous side in the mountains: Verenelisgärtli near the Glärnisch, and "St. Verenakehle is the name of the great avalanche chute on the Schafburg in the Säntis mountains."

The same paragraph runs the symmetric decay: "Odin becomes the wild hunter who molests lonely girls on the highways. Freia has turned into a she-devil"; and the eastward flip "Devas (Sanskrit, = angel) becomes the devil in Persian." The saint of healing springs and the lethal avalanche chute are one goddess under ambivalence.

occurrences.title: Ver sacrum - the sacred spring of Rome, youth sacrificed at the vernal equinox
occurrences.label: Ver sacrum - the sacred spring…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This idea of youth being sacrificed was called in Rome the ver sacrum, the sacred spring.
body: "Of what did the vernal sacrifice consist in antiquity?... It was particularly the sacrifice des primeurs, the first fruits of the field, the first vegetables, the first lambs and other young animals, and so on. And the first-born son, Christ the Son of God, is also sacrificed at the time of the vernal equinox. This idea of youth being sacrificed was called in Rome the ver sacrum, the sacred spring".

Jung's reading: "the best things of the moment were sacrificed in order to propitiate the gods of the future, to ensure a fertile continuation of the year" - the natural law behind the Christian self-sacrifice and behind the vision's crucified woman whose time of fructifying the earth is over.

occurrences.title: The card in the baptism goblet: aqua permanens against metaphysics (Vienna, ~1900)
occurrences.label: The card in the baptism goblet
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters
jung.locator: Letter 60, 'The Card in the Goblet' (pdf pp164-165)

occurrences.quote: That goblet with the card remained as a symbol of the aqua permanens that keeps evil metaphysical spirits at bay.
body: Pauli's founding memory of his epistemological stance: at his baptism — performed in "an antimetaphysical manner rather than in a Catholic one," his physicist godfather Ernst Mach having had "a much stronger personality than the priest" — a card reading "of metaphysical origin" was left standing in the goblet, "and despite all the great mental changes I went through later on, it remains a label that I myself bear."

Mach — "if you look at your own description of the extraverted sensation type, then you will see E. Mach" — regarded metaphysics as "the root of all evil in this world — in other words, in psychological terms, as the Devil himself." The anecdote opens Pauli's letter section "The Card in the Goblet," which Jung's mandala-with-empty-center note answers (pdf p164: "with me the center of the mandala is empty").

occurrences.title: Zosimos' vision: the boiling men in the embalming vessel (Egypt, ~3rd c.)
occurrences.label: Zosimos' vision — the boiling men…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Panopolis / Alexandria, Egypt (Berthelot III i 3 / III vi)
body: Second vision: the same bowl-shaped altar with boiling water and "a numberless multitude of people in it," burning and yet alive. A grey anthroparion ("a barber grown grey with age") explains: "The sight that you see is the entrance, and the exit, and the transformation... This is the place of the operation called embalming. Those who seek to obtain the art enter here, and become spirits by escaping from the body" (cw13 ¶86).

A brazen man with a leaden tablet commands the punished to write their inspirations with eyes upraised and mouths open — Jung: "might be compared with the technique of active imagination". The brazen man "is the priest who sacrifices and is sacrificed, and spews forth his own flesh". The vessel is the krater/vas Hermetis.

occurrences.title: Breaking the vessels of the dead - Jung's East African observation (~1925-26)
occurrences.label: Breaking the vessels of the dead - Jung's East…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Everything is broken up because the vessel has a soul which goes to heaven when they break it, to meet the dead and to serve them again.
body: Ethnographic ground for the burnt-snake rite and the smell-soul theory: when a woman died in the part of Africa Jung traveled, her cooking vessels, cooking stick, implements and jewels were set before her hut for about two months, untouched "until the soul had gone to heaven" - then everything broken, "because the vessel has a soul which goes to heaven when they break it, to meet the dead and to serve them again".

Jung: this is the logic "of those terrible human sacrifices" - the vessel's soul released by fire or shattering to serve the dead, the same age-old theory "that souls are subtle bodies which are smoke-like or smell-like". Cf. Sir Oliver Lodge's spiritist molecules in Raymond, "the ghosts have the same age-old theory of man."

occurrences.title: Cista and serpent on Ephesian silver coin
occurrences.label: Cista and serpent on Ephesian silver coin
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: there are in fact representations of the magic basket with a phallus lying in it surrounded by fruits.
body: The synthema (confession) of the Eleusinian neophyte, handed down by Clement, beside the Ephesian cista coin (pl. at pdf p304). Dieterich reads the "working" as phallic activity; the basket with phallus surrounded by fruits is attested; Clement reports a snake in the mystical basket — "the danger that comes from the regressive movement of libido" (¶530).

image.title: Thyateira - 133-132 BC - silver cistophoric tetradrachm - cista mystica with serpent - quiver with two serpents - Berlin MK AM 18204059

occurrences.title: Vision: the double goblet — intercommunicating cups, above emptied below
occurrences.label: Vision — the double goblet
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The next vision is a double goblet.
body: Second picture of the anticipatory series: a double goblet. Jung's amplification: an old Greek hospitality form — two bowls connected so host and guest drink intercommunicating cups, "done to be sure there was no poison in it" (p111); the open-handed greeting and the knife-concealing pocket likewise began as compensations for the contrary. The symbol's paradox: "when the top is filled, the lower bowl is empty... Only one part at a time can be filled. It might mean that what is poured in from above is poured out from below" (p111). His reading at the time: "the transition from above to below; one could expect that what had been above would now be below" (p111) — confirmed retrospectively by the wigwam vision following it: "The good shepherd, the poimen, above, is the primitive seer below. What is poured into the goblet of the Christian idea above becomes the instinct of the earthly seer below" (p111), with the primitive libation poured on the earth as parallel.

occurrences.title: Dead father escaped from the hot-water can (woman patient's dream, told 20 Feb 1929)
occurrences.label: Dead father escaped from the hot-water can
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: Oh, you know, Jung lifted the lid and I escaped.
body: A woman who had lost her father dreamed she met him: after his death he had reincarnated as a poor young clerk. Asked how he got out — she knew he had been in her hot-water can — he answered: "Oh, you know, Jung lifted the lid and I escaped."

Jung reads it straight through primitive psychology: "There the ancestors are living in pots and jars. That is why the Indians in Central America make their water-jugs like human faces... they are the spirits, the lares and penates, gods of the hearth sitting near the fire." Told this, the patient "was much enlightened and made a father transference to me... She associated her father's reincarnation with her own rebirth and renewal. That is the archetypal idea in dreams."

occurrences.title: Krater with snake and lion — Mithraic monuments
occurrences.label: Krater with snake and lion — Mithraic monuments
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "On the Mithraic monuments we often come across a strange symbol: a krater (mixing-bowl) with a snake coiled round it, and a lion facing the snake like an antagonist. It looks as if they were fighting for the krater" (¶671). Jung's decoding: "The krater symbolizes the maternal vessel of rebirth, the snake fear and resistance, and the lion raging desire" — a scene in which the opposing instinctual forces contend for the maternal container of transformation.

The same chapter reads the snake at the tauroctony: it glides to the blood flowing from the bull's wound — "the bull's life—its blood—is offered to the snake... a sacrificial offering to the powers of the underworld, like the blood drunk by the shades in the nekyia of Odysseus" (¶671). Bull's blood + snake = "a union of opposites," the cause "of the miraculous fertility that results from the sacrifice of the bull."
Verbatim: "The krater symbolizes the maternal vessel of rebirth, the snake fear and resistance, and the lion raging desire" (¶671).

occurrences.title: The liknon (winnowing-basket), cradle of Iacchus — Eleusinian procession
occurrences.label: The liknon, cradle of Iacchus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the cradle of Iacchus (λíκνον, mystica vannus Iacchi)
body: In the Orphic legend Iacchus was reared by Persephone in the underworld and, "after slumbering for three years, he awoke in the λíκνον" — the winnowing-basket as cradle of the buried-and-risen boy (¶528); cf. the Farnese stucco relief where Silenus holds the covered liknon before the veiled neophyte (¶536).

occurrences.title: The Lovatelli urn (Rome, ~1st c. CE)
occurrences.label: The Lovatelli urn (Rome, ~1st c. CE)
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The index files the Lovatelli urn at book p342, inside the Eleusinian-mysteries discussion (339–44): the famous Roman marble urn (Torlonia collection) carved with the ritual scenes — the maiden in the liknon/cista, the phallic pastries of the Haloa ("pastries, phallus-shaped, 342", index p613). It stands for the mystery vessel: womb, basket, and initiation box in one (cf. "vessel: symbol of uterus, 203", index p654).
Verbatim (index): "Lovatelli urn, 342"

image.title: Lovatelli urn (Rome Mus Naz 11301) 03

occurrences.title: The overturned bowl in the heart — initiation vision of Tewekkul-Beg (Sufi tradition)
occurrences.label: The overturned bowl in the heart
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: medieval Sufi tradition (date not given by Jung)
occurrences.quote: I beheld there in my innermost self something resembling an overturned bowl; when this vessel was righted, a feeling of boundless joy flooded through my whole being.
body: Jung's example of the mystics who "endeavour to recapture the primitive reality of the imago by means of an artificial introversion, in order to counterbalance extraversion" (¶47). The master Molla-Shah binds the novice's eyes, bids him gather the forces of the soul into his heart and create the master's image within; the heart opens and he beholds a vessel that must be righted before joy floods him. The doubled scene — "another Tewekkul-Beg were seated before another Molla-Shah" — is the interior mirroring of the initiated relation.
The master names it "the first phenomenon of his initiation"; other visions follow "once the way to the primitive image of the real had been opened" (¶47).

occurrences.title: FIG 14 — the toppling vase: a patient's first vessel (London, 1935)
occurrences.label: FIG 14 — the toppling vase
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: shown at the Tavistock lecture, London (painting by Dr. Bennet's patient)
occurrences.quote: The motif of the vessel is itself an archetypal image which has a certain purpose.
body: A clumsily painted bowl or vase, shown by Dr. Bennet. From its composition alone Jung diagnosed a schizophrenic condition: disparate unmotivated elements and "breaking lines" running through the field "like the breaking lines in a mirror" (¶407). The vessel is read as the attempt at self-cure — a container for all the incompatible units that the ego, which "can be identical only with one part at a time," cannot hold (¶408); the globe in the middle hints at a non-ego centre. As mandala it is temenos: magic circle drawn "to protect the centre of the personality" (¶409-411).
But the picture fails: "the design shows no balance, and the vase is toppling over... towards the side of the unconscious" (¶411).

occurrences.title: FIG 15 — the vase stands firm: souls, stars, and the averted anima (London, 1935)
occurrences.label: FIG 15 — the vase stands firm
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: shown at the Tavistock lecture, London (painting by Dr. Bennet's patient)
occurrences.quote: At the foot of the vase are eight figures of the crescent moon; the moon is also a symbol of the unconscious.
body: The same patient's second attempt at symmetry: the monstrous disparate things are assimilated; snakes and deep-sea fish — "animals of the underworld" — are gathered into a vase that now stands firm. Remarkably he "gathers in the stars" ("the cosmos, his world, is collected into the picture... an allusion to the unconscious astrology which is in our bones"), while at the top a naked anima-figure turns her back, and eight crescent moons stand at the vase's foot.

Jung's reading: the turned-away anima is "a typical position" in early objectivation; her arrival is "rather a positive sign — she also is a sort of vase, for in the beginning she incorporates the whole of the unconscious" (¶412). He prognosticates continued construction "if no particular trouble interferes."

occurrences.title: Amphora as 'vase of sin' — Gnostic gem, British Museum
occurrences.label: Amphora as 'vase of sin'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: A single gem among "the Gnostic gems in the British Museum... an amphora representing the 'vase of sin,' the womb with the ligaments on each side" (p354) — quoted while Jung assembles the cauldron's pedigree: Celtic symbol, alchemical crucible and alembic, womb, "the vase of transformation, the womb into which Nicodemus would not go: 'Can a man enter a second time into his mother's womb?'"

It was also the krater for mixing wine and water, and — his bridge to analysis — "there must have been a mystical society called the Krater, for there is a letter written by the alchemist Zosimos to a lady, advising her to go to the Krater to be reborn. In modern language: 'I would advise you to undergo some analysis in order to get a better attitude'" (p354).

occurrences.title: Zosimos' letter advising the woman to 'go to the krater'
occurrences.label: Zosimos' letter advising the woman to 'go…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: I have quoted the letter written by Zosimus, an early alchemist, to a woman friend, advising her to go to the krater.
body: In explaining the patient's volcano vision, Jung reaches for the positive meaning of the crater:

The krater, he says, "was either an actual initiation rite, or it was the name of a society" — but since Zosimos was an alchemist, "one may assume that the krater was the mixing bowl in which the constituents were brought together so that a new being resulted from it; so the positive meaning of the crater is the mixing bowl". The crater/volcano of the visions is the same vessel: "the crater is really a sort of retort in which heterogeneous elements are blended, thus making the Lapis Philosophorum"; the baptismal font as crater ("in the old mystical sense"). The woman friend of the letter is the alchemical sister of the patient being taught by the well-woman of the crater.

occurrences.title: Viennese patient's animus drawings: Kundalini from the god's head, quaternio minus one, the world-bridge
occurrences.label: Viennese patient's animus drawings
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: seen February 1931 (series began at her 46th year)
body: A woman of about Jung's age, "a bit mad in a very quiet and friendly way", producing elaborate drawings of her animus's great adventures, begun at forty-six after her lover's death — "in the meantime the lover had become identical with her animus". The first picture "contained practically the whole theory of these visions": a Kundalini yoga image "growing out of the head of the animus... exactly like the famous Dionysian head at Leiden where the hair is twisted up like a flame"; the symbols rise to "two triangles in which there was a cross, and over the cross was hanging a green snake".

Then mandalas "with three corners instead of four — always omitting the fourth" (sensation missing; Jung to her, in Faust's words: "There are three. Where has the fourth remained?"), and in the most perfect one "a heart in the center encoiled by a red snake... no peace, no rest." Her culminating picture: the animus as divine hero "throws himself over for a bridge, feet on one side, head on the other", bridging the great chasm of the world for humanity — "He reconciles the pair of opposites."

occurrences.title: Villa dei Misteri frescoes — Dionysian initiation of women (Pompeii)
occurrences.label: Villa dei Misteri frescoes
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The fresco cycle of the women's Dionysian mysteries, shown as photographs across two sessions. Scene by scene: Silenus, "the rather fat god, a perfect wise man, drunk with the sacred wine of inspiration", making music that arouses feeling; the communion scene with the two little goats — "The woman is to be initiated; she is receiving the inspiration that comes through communion with the animals"; then the union with the god "in the forms of Dionysus and Kore. Kore is the cult name for Persephone... The initiate is transformed into the divine figure, Kore, and as such she is celebrating the union with the god".

Jung immediately Easternizes: "this is the central idea of the Yoga in India, where the union is between Shiva and Shakti." The frescoes show what the patient's visions re-enact — initiation as re-identification with nature, "a great blessing... they felt the god in the complete identity with nature", the basis of the mystery cults' "hope of immortality" (p215). Linda Fierz-David's later Zurich seminar grew from these very lectures (ed. n.).

occurrences.title: Dream: vines growing from the heads of the congregation in the puritan church
occurrences.label: Dream: vines growing from the heads…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: she also noticed the extraordinary fact that from the heads of those people vines were growing all over the church. Then she discovered that in a corner somebody had brought in cocktails, and presently a girl pulled out a guitar and began to sing very frivolous songs.
body: A puritanical lady dreams she drives to the Episcopal church in her father's fine limousine, arguing convictions with her husband; the congregation is assembled but "they all looked half dead", and:

Jung: "Here we see Dionysus brought into the puritan church and it upsets the whole situation." The dream compensates a God-concept "limited by puritanical prejudices": the god who appears in the visions of the seminar patient is "naturally just the opposite" — the chthonic vegetation principle erupting inside the very container that excludes it.

occurrences.title: The glorification of the body as the Assumption of the Virgin — Reusner's Pandora (1588)
occurrences.label: The glorification of the body…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: The Pandora woodcut reproduced as Psychology and Alchemy fig. 232, "showing the glorification of the body in the form of the Assumption of the Virgin (from Reusner, Pandora, 1588)" (cw11 ¶? pdf p694). Alchemy's own Assumption: the corporeal raised as the Mother is raised. The Pandora plate is titled Speculum Trinitatis (Pandora, 1588, p. 253): "232. Glorification of the body portrayed as coronation of the Virgin Mary. — Speculum Trinitatis from Reusner, Pandora (1588)."

Jung's reading (cw12 ¶500): the Cantilena "ends with the apotheosis of the virgin-mother," which the Pandora depicts as the assumptio Beatae Mariae Virginis — body and soul reunited and taken up, marked "terra" and "corpus Lyb" (body) and "die wonn der jung-frowenn wardt"; the dove descends, God the Father blesses, she is crowned, "Mater" enthroned beside the orb-holding King: "in her the earth substance, becoming transfigured in her…"

The same footnote gathers the patristic virgo terra behind it — Augustine's "Truth is arisen from the earth, for Christ is born of a virgin" and Tertullian's "That virgin earth, not yet watered by the rains nor fertilized by the showers" — and points forward to the 1950 dogma Jung treats in Answer to Job's epilogue.
The plate's host tract: speculum-trinitatis-pandora-1588 (anon., bound into Reusner's Pandora, 1588).

occurrences.title: Mary as the black earth not yet fecundated by rain — Augustine, Sermon 189
occurrences.label: Mary as the black earth not yet fecundated…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the Virgin Mary was really the black earth not yet fecundated by torrents of rain
body: Jung's textual warrant for the black Madonna: "In an early Christian manuscript, St. Augustine said that the Virgin Mary was really the black earth not yet fecundated by torrents of rain; he used that simile in one of his sermons" (p132). Mary = the dark, untilled earth — the chthonic mother the church later denied: "Mary was the earth, the dark principle, but since that was close to the chthonic cult of Demeter, it was absolutely denied by the church... The sermons of St. Augustine would not have been particularly welcome a bit later on" (p132). Within the patient's dream-sequence the blackness is the condition of fertility: "Without the blackness of the earth, no wheat could be grown" (p133) — the chain that binds the black veil, the Madonna, and the harvest of wheat.

occurrences.title: The Black Virgin of Einsiedeln
occurrences.label: The Black Virgin of Einsiedeln
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: medieval image (baroque dressing); black-basalt Isis type much older
occurrences.quote: There are a number of statues of Mary which are black; at Einsiedeln, for instance, there is a black Virgin.
body: Asked about the patient's black face with white halo, Mr. Baumann supplies the Swiss witness:

Jung adds the genealogy: "there are also much older ones of black basalt which date from very early times. The Egyptians made statues of Isis in black basalt, meaning that Isis was the fertile earth, the black soil of Egypt"; through the likeness of Isis-Horus to Mary-Jesus "the early church simply took over many statues of Isis and Horus and called them Mary and Jesus; there is one in the Lateran Museum". St. Augustine: "the Virgin Mary was the earth which had not yet been fertilized by the spring rains" — hence Jesus "the son of the earth", the wheat-Host beside Iacchus' ear of wheat and Mondamin's corn. Jung admits no historical explanation for baroque black madonnas, only the psychological one: the Renaissance regression to antiquity, checked by the Reformation.

occurrences.title: Pagan virgin and well under the crypt of Chartres
occurrences.label: Pagan virgin and well under the crypt…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Gothic crypt (12th c.) over a far older sanctuary
occurrences.quote: The crypt at Chartres was previously an old sanctuary with a well, where the worship of a virgin was celebrated—not of the Virgin Mary, as is done now—but of a Celtic goddess.
body: "The crypt at Chartres was previously an old sanctuary with a well, where the worship of a virgin was celebrated — not of the Virgin Mary, as is done now — but of a Celtic goddess." Jung generalizes: under every medieval church there is a secret place where the mysteries were celebrated; the sacraments were the mysteria; in Provençal the crypt is le musset, "mystery-place" (also at Aosta) (¶254).

Within the Toledo amplification this is the Christian-architectural form of the serpent's cistern: the cathedral above, the older chthonic worship below — "something below the Christian Weltanschauung, something older than Christianity" (¶256).

occurrences.title: Christ in the Virgin's womb — Upper Rhenish Master (Germany, c. 1400)
occurrences.label: Christ in the Virgin's womb
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The unusual late-medieval iconography showing the Christ-child within the Virgin's belly, reproduced as Plate III (from Wachlmayr, Das Christgeburtsbild der frühen Sakralkunst). Jung invokes it at the point where Miss Miller's adolescent problem — "How am I to be creative?" — meets the mythological consolations: "Did not the Word become flesh? And did not the divine pneuma enter into the Virgin's womb?" (¶70).

His reading of the image's enduring power: "Why do we cherish the image of the Immaculate Mother even to this day? Because it is still comforting and speaks without words or noisy sermons to the comfortless, saying, 'I too have become a mother' — through the 'Idea spontaneously creating its own object'" (¶70). Reappears when the tube/hose of the Holy Ghost-dove fecundation paintings is discussed (¶150).

occurrences.title: The Collyridians' Eucharistic feast in honour of Mary (Epiphanius, Panarion 79)
occurrences.label: The Collyridians' Eucharistic feast…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: This plainly amounted to a Eucharistic feast in honour of Mary, at which wheaten bread was eaten
body: The sect of the Collyridians worshipped Mary "after the manner of an antique goddess": on certain feast days priestesses decorated a wagon or four-cornered seat, covered it with linen, placed offerings of bakemeats upon it "in the name of Mary," and afterwards partook of the sacrificial meal. "This plainly amounted to a Eucharistic feast in honour of Mary, at which wheaten bread was eaten" — devotees mostly women; Epiphanius rebukes that "the whole female sex is slippery and prone to error," and insists: "Let Mary be held in honour… but let no one adore Mary."

Jung sets this beside the Council of Ephesus (431), on streets that "had once rung with hymns of praise to many-breasted Diana," declaring Mary θεοτόκος: "Thus the archetype reasserted itself" — the feminine divinity returning at the very moment the masculine Trinity closed its ranks (his ¶195: archetypal ideas are "part of the indestructible foundations of the human mind").

occurrences.title: The Edda's winter-bound earth-maiden delivered by the spring sun (cited cw4 1912)
occurrences.label: The Edda's winter-bound earth-maiden delivered…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The earth, in the form of a maiden, is held prisoner by the winter, and is covered with ice and snow.
body: Jung's interpretive key to the Sleeping Beauty/Snow White cycle: "its astronomical or meteorological components, clearly brought out in the Edda.
