The earth, in the form of a maiden, is held prisoner by the winter, and is covered with ice and snow. The young spring sun, the fiery hero, melts her out of her frosty prison, where she had long awaited her deliverer" (¶494). The fertilizing spring sun has been associated "from ancient times" with the bull, "the animal embodying the mightiest procreative power" (¶497). In 1912 the seasonal reading stands beside, not yet instead of, the infantile-birth reading of myth (¶478).

occurrences.title: Jung's dream: the patient as golden goddess on the castle tower (Zurich, ~1931)
occurrences.label: Jung's dream — the patient as golden goddess…
occurrences.subject: jung
body: During a stalled treatment (the Java-born patient of the appendix), Jung dreamt: "On the hill was a castle with a high tower. Sitting on the parapet of the topmost pinnacle was a woman, golden in the light of the evening sun. In order to see her properly, I had to bend my head so far back that I woke up with a crick in the neck" (¶549). Waking, the Schenkenbach verse — an invocation to the Virgin Mary — came to him: the dream "had put my patient on the highest peak, making her a goddess, while I, to say the least, had been looking down on her" (¶550). Telling her the dream broke the mutual unconsciousness; the real analysis then began (¶551). The dream documents Jung's counter-transference corrected from within.

occurrences.title: The Jungfrau — virgin mountain and the virgin earth of Switzerland (folk-astrological tradition)
occurrences.label: The Jungfrau — virgin mountain…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~late-medieval folk-astrological tradition ('from olden times'); Jung's review 1928
occurrences.quote: These are living reminders that the virgin mother is the earth.
body: In "The Swiss Line in the European Spectrum" (review of Keyserling, 1928) Jung reads Switzerland's national earthiness through its loveliest mountain: "Our loveliest mountain… is called the Jungfrau — the 'Virgin.' The Virgin Mary is the female patron saint of the Swiss." Old astrologers, he says, assigned Switzerland either Virgo or Taurus — "both are earth-signs."

Jung's reading: the Marian toponym is a survival of the virgin-earth motif, witnessed patristically — Tertullian's "that virgin earth, not yet watered by the rains" and Augustine's "Truth has arisen from the earth, because Christ is born of a virgin" — "living reminders that the virgin mother is the earth" (¶914). From this earth-boundness come both the Swiss vices and their function: Jung's yin-people set against Keyserling's yang-aristocrat (¶913), redeemed by his confession, "I believe only in the Word become flesh, in the spirit-filled body, where yang and yin are wedded into a living form" (¶917).

occurrences.title: Korion festival at Alexandria: the virgin Kore gives birth to the Aeon
occurrences.label: Korion festival at Alexandria
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Epiphanius describes the pagan festival at the Korion in Alexandria: all-night songs and flutes, then, after cock-crow, torches carried down to a subterranean sanctuary to fetch up a naked carved wooden image marked with five golden crosses — forehead, both hands, both knees — carried seven times round the precinct and returned to the crypt. Asked the meaning, the worshippers answer: "Today, at this hour, the Kore, that is to say the virgin, has given birth to the Aeon".
Jung: the mother-goddess — like the star-crowned woman of Rev. 12 — is "usually thought of as a virgin"; the Christmas message "the virgin has brought forth, the light increases" is pagan.

occurrences.title: The Lauretanian Litany (Litany of Loreto)
occurrences.label: The Lauretanian Litany (Litany of Loreto)
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Analytical Psychology: Notes of the 1925 Seminar

body: The Marian litany of Loreto — tower of David, mystical rose, virgin powerful through chastity. Jung cites it at the climax of his historical argument on the repression of instinct: "In the year 700, the burning of witches was not allowed, but 700 years later, down to 1796, witches were burned. It had its climax at the same time as the appearance of the Lauretanian Litany,16 which expresses the culmination of the cult of the Virgin" (sem-1925).

His reading: "When such cruelties as witchburning appear in society, it means on the psychological side that instinct has been tortured, and in fact instinct is tortured by an extreme over-valuation of chastity. Really hellish tortures have followed in its wake." He endorses Schmitz's genealogy: patriarchy → paternity-interest → chaste wife → "the virgin powerful through chastity, such as Athena."

occurrences.title: Litany of Loreto — hortus conclusus, rosa mystica, vas insigne devotionis
occurrences.label: Litany of Loreto — hortus conclusus, rosa…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Against Dr. Schlegel's "church as mother," Jung points to where the feminine actually survived: "the later Catholics… brought in the feminine element, even using the symbols of the secret philosophy. The Litany of Loreto contains all the symbols of the secret philosophy, the hortus conclusus, and the rosa mystica, and the vas insigne devotionis".

The context is the exclusion structure of "On the Tree on the Hill"'s discussion: "Mary never entered the Trinity, the feminine element was excluded. And even the Holy Ghost… is made a neuter… That one exception, the Theotokos, the idea that the mother of God was identical with Sophia, is heretical". The Marian litany is the side-door through which the repressed female principle re-entered the masculine religion — with the editorial note that Jung saw Pius XII's 1950 Assumption dogma as a belated recognition of the feminine aspect of the godhead.

occurrences.title: Dream: the woman in blue with the child on her lap — Madonna of the inferior function
occurrences.label: Dream — Madonna of the inferior function
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Then I saw a woman who seemed to be raised above the crowd. She was dressed in blue. On her lap a tiny child was kneeling. She was sheltering it in her arms.
body: Following the mole down, she lands in a great medieval crowd and sees a woman raised above it, dressed in blue, a tiny child kneeling on her lap. Jung: to go down to the collective level is to go back in time — her feeling-life reaches the fourteenth century, the culmination of the cult of Mary (Lorettanian Litany, p124). The shepherd's lamb is now humanized: "it is the Mother Mary, and instead of a lamb, it is a child" (p125) — "regressive progress... the more she goes back in time, the more time comes to meet her" (p125). Not for her actual child: the maternal attitude belongs "to the pregnant lamb, and to this bambino... the thing that is weakest in herself" (p126) — the inferior function. The frame is the Mater Dolorosa: "That child you are going to care for is a child of sorrow and pain" (p127). The effect: "For the first time in my life I felt that people could no longer destroy me" (p128) — reinforcement by the archetype, "the instinctive store of energy in man" (p129).

occurrences.title: The Virgin Mary as rain-fed earth bearing Christ the wheat — St. Augustine
occurrences.label: The Virgin Mary as rain-fed earth bearing…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: A passage Jung "has often quoted": Augustine compares the Virgin Mary to the earth — fecundated by the spring rains, bearing Christ, "our truth," as the wheat. Ambrose parallels her womb with "a heap of wheat and the lily" (De instituto virginis, cited CW6 ¶394, footnote pdf p864).

In the seminar it serves the argument that a revelation is modified by its audience's mind: antique Christian congregations of "subtle minds" could take such chthonic analogies "on the wing" without dogma; the same image in later centuries "would have led back into a chthonic cult." The barbarian mind, by contrast, "demands things cut and dried" — the road to transubstantiation.
Verbatim: "St. Augustine compares the Virgin Mary to the earth: she is the earth fecundated by the spring rains, and from the earth, Christ, our truth, is born: he is the wheat".

occurrences.title: The mater dolorosa dethroned — the swan brings the newborn babe (Visions)
occurrences.label: The mater dolorosa dethroned
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: vision read 17 February 1932 (painted late 1929/early 1930 for Jung)
occurrences.quote: Oh you two women who have created me, behold me now. Did you create me only to be crucified?" I answered Christ: "Yes, from my womb I bring forth suffering. I will create you again with my body and again you will be crucified.
body: Before the dark Christ on the crucifix the mater dolorosa weeps — "Now he is up there upon the cross. Something has broken between us." The patient takes her by the hand — "Woman, are you afraid to stand alone?" — and answers the dying Christ:

Mary calls the menacing crowd; the patient veils her face (taking the veil, renouncing the respectable role), leaves the church, bathes her face in a stream — nature "worshipped consciously" — and a swan brings her a newborn babe in a basket. Jung: she places herself beside the mother of God — the assimilation of medieval Christian psychology; the Christ-life is "the ordinary human life" consciously accepted, and one who lives it "is his own church"; the swan, living between water and air, is "more chthonic than the dove".

occurrences.title: Mary's conceptio per aurem — the hymn 'Quae per aurem concepisti'
occurrences.label: Mary's conceptio per aurem
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: hymn in liturgical use, ~15th–16th c. (dating inferred)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: "According to that famous hymn: Quae per aurem concepisti, which means, 'Thou that hast conceived by the ear.'... So Mary conceived through the ear, she heard the Word, the Word came to her." — Miss Wolff supplies the ear; Prof. Fierz the angel.

Jung uses it as the exact formula for Zarathustra's anima, who "has heard the Word, has obviously been impregnated": "in a man's case... his anima has heard something, she had an audition, she conceived the Word." The child conceived by the Word "will be a logos, a word of authority" — the voice not his own that solitude forces one to admit. Buddha's irregular conception (side / dream of the white elephant, editor's note) stands beside it.

occurrences.title: 'She sits so high above us, no prayer will she refuse' — Schenkenbach's Reiterlied
occurrences.label: She sits so high above us, no prayer will she…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Two lines of a Swabian rider's song (Reuterlied, ca. 1520) that surfaced in Jung as hypnagogic amplification of his tower-goddess dream: "She sits so high above us, / No prayer will she refuse." Jung identifies them at once: "This is an invocation to the Virgin Mary" (¶550) — the folk-song formula carrying the Queen-of-Heaven archetype that the dream had constellated around his patient. A neat miniature of amplification operating involuntarily: the collective image supplies the reading of the private dream.

occurrences.title: The Proto-Evangelium — the woman and her seed bruise the serpent (Genesis 3:15)
occurrences.label: The Proto-Evangelium
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

body: The so-called Proto-Evangelium: "the Second Eve corresponds to 'the woman and her seed' mentioned in Genesis 3:15, which shall bruise the serpent's head" (¶625). As Adam was believed originally hermaphroditic, so "the woman and her seed" are thought of as a human pair — the Queen of Heaven and Mother of God together with the divine son who has no human father.

This is the Marian prefiguration on which Jung builds his reading of the Incarnation's precautions: Mary "chosen as the pure vessel", protected against Satan's tricks by immaculate conception and everlasting virginity — measures that "queer the pitch for a genuine Incarnation", since mother and son "are not real human beings at all, but gods" (¶626).

occurrences.title: Sleeping Beauty behind the thorny hedge (Grimm, cited cw4 1912)
occurrences.label: Sleeping Beauty behind the thorny hedge
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The tale of Sleeping Beauty has obvious connections with an ancient spring and fertility myth, and at the same time contains a problem which has a remarkably close affinity with the psychological situation of a rather precocious little girl of eleven.
body: Produced "as though by chance" by the 11-year-old patient — as an example of a fairytale without meaning — while her burning-house dream was being analysed (¶493). Jung takes the accident as anything but: "in psychology there are no blind accidents" (¶495); the child was partially identifying with the enchanted sleeper. He reads the tale within "a whole cycle of legends in which a virgin, guarded by a dragon, is rescued by a hero" (¶494), keyed by the Edda's seasonal myth: earth as winter-bound maiden, the spring sun as fiery deliverer. The complex it names is hers — "the expectation of coming events" (¶497), a precocious girl's own waiting.

occurrences.title: Snow White in the glass coffin (Grimm, cited cw4 1912)
occurrences.label: Snow White in the glass coffin
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: As a further example of an incomprehensible fairytale she cited Snow White, who lay enclosed in a glass coffin, in the sleep of death.
body: The child's second volunteer: still doubting that fairytales mean anything, she cites Snow White, "who lay enclosed in a glass coffin, in the sleep of death." Jung: "It is not difficult to see that Snow White belongs to the same cycle of myths as Sleeping Beauty" — with "even clearer indications of the myth of the seasons" (¶496). Methodologically it is the decisive confirmation: she did not realize the identity of the two tales, so the second example "accentuating as it does the meaning of the first" cannot have been suggested (¶497) — two spontaneous products from the same unconscious source, the complex of expectation.

occurrences.title: The Virgin as vas of the divine child — Venetian Rosario (1524)
occurrences.label: The Virgin as vas of the divine child
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the Virgin as the vas of the divine child
body: Plate 87: "The Virgin as the vas of the divine child," from a Venetian Rosario della gloriosa vergine Maria (1524). It follows the dream-31 commentary on the birth of the centre from the amorphous mass: "That this birth can issue from an amorphous mass has its parallel in the alchemical idea of the prima materia as a chaotic massa informis impregnated by the seeds of life" (¶244).

The Marian parallel confirms the vessel-family's Christian branch: the Mother as container in which the divine child takes form — the same structure as the alchemical vas bearing the filius philosophorum (¶338) and the dreamer's "uterus" point (dream 32).

occurrences.title: Virgil's Fourth Eclogue — the return of the Virgin (Rome, ~40 BCE)
occurrences.label: Virgil's Fourth Eclogue
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The messianic eclogue: "Now has come the last age foretold in the song of the Cumaean Sibyl; the great cycle of centuries begins anew. Now the Virgin returns, and the reign of Saturn is restored... Only do thou, chaste Lucina, favour the birth of the child, through whom the iron brood shall cease to be, and a golden race arise throughout the world" (¶119).

Jung's reading: proof that "even before the spread of Christianity, mankind was seized by wild, eschatological hopes of redemption" — the pagan expectation into which the Christian redeemer-figure was born, and the classical counterweight to Faust's opposite road (¶¶119-121).

occurrences.title: The beautiful woman standing in the dragon — gospel miniature, Bruges
occurrences.label: The beautiful woman standing in the dragon
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: there is a miniature which shows the 'woman,' beautiful as the mother of God, standing with the lower half of her body in a dragon.
body: In a 14th-century gospel copy at Bruges, a miniature shows the "woman" — beautiful as the Mother of God — standing with the lower half of her body in a dragon.

The footnote is one line, but the image is the Rev. 12 woman caught mid-metamorphosis: the radiant virgin and the devouring beast share a single body, the Terrible Mother and the benevolent mother not yet split.

occurrences.title: The woman in white with the child on the raised platform above the mad market (patient vision, 4 October 1933)
occurrences.label: The woman in white with the child…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I went to her and said: \"Why are you here?\" She answered: \"They wish it.\" I said: \"How can you stand this sight? Does it not sicken you? Have you no feeling?\" She said: \"No.\" I left her in disgust.
body: In the market place "thronged with a multitude of men and women surging and shouting and cutting themselves with knives" — the shadow aspect of collective life, dvesa — sits on a raised platform a woman in white with a child upon her knees. Asked why she tolerates it, she answers only: "They wish it... No." Jung reads her as Mary, mother of the Purusha: "she is the symbol of individuation for women as Christ is for men," free from participation mystique with the mad crowd, au-dessus de la melee — while the patient's disgust shows she is still fascinated by the spectacle herself.

occurrences.title: The Visio Arislei: the king's glass house, Thabritius and Beya
occurrences.label: The Visio Arislei — the king's glass house…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Arisleus is in danger of succumbing to the fate of Theseus and Peirithous … a repetition of the cosmic embrace of Nous and Physis.
body: One of the oldest allegories of the opus: Arisleus flees to the kingdom of the Rex marinus, where nothing is begotten because "only like mates with like." On the philosophers' advice the king unites his two children — Thabritius and Beya, hatched in his brain — in incestuous marriage; the son dies in the embrace; the party is imprisoned in a triple glass house (Beya's womb) for eighty days of heat; Pythagoras, seen in a dream, sends Harforetus with the food of life; the fruit of the immortal tree ripens and Thabritius lives again.

Jung: "its whole character relates it very closely to those visions known to us from the psychology of the unconscious" (¶392); he reads it as the descent of consciousness into the unconscious, mortificatio, and renewal (¶436-441), with the Ruska-discovered Codex Berolinensis preface naming the tree whose fruit ends all hunger (¶449).

occurrences.title: Orfeo Angelucci — the igloo craft, weeping for earth, and the hydrogen-atom stigma (23 Jul 1952)
occurrences.label: Orfeo Angelucci — the igloo craft, weeping…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: lonely spot, California; then 'over a thousand miles' above earth
occurrences.quote: He interpreted this as the 'symbol of the hydrogen atom.
body: After an "abaissement du niveau mental" — which Jung flags as "a very important precondition for the occurrence of spontaneous psychic phenomena" (¶795) — Angelucci enters a glowing "igloo" whose walls are "ethereal mother-of-pearl stuff," is carried into space, and sees earth from above while the voice weeps with him: "For all its apparent beauty earth is a purgatorial world among the planets." Jesus is re-explained as "the 'Lord of the Flame,' 'an infinite entity of the Sun'"; every person has "a spiritual, unknown self which transcends the material world." After a baptism of "true light" he returns; next morning finds "a stigma the size of a twenty-five-cent piece, an inflamed circle with a dot in the middle" — "the 'symbol of the hydrogen atom.'"

Jung's reading: "He was marked not by the Christian stigmata but by the symbol of the self, of absolute wholeness or, in religious language, God" (¶806) — the passage that fuels the Christ-lapis equation.

occurrences.title: Orfeo Angelucci — green fireballs with a voice: 'Don't be afraid, Orfeo' (Burbank, 23 May 1952)
occurrences.label: Orfeo Angelucci — green fireballs with a voice
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: road near Burbank, California (Lockheed night-shift worker)
occurrences.quote: Don't be afraid, Orfeo, we are friends!
body: The founding vision of Angelucci's prophetic career: a faintly red-glowing oval disk hovering near the ground shoots upward, releasing "two balls of green fire from which a man's voice issued, speaking 'perfect English'": "Don't be afraid, Orfeo, we are friends!" A voice bids him drink from a crystal cup on his fender; between the twin disks forms "a luminous three-dimensional screen" showing a man and a woman "being the ultimate of perfection," in telepathic contact; the beings see earthlings "as each one really is," recording everyone on "crystal disks," and ask to be looked on "simply as older brothers."

Jung lets him speak at length as "a unique document that sheds a great deal of light on the genesis and assimilation of Ufo mythology" (¶802) — the naive, self-taught dramatization of the individuation process "in an unconscious, symbolical form" (¶809). First sighting: 4 Aug 1946.

occurrences.title: Orfeo Angelucci — planetoid of Orion and Lyra, the noce céleste (September 1953)
occurrences.label: Orfeo Angelucci — planetoid of Orion…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: heaven 'as Orfeo imagined it' / small planetoid
occurrences.yearDisplay: early September 1953 (somnambulistic state of about a week)
occurrences.quote: a noce céleste was celebrated, a mystic union analogous to the coniunctio oppositorum in alchemy.
body: After a public sighting shared by eight witnesses (2 Aug 1952) and a meeting with a rippling-edged figure "who wished to be called by the name of 'Neptune'" (¶800), Angelucci fell into a week-long somnambulistic state and remembered a sojourn in heaven "with countless flowers, delightful odours, colours, nectar and ambrosia, noble etheric beings and, of course, almost incessant music." The friend was really Orion; "Neptune" had been his own heavenly name. His erotic response to Lyra horrifies the company; corrected, he celebrates "a noce céleste, a mystic union analogous to the coniunctio oppositorum in alchemy."

Jung closes the account here: "Without having the faintest inkling of psychology, Angelucci has described in the greatest detail the mystic experience associated with a Ufo vision" — the pélerinage de l'âme whose goal is the union of opposites (¶802).

occurrences.title: Vision 20: the unknown woman on the globe, worshipping the sun
occurrences.label: Vision 20 — the unknown woman…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "A globe. The unknown woman is standing on it and worshipping the sun." (cw12 ¶110).

The anima is distinct from the sun: "the latter is a personification of the unconscious, while the sun is a symbol of the source of life and the ultimate wholeness of man" (¶112). "The dreamer's anima still seems to be a sun-worshipper, that is to say, she belongs to the ancient world" — scholastic intellect drove her to regress, as the Renaissance's Hypnerotomachia shows with Polia at the court of Venus. Early Christians themselves "had some difficulty in distinguishing the ἣλιος ἀνατολῆς (the rising sun) from Christ."

occurrences.title: Vision 22: the ape-man in the primeval forest and the Dionysian danger
occurrences.label: Vision 22 — the ape-man…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "In a primeval forest. An elephant looms up menacingly. Then a large ape-man, bear, or cave-man threatens to attack the dreamer with a club… Suddenly the 'man with a pointed beard' appears and stares at the aggressor, so that he is spellbound… The voice says, 'Everything must be ruled by the light.'" (cw12 ¶117).

Behind the nymphs "there lurks the Dionysian mystery of antiquity, the satyr play with its tragic implications: the bloody dismemberment of the god who has become an animal" (¶118) — Nietzsche, who knew "that the dismal fate of Zagreus was reserved for him." The pointed-beard intellect exorcizes: "the devil is the 'strange son of chaos' who can most readily be trusted to deal effectively with his mother" (¶119).

occurrences.title: Vision: the bear with four-coloured eyes, the tunnel, the treasure in the east (visual impression 39)
occurrences.label: Vision — the bear…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: In alchemy the bear corresponds to the nigredo of the prima materia
body: A waking dream: falling into the abyss, the dreamer lands before a bear whose eyes gleam alternately "in four colours: red, yellow, green, and blue. Actually it has four eyes that change into four lights." The bear vanishes; a long dark tunnel leads to shimmering light, a treasure, and on top of it the ring with the diamond — "this ring will lead him on a long journey to the east."

Jung: the bear "stands for the chthonic element that might seize him," but proves only "leading up to the four colours… which in their turn lead to the lapis, i.e., the diamond whose prism contains all the hues of the rainbow. The way to the east probably points to the unconscious as an antipode. According to the legend the Grail-stone comes from the east and must return there again. In alchemy the bear corresponds to the nigredo of the prima materia (fig. 90), whence comes the colourful cauda pavonis" (¶263).

occurrences.title: Jakob Böhme's glimpse of the centrum naturae — sunbeam in a tin platter
occurrences.label: Jakob Böhme's glimpse of the centrum naturae
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: That Jakob Böhme should obtain a glimpse into the centrum naturae by means of a sunbeam reflected in a tin platter is also understandable.
body: Jung cites Böhme's famous vision among the gradations of enlightenment: Christian visions of the Trinity, the Madonna or the patron saint are "more or less as it should be"; Böhme's sunbeam is "understandable"; Eckhart's naked boy and Swedenborg's purple-coated God strain digestion; the Zen anecdotes stand "right in the middle" of the grotesque.

Note: the tie to lumen-naturae is inferred from Jung's wider corpus (Aion, Mysterium Coniunctionis); in this chunk the vision functions only as a satori-parallel. The reflected light of nature in a household vessel — the tin platter — is the locus's emblem.

occurrences.title: Vision 19: death's-head changing into a red ball, then a woman's head emitting light
occurrences.label: Vision 19 — death's-head changing…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "A death's-head. The dreamer wants to kick it away, but cannot. The skull gradually changes into a red ball, then into a woman's head which emits light." (cw12 ¶107).

Faust and Hamlet skull-soliloquies stand behind it. "Evidently an enantiodromia, a play of opposites, has occurred: after being rejected the unconscious insists on itself all the more strongly. First it produces the classical symbol for the unity and divinity of the self, the sun; then it passes to the motif of the unknown woman who personifies the unconscious." (¶108).

occurrences.title: 'We have to discover our shadow. Otherwise we are driven into a world war' — Visions Seminar (18 Feb 1931)
occurrences.label: We have to discover our shadow. Otherwise we…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: We have to discover our shadow. Otherwise we are driven into a world war in order to see what beasts we are.
body: The shadow-doctrine's dated political forecast, eight years before 'The Fight with the Shadow.' In discussion with Prof. Demos about the "acrobat" balance between god and devil, Jung generalizes: modern people are "inflated because we don't know or because we have forgotten what we are" — hence Nietzsche, Freud and Adler "tell us what we are, quite mercilessly." Then the aside, in his own voice, naming the war to come as the price of the undiscovered shadow. The same passage coins the era-diagnosis: "Our ignorance of the human being as he is really meant to be is a violation of the blood… when we try to live above our level" — the 'where there is a will there is a way' spirit read as God-Almightiness (the doctrine he will formalize in cw10 ¶437, 1946, as the psychic result of de-projection).

Timeline weight: this is the earliest in-corpus date at which the shadow-concept and the war-forecast are joined in one sentence; the Wotan's-fires aside follows a month later (wotans-fires-national-socialists-zurich-1931), the 1918 forecast beneath both (blond-beast-underground-prison-forecast-1918).

occurrences.title: Vision: the black eagle seizes the golden ring; the ship follows (visual impression 58)
occurrences.label: Vision — the black eagle seizes the golden ring
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Out of the egg… will rise the eagle or phoenix, the liberated soul
body: "The dark ring, with an egg in the middle." Then: "A black eagle comes out of the egg and seizes in its beak the ring, now turned to gold. Then the dreamer is on a ship and the bird flies ahead." Jung: "The eagle signifies height. (Previously the stress was on depth…) It seizes the whole mandala and, with it, control of the dreamer." Birds are thoughts and the flight of thought; the ship is the methodical vehicle over "the sea and the depths of the unconscious" (like Hinayana/Mahayana); "Man cannot walk the rainbow bridge like a god but must go underneath" (¶305).

The egg is "the chaos apprehended by the artifex, the prima materia containing the captive world-soul"; from it rises "the eagle or phoenix, the liberated soul, which is ultimately identical with the Anthropos who was imprisoned in the embrace of Physis" (¶306).

occurrences.title: The fish's eye in the pool — woman's verse vision (no Ufo connection)
occurrences.label: The fish's eye in the pool
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The disk becomes a blazing golden sun, / Compelling deeper contemplation.
body: Jung cites, as an example of "the ever-open eye of the fish in alchemy, or the unsleeping 'God's eye'" experienced today "not as external light-phenomena but as a psychic revelation" (¶807), a woman's poem: light strikes a deep blue pool's pebbled bottom; "A jewel flickers... A staring fish-eye's glance / Attracts my mind and heart— / The fish, invisible as glass"; the fish dances, the disk becomes "a blazing golden sun, / Compelling deeper contemplation."

His reading: the water is the unconscious depths, the light a ray of consciousness; from the fish-eye arises "a world-illuminating sun, an Ichthys, a sol invictus, an ever-open eye which reflects the eye of the beholder... a rotundum that expresses the wholeness of the self and cannot be distinguished, except conceptually, from the deity" (¶808). The sky Ufo "follows the old rule and appears in the sky"; this vision puts the same rotundum in the depths.

occurrences.title: Hildegard of Bingen's vision of the light (Bingen, 12th c.)
occurrences.label: Hildegard of Bingen's vision of the light
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 12th c. (Scivias period; Acta S. Hildegardis, Migne PL 197, col. 18)
body: Quoted by Jung for the light-vision phenomenon: "Since my childhood I have always seen a light in my soul, but not with the outer eyes, nor through the thoughts of my heart; neither do the five outer senses take part in this vision... The light I perceive is not of a local kind, but is much brighter than the cloud which supports the sun... While I am enjoying the spectacle of this light, all sadness and sorrow vanish from my memory" (cw13 ¶42).

Jung: the vision of light "proves to be something unconditioned and absolute, a combination of supreme power and profound meaning" at all times and places (¶42); such states bring in "a solution of psychic complications" and liberation (¶43).

image.title: Hildegard, receiving the light from Heaven.

occurrences.title: Ignatius Loyola's vision of the many-eyed snake
occurrences.label: Ignatius Loyola's vision of the many-eyed snake
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: Ignatius Loyola and his vision of the snake with multiple eyes, which he at first regarded as of divine, and later as of diabolical, origin.
body: Jung uses the vision in "The Holy Men of India" as his example of interpretation at work on religious experience: "at least a part of his experience is a humanly limited interpretation." The same numinous content is assigned first to God, then to the devil — with I John 4:1 as the standing injunction: "Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are of God."
This is Jung's critical counter-weight to Ramana's unproblematic "self = God" equation: experience is always emotion plus interpretation.

occurrences.title: Vision: mother's hand with haloed fingers; the golden pheasant
occurrences.label: Vision — mother's hand with haloed fingers
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A patient in hypnagogic condition sees his mother painted like a Byzantine church mural, one hand wide open, fingers swollen into knobs each surrounded by a small halo; associations: frog-suckers, phallus; then a skyrocket rises from her hand and turns out to be "a shining bird with golden wings—a golden pheasant".
Jung's reading: "Fire is bored with the hand; therefore fire comes from the hand; and Agni, fire, was worshipped as a golden-winged bird" (¶271) — the hand's spermatic-creative significance.
Verbatim: he saw what looked like a skyrocket going up from his mother’s hand, which on closer inspection proved to be a shining bird with golden wings—a golden pheasant (cw05 ¶271).

occurrences.title: Vision 21: surrounded by nymphs — 'We were always there, only you did not notice us'
occurrences.label: Vision 21 — surrounded by nymphs
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "The dreamer is surrounded by nymphs. A voice says, 'We were always there, only you did not notice us.'" (cw12 ¶114, pdf 112).

Regression to an unmistakably classical image; the voice in dreams carries final, indisputable authority. The splitting of the anima into many figures equals dissolution into the unconscious — parallel: "the Paracelsan regio nymphididica, mentioned in the treatise De vita longa as the initial stage of the individuation process" (¶116). Jung adds the alchemical corollary: the vessel must be round like the head, and "the work is crowned by the production of the rotundum."

occurrences.title: Hildegard's Scivias milk-and-cheese vision — human seed in clay vessels (Bingen, 12th c.)
occurrences.label: Hildegard's Scivias milk-and-cheese vision
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: Flying Saucers fn3 (pdf p631), 'Ufos in history' section (index print pp.403–404)

occurrences.quote: You look further and see people on the earth who carry milk in clay vessels. From this they prepare cheese.
body: Jung quotes Hildegard's Scivias vision (via the Scivias edition, pp.128f.) alongside Macrobius's Somnium Scipionis (I, 14, 19) in the "Ufos in history" section: medieval cosmology already knew the descent of soul-stuff into generation. People on the earth "carry milk in clay vessels," and from it prepare cheese — these are "the people, men and women, who carry human seed in their bodies"; the fatty milk makes energetic people, the thin milk weakly people, the corrupt milk malformed people, and of the good "the devil does not find his place in them."

The body is the vessel that curdles seed into destiny — a microcosm-milk vision paired in the same footnote-cluster with the Quickening plate (Rupertsberg Codex) Jung reproduces in the essay proper (cf. mandala-hildegard-quickening-womb-scivias-12c, ¶765–769).

occurrences.title: Vision 5: the snake describes a circle round the dreamer
occurrences.label: Vision 5 — the snake describes a circle round…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "A snake describes a circle round the dreamer, who stands rooted to the ground like a tree." (cw12 ¶62).

Jung: "The drawing of a spellbinding circle (fig. 13) is an ancient magical device… He thereby protects himself from the 'perils of the soul'" — the same act that sets a place apart as holy, like the Roman sulcus primigenius at a city's founding. The dreamer has "succeeded in establishing a protected temenos, a taboo area where he will be able to meet the unconscious" (¶63). The snake is anticipatory: the circular movement will later grip the dreamer himself (¶129).

occurrences.title: Vision — the spark that became a star in the fathomless dark (Wickes)
occurrences.label: Vision — the spark that became a star…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'On the shaft there hung a human figure that held within itself all the loneliness of the world... Alone, and hoping for nothing, the One hung and gazed down into the void... Then deep in the fathomless dark was born an infinitesimal spark. Slowly it rose from the bottomless depth, and as it rose it grew until it became a star. And the star hung in space just opposite the figure, and the white light streamed upon the Lonely One' (¶344 n.47). Jung: 'a typical piece of individuation symbolism' — the Gnostic spinther, Eckhart's scintilla vitae. Cf. Zoroaster, who drew down sparks from a star and was scorched.

occurrences.title: Vision 7: the veiled woman uncovers her face and it shines like the sun
occurrences.label: Vision 7 — the veiled woman uncovers her face…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "The veiled woman uncovers her face. It shines like the sun." (cw12 ¶67).

"The solificatio is consummated on the person of the anima. The process would seem to correspond to the illuminatio, or enlightenment" (¶68) — against the rational 'elucidation' of the conscious mind, which "only satisfies the little tip of personality that is contemporaneous with ourselves, not the collective psyche that reaches back into the grey mists of antiquity."

occurrences.title: Swedenborg's vision: the man in the purple coat
occurrences.label: Swedenborg's vision: the man in the purple coat
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: Swedenborg's 'man in the purple coat,' who wanted to dissuade him from overeating, and whom, in spite—or perhaps because—of this, he recognized as the Lord God.
body: Jung's exhibit, in the Suzuki foreword, of an enlightenment occasion that "borders on the grotesque":

Graded between Böhme's sunbeam glimpse of the centrum naturae ("understandable") and Eckhart's "little naked boy" ("harder to digest"), Swedenborg's banal divine visitor sits at the edge of the grotesque — precisely where, Jung says, the Zen anecdotes live. The point is comparative: satori's occasions are as undignified as any theophany — "the answer which appears to come from the void, the light which flares up from the blackest darkness" (¶896).

occurrences.title: Symeon the New Theologian's vision of the inner light (Constantinople)
occurrences.label: Symeon the New Theologian's vision…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: index 'Symeon, "the New Theologian," mystic experience of light, 91f' (pdf p645); c01 mention at ¶141 (pdf p101)

body: The mystic experience of light of Symeon "the New Theologian" (index, book p91f). Jung quotes the vision at ¶141: "I realized suddenly that it was within me, and in the midst of my heart it shone" — the divine light as inner fire-substance, the same lumen Jung sets beside Hildegard's vision ("mystic perception of light, 91, pl. XXXa", index p565) and the pneuma-doctrines of late antiquity.
Verbatim (index): "Symeon, “the New Theologian,” mystic experience of light, 91f"

occurrences.title: Living stones streaming into the tower — Shepherd of Hermas
occurrences.label: Living stones streaming into the tower
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: human beings, streaming from the four quarters, inserted themselves as living stones, melting into it 'without seam
body: The vision behind the lapis angularis: "the temple built upon the foundation of the saints inspired in the Shepherd of Hermas a vision of the great building into which human beings, streaming from the four quarters, inserted themselves as living stones, melting into it 'without seam'" (¶11). "The Church is built upon the rock that gave Peter his name (Matthew 16:18)."

Jung sets it against the alchemists' cornerstone-Christology: "the lapis is frequently compared to Christ as the lapis angularis," and Mercurius as the peace-maker of Ephesians 2:13ff. who "might create in himself one new man in place of two, so making peace" (¶10). The tower of self-inserting living stones is the ecclesiastical twin of the lapis' "one homogeneous substance."

occurrences.title: Vision 6: the veiled woman on the stair — first appearance of the anima
occurrences.label: Vision 6 — the veiled woman on the stair
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "The veiled figure of a woman seated on a stair." (cw12 ¶64).

"The motif of the unknown woman—whose technical name is the 'anima'—appears here for the first time" (¶65). Personification signals autonomous unconscious activity with an anticipatory character; the stair indicates ascent or descent. Jung then opens the initiatory row: the Stairway of the Seven Planets in Apuleius, the ladder as burial gift for the ka in Egypt, Zosimos' visions, and the solificatio in which "the initiand was crowned as Helios" (¶66).

occurrences.title: The 'Great Vision': the World Clock (second dream series, vision 59)
occurrences.label: The 'Great Vision': the World Clock
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: It is a three-dimensional mandala—a mandala in bodily form signifying realization.
body: A vertical blue disc with white border, divided into 4×8 = 32 partitions with a rotating pointer; a horizontal circle of four colours bearing four little men with pendulums, encircled by the ring once dark, now golden; three rhythms — small, middle, and great pulse. The dreamer carries away "an impression of 'the most sublime harmony.'"

Jung calls it "a three-dimensional mandala—a mandala in bodily form signifying realization… Whatever a man does in reality he himself becomes" (¶308). The self is "the centre and the circumference of the conscious and unconscious systems"; two heterogeneous systems intersect in it (¶310). The figure may even be "a small-scale model or perhaps even a source of spacetime" (¶312). The 32 partitions lead to the Sepher Yetsirah's thirty-two paths of wisdom (¶313); Guillaume de Digulleville's rotating siècles supply the historical parallel (¶315ff.).

occurrences.title: Vision of one's own younger selves (country doctor, early 19th c.)
occurrences.label: Vision of one's own younger selves
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: The boy or man that I was then, I see him still as he was.
body: Walking home exhausted at night, "a man living a very strenuous life... became aware of a shadow figure parallel with him in the middle of the road. He recognized the figure as himself about ten years younger" — then it returned as himself twenty years younger, "and so on down to a boy of eight or ten."

Jung adduces it as evidence for "a certain tendency in man to personify his ages," decoding dream 1's dead boy: "the allusion to the dead boy is an allusion to the patient's own dead youth. He has arrived in the second part of life, where one's psychology changes: youth is dead." A double staged along the time-axis rather than beside the body.

occurrences.title: Chroshtag the Call and Padwahtag the Answer — the voice that wakes the sleeping Ormuzd
occurrences.label: Chroshtag the Call and Padwahtag the Answer
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: They are Chroshtag (\"the call,\" in German der Ruj) and Padwahtag (\"the answer\"), and these two are companions of the wise leader.
body: At the awakening of the sleeping Ormuzd, two companion gods appear: Chroshtag ("the call," German der Ruf) and Padwahtag ("the answer"). Reichstein, and Jung with him: "Chroshtag personifies his first form in the world of phenomena. (He is the voice, the Logos.)" The symbolism, Jung says, "arises from an inner experience, according to which one hears the wise old man call out, or speak, before one sees him" — the messenger may be a letter, for writing "is an invention of the old wise man."

Jung draws the yoga parallel explicitly: "The important moment, which represents the beginning of the release, is paralleled in Indian Yoga by the moment when Kundalini is awakened. Here Chroshtag awakens the sleeping Ormuzd."

occurrences.title: 'God's voice' in the breastbone — the widow with voices down the body midline (Zurich)
occurrences.label: God's voice' in the breastbone
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: chronic ~30 years; treated ~14 years; told 1939 and 1956
body: A widow of limited intelligence, after one acute schizophrenic interval, suffered thirty years of chronic hallucinations: "voices... distributed all over her body and congregated more particularly round the body openings and also round the breasts and navel" (¶574). At the earlier telling, Jung notes her mentality was "early medieval, and I was able to establish a fairly good rapport with her only by adapting my terminology to that of the early Middle Ages. There were no hallucinations then; it was all devils and witchcraft" (¶540). One voice was "fairly reasonable and helpful"; Jung "tried to cultivate that voice" (¶540). It was "God's voice," "localized in the middle of the breastbone," and it prescribed the therapy itself: at each consultation Jung was to have her read a chapter of the Bible, memorize and reflect on it (¶574). After about eight years "the right half of her body was completely freed of voices, up to a line running exactly down the middle of the body" (¶574).
Jung's reading: the unforeseen gain came "simply from the fact that her attention and interest were kept alive" (¶574) — work with the one rational complex against the invasion.

occurrences.title: Hosea marries a prostitute by divine order — the prophet's symbolic act
occurrences.label: Hosea marries a prostitute by divine order
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The worst case was the prophet Hosea, who married a prostitute as a symbolic act because the Lord ordered him to do so
body: Jung's model for how dream-figures act meaningfully: "these figures in the archetypal pattern are acting symbolically, exactly as the prophets in the Old Testament acted symbolically... The worst case was the prophet Hosea, who married a prostitute as a symbolic act because the Lord ordered him to do so, expressing in that way that the people had prostituted themselves to the heathen" (p104). The prophets were poimen, spirit-leaders (p107); their gestures are "a manner of speech" — as in the dream, where the unknown man picking up the lame sheep and she the pregnant lamb "would thereby convey a certain idea... this I do in order to show you that one should feel compassion" (p104). The locus grounds Jung's rule that symbolic action communicates what conceptual language cannot.

occurrences.title: Jeanne d'Arc's voices — revelation through the ganz andere
occurrences.label: Jeanne d'Arc's voices
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The Maid's voices — her conversations with the saints, for which she "was pronounced a heretic for having had a conversation with the saints without the interference of the church"; "in her canonization process, they said that she had had an intuition" (Miss Wolff's example, confirmed by Jung).

Jung returns to her at once: "I believe that the early experiences of Jeanne d'Arc were truly revelations because one cannot assume that a peasant girl in the 15th century had any kind of political aspirations... if you were called to do something similar you would have certain qualms about it I am sure. So we can assume she had too; it must have been a pretty rough business". She belongs to his intuition-vs-revelation discrimination: revelation comes with the authority of a reality, "against one" (objicere), and is resisted for years.
Verbatim: "she got her revelation through the ganz andere, so she was pronounced a heretic".

occurrences.title: Clock tick-tock as marching battalion — Rhineland family murderer (~1920s)
occurrences.label: Clock tick-tock as marching battalion
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A man "of up-to-then blameless character" bought a knife "without having any particular object in mind", then fell asleep by a pendulum clock: "He heard the ticking of the clock, and this tick-tock was like the sound of a battalion of marching soldiers... When it ceased completely he suddenly felt, 'Now I must do it.'" He killed his entire family, even his dog, and stabbed his wife eleven times (¶817).

Jung's reading: the wife, of a sect dividing the world into "saints" and "children of the devil", had unconsciously "instilled the criminal instinct into his subconscious mind"; he "recited a saying from the Bible at each stab" (¶818). The automaton-voice (machine-clock becomes marching troop, then command) through which another's evil acts — cf. the baker of the same sect who murdered three in a cataleptic state (¶820).

occurrences.title: 'Press your sides and shout like a steer' — breath-call to the gods, Mithraic Liturgy (Egypt, ~2nd–4th c.)
occurrences.label: Press your sides and shout like a steer
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

body: The invocation-by-breath passage of the Mithraic Liturgy, quoted by Jung: "We have a description of it in the Mithraic liturgy, where it says: 'Hold both your sides and press them with all your might and shout like a steer,' so that the gods may hear you" (sem-kundalini pdf p157).

His frame is the anāhata (air-center) psychology: feelings "come out in the breath; you can express them—you press, and out comes the feeling in the form of sound. That was the original method of calling to the gods." Most people, he adds, are "still about there": exhaling thoughts and feelings without consciousness of what they do — pre-conscious speech, why "the self is only beginning to be visible from the anvhata".

occurrences.title: Schreber's system of voices — compartments that go air-tight (Memoirs, 1903)
occurrences.label: Schreber's system of voices
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: These compartments became air-tight.
body: Daniel Paul Schreber, "a famous lawyer" who became insane, differentiated and named his voices: "those that are hanging under Cassiopeia" (a society speaking one style); a bookkeeper's group "as if reading from a book where all new facts are recorded in Heaven"; when he played the piano with warm feeling, voices shouted down "Got it"; and little people floating in the air who, bumped into, said "Oh damn!" and vanished into him.

Jung's reading in the worm-lecture: "There were little compartments that exploded in him and melted into him, but later on as his illness progressed these compartments became air-tight" — the living image of segmented, dissociated consciousness, the fate the healthy dreamer flirts with when the "worm" of preconscious life comes up. Jung had read the memoirs around 1905 and brought them to Freud's attention.

occurrences.title: Socrates' daimonion — the swine omen in Athens
occurrences.label: Socrates' daimonion — the swine omen in Athens
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Jung's exemplar of the daimonion: walking with friends in Athens, Socrates' daimon whispered "Take the other road to the right, leave this road." He obeyed; down the road they had left "rushed a herd of swine, trampling down all the passers-by into the mud."

Jung: the daimon is "the prophetic voice of the seer in our unconscious, usually symbolized by the wise old man. So the daimon is the Superman, the thing that is greater than man, yet it seems to be in man." Socrates' usage defines daimonion as neuter mana — neither succubus nor incubus — the concept in which the Superman and the jester of Zarathustra meet. Identification with this voice is inflation (Nietzsche's megalomania).

Verbatim: "his daimon whispered in his ear: 'Take the other road to the right, leave this road.' Socrates obeyed and suddenly down the road they had left rushed a herd of swine, trampling dovwn all the passers-by into the mud." (pdf p161, OCR as in text)

occurrences.title: The patient whose 'telephone' voices told the truth
occurrences.label: The patient whose 'telephone' voices told…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: A "crazy woman" full of absurd megalomanic ideas heard voices she called her telephone — and "they were voices of perfect normality and insight." When her megalomania ran away with her, the telephone corrected her: "You are leading the doctor by the nose; it is all bunk, you really belong to the lunatic asylum." Later: "The doctor is quite right; of course you are mad, and you need to be locked up."

Jung uses the case to make madness discussable as split: "we can assume that behind madness there is a sort of nirvana condition," voices that remain entirely reasonable — the same structure as the typhoid patient who became gentle under fever and the sane self behind Nietzsche's condition.
Verbatim: "I remember the case of a crazy woman who was full of the most absurd megalomanic ideas, but the voices she heard, which she called her telephone, told her the truth."

occurrences.title: The crater of life — volcano with the crux ansata of smoke, green oasis (Visions)
occurrences.label: The crater of life
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: vision read 17 February 1932 (painted late 1929/early 1930 for Jung)
occurrences.quote: I stood on the edge of a volcano. I looked into the crater and saw a sea of boiling fire. Dead bodies were cast up and fell back again. A great cross of smoke with the Egyptian symbol of life above it arose, hovered in the air, and vanished.
body: Immediately after the rebirth (babe brought by the swan), the enantiodromic danger:

Jung: rebirth is "against nature" (Nicodemus' doubt), so nature takes her revenge — as Python pursued Apollo, Herod the children, the dragon the woman's man-child. But she stands on the edge, detached, "a sign of maturity": seeing the situation "as a sort of symbol, you have won". The smoke-ankh marks "the crater of life"; the crater is "the vessel in which the different elements or constituents are mixed" — the Zosimos krater, the mixing bowl; fire center of the Kundalini system. "The fire in the crater died down and instead of fire I beheld a beautiful green oasis" — the desert-destroyer becomes the fertile mother; the villagers call the mountain simply "the Great Mother… She only smokes".

occurrences.title: Zarathustra's descent through the volcano — 'Es ist Zeit, höchste Zeit'
occurrences.label: Zarathustra's descent through the volcano
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: A later chapter Jung cites for the archetype's impatience: Zarathustra "is seen descending to hell through the volcano," a voice crying that it is time.

Jung: "That shows how impatient he is to tell his message, as if he felt his impending doom, the degeneration of the brain which began soon after. In Ecce Homo you already see traces of it, the first symptom occurred only four or five years later" — the descent read as premonition of the 1889 collapse.
Verbatim: "I mentioned that later chapter where he is seen descending to hell through the volcano and where a voice says: 'Es ist Zeit, hochste Zeit.'"

occurrences.title: Wachandi rite of spring — hole in the earth as woman
occurrences.label: Wachandi rite of spring
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Spring fertility-magic: a hole shaped and bushed to look like a woman's genitals; men dance all night with spears thrust into it, shouting "Pulli nira, pulli nira, wataka!"; during the whole ceremony they may not look at a woman (¶221).

Jung's reading: "a sacramental mating, with the hole in the earth representing the woman, and the spear the man" (¶214); the hole is "an analogy of the mother's genitals... a kind of mother-substitute" by which incestuous energy is desexualized and canalized (¶226).
Verbatim: In this rite of spring there is enacted a sacramental mating, with the hole in the earth representing the woman, and the spear the man. (cw05 ¶214).

occurrences.title: 'In thy heart are the stars of thy fate' — Schiller's Wallenstein
occurrences.label: In thy heart are the stars of thy fate
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: The astrologer Seni's line to Wallenstein, quoted by Jung as the hinge between the astrological and psychological world-pictures: "That is a translation of astrological into psychological terms. But this was very late, in the beginning of the nineteenth century. Until then, people assumed that it was not psychological motivation but the movement of the stars which caused the personal reactions." Already cited in Symbols of Transformation (CW 5, par. 102 n. 52).

occurrences.title: Rite de sortie — the warrior locked up and fed on vegetables
occurrences.label: Rite de sortie — the warrior locked up…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "When a warrior comes back from a war filled with the mania for killing, they lock him into a hut and feed him for two months on vegetables in order to remove his blood lust. That is a very apt method for cooling those people down so that they can fit into the community again; otherwise they would go on dancing war, killing right and left."

The counterpart of the rite d'entrée — hunting and war dances worked up to ekstasis, the hunter identical with the hunted buffalo carrying his own arrow. "This explains the terrible slaughters that primitive people sometimes perpetrate; it is not cruelty, it is just going on with the dance. That occurs in the Bible-in the way the Jews slaughtered the Canaanites."

occurrences.title: Wasserstein der Weysen (1619): the stone as 'Prototype of the heavenly Stone Jesu Christ'
occurrences.label: Wasserstein der Weysen
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: How that the terrestrial Philosophical Stone is a veritable Harmonia, Contrafactur, and Prototype of the true spiritual and heavenly Stone Jesu Christ.
body: An alchemical book of devotions of 1619: on page 67 the anonymous author promises to show how the rejected cornerstone (lapis angularis = Christ) "accords and is in exceeding subtle and artful agreement with the terrestrial and corporeal Philosophical Stone" — a demonstration occupying nearly fifty pages and concluding that the terrestrial stone is "a veritable Harmonia, Contrafactur, and Prototype of the true spiritual and heavenly Stone Jesu Christ."

The book "made a great stir, and even Jakob Böhme is to be counted among its admirers"; the historian Kopp was scandalized by "the blasphemous mixture of alchemical ideas … and religion." Jung: "We should not judge medieval naïveté too severely, but must try to understand what such an unwieldy language was intended to convey."

occurrences.title: The swelling watch that says 'half three' — 'school dream' of a boy
occurrences.label: The swelling watch that says 'half three'
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: she's got a wristwatch; in the beginning it's very small, but then it suddenly gets so big that it has to be carried. Ellen says the time is half three.
body: Dr. Pitsch's "school dream": Indian-ink blots on the sleeves (the dark secret of puberty), the dark stable where the first step is missing, the man with the dog whose arrival turns the wall to glass behind which vegetables and flowers are sold, the father with two boys boring a well ("a Laocoön group without snakes"), the lost coat, and in the former home two girls — Regula without a watch, Ellen with one that swells:

Jung's crescendo: the man-and-dog is consciousness with the bound animal unconscious ("the dog is a part of man, a kind of shadow"; Vendidad; Anubis). The two girls are the two anima figures — "the Osiris situation" (Isis and Nephtys). And the watch: "It is the watch we carry within ourselves, the Self... It is a mandala and represents the dynamism of fate, it is heaven's watch, the zodiac... The Self revealing itself in time is represented by the instrument that determines time and fate, the watch". "Half three": the male number three not yet complete. The two strange names from A Thousand and One Nights he cannot say at the father's table.

occurrences.title: Aqua nostra as spirit-water: fire, baptismal water, Holy Spirit — Rosarium ch. 2 (1550)
occurrences.label: Aqua nostra as spirit-water — Rosarium ch. 2
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The aqua nostra (our water), as is evident from the text and from numerous other sources, is also fire, the baptismal water, and at the same time the Holy Spirit this contains.
body: The Rosarium's central identity: dissolution of the imperfect body returns it "to the watery initial state, i.e., into the prima materia," and the aqua nostra is simultaneously fire, baptismal water, and the Holy Spirit it contains — a "spirit water" united with the prima materia "in the same way as the spirit of God brooded over the water of the beginning and from it created the world" (Genesis 1:2 read as chemistry).

Jung's reading (¶1787): creation "outwardly through a chemical operation and inwardly through active imagination" — the text enjoins, "And imagine this with the true and not with the fantastic imagination." Medieval man thought from spirit into matter; we think from matter into mind, and so find the reciprocal transformation of matter by mind unthinkable. The art itself "is a gift of the Holy Spirit" (¶1785, quoted text).

occurrences.title: Baptism mosaics — Baptistry of the Orthodox, Ravenna
occurrences.label: Baptism mosaics — Baptistry…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: ...the fourth is St. Peter drowning in a lake during a storm, and the Saviour is rescuing him.
body: Four mosaic scenes — two of Christ's baptism in the Jordan, one of St Peter drowning in a storm-tossed lake with the Saviour rescuing him — cited by Jung as evidence that baptism "was still a mystery cult" in the fifth century: "Baptism is a symbolical drowning... It is a symbolic death out of which new life comes." Russian sects, he notes, held initiates under water until some actually drowned. The baptistery is also the site of Jung's famous Ravenna vision of mosaics later found not to exist (MDR 314-18, fn27).

occurrences.title: The benedictio fontis — Holy Saturday rite of the descensus Spiritus Sancti in aquam
occurrences.label: The benedictio fontis
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: attested in early sacramentaries (~6th–8th c.); still performed

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: The rite consists in a repetition of the descensus spiritus sancti in aquam
body: The Catholic rite performed on Holy Saturday before Easter: "The rite consists in a repetition of the descensus spiritus sancti in aquam. The ordinary water thereby acquires the divine quality of transforming and giving spiritual rebirth to man."

Jung's point is a derivation-with-reversal: "This is exactly the alchemical idea of the divine water, and there would be no difficulty whatever in deriving the aqua permanens of alchemy from the rite of the benedictio fontis were it not that the former is of pagan origin and certainly the older of the two." The miraculous water of the first Greek alchemical treatises (1st c.), the Gnostic legend of the spirit's descent into Physis that influenced Mani, and Manichean channels into Latin alchemy form the older, pagan line of which the Church rite is the liturgical twin. The alchemists' water was named "spiritualis sanguis" — Christ's blood the Christian parallel.

occurrences.title: The black water — Apocalypse of Baruch
occurrences.label: The black water — Apocalypse of Baruch
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In the Apocalypse of Baruch the black water signifies the sin of Adam, the coming of the Messiah, and the end of the world.
body: In the Jewish apocalypse ascribed to Baruch, black water is one of the symbolic waters of the world-drama. Jung adduces it in a note to the Death section of the transference essay, where the king of the "Tractatus aureus" drinks the "aqua pernigra": there the king "represents the new birth, the self, which has assimilated the 'black water,' i.e., the unconscious".
The passage binds the alchemical black water to Adam's fall, messianic advent and eschatology — the aqua pernigra carries the whole weight of the nigredo.

occurrences.title: The blue rock towering to the sky with healing waters (patient vision, 4 October 1933)
occurrences.label: The blue rock towering to the sky…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I looked up and saw a great blue rock towering into the sky. It sent forth streams of water which rushed down on either side of me. I was healed of my wounds.
body: Recoiling in horror she leans against the wall of rock (the mandala re-entered — a regression "through the ages" to the sheltering cave, svadhisthana) and sees a great blue rock towering into the sky, sending down streams of water on either side of her; her wounds are healed. Jung reads the blue (air-region, anahata color) rock as Christ himself — the Negro spiritual "I found a home in that rock," Moses' rock, the brazen serpent, the pierced side's blood and water, the four rivers of the heavenly Jerusalem: "whatever is in the center always has reference to the Self."
The water is the baptismal uterus resurrectionis — rebirth through return to the undisturbed origin.

occurrences.title: Leading the linen-covered cow to the crossroads to make rain (Russia, 1931)
occurrences.label: Leading the linen-covered cow…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Russian countryside (reported by an American traveller)
occurrences.quote: They were leading the cow to the crossroads to sprinkle her milk in the dust to the four corners of the world, in order to make the rain ashamed.
body: A first-hand 1931 report Jung relays: Russian peasants stop an American's car to let pass a procession leading a cow covered with white linen to the crossroads, where her milk is sprinkled in the dust "to the four corners of the world, in order to make the rain ashamed, to show it they could do better." The old woman's gloss is the historical punchline: "the Bolshevists had destroyed God, and they had nobody else to ask." Jung's exhibit of the salamander-restitution: destroy the civilized religion and the collective unconscious produces a more archaic, thoroughly alive replacement.

occurrences.title: Divine water gestated in sea-water — treatise of Ostanes
occurrences.label: Divine water gestated in sea-water
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The treatise of Ostanes directs that, in preparing the divine water, 'the vessel with the ingredients should be immersed in sea-water, and then the divine water will be perfected... gestated in the womb of the sea-water' (cw14 ¶317). Its self-description: 'This [divine] water makes the dead living and the living dead, it lights the darkness and darkens the light, concentrates the sea-water and quenches fire.' Because such water occurs in the oldest texts, Jung takes it as 'of pagan rather than of Christian origin' (¶317), kin to the Chinese 'flowing pearl' of the 142 CE treatise and to Komarios' 'blessed water' that brings the spring.

occurrences.title: Girl's dream 5 — the drop of water full of branches (origin of the world)
occurrences.label: Girl's dream 5 — the drop of water full…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1938-39 (dreams dreamt at age eight; presented at ten; died of an infectious disease about a year later)
occurrences.quote: A drop of water is looked at through a microscope: it is full of branches. This is the origin of the world.
body: Dream 5 of the Christmas booklet: "A drop of water is looked at through a microscope: it is full of branches. This is the origin of the world."

Jung pairs it with the mouse dream as spontaneous cosmogony: "the cosmogonic myth of the creation of the world and of man, which appears in dreams 4 and 5" — comparable, he says, to what a primitive medicine-man would teach at initiation: "what God or the gods or the 'founding' animals have done, how the world and man were created, what the end of the world will be, and the meaning of death" (¶536). The microscope image lets the tree-branch motif stand as the world's first figure — life at its smallest already world-shaped.

occurrences.title: Mother drowning in the bath — dream of the thirteen-year-old girl
occurrences.label: Mother drowning in the bath
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A brilliant, over-developed girl of thirteen, forced by her mother — a woman of "intense will to power" — to be a prodigy, dreamed: "I saw my mother slipping down the bath and I knew she was drowning, but I could not move. Then I grew terribly frightened and started to weep because I had let her drown."

Jung's reading: "it obviously means the death of the mother. Such is the answer of the child's unconscious to the mother's blind ambition. Had she not tried to 'kill' her daughter's individuality the unconscious would never have reacted in that way" (¶223). Yet he warns against generalizing: death-dreams of parents are common and meaning varies with the conscious situation.
Quote. "I saw my mother slipping down the bath and I knew she was drowning, but I could not move."

occurrences.title: The fiancée swallowed by the ice — depressed patient's fantasy (Zurich, ~1910s)
occurrences.label: The fiancée swallowed by the ice
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: she jumps into the crack, and he watches her sadly.
body: A male patient with psychogenic depression produced the fantasy in his "visualized mood": "He sees his fiancée running down the road towards the river. It is winter, and the river is frozen. She runs out on the ice, and he follows her. She goes right out, and then the ice breaks, a dark fissure appears, and he is afraid she is going to jump in. And that is what happens: she jumps into the crack, and he watches her sadly" (¶343).

Jung's reading: the fantasy is "two-dimensional" because the patient merely "perceives and passively endures" (¶344). The fiancée is "also a symbol for his anima, that is, for his relation to the unconscious" — the fantasy shows the anima "disappearing again into the unconscious" while he watches "without lifting a hand. But he could easily step in and arrest the anima" (¶355–356). The demanded cure is active participation: to behave in the fantasy as in reality would be "assigning absolute reality value to the unconscious" (¶350). The fragment became the textbook demonstration of how libido is recovered by making the fantasy conscious (¶357).

occurrences.title: The 'union of irreconcilables': marriage of water and fire (Indian painting)
occurrences.label: The 'union of irreconcilables'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: a circumspect and farsighted synthetic procedure… the paradoxical union of irreconcilables
body: Plate 72: "The 'union of irreconcilables': marriage of water and fire. The two figures each have four hands to symbolize their many different capabilities.—After an Indian painting."

Jung sets it at the climax of the dream-18 commentary: "If reason is not to be outraged on the one hand and the creative play of images not violently suppressed on the other, a circumspect and farsighted synthetic procedure is required in order to accomplish the paradoxical union of irreconcilables (fig. 72). Hence the alchemical parallels in our dreams" (¶186). The four-armed deities — water and fire married — carry the quaternary completeness of the coniunctio.

occurrences.title: The priests sing like frogs — Rig-Veda rain charm
occurrences.label: The priests sing like frogs
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the priests, as a rain-charm, formed a choir to sing like frogs because frogs were the sign of rain.
body: In the old Vedic songs the priests, as a rain-charm, formed a choir and sang like frogs, frogs being the sign of rain; wind and falling water were imitated to call up clouds. Jung's textbook case of sympathetic magic — "which can be rationalized to a certain extent" — and the direct parallel to the Indians smearing sheep's blood "in order to put the sun to shame and induce it to rise."

occurrences.title: Water turned to ice and the lapis lazuli ground — Second and Third Meditations, Amitāyur-dhyāna Sūtra
occurrences.label: Water turned to ice and the lapis lazuli ground
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)

occurrences.quote: When you have thus seen the water you should form the perception of ice. As you see the ice shining and transparent, so you should imagine the appearance of lapis lazuli.
body: The meditator solidifies the imagined water into ice, the ice into blue transparent lapis lazuli — the "ground" of the Buddha-land, shining "like a thousand millions of suns." Jung: "A different reality is created, so to speak, out of soul-stuff"; the yogi "makes, so to speak, a solid body for his vision," endowing his psychic world with concrete reality in place of the outer world (¶929). The blue translucent floor is "like a lake of glass" — also "a favourite symbol of the unconscious in our Western dreams" (¶937); through it the gaze penetrates "into the depths of the psyche's secrets" (¶938).

occurrences.title: Isis the Prophetess to Horus: the angel Amnael and the shining vessel (Egypt, ~1st c. A.D.)
occurrences.label: Isis the Prophetess to Horus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Hormanuthi, Egypt (Berthelot, Alch. grecs I xiii)
body: In the Isis treatise Jung cites: retiring to Hormanuthi, "Egypt's [city] of the sacred art," Isis is desired by an angel of the first firmament; refusing him, she demands the preparation of gold and silver. A greater angel, Amnael, comes the next day "as the sun was crossing the midpoint of its course," bears the sign on his head and shows "a small, unpitched vessel filled with a translucent water," revealing the secret she may pass only to Horus (cw13 ¶99).

Jung: the angel is winged spirit, like Mercurius the pneuma; the shining water is the divine water of the art, the arcanum after prima materia (¶96 fn24). Amnael's meridian relation makes him "a kind of solar genius or messenger of the sun who brings 'illumination'" (¶105); his indecorous behaviour — angels and the daughters of men, Genesis 6:2 (¶105).

occurrences.title: 'Some moisture in the air' — Catholic woman's fantasy of the first trans-subjective fact
occurrences.label: Some moisture in the air
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: I think I told you of that Catholic woman who discovered in her fantasy, after long vain attempts, that there was some moisture in the air. That was the turning point, that did it.
body: Jung's minimal-case demonstration of what he here calls the trans-subjective experience: a Catholic woman seeking something "not of her own make" in fantasy, "after long vain attempts," finds only "some moisture in the air." Precisely because she did not invent it — "It simply was there" — the smallest objective fact outweighs all the self-made images of God.

"This may come to you in a very banal form… and if you are not in the mood, you will not see it at all; it may be in a dream, or it may come in the way of a fantasy." The moisture is the criterion: something within the psyche "which is not your own make, and not your ego."

occurrences.title: Moses at the stream of life — the fish that came alive (Koran)
occurrences.label: Moses at the stream of life
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Arabia / the confluence of the two seas
occurrences.quote: There is a legend in the Koran that Moses came to the stream of life in the desert but did not recognize it, so he had to return to it because something important happened there: a fish he was carrying in his basket was touched by a drop of the water of life and thus came to life, and then it slipped…
body: Explaining the stream at which the patient bathes her face after leaving the church ("A stream always means natural life, the waters of life, and crossing the stream of life is a very important motif"):

The missed ford must be sought again — "so Moses understood that there was the water of life". Jung gives the modern dream-form of the same motif: a street dug up with "a high-tension cable laid across the ditch" that the dreamer's car cannot cross — "the place of the ford, fording the great river in modern form". In the vision the patient, unlike Moses, stops at the stream and worships: nature consciously received.

occurrences.title: River of the water of life with the tree of life — Revelation 22
occurrences.label: River of the water of life with the tree of life
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal
body: Cited at the close of the water amplifications for the sinking-dream: "And he shewed me a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal... on either side of the river, was there the tree of life, which bare twelve manner of fruits, and yielded her fruit every month" (22:1-2). Against the dream's negative water — devouring, flooding, deadly — stands the positive aspect: changeability, healing power, rebirth; "what she fears will change and bring her salvation." Paired with John 3 (born of water and the spirit) and the baptismal water of the Church.

occurrences.title: Peratic crossing of the Red Sea — 'genesis outside of generation'
occurrences.label: Peratic crossing of the Red Sea
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Hippolytus' Peratae read the exodus from Egypt as 'the exodus from the body, which is Egypt in miniature'; the crossing of the Red Sea is 'the crossing of the water of corruption, which is Kronos', and the arrival in the desert 'a genesis outside of generation' (cw14 ¶257). There 'the gods of destruction and the god of salvation are all together' (¶258). Jung reads the Red Sea as a death-water for the 'unconscious' and a baptismal water of rebirth for the 'conscious', making it the Gnostic twin of the alchemical aqua pontica and a figure of the transcendent function (¶257).
