occurrences.title: Dream series: every road leads into the water (Zurich man, 1932)
occurrences.label: Dream series: every road leads into the water
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich (a man known to Jung, not in analysis)

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: ...to his great amazement, all these roads inevitably led into water, the second cakra.
body: Recurrent, formally identical dreams of a man outside analysis: movement along a road or path, then the amazement that "all these roads inevitably led into water." Jung reads them as spontaneous svādhiṣṭhāna material — the way out of muladhara existence leads into the water, with the danger of the makara/leviathan: "The way into any higher development leads through water." Today, he adds, "instead of the sea or leviathan we say analysis, which is equally dangerous."

occurrences.title: Rudra songs: the fertilizing water/urine (Rig-veda, cited cw4 1912)
occurrences.label: Rudra songs: the fertilizing water/urine
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The fertilizing significance of urine is also mythological; we find excellent proofs of this in the Rudra songs of the Rig-veda.
body: The child's first birth-theory — the man's urine enters the woman's body and the embryo grows from it; hence the child is "in the water, i.e., urine, from the beginning" (¶511) — is not invented but archaic: "The fertilizing significance of urine is also mythological; we find excellent proofs of this in the Rudra songs of the Rig-veda." The variant in which the urine is drunk as the doctor's syrup and the baby drunk down by the mother threads the same water-fertility logic her drowning-uncle associations touched (¶508–510). The vault's water family already holds the Vedic rain-charm strand; this is its purifying-fertilizing double.

occurrences.title: Water-motif dream series — 26 dreams in two months (patient-anon)
occurrences.label: Water-motif dream series
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: In a dream series extending over a period of two months, one of my patients had the water-motif in twenty-six dreams.
body: A two-month dream series of a male patient in which the water-motif appeared in twenty-six dreams, enumerated by Jung position by position: surf on the beach, glassy sea, rain on water, voyages to America, ship passages, the Rhine, brooks, steamers, islands, a voice crying "This is the way to the sea, we must get to the sea!", sunken treasure, the father telling of the land where the water comes from, and finally a small river debouching into a larger one. Jung uses it to show the continuity of the unconscious theme and the statistical evaluation of motifs across a series.

Jung's reading (¶15): "the sea always signifies a collecting-place where all psychic life originates, i.e., the collective unconscious"; water in motion = the stream of life or energy-potential. After the series, the water-motif "gradually retreated to make way for" the unknown-woman motif (¶16).

occurrences.title: The divine water that is 'the whole' — Zosimos, Peri tou Aeiou Hydatos
occurrences.label: The divine water that is 'the whole'
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Zosimos's fragment on the divine water (ὕδωρ θεῖον), the aqua permanens: "This is the great and divine mystery which is sought, for it is the whole [hen to pan]. And from it is the whole and through the same is the whole. Two natures, one substance [ousia]... This is the silver water, male and female, which forever flees... It is the whole in all things. And it has life and spirit and is destructive" (cw13 ¶370).

Jung: "the water is wholeness" — a totality image already in 3rd-c. Greek alchemy; the quicksilver is a pneuma (¶371); the 'whole' is a microcosm whose attraction of the macrocosm works "a kind of apocatastasis" (¶372).
Verbatim: Two natures, one substance [ούσία]. But the one [substance] attracts the one, and the one rules the one. (cw13 ¶370)

occurrences.title: Four-year-old girl: wedding carriage, the devil as coachman, all goes up in flames
occurrences.label: Four-year-old girl
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: age four, remembered in adulthood; presented 31 Jan 1939

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Dream 1 of two, presented by Cornelia Brunner: through the gently rising shutter the child sees a wedding carriage in the garden; "A wedding couple is sitting in the carriage, with the devil on the box as coachman. All of a sudden the carriage is ablaze, and disappears in the rising flames. I am very scared."

The paper amplifies the carriage (wheels → sun wheel → mandala; Nerthus and Frey wagons), the devil's whole genealogy, and fire as purifying lysis. Jung: the child, safe behind the window, has a vision of the future — "a kind of vision of the future. The child anticipates her future life" (p201). The knowledge that wedding and hell-fire belong together "is a knowledge born with her... in the make-up of her brain" (pp202-203). The burning is the admixtio diabolicae fraudis purified: "The ashes fall down to earth, and the purified subtle body rises into the heights" (p209).

occurrences.title: 'When the brain is properly tended... one will certainly attain the miracle' — Wei Po-yang
occurrences.label: When the brain is properly tended... one will…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: When the brain is properly tended for the required length of time, one will certainly attain the miracle.
body: Wei Po-yang states that "when the brain is properly tended for the required length of time, one will certainly attain the miracle." Jung at cw14 ¶626 cites it beside the Greek enkephalites (brain-stone, equated with the stone that is no stone, one of Zosimos' terms for the brain — "not given and given by God," the "Mithraic secret").

occurrences.title: Coins cast into the sacred well of the Amphiaraion — Oropos
occurrences.label: Coins cast into the sacred well…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: There were any number of entrances to Hades in antiquity
body: The healing-well as katabasis spot — "Presumably this Oropian well was also the scene of his katabasis" (¶572) — where incubation-healed patients pay the earth with metal. Jung follows the whole chasm-series: Aidoneus' gorge near Eleusis, the Hermione chasm of Heracles and Cerberus, the Areopagus fissure (¶572).

occurrences.title: Fount of the Saviour in secret Judaea — Gloria mundi
occurrences.label: Fount of the Saviour in secret Judaea
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Gloria mundi invokes the aqua permanens as 'a very limpid water, so bitter as to be quite undrinkable... O water of bitter taste, that preservest the elements!' and locates its origin in 'that "fount in Judaea" which is named the "Fount of the Saviour or of Blessedness"' (cw14 ¶341). Jung insists the spring lies in a 'secret place' — accessible to no creed: it 'springs from the lumen naturae' (¶341), a 'secret Judaea' in man's inner life where 'the aqua solvens et coagulans, the medicina catholica or panacea, the spark of the light of nature, are to be found' (¶344). Alchemy as knowledge parallel to revelation (¶346).

occurrences.title: The temenos of Gaia Olympia and its fissure — Athens (Pausanias)
occurrences.label: The temenos of Gaia Olympia and its fissure
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the deadly flood flowed off into the fissure, back into the mother again
body: The fissure as one of "the doors of life and death" (¶578): the Deluge flowed off "back into the mother again, for it was from the mother that death came into the world in the first place"; honey-cakes are offered "that she may spare one from death" (¶571).

occurrences.title: Money-offerings into the lacus Curtius — Rome
occurrences.label: Money-offerings into the lacus Curtius — Rome
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: He was the hero who went down to the underworld in order to conquer the danger that threatened the Roman state after the opening of the chasm.
body: Curtius "was the hero who went down to the underworld in order to conquer the danger that threatened the Roman state after the opening of the chasm" — the yearly coin thereafter substituting for the human sacrifice (¶571); cf. the obolus to Charon, "the second Cerberus" (¶577).

occurrences.title: The deep well in the cathedral of Lourdes — homosexual youth's first dream (Zurich, c.1920s)
occurrences.label: The deep well in the cathedral of Lourdes
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich? (dreamt the night before Jung's first consultation)
occurrences.quote: In the centre there is a deep dark well, into which I have to descend.
body: A youth of twenty, "entirely boyish", homosexual, with "pronounced intellectual and aesthetic interests", dreams before his first consultation: a lofty cathedral in mysterious twilight, identified as Lourdes, with "a deep dark well, into which I have to descend." The patient himself glosses: "Lourdes is the mystic fount of healing."

Jung's reading: the treatment is figured as "a sacred religious act" in an initiation sanctuary (¶169); the cathedral condenses his childhood fascination with Cologne Cathedral — "I wanted to be a priest in a cathedral like that" (¶170) — i.e., the Church as mother-substitute ("the immaculate womb of the divine font", ¶171) and the puberty-initiation archetype, "engraved on the unconscious as a primordial image" (¶172). The dream compensates his conscious resistance: it "takes the part of the educator" (¶182).

occurrences.title: Synesius hymn: 'Fountain of fountains... monad of monads'
occurrences.label: Synesius hymn — Fountain…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Cyrene/Egypt (cited via Wirth, Aus orientalischen Chroniken)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: In a hymn Synesius addresses the divine as "Fountain of fountains, source of sources, root of roots, monad of monads art thou". The context is the Sassanid court debate (5th c.): the fountain of the Babylonian Hera was said to contain "the one fish... that is caught by the 'hook of divinity' and 'feeds the whole world with its flesh.'"
In Christian language pege ("fountain") means Mary — so invoked in orthodox and Gnostic circles (Acts of Thomas) — while in Christian symbology the crucifix is the hook that catches Leviathan.

occurrences.title: The three wells of Jacob — Nicholas of Cusa
occurrences.label: The three wells of Jacob — Nicholas of Cusa
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Et ita notemus puteum sensibilem Jacob, puteum rationalem, et puteum sapientialem.
body: Cusanus' exegesis of Jacob's well (John 4), cited by Jung in the Purification section: beside the sensible well "the animals drink"; above it the rational well where "the sons of men" drink — the philosophers; highest the sapiential well where drink "the sons of the exalted, who are called gods and are the true theologians." Christ "secundum humanitatem puteus quidem dici potest altissimus" — the deepest well, whose "fons sapientiae praestat felicitatem et immortalitatem" (the fountain of wisdom grants happiness and immortality).
The intellect itself carries a "principium fontale" generating "aqua intelligentiae" — psychology of the inner well before Jung's own.

occurrences.title: The well of delight poisoned by the rabble — Zarathustra, 'The Rabble'
occurrences.label: The well of delight poisoned by the rabble
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: Life is a well of delight; but where the rabble also drink, there all fountains are poisoned.
body: "Life is a well of delight; but where the rabble also drink, there all fountains are poisoned." Jung's reading is total: "when Nietzsche talks of the rabble, he means the rabble in himself"; what he will not accept "falls back into that well and poisons it" — repression distils the impurity at the bottom.

The chapter then swings on its own axis: at the ekstasis on the loftiest height he finds the well again — "here on the loftiest height bubbleth up for me the well of delight! And there is a life at whose waters none of the rabble drink with me!" Zarathustra "is the well itself, as a matter of fact," the spirit as fountain, "and the spirit is a fountain because the spirit is essentially life". The cost: identification with spirit at the price of the body — "Almost too violently dost thou flow for me".

occurrences.title: The wheel picture shown by Brother Klaus (Pilgrim's Tract)
occurrences.label: The wheel picture shown by Brother Klaus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: We know from experience that the protective circle, the mandala, is the traditional antidote for chaotic states of mind.
body: The "Pilgrim's Tract" (Ein nutzlicher und loblicher Tractat von Bruder Claus und einem Bilger, 1488) records that Brother Klaus showed a visiting pilgrim a picture of a wheel that had long preoccupied him. Tradition connected the wheel with the great vision and the Trinity picture at Sachseln; Blanke doubted the connection.

Jung's reading: against Blanke's scepticism, the connection is "very probable on psychological grounds" — visions like Klaus's cause disintegration (the heart bursting into little pieces), and "the protective circle, the mandala, is the traditional antidote for chaotic states of mind", which is "only too clear why Brother Klaus was fascinated by the symbol of the wheel" (¶19).

occurrences.title: The wheel with twelve buckets that fishes souls from the deep — Acta Archelai
occurrences.label: The wheel with twelve buckets…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: scooped up the souls from the deep and deposited them on the moon-ship
body: The strange apparatus of the "son of the living Father" in the Acta Archelai: "He constructed a great wheel with twelve buckets which, as they revolved, scooped up the souls from the deep and deposited them on the moon-ship" (¶34).

Jung juxtaposes it with the alchemical rota as "the symbol of the opus circulatorium" and with the Manichaean angels who, alternating male and female form, excite the archons' sweat — "rain" for the Manichaeans, "dew" for the alchemists (¶34). The bucket-wheel of salvation and the circulating vessel are one archetype of rescue-by-rotation; cf. the twelve urceos of the Manichaean world-wheel already harvested from Aion.

occurrences.title: Vision: the white bird killed, the swan from the black pond, three flaming crosses (27 Nov 1930)
occurrences.label: Vision — the white bird killed, the swan…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: A white bird flew down and lit upon the top of the Indian's head. He tore it off and ground it underfoot with his heel. Then all became dark, it was night.
body: A white bird lights on the Indian's head; he tears it off and grinds it underfoot. Night falls; the face of God appears and curses him: "Now you must wander until you find again the white bird you have killed" — Jung compares him to Ahasuerus. Indian and Chinaman walk round the pond (circumambulation as fertilizing rite); a swan rises from the black water behind a hand and says "Lo, I have come unto you"; the Chinaman pushes the Indian into the pond; he emerges by the crane, which tells him "Wipe the tears from your face"; a camel carries him into the desert; at dawn, three flaming crosses in the sky.

Reading: the white bird is the Holy Ghost ("a white bird alighting upon a person means the Holy Ghost to anyone with a Christian education", p183); the swan is the same spirit reborn from below — "The Holy Ghost is by no means only an air bird, he is also a water bird" (p187); the crosses flanking recall the thieves at the crucifixion and the Mithraic dadophori (p198-199).

occurrences.title: Adolescent dream 2: the sand teems with snakes; a white boa with black crosses
occurrences.label: Adolescent dream 2 — the sand teems with snakes
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

body: Second adolescent dream: again the desert, the sun no longer shining; the boy wears high boots against the snakes with which the sand teems. "Suddenly, a terribly big boa appears; it is white as snow and her back is full of black crosses." It winds around his legs and neck and strangles him; he wakes with his bones cracking.

Jung: the multitude of snakes is an exteriorization of the conflict between consciousness and the instinctual system — "the snake always means the cerebrospinal nervous system" (p232). The chaos condenses into one primeval being. The boa unites the opposites: white (the colour of cave animals, of the unconscious source) and black; source and tiger in one; a symbolic, sotēr-like snake replacing the well — "for Christ is the fountain of life, the water of life" (p237).

occurrences.title: The white maidens' airship — boy of three to four, repeated dream
occurrences.label: The white maidens' airship
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: who repeatedly dreamt that the white maidens came down every night in an airship and invited him to come with them up to heaven.
body: Jung's contemporary child-case for the plurality of the anima: "a little boy between three and four years old, who repeatedly dreamt that the white maidens came down every night in an airship and invited him to come with them up to heaven." The motif is Erlkönig's — "Du liebes Kind, komm, geh mit mir!" — the elves, Barrie's Green Folk, the houris: "a sort of eternally existing society... usually dance."

Reused on 30 June as the paradigm of "reminiscent feelings of a perfect state, a sort of paradise state" — "They were probably the Erlkonig's daughters, those wonderful spirits whose playmate he once had been" — archetypal playmates of the primeval world that also anticipate death.

occurrences.title: White snakes issuing from corpses in the cave (Visions patient)
occurrences.label: White snakes issuing from corpses in the cave
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: As I hesitated I saw white snakes issue from the bodies of the human creatures that lay upon the ground... The snakes with awful touch of velvet writhed around me.
body: The last vision-text of the seminar. Descending again in darkness past steps, the patient comes to a dark opening in the rocks strewn with "ugly shapeless human forms" — the unrelated, libido-less world, "a shadowy Hades". Then life stirs in the corpses:

Jung's amplification: snakes as souls of the dead, spirit snakes of folklore; the African medicine man's demon snakes; the soul-serpent of Aesculapius; Erechtheus and Cecrops as serpents of the Acropolis; the serpent as the duration of time. Having withdrawn all life from other humans, she is persecuted by the life in them — the claim everything alive makes. The velvety touch is elaborated through ectoplasm (whitish worms, reptile skin), Flournoy's melting three-fingered hand, Picasso's duplicated forms, and the Kundalini exteriorized in schizophrenia.

occurrences.title: The white temple: priest-animus, tongues of fire, Paragonians leading lame dwarfs (Visions, 16 Mar 1932)
occurrences.label: The white temple — priest-animus, tongues…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Then from out the temple walked many beautiful and strong young men. (A horde of animi!-naturallywith the erotic cast.) Each man led by his hand a small lame dwarf. The priest said: \"Let the dead return unto the dead.\
body: The enantiodromia after the Chinese statue: "I stood before a white temple. Through the door I could see into the temple which was lit up by the red light of the sacrificial fire." A priest announces: "Hail to you, the word shall be uttered by tongues of fire."

Jung: the priest is the animus, powerful again because the jewel fell back into the collective; the "word" is the Logos, Pentecost symbolism - back into history, the general religious assumptions. Out of the temple walk beautiful strong young men ("a horde of animi... with the erotic cast"), each leading a lame dwarf - coexistent pairs of opposites, "less an enantiodromia here than coexistent pairs of opposites". At the priest's word "Let the dead return unto the dead" they bury the dwarfs alive, tearing the united opposites asunder so the battle may begin again.

occurrences.title: The Great Whore of Babylon — Burgkmair engraving, Augsburg 1523
occurrences.label: The Great Whore of Babylon
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Engraving (fig. 22) of Revelation 17: the woman arrayed in purple and scarlet on the scarlet seven-headed beast, golden cup in hand — "Mystery, Babylon the Great, the Mother of Harlots".

Jung's reading: the seven mountains = Rome, the mother-city whose "sons" the kings commit fornication with; "In this primordial image of the woman on the dragon we recognize Echidna... Babylon is the symbol of the Terrible Mother" (¶315); her wine is a libido-symbol. She is cast out so that the heavenly mother-bride, New Jerusalem, may be attained (¶316-318).
Verbatim: Babylon is the symbol of the Terrible Mother, who leads the peoples into whoredom with her devilish temptations and makes them drunk with her wine (cw05 ¶315).

image.title: The Apocalyptic Riders, from The Apocalypse
image.credit: Hans Burgkmair the Elder / Silvan Otmar

occurrences.title: The widow marries her son: Beya and Gabritius — Delphinas via Maier
occurrences.label: The widow marries her son — Beya and Gabritius
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: she is identified with Beya—'the widow marries her son.
body: Maier reports the treatise of the anonymous "Delphinas," who "insisted particularly on the mother-son incest," and constructs the genealogical tree of the seven metals: the lapis at the top, whose father is "Gabritius," born of Isis and Osiris; after Osiris' death "Isis married their son Gabritius; she is identified with Beya — 'the widow marries her son'" (¶14). Maier adds an "Epithalamium in Honour of the Nuptials of the Mother Beya and Her Son Gabritius," which "was begun with the expression of great joyfulness, ended in the bitterness of mourning": "when the son sleeps with the mother, she kills him with the stroke of a viper (viperino conatu)" (¶14).

Jung links the murderous bride to Isis "who laid the 'noble worm' in the path of the heavenly Father, Ra" (cross-link isis-serpent-wounds-ra-egypt.md) and to Kerényi's Medea combination — "love, trickery, cruelty, motherliness, murder of relatives and children, magic, rejuvenation, and — gold" (¶16) — the core of the drama "instigated by the mother-world, without which no union seems possible."

occurrences.title: The wig turns from black to white at the judgment of the dead
occurrences.label: The wig turns from black to white…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~13th c. BCE (tomb painting); Papyrus of Ani (~1250 BCE)

jung.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East (CW11)
jung.locator: 'Transformation Symbolism in the Mass' n.17 (pdf p722-723)

occurrences.quote: When the dead man is led before Osiris his wig is black; afterwards (at the sacrifice in the Papyrus of Ani) it is white.
body: A footnoted transformation-marking rite: headgear as colour-code of the soul's passage.

Jung links this to the "shaving of a man" and "plucking of a fowl" of the magical sacrificial recipes — hair/shaving as the stuff of transformation. Psychologically the black-to-white change of the head is the nigredo-to-albedo sequence acted out on the dead man's own body before the god; cf. the homo albus the alchemists expect at the end of the work.

occurrences.title: The wild huntsman — Ernst Jünger, On the Marble Cliffs
occurrences.label: The wild huntsman — Ernst Jünger…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: a wild huntsman comes into the land, bringing with him a wave of possession greater than anything known even in the Middle Ages.
body: Jünger's 1939 allegorical novella, in which a wild huntsman comes into the land. Jung, writing "After the Catastrophe" in 1945, cites it as one of the few works where "the European spirit spoke… plainly" and was "tragically misunderstood": "in his book On the Marble Cliffs a wild huntsman comes into the land, bringing with him a wave of possession greater than anything known even in the Middle Ages" (cw10 ¶435).

Jung's reading: Jünger "sensed that very clearly" what Nietzsche and Wagner had only prefigured — that "Wotan the storm-god had conquered," the orgiastic frenzy spreading "like an epidemic" while the Castle of the Grail "vanished into an unknown land" (¶435). The literary wild huntsman (Jünger 1939) thus completes the row of Wotan-omens Jung assembles: Nietzsche's huntsman nightmare, Goetz's one-eyed hunter, the Völuspá's Naglfar.

occurrences.title: The wild man of the woods and the field of cats — Prince's patient, dream 5 (Boston, ~1905–06)
occurrences.label: The wild man of the woods and the field of cats
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: there in her path was a frightful creature like a wild man of the woods. His hair was hanging down his face and neck; he had a sort of skin over him for covering; his legs and arms were bare and he had a club.
body: Dream 5: the ever-recurring rocky path (Watts's "Love and Life" minus Love) suddenly fills with cats; turning back, she finds "a frightful creature like a wild man of the woods" — hair hanging over face and neck, a skin for covering, bare limbs, a club — and behind him hundreds like him. The choice: go forward over the cats without a sound or be smothered; she wakes with complete aphonia. Jung, against Prince's moral-precept reading: "The dream has not been analysed at all" — the cat phobia, the treading, the skin, the club, all unexamined. What the painting omits — the figure of Love — the dream supplies as cats: "the cats symbolize love" (¶183), referring to his own earlier cat-phobia study. The aphonia is the symptom "which captured the interest of the analyst, as she reckoned it would" (¶184).

occurrences.title: Ayik, the dark god who is a puff of cold wind (East Africa)
occurrences.label: Ayik, the dark god who is a puff of cold wind
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: they say is nothing but a puff of cold wind... He is the maker of fears.
body: "We found a tribe in Africa who had a bad dark god, that they say is nothing but a puff of cold wind. When you are walking in the night, up it comes from nowhere, and that is Ayik. He is the maker of fears." Baynes supplies the name from the 1925-26 trip. Jung's exhibit for the wind-theory of spirit: the primitive, embarrassed before an invisible psychical effect, explains it by the only invisible agency he knows — the moving air; a cold wind is the sign of a ghostly presence, felt in spiritualist séances "in every culture, whether you are attending a spiritualistic meeting in China, Tibet, with the Bedouins on an African desert, or in New York."

occurrences.title: The spirit descends as wind into Mary's womb — Immaculate Conception iconography
occurrences.label: The spirit descends as wind into Mary's womb
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: In medieval representations of the Immaculate Conception the spirit descends as wind: the pneuma comes down from the Father into the womb of Mary.

Jung's point is linguistic and archetypal at once: the Greek pneuma "referred wholly to the wind" before Christianity gave it its specific meaning — hence John 3:8's undecidable "The wind (or the spirit) bloweth where it listeth." The iconography preserves the older layer. It stands in his wind-sun series (morning wind as emanation of the sun-father; Mithraic liturgy; the lunatic's sun-phallus origin of wind) around Zarathustra as the spirit who is both newborn sun and great wind.
Verbatim: "in medieval representations of the Immaculate Conception, the spirit descends as wind: the pneuma comes down from the Father into the womb of Mary".

occurrences.title: The son inhales the father's last breath (Indian deathbed custom)
occurrences.label: The son inhales the father's last breath
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 Seminar)

occurrences.quote: ...the oldest son must watch during the last moments in order to inhale the last breath of his father, which is the soul
body: "When the father dies, the oldest son must watch during the last moments in order to inhale the last breath of his father, which is the soul, in order to continue his life" — Jung's ritual instance for the breath-soul at the threshold of anāhata (air center), set beside Swahili roho (the stertorous breathing of the dying AND the soul), Arabic ruch, Hebrew ruach, Greek anemos/pneuma: "the original idea of spirit or of psychical things is the idea of breath or air."

occurrences.title: Wenonah conceives Hiawatha from the West Wind — Song of Hiawatha
occurrences.label: Wenonah conceives Hiawatha from the West Wind
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: from “wind and water” man shall be born anew.
body: Mudjekeewis, having slain the bear and become "the West Wind, the fertilizing breath, the father of the winds" — the Zosimos parallel: the entrant of the womb becomes pneuma (¶484) — begets the hero on Wenonah by breath alone. "From 'wind and water' man shall be born anew" (¶485).

occurrences.title: Winged and wingless birds/dragons — De Chemia Senioris
occurrences.label: Winged and wingless birds/dragons
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Another favourite theriomorphic image is that of the two birds or two dragons, one of them winged, the other wingless.
body: Two birds or two dragons, "one of them winged, the other wingless," from the ancient text De Chemia Senioris antiquissimi philosophi libellus (Muhammad ibn Umail). "The wingless bird or dragon prevents the other from flying. They stand for Sol and Luna, brother and sister, who are united by means of the art" (¶3).

Jung cites it as the archetypal form of the spirit/soul polarity in theriomorphic dress, alongside Lambspringk's reversed fishes (mare nostrum = the body) and his stag (soul) and unicorn (spirit) in the forest (body) — the latter already harvested from cw13. The winged/wingless motif returns in ¶141, where the winged dragon (quicksilver) becomes a poison-breathing monster only through union with the wingless dragon (sulphur).

occurrences.title: The blind old wise man with Chinese dragons gives the ring of the way (Visions)
occurrences.label: The blind old wise man with Chinese dragons…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: vision read 9 March 1932 (painted late 1929/early 1930 for Jung)
occurrences.quote: Soon I came upon an ancient blind man who barred the way. Upon his robe were Chinese dragons. He put a ring on the finger of my right hand. I looked at the ring and saw written thereon the words: 'This way is for those who know. If you violate it then you will know death.
body: Holding the burning jewel, she breaks a taboo and advances into a sphere only the animus has explored:

Jung: "this old man with the Chinese dragons on his robe is obviously the old wise man" — physically blind, therefore seeing inward, "the legendary seer who knows the truth"; "he is the guardian of the threshold across which she is now stepping". The dragons "point to the East which means here the unconscious"; she needs not intellectual science "but the wisdom of the ages". The ring = union and bestowal of wisdom, like the Bey of Tunis' "Tout passe" ring. "This way is for those who know" = Tao — "the sign for Tao is written with the sign of the head and the sign for going" — glossed by Lao-tze's "I value the all-giving mother" (Tao-te-king ch. 20).

occurrences.title: Wish-fulfilment dream — nurse subject 24, lying in the grass with her beloved (Burghölzli, ~1904-05)
occurrences.label: Wish-fulfilment dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: pdf p69 (print ¶ 271 area — unmarked in chunk)

occurrences.quote: After the unhappy end of her love-affair the subject had a wishfulfilment dream: she was lying next to her beloved in the grass.
body: Subject 24 (nurse, 18): after her father cursed her love-affair and it broke off, the association experiment revived the complex — "The experiment was a revival of a complex that had become somewhat latent". In her explanations she reports the dream: in the orchard of her parents' house, under the beautiful tree surrounded by grass where she "often used to dream" watching trains go by, she lay next to her beloved in the grass. To the stimulus-word dream she reacts "with Pleasure and her eyes shine at the memory of that wish-dream." Jung's first published use of a dream as index of the constellation behind the reactions — the wish-dream read through the test, not interpreted from it.

occurrences.title: Witch's cave with rotating grids — dream of a boy of six (3 December 1940)
occurrences.label: Witch's cave with rotating grids
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
jung.locator: pdf p444–456 (presented by Dr. Kenower W. Bash)

occurrences.quote: In its last part, two interlocking rows of iron bars protrude from the wall; these two grids rotate, so that for one moment they open the exit and then block it again.
body: A six-year-old boy and a boy his own age are captured by a witch into a middle-sized, round, blood-red cave; the only exit is a tubelike passage, sloping down then up, blocked by two interlocking rows of iron bars that rotate — opening the exit one moment, blocking it the next. He wakes in great anxiety. Jung: the dream is "only an image," a confrontation without lysis; "he is not yet born. He is still in utero." The companion is the double — primitives see the afterbirth as the "other," the twin; "the other is the shadow." The grids were placed by somebody (the witch-mother): concrete prohibitions, incitement and forbidding at once; the passage slopes because the mother is lying (unconscious). Creeping through is possible only at a well-chosen moment — the kairós demanding absolute attentiveness; the unborn under emotion are "still under the Heimarmene."

occurrences.title: The witch's house - cross in blood on the door, charred snakes, the blasted shelter (Visions, 11 May 1932)
occurrences.label: The witch's house - cross in blood…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I touched the door with my knife and the door opened. Within was a dark room. In the corner burned a fire. I beheld in the fire the charred bodies of many small snakes.
body: With the knife picked up on the mountain ("the mind is discriminating, cutting... instruments are always male," pdf p753) she descends to a town and finds a house marked with the sign of the cross written in blood - apotropaic, "like the Passover in the Old Testament... an apotropaic charm against evil spirits". The magic knife opens the lock "like... the mandragora root, which opens all doors." Inside: a dark room, a fire, "the charred bodies of many small snakes" - a witchcraft sacrifice; snakes as incarnated spirits of dead heroes, burned so the spirit rises "as the subtle body". She rubs the ashes on her left palm - the unconscious side, "the path of the left hand in India... the Tantric Shakti worship" - heats the knife red-hot, touches the roof, and the entire house falls away, leaving her on the night desert with the fire.

Jung's diagnosis: a house "characterized by a Christian symbol outside and witchcraft inside" is the collective religious shelter whose mana has fallen out: "as long as a symbol has life so that it really conveys a solution... there is then no witchcraft". Blasting it = the Promethean-luciferian act: "before she can realize the nature of Tao, she must destroy all the ideas behind which she has been sheltered hitherto".

occurrences.title: Mother as witch and dangerous animal — three sisters' dreams; the mother's lycanthropy
occurrences.label: Mother as witch and dangerous animal
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: dreams at puberty; case retold 1924; mother's insanity years later
body: Three daughters of a "most devoted mother" confessed shamefacedly at puberty that for years they had suffered horrible dreams of her — as a witch or a dangerous animal — though she was "so lovely and so utterly devoted to them." Years later the mother went insane, exhibiting a lycanthropy: crawling on all fours, grunting like pigs, barking like dogs, growling like bears.
Jung's reading: the dreams registered the parental unconscious behind the conscious devotion — the infectious nature of complexes (¶107); primitive identity transmits what consciousness hides.
Quote. "They dreamt of her as a witch or a dangerous animal, and they could not understand it at all, since their mother was so lovely and so utterly devoted to them."

occurrences.title: Mother as witch, ghost, pursuing demon — clinging daughter's dreams (Zurich, ~1900s)
occurrences.label: Mother as witch, ghost, pursuing demon
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: She appeared in the dreams as a witch, as a ghost, as a pursuing demon.
body: A young woman "who clung to her mother in an extremely sentimental way" always had "very sinister dreams about her": the mother "appeared in the dreams as a witch, as a ghost, as a pursuing demon" (¶280).

Jung's reading: the mother had "spoilt her beyond all reason," blinding the daughter by tenderness to the harmful influence — hence "the compensatory criticism exercised by the unconscious." Because "the ‘witch’ is a collective image" (¶284), the dream also testifies beyond the personal bond: the daughter's blind dependence extended to the wider social group, since "she was still living in an exclusively infantile world, where the world was identical with her parents."

occurrences.title: Saul and the witch of Endor — necromancy at the end of wits (I Samuel 28)
occurrences.label: Saul and the witch of Endor
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: scene reign of Saul ~1000 BCE; text ~6th c. BCE

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: Saul, deserted by every ordinary means, goes by night to the woman of Endor to bring up the ghost of Samuel for counsel (I Sam 28:7). Jung cites her as the first term in a mythological row: "If a man does not know how to solve his problem, he turns to the witch, as Saul in the Old Testament turned to the witch of Endor" — the others being Wotan and Erda, St. Catharine in Anatole France's penguins, and Mother Isis.

The row frames dream 30: when "the male principle no longer helps; he must go to the female principle," and analysis itself is "calling up the dead, calling the unconscious, all magic ritual from beginning to end".

occurrences.title: The witch-hunting mania — Germanic countries (15th c.)
occurrences.label: The witch-hunting mania — Germanic countries
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: An instructive example of epidemic insanity was the witch-hunting mania in Germanic countries in the fifteenth century.
body: Jung's stock example of "epidemic insanity": "the witch-hunting mania in Germanic countries in the fifteenth century. This was the cause of a veritable campaign of enlightenment initiated by the Papal Bull Summis desiderantes in 1484" (Innocent VIII's bull to Kramer and Sprenger; the Malleus maleficarum follows in 1486–89).

Jung's reading: an induced collective psychosis of the same order as his other epidemics — Hitler's psychic epidemic is its twentieth-century twin (¶1385, ¶1389), while the explosive spread of Christianity and Islam shows the benign face of the same "release of unconscious dynamism" (¶1389). Companion loci in the witch family: the Malleus material Jung analyses elsewhere.

occurrences.title: The witches' sleep — ekstasis as symptom of witchcraft (Malleus Maleficarum)
occurrences.label: The witches' sleep
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: The Hexenhammer lists among the symptoms of witchcraft a trance-state the inquisitors called the witches' sleep. Jung reads it as ekstasis: "when a panic or a terrible pain reaches the culmination, it ceases and people become ecstatic. Pain cannot be endured in ever-increasing intensity beyond a certain point. Then it turns and becomes ekstasis".

The passage anchors his claim that the dreamer of dream 30, reduced to the helpless boy, "falls down into the archetype of the boy" — and that after numbness and exhaustion "the ekstasis comes and the mother appears." The deepest blackness turning to light is "the sun myth"; the Malleus passage shows the same pattern read diagnostically, as possession.

occurrences.title: Vision: the three witches' tooth, the wild beasts, the circle of fire — 'I am the sacrifice' (9 Dec 1930)
occurrences.label: Vision — 'I am the sacrifice'
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Then the youth said, 'I am the sacrifice,' and the fire consumed him. A white bird issued from his breast and flew up beyond the reach of the flames.
body: The youth stands on a boat's prow and throws his spear into a cliff face — a trickle of water comes out; the boat falls away. Seeing a woman's face in the water he dives, finds a cave with three witches "who came from the land of the blessed", tears the single tooth they share (robbing fate of one bad aspect), and flees; wild beasts maul him. An old man drives the beasts away, wraps him in a blanket, lays him face to the sky — and at night a circle of fire descends and burns around him.

Reading: the three spinners of fate; tearing the tooth is hubris — "the punishment for the assumption of divinity is dismemberment, as, for instance, Dionysus Zagreus was dismembered" (p230). The old man is the wise old man of fairy tale ("always in the supreme moment something helpful appears"), lord of animals, who makes the youth "not a sacrifice to blind passions but a conscious fulfillment of fate"; the bird is "the escape of the immortal soul, represented since time immemorial by the soul-bird". Through the fire the animus attains divinity and unites with her — she becomes entheos (p231).

occurrences.title: The tormos witches that eat darkness out of burning stones — Senior
occurrences.label: The tormos witches that eat darkness out…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: they conceive in the baths and give birth in the air
body: Marchos' parable in Senior: "There is an earth near us, which is called 'tormos,' where there are serpents [or witches] that eat the darkness out of the burning stones, and on these stones they drink the blood of black goats. While they remain in the darkness, they conceive in the baths and give birth in the air, and they stride on the sea, and they inhabit vaults and sepulchres, and the serpent fights with the male, and the male continues forty nights in the grave, and forty nights in the little house" (¶77).

Jung notes the Latin "serpent" renders Arabic jinn — female desert demons — under "the widespread primitive idea that the spirits of the dead are snakes," with goat sacrifice to chthonic numina. Continuation: the male's seed cast "upon the marble into the image [or spirit that dwells in the marble]," gathered by ravens who fly to unclimbable mountain tops and "become white, and multiply" (¶80) — resurrection as coniunctio of white dove and black raven, the ravens as "dark messengers of heaven, who at this point themselves become white" (¶81).

occurrences.title: The wolf that guides the lost monk to the Lower World (Black Forest, ~1450)
occurrences.label: The wolf that guides the lost monk…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: a wolf becomes his guide to the Lower World
body: A single sentence in the steamroller-dream discussion: "The patient thinks also of another old story, dating about 1450, of the monk who lost his way in the Black Forest and a wolf becomes his guide to the Lower World."

Its place in the argument: the dreamer stands at the bifurcation in the wood — Dante's selva oscura, "the divine comedy of Man" — and the old story supplies the guide-animal for the descent into the unconscious; the wolf as magical-companion/psychopomp, the dangerous animal turned way-showing companion (the same reversal by which Dr. Shaw's bull must not be killed).

occurrences.title: Little Red Riding-hood: the devouring wolf cut open (Grimm, cited cw4 1912)
occurrences.label: Little Red Riding-hood
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In the fairytale of Little Red Ridinghood it is the fantasy that the mother has to eat something which is like a child, and that the child is born by cutting open the mother's body.
body: The fairytale every child knows: the wolf eats the grandmother, takes her shape, eats the child; the hunter kills the wolf, cuts open the belly, and Little Red Riding-hood "sprang out safe and sound" (¶476). Jung's 1912 reading is genealogical: the tale carries the infantile birth-fantasy — "the mother has to eat something which is like a child, and the child is born by cutting open the mother's body," a fantasy "one of the commonest and... found everywhere" (¶478), kin to the solar motif of Jonah and the sun-swallowing sea monster. The child dreamer's wolf, by contrast, is put "in the father's place" (¶478, ¶481) — Jung's note on the problem of bisexual symbols. Wolf as devourer-mother here, as angry father there: one motif, two parental valences.

occurrences.title: The she-wolf suckling Romulus and Remus (Roman founding legend)
occurrences.label: The she-wolf suckling Romulus and Remus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: All the promise that was in those children fed by the Roman wolf is equally valid for this spirit child.
body: The Roman relief of the mother wolf feeding the twins — the legend Jung reaches for when the patient's abandoned spirit-child "crawled to an iron wolf which stood near by and the wolf suckled it." The twins, exposed and miraculously fed, found Rome; "the wolf intervenes because the child is a hero."

Jung's reading: the hero child is always fed in some miraculous way by a divine animal; from the wolf's milk the child "will inherit the fighting qualities of the wolf, it will be a sort of werewolf." Mrs. Sigg adds that the particular gift of the Roman spirit was the law — "the spirit of the law might be feeding the child." Against this background Jung measures the new, warlike god-child of 1932 against the gentle Christ-child with ox and ass.

occurrences.title: The strawberry-wood wolf dream — 11-year-old girl (Zurich, girl's 5th year ~1906)
occurrences.label: The strawberry-wood wolf dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich (case of Miss Mary Moltzer, reported Fordham 1912)
occurrences.quote: I was in a wood with my little brother, looking for strawberries. Then a wolf came and jumped at me.
body: A recurrent-memory dream: "I'll never forget the dream as long as I live." In a wood with her little brother looking for strawberries, a wolf jumps at her; she flees up a staircase, falls, is bitten in the leg, wakes "in deadly fear." Jung reads it against Little Red Riding-hood and the Jonah/sun-devouring cycle (¶476–478), then lets the child's spontaneous associations confirm the armature: the bite first recalls the Swiss stork-birth variant (¶479), the wolf "my father when he is angry" (¶480). The dream-year is the year her younger brother was born (¶484), so the bite compresses the sexual problem — "curiosity about the procreation of life" — into fear of the father as moral educator (¶485). Jung refuses to stop at education: the deeper root is "that tragic conflict between nature and culture" (¶486).

occurrences.title: The wollunqua — primordial serpent ancestor of all living things (Australia)
occurrences.label: The wollunqua — primordial serpent ancestor…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "There are similar myths in Australia, where they believe in the so-called wollunqua serpent, which is the primordial animal, the father or the mother of all living things; even men and women are descended from it. So that also is a snake that carries all people upon its back".

Jung cites it immediately after the python-flood myth as amplification of the patient's vision of the way as a living serpent — the rainbow-serpent type of Australian Ur-animal on whose back the whole tribe rides. Read together with the zodiacal serpent carrying the apostles and the time-dragon carrying the vanished past (pp1290-1295): the path itself is the primordial ancestor.

occurrences.title: The woman crowned with light rising from the sea, holding up the treasure - first vision of the Self (Visions, 18 May 1932)
occurrences.label: The woman crowned with light rising…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: At last the waters parted and from them arose a woman crowned with light. In her hand she held something which she lifted toward the sky.
body: Left alone on the shore after the communicants drop away, she gazes long at the waters: "At last the waters parted and from them arose a woman crowned with light. In her hand she held something which she lifted toward the sky" (plate 23) - "a most impressive experience" she painted.

Jung: classical title Aphrodite Anadyomene, literary Ibsen's Lady from the Sea - "but Dr. Curtius has mentioned the subtle body... Oh, if you write Self with a capital, that is something else. You are right, it is the first experience really of the Self, of something rising in her, being born in her out of her unconscious, which is not herself, which she merely beholds". "It is beyond the pair of opposites... The figure that appears is the idea of the Self, the objective Self, which is not identical with the ego; it is the psychological non-ego" - the transcendent function between the two parting waves of Eros and Logos. The held thing - jewel, child, or flower - is "the diamond center... the Lotus or the Golden Flower"; the rising = the Kundalini at the heart center, the figure "impersonating the mystery, the divine process which takes place within us besides our ordinary human psychology". Its shadow follows at once: pegasus-crucified-woman-star-vision-zurich-1932.

occurrences.title: The clock too high: 'definite hours paid with definite life' — dream (~1958)
occurrences.label: The clock too high — dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: The definite hours have to be paid for with the definite life, the indefinite hours have to be paid for with the indefinite life.
body: A late dream fragment in the Jaffe side of the correspondence (the chunk's opening pages of the dream are lost to OCR/blank scans): in empty curved space the dreamer tries to read the time on a clock, "but the clock is too high, so that doesn't work." The "dark unknown woman" then appears, crying because she cannot find a publisher for her book — full of time symbolism, how a period of time is constituted when certain symbols appear in it. A voice reads aloud from its final page:

The Pauli-series counterpart of Jung's world-clock material: the unreadable clock, the dark woman as bearer of time-symbolism, and the price of hours. Jaffe cautions that without the dreamer's associations such symbolic figures are risky to read — "this more or less covers the... confusion."

occurrences.title: Dark Man Cutting a Zone of Light — Pauli's periodic-symbol dream (13.3.1936)
occurrences.label: Dark Man Cutting a Zone of Light
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: a dark man appears... who is cutting pieces out of a zone of light at regular intervals.
body: Pauli's own analysis of how his recurring periodic symbols arise: comparing the 23.1.1938 clock dream with this earlier one, he shows "in it a dark man appears (associated by me with the 'shadow' archetype), who is cutting pieces out of a zone of light at regular intervals". In the 1938 dream "the 'oscillation' was horizontal, whereas it is vertical in the '939 one (but I also know rare cases where it is slanting)".

Pauli's intuitive reading binds the class to the death-attitude: "one oscillation signifies one human life, but one which is to be interpreted only as part of a larger whole" — beyond which the "time concept of the anima" holds. The dream belongs to the same world-clock/rhythm class as the ~1933 vision and 1938 dream.

occurrences.title: Three Rhythms and the Four-Part Clock that Fails — Pauli's second world-clock dream (23.1.1938)
occurrences.label: Three Rhythms and the Four-Part Clock that Fails
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

occurrences.quote: In contrast to the earlier world-clock vision, the sense of harmony is missing.
body: Pauli's second great clock dream, sent to Jung in October 1938 with a long self-commentary: three "spiritual layers" beyond personal life are figured, and "an attempt is first made to relate the two lowest of the 3 layers to a four-part object (clock), but this does not work" — hence, "in contrast to the earlier world-clock vision, the sense of harmony is missing". An ecstatic "voice" cries at the end over puzzling "rhythms" connected with "paying"; Pauli connects "a certain life" with the quickest rhythm, an indefinite life with the other two. The dream was constellated by the I Ching (three draws, divisibility by four).

Pauli read the wave/oscillation symbols as representations of spheres beyond personal death; Jung had already published the first vision as the climactic image of Psychology and Religion. Pauli explicitly reports that "the Trinity turned into the 3 rhythms (the 'world clock')" in a related dream.

occurrences.title: 'Oh, world, I am not afraid': the giant in the river of boiling blood and the blinding egg (patient vision, 21 May 1931)
occurrences.label: Oh, world, I am not afraid
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: I was in a river of boiling blood. The giant stood over me and cast such a great shadow that I could not see the stars or the sky.
body: The giant she meets is the world itself — "Hideous, he appeared. His skin was white and flabby": he threatens to rub her face in the dust and flay her; all things go dark and seethe, and she lies in a river of boiling blood under his shadow, which hides the stars. The image of progress hurt by the power of the past: even the most reasonable step forward collides with the friction of what has been. The giant disappears and "a great egg, blinding in its whiteness" remains — the new birth out of the ordeal.

Her much later picture (plate 28) reverses the scene: the tiny woman carrying the huge white giant with hanging arms — Jung's exhibit of the transitus, "the carrying of the symbol," as Attis' pine, Mithras' dead world-bull, and Christ's cross (= carrying the mother; "the world is the mother-Mother Earth").

occurrences.title: The world carried by an elephant standing on a tortoise (Hindu cosmology)
occurrences.label: The world carried by an elephant standing…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: The world is carried on the back of an elephant that is standing on a tortoise.
body: Schmitz recalls the myth "that the tortoise is the mother of the whole world, that everything living is born from the tortoise"; Jung locates it: "You find it in Hindu myths chiefly. The world is carried on the back of an elephant that is standing on a tortoise."

The editorial note shows Jung conflating the sixteen world-elephants of the Matangalila with Vishnu's tortoise avatara (Kurma) supporting Mount Mandara. His reading: "A tortoise is a most fundamental being — the basic instinct that carries our whole psychological world. For the world is our psychology, our point of view. And as our point of view is carried by our instincts, so the world is carried by the tortoise."

occurrences.title: Black Elk's boyhood great vision (Oglala Sioux)
occurrences.label: Black Elk's boyhood great vision (Oglala Sioux)
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: This is clearly an autochthonous invention from the same archetypal idea.
body: The vision of the Oglala medicine man Black Elk, "made of absolutely the same stuff" as Ezekiel 1: four living creatures, wheels, fire and splendor. Jung's clinching argument against literary borrowing: "we could not assume that this Indian seer, when the white man was not yet in his country, could have read Ezekiel; he was a boy nine years old when he had the vision and it all came out of himself."

Jung's reading (with the patient's four-gods vision as third term): "These visions have been repeated in the age-old archetypal pattern again and again, and they will be repeated through all eternity, because they correspond to something absolutely basic" — an eternal vision repeating in all times and countries "quite independent of any sort of tradition."

occurrences.title: Buddha sets the wheel of the law in motion — Deer Park, Benares
occurrences.label: Buddha sets the wheel of the law in motion
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: in the Gazelle Garden of Benares, Buddha, the perfect one, sets in motion the wheel of the law
body: The dharmachakra episode: in the Gazelle Garden of Benares "Buddha, the perfect one, sets in motion the wheel of the law that he evolves, and everything takes its law-abiding course." Jung pairs it, in glossing the patient's great wheel, with the wheel's second Buddhist meaning — "the wheel of death and birth, the wheel of reincarnation or of illusion-reincarnation being simply another stage of illusion"; whoever lets go of the revolving wheel "will extinguish himself utterly in nirvana, in the positive non-being."
The chunk opens with the same Benares setting as psychological event: Buddha's discovery of the middle path — "not this and not that" — after both the worldly and the ascetic way proved errors.

occurrences.title: The great wheel with heads and clutching hands (Visions Seminar, 7 December 1932)
occurrences.label: The great wheel with heads and clutching hands
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The wheel of fortune is the wheel of life, and it is also the sun's course, the rising, the culmination, and the downfall.
body: A new attempt at the mandala after the monster-birth failed to let her form one: "I came to a great wheel which blocked my way. On the outer rim of the wheel were the heads and clutching hands of men and women rotating swiftly with the wheel." She can only squeeze past in iron armor that shields the small flame from her breast — and no armor is to be found until the four gods bring up the square sheet of metal (see armor-square-metal-four-gods-vision-zurich-1932).

Jung's reading: the wheel of fortune is the wheel of life and the sun's course; in Buddhism the wheel of the law set moving at Benares and the wheel of death-and-rebirth — "reincarnation being simply another stage of illusion." To mount it would be to swing back into identity with emotion; the armor (individuation) is the right protection, though the hollow sound of the hands striking it leaves a doubt.

occurrences.title: Ixion on the sun-wheel — dream of an American Negro patient (~1900s)
occurrences.label: Ixion on the sun-wheel
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1900s (Jung's US research on mentally deranged Negroes)
body: The clinical datum that forced the archetype concept: Jung "was able to convince myself that the well-known motif of Ixion on the sun-wheel (cf. pl. XLVIb) did in fact occur in the dream of an uneducated Negro" (¶154), found during researches on mentally deranged Negroes prompted by the sun-phallus hallucination of his Zurich schizophrenic.

His conclusion is the hinge of the volume: "These and other experiences like them were sufficient to give me a clue: it is not a question of a specifically racial heredity, but of a universally human characteristic. Nor is it a question of inherited ideas, but of a functional disposition to produce the same, or very similar, ideas. This disposition I later called the archetype" (¶154).

occurrences.title: Manichean wheel with twelve buckets that raises the souls of the dying
occurrences.label: Manichean wheel with twelve buckets…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Hegemonius, Acta Archelai pp. 12f. (also Epiphanius, Panarium LXVI); Syro-Mesopotamian Manicheism
occurrences.quote: set up a wheel with twelve buckets, which is turned by the rotation of the sphere and raises the souls of the dying; these are caught by the rays of the greater light, which is the sun, and purified and passed on to the moon
body: The Living Father, seeing the soul tormented in the body, sends his beloved Son, who "made a device for the redemption of souls, and set up a wheel with twelve buckets, which is turned by the rotation of the sphere and raises the souls of the dying; these are caught by the rays of the greater light, which is the sun, and purified and passed on to the moon, and thus is the disc of the moon filled."

Jung quotes this (Part II ch. 5, n. 110) as a direct Gnostic-Mythological parallel to the alchemical opus circulatorium — the wheel/rota that elevates the divine soul out of matter — and immediately adds: "There are secret connections, or at least striking parallels, between alchemy and Manicheism which still need investigating" (n. 111).

occurrences.title: Tibetan World Wheel (sidpe-korlo) — painted banner, private collection
occurrences.label: Tibetan World Wheel
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The sidpe-korlo or World Wheel, "which represents the course of human existence in its various forms as conceived by the Buddhists" (cw12 ¶123).

Jung keeps it strictly distinct from the khilkor (mandala): "the World Wheel is based on a ternary system in that the three world-principles are to be found in its centre: the cock, equalling concupiscence; the serpent, hatred or envy; and the pig, ignorance or unconsciousness (avidya)." — "Here we come upon the dilemma of three and four, which also crops up in Buddhism."
