occurrences.title: Eating the snails from the glucose-coated tree (woman patient's dream, told 29 May 1929)
occurrences.label: Eating the snails from the glucose-coated tree
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

occurrences.quote: Help yourself.' She had to collect and eat those snails... she had to assimilate the brainless animal—something like the worm.
body: Jung led her in the dream up to a tree coated with glucose where snails had climbed; disgusted, she is nevertheless handed a plate with knife and fork by the dream-Jung: "Help yourself." She must collect and eat the snails.

Told in the worm-lecture: "Many people dream that they must eat something very impure." The meaning: "She had to assimilate the brainless animal—something like the worm" — the preconscious, ganglion-level life that the waking ego finds disgusting. The dream belongs with the patient's terror that "a worm might get into their brains" when touching the collective unconscious: what is feared from outside is asked to be taken in and integrated.

occurrences.title: Wotan disguised as Christ on a white horse — sect meeting-house, North Germany
occurrences.label: Wotan disguised as Christ on a white horse
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Wotan the wanderer was on the move.
body: A sighting Jung reports in passing: in the meeting-house of a sect of simple folk in North Germany, the reawakened god "could be seen, looking rather shamefaced, in the meetinghouse of a sect of simple folk in North Germany, disguised as Christ sitting on a white horse" (cw10 ¶373). The Wandering phase of the Wotan-event — rucksack youths, then the unemployed — had filled the roads "from the North Cape to Sicily" before the marching began in 1933.

Jung's reading: the god returns wearing the ruling local symbol. The sect "disguised" Wotan as Christ without knowing "Wotan's ancient connection with the figures of Christ and Dionysus" — the god of the Wagalaweia riding the apocalyptic white horse of Revelation. The shamefacedness is Jung's touch of tact about possession.

occurrences.title: Langmann's funeral sermon for Gustloff — Germany (1936)
occurrences.label: Langmann's funeral sermon for Gustloff — Germany
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: He sped the deceased on his journey to Hades, and directed him to Valhalla.
body: An evangelical clergyman and Church dignitary, Dr. Langmann, preached the funeral oration for the assassinated Nazi leader Wilhelm Gustloff "in S.A. uniform and jackboots." He "sped the deceased on his journey to Hades, and directed him to Valhalla, to the home of Siegfried and Baldur, the heroes who 'nourish the life of the German people by the sacrifice of their blood' — like Christ among others," ending "Lord bless our struggle. Amen."

Jung reprints the report (added to the 1947 London edition of "Wotan") as documentary proof of his thesis: "As a service held to Wotan it is no doubt very edifying — and remarkably tolerant towards believers in Christ!" The Wotan archetype did not merely grip the streets; it seized the pulpit, and Christianity itself was re-mythologized as one cult of the god among others.

occurrences.title: Wotan und germanischer Schicksalsglaube — Martin Ninck's monograph
occurrences.label: Wotan und germanischer Schicksalsglaube
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: The Swiss philologist Martin Ninck's Wotan und germanischer Schicksalsglaube (1935) collected the whole Wotan tradition — epithets, cult, legend — as evidence that Wotan is "the personification of the moving spirit behind Hitler."

Jung leans on it in the seminar weeks before publishing his own Wotan essay (March 1936, CW10 ¶371–99; cf. footnote pdf p888). Wotan as here summarized: "the noise in the wood, the rushing waters, the one who causes natural catastrophes, and wars among human beings"; Roman-identified with Mercury-of-sorcerers; psychopomp; kin to the Thracian Dionysos. Jung is "very grateful to the Germans for their paganistic movement" — at its head Hauer, now "a savior of the fools" — because naming it Wotan means the dreamers "cannot help telling the truth."
Verbatim: "old Wotan is in the center of Europe; you can see all the psychological symptoms which he personifies... all that is living again".

occurrences.title: Nostradamus quatrain on Germany's near-paganism — 'Wotan' motto
occurrences.label: Nostradamus quatrain on Germany's near-paganism
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Coming very near to happy paganism.
body: The quatrain Jung set as the epigraph of "Wotan" (1936): "In Germany shall divers sects arise, / Coming very near to happy paganism. / The heart captivated and small receivings / Shall open the gate to pay the true tithe." A sixteenth-century prophecy, read in 1936 as a diagnosis: the sects (German Faith Movement, German Christians, paganism-in-uniform) arriving at "happy paganism" — the old god returning under Christian names.

Jung's essay is the fulfillment-commentary on this text: Wotan as an "ergreifer" of men, the Germanic storm-god active again (cw10 ¶371ff). The motto also links him to his Aion-era use of Nostradamus (cf. antichrist-nostradamus-letter-henry-ii-1558) — prophecy as perception of archetypal weather.

occurrences.title: The hewing down of Wotan's oak — Christian missionaries at Geismar (~724)
occurrences.label: The hewing down of Wotan's oak
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~724 (traditional date of Boniface's felling of the oak)
occurrences.quote: rather like the hewing down of Wotan's oak by Christian missionaries. On both occasions no avenging bolt from heaven struck the blasphemer down.
body: The missionary felling of the great oak sacred to Wotan (Donar's oak at Geismar, in the Boniface tradition) — the act by which Christianity formally deposed the Germanic god. Jung names it in 1931 as one of the two "symbolic gestures of great significance for the Western world," paired with the enthronement of the Goddess of Reason in Notre Dame (1793): "On both occasions no avenging bolt from heaven struck the blasphemer down" (¶174). The god was cut down, not killed; the two acts bookend the dechristianization Jung dates from ~1800, and the repressed Germanic lower half of ¶17 (1918) — the prowling "blond beast" — is what returns when the Christian view of the world loses authority. Feeds the Wotan complex: the 1936 Wotan essay (CW10 ¶371ff) is this passage's sequel.

occurrences.title: Das Reich ohne Raum — Goetz's novel (Potsdam, 1919)
occurrences.label: Das Reich ohne Raum — Goetz's novel
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: A novel of the Wotanic "realm without space," in which Goetz "saw the secret of coming events in Germany, in the form of a very strange vision" — by which Jung reports having been early struck (CW10 ¶384; footnote pdf p904; cf. 5 June 1935).

Mrs. Baynes: Goetz takes Wotan as a symbol of the new integration of the psyche. Jung's correction: "He is just not an integration, but a disintegration... The storm does not cause integration, but destroys whatever allows itself to be destroyed" — waters breaking loose after long accumulation, the boiler exploding. Wotan as Wal-Vater wanders "without visible goal because it is the wandering of nature." Jung: "I am convinced that behind it something else follows, but it won't be Wotan. It cannot be".
Verbatim: "since Wotan is a historical figure we cannot hope that it is a progression. I am convinced that behind it something else follows, but it won't be Wotan".

occurrences.title: 'Give up Wotan as a devil' — the Saxon adjuration of the pagan gods
occurrences.label: Give up Wotan as a devil
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: In the formula of conversion, the adjuration of the pagan gods, newly Christianized Germans under Charlemagne were obliged to declare that they would give up Wotan as a devil.

Jung's chain: "Wotan the wild hunter becomes later on the devil. Already in the formula of conversion... the Germans in the time of Charlemagne were obliged to declare that they would give up Wotan as a devil. Wotan and Erda and the others are really like devils, and so the later medieval idea that Wotan was identical with the devil came into existence". The renunciation is the historical hinge for his reading of 1936: the repressed god returns as the "national God, Wotan for the German as Jahveh was for the Jew."
Verbatim: "the Germans in the time of Charlemagne were obliged to declare that they would give up Wotan as a devil".

occurrences.title: Wotan as thawing wind and wanderer-omen of war (Germanic legend)
occurrences.label: Wotan as thawing wind and wanderer-omen of war
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: There are legends of his having been seen as a wanderer, and soon after a war would break out. When Wotan appears, it is like the thawing wind in Spring which melts the ice and snow.
body: On Nietzsche's "'Woe to us! Hail to us! The thawing wind bloweth!'", Jung names the god behind the weather outright: "Here we have Wotan, the thawing wind." The god stirs when everything is "at a standstill... undecided," and his appearance is a war-omen:

Jung lets this legend-locus double with the Holy Ghost as pneuma, "a thawing wind", and with Germany's "old wind-god that blows all the dry leaves together" — the storm that precedes the war he saw coming in February 1939.

occurrences.title: The wild hunter in the wood — Nietzsche's Wotan nightmare
occurrences.label: The wild hunter in the wood
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Nietzsche's boyhood (b. 1844; sister's memoir I, pp.18-19)

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

occurrences.quote: In a dark wood he heard a terrible cry issuing from a nearby lunatic asylum, which means that there already he went into the unconscious-the wood.
body: Nietzsche's own dream-story (real event and fantasy at once), told in Jung's "Wotan" essay and recapitulated opening this seminar chunk: walking at night with a friend, he hears a terrible cry from a nearby lunatic asylum, the two nearly lose their way in the dark wood, and they meet "an uncanny man, the wild hunter. That was Wotan." The hunter wants to lead them to Teutschtal — a real village but "of course also symbolic" (Teutsche = the Romantic cult of Germanic blood) — then whistles horribly and Nietzsche loses consciousness.

Jung's reading: the cry from the asylum = "the shrieking and whistling of the wind in a storm in a nocturnal wood, the unconscious... It is Wotan who gets him, the old wind god breaking forth, the god of inspiration, of madness, intoxication and wildness, the god of the Berserkers". "A horrible foreboding of his insanity"; Zarathustra's later coffin-dream repeats it, and the howling dog of "The Vision and the Enigma" recalls it.

occurrences.title: 'Those swastika people are building Wotan's fires again' — Visions Seminar (11 Mar 1931)
occurrences.label: Those swastika people are building Wotan's…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: And in Germany those National Socialists, those swastika people, are building Wotan's fires again.
body: The first in-corpus naming of Wotan as the live German phenomenon — five years before the Wotan essay. Asked what new religious form might follow Protestantism's destruction of the symbol, Jung says he does not know, "but it is quite possible that it will regress pretty far," citing Russia: "the destruction of their religion forced the people to regress to paganism. And in Germany those National Socialists, those swastika people, are building Wotan's fires again." The logic is the compensation-law of cw10 ¶175: libido released by the collapse of a cult "runs loose" and re-animates the old gods — thirty years of Protestant patients in his practice, "not more than four or five real Catholics," as the Swiss corollary.

Timeline weight: with the 18 Feb 1931 shadow/world-war aside and the 1932 two-fishes aeon clock (same seminar), this is the pre-history of the 1936 essay — Jung did not move from Aion to Wotan but from these asides to both. The companion swastika reading of 1935 lives at swastika-nazi-black-left-turning-germany-1935.

occurrences.title: The wounded physician — Greek myth (Chiron/Asclepius complex, unnamed by Jung here)
occurrences.label: The wounded physician — Greek myth
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: It is his own hurt that gives the measure of his power to heal. This, and nothing else, is the meaning of the Greek myth of the wounded physician.
body: In "Fundamental Questions of Psychotherapy" Jung grounds the analyst's obligation to his own wound in Greek myth: the analyst must keep learning endlessly, and "a good half of every treatment that probes at all deeply consists in the doctor's examining himself, for only what he can put right in himself can he hope to put right in the patient." It is no loss if the patient hits him: the wound is the measure of the healing power. The myth is invoked, not narrated — the identification with Chiron, the wounded teacher of healers, is ours, not Jung's, in this passage.

occurrences.title: The wretched man's cry: 'who will deliver me from the body of this death?' — Romans 7:24
occurrences.label: The wretched man's cry — Romans 7:24
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In despair we would have to cry out with St. Paul: 'Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?
body: Paul's cry of the divided man — "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?" — answered in the next verse by "the law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus." Jung deploys it at the climax of the Freud critique: Freudian psychology "points no way that leads beyond the inexorable cycle of biological events," and faced with that circuit "we would have to cry out with St. Paul" (¶780). The release is "that opposite urge of life, the spirit" — "It is not the children of the flesh, but the 'children of God,' who know freedom."

Here the fleshly bond runs both ways — "back to father and mother or forward to the children," 'incest' with past and future (¶780) — making Romans 7 the formula of the parental constellation itself, and the spirit the function that breaks it.

occurrences.title: Yesod as the Son of Man with seven stars — BN MS Français 14765, pl. 8 (Mysterium Plate 3)
occurrences.label: Yesod as the Son of Man with seven stars
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "In the MS in the Bibliothèque Nationale, Fr. 14765, pl. 8, Yesod is depicted like the Son of Man in Revelation 1:12 ff., with the seven stars in his right hand, the sword issuing from his mouth, and standing between the seven candlesticks. See infra, our Plate 3".

Yesod — 'foundation', the genital region of the Original Man, the Sefira through which the King's influx reaches Malchuth — imaged with the full apocalyptic attributes of the Son of Man. The kabbalistic members of Adam Kadmon are Christianized as the Revelation Christ: the two anthropos-traditions fused in one late-medieval picture.

occurrences.title: The Yetzer Hara legend — the pious man prays the evil spirit back into the world
occurrences.label: The Yetzer Hara legend
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Well, J ezer Horra is the evil spirit of passion.
body: The old Jewish legend Jung invokes for the red jewel in the ice — the drop of hellfire without which no heart warms:

A pious man, "on very good terms with God", prays the evil spirit of passion out of the world — and the world goes dead: the roses lose their perfume, the wonderful old wine "had no taste, there was no kick in it", his beautiful young wife's kiss "meant nothing". He climbs the roof again and beseeches God to let Yetzer Hara out — "and because he was a pious man God let out the spirit of passion, and since then it has been in the world". Jung's moral for the ice-jewel vision: "that is the drop of hellfire… without it no ice can be melted… heart will not touch heart and no fire will be kindled".

occurrences.title: Dragon and Tiger, yin and yang devouring each other — Wei Po-yang's Ts'an T'ung Ch'i
occurrences.label: Dragon and Tiger, yin and yang devouring each…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Ts'an T'ung Ch'i, ~2nd c. CE (Davis trans., Isis XVIII, 1929)
occurrences.quote: Yin and yang drink and devour one another.
body: The treatise of Wei Po-yang: "Yin and yang drink and devour one another"; "Yang donates and yin receives"; "The Dragon breathes into the Tiger and the Tiger receives the spirit from the Dragon. They mutually inspire and benefit"; yin and yang are the "charioteers" leading from inside to outside; "The way is long and obscurely mystical, at the end of which the Ch'ien (yang) and the K'un (yin) come together." The dragon (yang) reigns over the East, the Tiger (yin) over the West — as Mercurius duplex is "orientalis" and "occidentalis."

Jung's reading: the Chinese structural equivalent of the coniunctio; also the scarlet Chu-Niao bird of five colours symbolizing totality (five elements, five directions). Parallels: chen-yen-true-man-wei-po-yang-china-2c, nigredo-blunder-wei-po-yang-142, tao family.

occurrences.title: Ymir — primordial giant of the Edda, world built from his body
occurrences.label: Ymir — primordial giant of the Edda, world…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: In the Edda, Ymir, a primordial giant, develops out of the primordial waters, out of whose body parts the world was built.
body: Head of the seminar's giant-material: in the Edda, Ymir, a primordial giant, develops out of the primordial waters, and the world is built from his body parts. The giants — eldest beings, coarse, amoral, but possessing "a knowledge of primordial things, an uncreated and traditional wisdom" — dwell in Utgard outside the circular earth or under the hollow mountains; the gods raise Midgard against them; gods and giants destroy each other at the Götterdämmerung. Giants and dragons turn into each other; heroes later end their human sacrifices.
The frame for the girl's dream: the father appearing as the giant = the chaotic, untamed instinctual nature of man confronting the child from the parents' bedroom.

occurrences.title: Dionysius Zacharius: the Easter transmutation witnessed (1550)
occurrences.label: Dionysius Zacharius
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Vidi perfectionem… conversum in purum aurum prae meis oculis
body: "After a fit of despair he revived with the help of the Holy Spirit and, applying himself to a serious study of the literature, read diligently, and meditated day and night until his finances were exhausted. Then he worked in his laboratory, saw the three colours appear, and on Easter Day of the following year the wonder happened: 'Vidi perfectionem'—'I saw the perfect fulfilment': the quicksilver was 'conversum in purum aurum prae meis oculis'" (¶365).

Jung's point is not the chemistry but the sequence: despair → Holy Spirit → study and meditation → the three colours → completion at Easter. "There is an unmistakable hint here that the work and its goal depended very largely on a mental condition" — the rubedo arriving as psychically conditioned event, dated like a resurrection.

occurrences.title: 'One became two' — Nietzsche's Sils-Maria poem
occurrences.label: One became two' — Nietzsche's Sils-Maria poem
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

body: Nietzsche's little poem written at Sils-Maria between 1882 and 1884: "Then suddenly, friend, one became two — And Zarathustra passed by me." Jung reads it as evidence that Nietzsche "had himself a pretty clear notion that he was not identical with Zarathustra": "Zarathustra then became manifest as a second personality in himself." Yet in 1883, "the time of the blooming of materialistic philosophy," when "nobody had an inkling of psychology," "he had to identify with Zarathustra in spite of the fact that he felt... a definite difference between himself and the old wise man".

The figure is archetypal: "It brought something of the breath of centuries with it, and it filled him with a peculiar sense of destiny: he felt that he was called to mend a damage done in the remote past of mankind." Editor compares Jung's own Personality 1 / Personality 2 (MDR).

occurrences.title: Zarathustra's 'ugliest man' and the higher men — the suppressed counteraction (Nietzsche, 1883-85)
occurrences.label: Zarathustra's 'ugliest man' and the higher men
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)
The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche (CW8)

body: In "The Transcendent Function" Jung reads Also sprach Zarathustra as a clinical document of the psyche's self-regulation suppressed: "The discovery of the 'higher' man, and also of the 'ugliest' man, expresses the regulating influence, for the 'higher' men want to drag Zarathustra down to the collective sphere of average humanity as it always has been, while the 'ugliest' man is actually the personification of the counteraction. But the roaring lion of Zarathustra's moral conviction forces all these influences, above all the feeling of pity, back again into the cave of the unconscious" (cw08 ¶162).

The suppressed counteraction did not disappear: it resurfaces as Nietzsche's war on Wagner (unforgiven for Parsifal), then against Christianity and St Paul, and finally — at the collapse — as identification with the Crucified and the dismembered Dionysus (¶162). In "Psychological Factors" (¶254) the same text serves as the prime example of identification with archetypes transforming personality.

occurrences.title: Seven eyes of the Lord on the foundation-stone — Zechariah 4:10
occurrences.label: Seven eyes of the Lord on the foundation-stone
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

occurrences.quote: They are seven eyes, and according to the testimony of the prophet, they are on the foundation-stone of the new temple.
body: The alchemists referred to Zechariah: the eyes of the Lord "run to and fro through the whole earth" — seven eyes, which according to the prophet's testimony are on the foundation-stone of the new temple. Jung reads the eye as "the self-perception of an unconscious illuminated or capable of being illuminated": the alchemists therefore saw corresponding phenomena in chemical transformations — the lighting-up of the dark, simmering compound, described as oriental jewels, "fish eyes."
With Ignatius' hundred-eyed snake and the piscis rotundus, it grounds the seminar's thesis: concordant God-images arise from such inner perceptions, not from invention.

occurrences.title: Zosimos to Theosebeia: be baptized in the krater
occurrences.label: Zosimos to Theosebeia: be baptized in the krater
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: she should, he says, hasten to the Poimandres in order to be baptized in the krater.
body: In his letter to Theosebeia, Zosimos — "a Gnostic who was influenced by Hermes" — recommends the krater as vessel of transformation and urges her to hasten to the Poimandres to be baptized in it.

The image comes from the Hermetic treatise "ho krater": after creating the world, God filled the vessel with nous and sent it to earth as a baptismal font, so that whoever wished to rise from the state of anoia (insufficient consciousness) could dip himself and partake of ennoia — enlightenment. The nous is a dyestuff, a tincture; its equivalent is the stone-extract, "which is also a pneuma and, as Mercurius, possesses the Hermetic dual significance of redeeming psychopomp and quicksilver" (¶409).

occurrences.title: Zrvan Akarana — unlimited duration containing all that happens
occurrences.label: Zrvan Akarana — unlimited duration containing…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

body: "Zrvan Akarana means unlimited duration that contains all that happens." Jung reports an old French scholar's guess that it contained Ormuzd (light) and Ahriman (darkness) as the pair of opposites — refuted by the texts: "one version has it that Zrvan, the devil, made time and another that Akarana, the god of duration, made it, so opinions are divided about the origin of that awful thing, the flow of energy. One can never make out who is responsible. Nowhere is there such a marvellous dualism." The diagram of the two makes a cross — prefiguring the crucified god between sun and moon. Zrvan later became the god Aion of the Mithraic cult (lion-headed-god-mithraic-aion-vatican-2c-3c).

occurrences.label: Zuni four cave worlds
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: traditional (as told in seminar, after Baumann)

jung.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940
jung.locator: Brunner's parallels to the transparent mouse (pdf p374)

occurrences.quote: through which the humans climb up on a plant from the dark to the light of day, in order to take off their slimy and scaled clothes.
body: The Zuni know of four cave worlds lying one above another — in one version: the inner world of raw dust, of soot, of mist, and of wings — through which humans climb up on a plant from the dark toward the light of day, taking off their "slimy and scaled clothes." An emergence cosmology staged in four, matching the dream's four transformation stages (mouse-worms / snakes / fish / man) and Jung's later four-worlds reading (earth, water, air; fire missing).

occurrences.title: Zwiefalten Abbey breviary: rectangular mandala with the Lamb
occurrences.label: Zwiefalten Abbey breviary
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the deity is enthroned at the centre
body: Plate 62: "Rectangular mandala with cross, the Lamb in the centre, surrounded by the four evangelists and the four rivers of Paradise. In the medallions, the four cardinal virtues." Jung: "equally in the Western mandalas of medieval Christendom the deity is enthroned at the centre, often in the form of the triumphant Redeemer together with the four symbolical figures of the evangelists" (¶169).

The dream's square-with-gibbon "presents the most violent contrast to these highly metaphysical ideas" (¶169) — the Lamb replaced by the reconstructed ape. The plate anchors the Western squared-mandala family: centre + cross + tetramorph + four rivers.
